consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a confession made out of court in a document that one is of age prejudices him, and when it does so.
2. A confession made in the absence of the party does not prejudice him, except in certain cases.
3. Whether a sworn confession by a minor prejudices others.
4. One who alleges minority, where age itself is the basis of the claim, is bound to prove it.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The point on which legal advice is requested is as follows. When a certain lady, Francisca Micheloti of Gubbio, intended to bring an action against Gerius and another of Gubbio, whom she alleged to be her debtors, she appeared before the competent judge and requested to be declared a minor upon visual inspection and to be appointed curators for litigation. That judge, with no one summoned or appearing on behalf of her debtors, declared her a minor upon visual inspection and appointed certain curators for litigation and causes to her. These curators, thus created and appointed, caused the said Gerius to be summoned to appear in court to answer and state whether he possesses a certain house. Gerius, or his procurators, appeared and raised an objection against the said curators thus appointed by the said judge, alleging that the said curators were not legitimately appointed and constituted; all the more so, etc. The form of the exception is as follows. Having been constituted before the aforementioned judge, sitting on the bench as above, Ser John, acting as procurator and in the procuratorial name of the said Gerius, stated, objected, and offered himself, in the said name, ready to swear on the Holy Gospels of God that it has newly come to the knowledge of himself and the said Gerius that the said lady Francisca is of full age and has conducted herself as one of full age; and he offers to prove this within a competent term to be fixed by the said lord judge, which term he requests to be granted to him forthwith. Since the said procurator, in the said name, intends to prove the aforementioned matters to bar the said lady from the threshold of the court, and that she ought to litigate through a procurator and not through curators, the said procurator, at the prompting of the said judge, swore on the Holy Gospels of God, with his hand touching the scriptures, that the aforementioned matters narrated by him are true. The judge fixed and prescribed a term of three forthcoming days for him to prove the matters narrated by him, and this was done in the presence of Angelico, who asserted himself to be the curator of the said lady and contradicted the claim. The said procurator appeared before the aforementioned judge within the said term and, in proof of the said exception, produced a certain public instrument in which the said lady asserted that she was twenty-five years of age. That instrument was transmitted to the consultant; and the other acts are also returned. In order that the consultant may avoid labor, the arguments alleged and the responses made by the parties are distributed here. The objection is raised on the ground that the said assertion of her concession made in the said instrument was made outside of court and in the absence of the opposing party; and thus it does not prejudice the case, as stated in the law *Certum*, § *Peius*, in the Digest under the title *De Confessis*. It is furthermore stated that even if it had been made in court between other persons, it would not prejudice the case, as stated in the final law in the Digest under the title *De Interrogationibus et Actionibus*. But this was of such a nature; therefore, etc.

I answer that the aforementioned allegation holds when an obligation arises from the confession, which consists in the will of two parties; but when an obligation arises from the confession, which consists in the will of one party, then even if made out of court and with the party absent, it prejudices [the party]: as in ratification, acceptance of an inheritance, and similar matters, which can everywhere be done in the absence of the party, as noted by the gloss in *Pomponius scribit*, § *si negotium*, D. *de negotiis gestis*, in the principal part; the great gloss. Thus holds Bartolus in the said law *Certum*, § *penes*, D. *de confessionibus*. But this was of such a kind, therefore, etc.

I also answer in another way: it is true that a confession made out of court in the absence of the party does not prejudice [the party] when the obligation arising from the confession is treated principally and in itself; but since the condition of the person, upon which the confession or assertion was made, even out of court and in the absence of the party, comes into court incidentally, as in the case proposed, then it also makes faith against other persons, until the contrary is proved; for from the said confession or assertion is induced a quasi-possession of majority of age, which makes faith until the contrary is proved, as is the case in the law *Non epistola*, C. *de probationibus*. Thus holds Innocentius, Extra, *de praesumptionibus*, c. *Illud quoque*, in the gloss which begins, "which nomination induces a presumption," etc. Thus holds he also more at length in c. *Per inquisitiones*, Extra, *de electionibus*, and there also is the gloss of Bernardus. Therefore, the exception is proved at least until the contrary is proved.

And it is also answered in another way, that the law *Si*, D. *de interest actione*, alleged for the contrary, speaks when the confessor evidently confessed a lie; which confession rightly does not prejudice as regards other persons; but when the confession was made upon that which is doubtful, whether it is true or not, as was in this case, it is believed until the contrary is proved; therefore, etc. Much supports the foregoing: the law *Si alterius*, the gloss placed there according to the opinion of Azo and mine, C. *si minor se maiorem dixerit*.

† It is also alleged on behalf of the opposing party the statement of Bartolus, which is found in the law *De aetate* in the Digest title *De minoribus*, where he treats the effect of proof of age. There he states that a confession made by a minor in one instrument does not prejudice him with regard to others. It is responded, with all due respect, that in our case his statement is negated by what has been written above. It is also responded, in another manner, that that statement could have application when it is taken as established that he is a minor; because his confession, even with an oath, does not prejudice him with regard to others. This is evident, since he cites Cynus in the tenth question, in the *Authenticum Sacramenta* in the Code title *Si adversus venditionem*, and he cites the aforementioned law *Si* in the Digest title *De interrogationibus et actionibus*. But in our case this is not established; therefore, that statement does not stand in the way. Indeed, Bartolus himself seems to imply in the aforementioned law *De aetate*, in the aforementioned member concerning the effect of proof of age, that a confession made regarding age prejudices him with regard to others, when he cites the aforementioned law *Si alterius* in the Code title *Si minor se maiorem dixerit*. This is also proven more strongly in this case. For in the aforementioned law *Si* in the Digest title *De interrogationibus et actionibus*, although the confessor does not prejudice himself by reason of the confession, he nevertheless prejudices himself by reason of the acceptance of inheritance; and there the glossa states, and the reason is, which was said for this part: because from this confession results an obligation, which consists in the power of one. Thus hold the doctors there. It is responded in another manner, that that statement of Bartolus has application when a minor confesses and swears not to go against [the agreement] concerning one contract with respect to that contract; a confession or oath which, rightly, does not prejudice him with regard to others. This appears, because there he cites Cynus in the aforementioned *Authenticum Sacramenta*, which authenticum speaks of a confirmatory oath of a contract. That statement can also have application, that a minor does not prejudice himself with regard to others, so that he cannot prove the contrary, as in the aforementioned law *Si alterius* in the Code title *Si minor se maiorem dixerit*.

† It is also alleged on this side that at least from this confession, or assertion made out of court, half-proof is induced: and thus the oath should be administered to Gero himself and to his procurator, because he induces half-proof for himself, as the learned hold in l. in bonaefidei, C. de iureiur.; the learned in l. admonendi, ff. eo. ti. de adult.; l. capite. In the fifth place it is answered that this would be true unless this half-proof were rebutted by another presumption, which results from the pronouncement of the judge made concerning age, and thus it should not be referred, as is the gloss, C. qui aduersus, l. 1. To which it is answered by the other party in two ways. First, because it is denied that from this pronouncement of the judge there results not even half-proof, but not even a presumption, which was made with Gero himself absent and not cited. Therefore, etc., as the laws wish. Second, because, granted that a presumption were induced, from which the half-proof resulting from this confession of this lady Francisca would be rebutted, then the question would remain in the simple terms of the common law,

† namely, that she would seek to be declared a minor and to have a curator appointed for her, so that she might bring an action, and the adversary would deny this; and since age was the basis of her claim, she ought to prove it, as stated in l. si minorem, C. de in integrum restitutione minorum. Thus holds Jacobus Butrigarius there, whom Bartolus follows in the aforementioned law de aetate. Now the question arises: what are the duties of the judge regarding the said exception and cause, having examined the records and proceedings in the aforementioned case.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A judicial pronouncement made regarding age based on the appearance of a person, without summoning those who ought to be summoned, does not prejudice them by imposing upon them the burden of proof.
2. The appointment of a curator for a person over twenty-five years of age is not valid, unless a sentence was rendered after the issue of age had been debated with the parties summoned.
3. One who seeks a curator must first establish his claim based on age, and therefore is bound to prove it.
body: In the Name of God, Amen.

† If a curator is appointed after [the minor] has passed his twenty-fifth year, the appointment is invalid and does not bind: because it is impossible, unless a sentence had been rendered on the disputed issue of age with the parties summoned, without any error being expressed: for such a sentence is held as truth between the parties. D. de minoribus, l. de aetate; D. de feriis, l. 2; D. ad Trebellianum, l. 3, §. puberi; D. de tutoribus et curatoribus, l. Seyae egressae; C. quando provocatio non est necesse, l. 2; C. de petitione hereditatis, l. si putas; C. de curatore furiosi, l. 1, with similar authorities. In our question, it is not alleged that a sentence was rendered regarding minority with the parties summoned: but rather with no one cited: and therefore the age is to be examined in the same manner, and the matter is litigated anew, as if nothing had been adjudicated. D. de minoribus, l. etiam, §. si. Although in the appointment of a curator no one needs to be cited, nevertheless if the age is brought into doubt, it must be examined. Thus D. de bonis possessionibus, l. 3, §. pen.; and C. quorum bonorum, l. 1. For even when something is decided from appearance, the party whose interest is affected ought to be moved. D. si regum, l. si in ruptione, §. ad officium; D. de venditionis inspectione, l. 1, §. denunciari. And although it is presumed in favor of the judge’s decree, nevertheless when the adversary denies, it must be determined after the cause is known. D. de in integrum restitutione, l. omnis. Hence, in our case, let us see upon whom the burden of proof lies. And certainly, in the appointment of a curator, if the minor were to object, he would prove that he is a minor, as in the aforementioned l. de aetate, and noted in that title, l. si minorem te, and in that title, l. cum te, and D. de probationibus, l. cum de aetate. But in a curator already appointed, it seems to be presumed in favor of the judge’s decree. l. actor rem rationem habet; and l. minor 25 annorum, l. ex aspectu, with similar authorities. The question stands on this: whether a pronouncement based on appearance prejudices those not cited by burdening them with the onus of proof: and I believe that it does not, because it would be unjust to burden one not cited, on the ground that it is against him, as in l. de unoquoque, and l. nam ita divus, and l. in causae, §. causa cognita, de minoribus. And therefore the judge will impose the proofs on either one or the other, as it seems to him, according to the gloss, or certainly,

† Because the petitioner bases the origin of the petition on age, he must prove minority of age, as stated in the aforementioned laws; and it is established by what is noted in the Digest, *De iuris et facti ignorantia*, law 2, § *quod observari*, in the gloss beginning *ex hoc dicunt*. However, this is proven by the judge’s visual inspection, with the parties present or summoned, and upon his decree.

† Likewise, by other modes, concerning the excused tutor, l. 2, §. aetas, l. 2, de his qui vetita, l. 3, C. si minor se manumiserit, and facit, C. de probat., l. 1, cum similibus. Whether a confession regarding majority of age prejudices oneself as regards other absentees: the glossa says that it does not, in l. de aetate. And this is true as regards full prejudice: but it does well make an indication. arg. l. si duo patroni, verb. multum tamen fidei, ff. de iureiurando. And thus it is understood, that not, in auth. sacr. pu., per glossam and Cy. Bal. de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a daughter provided with a dowry by her father or mother shall not succeed to either, if a brother survives: a brother born of another wife does not exclude the daughter, who is also his sister, upon the death of the mother.
2. A statute excluding a woman on account of a brother is understood to apply only when the brother is capable of succeeding.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

Having examined the statute of the City of Cortona, which provides that a woman endowed by her father or mother shall not succeed to either, if a brother survives, the following case is proposed: namely, that the said Joanna, daughter of the late Nicolutia, married Matthew Pauli by the will of the said father, who gave her in dowry certain specified goods, and generally all his rights. However, the said Nicolutia had been endowed with 60 livres, by reason of which dowry, in order to obtain it, the said Matthew, on behalf of the children and successors, as heirs of the said Joanna, their late mother, brought a hypothecary action, after having made excussion. It is objected that, since a brother of the said Joanna survives, namely Bernottus, though born of another mother, the said Joanna does not succeed to Nicolutia, her late mother. The question is asked, what is the law, having regard to the above-mentioned statutes and the acts and proceedings in the said cause? And it must be said without doubt that the said Joanna succeeded to her mother without any obstacle from the statute, and that the said Matthew can claim the 60 livres indirectly by bringing a hypothecary action against the possessors. And this is clear from the common law, because in intestate succession the cause of the children is prior, in the Authentica de hereditatibus ab intestato, after the principal; for a daughter ought to have the goods of her mother, not a stepson. Codex, common title on successions, law Vitricus. The statute does not stand in the way for multiple reasons,

† First, because a statute that excludes a woman on account of a brother is understood to speak when the brother is capable of succeeding; therefore, and so forth. This statement is proven by its own reason. D. de bonis liberorum, l. Si mater; § Si deportatus, D. de lib. et posth.; l. Gallus; § Quid si tantum. He who is not admitted to succession, nor is there hope that he will be admitted, does not prevent another from succeeding, as D. de contrahenda, l. 1, § Filium. It does not seem that a brother exists in the nature of things who does not succeed. D. ad Trebellianum, l. 2, § Videndum. Moreover, when succession is discussed, the quality of the words must be referred to the person, and with respect to the person whose succession is being discussed, as C. de cognatione, l. Ut liberis. Moreover, this brother was never in the nature of things during the lifetime of the lady Nicolutia; and thus the inheritance of the lady Nicolutia had already devolved to the said lady Joanna, as if she had a brother; and thus, since the day for acceptance had passed beforehand, the brother is not objected against the sister, as Inst. de legatis, agnatis, successione, § Proximus. It supports D. de in ius vocando, l. Si quis filio, after the principle; D. de suis et legitimis, l. Item praetor. Moreover, Joanna was endowed with a double dowry, and one dowry was the maternal inheritance and goods, C. de dotis promissione, l. 1. Since therefore she can be endowed with whatever goods, it cannot be said that she does not have a dowry, which the father’s will established for her. D. familiae erciscundae, l. Pomponius; and l. 1, D. de collatione dotis. It is therefore evidently concluded in favor of the said Matthew, presupposing that the said 60 pounds were the dowry of the said Nicolutia. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the testator placed a thing, which he possessed, in a conditional restitution, whether the substitute, suing against the external possessor with title, is bound to prove the testator’s status and that the thing was possessed by the testator at the time of death and long before, and not to prove the title and that the condition of the substitution existed.
2. A thing subject to restitution cannot be prescribed to the prejudice of the person to whom restitution must be made, since in the meantime he cannot bring an action.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the case of Basil, son of the procurator of the said Cęcha, several matters arise for consideration, and first,

Whether, when a testator placed a thing that he possessed in a conditional restitution, it suffices for the substitute, acting against an external possessor, to prove these three things substantially: the will, the fact that the thing was possessed by the testator at the time of his death and long before, without otherwise proving title, and that the condition of substitution existed. And I speak of an external possessor holding with title, and the matter is highly doubtful. For in a vindication of property, mere possession proved is not sufficient. C. de rei vindic. l. nullo. Moreover, an action on the will does not lie against an external possessor. l. 1, § si heredi, ad Trebellianum. Furthermore, a hypothecary action does not lie for the thing itself bequeathed. C. comm. de legatis, l. 1. Moreover, he does not have the benefit of the edict, because he is a legatee, as noted in the said l. edicto. Moreover, he does not have the action from l. si coloni, nor the officium iudicis; since the possessor has a just title, as noted by the doctors, C. de furtis, l. 2; de acquis. possess., l. literæ quæ nobis. I do not see by what right the possessor can be sued, unless it is proved that the deceased was the owner, or quasi-owner; but this is not proved by possession alone. C. de probat., in l. cum res; and noted by the doctors in l. penult., de cond. inst. Moreover, just error, which is held as title, is not proved. de usur., l. Celsus. But Bartolus says there that just error is proved by reputation; for which supports the gloss, de negot. gest., l. at qui natura, § cum me absente. Moreover, he says in the said l. rem quæ nobis, that if a position is made that at the time the deceased apprehended the things, they were not in the goods of anyone, that proved possession proves direct ownership, unless it is proved that they belonged to another previously. And he holds the same opinion in l. nam et si fur, si certum petatur. And if this position is true, let this article still be made and placed in the records; nevertheless, regarding immovable property, this opinion of his is quite doubtful. But if it is true, this is the only mode of assisting this client, and prescription does not protect the possessor, which did not run against the substitute, unless after the case of substitution had occurred, as noted in l. si, § si autem ob avaritiæ, C. comm. de legatis. And these matters are sufficiently doubtful in common law.

† But by the form of the statute it seems to be determined that by possession of 10 years, even without title, ownership is presumed, indeed even induced; and therefore, since the thing subject to restitution could not in the meantime be prescribed to the prejudice of him to whom restitution ought to be made, and who in the meantime could not bring action, as in the Authentica Res, quae communia, de legibus, it seems undoubtedly to be said that, in that which was conferred upon the said Lord Cæcha by right of substitution from the person of Lord Mita, the said Lord Cæcha has a right to the thing, by the said law Si communia, de legibus, § Si autem ob avaritiae. The portion conferred seems to have been one-half, in the other half which the said Cæcha could formerly have claimed; and because she did not claim it, both the prescription of the common law and the prescription and disposition of the statute seem to stand in her way. And thus it seems to me, joining the common law with the statute of the city of Cortona, to be said in this case. And so the delay of Lord Mita, and the prescription against her, do not suffice; and it did not prejudice Lord Cæcha, because while Lord Mita was alive she could not bring action for the share of Lord Mita; but only afterwards, after death, by virtue of the substitution made concerning both males and themselves. It is fitting, de legibus 2, law Peto, § Praedium. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A son of a second marriage cannot, in the person of his mother, claim the legitime in the property of the sons of the first marriage.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. The statement of facts is as follows.

† Lady Benvenuta had three sons by Vanne di Alessandro, her first husband, namely Angelo, Cola, and Jacobuccio. Upon the death of the said Vanne, the said Benvenuta gave herself in marriage to a second husband, namely Manutio di Gionta. By this second husband she had two children, namely Gionta and Orfina. Afterwards, Cola and Jacobuccio died having made a will, in which will they appointed the said Angelo as their universal heir. Thereafter, the said Lady Benvenuta passed away, with the said Angelo, her son by the first marriage, and the said Gionta and Orfina, her children by the second marriage, surviving her. After these events, the said Angelo passed away, having instituted certain relatives of his as his heirs. Now, Gionta and Orfina wish to claim the legitime which they allege was owed to their mother in the property of the predeceased Cola and Jacobuccio. The question is asked whether they can make this claim or not. It is presupposed that Cola and Jacobuccio did not possess property acquired from any other source, but solely paternal property; and furthermore, that in such property, since she married a second time, she does not succeed in ownership, but only in usufruct, which was extinguished by the death of the mother. And therefore, over the property of the said deceased Alessandro, the said Gionta and Orfina can claim nothing. C. de sec. nup. auth. ex testamento. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Where the testator's intent is not clearly apparent, the bishop may, if the parties are willing, reach a settlement, by authority of the text *interponere*, and such settlement shall be valid in perpetuity on account of his authority.
2. Bad grammar is not tolerated.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the will of Bartoluccio, and the institution of heirs written by the notary’s ignorance under these words and with these writings: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The tenor of the will of Bartoluccio is found to be sufficiently confused, due to the excessive ignorance of the notary, which ignorance destroys the world and places the consciences of good men in great peril. In all his other goods, he instituted Bartholomew, Francis, and Amator, his sons, as heirs; adding that if any of them should die without sons, the other should succeed. He also added that his son Amator could not sell any of his goods without the license of two of his close blood relatives, nor in any way encumber, alienate, or donate them. And also, the rector of the church of Mark and James ought to have food, clothing, and dwelling from his goods. These are the words of the foolish notary. It is asked, what is the meaning of these words. For if we say that alimony and habitation were left to the rector, this would be bad grammar in perpetuity: because one ought to say “to the rector,” and not “of the rector.” D. de aur. et arg. leg. l. Plautius. Moreover, it would be a certain injustice that the father, while his sons were living, would wish to burden them in perpetuity, contrary to l. si unquam, C. de revoc. don. But if we say that nothing was bequeathed to the rector, or if that genitive is construed so that the sense is that alienation cannot be made without the consent of the blood relatives and the rector, and that what follows concerning food, clothing, and habitation refers to Amator and not to the priest, this greatly burns the conscience: and it seems to be contrary to the truth; since Amator did not need this prelegacy, because he was instituted as heir for a share. Since therefore the case is doubtful, I think that the lord bishop ought to investigate whatever he can regarding the mind of the testator: and if nothing else appears to him, if the parties wish to settle, he may interpose his authority to the settlement: and it shall be valid in perpetuity on account of the authority of the bishop. D. de transact. l. praeses, with similar authorities. Baldus.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. The fact, concerning which legal opinion is requested, is as follows.

Premised is a valid municipal law, which provides that in testaments, codicils, and any last will, five witnesses suffice. Acomandius Acommandutii, having two underage sons, namely Nicolaus and Ioannes, made his solemn and valid testament; in which he made a division, institution, and substitution among the said sons in the manner hereinafter written, namely: First, etc., and it follows in the manner hereinafter written, namely:

Furthermore, he left and judged that, since he intends to divide his goods among his sons, they should not have cause for any scandals and discord to arise between them, but that they might live concordantly. For one part, namely for the part of Nicolaus, he assigned to the said Acommanducii the things and goods hereinafter written. First, one piece of land, etc. And after the enumeration of all things computed into the part of the said Nicolaus, he adds: “And in the said things, and the said part, and immediately of all other movable things, massarities, money, and whatever other things and names of debts, wherever they might be and could be found, I institute my son Nicolaus as my heir; and he may not demand more of my goods. And these provisions shall have effect, namely of the said parts, in the case in which they wish to divide.”

Furthermore, he left and judged that in the other part, for Ioannes, son of the said Acommanducii, and for his part, he placed the things hereinafter written: and he willed that they be his. First, he placed for the part of the said Ioannes one tenement of land, etc. And at the end of all things enumerated into the part of the said Ioannes, he says thus: “And in the said part, and also immediately of all his movable things, massarities, and all debts, and whatever other things of his, wherever they are and can be found, I institute the said Ioannes, my son, as my heir; and he may not demand more of my goods.”

Furthermore, he willed and commanded that if one of the aforementioned his sons should die in pupillary age, he substituted the other surviving son to the one dying, and thus substituted them to each other.

Furthermore, he willed and commanded that if the said his sons should both die without sons, or those legitimately descending from them, or if their sons not existing, there were no other sons or nephews of the aforementioned Nicolaus or Ioannes, or if they did not make a last testament in health of body, that half of the aforementioned their goods should come, and ought to come, in the said cases, namely when none of the aforementioned Nicolaus and Ioannes, nor the sons of the said, should survive, and when none should survive, and did not make a testament in health of body and last, and if they did make one, when they suffered from illness and could not conveniently leave home, it should come, and ought to come, to the Hospital of Mercy of Perugia. And the other half should come, and ought to come, in the said cases to the Hospital of Notaries of Perugia. And he willed and understood that the aforementioned illness be understood as when they were so burdened that they could not conveniently leave home.

After this, the said Ioannes died in pupillary age during the lifetime of the testator and the said Nicolaus, brother of the said Ioannes; after whose death the said Acommandus, before four witnesses, made codicils. In which, among other things, it is contained thus:

“Furthermore, I revoked and annulled the legacy of substitution of the inheritance made in the said testament, and I substituted Nicolaus, my son, as universal heir; and if the said Nicolaus should die without legitimate sons, I substituted the Hospital of Mercy and the Hospital of Notaries of the city of Perugia. Furthermore, I made, etc. Furthermore, I left, etc. And I confirmed and ratified the aforementioned testament, and in all other things contained in the said testament, left. Done, etc., present Bartolinus Massali, Agnellus Cum Soli, Iacobus Cæchi, Blasius Petri, witnesses requested and called by the said Acommanducius. I, Herculanus Petri, prior of Solis, and prior of Saint Anthony of Perugia, notary by Imperial authority, was present at all these things, and requested by the said Acommanducius, I wrote and published them.”

After the aforementioned, the said Acommanducius died, having substituted to himself the said Nicolaus, his son, and heir in solidum, and he, acting as heir and managing the said paternal inheritance, who, Nicolaus, being sound in body and mind after the death of his said father, made his last testament; in which he instituted certain heirs for himself, as appears in the testament itself. Finally, with the passage of time after the aforementioned, the said Nicolaus was defamed for conspiracy and plot to subvert the good and peaceful state of the city of Perugia; the penalty for which, by the form of the statutes of the city of Perugia, is that the head of the offender be amputated, so that he die; and that all his goods be published to the said commune. He was captured and, on account of the said crime, detained by the officials of the said commune. And being thus captured and detained, and knowing himself detained on the aforementioned occasion, by virtue of the substitution made to the said Nicolaus from the said hospitals, wishing to render fuller faith to his father Acommanducius, and knowing himself not bound before his death to the aforementioned restitution, having seen, known, and inspected the words of the testament of Acommanducius, his father, he restored the inheritance of Acommanducius, formerly his father, and all and singular movable and immovable goods, rights, and actions of the aforementioned inheritance, by full right, to the said hospitals, namely to each for a half; and he granted license to apprehend and enter into the tenure and corporal possession of the said inheritance and goods by their own authority; and he willed that from now on the restitution of the aforementioned inheritance be made, and be understood to have been made, by the said Nicolaus, in deed and word, to the hospitals above mentioned, to each of them for a half, etc.

These things thus being done, the said Nicolaus was found guilty of the said maleficium and was condemned to amputation of the head; and all his goods were published and confiscated to the commune of Perugia by sentence, according to the form of the statute of the commune of Perugia, and he was beheaded.

Now the question arises between the said commune and the aforementioned hospitals concerning the goods of the said Nicolaus, which formerly were of the said Amanducii; because the commune claims them to pertain to itself by virtue of the aforementioned sentence; whereas the hospitals claim them to pertain to themselves by virtue of the said testaments and codicils, and the restitution made to them by the said Nicolaus.

It is asked, having seen the points aforementioned and the allegations of the parties, to whom, in what manner, and for which part the said hereditary goods, formerly of Amanducii, which came to the said Nicolaus, his son and heir, ought by right to pertain and appertain.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The fiscus succeeds to the legitima and to the goods acquired by him who, being burdened with the restitution of the inheritance, was condemned to the death penalty without issue.
2. The Trebellian portion is not deducted from legacies left for pious causes.
3. "Natural" is said in two ways.
4. Alienated property is imputed to the legitima.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. If

If the codicillary substitution in favor of the hospitals had not been made, it could have been doubtful whether, by virtue of the substitution made in the will, the hospitals could be admitted or not. On this doubt, various opinions of great doctors appear. And truly it would be a disputable question in the lecture hall: but our lords, the priors and the treasurers, do not desire disputation, but a decision of the truth, which is as follows, namely, that the said hospitals, by virtue of the said codicillary substitution, come to the goods of the said Amanducius left to the said Nicolaus, after deducting the legitimate portion of the said Nicolaus, which pertains to the commune of Perugia.

† The Trebellianic portion is not deducted from the bequests to pious causes, according to the true and common opinion of modern jurists. The legitimate portion of Nicholas is one-sixth of the goods of Amanducius; for Nicholas’s sister likewise must have her legitimate portion, since there are no surviving males. And thus, since she is admitted to a share, she constitutes a share. In this fideicommissum, the goods purchased by Nicholas do not come into play, but they pertain to the commune of Perugia in the legitimate portion up to the concurrent quantity. And so it is to be decided decisively and briefly. These matters are proved in order: and first, that the fideicommissum is due to the hospitals, is proved because Nicholas died naturally without children; for even death of the body, which occurs by the sword, is called natural, because it is true and not fictitious, since the soul is separated from the body by the judgment of God, as noted in the Institutes, On Diminution of Status, after the beginning. Therefore, the condition exists through natural death by decapitation, not through civil death by condemnation. D. de iure fideicommissorum, L. Statius, § Cornelio. Nor is force to be made in any other way than in natural death.

† Natural. It is called natural in two ways: in one way, as distinguished from accidental; and in this sense, this death is not called natural. In another way, as distinguished from civil and fictitious; and in this sense, this death is rightly called natural: and thus, by it, there exists a true, and not fictitious, condition of substitution. Secondly, that the Trebellian portion is not to be deducted, is proved by l. si quis ad declinandam, in fine, together with similar authorities, C. de episc. et cler. non ob.; c. si pater, de test., lib. 6, by contrary reasoning, because it states that the contract ceases there, when it would be contrary to law. Thirdly, that the legitime is due to the Commune of Perugia, is proved, ff. ad Trebel., l. Marcel., in fine. Fourthly, that it is the sixth part of all the goods, after deduction of debts, is proved: because two parties share it, namely, the daughter and the fiscus on behalf of the son. Since, therefore, a third part is between both, the half of the third part is the sixth part, as in Auth. nouissima, C. de inoff. testa. Fifthly, that the goods newly acquired by the son do not fall into the fideicommissum, but belong entirely to the Commune of Perugia, is proved, ff. de vulg. subst., l. cohæredi, §. cum filii, versi. nec fideic.

Sixth and last, that what has been alienated is to be imputed to the legitime, is proved in the Authentica *de testibus*, and in the passage *ea quae parit*, §. *quoniam ob rem*. It is supported by what we know from the Digest, *ad Trebellianum*, l. *Marcellus*, §. *res quae*. And this we say and advise, we doctors, having seen the written documents, the testament, the codicils, the opinions, and the point at issue, and having carefully considered what ought to be considered in this matter. Bal

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Legacies repeated in a second testament, by which the first is derogated, are due; otherwise, with delegations made in the first but not repeated in the second.
2. That which is purchased with his own money by a hospitalier who has property of his own is acquired for the hospitalier himself.
3. A hospitalier who has property of his own, if he pays something because he was a surety for someone, cannot have the hospital oppose that it was paid out of the hospital's money.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

Having examined the wills of Aretius Bollus, also called Tignoni of Canaria, I, the undersigned Baldus, declare that the last will is to be observed, which was made in 1380, during the time of Pope Urban VI, on February 10. And that legacies which are not contained in this last will, although they are contained in the first, are not due, as C. de sacrosancta ecclesia, l. 1, and l. quod iterum, ff. de adimendo legatis, and ff. de legatis 1, l. si quis in principio testamenti; and therefore 40 Taseria of grain, and 10 Taseria of spelt, and such legacies which are in the first will and not in the second, are not due, nor can they be claimed.

† It is also alleged that the said Tignonus sold his own house to Marino Cecali Vignoti for the price of 27 gold florins; and that from the said price, and three gold florins, he purchased a share of a certain mill. Now the question arises whether the commune of Canaria can claim anything, because the said Tignonus was a hospitaler and had been assigned to the hospital of the said commune; and it must be said that it cannot, because the said mill was not purchased with the money of the said hospital; and because the said Tignonus had his own property, from which he could purchase, as in the chapter *Ut lex continentiae*, question 37, question 1. Furthermore, it is alleged,

† That the said Andreutius, called Tignonus, was arrested on account of a certain suretyship which he had given for a certain nephew of his, and was finally released, because payment was made for him: now the commune of Canaria says that the payment was made from the goods of the hospital. The question is asked, what is the law. I answer, he has the payment from another source; the commune of Canaria has an oblique action, and does not sue correctly: hence it is proposed by the opposing party that, if what was paid from borrowed money is concerned, the said commune of Canaria would have no right, unless it proves that it was paid from the revenues of the hospital, as in C. de arbit. tute. l. si defunctus and C. de episc. et cler. auth. licentia. I, Baldus.

In the Name of the Lord, Amen. The point of the question is as follows. It is proposed by Berleopardus of Pisa, procurator, and procurator in the name of Ser Raynerius of Campiglia, that the said procurator produces a certain document written by the hand of Nannes Philippus, the tenor of which is as follows: In the name of God, Amen. On the 10th day of January, in the year 1378, let it be manifest to any person, place, or judgment that will see this present writing, how I, Giovanni de Philippo of Urbetello, settle the account with Ser Raynerius de Cechino of Campiglia, inhabitant of Urbetello, today, the 10th day of January, for which settlement made, every account of every money which he has lent to me, and which I have received from him up to the above-written day. I, Nannes, confess, and thus is the truth, that I, the above-written Nannes, remain and am bound to give to the said Ser Raynerius 670 gold ducats, which 670 gold ducats I, Nannes, the above-written, agree and promise to give, render, and pay to the said Ser Raynerius on the Kalends of August next coming, to his heirs or to another legitimate person appearing for him, and thus I wish to be obligated, I, Nannes, the above-written, and my heirs, and all my present goods, and those that are to come, and thus I swear on the Holy Gospels of God as a real man never to go against this writing, and for greater faith and caution. I, Nannes, the above-said, have made this present writing with my own hand, and placed upon it my usual sign, not counting on this account in money, which I, Nannes, the above-written, received from the said Ser Raynerius for the house in which he resides, which I sold to him, and in which resides Lo de Abruna, etc. And I, Lapo de Francesco of Arezzo, was present to see the said account made, and the said writing made by the hand of the above-said Nannes, which Nannes, in the presence of the above-said Lapo, confessed that he ought to give to the said Ser Raynerius the above-written 672 florins at the above-mentioned term, for greater faith and testimony: I, Lapo, the above-said, have written this writing below the writing made by the said Nannes with my own hand, and signed it with my sign to the above-said day above. And I, Thomio de Maschetto of Urbetello, was present to see the above-said account made, and I was present when the said Nannes promised to give to the said Ser Raynerius the above-written 670 gold ducats at the above-said term, thus in my presence, the above-said Thomio, the said Nannes wrote with his own hand, and for greater faith and testimony of the above-said things. I, Thomio, the above-said, have written this present writing with my own hand, and signed it with my own customary seal, and this writing was made by the will of the said Nannes.

Which writing Nannes recognized under the tenor of the words inscribed below. Nannes Philippus, the above-said, not revoking the appeals interposed by him, but rather confirming them, constituted in judgment before me, John, the above-said, as above, sitting, says and recognizes the said writing produced by Berleopardus, as above named, and written by his own hand of the said Nannes; however, he says that the contents therein are not according to the substance of the truth; because he says it was fictitiously made, and under usury, and the money contained therein is doubled. He also says that the money which he received from him was the money of two counts, and the witnesses subscribed in the said writing were not present at the calculation of the above-said account; and the said Nannes was deceived in the said account in a great quantity, and he wishes to recognize and see his error. And furthermore, he says that where it is contained in the said writing that he swore, it is not true; nor did he ever swear the above-said; however, it is true that he wrote that he had sworn; and since the above-said are true, the said Nannes is prepared to prove them within a competent term to be fixed for him, in the presence of Berleopardus, the above-said procurator.

It is also proposed by the said Berleopardus, the above-said procurator, that the said Nannes ought to be condemned; and he protests that he be pronounced confessed; and condemned to the restitution of the quantities contained in the above-scribed writing, and in legitimate expenses.

It is contradicted by the said Nannes, and he says that he does not come to be condemned in the sum contained in the above-said writing; although it is proposed by Berleopardus, the procurator, that the said Nannes recognized that his said writing was fictitiously made, and that he was deceived, as appears more fully above in his response.

It is also proposed by the said Nannes that the said Ser Raynerius is a public usurer; and that the said writing is usurious. And that the said Ser Raynerius is and is reputed to be a usurer. He intends to prove this legitimately by suitable witnesses. On this proof to be made, the said Nannes produced articles; on which articles the said Ser Raynerius responded with an oath; and after the said response was made on the said articles, Nannes wished to produce witnesses to prove that Ser Raynerius is a usurer; by the said Berleopardus, the procurator, it was protested that the said witnesses ought not to be received, nor admitted, nor examined, for two reasons. And first, he says that in a confession there are no parts of the judge. Second, he says that the said Nannes is perjurious; since it is contained that the said Nannes swore not to go against the said writing, and he contravened it, as appears in the response, he ought not to be heard in law; nor ought the said witnesses to be received, nor admitted. And thus he was protested, as above. Nevertheless, the cognitor of the question nevertheless received the said witnesses, admitted them, if and insofar as he is bound and ought to do so by law, and not otherwise.

By the said Nannes it is replied, and it is said, that if a perjurer ought not to be heard, that also the said Ser Raynerius ought not to be heard; since in the response made by the said Ser Raynerius with the above-said oath to the above-said articles produced by the said Nannes, the said Ser Raynerius swore that he is not a usurer. And that he is a usurer, of this there is public voice and fame; and this he intends to disprove; and consequently, if both are perjurers, neither ought to be heard; and if neither ought to be heard, the cognition of the suit and the question ought to be known by the cognitor at the petition of the parties causing the suit; and the parties causing the suit do not take interest in the judgment for the above-said reason.

Now it is asked, what is the law: whether the above-said Ser Raynerius and Nannes, or either of them, is and ought to be reputed and pronounced perjurious on account of the above-said, or not. Also, if they are perjurers, or either of them, what ought to be done by the cognitor. Also, if the said witnesses ought to be received and examined, or not.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A person who has taken an oath cannot act against his own oath, even if he claims that the contract was usurious, unless he first obtains absolution.
2. When perjury is set off against perjury, and in what cases a perjurer is to be heard.
3. Proof that someone is a usurer ought not to be admitted in a secular court.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† He who swears to pay cannot go against his own oath, even if he claims that the contract was usurious, unless he is first absolved from the oath by the bishop, as stated in Extra, De iureiurando, c. 2 and c. Debitores. Therefore, unless he petitions to be absolved from the oath, he should not be heard raising an exception; nor should he be admitted to prove the exception. Hence, unless something new is introduced in the episcopal court, the case of usury pertains to the episcopal court, and the debtor will be compelled to pay, saving to him the right of the condictio indebiti, if he later proves that the contract was usurious, according to the aforementioned chapter Debitores and the note in the Digest, De conditione indebiti, l. Neratius. That he swore is apparent, because he said, “I swear,” etc., in Extra, De iureiurando, c. Et si Christus. Although he did not touch the writing, the Gospels, or the sacred books, as noted in the Authenticum, Sacra publica, through the doctors. It is not an objection if it is said,

† That perjury is compensated by perjury: because this is not true when perjury is committed concerning different matters, but only when it is committed concerning one and the same act. Furthermore, the objection that a perjurer ought not to be heard does not hold; for rather, he is heard in temporal matters, although not in spiritual ones, as noted above in the title *De iureiurando*, in the chapter *Alias*, and according to Innocentius in the chapter *Dilecto*, *De prebendis*.

† Moreover, perjury on the part of the plaintiff is not established: because, in order to prove that someone is a usurer, one should not be admitted in a secular court, even if it has already been established that he was a usurer; by reason of calculation, he could be placed and recognized by the secular judge. Sol. Mat. l. Titia. per Bar. A S. The point of the question is as follows. A certain Vannes Salvi of Cortonio died without having made a will, leaving behind him his sons, males, Salvi and Peter; and Lady Blasia, his daughter, now the wife of Martin. When Lady Blasia married, she received as dowry one piece of land from the common goods of herself and her brothers, and 25 pounds, of which piece of land and 25 pounds the husband confessed that he had received from the said brothers, namely Salvi and Peter. Furthermore, she had another piece of land, which the same husband confesses he received from the prior of the fraternity, or from the fraternity itself, to which fraternity that piece of land belonged. The father died thirty years ago, or thereabouts. Peter, brother of both, common to both parents, of Blasia and Salvi, died two years ago, or thereabouts. Lady Blasia claims to be heir to both Vannes, her father, and Peter, for an equal share with the said Salvi. It is alleged by Salvi that she should not be an heir, given the statutes stating that a dowried daughter shall not come nor return to the succession of her father or mother, etc. By Lady Blasia it is said that she was not dowried by her father, as is expressed and required by the statute; but rather she, to whom the inheritance of her father was due, was effectively dowried from her own goods, and not from her father’s goods. Moreover, she is not sufficiently dowried by those; but in defect and supplement of what ought to have been given to her as dowry, the fraternity gave one piece of land, which is of such value as the piece given from the former goods of the father. Or if it were of greater or lesser value, the difference in price between the piece of land and the other piece would be slight; and thus she is not considered dowried, who was not fully dowried. It is also alleged that the aforementioned statute, in that part where it speaks of a brother dowering his sister, does not exclude her from succession except in the part that was given to her as dowry, up to the concurrent quantity with what is due to her from the common goods or inheritance with her brothers. It is also said that she is not dowried, who in the case of restitution of dowry would not recover the dowry; and that the prior of the fraternity in the said case stipulated that the dowry be returned to him. Moreover, to the said giving of the dowry, or any act, there was no presence nor consent of Lady Blasia, who at that time was about fifteen years of age; and by the statute her obligation is null. It is asked whether the said Lady Blasia is admitted to the succession of both her father and her brother, or not.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A daughter, after the death of her father, is not excluded from the succession of her father, nor of her brother, even if she has been provided with a dowry by her brother.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† According to the matters proposed, this woman was not dowered by her father; therefore, she can succeed to her father, unless the prescription of thirty years stands in her way, as in C. de iure deliberando, l. licet. But she was properly dowered by her brother, not fully, but in part, because it was from common goods, C. de dote promissa, l. si. However, the statute does not seem to speak to the effect that she is thereby excluded from the succession of her brother; rather, it fictions that she is dowered from her own property. Also according to the note in the said l. si. But if the statute were understood from the general principle of the statute, that she is thereby excluded from the succession of her brother, she could sue for the supplement of the competent dowry. ff. de legatis 2, l. 1; de legatis 3, si filiae; ff. de iure dotium, l. cum post, §. generaliter; C. de inofficioso testamento, l. omnimodo; de actionibus et obligationibus, l. obligamur, §. lege succedere; auth. ut heres non posset. It is certain that the dowry given from outside by a prior brotherhood does not come into consideration, ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. sed si plures, §. in arrogato, because it is received by the right of piety, not of cognation, ff. de iure dotium, l. profectitia; ff. de conditionibus indebiti, l. cum his, §. si mulier. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given the rule that dowried daughters do not succeed when collateral brothers are alive, dowried daughters will be excluded by more remote collateral relatives than carnal brothers.
2. Although an outlawed person cannot alienate property during the period of outlawry, he may nevertheless bind himself personally, so that the alienation may become valid once the outlawry is removed.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Because Cechus died before Vanna, with male sons surviving, who appear to be included in the benefit of the statute intended to exclude entirely daughters who have received dowries, it follows that he who purchased from Blasio, who seized Vanna’s inheritance, purchased justly from him as from the owner and heir, as is stated in the Institutes, On the kinds of heirs, and in the Digest, § If, Code, On the sale of inheritances, law If, Digest, On the same matter, law Vendor. That he is included in the benefit of the statute seems certain, because he is among the collaterals, as is clear in the Institutes, On degrees, after the principal rule, Digest, On the same matter, law By the advice of the jurists. For the general term “collaterals” is to be understood generally. Argument from law On the unlawful calling, law Parents, and Digest, On the testament of a soldier, law In fraud, § If.

On the contrary, it appears that the statute, when it excludes a dowered daughter from her father’s succession, speaks conditionally, if flesh-and-blood brothers survive; but here no flesh-and-blood brothers survive; therefore, daughters are not excluded: as in the Code, On collations, law That one; Digest, On the inofficious will, law 1; Institutes, On intestate heirs, § Moreover, the ancient custom; Code, On the dowry of a free woman, law The greatest defect.

I am in doubt: for what effect does the addition of “collaterals” produce? Words ought to have some effect. Collaterals, namely males, are preferred to females; therefore, not only are flesh-and-blood brothers preferred, but also other collaterals descending or proceeding through the male line. But according to this, what effect do those conditional and restrictive words, “if flesh-and-blood brothers survive,” have? Certainly none, unless it is said that the dowered daughter is excluded by flesh-and-blood brothers, and no less by other descendants, and even by the transverse relatives of the deceased; because the statute intends to expand the right of the male and agnatic line. It supports what is noted by Cynus, Code, On adultery, law Public, and law 1, Digest, On the inspection of sales. Therefore, she is excluded by transverse relatives of a higher degree, such as by the son of the father; likewise by transverse relatives of equal degree, and by the paternal uncle’s son; and much more strongly by a flesh-and-blood brother. And thus I believe this to be the intent of this poorly worded and poorly composed statute: the words are merely superfluous. Digest, On municipal matters, law 1; Digest, On legacies, law 1, law If at any time. And so the first opinion is true. And

† Although the said Blasius was under a ban and, by the form of the statute, could not alienate, nevertheless he could personally obligate himself; hence, the ban being removed from the equation, the alienation becomes valid. D. de rei vend. l. si a Titio; D. de except. rei vend. l. 1, § si a Titio; and fully noted by the Modernists. D. de usuc. l. cum iuxta praedium.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An exemplified instrument is not believed if the original is found cancelled in its form and substance; and what is the law if both are original instruments, one of which is found cancelled.
2. Whether cancellation causes prejudice in the edict of the divine Adrian for the purpose of rescission.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The point on which counsel is sought is as follows: Having seen a certain petition produced in the name of Menecy, Laurentius, and Benedict, the minor heirs of Ser Angelus Tudinius by the testament of the said Ser Angelus, for the purpose of taking possession of the inheritance of Ser Angelus in the said petition, and having seen the contents thereof, and having seen the appearance made on behalf of Franciscus Lippi of Todi, asserting himself to be the heir by the testament of the late Marinutia, formerly the wife of the said Ser Angelus, and having seen the exceptions objected on behalf of the said Franciscus against the said petition, and having seen the replies made on behalf of the said Menecy and of the late Petruccia, heir of the said Benedict, and of the heirs of the said Ser Angelus, against the aforesaid exceptions, and having seen the terms and delays granted in the said cause to the said parties for proof, and having seen the acts and facts done in the said cause by the aforementioned parties, and having seen the testimonies of the witnesses examined in the said cause both on behalf of the said Menecy and Petruccia and on behalf of the said Franciscus, and having seen the testament formerly made by the said Ser Angelus, and having seen a certain original in the form of a testament formerly made by the said Marentia, as is alleged, which original is found to be written in the hand of the said Ser Angelus, and at the end of the said original is written in the hand of Ser Ioannes Ruchius, notary of Todi, now deceased, in the form in which it is transmitted to you, and having seen other instruments and rights produced in the cause by the aforementioned parties, and having seen the exceptions and replies made on both sides against the things produced, and having seen a certain fragment which is said to have emanated from the said original, written and published by the hand of the said Ser Ioannes Nuchius, and having seen the statutes of the commune of Todi, all of which are transmitted to you, Lord Consultant, who are the judges of the said cause, and what sentence ought to be rendered in the said cause, let counsel be given in the Name of Christ.

† If one instrument is original and the other is a copy, and if cancellation is found in the original regarding both form and substance, the copy is not believed, as noted in C. de edendo, auth. Si quis in aliquo documento, and C. de testibus, l. Publicati. And if there are two originals, and one is cancelled while the other is not, it seems that the non-cancelled one should be relied upon. D. de his quae in testamento delentur, l. Si, and there by Bartolus. But elsewhere he says that either both originals are protocols; and then the non-cancelled one is relied upon; or one is a protocol and the other is taken by the hand of the same notary; then the protocol is relied upon; therefore, if it cannot be known which is the protocol, neither is valid, D. de legatis 2, l. Sempronius Proculo. But there he speaks where there is a discrepancy in form; he does not speak of cancellation. And therefore it seems that the non-cancelled one should be relied upon, because cancellation does not always invalidate, as noted in D. de pactis, l. Postquam. And some notaries have the custom of cancelling when they return the instrument; nevertheless, they act improperly. Yet it may be doubted

† whether it may, or whether it prejudices the edict of the divine Adrian: and certainly it would prejudice, unless faith were placed in the cancelled document by means of the non-cancelled one, as in l. edicto. §. 1. de edicto diui. Adri. tol. Here one may doubt, because the non-cancelled document, by reference to the cancelled protocol, is rendered somewhat vitiated: and therefore in the possessory action under the edict of the divine Adrian it does not seem sufficient, according to the opinion of Bartolus in l. 1. §. si in duobus. ff. de bonis possessionibus secundum tabulas. For on account of the conflict of cancellation, which is opposed in the edict, the discussion of the truth pertains to the examination of a higher inquiry: which examination does not pertain to that edict, but is reserved for the petitory action, as in l. 2. C. de edicto diui Adria. Wherefore it seems that it may be defended in law: and on account of the said variety of the cancelled document and the one taken, such a document is not heard in obtaining the benefit of that edict, and the adversary, who has an undoubted instrument, is preferred. And it supports this, extra de religiosis domibus, c. cum venerabilis. For by the quality of proof, he is stronger who proves more clearly: so by the quality of possession, he is stronger who proves more justly: so by the order of time, he is stronger who proves the more ancient possession. C. de rei venditione, l. quoties. extra de probationibus, c. licet causam. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When the time fixed by the testator for the payment of legacies ought to begin.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If the testator commands, under penalty of deprivation of the inheritance, that legacies be satisfied within a year, and does not state when this year begins, we understand it to run from the day of the acceptance of the inheritance and the acknowledgment of the legacies. Hence, it is necessary that there be proof of the acceptance of the legacies, and the day inducing delay does not run before the heir is bound. See Digest, On the Right of Dowry, law *Tali*. And therefore the monastery of Saint Nicholas of Campo Longo does not lose its right under the testament of Coli Corraductii: who, now that he is heir, may freely sell for the satisfaction of the legacies. See Codex, On Fideicommissa, law *Quotiens*, at the end; and Authenticum, On Heirs and Falcidia, section *Si quis autem non implens*.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A legitimated child does not exclude the substitute.
2. When a son is legitimated after the father's death, those who have an interest must be cited.
3. Legitimation does not operate retroactively. Add also the two following consilia.
body: In the Name of God and of His most Holy Mother, the Glorious Virgin Mary, and of the entire heavenly court. Amen. Having seen the testament of Lord Albert of Campanea, having seen the donation made by Bernard to Lord Francis and his heirs, having seen the Imperial privilege granted to the Lord Count, having seen the legitimation made by the said Lord Count in the person of Michael, all things having been diligently examined, and mature deliberation having been taken, to me

It appears that the aforementioned Michael, thus legitimated, can neither bring an action nor demand anything from the heirs of Lord Francis regarding the goods which they, or their father, possessed by virtue of the testament of Lord Albert, or by virtue of the donation made by Bernard; which is evidently demonstrated and can be shown. By virtue of the testament and by virtue of the donation, the said goods ought to pertain to the said Francis and his heirs, if the condition was fulfilled, namely that Bernard died without legitimated sons, as appears from the very text of the testament or donation. Now the condition has been fulfilled and purified, because Bernard left no one but Michael, who was spurious and not legitimate; therefore, the testament and donation ought to take effect. Now it remains to respond to the legitimation made by the said contemptor. And first, such legitimation appears invalid, because in the said legitimation those whose interest it was were neither cited nor called, namely the sons of Lord Francis, agnates of Bernard; hence the legitimation is null.

For according to the common opinion of the doctors, a son is legitimated after the death of his father; and then those whose interest is affected must be summoned, as the learned Bartolus writes in *l. Gallus*, § *Quid si*, D. de liberis et posthumis. And this is the common opinion. But here no one was summoned; therefore, and so forth. If it is said that the lord cautiously legitimated him, notwithstanding that the agnates were not summoned, as is contained in the imperial privilege: to this I respond that perhaps the Emperor could not swallow up the right of another who was not required; and especially a right acquired from a contract of donation, in which consensus is involved, which is a matter of the law of nations. But because these points are somewhat doubtful, I can respond differently, that here no specific law was derogated from specifically, but generally. And the gloss in *Auth. Quibus modis*, § *Si*, and C. de incestis nuptiis, *Auth. Ex complexu*, wish that derogation be made specifically; but because this is not the common opinion, I respond differently, and most clearly. In the imperial privilege there is such a derogation, and also in legitimation, namely, *non obstantibus legibus* [notwithstanding the laws], which provide that bastards cannot be legitimated without the consent and will of the legitimate and natural children; therefore, derogation is made to the consent and will of the legitimate and natural children. Now, the sons of Francis, who were not summoned, are not the legitimate and natural sons of Bernard, but his agnates, concerning whom the privilege made no mention in derogating. Moreover, derogation is made so that the consent and will of the legitimate children are not necessary; but derogation is not made to the effect that they need not be summoned, nor that such legitimation, when it was being carried out, since it involved their prejudice, should not come to their knowledge. Hence, the privilege does not touch our case, since this privilege is odious and is not extended to another case or to other persons. These are common legal principles.

† Moreover, upon more subtle investigation, this legitimation was made after the right had already been fully acquired by Lord Francis and his sons; therefore, this legitimation does not prejudice them, by the argument of that which is noted in the preceding discussion, l. legat. §. quid si nepos. Whether we say that this legitimation has the force of restitution, and thus does not operate retroactively; hence it is true that, if it does not operate retroactively, Bernard died without a legitimate son, since at the time of his death Michael was not yet legitimated. And whether he had a legitimated son or not, we must examine the time of his death, as in l. ex facto §. si quis autem ad Treb. Or whether we say that this legitimation has the force of fiction, and thus operates retroactively, so that Bernard appears to have had a legitimate and natural son at the time of his death, and thus the condition of the will and donation fails, and this fiction is removed first because Jacobus de Belvisio in Auth. qui modo nat. efficiantur sui §. tribus holds that legitimation does not have the force of fiction, nor does it operate retroactively, which is perhaps true. But even assuming that it has the force of fiction, it does not operate retroactively because in the meantime the status has changed: for by prescription the ownership of the said goods was acquired by Lord Francis and his sons; therefore, this legitimation could not be drawn back. By the argument of that which Cynus fully notes in l. si C. ad macell. And by this, it is no obstacle to what Lord Bartolus writes in d. l. gallus. Assuming that legitimation has the force of fiction, it cannot be feigned that Bernard had a legitimate son in the past, since at the time of his death he was not yet legitimated. For this fiction to have place, it was necessary that he have him legitimate both at the time of his death and afterwards, and that he be feigned to have had him legitimate at the time of his death and in the past; but Bernard never had him legitimate, because he was legitimated after his death; therefore, it cannot be said that he had him legitimate at the time of his death, since fiction must have two attainable extremes in order to operate retroactively, the extreme from which and the extreme to which; but here the extreme from which is lacking, as noted by Cynus in l. si C. de sententiis passis, and by Lord Bartolus fully in l. si is, qui pro emptore. Since therefore Bernard did not have a legitimate son at the time of his death, either truly or fictitiously, the condition of the will and the donation stood; and thus Michael can claim nothing. Moreover, for the condition of the will or donation to fail, it is necessary that Bernard have a legitimate son born and begotten of him, as appears from the words of the will and donation, and thus this son must have two conditions, or qualities, to exclude the substitute or donee, namely Lord Francis and his sons: first, that he be legitimate; second, that he be born of Bernard. A privilege can indeed make one legitimate, but not that he be born of Bernard, since the law cannot dispose concerning rights of blood. For here the testator and donor seem to have had regard to naturalness, which ceases in a spurious child born in prohibited intercourse, as is Michael. And for this supports the question disputed by Jacobus de Belvisio in Auth. de sanct. episc. §. hoc praesenti col. 9, l. si ita quis §. is, cui ff. de legat. 2, although there Lord Bartolus says otherwise. But the opinion of Lord Jacobus de Belvisio is common, especially since it is said that the heirs of Lord Francis can prove by reputation that the said Michael is the spurious child of another, according to the statute of the city of Verona speaking on this matter, by which, and by many others that could be alleged, I think the heirs of Lord Francis support better and stronger rights than Michael himself. I, Agentius, etc. I, Paganinus, etc. And I, Ubertinus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Legitimation does not operate retroactively to the prejudice of those in whom a right has vested. And see on this matter below in the three immediately following opinions, in opinion 30.
2. One who has the power to legitimize spurious children, whether the parents are alive or already deceased, cannot legitimize them to the prejudice of those in whom a right has vested.
3. In the legitimation of a son after the father’s death, the consent of the agnates in whom the right of succession has vested is required as a matter of law.
4. The general words of a privilege must be strictly construed: and according to the common law, they are subject to limitation.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Regarding the legitimation of Michael, who is said to have been legitimated by Lord Cont of Parma, and with Bernard, father of the said Michael, having predeceased, twenty years or thereabouts have now elapsed. Lord Francis, the uncle of the said Bernard, succeeded to his intestate estate, and held and possessed his goods until he died, and today his heirs hold them. It is doubted whether the legitimation operates retroactively, so that he might thereby take away the inheritance of his father, already acquired by others, either in whole or in part, considering the power granted by the Emperor to Lord Cont, the words of which are written above in his privilege; and also considering the legitimation made by the said Cont, and its form, and the power viewed as granted and conferred upon the legitimated person in succeeding to his parents, it is doubted whether this prejudices the heirs of Lord Francis with respect to certain legacies made to him by Albert of Campanea in the case where the said Bernard, son and heir of the said Albert, should die without legitimate children begotten by him; and especially considering a certain promise made by the said Bernard to the said Lord Francis, by reason of a donation inter vivos of transferring the possessions which he holds in the land of Fauenzola, on the condition that if the said Bernard should die without legitimate children born to him, and from a lawful marriage. In the Name of Christ.

† Having invoked [the Divine Name], I first decide this last doubt, and I say that the aforementioned legitimation does not prejudice the lord Francisco, or his heir, beyond the aforementioned allegations: which I demonstrate from four points. First, because, considering the condition of the legacy, it is required that, according to the time of death, Bernard had children then legitimate, which was not the case here: therefore, the condition does not fail, but was fulfilled. That he ought to have legitimate children according to the time of death, I prove, because the quality added to the word "even" is required to be produced according to the time of the word to which it is joined, as in D. de noxa, l. in delictis, §. si extraneus, and l. ut praetor, §. Iulianus, and D. de testamento militis, l. si miles. But in our case, the existence of legitimate children is required according to the time of Bernard's death, because he says, "if he should die without legitimate children." Hence, just as the existence of the words is required then, so too is the quality of legitimation cohering to the children. Second, to the same effect, which is doubtful to no one, because the condition of the legacy existed, because he died without legitimate children: therefore, it cannot subsequently fail by a new supervening case. C. quoniam dies legati, c. l. cum uxori. Third, because the will of the testator, which always prevails in last wills, as in all laws, was that the condition should fail if sons were born legitimate from marriage, when he added "from the same" generally. For those words come as qualifying and limiting the preceding words, and as implying. For he did not will that the condition should fail by a legitimate son: but by one born legitimate to him: thus it is required that he be natural and legitimate, as the doctors note in Auth. nisi rogati, C. ad Trebellianum, and by John Andeolus in c. in praesentia, de probationibus. And this naturalness and legitimacy must concur according to the time of death, by the laws alleged above in the first argument. This is confirmed, because the said Albert prohibited the said Bernard from keeping a concubine: therefore it follows that, when he says, "if he should die without legitimate children, etc.," he did not understand those born from a concubine: and especially bastards, as the doctors note, C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus sub conditione factis, l. generaliter, §. si, and there by my lord. Fourth, this is validated by the promise made by the said Bernard to the said Francisco, which was conditional: and its condition was, if he should die without legitimate children born from him, and from a legitimate marriage. Hence, it is noted that he speaks of a legitimate marriage, which fails in our case, therefore, etc. And from the foregoing it is clear that this second point seems indubitable: and thus it should be held for the heirs of the said Francisco. There are also some things which I will add in the following.

† Now I proceed to the strength of the legitimation performed, and to the power of the Lord Count, assuming the power of the Lord Emperor, concerning which I do not extend myself: similarly, assuming the privilege of the Lord Count to be valid in what was granted to him, I say that the Lord Count granted more to the said Michael than he could grant by virtue of the privilege granted to him by the Prince. The Lord Count grants to him that the said Michael, by the legitimation performed by him, succeeds the said Bernard, his father, who died before this legitimation, as is stated above, having been dead for many years: but he could not do this, because, examining the entire privilege of the Lord Count, no power is found to have been granted to him to do this: therefore, etc. For although at the beginning of his privilege power is given to him to legitimize bastards whose parents are living or already dead, it does not follow that therefore power is given so that those legitimized after the death of their parents succeed them: and take away an inheritance already acquired by others. And the reason is, because it does not prove that this is so, when it is absent for this purpose, as in *l. ad probationem* and *l. neque natales*, *de probationibus*; and *l. non hoc*, C. *unde cognoscatur*. Nor can it be said that this power is granted to him in such a manner, when it says literally, "that they, in equal portions, succeed their parents and agnates," because those words similarly grant that power: which I demonstrate, for from those words a double interpretation may arise: one, that it refers to legitimation performed while the father was living, and this is a good interpretation indeed. The other, that it refers to legitimation performed after the father's death, as in our case: and thus when the inheritance has already been acquired by another. And this interpretation is not good: nor is it to be chosen from those words as being contrary to law, but rather contrary to reason and absurd, as in *l. benignus*, ff. *de legibus*; and *l. cum patre*, *de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*. That this second interpretation is absurd and vicious, I demonstrate briefly from several points. First, because the written words of a prince are to be interpreted in such a way that no injuries arise therefrom according to the laws, C. *unde vi*, *l. meminerit*; and *ad l. muscae*, *l. 2*.
