Second, because privileges of a prince are to be understood without injury to a third party, and without prejudice to a right already acquired by another, ff. *ne quid in loco publico*, *l. 1*, § *merito*; and § *si quis a principe*; and C. *de emancipatis liberis*, *l. nec auus*. Third, because otherwise the freedom of testation granted by law to the deceased would be taken away, contrary to *l. 1*, C. *de sacrosancta ecclesia*; *l. pactum*, *quod dotali*, C. *de collationibus*; and *l. pactum*, *de pactis*. Fourth, because one who did not sin would be punished, contrary to *l. mandata impleuit*, C. *de his qui vetita aetate impetrant*; and contrary to *l. sancimus*, C. *de poenis*; and the law *eum qui nocentem*, ff. *de poenis*. I declare the foregoing: for the deceased, by dying having made a will, or intestate, wished his goods to pass to the aforesaid heir, or to the legatee, as in the first doubt deposited above: or to the then nearest agnate, as in ff. *de iure codicillorum*, *l. si quis cum nullum*; and *l. conficiuntur*. Not to the bastard, whom he knew was excluded from his inheritance: therefore, etc. Fifth, this is to be observed here: because a son is not legitimized against his will by a rescript of the Prince obtained by the father, but only with his consent, as in Auth. *quibus modis naturales efficiuntur sui*, § *generaliter*; and noted by Guillaume de Cuyac in *l. benignus*, ff. *de legibus*. Therefore, neither is a father legitimized to a son by a rescript of the Prince obtained by the son, unless the father consented. The consequence is good, because the reason is the same in both cases, therefore the same law. Also, because successions intestate ought to be mutual, equal, and reciprocal, as in Auth. *quibus modis naturales efficiuntur sui*, § *filium*; and § *penultimus*; and C. *de legatis hereditatibus*, *l. si ab eo*. And especially in correlatives. And father and son, grandfather and grandson, are such, as noted by Jacobus Butrigarius in Auth. *defuncto*, C. *ad Tertullianum*. Similarly in other correlatives, such as husband and wife, what is disposed in one is understood to be disposed in the other, as in C. *de iure viri*, *l. finalis*; and *idem actore et reo*, as in C. *de fructibus et litis expensis*, *l. finalis*; and the same in buyer and seller, ff. *de rescindenda venditione*, *l. cum emptor*; and ff. *de acceptilatione*, *l. finalis*. And for the foregoing, a good text, C. *de cupressis*, *l. 1*, lib. 11. But in our matter, the father of the said Michael did not consent to this legitimation, nor could he consent as a dead father: nor did his heirs, therefore the legitimation is null to his prejudice. Sixth, I introduce similar cases well concluding to the matter of legitimation: for adoption is an act by which one becomes legitimate, ff. *de adoptionibus*, *l. 1*. And yet by adoption one does not become a legitimate successor to another, unless that person consented to the adoption, as in ff. *de adoptionibus*, *l. si is qui filium*; and *l. si is qui nepotem*, with the notes there in the gloss. Seventh, to our case I introduce what is noted in the great gloss, C. *de adoptionibus*, *l. cum in adoptivis*, vers. *si vero pater*. By which strongest argument you will find the decision of our doubt, for a son given in adoption while in power passes into the power of the adoptive father, as formerly, and becomes his legitimate successor; nevertheless, if he is emancipated while the natural father is living, he becomes the legitimate successor of that natural father: but otherwise if he is emancipated after the natural father's death, as the gloss there wishes.

Eighthly, because the consent of the agnates of this Michael did not intervene in this legitimation, and I speak of the said Lord Francis, who succeeded to his father, and of his heirs, who were necessary so that the legitimation of Michael could prejudice them, as is the text with the gloss in the Digest, *De adoptionibus*, law *Nam ita Divus*. I declare this, for there the adoption was invalid, as in the preceding law, and the arrogator having died, the arrogated person petitioned by imperial rescript for it to be confirmed, so that he might succeed to the arrogator. The text says that those who would be injured by such confirmation must be summoned; and these are the agnates of the arrogator, to whom the right of succession has been acquired. And the gloss there asks whether the consent of those agnates is necessary, and says that it is, according to Johannes. And although some reject that gloss, saying that just as the agnates of the arrogator are not necessary in constituting [the arrogation], so neither are they in confirming it, *Codex*, *De nuptiis*, law *Si ut proponis*, and in the *Authenticum*, *De defensoribus civium*, section *Iunctim*, yet from the beginning, and in the initial arrogation, their consent was not necessary, as in law *Cum adoptio* in that title. Therefore, and so forth. Nevertheless, my lord and uncle, who illuminated that gloss and preserved its ministerial provisions, said that those who reject it speak the truth if the matter concerned an arrogation confirmed during the arrogator’s lifetime. But the gloss in law *Nam ita Divus*, upon which it is placed, speaks of the arrogator having predeceased. Hence the law wishes that the agnates, to whom the right of succession has been acquired, be cited, because their consent is necessary, as in the gloss, and rightly so, because the emperor did not wish that by his enabling and confirmation the right of succession already acquired to those agnates should be taken away. Thus there the case appears clearly decisive of our question, so that we conclude by saying that the legitimation made by the said Count of the said Michael does not prejudice Lord Francis, who did not consent, nor could he, because he is deceased, nor his heirs. Nor do the words of the rescript stand in the way, because they must be understood as referring to those legitimated during the father’s lifetime and with his will, who afterwards succeed together with the legitimate children, as is contained in the privilege; nor is it surprising,

† Because the general words of a privilege, which derogate from the law, must be strictly interpreted and, according to the common law, admit of limitation, as is clear in l. 1, C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, together with the gloss, and l. si quando, in principio, C. de inofficioso testamento, and de noxalibus, l. 2, and the common authorities on succession, Authent. omnes peregrini, and ff. de mutatione et homine, l. et gradatim, §. sed si lege. Nor do the clauses appended in the letters of privilege stand in the way; for they do not extend to this case of rights already acquired by the agnates: since no mention is made there of a similar case, but rather there is an opinion as to whether general clauses appended ex certa scientia suffice in the legitimation of spurious children: and many most learned experts say that they do not: for the laws impeding legitimation must be specifically removed. On this point I do not insist, because it is not opportune to examine it at present: since, as I have said, there is no derogatory clause from the laws vitiating rescripts, by which alien rights are absorbed and already acquired by another, as in l. quotiens, and in l. nec damnosa, and l. rescripta, C. de prima imperatoris officio. I therefore conclude that this legitimation does not benefit the legitimated person with regard to paternal succession, which I also confirm from the fact that legitimation does not make the legitimated person the heir of the father by operation of law, but only, where it is valid and concerns the father’s succession, grants the faculty of entering upon the inheritance. But in our case, since the inheritance of the said Bernard is not vacant at the time of the legitimation, I do not see how it can be entered upon by Michael, the legitimated person. Nor does it avail anyone to reply that it is fictitiously assumed above that it was not entered upon by the said Lord Francis; because nothing is expressed or provided for in the said privilege granted to Conti regarding such a renunciation of an already made entry upon the inheritance, and therefore the words of his privilege cannot in any way be extended to our case. And there ends the matter.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A person cannot truly be legitimated before, nor after the death of his father; nevertheless, the Emperor may enable his subjects to succeed, and to perform legitimate acts, and to hold secular honors.
2. Legitimation does not operate retroactively so as to prejudice those who come in intestacy, in whom the right to the inheritance has vested.
3. Legitimation effected during the father’s lifetime, or because he disposed in his will that the son be legitimated, requires no citation; and if it is made outside these two cases without the citation and consent of those who have an interest, the legitimation is invalid.
4. Whether an imperial privilege derogates from the laws prescribing the requisition of those who have an interest: not decided.
5. In privileges, a derogatory clause is not sufficient unless certain laws are expressly mentioned.
6. How filiation is to be proved.
body: In the Name of the Lord, Amen. And of the Blessed Virgin, and of both Johns. In the question proposed, several points are to be examined. First, whether Michael could be legitimated after the death of his father. Second, whether this legitimation, assuming it could take place, prejudices those who would succeed intestate, to whom the right in the inheritance had already been acquired before the legitimation. Third, whether those whose interest is at stake, namely those succeeding intestate, are required and were necessarily involved in this legitimation. These three points touch upon the article of legitimation.

† Regarding the first point, namely whether Michael could have been legitimated after the death of his father, it must be observed that this depends on whether the Emperor, or another person by virtue of an imperial privilege, can truly legitimate someone after the father’s death; or whether he can enable such a person to succeed, to hold honors, and to perform legitimate acts, notwithstanding any defect of birth.

Considering the first alternative, the Emperor cannot do so, nor could he even during the father’s lifetime, even if the father requested it, much less after the father’s death. This is demonstrated as follows: for a true legitimate child is one born of a lawful marriage. D. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt, l. filium; and l. quia semper, D. de in ius vocandis; D. de liberis agnoscendis, l. 1, § Iulianus; D. de cariss. edicto, l. 1, § si quis; and l. si, D. de probat.; C. de nuptiis, l. si vicinus; Qui filii sint legitimi, c. 2, and throughout the title. Therefore, I argue: the Emperor has no power over marriage; therefore, he has no power to truly legitimate. The antecedent is proven because marriage, as a sacrament of the Church in which grace is infused (although there is an opinion on this point, see our commentary on De sacra unctione, c. 1), belongs to the forum of the Church and pertains to the Church alone; just as in Qui filii sint legitimi, c. lator; and De ordinatione et cognitione, c. tuam. Thus, the Emperor has no power over the sacrament of marriage. The consequent is proven because he who has no power over marriage has no power over things dependent upon it, since accessories follow the nature of the principal. D. de regulis iuris, regula cum principalis; and regula accessorium, eodem titulo, lib. 6. Indeed, not even the Pope can truly legitimate children born from those between whom marriage could not exist due to an impediment of divine law, where the Pope could not dispense; because legitimacy depends on marriage, as shown above; although he can enable them for any spiritual acts.

Considering the second alternative, I say that the Emperor, and another person by virtue of an imperial privilege, can enable subjects of the Empire, in places subject to the Empire, to succeed and to perform any legitimate acts and secular honors, notwithstanding any defect of birth, so that they are regarded as if they had been born of marriage. And this can be done during the father’s lifetime and after the father’s death. This is demonstrated because the Emperor, as lord of the world in secular matters, can do all things that depend on the supreme power of the law, and contrary to and above the law, as full lord of temporalities. D. ad legem Rhodiam, l. praecatio; C. de quadriennali praescriptione, l. bene a Zenone; see our commentary in l. si, C. si contra ius vel utilitatem publicam; 7 q. 1, c. in apibus. Therefore, the Emperor, by modifying [the law] as stated above, can enable bastards, spuri, medians, and any illegitimate persons to succeed and to perform legitimate acts and secular honors, just as if they had been born of a lawful marriage; but he cannot truly legitimate them, because he could not make an illegitimate person legitimate. Thus decided Hostiensis in c. per venerabilem, Qui filii sint legitimi. And according to this understanding, the texts in Auth. qui modo naturali efficiantur legitimi and the rubric De natalibus restituendis are to be understood.

Thus, the first decisive conclusion of the first point is concluded, namely that this Michael, after the death of his father, could have been enabled by imperial privilege to any succession, just as if he had been born of a lawful marriage; and every legal impediment could have been removed. But he could not have been truly legitimated by the Emperor, as shown above. Regarding the second point,

† Whether legitimation, or more accurately habilitation, operates retroactively so as to prejudice those who have come to possess hereditary goods as intestate heirs, in whom a vested right has arisen in the inheritance, it must be observed that the doctors have varied on this point: some say that this person recovers all goods, like a posthumous child, who, being born after the fact, breaks the father’s will. D. de lib. et posth. l. cum quidam; D. de acq. haer. l. quod dicitur. And he recovers just as if he had been returned from enemies. D. de iniur. rupt. et irrit. test. l. si quis exheredatus, § sed et si pater. Also, because upon legitimation following, the law fictions that he was not a spurious and illegitimate child. D. de nat. rest. l. sic. No. Bar. in l. Gallus, § quid si tamen, D. de lib. et posth. and holds this opinion: but he says that he saw the allegations of Azo and the Decretist, and could not see what they determined. For this conclusion it is made, because this act of legitimation, or habilitation, ought to be drawn back. For not only in judgments, but in contracts and malefices, the retroaction proceeds, having concordances in C. ad Maced. l. si; and in c. ratihabitionem, de reg. iur. lib. 6. Just as we also say in the case of one captured by enemies, as l. retro, D. de capt. et postlim. reu. just as the power of postliminium, when in his person it removes the right of servitude induced by captivity, makes his condition as if he had never been in that servitude. l. postliminium, D. de captivis, et postlim. reu. 16. q. 3. c. prima actione. Thus the power of legitimation, or habilitation, makes it so, as if he had never been illegitimate. D. de in ius voc. l. si quis filio, § pe. And just as by that right one returned excludes those later in degree, as l. sed filio, § sed si pater, D. de iniur. test.; D. de bonis lib. l. si necesse, § si deportatus, D. de bonorum pos. secundum tab. l. qui ex liber. § 1. Thus by legitimation, or habilitation, a retraction is made, and an exclusion of any subsequent agnates is made. And the text seems open in Auth. quibus mod. nat. effici sui, § reliqui, there, “we give them, once made legitimate, to have succession, even those which those have who were born legitimate from the beginning.” And there in § illud, otherwise beginning, “if anyone therefore of nature in the first,” there, “differing in no way from sons.” To the same effect. D. de lib. et posth. l. filio. And C. de consulibus, l. 1, in fin. lib. 12. Some say that Franciscus Accursius held this for § reliqua, immediately alleged. Bartolus of Brescia disputed this question, and it was this in the order of his questions, and begins “a certain one having sons,” and terminated in the contrary. And he says that Huguccio held thus. Tancredus in his q. against the same held. It is placed by Io. An. in the rule sine culpa, de reg. iur. lib. 6. In the work of the Mercurials, he formed a question concerning the firstborn, however natural, and afterwards born legitimate, and natural from marriage, the supervening one did not prejudice the right acquired by the one born in the meantime, legitimate and natural, so that the supervening legitimate does not take away the right acquired at an earlier time. Three texts are induced to this conclusion: s. c. si parte; and c. quamuis, de rescript. lib. 6; and c. si appellatus, de praeb. lib. 6. And they are induced in this manner. Either it would be said that this legitimation, or habilitation, is a grant of new law, and then it makes c. si pro te. For the Pope mandates that Titius be received as a canon, if the chapter consents: before the chapter consents, another is received, and purely by the mandate of the Pope: afterwards the chapter consents to the reception of the first, the prebend is vacant: the first purely received is preferred, and the other reception is made without prejudice to the right acquired before by the purely received one. Thus in the case at hand, this habilitation, which follows the right acquired by those coming intestate, will not prejudice them, if it is said that this legitimation, or habilitation, is a restoration, then it makes c. quamuis. A certain one was deprived of the grace granted to him in a certain church: afterwards grace was made to another by a person, who first prevaricated in the same church: afterwards the Pope restored the first deposed one: this restoration does not prejudice the right acquired in the meantime by the other. It makes C. de natal. restit. l. 2, there, “restored to their ancient natal rights,” etc. It makes in Auth. qui. mo. na. effi. sui, § si quis ergo, there, “wishes to restore the offspring to nature,” etc. If it is said that legitimation, or habilitation, was, then the chapter si apostolicae, de praeb. lib. 6, where if the reservation of the legacy preceded, and the Papal confirmation followed, and after the reservation and before the confirmation another obtained from the Pope, this middle one will be prior: For the supervening confirmation does not take away the right acquired in the meantime by the one who obtained it. Thus in the case at hand, the supervening legitimation, or habilitation, does not take away the right acquired by those coming intestate. To § reliqui, the solution is clear, for it was the mind of the law that, just as succession is deferred to those born legitimate from the beginning, so to those legitimated: but the text does not say that they are considered legitimate from the beginning, according to which they have successions, which those have who are legitimate from the beginning, and thus it is solved to § illud. l. 1, C. de consul. It makes, that when it is said at the beginning that the possessor first obtained the dignity: thus in the case at hand, the possessor first obtained the succession: and thus he is stronger, as the rule qui possessor, with concordances, lib. 6. But in fin. it seems to make against, inasmuch as there the possessor consul, who first obtained the patriciate, is preferred to the second who first obtained the patriciate, if we followed the second lec. which the gloss there places, the case would be denied, and thus it would not be necessary to respond, because it would make for: according to the common lec. it ought to be solved, that there by order of the consulship the magistracy was due. It makes l. rescripto, D. de mun. et hon. If therefore it was done otherwise, from which he first obtained the magistracy, he is rightly preferred to him, to whom in obtaining he ought to have been preferred, or there was the custom of the consulship, which had the custom of many churches, that among canons of that order the priorate is not inspected in order, or there from the consulship the consul had the right. To that which is said of retroaction, that in fictions which are said to be drawn back, it is necessary that the same cause and existence persevere, otherwise if from the power of the daughter she is emancipated, the fiction admits its matter. C. de rei ux. act. l. una, § videamus. Nor ought it to be drawn to the time, from which a repugnance could follow. D. de usucap. l. is. C. de inoff. test. l. 2. And l. donationes, C. de don. inter vir. et ux. Here, however, a repugnance would arise, because the concubine at that time could not naturally be a wife, because then she was married, and thus it is concluded that the legitimation of Michael, thus supervening, does not derogate from the right acquired by those coming intestate.: but supposing that the opinion of others proceeded, a third point arises,

† And whether, at the time of legitimation, those who have an interest ought to be cited, and here it must be observed that sometimes a person is legitimated while the father is alive and requesting it, and then no one is cited, because it is principally in his interest, as in l. cum adoptio, ff. de adoptionibus. Likewise, if the father has disposed in his will, the son may request to be legitimated after the death, nor is anyone else to be called. C. de naturalibus liberis, in auth. si quis, and in the corpus, from which it is derived that sometimes the father made no disposition in his will, and then the son cannot be legitimated unless those who are thereby harmed are required, and those to whom a right has accrued; indeed, their consent is required. ff. de natalibus restitutionibus. This is concluded by Bartolus in l. Gallus, § quid si tamen, ff. de liberis et posthumis, and thus it is concluded. The third conclusion of the third point,

But now it must be examined whether the imperial privilege derogates from the rights disposing of the requisition of those who have an interest. Here it must be noted that in the privilege there is inserted a derogatory clause concerning the necessity of the consent of the legitimate and natural heirs, and their requisition, and not that of others who have an interest; and thus that clause does not concern our case. For what is not expressed therein is subject to the disposition of the common law. D. 50, 17, l. Si cum dotem; D. 38, 16, l. Commodissime; and l. Si vero. C. 4, 39, l. Maritus. Nor does the consequence hold: "It derogates to the greater obstacle, therefore to the lesser," because in matters of strict law, the consequence from what is expressed to what is not expressed does not hold. D. 50, 17, l. Quicquid; and l. Ita stipulatus, §. Grisogonus; D. 50, 4, l. Constit.; and l. Si. D. 19, 1, 13. Such are privileges. D. 50, 17, c. Privilegia. Moreover, in matters that are exorbitant from the common law, such a consequence ceases, and they are to be restricted. D. 38, 16, l. Cum quidam; Regula Quae a iure; Regula In poenis; Regula Hodie, De regulis iuris, lib. 6. This is especially so when it is a matter of taking away another's right, which the prince does not intend unless he expresses it. D. 43, 8, l. 2, §. Si quid; C. 10, 1, c. Pastoralis. Especially since the prince cannot deprive anyone of his right without cause, as in l. Quotiens, C. 1, 4; as noted in l. Si, C. 9, 1; and by Innocentius in c. Quae in ecclesiarum, De constitutionibus.

Furthermore, the derogatory clause concerning consent does not derogate from the requisition. And these are two distinct acts: to require the consent of the person himself, just as to require counsel and to follow counsel, Extra, De arbitris, c. Cum olim; De electione, c. Cum in veteri. And if one of two servitudes is removed, the other remains. D. 8, 3, l. Si domus tua; De auctoritate et usu pallii, c. Ex tuarum. Therefore, although consent may be derogated from, nevertheless by virtue of the clause it cannot be done without requisition, since they are distinct acts; and when one is expressly omitted, the others are omitted by the certain knowledge of the one issuing it. D. 5, 2, l. Cum praetor; D. 4, 39, l. Maritus; De praesumptionibus, c. Nonne. Especially in matters that are odious and to be restricted, such as these. Although it is said, "To what purpose is the requisition, if it can be done against their consent?" I answer that such a requisition could oppose something on account of which the prince would not have legitimated, just as we say of those requiring counsel, that one is not bound to follow it, and yet is bound to require it, as noted in c. Cum olim, De arbitris; and in c. In veteri, De electione. Just as in the case of an arbiter, whose requisition is required, who nevertheless could not contradict the majority present, D. 4, 8, l. Item si unus, §. Si in plures; and as noted in c. 2, eod. tit., lib. 6. Thus that clause does not derogate, nor does the subsequent general clause derogating from the law in general, since a subsequent general clause expressly stated is not extended to greater matters, De procuratoribus, c. Quo ad agendum; De rescriptis, c. Sedis; and c. Cum in multis, eod., lib. 6.

† Moreover, according to the mind of the commentator on privileges, a derogatory clause against laws is not sufficient unless certain laws are expressly named. D. Si quis cautionibus; L. Sed et si quis, §. Quaesitum, D. De procuratoribus; L. Qui ad agendum, Lib. 6, D. De acquisitione hereditatis; L. Si quis mihi bona, §. Iussum, C. De bonis sublatis; L. 2, Lib. 10, De confirmatione utili vel inutili; C. Bonae, De dolo et contumacia; C. 2. By analogy, just as a father expressly disinherits his sons, as in L. 2, D. De liberis et posthumis, so too does the prince expressly disinherit the law. This opinion is followed by the Archdeacon, where the order of law is overturned or injustice arises, which occurs here, namely that no one is required to be heard when it concerns the removal of his own right, and that he is deprived of his right without cause. For here, if the prince could do this, an expressive clause should be inserted, and general words would not suffice. The notes in L. Si quis in principio, D. De legibus, and L. Finis, C. Si contra ius vel utilitatem publicam, and C. Uno, De excessibus praeparatorum, Lib. 6, support this. This also supports the opinion distinguishing whether the prince grants a privilege by his own motion, in which case the quality of the expressly derogatory clause is not weighed, or at the instance of another, in which case it is weighed so that it be expressive, especially when another’s right is absorbed, as here. In support of this is C. Si motu proprio, De rescriptis, Lib. 6, and in the gloss on C. Si Romana, eodem titulo. On this point, however, there are various opinions of the noted jurists in L. Si quis in principio, D. De legibus, and in C. Uno, De excessibus praeparatorum, Lib. 6. Therefore, I do not firmly adhere to this view, but leave it to the discretion of the judge.

† Item, it is asserted here that it can be proven by public voice and fame that Michael was the son of another, and by the assertion of Bernard, the putative father, that he was not his son. It must be observed that filiation on the part of the father is not probable of necessity, as in *l. Lucius*, D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus; and *l. filium*, D. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt; noted in X. de probationibus, c. *Per tuas*; de filiis presbyterorum, c. *Michael*. But it is proven in a petitory action, provided that marriage is proven, and that the child was born in the home while the marriage subsisted, and while the husband and wife cohabited together, as in *l. iubemus*, C. de nuptiis; and *l. filium*, C. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt. It is also proven in a possessory action, provided that quasi-possession is proven on the part of both, namely, that he was in quasi-possession of being treated as a son by the father, and thus by the father, and thus reputed. Thirdly, it can be proven by public voice and fame. Fourthly, it can be proven by combining all these modes. Here in our case, it is proven by public voice and local fame that this man was the son of a stranger; from which it is inferred that he was not the son of Albert. This proof is aided by the assertion of Bernard, who asserted that he was not his son. In this proof, one cannot proceed except in a possessory action, or by public voice and fame, [to establish that he is] natural or spurious, and thus the marriage does not proceed even by the sole proof of public voice and fame, and quasi-possession, and common reputation. Since therefore it is established here by public voice and fame that he is the son of another, and it is established by the assertion of Bernard that he is not his son, which assertion binds strongly, as in c. *Per tuas*, X. de probationibus, where the putative father denied the son in a similar case, and afterwards, overcome by the insistence of the concubine, recognized the son: according to the common opinion of doctors there, the denial of the father was upheld, if interpretation had not intervened in doubt due to the subsequent recognition because of the danger that threatened in contracting marriage with a cousin; because it is not likely that a father would deny a son whom he naturally loves as himself, D. quod metus causa, *l. isti quidem*, in fine, since he is considered one person with him, as in *l. si*, C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus. Here, the assertion of Bernard, together with the public voice of the neighborhood, will prove him not to be the son, unless stronger proofs are to the contrary. Nor does the denier here incur the penalty of the statute, since he proves in a probable manner: the statute speaks of one who simply denies, [where] proof is made to the contrary; this proof is denied, which is proven by proving filiation of another; and thus indirectly by the assertion of Bernard, the putative father. If the privilege had a most sufficient derogatory clause, it would not operate concerning this denied son, unless it otherwise appears that he is the son, since by the assertion of Bernard, and by public voice and fame, it is proven that he is not the son.

Furthermore, I consider that the said Albert, father of Bernard, in his will left certain legacies to Bernard, his son, with the addition that if he should die without legitimate and natural sons, it should devolve to Francis, his brother. This being assumed, that Francis, his heir, possesses those goods by the disposition of the testator, the fideicommissum being purified by the condition that he died without legitimate sons; nor does [the existence of a] natural son alone make it vanish, because he added "legitimate"; otherwise, if [he had said] "without children," D. ad Trebellianam, *l. ex facto*, § *si quis rogatus*; and *l. Lucius*, § *ultimo*; and *l. cum pater*, § *volo*, D. de legatis 2; noted in *l. quamvis*, C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus. But these rights acquired by Francis by the will of the testator are not taken away by the prince, even if he could take them away, considering the words of the privilege, and considering the words of legitimation or habilitation; for, considering the words of habilitation to any successions, just as if he had been born of a legitimate marriage, and makes him heir, as if he were legitimate; but if he were a legitimate son and instituted heir, nevertheless the legacies and fideicommissa would be due, since the will of the deceased is to be observed as if it were law. *l. 1*, C. de sacrosancta ecclesia; in Auth. de nuptiis, § *deinceps*. Nor do the words of legitimation or privilege imply this: to which [words] we must adhere. D. de legatis 3, *l. non aliter*; *l. 1*, § *si is qui navem*, D. de exercitoria. Nor was it the mind of the prince, whether legitimating legatees or fideicommissaries, to deprive particular persons of their right, where no prejudice would be done at all to the primary succession of the legitimated; for example, if he had thus distributed all his goods particularly; for it is not the mind of the prince to take away another's right, especially without cause, unless he expresses this specifically, as in *l. 2*, § *si quis a principe*, D. ne quid in loco publico; and D. de inofficioso testamento, *l. si quando*; X. de privilegiis, c. *Pastoralis*.

Item, the prince by this privilege does not grant more than the paternal disposition would grant by instituting the son as legitimate heir, which is proven by the intention of the privilege from the mind and words, to which we must adhere. X. de privilegiis, c. *Si Papa*, lib. 6; de verborum significatione, c. *Intelligentia*. Moreover, the legitimate institution of the son is not exclusive of legacies and fideicommissa; on the contrary, the heir is obliged to pay them. C. communia de legatis, *l. 1* and *2*. Therefore, the rights acquired by Francis and his heirs are not absorbed by the subsequent legitimation. From these, I infer these conclusions. First, that the Emperor can so habilitate that he prejudices anyone, both before death and after, those required and those not required, as to the faculty of succession; because such donations and successions are introduced by civil law; the conclusion is proven by the text in *l. 2*, D. de natalibus restituitis; and this would be done where the prince expresses it by sufficient clauses. Second, that the legitimation, concerning which inquiry is made here, made after death, as is assumed, does not draw back prejudicing those coming as intestate possessors; however, because by its nature, as such, it does not prejudice the right acquired in the case in which it could prejudice, this does not prejudice due to the defect of the requisition of those whose interest it is; which the clause does not exclude, although it excludes consent; however, because the clause does not specify what is necessary; however, because it is proven that he is not the son, probably, and insofar as it would be valid, it would not derogate from legacies and fideicommissa. Item, it would not prejudice those coming as intestate heirs at all. And all these things are demonstrated more fully above. I, John of Lignano, etc. I, Francis of Ramponibus, etc. CASE.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A legitimated child does not exclude a substitute heir.
2. The Emperor may legitimize spurious and incestuous offspring.
3. The Prince is not understood to have delegated to another that which he cannot do without sin.
body:
In the Name of Christ, Amen. The case is proposed as follows. Two brothers, one called Lord Albert of Campagna, and the other called Lord Francis of Campagna. Both were legitimate natural sons of the late Lord Rufinus of Campagna; they held and possessed the hereditary goods of their late father Rufinus undivided, and also acquired many other goods from the partnership while they were in communion, and they always remained in communion and partnership until the death of the said Lord Albert, who died first, having made a will of the tenor written below, word for word: this Lord Albert instituted Bernard, his legitimate and natural son, whom he had as his only male child, as his universal heir; and he made a substitution, of which mention is made in the will written below. And the said Lord Francis, his brother, survived the said Lord Albert; and Bernard, son of the said Lord Albert, survived him. This Bernard, although he had a legitimate wife, kept and had a certain Amasia, or concubine called Constantia, from whom was born a certain Michael, a spurious son of the said Bernard and the said Constantia; yet this Constantia did not have a husband. Then the said Bernard died intestate, leaving the said Michael, his spurious son, under fourteen years of age, surviving the said Lord Francis, his Bernard’s uncle, and also surviving the three legitimate and natural sons of the said Lord Francis, who were full brothers and blood relatives of the said Bernard; who also stand and live, and are called one John, another Peter, and another Bertus.

Furthermore, the same Bernard in 1342 had taken and had as wife Lady Catherine; during the marriage, the same Bernard took and kept a concubine named Constantia, from whom Constantia in 1350 was born Michael. Furthermore, the same Bernard died in the month of July of 1362, having left no legitimate son to himself, but having left Lady Catherine, his wife, and also having left the aforementioned Constantia, concubine of the same Bernard, who died before the death of the said Lady Catherine in the same month of July of 1362, leaving the spurious son Michael born from herself. Furthermore, that the same Lady Catherine, wife of the aforementioned Bernard, after the death of the aforementioned Constantia, died in the month of August of 1362, leaving no son. Furthermore, from 1362, Francis, inscribed and named in the will written below, and brother of the aforementioned testator Albert, quietly and peacefully had, held, and possesses the goods and inheritance of the said Bernard continuously throughout the entire time of that same Francis, and until his death, namely until 1369, when he died. Furthermore, that after the death of the said Francis, namely from 1369, the sons and heirs of the said Francis succeeded, and peacefully and quietly held and possessed the same goods and inheritance of the said late Bernard until 1381, and now it has been several years since the said Lord Francis of Tampanea died, leaving three legitimate and natural sons, with the said Michael, spurious son of the said Bernard, surviving. Now, about a year ago, the said Michael provided for himself with a remedy of legitimation, so that he might be held as legitimate, and as a legitimate person succeed to the inheritance of the said Bernard, his father, and to the said Bernard, his uncle; this Michael was legitimated by a certain Count Palatine; and thus after the death of his father Bernard, who Count has the faculty and mandate from the Emperor to legitimate; and after the death of the father, as is more fully contained in the said legitimation with the privilege of the said Count attached to the said legitimation and transmitted to us. From this legitimation, the said Michael claims to succeed to his father Bernard, and after the aforementioned legitimation, he sued for the inheritance before the judge, and involved himself in it. To this Michael, the aforementioned John, Peter, and Bertus, sons of the aforementioned Lord Francis of Campanea, oppose themselves, saying that the said Michael ought not to succeed to the inheritance of the said Bernard by law, notwithstanding the said legitimation, which the late said Lord Francis, his father, made for him, and that as the nearest relatives by law they ought to succeed to the said Bernard; and that by law they succeeded to him at the time of his death.

It must be premised for clarity, that the Emperor can legitimate spurious children, even incestuous ones, as in D. de ritu nuptiarum, law Qui in provincia, §. Divus Marcus, where the text is formal. And although it does not confirm the marriage, which is the producing cause, it nevertheless confirms the product, that is, the filiation, as noted there in the glossa ordinaria. But Hostiensis says that the Emperor does not legitimate truly and properly, but improperly, and in a certain respect, namely with regard to the right of succeeding, and with regard to honors, and other temporal things which the prince can confer. Thus he notes in his Summa, Qui filii sint legitimi, and in his Apparatus, under that title, c. Per venerabilem. And there John Andrea follows in the Novella. For if the Emperor cannot know whether anyone is legitimate, as in c. Lator, Extra, Qui filii sint legitimi, de ordine cognitionis, c. Tuam, therefore much more strongly he cannot dispense, because to whom knowledge of the case is denied, therefore much more strongly dispensation is denied, according to Hostiensis. These words are very colored, nevertheless the text in the said §. Divus says that the Emperor legitimates incestuous children, as if they had been legitimately conceived. Therefore, it washes away the stain of conception not in the producer, but in the product, and of that text Hostiensis does not remember. Therefore, the legitimated is legitimate not by nature, but by grace; not by generation, but by regeneration; not by the felicity of being born, but by the gift of the prince, as in C. de natura liberorum, Authent. Ita si quis, and in Authent. Qui modo nunc efficiantur legitimi, §. Si vero solummodo, col. 6. But this gift no one makes except the prince, as appears there, when it says, receiving this from the Empire. And C. de adoptionibus, l. 2, and l. Arrogationes, and note by Innocentius, Extra, de fide instrumentorum, c. Cum P. tabellio. Counts also, who have this authority from the prince, can legitimate, to the extent permitted to them; because the prince can grant this according to the note in D. de tutoribus et curatoribus datis ab his, l. 1, in the glossa ordinaria, in a similar case. And the glossa is moved because a concession sometimes does not harm. And he weighs this reason for what I will say below. But the limits of this concession must be diligently observed with regard to form, as in Extra, de privilegiis, c. Porro. Hence, whatever is not committed is understood to be prohibited. C. de rebus creditis, l. Nec filius. Furthermore, with regard to justice. For what the prince himself would not do, is not given to another in commission, as in l. Si pater, quae in fraudem creditorum, de conditione indebiti, l. Si non procurare. It supports what is noted in D. de pactis, l. Tale pactum, §. Sin, C. unde vi, l. Meminerint. Furthermore, that which the prince cannot do without sin, is not understood to have been committed to another. D. quod quisque iuris, l. 3, §. Si procurator.

Having premised these things, I come to the solution of the question: in which I find that Lord Dynus alleged for the part of the spurious child, that he should succeed: and assuming the power of the efficient cause, he is moved because he is restored to his natural rights. And restoration removes all obstacles. C. de sententiis passivis, l. Si quia posthumus, therefore it breaks the will and the donation. C. de revocatione donationum, l. Si unquam, D. de in iustum testamentum, l. 3. From these it appears, because restoration does the same thing as postliminium. Tit. Si quis, §. Pe, because it fakes retroactivity, as in the said §. Divus, and in Authent. Qui modo nunc efficiantur legitimi, §. Sit igitur licentia, col. 6. And the text there says that they differ in nothing from legitimate sons; therefore they succeed.

But against this is the truth itself: because a rescript of the prince does not derogate from a will. C. de testamento, l. Si testamentum. Nor from a perfect donation, or any contract, from which a right has been acquired by a third person; because such rescripts are contrary to law: I say, contrary to the law of the constitution, and to the law of contract and obligation; therefore they are not valid, as in l. Rescripta. Hence, after the inheritance has been entered upon, and thus after the contract, from which the right of legatees and creditors has been acquired, Inst. de obligationibus quae ex quasi contractu, §. Heres. Furthermore, if the right of dominion has been acquired by the one entering upon the inheritance, the spurious child cannot be legitimated to the prejudice of those to whom this right has been acquired. It supports what is noted in D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, §. Et quid si tantum, and C. de revocatione donationum, l. Si donationem. For what is perfect is not directed to the imperfect by a supervening case. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. Si Gaudentius, de donationibus ante nuptias, l. Iure iurando. Furthermore, after the inheritance has been entered upon, no times harm, so that the inheritance, as it is fixed, remains so. D. de haereditate instituta, l. Si in conditione, §. Solumus, de vulgari substitutione, l. Ex facto, §. Si, C. de usufructu, l. Inter antiquam, in fine, de vulgari substitutione, l. Verbis civilibus. For the entry itself has a right inseparable by nature and time. D. de minoribus, l. Et si sine, §. Sed quod Papinianus, unless it is torn away according to the rules of civil law. C. de fideicommissis, Authent. Hoc amplius, D. de vulgari substitutione, l. In substitutione filii.

Furthermore, it is absurd that a Count Palatine can draw the privilege of the prince to an unjust right. The said l. Ex facto, in principio, and there the text is noted. For privileges of princes desire the highest equity, which the prince cultivates and enjoins to be cultivated; although the eyes of judges, being blind, do the contrary to what has been acquired, as is read and noted in C. familiae erciscundae, l. Inter filios, in the glossa ordinaria. To this is added the consideration of the glossa in the said l. 1, de tutoribus et curatoribus. For if it holds that the collation of this authority is because it harms no one by injustice, therefore if the use of this authority were injurious, because it would take away the right rooted in the just successor, such use is impossible. To this it supports, because afterwards it says in the said Summa, that the prince himself could not do this without sin, as he places in §. Qualiter et a quo, verso Per specialem, in the said title Qui filii sint legitimi, in the Summa, that what is not permitted is not committed; because the abuse of superiority does not seem to be committed, but rather he who abuses the granted power is to be deprived of authority, Infra, de officio praefecti praetorio orientis, l. Si quos. Indeed, Caesar chose this count as a good man, a censor and guardian of equity. D. de operis liberto, l. Si libertus. It does not become a good man to extinguish wills and dominions against the law of nations, and entries upon inheritances against civil law, nor to excite past calumnies. C. de curialibus, l. Pe. And if the prince were asked, he would not wish to do it, as in §. Si quis a principe. And the prince is not understood to commit what is not to be done, which he himself cannot do without the gnawing of conscience; for he who holds the supreme power ought to observe the highest honesty and the highest equity as a rule; for reason must be rendered from the head. Therefore, the will of the prince is lacking, and the number, and the authority, and thus two things are lacking which have the power to canonize human acts. C. de donationibus ante nuptias, l. Cum sponsae, de rescriptis, l. Super literis. And what the living prince would not do, the foolish prince ought not to do. I.e., the image of the foolish prince in the privilege granted to the count: lest the image have more power than the truth. D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Filium quem pater, in principio. In the first cause, i.e., in Caesar, see the will. In the second cause, that is in the count, see the impotence, for he lacks the commission, because he uses no reason, nor the intention of the prince, which is presumed to be such as is suggested by reason. And even if the prince were to commit something unjust to someone, it would be understood to commit and grant that which contains the least iniquity. It supports D. de administratione tutorum, l. Impuberi filio Centurio.

Consider also, that the illegitimate never breaks wills, as noted in l. 1, §. 1, D. de contrahenda emptione. Observe, that the dead do not rise again in relative fiction. C. de captivis, l. 1, de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, §. Si eius, de operis liberto, l. Qui libertinus, §. Posthumus. Look back, that relative legitimation requires extremes, actual and potential, and is not made except with the parent living; but absolute legitimation with the father dead does not require extremes. D. ad Trebellianum, l. Si exhaereditatus exigit. Nevertheless, in the acts of the legitimation itself, lest it fall into many absurdities. C. de dote promissa, l. Quia rerum absurditates, laws abhor: but here it would include absurdities of different kinds and forms. I.e., the extirpation of the will, dominion, and quasi-contract, and the eclipse of nature’s remedy. Wherefore I say, that consulting, I assert, as I said in my lecture on l. Gallus, that the said legitimation, with regard to the force of succeeding to the inheritance not lying, but entered upon, has no force. It supports c. Quamvis, de rescriptis, lib. 6. The arguments of Lord Dynus to the contrary are not worth a fly, because his arguments would proceed supposing that the legitimation was a valid act in effect, about which it is asked, but here it is not valid.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. An action that can be brought by the ordinary course should not be pursued by an irregular and extraordinary one.
body: In the name of God, Amen. The case is stated as follows. A petition for witnesses for the perpetual memory of the matter, because the petitioner does not assert that he possesses, does not proceed according to law, since no action would be granted from matters to be proved, and because he does not possess, no exception would be granted, Extra de test. c. significavit. According to Innocentius.

† Moreover, since the matter may be pursued regarding the goods through the ordinary course of action, this irregular and extraordinary course ceases to apply; therefore, the action must be brought forward, and proof must be adduced concerning the action, for the judge ought not to receive evidence where an action can be instituted via the ordinary route. D. ad l. Aquil., l. Aquilia si deletum; and what is noted, D. de testib., l. curent; and D. de usur., l. pupil; D. ut lit. non contest., l. quoniam frequenter; in Auth. de test., §. pe; C. de eden., Auth. si quis in aliquo. Nor is this canon properly a case of status, because a certain person offered in evidence has died; rather, it is principally a case concerning goods. C. de reb. cred., l. cum proponas, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the buyer can be sued by a pledge action or another conditional action on account of the possession of the thing sold, once the price has been paid or set off.
2. How the simulation of an act is presumed.
3. A witness who does not testify regarding the form of the instrument cannot testify regarding the simulation of that form, nor does he prove anything, because he does not fully narrate the fact.
body: In the name of the Lord, amen. The point of the question pending before the venerable man Lord Franciscus de Machadelo, vicar general in the bishopric of Perugia, between the defendant ser Christofanus of Perugia, as agent acting on the one side on behalf of Lady Bernarda, wife of the late Alfanus Civelli, son of Lord Lucas of Perugia, as guardian and in the name of guardianship of Civellus, her son and the son of the late said Alfanus; and Rantius Cercoli of Perugia, and ser Nicolaus ser Iacobi, his procurator, defending on the other side, is as follows: namely, having examined the acts and proceedings in the said cause, and having heard the allegations of the parties, and taking it as established that the episcopal constitutions are valid, it is asked: What are the duties of the said Lord Vicar in pronouncing definitively, and what of the matters expressed, etc.? Whether a buyer can be sued by the actio pignoratitia or by another condictitious action by reason of possession, the price having been paid or set off? Also, whether and when the simulation of a contract is proved from preceding or following negotiation and deliberation? It must be seen

† whether by law a buyer can be sued by the actio pignoratitia or by another condictitious action, such as the triticaria, by reason of possession, the debt having been paid or set off. And the text seems to indicate not, ff. de pig. l. 2, where it states that one cannot bring an action, therefore neither the direct nor the equitable action [actio utilis], which is gathered from the force of that phrase, "he will not be able." And the reason is that the actio pignoratitia arises from a contract truly or fictitiously concluded between the plaintiff and the defendant; but here no contract of pledge was concluded between the possessor and the plaintiff; therefore the actio pignoratitia is not granted. Likewise, since the actio pignoratitia is a personal action, it does not follow the land, l. 1, § si haeres, ff. ad Tre., C. de ac. et ob. l. si eum; and that the actio pignoratitia is personal is evident, because it arises from a contract and a personal obligation, Inst. quibus modis re contr. oblig. § creditor; therefore it is not granted except against the contracting party or his heir, C. si cer. pe. l. 1, C. de distrae. pig. l. fi., and what is noted in the first constitution, § tertii insuper. Likewise, just as he who buys a pledge from a debtor is not bound to the creditor by the actio pignoratitia contraria, so neither is he who buys from a creditor bound to the debtor by the actio pignoratitia directa. And this the true nature of a personal action compels us to answer: for by no law is it provided that it is in rem scripta, because it does not adhere to the thing; for every action that arises from a contract is personal, as in Inst. de ob. § sequens. But the contrary argues against this: because the actio pignoratitia utilis is granted against a creditor of the creditor, and thus against a singular successor, ff. de pign. l. grege, § 2, and there is the ordinary gloss, and ff. de pigno. actio. l. debitor a creditore, § fi., and C. si pignus pigno. da. sit, l. 1 and l. fi.; for because a successor represents the name and image of his author, de praescrip. 30 anno. l. cum notissimi, he ought to be judged by the same law with him, for he does not have more right or more equity than his author has, ff. de pig. l. lex vectigalis, ff. de peri. et commo. rei ven. l. necesse, § fi. And although the laws speak expressly of the creditor of a creditor, the same seems to apply to one who buys from a creditor, who succeeds actively and passively to the right of the first creditor, ff. de rescin. ven. l. fundus, qui Lucii Titii erat, ff. de contrah. emp. l. qui tabulas; and sometimes without a contract concluded between the plaintiff and the defendant, the actio pignoratitia arises from the act of the one representing them, ff. de dam. infec. l. vtrique, ff. vt in posse. leg. l. is, cui, § quaeris, ff. de pig. actio. l. solutum, § vnde si domum; and this opinion seems approved by the equity of the canons, as in Extra, de pig. c. cum contra. The said l. 2, ff. de pigno. does not stand in the way, because there the surety does not derive his title from the debtor, as in l. 1, C. de dolo, through which he would have a right of pledge once the creditor had been satisfied, arg. ff. de sol. l. Modestinus; but the surety of himself was a chirographic and simple creditor; it is otherwise, however, when one succeeds in a pledge. Likewise, at least by reason of possession, an unlawful possessor ought to be held liable by the condictio triticaria, as in ff. de tri. l. 1, at the end, and l. 2. Because I do not wish to decide that question now, as it is not expedient, I come therefore to the other point, namely, whether the pledge has been proved. And it seems that it has, because from preceding negotiation and deliberation, simulation of a subsequent act is presumed, ff. de ac. haer. l. Celsus, ff. mand. l. 4, § si ab igno.; for things said in preceding matters seem to be tacitly repeated in subsequent ones, ff. de pec. l. item quia, § fi.; for the intention is proved from preceding matters, ff. de exce. doli, l. apud Celsum, at the beginning, and l. Fulcinius, § quid sit lactitare, ff. qui. ex cau. in pos. eat. Likewise, from subsequent words and deeds, simulation of a preceding act is presumed, ff. quibus mod. pig. vel hyp. sol. l. sic ad, § superuacuum, C. de natu. lib. l. si quis scu. § et quod de sub eunda. Likewise, from preceding and subsequent matters, an intermediate act is presumed to be fictitious and colorable, de distr. pig. c. et qui sub imagine; whence not the writing, but the truth is looked to, C. plus valere quod agitur, l. emptione, Extra, de pig. c. illa nos., de emp. et vend. c. nostram. Moreover, one witness, namely Martinus, deposes openly that at the time of the instrument it was agreed that it should be a pledge; wherefore in uncertain, not certain matters, there is room for conjectures that arise from the instrument, ff. de ver. obli. l. continuus, § cum ita. Likewise, that instrument had its origin in an illicit cause, as in the Authentica alearum vsus; or, because it is difficult to prove simulation, arguments suffice, C. mand. l. per diuersas, and l. ab Anastasio, de re mi. l. non omnis, § ab arbitris; nor does an agreement made under the name of a price stand in the way, ff. de pigno. l. si fundus, § fin., because a pact of selling can be inserted into a pledge; nevertheless, it remains a pledge simply, the price not having been declared. Likewise, to press someone for money, as the witnesses say, that is, to make secure regarding money, is done by giving a pledge, ff. qui satisdare cogantur, l. prima; for a buyer is not made secure regarding money, but regarding the thing, l. habitationum, § fi., ff. de pe. et commo. rei ven. Let the greater amount of the price and the pact of returning enter in; for from accidental pacts we sometimes know the essence [spiritualia], as in c. illos vos., and l. fi., ff. de condi. ob cau. The contrary seems true: for it is certain through the instrument that it is a sale, since from an instrument three presumptions approved by law arise: because it is presumed to be true, and solemn, and made by the will of the parties, C. de proba. l. cum pręcibus, C. de contra. et committem. sti. l. optimam; for from the fact that a notary is requested by the parties, it appears to have been made by the will and consent of the parties; for this reason a rogatio is required, as in the Authentica de tabel. § nos autem; therefore one must stand by the instrument unless the contrary is clearly proved by multiple concurrent witnesses, as noted in Inst. de inutili. stipu. § item verborum, Extra, de fide instrumen. c. cum Ioan.; nor do conjectural proofs suffice; this is supported by what is noted in ff. de pac. l. iuregen. § quod fere, C. de non nume. pecu. l. generaliter, because certain proofs prevail over doubtful and uncertain proofs, C. de edi. diui Adri. tol. l. fina. I speak of the conjectures of man, I do not speak of a presumption of law, which is held as clear proof, as noted in C. de pericu. tuto. l. penul., de le. 1, l. licet Imperator. But here simulation has not been proved by multiple witnesses,

† because a witness who does not depose concerning the form of the instrument cannot depose concerning the simulation of that form; nor does he prove who does not fully narrate the fact, as noted in ff. de infami. l. Lucius. For no witness made full mention of the form of the contract; and although it might be proved that words were spoken regarding pledging for 130 florins, nevertheless it is one thing to have spoken, another to have done or contracted, C. de aedi. aedic. l. sciendum, § dictum, de conditio. indebi. l. eleganter, near the beginning. For when something is added, there has been a departure from preceding statements, and a new contract has been concluded, ff. loca. l. cum in plures, § lege dicta, and § locata horr. i., ff. de praetorijs stipulatio. l. Valerianus, ff. de contrahen. emptione, l. pacta conuenta, § Paulus. Here, however, a price to be declared was added, which smacks of a sale, C. de contrahen. emptione, l. fin., C. de praediis curalium, l. fin.; and the order of the words began from a sale. And although it may seem imperfect since the price was not declared, nevertheless that belongs to another path of action and to claiming the thing by rei vindicatio; for a question of pledge is separate from an action of ownership. That step of rei vindicatio, when part of the price has been paid and the remaining part has neither been paid nor declared, does not belong to our question, but requires a different inquiry. It is also proved that he promised, through a certain person, to return in the amount of 130 florins; the nature of that agreement does not agree with a price to be declared further beyond. Likewise, neither does it by necessity imply a pledge, C. de pac. inter empt. l. 2. Likewise, a witness who was not present at the act, but withdrew, cannot truly and fully prove, as in C. de testa. l. cum antiquitas; he can, however, prove conjecturally, but naked conjectures do not harm an instrument. I conclude therefore that the defendant must be absolved, because it has not been fully proved, and because the transaction relapses into another form; the form and matter of a transaction is changed; similar is Inst. mandati, § in summa, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a daughter can omit a bequest of 50 pounds, and claim the third owed to her by natural law in the goods of the father.
2. Whether the time of the death of the testator is to be looked to when a supplement of the legitime is claimed.
3. Whether the prescription of long time stands in the way of one who does not wish to claim the legitime in the goods of the father.
body: In the name of the Lord, Amen. The point of the question, on which legal counsel is sought, is as follows: Titius, having an only daughter, passed away having made a will, in which among other things he left to the said daughter of his by title of institution fifty pounds of pence, and instituted Sempronius, the brother of the testator himself, as universal heir. After his death, the said Sempronius entered upon the said inheritance under the will, and possessed the goods of the said inheritance during his lifetime; and after his death, his sons, his heirs, possessed them without the knowledge of the said lady daughter, who demanded nothing for thirty years or thereabouts. Finally, the said daughter seeks what is owed to her by natural law in the goods of her late father.

† It is now doubted and asked: can the said daughter seek precisely a third part in the goods and omit the said fifty pounds, or ought she to calculate for herself the said sum into the said due portion and seek a supplement; and if it were a matter of the said supplement, whether the said sum amounted to the due portion, the valuation of the goods of which time ought to be taken into account, since with the passage of time the prices of things have increased; and whether, at least insofar as she could sue precisely for the goods, the prescription of long or longest time would stand in her way? That the daughter can omit the bequest of fifty pounds and seek a third part in the goods that belonged to the father, the testator, the text in § repletionem in l. sancimus C. de inoffi. testa. seems to prove, and there Guil. de Cun. seems to hold this; Bart. seems to think the same in l. in quarta ff. ad l. Aquil. The contrary seems to hold—namely, that the said daughter has another thing or money, etc., and a burden is imposed therein in quantity or time: l. lex non amplius de leg. 1 makes for this, and what is noted there by Bart. where he touches on the difficulty of performance because of the deduction of debt, the deduction of which is also made in calculating the ratio of the said due portion, as in l. Papin. § quar. Moreover, what is left by the testator in general terms is sought by the action on the will; nor is it supplied by the law, as in the said laws, but what is supplied only benefits; hence where the bequest extends, the condictio of the law does not embrace it; therefore, etc. Moreover, where a sum is left, it seems to be left in place of the valuation and price of a part of the goods, arg. l. plerunque de iure dot. ff. and l. quoties under the same title; and thus also a bequest of a sum made in place of a thing is said to be from the thing, by the argument of l. si rem et pretium ff. de petitio. haeredita. and l. quod procurato[rem], l. Iulianus § si procur. ff. de actio. emp. along with similar laws; thus therefore it can be said that the said sum, if it is paid, is from the substance and property of the father. The said § repletionem, where it is said that the replenishment is made from the substance itself, does not stand in the way: because the Emperor said it in respect of that, since he declares himself there 'from the substance itself' when he says 'not if anything from other causes, etc.'; and what follows gives an understanding to what precedes, as in l. si seruus plurium in fi. de fundo instr. Therefore the Emperor did not look to what things or what sums the said due portions are left in; nor is it to be believed that he regarded it otherwise, especially since above, under the same title, the laws have expressly promised to parents that a division be made among children, and in the action familiae herciscundae and communi dividundo a judge often undertakes to award a thing to one and certain money to another; and in this the power of the testator ought not to be less than that of the judge, as noted in l. solent C. de alim. cib. leg. and in Auth. de nupt. § disponit. And by the aforesaid, an answer seems to be given to the said Guil. Bartolus, however, touches only upon the supplement to be made beyond that which was left; and thus if it be presupposed that the said bequest cannot be omitted by the daughter, and the whole due portion cannot be sought in other goods.

† To the second query, namely whose valuation ought to be considered, it seems clear that the time of the death of the testator ought to be considered: because the text and the case seem to be in l. ratione, el. 2, and l. in lege Falcidia § final. and l. in quartam in prin. ff. ad l. Fal.

† To the third, namely regarding prescription, it also seems clear that prescription even of long time ought to stand in the way of the daughter: since he possessed those goods in good faith pro herede from the just cause of the will itself.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a father may choose in which property he shall give the legitime to his son.
2. The quantity of the father's goods is considered at the time of death, when the legitime is claimed.
3. The right to sue for the legitime is not prescribed by the lapse of a long time.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If the money was part of the estate’s assets at the time of death, the son could not choose what the father was permitted to choose, namely in which item he should grant his son the legitime, as stated in the cited passage of the Code, *De re vendicata*, in the law *Cum a matre*. This is supported by what is noted in the Digest, *De minoribus*, in law 3, § *Si ut*, and in the law *Si quis priore*, *Ad Trebellianum*; and in the Authenticum *Ut cum*, *De appellatione cognoscenda*, § *Caeterum*; and in the Code, *De familiae hereditate*, in the law *Filium, quem habentem*. But if the money was not among the deceased’s assets at the time of death, neither can the son demand the legitime from the substance of his father’s estate. See the Code, *De inofficioso testamento*, in the law *Cum quaeritur*, and in the law *Sancimus*, § *Repletionem*; and in the Authenticum *Novissima*; and in the Authenticum *De triennio et semis*, § 1, in the phrase *Propriae substantiae*. This is supported by law 2 of the Code, *Quando et quibus quanta pars debetur*. And thus is understood the statement of Guillaume in the aforementioned law *Sancimus*, and of Bartolus in the law *In quartam*, *Ad legem Falcidiam*.

† And the quantity of the goods is considered at the time of death, but the quality of the goods is considered at the time when the claim is made. D. de tritico, l. in hac; and l. si, D. de rei venditione. Not only with regard to the Falcidian portion, l. in ratione, D. ad Trebellianum; l. mulier, §. sed et enim.

† And prescription does not run against the right to bring an action for the legitime by long, but by very long, time. C. de iure deliber. l. licet. C. de constitu. pec. l. 2. Although Bartolus said that it is prescribed by five years, just as the complaint of an undutiful will is prescribed, by l. si quis filium, in fine, de inofficio. testa., which law, with all due respect to him, does not say this. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. It is presumed that an emphyteutic contract was concluded from the payment of the canon for a period of 40 years.
2. Whether prescription is transmitted to the heirs.
3. The emphyteuta is said to be a tenant for his own benefit; and therefore he transmits [the right] to the heir.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The points have been subtly addressed: first, whether an emphyteutic contract is presumed to have been concluded from the payment of the canon for a period of 40 years. And it must be said that yes, as noted in l. 2, C. de iure emphyteutico, through l. 1, C. de fundis patrimonialibus, lege iubemus, lib. 11. From this prescription arises an action on both sides, in that each party has acquired rights by prescription: for the emphyteuta prescribes the land with respect to useful dominion; and the owner prescribes the canon, or rather it is more a proof of the contract than a prescription. D. de usuris, l. cum de in rem verso. And then, just as from an oath in proper form arises an action on the part of the one swearing and of the one against whom the oath is sworn, as in l. si duo patroni, §. Marcellus, D. de iureiurando, so here, because this contract is presumed proven by the aid of payment and time, it binds both parties reciprocally, just like a contract of lease, as in Inst. de locato conducto, §. adeo. The separation from this contract should not be defective, as noted in D. de rescindenda venditione, l. 1. Therefore, whether we call it proof or prescription, it produces its effect reciprocally. To this effect, C. de agris et censibus, l. domini praediorum. For prescription is equivalent to truth, as noted in D. de servitutibus et aqua, l. 1. It is also equivalent to an agreement, as noted in C. de dotis promissione, l. 2. And thus one can prescribe so as to be an emphyteuta, just as one can prescribe so as to be a usufructuary. C. de praescriptione longi temporis, l. si. But since he is an emphyteuta, he does not prescribe ownership, nor the canon. C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. male agitur. Regarding the canon, however, say as in l. comparuit, in the same title. And it is to be noted that even where writing is required, the conjecture of time operates the same way. C. de apocryphis publicis, l. quicunque. And the reason is that legal presumptions are most clear, as noted in C. de procuratoribus tutorum, l. penultima. But it is asked whether the prescribed emphyteusis is real, just as an agreement is presumed to be real. D. de pactis, l. iure gentium, §. praedictorum. For since emphyteusis can be transmissible to heirs, and not transmissible according to the quality and form of the agreement, C. de iure emphyteutico, l. 1.

† It may be doubted whether the prescription is judged to pass to the heirs, or not; for in dissimilar cases, neither custom, nor prescription, nor a certain presumption applies. D. de annuis legatis, l. Seius, §. medico; C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. 1, according to Cynus. And it seems that one should say that such [prescription] is presumed as that which is placed before [it], as stated in the aforementioned law Cum de in rem verso; or that in case of doubt, a real [prescription] is presumed: for if the prescription to be completed passes to the heir, the time of the deceased also benefits the heir, as in l. Pomponius, D. de acquirenda possessione; all the more so does a completed prescription. Moreover, because rights are presumed to be perpetual, not temporary: this is supported by what is noted in D. de censibus, l. forma; D. de servis legatis, l. pater; Extravagantes de institutionibus, c. Cum venisset; de electione, c. Querelam. Or that in case of doubt, we should follow that which is more frequently observed in the region, according to the majority. D. de regulis iuris, l. Semper in stipulationibus; D. de fundo instructo, l. Cum delationis, §. asinam molendinariam.

† The emphyteuta, so to speak, is a tenant in his own right; and therefore he transmits [the right] to his heir, as is argued from C. loca. l. viam veritas. ignoras. and ff. de probatio. l. si pactum. And it supports what is read and noted in 12. q. 2. c. longinquitate. and l. 2. §. circa. de excep. doli. and l. in summa. in prin. ff. de aqua plu. and de agri. et cen. l. litibus. and l. cum satis. §. cum dicunt. where it appears expressly that the right arising from prescription affects descendants and heirs to the extent that, as in the aforementioned l. iubemus. de fundis pat., the case is such that it operates on both sides, because correlative prescription does not limp. From which I infer that the form which, over forty years, joins the present to the past, etc., must be observed in the future. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether and when a creditor may compel the debtor of his debtor.
2. Whether an award deserves execution according to the form of the award, if no challenge is made.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

There are three cases. Sometimes a person wishes to compel the debtor of his debtor, but does not have an expressly bound obligation: then the rule applies, C. when the fiscus, or private person, l. si in causae. Sometimes you have a tacitly bound obligation: then the law applies, non prius, co. titu. and de iure fis. l. moschis. Sometimes you have an expressly bound obligation, generally or specifically: and this is the case in which some have said that the excussion of the primary debtor is necessary, when the action is hypothecary, in Auth. de fideius. §. sed neque. Others have said that excussion is not necessary, because the action is useful, which corresponds to the direct pledge right of the debtor, l. si conuenerint, in prin. And this is the true opinion, according to Ia. de Beluiso, Nico. Mat., Bar., and many other doctors, and so also holds Spe. de pi. ver. sed pone. As if someone were to act on ceded rights. Against this, however, it is argued above de haere. actio. l. haeredem mariti. But this does not obstruct, because there it denies that the action for dowry competes against the husband’s debtor, yet it does not deny the useful action, which corresponds directly to the debtor. So holds Iaco. But. in lec. Cyn. disputes, but does not affirm. C. quae res pigno. obl. pos. l. nomen. But the truth is as I said, and as can be said, actio. l. hęredem mariti, and officium iudicis. de admi. tut. l. si minoris. ff. de mino. l. quod si minor. in prin. Thus, the action and the office of the judge are executive, namely that from the sentence one can hypothecate; and the creditor has, like the debtor, ready execution, because such is the right of the creditor as the obligation, as in the rule of law, is qui iuris.

† It is to be doubted, however, whether the award deserves execution, unless a refutation is made according to the form of the award. And it seems that this is so, because there are several chapters and precepts of the arbitrator: and from one of the separated parts nothing is inferred to another, as in l. si maritus, de donationibus inter virum et uxorem. To the contrary it seems, because this award has the force of a transaction, in Auth. ut differentiae iudicentur, § 1. But he who acts on a transaction must first fulfill his part, as is fully noted in C. de transactionibus, l. sive apud acta. To this it contributes that things are connected, one on account of the other, as noted in ff. de edicto edilitio, l. ediles, § fin. And because the mode of the sentence must be observed as the form, C. de sententiis, l. cum eorum. Also, it is not permitted to the creditor more than to the unhearing party, ff. de manumissionibus, l. Gaius. And it contributes, ff. de transactionibus, l. si. Also, I condemn to 30. It seems to have a day, if on the day when the general refutation is made, therefore it is acted upon wrongly before the day. I. certae conditionis, in principio, ff. si certum petatur, de legibus, l. homini, § ita cui. What therefore remains, if the debtor who can refute is not found, a curator bonis will be appointed, who can make this refutation, since otherwise it cannot be done, so that he may be compelled to pay, although the action has arisen, arg. l. praetor, in principio, de collatione bonorum. It contributes what is noted in d. l. si in causa, in glossa ordinaria, and l. ab hostibus, in principio, qui ex causa maiestatis. And he will refute by mandate of the judge, ff. de minoribus, l. ait praetor, § permittitur. Because in this necessary act he is equated to a tutor, as noted in ff. de administratione tutorum, l. inter bonorum. And he is a legitimate administrator, as noted in l. 2, ff. de curatoribus bonorum damnatorum. He can well acknowledge good faith, ff. de administratione tutorum, l. quoties, § igitur. Therefore, this refutation having been made by the procurator appointed for the goods, he cannot knowingly allege any cause why he does not pay. Having seen the statute, which speaks specifically of the execution of arbitral awards, and because in any part it suffices that the suit be offered, ff. de pignoribus actionibus, l. si rem, § si, I say that the said refutation having been made by the said curator, which is to be done in the obligation according to the form of the award, hence to make it, as to pay any debt, pertains to the said curator, because when a fact is due which can be done by another, he can do it just as in giving, to give. And I conclude that execution in the said 300 gold florins against the said Seretus ought to be made at the petition of the first creditor, or his procurator, even without any cession of actions. It contributes what is noted in ff. de damno infecto, l. damni infecti stipulatio competit, § si, in glossa, there, or in subsidium, etc. Which gloss is noted for many things. That is certain, that the hypothecary creditor is preferred to creditors not having a hypothec, as is fully noted in l. privilegia, de privilegiis creditorum. It also contributes what Innocentius says in c. de his, de sepultura, etc. I, Baldus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether profit, when two brothers stand together and profit together, ought to be divided per stirpes or per capita.
2. Whether a legacy made to daughters is due to posthumous children.
3. Whether fruits from a legacy made to daughters, which the father and brothers living in common received, ought to be shared in the division.
4. Goods are divided among heirs and partners per capita by reason of labor, but by reason of ownership they are divided per stirpes.
