5. Half of the fruits from a flock left to one of the partners, the other half is divided among the partners.
casus: CASE. In the name of the Lord, Amen. The fact is such: a certain Salibene and a certain Nicola were brothers: namely, Nicola died, now 25 years ago, leaving his son John. Finally, Salibene died, now 26 years ago, with three sons surviving him, who together with the said John remained at one bread, one wine until then, and at the time when the said Salibene died, there were certain animals in the goods, namely oxen, sheep, etc. Afterwards, on account of wars, the said animals were plundered, and five houses with their outbuildings and clothes were burned, afterwards all these became laborers, and they recovered the said houses, and bought certain animals. Now a certain doubt arises, whether the son of the said Nicola comes for half of all the goods acquired after the death of the said Salibene, and those three sons of the said Salibene for the other half, or whether each of the sons of the said Salibene comes pro rata, and the said John pro rata, namely for a fourth portion, namely in the goods acquired from the day of the death of the said Salibene, what is the law. Also a doubt arises, namely that a certain person answered etc. to the above-mentioned Salibene for his daughters one Pedia of land, and at that time the above-mentioned Salibene had two female daughters, and two sons, finally the wife whom he then had died, and he received another after 10 years, from another wife he had, and has three sons, namely two females, and one male, now it is asked, if the said sons, who came from the second wife, if they come, or succeed in the said legacy together with the other sons. Also it is asked, because the fruits received from the said Pedia of land left to the said daughters of the said Salibene were consumed, and converted to the utility of all the sons of the said Salibene, and of the said Nicola, now it is asked if they come to division, it is asked if they ought to communicate the said fruits received from the day of having the legacy until now. Also it is asked, because the said sons of Salibene are three men able to work, and the son of the said Nicola is one, and they sowed, their goods are now to be divided, how ought the hanging fruits to be divided? Also certain sheep were left to one son of the said Salibene, and the said sheep were kept together with the other sheep of the house, now he asks for the sheep left to him with the fruits received from the day the legacy was made until now, which time is 30 years.
body: In the Name of God, Amen.

† On the first point, it must be said that all profit, after deducting expenses, must be divided per capita, not per stirpes, and if all are capable and qualified to share in the profit, each ought to receive an equal share, as stated in the Digest, *pro socio*, l. *si non fuerint*. However, to those under fourteen years of age, a portion according to the number of persons is not due, because the labor of children cannot merit an equal share, both because they cannot enter into partnership, and because their services are unequal to those of robust adults. Digest, *de rei vend.*, l. *caeterum*.

† On the second point, it appears to include daughters born of any wife, according to the law *placet* in the title *De liberis et posthumis*. To the contrary, it seems that posthumous daughters, that is, those born after the will was made, are not included, as stated in the law *qui filiabus* in the title *De legatis primo*. What is more correct is established by the law *qui quartam*, section *si*, and the notes thereon, in the Digest, title *De legatis primo*.

† On the third point, it must be said that the father had the usufruct. L. cum oportet, de bonis quae liberis. If the father, whether liberally or jointly, consumed [the fruits] within the same household, they ought not to be reclaimed. D. de negotiorum gestis, L. Nescinius Appollinaris. But after the father’s death, the fruits ought to belong to the aforementioned daughters, since they were not maintained in the household, but by their husbands.

† On the fourth point, it must be said that the shares pertaining to the care of the laborers, i.e., half of the fruits, ought to be divided per capita; but the other half, which pertains by reason of ownership, ought to be divided per stirpes; because the fruits of the patrimony are divided according to the hereditary portion, just as the paternal or avuncular patrimony itself is; but the fruits of labor are divided according to the number of laborers, arg. de annuis leg. l. Seio. And thus half is attributed to ownership, and half to the labor of the persons. C. pro socio. l. 1. On

† Fifth, it must be said that half of the fruits of the livestock belongs to him to whom they were left by right of ownership; the other half must be divided according to the number of persons, by the law cited above and by D. pro socio, l. cum duobus, § si coeunda, etc. I, Baldus, etc.

2. An heir succeeds according to the will, unless he is outlawed for the crime of lèse-majesté or treason.
1. IN the name of the Lord Amen. It is proposed that a certain Mandus An
casus:
CASE. In the Name of the Lord, Amen. The facts are as follows: A certain Master Cagnus Coradi de Gallo made his last will and testament. Among other things, in all his other universal and individual goods, movable and immovable, rights, and actions, which are, are found, or can be found, he left, instituted, and made as his universal heirs: Bartholomew, son of his predeceased Lord Raynuit, for one-third part of his inheritance; Coradinus, Danialdus, and Guidonus, and the womb of Lady Francischina, wife of his predeceased son Ser Francis, if said womb should come to light and be a male child, or male children, whether one or more, in equal shares for another third part. And if any of the said sons of the said Ser Francis, predeceased, whether born or posthumous, or born in the interim, should die in pupillary age, or later at any time, without children legitimately born from themselves, or from either of them, he substituted for himself, dying or dying, vulgarly, pupillarily, and by fideicommissum, the other surviving sons of the said Ser Francis, or their children, in stirpes, and not in capita. And if all the said male sons of the said Ser Francis, whether born or to be born, or to be born in the interim, should die in pupillary age, or later at any time, without children legitimately born from themselves, he substituted them vulgarly, pupillarily, and by fideicommissum, to his other heirs named above, and their legitimate heirs in stirpes, but not in capita. And if the said Ludovicus, son of the said testator, predeceased, should die in pupillary age, or later at any time, without heirs legitimately born from himself, or coming to light, he substituted for himself, dying, vulgarly, pupillarily, and by fideicommissum, his other heirs named above, for two parts of the said inheritance, and their children, and to each of them legitimately in stirpes, and not in capita. And if the said Bartholomew, son of his predeceased son Lord Raynerius, should die without an heir legitimately born from himself, or coming to light, he substituted for himself, dying, vulgarly, pupillarily, and by fideicommissum, his other universal heirs named above, and their legitimate heirs, in stirpes and in capita.

After this, the said Master Cagnus died; twelve years have now passed with the aforementioned heirs existing. After this, the aforementioned Bartholomew, Guido, and Raynaldutius died, with the said Coradinus, Ludovicus, and Francis, posthumous son of the said Ser Francis, predeceased son of the said Lord Cagnus, surviving them. After this, five years have now passed since the said Coradinus was condemned for failure to appear in person; and in the said condemnation are these words at the end: “And that all and each of his goods shall come to the said commune, we confiscate and apply those goods of his to the said commune; and from now on they are and shall be considered confiscated and applied to the said commune in every way, manner, and form, etc.” Finally, in the last past year, in the month of September, the said Ludovicus died without children, with the said Coradinus, condemned as above, and the said Francis, heir substituted to him by their grandfather, surviving him. Now it is asked: whether the said inheritance of that Ludovicus pertains to the said Francis, in what share, or to the said Coradinus, condemned, and the said Francis; and whether the said Coradinus is deprived of the said succession on account of the said personal condemnation; and whether the said commune, to which the said goods of the said Coradinus were confiscated in the manner written above, at the time the condemnation was pronounced against the said Coradinus, can succeed in the person of the said Coradinus to the inheritance of the said Ludovicus. It is asked: what is the law?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Regarding the said condemned person, the said succession does not seem to pertain to him, at least as far as the goods located in the land of Gualdo are concerned; because one who is outlawed to death is considered dead for the purpose of succeeding: as stated in the Digest, *De contrahenda emptione*, Law 1, § *Si*; Digest, *De libris et postulis*, Law *Gallicanus*, § *Quid si tantum*; Institutes, *Quibus modis ius patriae potestatis solvitur*, § *Relegati*; Code, *De hereditatibus instituendis*, Law 1. But Jacobus de Arena says that outlaws do not lose common rights, but only municipal rights: Digest, *Ad legem Trebonianam*, Law *Ex facto*, according to Jacobus de Arena. And Bartolus says the same, disputing, and this is true. And thus they do not lose the right to succeed by will, since such succession is of common law. Nor does it apply to the fisc, because acquisition supervened after the sentence: Digest, *De manumissionibus*, Law *Si tibi*, § *Is, cuius bona*; and Digest, *De legatis tertio*, Law *Si deportati servo*. But it is answered that this condemned person, for treason, is similar to one condemned for the crime of lèse-majesté, who is declared incapable above, under the Law *Julia maiestatis*, Law *Quisquis*; and *De legatis secundo*, Law *Cum filius*, § *Repetendorum*; and Institutes, *De hereditatibus ab intestato*. On the contrary, this person cannot remain in part in the city and in part be a public enemy: Digest, *De capitis diminutione*, Law *In admissione*, § *Qui deficiunt*. These matters are therefore quite doubtful. One thing, however, is certain: the son does not succeed, because in a conditional right adhering to the person, the fisc does not succeed. This is supported by: Digest, *De novis querelis*, Law *Quotiens*, § *Si*; and Law *Si qua poena*, *De his qui sui iuris sunt*, according to Guillelmus and Cynus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the law *Qui patri* applies to a coheir in a certain quantity, and whether a substitute in a certain quantity succeeds.
2. A conditional legacy is transmitted.
casus:
CASE. Drea Merantis of Rieti, having two daughters and one underage son, coming to death, among other things, disposed thus, namely:

Item, she left to Matuicia 200 gold florins.

Item, she left to the same Matuicia, for clothing when she is given in marriage, 16 gold florins, in which [sum] she instituted Matuicia, her daughter, as her heir; and let her be content, and she may not ask for more of her goods, nor have [them] during the life of her son Girard, written below: and if it should happen that the said Matuicia dies without legitimate sons born of her own body, let Girard, her son, succeed her in all goods, etc.

Item, that after a certain other legacy, which she makes to her wife, and of the testator, she thus says:

Item, to Lucia, her daughter, beyond the dowry, which she later gave to Jeremiah, her husband, 5 gold florins, in which 5 gold florins she instituted Lucia herself as her heir in dowry; and let her be content, and she may not ask for more in the goods during the life of Girard, son of the said Mandus.

Item, she left, willed, and commanded, that the said Lucia, if it should happen that she is violated in any way, that she have recourse and habitation in the house of the said Mandus, where she now resides.

Item, she willed and commanded, and whenever it should happen that the said Lucia dies without legitimate sons born of her own body, that Girard, her son, and his sons, and heirs descending from the body of the said Girard, succeed her, etc.

After many other legacies, as she says, in all her other goods, movable and immovable, rights, and actions, she instituted and made Girard, her son, her universal heir: and if it should happen that the said Girard dies without sons born of his own body, or to be born, however, in pupillary age, let Rita and Vanna, daughters of Cola Vendicti, succeed the said Girard in 25 gold florins for each of them. In all her other goods, let Lucia and Matuicia, daughters of the said Mandus, succeed for an equal portion, provided that the said Rita, Vanna, Matuicia, and Lucia, or any one of them, may not nor ought to molest or disturb the said Matuicia in the usufruct of the goods of the said Mandus, etc.

The said testator Mandus died; after his death, Matuicia and Lucia died, with the said Angelo and Margarita, children of the said Lucia, daughter of Mandus, surviving her. Finally, the said Girard died in pupillary age, with the said Angelo and Margarita, children of the said Lucia, and Rita and Vanna, daughters of Cola Vendicti, substituted to the said Girard in 25 florins, as above, surviving.

Now it is asked, whether, by the species of the said pupillary substitution made to the said Girard, the said Lucia, substituted to the said Girard, transmitted [the inheritance] to Angelo and Margarita, her sons, because she was a coheir in a certain quantity, and substituted to the said Girard by the Law *Qui patri*, Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatis*; and if she transmitted, whether in whole or in part; and if the said law does not have place in a coheir of a certain thing, whether the said Rita and Vanna, substituted in a certain quantity, succeed in such a way that there is no place for intestate succession, whereby [the fisc] occupies the whole inheritance, or only 25 florins for each, in which the substitution was made. It pleases to consult, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† I do not believe that the law *qui patri*, D. de acquisitione hereditatis, has application in the case of a coheir in a certain quantity, namely, that the deceased, before the ward, having already accepted the inheritance through the ward, transmits the pupillary substitution, because this person is not properly a coheir. And thus the case of the said law *qui patri* ceases with regard to the aforementioned matter. For this person is reduced to the status of a passed-over legatee with regard to the complaint, since the universal heir has intervened. C. de hereditate instituenda, l. *quoties*, as noted in l. *si quis priore*, D. ad Trebellianum. Moreover, the law *qui patri* ceases with regard to the reason.

† And therefore we remain under the rule that a conditional legacy is transmissible. D. de suis et legitimis heredibus; D. si ex pluribus, de vulgari et pupillari substitutione; D. sed si plures, de re iudicata; C. quæ legata, de caducis tollendis; § si nauter, Rost. n. legis qui patri. The reason is that the coheir, by acknowledging the paternal obligation arising from a quasi-contract, is bound to accept the pupillary substitution; therefore, upon death, he transmits this necessary obligation, and consequently the substitution, or at least the effect of the substitution through the right of accretion. But this reasoning does not apply to a legatee, or quasi-legatee, or to a quasi-heir in a specific thing; because such a person, by acknowledging his legacy, obligates no one else, but only himself, and he may accept one legacy and reject another. D. de legatis 2; D. neminem; D. sed ex duobus. From these it appears that those who predeceased did not transmit the right of accretion, which had merged into the universal and solidary institution of an heir; nor did they transmit the right of substitution, because it was conditional and in a caducous hope. Whether a caducous substitute in a specific quantity succeeds may be doubted by D. cohæredi, § si, de vulgari et pupillari substitutione. But there the text speaks of a direct pupillary substitution, which is reduced to the pattern of the principal institution. D. ad legem Falcidiam; D. in ratione, § si filiae. But this substitution is to be considered a legacy in the second tablets; and therefore it is not due any more than a legacy, according to the noted D. de legatis 3; C. quod fideicommissum, de inofficioso testamento; D. ex tribus, per Cynus, ad tres; D. cohæredi, § et generaliter, per Decius. It supports what is noted in C. facit hæres, quoties. It follows that the father died testate, but the son intestate; and therefore succession is to him as to an intestate, i.e., quasi-intestate, by those to whom the inheritance of an intestate, or quasi-intestate, is granted, as in D. 1, de suis et legitimis heredibus, and the law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Writings made to induce an obligation shall be upheld against the writer, so as to prejudice him and his successors.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The said writings must be upheld against the heirs of the said Ser Nicolò. For a writing made to prove an obligation, when the cause prejudices the writer, and consequently his successors, as in the Digest, *de deposito*, l. *publica*, § *si*; and noted in the Code, *de probat.*, l. *instrumenta*. And the same applies to the ledger of a massarius (steward) of any city or territory. For the account book will be upheld against the writer. Digest, *de eodem*, l. *quaedam sunt personae*, in the beginning; and l. *argentarius*, Digest, *de donationibus nudis*, according to Bartolus, although it is considered private, unless it was made by a notary. Digest, *de iure fisci*, l. *in fraudem*, § *neque*. And it is supported by the Code, *de exact. trib.*, l. 1, lib. 10; and Code, *de apocr. public.*, l. 1; and Authentica, *de mancip.*, in the beginning, § *coges*; Code, *de non numer. pec.*, l. *in contractis*, § 1; and l. *generaliter*. Nor does it matter if it is said that the said writing is uncertain: for rather it is certain by reference to a certain thing, namely, the account book; hence, what appears in the book is deemed to be contained in the response letters approving the faith of the book, as in l. *in summa*, *de re iudicata*; and Code, *de senatusconsulto quod sine certa quantitate*, etc. This is the sentence. Insofar, therefore, as it can be understood that Ser Nicolò owed to the said Ser Nardo according to the existing books, it supports what is noted in the Authentica, *de iureiurando a marito praestito*, near the beginning. Insofar as it does not appear that payment was made, it cannot be claimed: for it is not permitted to simultaneously approve and disapprove a writing. d. l. *publica*, § *si*. I, Baldus, and others.

casus: AS VS. The point on which the opinion is requested is as follows. A certain person is inquired upon because he arranged and treated with a certain Lenae regarding the commission of adultery with a certain married woman: and with the intervention of the procuring, urging, and persuasions of the said Lenae, he who was to commit the adultery wished to proceed to acts proximate to adultery, which according to the form of the common law should be punished extra ordinem, according to what is contained in l. 1, Digest, *de extraordinariis criminibus*. And it did not rest with him that the said adultery was not committed; rather, he did all things proximate to adultery that he could do to perpetrate such adultery. It is asked whether the aforementioned arranger and negotiator benefits from the benefit of concord, considering the form of the statutes of the commune of Perugia under the rubric *de concordiis*: and considering also that adultery did not actually follow, etc. If anyone has taken every care to commit adultery, but has not yet committed it, can he be punished, considering also the disposition of the statute, which provides that if the parties have conciliated regarding malefices, the penalty is remitted? Can he be condemned if they have conciliated? And he concludes that he cannot. And this opinion is also below in number 33.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the statute, it appears to me that a settlement cannot be made regarding an attempt solely in the crime of sodomy, which is the most monstrous, ff. de extraor. cri. l. 1. §. fi. Whatever therefore follows in the same statute does not pertain to attempted acts, but to consummated ones. Whence if someone applied effort toward committing adultery, yet it was not committed, he is said to have made an attempt, but not to have carried it out; and therefore a settlement is valid, because the negotiation took place without consummation. Whence in statutes that which is not yet done is not held as done, for that would be a kind of fiction, ff. de fideius. l. fideiussorem., according to Bart. ff. de adul. l. et si amicis., and with the glossa ordinaria that when a settlement of adultery is prohibited, one may be made concerning an attempt, as regarding touching for the sake of adultery, because no one abducts a girl for the purpose of lying with her [?], in l. transigere, vel pacisci. C. de trans. In doubt, therefore, the statute must be understood as concerning a consummated act, because the word 'ad' includes, not excludes, the terminus ad quem; whence it is not called adultery unless adultery is committed. In doubtful matters, punishments are also to be mitigated; what is noted by Bar. de extraord. cri. l. saccularii supports this; what is noted by Cy. in l. si quis non dicam rapere. C. de epis. et cle. and l. is, qui cum telo. C. de sica. also supports this. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. An offense purged in one place cannot be punished in another place, even though the offender may acquire a forum in several places.
casus: CASE. The fact is as follows: A certain Perugian committed a homicide against a certain other Perugian in the territory of Assisi. For this matter he was condemned in his person by an official of the commune of Assisi. Thereafter, by the ordinances of the commune of Assisi, he was absolved from the said personal condemnation under this condition, that the said homicide must pay 50 gold florins to the commune of Assisi; and he has already paid them. It is now asked whether he ought or can be condemned by the officials of the commune of Perugia, since, as has been said, he was condemned in Assisi; and what the law is.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be considered that an offense purged in one place through a real penalty, that is, through an effective endurance [thereof], cannot be punished in another place, even though someone may acquire a forum in several places. And the reason is that by payment he is freed and considered as acquitted, as noted in C. ad l. Aquil. l. ex morte and ff. de execu. rei iudica. l. si quis cum totum. §. plane; for they are not only freed from the forum, but from the penalty, because the penalty purges the offense. Iac. de Bel. expressly holds this in l. 1. C. vbi de cri. agi oportet, in public disputation. Bar. also expressly holds this in ff. de adul. l. et si amicis. And although a Perugian has committed an offense against a Perugian, nevertheless, if he has been forestalled in the place of the delict, he cannot be punished further, l. licet. §. possumus. ff. naut. caup. sta., since by the common law no one ought to be punished elsewhere if he is open to being remitted to the place of the offense, as in Auth. vt nulli iudi. §. si quis vero comprehensorum. And although by custom an equal does not remit to an equal, nor a superior to an inferior, nonetheless the penalty is not to be duplicated, because vengeance once suffices, ff. de iniur. l. quod senatus. Nor should it be considered that a penalty was imposed on a homicide who had not yet been banished or condemned; I think that by no law can proceedings be taken in the city of Perugia, since the action is forestalled not only according to the said law, but the place of the delict is the more principal place for punishing a crime. And therefore the text speaks alternatively, not copulatively, in l. 1. vbi de crimine agi oportet, when it says 'either/or' (vel) and does not say 'also' (etiam), so as to give to understand that one place suffices, and that one penalty suffices for one offense. I, Baldus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When several arbitrators are appointed jointly, if one is lacking, the others cannot render a sentence or award.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† According to civil law, the award of the said three arbitrators is not valid in the absence of the fourth: because it was tacitly agreed that all should render judgment; because they were elected jointly, as stated in the law and number, Digest, On Arbitrators, l. non distinguemus, §. cum in plures. But according to canon law, it ought to be valid upon the fourth being summoned, as in c. ult., On Arbitrators, Book 6, and what is noted in a similar case in c. fin., On Wills, same title, Book 6, it may be said that c. ult., On Wills, does not apply, because that provision is special in favor of last wills. Since, therefore, the form of the compromise is not taken from any one individual, but from the entire number, it is not valid, because it is done with one absent, argument from Digest, On Arbitrators, l. Pedius, §. 1. And because in this case civil law is not found to be corrected by canon law: when arbitrators are appointed by compromise, there is a tacit condition that they arbitrate as compromised, i.e., the form being observed. Code, On Contracts of Sale, l. si nam. It departs from the person even of one among many; because plural language requires truth in all, argument from Digest, On Doubtful Matters, l. si is, qui, 200, §. utrum, and l. Iulius Phebus, ad Trebonium. Moreover, if it is special in the case of executors of last wills, therefore the common law is to the contrary. And so, since they chose the mere path of arbitration with three without the fourth, it can be plausibly said that the award is not valid.

The second reason is, because this compromise was made, and the award rendered concerning the law of the city of Spoleto, therefore the pact of the priests cannot impede public law, which even he himself may contravene as one of the people. As fully noted and read in Digest, On Pacts, l. iuris gentium, §. Item si paciscar, etc. I, Baldus.

THE

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether one who orders and attempts adultery, given that it did not follow through, can be punished notwithstanding a concord made concerning the same, in light of the statute on concords. He concludes that he cannot. And this conclusion is found above in number 30.
casus: CASE. In the name of Christ, Amen. The words of the statute being presupposed. The point on which counsel is requested is as follows. A certain person is required to have arranged and treated with a certain procuress (lena) regarding committing adultery with a certain other married woman, and through the intervention of procuration, and the urging and persuasions of the said procuress, he who wished to commit adultery proceeded to acts proximate to adultery, which according to the form of the common law ought to be punished extraordinarily, according to what is said in l. 1, Digest, On Extraordinary Crimes. And it did not rest with him that the said adultery was not committed; rather, he did all things proximate to adultery that he could do to perpetrate such adultery. It is asked whether the aforementioned arranger and negotiator benefits from the advantage of conciliation, considering the form of the statute of the commune of Perugia under the heading On Conciliations. And also considering that adultery did not in fact follow, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Having presupposed the words of the statute under the title concerning concords, I say that those words regarding aid, counsel, and favor given and rendered by command, discussion, and arrangement for the said malefices are not verified where the malefice is not consummated. The reason is that where the principal ceases, the accessory ceases. D. de furtis, l. si is qui, §. tutorem. And if it sometimes happens otherwise, this is by fiction. C. de furtis, l. si quis servo. This fiction has no place in the penalties of statutes, because it would be an execution. D. de negotiis gestis, l. 3, §. hæc verba; C. de his qui vetita, l. fi. But the principal delict, namely adultery, ceases, and likewise the accessory, which is said to be for the said malefices, signifies the definition of the malefice and a completed thing. D. quod quisque iuris, l. 1, §. hæc verba; D. arborum furtim, l. cedere, §. subsecare. This is also evident from the nature of this word "ad" [to/towards], which includes the final term; if the inclusion tends towards exclusion, or towards mitigation of the penalty. Arg. not. C. de nuptiis, l. a caligato, per Cynus. And it is evident from the word "ad" that it requires a completed thing. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. non putabam. It is necessary that the term from which is contiguous to the term to which, which cannot be if the term to which is not in the nature of things; because that which is not has nothing contiguous to it. Therefore, adultery is not said to exist where there is no adultery, just as it is not said to be "to the church" where there is no church, because those things which are said "to" something require two extremes. Note that the said statute does not say "for the committing of the said malefices," so as to punish the attempt, but it says "for the said malefices," and therefore it is necessary to see whether that by which the malefice was surrounded is true or not. It is clear, however, that it is not true, because it was not in the act of its perfection and proper definition, and therefore the law and the interpreter of the law act less, as in l. si quis non dicam rapere and l. is qui cum telo, per Cynus and others. The preludes of malefices, having strayed to other terms, are confounded, as in l. illud, §. fi. Et nota undequam plura and l. quæ de crimine, and per Bartolus de adulteriis, l. et si amicis. And because the statute excepts one case of a future malefice, or an imperfect past malefice, hence in other cases it seems to have considered the effect of the thing, i.e., the consummation of the delict, as in D. de funerariis instrumentis, l. quæsitus, §. respondit domo, ultimo, versi. nam qui hoc inquirit, etc. I, Baldus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Having made a compromise, whether in two [arbitrators] who agreed in their sentence, a third is chosen; if the third, together with one, delivers a sentence, and the other [does not], for the sentence must be adhered to, he concludes that the award given by the third [is valid].
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Without doubt, the said arbitration agreement was valid, because it concerned a matter capable of being submitted to arbitration, because it was between competent persons, because it was in the proper, competent, and appropriate form, and because it is presupposed that the third arbitrator, whose authority must be obeyed, pronounced his award together with one of the parties, while the other pronounced to the contrary, as stated in the first part of the concordance. See D. de arbitris, l. Item si unus, §. Principium; and C. ult., de arbitris, lib. 6. And although this does not prejudice the right of the buyer, unless the sale was simulated, as in D. de pignoribus, l. Si superata, nevertheless, if it prejudices the seller who submitted to arbitration, execution ought to be carried out against him; and if he cannot deliver the thing, execution shall be made by way of estimation. A similar case is found in C. de conditionibus ob causam datam, l. Ea lege. Nor can reduction be sought by the buyer, since he is not harmed, because it is not in his interest; therefore, see also D. de appellando recipiendo, l. 1, in principio. And thus it does not impede execution, as in C. de extraordinaria cognitione, l. Si, because execution is not made on the person but on the thing by way of estimation. See C. de executione rei iudicatae, l. Si legis; D. de re iudicata, l. A Diuo Pio, §. Si superveniet. Or, in this judgment and execution, there is even a singular interest, as in l. 1, in principio, de actione emptoris. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A simulated refutation does not harm the one who refutes.
2. Simulation may be proven by the confession of a party made in the absence of the adversary, accompanied by an oath.
3. An arbitrator may believe a single credible witness, supported by the oath of a party.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Three things are to be considered.
† First, that a simulated refutation does not harm the one who refutes. C. that which is done through the whole has greater force.
Secondly, that a simulation may be proved by the confession of a party made in the absence of the adversary, with an oath. Dist. 7, c. *Quoties cordis oculus*.

Thirdly, that an arbitrator may believe one good witness with the oath of the party, as in l. admonendi and l. in bonae fidei and the argument in de dote praelegata, l. Theopompus. It is not said that he commits fraud, but rather that he repels fraud and his award is true and equitable, because it rests on sufficient proof by one man; and therefore I previously advised on this case due to this confession, that the arbitrator was not in fraud nor in gross negligence, but rendered a true and equitable award, at least according to the equity of his own mind; and therefore certain others, who advised otherwise, did not properly note the facts. It is supported by Extra de successionibus ab intestato, c. si; ff. de edicto edilitio, l. quæro in fine; de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Titio fundus; ff. communia, l. argentis; and in arbitral matters, it is presumed for the arbitrator not only as to the intent of the mind, but also as to the intent of the act. de eo qui furtum ostendit susceptum, c. si, per Innocentius. Therefore, the reduction being abandoned, execution shall be made according to the form of the statute, as noted in C. de appellationibus, l. eos in principio; and C. de ordine cognitionum. I, Baldus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, when a pupillary substitution has been made and the inheritance has lapsed, the mother is admitted to the succession, excluding the children of her sister by another mother, as well as the maternal uncles and aunts.
2. The judge, in cases of doubt, must adhere to natural equity, as the words of the law permit.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† There is no doubt under the common law that, if a pupillary substitution has become void, the mother succeeds intestate to the exclusion of the children of the sister born of another mother, and all the more so to the exclusion of the maternal and paternal uncles and aunts of the pupil, as stated in C. ad trebellianam, auth. Defuncto; and in de legitimis haeredibus, auth. Cessantis; and in the Corpus, from which it is derived. Moreover, if the mother were not surviving, or were excluded by chance or by law, it is certain that the children of the sister exclude the uncles and aunts of the deceased whose succession is in question; because although they are of the same degree, they are not equal in succeeding, as in auth. Post fratres, and noted by Cynus in C. communia de successionibus, auth. Itaque indistincte. And thus in the case recently committed to me for consultation from Bologna. However, it must be examined according to the form of the statute whether the mother succeeds universally to an underage child intestate. And it seems that she does not, because it is true to say that such an underage child died intestate. Although this is not a proper location [of terms], it is not abusive, but in legal usage. D. de suis et legitimis haeredibus, l. 1, in principio; quomodo et quando sibi succedatur. For he did not die by will, nor by various figures, i.e., by successions validly figured or anomalous; therefore it necessarily follows that he died intestate, as noted by Cynus in de iure deliberandi, l. Cum antiquioribus, there: but the opposite is proven in l. 2, and in D. de petitione hereditatis, l. Credendum; de petitione tutelae; and l. 2, § Si mater; and § Videndum; D. ad Senatusconsultum Tertullianum. To the contrary, it seems that a pupil is not said to be intestate, but intestabilis [incapable of making a will], and these are different, as in the said l. 1, and noted by Cynus in l. 2, C. qui testamento facere possint. Doctors are varied on this point. For some, due to the inequity of the statute, understand the words "intestate" by referring them to the person, and if a pupil is said to be intestabilis, not intestate, unless perhaps his father made a will for him and it became void; and these say that the mother is admitted, and otherwise I have consulted unless the common usage of speech is proven. To the contrary, from D. de superioribus legibus, l. Labeo: for the usage of speech invents the significations of words. D. de legibus 3, l. Librorum, § Quantum Cassius. Others understand the words of the statute by referring them to the cause, for even in the case of a pupil we are in the cause of intestacy, because the final cause of succeeding is that someone has not made a will, and it is equitable to succeed; and according to these, even by proper usage, the mother is repelled. It is one thing to say "dying intestate," referring to the act of the person. It is another to say "dying intestate," signifying the cause and effect of the matter. And in this doubt, due to the contrary opinions of doctors, it is often pronounced sometimes for one party, sometimes for the other; the text in the said l. 1 can be induced for and against. The word "if" also, if placed privatively, requires a preceding habit, and thus does not apply to a pupil. But Jacobus de Arena, however, in our statute, more certainly favors the mother; because the statute makes two cases, one of dying in pupillary age, the other of intestacy, in § Sed quod si qua. For if the word "intestate" included pupils, the statute would have superfluously mentioned pupillary age according to the intent of the statute; hence it seems the statute considered this difference, and afterwards when it speaks of the mother, it speaks taking only the word "intestate," and not the word "pupil." And thus the mother seems to succeed in whole, as is the case under the common law, since the statute does not hinder the mother, as in l. Si servum, § Non dixit, de acquisitione hereditatis. This statute is very dry without any radical moisture of any equity, and against natural reason. D. de inofficioso testamento, l. Nam et si parentibus. And it speaks very precisely and absolutely against the mother, not with respect to other persons in that word, "and if any widow," in the first response. But in the third response, in the words "nor the mother," it changes the case, when the mother succeeds in nothing; hence in our case it seems to me, saving the substance of truth, that if the said usage of speech is proven, the mother would not succeed, except in the portion fixed by the statute. C. de secundis nuptiis, l. 1; and the children of the sister would succeed in the rest of the whole, because after the mother they are preferred to the uncle and aunt under the common law, which I do not find changed by the statute. But if nothing else is proven regarding the intent of the statute from the common usage of speech, then it seems that the mother is not excluded, unless perhaps the contrary is said, because it is clear that he made a will, and this is in the case of a void will and intestacy reduced. I doubt greatly, because in present substitutions the pupil remains intestabilis; if otherwise, I favor the mother if the said usage of speech is not proven, but if proven, I favor the children of the sister, as appears from the above. I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, have subscribed to the end, and sealed with the seal of my name, always saving the substance of truth. And for certain, this question is quite doubtful, and much can be said for and against.

† In case of doubt, he who has the power to judge must adhere closely to natural equity, if the words of the law permit. D. ad Trebellianam, l. Qui filium, § Imperator. And see what is noted in Inst. de hereditatibus ab intestato, in principio, and c.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a wife has two children from her first husband and three from another, and after the death of such mother one of the three dies, how shall the dowry and her property be divided among the said children.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

It is proposed that the said Margaret had two husbands, namely Cechus Lelli of Trosciano, from whom she had two sons, namely Bartholomew and Jacobutia; and after Cechus died, she took as her husband a certain man named Farolfus of Cantario, and from him she bore three sons, namely Petrutius, Nutarellus, and Floran. Then the said Lady Margaret died intestate. 3. The said Flora died; now it is asked how the dowry and succession of the said Lady Margaret are to be divided among the said sons. I answer that regarding the said dowry and succession, five parts ought to be made, and in two parts Bartholomew and Jacobutia succeed. In the three parts, however, Petrutius and Nutarellus succeed in their own person, and the said Flora, joined to them by both parents, and also the father of Flora succeeds with them in the portion of the said Flora, as in the Authentica Defuncto, and in the Authentica De herede ab intestato post principium, and in the Institutes De haeredibus ab intestato § Cum filio, Codex De suis et legitimis, Authentica In successione, Codex De legitimis haeredibus, Authentica Cessante. And this holds if the said Flora entered upon the maternal inheritance; but what if she did not enter, nor did she transmit the right of deliberation? It seems that only four parts are made, but the contrary is true, especially if she was an infant. For then the father can enter upon the inheritance, as in the Codex De iure deliberando, law Si infanti. And if the father did not enter, it would accrue to those joined by both parents, because those joined by legal connection are more effective, which in inheritances creates a right of accrual. And Digest De coniungendis cum emancipatis liberis, law 1, § Si quis ex nepotibus. Notwithstanding the Codex Ad senatusconsultum Orphitianum, law Non pro matrimonio, because there all were equally joined. Concluding, therefore, it must be said that to the said Bartholomew and Jacobutia pertain two parts of the five parts of the said goods, and no more. I, Baldus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a priest, who cannot serve at the altar to which he was elected by right of patronage due to private enmities, is deprived of the benefice after two months.
2. Whether the prior is bound to elect a priest from the testator’s lineage, given the testator’s disposition that the election be made from the family, or whether he may retain the benefice for himself.
casus: CASE. On which counsel is requested, the case is as follows. A certain man made his will, in which, among other things he disposed, he disposed and ordained that in a church, to be designated by his trustees, a certain altar be appointed and established by his said trustees and heirs, or the heir of the heir, one priest from the progeny of the said testator, who shall minister the divine cult, and in that altar, according to the form of the said testator and the last will of the testator, the heirs and the heirs of the heirs, executing the will of the said testator, elected and constituted in the said altar a certain priest from the progeny of the said testator, who priest, thus elected and appointed, was put in possession of the altar and the appurtenances of the said altar. Finally it happened that mortal enmity arose among the blood relatives of the said testator, and also the said priest, in the land where the said altar was constructed and established, to which the said priest had been appointed to serve, so that it was necessary for the said priest and his blood relatives to absent themselves from the said land, since on account of the said mortal enmity they could not remain and stay without danger to their persons; and thus, on account of the absence of the said priest due to the aforementioned cause, the altar became vacant. Finally, and then, the prior general of the Order of Mount Fano of the district of Fabriano asserted that on account of the absence of the said priest, the said altar had devolved to the said prior by virtue of the will of the said testator, because he said it was vacant in the celebration of divine services, and thus, in fact, he took possession of the said altar and its appurtenances for himself, nor did he elect, place, and constitute a priest for the said altar according to the disposition and will of the said testator. Now it is asked whether the said priest from the progeny of the said testator, elected according to the form of the will of the said testator, on account of his absence, which was necessary due to the said enmity which compelled him to absent himself, falls from the election, nomination, and governance of the said altar and its appurtenances, or not. And whether the said prior of the Order of Mount Fano lawfully detains and possesses the said altar, because he retains it for himself and does not observe the form of the statute and the last will of the said testator in electing, naming, and placing a priest for the service of the said altar and the celebration of divine services, nor does he make continuous residence in the place according to the disposition and will of the said testator. Furthermore, it is asked whether the said heirs and the heirs of the heirs of the said testator can lawfully, again and anew, elect, place, name, and ordain in the said altar a priest, and for the priest of the said altar, the said priest from the progeny of the said testator, who was otherwise elected and appointed by them according to the will of the said testator, as is premised, put in possession of the said altar, given that he was compelled to absent himself from the said land on account of the said enmity. Wherefore, please, having seen the said will and having seen the narration of the present bearer, advise, as the Most High shall minister to you, and also on other matters as your wisdom shall know to be expedient, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The will of the testator must be observed, as in the Authentica de ecclesiis, title, §. si quis ad aedificationem, col. 9. However, since the altar is spiritual, it cannot be conferred by laymen; but they say that rectors present the altar to the bishop, and the bishop, if the person presented is suitable, is bound to institute him. Extra, de iure patronatus, c. consuluit. Nor can the testator prohibit the bishop from exercising the right of patronage, as in the Authentica de sancta ecclesia, §. si quis; Authentica pro redemptione; Digestum, de legibus, l. nemo potest. I say that it cannot be conferred as a benefice or canonical title, so that the altar is said to have a rector, unless he is instituted by the bishop, as I have said above; but to serve the altar simply, not however such that the priest serving thereby is said to have a benefice or this title, it can be done by executors or heirs, argument from the said §. si quis ad aedificationem. Now it is asked, if this priest, on account of his private enmities, cannot serve, whether after two months it becomes vacant according to the form of the testament. And it seems that it does, because private enmity is reckoned as fault, otherwise in public enmity. Digestum, solutione matrimonii, l. pe; Digestum, locati conducti, l. Item quaeritur, §. exercitu; and l. si merces, §. culpae. On the contrary, it seems that because of enmities, provided they are not affected or simulated, one is excused from the necessity of residence, as in c. bonae electionis, de electione. I say that, on account of the order given and the form laid down by the testator, the heirs ought to have seen to it that the altar was served by another, argument from c. peruenit, extra, de electione, §. si mater, with the following §.

And therefore the prior of the mountain of Fano succeeds; nevertheless, he must choose a priest from the testator’s lineage, if one suitable is found there, because the substitute is bound by the same form as that to which the instituted heir is bound. D. de legatis 1, l. Imperator; D. de legatis 2, l. Cum pater, § Ab instituto. And he must be compelled to do this by the bishop, and if he does not wish to obey, he would forfeit this right through deprivation. C. de fideicommissis, Auth. Hoc amplius; Extr. de testibus, c. Si heredes; Extr. de nominatione, c. Licet. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The sum, as in the statement of the case.
casus: CASE. The fact proposed is as follows. A certain John and Simon of Saint Elpidio ad Mare, brothers who held common property and conducted business jointly, were condemned for the crime of lèse-majesté, because they were said to have plotted and arranged the rebellion of the said land, wishing to subject it tyrannically to wickedness and to kill the vicar appointed there for the Holy Roman Church, and to give effect to their plot, they had ordered that, insofar as it was in their power, etc. For these reasons, the power of the said land and the one elected by the said vicar appointed for the Holy Roman Church condemned them, and each of them, to the penalty of death and the confiscation of all their goods, wherever they may be and can be found, to be applied to the said commune and the vicar appointed for the Holy Roman Church. It is presupposed that jurisdiction to punish and to cognize, by himself and officials appointed by him, of every offense, with the concession of mere and mixed empire and the power of the sword, and with the power to confiscate and apply to himself and the said commune all things that would come to be applied to the Roman Church, had been granted to the said vicar by the Supreme Pontiff. Now, after the said sentence was given, the power, the commune, and the vicar of the land of Saint Elpidio request the lords, the commune, and the officials of the city of Fermo, that certain goods and merchandise placed and brought into the said city by the said condemned John, by executing the said sentence, they should give and assign to the syndic and procurator of themselves and of the said vicar and commune of the land of Saint Elpidio, to whom it is said to belong by right by virtue of the said offense and sentence passed. Which matter, since the said lords of the city of Fermo committed it to certain judges for determination, a sequestration of the aforementioned goods was made. After which, certain persons appear, saying that they are creditors of the said John, the said John confessing, and by his own will possession or tenure of the aforementioned merchandise is given, especially by virtue of certain private documents made after the time when the offense is said to have been committed.
† Now it is asked whether the goods and things located in the city of Fermo fall within the aforementioned consideration as being outside the jurisdiction of the said judge.

Secondly, it is asked whether, at the request of the said communal authority and the vicar, the officials of the city of Fermo are bound to execute the said sentence upon the aforementioned goods and to assign them to the syndics and the procurator already mentioned.

Thirdly, it is asked: even if the aforementioned goods are subject to confiscation, to which community or treasury should they be applied, whether to the city of Fermo, where the goods are located, or to the community and vicar of the said territory of San Elpidio, where the sentence was pronounced? It must be premised that the said goods are movable property and merchandise brought into the said city of Fermo not with the intention of retaining them there, but of transferring them to entirely foreign places, presupposing that each of the aforementioned territories acknowledges the rule and dominion of the Church.

Fourthly, it is asked whether the said condemned person may confess himself to be a debtor of a third person to the prejudice of the said community to which he is condemned, and what is presumed by law.

Fifth and lastly, it is asked whether the said commissioners, to whom the aforementioned cause has been entrusted, may intervene in any manner regarding the rights and validity of the said sentence, or whether they are to judge only whether it is to be executed or not executed.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the first point, whether goods situated outside the territory are subject to confiscation in a universal confiscation. It must be said that if the person is such a banished individual as to be equated with one deported, according to the noted institution *Qui modis ius patriæ potest solui*, § *Relegati*, all his goods are subject to confiscation. L. *Deportatorum*, C. *De poenis*; ff. *De capite diminuto*; L. *Tutelas*, § *Peccato*, because the fiscus is not divided, but is everywhere. Moreover, deportation cannot be local, but extends throughout the entire territory of the authority by which it is imposed, for example, that of the Pope or the Emperor; nor does it result in one remaining in the city in part and dying in part. ff. *De capite diminuto*, L. *Ammissione*; ff. *Qui deficiunt*; ff. *De posthumis*; C. *De iniuria testamento*, L. *Si quis filio exheredato*; ff. *De testamento*, L. *Eius qui*; C. *Ad legem Iuliam de vi*, L. *Si tutores*. In our case, he must be equated with a deported person by the nature of the crime. C. *De abolitione*, L. 2, in fine; C. *Ad legem Iuliam maiestatis*, L. *Quisquis*, in the said § *Qui deficiunt*.

But there is doubt in the corporation, to which, however, it is made, whether where the offense was committed and condemnation ensued, or over the goods, assuming that both chambers are procurators of the Emperor for their own interest. The doctors say that the case of goods, i.e., where the goods are, with respect to the goods, the condemnation is real: because it follows the thing, as the moderns fully note in l. cunctos populos, de summa Trinitate. And they allege many things, which I do not care to refer to, but they speak of things coherent to the territory, but in movable things it seems that a distinction should be made, whether they are there, as in a fixed situation: or temporarily, because things which are claimed according to place are assigned to that place where they are destined. ff. de haeredibus instituendis, l. ex facto, §. rerum; auth. ff. de pignoribus, l. debitor; ff. de legatis 1, l. huiusmodi, §. legatur. In this case, therefore, where the things have been transferred elsewhere, not for the purpose of bringing them back from where they were transferred, it does not seem that the fisc of this land should have them, unless they were transferred after the offense, because then they are claimed as if affected on account of the crime of lèse-majesté, as ff. de rebus in rem versis, l. si. And this is the first point.

† Regarding the second point, it depends, and first I say that obedience is due if the case involves confiscation to the Camera, which is what is sought here; otherwise not, because the Camera is twofold, namely universal and singular, and the Camera of the fiscus is a member and not a head, having limited right, as is stated in the law Extra territorium and in the constitution Ut animarum, Book 6. And by these authorities the response has been given.
† Thirdly, on which point I say that a confession is not valid to the prejudice of the fisc, as is clear from the law *Post contractum*, in the Digest, under the title *De donationibus*.

† On the fifth point, I say that a mere executor does not adjudicate nullity, but an executor who possesses jurisdiction should not execute that which is null. D. de iudicibus, l. si praetor. For he is a mere executor who is bound to obey the one who commands, but he who executes by his own authority is not a mere executor. On this, fully, note the opinion of Innocentius, D. de iureiurando, c. de caetero. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, and when, legitimation made by the Emperor extends to property situated in the territories of the Pope.
casus:
CASE

In the name of the Lord, Amen. The point of law is as follows: Lord Matthew of Nanea, having taken holy orders, had two sons by a certain woman named Golata. Among the said sons is a certain one named G., whom the said Lord Matthew had legitimized through the hands of a certain person claiming to have authority from the Emperor. This legitimation was performed in the lands of the Church. Now, the same Lord Matthew, being at the point of death, with the said son G., as is reported, surviving him and legitimized, and with his carnal brother Angelo surviving him, and with Simon, John, and Martin, sons of the said Angelo and nephews of the said Lord Matthew, surviving him, and while making his will in the presence of the said Angelo, his brother, he instituted the said G. as heir to a certain portion, and Angelo to a certain portion. In this will, the testator wished that Angelo promise not to molest the said G., his son, and thus he promised in the same will, written by his own hand, and swore not to molest the said G. in the institution made concerning the said G. After the testator died, and while the said G. and Angelo and the said sons were still living, the said Angelo finally passed away, leaving the said Simon and the others, and the said G. It is claimed on behalf of the said G. that he should succeed to his father’s inheritance, because he was legitimized, and because Angelo consented and swore on behalf of Simon and the others. It is responded that the said legitimation is not valid in law, nor is the promise made and sworn by Angelo not to molest valid, and even if it were valid, it is not to the prejudice of Simon and the others. Now it is asked whether the said legitimation is valid, since it was done in the lands of the Church, and concerning that which is under ecclesiastical dominion. Also, whether the said promise or renunciation made by Angelo would avail anything. Also, whether the said G. succeeds in any way as born from one who is in holy orders. Also, if the said G. does not succeed, to whom the goods, in which G. was instituted, shall devolve, and what is the law.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The Emperor possesses Imperial majesty everywhere, because majesty is not divided, just as neither is a character nor fame; but he does not possess Imperial administration everywhere. For it is divided, and he holds Empire together with the Apostolic See, so that the lands of the Roman Church are subject neither mediately nor immediately to the Emperor. It must therefore be considered that some things do not admit of division, such as fame, and then the restitution of the Emperor is valid in all places. D. de posth. l. 1. §. de qua. D. de re iud. c. cum te. But some things admit of division, such as succession, and then it must be considered that, with respect to goods existing in the Imperial territory, legitimation is valid even for those born of incest. D. de ritu nup. l. qui in provincia. §. diuus. But with respect to goods existing in the patrimony of Blessed Peter, it may be reasonably doubted; for if one cannot be removed as a spurious child on one part and made legitimate on another, then it is valid in its entirety. D. de don. l. inter vir. et vx. l. si sponsus. §. generaliter. Moreover, to legitimize is an act of the supreme will of jurisdiction, and therefore it extends everywhere, just as emancipation does. C. de eman. liberorum. l. 1. and arrogation. C. de adop. l. 2. D. de offic. procons. et de leg. l. 3. hoc tit. Jacobus de Belvisi notes what is stated in Extravagant, Qui filii sint legitimi, c. per venerabilem. And thus Bartolus advised to the contrary, because thus legitimation does not properly make someone legitimate, as is noted in Extravagant, De electione, c. innotuit; but it confers the rights of legitimate persons. Therefore, since the right of the conferring party is limited, the right of the receiving party will consequently be limited, according to the argument from C. de leg. l. vxor. patrui. and D. de contrah. empt. l. qui tabernas. Moreover, just as the Pope does not legitimize in the lands of the Empire, so neither does the Emperor do the contrary, according to the aforementioned c. per venerabilem. For in the lands of the Pope, the Emperor is reduced to the status of a private person, and if he cannot pronounce law, he cannot therefore grant privileges. And thus Jacobus de Belvisi holds in the constitution C. tenendo, that the donation was an operation previously made, or a resignation into the hand of the superior. And Bartolus on another occasion advised for this side. Therefore, I distinguish thus: some legitimation is permitted by common law, such as that of natural children, and these are valid with respect to all things, because the Church has approved the common law and uses it; some are prohibited, such as those born from illicit intercourse, and then, although the Emperor dispenses from the fullness of power, this dispensing right must be restricted to goods which the Emperor can grant, not to others, for example those which are in the kingdom of the Franks. But the kingdom of the Franks is sufficiently analogous to the free kingdom of Blessed Peter. And therefore it is not permitted for the Emperor to thrust his sickle into another’s harvest, and thus not his own, as in l. cunctos populos, De summa trinitate, and in c. vt animarum. And I have experienced that the Pope does not wish to grant to anyone that he may legitimize in the lands of the Church. The remaining points are determined by l. 1. in fine, De naturali. A scruple remains, however, because the Pope caused legitimation when jurisdiction appears to have been prorogated; but in this it must be considered whether it can be prorogated by a cleric. I, Baldus, and others.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a confession made in response to a pleading for the purpose of deciding the case can be retracted.
casus: CASE. In the Name of the Lord, Amen. The point is this: a certain person was proceeding by enumeration; the adversary made a position that the thing was without that which had been enumerated; the plaintiff, responding to the position, said it was true; afterwards he wished to revoke his response, saying that he had erred, because he did not understand that those words “without the same” implied a negation, namely that enumeration had not intervened. It is asked whether he may do so. And so forth.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A confession knowingly made to a position for the decision of the lawsuit cannot be revoked, unless it is revoked before it diverges into other acts, as in D. de re iudicata, l. post rem; D. de confessionibus, l. non fatetur; and C. eodem, l. 1. And note in C. ult. de iureiurando, lib. 6. But if it was made through error, either through probable error of fact, or through improbable error of fact, or through error of law. Or it is doubted whether it was through error of fact or with certain knowledge. If indeed through probable error of fact, and in another’s fact, it can be revoked, and the error is proven by proving the contrary, and by proving that the matter stands otherwise. D. de iure et facti ignorantia, l. si post divisionem; and l. error. But if through improbable error, or through error of law, the confession decisive of the entire lawsuit cannot be revoked, as in l. non fatetur. This is true, unless such error removes the understanding of the respondent from the response itself, because he, since he does not understand the position, is not said to confess it. Understanding is necessary in a response, arg. D. de in integrum restitutione; and l. diuus. And that someone did not understand the words of the position, which consist in the interpretation of law, such as that the word “absque” [without] is a negative word, is proven by the respondent’s oath together with certain presumptions. For it is not likely that one who alleges a reckoning with an oath immediately, upon swearing, feels the contrary, D. de condictionibus et de, l. non ad ea. And therefore in this question, I believe that it is proven that the money was counted, or that the substance of the obligation subsisted, i.e., the cause, insofar as it is proven. The said response of the plaintiff does not obstruct, that the defendant is condemned. And this holds equity in itself, nor does the defendant profit from the presumption of the ignorant creditor. The last case is when it is doubted by presumptions, and it is left, even having made the distinction of one’s own fact and another’s, D. de novatione, l. si quis leg.; C. de his qui sibi adscripserunt, l. senatus. With these things, I conclude that, the truth of the debt being proven from a true reckoning subsisting, the defendant ought to be condemned, notwithstanding that the respondent, confused by error, did not know what he had responded: because he did not understand, as is proven by his oath and confirming presumptions, arg. D. de accusationibus, l. si cui, § 1; and Extr. de accusationibus, c. cum dilecti; and D. de transactionibus, l. cum Aquili. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A son cannot be burdened in his legitime by a testament made for pious causes.
2. Property alienated by the son before the time of restitution is counted toward the legitime.
3. Whether the legitime may be deducted from the person of one who died in pupillary age, having made a pupillary substitution.
casus: CASE. The point of the emerging question is this: The said Albe. of such a place, not wishing to die intestate, made his testament and last will: in which testament and last will he made many legacies. In the said testament it appears sufficiently that, in all his other goods, both stable and movable, present and future, actions and rights, and his entire inheritance, he instituted Pet. and Ioan., his legitimate and natural sons, as universal heirs in equal portions, with the condition added that if one of them should die without children, he substituted the other to himself both pupillarily and vulgarly; and if both should die without children, then the church of §. Secondiani of such a place should succeed, with this condition that two Chaplains be elected by the said bishop and the said archpriest, who shall be in office for the time being, and that these two elected Chaplains, beyond the first number, celebrate divine offices in the said church, one continuously at the altar of §. Herenei, and the other at the altar of Saint John, and with this condition that the said Pet. and Ioan., or one of them, may, when some necessity exists, sell and alienate from the goods and inheritance of the said [testator], and from whatever they please, and make any contract as it seems to them, notwithstanding the above. Finally, one of the said sons, after the death of the father, having come of age, died without surviving children, [survived by] his brother, who brother had alienated many paternal goods. Finally, this surviving brother, having come of age, died without children. Now the nearest relatives intestate of the said sons demand the legitime of the said sons, saying that the father could not deprive them of their legitime. Now it is asked about two things: first, whether the said legitime is due and can be demanded in law to the prejudice of the said church. Also, if it is due, whether it can be compensated and computed with the goods alienated by one of the said sons, who died afterwards, from the goods of the said inheritance after the death of his father, without proof of the necessity for which he sold. On all and each of these things, a sound opinion is requested to be given, and thus, if the legitime is due, what part of the inheritance it is, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the legitime, children cannot be burdened, even if the testament is made for pious causes or for the soul, as in c. Si pater, de testibus, lib. 6; C. de inofficioso testamento, l. Sancimus; and Auth. Novissima, extra de testibus, c. Raynutius and c. Rayhaldus. And therefore, to the blood relatives of the last dying child, the legitime of their share is due, namely, a third of their half, without doubt.

† in which, however, the alienated portion is counted, as in Auth. de testamento et ea quae parit, §. quamobrem, ad Trebellianam, l. Marcellus, §. res quae. For since the son is owner in full in the meantime, before the case of substitution occurs, he may alienate revocably, insofar as he has not been restored to anyone. Nor is he obliged to sell his legitime as an undivided share, because in the meantime he has no fideicommissary co-owner competing with him; and therefore the fideicommissary does not for the time being make a portion for him, wherefore also in one thing he may choose his legitime in the meantime, before a portion is made for him by the contrary action of the fideicommissary. d. §. quamobrem. And thus I have often advised.

But a difficult doubt arises concerning one who died during the age of puberty, whether any portion of the legitime may be deducted from his person: for the legitime is not deducted from a pupillary substitution, but from a fideicommissary one; therefore, nothing is defalcated, as stated in the title *de inofficiosa testamento*, in the law *Ex tribus*. Moreover, a brother who was substituted pupillarily cannot deduct the legitime as a brother, because the legitime is not owed to collateral relatives; thus, the entire inheritance of the minor passes into the fideicommissary restitution, because that which is acquired through pupillary substitution passes into the universal fideicommissum, if the father first substituted pupillarily and subsequently validly by fideicommissum, as held in the *Digestum*, under the title *ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum*, in the law *Ita tamen*, section *Qui suspectam*. However, according to Bartolus, that text seems to say the contrary. Nevertheless, if the goods of the testator pass, in which all of them the substituted heir may be burdened, then the only doubt remaining concerns the legitime of the minor’s legitime, from which it is deducted, as stated in the title *de vulgari substitutione*, in the law *Cohaeredi*, section *Cum filiae*. But it is said that no deduction is made from one who is expressly named, after examination, according to Bartolus there, citing the law *Si fundum per fideicommissum*, section *Fin.*, together with the following law, under the title *de legatis primo*. And Dinus so advised, and Cynus approves this in the reading of the aforementioned law *Ex tribus*. And this is to be held, etc. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given the statute of the merchants, which provides that a certain shop, although not belonging to them, but because they have always held it, cannot be seized except by the merchants themselves, if the rights to said shop have been purchased for a certain period by someone other than a merchant, whether the merchants can prevent this.
2. Whether the person who holds the aforementioned rights can assign them to a surety who wishes to remain indemnified, since he is a merchant, and whether the latter, by accepting such assignment, incurs the penalty of the merchants' statute.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Assuming that Gaietanus truly purchased for himself the fruits of a certain common pharmacy in Perugia for a period of five years at public auctions, as is customary; that Gaietanus is not a merchant; and that the census of the Benegratis, a merchant, acted as surety for him; and that certain other citizen merchants, who held said pharmacy, did not appear at said auctions but allowed the fruits of said pharmacy to be sold. The question is whether Gaietanus can be impeded in any way by said merchants. It must be said that he cannot: because the statutes of the merchant guild do not bind him, as noted in C. de iurisd. om. iud. l. fin. and de constitu. pecu. l. 2; and because merchants cannot make statutes concerning the property of their superior, namely the commune of Perugia, as stated in ff. de arbi. l. nam magistratus.

Secondly, it is asked, since the said Gaietanus has freely stated his rights, and since the said surety requests to be kept indemnified: whether, for the sake of said indemnity, the said Gaietanus can grant the said apothecary to the said surety by granting him his rights; and it must be said to him that he can grant it, and receive the consideration without penalty, unless it had been sought by the principal through an interposed person, and this were proven. For in doubt, fraud is presumed. Ad Vell. l. iur. vxor. §. si. C. de secundis nuptiis. l. hac edictali. ff. de mandato. per diversas. §. exceptis. For it does not take away from those merchants or certain servants, but rather comes already offered by Gaietanus by not objecting during the time of auctions, nor protesting that he consented by right of his own, which can be said in a manner, arg. C. de aedificiis privatis. l. in totum. de iure patronatus. l. adige. in princ. de remissione pignoris. c. eo tempore. ff. de in diem addendo. l. necesse. And it is likely that they knew those things which are done publicly, and in the place where they habitually frequent. C. de defensione civium. l. iubemus. And thus it is lawful to do something through another, and in the law of another, which is not lawful directly for oneself, provided that fraud does not intervene. ff. quae res in pignus obligari possunt. l. Aristo. And therefore, Gaietanus having been put in possession of the apothecary, and the said merchants having been expelled: afterwards if the said above-mentioned person takes use of the said chamber in the manner aforesaid, or otherwise, unless fraud is proven to have been employed, he can do so freely and without penalty, and much more so without any title: for the first, he can serve there the said Gaietanus, because this is not prohibited by the latter. §. qui loquuntur. de cameris communis Perusii in special, and the statute says nothing about common chambers, they are not understood to apply to them. l. si peculium. §. si quid. de peculio legato. Because damage results to the common good. s. by enticing people they are repelled, and it makes well de distractione pignoris. l. et qui sub imagine. I, Baldus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a guardian has promised a ward in marriage under a penalty, he may without penalty promise the said ward to another.
2. Whether betrothals are binding before the age of seven.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Marriages ought to be free from contractual penalty, although not from legal penalty. On the words of the obligation, law Titia, Code, on betrothals; law if, Extra, on betrothals; chapter Gemma. And therefore the penalty incurred by the guardian cannot be claimed, because the guardian’s promise is in this case equivalent to the promise of the principal person, as stated in the aforementioned law if, according to Cynus and others, on conditions and demonstrations; law my heir, section final. Therefore, this girl may again be betrothed to another by the guardian, with the mother and relatives intervening. Argument, Code, on marriages, law widows. Nevertheless, betrothals cannot take place before the age of seven. Digest, on betrothals, law betrothals.

† On the contrary, however, the Moderns say that if such affection of mind appears in the girl that the intellect supplies for the age, and thus she is near seven years old, the betrothal is binding, although this rarely happens; whatever may be said on this point, nevertheless the tutor is not bound to the penalty, as I have said: and if the tutors deliver the said girl and take care that the goods are preserved intact from the creditor of the administrator of the guardianship, the preservation shall be valid, etc. And thus I, Baldus, say.
In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† This contract either did not bind, or at least was defective, such that ratification was necessary, and sufficient solemnity, and in any of these presupposed modes he could not act, either because from no contract is any action given, as is stated in the delegation and constitution l. non dubium; or because ratification must intervene while the state of the thing sold is intact, not when it has been deteriorated on account of wars, or similar cases, for the ratifying party ought not to await the case, and ratify while the thing remains in the same state. ff. rem ra. ha. l. quoties enim. §. 1. And therefore, if what is proposed to me is true, that the thing was much better at the time of the contract, now the ratification is late, which is excluded by the change of terms. ff. de solu. l. ratum. and l. quod dicamus. And thus I say, Bald.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a first will is made, in which one heir is instituted, and afterwards a second will is made, in which another person is instituted, who at the time of the making of the will, without the testator's knowledge, was already dead, whether the first or the second will is valid, or neither.
casus:
and others.

A certain man named Lucas of Florence made a testament in the city of Venice, in which, disposing in the last place, he said, in all his other goods he instituted Andrew as his universal heir. And if it were not valid by the law of testament, let it be valid by the law of codicils, and in every way in which it might better be valid, cancelling and rendering void every other testament, etc. After the passage of time, he made another testament, among other things, lastly he instituted Andrew, his brother, as universal heir in all his other goods, insofar as the said Andrew should die without legitimate and natural children, he would come, etc. And he asserted that this his last will and last testament was his will, which he wished to be valid by the law of testament, and of any other last will, as it may better be valid. And if it were not valid by the law of testament, let it be valid at least by the law of codicils. And as it may better be valid, cancelling, and rendering void, and annulling every other testament, and last will hitherto made by him, ordering and commanding them to be of no value, this first prevailing over all others.
