Finally, the aforementioned testator having died, it appears that the said Andrew, instituted as heir in the said second testament, had died at the time of the second testament, and well before the aforementioned testator knew it, whence arises the question, which of the aforementioned testaments is valid, whether the first, or the second, or neither, and what is the law in the aforementioned matters, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A testament in which an inheritance is left to a deceased person is void, as stated in the Institutes, De haeredibus instituendis, in the section Si iam mortuo; in the Code, De iure codicillorum, in the law Quidam referunt; and in the Digest, De capite tollendo, in the section Sed cum triplici. And therefore, from its own immediate nature, it does not revoke the first testament, because that which is null is not revoked, but that which has some validity. Digest, De libellis et postulationibus, law Si filius, qui in potestate; Digest, De iniusto testamento, law Cum in secundo; Institutes, Qui testamento infirmo, section Ex ea. And because it appears that the testator’s intention was not to depart from the first testament unless the second were valid, Digest, De legatis tertio, law Si mater; and what is noted in the Digest, De aditione legatorum, law Ex parte. For a testament is not revoked by mere repentance, but by an act similar to the previous one, Institutes, De haeredibus instituendis, law Sed si in conditione; Digest, De libellis et postulationibus, law Si ita scribitur, section Regula; Digest, De testamento militis, law Militis codicillis, section Veteranus. Moreover, those words, “revoking and annulling,” appear to have been added in favor of the instituted heir, argument from Digest, De legibus, law Si servitus, section Qui Margaritam. Therefore, if it cannot operate in favor, it does not operate to the detriment, because when the cause of ademption ceases, the ademption of the legacy ceases, argument from Digest, De aditione legatorum, law Quod si iterum; Digest, Ad Trebellianum, law A filia, section Alumno. That clause, “revoking and annulling, etc.,” is placed in consequence, not principally and in itself; hence, if the principal and antecedent is invalid, the consequent does not hold, argument from Code, De conditionibus ob causam, law 1; Code, Si poena apud mortuum interueniat, law 3. For appendices are vitiated when the principal is vitiated, argument from Digest, De acquisitione haereditatis, law Si quis haeres. This is supported by the fact that the testator appears to have been moved to change the testament by error concerning the life of his brother; therefore, the first testament remains, Institutes, De haeredibus instituendis, law Si. And the legacies of the second testament are not thereby annulled, as is clear there, and what is noted in the Code, De fideicommissis, law Eam, quam.

To the contrary, the case in the Code, De testamento, law Sancimus, and what is noted in the aforementioned section Ex eo, seems applicable, due to the passage of ten years and that precise clause, “revoking and annulling.” The objection based on the aforementioned law Si, Institutes, De haeredibus instituendis, does not hold, because there the testator had not changed his affection toward the first instrument, as is clear from the preamble of the testament and the testator, which he promised as the final cause; here, however, the affection was changed, and also the form of the institution, and not only in favor of the instituted heir, but of the children: which are due in the testament by the codicillary clause, Digest, De legatis secundo, law Lucius, section Filia. By which clause it appears that the testator chose rather to die intestate than to die with the first testament, argument from Digest, De maioribus testamento, law Si quis locuples. Therefore, it is the case in the law Sancimus, and it is a special case. And by this, the aforementioned law Si ius, Digest, De legatis tertio, would be answered. I, Baldus, and others.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that those who die intestate without children are succeeded by the nearest relatives on the paternal line, or the paternal grandfather’s line, the mother is excluded from the succession of her son who dies in pupillary age.
casus:
CASE. A certain person named Blasius died, leaving a sole daughter, a minor named Francisca, and his sister, Antonia, who was the aunt of the minor. The minor died while still a minor. A dispute arises between the mother of the minor and the aunt: because the aunt claims that she, as the closer relative, is admitted by virtue of a certain statute placed under the heading “Concerning those dying intestate and without children.” It is said on the other side that the mother comes to the whole, and especially to the legitimate portion of the said minor, succeeding the deceased who died in minority, and this by virtue of a certain statute with an addition made by the approvers of the statutes of the Roman Church, which statute is placed under the heading “Concerning a dowered woman,” notwithstanding the statute alleged by the aunt, in which no mention is made of the mother. Also, because that statute has no place except in those who could make a testament and died intestate. Also, because where the mother was recited in that statute, the legitimate was expressly reserved for her. Now the question is, having seen the statutes, to whom the inheritance should be deferred, to the mother or to the aunt, and in what proportion. The tenor of the statutes is as follows, namely:

Heading: Concerning those dying intestate.
We also statuate and ordain that if anyone, male or female, of the territory of Saint Severinus and its district dies intestate, male or female, without legitimate children, that all goods of one thus dying intestate shall come and devolve upon the closest blood relatives descending from the paternal line or the paternal grandfather’s line, since it is sufficiently suitable to reason that such goods return to the first statute from which they had their beginning, and the aforementioned shall have place in the present and future, etc.

Heading: Concerning a dowered woman.
Also that no woman dowered by father, mother, brother, etc., shall have at least this chapter, that the mother is not admitted, nor can the mother have any succession in the goods of a predeceased son or daughter, if the said son or daughter made a testament, and having made a testament, died, notwithstanding any chapter making or speaking to the contrary. This is the addition of the Roman Church. Saving the right of the legitimate due to her by law to claim, and this chapter shall be precise and have place in the present, etc.

On the matter, add below in counsel 339.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If we hold that opinion, namely that a ward is not properly said to die intestate, the mother would be admitted in full, excluding the aunt, as in l. 1, de suis et legitimis heredibus, and notably by Cynus, C. qui testamento facere possunt; l. 2, C. de iure deliberandi; l. cum antiquioribus, which is the common opinion, taught at Bologna. But if we hold that, speaking broadly, a ward does die intestate, so that the syllable “in-” is placed for “non-,” i.e., not having made a will, and the aforementioned l. 1, according to Bartolus, then the aunt would succeed. Nevertheless, in this case, I believe the mother ought not to be defrauded of her legitime, arguing from another statute. For if the legitime is due from a necessary will, it follows that it is also due intestate, because the legitime of the testator arises from the legitime of the intestate. C. de inofficioso testamento, l. cum quaeritur. Hence, the legitime granted by the making of a necessary will is granted intestate on account of the aforementioned rubric. And thus I hold, although otherwise I have consulted according to the doctors of Bologna in favor of the mother. However, in our statute, the same cannot be said by those words, “without children,” which are most properly verified in the age of wardship. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Centurio; and notably, C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. precibus, in the major gloss. Therefore, the mother ought to have the third part, and the aunt two parts. And it helps, C. de donationibus, l. si amanuensis. For the final reason is the children, not the age, de pactis dotalibus, l. inter, §. cum inter; de hereditatibus instituendis, l. Lucius. Hence, the statute weighs the children, i.e., whether one has them or does not have them. C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. generaliter. Wherever there are no children, there the statute intends to provide for the paternal stock, or agnatic line, with the modification, however, of the legitime, as I said above. It helps, Inst. de substitutionibus, l. 1, §. sed nostra. When the reason is inscribed in statutes, we attend more to the nature of the reason than to the strict nature of the words, de excusationibus tutorum, l. scire oportet, §. quod si maximus; C. de libertate praetoria, l. 3.

A S VS. In the name of God. Amen. The point is this: because a certain public instrument is found, by which Do. Magdalena, with the consent of her brother Taxinus, and of her legitimate Munduald Andrew, on one part, and Blasiu, tutor of the said Lady Magd., on the other, promised regarding every site, question, and controversy that might exist between them on account of the administration of the tutorship of the wicked man Guilelmus: another public instrument is found, in which it is contained that Lady Magd., with the consent of Taxinus and Andrew Munduald, confessed to have had and received, and had and received, 455 florins, 14 soldi, and 10 denari in one hand, on account of the said administration of the tutorship, coming to the said Blasius; and 225 in the other hand, for the interest of the moneys during the interim; and of these they called themselves well paid and satisfied. Also, another public instrument is found, a laud (arbitral award) made by Guilelmus, upon the said matter, in which it is contained that, having seen the payment of 355 florins and 14 soldi and 10 denari, he absolved the said Blasius, tutor, from everything for which he was bound on account of the said administration, as well as from the inventory and the rest; and that the aforementioned parties made an end and release to the said Blasius, and thus it was adjudicated to the parties present and ratifying. On the same day, the aforementioned parties also made an end, release, and perpetual pact with the said Blasius regarding the said sums. And also regarding the contents of the laud. Also, a certain public instrument is found, in which it is contained that Lady etc. and the aforementioned parties made a general and most general end and release to Bonetus, regarding everything administered by him while he was tutor, which instrument is full in the customary form. Now it is asked whether the aforementioned tutors can in any way be molested by the said Magdalena, and what is the law, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. General words cannot be restricted unless a restricting reason intervenes.
2. Whether tutors are fully liberated by a general liberation, so much so that they cannot be sued any further.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Because general words cannot be restricted unless a restrictive reason intervenes, especially where a release is at issue, which is favored. D. de pactis, l. emptor; § Lucius, D. de liberatione legata, l. Aurelius; § Titius testamento, D. de transactionibus, l. actione.

It must be said that Blasius and Biundus are fully liberated and most generally absolved; for neither fraud nor error is presumed to have intervened, according to the noted authorities: *de pactis*, l. *tres fratres*; *de transactionibus*, supra; the text of the Code, *de condictionibus causa data causa non secuta*, l. *si ex maiore*; *de conditionibus indebiti*, l. *sin.*, § *idem quaesivit*; the Digest, *de transactionibus*, l. *cum Aquiliana*.
In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† Titius was the creditor of Sey in several sums and for various causes; he made and established an account with him, and finally, at the instance of Sex, he wrote as follows: “Senis, the money-changer, ought to give me, Sey, on this day, as the balance of the account made between him and me up to this day, 100 gold florins, which he had received from me on his ledger, and of all other quantities of coins received by him from me up to the present day, having deducted and set off the coins which he gave and paid to me up to this day, there remains to be given by the said Sey to me, Titius, up to this day, 40 livres of Bologna. Which quantity of coins the said Sey promises to give and pay to me, Titius, when Lucius, my friend, shall have restored to the said Sey 40 livres of Bologna, which he is bound to give to him on account of a loan; and I promise to the said Sey not to demand from him the said 40 livres of Bologna unless the said Lucius shall have restored the said 40 livres to him. And this for the reason that the said Sey lent the said quantity of coins to the said Lucius at my request and command.”

Fifteen days having elapsed after the execution of the said writing, the aforementioned Titius sued the said Sey before the ordinary judge of the place, and filed a libel against him, stating as follows: “Before you, etc., Titius brings a claim against Gayus, that he lent to him 40 gold ducats; therefore, since the same Gayus, having been repeatedly requested concerning the restitution of the said money, refused and refuses to restore the said quantity of money to Titius, he asks that he be condemned, etc.”

It should be known that the action concerns a loan made before the execution of the said writing. And in this case, it is asked: First, whether from the said writing a general discharge accrues to Sey, both for the said 100 gold florins and for all other quantities subsequently received by him before the execution of the said writing, and thus for the said 40 ducats lent to Sey before the execution of the said writing.

Second, it is asked whether the said [Sey] can raise the exception of non-payment of money against the said writing, and especially considering the words of the writing itself, where it says, “having set off the coins which he gave and paid to me,” and thus whether he can sue for the said 40 gold ducats against the said Sey, who objects to him the exception of payment contained in the said writing, etc.

Third, it is asked whether, in the case where he can raise the said exception, it appears that Titius raised it in his said libel filed against Sey, inasmuch as it is stated therein that, having been repeatedly requested concerning the restitution of the said money, he refused to restore it, and it appears in the case that no mention was made of the said writing, and thus whether it appears that satisfaction has been given to the law in *Contractibus*, § *Super ceteris*, and § *In omni*, with its material, C. *De non numero petendo*, and the material of l. *Si non singuli*, in the gloss on the word *restituere*, C. *Si certum petatur*, with its authorities.

Fourth, it is asked whether, in the case where he can raise the said exception or complaint, and it appears that he raised it, whether Gayus can deduct from the said 40 ducats the 40 livres of Bologna contained in the said writing, which the said Sey remains bound to give to Titius, as appears in the case, or whether he must be compelled to pay the said 40 ducats and also the said 40 livres of Bologna upon the occurrence of the condition comprehended in the case.

Fifth, it is asked whether, since the said writing appears to contain 100 florins, of which it is mentioned in it that they were deposited, inasmuch as it says, “which he had received from me on his ledger,” it must truly be understood as a deposit. And whether the exception of non-payment of money can be raised for them, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The rule of calculation does not operate except in that which has been calculated.
2. Whether the exception of money not paid can be raised within 30 days.
3. Whether a creditor, who can raise the exception of money not paid, is deemed to have raised it in the libel, in which it is stated that, having been repeatedly requested concerning the restitution of the said money, he refused to restore it.
4. In the case where one can, as above, raise the exception of money not paid, or bring a complaint, whether he is deemed to have raised it, and whether the plaintiff can deduct from the said 40 ducats, 40 livres of goods which are contained in the record.
5. In case of doubt, a contract is presumed to be a loan rather than a deposit.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. This question arose from the understanding of the text and glosses of the Digest, under the title "On the Resolution of Obligations," in the law "If from several causes," in the first place. It must be known,

† that the reason of the calculation does not operate, except in that which has been calculated, as there, and in D. de pactis, l. emptor, § Lucius. Nevertheless, where the writing attests to a general computation, it ought to operate generally, as there noted. And if the exception of a non-specified sum of money is not raised, without doubt the debtor would be discharged, save from the residue. C. de distractione pignorum, l. si residuum, in the first gloss.

But it is doubted whether the exception of money not paid can be raised within 30 days, for in l. si ex pluribus there are two contrary glosses: one says that it cannot, because the debtor is released by pact; ff. de pactis, l. tale pactum, in the beginning; the other says that it can, because it is not a pact, but a confession. Bartolus says that where mention is made of a pact or acceptance in the release, the exception ceases; otherwise, if it is a mention of a confession, even if the confession arises from a preceding reckoning or calculation. Andreas de Pisis says that wherever a confession is compromised, the exception has place, because that pact is in view of a future payment, just as the confession itself is; arg. de non numerata pecunia, l. si; and arg. ff. de constituta pecunia, l. ult. It would be foolish to advise against the gloss, which speaks formally of a confession arising from a cause of reckoning, the gloss referring to the text, since the text says after the exception has been proposed, and extra, and thus I say in this passage.

It remains to be seen whether the creditor, by bringing an action, appears to have interposed a complaint. And this question may be understood with respect to the larger sum, for which he did not sue; and there is no doubt that he did not, according to Inst. de actionibus, § si minus, in the gloss. Again, it may be understood with respect to the sum claimed; and it seems that he did, because it makes no difference whether he says “I complain” or “I claim,” since there is no difference between equivalent terms, C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. omnes. And because he appears to have tacitly included all right of claiming, arg. de exceptionibus rei iudicatae, l. an eadem, § actiones. The contrary can be persuasively argued, because if a confession is raised against this plaintiff, he must necessarily reply on the ground of non-numerata pecunia, Inst. de replicationibus, in principio; ff. de pactis, l. si cum te; because he does not yet appear to have directed the complaint by confession, unless he replies, and then thirty days will have elapsed, and thus he will not be able to reply, C. de exceptionibus, l. si pactum. And it seems that this can be sufficiently defended in law, because the mode of proceeding must always be examined, as in no. 3, q. 6, haec quippe; and it supports this, C. de postulando, l. si sub specie.
It remains to be seen whether the banker may set off. L. 40, D. De bonis quae sub conditione possidentur; and it must be said that he may. L. Pecuniam, D. Si certum petatur.

† On the last point, because the contract of loan for consumption (mutuum) is more frequent and more useful to the contracting parties than the contract of deposit, it must be said that in case of doubt, a loan for consumption is presumed, not a deposit. D. si certum petatur, l. si quid, in the glossa ordinaria, in the ultimate opinion, in the gloss; for since the ultimate opinion remains, it finally approves it, as noted in D. ad Trebellianum, l. qui filium, at the end. And therefore Innocentius says that the ultimate opinion, which he attributes to no one, is his own opinion, and according to it we ought only to allege the plaintiff. And thus I, Baldus, say, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a publicly contracted marriage is to be preferred to a clandestine marriage, of which there is proof by the confession of the parties and public reputation.
casus: CASE. In the name of Christ, amen. A certain man named Dominicus Andreutii of Assisi, being a domestic and familiar of the lord John Loli and Solutius of Assisi, and having a certain sister of the blood residing together with him named Thomasa, with the said lord John her brother and the said Dominicus, and the said Dominicus and Thomasa loving each other cordially, the said lord John being unaware, came to the following act between them, namely, that by mutual consent they contracted marriage with each other by words of the present tense, with the placing of a ring by the said Dominicus on the finger of the right hand of the said Thomasa. After the aforementioned Dominicus had carnally known the said Thomasa as his legitimate wife in their dwelling houses, the said lord John her brother being unaware, on account of which carnal knowledge the said Thomasa became pregnant and with child. Since this marriage thus contracted between them and consummated by carnal copula cannot be proved by witnesses, because the said lord John, brother of the blood of the said Thomasa, did not intervene successively after the aforementioned acts done and performed by the said Dominicus with the said Thomasa, the said lord John married the said Thomasa to a certain Pannutius, whom he immediately betrothed with a ring, and desiring to take her to his home as his wife, it was announced to the said Pannutius that he should not bring her in, since she was with child; whom the said Pannutius did not bring into his home, nor did he consummate marriage with her by carnal copula. It is now asked, from the aforementioned narrative, what is the law, and what course the said Dominicus, who betrothed the said Thomasa in the aforementioned manner and affects to have her as wife with the consent of the said Thomasa, who desires to have the said Dominicus as her legitimate husband, so that he may be certain regarding the marriage, ought to take. Finally, please draft a petition in the episcopal court, if it shall be necessary, for the marriage contracted with the said Dominicus, so that the said Dominicus may obtain victory, and to the bearer of these presents, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If the said Thomas confesses that she previously contracted marriage with the said Dominic and consummated it by carnal intercourse, it seems that this confession should be upheld, supported by public reputation. This is established by the gloss on the Code, *De fideiussoribus*, in the law *Pe*. To the contrary, it appears from the text in the Extravagant, *De eo qui cognovit consanguineam uxorem suam*, chapter *Super eo*; and according to the rule which the doctors set forth in chapter 1 of the Extravagant, *De clandestinis desponsis*, where they state that a publicly contracted marriage always prejudices a clandestine one, even if faith were made regarding the clandestinity by one witness and reputation, according to Nicolaus. Nor is confession upheld to the prejudice of a third party, as stated in the aforementioned chapter *Super eo*. But if no one outside the confessing parties were prejudiced, then the confession would be upheld. And thus the gloss alleged to the contrary is understood. However, because the second husband never abducted her, nor alleges marriage, nor wishes to keep her, being led by conscience, all things considered, it is in the interest of the heirs to adhere to the truth, and judgment may be pronounced in favor of the petition of the said Dominic, after citing the said Pannutio. I, Baldus, say so, and so forth.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What is meant by the liberality of the prince.
2. Several things are considered as one for the sake of one.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† First of all, it must be considered whether the said grant is, or is not, to be called an imperial liberality. And this question seems to have been raised, for that would be called an imperial liberality which proceeds from the majesty of the prince, as in C. de quadrien. praesc. l. bene a Zenone, §. quae omnia reservantes, in the words "ex nostra aula procedentes" before the name. For thus nothing is said to be imperial except that which proceeds from the august fortune, as noted in the proemium of both the Digest and the Institutes, and it is clear from ff. de leg. 2, l. quod principi; and l. digna vox; and l. si. C. de donat. inter virum et uxorem, l. pen. Moreover, if we were to say otherwise, it would follow that each individual city would have the privileges of the Caesar, which is ridiculous to say, as in ff. de administr. l. simile; ff. de verb. sign. l. eum, qui vectigal; C. de bon. vac. l. 1, lib. 10. For cities are regarded in the place of private persons, as fully stated in C. de iur. rei publ. lib. 11, in the rubric. Thus, therefore, this donation must be understood as a donation perfected from a private person to a private person, in which a lapsed or failing share does not accrue to the co-partners by right already acquired, but returns to the grantor. This fails in the case of a simple usufruct. ff. de usufr. accresc. l. 1, §. interdum; ff. de verb. oblig. l. si mihi et Titio; and see C. quando non pet. partes, l. 1, according to Cynus and others.

I state the contrary, that this is an imperial liberality by reason of the influencing cause, by reason of the grantor, and by reason of the effect of the thing. And I presuppose that whatever is done by the authority of the prince, the prince himself is deemed to have done, as in C. de veteri iure enucleand. l. 1, §. omnia; and in c. cum aliquibus, de rescriptis, lib. 6. Moreover, I presuppose that to have territories, castles, and empires is to have regalia, as in 10. col. quae sunt regalia, c. 1. But regalia cannot be granted even by royal authority. l. prohibere, §. placet, quod vi aut clam; as in Auth. de defensor. civ. §. iunctim. This authority, however, must be claimed as deriving from a certain influence proceeding from the Caesar; therefore, the liberality itself is imperial by reason of the superior influencing cause, from which, as from a first cause, and which has the greatest power, such influence is generated by authority. Moreover, it is imperial by reason of the granting city, which has, in its territory, by natural custom, and more strongly by the described imperial laws, as read and noted in Auth. de defensor. civ. §. nulla, in the gloss on the word "iurisdictione," by which they are granted full administration of imperial rights in their territory, and they must confess this, otherwise the Commune of Siena would be a robber of jurisdictions and other regalia, and would live tyrannically; for peoples cannot be tyrants, as reported by Cynus in l. si qua, ff. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt; and Augustine in De civitate Dei. For all, whether one or many, tyrannize if they plainly, or by fraud, principally assume the role and image of the prince, according to Aristotle; therefore, the said donation is considered a liberality of the reigning prince. Moreover, it is an imperial largess by the real effect: for if we consider what is granted, certainly regalia are granted. What then matters from whom it is granted, since the effect of the thing passes to the receiving person? For where the effect is not changed, the name also ought not to be changed. l. 1, C. de impon. lucra describ. lib. 10. If it is so that the liberality is imperial, we have an express law that it does not return to the donor, but accrues to the partners. C. si liberalitas imperialis socius sine haerede decesserit, l. unica, lib. 10.

But let us suppose that this is not understood by mere interpretation as an imperial liberality; is it not similar to one? Certainly it is: for both agree in one conclusion and the same spirit, in which the law lives, not in the mere bark of the words. 1 q. 1, c. Marcionem et Basilidem; de verb. oblig. l. Titio; ad l. Aquil. l. illud; C. de interd. l. 1; and ff. de font. l. 1, §. hoc autem interdictum. Furthermore, whether it is an imperial largess or similar to one, it must nevertheless be considered regarding the right of ascending and reverting, whether it accrues and reverts, and it seems that the right of accrual has no place for three reasons: first, from the general nature of contracts, because in contracts there is no right of accrual, as in d. l. si mihi et Titio; C. fam. ercisc. l. si familiae. For a donation is a contract, and of strict law, and does not extend beyond the nature of the words. ff. de verb. oblig. l. quicquid astringit; nor ought it to be sought for one by another, as in d. §. alteri. Second, from the nature of legitimation for succession: because it is for oneself and male descendants, therefore, conversely, upon the failure of these, the concession expires and reverts to the lord, as in Auth. de non elig. §. emphyt.; ff. de pact. l. epistola, §. si; ff. de pact. dot. l. inter, §. cum inter. Third, from the division of things which are not of the same integral body, for in things entirely different the right of convention does not occur; and conjunction being removed, the right of accrual does not apply, as in ff. de usufr. accresc. l. pen.; ff. quib. mod. ususfr. amitt. l. si sub conditione; de leg. 1, l. huiusmodi, §. quibus ita, where it seems expressly stated.

I state the contrary for three reasons: first, from the force of the compressed name under which the donation is titled; second, from the force of the family to which the donation is perpetuated; third, from a certain nature in which the donation is rooted. And first, it has the right of convention, which collective names induce; because by collective names there is made the greatest conjunction, as if by one body, and the general and unique word is noted. And second, I have the right of perpetuation or extension, demonstrated by an extensive, indelible, and representable word, even in one. And third, I have a natural flowing and descending into posterity, demonstrated by a natural word, which words I thus declare. For I consider in this agnomen, i.e., the common name of agnation, i.e., "schiattale" [lineage/descendants]. Thirdly, first, a certain extension of agnation; second, a certain duration of the genus; third, a mode of transition. And I argue thus:

† Whatever rights accrue to several persons as to one, there is considered to be one entity; there, the many are regarded as one, and in both cases only one. D. de pactis, l. si plures. But to all of the Schiattali, it accrues as to one Schiattale, and the whole Schiattale appears to be one. D. de interdictis, l. proponebatur; D. de usucapione, l. rerum mixtura. And it is as when something is left to a genus or a family. For the failure of one does not induce lapse, but it remains for the others according to the will, as in l. civibus, D. de rebus dubiis. And this is expressly clear. D. de legibus, l. cum ita, §. in fideicommissa; and l. peto, §. fratre. As long as anything of the Schiattale remains, the entire donation remains valid; because the whole Schiattale remains, the entire donation remains valid, and the whole Schiattale remains valid, just as the whole genus in one individual. l. sicut, §. fin., D. quod cuiusque universi nomine. Therefore, it is clear from the title. D. de verborum significatione, l. pronuntiatio, §. familiae agnationi; for the title was given to the agnatic family. And because agnation is great, just as the city is small, according to Aristotle, it is the best argument from the donation to the city to the donation to the agnation. Moreover, in contracts we argue from similarity, as in D. de deposito, l. 2, §. si quis servum; and note in l. de quibus, D. de legibus. But in fiefs we have this expressly stated, that in a fief the stems succeed the stems; for this is called an ancient fief, which proceeds from the stem, as in c. 1, de gradibus succedendi in feudum, col. 10. And although this donation is not feudal, it is nevertheless censual and similar to a fief, and therefore it looks to its own stem and does not revert to the lord, as in c. 1, an agnati vel filius, col. 10. Moreover, these had the power of alienating among themselves; but he who dies intestate seems to leave it to him who is nearest to him, D. de legibus, eo, §. pe. Hence, it pertains to him of his own Schiattale who is nearest and more closely connected, arg. D. de vulgari substitutione, l. cohaerede, §. qui discretas. And thus it pertains to the said Nicolaus da Limbenis; but natural sons do not succeed in dignity and jurisdiction, nor are they of the legitimate Schiattale, unless speaking abusively of the Schiattale simply. C. de naturalibus, lib. 1, fin.; and 3. Compilatio, si de feudo fuerit controversia, c. naturales. It supports what is noted in D. ad Trebellianum, l. ex facto, §. ex facto. I therefore conclude that it neither returns to the city nor goes to the natural sons, but recedes to its own stem, not destitute, but temporarily interrupted, and remaining valid in its root, etc. I, Baldus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When a penalty attached to an agreement may be claimed.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be considered that sometimes a penalty is attached to a potestative agreement, such as not to load the ship with another’s goods. Moreover, if the contrary occurs, the penalty is incurred, especially if it is in the interest of the stipulator that the contrary not happen, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. eadem § Cato, with its subject matter. Sometimes a penalty is attached to a non-potestative act, such as diverting to Alexandria or to another place, C. de inst. et subst. l. si pater. And then it matters whether it was due to a fortuitous event that nothing else could be done, and then the penalty cannot be claimed with effect, as in D. si quis caut. l. 2 and l. sed et si quia § quaesitum. Or whether it was due to the act of the promisor; then the penalty can be claimed with effect, C. de contrah. et committ. stipul. l. magnam. Or there is doubt, and then the promisor must prove his excuse, C. de pign. act. l. quae fortui. But it must be seen whether, if repeatedly contracted, the full penalty is incurred from each chapter not observed, and it must be said that it is, because so says the tenor of the stipulation. Some say that it cannot exceed four times the interest, C. de sent. quae pro eo quod interest l. 1 in fin. Others say the contrary, because in penalties interest is not considered, D. de verb. oblig. l. stipulatio ista § alteri, unless the penalty was attached by multiplicative terms, C. de spons. l. si. And this opinion is the more correct according to the strictness of civil law, and is commonly approved. From these things the answer to all the above doubts is clear, and the above are confirmed in l. traiectitiae § de illo de acq. et obl. cum si. super illo de lit. priv. cum debeat eis cred. per patronum navis. It must be said that unless he had been advised beforehand about them, D. de deposit. l. si quis inficit. D. de proc. l. si proc. absentem. D. de surr. l. eum qui § si epistola.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether those who navigate ships to Ancona, on the condition that the goods are to be brought in, and the freight paid, elsewhere and not at Ancona, nor in the Anconitan sea, and whose goods have not been brought to Ancona, nor into the Anconitan sea, are bound to pay the customs duty.
2. How a district at sea is to be determined.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is asked whether Florentines, or Perugians, or others like them, who hired ships at Ancona on the condition that their goods were to be taken on board and paid for elsewhere, and not at Ancona nor in the Anconitan sea, and whose goods were not brought to Ancona nor into the Anconitan sea, are bound to pay the said customs duty. And it must be said that they are not: because a law cannot be imposed on non-subjects, as is stated in C. de summa Trinitate, l. cunctos populos; de constitutionibus, c. ut animarum, §. statuto; de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. extra territorium; and noted by Innocentius, extra, de foro competenti, c. postulasti; and by Bartolus in l. ne quid, ff. de regulis iuris et naufragiis. As for subjects, however, or those who call at or put into their sea not by chance but by design, the law is valid. For I except cases of fortuitous accident. l. Caesar, de publicanis; and C. de furtis, auth. nauigia; and ff. ad legem Rhodiam de iactu, l. deprecatio ista iniquam. A subject is bound to pay the burdens. He who sends in goods does not have the ship steered for his goods, as ff. locati conducti, l. cum in plures, §. vehiculum. And if the statute expressly stated that if the master of the ship paid the tithe of the goods, it would be reasonable and inequitable, C. ne filius pro patre, auth. et omnino; and noted in the aforementioned l. ne quid. But if it is known,

† How are districts cognizable at sea? I answer: to the extent that the land binds the sea, and the sea is subject to that interdiction, as is stated in c. Ubi periculum, §. Porro, de electionibus, lib. 6, in the glossa ordinaria. The reason why it is said to be a place of solution is on account of l. Contraxisse, de actionibus et obligationibus, and l. Si servus, de bonis aucthoritatis iudicis possidendis.

Furthermore, if it is asked: if payment of the guardage is due where customs are not paid, and the ship has sailed to Ancona, disregarding the letters of which he had been advised by the owner of the goods, to whom is the damage attributable? It must be said that the ship’s masters are liable for fault, as in ff. locati conducti, l. Colonus, §. Navem, and it is fully noted in l. Si uno, §. Item cum quaedam.

I have made the aforementioned remissions and deletions for the sake of a clearer narration; nevertheless, to make it even clearer, I raise the matter into doubt again. An agreement was made at Ancona to load goods there, to pay beyond the sea, and to load again beyond the sea, and to unload at Candia, which place is not, either with respect to land or with respect to sea, within the jurisdiction of the commune of Ancona. It is asked whether, by reason of such a contract, merchants can be distrained at Ancona by virtue of the said statutes. It must be firmly said that the merchants are bound, even though they are not subject to the laws of Ancona, because this is a lesser burden imposed upon the thing, or at least upon the person for the sake of the thing; hence, those who are not subject to that commune are not bound by it, nor are their goods carried from there or brought back thither. ff. de muneribus et honoribus, l. Rescripto, §. Si. And I say this by way of further clarification than what I said above. It is added that it is fully noted by the doctors in l. Cunctos populos. And this is considered according to the words of the statute as they stand. For I do not deny that other sufficient modes may be found to save the intention of the enactors; however, none have been seen up to this point. I, Baldus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, the petition proceeds that witnesses be received from time immemorial.
2. One who is bound to prove a fact with a specific time limit does not suffice by merely proving the fact.
3. Whether witnesses received from time immemorial prove in another trial.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Sometimes it is requested that witnesses be received and published for eternal memory for the purpose of defense, sometimes for the purpose of attack, or for preparing a claim; that is to say, sometimes the defendant requests it, sometimes the plaintiff: in the first case the request proceeds, in the second it does not. C. de testi. auth. si quis aliquid. and in the concordance, whence it is derived. C. de us. pupil. l. pupillus. and note ad l. Aquil. l. in l. Aquil. si deletum. and extra de testi. c. significavit. and c. Albericus. and ff. de testi. l. current. And the reason for the difference is that the defendant lacks an ordinary remedy. C. ut nemo invit. l. 1. C. de exc. doli. l. patri. §. si. And therefore, lest the faculty of proof perish through fortuitous events, such reception and publication is granted; but in the plaintiff, who can be dealt with according to ordinary law, it is not granted to produce witnesses after the litis contestatio, because the time and order of trials would be perverted, extra de lit. non contest. per totum. C. de sent. et interl. l. prolatam. Wherefore it seems that this request was not founded in law, nor was the procedure regular, since the party does not claim to possess, and consequently does not state that he is a defendant, but simply a plaintiff; and I have often seen such a libel condemned in fact, and proven so. But Bartolus in the said Auth. si quis, and others hold that in wills such a request proceeds, either in favor of the last will, or because one is not certain of the rights of the testament before it is established that it has been proven, according to Bartolus. That last reason does not hold, because just as a will can be entered upon with the tablets closed, as in §. in novissimo, so also with the witnesses closed. Nevertheless, his statement seems true by l. publicati. C. de testa. But one could respond that there the examination of witnesses was requested for the confirmation of the writing, just as also extra de fide instru. c. cum P. tabellio. Otherwise it seems, where the cause of payment is weighed by witnesses: for then it is not provided by law that witnesses be received before the litis contestatio. For the plaintiff must impute it to himself if he does not act ordinarily, when he can, and has a pure and purified right at present. I say that we have the glossa ordinaria, which states that for obtaining the benefit of the edict of the Divine Hadrian, such a request proceeds, and no distinction is made between old age or health, whether it is a will or not. C. de ed. div. Adri. l. edicto. in the gloss which begins, signorum. versi. sed quid si nuncupativum. For no other benefit is applicable unless the witnesses are first received and published, since no other writing has been made; and this is true in the heir and the universal fideicommissary: otherwise in legatees, in whom the plaintiff is distinguished from the defendant, just as in contracts; and this is the truth. It is therefore clear that the said request proceeds.

But it must be considered whether what was alleged and asserted has been proven. Here it must be observed that, although the day and the consuls are not of the substance of the testimony, even though they are of the substance of the instrument, nevertheless, if one binds himself to prove a fact together with the time, it is not sufficient to prove the fact alone, as in c. Abbate, de re iudicata, lib. 6. But if the plaintiff binds himself to a certain time, and has not proven it, and the act is repeatable, therefore, since it could be one thing or another, the witnesses, if it were something else regarding that point, would be unsworn; therefore, they should not be published, because if unsworn, they were not lawfully received; therefore, the publication is void by operation of law, and what is done voidly ought not to be done. L. 1, ff. de servis, and L. si feriati. To the contrary, it seems, because two deductions appear: S. testamentum factum a tali tempore, factum de arbitris; L. Celsus. Therefore, it suffices to prove the fact, even if the witnesses do not recall the time, de accusatione, c. qualiter, according to Innocentius. Furthermore, regarding the substance of publication, since even witnesses who say they know nothing are published, for all must be published, however they may depose, for or against, because the truth must be published, as is clear in the aforementioned laws. Hence, although they say they do not know or do not recall regarding the time, nevertheless they must be published for the eternal memory of what they say.

Whether they prove or not, this must be inquired into in another judgment; it is not a matter of the substance of the publication that it be proven, just as when letters of contestation are published and the solemn order is observed. Whether, therefore, they are published for perpetual memory of proof or not, is a question of law; nevertheless, they must be published in such manner as they depute, whether they prove or not. And therefore the judge who published acted well; the other points are clear. That among heirs and for pious causes two suitable witnesses suffice. I, Baldus, etc. This opinion 5 6 is found in opinion 339, beginning "Opinio communis" and c.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What is required for the entry into possession by virtue of the first decree to be valid.
2. Whether and when the person entered into possession by virtue of the first decree acquires the fruits.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† For this purpose, in order that the *missio* based on the first decree may be valid, several things are required. First, it is required that the cause be alleged; because from a cause not alleged, a decree or interlocutory judgment cannot issue. D. de damno infecto, l. 4, §. hoc interdictum. Second, it is required that the cause be true, because a false cause vitiates the *missio*. D. ne vis fiat ei, l. 1, §. haec verba; D. ad Carbo, l. 3, §. puberi. Third, it is required that the defendant be cited or warned, as in l. si, C. si per vim, vel alio mon. Fourth, it is required that the cited party be contumacious, or quasi-contumacious. D. de minoribus, l. minor; etiam si quasi contumax; and l. praesenti, §. sane, D. de his qui ad ecclesiam confugiunt. Fifth, it is required that some summary proof be made, at least by oath, in Auth. he exhib. re, §. si vero; and l. Thesauris, D. ad exhibenda. Sixth, it is required that it be clear to the judge; because the judge ought not to proceed on the fact, but on the records. l. haec, Auth. §. 1, D. qui ex causa in possessionem eant.

† And the person sent into possession does not acquire the fruits: this rule fails if the custom or statute of the place provides otherwise, as noted in § Si quis, in the Authentica De exhibendis rebus, in the glossa ordinaria. It also fails if the judge has decreed this on account of the defendant’s minimal contumacy, and he has issued an interlocutory judgment, as in L. Fulcinius, § Si, Qui ex causa, in possessionem. For then the fruits were taken from the defendant by way of a certain penalty, even though they are applied to the other party. L. 1, § Hoc iudicium, D. Si quis ius dicenti non obtemperaverit. To this effect is what Innocent notes on Verba sigilli, c. Dilecto. And it must be considered that excessive contumacy does not apply to a minor who is defended, and therefore on this ground a minor could not be penalized in fruits for minimal contumacy, especially a ward. D. Si quis ius dicenti non obtemperaverit, L. 1, § Si procurator; D. De lege 2, L. Quod solidum, § Etiam quod poena, in C. 1, Ut lites non contemnantur, according to Innocent. But this applies only on the ground of custom or statute. However, a minor could well suffer this penalty or loss of fruits, because the statute is common to minors and adults alike, and the law equally admits both. L. Sine, § Lucius; and as noted in L. 2, Quae sit longa consuetudo. And this is true if the procedure followed the form prescribed by the statute. For if the statutory path has been chosen, the path of common law is excluded; the path which the plaintiff has chosen shall be open to him, as in D. Quod metus causa, L. Si mulier, at the end; and he assumes no cumulative effect from the other path, as in D. De petitione hereditatis, L. Si quis, § Si; and in § Eligere; and in L. Habebat, D. De institutione cum si. And although it appears that in our case this was done, by alleging the instrument of contract, yet there is also implicitly contained therein a cession by right of testament, which would be valid if faith had been given in these instruments before the interlocutory judgment. See on the contract, and the first cession, and the second cession, and the testament. And if faith was not given, it is otherwise, because the words of the statute regarding the execution of the guarantee say, “the instrument having been seen.” C. De edicto Adriani, L. Si. For giving faith afterwards would avail little. C. Appellanti, D. De appellationibus, in the Clementina. Moreover, it appears whether the person sent into possession acquires the fruits or not, because if the procedure followed the order prescribed by the statute, he acquires them; otherwise, he does not. See the statute for yourselves. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Natural children may be instituted as heirs in solidum in the absence of legitimate children.
2. The words “instituted” and “substituted” signify nothing other than a vulgar substitution and a substitution by fideicommissum.
3. Whether and when a son to whom a vulgar substitution was made transmits the right of deliberation to his uncles; the substitution does not impede the transmission of the right of deliberation. See also no. 5.
4. Whether and when one who has once become an heir can cease to be an heir.
5. Whether a child legitimated after the father’s death can come to the paternal estate, in which he had been instituted.
casus: CASE. The point of the question is as follows, on which a legal opinion is requested. The said Bartholomew, Lord of the Cancellarii, made a testament, in which he made an institution of the following tenor, namely: In all his other goods, movable and immovable, rights and actions, of whatever condition, wherever they may consist or be found, both present and future, the said testator instituted and wished to institute Gerius, his legitimate and natural son, as universal heir. And if the said Gerius should die intestate, or otherwise at any time without legitimate and natural children, he substituted to him, although he was his brother and the legitimate and natural son of the said testator, vulgarly and by fideicommissum, if he survived. But if none survived, then, and in that case, he instituted and substituted Dionysius, the son of the said testator, and Beso, the son of the said Gerius, as universal heirs in equal shares, and wished them to be so, in which case he now deprives the said Dionysius of the above-mentioned legacy of 300 gold florins, which he left to him by right of legacy. If any of the said Dionysius and Beso should die in pupillary age, or intestate, or at any time without legitimate and natural children, then, in that case, he wished that the share of the inheritance of the one thus deceased should come and ought to come to the other of them surviving. Now it happens that the said Bartholomew, the testator, died, leaving behind him the said Gerius, and the substitutes Dionysius (who was, however, the natural son of the said Lord Bartholomew) and Beso (who was, however, the natural son of the said Gerius). Then the said Gerius died intestate, with the said Dionysius and Benedictus surviving, and no other brother of the said Gerius, and no son of the said Lord Bartholomew, but leaving three brothers from both parents, the said Lord Bartholomew and the uncles of the said Gerius. After the death of the said Gerius, the aforementioned Dionysius and Benedictus, although natural, were legitimated. From the foregoing, it is asked whether the aforementioned Benedictus and Dionysius, after the aforementioned legitimation and the authority to legitimize granted by imperial majesty, and after the institution and substitution of the said [testator], ought to be admitted to the inheritance of the said Bartholomew, and to the whole, or to a part, and to what fractional part, and whether the said uncles ought to be admitted to any part, and to what part, this being presupposed, that the said Gerius died heir, having not accepted the inheritance of the said Lord Bartholomew. Furthermore, it is asked, if the said Gerius died before the death of his father, whether a greater right in the inheritance of the said Lord Bartholomew is acquired by the said Dionysius and Benedictus, or not.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† I begin with the second point, and I say without doubt that if Gerius had died during the lifetime of the aforementioned Bartolus, the said Dionysius and Benedict succeed alone and in solidum by virtue of the words “I institute” and “I substitute.” For natural heirs may be instituted in solidum in the absence of legitimate heirs. And they exclude the agnates of the testator from the will, as is taken from C. de naturalibus liberis, Auth. licet and in the gloss on the same. And this is most certainly true, and on this point the glossa ordinaria in l. si, ff. de regula Catoniana, makes it so. ff. de haeredibus instituendis, l. 3, tit. 1, si quis haeres, in pe. carta.

† In the first point, namely that Gerius survived his father, it must be considered whether Gerius died before he had entered upon his father’s inheritance, or indeed after such entry. And if he died before entry, it must be considered what is the law if he died ignorant of his father’s death. Likewise, what is the law if he knew of his father’s death? And for clarity, I premise that it is said that he instituted and substituted. Certainly, this is nothing other than to say that he substituted in the ordinary way and by fideicommissum. For the word “instituted” is direct, and the word “substituted” is oblique, so that there may not be a redundancy of words, as in D. 36.1.17 (recusare), § Titius. And this ordinary substitution is explained as that of a sui heres, as noted in D. 28.2.18 (Papinianus), § quarta, and in D. 28.6.1 (si filius pro patre), de vulgari substitutione.

† Therefore, Gerius did not transmit the unaccepted inheritance to his uncles, nor the right of deliberation, if he was ignorant; for neither a sui heredes nor an extraneous heir who is ignorant transmits the right of deliberation, as stated in C. de iure deliberandi, l. cum antiquioribus. If, however, he knew of his father’s death but nevertheless did not involve himself, it is doubtful whether he transmitted the right of deliberation to his uncles. For Bartolus says that a vulgar substitution does not prevent the transmission of the right of deliberation, C. de iure institutionis, l. 3. Which certainly I would not say here at all, because it matters greatly whether the vulgar substitution is made in default of acceptance, as if one says, “If Titius shall not be heir, I substitute such a person,” and then the opinion of Bartolus may be accepted as true; or whether it is made in default of acceptance and in default of the person declaring, and then there is no transmission, because it would be to swallow up the will of the deceased, who preferred the substitute by direct words to anyone else, and could prefer him. ff. de verborum significatione, l. verbis legis; and in Auth. de nuptiis, §. disponat. Because in the case at hand no transmission would take place. Nor does it avail to object from de milite testamento, l. ex militari, §. si, and l. apud hostes; because, as I have said, this sui heres had a vulgar substitute precisely and expressly.

It remains to be seen what is the law if Gerius has intervened. And here it must be premised for clarity that one who has once become an heir cannot cease to be an heir, except by legal deprivation, as in C. de fideicommissis, Auth. hoc amplius, on account of a statute annulling; ff. de vulgari et extraordinaria substitutione, l. ex facto, §. quemadmodum, on account of a distribution made by a soldier; ff. de militum testamento, l. miles ita haeredem, §. et quia, as we said in Pagano, ergo secus; ff. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. haereditas ex die, and note C. eo, l. extraneum. By natural death, however, one who has once been an heir ceases to be an heir as regards himself, because death dissolves all obligations, as in Auth. de nuptiis, §. soluto, and l. qui libertinus, §. posthumus, de bonis libertorum. Nevertheless, by legal fiction, he is not said to cease, but to transmit, and to make another heir such as he himself is, as fully noted in l. 2 and 3, ff. de petitione hereditatis. It is doubted whether the testator can effect this transmission by appointing A.

† heir during his lifetime, and B. heir after the death of A. And some say precisely that not, in the said law *Haereditas ex die*, D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione; law *Verbis civilibus*. But William of Conchis says that yes, in the said law *Extraneum*. It supports what we note in the said law 2 and law *Ante*, § *Si*, D. si pars hereditatis petatur. For since this can be done by a penal disposition, D. de his quae poenae nomine, law 1, much more ought this to be possible by a favorable disposition, for favorable dispositions produce their effects more quickly and effectively than penal dispositions, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, law *Si*; D. de manumissionibus, law *Causam*, § 1. This is also the opinion of Dyonisius in the law *Haereditas ex die*, D. de heredibus instituendis, that one can be an heir for a temporary period of uncertain duration by reason of a sentence, but here the institution is by reason of the death of the person in whose favor the mention of death was made, argument from D. de legibus 1, law *Filius*, § *Divi*, non obstat D. de minoribus, law *Et si sine*, § *Sed quod Papinianus*, where it is said that he who once is an heir cannot cease to be one, because it is true that an heir cannot cease to be an heir under civil law by virtue of praetorian law, otherwise through restitution in integrum, which is of praetorian law, as in Inst. de bonorum possessionibus, § *Quomodo autem*. But by the natural artifice of civil law, one can well cease to be an heir: for what if the heir dies without an heir, namely he ceases to exist, and another does not begin, thus one can cease and another begin, nor is there any law which expressly contradicts this. And if this opinion is true, then it is said that natural heirs, even of the second time, directly exclude collateral agnates, as we note in the said law *Si*, D. de regula Catoiana. But let us suppose that it is not valid by direct right, but by fideicommissum; then the said natural heirs, if they were not legitimated, would have from the fideicommissum half of the estate, as in the chapter *Raynutius* and *Raynaldus*, and of the other half, if Gerius were not married, the natural son of Gerius alone would have two ounces, as in the Authentica *Licet* cited above. Because the legitima and the trebellianica were in the goods of Gerius, who died intestate, but this also without any legitimation having been made, whereas in our case legitimation was made.

† The question therefore arises concerning the effect of legitimation, given the words “instituted” and “substituted.” Some say without distinction that the legitimated person is equated with one who has returned from beyond the frontier (postliminium), just as in the case of restitution. D. de in iustis testibus, l. si quis filio exheredato, §. fin. And thus, restitution, notwithstanding intervening periods, is drawn back to its original beginnings, and this is the opinion held by Decius in his consilia. Others say that the restitution of birthrights does not absorb rights rooted in another party during the intervening time. C. quamvis, de rescriptis, lib. 6. And that no sentence is passed. D. de sententiis, l. fin. A third group distinguishes between a person legitimated by paternal disposition, who takes away all rights from any others, so that the father’s judgment is confirmed and held valid, since it is both the father’s and the prince’s, provided that… C. de naturalibus liberis, Auth. si quis; and between a person legitimated without the father’s provision, who does not take away the rights of agnates unless they consent. This is the opinion held by Bartolus in D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, §. et quid si tantum. Following this distinction, it must be considered that the father, by instituting a natural child, or even a spurious one, implicitly wills whatever is necessary for that purpose. And therefore I say that the statute of the instituted person is confirmed by legitimation, just as one who chooses confirmation consents, because it is ordered toward that end, and the distinctions of the doctors apply in intestate succession, not in testamentary succession. And so I hold, just as one who thinks of giving an inheritance also thinks of giving freedom, without which even the grant of an inheritance is useless. C. de necessariis heredibus instituendis, l. quidam. It follows. D. de testamento tutorum, l. quæro, §. Lucius. I therefore conclude from all the above, taken collectively, that the said legitimated persons succeed to their fathers, as if they had been born legitimate, and to uphold justice in the aforementioned goods, and this especially by virtue of the form of the privilege, which exceeds the most well-known reasons of the common law, and considering the causes of both testate and intestate succession together, and also considering the cause of intestate succession alone with regard to Gerius, and testate succession with regard to Lord Bartholomew. I, Baldus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A special legacy derogates from a general legacy.
2. A son cannot be burdened in the usufruct of his legitime.
3. The wife, left as mistress, housekeeper, and usufructuary, until, etc., the son, instituted as heir and to whom a substitute is given, should it happen that the son dies, the mother, and thus the wife, must have the usufruct of all goods except the legitime and the other quantities.
4. The mother, who did not claim during her son's life the alimony due to her, may claim it after his death, unless remission is proven.
casus: CASE. In the name of Christ, amen. Mannes Pandolphi in his will, among other things, left his wife Anesa as lady, manager, and usufructuary of his house and all his goods, provided that the said his wife wishes to remain in his house with his son or sons, and observes an honest and chaste widow’s life. He also left to Lady Agnes 100 pounds of denarii. In all his other movable goods, rights, and actions, both present and future, wherever they may be and may be found, and may be found, he instituted and made Pandulphus, his son, universal heir. And if the said Lady Agnes, his wife, were pregnant and bore a son or sons coming to light, he instituted them as heirs together with the said Pandulphus in equal shares; but if she bore a daughter or daughters coming to light, he instituted them as heirs in 200 florins each. Then, if the said his sons, born or to be born, should die in pupillary age, or later at any time without legitimate children, he left certain legacies, as contained in the will itself. In all his other goods, he substituted Victionus Cicareli, Nicolaus Paulutii, and Transaricus Gilucti, and in the said case he also left all his goods to them, so that the said Victionus, Transaricus, and Nicolaus are bound to give and distribute the said goods to the poor of Jesus Christ for the soul of the said testator and his dead, and he wished them to be tutors to the sons, as these and other matters are more fully contained in the said will, a copy of which is sent to you together with the point of law. Then, in fact, it happened that the said testator died, survived by the said Pandulphus, his son, and the said his wife. Then, after many years, the said Pandulphus, son of the testator, died in pupillary age, and the said his wife was not pregnant, and she did not bear a son or another daughter, and in the testator’s house, while the said Pandulphus, the common son, lived, she remained with him, and now she remains in the house, observing an honest, chaste, and widow’s life. Most recently, the aforementioned Victionus, Nicolaus, and Transaricus wish to give and distribute the said goods according to the judgment of the testator, and the legatees, to whom the testator left legacies after the death of the sons, demand the legacies. But the lady, wife of the testator, says that she is the lady, manager, and usufructuary of all the testator’s goods according to the judgment of the said testator, as long as she wishes to remain in the testator’s house, chaste, honest, and a widow. Hence she says that the said goods should not be distributed to her prejudice, as long as she remains as stated above, and that the pecuniary legacies, especially from the hereditary goods, should not be paid during the existence of her said right to her prejudice; because there is no money in the inheritance. Having seen this point of law and having seen the will, what the said Victionus, Nicolaus, and Transaricus ought to do with the said goods, and what the said Lady Agnes, wife of the testator, ought to have from the said goods, and what the aforementioned legatees ought to have, your wisdom, with good and clear laws and lucid reasons, please declare and advise copiously. Moreover, the said lady, during the lifetime of her son, did not have alimony from the goods of her son and husband when he was ill. It is asked whether she can have or retain something from the said goods for alimony, while the son was alive and she remained with him.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It must be premised for the sake of clarity that if the usufruct of goods is bequeathed generally to one person, and certain specific things or quantities are bequeathed specially to others, whatever is assigned specially to others diminishes the general legacy, because the specific derogates from the general. D. de peculio legato, l. servo manumisso; and note D. de legatis 2, l. si domino Stichus. There are added the common laws which state that the specific derogates from the general. D. de alim. legatis, l. alimenta, § basilicae; and l. Stichus nutritius. D. de verb. oblig., l. stipulationes. It is most expedient to compose it thus. D. de vulg. et pupill. sub., l. cohaeredi, § qui patrem; D. de legatis 3, l. heres meus, § duae statuae; and in c. generi, per Dy.
† Furthermore, it must be premised that a legitimate son could not be burdened in a legal usufruct, as stated in the Digest, De usufructu legato, in the law *Uxori*.

From these, the questions are answered, namely that, except for the things and quantities specified, and except for the legitimate portion, the wife of the deceased son must have the usufruct of the remaining goods, and that the remaining goods cannot be alienated to her prejudice. Digest, On Usufruct, law *Fundi Trebatiani*. However, specific legacies may freely be delivered to the legatees by the executors.

† Moreover, if during the son’s lifetime maintenance was not paid to the mother, it can be claimed, as in D. de usufructu legato, l. Si usufructus mihi in biennium, unless it is proven that it was remitted to the son, as in D. de negotiorum gestis, l. Nescennius Appollinaris. But the lady cannot be expelled from the house of habitation, because habitation was left to her by name. I, Baldus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Generality restricted to a cause operates only with respect to those matters that belong to the same cause.
2. By virtue of a commission made in this form, we commit: the appeal and the entire case. N., who is to take cognizance, etc., as is contained herein in the narration of the case. What the judge may do.
3. Certain offices are real in the strict sense, others personal in the strict sense.
casus: CASE. The facts are as follows: On behalf of the men of the castle of Albereto in the county of Rimini, a mortal action was brought against the families and men of the village of Mautriglia, and it was sought that those families and men be compelled to pay certain burdens and charges concerning the common of Rimini touching the said castle of Albereto, and a sentence was rendered against the aforementioned parties, from which they appealed. Now, while the appeal was pending, the men and the commune of the castle of Faytano petitioned Lord Galeotto that he would deign to commit the aforementioned cause, stating in their petition that the aforementioned families and men were and are of the castle of Faytano, and there they hold possessions and bear royal and personal burdens, although they transfer their residence to the village of Mautriglia for the utility of the possessions which they hold in the said village. And therefore they say that the Lord should not have committed the cause by right of petition. In the form written below, the said Lord Galeotto commits the said appeal and the entire cause to Lord N., his vicar, who shall know and terminate the entire cause and every controversy that might arise therefrom in any manner summarily, etc. Now it is asked whether the said commission and the sentence rendered by virtue of the said commission held or not. And it must be known that this sentence was contrary to the first sentence, rendered in favor of the men of the castle of Albereto, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† A genus restricted to the cause does not operate, except in those matters which are of the same cause, as C. de transactionibus, l. de certa; de pace, l. emptor, §. Lucius; ff. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. si is, qui anno. And therefore those words, "every case which could arise therefrom," are restricted to those which, from the appeal which the suppliants introduce for the first and principal matter of the supplication, are introduced by right, and by the introduction in court arise from the force of the appeal. For those words, "in whatever manner," are understood of the mode adjacent: mode is the determination adjacent to the thing. ff. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, §. modus; and noted, ff. de condictione indebiti, in the rubric. If, therefore, one omits the appeal and assumes another way, the first sentence passes into res iudicata by the running of the fatal terms, and the judge commissary, if he has no commission concerning the separated matters, as is read and noted, C. si a non competente iudice, l. si de proprietate. But let us suppose that he were a commissary; the question is asked concerning the justice of his pronouncement, and it must be admitted that that which no proof can bring about, the judge cannot conclude from the proven facts, nor can he render sentence. ff. inter actiones, l. confessionibus.

† Moreover, it must be premised that some offices are purely real, such as those imposed on lands or buildings; some are purely personal, such as those imposed on persons merely, without regard to property; and some are mixed, imposed on persons by reason of their property, involving a consideration of both the person and the patrimony. On offices and honors, l. *Munerum*, throughout; l. *Et l. Scripto*, § *Fin.*; and noted in the Code, On offices, in the Rubric, Book 10; and on the immunity of boundaries granted, l. *Per Bithiniam*, Book 10.

Having premised the above, it must be known that the sentence pronounced against the community of Alberteti for the common Faytani regarding real burdens, by reason of possessions or buildings in the village of Madrilla, namely that the inhabitants of the aforementioned village do not perform real obligations in the territory where the possessions are located, is contrary to justice. And if the sentence were understood in this manner, it would contain an express error in the sentence, as stated in the law *de muneribus* and the law *prohibitum*, in the Code *sine censu* or elsewhere, in the law *omnis*. Nevertheless, I do not believe this was the intent of the pronouncing judge, but rather that he referred to the real burdens of the possessions existing in the district of Faytani.

Concerning mixed burdens, namely collections, it must be known that where one has the greater part of his fortune, there he is understood to have his domicile, especially if he resides there habitually in body and mind, as noted by the gloss and Bartolus in the Digest *ad municipalia*, in the law *Eius qui*, § *Si*, and § *Si quis sortitur*. The inhabitants of Mautrigla have the greater part of their fortune there, which is presumed unless the contrary is proven, as noted by Bartolus in the Digest *ad municipalia*, in the law *De iure*. It is not presumed that one has anything elsewhere unless it is proven, as in the law *Si non*, § *Unicus*, in the Digest *Qui satisdare cogantur*, where it states "they are bound." Therefore, if the families in question have the greater part of their fortune in the village of Mautrigla, they are compelled to pay the mixed burdens, i.e., collections, there, as stated in the law *Rescripto*, § *Si*, concerning burdens.

† However, regarding personal matters, such as guardianship and similar issues, it should be known that where a person habitually resides, where he eats and sleeps, makes his hearth, and attends divine services, even if he has no other domicile because he possesses no property, he nonetheless acquires jurisdiction there, and may be commanded to appear. C. *Ubi senatores*, vel *clarissimi*. L. 2. And note the opinion of Innocentius, *extra de foro competenti*, c. *Ex parte*. And if he is burdened in two places simultaneously, then what is the law, note C. *De incolis*, L. *Cives*, lib. 10. Therefore, the aforementioned sentence, if understood adversatively, that it opposes the Commune of Albret, and imposes silence upon him regarding the aforementioned matters to which, by law, the men of the said village are bound, ought rightly to be corrected, especially if the Commune of Albret imposes burdens on the said universality and village, and not on individuals, but that the universality ought to have this done by each individual: for the said universality, and the universality as a municipal body, is subject to the castle of Albret by reason of territory, and therefore all public duties may be imposed on it under the name of the universality, which is subtle and notable, and is proven. D. *Ad municipalia*, L. *Qui ex Nico.* And note, in the same title, L. *Ei qui*, § 1, by the gloss and by Bartolus; and in the same title, L. 1, and by the gloss in Auth. *Qui mores*, na. effi. sui, § *Si quis igitur*, col. 7. And observe, because on this point there has been no judgment, and therefore also as a precaution, not out of necessity, this is a remedial mode of correcting error, unless a constitution of a superior authority contradicts it. L. 3, § *Divus*, *De sepulchro violato*. Furthermore, it should be known, as I said, that the sentence was thus rendered due to the commission: for the following are referred to the appendices of the appeal. It supports what Bartolus notes, *De verbis obligatis*, L. *Qui Romae*, § *Calimachus*. And this is clear, because the cause of the appeal was prejudicial to the new petition, and therefore it is not understood that it was committed to proceed improperly and omit substantial matters, as D. *De excusationibus tutorum*, L. *Dixit*, non. n. in judgment by acts, that in the libel of the Commune of Faytani mention was made of the appeal interposed by the men of the village, nor that they prosecuted it, whence the sentence passed into *res iudicata*. C. *De appellationibus*, L. *Cives et incolae*, and L. *Hi qui ad civilia*. And thus the later sentence, even assuming jurisdiction, is not valid to the contrary: as L. 1, *Quando provocatio non est necessaria*, because the finished lawsuit absorbs the lawsuit to be finished, especially if it is prejudicial and greater, as the lawsuit of appeal, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a mother, having assumed guardianship, enters into a second marriage, she is admitted to the succession of her underage son who dies.
1. If a statute prescribes a form different from that of the common law, whether it suffices if the common form is observed, or not.
2. If a statute provides that if any person dies intestate without children, etc., whether such a statute is to be understood as applying to a ward.
3. Given a statute providing that brothers exclude a sister from intestate succession, whether the sister is excluded only by uterine brothers.
casus:
CASE. In the Name of Christ, Amen. The facts are as follows, namely: A certain Francis Cioli of the Commune of Todi made a testament, in which he left and ordered to his daughter Catherine, born of his first marriage, one hundred pounds of denarii as dowry, and in those one hundred pounds he instituted her as heir, and willed that she could not have more of his goods on account of the legitime, the Fideicommissum Trebellianum, or any other case, whether by law or by fact, and in those one hundred pounds he willed that she be tacitly satisfied and content. And that the said lady could not, nor ought to, by law or by fact, disturb, molest, or harass his inscribed daughters, and if she should do the contrary, she shall fall from the said legacy, and his inscribed daughters shall succeed, and in all his movable and immovable goods, rights, and actions, present and future, he instituted Helen and Bartholomew, his daughters born of his second marriage from him and from the lady Gratia hereinafter written, as universal heirs, as appears more fully in the aforementioned testament, etc.

It is also stated that before the said testament, the said Francis composed certain codicils, in which, among other things, he left and ordered that two hundred and sixty pounds of the dowry of the lady Besondicta, formerly mother of the said lady Catherine and first wife of the said Francis, be restored to the said lady Catherine, his daughter born of his first marriage. And that before the aforementioned testament was composed, and before the aforementioned codicils, the said Francis had emancipated the said Catherine, his daughter, and given her in marriage, and had given dowries to her.
