And after these things, the said Francis died, the aforementioned testament not being changed, with the said Helen and Bartholomew, his daughters and daughters of the said Gratia, wife of the aforementioned Francis, born of his second marriage, and heirs or those instituted as heirs in the aforementioned testament by the said Francis, surviving and outliving him, and also with the said lady Catherine, his daughter born of his first marriage, instituted as heir in a certain thing in the said testament, surviving and outliving him, and also with the said lady Gratia, his second wife, surviving and outliving him. And that after the death of the said Francis, the said Helen and Bartholomew, heirs instituted in the aforementioned testament, became heirs of the said Francis, their father, and possessed and held the goods of their father's inheritance by themselves and their tutors for many and many years, namely from the death of the said Francis until the death of the said Helen and Bartholomew. And that the said lady Gratia, mother of the said Helen and Bartholomew, assumed guardianship, made an inventory, and managed and administered the said guardianship, and afterwards the said lady Gratia, wishing to proceed to second vows and a second marriage, constituted herself before the ordinary judge and petitioned that certain tutors be given and constituted to the said Helen and Bartholomew, namely the lady Cecha, their maternal grandmother, and Nicholas, son of the late John Bonis of Todi. And that the said lady Cecha and Nicholas were constituted and given as tutors to the said Helen and Bartholomew by the said judge, and at the petition of the said lady Gratia in due form. And that the said lady Cecha and Nicholas made an inventory of the goods of the said wards, and by reason of the administration of the guardianship received from the said lady Gratia, and made a discharge to the said lady Gratia for the things administered by the said lady Gratia, formerly the guardian, and for the goods and things that had come into the hands of the said lady Gratia. And that after these things, the said lady Catherine sued in the court of Todi against the heir of the said Francis, her former father, for the said two hundred and sixty pounds which the said Francis ordered to be restored to her in the said codicils, and there was litigation in contradiction regarding the said restoration made in the said codicils with the tutors of the said Helen and Bartholomew.

After these things, the said Bartholomew died in infancy, with the said Helen, her sister carnally related on both sides, and the said lady Catherine, related on the father's side only, and the said lady Gratia, stepmother of the said ward Helen, surviving and outliving her, and with Blasius and Stephen, sons of the said daughter of the lady Gratia, born of a second husband in a second marriage, and uterine brothers of the said Helen and Bartholomew. The said Helen, sister carnally related on both sides to the said Bartholomew, legitimately entered upon the inheritance of the said Bartholomew for the share falling to her. Then the said Helen died after the death of the said Bartholomew in pupillary age, with the said lady Gratia, her mother, and the said lady Catherine, her sister carnally related on the father's side only, and the said Stephen and Blasius, her uterine brother and common child of the said Nicholas and the lady Gratia, surviving and outliving her.

Now it is asked, having seen and considered, and having seen the statutes of the Commune of Todi placed under the rubric *De successionibus ab intestato*, which are transmitted to you, since the said lady Gratia says that the inheritance of the said Helen and Bartholomew pertains to her, and says that the said statute of the Commune of Todi does not apply to a ward dying, because a ward is not properly said to die intestate, and because he cannot die with children. And therefore she says that she succeeds according to the form of the common law, and not according to the form of the said statute, since also the said Blasius and Stephen say that they succeed as uterine brothers of the said Bartholomew and Helen by the common law, notwithstanding the said statute, especially since carnal sisters and aunts of a deceased person, while some carnal brother of such deceased person survives, as appears from the form of the said statute, and then the said lady Catherine says that the inheritance of the said Helen and Bartholomew pertains to her, and that she succeeds to them as the nearest agnate according to the form of the statute, and by virtue of the said statute, and having seen the chapter of the statute under the rubric *De ratione cedenda a tutoribus et curatoribus*, etc., the form of which is said by the part of the said Catherine not to have been observed in the discharge made to the said lady Gratia, while on the contrary it is said for the part of the said lady Gratia that the statute claims place when the guardianship is finished, but not while the guardianship is ongoing, when she wishes to proceed to second vows and gives other tutors to the ward. What is the law regarding the inheritance of the said Helen and Bartholomew, namely to whom, or to whom, does the said inheritance pertain, whether to the said lady Gratia, their mother, or to the said lady Catherine, their carnal sister, however on the father's side. Or whether to the said Blasius and Stephen, uterine brothers of the said Helen and Bartholomew, and for what, or what share only.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Under the common law, a mother who has assumed guardianship and, wishing to enter into a second marriage, has requested that a guardian be appointed; and once such guardian has been appointed, she lawfully renders an account of her administration, and succeeds to the inheritance of the minor upon his death; otherwise, if she had entered into a second marriage without having requested a guardian, or having requested one but not rendered accounts, as stated in the Authenticum *De nuptiis*, § *Si autem tutela*, col. 4; and in the Code, *Ad Tertullianam*, l. *Omnem*; and *De legitimis haeredibus*, l. *Sciant cuncti*. In the rendering of accounts by the mother, good faith is required rather than a scrupulous inquiry. D. *De manumissionibus testamento*, l. *Qui filium*; D. *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, l. *Quamvis*; D. *De legatis primo*, l. *Servus vetitus*. However, if a certain form for rendering accounts has been prescribed by statute, it is necessary to comply with that form. D. *Ad municipalem*, l. *Constitutionibus*; C. *De iudiciis*, l. *Certam formam*, lib. 10; nor are women excused from general forms. C. *De iure et facto ignorantia*, l. *Si*.

Let us therefore examine, comparing the statute with the common law, whether this mother, who renders an account simply according to the common law, but does not render the cause according to the form of the statute, is thereby deprived of the succession of the minor by the common law, because she neglected the statute, and whether it should be seen that she is deprived: for it is held that not rendering an account is equivalent to rendering it vitiously or uselessly. D. Qui satisdare coguntur, l. Quoties; D. De conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Cum servus; and l. Qui sub conditione rationum reddendarum. To the contrary, because the common law requires nothing else than that the account and the rest be rendered. D. § Subordinato tutori; D. § Cum autem tutelam, in fine. Nor did the entire common law consider the scrupulousness of the statute, to which it would be unjust to constrain the female mind. It supports what we noted in l. Finis, De regula Catoiana; and in c. 1, De constitutionibus, lib. 6. Moreover, the statute speaks of the guardianship being finished, so that the account is to be rendered with the inquiry of the judge; but here there is a substitute judge, the guardian, and this is a case in which the common law provides a special form, and therefore by the general words of the statute it is not understood that there is a departure from the special provision. L. Sanctio legum, De poenis. Moreover, having given security, we do not dispute about the mode. D. De verborum obligationibus, l. Cum servus; D. De pignoris actione, l. Solutum, § Solutam. Moreover, the statute does not say that if the rest are otherwise rendered and the account is not given, release does not occur between consenting parties, but that as to that form they can be constrained and are bound even to offer themselves; yet it does not restrict the rendering of the account and the rest made by an extrajudicial mode with the consent of the legitimate persons, namely the subsequent guardian, as here: although the law does not proceed further, nor do we, because we should not exceed the words of statutes, especially for the correction of the common law, as by the doctors in l. Omnes populi, cum sequentibus. Also, it must be observed that in this case, when the mother wishes to marry a second time, and therefore asks for a guardian to be appointed, she simultaneously ceases to be one and another begins; thus, to one having a guardian, a guardian is asked for, but immediately that he is given, he begins to be, and the mother is removed from being one, and thus it should be understood as we noted in Inst. De curatore, § Sed interdum; and it is expressed in the said § Si autem tutelam. Otherwise, the mother could not render an account, and if she remained guardian. L. Nisi fieri ea, De tutelis; and Ratio, De distrahendis. Let it therefore be concluded that, according to the common law, she succeeds alone, excluding only the consanguineous sister, and the uterine brothers, as in Auth. Defuncto. Now, therefore, we must proceed to the statute: the words of the statute say,

† If a person dies intestate without children, etc., the question arises whether this is understood to apply to a minor under guardianship. Bartolus says yes, for a minor under guardianship dies intestate, and succession occurs according to the rules for intestacy. D. ad Trebellianum § confestim; L. 2; L. credimus, Q. qui petunt tutelam. The contrary view seems to be that he is not properly called intestate, but rather incapable of making a will. L. 1, D. de suis et legitimis heredibus; in the beginning of the same title, there it clearly states, etc. But certainly, to that which is said there, that he is not properly intestate, immediately follows the adversative clause: but if we must also consider these as intestate, here consider first the force of the adversative word in law: for it corrects the preceding statements; secondly, consider the word "must," because it implies the necessity of accepting the term "intestate" more favorably, broadly, and generally, even extending to minors under guardianship and the insane. Moreover, the common understanding of ordinary people interprets it thus, therefore it should be understood in the words of statutes. L. 3, D. liberorum; § quod tamen Cassius, D. de verbis significationibus. And that this is the common usage of speaking and understanding, Bartolus holds there by that text, and many follow him; I have also seen many opinions supporting this side: but on the contrary, I have seen many more opinions of venerable doctors, that a statute excluding the mother, as being odious and contrary to reason and natural law, does not cover the case of an underage person. And in the City of Todi, I previously advised thus, and I advise so now. And first, from the nature of the proper meaning of the words "intestate," d. l. 1. For although where the favor of the mother is concerned, the meaning is extended, and otherwise where hatred and exclusion are involved, arg. in L. cum quidam, D. de liberis et posthumis. Thirdly, from the condition of children, for those words, "without children," apply to an adult, as noted in L. precibus, in the large gloss, D. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus. Certainly that gloss argues to the contrary, because it says that they apply to both: i.e., to him who has no children, and to him who cannot have children. Thirdly, by the ordinary gloss, C. de iudiciis delictorum, L. cum antiquioribus, vers. et si quidam, which gloss you may see. Fourthly, by the last law, C. de testamento militis, in the literal sense. Fifthly, because the same reasoning does not apply to a minor under guardianship and an adult, for a minor under guardianship cannot provide for his mother, if the mother were excluded, whereas an adult can by making a will, and if he does not, he seems tacitly to dispose according to the law, L. eo, § pen., D. de legatis 2. Sixthly, because that word "for" denotes an extensive similarity, which has no place in statutes exceeding due reason. D. de verbis significationibus, L. mercis, so. ma.; L. si vero, § di. viro. Seventhly, that which is not noted by Cynus in L. 2, C. qui testamento facere possunt, and by what the Ultramontanes note in L. 1, C. quoniam imperator, inter viduam et filium, and there William of Cuneo and Richard determine, I hold that the said mother succeeds, otherwise the father comes into the goods, with only the blood relatives excluded, the uterine brothers, as noted by Cynus, auth. itaque; and noted in Inst. de servorum agnatione, § totis. With the love of the Reverend Lord An., I have thus extensively discussed the following in all respects, the substance of the truth.

† And by this statute, because it excludes agnate offspring, and the higher provisions are consistent with the lower, and the lower with the higher, it is not understood that a uterine brother excludes only an agnate sister, cf. D. de haer. inst. l. qui non militabat. §. filius. C. de fa. her. l. toties. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The action of a daughter for the payment of her dowry from her mother’s estate, when it is acquired by the father through stipulation.
2. Whether a daughter may make a donation causa mortis to her father, who is present and gives his authorization.
3. Whether one may impose authority for one’s own benefit.
4. Whether an infant transmits a maternal inheritance.
casus: CASE. In the name of God, Amen. The facts are as follows: Nardus married his legitimate and natural daughter Matthea to Vicocellus, for whom he confessed to having received from the said Nardus 200 pounds as dowry, which dowry the said Vicus promised, by himself and his heirs, to restore to the said Nardus, in the name of the said his daughter receiving and stipulating, in the case in which the said Vicus should die before the said do. Matthea, with common children surviving, or not, after the said Vicus, coming to his death, had made his will, in which, among other things, he left and bequeathed to the said lady Matthea, his wife, beyond her dowries and her dotal rights, all linen and woolen cloths, and all the furniture of the said lady, and made for her person, and her own gifts, which she had brought from her father’s house, and in all his goods he instituted as heir Jacoba, his daughter, and daughter of the said do. Matthea, and the posthumous child to be born from his said pregnant wife, if she bore a female, and if she bore a male, then he instituted the said Jacoba and the posthumous child to be born in 5 pounds for each of them, and he instituted the male to be born as his universal heir, and to him he substituted vulgarly and pupillarily Paul and his sons for one half, and finally Bartholomew for the other half. Having made this will, the said Vicus died, survived by the said do. Matthea, his wife, pregnant, and the said Jacoba, his daughter; then the said do. Matthea gave birth to a male child named Vicus; afterwards the said do. Matthea made a donation causa mortis to the said Nardus, her father, present and authorizing, of all her dotal rights and other her goods and rights, for the said Nardus receiving, and 10 pounds of her goods and rights receiving for the said Jacoba, out of 25 pounds receiving for the said Vicus, her posthumous son, for all the right competent to the said children in the goods of the said lady. Finally, the said lady Matthea died, and subsequently on the same day the said posthumous Vicus died, not yet being one month old? and lastly the said lady Jacoba died, under two years of age. The inheritance of the said lady Matthea, their mother, not having been accepted by them or any of them. These being dead, the inheritance of the said Vicus, the testator, devolved to the said posthumous children by virtue of the said will, and they apprehended the said inheritance, or hereditary goods. Now, from the foregoing, a question arises between the said Nardus and the said substitutes: for the said Nardus says that the said dotal rights and the said things bequeathed to the said do. Matthea belong to him, both by virtue of the said donation and by virtue of the dotal instrument, in which it appears that the dowry was common to the father and the daughter, and thus, she being dead, it consolidates in the father, for which dowry he says he can sue within a year and demand it by virtue of the will of the said Vicus, notwithstanding that, by the disposition of the common and municipal law, the dowry could not be demanded or exacted within a year. And this by those words added in the will, where it is said, “he bequeathed her dowries,” etc. Also, because the said Nardus occupies the said rights and goods by the right of peculium, excluding the said children, since he has no heir by will or intestate in the said goods, because she was in the power of her father, and thus, from one or the other of the said reasons, he says that the said rights and goods belong to the said Nardus. On the other hand, the said substitutes say that the said Nardus has no right in the said rights and goods, but that they belong to them, the substitutes, as goods and rights of the said Jacoba and Vicus, children of the said Vicus, and as heir of the said do. Matthea. Both because the said donation causa mortis is invalid by law, which the father could not authorize to himself; both because the dowry was not common, but proper to the daughter herself; both because the said Jacoba and Vicus succeeded intestate to the said Matthea, their mother, and the said Nardus is entirely excluded. This maternal inheritance, even if not accepted, they say, the said substitutes would have transmitted to them, or at least they can say that they ought to be admitted to the said inheritance by the right of deliberation, since it is within a year. Now, having seen the foregoing narration, and the said dotal instrument, and donation, and will, it is asked, what is the law in the foregoing. I answer by alleging the law to each of the above parts, and proving the said laws. Finally, it is asked, insofar as the foregoing would not benefit the said Nardus, whether it would be good that nothing be said within a year, i.e., whom he would ask for the right of deliberation within a year, within which the right of deliberation is demanded, the substitutes could come, and thus after the year the said Nardus could demand the said rights and goods as intestate heir of his said daughter, as if the inheritance had not devolved to the son, a minor infant, and as if they had never been, since the mother’s inheritance was not accepted by them or another for them. Concerning which, please give your useful advice and provide a remedy, what is to be done for the part of the said Nardus. Also, please consider the substitution made by Vicus to his sons, whether the said substitution excludes the said Nardus, paternal grandfather of the said sons, in whole or in part, or whether by virtue of such substitution the said substitutes can take the said goods and rights of the said lady Matthea, and give advice and remedy to the said, and supply the fact and the law, as it will seem to your discretion to be fitting, so that it may avail for the protection of the said Nardus by law.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Upon the dissolution of the marriage by the death of the husband, with children surviving, the tenor of the said paternal stipulation gave rise to an action for the dowry belonging solely to the daughter, who is capable of the said dotal stipulation. D. 38, 15, 3. There are three cases, for sometimes the father stipulates for the daughter, sometimes for himself alone, and sometimes simply. In the first case, the action belongs solely to the daughter; in the second, solely to the father, unless in the case of consolidation. C. 5, 13, 1. In the present case, see D. 38, 15, 7, § quod si in patris; and C. 5, 13, 1. In the third case, the action is common to the father and the daughter under his power. D. 38, 15, 7, § quod si in patris; and C. 5, 13, 1. Therefore, in our case, according to the tenor, the action for the dowry is valid. The legacy was to the son alone, although it was also written in the person of the daughter. And it is valid on account of the benefit of representation, as D. 23, 3, 1; and D. 23, 3, 2, § mella; and D. 23, 3, 1. For on account of the word "ultra," which is inclusive, the dowry is also included.

It remains to be seen whether the aforementioned daughter may make a donation causa mortis to her father, who is present and giving his authorization. The glossa ordinaria states that she cannot, in l. 1, in principio, ff. de auctoritate tutorum, and the doctor in l. tam is, §. 1, de donationibus causa mortis, because no one can provide authority for his own act, as in c. Si una, de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, and in the decretal, and there fully noted under the word “mense suo.” That the father’s consent is not called authority is clear from ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. 1, §. 1; Institutiones, de inutilibus stipulationibus, §. pupillus, in fine; and noted in Codex, de iure deliberandi, l. Si infanti, in the glossa which begins “Ex quo videtur,” near the end, ff. de adoptionibus, l. Si pater naturalis, according to Guillaume de Coucy, beyond the manner stated.

Therefore, the rule stands that no one may interpose his authority for another to his own advantage, as noted by Guillaume in the Digest, *De adoptionibus*, in the law *Si consul*. And this is the common opinion, following the gloss that a son under paternal power cannot make a donation *causa mortis* to his father with the father’s authority, because there must be a personal distinction between the acquirer and the authority, as stated by these authors in the Digest, *De auctoritate tutorum*, in the section *Si*. And thus the donation made to the said Nardo did not hold, and so hold Dyonisius, Bartolus, and Petrus in disputing, and Johannes Andreae in the *Speculum*, *De instrumentis exhibendis*, in the section *Porro*, in the additions. And this is supported by the Institutes, *De inutilibus stipulationibus*, in the section *Item inutilis*; and by the law *1*, *De contrahenda emptione*; and by what is noted in the Digest, *De condictione indebiti*, in the law *Frater a fratre*. But Petrus de Bellapertica holds that he may do so; otherwise, that which is introduced in favor of the father, so that it may not be turned to his detriment without the father’s consent, which it ought not to be, would be defeated, as in the Code, *De secundis nuptiis*, in the law *Generaliter*, in the section *Si*; and for this view, see the Digest, *De inofficioso lucro descriptione*, in the law *Una*, near the beginning, book 10; *De in rem verso*, in the law *Si pro parte*, in the section *Idem tractat*; *Nisi donare*; and the Code, *De fideiussoribus*, in the law *Si quis pro eo*, section 1. Therefore, a daughter may grant to her father in dowry that he may act, that he may stipulate, because it is acquired for the father, as in the Digest, *De solutione matrimonii*, in the law *Quoties*; and in the law *Non solum*; and in the Code, *De iure dotium*, in the law *Auia*. To this effect, see the Authenticum *Ut liceat matri et aviae*, after the principle, where it says: “But the property,” collection 8, title *De dote*, number *Proprie filiae*, as in the Digest, *De minoribus*, in the law *Denique eius*, in the section *Sed utrum*. It does not imitate the nature of other *profecticia*, as in the said law *Pomponius*; and see the argument in the Digest, *De capite diminuto*, in the law *Eas*. Moreover, the doctors say that this is not properly authority, but consent, which may be given for one’s own utility, as in the Digest, *De contrahenda emptione*, in the law *Fistulas*, in the section *Fundum*. Furthermore, paternal power is ordered to the father’s utility, and therefore, if the father authorizes for his own advantage, it is otherwise in the authority of a tutor and a prelate, which is not ordered to this end, as in the Digest, *De negotiis gestis*, in the law *Qui sine usu*. This opinion is held by Guillaume de Cugno. It may be said that either the father authorizes in good faith, and then the opinion of Petrus is true; or in fraud of the children, as in our case, because it is in fraud of the nephews and daughters. Then the opinion of the gloss and Dyonisius is true, that it is not valid. And this distinction is quite equitable; nevertheless, from the subtlety of the law, the opinion of Petrus and Guillaume is more true without distinction. And it is one thing in a tutor, as in the Authenticum *Minoris debito*, in the words *Sed et si cessionem*; and another thing in a father. Whether a son under power may cede a life against a third party, and no law prohibits it, I speak of a son of legitimate age. And from this donation *causa mortis*, the legitime of the children is deducted, as in the Code, *Ad legem Falcidiam*, in the law *Si mortis*. But in Besse it is valid, as he said, because it is true that the father’s will does not cease; therefore, the donation is valid, as in the Digest, *De donationibus*, in the law *Filius*, in the section *Pari ratione*. The sole cessation of paternal will is the impeding cause, as is notably clear there. But assuming that the said donation were not valid,

† Other points arise concerning the transmission of an unaccepted maternal inheritance to children who die in infancy: whether they transmit anything to the pupillary substitutes. And it is certain that, by their own knowledge—not because they cannot know, but by the knowledge of the father or tutor—they transmit the right of deliberation, which expires, Auth. de reb. dub. §. qui duos, according to Bartolus. Others contradict this, stating that an infant does not transmit an unaccepted inheritance, by l. si infanti, §. 1. And it is said that the law, with the older authorities, does not speak of an infant. I say that this grandfather should remain silent until the grandfather is released. And thus, the substitute being excluded, the grandfather himself will come to the dowry, concerning which inquiry is made, given that the donation would not hold; which the aforementioned Ultramontane doctors then say holds, and for this side it serves that we in l. 2, C. de inof. do., according to Jacobus de Belvisio in his public and beautiful disputation. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the memory of one who has committed the crime of lèse-majesté can be condemned, and the form of the inquiry concerning the same.
casus: CASE. The point, or narration, upon which legal advice is requested, is as follows. It is reported that a certain person committed the crime of lèse-majesty, who, for this reason, was seized by the fury of the people. Now it is asked whether proceedings may be had for such a delict, and whether his memory be damned and his goods confiscated and applied to the treasury; and, if proceedings may be had, whether it is necessary for the delict to be proven for condemnation and confiscation of goods; and what is the form of the procedure and condemnation; and who ought to be cited for this.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If anyone has committed the crime of lèse-majesté against the prince or the Roman Republic, his memory may be prosecuted, he may be condemned to death, and his goods confiscated; but if not against the prince or the Roman Republic, then the crime is extinguished by death, as in D. ad l. Iul. mai. l. fin. and Inst. de haer. ab int. § per contrarium. And there the form of procedure and condemnation is set forth, and those who have an interest must be summoned: as in l. 4 § tutor de damno infecto. On this matter, see D. de accusat. l. ex iudic. Inst. de publ. iud. § publica. The title of the inquisition attends to inquire against the memory of such a person, concerning him, about him, and upon him, which also c. and at the end it adds, and having found the crime, it intends to condemn his memory and declare his goods confiscated and incorporated into the fisc in every manner, way, and form by which it can best be done. From this also appears the form of the sentence, which the gloss places differently in the said § per contrarium. And it accords with what is noted in C. si reus vel accusatus mortuus fuerit l. 1. But concerning the crime, one must speak through proofs, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Up to what sum a donation is valid without insinuation.
2. Whether a blood relative may draw up an instrument.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Up to five hundred gold coins of legal currency, that is, at the rate of 72 florins per pound of gold, a donation is valid without insinuation; but beyond that amount it is not valid, even if there is a clause of distribution, which was the case in the donation, etc., as noted by Cynus and others. C. de donat. l. sancimus. §. si quis. From this it appears up to what sum this donation is valid. And it should be known that although the notary is the nephew of the donee and the first cousin once removed of the donor, he may nevertheless draw up the instrument of this donation: as in ff. de falsis. l. pater. and l. uxori. I, Baldus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How a partnership is contracted, and when it is contrary to partnership in this manner, that one contributes labor and the other money, how the loss of lost money is to be divided, and when it is to be divided.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Let us see what this partnership is.

For a partnership is contracted sometimes when both parties contribute a thing or a quantity, sometimes when both contribute labor, and sometimes when one contributes a thing and the other contributes labor. D. loc. cond. l. socie. and l. si non fuerunt. §. 1. C. eod. tit. And if this is well considered, this partnership was of this third kind, because my Lellus contributed money, and John was to contribute labor, namely by trading with the said money; nor did this partnership extend to other things of the said John. If, therefore, it were established that the said John had converted that money into the purchase of goods for the purpose of trading, and those goods were lost, the loss would be common, that is, of both parties in equal halves. Hence, if these ten florins had been converted and all the goods were lost by fortuitous event, John would be released from the restitution of one hundred florins out of the two hundred to Lellus, both by the perishing of the specific items and by the nature of the partnership joined together, as D. loc. cond. l. in naue saupheli. D. pro soc. l. cum duobus. §. damna fatalia. For each would lose one hundred denarii due to the fortuitous event concerning the two hundred denarii, because they are affected by equal loss. But because it is established by the statements of the witnesses, and considering the acts transmitted to me in no other way, that those two hundred were converted into goods, the fortuitous event does not release the debtor of a certain quantity, as C. si cert. pet. l. incendium. And the said John ought to be condemned according to the form of the petition of the said Lellus. For the witnesses, in the narration of the cause, depose by hearing what was said, which testimony does not prove, as is fully noted in l. 2. §. pe. de aqua plu. l. si arbiter. D. de proba. C. de testi. l. testium. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a father has provided a dowry for his daughter, and in the event of the dissolution of the marriage without issue has stipulated that the dowry be returned to him, and if the marriage is dissolved by the death of the daughter while sons from the said marriage are living in infancy, and having died in their minority without having accepted the inheritance, nor after their death by the father, to whom does such dowry belong, whether to the father of the dowried daughter, or to the paternal grandfather of the said sons.
casus: CASE. The fact upon which counsel is sought is as follows. John had a daughter named Nicoleta, whom he married to a certain person named Ser William, and gave her a dowry, and stipulated that it be returned to him if the marriage were dissolved without children between the said Nicoleta and Ser William. The said Nicoleta died, leaving John her father, and the said Ser William her husband, and three children born to her. And the said Ser William, with two infants and one older child, although a ward, died after the death of the said Nicoleta. All the said children died within two months after the death of their said mother: two infants, and the other ward, without having accepted the inheritance of their said mother, either by them or by the said Ser William, their father. After the death of the said infants and ward, the said Ser William, their father, was killed by force about two months after the death of his said children, and of the children of the said Lady Nicoleta, his former wife, and died, leaving John, his former father-in-law, father of the said Lady Nicoleta, and leaving Ser Nicholas, father of the said Ser William. And the said Ser William, while he lived, did not accept the inheritance of his said children, or of the said Lady Nicoleta, his mother-in-law, as if it had already been acquired by his said children, the infants and the ward, or by any other mode of law. It is asked what is the law regarding the dotal goods and the inheritance of the said Lady Nicoleta: whether it is as if it had not been devolved to the said infants and ward, since it was not accepted by them while they lived, nor by the said Ser William, their father, while they were living, nor afterwards during the life of the said Ser William, and thus it pertains to the said John, father of the said Lady Nicoleta, or whether it pertains to the said Ser Nicholas, father of the said Ser William, so that he may still accept it by some right, or to whom it pertains, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Considering the theme, the first part of the theme pertains to the first part of the law *Si infanti* in the Code, *De iure deliberandi*, because it speaks of an infant. The second part of the theme pertains to § *Si autem*, “seven years of age,” which section speaks of an older infant.

† And it must be premised for clarity, that when an infant dies, the parent who had him in power will occupy the devolved inheritance by right, as if it were peculium, according to the law of the Codex; but today, as the gloss says in l. Si infanti, he is considered as heir. From this it appears that formerly the grandfather, having the infant in his power, was preferred to his son, who did not have the infant in his power; but today, because the father is preferred to the grandfather as heir, since he is closer in degree, as in Auth. Defuncto. Therefore, it must be said that if Ser Gul. acted as heir of his wife, the entire said dowry would belong to Ser Nicola as heir of Ser Gul. But if Ser Gul. did not act as heir, and thus the question arises between the paternal and maternal grandfathers, then there are two opinions. For some prefer the paternal grandfather to the uncle by right, on the ground that the power of reason ceases. Since the intermediate person is impeding, the right reverts to the paternal grandfather himself: and this is held by Nic. de Mat. Others, in succeeding to the infant, and consequently to his wife, join the paternal grandfather, considering only the natural cause. Thus the dowry will equally belong to these. And this is commonly held by the doctors in l. Si infanti, that since succession is by hereditary right in equal degree, they succeed equally, because the law treats the inheritance as acquired by the infant, as is clear in the text there, "to take as if already acquired by the infant." And this I hold in l. Si infanti. Following natural equity, I come to the second part of the theme, namely, concerning the older infant, to whom the maternal inheritance not entered upon is not feigned to have been acquired: as in l. Non pro numero, ad officia. And I say that the portion, as caducary, accrues to the other portions, and consequently the same division must be made, as I said, of the infants' portions, because among coheirs, both by will and intestate, there is room for the right of accrual. And thus I, Bal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that if anyone dies intestate without sons and daughters, the nearest blood relatives on the father’s side shall succeed to the patrimony, and the nearest relatives in marriage, provided, however, that males are preferred to females: whether a natural daughter succeeds to the exclusion of the nearest relatives, and who is admitted, whether the son of an aunt or the daughter of an uncle, and whether the mother is excluded.
casus: CASE. The point of the question is this. A certain Stephanutius of the Old City died without legitimate or natural children, intestate, but with a daughter surviving him from a concubine, whom he did not keep in his house, who died after the said Theo by 20 days in impupillary age, and with the said Theo surviving, the legitimate and natural mother of the said Theo, Domina Melontana of Matte, and with Domina Mema, formerly legitimate and natural daughter of the uncle of the said Theo, and with Stephano Mulialdi, formerly legitimate and natural son of Domina Inscia, aunt of the said Theo. Now it is asked, who succeeds in the goods of the said Theo, first seeing and taking as true the words of the statute of the said city, which are in this form. If anyone dies intestate without sons or daughters, the nearest blood relatives on the part of his father shall succeed in the patrimony, and the nearest on the part of the mother in the dowry. So however, that males are preferred to females.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The daughter of the said concubine, conceived outside the home of the father and born there, is not considered a natural child for the purpose of succession, but is regarded as a spurious and uncertain daughter; and therefore she does not exclude the benefit of the law, which was enacted for the burden of families, as in l. filium, de his qui sunt sui vel alieni iuris, and de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. generaliter, §. si, and note in c. 1, de Baptismatis, in the Decretals; ff. de ritu nuptiarum, l. lege, §. distinguitur. And I prove this by an effective reason: for the statute considers agnation, not cognition, in the succession to patrimony, if the spurious or natural child is not acknowledged, as in ff. unde cognati, l. si spurius, and l. hac parte. And therefore the natural child, who most certainly does not have the civil rights of natural children, as is the case with this one, does not exclude the closer agnates, i.e., consanguineous relatives; and because the daughter of the paternal uncle, and the consanguineous relative, and the son of the maternal aunt, differ in agnation from their father, and in cognation from their mother; hence the son of the maternal aunt is not a consanguineous relative of the said Theo, it follows that the daughter of the paternal uncle succeeds, and not the son of the maternal aunt, in the patrimony in question. ff. de adoptionibus, l. qui in adoptionem. Consanguinity is said to proceed from the male sex, not from the female sex, in Auth. de consanguineis et uterinis fratribus, in the rubric and black letter; de suis et legitimis heredibus, l. post consanguineos, §. 1; and C. de legatis et heredibus, l. in l. 12, tab. From these it appears that the statute excludes the mother, according to what is proposed to be contained in the statute, unless something else is provided in another part of the statute or in another statute. And that the daughter of the aforementioned paternal uncle, namely Mamma, succeeds, because of the word “closer consanguineous relatives,” which is in the statute. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a usufruct of a certain thing is bequeathed to someone until a certain person marries, and that person dies, whether it is extinguished by death.
2. A bequest of the usufruct of a single part, in which the testator holds only a half-share, is understood to apply only to the usufruct of his own share.
3. The mother is the next of kin in the succession of children.
casus: CASE. In the name of God, Amen. The point is this. Bernardus Colae, being in his last illness, made his will by the hand of a public notary, in which, among other things, he bequeathed to Franciscus Titij, by way of legacy, in case he should not die from the illness he now has, all the equipment and tenancies pertaining to his farm; and if he should die from it, he wished the said will to be void and of no value. He also left to the said Franciscus the usufruct of the apothecary of the said farm, situated in the castle of the parish, from one etc., until Bartholomea, daughter of the said Bernardus, marries. In all his other goods, he instituted Bartholomew, Joanna, and Petrutia, his daughters, as heirs, and substituted them to one another, as is contained in the will presented to you. And if it should happen that the testator should have other sons or daughters from his wife, Lady Cecha, or from any other legitimate wife, he instituted them as universal heirs with equal portions together with the aforementioned Bartholomew, Joanna, and Petrutia, or with one or the other of them. After the said Bernardus died, with his wife Bartholomew pregnant, the said Lady Cecha, before the competent judge, requested the guardianship of her said wards and the curatorship of the womb, and this was executed. After the said Bartholomew died at the age of ten years, and Petrutia at the age of three, with the said Joanna and Margaret, born from the aforementioned womb, surviving. It is now asked whether the said Franciscus is deprived of the usufruct of the said farm by the death of the said Bartholomew. It is asked whether any action is available to the said Franciscus in the goods formerly of the said Bernardus, if all the said daughters of Bernardus should die in their minority, or whether any action would be available to the said Lady Cecha, mother of the said wards.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. First, the legacy of the massarities pertains to Francis without doubt, because the testator so willed. It follows to consider

† On the usufruct of an apothecary shop. And first, whether the legacy is extinguished by the death of Bartholomew, since she cannot marry at all. And it must be said that the legacy is not extinguished, but endures as long as Francis lives, as in D. de usufr. l. ambiguitatem.

It remains to be seen that the apotheca was not entirely the testator’s, but only a part thereof; whether it appears that the testator bequeathed the usufruct of the entire apotheca. And it must be said that he did not, but only the usufruct of his own part, according to the rule in Leg. 1, L. Servus electione, §. Si, per Dynus and others, although the gloss there says otherwise.

It remains to be seen who shall succeed after all the sons have died, and it must be said that only the mother shall succeed, as in the Authentica *Defuncto*. For she is the nearest relative. D. 38, 2, 1, with many others. And because she is the heir of the sons, she may sell and do whatever she wishes, without prejudice to the aforementioned usufructuary, as in D. 7, 1, *Filiae fundi Trebatiani*. The usufructuary must give security for using and enjoying the property according to the discretion of a good man, and for restoring it upon the termination of the usufruct. D. 7, 1, 1; C. 7, 1, 5; C. 6, 62, *Scire*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In what order one arrives at the first decree.
2. Whether the sentence, by which the first decree is confirmed, is interlocutory.
3. What is required as to substance for the first decree.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It must be premised for the sake of clarity that, in order to arrive at the first decree in personal actions, a certain order must be observed. For, first of all, the judge must be approached, and the plaintiff must make some demand, as in the Authentica de exhibendis rebus, § si vero, in the gloss on the word declarati, which says: i.e., demanded; and in the Digest, de damno infecto, l. 3, § hoc iudicium, on the words si id postulatum. This demand must be certain if anyone wishes to be put in possession for a certain amount of debt. If this foundation is lacking, the judge proceeds foolishly and stupidly, because he has nothing upon which to proceed, as in the Digest, communi dividundo, l. ut fundus; the Code, de fideicommissis liberis, l. si; the Decretum, de veris sigillis, c. saepe. In the Clementina, modo ego, I saw the first process, and it is true that I find well that on the evening of January 30, a certain person, as procurator and so forth, asked that 56 gold florins be given, paid, and counted to him, on account of a certain partnership and profits of six years and so forth, which he asserts to be 60 florins, from the heirs of Vitalis, referring to the instrument of the said partnership, which he produced. And in the same instant, the judge, by interlocutory judgment, pronounced that the plaintiff should be put in possession according to the said petition, upon the faith of the instrument of the said asserted procurator. However, I do not find that any petition was presented to him, and then followed a corporal immission by the executor, preceding the appearance and contradiction of my lady, or of her procurator, offering himself to the judgment in his own name on behalf of my lady as heir of her father. In the acts, it is well mentioned that he was present at the production of the instrument, but not that any petition was presented to him. Nevertheless, I insist on this point, because simultaneously and at one and the same time the judge demanded and the instrument was produced, but an oath was required from the judge, against which he pronounced the plaintiff to be put in possession, who ought not to be put in possession except by the contumacy of the defendant. And for certain, the judge did not proceed rightly or correctly, but in fact rashly, and without observing the order of law.

† And to this it must be premised as a substantial point that which is required in the first decree, namely, that the defendant be contumacious, as stated in the aforementioned § si vero; and in the Code, On Judges, l. properandum; § sui autem reus; in the Code, On Those Who Are Admitted to an Inheritance, l. praesenti; in the Digest, On the Causes by Which One Comes into Possession, l. 2; and l. hoc autem; in the Digest, That Litigation Not Be Contumacious, c. quam frequenter; § si; noted in the Digest, On Damages Given, l. si; in the Digest, On the Meaning of Words, l. finita; § si plures; in the Decretals, c. dilecto, according to Innocentius. But it is certain that one is not contumacious who appears and offers to separate the law and to answer on the law, as in the Code, On the Right of the Fisc, l. fiscus defensionis, lib. 10; in the Digest, On the Rules of Law, l. non defendere videtur; and in the Digest, On Judges, l. rectis in veniendo. Nor is he contumacious, because he has not yet paid; nor is he contumacious, because the debt was not joined, nor confessed, nor was the instrument liquid in the entire quantity claimed, as in the Digest, On the Status of Freedmen, l. statu lib. ratiocinii; nor did the procurator show his mandate, as these prove: in the Digest, On the Law of Codicils, l. quidam referunt; in the Digest, On Deposit, l. si quis inficiatus; in the Digest, On Acquiring Possession, l. iniuste; in the Digest, On Things Adjudicated, l. si cum nulla; in the Code, On the Execution of Things Adjudicated, l. 1; in the Code, On Peace, l. si pacto, quo poenam; in the Code, On Prohibiting Seizure, l. 1; and l. nequibus; § pe; in the Digest, On Fideicommissary Freedoms; in the Digest, On Those Who, For What Causes, Come into Possession, l. hoc autem; § non defendi; in the Digest, On Judges, l. solui; l. vir bonus. It is no objection that the said lady denied that she was an heir; for the daughter could still have entered upon her father’s inheritance, as in the Code, On Repudiation of an Inheritance, l. si; and while the matter was still intact, she could have repented of her answer, as in the Code, On Interrogation in Actions, l. de aetate; § si; especially since the adversary knew her to be an heir, as appears from his own positions. Therefore, without doubt, the judge of the first cause proceeded precipitately and nullly, and thus the judge to whom the appeal was made ought to have pronounced.

† Now it must be considered, because the judge to whom the weak interlocutory judgment was confirmed, whether this confirmation is interlocutory, so that it can be revoked by the contrary command of the lord count. And it should be said that the confirmation of the first decree is interlocutory, because it does not decide the case, hence it can be revoked by contrary command, de re iudicata, l. quod iussum. And d. c. dilecto. per Inn. and l. arbiter. qui satis dat. cog. instrumentum etiam refutationis generalis generaliter operatur, de pactis, l. emptor. §. lucius. And the decree is rescinded as obreptitious. l. 1. §. haec verba. ne vis fiat ei et d. c. dilecto. per Inn. It is also certain that a procurator legitimately relieved is not bound to give security, insti. de satisdatione, §. vero aliquis. I, Bal. and c. C A §. IN the name of the Lord Amen. V. A, also called V. de la frustra depiziliano, for himself and his heirs on one part, and G. olm obiti de pistorio, formerly inhabitant of the said castle of Piziliano, for himself and his heirs on the other part, for the purpose of conducting trade over any trades and businesses, both of beasts and merchandise, as well as others whatsoever, about which they agreed to conduct business and trade, entered into a partnership with each other, in which said partnership the said G. contributed and placed for his capital 57 florins and just weight according to the common weight of Piziliano, as the said V. confessed and was content that he had received from the said G. in my presence as notary and the undersigned witnesses, and excepted non colla. And placed and consigned by the said G. in the said partnership quantity, and of the aforementioned confession, reception of the said quantity of money made by D. V. from the said G., entirely renouncing, the said Vitalis promised to put into the said partnership 25 florins of gold for his capital, and promised during the said partnership to exercise his person in buying and selling the merchandise of the said partnership inside and outside the castle of Piziliano, as he shall see fit for the best and most useful expedience, and faithfully, diligently to conduct business and trade, and to maintain the said partnership, and in it to solicitously seek profit and revenue, and to carefully guard and preserve the things and goods of the said partnership, which partnership by common agreement of the said parties they wished to last at their pleasure, and whatever from the said partnership, or on its occasion, came into the hands of the said V., to consign in full, to make no credits without the license of the said G. Moreover, at the request of the said G., every year to render an account of the transactions, and to assign the profit, or loss, which God forbid, at the end of the said partnership at the request of the said G. the said V. promised solemnly by himself and his heirs to the recipient for himself and his heirs the said G. well and legally to render an account of all transactions and administrations on the aforementioned occasion, and to bring in the rest according to the custom of a good man and partner, and to consign to him his capital with the share of profit, or loss, if there were loss, which all and each of the said parties promised to each other with solemn stipulation henceforth intervening by themselves and their, and any of their heirs to attend, and observe, and fulfill, and not to do or come against by themselves or another, or others in any way, or cause, ingenuity of law, or of fact to the penalty of 50 florins of gold. stipulated. promised. and reparation of damage, and expenses. and extra, and in the obligation of all their goods, and any of their present and future etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Plurality is not presumed unless it is proven.
2. Where there is conformity of name, identity of person is presumed.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Although it appears that P. G. de M. has been condemned, even though the identity of the person has not been specifically alleged, nevertheless, since it is not established that there are several persons of the same name, plurality is not presumed: for if it were presumed, the sentence would be void on account of obscurity. And thus, in case of doubt, we would presume the sentence to be void, which is ridiculous to say; see *de iudiciis*, l. *eum, quem temere*; in the gloss *de testamento*, l. *duo sunt Titii*. Therefore, plurality of the name is not presumed unless it is proved.

And where there is conformity of name, identity of person is presumed, unless diversity is proved, as in the Digest, title "De duobus reis," law "Qui habebat Flaccum"; and in the Digest, title "De manu testamento," law "Qui habebat." And thus identity of fact is presumed, unless plurality is proved, as in the Digest, title "De iureiurando," law "Qui iurasse," notable section "Si pater"; and law "Eum qui," section "In popularibus." And it is very well supported by what Cynus notes in the Code, title "De episcopis et clericis," law "Si qua per calumniam." The objection from Bartolus in the law "Divus," title "De custodia reorum"; and in the law "Demonstratio," Digest, title "De conditionibus et demonstrationibus"; and in law 1, title "De inutilibus stipulationibus," Digest, title "De verbis obligatis," does not hold, because he speaks of caution, not of necessity; for if he had understood otherwise, he would not have properly considered this point, as often happens in the course of lectures. Nevertheless, I say and advise thus. I, Baldus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who fails to make an inventory is bound to pay legacies beyond the assets of the inheritance.
2. A minor has restitution in integrum when he did not make an inventory, etc.
casus: CASE. In the name of the Lord, Amen. A certain person named Maximus, in his will, instituted his nephew Bartholomew as heir, who imprudently accepted the said inheritance, and without the benefit of inventory. Now the Lord Bishop wishes to compel the said Bartholomew to pay a certain amount of tithes bequeathed by the said Maximus, notwithstanding that the said inheritance is insolvent. Now the question is, what is the law?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the aforementioned point, it must be said that, under canon law, an heir is not compelled to pay beyond the assets of the inheritance, even if he has not made an inventory, as noted in c. *Quamquam*, de usu, lib. 6, and by Hostiensis in his Summa, de test., §. pe., ver. *Item si bona*. But under civil law, a distinction was made between debts and legacies: debts were payable in full (*insolidum*), whereas legacies were payable only to the extent of the estate’s assets (*pro iuribus patrimonii*). C. de iure deliberandi, l. *Si*; §. *Si vero postquam*, C. de regulis iuris, l. *Si universitatem*. However, under the law of the Authenticae, no distinction is made between debts and legacies, because the law fictions that the inheritance is solvent and that the heir has misappropriated assets, as in Auth. de hereditate et falcidia, §. *Si vero sancimus*.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If someone has given or promised a dowry, and is afterwards pronounced a usurer, whether and when creditors on account of usuries are preferred to the one who received it or to whom the dowry was promised.
casus: Case. In the name of God, Amen. The point of the question is as follows: a certain Blasius gave one of his granddaughters in marriage to a certain Petrus, namely born of one of his sons, and promised for her dowry gold florins in this form, namely a piece of land with its boundaries, and 30 gold florins upon the request of the said Petrus, and 50 gold florins after the death of the said Blasius upon the request of the said Petrus; and in the said promise the said Blasius bound himself and all his property to the said Petrus, who was present and accepting, and promised to draw up an instrument of the said promise upon the request of the said Petrus. At length the said Blasius died. After the death of the said Blasius, it was pronounced in the court of the bishopric of Perugia and Chiusi that the said Blasius had been a usurer, and that all his contracts were usurious. After the said pronouncement, the said Petrus took possession of certain property which belonged to the said Blasius by virtue of the aforesaid promise of the aforesaid dowry made to the said Petrus, which property the said Petrus holds and possesses. Now certain persons with whom the said Blasius had contracted usuries long before the promise of the said dowry had been made to the said Petrus claimed the said usuries against the said property possessed [?] by the said Petrus by virtue of the said dowry promised to him; and it being presupposed that discussion was made of the said inheritance of the said Blasius, and it being presupposed that the contracts of those demanding that usuries be restored were concluded long before the said promise of dowry was made to the said Petrus, it is now asked what the law is. I, Baldus.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. Under civil law, this question is determined in l. fi. §. 1. ff. quae in fraud. cre. and it is said there,

† that if a husband receives a dowry in good faith, not with the intention of defrauding prior creditors, the husband cannot be sued by the creditors, because he cannot have an undowered wife; nor is any distinction made there as to whether those creditors hold their claims on account of usury, or in what manner. If, however, the marriage were dissolved, the dowry would have to be restored to the creditors and not to the wife; but if the husband had received it in fraud of the creditors, then he would be liable to them; so states the text there. A fraudulent design, however, is not presumed unless it is proved, ff. de prob. l. quot. §. qui dolo. Under canon law, moreover, there is even greater doubt, because some say that for the restitution of usuries the usurer's goods are altogether tacitly obligated, and then the husband, just as any possessor, could be sued by the hypothecary action after discussion has been made. Others say that only those goods are really obligated that were purchased with usuries, as in extra de vsu. c. cum tu. A third group says that even goods bought with usurious money are not tacitly obligated, and therefore, if they reach someone under an onerous title in good faith, they cannot be taken away from him. Inn. holds this in the said c. cum tu., and Gem. in the same place, and dominus Fed. de Sen. in his consilia, consi. 61., which begins quid talis est, quidam vsurarius; and Io. An. says the same in c. quamquam. de vsu. lib. 6.; and this is especially to be maintained in favor of dowries, l. assiduis. qui po. in pig. hab., and as noted by Bar. in the said l. fi. §. j. Nor does it stand in the way that all instruments have been pronounced simulated, for this does not apply to instruments that are genuine by their very nature, such as an instrument of dowry, as in ff. de ritu nup. l. qui liberos, ff. de act. et obli. l. ex permissione, ff. de condi. ob cau. l. si donaturus, C. de impo. luc. descr. l. 1. lib. 10.; and it must be understood in this way, as noted in spe. de vsu. ver. pone, vsurarius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute that a dowried daughter shall not succeed, can she succeed who was left a dowery in a will?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† There is no doubt under the common law that Brunetta, daughter of Andreotto, succeeds to the place of Andreotto upon his death, having entered into the paternal degree, as stated in the Digest, *De in iustis testibus*, law *Posthumorum*; and in the Institutes, *De haeredibus ab intestato*, section *Cum filiam*. And therefore Ciolo ought to succeed to her at least in her legitime. Furthermore, it is not doubtful that she would succeed to the dowry of her grandmother pro rata, from which Brunetta, upon the death of her mother, would succeed in the dowry of Urimetto the Elder in the person of her mother, according to the Code, *De suis et legitimis haeredibus*, law *Apud hostes*, in the gloss *Pro ea parte*, for that part to which Brunetta, his daughter, would succeed if she were alive. But by the statute, since Brunetta was endowed by her grandfather in the grandfather’s will, she seems to be excluded from the succession of the grandmother, there where it says, “nor can she claim anything”; because the goods of the grandmother seem to be able to be called patronage, according to that well-known maxim of the one who made the statute. And it must be considered that the statute speaks alternatively regarding the endowment, but speaks conjunctively regarding the exclusion; hence, being endowed from one, she seems to be excluded from the succession even of the grandmother. Considering therefore the statute, it appears that Brunetta cannot claim by law except that which was left to Brunetta in the will of Ciolo, because, as I said, it is the common usage of speech that one is called endowed even if endowed in a will, although she is not of marriageable age, as in the law *Cum plures*, section *Pe.*, *De administratione tutorum*, according to Bartolus. Although, regarding the subtlety of words, a dowry is not said to exist where there is not, nor can there yet be a marriage, as in the Digest, *De fideicommissis*, law *Thais*, section *Spem deformem*; *De legatis tertio*, law *Uxor*, section *Codicillis*; through Dyachenko, Code, *De donationibus ante nuptias*, law *Si*; through Dyachenko, nevertheless, from this subtlety of words one departs by the common usage of speech, as noted in the Digest, *De legatis tertio*, law *Librorum*, section *Quod tamen Cassius*; and it supports what is noted in the Extravagantes, *De conversione infidelium*, section *Si*, at the end. It is also said that around the time of birth a marriage was contracted. Then, at fourteen years of age in the month of December, the marriage was dissolved. The question is raised concerning the fruits of the dowry. I answer: the heirs of the husband must have the fruit for as many years as the marriage lasted; afterwards, the fruits belong to the heirs of the wife, as in the laws *Divortio* and *Divisione*, Digest, *De solutione matrimonii*, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a building erected on emphyteutic land is emphyteutic.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A building has been erected on emphyteutic land; nevertheless, the census (ground rent) has never been paid solely for the building, but only for the land. The question arises whether the building is emphyteutic, just as the land is. It appears that it is, because the building accedes to the land and cannot be separated from it and its quality, even by express agreement, as stated in *l. obligationum fere*, § *placet*, *de actionibus et obligationibus*. These improvements made in an emphyteusis remain with the owner; this case is expressly set forth in *l. 2*, C. *de iure emphyteutico*, and in *l. 1*, § 1, *de superficiebus*. Even if the contract stipulated otherwise, because the land was granted under emphyteutic right and the emphyteusis under a proprietary right, thus says Bartolus in *d. l. 2*, that agreements and custom must be observed (*l. creditor*, *communis praediorum*). And I say that the upper part, with the consent of the owner, may be sold by the holder of that upper part under surface right (*ius superficium*), *ff. de iure emphyteutico*, *l. si*. And in our case, it is sufficiently gathered from the payments made for the land and not for the building, and from the attestation of those words, “on which said Peter has a building,” that the land is emphyteutic, but the building is not emphyteutic by original grant, but rather like those contracts in which it is said that the land is granted under leasehold right (*ius libellarium*), but the building under proprietary right, because the pension attests this, and it is confirmed by the word “has,” and by the distinction made in the instrument, and by the building alone in the hand of Ser Nicolaus Cola. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, having seen the ancient instrument and the instrument of payment in the hand of said Nicolaus Ser Cola.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the Friars Preachers may sell, compromise, and make agreements without a decree, and whether, having been enormously injured, they may seek restitution in integrum.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It must be known that the Friars Preachers differ from other churches, because they are bound to sell and ought not to possess for a long time, since they are mendicants; and thus they can sell without a decree of a superior, because this is commanded to them by the canons. Likewise, they can transact and make peace. And see the case in c. ult. de pace, lib. 6. I do not deny that, if they were enormously injured, they can petition for restitution. A continuous quadriennium, which is noted in l. Deo nobis, by Jacobus de Arena and Cynus of Bologna.

CASE. The fact is proposed to be as follows, etc. A certain Huguetius, formerly of Munctioli, had five legitimate sons, Nicolaus, Do. Diacultia, Do. Lixa, Antonius, and Cionus. This Huguetius died and departed from this life intestate, with the said five sons surviving and remaining alive. Of whom the first four, namely Nic., d. Dia., Do. Lixa, and Ant., were born of the first wife of the said Hug., who had predeceased. Cionus, however, was born of the second wife. After this, the aforementioned Do. Lixa died without children and without having made any testament, with the aforementioned Nic., d. Diac., Ant., and Cionus surviving. Finally, the said Nic. died, with several children remaining alive from him, to the said Do. Dia., Ant., and Cionus. After whose death, subsequently, Cionus died, with the said Do. Dia. and Ant. alive. After whose death, Dionysius died, Ant. having previously made his last will, in which he instituted the aforementioned Dia. as heir, since from this Antonius no son remained, who Dionysius died in pupillary age. From him remained the mother of the said Cionus, who still lives, and within a year from the day of the death of the said Hug., her husband, nor even afterwards, assumed the guardianship of the said Cionus, her son. Lastly, the said Do. Dia. died, leaving from her Galeotto Michilini of Facula, son of the said Do. Diacultia. It is now asked, what and how great a portion is due to the said Galeotto Michilini on the part of the said Do. Dia., his mother, in the goods and inheritance of the said Huguetius, and the fruits, and those of his aforementioned sons, it being taken for granted that the said Galeotto has entered upon the inheritance of the said Do. Diac., his mother. On which point counsel is requested, fortified with good and subtle allegations. And before the counsel, briefly state according to Baldus that in the fifth part of Nicola, his sons succeeded; in the fifth part of Do. Diacultia, Galeotto succeeds; in the fifth part of Lixa, Nic. Diacultia and Ant. succeed; in the fifth part of Antonius, Do. Diacultia succeeds ex testamento in solidum; in the fifth part of Cionus, Diacultia, Antonius, and the sons of Nicola succeed. Follows counsel in another manner.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Those related on both sides are preferred over those related on only one side.
2. The sons of brothers succeeded together with the uncle, per stirpes.
3. With the mother excluded and no guardian appointed, the way is opened for other successors.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

It must be premised for clarity that in the intestate succession, those united on both sides (utriusque coniuncti) are preferred over those united on only one side; and in the same manner, the children of those united on both sides are preferred, as stated in C. de legatis et hereditatibus, Authentica Cessante, and C. communia de successionibus, Authentica Itaque, where this matter is fully discussed. This holds true if they have entered upon the inheritance; but if they have not entered upon it, they do not transmit the right, except merely the right of deliberation, according to C. ad Senatusconsultum Orphitianum, Lex Non pro numero, and C. de iure deliberandi, Lex Cum antiquioribus.

Secondly, it must be premised that the sons of brothers, when succeeding together with their uncle, are called to inherit per stirpes, not per capita, as stated in the aforementioned authority *Cessante* and in the commentary on the law of intestate succession, § *Reliquum*, and in the Authority *Ut fratrum filii*, § 1.

Thirdly, it must be premised that where a mother is excluded on account of not having requested a tutor, the way is opened for other successors, as stated in l. 2, § videndum, D. ad Tertullianam, and as noted in l. nepotibus, C. qui petant tutelam. From these authorities it appears that in the inheritance of Lady Lysa Cioni, she did not succeed in any part, her brothers on both sides being conjunctly related to Lady Lysa, and the sons of the aforementioned brothers standing in the name of brothers; and by "brothers and sisters" I understand those referred to in l. Lucius, § quaesitum, D. de pactis, l. tres fratres, and in the Authentica de hereditatibus ab intestato, § penes. Therefore, the intestate successors of Lady Lysa were Nicolaus, Lady Diacultia, and Antonius, with Cioni excluded. To Nicolaus succeeded his sons, according to the Authentica de hereditatibus ab intestato, § penes; and in the inheritance of Nicolaus, they found the third part of Lady Lysa’s share. To Cioni succeeded Lady Diacultia and Antonius, and the sons of Nicolaus, with the mother of the aforementioned Cioni excluded, because she did not request a tutor nor assume guardianship within the year, as provided in l. 2, § si iure, D. ad Tertullianam, C. de legatis hereditatibus, and l. sciant. As for whether Antonius succeeded by will: if Lady Diacultia took possession of the inheritance of Lady Diacultia, Galeotus, her son, succeeded to the inheritance of Lady Diacultia. He found the said inheritances devolved to her in the order mentioned, and he is entitled to them and their fruits, because inheritances are increased by fruits, as stated in l. item veniunt, § fructus, D. de petitione hereditatis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A daughter burdened with restitution may, after her death, give all her goods in the meantime as dowry, and indeed in any manner whatsoever.
2. If goods subject to restitution have been given in dowry in good faith, they are not revoked upon the arrival of the time for restitution; otherwise, if they were alienated in any other way.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A daughter burdened with the duty of restitution after her death may, in the interim, not only give all her goods in dowry, but also alienate them in any manner whatsoever, as is stated in C. communia de legibus, l. si; §. si autem avaritiae cecitatis; and non ff. ad Trebellianum, l. Marcello; §. res, quae; de legibus 2, l. peto; §. praedium. But there is this distinction between a dowry and another alienation, because other alienations are revoked as void if the condition of substitution remains in force.

But the dowin, insofar as it has been given in good faith with due moderation, is not revoked as void, even if there exists a condition of a fideicommissum, as the Authentica Res, quae communia, De legatis, teaches. This is to be understood as follows: if the daughter dies, the remnants of the marriage remain in the marriage, namely the common children, the cause of the promise having ceased to have effect; and the dowin returns to the fideicommissum, because a temporary cause has a temporary effect, as the Digest, De iure patronatus, Law Adigere, § Quamvis, states. I therefore conclude in the case at hand: since all the goods were in the dowin, I say that the husband must gain one-third part of all the goods, if the wife died before the husband, because this third must be taken from the whole body of the dowin, which by agreement includes all the goods. For it is necessary that the part be derived from the whole, as the Digest, Ad legem Falcidiam, Law In ratione, § Et filio, words "ut enim opes," teaches.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A prescription introduced by common law or municipal law does not run against a son under paternal power.
2. Prescription is interrupted by the appointment of an executor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A prescription, whether introduced by the common law or by municipal law, does not run against a son or daughter. C. de anna. exce. l. 1. in fi. And therefore, as long as Ser Daniel lived, no prescription ran against my lady. But after the death of Ser Daniel, it began to run,

† However, because before the completion of 20 years there was a broken promise of the executor, prescription does not run, as in C. de praescrip. 30. ann. l. cum notissimi, and noted in l. si, de eo, per quem factum erit, according to Guillaume and according to Baldus in l. 2, § si; and therefore, in conclusion, it is that the prescription is not decided against my lady, and her petition proceeds notwithstanding the passage of time. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether witnesses examined concerning a crime may be examined concerning a contract.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The mode of defense is this: that on behalf of Angelutius, those witnesses who testified in that case are produced to prove the same thing, namely, that the penalty had been waived by agreement; for otherwise, the said witnesses would not be probative, since it is a different cause and action is brought for a different purpose. Now, it is first necessary to prove in this judgment that agreement or pact, and then the accused will come to be absolved. This is proven by the statements and the theory of the doctors, namely Innocentius in *causam*, *de testibus* and *de iureiurando*, *mulieri*; and although there are public attestations concerning the crime, this does not prevent them from being received concerning the pact, because it is a different chapter, as fully noted by Innocentius and others in *extra*, *de testibus*, *fraternitatis*, and in the Code, *de tempore appellationum*, *per hanc*.

CASE. The case is as follows. A certain Landutius Andreae made a will, in which he instituted his nephew, Lord Franciscus, as heir, and in the said will, among other things, he disposed of lands and houses, concerning which counsel is requested in this manner, namely: Furthermore, he wished, ordered, and commanded that the said houses of the said testator, in which this testator now dwelt, should in no way be sold, alienated, or pledged in any manner by his heir or any other person, but should always stand and remain for the perpetual memory of the said testator and his descendants, in which houses, namely from the front side towards the contract of the Burgus, there should be placed, as it were, the arms of the said testator inlaid in a certain stone, so that they may be seen well and clearly. Furthermore, he wished that if his said heir should at any time die without legitimate and natural sons, the said houses should devolve upon Landutius Petri and the legitimate and natural male sons of the said Landutius, so that they should in no way be sold or alienated, but should always pass to the sons born and to be born in the direct line of the said testator who are nearest. And if any sale or alienation were made by anyone, it should not be valid, but it should devolve and ought to devolve upon the fraternity of St. Mary of Aretio under the aforementioned condition. Now, the said Franciscus dies without sons, and he institutes the said fraternity as heir; then the said Landutius dies, to whom the said houses had been left, remaining without male sons after all the aforementioned persons. A certain man named Lucas, son of Baldinus Lucae of the acceptants, claims that the said houses pertain to him, since no one is a nearer male relative than he alone, namely, if he were born of the same consorts, in which degree he stands with the said Landutius. Now it is asked, up to what degree the said houses devolve upon the said Lucas, if he were in the said degree of kinship with the said Landutius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When the testator used words of this kind, “to the perpetual memory of the testator and of his [suorum],” what does the word “his [suorum]” signify?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. However, upon the death of Vannutius’s closest relatives, the will speaks in the clause of Landutius. D. de executione tutorum, l. 2, § non solum; D. de verborum significatione, l. liberorum; in Auth. de restitutione fideicommissi, § manifestum. And in this case, it is extended indefinitely to all descendants, because this is the testator’s meaning, although otherwise the term “son” is used strictly, as is evident in the cited laws.

But in the upper part of the testament, for the perpetual memory of the said testator and of his *sui*, it must be seen what is meant by *sui*, and whether it comprehends spouses or collaterals, up to which degree it comprehends them, and whether it extends itself infinitely in collaterals, as it does in descendants. And this is a fine point. This word, *suus*, signifies according to the dative and the substantive. For if I say, *his thing*, it is sometimes understood strictly for him who has the rights of *suietas*, as in D. de lib. et posth. l. in suis; and Inst. de haer. ab intest. § sui; D. de lib. et posth. l. Gallus, § in omnibus. Sometimes, even if he does not have the civil right of *suietas*, and thus broadly, D. de suis et leg. l. 1.
