Sometimes it is said most broadly, *his heir*, D. ad Treb. l. sibi haer.; D. de facto, § si. If, however, I say *his agnate*, it extends beyond to the tenth degree. The same today if I say *his cognate*, as Inst. de suc. agn. § si. But if I say *his nearest*, it is understood up to the seventh degree, and certain persons of the seventh, as in the said § si, ver. proximitas vero. Sometimes it is not understood otherwise, as C. de adult. l. quamuis adulterii. The difficulty of the point therefore lies in this, because the condition of *sui* is substantiated in itself, and does not have some substantive designating the truth of the word, unless we apply the latter words to the former indefinite words, because below it says *nearest*. But to this response stands in the way that word *perpetual* from D. de serv. urb. praec. l. eum debere. This is a question of will, yet as much as can be presumed from law, that *sui* seems to be determined by the word *nearest*. And because he who cannot be nearer to the seventh degree according to civil law, I think it should be restricted, so that we may declare the doubtful understanding in principle by the process of the writing, D. de leg. 1. l. si servus plurium, § si. Among these degrees, the nearest is he whom no one precedes, D. de verb. sig. l. proximus; D. de suis et leg. l. post consanguinei, § si. And what I said is expressly determined by the gloss, C. ad Turpil. l. si foemina. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. In how many ways can several executors be appointed, and whether, when two executors are left, each for a half, or each for a part, either can carry out the execution alone even after a year.
casus:
CASE. The case is as follows. A certain Pagnus made a testament, in which he instituted the poor of the fraternity of St. Mary of la Mia of Arezzo as his universal heirs, in which certain testament he left his wife, Lady Joanna, as usufructuary of all his goods for the whole time of her life. Then he made codicils, in which he left and wished to be given from his goods by his heirs to the religious man, Brother Angelo Megli, his nephew, and to Lady Joanna, his wife, two thousand gold florins, which the said Brother Angelo and Lady Joanna, and each of them for half, are to hold and must give, distribute, and expend to both miserable persons and relatives, as well as to any other persons whatsoever, to whom the said Brother Angelo, Lady Joanna, and each of them shall see fit and please. Then, when it was said that the said Pagnus was not of sound mind at the time the said codicil was made, it was reformed by the appropriate councils of the city of Arezzo, as is more fully contained in the words of the reformations transmitted. After the said Pagnus died, the rectors of the said fraternity entered upon the said inheritance, and are and were in peaceful possession of it, and the said Lady Joanna and Brother Angelo remained after the death of the said Pagnus for many years. Then the said Brother Angelo died, the said Lady Joanna surviving, and enjoying the usufruct of the goods of the said inheritance; the said Brother Angelo disposed of nothing of the aforesaid during his lifetime. The said Lady Joanna, being in her last moments, made her last testament, in which she left and made legacies from her own and dotal goods to various persons. And afterwards, concerning the said two thousand gold florins, which she said she could and ought to distribute from the goods of the said Pagnus, she made such disposition, namely: "Item, she asserted that it was established by the hand of Ser Nardo, notary of Arezzo, in a certain codicil made by the said Pagnus, in which he had left to the said Lady and Brother Angelo Megli, his nephew, the power to distribute from his goods two thousand gold florins, as thus or otherwise established by the hand of the said notary, wishing to put the codicil into execution, she distributed and bequeathed from the goods of the said Pagnus the underwritten quantity of money and gold florins, or rather from the goods of the said Pagnus, which are of the value of the underwritten quantities bequeathed, first to certain daughters of the household, etc."

Now it is asked whether the said codicils of two thousand gold florins are invalid by the said reformation, and if they are not, whether the said Lady could dispose in her last will of the said two thousand gold florins, or only of one thousand, so that the said fraternity is bound to pay the said legacies or distributions made by her in whole or in part to those who are named in the said testament, or distributively, or whether it is bound to give to other persons and distribute as the said fraternity shall will, and whether by the disposition made by Lady Joanna in her said testament an action lies against the said heirs of Pagnus for the said heirs of Lady Joanna, or rather whether it lies for those named in the said testament without distribution, and whether the heirs of the said Lady Joanna can claim dowries against the heirs of the said Pagnus in what quantity, since it appears that the said Lady Joanna left her dowries by right of legacy in her said testament, as is contained in the said testament, or whether the claim lies for the legatees.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be considered that when several executors are appointed jointly and severally, sometimes simply, sometimes the execution is divided among them by the testator, so that in the first case each appointed executor is not an executor pro parte, because each of them can fulfill the office entrusted to him; in the second case, if one dies or acts from afar, the survivor can nevertheless fulfill the office, but if they are present, it must be done by all. c. Religiosus, § Sane pluribus, De testibus, lib. 6. In the third case, each can execute pro parte, and nothing accrues to him by the death of the other. d. c. Verum si testator, ff. De manumissione testamento; l. Si ita fuerunt, ff. De legatis 3; l. Lucius, § Quisquis. Since it is said here that each of the executors can act for one-half, therefore Domina Joan was not left as an executor except for one thousand florins; for the other thousand, she alone had no power, nor could she make any execution. Therefore, it must be seen regarding the thousand [florins] in which she had power, whether she could make the execution in the manner and time in which she did it, and truly that she could, notwithstanding perhaps that the year had elapsed, because as long as she lives, she has the power of choosing even by making a will. ff. De legatis 2, l. Cum quidam; and l. Unum ex familia. To the contrary it seems, because after a year the office of the testamentary executor for pious causes expires. De episcopis et clericis, l. Nulli. But here it seems disposed for pious causes, as noted by Innocentius, Extra, De testibus, c. Cum tibi. Solution: It seems to be said that this testator does not seem to have considered only the pious cause, but also the connection of his own family, whence it is presumed more in consideration of the person than of the cause, as noted in the said c. Religiosus, in the glossa ordinaria; and C. De sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. Illud; and ff. De excusationibus tutorum, l. Tutor petitus, § Quae tutoribus. And therefore it seems she could distribute the one thousand florins even after the year, as the said l. Cum quidam; and there by Bartolus, argumentum: even by making a will, as the said l. Unum ex familia, § Itaque. And persons thus declared have an action from the will against the brotherhood as universal heir, as if they had been declared in the will. l. Ea; l. § Si de falcidia; and l. Utrum, § Cum quidam, De rebus dubiis. I say that for pious causes she could not distribute after the year, because the execution had devolved to the bishop, as the said l. Nulli. But within the year she could make distribution of the one thousand florins, however, as I said, even in the will. But the reformation made in this matter is of no value, as C. De testibus, l. Testamentum. To what I said about the year, it contributes Extra, De testamentis, c. Nos quidam; and what is noted there by Innocentius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When a statute requires presence, consent, or authority, whether one can authorize, consent, etc., for oneself.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It must be premised for clarity that sometimes a statute speaks of presence, sometimes of authority, sometimes of consent, and sometimes alternatively of consent or authority. If the statute speaks of presence, one may invoke presence for one’s own benefit, even if the presence solemnizes the act, as in D. 50.16.1 (Digest, On the Obligation of Words), in the principal part. If, however, the statute speaks of consent, then either, by reason of the quality of the person who must consent, the consent is authorized, such as the consent of the legitimate father-administrator in the act of his son; and then the gloss and Decius speak in D. 26.1.1 (Digest, On the Authority of Tutors). But if the consent does not contain authority in itself, but only will, one may also consent for one’s own benefit, as in D. 18.1.17 (Digest, On Contracting Sale), § fundum. If, however, we are speaking of strict authority, then one cannot authorize oneself, as in the aforementioned D. 26.1.1. The same applies if the statute speaks conjunctively of authority and consent; but if it speaks alternatively, namely as if it were consent, it is concluded from these things that, having seen the said statute, the husband may invoke his presence, even when the husband himself is instituted heir by his wife, as occurred in the testament of Lady Francischina. It is true that the legitimate portion and the third are due to his husbands, as in Auth. de tut. § et se post patri. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the way is barred to the instituted heir when the first substitute dies while alive. Secondly, whether it is opened.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Although the first substitute dies while the instituted heir is still alive, and thus the first substitution becomes void, the way is not barred for the second substitute, but rather opened, as C. de caducis tollendis § 1; secondly, this is noted in the glossa ordinaria, ff. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. qui habebat; to this effect, ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Publius § 1 at the end. Therefore, although Luca predeceased, Ursa succeeds, the condition of the substitution being attached, and the property subject to restitution could not be alienated, unless until Trebellian, ff. ad Trebellianum, l. Marcellus § res, quae etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a will is valid in which a son is instituted heir under a casual condition.
2. If the testator left his wife as dominus, massaria, and usufructuary, and after her death, or after the said wife had relinquished the said rights, he instituted his daughter, which of these should be called the universal heir.
casus: CASE In the name of God, Amen. The point on which counsel is requested is as follows. A certain man named Nardalus Vanotii of Orte made his will, in which among other things he disposed in this form: "Furthermore, I leave my wife, Lady Angela, as usufructuary of all my goods for the whole time of her life, if she lives as a woman according to chastity and honesty, and wishes to remain in my house. And after her death, in the said goods left to her, and in all my movable and immovable goods, rights, and actions, wherever they may be and can be found, I institute my universal heirs to be Prona, my daughter, and Peter Meri of Lord Tebald, in equal shares, as is contained in the aforementioned will." Now the question arises on two points: first, whether the said will is valid; second, if it is valid, who is said to be the universal heir, assuming as certain that the said testator died, and after his death the said Peter died before the event occurred, on the occurrence of which the institution of him was made.
body: Having examined the aforesaid point, for the clarification of the said point

† it is first to be seen whether the said testament is valid. And it seems that it is not, because, as appears from the series of the said testament, the said Prona, daughter of the said testator, was not instituted unconditionally (pure), but after the death of the said Angela, her mother and formerly wife of the said testator, or after the said goods have been abandoned by the said Lady Angela; and thus she is instituted under a casual condition, and consequently the testament is not valid, as in l. si pater, ff. de inst. et sub., [and] ff. de haer. instit. l. suus quoque. And the Ultramontani hold this opinion, namely that such a testament is also not valid, in the said l. si pater; and Gul. de Cu. in l. quoniam in prioribus, C. de inof. te., holds [the same]. The gl. in l. si pater and the said l. suus quoque holds the contrary, which says that today by the said l. quoniam, with respect to the legitimate portion owed by natural law, because the legitimate portion is owed to a son or daughter, every condition and postponement is rejected ipso iure; and Azo holds the same in sum. of that title de inst. et sub.; and this second opinion seems truer. And the text in l. sancimus, §. cum autem, C. de inof. te., seems to support this opinion, where if someone is asked to make restitution to a son after the death of the person so requested, with respect to the legitimate portion owed by natural law every postponement is by law itself discarded, and the son must have the legitimate portion immediately; the remainder above the legitimate portion he will indeed have after the death of the person requested according to the testator's disposition. It is therefore concluded from the aforesaid that the said testament is also valid, since the said Prona remains instituted unconditionally in the legitimate portion, although she ought not to be admitted to the remainder of the inheritance except upon the occurrence of the condition of the aforesaid testament, as in the said l. sancimus, §. cum autem.

† Secondly, it is to be seen who is the universal heir of the said testator, regarding which it seems should be said according to law that the universal heir is the said Angela. For although elsewhere we have the doctrine of the gl. and Doctors as to what the said words import, 'I leave my wife mistress and usufructuary', whether children or strangers have been instituted, as noted by the gl. and Doctors in auth. hoc locum, C. si secundo nup. mulier, and Dy. in l. Titia cum testamento, §. fi., de le. 2, and in Spec., [tit.] qui fi. sint le., ver. quid si ita, §. 1; nevertheless, those laws speak where a son or a stranger has been instituted unconditionally as universal heir, as appears in them; but in our case no one has been instituted unconditionally as universal heir, because neither the said Prona has been instituted unconditionally as universal heir, nor the said Petrus, but only after the death of the said Angela, or after the goods have been abandoned; therefore etc. I will say, therefore, in our case that the said Lady Angela, who was left mistress and usufructuary of all his goods during her lifetime, as long as she lives chastely and honestly, is immediately universal heir, as if the word 'I leave', since it is joined to the totality of goods and there is no other universal heir, were drawn to the institution of an heir, as is noted in l. his verbis, in prin., ff. de haere. insti., and in Auth. de haere. et fal., §. si vero. The universal heir is therefore none other than the said Angela, and the said Prona must have her legitimate portion immediately, with every postponement and condition removed and rejected from the legitimate portion; but to the remainder of the inheritance she cannot come except upon the arrival of the event of restitution, namely the mother's death, or that the goods have been abandoned by the mother, as in the said §. cum autem, in l. sancimus. And the legitimate portion of this Prona is the third part of the goods which the father had at the time of his death, after deducting debts and funeral expenses, as in auth. novissima, C. de inof. test., and in Auth. de trien. et se., §. 1, joined with l. Papinianus, §. quarta, ff. de inof. test. Concerning Petrus, because he was instituted together with Prona, no account is to be taken, since he died before the fulfillment of the condition under which he was instituted; and consequently the institution made of him vanished, and he transmitted nothing to his heir, as in l. j., §. si autem, C. de cadu. toll., and l. haeredes mei, §. cum ita, and what is noted there, ff. ad treb., and ff. de vul. et pup. l. sed et si plures, in prin., with the like. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a syndic can bind all members of a corporation, even those who do not consent.
casus: CASE. The point on which counsel is sought is as follows: The men of the village of San Cristofano del Colle, and also of San Nicolao del Colle, appointed syndics to make peace among themselves and to purchase one Palace with a certain territory, so that they might build a castle there, as will be shown below in detail. Finally, a fortification or castle was built in the village of San Nicolao del Colle, where the said Palace and territory were, with the license and will of the officials in charge of the custody of the city and community of Perugia. Now, the villages of San Cristofano and San Nicolao appoint syndics to obtain the legitimate guard and to pledge all and each of the men of the villages of San Cristofano and San Nicolao who have not paid the taxes imposed for the building of the said castle or fortification. And among others, two are burdened, who oppose this, contradicting it, and allege that they are not bound, because they never consented to the union and the agreements made, of which mention is made above, and thus they could not be prejudiced, since they do not intend to reside in the said castle of San Nicolao, nor do they have their homes in the village of San Cristofano, and there they wish to pay the duties and taxes, provided that they wish to pay those which are imposed for the building of the said castle of San Nicolao, etc. Now the question is, having seen all the aforementioned ordinances and the form of the agreements, and having seen the statutes of the community of Perugia speaking on this matter, whether the said two can defend themselves in law and are not bound to pay for the building of the said castle.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† We must consider whether the said syndic was made in the legitimate form of the universitas, and whether he was constituted in a sufficient number; for then that which is done by the greater part of those having voice, when two parts are assembled, is referred to all, as in D. de regulis iuris, l. Aliud, §. Refertur. Here the question arises whether this is true when the greater part enters into new contracts in the name of the universitas; and it is true, because the glossa ordinaria says in the said §. Refertur that that §. has place in contracts; for it is certain that universitates can contract, as in D. si certum petatur, l. Certas; D. de contrahenda emptione, l. Sed Celsus; D. de dolo, l. Sed ex dolo, §. Si; C. de venditione cum in rubro et nigro. And this cannot be carried out in fact by all on account of the difficulty of assembling them, hence recourse is had to the rule of l. Quod maior, and the addition to §. Refertur. To the contrary it seems, because no one is compelled to contract against his will, D. commoda, l. Commodata, §. Sicut; C. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. Sicut; C. de iure deliberandi, l. Nec emere. Moreover, the act of the universitas does not bind individuals when they have not consented, D. de maioribus et conveniendis, l. 1, §. 1, and note in l. 2, C. quae sit longa consuetudo. But to this it seems that individuals are not bound to the one contracting with the universitas, but the universitas itself is bound; however, since there is nothing in the chest of the universitas from which payment can be made, those of the universitas distribute among themselves by weight and measure, hence individuals are bound to contribute to the body of the universitas, D. quod quisque universitatis, note in l. 1, §. Quibus, note by Innocentius in c. Gravem, de sententia excommunicationis. Moreover, the purchase of the said fortification seems to have been publicly and privately useful on account of the imminent war and the social troubles afflicting the country, and that which is usefully done by the greater part ought to be ratified by the lesser, argument from D. de negotiorum gestione, l. Pomponius, and fully noted by Innocentius de constitutionibus, c. Cum omnes. Before coming to the solution, it is necessary to premise that that which is done by the greater part of the men who make up the body of the universitas, in some respects is compared to that which is done by the owner, namely as regards those doing it, and in some respects is compared to that which is done by the administrator, namely as regards certain absentees; therefore, such an act should be done as would be done by the administrator, binding the owner. When therefore such contracts are made, a good judge will determine variously from the persons and causes, D. de rei venditione, l. In fundo. For if the expense which unduly burdens the absentees, because they hold the greatest part of the sum of the castle, and they were not consulted, it is unjust to compel them, argument from C. qui bonorum cessio possit, l. Si; D. de pactis, l. Maiorem, and l. Cum in eo, especially if they have other safe refuges, to which if the matter is referred, it is uselessly managed, D. de negotiorum gestione, l. Sed an ultro, §. Pe; D. de iure et facto ignorato, l. Iniquissimum, unless such necessity existed that it had to be done thus and not otherwise; for necessity has no law, l. 1, de officiis consulum. But if it is expressly for the common good, not unduly burdensome, and expedient for the whole body there, which regards the common good, not that of the buyers, yet it is of singular interest. Utility, which is not subject to one, is not called the utility of the universitas, D. de usucapione, l. Rerum mistura. But when it is subject to one name, and the effect regards all, even the absentees must contribute according to the rule given by Innocentius. It is certain that when these burdens, which have an impositive cause, are imposed, those who are not of that body are entirely exempt. But if the city imposed them, all who are under the city would be bound. And from this it appears whether those received into the city are bound or not; for the imposition of the city introduced nothing, although the officials of the city presumed to build that castle. For by this it was not their intention to make them exempt and citizens of that castle, as D. ad municipalia, l. Praeterea; C. de sententiis, l. Decurionibus, lib. 12; D. de legibus, l. Ab omnibus. Hence, as to this last point, the law is this: if they are exempt and citizens before, they are bound as to burdens. And in this regard, the instruments and statutes speaking on the matter must be examined. But beware, if all of the village except one wish to acquire a new domicile in the village or in another castle, and one alone wishes to remain in the village and old domicile, his voice is stronger in contradicting by himself than that of all others against him; for domicile is established by fact and one's own mind, not by the mind of another, as D. ad municipalia, l. Non utique, and l. Domicilium. Hence, if the whole colony transfers itself to another place with only one remaining, he does not follow it, nor is he of that body, nor is he bound to the burdens of this transfer, D. de assessore, l. Si eadem. No one is therefore bound to follow a new centuria and new inhabitancy, and he who would say the contrary would be a beast. Hence, since the new castle, from which a new domicile arises, is outside the body of the old village of Saint Christopher, assuming it is a village, they did not consent to pursue it or invoke it, because no one is bound to contract new domiciles or follow those contracting them, nor to be bound by them, as has been said. The discretion also sometimes regarding custody, fortification, and garrisoning regards the repair and adaptation, not the total invention of new works, as in c. 1, §. Pe, de religiosis domibus, lib. 6; D. de itinere actuque privato, l. 4, §. Pe. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a son’s will, in which he omits his mother, is void, and whether it suffices to leave something to her under the title of legacy.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is true that if a son omits his mother by not instituting her as heir, nor disinheriting her, his will is null; nor does it suffice merely to leave her something under any title of legacy, as in the Authentica "Ut cum" on the cognizance of appeals, §. Aliud quoque capitulum. There the matter is fully discussed and determined by Jacobus de Belvisio, although Bartolus says the contrary erroneously in the law "Siue" on the right of patronage. Therefore, this mother succeeds as an intestate heir, the institution of the said brother Gabriel being broken. And according to the common law, she is bound to restore the inheritance, the codicillary legacy being retained, which is the legitime, namely one-third, as in the Authentica "De trien." and thus it is according to the common law. The municipal law does not apply, because it does not speak to our case, since the father of the said son died testate. To this end, the last chapter of the statute speaking on the matter of usufruct, even if it must be had by virtue of the legacy, especially on account of the codicillary clause: I say this on account of the notable gloss and doctors in the law "Maximum vitium" at the end, on the freeing of those omitted, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a pact concerning the succession of a third party, regarding whose life the contracting parties were uncertain, is valid.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the first point, it was said that the pact concerns the succession of a third party, whose life was uncertain to the contracting parties. C. de captiuis et postliminio reuersis, l. nec nos præterit. Moreover, the final cause, namely the will and succession to the devil, fails upon his arrival; and therefore the pact granted to him as a successor fails: as ff. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. si. For it is certain that a Catholic son is superior to the devil both in degree and in right, as C. de legatis et hereditatibus, auth. post fratres, and in the concordant authorities, from which it is gathered. From these, it is concluded that the said Cegolus is not effectively bound to the said one hundred and nine florins.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether in the vindication of a thing on a hereditary ground it is called a hereditary question.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† The said case, in which a claim is brought by vindication of the thing (rei vindicatio) arising from the ground of hereditary ownership, expressed in the libel and in the acts of the proceedings, does not seem capable of being submitted to arbitration: because it is a case in which the plaintiff asserts that he succeeds to the ownership by reason of proximity of intestacy and as heir to his mother, as appears from the acts of the proceedings; for ownership arises for the successor from succession, ff. de acqui. pos. l. cum haeredes, and from ownership arises the rei vindicatio, as noted in ff. de eden. l. 1 in prin. Therefore, the ground joined to the conclusion renders this question hereditary by way of the cause [of action], ff. de acqui. pos. l. 3. §. ex plurimis and ff. de pub. l. sunt et quia aliae; and because he acted in this way and declared this by formulating articles, it does not seem capable of being submitted to arbitration. To the contrary stands ff. ad exhib. l. ex eo. §. fi., because he did not sue as heir, but as owner, and the defendant is sued on the basis of present possession, not past possession; and therefore we measure both principles of the rei vindicatio here from the person of the claiming heir and of the defendant who is sued; whence it does not seem that the proper question is a hereditary one, in which the dispute is over singular ownership and where proof from any source whatsoever suffices, de pet. haeredit. l. et non tantum. §. quod si pro emptore. Likewise, the statute must be understood as concerning hereditary questions principally, not incidentally, de li. agno. l. si quis a liberis. §. si vel parens; and an arbitration can be requested up to the publication of the witnesses, l. si rem. §. fi. in glo. fi. ff. de euictio, or up to the conclusion in the cause. What shall we say? I reply: having considered the libel and its general conclusion regarding restitution on every ground, and having considered the allegation of grounds and the libel, I say that there is no place for arbitration, since the plaintiff could prevail on a hereditary ground if he were to prove it in a petition of inheritance: therefore it is a hereditary question, ff. de petit. haere. l. minimam; ff. si pars haere. peta. l. 1 in princi. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether place and time should be specified according to the form of the libel, etc., in the impeachment of a usurer witness.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

Whether it is necessary to include in the libel of impeachment against a manifest usurer the place and time, and with whom, as if the matter were being pursued criminally, as in l. libellorum; or civilly, as in Extra de procuratoribus, c. tuae; or as in the case of a crime from writing, as in Extra de testibus, c. praesentium; de exceptionibus, c. pia; de probationibus, lib. 6; and in c. constitutionem, de electionibus, in the Clementines. Or whether it is not necessary, because the action is not for punishment, nor is a crime imputed to the defendant, but rather the delict of a third party, as in ff. quod metus causa, l. si cum exceptione, §. in hac; and because from this objection the defendant is not defamed, hence it is not necessary to oppose the place and time, as noted in ff. de dolo, l. Item exigitur, according to Bartolus in l. praetor edixit, in principio, de iniuriis; according to Bartolus in l. praetor. It must be said that it is not necessary for the libel to be circumstanced, because a universal cause is objected, and the crime is alleged in general, as in c. alter, de re iudicata, lib. 6. It supports what is noted by Bartolus in l. haec etiam, de suspectis tutoribus; and l. 2, §. si publico, ff. de adulteriis. Otherwise, what shall we say if it is unknown from whom he extorted usury? For example, a Florentine practiced usury in England, and made his will in Florence, and it is established that he lent money at interest in England, but it is not established to whom he lent; will the will be valid on account of this uncertainty? Certainly not. Therefore, if the person from whom he extorted is not to be named, the libel proceeds without circumstances. It supports de iudicibus, l. cum sit, from which we see that it appears that action is even taken against the usurer himself; because it is said that in a usurious contract, where restitution of usury is sought, the month and place of the extorted usury are not inserted; because the crime is not intended for condemnation, but for the condictio indebiti. Hence, Speculum, who omitted nothing in the form of libels, did not place these circumstances in such a libel, as appears in Speculum de usuris, fourth part, in principio. From these reasons, it is clear that the said libel proceeds. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
0. the matter, which is expected to be raised in the prince's consistory.
1. Whether the original document may be entrusted to another, and what is required of the subscribers.
casus: In the name of God, Amen. The facts are proposed as follows. In the court of the Prelate of Perugia, a certain question was being debated between Nicolaus, son of Baldus of Perugia, concerning a certain house on one side, and the daughters of Bartholomew Marini, and the lady Mattheola on the other side, before the Lord Vicar of the said Court. The said Lord Vicar gave a definitive sentence against the said Nicolaus, who appealed from the said sentence to the Supreme Pontiff; and finally he appointed a certain procurator to prosecute the said appeal. The said procurator, towards the end of the year, within a month and a half, or thereabouts, appeared at the door of the lodging of the Lord Pope, and requested, as is said, one of the doorkeepers of the first gate, to permit him to enter to the Supreme Pontiff; because he wished to ask that a judge be given over the said appeal. He requested a notary, as appears from the said appearance by a certain document written by the hand of the said notary. Finally, on the last day of the said year, the said Nicolaus appeared before the said Lord Vicar, and produced the said appearance made by his said procurator. It is said on behalf of the said two parties, that the said opposition is abandoned, since it was not prosecuted within the year, and there is no proof of any other prosecution, except only the said single presentation at the said door, and that the said document is not valid, nor should faith be given to it, since a document written by the hand of another, notwithstanding the subscription of the said notary; because, assuming that he subscribed himself, he could not delegate another to write. Now the question is, what is the law.
body: If the diligence of the appellant is established, the time periods do not run. In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Neither law nor necessity can be imposed upon the Lord Pope; and therefore, if the diligence of the appellant is established, the time limits do not run in a case which is expected to be brought before the consistory of the Prince. C. de temp. app. auth. sed lis; and q. 6. c. anteriorum; extra de app. c. ex insinuat. However, it is not sufficient to go to the Palace of the Prince once to protest, but one must strive often and most insistently; because in introducing and exercising an appeal, the utmost diligence is required, as l. 1. ff. de libellis dimisso, in the words "instanter" and "saepe". Nor should one immediately protest and withdraw when access is denied; but one must knock at the door of the Pope and press with utmost effort, which is proven by open appearances. ff. de pigno. l. 4. And one must appear at the time when audience is granted, i.e., when it is customary to be granted. ff. quando ap. sit. l. 1. §. quid igitur. Where exact diligence has not been observed, the appeal would appear to be abandoned by the lapse of time, as noted in C. de appe. l. eos. in principio; and ff. de excus. tuto. l. scire oportet. §. sufficit, a text which serves this purpose excellently. To this effect: ff. de usuris. l. mora, at the end of the beginning. Moreover, it does not appear here at what hour the appearance was made; it must necessarily be established that it was at a suitable hour, as d. §. quid igitur; de offi. dele. c. consuluit. And therefore, if it clearly appears in all respects, the said appeal is abandoned. And this concludes the first point.

† On the second point, I say that the original document cannot be entrusted to another, as in the Authentica de tabellis, §. nos autem; however, if it is established that it was written by the hand of the requested notary, and another notary takes it, and the original notary removed the original—perhaps because he himself was impeded—then such a document would make faith; nevertheless, the subscribing notary must make mention that he took it from the true original, as noted in the said §. nos autem by Lauro de Bellis. One must, however, incessantly pursue the appeal, as in the Authentica de his, qui ingrediuntur ad appellandum, §. 1, and there by Lauro de Bellis.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When an appeal is prohibited by statute, against the sentences of the consuls and other chamberlains, and recourse is allowed elsewhere. The section "recourse" appears to be permitted, if the words of the statute are deficient; what will be the meaning of such a statute?
2. Relatives placed indefinitely are to be repeated.
1. The fact is this: Appollonius Massarelli of Assisi, his
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† By statute, appeal is prohibited from the sentences of the consuls and of the other chamberlains, as in the statute *volumus*. And from their sentences, it is prohibited there, and recourse, there, when it says, nor in any manner is recourse to be had. And against this it is objected, and rather it seems that recourse may be had to the prior lords, or to the chapter of the people, as in the same statute, verse *volumus tamen*. Therefore, distinguish the persons, and you will reconcile the paragraphs, for either the instance is made to an artisan, or to the craft, or to another artisan, who litigated before such a chamberlain: or to another person. If to an artisan, recourse is promised; if not to an artisan, it is not promised. And this seems to be gathered there, when it says, to an artisan or to the craft: or who before, as if *anes* [anyone] were understood as the antecedent of this relative, who is of the same quality: so that the sense is, to an artisan, or to the craft, or to another artisan, who before, etc.

For even relative terms, when placed indefinitely, are to be repeated with the same quality in different subjects; similarly, this alternative word, "or," is accustomed to alternate between equals, as is proven by these authorities: D. de vino, tritic. vel oleo legato, l. si, §. cui dulcia; and D. de pen. legat., l. nam quod liquide, §. si cui penus; and D. de re dubia, l. 1. But this interpretation is not pleasing, for in interpreting laws or statutes, absurdity must be avoided; and the same applies to privileges and rescripts. Thus, a law should be understood in such a way that the legislator cannot be reproached by a wise person, as in D. de leg. praest., l. Sabinus, Ariston; and D. de vulg. sub., l. ex facto, in princ. But the aforementioned exposition would be absurd, because the law should be general and not favor some kind of monopoly, as in X. de testib., c. cum omnis. Hence, Dynus says: "The law will be..." For since artisans are more strictly bound to the chamberlains than others are, therefore, all the more strongly, they ought to abide by the judgment of the chamberlains, no less so, as in C. de iur. omn. iud., l. si. And therefore, I do not make a distinction of persons, but of facts and sentences: either the chamberlain proceeded or adjudicated without cognizance of the rights of the parties, or with cognizance of the cause. In the first case, recourse is permitted, as there it says, "without cognizance." Nor is this surprising, for such is not a sentence if it is rendered with precipitous haste, contra l. 2, and ultra ex peric. recit., and contra l. prolatam, and 2 q. 1, c. nos in quemquam, and de const., c. Ecclesia Sanctae Mariae, C. de accus., l. 4, and C. unde vi, l. meminerint, and l. si, C. si vim, vel alio modo.

CASE. Appollonius made a will and died, no posthumous child having been born. Then his daughter Amerita died, being in pupillary age, with her mother Nesutia, usufructuary and guardian, surviving, and with Christian, universal heir and son of the said Appollonius and carnal brother of the said Amerita, surviving, and with Francisca and Lena, daughters of the said Appollonius and married, surviving, as is contained in the testament. Then the aforementioned Christian, universal heir, died, being of an age over 14 years, with the said Nesutia, mother and former guardian of the said Christian, surviving, and with Francisca and Lena, his sisters, surviving, and with Cello, Massii, and Baziati, substituted in the testament, surviving. Now it is asked: what are the shares of the said Nesutia, and whether she succeeds in the goods of the said Christian, and whether she ought to be usufructuary of all the goods of the said testator after the death of the said Christian, provided she lives chastely and honestly and observes a widow's life, and in what share she succeeds. It is also asked: whether the said Francisca and Lena ought to succeed the said Christian in the goods of the said testator, and in what share, and whether they ought to have the said share, if they do not succeed in anything, the usufruct not having ended and during the lifetime of the said Nesutia. It is also asked: whether the executors of the said testament can and ought to execute the bequests made by the said testator in the substitution of the said testament to the guardian altar of Saint Francis and Saint Mary, and to the fraternity of the disciplinarians of Saint Rufinus, during the usufruct of the said lady Nesutia, and whether the said executors can sell the said fourth part which ought to be given for the love of God.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The son deducts the legitime and the trebellianic portion when he is burdened with the obligation to restore the legitime, even in respect of legacies left for pious causes; but not the trebellianic portion.
2. How much is the legitime of a son who has three sisters, and how much is the trebellianic portion.
3. While the usufructuary is alive, the goods cannot be sold, except as to the bare ownership, even if they are to be distributed among the poor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is proposed that Christian died after the age of pupillarity, and thus the pupillary substitution had lapsed, and we are dealing with a fideicommissary substitution. Let us therefore consider how much ought to be restored by reason of the fideicommissum. It is certain that the son, burdened with the duty of restitution, deducts the legitime for all, even for God, the Church, and the poor; but Trebellianus does not deduct from the fideicommissum destined for pious causes.

† How great, therefore, is the legitimate portion of the son? I answer that, since there were four siblings, one male and three females, the legitimate portion of the male son is one-fourth of one-third. For the female daughters constitute a share for him by concurrence, since he has his legitimate portion in their dowries, and in the Authentica Nouissima, Codex, On Inofficious Wills, where it says, "from which the Trebellian portion is to be divided among them"; and it is one-fourth of the residue, Codex, On the Trebellian Portion, Law Iubemus. In the first place, therefore, the mother and sisters deduct from the person of Christian, to whom they succeed intestate, one-fourth of one-third. Likewise, they deduct one-fourth of the entire residue of the inheritance by virtue of the Trebellian rule, the portion left to the poor being saved.

† The remainder, however, is divided among the substitutes according to the form of the will, who are bound to the mother, namely the sons in half of the alimony, and strangers in half of the usufruct. L. Titia. §. si. de leg. 2. according to Bartolus, during which usufruct the executors cannot sell except the bare ownership, insofar as it pertains to the poor, and it pertains to distribute that to the poor. For the usufruct must be preserved, de usufr. L. fundi Trebani. Moreover, the wife must also have her dowry, similarly the daughters. Therefore, they also say that the legacies of the daughters are to be had. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the provision of a statute is to be applied to past events.
casus:
CASE

In the name of the Lord, amen. The fact is as follows: In the city of Cagli there is a certain old statute, which provides that if the wife predeceases in marriage, with no common children or children of children existing, the husband profits one-third part of the dowry, and the other two parts he is only obliged to restore; and that no pact to the contrary contained in the dotal instrument regarding the dowry being restored otherwise is valid. Also, afterwards a new statute was issued, which provides that if the woman predeceases in marriage with children, or other descendants from the said marriage, that the entire dowry remains with the said children or descendants, and their children, and no pact to the contrary appended in the instrument is valid: in such a way, the father, who gave the dowry, stipulated at the time when the old statute was in force that the dowry be restored to him in every case of the dowry being restored. Finally, it happens that, while the said old statute was in force, the marriage was dissolved by the death of the woman, with common children from the said marriage remaining. Then the new statute, mentioned above, is enacted, and while the said new statute and its observance are in force, the said children, who were begotten from the said marriage, die, leaving no descendants, but nevertheless the father. And thus, although the stipulation for restoration was interposed at the time of the old statute, nevertheless the case of restoration being made occurred at the time of the new statute. Now it is asked, whether the dowry ought to be restored considering the old statute, or whether the whole ought to remain with the husband considering the new statute: since the case of restoration being made occurred at the time of the new statute: although the stipulation for restoration was interposed at the time of the old statute, and on this point Master Rosellus consulted, as immediately follows, and afterwards follows the opinion of Master Baldus.
body: Having seen

† On the aforementioned point, and according to the said statutes, I state, in accordance with the form of the earlier laws, that the aforementioned dotal provisions must be observed: for the last statute, which states “if the marriage should be dissolved, etc.,” is understood to apply to the future, as in C. de legibus, l. leges; and Extra de testibus, c. cognoscentes. But in the case proposed, the marriage had already been dissolved; therefore, the law does not extend to that case. Moreover, in matters pertaining to the decision of a lawsuit, the old law is observed; but these matters pertain to the decision of a lawsuit; therefore, the old law must be observed. This is examined at length by Cynus in the said l. leges. And thus argued Jacobus de Belvisi. Thus the doctors commonly hold in l. omnes populi. Nor does it avail what is noted there by Bartolus, where he says that if a statute provides that if the wife predeceases without children, the husband shall acquire one-third of the dowry, that such a statute extends to dowries previously given, because that statute derives its force from the death occurring after the statute and the dissolution of the marriage: so it would be here, but the marriage was dissolved before this, therefore it does not extend to that case; since the nature of law is to give form to future transactions, as I said above. I therefore conclude that the dowry must be restored according to the first agreements, notwithstanding the second statute, etc. And thus it seems to me that the law should be stated. By Rosellus of Arezzo, Doctor of Laws, therefore I have subscribed and signed with my usual seal. Follows the opinion of Lord Baldus on the same matter.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a provision concerning the restitution of the dowry extends to a marriage already dissolved.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† It should be known that sometimes a dowry is reclaimed by the provision of the law, that is, from a tacit stipulation made by the law, as in C. de rei vx. ac. in prin.; at other times it is reclaimed by the provision of man, that is, by an express stipulation. In the first case, either the due date or the event for restoring the dowry anticipates the new law: and then we must look to the former, old law that does not prohibit it, and not to the new law, because the old law carries with it its effect with respect to the status of a perfected obligation, even if the new law provides by way of discharge. This is a noted text in Auth. de consti. quae ex ascripto, et liber. natas. in prin., at the words, cum vtique nos hunc habuerimus intellectum etc., which text is noted. Or, conversely, the law anticipates the event and the time of restitution, and then according to Bar. and Cy. the new law is looked to, as noted by Cy. in C. rem in praesenti, §. fi., and Bar. in l. omnes populi. In the second case, one must abide by the pact, provided that the pact was not prohibited by common or municipal law in force at the time the pact was made, as in C. manda. l. ab Anastasio, §. fi., for pacts and agreements must be observed, C. de iu. do. l. auia; ff. sol. mat. l. quoties; C. de pac. conuen. l. fi. in fi. Whence, although the old law is removed by the new law, the old pact is nonetheless not removed, because it would be contrary to the ius gentium to remove that natural obligation and that natural justice which arose from a consent not disapproved; noted by Inn. in c. quę in ecclesiarum. And that is true unless the law expressly provides concerning the pact itself, which it can do for cause; whence the new statute is certainly valid, and the old one was also valid, because it seemed to the legislators that such a statute is useful, good, and expedient, and therefore ought to be held as good and just in favor of children, by the argument of ff. de postula. l. 1, §. pueritiam; de act. et obl. l. obligamur, §. lege; de ritu nup. l. quod liberos. Which reasoning applies just as strongly to a dowry given before as to a dowry given after, because with respect to the subject matter there is no difference. Therefore, things which agree in equity will agree in effect, and things which are not distinguished by reason will not be distinguished by time; and because the derogation of the new statute regarding pacts is general, ff. de ma. testamto. l. in fraudem, §. fi.; de alea l. 1, §. quod autem, and l. 1, §. hoc interdictum; ff. de tute. Consider that by custom the dowry is retained for the children, and the tacit stipulation ceases; but an express stipulation would indeed have place, as noted in C. sol. matr. l. dos a patre, and C. communia vtriusque iudicij, l. fi. And this by law and general custom, which was in force at the time of the first law. Now a new law supervenes determining new cases; it is therefore asked whether that succession of the children in that dowry is a new case, for the stipulation is not said to be invalid, but its benefit is said to be transferred to the daughter’s children. Likewise, it is asked whether, from the intention of the new statute, namely that children cannot be derogated by a pact. For since, when children do not exist, the statute gives a third notwithstanding pacts, by an argument a contrario sensu, when children do exist, it ought to be retained for the children notwithstanding pacts, ff. de pac. dota. l. inter, §. cum inter, and it is express in eo. tit. l. Beblius Marcellus. For the argument from the contrary sense of the statute must operate to the same extent—and that it can be renounced—as the case expressly stated in the statute operates, as noted in C. de fur. l. apud antiquos. But that argument is invalid, because one statute speaks of the husband, and the other, namely the new statute, speaks of the children. Likewise, it is against the gl. or. in said l. Beblius, at the words ideoque respondit. Therefore, the new statute clarifies the old one and expresses its intention; it does not create a new matter. Surely, then, from the combination of these statutes it seems judgment should be given in favor of the children; indeed, it is entirely new, whence this statement is not true. But for another reason judgment seems to be given for the children, because the statute wills that they have this dowry because the mother took it from her father, and through her it flows to the children themselves; ad l. fal. l. in 4. per Bar. This passage is difficult. And the intellect has various considerations regarding this; and it seems to me that I advised otherwise not long ago: nevertheless, I do not find that a copy of the consilium remained with me, nor do I retain in memory whether I was consulted upon this, and whether I leaned in favor of the children or not. I should like to see, because inconsistency is unseemly in a matter of dowry, although the speculative and estimative faculty, which is the more useful part of the intellect because it is conclusive, is not always the same. Concerning the other point, there is no doubt: because the contract of dowry and the stipulation hold during the subsistence of the marriage, if nothing else impedes it, nor is a dowry contract presumed simulated by reason of the marriage, because marriage belongs to the nature of dowry, as in C. de dona. ante nup. l. fi. The opinion that it remains with the children upon dissolution of the marriage after the new statute pleases me entirely notwithstanding the stipulation, because the force of the law and of the statute can transfer it to another person, C. rem in praesenti, §. videamus. But if the due date and the event of restitution by virtue of the stipulation had already occurred before the statute, then I hold what I stated in the beginning. Baldus advised anew more clearly and subtly, as immediately follows; Baldus does not retract that consilium because he had not firmly settled upon it, but the following consilium, which is on the same fact, stands thus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that, in the absence of children, a husband whose wife has predeceased him shall acquire one-third part and restore two-thirds, notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, whether anything is to be restored when children are present.
2. Whether one may renounce a statutory disposition, with the resulting consequences, and conversely.
3. Whether a new statute extends to dowries stipulated before the statute.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† First, the statute provides that, if there are no children, the husband, upon the predecease of his wife, shall acquire one-third part, and shall restore two parts, notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary. For the question arises whether, if children are present, anything is to be restored, the custom referred to in the law *dos a patre* being set aside. And I see that the entire dowry is to be restored, as noted in the law *Beblius*, *de pactis dotalibus*. For the case of children is a case unforeseen by the statute; therefore, the custom ceasing, we are in the common law, and thus it ought to be restored. Law *si*, Code, *conio utriusque iudicii*; and in the text of the said law *dos a patre*. To the contrary, it seems, taking an argument from the contrary sense from the statute itself. Digest, *de pactis dotalibus*, law *inter socerum*, section *cum inter*; and it remains with the father for the children. It supports what is noted by Dy. in chapter *ob gratiam*, *de regulis iuris*, book 6; and in the law *quod favore*, *de legibus*, by Cy. I believe that from this statute an argument from the contrary sense is taken, as if from the contrariety of the final cause. For the final cause why two parts ought to be restored when there are no sons is the lack of children; therefore, when children are present, the contrary final cause produces the contrary effect. The major solution of the law *si cum dotem* does not obstruct, because there the unforeseen case was not contrary in the final reason for the restitution of the dowry, which was expressed in the contract. But here it ought not to be called unforeseen, because the conception of the mind understands both contraries simultaneously. But it is doubted whether one can renounce this argument from the contrary sense by agreement, just as one can renounce the custom of the law *dos a patre*. It seems that one can. Digest, *de pactis*, law *pacisci*.

† On the contrary, it seems that the statute provides for renunciation of its own provision; but this contrary sense is a tacit provision of the same statute, therefore one cannot renounce it, because this contrary sense appears to be the text of the statute itself, *de testibus*, l. *qui testamento*, §. *mulier*. And if this is true, even under the old statute, the dowry remains for the children with the father, notwithstanding a stipulation made to the contrary by the father of the woman. For if the father could renounce, he would gain nothing; and even the children, who are said to be the cause of gain, would be the cause of loss: which is most absurd. But this statute seems false, because this argument from the contrary sense is tacit, and therefore it is removed by the express. Likewise, the custom, mentioned in l. *dos a patre*, is derogated by pact, as noted there. From this it seems to be concluded that the said dowry ought to be restored according to the form of the stipulation, as in C. *rem in praesenti*, §. *videamus*. For contracts are understood from agreement, as in ff. *deposi.*, l. 1, §. *si convenerit*. And therefore it seems that recourse should be had to the second statute; however, that does not seem to have application, because the case for restitution of the dowry had already ceased and occurred before the new statute was made, and thus one must adhere to the old statute, indeed to the law, and not to the new statute, as in C. *de legibus*, l. *leges et constitutiones*, cum si. And although the father is bound to provide a dowry for his daughter, nevertheless, according to common law, he may stipulate in the case of restitution of the dowry that it be returned only if given solely to him, as in ff. *solut. matrimonii*, l. *si cum dotem*, in princ., and C. *commun. utriusque iudicii*, l. fin. Hence, according to the strictness of the law, the dowry in question seems to be in the case of restitution; nevertheless, because the intent of the old statute was certainly to the contrary, one might perhaps say the contrary on grounds of equity by l. *inter*, §. *cum inter*, *de pactis dotalibus*. The preceding opinion is more correct. There is no doubt about the third part of the dowry, that it remains with the husband, because the case of existing children, whose death is the cause for triggering the stipulation for restitution of the dowry, is similar to the case of children not existing at the time of the mother’s death; and in that case too there is a stronger reason for gain, therefore, etc., as in ff. *de legibus*, l. *non possunt*, and l. *illud*, ff. *ad leg. Aquiliam*, C. *de interdictis*, l. 1, cum si. Secondly, the new statute expressly contains this by edict,

But it is doubted whether this new statute extends to old dowries stipulated before the statute by the parties, in the case of a dissolved marriage with children, if it happens that they subsequently die; and it seems that the new statute does not recognize old stipulations. C. de leg. l. leges. C. de decurio. l. pe. C. manda. l. per diuersas. §. fi. To the contrary it is argued, because the restitution of the dowry is of the future: although the stipulation is of the past, as noted by Cy. c. rem in praesenti. §. fi. and Bart. in l. omnes populi. ad hoc facit. ff. de pac. dota. l. si inter virum, et vxorem. So, if this new statute is understood to be declaratory or interpretative of the old statute: then there is no doubt that it applies to past cases. ff. de libera. leg. l. Aurelio. §. Sticho. and in Auth. de filiis ante dotalia instrumenta natis. §. fi. But if we say that it is entirely new, then either the condition for the restitution of the dowry had occurred, and this acquired right is not taken away by a subsequent statute, nor does it seem to be the intention of the lawmakers to remove natural equity and a natural obligation already established, as in Auth. ex libe. et ascripti. natis. post prin. coll. 5. Or it had not yet occurred, because the son or daughter was still alive at the time of the new statute: although the marriage had been dissolved a year earlier, and then the new statute must be observed, and the reason is that the condition of the death of the children, like a conditional acquisition mortis causa, does not feign retroactivity; hence, impeded by the new statute preceding the death of the children, the stipulation for the restitution of the dowry cannot be incurred: because the time of the condition, and not of the contract, is considered, as ff. ad sil. l. 1. §. serui. and l. 1. ff. de reg. cato. ff., de haere. insti. l. sed si in condi. §. solennis. And by this our question is decided either one way or the other, according as the order and course of facts stands. In the second point, it is childishly doubted: because by law the dowry contract is valid during the subsistence of the marriage. C. de do. ante nup. l. fi. ff. so. ma. l. quoties. nor is simulation presumed. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the penalty for not requesting a guardian passes from one degree to another, for example, from the mother to the grandfather, or from the father to the uncle.
2. Whether the maternal grandfather is excluded from the succession of his grandson due to the delay in requesting a guardian.
3. The legitimate guardian must request that he himself be appointed guardian.
casus: CASE. The point is as follows. Wife of Cola was alive, from them was born Felia, Cola died, the lady Viua married Bartutiolo secondly, and from him she bore a daughter named Eufragina: finally the said Eufragina married Cellolo: then the lady Viua died, and the said Bartutiolo contracted a second marriage, from which was born Philip from the said Eufragina, and from Cellolo was born Ange. Cellolo died, leaving the said Ange. Finally the said lady Eufrugina assumed the guardianship of her said son, finally she passed to a second marriage without requesting a guardian for the said Ange her son, who Ange afterwards lived for over a year without a guardian, nor was a guardian requested for him either by the said Bartutiolo nor by another, and finally Ange died in pupillary age, it is asked, who is admitted to his succession.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Here several doubts arise,

† The first point is whether the penalty for not petitioning for a guardian passes from one degree to another, for example, from the mother to the grandfather, or from the father to the uncle, and so on among others between whom there is an order. The glossa ordinaria states that this is notable in C. qui dat. tut. pos. l. qui nepotibus. And it appears to be expressly stated in l. 2, §. si, ff. ad Tertullianam.

To the contrary, it seems that in the aforementioned §. si, the reason is that those following were not strictly bound by the law of their forum to petition for a guardian, and since the mother did not exist, they were therefore not excluded; but today they are strictly bound to do so, as C. de leg. haer. l. sciant. Therefore, if they do not petition for a guardian, they are excluded. Bartolus determines this question in l. 2, ff. qui pet. tut. in this manner: Either we are speaking of the mother and the grandmother, and they are excluded; or we are speaking of other persons, and they are not excluded; because the law sciant, which corrects the ancient law by adding to it, does not say this. ff. sol. mat. l. si vero, §. de viro. But in l. nepotibus, Bartolus simply states that if a slave is negligent, he is excluded. However, this distinction of his has neither truth nor reason; because if the latter is excluded by negligence, another blood relative ought all the more to be excluded than the grandmother, ff. de inoff. test. l. nam et si parentibus; and C. de cond. l. si, §. si; in Auth. de haer. et fal. §. si quis autem non implens; ff. de fal. l. si quis lega., §. si; de bo. dam. l. cum ratio; C. de impo. lucra. descri. l. 1, lib. 10.

And therefore the truth is this: Either the first person is excluded solely from the hope of succession to the minor; and in this case, the subsequent person, if similarly negligent, is not deprived [of that hope], and the reason is that, with regard to the petition for a guardian, the first person can purge the delay. I do not mean as regards recovering the lost hope of succession, but as regards the duty of petitioning for a guardian, as ff. ad Tert. l. 2, §. quid ergo. And this is for the benefit of the ward, so that he may not lack a guardian due to the delay of the city. l. dilatae petitionis. The delay can be purged both voluntarily and by the compulsion of the praetor; but not as regards the hope of succession, or the benefit of the negligent person himself, from which he is excluded ipso facto; because once the penalty has been inflicted by the law itself, especially a privative penalty, there is no place for the purging of delay, as d. l. 2, §. si mater; and C. de fideic. auth. hoc amplius.

Or, the first person is excluded not only from the hope of succession to the minor, but is also removed from the guardianship as suspect, as is the case here; because the mother, by passing to a second marriage, is removed ipso iure as suspect for three reasons: first, on account of dishonest morals; second, on account of diminished affection for the children; third, on account of the presumption of future dissipation of assets, as in Auth. de nupt. §. sin autem tutelam, col. 4; and C. de adm. tut. l. lex, quae tutores. And in this case, the person who, after the mother has been excluded, hopes for the succession of the minor, is deprived of it if he is guilty of similar fault, as l. sciant, joined with d. l. 2, §. non solum, ver. sed prioribus. For in place of the removed and suspect person, another must be petitioned for. And consider that, once the mother is removed and suspect, a new origin of petition arises from this; and it begins with the person immediately following the mother, who is the first in this burden. Hence, the rule concerning the first person does not fail, but rather is verified in him, excluding him for negligence. Also, because this case of transition is similar to death; because, as regards guardianship, the mother is considered as dead, arg. de lib. et post. l. Gallus, §. et quid si tamen. But if she were dead, the same diligence and penalty would apply to the subsequent person, who has now first entered the degree, as in Auth. de haer. ab int. §. ex his, col. 8. Having seen this theory, which is most true.

It remains to be seen regarding Bartutiolus himself: whether he was excluded from the hope of succession by the lapse of a year. And it seems that he was not, because where there is a legitimate guardian, as he is, there is no necessity to petition for a guardian, as is noted in C. ad Tertul., l. matres. That the maternal grandfather is a legitimate guardian is clear from the aforementioned § ex his, and is noted in Auth. matri, et auiae, and in Inst. de leg. patron. tute. Bartolus in d. l. 2, ff. qui pet. tuto., in the first column, says the contrary, etc. He states that a legitimate guardian is not deprived of administration by the lapse of a year, not because he did not petition for a guardian, but because he is punished with the same penalty for the fault of neglected administration. And because he entered into administration in fact without making an inventory, for he does not divide the estate; and because he did not administer legitimately, indeed, more justly, one who administers so rashly is excluded than one who intrudes, as is noted in d. § si mater, ver. quid si pater, and l. si ita autem, de adm. tu., and l. tutor, qui repertorium, in the beginning. For a de facto act does not excuse, when it ought to have been done according to law, as in d. § non solum. Since therefore this Bartutiolus was in delay, he lost the hope of succession of the impubes.

Furthermore, the marriages are against him, by which he brought a stepmother upon the nephews from his daughter; as in Auth. de nup., § optima. Just as the grandmother, who brought a stepfather upon them without petitioning for a guardian, is deprived of guardianship and succession; although regarding deprivation of succession on account of second marriage, nothing clear is found concerning a male in Auth. de non eligen. secundo nub., in column 1. And this is clear: because not only the mother, but also the grandmother renounces second marriages, as in Auth. matri, et auiae, and d. § ex his. Therefore, since this Bartutiolus was not suitable, he ought to have petitioned for a suitable guardian to be appointed; just as the mother, who was not suitable under the old law, ought to have petitioned for a suitable one to be appointed. This is proven manifestly, and it is certain that the mother and grandmother, by accepting guardianship, are legitimate guardians; just as this grandfather is, without acceptance, presupposing that he was not suspect in law. But they are deprived if they do not proceed to further solemnities, namely, to administering with a decree, not perfunctorily or nullly. Therefore, this Bartutiolus also fell from the hope of succeeding; because things are equal with regard to the reason of the law, which regards the utility of wards: to have no guardian is, otherwise, to have one in vain without the legitimate exercise of guardianship. The case is in d. § non solum.

From these, it is concluded, and this is the very truth, that this Bartutiolus, whether he was suitable for guardianship or not, fell from the hope of succeeding; hence the inheritance belongs to the son of this Bartutiolus, and to half to Lady Felice, who was also the daughter of the said Bartutiolus, in whom no reason for exclusion is found. Someone will say: if neglected administration absorbs the hope of succession, why is it not so in one who is negligent after legitimately accepting guardianship, making an inventory, and having administration decreed, even if we suppose him to be negligent thereafter for a year and years? Yet no law deprives him of succession. I answer: because this person performed the solemnities, and therefore was more obedient to the law.

Again, someone will say that the law Sciant speaks when the ward needs an appointed guardian; but when he has a legitimate one, that law does not speak; because a legitimate guardian is not to be petitioned for. l. fi., C. de adm. tu., according to Cynus.

Secondly, I concede that he is not to be demanded from another, but rather he himself must seek that he not be given [to another], but that at least with respect to administration it be decreed. L. si. C. de arbitrio tutoris. The full office is desired by all, just as from the mother according to Nicolaus de Tudeschis in the present lesson, from the grandfather, just as from the grandmother. And thus I advise, following Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, if something comes through a pupillary substitution, it passes into the fideicommissum.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It appears that the son could freely make a will regarding that which came to him through pupillary substitution; because that does not fall within the fideicommissum, in which sons are substituted as sons, and by consideration of the person, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. ita tamen, §. qui suspectam. But Bartolus says that pupillary substitution falls within the fideicommissum, if first he substitutes, then he requests, D. ad Trebellianum, l. Marcellus, §. quidam. I speak of the testator’s goods, not of others, D. de vulgari substitutione, l. cohaeredi, §. cum filiae. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a sentence pronounced purely, with the power of judging, declaring, and interpreting reserved to the will of the parties, but with the substance not changed, can have a condition added in a new sentence.
2. Whether a legacy, or a sentence, with the words "when she marries" or "if she marries," is conditional or pure.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The sentence pronounced in the first place under these words. Moreover, the said Lord Archbishop willed and ordained that the legacy, or bequest, made by the said Bert to all his daughters, and to each of them born of his second wife, the said Angelinus is bound and ought to pay and give to each the third part. It does not expressly contain any conditional, condition, or other delay: because he did not say, if they were to marry, or when they were to marry.

† And therefore this sentence is not understood to have been pronounced conditionally: but purely, unless perhaps the legacy, to which it refers, was in fact and in law conditional, as in the argument of ff. de verb. oblig. l. si ista stipulatus. §. grisogonus. in fine. I said "in law," however, because a condition cannot be opposed in law regarding the legitime. C. de inoff. test. l. quam in prioribus. If, therefore, this first sentence, having been solidified by the will of the parties, was pure: it could not be made conditional by the second sentence, because that would be to change the sentence, as noted in the final part of l. lecta. ff. si cert. pet. Since, therefore, those words "when it happened to marry" were added in the second sentence, which words are conditional, as in C. de nupt. l. sancimus. and in Auth. de sanct. ep. §. sed hoc sancti. It appears that this condition, which alters the substance of the obligation, could not be appended: because this would be a novation in substance, as in l. pecuniam sicut peta. And in this matter, this Archbishop had a thick head and small understanding, if the facts are as I stated, notwithstanding that the bishop reserved to himself, by the will of the parties, the power to declare doubtful questions and disputes. This word "disputes" should be written with a double 't'. i. i. disputes, and it is the common term of lawyers: who say in the vernacular "ogne debattico chefosse tra le parte," i.e., every litigation: because it is immediately followed by "not changed," but here, as I said, the sentence would be changed. Of this, nothing was reserved in any way: hence a sentence against a sentence is not valid, as in l. 1. C. quoniam prov. non est nec. and l. quod iussit. de re iud. and as noted in C. de trans. l. si divers. with many others. It follows, therefore, that Jacob, as heir of the sisters, united on both sides, and by right also if he is alive, as in auth. defuncto, may bring an action based on the first sentence as pure, notwithstanding the passage of ten years: I speak of the common law, as in C. de const. pec. l. 2. and l. sicut. C. de praescr. 30. an. The second sentence, however, held in that it declared regarding the third of five hundred pounds: although this is presupposed to turn on the testament to which reference is made, as in l. in summa. and l. haec sententia. Otherwise, if nothing appeared from the testament, the second sentence, being certain, would prevail, and not the first, being uncertain: and then the said Jacob, since the sisters did not marry, could not bring an action except up to the legitime of the sisters. C. de nupt. l. sancimus. It serves. ff. de arbitris. l. quid tamen. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. It is asked, by virtue of the first statute, whether the mother is entirely excluded from intestate succession; and there is doubt, since another statute provides that she shall come into the legitime, and the legitime is one-third of that which is due in intestacy; therefore it seems that the statute intends that she also succeed in the legitime in intestacy.
casus: CASE. IN THE NAME OF THE LORD AMEN. There are two statutes; by one it is provided that those who die intestate without legitimate children shall be succeeded by the nearest blood relatives on the part of the father or paternal grandfather: because it is equitable and fitting that goods should regard and follow the principle from which they derived their origin. Also, by another statute it is provided that, although the first statute mentions only that the nearest blood relatives shall succeed, nevertheless the same applies if blood relatives on the part of the father survive, so that the first statute comprehends both males and females. Also, there is a certain third statute, by which it is provided that many cannot come to the succession of sons or daughters by testament, except for the sole legitime.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The question is who shall succeed Ludouico Cola, who died intestate: whether Nina, his mother, or Lady Vanna, and Amolina, and the sisters of the said Cola, and the aunts of the said Ludouico. And here it must be considered the statute concerning intestate successions: and if we had no other statute, the mother would certainly be excluded, because the statute provides that agnates shall succeed. And by this it seems to exclude all others: because, with an agnate included, the extension of succession entails the exclusion of agnates. This is also the reason of the statute, that goods should return to where they are known to have had their beginning. That is to say, that they look to their own stock, from which they were cut. Therefore, by the force of the devolution of succession to agnates, the rest are understood to be excluded. D. de legatis 1, l. quod in rerum, §. si quis post, in fine; §. ergo et mater. Therefore it seems that this was the intent of the legislators by the force of the reasoning given back, just as in a fief the mother does not succeed: even in a fief of women, because it looks to its own stock. And although this reason is not compelling in others than in fiefs: yet since the statute describes this very reason, the law is written. D. de re militari, l. milites agrum; D. de iure patronatus, l. adigere, §. quamuis; D. de pactis, l. quod dictum. However, because by another statute it appears that the mother ought to have her legitime by will, and also instituted agnates necessarily follow, it follows that the mother is not excluded intestate: because there would be no legitime if the case of intestacy did not exist, D. de inofficioso testamento, l. cum quaeritur. For since the legitime is one-third part of the intestate succession, therefore she succeeds intestate in three thirds. That is, in the whole estate. This is a compelling dispute, and if this were not so, nevertheless there should be no doubt about the legitime: because deprivation, which cannot be made by will, cannot be made intestate, D. de legatis 2, l. codicillis, §. pe. And therefore if, insofar as the inheritance pertained intestate to Lady Annola and Vanna: which I do not believe, nevertheless the mother cannot be deprived of her share. The mother ought, if anyone holds that she does not succeed except in the legitime, to impute to herself what is due to her for the part of Nicolina. 5 florins left to her by right of institution, although by Lady Nicolina, but this benefits Ludouico nothing, who does not have these 5 florins from the substance of the father, and the goods of Ludouico.
