C. de inofficioso testamento, l. scimus, §. repletionem. Hence, as regards Ludouico, he does not impute to himself in the legitime from the resignation of reason. I say that the mother succeeds in the whole. Here there is no need to discuss the reason to be given back: but if we say she succeeds only in the legitime: then she is bound to render an account of the administration of Ludouico’s part, not of Nicolina’s part: who bequeathed to the mother a release, as D. de liberatione legati, l. Aurelius, §. Titius testamento. Furthermore, to Andrea succeed the nearest agnates according to the form of the aforementioned statute, and thus are solved the doubts formed to me in the note of my lord the notary. Also, the bequests made to the said two in the wills are valid notwithstanding the sale made by Cola, as C. communia de legatis, auth. res, quae, cum si. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that each partner is liable in solidum for the contract of any one partner: if someone has acted as surety for a particular partner, not on account of a specific person, but generally; and if, subsequently, against the partnership, in which many debts have been contracted, the surety is compelled to pay, and thus the partners are released, whether he may bring an action against the partner for whom he did not act as surety.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Peter stood surety for Martin before the auditors of exchange: not with respect to any certain person, but generally according to the ordinances of exchange. After Martin’s death, he had contracted a partnership with Gaius, and many debts were contracted in the partnership: which said surety was compelled to pay, and he paid, and thus by paying he released Martin, and Gaius, for whom he had not stood surety. Now, however, having been preserved by stipulation, or by the direct action on mandate, or on negotiorum gestorum, or by the useful institoria action, he sues against Gaius, for whom he did not stand surety, whom nevertheless he released by paying. It is asked whether he can do so, presupposing a statute that even from contract any one of the partners is bound in solidum. And it seems that yes. And I argue first from the statute, for this surety contracted with one of the partners: therefore each is bound in solidum. And that suretyship is a contract is clear, because contract is generally said to be any agreement, as is noted, D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. 1. Also, if he were not a surety, he would not be bound: because obligation arises from fourfold matter, namely from contract, or quasi-delict, or quasi-contract, as in Inst. de obligationibus, §. sequens. But none applies here except contract, therefore, etc. Also, the surety is bound by stipulation, but it is certain that stipulation is a contract of strict law, D. de verbis obligationum, l. 5, §. satis acceptio; C. de fideiussoribus, l. blanditus; D. de pactis, l. 1, §. conventionis. And this is the truth, that suretyship is a contract: therefore, etc. But to this it is replied, first easily, because at the time of the suretyship he was not a partner; secondly, during the time of the partnership new debts were contracted, but only by Martin: therefore by his contract made before the partnership, namely from preservation or mandate, Gaius was not bound: the partner, who was not, could not be bound. C. de decuriis, l. providendum, lib. 10. Also, the statute speaks of a contract which is by reason of the partnership, not by reason of the person of one not falling upon the other. D. pro socio, l. socium, qui, §. si; D. de duobus rebus, l. si id, quod; ergo, D. de procuratoribus, l. si procurator meus, §. si. Also, this surety did not stand surety for Gaius: but before Gaius, as before other creditors, hence it is not understood that he stands surety before him and for him. If, however, Martin conducted himself badly in the partnership, this Peter is bound to Gaius on this account, how then does he sue against Gaius? By fraud. For he commits fraud by suing against him to whom he is bound from the same fact. C. de furtis, l. apud antiquos; D. de exceptione doli, l. dolo. And for a more certain understanding, so that we may see whether this surety can sue against him for whom he did not stand surety. It must be known that he does not sue from stipulation of identity: because he did not stipulate from Gaius; from mandate: not because Gaius did not mandate; institoria: not because Gaius does not presuppose Martin for this. D. de institoria, l. cuicunque, §. non tamen omne; de actione negotiorum gestorum. It is doubted, because by paying for Gaius and releasing him, Gaius is bound to ratify: because it is usefully managed by his very act. D. de negotiis gestis, l. solvendo. And although he would not have ratified, there is no force: because by his very act the business is his own. This must be observed: because not always does he who releases me by paying have an action against me. If anyone, however, pays for me, because he is bound to release me and preserve me, this one by paying is released from me, and does not sue against me: because the same payment cannot release the payer and bind him who must preserve indemnis. For if the principal pays to release the surety: nevertheless he does not recover from the surety: because he was bound to release him. So it is, Peter was bound to pay for Martin, and was bound by him, which proceeds from Martin’s fault, to preserve Gaius indemnis. If therefore he preserved, he paid Gaius duly, and therefore does not recover from him: because he received what is due to him. D. de conditione indebiti, l. repetitio. And therefore from the claim of said surety said Gaius ought to be absolved, although if the surety had paid not as surety, but as if Gaius: from his own fault he was bound, and as a friend Gaius paid. Of this before his judge he could obtain justice: because it is outside the cause of suretyship, and does not pertain to his suretyship: nor to the writing of the book. In doubt, however, he would pay from the cause of suretyship. D. de mandato, l. Papinianus, where of this that is certain, that before the partnership it would be said to be done, that the first is finished before the second. l. si id, quod, §. illius, pro socio. This one therefore, whom I called Gaius, and of the name I did not care, but of justice alone, ought to be absolved, otherwise there would be circuits: for if Gaius would pay the surety, then Gaius would have recourse against Martin, for whom Gaius suffers damage: but Peter is surety of the dead, therefore Peter would be sued by Gaius. And thus lawsuits would be usefully exchanged, and the outcome of the controversy would be against Peter, which the law considers finally, and by cutting off superfluous judgments in the end, either concludes, and stops. It accords with the above, that it is read and noted, de duobus, who release themselves by nature of obligation, and noted by office of management: that one paying does not recover from the other, although he released him: because no business was managed between them. D. de negotiis gestis, l. ex facto, modo ordinario, and touched. C. de transactionibus, l. 1. To the same effect. D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. in lege Falcidia. These things ought to be pondered in the reason of that law.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the daughter of a sister is preferred in succession, or the uncle of the deceased.
2. Whether the Trebellian portion may be deducted if the inventory has not been completed.
3. Whether a substitution made under the condition that the son and all the brothers of the testator, who were substituted to the son, die without issue, constitutes a substitution of further descendants from the same house; and whether, if the son died without sons, and secondly one brother died with sons, and lastly another brother died without sons, further descendants of the lineage succeed in the portion of the last one dying without sons, or not.
4. Whether that which one has obtained by virtue of a substitution comes into the fideicommissum.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the first question, I answer thus: namely, according to the common law, the daughter of a sister, although dowered, succeeded to her uncle Angelo, excluding Angelo’s paternal uncles; because the son of a brother and the son of a sister, although they are of the same degree as paternal uncles, are nevertheless preferred in succession; because they enter both the paternal and the maternal degree, as is stated in the Code, On Legitimate Heirs, in the Authentica *Post fratres*, there: “But etc.” If, however, it is asked to what extent Angelo was free from the burden of substitution, I answer: in one-third, which is half of one-third. The dowered sister makes a share for her brother in one-third; since the sister herself is admitted to her share of one-third, because the dowry succeeds in place of the legitime, as is stated in the Code, On Inofficious Wills, in the law *Quam nouella*.

But regarding the Trebellianic fourth of the entire inheritance left to Angelo, there is great doubt whether it can be deducted if the inventory has not been made, or not. No. For we have no text expressly permitting deduction if the inventory is not made, nor expressly prohibiting it; therefore, the matter is doubtful. And the gloss in Auth. de her. et fal. §. si vero expressim determines that the Trebellianic fourth ceases, just as the Falcidian fourth does, because they are similar, as stated in ff. de fideic. her. §. sed dubio forte. And that where the Falcidian fourth ceases under the newest law, the Trebellianic fourth also ceases, in Auth. sed cum testator, and in l. sed ut allegas, C. ad l. fal. The gloss holds the contrary, namely, that nothing has been corrected in the Trebellianic fourth; because if the legislator had wished to correct it, he would have said so, as in C. de appel. l. praecipimus, and C. de sac. san. ecc. auth. quas actiones. The same is held by Decius, because he who is burdened in one respect is relieved in another; but the heir, being universally burdened, is compelled to accept the inheritance, and in this he is burdened; therefore, if he accepted voluntarily, he is relieved so that he may deduct the Trebellianic fourth. The same is held by Jacobus de Belvis in his disputation, and in his lecture on the said §. si vero expressim. The same is held by Rosellus in tit. Senatusc. The same is held by Bartolus, namely, that the Trebellianic fourth does not cease due to the inventory not being made, ff. ad Treb. l. Marcellus, §. quod autem. And he says that when the Falcidian fourth ceases by the judgment of the testator, the Trebellianic fourth ceases, because the power of the efficient cause, i.e., the testator, is the same in one as in the other; but where the Falcidian fourth is prohibited from outside, not from the testator himself, for example due to the negligence of omitting the inventory, although the Falcidian fourth is prohibited from the Falcidian deduction, the Trebellianic fourth is not prohibited. For this prohibition is not of man, but of law; but the law does not say this, therefore neither should we say it, as in ff. de adqu. her. l. si servum, §. non dixit. Others, however, teach without this distinction, holding that the Trebellianic fourth does not cease. Others hold the contrary. But the Lord Cynus in the said Auth. sed cum testator says that either the heir accepted under compulsion, and the Trebellianic fourth ceases under old, new, and newest law; or he accepted voluntarily, and then either he restored immediately, and he is not bound to make an inventory of the quarter which he restored, but only of the quarter which he retained; or he restored after an interval; and then, because he is bound to render an account, the head of which is the inventory, he is bound to make an inventory, ff. de cond. et dem. l. cum tale. And thus he is not presumed to have subtracted or devised fraud; and therefore he is unworthy of the benefit of the fourth, in Auth. de her. et fal. §. scimus, and ff. ad l. fal. l. beneficio, and l. hereditatum, §. si, ad Treb. l. Paulus. Namely, in one who does not make an inventory, fraud is presumed, ff. de adm. tut. l. tutor, qui repertorium, in princ. But it would be permissible to distinguish according to the equity of one’s own head; the distinction should be formed thus: either he restored before the time for the inventory, and then he is not bound to make an inventory, because he is heir only in name, since he restored, and because he transferred all burdens to another; or after the time for the inventory, and then it matters whether he is such a person in whom neither in law nor in fact is fraud presumed, but rather a certain simplicity, such as a woman, a minor, a soldier, and an absent person, who could not have subtracted anything; and then he could deduct the Trebellianic fourth, because in these persons fraud is not presumed, nor knowledge of the law, ff. de dolo. l. ubi, §. si. For where fraud does not proceed without knowledge and contentment of the laws, these are excused from presumed fraud; otherwise, where fraud would proceed from the nature of the act. Or there are others who are bound to know the law, and in whom fraud is presumed; and then they do not deduct the Trebellianic fourth, because they are presumed to have subtracted things sufficient for the Trebellianic fourth, although the intellectual body of the inheritance itself cannot be subtracted; nevertheless, things can be concealed, as in C. quoniam, et qui, quar. pars debe. l. 2. But because one ought to follow the equity of the law, not of one’s own head, as in l. 1, C. de leg., it is safer to proceed by the beaten path, i.e., by the text of the laws, and to consider them diligently. And the text in the body deprives heirs of the Falcidian fourth for three causes: for not making an inventory, in §. si vero non fecerit; also for the prohibition of the testator, in §. si vero expressum; also for the pious devotion of the heir, and because he knowingly began to pay without retaining the fourth, as in §. non autem dabimus, and in Auth. sed cum testator. For not making an inventory, the text says that the heir comprehends legatees and fideicommissaries. But it is certain that the name of fideicommissum contains universal fideicommissum just as particular, as in ff. si quis omis. causa test. in l. servum, §. institutus. Nor does it matter that there it speaks of the Falcidian fourth. For Falcidian, said from the sickle, is a general name. Moreover, the text in that title, §. illo adiecto, openly says that the heir, who fears not to profit, ought to make an inventory, calling all fideicommissaries; therefore, if he does not make it, or makes it and does not call them, it happens to him to lose profit, that is, to lose the fourth. And certainly there it speaks of every profit of every fourth except the legitime, which is not called profit, but another’s thing. Therefore, whether you consider the text, or the reason written in the text, you will clearly find that he loses every profit, therefore also the Trebellianic fourth, if, when he ought to deliberate to make an inventory, he does not; otherwise, if he ought not, for example because he burdens himself by restoring before the time for the inventory. And this is the very truth in law, although contrary to this is commonly observed according to custom introduced by error of opinions. And my opinion is confirmed because the Falcidian fourth is due by stronger right than the Trebellianic fourth. For the Falcidian fourth is due, as if it were not permitted to bequeath beyond the quarter, ad l. falc. l. 1, in princ., which is not found in the Trebellianic fourth; indeed, although he can be compelled to accept and restore everything; therefore, if the stronger right is taken away, much more will the weaker right be taken away. And the distinction of Bartolus is not true, because one is excluded more strongly by sinning than by the judgment of the testator. This will be clear later, because the testator could not prohibit the Falcidian fourth, ff. ad l. fal. l. de bonis, §. 1, and l. Seius, et Augerius. And in the delict of the heir, it was lost, as in l. Paulus, and l. rescriptum, de his, qui, vt indi. From these things, the response is clear, that the legitime was due to Angelo, but the Trebellianic fourth by no means, in law, if the inventory was not made; but according to custom, the same applies to the Trebellianic fourth, because in the text it does not distinguish in c. Raynaldus, and c. Raynaldus, de test. But it indistinctly grants two fourths without any mention of the inventory. And in sons, and similar persons, it is sufficiently equitable opinion, because in them there is rather a continuation of dominion, than an entirely new inheritance, C. pro herede. l. nihil, and l. in suis, de lib. et posth. Therefore also, ff. pro socio. l. merito, C. de impo. lucra. descrip. l. 1, li. 10, C. de condi. insti. l. si, in fi., and to this contributes c. si pater, de test., li. 6, taken from the contrary sense indistinctly; therefore, at least in canonical equity, which greatly favors children, the Trebellianic fourth is deducted even if they do not make an inventory, just as if they did; however, lest things be subtracted by subtle ingenuity, inquiry will be made, C. quoniam, et qui, quar. pars debe. l. 2, li. 10. And often I have thus advised indistinctly, and thus I hold in canonical equity approved by usage; although in civil law the opinion is truer, which I held, following, declaring, and founding the opinion of Cynus in the addition to the lecture of Cynus himself.

† Subsequently it is asked whether a substitution made under the condition that if the son and all the brothers of the testator, to whom the son was substituted, should die without issue, further descendants of the family are substituted; or whether, if the son died without sons, and secondly one brother died with sons, and finally another brother died without sons, further descendants of the lineage succeed in the portion of the last survivor who died without sons, or not. And it is certain that, by the force of the wording, the condition of the substitution has failed, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. Haeredes mei, §. Cum ita. But by the force of the testator’s intention, since the last person died without a blood heir, the substitution takes place, because there is no one to exclude it from that side. For the son of the predeceased brother was placed in the condition, but he was not substituted to the last survivor, as noted in D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. Lucius. It does not obstruct D. de legatis 2, l. Titia, §. Seia, as noted there regarding substitution, namely tacit substitution, which there speaks of arising from the contrary sense of the condition; but rather from the precept against alienation, as in l. Peto, §. Fratre, D. de legatis 2, according to the glosses of Dy. and Pe. It supports what is noted by Bar. in Sol. matr., l. Si cum dotem, in principio. And it is expressly stated that the sons of the predeceased are not understood to be substituted to the last survivor without issue, in the said §. Cum ita, and it is fully read and noted in l. 1, C. de his qui ante apertionem tabularum.

† Subsequently, it is asked: since the deceased, having children, substituted others to them in the event that all should die without sons, whether that which the latter acquired by virtue of the substitution made to the son of the first testator is included in this fideicommissum. And it is certain that it is included, because, as I have said, the sons of this man do not take as substitutes for their father, but as heirs of their father; and thus not as a debt owed to them, but by hereditary right. Hence, just as the remaining goods come into the fideicommissum, so does this; for children are freed from the fideicommissum, but do not burden it by introducing a fideicommissum between father and sons, as stated in the law *de legato* 1, and in the law *filius*, § *cum quis*. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws. And to the truth of this I have subscribed and signed with the seal of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that the husband shall acquire one-third of the dowry upon the dissolution of the marriage by the death of the wife without issue, if the wife did not give a certain dowry, but permitted the husband to possess all her goods, does the husband, by virtue of such a statute, acquire one-third of the goods of his wife?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

A husband took a wife, and he possessed the house and lands of the said wife as husband and as dowry, for a long time, with the wife knowing and suffering it. The marriage was dissolved without children. The husband said that he profits by a third part, as of dowry goods, according to the form of the statute, because the wife predeceased him. It is said to the contrary that he should not profit, because the statute speaks of dowry, but here no certain and determined dowry appears, nor even one promised or delivered. It is asked, what is the law? I answer: It is a matter of urbanity (custom) that a wife gives her goods to her husband as dowry, and from this urbanity Aristotle says that goods are presumed to be dowry. But because this is not proven, and it frequently and easily happens that this is absent, C. de probat. l. neque natales, and because rich women always retain many things for themselves, therefore the glossa says that the opinion of Aristotle is not true according to civil law, as noted in ff. de iure dot. l. mulier bona. And this is confirmed because dowry is a matter of fact. ff. de cap. dimin. l. eas. And facts are not presumed. ff. de publ. l. quaecunque. §. si. Moreover, that which is variable is not presumed, but dowry is variable, because sometimes it is greater, sometimes lesser, sometimes in things, sometimes in money; therefore it cannot be presumed. This supports what is noted by Cynus, de contrah. et comm. stip. l. 1. Moreover, dowry is a title, but titles are not presumed, as in Inst. de act. §. aliae. Moreover, the law is express. ff. de iure dot. l. si ego. §. dotis. Moreover, this supports the point, because from performance a title is sometimes presumed: but from suffering (toleration) a title is not presumed; although sometimes delivery is presumed, as noted in l. si certis annis by Cynus, because delivery is presumed from a preceding title. C. de acq. poss. l. enim. But negligence is nothing; and therefore it is not a title. Hence consider that negligence is not properly called suffering. Suffering, however, is not properly called delivery, but it comes almost truly from the nature of a preceding title, or from the nature of the thing, as in servitudes. ff. de usufr. l. 3. §. dare. C. de serv. et aqua. l. 2. ff. si servi. ven. l. si quis diuturno. A title, however, is per se, and is not presumed, neither from negligence nor from suffering. The exception applies when suffering is apt to induce mutual benefits. C. communi divi. l. pe. and C. de pet. haer. l. si filius. Moreover, in l. pe. there precedes the cause of division, i.e., community, and in l. si filius. there precedes the cause and title of acceptance, and thus suffering is not naked, but has a cause. Therefore it is concluded that suffering alone is not sufficient. Moreover, in uncertain dowry, the certain sentence of the statute does not apply. C. de sent. quae sine cer. quant. l. si. Therefore, he who wishes to obtain the retentive sentence must prove a certain quantity, so that he may retain that quantity. Moreover, it seems express. C. de fals. causa adie. lega. l. si non designata. For dowry not designated is not owed as dowry.

To the contrary, it makes a great difference whether the husband demands or asserts, and the wife defends, or conversely, the wife repeats (claims back) and the husband denies. For in the first case, the office of the judge is given to the husband to declare the dowry which was not specified. ff. de iure dot. l. cum post. §. gener. In the second case, it is otherwise, as in the said l. si. Since therefore dowry is established here, it must be declared by the judge, so that retention of the third part may apply, and a greater dowry is owed by a widow than by a virgin, and therefore the declaration must be congruous and substantial: so that the declaratory office of the judge endures for the retention of the third part; for just as the husband would be heard in demanding, so also in excepting. ff. rem rat. ha. l. amplius. And thus I hold, and confirm with many reasons, and first by the reason of general custom. For general custom is that marriages are not contracted without dowry; therefore dowry constituted is presumed, which is to be referred to the arbitrium of a good man, as in ff. de iure dot. l. siue generalis. ff. de leg. 2. l. 1. ff. de leg. 3. l. si filiae. I do not say that the dowry is constituted by the sole mother; but it is declared, how much it is likely to have been constituted previously, so that the husband is not defrauded by deceit; for often something is declared due to acceptances which would not otherwise be declared, de rei vend. l. vtrique. Secondly, because I consider that if I suffer my thing, I command possession in my name; I seem by suffering to will it. ff. de re iur. l. semper quo non prohibet. and arg. ff. manda. l. qui patitur. But the husband possesses the redotal goods in the name of the wife as to certain things; therefore the wife, by suffering them to be possessed thus for a long time, seems to consent that it is dowry. For the husband is the image of the wife, and represents her in dowry. l. sciendum. §. 1. qui sat. cog. and l. in rebus. C. de iure dot. 3. Because I consider that this is not suffering, but an act and deed of the wife through the husband possessing, because to possess is an annual act through the organ of the body, past or present. ff. de acq. poss. l. 1. in prin. and l. possideri. in prin. And therefore l. cum de in rem verso seems to apply, because from suffering joined with an act of will. Moreover, it is suffering joined with a receptive act: for the burdens of marriage exhibited by the husband, and the alimony provided and received by the wife, are in fact, and in the doer the law cum de in rem verso applies. According to all, it supports. C. de agri. et cen. l. litibus. lib. 11. For wherever from long suffering one has benefits, those benefits are in place of performance, as in the said l. si filius. and l. pe. communi divi. and noted in C. de rei vend. l. solennibus. and arg. ff. de evict. l. quidam ex parte.

The objection from de iure dot. l. si ego. §. dot. is not valid, where it is said that, in order for it to appear what is dowry and what is paraphernal, and what was delivered to the husband and what not, it must be set forth in a libel of attestation; for this does not exclude other modes of proving. Added to the above is the confession of the testament and codicils of the wife, as noted by Cynus, C. de non num. pe. l. generaliter. And therefore judges must have truth before their eyes; for those who examine truth do not easily come to fault, as in Auth. vt defunctae, seu fenera. in prin. col. 5. From these it is concluded that the husband will profit by the third part, or all the possession, as if all were dowry, or at least according to the congruous arbitrium of a good man.

But against this it is objected, that if there is no stipulation or certainty, dowry cannot be demanded. C. de dote promi. l. 1. I answer: Here the husband receives and retains, and in retaining, an uncertain dowry pact is valid, nor are there two special things there; because in retaining there is the common law, which is notable.

CASE. The point is this: A certain Marcutus Phinti de Nuco made his last testament, in which he instituted and made his daughters Lippa, Bella, and Margarita, and the future offspring of his wife, if it came to light, if it were female, his universal heirs. But if it were male, and came to light, he instituted and made his son his universal heir, and willed and ordered the said testator that then the said daughters should have and ought to have from the goods of the said testator, for their dowries, two hundred pounds of denarii for each of them, by right of institution, upon the happening of the said condition, if the said offspring were male from one of the said daughters; if the said offspring were female, she shall succeed to the deceased, or deceased ones, and that the male shall succeed to the said females, if he comes to light. But if all should die, and no heir remain, of the above, he substituted to himself as universal heir the fraternity of S. Matiae de Nuco. After the said testament was made, the said Marcutus testator died, with the said Lippa, Bella, and Margarita, his minor daughters and heirs, surviving him, and with Do. Paula, wife of the said Marcutus testator, pregnant by whom, a certain daughter named Joanna was born, and that the said Paula legitimately assumed the guardianship of the said four minor daughters. Finally, three of the said minor daughters died, with the said Do. Paula, their mother, and the said Bella, their sister, surviving them, after the said Bella was given in marriage to a certain boy named Bartholomew Mactioli de Nuc. And the said Paula, mother and guardian, gave and granted in dowry and for the dowry of the said Bella all and singular goods pertaining to the said Bella under whatever title or right; and the said Bartholomew took the said Bella to his house as his wife, and she remained with him for years, and became an adult. Then the said Bella died an adult, intestate, with no son remaining from her. From which the case of substitution occurred, and the goods and inheritance of the late said Marcutus are held and possessed by the said Bartholomew, late husband of the said Bella, and Mactiolus, his father. And there is in the City of Nucerii a certain statute, which provides that the husband profits by the third part of the dowry of a wife dying without children. From which the said Mactiolus and Bartholomew say that the third part of all the goods and from the inheritance of the said Marcutus testator pertains to them by virtue of the said statute, and the men of the said fraternity say that the said Bartholomew has and ought to receive from the goods of the late Marcutus only as much as is declared in a certain note, which is also transmitted to you.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a testator institutes several daughters as heirs and substitutes them for one another, and substitutes someone for the last one to die: whether the person substituted in the last place is understood to be substituted to the entire inheritance, or rather only to the share falling to her.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† In the said testament, there is first the institution of the daughters. Second, among them, a substitution: although sufficiently poorly conceived there, and void, and a useful substitution of the fraternity there. But if all [die]. Thus, three having died in pupillary age, the fourth daughter succeeded, excluding the mother: because those words, “let him succeed the one dying,” express the quality of pupillary substitution: by which one succeeds the ward. As in the Institution on pupillary substitution, after the principle; and in the Digest, in the same title, law *Moribus*, in the principle, with infinite similar cases. But it must be seen, since the fourth died in adult age, whether the substitution made by fraternity is understood to be made to her alone: the word “to herself” hints at this, however, as it seems to be read and noted. In the Digest, on vulgar substitution, law *Vel singuli*; and law *Qui duos*; and law *Pater impuberes*; and in the Digest, to the law *Falcidia*, law *Pater filiam*, section *Duobus*; Code, on impuberes and other substitutions, law *Penultimate*. And reason also suggests this: because that which is acquired from pupillary substitution does not come into the fideicommissary substitution for two reasons. First, because it is acquired as if from the testament of the brother. Second, because it would follow that all goods, however acquired by the impubes, would come [into the fideicommissum], contrary to law *Coherede*, section *Cum filiae*, words “nor in the fideicommissum,” on vulgar substitution. Also, the text says it does not come, unless compelled to accept. In the Digest, to the Trebellian law, law *Ita tamen*, section *Qui suspecta*. Therefore, only the portion of this adult comes into the fideicommissum, after deducting the legitime, indeed also the Trebellian fourth, because fraternity is nothing other than brothers: who are lay and secular men, like other colleges. In the Digest, to the Trebellian law, law *Omnibus*. And according to this, the fraternity would not succeed, except in the half of the fourth of all goods: but this is very inconvenient, and contrary to the mind of the testator, who wished the entire inheritance to devolve to the fraternity after the death of all, if they died without children. In the Digest, to the Trebellian law, law *Haeredes mei*, section *Cum ita*, where it is expressed. Therefore, let us see to whom it devolves. Answer: if you ask from which words: I answer, from those [words] he substituted a universal heir to himself: for since he did not speak of time, he included the whole. In the Digest, on the action for recovery of property, law *Si in rem agat aliquis*. If, however, you ask by what right: I answer, by the right of the testator’s will: because he so willed, and he could so dispose of his goods. In the Digest, to the law *Falcidia*, law *Qui fundum*, section *Qui filium*; Digest, on the significance of words, law *Verbis legis*; Digest, on usury, law *In fideicommissa*, section *Nonnunquam*. If, however, you ask whether that which is acquired from the pupillary [substitution] comes into the fideicommissum. I answer: either you ask whether it comes without deduction of the fourth, and it does not come, unless the substitute is compelled to accept: for then he does not deduct the fourth; or whether it comes with deduction of the fourth, and truly, that it comes, if first he substituted pupillarily, and afterwards requested universally. For whether we consider that the father, and testator, can do this for himself from his goods, or testifies for himself and others, he can do this in all things: because the power of ordering is given to the father, the succession is given to the son, not as the son wishes: for the ward does not have the will, but as the father wishes, to whom the law grants the supreme ordering of the testament, and because the father’s power is not cut off in the goods of the father himself: except in the fourths expressly stated by law. Note, if the sister had succeeded the last dying [daughter] intestate, their portions would not come into the fideicommissary substitution: namely, because she would have them by the judgment of the father, but by the judgment of the law intestate. For there is a difference between these, as in the Digest, to the law *Falcidia*, in the law *Ratione*, section *Quam filios*. But where the father makes degrees, and expressly states the order of devolving all goods, his judgment must be followed, saving the benefit of the law. In paternal goods, of which he himself felt, and could feel. Therefore, the father wished to restore his entire inheritance after the death of all, and the restoration under the Trebellian [law] must be made to the legitimate successors of the last dying. In our case, to the mother, who is closer. But let us see, is this so: because that which is acquired from the pupillary [substitution] comes into the fideicommissum. The contrary. For it has been shown above, whether by virtue of the pupillary substitution to be drawn to an oblique [substitution]: but as if the father had requested a certain thing, or a certain quantity of his goods to be restored in the case comprehended by the condition: or whether this is so, because all children after their death. In the Digest, on legacies, third title, law *Si fuerit municipio*, section *Si*. What seems to some, that thus from the person of all two fourths are deducted, as if all were burdened: no. For the father is not prohibited from substituting two to an impubes. One directly, another by fideicommissum, as in the Code, to the Trebellian law, law *Non iustam*. But if it is understood that the last [dying] is burdened with the portion of the brothers: then he would not deduct the legitime from that portion, because it is not due to him, since the portion of the brothers is outside his portion. Code, on inofficious testaments, authentic *Novissima*. And he would scarcely deduct the Trebellian fourth. It seems more probable to say that he appears to have substituted to all, and after all: because he substituted in the whole universality, not simply: for it matters much between universal and indefinite words, as noted in law *Marcellus*, section *Quidam*, to the Trebellian law. But against this stands the limiting diction, “to herself.” Or, as the last dying, he made a fideicommissary substitution both in his own part and that of the brothers, and from his own part he deducts the legitime and the Trebellian fourth. But from the brother’s part no legitime is due to him, unless one says that the heir slave appears to be requested from the person of the first: and thus this one, as requested from the person of the brothers, deducts two fourths: just as they would deduct, argument from law 2, section *Idem Neratius*, to the Trebellian law. For whenever the portion of an impubes is burdened from the person of the impubes, thus the deduction of fourths, as in the said law *Qui fundum*, section *Qui filium*. And this opinion seems safer and more secure, because all must be promised. In the Digest, to the law *Falcidia*, law *In ratione*, section *Quod vulgo*. This passage is difficult. I come to the gain of the dowry, and I say that the husband ought to have the third of all things given in dowry: for even if they did not amount to such a fourth, nevertheless the privilege of the dowry has place. Code, common matters of legacies, authentic *Res*, which is also in the body, whence it is taken.

CASE. In the name of God, Amen. The fact, on which counsel is sought, seems to be such, namely, A certain Luchetus, son of the late Geraldinus of the Decrebetellis family of Pistoia, in the year of our Lord’s Nativity 1383, in the month of August of the said year, died intestate, leaving from himself and his wife, the lady Francischina, a daughter, Urbanetta, an infant. Also a certain Thadeus, a spurious son born to the said Luchetus from a certain Justina, recently deceased, who Thadeus, on the fourth day of the month of December last past, after the death of the said Luchetus, his father, was, by authority of a privilege and imperial rescript granted to Lord Dilano of the Patiatricho family of Pistoia, and his sons descending through the male line, by the noble man Angelo, son and heir of Lord Dilano, legitimately born, and to common and first birthrights by natural law: whereby there was no difference between spurious and legitimate [children]; and also to the rights of succession of the said Luchetus, the late father of the said Thadeus, he was restored, by an instrument written by the hand of Ser Lippo, formerly Ser Corrado of Pistoia, notary. From the foregoing it is asked, whether by virtue of the said rescript and privilege, and the restoration made to Thadeus, the said Thadeus, together with the said Urbanetta, succeeds the said Luchetus intestate, having seen the said rescript and privilege. Secondly, whether, having seen a certain statute of the commune of Pistoia placed under the rubric “On the mode of succession of a woman, or women, intestate,” where it is said that no woman may succeed intestate to her father when there is any male son, the said Thadeus, by virtue of the said statute, privilege, and restoration, succeeds the said Luchetus in totality, and the said Urbanetta has a suitable dowry from the goods of her said father according to the disposition of the said statute. The words of Caesar thus say: “We grant and bestow that you may and can legitimize natural and bastard children, Manzares, and any conceived from illicit intercourse, whether their parents are living or dead, with the exception only of the sons of illustrious princes, counts, barons, and nobles; and restore and reduce them to all legitimate rights, and utterly abolish all stain of birth, restoring them to all and each rights of succession, and intestate [rights] of cognates and agnates, honors, dignities, and to all legitimate acts: as if they had been born from a legitimate marriage: with others coming intestate, and to whom succession ought to pertain by common or municipal law, being cited or not cited, as it may please you; provided that at the time of legitimation, and your said descendants, as is premised, do not prejudice legitimate sons and heirs, so that they succeed with equal portions to their parents and agnates, notwithstanding.”

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that no woman may succeed her father intestate: if there is a male son, a legitimated son who was under his father's power at the time of the father's death does not exclude a daughter who has already taken part in the succession naturally due to her. See on this matter above, consilium 19, together with the three preceding ones.
2. Legitimation is equivalent to postliminium.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

And it must be considered that, at the time of these laws, the prince, out of love for chastity and the honor of families, legitimated no bastard unless on account of a grave cause, innate clemency, and at the supplication of the parents. D. de ritu nuptiarum, l. qui in provincia, §. divus. In order not to provide fathers with an occasion for sinning, they restrained nefarious and shameless embraces, so that the commonwealth might not be filled with such disgraceful persons. C. de naturalibus liberis, l. si, in the word “vitium frenandum”; and in Auth. qui monachos efficiunt sui, §. si, col. 6, in the words “sit supplicum patrum”; and D. soluto matrimonio, l. 1; and in Auth. de nuptiis, in the beginning, where it says, “it is not rightly your study to grant mortality,” D. de nuptiis, l. hodie autem. How great is the reverence in the prince, how great his love for chastity and morals, and how incredible his clemency, we see not through a mirror in an enigma, but [rather] that hidden faith trusts more in power than in decency. But since in this matter nothing else can be lost except status, recourse must be had to l. sancimus. It appears that this legitimation causes the legitimated person to come into the right of the legitimately born son by diminution of right; because the words state that it cannot prejudice the children and heirs in concurrence, and because it says “children,” it signifies legitimate ones, D. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt, l. filium diffinimus. And because it says “heirs,” it also signifies those admitted to the inheritance; for they are properly and truly heirs, as C. si quis a se ab hereditate abstinerit, l. 1.

† Moreover, legitimation is equated with postliminium, as in *l. si quis filio*, §. *pe.*, *de iniusto testamento*; but one who returns by postliminium succeeds together with another, as in *ff. de liberis et posthumis*, *l. Gallus*, §. *sed si eius*. Moreover, legitimation is said to be a restoration; but through restitution, one recovers rights from which he was found to be excluded, as in *C. de hereditatibus*, *auth. idem de Nestorianis*. Moreover, the legitimated person is said to be posthumous, because he was conceived by nature during the father’s life; but he was regenerated by the artifice of law. Therefore, with law and nature joined together, it now appears that this person is posthumous, as noted by Bartolus in *l. Gallus*. Moreover, if the law did not provide that one should be a spurious child, no one would be a spurious child, as was the case when primitive nature alone and by itself perceived things in humans. Just as one becomes spurious by law, so too can one be reduced by law to that status in which he was not spurious, as in *Auth. qui monachos effici legi*, in the beginning, columns 6 and 7. Moreover, the removal of obstacles is followed by the establishment of a right. But here the stain is removed, as argued in *C. familiae herciscundae*, *l. in ipsius*. Moreover, this is held by the excellent doctor Dino in his consilia. Nor does it matter that no citation intervened, because citation is not here a matter of natural law, but of civil law, as noted in *ff. de bonis possessoribus*, *l. 3*, §. *si causa cognita*. And Bartolus says that if the prince wishes, he may, as noted in *l. 2*, *de naturali restitutione*. For here the question is not one of innocence, but of inheritance, and thus the chapter *Pastoralis*, *de re iudicata* in the Clementines, does not stand in the way. Moreover, it does not matter that the doctors speak of *ius gentium*, because this is true with regard to the definition of dominion, not with regard to the mode of acquiring it, as noted in *l. ex hoc iure gentium*. Moreover, dominion was not here irrefragably rooted in the legitimate child, because the status of legitimation was implicit in the spurious child, and there was a right to diminish the legitimate child’s share, as in *ff. si ex noxali causa agatur*, *l. fi*. From these points, it clearly appears that this legitimated person takes away, or makes a part of, the legitimate share of the sister born legitimate, and although this opinion is safe, nevertheless, etc., as in *l. prospexit*, *qui et a quibus succedant*.

The contrary is shown thus, and I premise for clarity that sometimes one has the right to accept (*ius adeundi*), sometimes the right of having accepted (*ius aditi*), and thus I say: if one has the right to accept or to deliberate, such that the inheritance is not properly said to be in his goods, as in *ff. ad legem Falcidiam*, *l. pretia rerum*; if it has not been accepted, then he has freely disposed of it as his own dominion, just like his other goods, as in *ff. de militum substitutione*, *l. sed si plures*, §. *filio*. In his own heir, I consider the right of deliberation, and the mixture of existence, and the more perfect mixture: the first is spoken of in *C. de iure deliberandi*, *l. cum antiquioribus*; the second is spoken of in *l. apud hostes* with its material; the third is spoken of in *Institutes, de hereditatum qualitate et differentia*, §. *fi*, and *natura ipsa*. If a son, therefore, is an heir, and more so an heir by the existence of his heir than by deliberation, if he chooses this path. Moreover, he is more an heir by real mixture than by existence, because it is fixed. And then the inheritance devolves to him inviolably and separately, as in *C. de repudianda hereditate*, *l. sicut ille*. Therefore, the term “sons and heirs” must be understood in the narrower and more favorable sense, as in *de regulis iuris*, *l. quoties idem sermo*, so that I do not remove with one word all the rules of law of which no mention is made in the *non obstante* clause. Such is the rule that he who once is an heir does not cease to be an heir, as in *de minoribus*, *l. quod sine*, §. *sed quod Papinianus*. And such is that other rule that what is ours, whether by our act, cannot be taken away, as in *de re iudicata*, *l. id, quod nostrum*. These two laws have not been derogated: because no mention is made of them in the *non obstante* caution, and to this reason no congruous response can be made. Moreover, there is another reason, because obstacles which are of natural or divine law must be expressed specifically; but the retention and defense of dominion is of natural law, pertaining to the rational mind, which all humans use, as in *l. ex hoc iure* with its sequel. Moreover, implicit derogation, with regard to §. *ultimus* of *qui moriuntur*, column 7, does not seem sufficient; because the gloss there says that it must be said specifically, “notwithstanding this law.” And the argument is in *ff. si quis cautio*, *l. et si quia*, §. *quaesitum*. Of this, note is made in *l. ultima*, *si contra ius vel utilitatem publicam*. Otherwise, note is made in *C. de naturalibus liberis*, *l. 1*. And because there are contrary glosses, and I do not intend to restrict the privilege, but to interpret it, I do not insist on this allegation: this, however, seems to be the case, that the *non obstante* clause refers to the validity of the legitimation, but not to the power of eviction of acquired dominion; because it would be to multiply inconvenience, and the prince does not wish to emulate errors, as in *C. de donationibus promissis*, *l. 1*. Nor did the prince say this; therefore, etc., as in *C. de emancipatis liberis*, *l. nec auus* with its sequel. Moreover, legitimation is a privilege granted to a spurious child, and a privilege is a private law; but law does not take away successions from one who has acquired them; therefore, neither does a privilege, as in *Auth. de testamento imperfecto*, *heredes ab intestato*, §. *fi*. Moreover, legitimation is a restitution, which does not extend to a right acquired by another, as in *c. quamvis*, *de rescindenda lite*, book 6. Moreover, this is held by the doctors in §. *et quid si tamen* in *l. Gallus*. Moreover, legitimation should be the dominion of the father and the prince, even if it were added, because here the father seems to have left it to the legitimate son, as in *l. 2*, *de iure codicillorum*. Moreover, here the wife is in the middle, whence derogation would be made to *auth. licet*, *C. de naturalibus liberis*; but this allegation is not well founded in law. Moreover, the words say, “they succeed with those to be legitimated.” And thus they note the case in which they can accept together, as in *ff. de iniusto testamento*, *l. si ego*. But this succession was entirely applied to the legitimate child. I solve by saying that if the girl was mixed into the succession due to her by nature, as in *l. cum rogatus*, *de bonis damnatorum*, the count could not deprive her by legitimation, and that a privilege, with sound understanding, should not be extended to this case; and if it were extended, nevertheless, this legitimated person would not have the benefit of the statute, because he is not contained within the proper signification of the term “son,” as in *l. filium definimus*, etc. And because the privilege said the contrary there, “when they themselves, etc.,” it makes a difference, as in *ff. de vulgari substitutione*, *l. ex facto*. Moreover, truth is not bound by fiction, as in *ff. de liberis et posthumis*, *l. filio*. Moreover, the legitimated person is assimilated to an adopted son, as noted in *l. filios*, *C. de muneribus et oneribus*, *l. 10*, where there is a notable gloss. Moreover, it supports what was said above, that which is noted in *C. de sententiis praesidentium*, *l. fi*, and I spoke where nothing had been disposed by the father concerning the succession of the spurious child; for if something had been disposed, there would be room for another consideration and disputation. And thus I say and counsel, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute which interprets legitimate age to be 18 completed years in all matters, contracts, and judicial proceedings or cases, whether a mother under 25 years of age, but older than [the age of minority],
2. may assume the guardianship of her daughter who is a ward.
3. Whether the paternal grandmother, the maternal grandmother, or both are admitted to the preference in guardianship.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is asked whether Do. Franc., the mother of the ward Urbaneta, can assume her guardianship by virtue of the statute on the age of majority, presupposing that the said mother is over 18 years and under 25, and presupposing that the statute or custom dictating this is valid, as noted in l. 2, ff. de eo, quod certo loco, in the glossa ordinaria. And I see that she should be admitted, because, the impediment of minority being removed, there is nothing that stands in her way; but the impediment of minority is removed by the statute, which provides in this form, namely: “We declare and interpret the age of majority to be 18 completed years in all affairs, contracts, and lawsuits, or cases.” The general sanction of this statute is found in l. in fraudem, §. si, ff. de testamento militis.

The contrary is the truth itself, because it must be considered that this statute speaks in cases, or members, namely: in affairs, in contracts, in lawsuits, in cases. And if the word “or” is interpreted exclusively, there are only three cases. This is clear from the form of the statute. But if it is so that guardianship is neither an affair, nor a contract, nor a lawsuit or case: therefore the statute does not speak of guardianship. The consequent is proven by what is noted in a similar case in C. de annuis pensionibus, l. ut perfectus, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. si. The antecedent is proven most clearly, in that guardianship can be considered in two ways: first, in a substantial manner, as it is in the law of office; second, in a consequential manner, as it is in the act of exercise. And when the first is removed, the second is also removed, because he who is removed from the first is removed from the power of administration, and consequently from the act. And he who is not fit for being, and for the form of being, is not fit to act, because operation implies form; hence operation is taken by the argument from form. And it is absurd for something to be in the second act, or operative, before it is in habit. This is proven by removal and by obstruction. For he who is removed from the office of guardianship is removed from its exercise, ff. de solutionibus, l. quod si forte, §. 1. And he to whom it is an obstacle to begin to be a guardian, it is an obstacle to administer as a guardian, ff. de eo, qui pro tutore, l. quaero.

Furthermore, guardianship can be considered as it is imposed on a necessary guardian. Second, as it is offered to a voluntary guardian, i.e., the mother and grandmother. Third, as it is administered. If, however, it is asked whether guardianship is an affair? Certainly not, but it is a right and power over a free person for the purpose of protecting, etc., ff. de tutoribus, l. 1, and Inst. de tutoribus, in principio. And in the same way, guardianship is not a contract: because a contract is of fact, de cura furiosi, l. consilio, §. si. But guardianship is of law. Furthermore, guardianship is not a lawsuit, nor a case: therefore, speaking of guardianship, we are in the common law. Therefore, a mother under 25 years cannot be a guardian, C. de legitima tutela, l. si. Because a case omitted by the statute omits the disposition of the common law, l. si cum dotem, in principio, ff. de solutionibus matrimonii, and l. si non, §. de viro, ff. de legibus, l. de quibus, in principio.

What an affair is, and how it is called, as if denying leisure, and thus it is of fact, and consists in fact, is clear, ff. and C. de negotiis gestis, per totum, and extra de verbis significatis, l. forus, and ff. de mandato, l. si procuratorem, §. 1, and l. si quis negotia, with infinite similar cases. Concluding, therefore, it appears that the statute does not speak of guardianship, because guardianship is not an affair, nor conversely, and it is expressly stated, ff. de negotiis gestis, l. qui aliena, §. quamvis. And to this reason no response can be made.

The second reason is that a woman holding guardianship is a special case for the mother and grandmother. Furthermore, that a minor holds guardianship would be another inconvenience, ff. de curatore furiosi, l. cuius bonis. But the law does not tolerate two special cases and inconveniences, as C. de dote promissa, l. 1. And this reason also is good and pressing.

The third reason is that he who can be restored to his original position (in integrum restitui) is not a legitimate defender, ff. de procuratoribus, l. minor 25 annorum. But this minor under 25 years could be restored to his original position if he were bound to do something, as ff. de arbitris, l. cum, l. ultimo responso. For example, if he acts temerely or negligently, for in negligence the statute does not say that he has the age of majority. And this reason also compels us to say this, because negligence is not among the four cases comprehended by the statute; and yet the judgment of guardianship can be purged.

The fourth reason is that in a guardian, not only age is considered, but also counsel, especially in a woman, as C. quando mulier tutelae officio fungi potest, l. 2. But the authority of the statute does not represent counsel where it is not, because the matter does not repugn, arg. de usufructu, ea rerum, l. 2.

The fifth reason is that an oath represents one as older; yet an adult swearing does not thereby become a guardian. Hence, a fictitious age is not sufficient, because the strength of mind and vigor of strength do not lie in fiction, but in the perfection of age, ff. de minoribus, l. 1.

The sixth reason is that the counsel of young women is not sufficient in itself, C. de nuptiis, l. in coniunctione.

The seventh reason is that the privilege of minors should not be extended to the injury of others, ff. de administratione tutorum, l. impuberi filio centurio.

The eighth reason is that a statute should not be drawn to an unjust interpretation, ff. de vulgaribus substitutionibus, l. ex facto. Hence, a bad interpretation is either foolish or rash, in Auth. constitutio, quae ex rescripto, and libera natos, post principio, col. 5, where there is a notable text.

The ninth reason is that no guardian administers unless the judge decrees the administration, C. de arbitris tutoribus, l. si. But a wise judge should not decree to a foolish or little-wise person, such as young women; because youthful heats are prone to ruin, de bonis quae libera, l. si, §. filius autem.

The tenth reason is that guardianship and curatorial governance require wisdom and integrity of mind, which in minors is not so invalid that they cannot renounce the benefit of age, nor any other aid, ff. de nova operis nuntiatio, l. doli, §. diversum, ff. de noxalibus actionibus, l. si iudex circumvento. Since, therefore, the renunciation of benefits does not fall upon a minor, neither does guardianship, as in Auth. matri, et aviae. And this is the truth itself.

† It therefore follows that, the mother being excluded, one must consider the paternal and maternal grandmothers, and which is to be preferred, or whether both are admitted to guardianship. And it should be known that such women are sometimes testamentary guardians, sometimes more than legitimate: they are preferred to all legitimate ones. Sometimes they are appointive: when they are appointed by the judge from the conscience of the law. They can, by law, be left and appointed, as stated in the above-mentioned authority in the word "promittitur." And if they concur, there is no doubt that both are called, as in Auth. de hær. ab intest. §. ex his, where it is expressly stated. But let us suppose that only one is appointed, and no mention is made of the other; the question arises whether the other can be appointed or joined, and the answer is that she cannot, because a guardian is not appointed to one who already has a guardian: although a curator may be joined to one whose property is widely dispersed, as C. in qui. ca. tutor habenti, l. propter late, and Inst. de cur. §. interdum; because curatorship is joined for the sake of solicitude, not for the fullness of power. ff. de app. l. cum in uno, §. tutor. Moreover, if any other person had been appointed on account of the delay of the grandmothers, they would have been excluded. ff. de tu. et cur. da. ab his, l. tutor si petitus. ff. ad Treb. l. 2, §. si mater. Secondly, either one is appointed in contempt of the other, the judge having determined the contempt, and the other having been cited, and then she who was absent in contempt makes herself alien to the guardianship, ff. de fidei. lib. l. si legatario, §. a duobus. Or this was not questioned before the judge, nor was she cited, and then one does not exclude the other, just as she does not from inheritance; because to whom the inheritance goes, to him the guardianship goes. ff. de reg. iur. l. quo tutela. And if it is said that a guardian is not appointed to one who already has a guardian, I answer that this is true, unless the one who ought to have been appointed from the beginning, who had the right to demand to be appointed, is not found to be excluded from that right. Therefore, I conclude that both grandmothers, if they are otherwise suitable, ought to concur in the present guardianship; however, in the case of a guardian to whom the right to demand a guardian did not belong, it is true that a guardian cannot be appointed to one who already has one, and thus I hold according to the said §. ex his. Just as grandmothers concur in intestacy and in the more potent guardianship, so too in this appointive guardianship, which is substituted in place of that one and is appointed from the conscience of the law, it is equally in the interest of both, and of the ward, to have them both, lest one alone might contrive, etc. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a person who is a native citizen of a certain place, against whom reprisals have been granted, and who is a citizen enjoying the privilege of the place granting the reprisals, may be arrested by virtue of such reprisals.
2. Castles exempted by the prince are not included within the city or its district.
3. During the time of fairs, a person may not be arrested by virtue of reprisals.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† That the said Grassus could not be seized on account of the said reprisals is manifestly clear for several reasons. And first, because, since he is a citizen, he ought to be treated as a citizen: and, if necessary, in the stronger sense, namely as an original citizen. D. 50.17.105 (Quidam cum filium). For this is a benefit, and therefore it must be interpreted most broadly, D. 1.17.1 (Beneficium), unless it were restricted by other laws. But original citizens of Perugia above all cannot be seized on account of reprisals granted by the Commune of Perugia; therefore, these men cannot be seized, who are of the same reason and condition, as D. 48.19.1 (Sed si accepto usu rogatus). Secondly, because the city is bound to defend its citizen against others, D. 4.15.1; by this law, D. 50.6.1 (De iure ad munera). Therefore, it ought not to injure him, as D. 9.5.1 (Frater a fratre) § Porro. Therefore, because the city is not understood to grant anything against itself, D. 33.6.1 (Si peculium) § Sicut; but this would redound against itself, which has an interest in having wealthy citizens.

Fourthly, because castles exempted by the prince are not included within the city or district, since they are separate. D. de assessoribus, l. eadem. Fifthly, because either this person is not at fault in any way, and then it is unjust to arrest him; or he is at fault in some way, and then he can be sued through ordinary legal proceedings, because he is a citizen. Therefore, the extraordinary remedy of praesalia ceases to apply, D. de condictione institutoria, because the reason of primary power is more appropriate. L. 1, § habet utique, D. si quis testamento liber iussus fuerit.

† Sixth, on account of market days. C. de nundinis, l. nundinę. For public utility is at stake in market days, and in favor of public utility, which takes precedence over private interest, reprisals cease temporarily: because these individuals are not enemies of the republic, nor have they been declared untrustworthy. Those, however, on account of public utility, namely that the province be purged of evil men, may be seized, when general security does not protect them, in Auth. de man. prin. §. neque autem homicidis. From all of the above, I clearly conclude that the said robber ought to be released, and goods ought to be restored to him, if any were seized on account of these reprisals; therefore, let reprisals be valid against those against whom they may be exercised, but they do not include this man and his like. And thus I say, I, Bal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Retaliations cannot be granted against any people unless justice has first been denied to them; but if a people has committed some injustice, retaliations are lawfully granted without seeking justice from the judge of that people.
2. Envoys have security under the law of nations in going, staying, and returning.
casus: CASE: The point is as follows: Gasfredutius, son of Iacobi, brought an action against the commune and the inhabitants of the city of Castello before the officials, on the basis of a commission granted to them by the authority of the general assembly, and let the bill of complaint be examined here. The commune of the city of Castello was summoned; the syndic of the commune appeared, and the territory raised the following objections: First, that reprisals cannot be granted unless it first appears that justice was denied in the city against whom they are sought, and therefore Gasfredutius should not be heard unless he first formally brings suit in the city of Castello and it appears that justice was denied to him there. Second, that in the articles of peace made at Bologna with the Roman Church, against their accomplices and followers on one side, and the commune of Perugia on the other, all robberies, rapines, and cavalry raids committed between the said parties were mutually remitted, and the city of Castello was then among the accomplices and followers of the Church. Third, regarding the award given and received by the commune of Florence and the commune of Perugia on one side, and the commune of the city of Castello on the other, which is relevant. Finally, a term was granted to Gasfredutius for proof, and the summons and letters of the officials were notified to the commune of the city of Castello. Finally, the said commune was summoned on behalf of the said officials at the petition of the said Gasfredutius, so that it might lawfully appear to witness the publication of the proceedings within the year. A term was granted to the city of Castello for proof, and to have proof of all its rights, and to introduce and adduce all its rights, and this was notified to the said commune by messenger and by letters of the officials within the aforementioned term. The syndic of the commune of Castello appeared and produced the promise made by the commune of Perugia on one side and the commune of Castello on the other in the commune of Florence, and the award given by the commune of Florence, which should also be examined. The question is: what are the duties of the officials, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Whenever anyone has received injustice from a people committing it openly, he does not have to bring an action before the judge of the people against the people for two reasons: because he commits injustice by plundering, hence no other evidence is needed. Secondly, because one is not bound to go against the people to the judge of the people: and therefore the injustice of the people is apparent by their offending, and the injustice of the judge is apparent by presumption, as in c. Statutum, § Cum autem, de rescindenda donatione, lib. 6. Therefore, when the people expressly offend, reprisals may be granted: because by that very fact it appears that the people are offending, as in Auth. Quae in provincia. Moreover, because there is no judge unless he is favorable. The chapters do not stand in the way: because ambassadors have a treaty by the law of nations, hence they are not in war, but in alliance. And therefore what has been taken must be restored to them: because it was done contrary to the law of nations.

† Because all ambassadors have security in going, staying, and returning through their embassies, previously signified to those to whom they are directed: where previously they were enemies and foes, as noted in ff. de pace, l. conventionum, in the last gloss. And therefore, the remission of things taken on the occasion of war does not include this special case of the official; hence, reprisals ought to be granted. And thus I, Baldus, say. The fact of the written opinion appears as follows: a census paid for a certain piece of land on several occasions in this form, namely, the said prior, in the name above mentioned, was confessed to have received from Antonio Nicolutii of Porta Solis in the parish of St. Lucy, given for the conservation of the present year, for a certain piece of land planted with vines situated in the Valley of Valliani, the boundaries of which on one side are the property of the monastery of St. Paul of Faenza, on another Massius Cicionis, on another the road of Lucas Ser Pauli called de Perusio: concerning which census, under the said protestation, which is in some right, devolved to the said church, did not receive the said census to the prejudice of the said church, and the said Antonio was confessed to hold and possess the property of the said thing by the said right. Now the said Antonio says that only part of the said thing is freehold, although the payment was made simply, and the faith of the above-mentioned deed encompasses the matter. And on the same point he consulted twice, as will appear below immediately, and the first opinion, because of what he added about the confession, was rather against the client, who for himself, and therefore I consulted again because of new reasons.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the payment of several years of a certain pension or annuity for a thing that was only partly emphyteutic prejudices the payment. The same holds in the following opinion.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† When the formal origin of the emphyteutic contract is established, from which it appears that the emphyteutic payment of the census or canon is understood simply as such, and to what extent, as it appears in the origin: because the payment is to be referred to the debt, not to the non-debt. D. de solutionibus, l. 1; C. eodem, l. 1, with its subject matter. And because, if anyone pays the canon for his own property, he does not prejudice himself. C. de locato et conducto, l. qui rem; and fully noted, D. de acquirenda possessione, l. si aliquam rem. And therefore, notwithstanding the said payment, the original truth, as the primary cause and foundation, must be examined. D. de donationibus, l. qui id quod. And the description of boundaries shows the body of the thing, but not the quality of the thing, because it must be understood according to the principal instrument to which it refers. D. de contrahenda emptio, l. qui tabernas; D. de legibus 1, l. si domus, §. si. However, confession must be adhered to, unless the contrary is proved by the original instrument, that is, by the reformation, to which adherence is due. And thus I say, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 0. In order to ascertain what emphyteutic properties are, and how many there are, recourse must be had to ancient instruments; and if the instruments cannot be found, proof must be made by witnesses; and if it cannot be proved either by instruments or by witnesses, recourse is had to presumptions.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† To ascertain what and how much property is held in emphyteusis, recourse must be had to ancient instruments, which are supported by the undoubted light of truth, as stated in the Digest, *De probationibus*, law *Celsus*, and to monuments. And if it appears from the instrument what, how much, and of what kind the emphyteutic property is, the instrument itself is to be relied upon, and there is no room for conjecture, because conjecture has a place in uncertain matters, not in certain ones. Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Continuus*, § *Cum ita*. But if it does not appear with certainty from the instrument, because the emphyteusis is very ancient, and the boundary of possession has varied, recourse is had to ancient witnesses, if any exist, and to reputation, of which there is no contrary memory. Digest, *De aqua pluviali arcenda*, law 1, in the end; Digest, *De probationibus*, law 2, *Arbiter*; *De aqua quotidiana*, law *Hoc iure*, § *Ductus aquae*; Digest, *De flumine*, law 1, § 1. For reputation is held to be equivalent to truth, so that in the Extravagant, *De veritate sigilli*, chapter *Quicquid per novale*. But if it cannot be made clear with certainty, recourse is had to conjectures, and among other better conjectures, which are to be used for proving, the proof of the quantity of the price of the estate is the proof of the estate itself: because these have proof of each other. This is stated by the notable gloss in law 1, Digest, *De superficiebus*. Therefore, he who examines equity must be moved by the conjecture of the agreed price, for it is not probable, nor tolerable, that a thing worth two thousand should be sold for four hundred; but there is in the thing only as much as is designated by the measure of the agreed price, and thus I say in the proposed question, that it is presumed that something of this body of deeds, which perhaps was formerly one estate by itself. For this is possible and probable, for unless we say so, the church would succumb in action due to the uncertainty of the place and the share, as noted in the Digest, *De rei venditione*, law *Si in rem agat aliquis*. Hence it is more just to win proportionally than to succumb entirely. Therefore, from the quantity of the price, the truth must be presumed that the contract was just on both sides, and not unjust, as the law says, that a small price is not sufficient for a large thing. Law *Ita autem*, in the beginning, *De administratione tutorum*. And the greatest is that which is four times greater. Digest, *Ad Trebellianum*, law *Lucius*, § *Si*. And all solutions of the census, which are found to have been made afterwards, are referred to their beginning, as in the Digest, *De minoribus*, law 3, § *Seio*; Digest, *De fideiussoribus*, law *Tuto*; Digest, *De donationibus*, law *Quicquid*, § *Si cum primus*; and Digest, *De solutionibus*, law 1, with the following law. And if anyone were to say otherwise, he would have to hold that that instrument would not be valid as being uncertain in the thing, as touched upon by Cynus in law 1, Code, *De contrahenda emptione*, law *Coniunctae stipulationes*. Which, however, I do not believe, but I say that it should be reduced to due consideration of equity and proportion. It is supported by what is accustomed to be noted by the doctors in law 1, Digest, *De rebus dubiis*; and Code, *Ne liceat potentibus*, laws 1 and 2; and Code, *De mandato*, law *Per diversas*; Digest, *De in diem addendo*, law *Cum duo*; Digest, *Finium regundorum*, law *In finalibus*; and law *Eos*; Digest, *De legatis*, 3, law *Qui concubinam*, § *Qui fundum*, and 2; and Digest, *De actione empti*, law *Titius haeres*. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If there are two partners, and one of them acts as a surety for something, whether, when, and what action the surety has against the other partner.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The obligation which gives rise to an action against the surety must be considered, and this is an obligation of mandate reduced to a stipulation for the preservation of indemnity. However, the mandate does not bind unless the principal debtor, who gave the mandate, or another person in whose name the mandate was given.

† Whether his partner is bound. First, it must be seen what is the law according to the common law. Second, what is the law according to the form of the statute. And according to the common law, it must be said that either the suretyship is useful to the partnership, or to one of the partners, but not advantageous to the other, or it is doubtful. In the first case, both are bound. D. de inst. l. quicunque. In the second case, only the one who gave the mandate is bound. ibid. l. §. non tantum omne. In the third case, either the suretyship must be conceived under the comprehensive name of the partnership itself, and both are bound. Or it did not apply except to one partner, and then he alone is bound, arg. supra de procu. l. si procu. meus. §. fi. where a similar distinction is made, if that partner, for whom the surety did not intervene, is the debtor of him for whom he intervened: because then, preserving the order of law, he would act against him, as against the debtor of his debtor. In the case at hand, however, it is proposed to the contrary, namely, that he for whom he did not become surety was a creditor by reason of the fault of the partner. l. de illo. pro socio. where it must be observed that the surety who is bound for the principal is bound: so also his partners, just as other creditors, therefore he is bound to him, and from the same fact he acts against him without alleging, let us suppose, that Peter would pay the surety by reason of Bernard’s fault: would he not recover from Bernard? Certainly yes, and if he has Bernard bound, therefore also the said surety: therefore the said surety demands by fraud what he will restore by fraud. For the suretyship is general in every negative cause, and in every person, and benefits all whose interest it is. Moreover, this new partnership does not regard the true mandate which was made before it, and because there was a novation of the contract. D. de fideius. l. stipulatus est opus. D. pro socio. l. id, quod. §. filius. C. locati. l. si cum hermes. The statute is not an obstacle: because it speaks of a partner, but with regard to this mandate, from which the action arises, he is not a partner, because they did not form a partnership for this act, nor does it regard the common interest, but the proper and singular interest of one partner, whence the partnership should not be liable. D. pro socio. l. cum duobus. §. fi. because they are conducting business separately, and not touching upon this matter, whence I do not see the cause of action founded, and therefore the defendant, being sued in that bad judgment, ought to be absolved, saving the substance of the truth: to which I always submit all my saying and my counsel. And so I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, and by what penalty an invader is held liable, who kills or maims.
2. Signs which show fear of death in him who flees when attacked, so that he may plausibly defend himself on the ground that he killed the attacker out of fear of death.
3. Signs which show fear of death in him who was the attacker.
4. One ought not to wait to be struck by an enemy.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.
