† He who, being unable to avoid death in any other way, kills or maims his assailant, is not bound by the penalty for homicide, as in c. 1, de homicidio, in the Clementines. And although the law says that the murderer should await what he has done, as in l. 3, C. de episcopis et clericis audiendis.

† However, an exception is made if it is for the defense of one’s own person, and especially when one feared death not with vain fear, but with a reasonable and terrifying fear; for you will find no one whom weapons and a drawn sword do not terrify, D. 43.16.3 § qui armati (De vi et vi armata). Hence, since he could not otherwise defend himself, he killed, being placed in a doubtful peril: he does not deserve punishment. D. 9.2.27 § qui cum aliter (Ad legem Aquiliam); and C. 9.16.1 (Is qui aggressorem) (Ad legem Corneliam de sicariis). Moreover, that he could not otherwise defend himself from death or grave injury is shown by the quality of the weapons. X. 5.12.1 (Significasti) (De homicidio). For it is not customary for a rod or a light blow to cause serious harm, especially when in the hands of a robust man, as is noted, D. 43.16.1 (Unde vi). Therefore, this homicide was committed with the permission of natural and civil law. D. 1.1.10 (Ut ulcisci) (De iustitia et iure). So much so that a contrary statute is not valid, which provides that one may not defend one’s person from injury, as X. 2.1.1 (Pastoralis) (De re iudicata) in the Clementines. For it could not be done even by consent, as is noted, D. 2.14.1 (Pactum inter haeredem) (De pactis). Furthermore, a statute is to be understood strictly regarding punishment, clearly applying to culpable cases, not to lawful ones. C. 9.1.1 (Si servi vestri) (De noxalibus); nor is innocence subjected to punishment. C. 3.32.1 (Si) (De actionibus). Rather, the statute seems to be glossed, just as the common law is glossed. For this statute appears to have been made to limit the common law; indeed, it is the common law itself, from which it does not deviate. As is noted in C. 1.1.1 (De constitutionibus) lib. 6; X. 5.39.1 (Cum dilectus) (De consuetudinibus). For a statute must be understood soundly, so that its reason and nature are not rejected, as in D. 1.3.1 (Erit autem lex). It is certain, however, that in corporal punishments, dolus (intent) is required. C. 9.14.1 (Nec exemplum) (De falsis); D. 9.16.1 (In lege) (De sicariis). For it is never found that one ought to lose a limb or life for simple culpa (negligence), since one ought not even to lose one’s reputation, as is noted, Inst. 4.13.1 § suspectus (De suspectis tutoribus); and noted in D. 4.3.1 § gravior (De poenis); and D. 2.5.1 (Mac) (De in iurandum litem). This is expressly read and noted in C. 1.1.1 § si quis hominem (De pace tenenda et eius violatione), col. 10. Moreover, if it is culpa not to defend another when you can, it is dolus not to defend yourself when you ought; and therefore natural and civil reasons concur in the defense of one’s own safety, provided it is done moderately. Furthermore, if the measure is exceeded, provided it is done immediately, one is not punished for the whole, but only for the excess of the measure. X. 2.27.1 (Olim) (De restitutione spoliati). It should be known that when one reasonably fears being killed, the measure is to defend oneself, and the deliberation is the fear of death itself, or of inevitable harm, which fear is shown by the quality of the persons, the instruments of audacity, the aggressor’s confinement of place, and similar circumstances, which appear from the surrounding facts, from which the mind of the defender ought to be moved, as is noted in the aforementioned C. 1.1.1 (De homicidio) in the Clementines.

And certainly, in the case at issue, the circumstances are not merely probable, but compelling: first, the necessity arising from being surrounded; second, flight and assault; third, the immediacy of the response; fourth, the physical strength of the aggressor; fifth, that he had already inflicted wounds; sixth, that he had initiated the brawl; seventh, the nature of the weapons. Finally, natural equity: for anyone concerned for his own life would have acted likewise. Hence, what is permitted to all ought not to be forbidden to one, as is fully examined in C. unde vi, l. 1, and in the cited chapter Significasti, de homicidio. And certainly, the sequence of the denunciation demonstrates this, as does C. de lib. cau., l. cum praecum, as well as the credibility of the witnesses and their depositions. Therefore, the accused ought to be acquitted with certainty, in accordance with the facts presented.

First, due to uncertainty, one ought not to wait for the enemy to yield when it is permissible for the enemy coming against you, unless he approaches within a stone’s throw; to yield, §. qui cum aliter. It is no doubt to anyone that one coming with such intent to kill or wound, in which wound death may lie, c. ultimo. de homicidio. lib. 6. comes to l. Cor. de sicar. l. qui cum telo. Hence it is lawful in time to prevent, since it is necessary to oppose this aggressor with a weapon as to a robber. C. quando licet sine iudi. l. ven. j. and l. opprimendorum. in the natural reason of that letter. and ff. ad l. Aquil. l. si ex plagiis. §. tabernarius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that no artisan on feast days, on which there are holidays in the maleficium courts, shall dare or presume to work, open his shop, or practice his craft. Whether Jews on the said days may take pledges, exercise usury, and return the same pledges to those who demand and pay for them.
2. The matters at issue are such as the foregoing demonstrate.
3. To lend at interest is to contract.
4. What an art is.
5. Moneylenders are not artisans.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The statute provides that no artisan on feast days, on which there are holidays in the maleficia, shall dare or presume to work, to open his shop, or to practice his craft. The question is whether Jews on the said days may take pledges, exercise usury, and return the same pledges to those who demand and pay for them, and keep their shops and warehouses open notwithstanding the provision of the statute. And it seems that they are bound by it.

† For such things are subject, insofar as the predicates demonstrate how they are subject. D. de interrog. act. l. si defensor. But it is certain that on the said days there are holidays in the courts: and as to the Jew. See C. de Iudaeis. l. sabbati. Therefore, with respect to this, that he cannot labor on the said days, open shops, or practice a craft. To the contrary is the truth itself for several reasons, and first, because they are not bound to observe the feasts of the festivals introduced by the holy Catholic fathers: because they are not compelled to venerate the Catholic faith, D. de Iudaeis. c. sicut 45. dist. c. qui sincera. And the constitutions of Christians bind them in temporal matters, not in their spiritual matters, nor in those relative to their spiritual matters, as in the observance of days, D. 8. dist. c. si solus Christus. And there, note. Secondly, because the observance of those dedicated days was introduced not only in honor of God, but for the salvation of souls: in which Jews are not included, D. de legibus 2. l. Lucius, and 2. Thirdly, because Jews are not called artisans: because they are not numbered among the registered crafts. D. de test. milit. l. ex eo.
† Because to lend at interest is to contract; but in contracts there are no holidays. C. de feriis l. dies festos.

† And this is evident from the definition of art. For where there is no rule, there is no art, as is noted in the Digest, De iustitia et iure, l. 1, ff. on the word "ars." For without skill, a rule is not art.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If any infant dies in infancy leaving a paternal and a maternal grandfather, which of these succeeds to the maternal goods of the said infant.
casus: CASE. The legal point upon which counsel is sought is as follows: A certain man named Giovanni had Francesca as his wife, and had by her one son named Domenico. Under the title of dowry of the said Francesca, the said Giovanni had one hundred. Later the said Giovanni died, surviving him the said Pietro his father, in whose power he was [?], the said Francesca his wife, and the said Domenico his son. Afterwards the said Domenico died in infancy, surviving him the paternal grandfather and the maternal grandfather. Now it is asked whether the paternal grandfather or the maternal grandfather succeeds to the goods of the mother of the said Domenico, namely Francesca.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† Having seen the said legal point and the matters narrated therein, it seems at first to be said that the paternal and maternal grandfathers are admitted equally: because, since they are in an equal degree, they are admitted equally and ought to be admitted; arg. in auth. post fratres. C. de leg. haer. Moreover, the distinction between agnation and cognation has been abolished, as noted in Auth. de haer. ab inte. § ex his, and what is noted in auth. in successione. C. ad Ter. supports this; therefore, those who are in an equal degree, whether on the side of agnates or cognates, ought to be admitted equally; and from this it is inferred that the paternal grandfather and the maternal grandfather ought to be admitted equally. But the contrary is to be said according to law: namely, that the maternal grandfather is preferred to the paternal grandfather in the said maternal goods upon the death of the said Domenico at an infant age. And that this is true is the case according to one reading maintained by Bart. in C. de bo. quae lib. l. quod scitis. Furthermore, it supports this because a dowry ought to return to the source from which it originated; arg. l. dos a patre. C. so. ma.; therefore, the said dowry of the lady Francesca ought to return to the maternal grandfather of the said infant, from whom the dowry originated. Furthermore, we see in a similar case that when the succession of a brother is in question, uterine brothers are preferred in maternal goods, and consanguineous brothers are preferred in paternal goods, while in property acquired from elsewhere they are admitted equally, as in l. de eman. C. de leg. hae.; and what is noted in the same title in auth. post fratres in gl. supports this; moreover, the gloss maintains this in the said l. quod scitis in dote, namely that in it the maternal grandfather is preferred to the paternal grandfather; therefore in our case it is clear that the said maternal grandfather, when the dowry of lady Francesca is at issue, is preferred to the paternal grandfather. It also supports this that Bart. maintains in auth. in successione and in auth. defuncto that in maternal goods—namely, in those donated by the father to the emancipated son himself—the father is preferred, and the mother, and in maternal goods the mother is preferred, as he stated in the said auth. defuncto. Nor does it obstruct this if it is said that the paternal grandfather, by the benefit of l. si infanti, can enter by his grandfatherly right upon the maternal inheritance devolved upon the infant, which he did not enter upon on behalf of his infant while alive: because the law si infanti is a new law, and it speaks of the father, and certain jurists say that it does not extend to the grandfather; for the text says iure paterno, etc. Or it can be answered that that law is limited by the said l. quod scitis, which is posterior, so that it does not have application when both a maternal grandfather and a paternal grandfather survive regarding goods coming from the mother. It can also clearly be answered in our case that we are not in the case of the said l. si infanti, because here the paternal grandfather is understood to have entered upon the inheritance on behalf of the infant grandson himself during the latter's lifetime; which is proved because Bart. says that a grandfather or a father, by not restoring the dowry, is understood to enter upon the inheritance on behalf of the infant; he expressly holds thus in l. infante and l. geritur. de acq. haer., although Bald. varied somewhat on that point. If therefore this paternal grandfather entered upon the inheritance on behalf of the infant, he cannot henceforth allege the benefit of l. si infanti; rather, we are in the case of the law quod scitis, so that the maternal grandfather is preferred in the maternal inheritance acquired for the infant. Whence, nevertheless, I concede that this paternal grandfather, by right of paternal power and as the legitimate administrator of this infant, acquired for himself the usufruct; noted in l. 1. C. de bon. mat. and in l. cum oportet and in l. cum non solum. de bon. quae lib.; and that in the said usufruct the paternal grandfather is preferred to the maternal grandfather, but as to the ownership the maternal grandfather is preferred, to whom the usufruct will be consolidated after the death of the paternal grandfather. And as written above, I, Marco of Perugia, the least of the doctors of both laws, state and advise, and in faith thereof I subscribe and affix my seal, subject to truer counsel. Speaking in the case of an infant, just as it speaks, I believe that the paternal grandfather can enter upon the inheritance upon the infant's death by his own right, as devolved upon him through the said l. infanti, which also speaks of the grandfather, as appears from the opening of l. si infanti; nor is it an objection that it was not entered upon, and thus an unadited maternal inheritance is not transmitted to a father or a paternal grandfather, as in l. non pro numero. C. ad or., because that does not apply in the case of an infant, as in the said l. si infanti; which case, as it speaks of an infant, is not found elsewhere. Likewise it does not stand in the way that the grandfather might be seen to have entered according to the opinion of Bart. in l. gerit, because Bald. in l. non hoc. Vnde legitimi holds the contrary, and in the said l. si infanti in the lecture which he delivered in Padua at home in question 11, and in l. non hoc. C. vnde legit.; and therefore, when requested, I refused to subscribe to the said opinion, etc. I, Francesco, etc. CASE. A certain man, sound in mind and sense though languishing in body, not wishing to die intestate, relying upon the wisdom, uprightness, and diligence of the venerable father Abbot of Santa Croce, his kinsman, entrusted his last will and disposition to the said lord Abbot to be arranged and disposed of as it shall seem fit and pleasing to him, to whom he fully committed his authority in the premises.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a person, though physically ill, is of sound mind and senses, and declares that he does not wish to die intestate, and entrusts his will to someone in whose wisdom, integrity, and diligence he greatly confided, such a testament is not void on account of the daughter being passed over.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is asked whether the disposition of the aforementioned daughter, who was passed over, is valid. And it seems that it is: because Innocentius says in the Decretals, *De testibus*, in the chapter *Cum tibi*, because this disposition does not contain an institution of an heir, but the goods will be given intestate by the executor to the poor, saving the rights of the intestate successor. Nor is the disposition considered captatory; rather, it is distributive in favor of the soul. The truth is in our case, in which the testator expressly says that he does not wish to die intestate; which is understood to mean that he instituted the Abbot as heir: as in the Digest, *De testamentis*, law 1. And thus there is no institution due to the omission, whence the testament is valid in nothing, as in the Authenticum *Ut cum*, *De appellationibus cogitandis*, in § *Aliud quoque*. And if anyone should say that this is not an heir, but someone having the power to order another heir, this disposition will be null: because it is captatory, indeed because the testator must name an heir. Code, *De testamentis*, law *Iubemus*. The chapter *Cum tibi* is not to the point: because there the text speaks of his will. Therefore, he must express something of his will, whence our doctors understand that there the testator did not leave the making of the testament, according to Raymondus de Peñafort and Cynus in the law *Captatorias*. And therefore, because the institution of an heir requires that the heir be declared in some way, it seems that that case does not speak of a captatory institution of an heir, because it is the head of the testament, whatever Bartolus says, whose statement I limit in the said law *Captatorias*. Furthermore, if we consider Innocentius well, he himself distinguishes: either a universal disposition is committed, and the executor is considered instituted as heir for the poor; or a disposition of certain things is committed, and then it seems that he dies intestate. And in the second case, the legitimate heir succeeds intestate, and pays the legacies after deducting the Falcidian portion, and this distinction he drew to the gloss of Accursius in the law *Quaerens*, *De hereditate quaerenda*. Since therefore a universal disposition was committed here, granted that, in favor of a pious cause, it was not considered captatory, but certain, and made of a certain heir, namely the executor, it is necessary that it be null due to the omission of the daughter: nor can it be drawn to intestacy. Code, *De conditionibus*, law *Si quis agere*; and Code, *De testamentis*, law *Non codicillum*. And therefore I conclude the disposition null: as in the Digest, *De liberis et posthumis*, law *Gallus*, in the principle and § *In omnibus*, and law *Inter caetera*. It does not avail by the law of intestacy: because the testator did not wish to die intestate, nor by the law of testacy: because he could not, due to the less than legitimate interpretative institution of an heir, as an incongruous ordering of the testament, for even when left to God, the omitted son can neither be disinherited, as is noted in the Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*, law *Papius*, § *Si imperator*. Furthermore, those words, "committed the will to the will, etc., to be ordered," show that, since the testator himself imposed his will upon the will of another, and that which he did not order, but committed to be ordered, which is impossible: because a testament is the certain knowledge of our will. But this word, "our," which is of the substance of the definition of a testament, ceases here. Whence this disposition is more than captatory, because it is truly and interpretatively captious, since it must stand by itself regarding the institution of an heir; that institution, and, so to speak, is a will without a will, which implies a contradiction, and that one should make a testament or last will for another is not found, except in the exemplary pupillary substitution, which is made for those lacking judgment, and from two comprehensive wills of the living and the dead, a last will cannot result, as in the said law *Si*, Digest, *Coniunctis praedictis*. Therefore, this testament lacks both piety and the authority of law: and therefore it is not valid, neither by the subtlety of law, nor by canonical equity, weighing the point proposed, etc.

A. Such a fact is proposed: Simon Nerii of Siena, having two legitimate and natural daughters, and having one male son named Blasius, made an institution and substitution by the words written below, namely: "Also, he instituted as his heirs in solidum, equally in all his movable and immovable things, rights, and actions, however and by whatever name they may be considered or could be considered, all his legitimate male sons born of the legitimate marriage of the said Lord Simon and of Lady Francisca, his wife, saving the indications and legacies written below. Also, he indicated and bequeathed by the right of institution to all his legitimate daughters born of the legitimate marriage of the said Lord Simon and of the said Lady Francisca, 100 gold florins for each of them: and he wished them, and each of them, to be tacit and content with the aforementioned. Also, he says, he wished, ordained, ordered, and commanded, that if all the aforementioned legitimate male sons born of the aforementioned legitimate marriage of the aforementioned Lord Simon and Lady Francisca should die within such an age without legitimate children descending from them, in that case he instituted and substituted for himself, and in his aforementioned legitimate male sons, heirs in solidum in all his goods and things, movable and immovable, rights, and actions, however and by whatever name they may be considered or could be considered, the nearest agnate of the said Lord Simon from the paternal line of the said. Always saving the aforementioned and below-written, he wished the aforementioned to be valid by the right of testament, and if they do not avail, or will not avail by the right of testament, let them avail by the right of codicils, and if they do not avail, or will avail by the right of codicils, let them avail by the right of donation causa mortis, and by every other right and form by which they may better avail."

After the said testator died, the said two daughters and the said Blasius surviving; then the said Blasius died at the age of 30 years, without children, and certain sons of John, formerly the brother of the said testator, surviving, who were paternal cousins of the said Blasius. This John was alive at the time of the death of the said Simon; but he predeceased the said Blasius. It is asked from the foregoing, whether the said paternal cousins of the said Blasius can come to the inheritance of the said Simon by virtue of the said substitution: for it seems that they can: because they are the nearest male agnates of the said Blasius, through whom male agnation is confirmed, and they are of the paternal line of the said Simon, and because the said testator in the said substitution used the name of the masculine gender, saying "nearest agnate," although he did not express any proper name, and because the said Blasius died within the legitimate age, which legitimate age is said to begin at the end of the 25th year, and thereafter the said legitimate age lasts until one hundred years, or until death. For in the aforementioned words there seems to be no doubt. Whence one should not depart from their meaning. For if the testator had intended and wished to provide for the case in which the same Blasius would die before the age of puberty, or before the 28th year, he could have expressed this. To the contrary, it is said by the carnal sisters of the said Blasius that the said paternal cousins do not come to the said fideicommissary inheritance by virtue of the said testator, otherwise the said substitution, saying that they are the nearest agnates, and that they are of the paternal line of their father, and that they are comprehended in the said substitution, since the masculine pronounced by the testator conceives the feminine, and especially because they say that the testator in the said substitution intended that if the sons died after the legitimate age, otherwise an absurd understanding would result. It is also alleged by the said daughters of the said testator that the said testament is subject to the defect of nullity, because they were not instituted purely, but conditionally, as appears from the series of the said testament. It is asked, what is the law.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the father substituted the nearest agnate from the paternal line of the testator, whether daughters are included under the term "nearest relatives," to the exclusion of male sons from the testator's brother.
2. Below, what is meant.
3. A daughter instituted by this wording, when, or at what time, is she to be understood as instituted, or whether under a condition.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the first point, I say that the daughters do not appear to have been substituted on account of the words “from the paternal line,” because agnation does not arise between the testator and them as proceeding from the testator’s side, but rather from the testator himself, who is the stock, root, and first principle of agnation with respect to his daughters; and this is shown by the principle of the degree in which they stand, as stated in the Digest, De gradibus, l. Iurisconsultus.

† On the second point, I say that, by the proper nature of the word "infra" when appended to a time, it signifies the inclusion of the entire period, as is established in the rescript *frequens*, Book 6 of the Code, *de non numerata pecunia*; in the law *cum ultra*, *de electione*; in the chapter *statutum*, in the same book; and in the chapter *cupientes*, section *caeterum*, *de electione*, together with the chapter *si*, Book 6. However, the testator’s intent appears to contradict this. For it must be believed that the testator intended to substitute for the younger rather than the older heir, which would be entirely contrary to the present case. Therefore, I say that the word "infra" is used here in an exclusive sense, meaning "before" or "prior to," as in the Code, *de posthumis hereditatibus instituendis*, in the law *si*, in the gloss. I believe this was the testator’s intention. Nevertheless, regarding the truth of the matter, the first opinion seems more correct, as in the Digest, *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*, in the law *ex facto*, section *item quaero*, where it states: "indeed, the entire space," etc. Briefly, I say that the word "infra" is used here to mean "before," as the text establishes in the Digest, *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*, in the law *qui habebat filium*. For the phrase "within puberty" signifies "before puberty"; otherwise, the discussion of pupillary substitution there would be in vain, since pupillary substitution ends at puberty. And it is certain that the case is correctly posited there.

† On the third point, I say that the will is valid, because the word "since" or "when" is to be understood here temporally, not conditionally. For an uncertain day does not always create a condition, especially when such a condition would induce nullity or absurdity. When the day of a legacy arrives. L. ex his verbis. And this delay is removed by L. quam in prioribus, C. de inoff. test. And thus the will is valid; however, as I said, the substitution expired in time. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a testator instituted two sisters and the nephews from them, one of whom had five sons, and one sister died together with four sons while the testator was still alive: upon the testator’s death, it is asked whether the sister and the granddaughter of the said testator come to the said inheritance by concurrence.
casus: CASE. A certain Lord Jacob, having two full sisters, namely Lady Paulina and Lady Nina. This Lady Paulina had five legitimate and natural children, namely Francis, Nese, Bartholomew, Nicholas, and Catherine. Now, the said Lord Jacob made his will in the presence of the said nephews and niece. And among other things, he disposed in this manner: namely, in all his movable and immovable goods, rights, actions, and names of debts, wherever they may be and may be found, he instituted and made Lady Paulina and Lady Nina, full sisters of the said testator, and their children, his heirs. It happens that Francis, Nese, Bartholomew, and Nicholas, and the said Paulina, their mother, died during the lifetime of the testator. Then the said testator died, with Lady Catherine, daughter of the said Lady Paulina and niece of the said testator, surviving. And the said Lady, his daughter. After the death of the said testator, the legitimate and natural father of the said Lady Catherine, as the legitimate administrator of the said Lady Catherine, entered into the inheritance of the said testator in the name of the said Catherine. Now it is asked whether one-half of the inheritance of the said testator, or one-fourth part, pertains to the said Lady Catherine.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Having carefully considered the wording and its weight, the sense is this: because the said Jacob instituted the lady Paulina, and her sons and daughters, as heirs, and so forth. For the word "their," being plural, is resolved into singularities, and returns the genus to the genus by referring the sons to their mother, and joining them to her according to the reasoning of understanding and of the words. Thus, there is found a conjunction among the said sisters, and a conjunction between the sons and their mother; therefore, the sons of their mother are compelled, by the utterance of the words, by the affection of the testator, and by the interpretation of the law, so that one sister with her children is instituted to one half, and the other sister likewise with her children to the other half, as in C. de impub. et aliis substit. l. si. And by this we have the matter of the right of accretion. For the mother's share accrues to her children, and among themselves it accrues to those who are from the same mother: because the bond of conjunction is greater among them, and omitting circumlocutions, thus hold the lords Dy. and Cy. ff. de vulg. sub. l. cohæredi. §. qui discretas. And this is the very truth: because from the greater conjunction of affection in the right of accretion arises the right of preference. It follows well that the said lady Catherine ought to have the half. The objection from de usufr. accre. l. si quis Titio does not hold, because this contrary is fully resolved by petitio. and Cy. in d. l. si. The remaining points, which are of the subtle matter of the right of accretion, are not necessary here; let the true conclusion suffice. And even if the opinion of Dy. and Cy. is not true in the question formed by them, nevertheless in our case their reasons, which are founded on the conjunction of affection, show that what I said is true, for nature, by the contestation of filiation, otherwise called conjunction, and affection, has united the sons to the mother. And this is the case in d. l. si. 1

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A mother, uncertain whether she wishes to accept the inheritance of her son or merely the usufruct, may, with no objection from the husband, take possession of the usufruct with a protestation that she does not intend to prejudice the succession.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If this lady has a contradictor, she must choose whether she prefers the formal usufruct from her husband’s will or the intestate inheritance of her son; but if she has no contradictor, she may possess the usufruct with a protestation, because she does not intend to prejudice herself in the succession. And these points are derived from, and noted in, C. de haer. act. l. debitum. And this is true for the part in which she succeeds, or in whole: if she succeeds in whole, which is when this occurs, it is clear from auth. cessante, C. de haere. For where she succeeds in part, for the other part the inheritance provides security. But where she succeeds in whole, the usufruct provides security to no one in the name of usufruct, because it is inherent in the ownership.

In the name of God, amen. The facts are as follows: Piccha, Clara, Valla, Hugolinus, and Ninus of Todi, while they were exiles and rebels of the city of Todi, and with all their goods confiscated, confessed before the commune of Todi that they had mutually received from Gualterius and Vivianus of Todi, paying for themselves and for Gualterellus Manutii from their common funds, five hundred florins, which they promised to restore to the said Gualterius and Vivianus for themselves and to the said Gualterellus, present and stipulating, at their request, obligating themselves jointly and severally. And a penalty was added in the instrument drawn up therefor, namely that if the said debtors did not observe the contents of the instrument or in any way acted against it, they would incur the penalty of double the amount; which is repeated as often as they act against the agreement, and whether the penalty is paid or not, the contents of the instruments nevertheless remain firm. And a command of guarantee (guarentigia) was made by the notary who had drawn up the instrument, without saying or asserting in the aforementioned instrument in any part that the same notary was an ordinary judge or otherwise a judge.

Afterwards, the said Gualterius and Vivianus, at the same time, by another instrument, but not by the hand of the same notary, had it promised to them by the said Piccha, Clara, Valla, Hugolinus, and Ninus that they would not at any time come forward nor oppose anything against the said loan instrument, under a penalty of one thousand florins; and in the same manner a command of guarantee was made.

Then it is noted by the said Piccha, Clara, Valla, Hugolinus, and Ninus that the said Gualterius and Vivianus, who had likewise stood in rebellion with them against the city of Todi, were recalled and readmitted to the city of Todi; and also the bans and condemnations against them were annulled, abolished, and erased, and they were restored to all their rights. But the said Gualterius and Vivianus, having been thus recalled and readmitted, by virtue of the said loan instrument for five hundred gold florins, sued the said Piccha jointly and severally. And by virtue of the statute of guarantee of the city of Todi and the said instrument, certain executions were carried out in the contumacy of the said Piccha, namely, because many citations were issued against the said Piccha with strict enforcement, and it was ordered by the judge that he be arrested. It was ordered by Bartolus that Piccha and the house of the said Piccha be pronounced and held liable, although not yet seized, which executions the aforementioned statute of guarantee of the city of Todi permits, provided that by the form of the statute of guarantee nothing can be opposed or otherwise proven, unless the exception of payment is raised, which must be proven by a public instrument. And the said Piccha raises another exception, namely, of simulation and of a condition due to a disgraceful cause, because the said loan instrument was in truth made so that the said Gualterius and Vivianus would place themselves in rebellion against the city of Todi together with them, and also for the repair of certain houses of the said Gualterius, Vivianus, and Gualterellus, the destruction of which they feared by placing themselves in the aforementioned rebellion, on the occasion of which rebellion they were destroyed.

On the following points, having seen the case as stated and the statute of guarantee of the city of Todi, namely:

First, whether the said loan instrument is valid, because it was made during the time of rebellion, whereby their goods were confiscated.

Second, whether the said loan instrument deserves execution by guarantee, and if the execution by guarantee made can and should be revoked.

Third, whether the said Piccha, the facts being as they are, can come against the said loan instrument with impunity, and how.

Fourth, whether the stipulation made by the said Gualterius and Vivianus in the manner aforesaid is valid as regards the father of the said Gualterellus, and if it is valid, to whom the action belongs.

Finally, how counsel is given to the said Piccha against the aforesaid, and what he ought to do in order to evade the penalty and the debt aforementioned.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A promise made from an illicit cause, whether express or tacit, is invalid.
2. In how many ways the payment of debts may be made.
3. A statute which prohibits the raising of the defense of simulation is contrary to natural law.
4. When the promisor may be admitted to allege his own turpitude.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It must be premised that promises, whether express or tacit, which arise from a base cause, are invalid. D. 50.17.129 (Si plagii); D. 2.14.1 (Iuramento); D. 2.14.1 § 2 (Et generaliter) and § 3 (Si ob maleficium); D. 44.7.53 (Si). And there are three cases: either a promise is made to someone not to commit a delict, or to commit a delict, or because he has committed a delict, for the sake of rewarding the offense. In the first case, the promise stands, but an exception is raised: for the cause is not base, but the recipient acts basely; because he ought to abstain from committing a delict not for a price, but gratuitously. As stated in the aforementioned § Si ob maleficium. The said cause is therefore not base because its contrary is base, and the nature of contraries is opposed. And if one of the contraries is base, its contrary will not be base. D. 1.3.1 § 1 (Ibi bonos). Not only in the second case is the promise void by operation of law, because it tends toward a crime, and those things which refer to a base cause cannot be brought to effect; hence, if someone promises, otherwise he will commit some mischief at the request of another, although a promise of indemnity has been made to him on this account, nevertheless he can obtain nothing, as D. 40.12.1 (Si remunerandi) § Rei turpis; and in D. 17.1.13 (Si tibi mandaveris) § Qui eadem; and it is expressed in D. 46.1.56 (Si a reo) § Quod vulgo; D. 35.2.1 (Dominus Sticho) § Fin.; D. 9.2.1 (Nec praetermittendum); C. 9.13.1 (Quoniam multa facinora); and in C. 22.1.1 (Sicut) de iureiurando, according to Innocent III; D. 33.8.1 (Quintus Mutius) § Fin. And the judge must interpose his authority ex officio, and such matters are to be rescinded by conjecture. D. 1.16.1 (Illicitas) in principio.

Thirdly, in the case of turpitudinous delicts, the remuneration is shameful and foul, and men wish to be remunerated in three ways by testament, by promise, and by delivery: by testament they cannot [bequeath] to those incapable, in Auth. quibus monachis, §. finalis, col. 7, de probationibus; l. qui testamentum, de legatis tertio; l. cum quis decedens, §. Titia, C. de naturali liberorum. But by testament to capable persons it seems that it can be done. D. de donationibus, l. affectionis. This fails in the case of soldiers, who ought to shine with honesty. D. de testamento militis, l. miles ita, §. mulier. Or it can be said that the law affectionis speaks of turpitude not condemned: as C. de naturali liberorum, Auth. licet. For it is shameful to have a concubine, yet a legacy and donation can be made to her up to the legitimate amount. D. de legatis tertio, l. Item in legato, §. paruique. It is otherwise in turpitude condemned, which is punished by law, as noted in Inst. ad orf., §. nouissime, and in l. si qua illustris, and in l. Claudius, D. de his qui ut indigni. By promising also no one is bound, as in the said l. si plagii, and there noted. And this is the true understanding of that law, when it says, or makes the cause by delivery, he is also not bound regarding eviction, yet dominion passes, as D. de conditionibus ob turpem causam, l. 1, joined with l. si usufructum, quem ad modum cautio. Now I return to the proposition. For if, as if they were placing themselves in rebellion, they received such a promisor and a cautio, the promise is not valid, nor is execution to be given by common law, since such a promise pertains to the execution of delicts, and to sedition, and to monopoly: against which the judge ought to oppose with all efforts, as in Auth. de mancipiis principum, §. deinde conueniens, C. de monopolio, l. 1. And note, c. Id venerabile, de electione, that in those things which are pernicious by example, even an oath is not valid according to Innocentius. And to a bad example favor is not to be shown, as D. de poenis, l. si quis aliquid, §. qui abortionis, there where it says, because it is a matter of bad example. Also it must be considered that in our case the substance of the obligation is lacking, namely the first cause, because it is turpitudinous. Also the cause of the stipulation, because it is simulated, for no loan intervenes according to the substance of truth, hence three cases are to be considered, for sometimes the origin and foundation are lacking, whence novation cannot be made by stipulation, then the obligation fails in effect. D. de exceptionibus doli, l. 2, §. circa. Sometimes a reasonable cause and foundation are present, yet the parties wish to insert the cause of a loan, and then they can, because the substance of the obligation does not fail, although as regards the loan no natural loan intervenes, yet a civil one intervenes, which cooperates with another, as C. si certum petatur, l. si ex pretio. Sometimes without consideration and thought of another cause a promise is made on account of a loan, and then the parties were acting among themselves that the contract was a true contract to be fulfilled by subsequent payment, then the rule of non-numerated money has place. D. si certum petatur, l. qui pecuniam; C. eodem, l. si non singuli; Inst. de verbis obligationum; D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. non figura; C. de non numerata pecunia, l. in contractibus. In our case, however, a turpitudinous cause is alleged: and let him blame himself who placed himself in rebellion, and these things are true, if the truth can be proven, but it must be seen whether the statute resists the exception and the proof. For truth avails little, which cannot be proven in law or in fact, de exceptionibus, c. cum ecclesiae, and noted, C. de transactionibus, l. ubi pactum. For that which is held is considered valid, if no one can allege this, as D. de manumissione testamento, l. qui habebat, §. si, and there the gloss singularis. That which is noted in §. pactus ne peteret is applicable. Moreover, if the statute prohibits opposing the exception of simulation, it will not be said by action that the contract is one of simulation, because to whom the exception is denied, the petition is denied, on account of which one comes to the exception, D. de minoribus, l. in casu, per Cynus. Also, to whom defense is denied, much more strongly is impeachment denied. C. de transactionibus, l. nec intentio codicillorum. Also, the sentence of the law is not of less power than the sentence of a man, but if a man, having cognizance of the cause, rejects the exception, one cannot again sue for the same effect. D. de compensatione, l. quod in diem, §. 1; D. de negotiis gestis, l. si autem, §. si; C. de fideiussoribus, l. si in fine. But every law would say, having cognizance of the cause, for the common usage. C. de legibus, l. humanum. For in the law, for the cognizance of the cause, there is either the reason of the law itself, or its authority. D. de legibus, l. non omnium; D. de postulando, l. 1, §. pueritiam; D. de testamento, l. ex

† Opinion. It must be considered, however, that a statute which prohibits the raising of the defense of simulation is contrary to natural law, because where consent is lacking, natural law is lacking. D. de pactis, l. 1, §. conventionis. Likewise, if it prohibits the raising of the defense of the turpitude of the actor, it is contrary to divine law, by which law things that are naturally turpitudinous are invalid not according to positive law, as in c. non est obligatorium and in c. nervi testiculorum, 13, dist. 4, c. erit autem lex. Hence, although the party raising the defense of simulation and turpitude may lack a judge, because the judge does not immediately permit the raising of the defense to be heard, nevertheless he does not lack natural justice, as in l. si, C. si contra ius, vel uti pu., per Cynus, and in c. quae in ecclesiarum, de constitutionibus, per Innocentius. Whenever the turpitude is that of the cause itself and of the person, the defense may be raised considering natural reason; otherwise, if the turpitude did not affect the cause itself, even if the person were turpitudinous, for even in the case of turpitudinous persons justice must not be denied. D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. sed et milites, in §. sed ignominia. Hence, even a perjurer is heard if the perjury does not touch the cause on which the action is based, as noted in D. de iureiurando; otherwise, if it touches the cause itself. C. de transactionibus, l. si quis maior. Where, however, the statute resists the party raising the defense, and even commands the judge not to hear it, the judge cannot hear it; but the prince or bishop may be heard on account of sin through the way of denunciation; because justice is lacking before the secular judge, as noted in c. licet, de foro competenti, and noted in c. significantibus, de officio delegati, per Innocentius.

† Nevertheless, there is doubt, because how, when bringing an action for rescission or for the rescinding of a contract, will the promisor allege his own turpitude? I answer that, because the action partakes of the nature of a defense and is directed toward it, and because a replication of fraud nullifies an exception of fraud, since the plaintiff deals with damage and the defendant with profit, as in l. cum mulier, § so, ma., according to Jacobus de Aretio and others. Other exceptions, which can be prohibited by natural reason or by reason of good faith and equity, never open a path to the bishop; rather, municipal law will be observed in every forum, as noted in l. ex ea, ff. de postulando. That which is noted in c. 1, de officio ordinarii, according to Innocentius, is pertinent. Where, however, the statute ceases to apply, for example because the instrument is not guaranteed, then even the secular judge cognizes the exception of simulation and turpitude, because the statute ceases to apply and common law takes effect. In such a case, if the party raising the exception is alive, he is not bound to the penalty of the contract. ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. qui Romam; ff. ad legem Falcidiam, l. Seius. And Augerius.

In the name of God, amen. The question is between Agnolo Mei and his wife, Lady Paula, acting on one side, and Iano Mei and his wife, Lady Jacoba, defending on the other side. The point of the question and of the aforementioned cause, having seen the writings and acts and proceedings made in the said cause, and having heard the allegations of the parties, which are the matters for the judge to pronounce upon in the said cause by the said judge, on which it was committed to give counsel to the eminent Master Baldo, Doctor of Laws, according to Bartolus, judge of appeals of the present Lord Podesta, on the 9th day of January, 1334.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When reduction is sought on account of the fraud of the arbiter, or arbitrator, what may be sought is more accurately a cassation, or declaration of nullity, or quasi-declaration thereof.
2. A procurator appointed prior to the award for the purpose of ratifying it does not appear to have a mandate to consent to injustice.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

I premise, for the sake of clarity, that where a reduction is sought on account of the fraud of an arbitrator or umpire, a reduction may be sought, or rather more accurately, a cassation or nullity, or a declaration of nullity. C. de arbitris, l. arbitratorum; ff. de arbitris, l. non distinguimus, §. cum quidam; and l. ita demum. This holds notwithstanding that any license whatsoever has been granted to the arbitrator or umpire; because, since he is chosen as a good man, it was not intended to permit fraud, but to prohibit it. The text is in the aforementioned l. ita demum. Nor does an oath stand in the way, because it does not appear that an oath was taken in a matter in which one is not so much settling as being deceived. de operis lib., l. si libertus; de iureiurando, c. quintauallis. And thus Raynerius de Ferriaco argues in his disputation beginning "Two parties compromised." And Johannes Callius argues in his disputation beginning "Two litigants." I possess these disputations, and no one possessing understanding doubts this point.

Secondly, I premise that a procurator appointed before the arbitration award for the purpose of ratification does not appear to have a mandate to consent to injustice and fraud. D. de cond. indeb. l. si procurator; D. quod quisque iur. l. 3, § si procurator; and noted expressly by Bartolus, D. quomodo et quando appel. sit l. 1, in fine. Thirdly, I premise that either this procurator ratified the award led by error, because he believed in good faith that the award was valid, and it is not valid on account of the error, D. de pact. l. tres fratres; or he did so knowingly, and it is not valid, because the procurator acted with fraud and appears to have acted against his mandate, D. mand. l. creditor, § Lucius. From these it appears that the bill of complaint proceeds with regard to fraud and corruption, because on account of these causes a sentence can be retracted. D. ad Treb. l. servo invito, § eum praetor; D. de iud. l. si praetor, § Marcellus; C. quando prov. non est necesse l. venales; 2 q. 1 c. in primis. And consequently, with regard to these two chapters, the case ought to be compromised, and it ought to be compromised only under these terms, not on any other matter, as is clear in the aforementioned disputations through the aforementioned laws. But it is objected that finally payment was not made within five days. I answer that this is not required by the statute for the substance of the petition, but for the substance of compulsion. Thus, C. de lit. contest. auth. offerantur. For sportulae are provided after the petition and after the time for petitioning. Again, it is objected that notice was given to the procurator; indeed, he was present, and thus the principal appears to be present. D. de lib. agn. l. 1, § 1. But I answer that the statute requires that notice be given to the party against whom the award is made, but this procurator is not the party against whom the award is made: because he is not mentioned in the award, and because it does not concern him. D. quando appel. sit l. 1, § impropria. Again, it is objected that the compromise was not legitimately petitioned for within the fifth day, since the lady Paula was a minor and in need of a curator. It is answered that Angelus compromised, and he is the principal person. And therefore he could petition for his own interest and that of his wife, and that for his own interest there is no doubt. Again, for the interest of the minor wife: because she is a co-litigant, and depends principally on the major, who bound himself for the minor, and is an author in his own right, whence the minor is in the case by way of a certain dependence on the major. See D. l. 3, § si rem. R. ha. Again, this petition is useful to the major, as in D. l. non eo minus, because it benefits and does not harm him by virtue of the petition. In the compromise, however, a curator will be required when there is an interest, because there the weight of advantage and disadvantage lies. And thus I say and counsel, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If one is placed in office, a salary is owed until the arrival of the successor becomes known.
casus: CASE. The point is as follows. The city of Spoleto being under the dominion and recognition of the lord Supreme Pontiff, the lord Urban appointed as Vicar of the said city a certain Peter, at the pleasure of the said lord Supreme Pontiff, without any other determination or taxation of salary. And that the said lord Peter could exercise the said office by himself and by a substitute appointed by him, as appears in the rescript of the lord Supreme Pontiff. Finally, the substitute of the said lord Peter administered the said office, sitting in civil and criminal matters, doing all things that are usually done in such offices among the citizens and subjects of the said city of Spoleto, proposing in the council those matters that were to be exercised by the council of the said commune, as is customary according to the form of the statute of the said city. Finally, in the course of time, the prior of the city of Spoleto and others who are appointed to issue bills for payments to be made for the money of the commune of Spoleto, issued to the said lord Peter two bills for the first two thirds of six months, with an additional quantity of money determined, of which bills for the said first third, the said Peter received in ready money. Finally, in the course of time, the commune of Spoleto, by council, deliberated also by the authority of the said substitute, that for the other second and final third of the said six months, the said lord Peter, Vicar, should be paid from a certain sum of money of the said commune, or in which the said commune claimed to have a right, that the said lord Peter, Vicar, should have from the said quantity for each third, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Until the arrival of the successor is made known, the salary previously appointed is due. D. de officio proconsulis, l. Meminisse; D. locati, l. Item quaeritur; §. Qui impleto, D. soluto matrimonio, l. Pene; §. Uxor, C. locati, l. Licet. But after it is made known that the successor has arrived, the salary is due, because it is owed on account of the office, and the office has expired, and because stipends are not owed to one who does not administer, as is fully noted in l. 1, §. Diuus, D. de nauigantibus cognatione, de assessore, l. Diem functo, and l. 1, C. de re militari, lib. 12.

CASE. Given the statute of the city of Triviso in the third treatise of the second book, c. 2, under the rubric “On the succession of males, with nephews and daughters excluded,” which begins “Ad decus et c.” The case is as follows: Titius died, leaving one male son by his first wife, and two daughters by his second wife, and likewise leaving said second wife. He died intestate, having constituted no dowry for his said daughters, nor designated any provision for them, either expressly or under the name of dowry. Then said daughters died in pupillary age, and thus, having reached marriageable age, survived by their said mother, who made herself heir of her said daughters. Now it is asked whether said mother, as heir of the aforementioned, has any right to claim something from the goods of their said father by virtue of said statute or any other law.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute concerning the succession of males to the exclusion of granddaughters and daughters, and the father having died leaving a male son and two daughters from another wife, who die in their minority, whether the mother may claim anything from the father's estate of the daughters, since nothing was assigned to them for dowry or for their legitime.
2. A testator who does not expressly provide is deemed to have tacitly ordered that which the law ordains regarding his succession.
3. It is a matter of law that the same applies to that which succeeds in place of the legitime as applies to the legitime itself.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Assuming that the statute is valid, it must be examined what the statute intends: and I consider that the statute first provides for male descendants by admitting them to universal succession, entirely excluding daughters. And this extends up to the words “but to daughters.” Secondly, it provides for the daughters themselves, and this in three causes. First, when they are dowered, by ordaining that the dowry remain with them. Second, because they are not dowered, by providing for them according to the discretion of their relatives. Third, by positing a special case, when they wish to enter a monastery. The first case lasts up to the word “however.” The second lasts from the word “however” up to the words “always considered.” Our issue concerns the word “however,” and whether the provision of this word is conditional. Thus, if a daughter dies before this arbitration is rendered, does she transmit nothing? Or is the disposition not conditional, but merely an obscure portion? And does a legal compromise expire upon the death of one party, just as a human compromise does?

To clarify the distinction, three cases must be distinguished: sometimes a commission is made to the discretion of someone between living persons; and then it has an implied condition, if substantial matters are compromised, namely, if it shall have been arbitrated. C. de contrahenda emptione, l. si; de verbis oblig., l. si quis arbitratu. Sometimes it is in a last will, and then either there is an express condition, if he shall arbitrate, and it is conditional as to whether and how much; or there is no express condition, and then it is not a conditional disposition, but an uncertain quantity prima facie: but according to the interpretation of the law, there is no uncertainty; for it is as much as it ought to be according to the discretion of a good man, as l. 1, ff. de legatis 2. Sometimes a commission is made by law. Here it must be considered whether this commission is reduced to the similarity of a last will, or to the similarity of a disposition between living persons: where I state for certain that a law disposing of successions is reduced to the understanding of a last will, and not to the instance of a contract, as ff. de iure codicillorum, l. si quis cum nullum; ff. de legatis 1, l. si fundum per fideicommissum, § Iulianus; ff. de legatis 2, l. codicillis, § pen.

For he who does not expressly declare his will is deemed to have tacitly ordered that which the law ordains concerning his succession, as is noted in the Digest, De collationibus bonorum, l. 1, § vel matrimonium. From this theory, in the question proposed, it is concluded that the ordinance of the statute is not conditional; because it is not in the petition of the relatives, but, insofar as it goes, only in the petition of good men. Therefore, although the portion is obscure at first sight, it is nevertheless not a conditional disposition, and thus it is transmissible to the heir, notwithstanding the Digest, De verbis obligatorum, l. qui Romae, § Augerius, where after death it cannot be declared; because there the text speaks of a contract and an express condition, whereas here there is no condition. Likewise, it is not an objection if it is said that the final cause of providing for the girl at the discretion of the relatives has ceased, since the girl has died; for I deny this,

† For since in this case the legitime is due by the authority of the common law, it ought to be of the same nature. But it is certain that a debt is transmitted to the benefit of the estate. C. de inoff. test. l. si quis filium. arg. de fuis, et legi. l. apud hostes. For if the inheritance were to pass to the mother: therefore much more so the legitime debts by natural law. For nature itself is the final cause, not an accident contrary to nature. i. marriage, and thus it does not obstruct de condi. et de. l. Titio. §. Titio genero. and in Auth. de sanc. epis. §. sed hoc praesenti. Likewise it does not obstruct ver. semper consideratione habita: because it speaks of another case. s. when a girl wishes to enter a monastery. For if such a case, or condition, exists: that verse has application. But we are not in that chapter of the statute, but in the general chapter, in which the statute does not speak conditionally; for it is one thing to insert a condition into the substance of the act: another to commit the declaration of the quantity, or portion, to discretion. The case is in d. l. 1. ff. de le. 2. And the foregoing are confirmed: for although one may argue from the words of the law to the words of the testator, as ff. de manu. testa. l. si ita fuerit. §. conditionem autem qui tex. is very notable for the purpose. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the term "sermo" (speech/utterance) has application in the masculine sense with regard to women.
2. Whether it suffices for the institution of an heir to be made by a notary, with the testator saying in his own voice, "I do this."
3. Whether parents ought to be provided for by the law of institution [of heir], or whether it suffices that they be provided for under any other title.
4. Whether the word "relinquo" (I leave/bequeath), when used with another heir instituted, implies the institution [of that heir].
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Regarding the first point, doubt arises from the use of the masculine gender in a matter involving a difference of sex. For women are of fickle counsel, and therefore one should not understand the sense to refer to the female sex, since in many articles of law the condition of women is worse than that of men, as in D. 1.5.10 (*In multis*). This is especially true concerning the giving of testimony, as in D. 22.5.1 (*Qui testamento*), § *Mulier*, and Inst. 2.7, § *Testes*. Moreover, this presence is required for the validity of the will; therefore, the person must be such that she does not need to be confirmed by another in a similar act, as in D. 4.4.1 (*Filium habeo*). To this effect is D. 34.1.1 (*Si*), and what is said in C. 1.3.1 (*Cum clericus*), § *Ipse non*. To this effect is that part of the brocard: "The masculine does not comprehend the feminine in a singular matter, and one that departs from the common law," as noted in C. 10.3.1 (*Quicumque*) by Cynus, and in D. 50.17.1 (*De verbis significandis*) by Dythmus and Bartolus, and in C. 1.6.1 (*Generaliter*) by Johannes Andreae. To this effect is D. 23.2.1 (*Si quis officium*), § *Si*, and C. 9.8.1 (*Quisquis*), cum similibus.

I say the contrary. For either the nearer female relative ought to be present for the testatrix, or not. If so, the statute is observed, as in D. 28.5.1 (*Ait divus Troianus*). But if she is to be present, then the presence of the aunt suffices, who was alone in the priority of proximity. To this effect is what is noted by Bartolus in D. 34.2.1 (*Stichum, qui meus erit*). The objection from D. 22.5.1 (*Qui testamento*), § *Mulier*, does not hold, because there the matter is not of testimonial presence, but of consanguineal presence, so to speak.

I therefore conclude on the first point that the first will was valid at the time it was made.

† On the second point, it should be known that an ancient question arose as to whether it suffices that the notary reads the institution of heir, and the testator says in his own voice, “I do so.” For the glossa says, as in l. iubemus, C. de testibus, provided that the testator can articulate, i.e., speak distinctly and clearly, as in l. hac consultissima, §. hac cum humana, C. qui testamento facere possunt; and in l. et fideicommissum, non est dubium, because legacies can be left by nod, as in l. si ad interrogationem alterius quis annuat, ff. de legatis 3; l. Pamphilo, §. fin.; and l. nuto, ff. ad Trebellianum; l. servo invito, §. cum praetor. But considering the form of the municipal law there, “he shall say with his own voice and will,” etc., it seems that it does not suffice to have answered the questions; because the words of the statute say, “no more or less than they say to him,” etc. But here the notary not only writes down the words of the testatrix, but beyond them writes down the notary’s own words, without which the testatrix’s words cannot be understood, and thus the form of the statute is not observed. But it can be said with probability that these words of the statute are to be understood according to the common law, de consuetudinibus, c. cum dilectus, C. de noxalibus; l. servi vestri. And therefore, on this account, the testament does not seem invalid, nor even on account of the intermediate act; because it was a necessary act, C. de testibus, l. casus, and l. cum antiquitas; and it was not an extraneous act, but one pertaining to the matter at hand; and this concludes the second point. Hence I conclude, according to the glossa which is in the aforementioned l. iubemus, that although the text there speaks of the testator’s tongue, nevertheless the glossa raises and resolves the question, as has been said, namely, that the notary writes, reads, and asks; and the testator says that he does so, namely, makes the testament, which can be done with two words, ff. de hereditate instituenda, l. 1.

† On the third point, it should be known that Bartolus states that it is not necessary for parents to be left an inheritance by way of institution; but it suffices if they are left something under any other title. Thus he notes in l. siue, ff. de iure patronatus. But Jacobus de Belvisis holds that unless they are left an inheritance by way of institution, it is null in §. aliud quoque capitulum, in Auth. vt cum de appellatione cognoscitur. And if it is null, according to the second will it does not break the first, as in l. si filius, de liberis et postumis. So much so that neither are legacies from the second due; because the rule “autem ex causa” does not apply. The first will remains valid, and the second is invalid on account of the first, and on account of the preterition joined together with it. To this effect is ff. de legatis 3, l. si iure; Inst. de exheredatione liberorum, in principio.

But it must be considered whether the sense of the words contains an implicit institution of the grandfather, and it appears that it does not: because the word "relicto" or "relinquo," when not added to a share of the universal estate to signify another heir instituted, does not include an institution: as is noted in the Digest, *De hereditatibus instituendis*, in the law *His verbis*. To the contrary, it seems, for the same thing is said, "I leave a third of the goods to my grandfather," and "I leave to him his legitime." For the same is stated in the Authenticum *De tertiis et semissibus*, § 1. But if he did not say "legitime" in formal words, it is said that it carries the same weight. Code, *De testibus*. But when the testator says, "I leave the legitime," it appears that he leaves it by the right of institution, and does not pass over. Code, *De impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus*, law *Humanitatis*, by supplying "something, unless," as the text lies, although some, on that text, say "relicta" means by the right of institution, or say that the word "alle" in the text is valid. Against whom I hold, because the word "relinquo" is added to a share, in which I come, another is instituted; therefore he who is instituted is seen, as is noted in the Authenticum *De hereditatibus et falcidia*, § *Si vero nulla*, column 1. And suppose that the testator says thus, "Baldus, I leave half of my goods, in the other half I institute Peter": are not Peter and I, Baldus, instituted? Certainly so, and it is clear by arguing from the whole to the part. For if I have no co-heir, I am heir in whole; therefore if I have in part, I do not have in part, I am heir in my part, and so it is in this institution: because the goods are divided into three parts, and a third part is left to the grandfather, in which, since he has no co-heir, he is heir in the other third. And in the residue, others. And this is clear: because the testator says, "In all others, etc." I say this is to be understood according to what is noted in the law *Cum a matre*. For favor is to be shown to wills, *De liberis et posthumis*, law *Gallus*, in § *Quid si is*, in the ordinary gloss, and *De inofficiosis testamentis*, law *Omnimodo*, and law *Scimus*. Otherwise, if the word "relinquo" were added to a certain thing, or quantity, and so it is understood what is noted in the said law *His verbis*, and Code, *De hereditatibus instituendis*, law *Quoties*. And the above opinion is confirmed by all laws which presuppose that it is sufficient to leave the legitime, as is noted, Code, *De sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, Authenticum *Si qua mulier*; Code, *De naturalibus liberis*, Authenticum *Licet*; Code, *De secundis nuptiis*, law *Hac edictali*. It makes for what is expressly noted, Code, *De re vendenda*, law *Cum a matre*; Code, *Familiae erciscundae*, law *Quoties*. And it is proved by this reason: The title of institution is required on account of the right of accrual, and on account of honor, *De legatis*, law *Filium*, and is noted in the Authenticum *Novissima*, by Cynus. But this one, to whom the legitime is left, has the right of accrual, as in the Authenticum *Ut cum de appellatione cognoscitur*, in § *Ceterum*; therefore the reason of the laws is satisfied. To this it contributes that it is read, and is noted, Extra, *De testibus*, chapter *Raynaldus*, in the principle. From which I conclude that the paternal grandfather was instituted in the legitime. And thus I conclude that the second will is valid in law as to all things, the first being broken, as in § *Posteriore*, Institutes, *Quibus modis testamentum infirmatur*. And although one could argue to the contrary from the law *Non amplius*, § *Finis*, *De legatis I*, with *Si*, nevertheless it is easy to solve, if it is considered who, and to whom, and from whom. To this it contributes, Code, *De impositione lucra descriptionis*, in the word "natural debt is performed"; Digest, *Solutione matrimonii*, law *Si cum dotem*, in § *Si pater*. And so it is held in the said law *Quoties*, Digest, *De hereditatibus instituendis*, in my work. Let it therefore be concluded that the second will is valid.

† On the fourth point, it is not expedient to write at length; nevertheless, for the sake of knowing the truth of the question, it must be known that the gloss in l. maximum vitium holds that legacies left to an omitted heir are due to him. Others hold that they are not due, by virtue of l. filium, in § omnibus, de legatis praestandis. The truth is that either the omitted heir impugns the will, in which case they are not due to him; or he does not impugn it, but assents to the will, content with the legacies, and then they are due to him. From these premises, the response to all points is evident. It is supported by ff. de minoribus, l. si filius. However, as I have said, there is no need to inquire into this matter, because according to the will, it does not suffer from the defect of omission.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What degree of patience the owner is bound to show toward the usufructuary.
2. When jurisdiction is granted to someone as a usufruct, whether he is bound to pay the toll.
3. When a passage right or toll is sold by the fisc to someone, no passage right or toll is owed on the property of the fisc.
4. In a partition award in which the usufruct of the revenues and profits of all and each of the pastures is adjudicated to someone, whether that which is collected from them is also included.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be premised for the sake of clarity. First, that the owner is bound to afford patience to the usufructuary, as stated in D. de usufructu, l. 3, § dare; and D. de servitutibus rusticis praediorum, l. 1, in fine; and C. de usufructu, l. corruptionem. This patience he is bound to afford in the thing itself, so that the usufructuary may cultivate, sow, and reap; and also outside the thing, so that he does not impede him on the way; because the usufructuary, being an uncle, is in need. D. si usufructus petatur, l. 1, § 1. But he must allow him to carry the produce to the granary. D. de usufructu, l. si fur decesserit; D. de emptione, l. qui pendentes; D. de donationibus, l. qui saxum; D. de dolo, l. si eum; in D. qui modis ususfructus amittatur, l. si usufructuarius in esset. In certain rural servitudes and such like duties of forbearance, the law is the same, as in D. de servitutibus rusticis praediorum, l. pecoris; and l. 3, § qui habet austum; and l. quintus; D. de contrahenda emptione, l. si aquaeductus; and l. licet; D. de usufructu, l. sed et si quid, § proprietatis. And this is the point of doubt regarding the use of the servitude and the enjoyment of its utility.

Secondly, it must be premised that sometimes the usufruct of jurisdiction is granted to someone, and this person is not bound to pay the public tax which pertains to him by contract; for this person is a tax farmer in respect of his own property, who makes the taxes his own. D. de publicanis et vectigalibus, l. cotem., §. agri; and §. qui maximos, l. cafat.; D. pro socio, l. verum, §. in haeredem; D. quod cuiusque universitatis, l. 1, ver. ut ecce. Sometimes the usufruct of a field or of the soil alone is granted to someone by the republic; in that case, the tax does not appear to have been granted or remitted to him. D. de publicanis et vectigalibus, l. licitatio, §. debitores; just as future taxes and levies do not appear to have been remitted to him, for the dowry is not liable for these, which are burdens of the thing or of the owner. D. de usufructu, l. si pendentes; in §. si quid cloacarii; arg. D. de impedimentis, l. neque; and note C. de pignoribus, l. in summa. And the reason is that, although the tax or toll adheres to the soil, it does not adhere to the utility of the soil, but to that of the treasury, as noted by Bartolus in D. locato conducto, l. locare. And thus the treasury has two rights, namely, the right to the fruits, which it granted to another, and the right to the toll, which, since it granted to no one, remains with the treasury. D. de servitutibus rusticorum praediorum, s. si domus. Therefore, these public rights are not disturbed by the grant of the fruits. D. de iure fisci, l. praediis. And this is true, unless the contrary appears from the meaning of the words, as I shall say immediately.

Thirdly, I premise for the sake of clarity that if the fisc sells tolls or a passage right to someone, no passage right is owed by such buyer with respect to the fisc’s property, because the fisc sells its own right; yet it does not have the right to demand it from itself. But if the fisc were to sell such things, then the buyer would pay. See the Digest, *Licitatio*, § *Nunc ad propositum*, *De fructibus*. The fisc owes itself three times; therefore, by selling to another, it does not transfer this right by way of translation. See the Digest, *De acquisitione rei donatae*, *Traditio*. But it may be bound by agreement not to demand passage or toll from the buyer. For it is taken as established that the proceeding, or the award, is thus: now, therefore, having premised these things, it must be examined whether the words of the award imply immunity or not. And that they do imply immunity, and thus by the force of the words the usufructuary cannot suffer this new and recurring burden, is clearly proven by several reasons drawn from three adverbs, namely: freely, peacefully, and quietly. To this it must be known that being subject to such passages and tolls is, because it is a certain servitude, and thus a perpetual jurisdiction. See the Decretals, *Quamvis*, *De officio delegati*, according to Johannes Andreae and Innocentius in the gloss, and the Decretals, *Rationes*. The contrary arguments, namely against the opinion given, which move me, are these:

† namely, the duplication, or the expression of those words “the usufruct, the revenues, and the profits of all and each of the pastures are adjudicated,” which seems to indicate that the arbitrator intended to grant something beyond a simple usufruct, and so that the expression of revenues and profits may have some effect according to common usage of speech, it is vulgarly said, “such tenement and of such revenue.” And in this are included the tolls connected with the writings of the same award, although the usufruct of certain goods is adjudicated. On both sides it is excepted, that the party against whom the adjudication was made may pass through the places, the usufruct of which is adjudicated to the other party, with beasts, and without any payment of toll, by which it seems that the arbitrator understood that by the sole adjudication, otherwise the adjudication of usufruct, the right of demanding toll passes to the usufructuary, an absurdity resulting in the utility. The absurdity of adjudicating the usufruct is inferred from the fact that since toll, or tax, is the eighth part of the thing which is carried, it would be absurd to say that the arbitrator intended that on every day on which the usufructuary, or one hired by him, entered the pasture, he should pay for the toll the eighth part of the beasts. Moreover, the uselessness of the usufruct will arise, because however small the toll might be, if nevertheless each time the usufructuary led the beasts to pasture, he had to pay at the end of the year, he would leave to the owner more than the value of the beasts pastured. And thus he would find the usufruct to his detriment, and not beneficial. Outside the point, it is newly opposed by our client, that such toll was never exacted at the time of the compromise and the award, and this admits the matter more adjudicated, but in either case the opinion concludes for our party, whether exhibited before or not. This question has two doubts. First, whether the right or benefit of demanding the said toll was transferred by the aforementioned adjudication to the commons of the Holy Cross and of the Free Castle. And to show this, three reasons first induced by me fall. Secondly, if they are not transferred, whether those commons are bound to the payment of the said tolls by the beasts which they hire by pasturing or using, or enjoying the pastures. And to this all the said reasons contribute. If you can, advise. First, namely, that they are transferred, or secondly, namely, that they are bound to pay, nor is it expedient that you labor in reading the compromise, although mention is made of it in the point, nevertheless I transmit a copy.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that, notwithstanding the existence of children, the husband shall acquire half of the dowry, if a woman having children from her first husband enters into a second marriage, the second husband must acquire half of the dowry, and the children cannot revoke such dowry.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The question is formulated by Jacobus de Belvisio. The statute provides that the husband shall succeed to one-half of the dowry, notwithstanding the existence of children, provided that the woman gave all her goods as dowry. The sons of the woman from her first husband claim that the dowry should be revoked, because the husband has more than what falls to any one of them. Against this is *l. hac edictali*, *de secundis nuptiis*. But the husband says that he has this by benefit of law, not by convention. But he speaks wrongly: because one who gives so much dowry is deemed to wish the husband to profit; for he who wills the antecedent wills that which follows from it, *arg. C. de praediis minorum*, *l. 1*. These are the words of Jacobus de Belvisio. This question was disputed in Florence by Master Franciscus de Arbergo of Arezzo, and he determined the same: because one who is prohibited from alienating must take care that it not be done by law. Thus this woman ought to have taken care that it not be done by statute, *de legatis 2*, *l. codicillis*, § *penult.*; and *quod non*, *ff. de verbis obligatorum*, in *l. si ita quis*, § *ea lege*, where is the notable gloss, by which he determined this question. Moreover, the statute must be understood as saving the common law, since it is not found expressly corrected, *de noxa*, *l. 2*, *extra de consuetudinibus*, *c. cum dilectus*.
