For the common law speaks in a specific case, the law *hac edictali* speaks in general; the specific derogates the general, *de aliis legibus*, *l. alimenta*, § *basilicæ*; and *l. Stichus*, *ff. de vulgari substitutione*, *l. cohaeredi*, § *discretas*, as noted in the said § *in principio*, *ff. qui satisdare cogantur*. If it is asked how this woman could do this, I answer: by agreeing that the entire dowry be returned. And it appears that she renounced the benefit of the statute, *ff. de pactis*, *l. pacisci*. To the contrary is the fact that this is a benefit of law: for by statute one may derogate from that law *hac edictali*, according to the note, *ff. de regulis iuris*, *l. nec ex praetorio*. Moreover, our statute says "irrevocably," hence this determination is general, whether there are children or not, *ff. de testamento militis*, *l. in fraudem*, § *finis*. Moreover, that statute breaks the pact in the words "notwithstanding." Therefore, that profit does not come by the tacit consent of the woman, *ff. de adoptionibus*, *l. si arrogato*, § *sed cum impuberi*. Moreover, she could not otherwise agree: because she would not have found a husband, or not so good a one, since in marriages much regard is had to the dowry, *ff. de legatis 3*, *l. si filiae*; *ff. de conditionibus ob causam*, *l. si donaturus*, § *finis*. By these arguments it seems, considering our statute, that the profit of this dowry does not belong to [the husband] by the municipal law *hanc* simply, because of that adverb "irrevocably," and because of that clause "Notwithstanding," which signifies that this statute is paramount, and thus not to be interpreted by the common law; since the common law wishes that a form reduced to a pact have no place to impede the effect of the statute. And this reason moves me more: because the common law and its interpretation warn against it, *C. de edictis divorum*, *l. 1*, in the beginning. Hence this statute, being so precise, does not receive a restrictive or derogatory interpretation. For it is clear that if we said the contrary, this would be only by an interpretation of the common law applied to the statute itself. But that interpretation has no place where the statute is precise. This question is very doubtful. But in doubt, one must serve the words of the statute, *de exercitio*, *l. 1*, § *si is qui nanciscitur*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If anyone has instituted an action in his own name, and after the joinder of issue has changed it and proceeded by means of a procurator, this change is not permitted, and the defendant is to be absolved, and the plaintiff condemned in costs.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The foundation of a judgment consists principally in the persons and in the narration concerning the persons. And therefore, if something is claimed under the proper name of someone, and afterwards the claim is transferred from the proper name to that of a procurator, there is a change of persons. D. de except. l. Modestinus; D. de pet. haer. l. Nec alias; l. Haeredum ullam, § Si quis absentis. And after the joinder of issue, since it concerns essentials, it cannot be done; because that which is claimed after the joinder of issue, and was not claimed before, cannot be seen to have come into judgment. D. de iud. l. Non potest. And therefore, after the joinder of issue, amendment is prohibited, as in l. Edicta act. Wherefore the defendant ought to be absolved from the observance of the judgment; because by amending, the plaintiff is deemed to have desisted. And because he acts temerarily, he ought to be condemned in costs. D. de iud. l. Destitisse; and l. Eum, quem temere, de reg. iur.; l. Qui in alterius. And even well-drafted and even proven capitulations avail nothing. And if the petition is ill-founded, as says Speusius, and also noted in c. Examinata, de instit., by Innocentius. Since therefore the truth of the amendment excludes the truth of the petition, the plaintiff bringing the action ought to succumb. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When the provision of a statute ceases to apply, the common law does not cease.
2. An error of the arbitrator, once it has been accepted by the parties, cannot be corrected.
3. In any spiritual matter, a bishop cannot be approached incidentally.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Although the denunciation, or notification, which was of the substance of preventing the reduction, was omitted after 10 days and for this reason the statute ceases to apply, nevertheless the common law does not cease, which holds that even those things which would otherwise be invalid or less effective are corroborated by consent, as in C. communia utriusque iudicii, l. 2, in the text and gloss.

† For the error of an arbitrator, once the parties have accepted it, cannot be corrected: and even if the error were established, how much more so where it is not established, ought one not to be admitted to prove that which, if proven, would not avail. D. de petitione hereditatis, l. si quis libertatem, §. final; C. de probationibus, l. ad probationem.

† of the lords. For by reason of law, a bishop may be incidentally sued; otherwise, by reason of marriage or another spiritual cause. Nor does the exception of pending litigation before a secular judge hinder this in such a case, as stated in *extra de ordine cognitionis*, chapter *Tuam*, and in the law *Lator*, under the title *Qui filii sint*, in the Digest.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The solemnity required in construction is not always required in destruction.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Although the rule of law seems to require that the solemnity required in construction be required in destruction, nevertheless it is otherwise in this case, and therefore the said cancellation is valid, and the lady died intestate. C. de testamentis, l. nostram and l. causcellauerat, and concerning those things which are deleted in a will. Notwithstanding the statute, which does not speak of the case of intestacy, but of the case of testacy; and because the statute is contrary to the common law, it should not be extended to its consequences. And thus I say and hold, I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A citation made to the house, under the name of the heir, or if there is anyone who wishes to be the heir, is considered as a certain and specific citation.
2. A minor can act according to the decree.
3. If a pledge has been made to the judge for a debt, it is valid according to the decree.
4. The son is presumed to be the heir with respect to a real judgment, not a personal one.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A citation made at one’s own home in the name of the heir by way of appeal, or if there is anyone who wishes to be heir: because it has presumably come to the knowledge of the person cited; it is considered as a certain and special citation, because we have the effect that results from a special citation, namely, notice. C. de anna. excep. l. vt perfectus. ff. de libe. agno. l. 1. §. 1. and in c. causam. de ele. in cle. and therefore if an edict was placed or affixed at the house, or otherwise notified according to the custom of the forum, or common law, for example by the live voice of a herald at the house, as noted in Auth. qui semel. it is said that a citation made by name is sufficient: because notice specially required by law is presumed to have been received, ar. ff. de insti. l. sed et si pupillus. if the citation was special, it is sufficient.

† As to the point concerning pupillary age, it is established that a ward suffers loss according to the decree from the debts of the deceased, as in the law *Apud Iulianum*, *Qui ex causa in possessionem eatur*, and in the Code, *De hereditatis actionibus*, the law *Sub praetextu*. As to the third point, I say
†, that if a debt exists, and the judge has been given assurance: it is valid according to the decree; otherwise, if it does not exist, l. 1. §. haec verba. ne vis fiat ei.

† And the son is presumed to be an heir as regards suffering a real sentence, or decree: but not as regards personal condemnation against him, unless intermeddling is proved. ff. de condi. fur. l. 2. solu. matri. l. si cum dotem. §. transgrediamur. And the reason for the diversity is, because the favor of the benefit of abstention is not necessary in the first case, since he in no way endangers his own property. But in the second case it is so, because it is to his interest not to be bound, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The granddaughter must receive her legitime from the entire estate.
body: In the Name of the Lord, Amen.

The granddaughter is entitled to her legitime, which, in our case, amounts to one ounce of two talents, calculated correctly, and she must receive it from the entire body of the inheritance. *De bonis*, lib. 1, *Libertus*, § 1, and there by Lacobus Arellius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How the sons of brothers succeed together with their uncle in paternal inheritance and in property acquired from other sources.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The sons of brothers, succeeding together with their paternal uncle, succeed to another paternal uncle per stirpes, not per capita, as in the Authentica de haereditatibus quae ab intestato deferuntur, §. si igitur defunctus; and in the Codex de legatis et haereditatibus, Authentica cessante, according to the gloss, Cynus, and all the commentators. From this it appears that Ventura succeeded, and his brother Vitalis for one-third part, and Thomas and Cyolus for one-third, and Stephanus Tangutius Pacae and Herculanus for the other third, and this in patrimonial assets. But in assets acquired from outside, or in partnership assets, the quality of the acts inducing the partnership and the quantity of the contributions give form to the partnership; hence they sought their gains and received the instruments per stirpes. Thus it was judged concerning the division of portions: because from the acts a year is presumed. Digestum pro socio, l. cohiri; and l. si non fuerit. But if the quality of the acts forming the partnership does not appear, [the division is] per capita, because the heads would be so many parts, in the same title, l. cum duobus, §. si fratres. For the person makes the place, and the benefits and the shares of the portions are counted from the number of persons. Digestum ad legem Falcidiam, l. in legem Falcidiam. And this is to be observed. Hence, the instruments which from the origin of the partnership show the shares, as long as the partnership lasts, induce the same shares. Digestum si certum petatur, l. si socius; Digestum pro socio, l. si societatem, in principio; and l. actione, §. item si. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the wife is with her son, with whom the dowry ought to be.
2. When a husband assigns a dowry to someone on behalf of his wife on account of the burden to be borne, whether and how he is to be kept indemnified.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is true that if the wife is with the son, the father is bound to assign to the son the dowry of the wife for bearing the burdens of marriage. D. 24.3.1 (*Si maritus*). For where there are the burdens of marriage, there the dowry ought to be. C. 5.13.1 (*Pro oneribus*). However, the father must be preserved, so that he cannot be sued further in the future. D. 23.3.1 (*Pater*, cum si). D. 24.1.1 (*Si is, qui*), § *Ibi*. And although it speaks there after the death of the father, the same applies if the son was emancipated by the living father, or was expelled from the paternal home, or lives separately with the consent of the father; for the reason is the same. Thus decided Dy.
† However, to preserve the father, it suffices that the husband and wife, under oath, deny that they support themselves and their dependents from it. L. quamuis, D. de solutione matrimonii.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute that a woman cannot sell without the consent of her husband, if a woman having a legitimate husband and a putative husband sells something and gives to the putative husband for the burdens supported, does such a sale hold?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a father, when making a testament, institutes the womb, and dies after a year, after whose death a son is born, whether he is said to be a passed-over posthumous child.
2. If a mother did not petition for a tutor for a son who died within a year, whether she is on that account deprived of the inheritance of the said son.
3. Whether a mother excluded by statute from the succession of an intestate son is excluded from the succession of a son dying during pupillary age.
casus: CASE. The statement of facts is presented in this matter: A certain Moricus, the late son of Ioannutius Moricani of the village of Campana in the pieve of San Faustino of the county of Todi, having his wife named Lady Cechella, in the running year of the Lord 1368, on the 21st day of the month of January, made his last testament concerning his goods, in which among other things he stated as follows: As to all his other present and future movable and immovable goods, deducting the testamentary dispositions, he bequeaths to the womb of the said Lady Cechella his wife, if she should be pregnant, and if she bears a male son or sons to him, he instituted and left him or them as universal heir or heirs, and if a daughter or daughters, etc. But if she should not be pregnant, or if she were pregnant and gave birth to a male son and he did not come to the light, or if he came to the light and died in pupillary age, or whenever he died without legitimate children born of him, Aurectus and Bartholomaeus, his brothers by blood, should come into and succeed to his said inheritance. And with this testament thus made, Moricus himself survived by a full year, within which no child, male or female, was born of his said wife; and after the lapse of the said year Moricus himself died. After his death, three months or about that after the death of the said testator, a male son was born of his said wife, and he came to the light, and lived for seven months after his birth. Finally that infant died, the said Lady Cechella, his mother and former wife of the said Moricus, surviving him; while her said son was living, she did not petition for a tutor to be given to him, nor did she assume his tutelage; but after the death of her said son, she entered upon and accepted his inheritance. Now, concerning the aforesaid inheritance, there is and can be a dispute between the mother herself on the one part, and the said Aurectus and Bartholomaeus on the other. And it is asked what the law is, namely to whom the inheritance itself belongs, having seen and considered the aforesaid matters, and the said testament, and that entry [aditione?], and the legal authorities operating in favor of each party, etc.
body: Giving counsel upon these matters, I, Johannes, having seen and considered everything written above, respond briefly to the questions and say that, having considered the words of the said testament, no mention is found to have been made therein of the son born after his father's death; because it appears that the said Lady Cechella was not pregnant at the time the testament was made, and if she was not pregnant, no mention was made of the posthumous child thus born. On account of this, Moricus died intestate, since through the agnation of this posthumous child, whom he did not mention, the said testament was and is broken, as in Inst. de exhae. li. § 1 and C. de posthu. hae. l. 1. Secondly, to the same effect: since the testament itself is broken, as aforesaid, and Moricus died intestate, the said son—that is, the posthumous child born to him—was the heir of his father even without any other acceptance or entry, as in l. in suis. ff. de lib. et posth. and Inst. de hae. abinte. § sui autem. And since this is so, it seems said beyond doubt that the said inheritance is due by law to the said mother through the person of her deceased son as succeeding to him as nearest in law, as in the Corp. Auth. de hae. quae ab inte. § consequens and C. de senat. consul. Tertul. l. 1 and in Auth. eod. tit. and l. 1 C. de his, qui ante aper. ta.

† Nor does any negligence on the part of the mother in not having petitioned for a tutor stand in the way—the negligence of which the law speaks elsewhere in C. de legi. hae. l. sciant and l. matres C. ad Ter.—because it is set forth in the statement of fact that the posthumous child died before reaching one year of age; and thus, since he died prematurely and the mother herself was forestalled by that death, it cannot at all be imputed to her: as in ff. ad Tre. l. 2 § confestim.

† Nor does the aforesaid statute of the commune of Todi stand in the mother's way, in which it is provided that the mother succeeds to one who dies intestate in only an eighth part of his goods. For if the said statute is carefully considered—which in this part is odious and exorbitant from the ius commune—it applies to one who dies intestate strictly and properly speaking; but an infant cannot make a testament, and consequently cannot be said to die intestate, because he lacked the capacity to make a testament, as in l. 1 in prin. de suis, et legi. haere. and in the matter of a statute and its disposition, especially when odious, we must adhere strictly to its words and to the proper signification of the words, as in ff. de sup. leg. l. Labeo in ver. verum and l. non aliter de le. 3 and l. constitutionibus ff. ad muni. Resuming the premises from this, since the infant himself, as aforesaid, could not have made a testament on account of the defect of his age, as in ff. de testa. l. qua aetate, and on this account could not be said properly to die intestate (of which the said statute speaks), it necessarily follows that as to another person dying—namely in the case of that infant, according to the form of the ius commune omitted in the said case by the said statute—the mother herself succeeds by virtue of the aforesaid laws, by the argument of l. commodissime ff. de lib. et post., l. si cum dotem in prin. sol. ma., and in l. si extraneus de condi. ob cau. And she succeeds to him by operation of law in the whole, and thus to the said Moricus who died intestate through the intermediary person of his said son, notwithstanding the above-written obstacles, which are removed by law, as has been said. And so I say and advise to be true, always saving wiser counsel. I, Johannes domini Petri, doctor of laws, from Amelia, so say and advise, as is written above, to which I have subscribed with my own hand and affixed my customary seal. Against this consilium makes l. placet and what Bartolus notes there, ff. de li. et posth., and by the same in l. 1 in 7. q. ff. de iu. cod. And because it is asserted to me that counsel was given in opposition to the premises through l. placet cum se. ff. de li. et posth., and on account of the word "fuerit" written above in the theme above-stated, namely "if she shall be/has been pregnant, etc.," which is said according to grammarians to be a future subjunctive verb, as if the said words might be justified in the future time, even though at the time of the testament the said woman was not pregnant, on account of the reasoning stated in said l. placet; therefore, for the corroboration of my said consilium and its clarification, I reply that the said l. placet cum se. has no bearing on the present case, since it speaks of a posthumous child in whom the testator's disposition is made good at whatever time he was born and from whatever wife, and this out of favor for the testament; but in the present matter the words of the testator stand otherwise, as appears above, because the testator instituted as his heir the womb of his wife, "if it shall be/has been pregnant." On account of these words, it must necessarily be understood of a present pregnancy, even if it is to be disclosed in the future. And this is proven, first, by the word "womb" (ventrem), which in law is understood to be full, as in l. ventre ff. de acq. hę. and l. cum quidam C. de insti. et subst. cond. factis; secondly, by the word "pregnant" (praegnans), which likewise denotes the same, as in ff. de pę. l. qui praegnantis, l. negat de mor. infe., and the said l. cum quidam, especially because according to grammarians it is a present participle formed from the first person of the imperfect indicative. From this, referring back to the past, it seems that the said woman must have been pregnant then, and the said testament was not made regarding the past or the future, even if the pregnancy itself was later to be disclosed in the future by the delivery of the birth. And so I understand the aforesaid words, and so they must be understood, notwithstanding the said l. placet, as was said, nor does the said word "fuerit" stand in the way, in which the intention of the consultant to the contrary seems to consist; because although, as he says, it is a verb of the future subjunctive tense, nevertheless, because the said future does not have duration like the future indicative, and is formed from the past indicative, as in ff. de ver. ob. l. si quis stipulatus, and what is noted there in prin., ff. de colla. bo. l. 1 § si emancipato, and consequently it ought to savor of the nature of that very past from which it is formed, as in l. cum stipulamur, and l. si a colono, and l. si stipulatus § cum stipulamur de verb. ob. There is no doubt that it refers to a past time and requires that at the time it was uttered, and before, it had the effect of pregnancy by reason of the said adjunct word "pregnant," to which is added what is noted in l. Imperator ff. de sta. ho., even though the birth is manifested after the fact. For the understanding of this future in support of this opinion, c. ex parte where it says "fuerit, etc." el. 1 and c. ex parte el. 2 where it says "numerus, etc." extra de app. serve well. From these points thus superadded for the clarification of my said consilium, I say and assert that in that part the said consilium contains truth and justice, notwithstanding other points subtly alleged to the contrary. I, Johannes domini Petri de Amelia, doctor of laws. There follows the consilium of dominus Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the words “I institute the womb, if she shall be pregnant” refer to the present time, the future time, or both.
2. A participle joined to a verb signifies the time of the verb. The rule is uniform, and a condition of time is understood to apply to any time.
body: It seems to me, Baldus of Perugia, the least of Doctors of Both Laws, that it should be said according to the law,

† That these words, "the womb, if she shall be pregnant," in their proper meaning, receive the understanding of the future according to the intellect of the laws, which is called the interpreter, and also of the present womb, not only of the future. Thus, let no testament be broken by the birth of any posthumous child, lest he who did not omit his sons suffer the penalty of omission. C. de posth. heredi. insti. l. fin. I am moved by these reasons, because it is the same to say "the womb" and "the posthumous." For the womb is put for the posthumous. ff. de acquirenda hereditate l. cum quidam. § quod dicitur. and l. venter. ff. si pars hereditatis petatur l. antiqui. Hence, if the testator says, "I institute the womb," it is the same as saying, "I institute the posthumous." But when the testator says, "I institute the posthumous," there is included in this whatever son shall be born at any time, as ff. de liberis et posthumis l. placet, where is the case for anyone intelligent to induce that law.

Secondly, I am moved by the fact that a participle joined to a verb signifies according to the tense of the verb. D. 29.1.13 (Titius); D. 9.2.1 (in delictis), § si detracta. Therefore, even if the word “praegnans” is a participle of the verb from which it is derived, it will signify the future because of the word “fuerit,” which is of the future tense and has a mode of signifying the future, and this mode of signifying is attributed by the intellect. For words are signs of those passions or considerations that are in the soul, as D. 34.1.1 (Labeo), § idem tubero. And the law cited by another consultant directly proves my point: D. 45.1.1 (si quis stipulatus sit Stichum). For there it is said that although it is of the future tense and of future signification, nevertheless, after the existence of the terms, those terms are unchangeable, and this is what that law states.

Thirdly, I am moved by the fact that conditions referring to the future, by their very nature, look to the future; for if the testator had intended only the present pregnancy, he would have said, “if she is pregnant.” Hence, these words, “if she shall have been pregnant,” manifest also a future sense, as D. 45.1.1 (si ita stipulatus fuero), § si Titius; D. 35.1 (de conditionibus et demonstrationibus), because words implicitly referring to the present and the future, when conditionally uttered, most clearly indicate the future, as noted in D. 35.1 (de conditionibus et demonstrationibus), l. cum talis, § pe., and there is a gloss, sin. From which it is evidently concluded.

Fifthly, I am moved by the fact that

† because when the reason is uniform, and the condition of times, it is understood of any time, and where the reason does not distinguish, nor the nature of the thing, nor the form of the words, nor do we distinguish, de bonis possessis, l. in benedictione, § de tempore. But here is a uniform reason of charity in judging of any unborn child, for he considered nothing but the filiation of the testator, therefore et cetera, ff. de legatis 1, l. qui filiabus, ff. de testamento tutorum, l. si quis ita, in § si posthumus. Sixth, I am moved by the fact that those words, if she shall be pregnant, are also referred to the time of death, per l. expressam, ff. de testamento tutorum, l. tutoribus datis. From which I conclude that the said posthumous heir is instituted, and by his birth the testament is not broken. And so I say, and I counsel, I, Bal. de Peru., Doctor of both laws, and to the faith I have subscribed, and signed with the seal of my name, always saving the sounder counsel, to which I always submit myself.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a cleric in benefice who attempts and proceeds to carry out high treason is deprived of his benefices by operation of law, especially against the Church.
2. Where a sentence declares that someone is deprived of his benefices, the benefices are vacant prior to the sentence.
casus: CAESUS. A certain Parish Priest of the province of Romagna, and diocese of Faenza, lived with a certain nobleman, and treated of occupying that province by treachery, and submitting it by theft to the tyrannical hand and power of the nobleman, one of the lands of the said province immediately subject to the Roman Church, from that side a great part of the citizens of that land, and after long treatment of the said treachery, the said Parish Priest, wishing to fulfill his evil intention, armed together with a great company of armed men of the said nobleman, went to that land, and went out through one of the gates of that land, and the said peoples, whom the same Parish Priest had with him, crying, and at his instigation, fought at that gate, and occupied that land, and submitting it to tyrannical wickedness, and expelled, as said, crying, long live the aforesaid nobleman: and for the said Parish Priest, and the said peoples, it did not stand, that they did not occupy by theft, and violence, and treachery, the aforesaid land, and expelled from it a great part of the citizens, from it it was subjected to the aforesaid tyranny, but for the good defense of the citizens, and devotees of the holy mother Church, defending between right. It is asked, if the said Parish Priest is deprived by the law itself, and by the fact itself, of the benefits which he held from the Roman Church, so that there is place for one wishing to obtain the said benefits as vacant, or by another judicial sentence preliminary, especially considering the provincial constitution, which begins, vestri cura. And the Papal constitution, which begins, dierum crescente malicia. Of which provincial constitution mention is made, which constitutions are insinuated to you in this present rubric.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The determination of this question is clear.

† It is certain that this private individual is, by this very act, an attenter, as one who has taken action, as one who has proceeded to the point of near-completion, and even as a consummator of the crime of high treason: to attenter means to attempt with some act, as in the law *Si quis non dicam rapere*, Codex, *De episcopis et clericis*; Codex, *Ne filius pro patre*; Authenticum *Habita*, *De libellis oblationis*; chapter 3, *De officio ordinarii*; chapter *Quamvis*, Book 6. To treat (tractare) is the same as to hold a consultation on how something may be done, as in chapter *Cum olim*, *De arbitris*; chapter *Dudum*, *De negotiis gestis*; law *Pomponius*, with the gloss, *De probationibus*; chapter *Si*, Digest, *De adulteriis*; law *Et si amicis*. To proceed is to begin to proceed, if one endeavors to bring a malicious purpose of the mind to fruition, as in chapter *Sine possessione*, *De iudiciis*; chapter *Venerabilis*, Digest, *De usucapione*; law *Possessio*, with many others. To consummate a crime is to do that which the law considers a consummated crime; hence sometimes the crime is a consummated counsel, when the law punishes the counsel principally, not accessorially, as in Digest, *De servo corrupto*, law 1, § *Persuadere*. Hence certain things are consummated in the cause, though consummated in the work: because the law notes a factious will, and much more strongly a factious faction, as in Digest, *Qui et a quibus*, law *Quaeritum*. For such organizers the law would make them guilty: because that which after the fact would not have a punishing judge, ought before the fact to have an avenger. Codex, *Ad legem Iuliam maiestatis*, law *Quisquis*; Institutes, *De hereditatibus ab intestato*, law *Per contrarium*. Therefore, the said Parish Priest is deprived by the law itself by this very act,

† because where the sentence of a man does not deprive, but shows that he is deprived, there the benefice is vacant. c. Pro humani. de hominibus. lib. 6. de electione. c. Ubi periculum. eadem causa. l. Si vacat, ergo conferri potest: nevertheless, when possession is sought, it is necessary to declare upon the delict. l. Palam. §. Si. ff. de ritu nuptiarum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. One is not liable for a fortuitous event, unless fault or negligence is present.
2. Fire is a fortuitous event.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Unless fault in commission, or negligence regarding the fire in this case of fortuitous event, is proven, Nicolaus is not liable; and I speak of the lightest fault in omission, not in commission. Liability arises not from the nature of the thing, but must be proven under the Lex Aquilia; nevertheless, there is fault. The laws proving this are readily available; it is unnecessary to cite them to those who are knowledgeable.

† It is certain that fire is a fortuitous event. D. quod vi aut clam, l. si alius; in § est et alia, C. de testibus, l. testamentum, in fine; D. de regulis iuris, l. contractus, in fine; D. pro socio, l. cum duobus, § damna fatalia; D. de officiis praefecti urbis, l. 3, § 1; D. de periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. si vendita insula, in glossa. Therefore, things which perished by chance and fortune do not fall under the risk of the said lessee, just as his own things do not fall under the risk of the lessor, as C. locati conducti, l. damnum, unless fault were proven, according to the Lex Aquilia, D. si servus servum, § si fornicarius, which is not presumed unless proven, D. de plenaria actione, l. si creditores. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A pledge, not a sale, when it is established to be genuine, may be opposed by set-off.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If in truth of the matter there was a pledge, and not a true sale, the exception of compensation is raised, and it has more force even in the secular court, which is being pursued. *L. emptione*. Otherwise not, as in *L. 2. C. de pac. inter emp.* Indeed, in the first case, they reduce that first principal by operation of law, and not the second principal which has been changed, for in two obligations one compensation is not objected, *de compen. L. quod Labeo*. And it is not to be argued before the bishop, because it was done in fraud of usury.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a judgment obtained through fraud may be ratified.
2. Whether a procurator, by ratifying, may exclude the right to demand the production of documents.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

A judgment was rendered through fraud, but an exception stands in the way. D. de arbitris, l. non distinguimus, § cum quidam; and l. ita demum. Therefore, since something can be ratified, and thus the fortunate party, who approved it, cannot act contrary to it: C. de arbitris, l. pe; Communia utriusque iudicii, l. 2. And the bishop can compel him to observe the oath, for by this process justice is not violated; and because the temporal judge cannot impede the spiritual in his jurisdiction, since he ought to be subject to it, not to preside over it: but here the fortunate party did not approve, but his procurator,

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a father left a legacy to his daughter under the condition "if she should marry", and in the event that she should die without children, it should revert to the sons or grandsons of the testator himself, upon whose death it should belong exclusively to the woman herself, whether it suffices that the other condition has occurred, namely that the sons and grandsons have predeceased.
casus: CASE. In the name of God, amen. The fact is presented in such form: Clemens Herculani made certain codicils of his of the tenor and content written below, namely: whereas Clemens Herculani de Periculo had executed his testament written by the hand of Meino, the undersigned, and in that testament made several bequests and instituted his son Petrus as universal heir, and now at present wishes to revoke some parts of that testament, and others not, except as contained below, but rather by confirming them, therefore the said Clemens, weak in body, yet sound in mind, and being in good and right conscience, codicilling makes the below-written codicils in this manner: namely, he left and adjudged to Lady Margarita, his daughter, her dowry, and beyond the legacies made to her by him in the said testament, one thousand pounds of pennies, [in place of] the others left to her by the said Clemens in his said testament, which he ordered and willed to be and to have to be computed in this amount of one thousand pounds of pennies. Which one thousand pounds of pennies she has and ought to have, and may demand and claim them against the heir of the said Clemens from his goods if, and insofar as, the said Lady Margarita shall have entered into marriage with another husband and legitimate spouse, and shall have remarried, and not otherwise; and if the said Lady Margarita should die at any time without children from the said marriage, to be contracted by her, if she contracts it, the said Petrus, his son, or the male sons of the said Petrus surviving, he substituted them, then surviving, in the said one thousand pounds of pennies, namely the said Petrus, his son and universal heir, and the male sons of his sons. If, however, the said Petrus, or his son, or the male sons of their sons should die without male sons, the said Lady Margarita surviving, he willed and ordered that the said one thousand pounds of pennies should belong exclusively to the said Lady Margarita, and that she might do with them whatever she wished. Likewise, he ordered, willed, and commanded that if the said Petrus, his son and universal heir, or his son, or the sons of his son should die at any time without male sons, in that case half of all the goods of the said Clemens, etc., ought to belong to the Hospital of the Misericordia for the enlargement and common benefit of the said hospital by full right, and he instituted the hospital itself as his heir in the said half in the aforesaid case. Now it happened that before the death of the said Clemens, Francisca, daughter of the said Petrus, wife of the said Seta, died, two children surviving, one male and the other female, and they still survive, and Mea, daughter of the said Petrus, surviving, and also surviving his said son and heir of the said Clemens, Ioannes, son of the said Petrus. Finally, the said Clemens died, the aforesaid persons surviving, who were surviving at the time of the death of the said Francisca. Afterwards the said Ioannes died, the said Petrus his father surviving, and Nicolaus, the male son of the said Ioannes, surviving. Afterwards three children of the said Ioannes died, namely the said Nicolaus and two female daughters in pupillary age. Now there survive Lady Mea, daughter of the late said Petrus, and the said children of the said Francisca, and three female daughters of the said Ioannes who are married, and one of them has borne a male son; the said Margarita also survives. Now it is asked, what is the law regarding the said legacy of one thousand pounds, the aforesaid Lady Margarita having remained always a widow at the time of the making of the said legacy and up to now, as she still remains.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† By the bequest of one thousand pounds, the male was burdened, and the female was burdened under the condition of marriage, and not otherwise; for this uncertain condition of the daughter agrees with the wish of the father, ff. ad Treb. l. mulier. §. cum proponeretur. The father also considered that a widow remarrying needs a larger dowry than a virgin, and therefore he increased the dowry for her in the testament. And that is the first clause, in which conditional legacy—the event of marriage having followed—if the daughter should die without children, he substituted the male and the male line; and that is the second clause. And there follows adversatively the clause: "if, however, the son should die, no male sex remaining from him or from his son, that the said 1,000 pounds shall belong exclusively to the said female daughter, and that she may dispose of her will concerning them." How, then, does the matter stand in this respect: whether that adversative clause applies only to the condition of the daughter's death, or indeed to the twofold condition, namely of death and of marriage, so that, with the obstacle of males removed, we may interpret the father's full affection toward his daughter, ar. ff. de le. 3. l. Paulo calimaco. §. Pomponius erripus. And natural equity supports this side, for upon the failure of males the father’s affection is consolidated upon the daughter. The word "propriae" [exclusively her own] also supports this. The word "voluerit" [she should wish] likewise supports it, de leg. 3. l. fideicommisso. §. quamquam. To the contrary is that phrase "and not otherwise," in Auth. de san. epi. §. sed hoc praesenti. col. 9. Also that a testator in substituting does not enlarge the first disposition, ff. de he. insti. l. ex facto etiam agitatum. Also because adversatives refer to the nearest things, not to remote things, because an adversative is nothing other than an adversative relation; therefore it is made to the nearest things, l. si idem cum eodem. §. fi. Also one is not understood to correct oneself, de cond. et de. l. nam ad ea. Also up to that point: "and if the said," a form was given to the legacy, afterwards it is given to the substitution, not to the condition of marriage, and thus it seems the legacy ought not to be due. It suffices that it is doubtful; nevertheless, I would say that in doubt the adversative relation should be made to all conditions, both of marriage and of death. It can be said with sufficient probability: because when a relation can be made to all things, let it be made to all things, so that we may adopt a more generous interpretation on account of the father's ardent love for the daughter, as in the said §. Pomponius, as in the text and the gloss. Thus, therefore, when the males do not survive, to whose honor the condition of marriage looks, let the legacy be freely owed to the daughter, nor should the condition of marriage be understood as repeated in the final bequest. Rather, the legacy is more bountiful, because the father left the disposition of the said 1,000 pounds to the free will of the daughter in the event of the death of the males. Whence we ought not so to restrict this legacy; and since it can be understood both with the condition of marriage preserved, and freely, let us similarly understand it freely on account of the prior death of the males, which is the final cause of the more bountiful paternal intention. To the contrary is that this adversative "but" is joined to the verb "should die" [decesserit], and thus opposes death; nor can it oppose marriage, preserving the rule of correct speech, de au. et ar. le. l. Plautius. Therefore the condition of marriage remains firm, and does not purify the legacy for her except after marriage and with marriage preserved. To this there can also be adduced all the laws that state that subsequent provisions are understood to be disposed with the preceding ones preserved, and this by virtue of tacit repetition, as in l. talis scriptura and l. licet imperator, de leg. 1., and de le. 2. l. legatorum. §. fi., l. cum pater. §. ab instituto, de ver. ob. l. Titia. §. idem respondit, l. si ita stipulatus. §. Grisogonus, de pac. l. item quia. §. fin., with similar laws. But to these it is answered thus: words must produce some effect, as in l. si quando, de leg. 1., de usuris l. si stipulamur, ad muni. l. 1. But if this were so, those words "if, however" up to the end of that clause would effect nothing. For suppose that the testator had entirely omitted those words: if nevertheless marriage had been contracted and the males had predeceased, the said daughter would have the entire said legacy without the burden of substitution, C. de cad. tol. §. si autem sub conditione, and noted in l. 1, C. de his, qui ante aper. tab. And thus the testator, who wished to make provision through the said clause, would have provided nothing, which is absurd. Therefore the said words show that, in the event of the failure of males, the testator wished to leave the property freely to the daughter, so that she could do whatever she wished, whether she married or did not, C. de iure dot. l. si mulier dotem. Otherwise, the other three hundred pounds left in the testament under an equal condition would also seem to be revoked, which ought not to be believed to have been of the father's intention. He said that the question is doubtful; nevertheless, in this doubt I believe it is rather to be held that the aforesaid legacy, according to the facts presented, is owed to the daughter even if she does not marry. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Mere reputation is not sufficient to prove a wrongful act.
2. When several persons commit a wrongful act, whether each is held liable for the whole, or in what manner.
3. Set-off is not admitted in cases of wrongful acts.
4. The making of a truce does not prevent restitution from being sought by civil means. Witnesses of faith may be plundered.
casus: CASE. The facts are as follows: During a war between the Muffata party of the city of Urbis Veteris and the Bretons on one side, and the party of the Mercurini on the other, for which war the entire community and the said city were divided and partitioned, between whom there are two partial nobles, one Muffatus, the other Mercurinus, with their castles, men, and vassals. It is true that each of them in making war or offense implicated themselves little or not at all. However, it happened that some men of the other of the said nobles, sometimes himself, sometimes with other associates, committed many offenses against the men and animals of the castle of the other noble; nevertheless, outside the territory of the castle of that noble, and unknown to him, and with spoils they received another into the castle of the offending noble, and not otherwise. Finally, after many and various offenses, the noble of the injured party, knowing that many men of his land had, or had in society, many beasts from the men of the land of the said offending noble, not however from those who committed the said damages and injuries, but from his other subjects, and also non-subjects, but inhabitants and districtuals in his castle, which castle is common between him and his other consorts, who are not subjects to the common as much as to his other consorts, took away the said beasts and restored all the real damages to his said men who were damaged. Now, however, the said nobles wish to reduce the said offenses and damages, insofar as they ought to restore and amend one to the other, and the other to the other. It is true that the first noble, the offender, partly denies the said offenses, and especially those which were done secretly; but of all there is public voice and fame, which fame I think can be better proved in the lands proper and in the lands of the friends of the injured party, than in the lands of the offender. Now it is asked whether the said public voice and fame should be proved, so that it would be held for full proof, or not. Also, the injured noble says that, granted that his men were present to commit the said offenses, nevertheless they were not principal, nor were they alone, but they were with other associates, and who did not go with the intention of making the said spoils, but otherwise, as they assert; in the end, however, no other spoils appeared that day except the said ones. For he says that the spoils ought to be restored, that his men are not bound to restitution except for that part, namely, which they had, that he does not believe they had anything, or perhaps for a quota with other associates. The injured party, however, says that he is bound for the whole of his, because they and other associates went out of his land and carried with them bread and wine, and they led the associates and placed them in ambush in the places where the said offenses were made. Now it is asked whether those men are bound to restore the whole, or for a quota, or something, if the above were proved by public voice and fame, as is said, and also by those who were spoiled. Also it is asked whether the said injured party ought to restore the said society taken by him and damaged to his men for the damage done to them, before the said his men are restored from being damaged. Also, because a truce between the Muffati and the Mercurini is established, in which the said nobles, each with his party or sect, are expressly named. And in the chapters of settlement, in the said truce, nothing was asked or said about the said restitution. Now it is asked whether the spoils made on both sides before the truce can afterwards be asked to be restored after the establishment of the said truce. Also, the noble Mercurinus says and alleges that if he or his men made any spoils, it was against another noble Muffatus or his men, that according to the constitution issued by Pope John 22, while he could lawfully do so, he is bound to no restitution, in which it is said that it is provided that any Christian faithful may offend real and personally all rebels and persecutors of the holy mother Church. It is sufficiently manifest from the fact that the vicar of our lord the Pope, who was in the city of Urbis Veteris, was expelled by the said Bretons and Muffati, and they retained, and then retain, the said city in rebellion or revolt against the said church; and consequently, the noble Mercurinus says that the war of the Mercurina party is just, since it is fought for the liberation of the fatherland from the hands of tyrants in defense of the holy mother Church, and thus he argues that he is not bound to restitution if he spoiled the men of the said noble Muffatus. Now it is asked what is the law.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the first point concerning reputation, it must be said that reputation alone is not sufficient to prove witchcraft, as is fully noted in D. de testibus, l. 3, § eiusdem quoque principis, on the word "confirmatur"; in X. de censuris, c. Veniens, in the gloss beginning "Sed cum crimen"; and in X. de probat., c. Cum causam, in the gloss.

† On the second point, whether each is liable in solidum, or whether each is liable in solidum individually, or whether each is liable individually, it seems that each is liable in solidum; but if one pays, all are released. C. de cond. fur. l. 1. To the contrary it seems, namely that the ringleaders are liable for the act of all, but the individual accomplices are liable for their own act, as noted in the case of Count Albert and the exiled Bolognans, ff. vi bo. rapt. l. 2. §. si quis. in the gloss ordinaria. And Bartolus says there that this is true both in the forum of causes and in the forum of conscience; however, he did not consider well the matter of restitution. l. 1. C. de cond. fur. And therefore, resolving these contradictions, it should be said thus: either all concur in the same act, for example, in stealing one ox, which they later sell and divide the price among themselves, or in burning one house, or in killing one man, and the spoils are divided among them, and each is liable in solidum by human and divine law. ff. ad l. Aquil. l. ita vulneratus. In the example of the letter "detrahe furata," or they divide themselves in committing the offense, and one robs one, another another, and then there is a difference between the ringleader and the non-ringleader, as the gloss says. Namely, to whomsoever the act is discerned individually, and they sin discretively and collectively. de iu. om. iud. l. si familia. in the gloss. Because on the third point it must be said

It is that one may not retain animals taken away, on the ground that others have caused damage to one’s own slaves, since one person ought not to be burdened for another, nor is compensation admitted in the wrongful acts of different persons. C. ne vxor pro marito, Auth. sed omnino; and in Auth. ne fiat pignus, in the rubric and the text; and note ff. quod metus causa, l. ex testamento; to this point note ff. de noxalis, l. qui autem, § si seruus meus. On the fourth point

It must be said that during a truce, war cannot be waged by means of arms, but one may recover what is owed through civil proceedings; for even after peace has been made, damages may be recovered if they were not expressly remitted, as is stated by Dyonisius in the title *De iniuriis*, in the law *Si unus*, § *Si ante*; and this is expressly provided in the Extravagant Decretals, in the title *De iniuriis*, chapter *In nostra*.

† On the last point, let the lord, whose cause is at issue, determine the matter, and let the power of the father and the wisdom of the son miraculously declare the world, and let us not stand in such great tears; otherwise, it is certain that the enemies of the faith can be plundered. 8. di. c. quo iure. 1. di. c. ius militare. C. de do. l. si quis pro redemptione. de vassallo mili. contu. c. 1. in finu. But who are the enemies, I believe, that the aforementioned according to my opinion. However, because I do not know more than I know, let Apollo solve it, as no. 79. dist. c. si duo forte. in fin. primę glo. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether goods purchased by a woman can be sold by her husband to her detriment, or to the detriment of her children.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Where a statute provides that the banished may be attacked with impunity, if someone was banished for a crime and was released through a reformation, and this is evident, yet not in the book of the banished, he could not be attacked with impunity; but if he is attacked in ignorance, the attacker is not liable to corporal punishment, but shall be fined extraordinarily.
2. Whenever the law represents as done that which is to be done by a human being, it must be held as done.
casus: CASE. Proceedings are being conducted by the lord podestà of Pisa against a certain Ioannes in the matter, of the matter, and concerning the matter, namely that the said Ioannes ought not to have killed Iuncta. It is objected on behalf of the said Ioannes against the said prosecution that proceedings cannot or ought not to be taken against him for the said homicide or by reason thereof, because at the time of the said homicide the above-written Iuncta was a banished person of the commune for a crime, and was, and is, recorded in the chancery of the commune as banished, and as a banished person for a crime, on account of which, both under the form of the statute on banning and under the form of the statute of the commune of Pisa, he could be attacked and killed with impunity; nor could or can proceedings be conducted for the homicide committed against him by the said lord podestà or his court. And this is asserted by virtue of the statute of the commune of Pisa placed under the rubric De dante auxilium ('On him who gives aid'), in which among other things the following is contained, namely: 'If anyone however is, was, or shall be banished by reason of any crime, he may be attacked with impunity by anyone, both in property and in person, and he shall not be heard at law, either in bringing an action or in defending.' Likewise by virtue of another statute placed under the rubric De occidente ('On him who kills'), in which it is contained at the beginning that if anyone kills someone, he shall be punished with the death penalty, and afterwards below it is said in it: 'saving the aforesaid cases, that if the person attacked was under the ban of the commune of Pisa for any crime committed by him, or on occasion thereof, proceedings ought not to be taken against the attacker.' On the other hand, it is asserted on behalf of the court against the aforesaid Ioannes that by virtue of the said ban and statute he cannot and ought not to be defended from the said prosecution and from the charges contained therein, for the reason that the said Iuncta, who was killed, at the time when he was killed and beforehand, when he was in the prisons of the commune of Pisa for the said ban and the condemnation that followed therefrom, was released from the said prisons by the commune of Pisa out of mercy on the feast of Saint Mary in mid-August pursuant to the terms of the statute of the commune of Pisa placed under the rubric De carceratis sub misericordia relaxandis ('On prisoners to be released out of mercy') in each year, on the aforesaid vigil 20 prisoners ought to be released out of mercy, and by the notary of the chancery they ought to be recorded as unbanned, and there is a release from all bans and condemnations on account of which they were imprisoned. From which things it is asserted on behalf of the said court that by virtue of the said ban the said Iuncta could not be attacked with impunity. Against which it is replied on behalf of the said Ioannes that the aforesaid does not stand in the way, because in the said chapter of the statute placed under the rubric De dante auxilium exbannito ('On giving aid to a banished person'), among other things, the following form is contained, namely: 'and I shall hold no one as banished or unbanned unless he has been written in the chancery in the register of the aforesaid chancery as banished or unbanned.' But since the aforesaid Iuncta was not, nor is, written in the aforesaid register of the chancery as unbanned, but is written in it as banished, and his ban stands in that form in which it was before the said release of the said Iuncta made by virtue of the said statute, he ought to be held as banished, and is so held, and could be attacked with impunity. It is asked what the law is, whether the said Ioannes could defend himself against the said prosecution or not, in view of the said statutes, copies of which are sent in those parts where it is appropriate, which are cited, and in view of the allegations of the parties, which allegations are sent to the consultant together with the above-mentioned point.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† This question arose under similar circumstances in fact in the city of Florence, and was committed to the counsel of the lords Iacobus de Belvisio and Iacobus Butrigarius, illustrious doctors, the tenor of which question and counsel is in all respects as follows: In the name of Christ, and of the glorious Blessed Virgin, and of the precious Cross, Amen. As it is presented under these terms, the fact is such: Balducius and Iohannes Clari, citizens of Florence, were wounded, each of them by ser Franciscus Averardi and a certain other person, concerning which wounds an inquest was made by the judge of crimes. On behalf of the persons under inquest, it is said that the aforesaid wounded Balducius and Iohannes Clari, at the time when they were wounded, had previously been, were then, and still are outlaws of the commune of Florence for a crime, entered in the books of crimes of the said commune existing in the chamber, which writing of the outlawry was produced in public form and shown to the judge of crimes taking cognizance of the case; and consequently it is said that the aforesaid Balducius and Iohannes could be injured with impunity according to the form of the statutes of the commune of Florence. On the other hand, it is said on behalf of the wounded men that, notwithstanding that they are found entered as outlaws, they could not be injured, for the reason that they were exempt, and entirely absolved and freed from the outlawry and the penalties and burdens inserted therein, and they cite a certain reformation of the commune of Florence, and the payment of a quantity of money which must be paid by an outlaw, made by virtue of the said reformation to the chamberlain of the chamber of the commune of Florence within the term contained in the said reformation; which payment was made and is in the books of the said chamberlain of Florence. From which they say that they could not be injured with impunity. It is asked what the law is. And first, it seems that by virtue of the outlawry they could in no way be injured, since the forces of the outlawry itself were removed by payment of that which is owed for all outlawry and its contents; hence one must not care about the cancellation, as in ff. de pact. l. si fundus [?] and ff. de condict. sine caus. l. si pecuniam [?]. Second, because the origin of the thing seems to have been removed and only the image remained; therefore it has no effect, C. de Latin. libert. toll. l. 1 in princ. Third, because there is the provision of law by which they are understood to be exempt, freed, and entirely absolved, to which provision and fiction of the law one must stand, C. de testam. mil. l. rem in praesenti in princ., ff. de vulg. et pup. subst. l. Lex Cornelia. Fourth, because when they proceeded to commit the offense, they ought to have deliberated more fully, as in C. de fals. l. Si ad te. Fifth, the word 'to exempt' without [qualification] is general and seems to signify cancellation and exemption from the outlawry, ff. ne quis eum qui in ius voc. l. sed eximent; therefore it was in no way permitted to injure them. Sixth, because in examining the words and ordinances of the statute, two things especially and principally seem to be required in order that it be permitted to injure [someone]: namely, the outlawry and the writing or figure of the outlawry. But one [or both] is removed, namely the outlawry, and the writing of the outlawry has been weakened; therefore it seems that they could not be injured, ff. de divor. l. fin. §. ait lex.

† Seventh, because whenever the law represents a fact that is to be done by a human, it must be held as done, ff. de manumiss. testam. l. Causam §. 1 and in Auth. de hered. et Falc. §. Is igitur a nobis; therefore cancellation must in all respects be held as had. To the contrary many things are moved: first, the remaining figure of the outlawry, which seems to excuse the doer, ff. de interrog. act. l. De aetate §. ex causa. Second, because in this statute it is so grasped, C. de servis export. l. Moveor, ff. de adquir. poss. l. 3 §. Si servus. Third, in that ignorance, and upon this one must insist with many arguments: and first, that wherever any act is done, if ignorance exists concerning that which makes it fail, [it excuses], but the outlawry in its original force would excuse, therefore ignorance concerning that which makes the outlawry fail excuses equally. And this is proved in l. Eius qui in provincia, ff. si cert. pet. and l. Si forte, ff. de offic. praesid., and Inst. de mandat. §. penult., ff. de solut. l. Si quis servo and l. Quod servus. Many arguments and laws support this ignorance as just: and first, because if the state of affairs which previously existed is changed, ignorance is just, ff. de solut. l. Cum quis §. 1, Inst. de mandat. in §. Item si adhuc, and the said l. Eius qui. Second, because this change consists in the act of another, therefore it is justly not known, ff. pro suo l. fin. Third, this is proved by two cases: the first is in the said §. Proposuisse [?], for it clearly states that the endorsement of the revocation ought to be in that place, so that one entering a shop could not pretend ignorance, so that the inspection of the one demonstrates the other; and therefore next to the outlawry the payment ought to have been inserted, so that upon the outlawry being seen, it would appear negated by that very sight. The other case is in ff. locat. l. Si quis ignorans; for it is established that there is a certain register of soldiers which contains all soldiers, as in l. antepenult., C. qui testam. fac. poss. and l. Ex eo, ff. de milit. testam.; for although by searching he could have had knowledge, and the man was a soldier, nevertheless he who is ignorant is excused, as in the said law; therefore so in the present matter. Fourth, this is proved because in offenses in which the atrocity is weighed, dolus is regularly required, that is, the purpose and intention of offending, so that gross fault is not equated with dolus, ff. ad l. Corn. de sicar. l. In lege Cornelia; hence any probable ignorance excuses from all punishment, ff. de liber. causa l. Igitur, ff. de abigeis l. 1 in fin., C. ad l. Fab. de plagar. l. Plagii, and ignorance is presumed, ff. de probat. l. Verius. Furthermore, it is permitted to injure one entered in the book of outlaws, but these men are of this sort; for writing is a matter of fact, wherefore fiction is not regarded, ff. quib. ex caus. maior. l. Denique, ff. de his quae in testam. del. l. 1, C. de edict. divi Hadr. toll. l. 2 and l. fin.; and the outlawry is presumed to endure in its being, since it does not appear abolished, C. de poenis l. Servus; to the same effect can be adduced ff. mandat. l. Si fideiussor §. Si cum debitor. Fifth, for this party there is the case of the law in ff. de adult. l. penult.; C. de incest. nupt. l. Cum ancillis and l. Qui contra are added. For which reasons, and because we must adhere to the words of the statute without extraneous interpretation or fiction, we, Iacobus de Belvisio and Iacobus Butrigarius, say and advise that the said persons under inquest are to be totally absolved. Which consilium was rendered by the said illustrious doctors in the month of June 1330 under the hand of Lambertus Meloni, notary of Bologna. Because, therefore, the arguments and authorities of such great men move me, I therefore say the same in the proposed question. What is noted by Cino on C. de repudiis l. Uxor, by Dynus on the said l. 3 §. Si servus, supports this. Bartolus on l. penult., ff. de adult. says that this man is punished for fault, not for dolus, wherefore he will be fined extraordinarily, but not with corporal punishment, because he ought to have been a diligent investigator, not an injurious striker; for if a denunciator ought to be a diligent investigator, ff. de iur. et fact. ignor. l. Nec supina, then all the more so a wounder, and all the more strongly a killer. Nevertheless, he is speaking where the outlawry never had force, but only the figure without the reality; but where it had force, in favor of liberation it is the same on account of ignorance as if it subsisted in its force. Nor indeed ought he to be punished in any way, since the statute wills that it can be done with impunity, ff. de aleator. l. 1 §. Quod autem. And this is greatly fortified by the section 'and no one is held by me as an outlaw or re-banned unless it was written in the chancery', etc.; for force and right are often in the writing, thus in this case. Conversely noted by Cino, C. de testam. l. Ambiguitatis, and ff. de usufruct. legat. l. Si alii, ff. de oblig. et act. l. Ex maleficiis §. Qui servum mihi; for even a judge would be excused if he carried out the execution [?] on the pretext of an outlawry in the books of outlaws when the absolution or examination of the outlawry was not shown to him, because we are compelled to follow appearances, but no divine necessity of [knowing] secret things is imposed on us, ff. ad l. Aquil. l. Si putator ex arbore. Lastly, that cancellation is one thing and payment another is expressed in ff. de legat. 1 l. Huiusmodi §. Si ita cui. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of both laws; in testimony whereof I have subscribed myself and sealed with the sign of my name, without prejudice to a better opinion, as in l. Claudius Felix; and although the substance of an obligation does not consist in an instrument, ff. de pact. l. Postquam, nevertheless it excuses from the penalty of the fault, as has been said.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. It is lawful to attach stipulations to donations or obligations of property made to any church.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† All the aforesaid pacts are valid, because it is lawful to append pacts in a donation and in the offering of one’s own goods, as is stated in C. de donat. l. legem; C. de donat. quae sub modo, l. 1; ff. de dolo malo, l. hereditatem. And although he offered himself and his goods, he did not profess religion, since he had a wife, retained some property of his own, and reserved to himself the right to make statutes in certain matters, as in Auth. de sancta ecclesia, § si, hoc presenti, coll. 10, and 6 q. 1, est ubi de hoc ergo pactum; c. ut lex continentiae, to be observed while saving the legitime of the children, which is owed to the children, as in Auth. de sancta ecclesia, § si qua mulier, to which the hospital contributes, and all other beneficiaries pro rata; ff. de bonis libertorum, l. si libertus, § libertus. Because the legitime, like a debt, concerns the entire patrimony, whatever is brought into it diminishes it, and by the word “sale” in a confirmative sense every disposition is included; de statu hominis, l. statu liberis, l. a liberis, alias ceteris, § quintus. And therefore regarding the said two hundred pounds, and regarding all that he reserved, he could make a will both concerning money and movable property. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The judge, to whom the power of choosing an arbitrator has been granted by the form of the statute, after having chosen him, may revoke him and choose another.
casus: A S VS. The case is proposed as follows: A certain controversy arose before the judge of the commune of Perugia, appointed by the lord podestà or captain of the said city, between Titius, acting as plaintiff on one side, and Sempronius, sued as defendant on the other. This cause ought to be compromised according to the form of the statutes of the said city. On behalf of the plaintiff, it was requested that the cause be compromised at the proper time, as required by the statute of the commune of Perugia. Finally, the defendant was summoned to appear before the lord judge to compromise the said cause. And after many and various summonses, since the defendant did not appear before the lord judge with his arbitrator, the judge, who by the form of the statutes had the power to choose an arbitrator on behalf of the said defendant, chose as arbitrator a certain person who was a blood relative of the said defendant and was absent. And when the said plaintiff requested that the said arbitrator be revoked and that another arbitrator who was present be chosen by the said judge, immediately thereafter the said judge, seeing that the said arbitrator was not present, chose as arbitrator a certain other person then present and accepting. Finally, immediately after the aforesaid events, the said plaintiff on one side and the said judge on behalf of the said defendant compromised in the arbitrator chosen secondly by the said judge; and the said arbitrators were present and accepting. Finally, on the day when the said compromise was made, the said two arbitrators chose a third, one named John. After this election was thus made, the said John, after an interval, namely after two days, revoked the second election made by him, and anew chose as arbitrator another person whom he had chosen in the first place. After all these things, the arbitrator chosen on behalf of the said plaintiff, and the aforementioned third arbitrator chosen by the plaintiff’s arbitrator, and also by the arbitrator chosen secondly by the lord judge, gave their award. And considering the form of the statute speaking of compromises, it is said that the said award is not binding; because since the judge, who had the power to choose an arbitrator on behalf of the defendant, once he had chosen, could not vary his choice nor choose another arbitrator. Moreover, the judge revoked the second election made by him of the second arbitrator, and returned to the first election made by him of the first arbitrator. On the contrary, it is said that the first election of the arbitrator made by the judge stands as interlocutory, which the judge could revoke immediately, and it was immediately revoked by the judge. Moreover, the judge in the power of choosing an arbitrator succeeds in the place of a father; but it is established that if a party named a certain absent person as arbitrator, he could withdraw from that nomination and election, and name and choose another. Nor does it obstruct that the judge afterwards, after an interval, revoked the second election made by him and returned to the first; because he could not do this, since the said revocation was made after the judge had compromised on behalf of the defendant in the arbitrator chosen by him in the second place. And also after the arbitrator chosen secondly by the judge, together with the plaintiff’s arbitrator, had chosen the third arbitrator, and thus the matter was settled both by the compromise made by the judge and also by the election made of the third arbitrator. It is asked, what is the law, having seen the said statute, outside in the following consilium.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† That the judge could not vary [his decision] is proven, because a statute that speaks of election is understood to speak of the first and only election, from the word. See L. *boves*, § *hoc sermone*; and by that first election, the right of choosing is consumed. D. *de procuratoribus*, L. *si is, qui stichum*. Moreover, he immediately ceased to be the *cognitor* of the lawsuit, from the moment that election was transferred to the arbitrator of the known cause, just as we say regarding arbitrators who are chosen even on grounds of suspicion: for immediately the jurisdiction of the judge is closed. C. *de iudicibus*, L. *apertissimi*; and L. *cum specialis*, D. *de appellationibus*, L. *legitima*, Book 6; *de officio delegati*, C. *suspicionis*. Therefore, he cannot change his mind, since he ceases to be a judge. D. *de arbitris*, L. *qualem*, § *dicere*; and plainly, as we note in L. *quod iussit*, D. *de re iudicata*; just as if he were to interpose that he is not a judge, or that he cannot proceed, *de officio delegati*, C. *significantibus*. Interlocutory decisions, which remove jurisdiction, cannot be revoked by the same person who issued them. This also supports the point, because whenever a right has been acquired by another through election, it cannot be revoked. Extravagantes *de electione*, C. *publicato*. But this is jurisdiction acquired by the arbitrator, even if absent and unaware. D. *de iudicibus*, L. *cum furiosus*. Therefore, it could not be revoked. Moreover, by the statute, as stated, the form cannot be departed from; every form is of the substance, D. *de arbitris*, L. *divus*, § 1; D. *ad municipalia*, L. *in constitutionibus*; C. *de iure fidei*, L. *certa forma*, Book 10. And it is similar to the case where a guardian is not appointed to one who already has a guardian, but an arbitrator is not appointed to one who has an arbitrator by the first election. For we are dealing with an arbitrator appointed and unique. To the contrary, that the judge can change the election of the statute within his simple limits, and thus it is proven, that as long as the judge retains something of his jurisdiction, he can revoke the election he makes of another; hence, a delegate of the prince, who sub-delegates, begins to exercise jurisdiction, otherwise so, as in C. *quamvis*, *de officio delegati*, § 6. It should be noted here: because there the case of this question appears, for from the mere commission the power of revocation does not expire, which would expire if the matter were not intact. Moreover, that one would be suspect, just as this one is, and thus the note of jurisdiction does not explicitly remain with this one, as with that one; hence, it is not true that from the mere election he has performed his office. Therefore, since the judge still endures, he cannot, namely, retain jurisdiction, since it is indivisible, without retaining the power to revoke the interlocutory, or quasi-interlocutory, decision; the text is explicit in the said C. *quamvis*. Furthermore, the law is explicit that, on account of the absence of the elected judge, another is ordered to be elected. D. *de iudicibus*, L. *si longius*, in the beginning. By waiting for him, more would be waited than seems fair to the judge. Thus it was in our case: therefore, the second election was valid, and what was committed to another is considered revoked by the first. D. *de iure*, L. *cum praetor*; D. *de legibus*, L. *quod in rerum*, § *si quis post testamentum*. Moreover, whenever the first act was not done well, or sufficiently, the words are understood to refer to the second act, and until it is done effectively. D. *de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, L. *conditio*. Hence, a perfunctory election does not remove the judge’s power; since therefore it seemed to the judge that the absent one should not be waited for, because compromises desire speed, the election could be changed while the matter was intact. This supports what Bartolus notes, D. *de appellationibus*, L. *ad principem*. And if it is said that jurisdiction was immediately acquired by the elected one, I answer that it was not acquired effectively and irrevocably, nor does his change matter in such a way, as noted in the said C. *quamvis*. Hence, the jurisdiction of the elected arbitrator was initiated by a certain designation: but it was not confirmed or rooted before the compromise, therefore it could be revoked. D. *de iudicibus*, L. *iudicium soluitur*; D. *de iure omnium iudicum*, L. *et quia*. And thus also a new guardian is appointed if the first is absent. D. *de tutoribus*, L. *quaesitum*; or if some other reason of equity moves the judge, D. *de testamento tutorum*, L. *si quis sub conditione*. And this is general in all things that make an act by one’s own right and ordinary course, because it must be done until it is done effectively. D. *de iureiurando*, L. *quae per salutem*; D. *de arbitris*, L. *quid tamen vnum*. According to what precedes, without doubt, another could be chosen in place of the absent one, especially since suspicion was alleged on account of consanguinity. The said L. *apertissimi*; and what is noted in the said L. *non distinguemus*, § *cum quidam*; and L. *licet*, D. *de arbitris*. The case of C. *publicato* does not obstruct, because there the electors have only the mere right of choosing, and they have performed that: but the judge has the right of choosing and proceeding further; hence, if it is expedient for a new election to be made, he can make it. D. *de regulis iuris*, L. *eius est nolle*.

I, Baldus, HAVE DECIDED.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A statute providing that the person to whom an inheritance is due, whether by will or intestate, must accept or renounce it within six months, binds those who are unaware that the inheritance has been devolved upon them.
2. The action which the heir of the deceased possesses is extinguished by confusion, and to what extent: whether a deduction can be made.
3. One succession does not extinguish another by confusion, nor does it extinguish personal rights.
4. Whether, due to the failure to compile an inventory, one is bound beyond the assets of the inheritance.
5. The son of a sister is admitted together with the brother of the deceased in an intestate succession.
6. The legitime and the Falcidian or Trebellian portion are not included in a fideicommissum.
7. A legacy made to a daughter, if she marries upon the failure of a condition, is not owed to the extent that it exceeds her legitime.
8. Anyone may make a will regarding his own property.
casus:
The point of the case is this: A certain Cechus, son of Nicolaus, made his testament, in which he instituted Sylvester and Francis, his sons, as universal heirs, and substituted them for each other; and among other things, he left to Masia, his daughter, for her dowry, five hundred pounds of wax and dotal movables, and the right of reversion of his habitation if she should remain a widow. Masia was never married, but is professed of the third order of Blessed Francis. Cechus died after making the said testament, now thirty-three years ago, or thereabouts, with the said Sylvester and Francis, his sons, and Blondella, Alenutia, and Asseduta, and the said Masia of the said third order, his daughters, surviving him. After Francis, who was over fourteen years old, died intestate without any children, now twenty-four years ago, or thereabouts, with Sylvester, his brother, Blondella, and the said Masia of the said order, his sisters, and the children of the said Alenutia, his sister, surviving him.
