After this, the said Sylvester died, now ten years ago, or thereabouts, with the said Masia of the said order, his sister, and his only daughter, surviving him, whom he instituted heir in one hundred solidi of Cordova in the testament made by him, in which he instituted his former wife, Ioannella, who is now deceased, and Masia, the aforesaid, his carnal sister, as universal heirs; the said Masia being instituted by the said Sylvester, her brother, with certain legacies and conditions, as and how it is contained in the testament of the said Sylvester, and especially that which begins “provided that,” etc. We send to you that testament. It is true that in the city of Narni there was and is a certain statute, which we send to you, that if anyone succeeds to anyone by testament, or intestate, or if an inheritance is devolved to anyone by testament, or intestate, he is bound and must, within six months computed from the time of the death of the deceased, either accept or repudiate that inheritance by himself, as is contained in the said statute. And the said Masia did not repudiate the inheritance of the said Sylvester, her brother, within the said six months: because she was not certain of the said conditions and legacies of the said Sylvester, but was ignorant of them, namely, that which begins “provided that,” etc.

It is asked: Whether she is presumed to have accepted it; and, assuming this as constant, whether she can claim the things left by Cechus, the former father of the said Masia, and claim the right belonging to her in the goods of the said Francis, her former brother, who died intestate, being over fourteen years old, without any children, in which the father could not burden him; and whether she can also claim the part of the contingent dowry of her mother, who died more than forty-six years ago, or thereabouts. And whether the children of the said Alenutia, sister of the said Francis, who died before the death of the said Francis, her brother, now twenty-two years ago, or thereabouts, can claim the part belonging to them in the goods in which the said Francis, their carnal uncle and carnal brother of the said Alenutia, their mother, was free; and in what part the said Francis was free. And, assuming that the said Masia can claim the things left by her father, namely, six pounds and movables, and the habitation of the house, and because the rest is said to be for dowry, and the said Masia, being professed of the said third order, was never married, whether she can claim it by the right of dowry, or as a debt by natural law. And, assuming that the said Masia is considered the heir of the said Sylvester, her former brother, can she make a testament regarding the rights which she has in the goods of her father, mother, and other brother?

It is also asked: If the said Ioannella, wife and heir of the said Sylvester, who is now deceased, is not found to have made an inventory, were the actions which she had in the goods of her said former husband, by virtue of the things left to her by her said husband in his testament, confused? Having seen the first part of the testament of the said Cechus, and the testament of the said Sylvester; and the renunciation in the instrument of the inheritance of the said Sylvester made by the said Masia in public form; and the statute of the said city, all of which are sent to your lordship.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the first point, I say that either the said Masia knew of the will, and then she is a necessary heir by the form of the statute. Or she was ignorant of the will: and then the statute does not make her an heir; because the statute must be understood as referring to an heir who can accept and renounce, for by doing neither within six months one becomes an heir; but the statute cannot be understood as applying to one who is ignorant, because he who cannot truly accept, nor even interpretatively, cannot accept fictitiously either; but one who is ignorant cannot truly accept, nor interpretatively: therefore not fictitiously either. D. si pars hereditatis, pe. l. illud; D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. multum interest; D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. is potest; and l. sed et si de sua; C. de iure deliberandi, l. cum antiquioribus.

† On the second point, I say that if he is heir for one-half, the action which he had against his brother is extinguished by confusion as to that one-half. D. de solutionibus, l. Stichum, § aliquando; C. de hereditatis petitione, l. si adulta; C. de iure deliberandi, l. quia non fecit inventarium, l. finalis. But as to the other half it is not extinguished by confusion; this is established by the law which begins "quae dotis," D. de solutionibus, together with its gloss. Nevertheless, although the action is extinguished by confusion, the right of deduction is not extinguished, so that such a debt may be deducted, just as any other creditor may do, as in D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. pater filium.

† On the third point, I say that the rights which he had in the inheritance of Francis he did not lose, as is stated in the Codex, on the petition of inheritance, in the law *Haereditas materterae*. For one succession does not merge with another succession, nor does it merge real rights, as is stated in the Digest, on the institution of heirs, in law 3, § *Qui fideicommissariam*.

† On the fourth point concerning maternal dowries, I answer the same as I said on the second point. C. de bonis autem iudicis possessis, l. 1; and l. si uxor tua. Nor does it avail that it is prescribed: because the natural debt endures, which can be deducted. ff. de negotiorum gestis, l. at qui natura; and l. si. ff. rem ramm habere, de fideiussoribus, l. si quis postquam tamen. To the contrary is de administratione tutorum, l. si pupillus, in fine. And because we are in the lands of the Church, canon law must be observed, which holds that, although an inventory has not been made, this heir is not bound beyond the assets of the inheritance: especially because she is a fictitious heir, as is noted in c. quamquam, de usuris, lib. 6; and in c. parochiano, de sepultura. Nor is she within the assets of the inheritance, unless the residue remains after the debts have been paid, as C. de legatis, l. si universae; and de verbis significandis, l. significatum, §. bona; de iure dotium, l. mulier.

† On the fifth point, it must be said that the daughter’s son succeeds together with the brother of the deceased in an intestate succession, as in the Authentica *De haeredibus ab intestato*, § 2, and in the Authentica *Defuncto*, and in the Authentica *Ut fratrum filii*, in the rubric and in the black letter.

† On the sixth point, it must be said that in the legitima and the Trebelliana, it was said by Franciscus, so to speak, that it is free, because the legitima and the Trebelliana do not come under fideicommissa. In c. Ray. and Ray. cum si.

† On the seventh point, it must be said that if she does not marry, she ought not to have the remainder left over as dowry, because the final cause is lacking, as in § Titio genero, according to Dy. For the cause of the dowry is presumed to be final, l. si ego, in the beginning, de iure dotium. However, a condition of marriage could not be placed in the legitime, as l. quoniam in prioribus. And therefore the daughter ought to have this freely. Nor does it matter that she is a sister of the third order, because she did not enter the monastery for that reason, as in § sed hoc praesenti, and in c. in presentia.

† On the eighth point, it is to be said that anyone may make a will concerning his own goods. And L. 1, C. de sac. san. ecc. de ver. sig. L. verbis legis, and in Auth. de nup. §. disponat. On the ninth point, it is to be said the same as in the second and fourth, by the same laws. I, Bal. de Perus., doctor of both laws, advise, and what is contained above, and to the faith thereof I have subscribed and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a young animal is driven out of someone’s territory and such an animal perishes, whether and when the person is liable for compensation.
2. When it is required that something be denounced, it suffices that it was denounced by any person capable of assigning blame.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. On another day, I was questioned by my very dear friend Jo. Tanguarini on this matter, and I gave him the same answer that he himself had stated in his award, namely:

† That Giliolus was bound by written law to make amends, or to compensate Andrea’s goods, and not Putius’s goods, since he told him at a suitable place and time that the aforementioned ox should be returned, or that the aforementioned ox should return, and he did not wish to return it, or to come back, wherefore the said ox was lost. Now, however, another fact is proposed, namely that it was notified to the said Andrea by the son of the lady Floris that he should go for the said ox, and it was a suitable hour, and likewise Andrea did not wish to go, and this is what has changed in the facts, which was not narrated to me on another occasion: wherefore, regarding those matters which are contained in the point written above, I say that the said Giliolus ought not to make amends for anything, neither to the said Putius nor to the said Andrea, neither strictly nor in equity. And this for many reasons, and first by law Quintus, in § Papi, although, D. ad legem Aquiliam, where it is said that if I find your livestock on my estate, I can expel it: nevertheless, I must exercise discretion in myself, so that I expel it without damage to you, and my expulsion is not the occasion of your damage, or so that I notify you to take away your livestock: because therefore Giliolus notified this to Putius, he is not bound to Putius. Likewise, it was notified to Andrea, he is not bound to Andrea. For there is no difference that someone notified Andrea, because it suffices that it be notified by anyone, as to fault.

† to be brought against the person of the said Andrea. D. de petitione hereditatis, l. item veniunt. § a quo. D. de usuris, l. si quis solutioni. § mora. For Putius and Andreas ought to have gone and preserved their property, and if they did not do so, which they could have done conveniently and easily, let them impute it to themselves, because those who allow their property to perish are in greater fault. D. de legatis, l. item quaeritur. § exerciti. and l. si quis fundum. § impetrator. According to the reading which understands, quo loco. D. de locato conducto, l. locatur dominis caprarum. For if the owner is at fault for the loss of the goats, let him impute it to himself; and because leniency is to be shown to Giliolus, who drove them away from a distance so that they would not return to eat his grain again. D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. si quis fundo. § 1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How many formalities are required for the confession of an inventory.
2. The written records of proceedings are believed, just as other writings sealed by witnesses.
3. Witnesses accepted by the judge are presumed to be competent.
4. Let it be conceded that an arbitrator may render an award wherever he understands the matter, yet in a suitable place, and not outside the province.
5. If a case is compromised, acts performed before the first or second arbitrator are valid before the third, if they are public.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The inventory of an heir is a matter requiring scrupulous care, and even the diligent are often deceived. It requires that many formalities be joined to its perfection, and three things are principally to be observed: namely, the time at which it was begun, or the month, and completed within another forty days; the subject matter, that the things to be listed are listed; and the solemn form, namely, that one notary intervene to write it, and that the heir write it himself, or, if he does not know how to write, he will have it written. A second notary is required for this very purpose, namely, that the sign of the cross be made, that creditors and legatees be cited, and that in the place of absentees three known, knowledgeable, and substance-possessing witnesses intervene, and thus two witnesses are employed to prove, and three to supply the absence of creditors and legatees by their presence; therefore, according to this, five witnesses are necessary. In this inventory, however, the sign of the cross is lacking; nevertheless, this does not vitiate it according to the learned, because it is ceremonial, or because the invocation of God at the beginning of the inventory and the sign of the cross are equivalent, as argued in *de auro et argento*, law *Titia*, § *si*. It also seems necessary that citation be made, because solemn citation must specifically be made personally, and if the person is not found, it must be made at his house, as in the law *ut perfectius*, which was not done here; but it can be answered that such citation suffices, Code, *quomodo et quando iudex*, authentic *qui semel*. Furthermore, in this inventory there are only four witnesses; therefore, it is not valid. Code, *de testibus*, law *si unus*. For according to Bartolus, five are required. But still it can be answered,

† That credit is given to the written records of the acts, just as others give credit to the written records of Vallata by witnesses, on account of the presence of the judge and the faith of the acts, as in C. de dolo malo, l. in donationibus; C. de testibus, l. omnium and l. sancimus. Moreover, because they can perform a double office, as argued in ff. de adoptionibus, l. si consul. Furthermore, in this inventory there is no subscription of the heirs; therefore it is not perfect, because it demonstrates a completed subscription. To this it may be answered that when it is done before the official records, the subscription of witnesses or parties is not required, as noted in a similar case in the aforementioned l. in donationibus. Moreover, because all things are presumed to have been done solemnly, since the decree of the judge was interposed, as noted in l. 1, C. de fidei instrumentis, and iure hastae fisci, lib. 10, in the glossa ordinaria. Furthermore, in the lands of the Church, the simplicity of truth is to be regarded more than excessive and scrupulous subtlety, de testamentis, ca. cum esses. And it supports what is noted in c. quamquam, de usuris, lib. 6, in the novella, and the argument in ff. de legatis, l. si servus vetitus; ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. quamvis.

† Moreover, it is presumed in favor of the witnesses that they are competent, since they have been accepted by the judge, as is sufficiently established in the Digest title *Arbitro*. Certain authorities state that an inventory is not valid unless the witnesses declare that they are not aware of any malice, as in § *Si* of the Digest title *Noxales*. However, it is not necessary to make such a declaration at the time of the inventory, but rather afterwards, if malice on the part of the person making the inventory is alleged in the proceedings of the opposing party, which is evident from what I said there regarding the oath. Furthermore, the Master of Notaries states that, according to general custom, we do not employ so many subtleties in these inventories. For the authority of notaries has gained greater force by custom than by strict law, as noted in the Code title *De fideicommissis*, in the gloss to the law *Si*. Therefore, all things considered, I hold that the said inventory is presumed to be effective and formal. To this effect is what is noted in the Speculum, title *De emptione et venditione*, § *Nunc dicendum*. And let these things be said concerning the inventory, etc.

It remains to be considered regarding the award of Lord Antonio, having regard to the words of the compromise, in which it is provided that they may make an award wherever it is understood that an award may be made outside the province in which the compromise was made in his favor. And it must be said that he cannot draw the parties by citation, much less can he render a definitive judgment, which prejudices more than a citation. D. de iudiciis, l. si locus; D. de arbitris, l. si cum dies, § si arbiter; and l. diem proferrei, princ. And although it has been said that wherever discretion is given, it is to be understood in a suitable place, as noted in D. de constitutionibus, l. si duo; D. de deposito, l. Lucius. Moreover, it was agreed that he was to judge according to law, but no one can judge according to law unless the parties have been heard and understood. L. fin., C. si per vim, vel alio modo. And because it was agreed that he was to render a sentence, it appears that he was not a mere arbitrator; hence, at least for a definitive judgment, he was required to cite the parties, as in C. quoniam, and when the judge, for even an arbitrator is bound to this when otherwise the compromise is made on a disputed matter, and not merely on a simple convention. Indeed, Bartolus says that this is always required, otherwise it is presumed that he awarded unjustly, because he did not hear the rights of the parties, as noted in l. si quis arbitratu, per Bartolus. And therefore the arbitral award is invalid by way of exception, or replication, or reduction to the arbitration of a good man. But pure arbitration is null by operation of law.

It remains to be seen, when a case has been referred to several arbitrators successively, whether the proceedings before the first or second arbitrator are valid before the third. And it must be said that if they are public and relate to matters of fact, they are valid. C. de arbitris, l. penultima; C. de testamentis, l. finalis; C. de appellationibus, l. qui ad civilia; and l. necessitas; and l. a proconsulibus; and l. ampliorem, under the words “and those which have been pleaded.” I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. One who is prohibited from alienating is understood to be prohibited from every kind of alienation.
2. Death placed by a person in a condition is understood to refer to natural death, not to civil death.
3. An heir instituted under a condition, if he enters upon the inheritance before the condition has occurred, whether he is bound to ratify it once the condition is fulfilled.
body: From all

† is understood to be prohibited from alienation. L. Peto, § Fratre, De legatis 2. The natural heir is not included unless he becomes a legitimate heir, ad Trebatium. L. Ex facto, Si quis non perdit. L. Is consequenter, § 1, Familiae herciscundae. L. Codicillis, § Pe, De legatis 2. L. Cum ratio, In fine, De bonis damnatorum.

† To the contrary, because if death by a human is placed in a condition, it is understood to be natural death, not inflicted and capital. L. ab hostibus, §. si, Sol. matr. And thus it is excluded. And also an inofficious donation is valid, but a complaint is required, L. 1, De inoff. doti. And it is noted that C. De pac., L. si. By this statute, existence is not given, and that which is null. C. De transac., L. ubi pactum, in gl. 1, Quod vi, aut clam, per Bart. But here it is valid due to the enumeration of things, as noted in Spe. De dona., ver. quod si aliquis valet iure fideicommissi in bonis testatoris, L. cohaeredi, §. filiae. And two quarters are deducted, and alienated things are imputed in §. res, quae in L. Marcellus, ad Treb., even in the deceased, as noted in C. De resc. vend., L. in representat. Legitimate age and they will be said, when court writings make insinuation, therefore it is valid regarding sacred things, San. eccles., per Gul. Not by the force of the clause, that so many are donations, but by the force of insinuation, as noted in Spe. De dona., ver. quid si aliquis donat omnia. And L. sancimus, per Cyn. He acted for the heir, De acque haere., Insti. De haeredum, quali. et differentia, §. si.

† And he became an heir, if he ratified expressly, as is contained in the will; otherwise not, because he did not fulfill the condition, and if the condition is not fulfilled, the acceptance does not bind. Therefore, there is doubt on account of the adverb "expressly" placed in the will, infra, under the heading "express words," on adoption, l. si pater naturalis, in the gloss. Whether it suffices that he ratifies by the very fact, or by the tacit consequence of an express acceptance. C. de inst. et subst. l. reprehendenda, in the gloss, de fideius. l. non recte, si cert. pet. l. et cum quid. The first part is safer, as in c. si quem, de procu., lib. 7, in the verse "say expressly." In any honest place, the ordinary judge may sit on the bench, as C. quomodo, et quando iudex, l. si vt proponis, and l. praeses. The same action of interrogation was valid, in c. cum episcopus, de offi. ord., li. 6. By acceptance, one patrimony is made of the heir and the testator, de vul. sub. l. sed si plures, §. filio. The acceptance holds, if, by the additions, there is no legal union from an invalid act, and if the condition is not fulfilled by the heir, it cannot be fulfilled by the heir of the heir; because a conditional inheritance is not transmitted. C. de cad. tol. §. in nouissimo, and §. sub hac conditione succedentes. Directly, I can take vacant possession from the hand of another, of whom leg. l. 1, §. alterius, cum si, and l. cum haeredis, de acque pos., and l. cum mitis, qui ex ca. ma. It is useful for one having several compatible claims to assert all of them. C. de codi. l. fi.

CASE. Hermanutius Lelli made a will, in which, among other things, he thus disposed: "Furthermore, I bequeath, order, will, and command that the underwritten fideicommissaries give, pay, and distribute from their goods to those men, persons, and places who and which shall seem and please to them, notwithstanding that the specific quantity is not stated." After other legacies, he concluded thus: "In all his goods, however, he instituted Paul, Jacobutius, and his sons jointly and severally in equal portions as heirs. And if any of the said sons should die in pupillary age, or afterwards at any time without legitimate children, he substituted the other surviving one of them. And if all the aforesaid sons should die in pupillary age, or afterwards at any time without legitimate children, he substituted the said daughter of his jointly and severally in half of the said goods of Paul and Jacobutius. The other half of the goods of the said persons, in that case, he ordered, willed, and commanded to be sold by his fideicommissaries, and the price thereof to be given and distributed by the same to those persons, and among those persons, which shall seem and please to the said fideicommissaries, notwithstanding that the persons are not declared here by name." The fideicommissaries were his brother Nicholas, his carnal brother, and any two others jointly and severally. These fideicommissaries, after the death of the said testator, for five years after the death of the jointly and severally liable party, and subsequently after the death of Jacobutius, and with Paul surviving, made distributions of certain possessions of the said Paul, giving and granting those possessions jointly and severally for a certain quantity to certain churches, under this condition, and by these words, namely: "And the said grants, gifts, and transfers were under these conditions, namely: if, and insofar as, Paul, son of the said Hermitius, shall have died hence within the next four years, within the said time, without legitimate and natural children; and otherwise not." The fruits of the said goods were reserved to the said brother Nicholas for the whole time of the life of the said brother Nicholas. When the said grants and distributions were made, the said Paul had attained his twelfth year, and he lived for a time after the said grants and distributions. Now it is asked: whether the said fideicommissaries could, by right, make the said grants, the facts being thus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Executors appointed under a condition cannot carry out the execution before the condition is fulfilled.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

These executors were appointed subject to a condition, and, like fools, acted before the condition was fulfilled, and thus before they had entered office, and they carried out the execution contrary to the form of the mandate; therefore, by operation of law, their act is invalid, and it cannot be validated, since it was done contrary to the form of the law and of the will. The testator who imposes a condition intends that it first exist, as is stated in the Digest, under the title "Of Conditions Inserted," law 2; in the Codex, under the title "To the Trebellian Trust," law "But if he makes"; in the Digest, under the title "Of Legacies," law 3; in the Digest, under the title "Of Legacies," law "If the son," section "The Emperor"; in the Digest, under the title "Of Legacies," law 2; in the Digest, under the title "Of Legacies," law "One from the family," in the beginning; and in the Digest, under the title "Of Legacies," law "When the father," section "By the son." Indeed, they behaved with bad faith in inducing a vow to capture the death. In the Codex, under the title "Of Pacts

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a vulgar substitution, contained in a concise clause concerning the death of the instituted heir, has place in a testament or fails. This and in itself. Consilium 5.
2. Namely, "should he die," and whenever it happens, whether it includes an express or tacit vulgar substitution.
3. The brother of the testator, to whom something has been left by way of institution, and who cannot claim more from the goods of the said testator, whether he can succeed notwithstanding such prohibition, when the universal heir died during the lifetime of the testator.
4. The syndic, on behalf of the brother to whom the inheritance had devolved, requested to be put in possession of the goods, with reservation of the right of each person having better rights, if it should happen that contradictors appear afterwards; whether, if they request before the secular judge to be put in possession, the substitutes can oppose the exception of incompetence through the said syndic.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The facts are as follows: A certain lady Butia de Cassia made her last will and testament, in which, among other things, she bequeathed to her nephew Marco, her brother’s son, two florins, and in those same two florins she instituted, made, wished, and commanded that he could not claim more from her goods, etc. In all her other movable and immovable goods, etc., she instituted and made Iacobus Ciolicolae de Cassia, her nephew, general and universal heir, with this condition added to said institution, namely, that if it should happen that the said Iacobus dies at any time without legitimate children descending from his own body, then Lucius Io. Coletae, Ioannetta Vannona, Nicoletta, and Mobile Tredoni, or their heirs, or the heirs of any of them, from the village of Strepeta in the district of Cassia, shall receive equal portions, and this is her last will, which she wished to be valid, etc. After the making of said testament, and before the death of said testatrix, the said Iacobus, the instituted heir, died after some years; finally, said testatrix died, a minor, with the aforementioned Lucius Coletae and the others named above surviving her.

It is now asked whether, by virtue of the said substitution made by the said words, namely that he dies, the said ladies should succeed according to the will, or whether there is room for intestate succession.

And it raises a doubt whether the said word “moriatur” (he dies), and “whenever it happens that he dies,” contains and includes a vulgar substitution, whether express or tacit; for if it contained an express one, there would be no doubt, because the substitutes would be admitted by § In primo, C. de caut. toll. attent., l. Talis ancilla, § Filia impubes, ff. de fideic. libert., l. Si pater filium, § Ult., ff. de vulg. et pupill., together with similar authorities, l. Lex Cornelia, in the gloss, in the same title. If it contains a tacit substitution, then the learned authors differ on this point. Some hold one opinion, namely that the substitute is not admitted, as Lambertus de Rampone, by l. Quod si filius, ff. de cap. et postlim. revert., and l. Si pater, at the end, in the same title. Ioannes Andeolus raises this question in his Novella, in c. Si pater, de testamentis, and cites the statements of the aforementioned doctor Dynus. He holds the same opinion by the text in the said l. Quod si filius, where it is said that there is nothing to be discussed regarding the second tablets. Cynus, in l. Precibus, distinguishes in the matter of vulgar substitution. And Bartolus, in l. 2, de vulg. et pupill., in his treatise on pupillary substitution, and in the said l. Lex Cornelia, with the following. On the foregoing, it pleases the consultant to write the truth, and what kind of substitution is comprehended by the said words, notwithstanding that the word “moriatur” is a direct word, as in the said c. Si pater. And let the laws on the foregoing be cited.

The second doubt is whether Brother Marcus, to whom two florins were bequeathed and who was instituted as heir in respect of these, and who, as you state, cannot claim more than this, and there are certain others to whom similar legacies were made, can succeed under the testament notwithstanding the prohibition of the testator, after the universal heir died during the lifetime of the testator. It is true that, as long as there is room for succession under the testament, and so on, as in the law *Quamdiu* and the law *Antequam*, common in the title *De successionibus*. It is true that the will of the testator prevails if it opposes this, as in the law *I*, § *Si ex fundo*, in the title *De hereditatibus instituendis*, and the law *Ex facto*, in the same title; the law *Quoties*, § *Si duo*, in the same title, with similar authorities; and the law *Quoties* in the Code, in the title *De hereditatibus instituendis*, with similar authorities. And on such matters, one may also give counsel.

† Concerning the other doubt, which is at issue and is pending in the court of Cassia, let counsel be given, namely: the syndic of the chapter and the convent of Saint Augustine of the Friars Hermits, acting on behalf of Brother Mark, to whom the inheritance of the said lady had devolved intestate, petitioned to be put in possession of the goods of the said inheritance as the nearest in degree. And after the usual citations were made, and even certain persons cited to whom it was said the inheritance might pertain, and also after proclamations: because nothing was opposed or legally objected by anyone, the judge of Cassia granted license to take tenure and possession of the said goods by the said law, *edicto*, reserving the right to each one having better rights, etc., since no contradictor appeared at that time. And the friars and the syndic are in possession of the said goods, having been given authority and granted leave. Then come the substitutes named in the said testament, and they petition to be put in possession of the said goods of the said inheritance, having shown the testament not cancelled according to the form of the law *edicto*, and they petition the judge to grant them license to take tenure, and they cause the syndic of the said place to be cited. The syndic appears before the judge, and he opposes the exception of declination of incompetent forum of the judge, since they ought not to be cited nor sued before a lay judge, as in the *auth. statuimus* and in the *auth. causa* which is made with a monk, c. *si diligenti*, cum *si*, de foro competenti. I answer that this is true when the judgment is not yet concluded before the judge, but the said judgment was already finished, so they cannot be removed from the said judge and transferred to a cause before an incompetent judge. Because they are legitimate contradictors and possessors of the said goods. Now it is asked whether the said taking of possession should stand in the way or not, so that the judge of Cassia is the competent judge by the law *heres absens*, ff. de iudicibus, and whether it is expedient that a revocatory action be brought, or that the validity of the said substitution be disputed, which are matters to be pursued by the aforementioned parties, which will be for the judge to handle in the proceedings, and concerning all the aforementioned matters, let it please the consultant to advise serially and particularly with the laws pertaining to the aforementioned according to the subject matter, as he shall see fit in his discretion.
In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Although it has been prudently and subtly alleged, the truth is that in this compendious substitution a vulgar substitution is contained, by which, if the instituted heir predeceases the testator while the latter is still alive, the substitutes succeed. Thus holds Cynus in l. precibus, and I have often advised: it is not entirely tacit, since it can be gathered from the words, de lib. et post. l. Gall. § 1. For the adverb "whenever" is verified by its indefinite, indeed universal, signification, whether the instituted heir dies before the testator or afterwards; l. quod si filius? does not obstruct this, because it speaks of a vulgar substitution which has its root in a pupillary substitution and is entirely tacit, such that, by the nature of the words of the will, a compendious substitution cannot be comprehended, and it is of another nature. And this appears, because the matter is one of intestacy, and thus is the truth; and therefore also on the last point it is more prudent not to insist, but to reconcile in an honest and cautious manner. I, Bal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Credit is given to the document found in the public archive.
casus: CASE. In the Name of God, Amen. Among other things found in the archive of the commune of Perugia and in the old cadastre of Pero Pironis Grini, pol. sol. and porte. si. florentii, it is found thus, namely: first, one petia of land, etc.; also another holding of land, both vineyard and non-vineyard, wooded and unwooded, situated in the dependencies of the village of San Pietro in Parere, in the place called Parere, bounded on one side by Venturellus, on another by the daughters of Nicolaus, on another by a ditch with one destroyed mill situated in the said ditch, and with the yards and squares adjoining the said mill, a part of which is held in enfiteusis by the canons of the prebend, which is the name of the commune, for four hundred pounds.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† This document must be upheld as genuine, for a census profession constitutes valid proof against the person who causes it to be written or consents to it. C. de donat. l. censualis; and what is noted by Bartolus, ff. de donat. l. nuda; C. de omni agro deserto, l. rura, lib. 11; and because all things are presumed to have been done solemnly. Since the public official of the archive and the notary received this confession in the name of the interested party, as in ff. de usur. l. 1; ff. de fideiuss. l. cum ostendimus, §. si; C. de contrahenda et concludenda stipulatione, l. 1; similarly noted in ff. de arbitris, l. litigatores, §. quod ait; to the same effect, C. de iudic. l. properandum, §. cum autem Hermodicium; and C. de libellis causis, l. cum precum; and what is noted in de non numerata pecunia, l. generaliter, according to Cynus. And thus, the objection from de confessis, l. certum, §. si quis absente, does not hold. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, if a person having a right in a certain thing sells or leases a part of it, and subsequently sells the entire right in the same thing without mentioning the previously alienated part, the whole passes in the second alienation.
casus: CASE. The officials of the commune of Perugia sold to Master Martin Francischini of Perugia the fruits, revenues, and profits of the future, and the common pasture rights of three Bubulcariae (pastoral districts) of land situated and included within Perugia, in that part of the village of the Abbey of Saint Christopher, in whichever of those names and places, and within whatever boundaries, the said Master Martin should choose and take in the said village, namely, of the land sown, etc., for a period of ten years. And they did this for the price and payment of 26 gold florins for each year of the said ten years, which the said Master Martin promised and agreed to give and pay to the said officials in the name of the aforementioned commune, every year of the said ten years, at the end of each year. And this sale was made in the year of our Lord 1376, on the 27th day of the month of February. The land of the said three Bubulcariae, and the fruits, revenues, and profits thereof, had never before been sold to anyone, nor had they ever been sold at any time. Later, in the year 1361, on the 27th day of the month of July, the officials of the commune of Perugia sold to Puto Buccholi of Perugia all and singular fruits, revenues, and profits, rights, and perquisites to be received, and which could be received and held, of the future, or the common pasture rights of the aforementioned village of the Abbey of Saint Christopher, for a period of ten years next to come, etc., for the price contained in the said instrument. And the said common pasture rights of the three Bubulcariae of land were not notified of the sale to the said Master Martin, as was required to be done according to the form of the ordinances of the commune of Perugia. Now, having seen all the aforementioned instruments, it is asked whether the said Martin ought to pay 26 florins for each year to the commune of Perugia, during the time of the purchase of the said pasture of the Abbey of Saint Christopher.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

Under the whole integral, any part of it is comprehended, as in D. de usufructu, l. 1, si alij. And therefore, by the sale of the post, everything which the fisc has by right within the post is included. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. in modicis; D. de acquirenda re, l. quaedam; D. de actione emptoris, l. fundum. For the price corresponds to the entire post, and was given for the whole post. D. de superficiebus, l. 1, § 1. Therefore, whatever is by right within the post comes into the sale; hence, the revenue owed to the fisc under the name of three Bubulcaria comes into the sale. D. de actione emptoris, l. creditor, in principio; nam l. cauetur, that if I sell a fund which I had leased, or part of which I had leased, the advantage of the rent, as a fruit of the land, is due to the buyer pro rata temporis, as noted in D. de actione emptoris, l. Iulianus, § si locator. This is especially so in the case of the fisc, where the buyer is compelled to stand in for the tenant. D. de iure fisci, l. 1. Hence, even if someone sold excepting the right of the tenants, the tenant cannot be expelled; nevertheless, he will pay the pension to the buyer. D. de actione empti, l. si mercedem, § 1.

In our case, however, it is manifest from those words, “regione che la contumacia.” For the indefinite is equivalent to the universal, as in D. de pignoris actione, l. si necessitas, § si annua; D. de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum, l. si servitus. It is not an objection that in the same instrument it is said that others who had leased cannot thereafter be burdened by the buyers; for this is said for the purpose of preserving the right of those persons, not for the purpose of finding a right for new buyers. For they are not burdened by this: because it does not matter to whom they pay, especially if they pay voluntarily; for they pay what is due, just as if it were said “saving the right of the first,” nevertheless the pension is due to the general buyer pro rata temporis, but he cannot expel the special lessee, nor ought he to burden them by fact; but he can claim what is due to him as a penalty, and much more so if they pay voluntarily. D. de verbis obligatorum, l. venditores. And these things are true, unless custom interprets this clause differently in similar cases. C. de fideiussoribus, l. 1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When something is said expressly.
2. When something is said commonly.
3. Whether witnesses not examined as to whether they are sufficient in the bequests for the purposes of the case.
4. Whether credit should be given to an example to which a party has objected, and the cause of the objection was not from malice.
5. What is left to a hospital that is not found, to whom such a legacy is due.
casus:
CASE. Have counsel from the consultant, and first, whether the will made by Vincentius, son of Master Iacobus, the transcript of which appears in the copy, as to the legacies contained therein, is valid in law, notwithstanding the following objections regarding the fruits which appear to be in it: namely, first, that the city or place from which the said testator is not declared in the said will; for he says at the beginning, “Vincentius, son of Master Iacobus of Bancha Salomoni.” Second, because in the said will the witnesses were not summoned. Third, because no certain place where the will was made is declared therein, nor is the house indicated before it appears that the said will was made. And have the consultant declare in memory that all the witnesses described in the said will are dead, so that the will of the said testator cannot be proved except by the said will alone. Also inquire whether faith should be given to the said transcript, notwithstanding the objections, as appears in the interposition of the decree to the protocol of the said will registered in the acts of the court of the episcopate by mandate of the vicar of the said episcopate.

Secondly, narrate how the condition appended in the substitution made in the said will has already arrived and been fulfilled. Therefore, inquire whether the said substitution, because it concerns a pious cause, is valid, notwithstanding that the opposing party alleges to the contrary that the said substitution does not touch the Hospital of the Holy Cross outside the gate, since the will contains that the goods are to be given to the Hospital of Saint Peter outside the gate, nor does it touch the hospital which is at the head of the bridge of Saint Peter, for two reasons. First, because for eighty years past no hospitality has been seen in the said hospital, nor do men come who remember having seen hospitality observed, although it is rumored that that house was formerly a hospital, which was commonly called the Hospital of Saint Peter of the Bridge outside the gate. Second, because certain pontifical privileges appear regarding the said hospital, in which the said house is not called the Hospital of Saint Mary at the head of the bridge of Saint Peter outside the gate of Spoleto, and also because at the time the said will was made, no hospitality was observed in the said hospital before, and least of all is it observed after.

Thirdly, whether the prior canon and chapter of the church of Saint Peter have an action in the said inheritance on behalf of the said hospital at the head of the bridge of Saint Peter, notwithstanding that it is not clearly established by succession or union made of the said hospital to the said church of Saint Peter, except by the possession of the said house or hospital, and of its donations, which the chapter of the said church of Saint Peter has had for a long time, or whether it pertains to the Hospital of the Holy Cross outside the gate of Spoleto, which hospital is commonly called the Hospital of Saint Peter outside the gate of Spoleto, and was so called before the will was made, and after, and is so called before, and hospitality was retained in the said Hospital of the Holy Cross; whether the Vicar of the Episcopate of Spoleto, as executor of the last wills of the deceased, and especially for pious causes, can and does it pertain to his office, and not at the petition of any other hospitals, to proceed to the execution of the said will or last will, and to apply the goods of the said inheritance to one of the said hospitals, or to both simultaneously, retaining or not retaining the canonical portion. And concerning this, show the acts initiated by the said Vicar from his said office regarding the said execution, and the objections of the opposing party.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.
† On the first point, it must be said,
† That which is expressly stated, that which is so stated, that which is appropriately understood. D. de lib. et posthu. l. nominatim.

† For what is commonly said is most certainly expressed. For one must have recourse to common and general understanding regarding similar things, because genera give understanding to individual genera, as stated in Leg. 3, l. librorum; l. quod tamen Cassius, de fun. instru.; l. cum delationis, §. asinam, de ver. sig.; l. ut Alphenus, extra de sponsa; c. ex literis. It is therefore sufficient to have said, Vincentius, son of Master Jacob of the Solomon Bank. For the place is established by the person, and the person by the place. This is supported by what is noted in C. qui test. fac. poss., l. hac consultissima; and C. de inge. et ma., l. ad recognoscendos. And this concludes the first point.

And regarding bequests to pious causes, witnesses are sufficient even if not formally summoned, as stated in the Extravagant Decretals, De Testamentis, chapter Cum esses, and chapter Relatum; moreover, since they allowed themselves to be written into the testament, even if summoned, it is presumed that they were present, as established in the Authenticum De Tabulis, section Nos autem; De Verborum Obligatione, law Sciendae; Fideiussoribus, law Cum ostendimus, section Ultima. And this concludes the second point.

And because it was stated "before the house of such a one," this is sufficient, as it identifies itself, according to the Authenticum Qui mox nati efficiuntur, section 4, Collatio 6; and in the Proemium Sexti; and in the Proemium Clementinarum, as noted in chapter Abbate sane, De Ratione Iudicii, Book 6. Hence, although the house is not specifically defined, it suffices that it is declared by equivalent description, since it states "before the house of the said Vincentius." For specification suffices, and specification of specification is not required, as held in the Digest, De Donationibus Praelectis, law 1, in the final paragraph. And thus it is commonly observed by custom, although some, for greater caution, include the location of the location. And this concludes the third point.

† But whether it should be believed by example, when a party had objected, and the grounds of the objection had not been examined, it must be said that, since it was not the original, that must be produced, and faith must be taken from it. Codex, On Wills, Law *Publicati*. And this is the fourth point.

† Another doubt follows, because the Hospital of Saint Peter is not found. To this I answer thus: either it is found, and the legacy is due to it; or it is not found, and such a legacy is due to the poor in general, just as if a legacy were left to a certain church of a saint, if it is found, it is due to it; if it is not found, it is due to the general church, i.e., the cathedral of that city, as in the Authentica de ecclesiis, titulus § Si quis in nomine, collatio 9. In our case, however, the Hospital of Saint Peter is found, which is a hospital in habit, although not in act; nevertheless, it is not capable, according to the noted opinion of Innocentius de non operante numero, chapter Cum ex iniuncto; it ought to be found, insofar as it has lapsed in fact, as noted in the law Sicut, quod cuiusque universitatis, number Whether. But whether the bishop, without being implored, may proceed ex mero officio in the cause of churches and the poor, it must be said that he may, and this is a special rule, as noted by Innocentius de iureiurando, chapter Ad iuramentum, extra, secundo. And thus all points have been clearly answered. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When the mother, one daughter, and one son die simultaneously due to the collapse of a certain house, leaving behind another son and a grandson through the daughter, how are they admitted to the mother’s inheritance?
body: In the name of the indivisible Trinity, Amen.

† The point on which legal opinion is sought is as follows: Lady Catherine of Saint Severino, and Lady Vanna, a person of full age, and Francis, a minor, legitimate and natural children of the aforementioned Lady Catherine, died together due to the collapse of a certain house, without having made any will, with Severino, legitimate and natural son of the said Lady Catherine, and Nicholas, nephew through the said Lady Vanna, her daughter, surviving. Between these, namely Severino and Nicholas, there is a dispute concerning the inheritance of the said Catherine. Now the question arises: what is the law? On this point it must be said that, according to law, the said Severino and Nicholas are to be admitted equally to the said inheritance. For in this case the said Lady Catherine transmitted the inheritance by right of representation (*votum transmittendo*), and to whom, by disposition of the law, one seeks to be admitted to the said inheritance, namely to the aforementioned Lady Vanna, who was of full age, as provided in *l. qui duos*, § *fin.*, and *l. cum pubere*, D. *de rebus dubiis*. And the said Francis, a minor, is presumed by law to have predeceased his aforementioned mother, as provided in *l. si mater* and the aforementioned *l. qui duos*, § *fin.*, in the same title. And thus the said Nicholas will have half of the said inheritance devolved upon the aforementioned Lady Vanna, his mother, although she was unaware that it had devolved upon her, even though she did not accept it, as provided in *l. una* and the commentators, C. *de his quae ante apertionem tabularum*. This law also claims its place when succession is intestate, as in our case, and the same is noted by the gloss beginning *et no.* at the end of the same gloss. This would also hold if it were said by the said Severino that the said Francis died being of full age, and that he claimed his inheritance solidly according to the form of the statute of the said territory, since between them the right of transmitting the inheritance ceases, and consequently the burden of proof would lie upon him to prove that the said Lady Catherine predeceased the said Francis. And thus he would fail, because in this case he upon whom the burden of proof lies fails by law, as provided in *l. ex testamento*, § *si quis autem*, D. *ad Trebellianum*, noted by Lord Bartolus in *l. quam de praeterea*, D. *de rebus dubiis*. I, Peter de Ripa, Doctor of Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a pupillary, vulgar, and fideicommissary substitute is admitted to this substitution, if the instituted heirs die in pupillary age, or later at any time without children, when all the instituted heirs have died before the testator, who died with the same testament.
body: In the name, and of the indivisible Trinity, Amen. From the fact, it is placed before us that the late lady Symonella, wife of the late Cola Grifutii of San Severino, made her last will and testament, and instituted in it as her universal heirs her two sons and the three sons of the said Cola, and to them she made a pupillary substitution, by a fideicommissum, vulgarly called a fideicommissum, the said Cola, if both the said sons should die in pupillary age, or later at any time without sons; finally, from the said Cola another son named Nicolaus was born, and all the said sons subsequently died while their mother, the said lady, was still living; lastly, the said lady Symonella, mother of the said testator, died without having changed the said will, the said Cola being still alive. Now the question arises, what is the law, namely whether the said Cola, who was substituted, is admitted to the said inheritance by virtue of the said substitution, and it must be said

† That which is according to law, namely that, under the pretext of the aforementioned vulgar substitution, which has been proven above, and which is also vulgar, contained in the aforementioned pupillary substitution made by the said mother: as is noted in the final law, Codex, On the Institution of Heirs; and in the matter of substitutions, that which is vulgar, contained in the aforementioned compendious clause, “whenever they shall have died,” made by the said common word, he substituted. According to Lauro de Arezzo and Cynus, reported in the law *Precibus*. This is also held by Master Raymond and Master Bartolus in the matter of the compendious clause; because the meaning of those words, says Master Bartolus, imports this: it is said, if the said sons, or both the said sons, shall have died without sons, otherwise whenever; because it is understood, whether they die during the life of the testator or after, as in law 3, Digest, On the Revocation of Legacies, with similar authorities. The said Cola may choose this vulgar substitution, after the said fideicommissary legacies. Argument: law *Titio*, Digest, On the Usufruct of Legacies; and it is the text in law *Recusare*, section *Titius*, Digest, On the Trebellian Trust; and in both places by Bartolus. This vulgar substitution, whenever the said instituted sons shall have predeceased their said mother, the testatrix, is not extinguished, although it is otherwise in the pupillary substitution. As is noted in the notable gloss, and there the text concerns our case, Codex, On the Removal of Caducary Rights, in section *In primo*, in the gloss beginning “Moreover,” there “but that,” where it is said, what if the pupillary heir, pupillary substituted, dies during the life of the testator? That the pupillary substitution is extinguished, and one cannot succeed from it. The contrary is true in the vulgar substitution, because, upon the death of the heir, by the authority of that law, the vulgarly substituted person succeeds; therefore, by those words, it is said that through the pupillary substitution one succeeds to the pupillus, and it is called the testament of the pupillus, as in law *Patris et filii*, On Vulgar and Pupillary Substitutions; law *Papius*, section *Si quis impubes*, Digest, On Inofficious Testaments. But when the pupillus dies during the life of the testator, he is in his power; hence it cannot be said that he could have made a testament, rightly because the pupillary substitution and the testament of the son are considered in the power of the father; during the life of the father, it is removed and expires. It is otherwise in the vulgar substitution, because through that one succeeds to the testator, not to the heir. Therefore, although the aforementioned heirs died during the life of the said testatrix, the aforementioned vulgar substitution is valid and endures, and from it the said Cola succeeds, as has been said above. Nor does the agnation of the said posthumous child obstruct, because the effect of that agnation, namely its nullity, ceased by pretorian law from that instant until the death of the said posthumous child, and not before, as in law 3, section *Si*, Digest, On Free and Posthumous Children, and there the gloss notes; it ceased by pretorian law after the death of the same posthumous child, who died during the life of the said testatrix, as in law *Posthumus*, and there Bartolus notes, Digest, On Invalid and Ruptured Testaments; and it is noted in law 2, On Free and Posthumous Children. That law *Posthumus* favors the instituted person, and thus the substitution to the said Cola; for the substituted person is called instituted, as is noted in the gloss in law 1, Codex, On the Edict of the Divine Hadrian. Nor does it obstruct if it is said that the said posthumous child was born after the death of his said instituted brothers; for it is of no consequence, since he died during the life of his mother, the testatrix, as is alleged above, and especially from the said section *Pro secundo* to law *Posthumus*, a clear response is inferred. Nor does it obstruct if anyone should say, because the said Cola was substituted only for the case of the two heirs dying, as there “if both the said sons,” etc.; therefore not, in the present case, where the said posthumous child was born and died. For the aforementioned vulgar substitution, made in the aforementioned case, comprehends the said other case having the same reason, as in law *Gallus*, section *Et quid si tantum*, Digest, On Free and Posthumous Children, and there Bartolus notes; let law *Final*, Codex, On Institutions and Substitutions Made Under Condition, be added. For there is no doubt that in this case, omitted, the reason is the same in all respects as that expressed above, since the said Cola wished to succeed in the case of the sons dying, argument from law *Tale pactum*, section *Si*, Digest, On Pacts; and law *Si non*, On Inofficious Testaments. And thus the said Cola, even if it were said that he was substituted for a part, insofar as his aforementioned substitution regards the defect of the aforementioned instituted persons, the contrary of which is written above in its entirety, nevertheless succeeds, as in law *Cohaeredi*, section 1, Digest, On Vulgar and Pupillary Substitutions. I, Peter de Ripa, Doctor of Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a will has been made and another son is subsequently born, the necessary heirs and those possessing the tablets [of the will] are affected.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The aforementioned opinion is subtle

It is so, and true: nevertheless, in this case, a bonorum possessio is necessary according to the edict, because by the latest civil law the testament was broken ipso iure by the birth of posthumous children, as in the Digest, Auth. Ut cum, on appeals, col. § Aliud quoque capitulum. And in the case of substitutes, one does not succeed by civil law, but by praetorian law, thus: D. l. Posthumus, De inofficioso testamento, as noted under Unde legitimi. I. Certum, in the gloss, and according to the doctors. The days, however, are utile, and do not run against the ignorant person. D. De iure et facti ignorantia, l. 1, in fine; D. De successionibus edictis, l. 1, § Largius, with similar authorities.
In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Because Nic. is sued on a hypothecary action, not on his own promise or contract, nor by any right not granted or ceded, as in l. nomen, C. quae res pignori obligatae possunt, with similar authorities, the Camerarius is not the competent judge, because it does not pertain to our art, C. de iure omnium iudicum, l. fin., and this is proven by the authorities cited in the cautionary statutes, l. 3, § caeterum, and there is a more notable text, which is in the law.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a judge who has a connection to a particular art should not be sued in respect of that art before the same judge.
body: In the Name of Christ.

† It is asked concerning the jurisdiction of the chamberlains, whether they can take cognizance against artisans holding things pledged or mortgaged to other creditors: and it must be said that one is sued by a real action as a possessor, not as a debtor, as in D. ad exhibendum, l. de eo, §. si; and therefore the mortgage, which does not extend to the affairs of the craft, does not pertain to the artisans, as noted in C. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. final; and it is the notable text in D. de nautico et chirographario, l. 3, §. caeterum. Wherefore it follows that Niccolò Guelfi cannot be sued before the chamberlain of the innkeepers in the case in which he is now being sued before him. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A statute that speaks of and punishes a striker does not apply to one who bit with his teeth.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Mordentibus is the act of animals fighting or contending with their teeth: as dogs, wolves, and lions. In a man, however, it is an act contrary to custom and contrary to human nature, as is manifest. To strike (percutere), however, is proper to man, namely, to inflict a blow upon another, as appears in the laws which make mention of striking, which set forth the example of a blow inflicted upon another by means of some instrument suitable for this, namely, hand, foot, and so forth, as appears. D. ad l. Aquil. l. sed et quaecunque, §. si. There it says: "the shape of the shoe, behold the instrument. He struck the neck, behold the act." L. item mella, §. si plures. For when it had said, "they struck," it adds the word "blow." Hence, a striking is nothing other than a blow. But the teeth of a man are not organs naturally tending to this, nor by their nature. The words of laws and statutes ought to be understood according to nature, according to custom, according to suitability, and according to the mode of common usage of speech. That which is noted in l. 2, si certum petatur, and in §. quod tamen Cassius, supports this. Therefore, speaking properly and interpretively, the name of striking does not signify a bite, even if the skin is touched and broken, and because the loss which comes from a man's bite is very slight, and therefore I say that it removes the entire penalty. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that an heir instituted by her husband shall pay the tax, and whether, if the wife was instituted as heir during his lifetime under a condition, etc., she is bound to pay the said tax.
casus: A V. §. Angelus, formerly of Bologna, son of John Raynutius of Cortona, a citizen of Perugia, of the gate of Ivory and of the parish of Saint Mary of the Market, being ill in body and so forth, made and procured this present nuncupative testament, which is said to be made without writing, in this manner. Namely, that first he judged and left his body to be buried, and so forth. Furthermore, he judged that all and each of his creditors, and those who ought to receive and have something from him according to the truth of the matter, whatever quantities of money or other things, he wished and ordered to be satisfied to them from the said [estate], and so forth. Furthermore, he left and judged to the sons of the master, who are accustomed to dwell and reside in the city of Castello, his nephews by right of institution, 200 pounds of denarii. Furthermore, he left and judged to Lord Jacob Andrutius, son of Peter of Perugia, of the gate of Ivory, of Saint Angel, 300 gold florins; and to Ravarulus Andrutius, son of Peter, brother by blood of the said Lord Jacob, of the said gate and parish, 200 gold florins. In all his other goods, and so forth, he instituted and made Lady Blasia, his wife, universal heir, during the life of the said Lady Blasia, and as long as she shall live honorably and shall not pass to second marriage, and so forth. But after the death of the said Lady Blasia, or if the said Lady Blasia shall not have lived honorably and chastely, or shall not have observed the widow's life, then in any of the said cases he substituted to the said Lady Blasia his aforesaid daughters, and so forth. And to the said Lady Blasia in the said cases, in any of them, he left and judged her dowries, which he confessed to have been and to be five hundred gold florins, and beyond the said dowries he left to her from his goods 200 gold florins, and all the Aredium, and all the Arnesia, and linen, and wood, and bed, which at the time of the death of the said testator were in the chamber; however, let it not be understood that what was in the said chamber comes into the said proximate legacy made for his said daughters, but let it be reserved for them and given to them, having been placed for them, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is asked concerning the tax, having regard to the statute, which simply provides that when a wife is instituted as heir, payment shall be made according to the valuation of the immovable property nearest at hand, as it is found in the cadastre, i.e., the public estimate. And it appears that the taxes must be paid precisely as the statute states: because that which can be resolved should not be taken into account, but rather that which exists in the meantime. D. de in diem adiect. l. 2; D. de rei vend. l. non ideo minus. The valuation of the things has been fixed: hence one should not consider how much the hereditary right itself is worth, but rather the valuation of the things themselves. D. quod met. cau. l. si mulieri. Hence, if the inheritance is onerous on account of personal debts, nevertheless payment would be due according to the valuation of the things. D. de iud. l. si fidei commissum, § 1. Moreover, the words of the law, once introduced into a contract, are to be observed as they stand, and the right of the buyers, who contracted most liberally, ought not to be harmed by a restrictive interpretation. D. de verb. oblig. l. quicquid astringendae, 3. responso.

To the contrary, that the tax is not to be paid so precisely, but is to be assessed at the discretion of a good man, is proved by the fact that the same law applies to a part of a thing and to a part of time. D. de testamento milit. l. miles ita haeredes, § 1. If one instituted as heir in part does not pay, he pays only for that part; therefore, the same applies if one is instituted for a time: considering the effect of the benefit, he pays only to that extent and no further. Moreover, since regard is had to the valuation of the thing, one must consider not the thing simply, but the thing with its quality and condition, as is clear from D. de don. causa mort. l. mortis causa, § fin. It is established, however, that temporary dominion is worth less than perpetual dominion. C. de donat. l. sancimus, § fin.; C. de sacr. eccl. l. iubemus, § fin.; D. ad l. Falc. l. non habetur pro puro. And there, Bartolus introduces that law concerning the tax, C. de sacr. eccl. l. iubemus, § fin. Therefore, the thing is not to be considered in itself simply, but as it is in the acquisition. Moreover, the condition "temporarily" can be understood inceptive, according to the gloss in D. de incidi. vi, l. fin., eod. tit. Hence, without the Mutian caution, one is not an heir, and thus before the condition is fulfilled, one is not bound to pay; but this gloss is commonly not approved.

In the second way, distributively, so that in the first year the legacy is pure, and for the others conditional. This is held by Bartolus in legacies and fideicommissa in D. de leg. 2, l. Titia, § fin. And thus the taxes are divided by years. D. de stipul. seruo, l. si seruus communis Meuij, et Castrensis peculii, § fin. And the day had not yet arrived, except for the first year: but this is contrary to nature, but not contrary to the effect of the institution. D. de acq. vel omitt. her. l. hereditas ex die.

In the third way, that it is a privative condition, and this diminishes its price, hence it is worth less than a slave simply, as in D. de condi. et demonstr. l. si seruus. Wherefore, the taxes are due when the things are estimated with their cause and hope, not simply, as argued from D. ad l. Falc. l. hereditas.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The impression and violent intent are proved by one witness of sight and several of reputation.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Having examined the records, it appears that the impression and the violent intent have been proven by one witness of direct observation and by several witnesses of reputation, as in the case of this question, as stated in the canon *Si quis*, in the title *De his quae vi*, in the Decretals.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Where alienation is generally prohibited by the testator, the institution of an extraneous heir is prohibited.
2. Given such a prohibition, whether heirs may make donations among themselves.
3. The objection that there are as many donations as there are things, whether it validates donations without insinuation.
4. A son generally requested to restore after death may alienate the legitime and the trebellianic portion.
5. An heir instituted under a condition of death, if burdened with a fideicommissum by killing, does not cause the condition of death to exist.
6. Whether insinuation may be made before any judge whatsoever.
7. Sons do not transmit the querelam inofficiosae donationis (complaint of an undutiful donation) not prepared against extraneous heirs.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Regarding the point on which counsel is sought, namely whether the institution of an alien heir appears to be prohibited by the general prohibition of alienation imposed by the aforementioned testator, Namnus, it must be said that it is so, as established in *l. peto*, § *fratre*, *de legatis* 2. And therefore, it would be said that the house pertains to the legitimate descendant, that is, to Barnabus, and does not pertain to the bastard, according to *ff. ad Trebellianum*, *l. ex facto*, § *si quis*, there: “but this by reason of dignity,” etc. And the aforementioned Barnabus may take possession by his own authority, because the testator promised this, *de legatis* 2, *l. Titia*, § 1. Nor is there any right that the house be separated; because the testator’s disposition remains valid with respect to the courtyard and foundations, as they are now, *ff. de legatis* 1, *l. domos haereditarias*.

† Regarding the question whether, notwithstanding the aforementioned prohibition, they may make donations to one another, it must be said that they may, as stated in the Codex, Title on Fideicommissa, law *Voluntas*. However, if the donation exceeds five hundred legal gold or silver coins, of which seventy-five make up a pound of gold, insinuation is required; because it is not permitted to donate above that amount without insinuation, as stated in the Codex, Title on Donations, laws *Sancimus* and *Si quis argentum*.

But there is doubt concerning that caveat, namely that there are so many donations, etc., whether on this account insinuation is not required; and Cynus says that this confused distribution effects nothing, and therefore insinuation is required. The same is said in the Speculum, unless the things were specially designated, or specified, and are not enumerated by a collective name: *De verbis obligatorum*, l. *Scire debemus*, and the note in the Speculum *De donationibus*, under the words “What if someone.” For then there are as many instruments, and as many donations, as there are things enumerated; and thus I hold.

† And a son, generally requested to restore [the inheritance] after death, may alienate the Trebellianic portion of his legitime: as in the Authentica de restitutione et ea quae pacta sunt, §. quamobrem.

† Furthermore, it is asked whether a brother instituted by a fideicommissum under the condition of death acquires that fideicommissum if, by killing him, he causes the condition of death to exist. And it seems that he does, for the condition has occurred, and it appears to be a case. D. 38.1.1 (Is confirmatus) § 1; and D. 10.4.1 (Cum ratio) in fine, De bonis damnatorum. I say the contrary, lest his own fraud benefit him. D. 24.3.1 (Ab hostibus) § Si vero uxorem; because it does not seem that the testator intended to confer honor upon him in this case, arg. D. 35.1.1 (Codicillis) § Penultimus, De legatis secundis. And thus the murderer loses the substitution made in his favor after the death of the brother killed by him, and this portion accrues to the other brothers, he being excluded. He is held to be dead.

† Furthermore, it is asked whether the donation made by Walter before the Captain of the land of the Borough was valid, and it must be said that it was: because it was insinuated, as it could be done in any place, there the judge sitting on the bench; because insinuation is of voluntary jurisdiction, as stated in the question and answer, l. voluit, § 1, de officio proconsulis, l. 2, de officio ordinario, c. cum episcopus, lib. 6.

† It is not an objection that the said Walter had sons then born, who did not bring the querela (action for omission), nor did they transmit the unprepared claim to an extraneous heir, as noted in l. posthumus, in fine, de inofficioso testamento; because 300 years have elapsed, C. de inofficiosa donatione, l. si. And therefore extraneous heirs do not bring the querela, but the donation stands firm, and for the same reason, namely prescription, the right of the donor is excluded, unless he possessed, because possession does not allow prescription to run against the possessor. ff. qui ex causa possessionis, l. si is, cuius rem. This must be understood according to the note in l. fin., C. de pactis, where it is said that the donation is valid, unless it was a simulated donation, and simulation was proven: for in doubt, truth is presumed. It is also asked about the testament of Walter, who substituted Christopher, Vigone, and Matthew, or their children in stirpes, and by the testament of Christopher that which is due from the testament of Walter could not be taken away. ff. ad legem Falcidiam, l. pater filium. After deducting the Trebellian portion and what is due by natural law, and in c. Raymundus and in c. si pater, lib. 6, and what was alienated by the said Christopher is imputed to his legitime, as ff. ad Trebellianam, l. Marcellus, §. res, quae, and d. §. quamobrem. And when the universal fideicommissary finds himself in possession, without defect he may retain and plead exception. ff. ad Trebellianam, l. filiam fratribus. As noted in l. edicto, C. de edicto divi Adriani, and precarious possession does not pertain to that edict: because it is extinguished by the death of the one who asked for the precarium. ff. de precario, l. cum precario, §. 1. And therefore Bernabò is a legitimate adversary for the two aforementioned reasons: because he possesses without defect, and because the testator possessed precariously, not as his own, whence his heir succeeded to the defect of the deceased, as fully noted in ff. de publiciana, l. eum in, §. in hac. And the brother transmitted the unaccepted inheritance, yet if he did anything as heir, as because he acts beyond his share, they are seen to have accepted, and he transmits the inheritance, de acquirenda hereditate, f. duo fratres. And fraud and theft do not come against a donation, unless the adversary’s fraud and simulation intervened, as noted in auth. sacramenta puberum. Even if no mention is made of minority, as noted in l. 2, C. de rescindenda venditione. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If the testator has bequeathed moneys which he ought to have from someone, against whom the legatee is bringing an action, whether against the heir or against the debtor.
casus: CASE. In the Name of God, Amen. The facts are proposed thus, upon which counsel is requested. Namely, Lady Nera, daughter formerly of the said Ser Odonis, Ser Conis of Castro, made her last testament with substitution of an heir, and among other legacies, namely, she also left, willed, and commanded in the institution of a legacy to Marrucina, her legitimate and natural daughter, for her dowries, seven hundred pounds of Perugino currency, which the said Lady Nera, the testatrix, is bound and ought to have and receive as the legitimate daughter and intestate heir of the aforementioned Lady, her mother, and wife formerly of Matatutius Marrucina of Monte Purtiano, paternal grandfather of the aforementioned Marrucina, from the said Matatutius, and from the sons, or from the heirs formerly of the said Matatutius, or from the possessors of the goods of the said Matatutius, for the restitution of the dowry of the said Lady, her perfect mother, or the aforementioned, as appears by public instrument of Manuser Manuellis Victalurii of Barthino, or of any other notary, giving and granting to the same daughter, Marrucina, all right, and every action, real, personal, useful, and direct, tacit and express, praetorian and civil, and every other, which, and that which she hopes to have in the aforementioned, and which she has, and ought to have against the said Matatutius, and sons, and heirs, or possessors of goods, to the same Marrucina by virtue of the restitution of dowries, and the aforementioned quantity, and in the said quantity, and possessions, and actions, she is tacitly satisfied and content, and that she cannot demand more of his goods, and if she should demand more, she falls from the said legacy, and from all succession of his. In all his goods, however, he instituted and made Baptist, his legitimate and natural son, universal heir. It is asked, because it is brought into doubt, whether the said legacy is valid, whether it is a legacy of the name of a debtor, or what kind it is, and against whom the action of the said Lady lies for the petition of the said quantity: whether against the heir and possessor of goods of the said Matatutius, husband formerly of the said Lady, perfect mother of the said testatrix, or against the heir of the testatrix.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† That the heirs of the said Nera can be sued for the payment of the said legacy, appears to be a case according to the letter of the law. D. de legatis 1, l. quidam in testamento. To the contrary, that this is a legacy of a debt by name, appears from the text according to the letter in l. si mihi Seius, debet legatum, nominis est. Therefore, the amount should not be demanded from the heir: although it suffices that the heir assigns the actions, as in C. de legatis, l. ex legato nominis. The solution in our case is that she bequeathed the debt by reason of those gerunds, giving, and granting, etc. For by this gerund it is signified and derived that she bequeathed something in the manner of bequeathing, because the testatrix says, I bequeath by giving and granting: but she does not simply say, I bequeath. And because she inserted the name of the debtor into the substance of the legacy. That is to say, the relative which here signifies: but in l. quidam in testamento, he did not attach the name of the debtor to the substance, but to the precept, by demonstrating, not by limiting, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a statute provides that wills are to be executed, with respect to which wills is such a statute to be understood?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The statute provides that wills shall be put into execution: this is understood to apply to those that are liquid immediately, or to those that are to be liquidated after liquidation. C. de compensatione, l. si; ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. quae sub conditione. And thus in the case of a judgment: because it becomes liquid immediately, if it contains a condition, it is put into execution after liquidation. C. de sententiis, l. cum iudex, and l. cum eorum; in l. 1, § biduum, quando appellandum sit. And a judgment in rem is put into execution by the office of the judge; in the same way, a will is here put into execution by verbal restitution, de iureiurando, l. nam et postea, § si, and hoc; ff. de iudiciis, l. sed et si restituatur.
