And what is noted there, where it is pleasing to see the gloss. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A general exception is admitted by way of a declaratory, supportive, and proven prosecution in order to conclude the argument.
2. If a wife purchases something after the death of her husband, it is presumed that she purchased it with her own funds.
3. Whether one who holds a title and possesses is understood to possess by virtue of the same title.
4. On account of the presumption of writing, the litigant is excused from expenses.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

One must begin with the libel, and the libel in which it was requested to declare that [the matter] pertains, belongs, etc., is general, as noted in the Digest, *De iudiciis*, l. *Si quis intentione ambigua*. And the nature of a general libel is that it can be clarified in the prosecution. Codex, *De iudiciis*, l. *Licet*. Nevertheless, that specification must conclude against the defendant to the condemnation of the thing; otherwise, all other things being equal, the defendant prevails, *De publicianis*, l. *Sive autem*, § *Si duobus*. Therefore, the foundations of both intentions must be carefully considered, namely, those of both the plaintiff and the defendant. Let us begin at the head, that is, with the plaintiff. The plaintiff alleges a universal conditional fideicommissum, and that its condition has been fulfilled, and concludes to a specific thing, nor does he say that the inheritance was restored to him by a person or by law, because he does not allege the case of the law. Codex, *Ad Trebellianam*, l. *Penultima*. And thus the libel is insufficient unless it is assisted by a declared and assisting prosecution, and proven to conclude to the purpose. Hence, let us examine the following, and it should be known that this libel is not based on the edict of the Divine Hadrian, *Tollenda*, especially when possession is not alleged in the libel, nor is it held as a claim of death, nor does it conclude in a vindication of the thing, because dominion is not alleged, nor in a publician action, because quasi-dominion is not alleged, but it concludes in a petition for a fideicommissary inheritance, which is excluded by the defendant’s title, unless the defendant’s title is invalidated. L. *Nec ullam*, in § *Omnibus*, *De petitione hereditatis*. However, it is necessary that the plaintiff first establish his own foundation, and therefore the records speak of these foundations, and we must inquire into them.

† First, the question arises concerning the right of the testator, whether it is proven or whether the contrary holds. Indeed, the purchase appears from a public instrument, which is on file at folio 79. And because it appears that they were purchased after the death of the husband, due to the adverb “quondam” (late/former), as noted in *l. eius, qui in provinciam*, *si certum petatur*, it is not presumed to have been done with the husband’s money; otherwise, it would be presumed that the woman had subtracted it from the husband, and fraud would be presumed, which is false. *l. Marcellus*, *rerum amotarum*. But while the husband was alive, the woman is not said to subtract, but to administer. *ff. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, *l. quintus*. And as if through an administrator, it is sought for the husband in a subsidiary capacity, not simply, as in *l. multum*, *si quis alteri, vel sibi*, *art. tit. de institutionibus*; *C. de rei venditione*, *l. si ut proponis*; and *l. uxor marito*, *de donationibus inter virum et uxorem*. Nevertheless, I doubt the aforementioned instrument, which states that it was said by Ciolo Gilii, and Master Baltramus by Ciolo Angeli. *ff. quemadmodum testamentum aperiri debeat*, *ad l. 1*, in the end. But there it speaks of a substantial witness and of a written document, here of an extraneous witness. It follows to consider the matter of possession, and Master Baltramus proves possession; nevertheless, it must be considered here that one witness does not sufficiently prove; however, with another probable circumstance added, it is strongly corroborated. *de successionibus ab intestato*, *c. si*.

† but it is probable that one having a title possesses by that title. As in D. pro socio, l. merito; D. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. 2; D. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. praedia; D. de rei venditione, l. quaedam mulier. But here I doubt whether this is true only when the order of time is proven, i.e., that the title precedes the possession; for otherwise the possession is unjust, or ineffective for the strength of the judgment. But here the order of time is not proven. Argument: D. de negotiorum gestis, l. eum actum; l. at qui natura, §. Scaeuola. It supports what is noted in C. ult., de rescriptis. Also, because this is so only when the possession falls under the same author. D. de usucapione, l. non solum. But here there appear to be different bodies, Ciolus of Gilii and Ciolus of Angelus, and they do not correspond univocally; therefore, neither in the body. C. de ingenuis manumissis, l. ad recognoscendos. For possession must be relative to its title, and qualified by the title; otherwise, one remains a possessor as a possessor, not as a buyer. D. de petitione hereditatis, l. si rem, et pretium; according to Odofredus, C. eodem, l. cogi; according to the doctors, on possession, Ciolus deponit, Bisaccia, fol. 60. But here it must be observed that possession is transferred by precarium if it was held at that time; otherwise, if before, and not at that time, or afterwards, and not at that time; because it cannot truly be delivered, it cannot be delivered by fiction. D. si certum petatur, l. si filius. Hence, among partners, we see present things become common; but future things do not become common; rather, action is brought to make them common, because where true delivery does not occur, fictitious delivery does not occur. D. pro socio, l. 2 and 3; D. si certum petatur, l. si socius. But here it is not proven that at the time of the contract, nor could this witness prove it, because he did not know one of the contracting parties, namely Lady Vanna; nor does it follow necessarily. But to this it can be answered, because he says, until he sold. And thus he testified sufficiently, although in general terms he included an extraneous time within the substantial facts. But because there is only one witness, and he has no corroborating witness, it is not sufficient. C. de testibus, l. iureiurandi. Ownership, however, is not proven, although he was not questioned; although in a case of knowledge, as noted by Innocentius, de testibus, c. cum causam, because ownership is not perceived sensitively, but intellectually. And in this intellect the witness could be deceived; hence, it is necessary that he express causes through bodily senses, which are not deceived regarding their proper objects, just as sight is not deceived in colors. And therefore, by the instrument and the said witnesses, it is not sufficiently proven for the plaintiff, and the defendant ought to be absolved due to the lack of proof by the plaintiff, and the title of the defendant, and his possession thereof, d. §. si duobus. However, the plaintiff, because he was moved by the writing, ought not to be condemned in costs, because he is excused from temerity due to the presumption of the writing. D. de interrogatione actorum, l. de aetate, §. ex causa. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, after the hospital has been constructed according to the testator’s intent, the bishop may interfere in its affairs.
casus: CASE. In the name of Christ, Amen. The fact, on which counsel is sought, is as follows: A certain person named Master Peter of Artono, of the district of Spoleto, in the year of our Lord 1454, made his last will, in which, among other things, he judged, left, and disposed that a house be built, or bought, before the gate of the Castle of Monte Franchi, or indivisely of the said Castle, in the price of which 200 gold florins shall be expended, in which four supported beds shall be committed and held in perpetuity, to receive poor pilgrims and other good men, and in which alms shall be made continuously in perpetuity of at least one cup of wheat for each week, and that from the said price, i.e., possessions constituting and valued at a thousand gold florins be purchased for maintaining the aforementioned. Also, he judged and left Lady Annanutia, his sister, as governor and patroness of the said house, and of all possessions and goods pertaining to it, for the whole time of her life; and after her death, he substituted to her the firstborn male son, and where males fail, let females be; and in all his other goods, he instituted and made Jacobus Benedicti, his nephew, and Lady Annanutia, his sister, his heirs in equal parts. After the said testator died, Lady Annanutia built and had built the said house before the said gate, and bought not a few possessions from the said thousand gold florins, and fulfilled in all respects the will of the said testator, and in the said house retained four supported beds, and hosted poor people and pilgrims until her death. Finally, the said Lady Annanutia died, with Peter, her second-born son, and the said Christiana, her daughter, and Federico, her nephew, alive, having made the last will mentioned below, in which she instituted the said Peter and Federico, her nephew and son of the late Gilii, son of the late said Annanutia’s firstborn, as her universal heirs. To her daughter, Lady Christiana, she left one house, in which she instituted Lady Christiana as heir. The said Peter retained similar hospitality in the said house, and did and observed all other things according to the will of the testator until his death. Finally, the said Peter died, with Ser Benedicto, his legitimate and natural son, alive, and with the said Lady Christiana, his sister and daughter of the late said Lady Annanutia, alive, who said Lady Christiana was born after the death of the said Peter; nevertheless, if she legally retained hospitality in the house, and managed, retained, and administered the goods bought from the said thousand florins for many years, recently the said Lady Christiana died, with Morico, her son, alive, and with Federico, son of the late said Gilii, son of the late firstborn of the said Lady Annanutia, and carnal nephew of the said Lady Christiana, alive, and with the said Ser Benedicto, son of the late said Pe., son of the late second-born of the said Lady Annanutia, and carnal nephew of the said Lady Christiana, alive. Now two questions are asked, and first, to whom, of the aforementioned Federico, Ser Benedicto, and by right, does the governance and administration of the said house and the aforementioned goods pertain by virtue of the aforementioned substitution? Whether from the fact that they are heirs of the aforementioned Annanutia, or from the institution of the heir by the said Peter, since the aforementioned Jacobus is not known to have accepted the inheritance of the said Master Peter and died. Secondly, whether it pertains to the diocesan or bishop to order or constitute some governor to retain the aforementioned hospitality in the said house, since the said house was not constructed or appointed for the aforementioned hospitality by license or provision of the diocesan bishop; although he may provide and order, not as executor of legacies for pious causes, that the pious will of the said testator be fulfilled, on all of which please give your sound counsel, if you feel that the aforementioned governance pertains by right to the aforementioned Federico and Ser Benedicto, or to one of them.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

The order of the testament must be followed, as in the Authentica *de ecclesiasticis titulis*, § *si quis*, under the words “et si quidam,” column 9. It pertains to the authority and office of the bishop to intervene, even if the testator had forbidden it, as there; and in the Codex *de episcopis et clericis*, Authentica *licet testator*. It suffices that, for the hospital to be established by divine law, the provision of the bishop accedes, even if it does not proceed. For it suffices that pious acts be confirmed and approved by the authority of the bishop, as in the Extravagant *de testamentis*, chapter *Nos quidem*, and in chapter *Cura*, *de iure patronatus*. Therefore, the said hospital is a pious and ecclesiastical place, not profane. Regarding it, two things are to be considered: namely, the right of patronage and the administration of the hospital. For these are distinct, since the right of patronage is the right of presentation, whereas administration is the right of governing. The former right passes even to a minor, the latter is not entrusted except to those who are discreet and suitable. Digest *de cura furiosi*, law *Cuius bonis*; *de iure patronatus*, chapter 2, in the Clementines. Our question, however, concerns both the right of patronage and the right of administration, because the testator disposed of both together, and his testament is to be observed, unless as regards administration the successor were not suitable. Digest *ubi pueri educandi sunt*, law 1; *de confirmatione tutorum*, law *Utilitatem*; *de religiosis donationibus*, chapter *De xenodochiis*. Therefore, the testament must be examined, and it must be considered that the testament contains three substitutions: the first and the last are express, the middle one is tacit. The first was in favor of the firstborn son, but the term “son” does not include the grandson, because the testator spoke distinctly of the firstborn. For this is a distinctive term. Codex *ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum*, law *Iubemus*, at the end. The second express substitution was after the male line, and this ceases, because males exist. The third, however, was in favor of other males and the firstborn, and this applies. Digest *de legatis secundis*, law *Titia Seio*, § *Seia*; *non quoties lex non providet*, as in Digest *de vulgari substitutione*, law *Vel singulis*. Meanwhile, the testator appears to have provided for them and substituted those whom he preferred to the last substitute. Therefore, having regard to the judgment of the testator, and by tacit substitution, the right is devolved to the grandsons, and to the sons of the males, the right and all administration of the testament, saving the right of the diocesan bishop in examining and approving the more suitable of the aforementioned Federico and Ser Benedetto as administrator of the said hospital and its goods, and in demanding an account if they administered poorly. For the Orphanotrophus is compared to the tutor of minors, as in law *Orphanotrophos*, Codex *de episcopis et clericis*; in chapter *Quia contingit*, *de religiosis donationibus*, in the Clementines. This hospital has a rector appointed by the testator, if he is suitable; otherwise, recourse is had to an appointee, just as we say in the case of a tutor, Digest *de excusationibus tutorum*, law *Non solum*, § *Si libertus*. Therefore, neither the heir nor the bishop can infringe upon what the testator has done, as in the Authentica *de nuptiis*, in § *Disponat*; Digest *de petitione hereditatis*, law *Haereditas*; in law 1, Digest *de annuis legatis*. Quintus, at the end, saving what has been said regarding insufficiency or negligence, as in the said § *si quis*, under the words “et si quidam,” *de ecclesiasticis titulis*, column 9. And in doubt, the senior of these two is preferred, as in law *Ultima*, Digest *de fide instrumentorum*; and *de maioribus et obediendis*, chapter 1, according to Innocentius; and chapter *Masculus foeminae*, in the same title.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A doubtful legal issue may be clarified by the immediately connected subject matter.
2. Legacies left for pious causes require no other confirmation than the death of the testator.
3. A lessee cannot raise the question of ownership.
4. In legacies of property consisting of profits, a cession is not necessary.
5. In the case of two co-debtors, a renunciation of the benefit is sufficient without formal notice.
6. Whether heirs may demand the division of the testator's debt.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. The allegations made on both sides are so profound and notable that it is not expedient to allege further, but rather to arrive at the decision on the points formally touched upon.

† And first, regarding the place, I say that the same place is understood which is contained in the preceding and immediately conjoined subject matter, whence in §. si initium tabularum. an argument is drawn from time to place, and C. si cer. pe. l. eo, quod a multis supports this.

† Regarding the second, I say that in bequests to pious causes no other confirmation is necessary than the death of the testator: because in legacies where the Falcidian law ceases, the adition of the inheritance is not required, as noted by Ia. Bel. in Auth. de hae. et fal. §. hinc nobis. and Bar. in l. 1. ff. si quis omissa causa testamenti. The better reason is that it is ordered into execution by the office of the bishop. ff. de pet. hae. l. haereditas. in fi.

† To the third, I say that a lessee cannot raise the question of ownership: because that would be a kind of spoliation. Cyn. in l. 2. C. si cer. pe. in §. qui ad agendum. and that is the case in C. de agri. et censi. l. litibus. and noted in C. loca. l. si quis conductionis. with similar texts.

† To the question whether a cession is necessary, it must be said that he who bequeaths the property is deemed to bequeath it with its benefits. C. de leg. l. monumenta. and l. vxor patrui. The emoluments, moreover, are the very rents, whence a cession is not required with respect to beneficial actions. eo. tit. l. ex legato nominis.

† To the other point regarding two joint debtors, it must be said that a renunciation suffices, nor is certification required, except in the case of a woman and a minor; and noted in ff. de verb. obli. l. sciendum. and l. 2. §. fi. de iu. fis. and in c. 2. de pac. li. 6. by Io. An. Likewise, he who pays is presumed to know why he pays. C. si cer. pet. l. pe. in fin. and furthermore he is deemed to ratify. C. de condi. inde. l. indebitum. §. 1.

† Regarding the other point concerning division between heirs, the allegation is precluded if it is true in fact: because it is divided actively and passively, de hę. act. l. pro haereditariis; whence the records should speak on this. Regarding the other point concerning the curator, one must stand by the decree, as in ff. de postu. l. item quibus. and a mere present petition, not joined with fraud, just like an exaction, produces no effect, de leg. 2. l. qui solidum. insti. de act. §. triplici. And this I say and speak to the prudence of so great a man, who has to judge the case, and to whose decision it will rest; you are better able to know that the remaining points of this question are untouched and subtle. But the course of the facts is that the said Dominicus is the heir of one of the debtors obligated in solidum, and therefore if he is heir in solidum, which is presumed unless a co-heir is shown, l. 2. si pars hęr. pe. he is liable in solidum; otherwise only for the hereditary share, as has been said, as appears in ff. ad l. Fal. l. in l. fal. and this must be observed; concerning Marcellus there is no doubt that by bequeathing he entered upon the inheritance, as in l. si auia. and if the son was an infant, he could do so even after the death of the infant, as in l. si infanti. If, however, he were older, the same applies during the son's life, as in l. non solum. de bo. quę lib. But once he is dead, many great doctors say there that he cannot enter upon the inheritance, and consequently he could not bequeath the rights of lady Nanna, extra de testis. c. filius, and thus according to that opinion Dominicus would have to be absolved: because it was not articulated concerning infant age, indeed nor concerning patrimony and paternal power, which is required here, unless because this is presupposed by those alleging, unless we wish to hold that the father may enter upon the inheritance without distinction, or that the mother's inheritance is transmitted to ascendants through the gloss in l. apud hostes, which seems contrary to the case of the law in l. non pro numero. ad Orfi. and according to the doctors this right could not be derived to the hospital through the husband: because they did not earn the rights of the heir, according to the gloss thus, because either from transmission by benefit of the law, since he was not only able to enter whenever; certainly in this case the advocate of the plaintiff was prepared in capitulating, and from the proceedings it is not well gathered that Marcellus, through the intermediary person of the son, was the heir of lady Nanna, and that he could make testamentary disposition concerning the rights of lady Nanna regarding a fourth part, whence it is proved through the cession of lady Cecha. And therefore, except in that fourth share coming from the right of the cessionary and bequeathed, Dominicus ought to be absolved: because Marcellus could not bequeath a right that was not his own as to him by right of transfer. I do not deny that the points are exceedingly doubtful, and there are as many opinions as there are heads, both of the ancients and moderns; nonetheless the aforesaid opinion is true through l. si infanti. §. si vero vel non sit tutor. and so Bartolus would hold in l. cum non solum. and Ray. and Cy. and the said lex non pro numero supports this. Distinguished Father and my Lord: a certain lady named Catharina, under 25 years of age, placed under the power of Iacobus her father, married to a certain Angelus of Foligno, donated mortis causa to Girardus her paternal uncle, with the consent and will of the said Iacobus her father, one hundred gold florins; and having seen the instrument of the said donation, and having seen the statute of the commune of Foligno, you advised that the said donation was valid, and would be confirmed by the death of the said lady Margarita alone, as is contained in our consilium which the bearer of the present letters carries, which you returned to Barcorius, chancellor of my Magnificent Lord Corrandus de Trincis, kinsman of the said Girardus. Now, however, the said instrument is called into doubt, and it is said that such donation is not valid, on the ground that in the said donation the form of the constitution of the Roman Church under the rubric, 'what form should be observed in alienations of goods and contracts of minors,' was not observed, a copy of which is sent to you, along with a copy of the said donation; which constitution wills that donations, sales, alienations, etc. are not valid if the form of the said constitution is not observed. For which opinion the case in l. alienatum. §. donationis. ff. de ver. si. seems to stand, and as noted there by the gloss in the distinction it posits there, namely, either the word 'donation' is uttered by the law, and must include every donation, or by man, and then it does not; the gloss also supports it in l. 2. ff. de do. praele. and l. causa mortis. §. filius ff. de don. causa. mor. with similar passages, in that it says that it approaches more to a contract inter vivos than to a last will, etc. To the contrary, I argued through the aforesaid gloss in the said §. donationis, which is commonly rejected by the doctors, and especially by Ia. de Are. and by Bar. in l. filius f. ff. de dona. because the words of the law must be taken in their proper signification, as in l. non aliter. ff. de leg. 3. and in l. 1. §. si is, qui nauem. de exerci. But a donation causa mortis is not properly a donation, as in l. 1. ff. de dona. Therefore such a constitution does not extend to an improper donation, that is, to a donation causa mortis, but to a proper one, namely pure and irrevocable, that is, inter vivos, as in the said l. 1. And this the aforesaid constitution seems to intend if one inspects it well, as well as the words joined to the said word 'donation' etc., and the final cause of the constitution itself, namely lest they may be harmed or injured in contracts and business dealings, etc. Otherwise it would follow that even a paterfamilias under 25 years of age could not make a legacy, since it is a kind of donation, etc., which would be absurd. And now let it be understood, and therefore may it please you to advise, or to add to your consilium what seems best to your Lordship. Your least servant, Ioannes Milutii de Trivio, at Foligno, the 18th day of November. Copy of the constitution of the Roman Church: 'What form is to be observed in alienations of property and contracts of minors, etc.': in order that succor may be brought to the vulnerability of minors by all suitable and expedient means, lest they may easily be damaged or harmed in their contracts and transactions, as we have found to have occurred in many cases, we enact and by the present constitution establish that donations, alienations, sales, remissions, cessions, and acquittances of whatever things, actions, or rights, under whatever form of words contracted by poor persons, but of full age, without an oath bodily taken, and also without the knowledge of two or three of the nearer blood relatives, if they exist, or at least affines, if blood relatives do not exist, and without the decree of a competent judge and an entry to be made in the public acts with any corporate bodies, colleges, communities, and any individual persons, cannot be made nor celebrated in any way; and if they have been made or celebrated without having observed all the aforesaid formalities, let them be presumed and feigned to have been fraudulently exacted, and obtain no validity; and nonetheless, let whoever contracts with a minor contrary to the form noted above be punished at the discretion of the judge.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a donation causa mortis is comprehended under a statute disposing of donations.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. This constitution cannot be understood as applying to a donation causa mortis, because, since it speaks of an oath by which the act is irrevocably formed, it does not accord with this donation causa mortis, but rather with one inter vivos; on donations causa mortis, l. Ubi ita donatur. Moreover, this constitution, which comes supplementarily to the common law, must be restricted, not extended, to a donation causa mortis, which is not a simple donation, although it is a contract quasi innominatum; on donations causa mortis, l. Senatus, §. Nec dubitat Cassianus, and to this effect, ff. on donations, l. Filius. Furthermore, because a donation causa mortis does not require insinuation; C. on donations causa mortis, l. Fin. For in these solemnities, which are not to be observed, it accedes to the last will, as appears there. And this is declared by the statute under the heading "On Donation," which can be interpreted as another constitution among its subjects, and also because customary observance is that statutes are to be observed, as l. Omnes populi, cum si non obstat, the most general word, "alienations," etc., because by the said formal words it is restricted to those things which are compatible with the form; l. Item autem, in the beginning, on the administration of a tutor. Here the constitution is to be considered, but the statute is not doubtful; but assuming the validity of the statute, that this donation causa mortis is valid, because the words are so expressed, to which one must adhere; l. 1, §. Si is qui navem, and l. Fratres, on penalties, cum si. According to the constitution, it is doubtful because of the general word "donations," because of the more general word "alienations," because of the most general word "under whatever form," or contract of words; for a donation causa mortis accedes to an innominate contract, as ff. on donations causa mortis, l. Senatus, in §. Nec dubitat Cassianus. Nevertheless, I say the contrary, for certain contracts are not confirmed by the authority of the father; ff. on verbal obligations, l. Fin.; ff. on numbers, l. 1. But a donation causa mortis is confirmed by the authority of the father; ff. on donations causa mortis, l. Tam is, §. 1. In which case that reason ceases, viz., "to the weakness," etc., because it gives him greater authority to use his own counsel, and not weakness; because in the constitution mention is made of an oath; because in a donation causa mortis it does not apply, as on donations causa mortis, l. Ubi. Notwithstanding the general words; because by the said form they are restricted to those things which are compatible with the form, as l. Ita autem, in the beginning, on the administration of a tutor; on military matters, l. Milites agrum. And because a donation causa mortis, as regards privileges, accedes to the last will, Inst. on donations, §. 1, and l. Fin., C. on donations causa mortis. And therefore the said constitution, "I, Baldo," is not understood to apply to it.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Sureties given for a certain craft are bound in every respect, and if they have submitted themselves to the jurisdiction of that craft, they may be sued there.
casus: A certain Bernardus of Monte Pulciano and Luculus Suragus of Perugia were confessors, obligating themselves jointly and severally, having received from Lady Angela one hundred and fifty florins, and they had and received, in the presence of a notary and witnesses, as the instrument says, those one hundred and fifty florins, promising to restore them to the said Lady at any of her requests. With the passage of time, the said Bernard, obligating himself and his goods, promised to the said Luculus to free him from the aforementioned obligation, and to extract him from the obligation, and to keep him indemnified at the request and term of the said Luculus, and he did this for this reason: because the said Bernard, at his request and command, had caused the said Luculus, otherwise called Nicolaus, to obligate himself and to come to the hands of the said Bernard for the said quantity of 150 florins, and the whole sum came to the hands of the said Bernard, and nothing to the hands of the said Luculus, because the said Bernard confessed that he had received it for the purpose of practicing the art of exchange in the city of Perugia, and that the said one hundred florins had been converted to the proper utility of the said Bernard. It happens that the said Bernard, breaking faith, departed. Now it is asked whether the said Luculus can act: because the act done by the said Lady Angelina in the court of the captain, having recourse against the sureties of Bernard, practicing the art of exchange in the city of Perugia, that he is bound to give sureties, to exercise the said art well and legally, since the said Bernard in the instrument of conservation confessed that he received the said quantity for exercising the art of exchange. Moreover, it is asked in the second place, whether the auditors of exchange have jurisdiction over this, and whether the said Luculus can have recourse against the said sureties, and before the said auditors.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Because the guarantors have bound themselves for every cause to the notary receiving on behalf of all those who have an interest, they can undoubtedly be sued, since this arises from the occasion of the art of exchange. D. loca. l. quaero; in Auth. de fideius. in §. sed neque; D. de adop. l. his verbis. And it supports what is noted in D. de arbi. l. litigatores, §. quod ait. The same applies if these guarantors have subjected themselves to the jurisdiction of the auditors of exchange; they can be sued there. C. vbi causae fis. l. cum vende; de iur. om. iud. l. est receptum; in Auth. de fideius. in §. argentariorum; C. de consti. pe. l. 2, in fi. It supports what is noted in D. si quis in ius voc. non ierit, l. 1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given the aforementioned statute, which provides that inquiry may be made into acts of violence and the like, whether inquiry may be made into the rape of virgins, married women, and widows.
2. Adultery differs from rape.
3. The heirs of a deceased person who was killed may be compelled to avenge the death of the slain person.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.
† It is asked whether an inquiry may be made similarly concerning the rape of a virgin, or concerning the rape of a married woman or a widow, having regard to the aforementioned statute.

The question stands thus: whether rape constitutes violence, or whether it is one thing in itself, or another thing, or something else. And it is certain that adultery differs from rape, and they are not the same, as is noted in the Code, *De transactionibus*, in the law *Transigere, vel pacisci*. For violence is inherent in rape. Thus, therefore, the rapist is called a violator. Digest, *Ad legem Iuliam de vi publicae*, law *Qui centum*, section *Qui vacantem*; and Digest, *Ne quis eum*, law *Sed eximendi*; Code, *Ad legem Iuliam de vi*, law *Si confidis*. And therefore I say that inquiry cannot be made regarding rape, nor even if inquiry is made simultaneously regarding adultery and rape, because the beginning of the statute speaks conjunctively, and then adds and says that the power, etc. And thus the objection based on law 1, Code, *De raptu virginum*, and Digest, *De adulteriis*, law *Vim passam*, section *Praescriptione*, does not hold. Moreover, the words of the statute must be observed, as in Digest, *De poenis*, law *Fratres*. Nor can the power compel one to accuse, etc., by the rule that no one should be compelled to act or accuse against his will.

† Although some say that there is something special in homicide: so that successors may be compelled to avenge the death of the deceased on account of the benefit of the succession, which they hold. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A person who has been restored to good reputation after having been infamous may execute legal instruments.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Wherefore, since the Lord Pope restored him to good fame, and then Ser Herius, notwithstanding the condition, could draw up instruments; but before that, during the infamy, they are not valid, because to the reputation and honors which are conferred by Roman law, only the Roman prince, i.e., the Apostolic See, or the Caesar, restores, ff. de postul. l. 1. §. de qua restitutio. de re iud. c. tenere. per Inn. And because this is the truth, I do not extend myself in more prolix words, nor to those things which Bar. says in l. infamen. ff. de publ. iud. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Two species are required.
2. He who commits a continuing offense for one month, with continuation into another month, commits but one offense in number; therefore, if he does not prove the beginning of the time, i.e., the principal month, he does not prove the wrongful act.
3. Storms, rains, and illnesses excuse from legal penalties.
4. Excessive and unusual rain is counted among fortuitous events.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

There are two species of cessation: one is culpable, as when someone ceases because he is in default; the other is without fault, as when someone ceases due to an impediment of chance, which is just; otherwise, due to the nature of things, because nature ceases to produce. If it does not produce what it usually produces, in penal matters it is not said to have ceased, unless it has ceased culpably by him who wished to cease. D. 43.17.1 (Is cui); D. 9.4.1 § 1 (Si cum duobus); D. 49.15.1 (Sed et si quia) § Quaesitum; in the gloss on *deseritur*.

† Furthermore, I premise that in a continuing delict, such as in an omission, he who alleges one month with continuation into another month alleges only one delict in number. Therefore, if he does not prove the beginning of the time, i.e., the principal month, he does not prove the wrongful act, according to the gloss in *l. eum, qui in popularibus*, *de iureiurando*; nor does he prove the time to which he binds himself, *ff. de negotiis gestis*, *l. cum actum*, and *l. at qui natura*, § *Scævola*. This is because what he proves is not the time of the commission of the delict, but the time of its persistence, which time was not alleged, so that an action may be granted from that time, according to the old view.

† I further premise that storms, rains, and illnesses excuse one from legal penalties. D. de publicanis, l. Caesar. I further premise that while a suit is pending before a judge and the matter remains uncertain, the debtor is not in default. D. de usuris, l. in fideicommissi. I further premise that if a judge issues an injunction, the party is not in default in the meantime. L. mulier, D. de lege commissoria.

And that excessive and unusual rain is among fortuitous events. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. fistulas; §. frumenta. D. si quis cautio, l. 2; §. pe. Therefore, having proceeded with due deliberation and weighed the form and substance of the action, and because by the nature of the matter, for the imposition of a penalty, more than slight fault is required; for, as Cynus says in l. si quis non dicam rapere, the slightest fault is not punished criminally, but at least slight fault; and this fault is excluded on account of the unsuitability, or incongruity, of the times due to the hostility of the weather, and because the goods were not ripe on account of the rains, and on account of the custom, which sets the month of August as the term for bringing in the harvest, and on account of the judge’s command, it is without doubt that these accused are to be entirely absolved, and for the observance of custom, it is well done. C. de agris et censibus, l. domini prædiorum, lib. 11. I, Hal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The local law must be observed in prohibitions.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† Whosoever wishes to do anything subject to prohibition, such as grinding grain, baking bread, trading, doing business, importing, or exporting merchandise, whether he be an inhabitant of the territory or from Hungary, they ought to observe the local law, especially one confirmed by custom. For the law does not operate by reason of the person, but by reason of the act which he performs, ff. de offic. praet. l. 3; and therefore foreigners are included under that general term, with the exception of clerics. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A statute prohibiting sale does not prohibit exchange.
2. An oath does not bind one who is mistaken.
casus:
CASE. The point at issue is as follows. The statute of the town of Gualdo provides that no one owning a house in the said town may sell it to anyone under any pretext whatsoever; and if it is sold, the sale is void by operation of law, etc. Now, a certain Massarellus and Massutius Thomas of the said town, who owned a certain house in the said town, granted it to a certain Petrutius Cecharelli of the said town by way of exchange. And the said Petrutius, being under 25 years of age, with the consent of his curator, granted to the said Cecharelli and Massutius certain plots of land and woods worth more than half the price that the said house was worth at that time, and even more. Moreover, the said Petrutius swore to observe the terms contained in the said contract and not to violate them. Now, the aforementioned Petrutius, having reached the age of majority, seeing that he has been enormously prejudiced by the said contract, wishes to return the said house and recover his possessions. He appears before the vicar of his diocesan bishop, produces his bill of complaint, and requests to be released from the said oath, as will appear from the said bill.

Now, having examined the said statute, the said contract, and the said bill, the questions are: First, whether the said contract is void due to the said statute; or whether the said oath ought to be released, and what is the proper form of pronouncing judgment. Second, whether, if it were not void due to the said statute, it should be annulled upon proof of the said prejudice. And whether this constitutes a sufficient cause for releasing the said oath. Third, and finally, by what means or by what action should the said Petrutius subsequently proceed before the secular judge, and whether restitution in integrum is necessary.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A statute prohibiting sale does not encompass transfer by exchange. L. si. de condi. ob causam. FF. Thus says Speusippus, by that text in Speusippus, de emptione et venditione, §. nunc dicendum, ver. sed pone statutum. An oath may also be relaxed for a minor on the pretext of age: because an oath makes him an adult; but if he has been circumvented by the cunning or fraud of an adult, then in the Authentica sacramenta puberum, cunning to circumvent a minor is fraud, and therefore the oath should be relaxed: because an oath ought not to support fraud and wrongdoers. An oath not to act against the reason of a lower price is valid,

† If it has been provided for the value of knowledge, but if aid must be given to an erring minor: because the erring person does not consent. It is established as noted in l. 2, C. de rescindenda venditione; by this constitution, the oath is to be relaxed. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When the rumor or conjecture ceases, the son is not considered to have died before his father or mother.
casus: CASE. The point of the question is as follows. A certain lady Catherine, having a lawsuit with a certain lady Baria, her sister, before arbitrators, produced a petition, which I transmit to you: in which, in effect, she states that Francis, their father, died, with Matthew and Christopher, his legitimate and natural sons, brothers of the said lady Catherine, related on both sides, and of the said lady Baria on the father’s side only. And by this she wishes to conclude that the entire inheritance of the said Francis devolves upon the said lady Catherine, as heir, in place of her said brothers, as you will see contained in the petition. It was responded to by the said lady Baria, that then Francis died with no male son remaining. Now it is asked, since the death of the said sons is alleged in the said petition, although after the death of the father by the said lady Catherine, and it was denied by the said lady Baria, what is to be presumed in law regarding the death of the said sons of Francis? And whether the said lady Catherine or the said lady Baria, who denies that they died, must prove that they survived the said Francis? It is presupposed that the said brothers, during the lifetime of their father, were in distant parts, during the time of their father, that they were dead, and thus it is held and maintained today, and the said sisters held the inheritance of their said father without any mention being made of the said sons, as if they were not in existence.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If it can be proven by reputation or by certain presumptions that the sons predeceased, I will adhere to the reputation and presumptions. C. 5.30. *Si quidem*. Through the gloss and the doctors in *Qui ex liberis*, in the beginning, *De secundis tabulis*. Otherwise, I presume that nature preserved its course and did not disturb the order, and thus that the sons survived, since they were of age. *Ad legem Falcidiam*, *Haereditatum*; *Qui duos*, § *Final*, *De rebus dubiis*. Although those laws speak of another case, namely when persons are simultaneously crushed by a collapse, here the swiftness of the deaths appears; yet due to absence, it is doubtful who died first. C. *De capite minuendo*, *Nec nos*. Or it may be said that the burden lies upon him who asserts the order of death against the possessor, where the order can be proven by witnesses, as here; but where it cannot be proven by witnesses, as in a collapse or shipwreck, then the presumption is followed, which presumes concerning the fact; and this is the more correct view according to the aforementioned law *Nec nos*. Nor does the aforementioned law *Qui ex liberis* stand in the way, because there a special favor is shown to the testament, lest the substitution perish in doubt. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A statute commanding that alienations be perpetual excludes all special voluntary alienations.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† This statute, which commands that alienations be perpetual, clearly excludes every species of voluntary alienation. C. non licere habi. me. l. 1. C. de iur. fis. l. certa forma. And although the term “sale” is used strictly with regard to the penalty of the statute, as noted in Speculum de emptione et venditione, § nunc videndum, ver. sed pone statutum, nevertheless, with regard to preventing alienation on account of public utility, it is interpreted broadly, so that it also prohibits exchange, and it is not validated by an oath whenever it is principally contrary to public utility; and the bishop ought in this matter to follow municipal law and to relax the oath. C. de agris et censibus, l. quemadmodum. Especially because the minor was deceived, and in an evident matter it is presumed that he was circumvented by the sagacity of the adversary, in which case, even under the common law, he would be restored in integrum with the oath relaxed by the bishop: but because the statute forbids it, the contract is null, and the relaxation of the oath does not yet avail the defendant, for that which is contrary to the law is void, de pactis, l. iure gentium, § pactorum. And this supports the foregoing: ff. de statu liberorum, l. statu liberum a ceteris, § quintus; and in l. 2, § de usucapione pro empto. And thus I hold. And because an oath extorted by fraud or excessive malice does not render him a major, even if he was one, see l. 2, de rescindenda venditione, in the gloss. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Profits acquired from a partnership are divided per capita, that is, according to the number of persons, even if they are not of equal industry.
casus: CASE. In the name of God, Amen. The facts are stated as follows: Matthiolus Petrioli and Vitalis Petrioli, natural brothers, died; all [the descendants] came from the said Matthiolus. There remained two legitimate sons, Seruiolus and Thomas. From the said Thomas there remained four sons, namely Stephanus, Cagnutius, Herculanus, and Pace. From the said Vitalis there remained one son, namely Antonius. From the said Ventura no son or daughter remained. After the death of the said brothers, all the aforementioned sons remained in common, and they jointly shared and participated in all their goods and profits, and also in the profits of the other deceased sons, and also from the said sons. Now they come to the division of the said goods, both patrimonial and acquired. It is therefore asked, what division should be made by them of the said goods, whether per capita or per stirpes, presupposing that the goods acquired by them were acquired by their own labor, and not from the fruits of the patrimonial goods; because the latter were not sufficient to sustain their lives, let alone that there should be any surplus.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The profits of the partnership are to be divided equally among the partners per capita, that is, according to the number of persons; because this is the nature of partnership in case of doubt, so that the shares are equal. D. 17, 2, *Si non fuerunt*; J. *Responso*. Even if they were not equal in industry or strength: because partnership is a species of brotherhood, and just as things are to be divided equally among brothers, unless something else has been agreed upon, so it is among partners. D. 17, 2, *Verum*. And just as one brother naturally ought to seek the benefit of his brother, L. *Creditor*, § *Si*, D. 40, 4, so too must a partner strive for the common profit. D. 50, 17, *Si negotia*. Since therefore these men were partners in labor, they are also, by equal right, to share in the profits, and an accidental partnership is easily presumed where a natural consortium is found. And thus commerce follows the natural consortium, provided that acts indicating partnership are added. D. 17, 2, *Cum duobus*, § *Si fratres*. Wherefore it is concluded that the said division ought to be made per capita. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. By asserting that he made a will in a certain manner among his children through these words, it appears that he executed that will.
2. A daughter who receives a legacy and possesses it, which would otherwise be common to all the heirs, but is her own in full, is presumed to know the will.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† When a wise man gives counsel, it is remarkable if he advises in cases of law directly contrary to the case of the law. I said that if someone asserts that he made a testament in a certain manner among his children, that by these words it appears that he made a testament: because these words, principally and absolutely uttered, have the force of a disposition. D. de donationibus, l. ex hac scriptura. Especially among children, in whom indications of will outside myself suffice. C. de fideicommissis hereditatibus, l. si. Says my friend, those laws speak that words are uttered in a last will, otherwise if between living persons, as in c. si. de successionibus ab intestato, in the gloss which begins, videtur, quod talis. I believe, with due respect to his peace and honor, that he considered the pact, and in his response did not weigh the gloss of the same chapter which begins, quasi dicat. Nor did he note his own reason, why the monastery prevails in favor not proven by the bishop coming ab intestato in the name of the church subject to him. For this reason the monastery prevails: because it proves the testament fully, the oblation not fully, and therefore the pope does not base himself on the oblation, but on the testament, which is proven by indications of confession: which indications he calls there supports. And therefore Jo. An. on the said gloss says that the gloss opposes badly, since the same thing is intended by this chapter, which the laws say, which the gloss alleges as contrary: for they are not contrary, but concordant, because by these enunciative words a testament is made, if they have other coherences: but these words were proven of the testament: because these words, by legal interpretation, are a testament, just as, however, words which are uttered of a contract, then it would not be a testament. l. verba gesserunt. Hence in the said chapter is the case, that such confession makes one die as having made a testament, and not intestate. And so holds Innocentius and all.

†Furthermore, I stated that the daughter who receives a legacy and possesses it, which would otherwise be common to all heirs in solidum, is presumed to know the will as her own and to recognize the final judgment. This is clear from the noted authorities in *l. cum haeres*, *de lib. leg.*, D. *de trans.*; *l. non est ferendus*, C. *si cert. pet.*; *l. 1*, in the end, according to the noted authority, D. *de inof. test.*; *l. si ut proponis*, § 1; and *l. nihil interest*; and *l. filius cum sit*. But that able man says that this is true when she knows the validity of the will, otherwise if she is ignorant. On the same title, *l. mater decedens*, § *praeterea*. A woman is presumed to err in law when she does not pursue her right, but departs from the established right, for example from a complaint or the right of defending against nullity; and it is stronger here because she erred in fact: for to believe a will was made when it was not, or to believe it was made solemnly and that something was inserted which was not, for example that something was left to the daughter by way of institution, when it was left by way of legacy, is an error of fact. *l. 1*, D. *de iur. et fact. ign.* Note what he says, "error of fact." He speaks truly when alleging error; otherwise an error of fact would not be presumed, D. *de adul.*, *si adulterium cum incestu*, § 2. But here it was not alleged, hence she bases herself poorly on error of law. It is not true that it harms in quasi-profit, especially in favor of the testator, as C. *de iur. et fact. ign.*, *l. 2* and *3*. And on both sides, furthermore, it is not true that she erred in fact, in which she acknowledged good faith, to which it pertains to confess the truth and not to dispute on hairsplitting points. D. *de manum.*, *l. si fideiussor*, § *quaedam*. Furthermore, even if the writing were not solemn, nevertheless joined with the confession of the testator, which is to be referred to her sound understanding in consonance with the truth, it fully proves. D. *de cond. et dem.*, *l. si ita scripsero*. Furthermore, these enunciative words, by proving from themselves, dispose, as has been said. Thus I stated that the brothers defend in good faith, with long possession. My friend says that there is no good faith where there is error in law regarding prescription. But note, if the prescription is against the law of nations, error of law harms; but if it has natural equity, as from a non-solemn will: then because the prescription is good and equitable, and it is not said that one errs in law, but is presumed to have good faith, which arises from the law of nations, see what is noted in D. *de iur. et fact. ign.*, *l. si post divisionem*. Thus I would believe that the notary, who says it was committed to him, speaks the truth; this is not error, but good faith to believe an honest and approved man. D. *comm. div.*, *l. argentum*. And therefore my friend advised against the truth of fact and law, which could not be; wherefore the defendant ought to be absolved, and the recent consultation is void, without touching that which he says about intrusion: because he does not speak the truth, as noted in D. *de iud.*, *l. si cum dotem*, § *transgrediamur*, sol. mat. in the gloss of the *Ordinatio*, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A minor who has suffered prejudice, because he did not pay within the prescribed term, may seek restitution in integrum by way of exception.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Because the ward has suffered injury, he may be restored to his original position with respect to what he did not pay within the term; and he may invoke this full restitution as a possessor by way of exception. D. 12.1.10 pr. (nam et postea); D. 4.4.1 § si minor; and note Inst. 4.6.1 § rursus, according to Dynus. And in this manner he shall pay after the term, and the contract shall be valid. D. 4.4.1 (Emilius Largianus).

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether by these general words, and in any other manner and cause, all burdens acquired from whatever source are included, even those outside the donated property.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† Assuming, without prejudice, that it has been proven that the said donor previously accepted the fraternal inheritance, a doubt arises whether, by virtue of those general words, “and in any other manner and cause,” which are very broad words if they had not been placed in connection with the inheritances granted to the donees, they include all burdens, from whatever source incumbent upon the donor. But because they are placed in connection with the preservation of the respect due to correct speech, they do not seem capable of being understood except as referring to burdens arising from inheritances, by reason of testaments, or contracts, or delicts, or quasi-delicts, provided that they are burdens of those inheritances. Hence, the nature of the preceding matters declares the intent in the subsequent ones: see *l. si ex pluribus*, D. de solutionibus; *l. emptor*, § *Lucius*, D. de evictionibus; *l. Lucius*, § *fi*, with the gloss, D. de conditione indebiti; *l. fi*, § *idem quaesivit*, D. de transactionibus; *l. cum Aquiliana*, C. de exceptionibus; *l. si ex maiore*, D. de vino legato; *l. Aurelio*, § *Sticho extra haereditates*. Therefore, no caution is made regarding the burden; yet the burden is an hereditary one, being a dowry bequeathed: D. de actionibus et obligationibus; *l. hereditarium solutione impletum est*. Burdens that are separated are not said to be mixed: C. de hereditate acquisita; *l. si adulter*, § *fi*, with similar cases.

CASE. The doubt on which counsel is sought is this. In the territory of Fabriano, on account of war, a certain reform was made in favor of debtors who contracted debts during the war. Now it has happened that a certain Vannutius, a debtor, wishing to prove a debt contracted before the war, did so in this form: “Also, the said Vannutius lent the said 10 florins to the said Perrozo before the war began, with the commune of Fabriano and Lord Rudolph as sureties.” When questioned, the witness says that he knows this only from what he has heard, namely, that he heard that the said war had begun between the aforementioned parties, and that before the said war, the witness himself saw when the said Vannutius lent the said quantity of florins to the said Perrozo. He was not questioned further, nor does he say anything more. Now it is asked whether this witness proves the debt contracted before the war, so that the reform mentioned above does not apply in such a case, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A witness who testifies that something was done before the war must state whether he heard that it had begun, and prove that it was done before the war.
2. A witness who, when questioned, did not give a reason for his silence does not prove according to the common opinion.
body: Because I do not have time to speak at length, and the case is minor, I shall express myself in few words. If I consider correctly the proposed theme, two doubts arise from the same source, although one has more doubt than the other,

A doubt arises from l. solam, C. de testibus. For it is certain that a testimony produced alone, without other supporting evidence to corroborate the case, is of no weight. Thus, in the case at hand, the witness does not appear to have proven either a loan contract or a contract made before the war. Moreover, for another reason, he does not appear to have proven that the loan was made before the war: because whenever a certain time is of the substance of the act, that time must be proven precisely, as stated in l. cum actum, C. de probat.; l. actor, which asserts, ff. sol. matr.; l. de diuisione, cum si. Thus, in the case at hand, it is of the substance of the act to prove that the loan was made before the war; but nothing regarding the war has been proven except by hearsay: because the witness says that he heard it. He therefore says briefly. Notwithstanding these objections, I say that this witness has proven the claim produced. The witness need not be verbose, nor give eloquence beyond what is required, if he does not attend to the reason in his statement, since this is not demanded of him by the examiner. We adhere to the statement without any other reason, as in extra, de re iudicata, c. sicut nobis. This is notably stated by the gloss in the aforementioned l. solam. To the contrary: no one is presumed to be forgetful of eternal salvation. 1 q. 6, c. scimus. Speusius places this in tit. de testibus, § 1, ver.

† Moreover, it is the common opinion of all that a witness who is not asked does not give a reason, as stated in the aforementioned law *Solam* and in the law *Testium* in the title *De iure fisci*; in the law *In fraudem* in the title *De iure iurando*; in the law *Iusiurandum*, section *Qui ius*, in the title *De non obli. operis novi*; and in the law *De pupillo*, section *Qui opus*. And if it is said that the aforementioned Vanus applies when a witness gives no reason at all, but not when he gives one, albeit less suitable, as was the case here, the witness says that he heard it said. Certainly, if one carefully considers what this witness said here, he principally asserts two things: nor is one the reason for the other, but each statement was made on its own. It is clear that he said he had [knowledge] in the plural, and thus intended to say several things, and not one. Moreover, between the first statement and the second, he admits a conjunction, and it is of the nature of such a conjunction to join diverse things, not to indicate them by way of reasoning. Furthermore, it is commonly said that the consequence follows, but does not proceed; otherwise, the antecedent would be produced in existence before the consequent, and the effect before the cause, because the cause is contrary to nature and does not obstruct, as stated in the law *De divisione* and the other authorities cited above for the contrary. Because, according to the intention of the one asserting, the precise time is proven. For if it was not necessary to prove, for the exclusion of the aforementioned reformation, that the loan was contracted at a certain and limited time, it suffices that it was contracted at any time before the war; it is not required that one year be distinguished from another, or one month from another, or one day from another, and it is required, as can be seen in cases of contrary laws, to admit that the precise month or day must be proven. For the fruits of the last year of a dissolved marriage are divided pro rata temporis; it is necessary to know at what time the marriage was dissolved, because the division of fruits is made according to the proportion of time, and thus before the division or after the division; so that we may know whether the child was born free. It must be known whether, at the time of the deposit of the child, it was free by law, as stated in the law *Matrem*. Thus it is in the law *Eum actum* in the title *De negotiis gestis*: wherever it is a matter of proving a precise time, but as I said, in the case proposed, the act in question does not have effect if more time is involved in one instance than in another, for example, that it was before the war by a thousand years. I admit that he should have done so, because then it seems to exclude that it was not at other times. But he acts cautiously, not binding himself, but stating generally that the general statement of the witness correctly responded, and therefore does not prove less, since he was not further questioned without cause about the reasons for his knowledge, as I said above. The same as in the preceding opinion.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. The loan was proven by the recitation of the cause of his vision, as in C. de testibus, l. testamentum; but the time was not proven, because an ignorant person does not prove, [although] the restrictive dictum nevertheless shows: because he did not know by truth when there was war, and therefore he cannot prove that it was before the war, when he proves that it was before that time in which he heard it said that there was war, because, however, when he heard it is not explained. The proof of the time remains confused, because it is not valid as to a certain proven time; but he proves the fact, as if he were to say, I saw the loan being made, but I do not remember the time: as noted in In. extra de accusatione, c. qualiter.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A renunciation, when made without cause, is understood to be a donation, and therefore, if it is inofficious, a complaint has place.
2. A son as heir can come against the deed of the father by reason of fraud committed.
3. A renunciation restricted by no limits relates to all things.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† A renunciation made without cause is understood to be a donation, as in ff. de iu. l. si quis absente, and ff. qui. mo. pi. vel hypo. l. 1. §. 1, ff. de pac. l. tale pactum, ff. de prob. l. procula. And therefore, if the time periods permit, a complaint of an inofficious donation also has place, C. de inoffi. testamen. in auth. vnde si parens; and those time limits do not run against minors by operation of law, C. in qui. cau. in inte. re. non est necess. l. fi. Therefore, the lady Christophora has a right in this, provided that she is universal heir: for if she should repudiate the paternal inheritance, she could not sue for the legitime, because the legitime from the inheritance itself is not owed to one who repudiates the inheritance, although in a certain case this may be found, ff. de bon. li. l. si partis, l. si libertus patrono. §. 1.

† And if it is said, if she is the heir of her father, how can she come against the deed of the father? I answer: by reason of the fraud committed against the heir himself, C. si in frau. patroni. l. 1. If, however, there was nothing else in the father's estate than that which was donated, it is not necessary that the other enter upon the father's inheritance, except that she claim the legitime, which alone belongs to her, said auth. vnde si parens. However, if the said lady Christophora is the father's heir, she is bound for the dowry provided by her brother, who endowed the sister—namely the lady Antonia—in the name of the common father; for by this very fact it is seen to have been turned to the father's account, ff. de in rem ve. l. et ideo. §. fi. with l. se., provided however that the brother remits to her the stipulation conferring the right of restitution, de le. 3. l. vxorem. §. pater. Moreover, the natural legitime is understood after debts have been deducted, and consequently after the said debt of the dowry has been deducted, l. Papi. in §. in quarta, ff. inoffi. test. Whence, if beyond debts let us suppose there are 12 hundredweights, and there are brothers, and the said sister, the sister's share for her legitime is one uncia, C. de inoffi. test. auth. nouissima; because it is a fourth of a third, namely one out of four according to the quaternary number of the children. If restitution is sought by a minor against a judgment rendered in a complaint, she ought to prove that she is a minor, and that she has unjustly succumbed, de min. l. minor autem magistratus. For if the judgment is unjust, she is not said to be injured, even though she succumbed, ff. de au. et arg. leg. l. Titiae amicae.

† A general renunciation restricted by no limits relates to all things, ff. de pac. l. emptor. §. fi.; it is otherwise if it has terms of restriction, ff. de so. l. si ex pluribus, C. de exce. l. si ex maiore, C. de trans. l. si de certa. This renunciation of ours is very general. A dowry given for a daughter by the mother during the subsistence of the marriage is presumed to be from the husband's property, except to the extent that she herself possessed paraphernal property, which must be examined by the judge, de do. inter virum. l. quintus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Alienated on the occasion of paying fines and condemnations are imputed to the legitime and the Trebellian portion.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The property alienated by the aforementioned Marcutio on the occasion of paying the ban and condemnations is imputed to the legitime and the trebellianic portion of the said Marcutio, as is noted in the Digest, under the Trebellianic portion, in the law *Marcellus*, § *res quam*, and in the Authenticum, on restitution and that which produces, § *ob rem*. Although he could not alienate it during the lifetime of his husband, because it belonged to the husband, nevertheless, since the husband first succeeded to it, the alienations are confirmed. Digest, on usucaption, law *cum*, word *praedium*; and Digest, on pledges and actions, law *rem alienam*. Therefore, let those be cited who wish to be heirs of Marcutio, so that they may come to restore the inheritance to the substitute in the testament of Lord John. And if no one appears, let the heir have the inheritance as restored in word, and then let the writ of possession be sought from the edict of the Divine Hadrian. Thus, Code, under the Trebellianic portion, law *pe*; Code, on conditions, law *fina*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether grandchildren are included in the substitution by the term "son."
casus: CASE. The point, or case, is as follows: Agnesa had a certain uterine brother named Ventura, who Ventura had a son named Andrea, who Andrea had a son named Vannutius, who Vannutius had a son named John. This Agnesa, coming to death, made a testament, in which testament she instituted her husband as universal heir, namely for his lifetime. After the death of her said husband, she substituted for herself the aforementioned Ventura and Andrea, son of the said Ventura, if he should be living at the time of the death of her said husband; and if he should not be living, she substituted for the said husband the legitimate sons of the said Andrea. Finally, this being done, the said Agnesa dies, and the inheritance was accepted by her said husband. Finally, this husband, heir instituted by the said Agnesa, wishing to avoid the vow of capturing death, came to an agreement and transaction with the said Ventura, who was substituted to him in the first place, namely that the said Ventura remitted to him all the right which he had in the inheritance of the said Agnesa, and bound himself and his heirs not to come against the said transaction under a penalty of a thousand. And this transaction was entered into for a quantity three times less than the value of the said inheritance of Agnesa. Finally, it happened that, during the lifetime of the said husband, heir instituted by the said Agnesa, by the force of his illness, first the said Andrea, the same son of the said Ventura and substituted to the said husband, dies. Then the said Ventura dies, who Ventura instituted the aforementioned Vannutius, his nephew, as universal heir, and who was substituted in the third place. With the lapse of time, the aforementioned husband of the said Agnesa, who was heir instituted for his lifetime by the said Agnesa, dies. Now the aforementioned Vannutius, the same one substituted in the third place to the aforementioned husband, seeing himself bound not to accept the said inheritance of the said Agnesa by virtue of the said transaction made by the aforementioned Ventura, his first grandfather, who had instituted him universal heir, accepted the inheritance of the aforementioned Agnesa. Now the aforementioned John comes and wishes to claim the said inheritance from the heirs of the said husband. It is opposed to him that he cannot claim it, because he was not substituted. It is explained on behalf of the said John that rather he was substituted in this manner, namely that the said Agnesa first substituted Ventura, brother of the testatrix, secondly substituted Andrea, son of the said Ventura, and if such should not survive, she substituted the sons of Andrea. Now he says, I am the son of the said Andrea, and thus the grandson of the said Andrea, and by the appellation of sons, grandsons are comprehended; I ought to be admitted by the substitution made of the sons of the said Andrea, since I am a grandson through the son of the said Andrea. Secondly, it is objected to him that he cannot claim the inheritance of the said Agnesa, because he did not fulfill the condition appended in the testament, which condition was in giving. It is replied on behalf of the said John that, since he is a minor and an infant, he ought to be restored against the omission of fulfilling the condition. Now it is asked, whether the said John can claim the aforementioned inheritance by virtue of the said substitution made of the sons of the said Andrea, notwithstanding the transaction made by the said Ventura with the said husband; and also whether he can claim it without prejudice to the said Vannutius, his father and universal heir of the said Ventura, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain

† The great doctors say that Andreas de Pisis and many others hold that in substitutions the grandson is not included under the name of son, just as in institutions the grandson is not included under the name of son. L. Gallus, in the beginning, and § 1, On Free and Posthumous Children. Bartolus says the contrary in L. Liberorum, On the Signification of Words, by means of L. Lucius, On the Institution of Heirs. And this opinion is true, since descendants are understood to extend to infinity, all seem to be substituted, which is false; it does not obstruct. L. Lucius: because it is understood to refer to children, i.e., of the first degree. C. ad Trebellianum, L. Iubemus, at the end. And this is the truth, unless conjectures reveal the breadth of the will: for example, because he called the grandson a son. Moreover, the question asks about a collateral grandson, indeed about a grandson, nay, about a posthumous child: and therefore I think he is not included in the substitution by the force of the appellative name. D. De his qui sui iuris, L. Filium diffinimus; D. De legatis 1, L. Si filiabus; D. De testamento tutorum, L. Si quis ita. But there is doubt whether by the force of the plural number, and this in such a way that the plural number operates something. D. Ad Trebellianum, L. Si; and D. De secundis nuptiis, L. Fundus qui locatus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether sureties given generally for a certain trade, yet not equipped for that trade, are liable for delicts committed outside that trade.
2. What the term "in a certain respect" signifies.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The generality of words often creates peril. C. de do. promis. l. si. Yet sometimes it is restricted to what was contemplated. ff. de transac. l. Aquiliana. ff. de pac. l. tres fratres. ff. de testa. tu. l. si quis ita. ff. de sol. l. si ex pluribus. And it matters greatly between a necessary obligation, which is strictly interpreted, even if expressed in the broadest terms, by restricting it to the nature of the necessity. ff. de dam. insec. l. inter quos. §. et quod in stipulatio. and a voluntary promise, which has no restrictive limits. ff. de pac. l. emp. §. si. and l. si. C. quae res pi. ob. pos. l. si. de lega. Moreover, sometimes the species follows the genus and has the effect of narrowing it. ff. de verb. sig. l. si cum fundum. Sometimes the species proceeds; then it follows the genus, and they are held expansively, unless a restrictive reason applies equally to both the genus and the species. ff. de acque poss. l. si is, qui animo. ff. de pac. l. quod dictum. Since, therefore, the surety should not have been given except on account of the art of exchange: because an extraneous cause is not contained under this, if he had written the exception of the estates in the exchange books, whether the sureties would be bound: certainly not at all. Hence, although the language is profound, it is restricted, or rather more correctly explained by the cause. Moreover, this is understood to have been done, which is accustomed to be done. C. de fideius. l. si. And although it is contained in the exchange book, not from the book, but from the cause, is the obligation to be considered, as C. si cer. pet. l. eo quod a multis. Therefore, reason informs and narrows the pact. Furthermore, here the genus is openly restricted, where it says, according to the form of the ordinances of the said art.

† For the word "according to," after the species, has the nature of demonstration. L. eum, qui. §. Iul. de consti. pe. But after the genus, it has the nature of limitation, de verbo. sign. c. Abbate. cum sim. For what is done outside the camporium does not pertain to the campsores. ff. de trib. l. 1. §. si plures. and l. fi. de iur. om. iud. And therefore, the said sureties cannot be sued for debts not arising from the camporium. ff. de annuis leg. l. fin. It appears, therefore, that the aforementioned sureties are not bound for the said cloths, having seen the aforementioned instrument.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A cousin, whether maternal or paternal, is a competent witness.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Whether a cousin or a paternal cousin is a suitable witness: there is no doubt, unless some other reason were present, as in no. C. de testi. l. eos. per gl. et doc. For he is a person of full legal capacity by presumption of law, de probatio. c. ab ea parte. and the amount is small. And therefore the judge who administered the oath did what he ought to have done. l. in bonae fidei. and l. admonendi. for where a small prejudice is at issue, lighter proofs suffice. And this is held by Nic. de Mat. not only in the case of a cousin, but also in the case of a fleshly relative living and conducting business independently. C. de proba. l. sciant cuncti. and although it was discretionary for the first judge, nevertheless he used his discretion correctly, because he ought to have done so: on account of the degree of kinship. The only requirement of solemnity is that the person be otherwise worthy of belief. This is the case in l. lege Iul. ff. de testi. by contrary reasoning, for although he is not precisely compelled in a criminal or civil case: nevertheless if he testifies, his testimony is valid; otherwise the law would not say, "they are not to be compelled": but it would say, "they are to be compelled," and this is a good argument a contrario sensu. ff. de testa. l. qui testamento. §. mulier. By this it is expressly stated to the contrary de pręsumc. literas. The gloss of the said law l. Iul. is not an objection, because it speaks of one who is unwilling, whose statement is not valid either for or against, neither in a civil case nor in a criminal case. And he is called unwilling when, having been summoned, he alleges his privilege: but if he does not allege it, he is called voluntary, as expressly noted. ff. de his, qui. u indig. l. post legatum. §. is no. and de excu. tut. c. voluntaria. and it is clearly apparent. ff. de iudi. l. 2. in prin. cum si. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 0. The borrower is not liable for accidental loss, unless some fault on his part has occurred.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The case of fortuitous event does not arise, nor does it apply under the common law, i.e., by the nature of the contract, as in D. de comm. l. si ut certo, § nunc videndum; and D. de re iudicata l. contractus. Nor does any agreement speak of a fortuitous event: D. si quis cautio l. sed et si quia, § quaesitum; C. de comm. l. 1. Therefore, the goods burned, which belonged to the said lady and were in the said house, were burned at the risk of the said lady, unless it is proven that some fault of the said Nicholas, or of those whose services he was then using, intervened in the fire: D. quod vi aut clam l. si alius, § est et alia; C. ad leg. Aquil. l. 1; D. ad leg. Aquil. l. si servus servum, § si fornicarius; de incendio, ruina et naufragio l. qui aedes, existing in the house of the said lady, the lessor. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A legacy made to someone for his own use, if he did not devote it to that use, ought to be converted to other uses.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The intention of the testator is to be ascertained from the general intention, purified by the special provision, which prevails over a contrary determination.
