† And therefore, from the general head, it is said that proper legacies, which do not serve their proper uses, are converted to other uses, On usufruct, law 1, Legatum; Digest, On the administration of civic things, by law Legatum; and in the decretal Quia contingit, On religious things. Although the legatee is a private person, the general intention of the legatee is not removed; therefore, what the brothers do not have, the letter of the testator should nevertheless have, with the cooperation of the bishop; because for the light of his conscience he should not burden himself, but should expend it on pious uses. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a sister of the full blood or a cousin is instituted as heir, and the mother is passed over, the will is void.
2. If the passed-over mother remains silent for many years, the will is valid with respect to equity, if the bonorum possessio secundum tabulas is sought therefrom.
casus:
CNISIVS. The fact, on which counsel is sought, is as follows. A certain man named Cirisciolus had two sons, namely Mannutius and Roctius. Roctius died before the death of the said Cirisciolus, with his daughter Andreola surviving him. Afterwards, this Cirisciolus made a will, and instituted the said Mannutius, his son, as his heir, and provided a dowry for the said Andreola, his granddaughter, and then died. Finally, the said Mannutius died intestate, with Massarello and Paulutio, his sons, surviving him. Then this Andreola remained a widow, and returned to the house of the said Paulutio. Lastly, this Paulutio made a will, and instituted as his universal heirs the said Lady Joan, his full sister, and the said Lady Andreola, his cousin sister, in equal shares, without any mention being made of his living mother. And at the end of the said will of Paulutio was appended that customary clause, namely, that if it were not valid by the law of wills, he wished it to be valid by the law of codicils. And he died. After the death of the said Paulutio, the said Lady Joan and Lady Andreola stood together, and enjoyed the usufruct, and possessed for two years, or thereabouts, the hereditary goods of the said Paulutio. Afterwards, Mactiotius took the said Lady Andreola as his wife, and Fran., son of the said Mactiotius, took the said Lady Joan as his wife. And the said Mactiotius, as head of the household, possessed, held, and collected the said inheritance of the said Paulutio, and the goods of the said inheritance; and the said Andreola together with the said Joan held and possessed until the death of the said Andreola, and still the said Mactiotius thus possesses. And this Lady Andreola died, with her son Massarello surviving her, and afterwards the said Mactiotius, as father and legitimate administrator of the said Massarello, his son, and of the son and heirs of the said Andreola, his mother, heir of the said Paulutio, for one half, and the said Lady Joan, with the presence of her husband and other blood relatives, heir of the said Paulutio for the other half, made a certain release to a certain man named Mactuitius for 60 lire of the currency of the region.

It is now asked, first, whether by the things said above the inheritance of the said Paulutio has been entered upon, or whether it appears to have been entered upon by the said Andreola, and consequently by her heirs; secondly, whether the said will is invalidated in whole or in part, and for what share, since the said mother lived after the death of her son, the said Paulutio, for six years and more, and said nothing about the said inheritance of her son; thirdly, whether the heirs of the said Andreola succeed in anything in the said inheritance by the law of codicils; and lastly, whether the release made by the said Lady Joan, heir of the said Paulutio for one half, and by the said Mactiotius, father and legitimate administrator of the said Massarello, his son, and heir of the said Andreola, heir of the said Paulutio for the other half, has any effect on the case, since it was made after the death of the said Andreola, heir of the said Paulutio; and whether time runs in any respect for the said Massarello, since the said Lady Joan entered upon and took possession of the said inheritance last year by order of the judge of the communal court of Todi, without anyone being cited or required.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If a brother institutes his full sister and his cousin as heirs, passing over his mother, the will is today void by operation of law. But formerly, under the old law, it had some validity; however, a complaint was granted to the mother, as stated in the Institutes, *De inofficioso testamento*, § *Mater*, and in § *Aliud quoque capitulum* of the Authenticum *Ut cum de appellatione cognoscatur*, and in the Authenticum *De hæredibus et falsis*, § *Exhæreditatos*, column 1.

But if the mother survived for several years and did not declare the will null on grounds of equity—namely, if possession of the goods is sought according to the tablets, as stated in the law *Filio praeterito* from the title *De iniusto testamento*—for it is confirmed by praetorian law; but first it must be confirmed by civil law, so that the inheritance may be entered upon from it. And it is certain that it is not confirmed by the strict letter of the law, but by equity written in the responses of the jurists, which are part of civil law, and thus it appears to be confirmed; hence, by equity, such a will is not null. Moreover, the mother raises an objection after several years, and did not declare it null, as noted in the Code, title *De coronis*, law *Post*. This person suffered from the subtleties of the law, for when a will is invalid because a *sui heredes* (necessary heir) is passed over, it never recovers validity under civil law, but possession of the goods according to the tablets is necessary, as stated in the law *Posthumus* from the title *De iniusto testamento*, and in the law *Si impubes*, section *Si autem*. But if it is invalid due to the passing over of the mother, it seems to recover validity by the equity of civil law, because the mother is deemed to have tacitly approved it by not disapproving it. And the reason for the difference between a *sui heredes* and a mother is that a passed-over *sui heredes* is by the very law a necessary heir under civil law, as stated in the law *In suis* from the title *De liberis et posthumis*. And therefore another cannot be an heir under civil law, as stated in the law *In suis* from the title *De liberis et posthumis*, and therefore another cannot be an heir under civil law, as stated in the law *Quod contractus*, section *Vni duo*, from the title *De regulis iuris*, because a *sui heredes* excludes all others by the force of his status as *sui* under civil law, as stated in the Code, title *Unde liberi*, law *Qui sepraesens*, according to Jacobus and Cynus, and commonly by all doctors. But a mother is not a *sui heredes* by law, and therefore she does not obstruct another from succeeding under civil law, according to the theory of the doctors in the aforementioned law *Qui se praesens*. Moreover, in the case of a mother, the right to declare it null takes the place of the complaint (*querela*); hence it is not null unless it is declared null by the mother herself. But here it was not declared null, but remained silent, and she seems to have accommodated her consent. Digest, title *De probationibus*, law *Procula*. Another opinion is that in these cases, the instituted heir, when the observance of the legal portion is lacking, does not succeed except through possession of the goods, as noted in the Code, title *Unde legitimi*, law *Certum*. But I answer that this argument concludes according to the strict letter, not according to equity, as argued in the Digest, title *De heredibus instituendis*, law *Qui solvendo non erat duos Appolonios*. In conclusion, I say that if the objection of the gloss is true, both sisters are heirs for one-half each; but if the opinion of the others is true, the full-blood sister would be heir in total, but would be bound to restore to the cousin sister one-half part by virtue of the fideicommissum, for she does not deduct the quarter before the part, because it does not appear that she is burdened except by one-half, and thus the Trebellian rule has no place. And these points are proven by the fact that the noted doctors go beyond the gloss in the constitution *Ex causa*. And this seems to be the truth itself.

CASE. A certain John and Francis of Spoleto sold certain properties to a certain Conrad for the price and sum of 130 florins, as appears from a public instrument, etc. With the passage of time, the said sellers stated that the contract celebrated in the form of a sale was simulated, and made in simulation in place of a pledge, saying that at the time of the contract, and before the contract, it was agreed between them that the said properties sold were in place of a pledge, and whenever the aforementioned price was returned to the said buyer Conrad, Conrad would return and restore the said properties sold. And thus the said John and Francis, the aforementioned sellers, allege this in their petition before the ecclesiastical judge, requesting that the fruits perceived in the meantime be offset against the amount of the price. And to prove their intention, they introduce witnesses, who testify that when the aforementioned sellers were obligated to the said Conrad in a certain quantity of grain, they brought the aforementioned sellers and buyer to an agreement, that for the said grain they should receive 130 gold florins, and that for the said sum of 130 gold florins a certain contract of purchase should be celebrated, which in truth should be a pledge, which came into the contract, that if within a hundred [days/terms] he returned the said price to the said buyer, the said buyer would be bound to return and restore the said properties sold. And they say that they went to celebrate the said contract, and immediately afterwards returned, and said that they had celebrated the said contract in the form of a sale, although in truth it was a pledge. However, the aforementioned witnesses say and assert that they were not present at the contract. Now the question arises on two points: first, since the party in the petition alleges a contract between them, that whenever the price was returned, the properties should be restored, and the witnesses say that within the said term then declared between the parties it was agreed; secondly, since the witnesses do not testify about the time of the contract, but rather assert that they were not present at the time the contract was celebrated, but say that when it was agreed that it should be a pledge, whether the intention of the plaintiffs is sufficiently proven, given that a pure and simple contract of sale, freely celebrated, etc., is found.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a certain quality is required, it is not valid unless it has been proven.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† In the petition, the quality of fraud is alleged. And since it is not proven that this quality was committed in fraud of usury, except by one witness, therefore it is not proven, because he bound himself to the said [requirement]. L. Praetor, § Docere, D. De vi bonorum raptorum. And this quality confers jurisdiction upon the bishop, for a pledge without usury does not pertain to the bishop. There is usury when the matter concerns the gaining of fruits; otherwise there is not, even if it were valid that more is being claimed. D. De emptione et venditione; C. Ad nostram, De pignoribus; C. Illo vos. This substantial difference appears when one said he did not believe that it was in fraud of usury, unless the pledge included usury of the aforementioned price, so as to be usurious; for a pledge does not include usury, just as a hypothec does not. And even if it were agreed that it was a pledge, it does not follow that it was a loan contract. And this is expressly stated by Innocentius, De foro competenti, C. Cum sit generale, in the gloss beginning "Not. captores." It is necessary, however, that always, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When an oath contains an implied condition, if that condition has not been fulfilled, absolution from such oath is not necessary.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Oath

† sometimes it has a tacit condition, as in this case, if the award was equal according to the arbitrator’s judgment, as in D. de operis liberti, l. si libertus. And thus, in such a case, absolution from the oath is not necessary, if the award is so unjust that a petition for reduction may be made. D. pro socio, l. unde si membra; D. de iniuriis, c. Quintavallis. Where it is said that a lawful oath does not refer to an unlawful command. And this supports what is noted in D. de regulis iuris, l. non videtur, § qui iussu. And by this it appears at first sight that the bishop cannot intervene by reason of the oath, since this case was not sworn to; otherwise bishops could assume all temporal jurisdiction by reason of the oath, which is absurd. On the contrary, it is argued: just as it is lawful for the fortunate party to seek reduction, so too it is lawful for Catulius to seek a declaration that the fortunate party is an perjurer, because the award is equitable. And this matter will be prejudicial, greater, and pertaining to the Church by reason of the oath, which jurisdiction cannot be preempted or impeded by a secular judge, for the jurisdiction of blessed Peter is greater than that of the secular judge by reason of spirituality. And therefore the bishop, having summarily cognized and justified the award before himself, may command the secular judge not to hear the one coming against his own proper oath; but the executor ought not to issue an injunction. C. fin. de foro competenti, lib. 6. Because this oath was not pure, but with a tacit condition, it is therefore necessary that the case be terminated before the bishop, where it is requested that it be pronounced that the fortunate party comes against his own oath, and that an injunction be issued, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. No one is compelled to bear burdens, except in proportion to his hereditary share, when the inheritance has been purely conferred upon several persons, or has become pure by the fulfillment of a condition.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† When an inheritance has been purely conferred upon several persons, or has become pure by the fulfillment of a condition, one is not compelled to bear the burdens except in proportion to his hereditary share. C. de haeredi. l. pro haereditatum. And the contrary does not obtain from ff. de l. fal. l. qui fundum. §. si tu ex parte, because there the inheritance had not been conferred upon all. From this it is concluded that Do. Ioanna is not bound except in proportion to her hereditary share, on the ground that the existence of the condition of substitution was either proved or confessed. It remains to consider the condition inserted in the legacy of alimony, the existence of which has not been proved, nor is the case impeding it proved; and therefore alimony is due in no part, as is fully read and noted in C. de leg. l. 1 and de conditio. et demonstra. l. illis libertis. And by this it is unnecessary to treat of the ritual of the procedure, since the substance of the obligation is entirely lacking.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A donation made is not revoked, even if the donee dies, and his inheritance devolves to strangers.
2. Nor is it revoked by the subsequent insanity of the notary who was requested.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

Having examined the donation made by Santella to her brother of paternal and maternal goods, through her own notary, there is no doubt that effect must be given to the said donation, and that it cannot be revoked, even though the said brother has died and his inheritance has passed to strangers, as in C. de donat. l. si auia vestra. And it suffices that the notary was of sound mind at the time,

† which he wrote: although he later became insane or mad, since the death of the notary does not prejudice the matter, neither does madness; this is most certainly true, as is stated in the gloss on the chapter *Ut officium*, *De haereticis*, Book 6.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the instituted heir dies before the testator, who comes to the inheritance: the substitute, or those coming intestate?
2. A genus differs from a universitas, for a genus is preserved in a single species, whereas a universitas is not.
3. A question of fact, for example, whether a priest ought to have the fruits of a certain altar, etc.
4. Goods for the utility of an altar cannot be alienated, otherwise for necessity.
5. The closer degree is admitted to present [a candidate].
6. Acquisitions made after the testament come into direct substitution.
7. Whether one renouncing succession is understood to have renounced the legitime.
8. The goods of a testator who did not restore them to the altar: does the substitute fall from the legacy?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Regarding the question of who is the presumptive heir of the said Butius, son of the testator, during the lifetime of Butius after the death of his mother Tucta—whether it is the altar to which substitution was made, or those who would come to him intestate—doubt is not without merit, and it appears that those who would otherwise come intestate succeed, for several reasons.

First, because whenever institution and substitution fail, we are in a case of caducity, and those who would come intestate enter, as stated in C. de caducis tollendis, l. 1, § cum triplici, and § quod pro secundo. For the path of intestacy is opened by the defect of the testate cause. C. de fideicommissis, l. eam, quam. But here, in the testament, the universal heir predeceases, therefore the entire right of the testator is dissolved. ff. de re iudicata, l. si nemo. Namely, because what is left in a testament has a tacit condition, if the inheritance is taken from the testament. ff. de legatis 1, l. haec verba. Therefore, they will not be valid otherwise. ff. quando dies legatorum cedat, l. haeredis aditio.

Second, because every fideicommissary substitution is sustained under an institution, but this one is fideicommissary, as is proven; therefore, the caducity of the institution induces the caducity of the substitution. That it is fideicommissary is proven thus: a substitution made by common words in certain things is to be considered fideicommissary. l. cogi, § et generaliter, ad Trebellianum, and there by Dynus. But this substitution regarding the altar was made concerning certain things, because in immovable property, and by common, indiscriminate, and ambiguous words, because by the word "be of the altar," which can be understood in direct right and in fideicommissary right; therefore, added to certain things, it savors of a fideicommissum, and consequently does not exclude intestacy, as ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. cohaeredi, § cum filiae. And this is beneficial, because in a fideicommissary substitution, movables do not come; because the testator wished, and it is noted in a similar case that fruits are to be separated, as l. precibus, and in l. Centurio.

Third reason, because to say the contrary is to do violence to the will of the testator, who decreed that only immovable goods should come in the substitution; therefore, he wished to substitute directly; because then it would be drawn to the whole. de vulgari substitutione, l. cohaeredi, § fin.

Fourth reason, because the testator wished to substitute to his mother after the inheritance was accepted; for he preferred her to the altar, although every such oblique substitution is excepted from pupillary and exemplar substitutions, which by their nature require the acceptance of the inheritance, de vulgari substitutione, l. moribundus, and l. verbis civilibus, and ff. de captivis et postliminio reversis, l. quod si filius.

Fifth reason, because according to the purity of conscience, it must be done formally to the extent that the testator ordered, as ff. de verbis significandis, l. verbis legatorum.

Sixth reason, because we should not in doubt exclude the rights of blood by an interpretative, guessed, and incongruous sense. C. quoniam et quibus quibus pars debetur, l. 1. C. de codicillis, l. fin. cum si, and in Auth. de testamentis imperfectis, in principio. For if the testator does not exclude, neither should we, nor can we, exclude. as l. cum quidam, de liberis et posthumis. Because exclusions are odious and of strict law, as l. maximum vitium.

Seventh and last reason, because immovables were inserted for the purpose of diminishing the maternal obligation, and every obligation refers to a fideicommissary substitution, because a direct one does not pass to the rules of obligations, but by the right of entering. ff. ad legem Falcidiam, l. in ratione, § quod vulgo. Therefore, whether we inspect the nature of the words, the mind of the testator, or the mind of the law, it appears that the altar was substituted by fideicommissum in the immovable goods, and not directly in the entire breadth of the inheritance. ff. de verbis significandis, l. momentum. ff. de peculio, l. quam Tuberonis, § 1. l. in peculio. de re iudicata, l. a Divio Pio. For no substitution in which rights and actions do not come is one of rights and actions, but only of the bodies of immovable things; therefore, it is no longer direct. It does not operate more than if another heir were instituted, who, if no one were instituted prior, no. in l. in his verbis, de haeredibus instituendis. But if they said thus, "all my immovable goods be Peter's," no one says Peter is instituted heir; because the words do not sound this, nor does jurisprudence dictate it; therefore, much less with another heir preferred, and this reason seems to demonstrate conclusively for this part.

On the contrary, it is argued by example and proven by reasons that the said substitution is to be considered direct, and by the nature of the direct, it is drawn to all goods, and suffers neither the Falcidian deduction nor any other diminution. Suppose the testator had said, "whenever my mother dies, my immovable goods be John's," the mother dies before the testator, and thus the inheritance is not accepted; unless we say that the vulgar substitution has place, we corrupt the signification of the adverb "whenever," which is said whether before the inheritance is accepted or after, and therefore in this concise phrase the vulgar is included, as noted in l. precibus. For in the place of a caducous institution, a non-caducous substitution is supplied, as d. § pro secundo. For this reason he substituted, so that the goods do not remain in a case of caducity. Nor is this absurd, that a particular direct is drawn to a total direct. d. l. cohaeredi, l. fin., and l. 1, § si ex fundo, with similar. And although the testator here did not say "whenever she dies," it is understood, de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. quibus diebus, § quidam Titio. C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. antepenultima.

Furthermore, here the testator used the word "be" (sint), which is a word signifying direct dominion; therefore, it is direct. l. 2, § in locum, ff. de religione, l. 2, § 3, qui in perpetuum, si ager vectigalis vel emphyteuticus, and d. l. his verbis.

Third reason, which touches the heart of this question, is because the testator says thus: "a laquale ditta donna, quando morisse, sustituisse vniuersale herede lo dit to altare de §. Iacobo, s. melodicto stabole feci cifra, sicut est" [from which said woman, when she died, I substituted universal heir the said altar of St. James, or the aforementioned stable, I made a cipher, as it is], from which uncertainty arises, whether he says, i.e., whether it is a simple period, or a period by conjunction. But I argue that it does not have the figure of the letter, that it is not to be cared for what it says, but what it ought to say verisimilarly, and certainly, since the testator said, "I substitute universal heir," no one doubts that it ought to be extended to all things in doubt, saving the maternal right.

For there is a difference between the universal and the genus: for the genus is preserved in one species of the universality, not as is stated in l. sicut. I imagine the thought of this deceased person to be that he wished for the stable goods to come precisely to the altar, and for certain other goods insofar as they existed, arg. ff. de petitione hereditatis, l. vtrum, there I think, and c. de legatis 1, l. si seruus plurium, §. fin., and l. cum pater, §. cum imperfecta, de legatis 3. Where therefore the eye does not certify, let the intellect certify. l. 1, ff. de his quae in testamento delentur. For this reason the testator deducted movable goods, because he preferred the mother in the power of distributing movables; however, where the mother is not present, the reason for the deduction ceases, and the writing encompasses everything, arg. ff. ad Trebellianum, l. Titius rogatus; arg. ff. de hereditate instituenda, l. si quis ita fuerit institutus excepto fundo. Moreover, the word "heir" is a civil term, and most direct in voice, signification, and power. d. l. his verbis; and ff. de vulgaribus substitutionibus, l. verbis civilibus; and note inst. de pupillaribus substitutionibus, §. qua ratione. Provided that the case and time allow the direct sense with the effect of substitution, as is the case in our situation, and an unintelligible cipher does not vitiate that which is otherwise understood; for a cipher is properly that which is no part of speech, i.e., neither a noun nor a verb, de bonis possessionibus, l. sed cum patrono, §. notis. From these things it appears most evidently that the said substitution is drawn to the vulgar, and encompasses all things, and this is the very truth. Behold, therefore, the second degree has become the first due to the contingent case in the person of the said Lady through the fideicommissary and substitution, with the restrictive terms removed due to the defect of the final restrictive cause; this would result in the altar obtaining it in effect, but it is not necessary to inquire into this here, because, as I said, the substitution is direct. Now let us proceed further and see

† Concerning the altar and its goods. It must be considered that whether this is called the dowry of the altar or the prebend of the altar, the risk pertains to the curator or priest of the altar. For whether it is a dowry, which is the price for the spouse of the altar, or a prebend annexed to the altar, it ought not to be severed, as in c. maioribus de prebendis. And this holds if this priest has the altar in title, because he is instituted by his superior as perpetual curator of the altar: for then the goods of the altar are separated from others as to property, as to governance, and also as to utility, and then the altar has the risk of its own right in the disposition of the rector; the text is noted in c. 1 de successione ab intestato. But if he does not have the altar in title, and thus is not properly a rector, but is only deputed there to officiate at the altar, and received alms as a stipend, then whatever remains from the alms belongs to the church in which the altar is situated: hence there is a great difference between a dowry, a prebend, and a stipend; see de prebendis, c. cum secundum appellationem. Also relevant is that saying of the Apostle, “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content.” Also relevant is what I noted in c. praesenti de officio ordinarii lib. 6, and what Innocent noted de iudicibus, c. cum deputati. The truth is that the priest ought to be supported from the fruits, and the remainder remains with the altar. And because the altar is under the church, it pertains to the church, regarding alms, see l. annua § 1. For the superior disposes of the goods of the inferior as legitimate administrator by right of superiority, as C. de bonis matri., l. 1, and C. de senatu et pas., l. si de rescrip., c. edoceri. The objection from ff. de donationibus, l. donationes in concubinam § species, does not hold, because there property was left for the maintenance of the husband, and to the same person, ff. de usufructu, l. Proculus. Here, however, property was left to one person, namely the altar, because it acts in the place of a person, in Auth. de ecclesiis tit. § si quis in nomine, ff. de fideicommissis, l. mortuo, so that it might support another person, namely the priest, de usuris, l. in fideicom. § cum Pollidius. Therefore, the priest can demand nothing beyond alms and sustenance, because, as I said, he is rather a mere officiant of the altar than a mere curator of the same. And this follows from the ordination of the deceased, which is lawful; the text is noted extra de prebendis, c. significante, and c. episcopus, and de clericis non residentibus, c. conquerente.

It remains to be seen whether goods may be alienated for the utility of the altar; I do not speak of necessity, and it is certain that they may not, as in the Authentica *De alienationibus emphyteuticis*, § *Sanctissimas*, unless with the authority of the Pope, as in the Clementina *Quia contingit*, *De religiosis domibus*.

It remains to be seen whether the uncle should be admitted to present himself together with the nephews of the deceased. And it seems that he should, because they are of the same degree; the testator appears to have considered the degree when he stated that the estate should remain with the nearest relatives. The safer opinion is to prefer the degree, which is preferred by law due to its privileged quality; hence, the nephews are preferred, because words must be understood in a civil manner. C. de legatis et hereditatibus, auth. post fratres ex utroque.

† It is doubted whether goods acquired after the making of the will are included, and it is certain that they are so included in a direct substitution: and because future goods are included in a universal disposition. L. Lucius, de fundo instrato.

† It is doubted whether the said Lady made a renunciation, and certainly there is no need to inquire about the legitime, because she died while her son was still alive; but if she had survived him, this question was discussed in the gloss on l. si quando, §. fi., C. de inoff. testa.

† To the next question asked, whether the lady Massia and Catherine, by not restoring certain goods of the said testator to the altar, fell from their legacy: I say that they did not, because it is not sought from the will, but as any possessor; hence they do not come against the will, nor do they contradict the legacies made by the testator, nor do they claim for themselves that those things are due to them contrary to the will; therefore, the penal cause ceasing, the penalty ceases, *de his quae poenae nomine*, D. 50.16; and *l. quaero*, § 1, *locati conducti*, D. 19.2; *l. quidam cum filium*, D. 30.1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that if any persons die intestate without sons or daughters, the nearest blood relatives on the father’s side shall succeed to the patrimony, and those on the mother’s side to the dowry, if someone dies while his mother and certain blood relatives are still living, who succeeds to the goods of the patrimony?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The statute provides that if any persons die intestate without sons or daughters, the nearest blood relatives on the father’s side shall succeed to the patrimony, provided, however, that males are preferred to females. And it has now happened that a certain Teus died, with his mother, Lady Mellotana, surviving, and with certain blood relatives of the said Teus on the mother’s side also surviving. The question now arises as to who shall succeed the said Teus in the goods of the patrimony: whether those related on the mother’s side, or Lady Mellotana. And it seems that only those related on the paternal side [should succeed], because they are related on the father’s side, and also on the second ground, because there is a male who is preferred to a female, since the statute speaks thus, and the law, though harsh, must nevertheless be observed, as in l. prospexit, Qui et a quibus. Nor should we depart from the words of the law, as in l. 1, §. sus, Qui navem, de exercito. But the contrary appears evident, because the statute cannot be understood as excluding the mother, because by law she would not be the nearest relative on the mother’s side; for no one is nearer to himself than himself, because in this subject the concept of degree does not apply, since she herself is the principle of derivation, not the derived. The statute, however, is derived from the mother, speaks of the mother herself, and does not speak of the common law, which we follow when the statute ceases to apply. l. si vero, §. de viro, Soluto matrimonio. To this effect serves the word “ex,” which is separative, de incendio, ruina, et naufragio, l. 1, §. ex incendio. Nor does the last part, which stated that males shall be preferred to females, constitute an objection, because it is to be understood according to the principle of the statute, when a division is to be made among the nearest relatives on the father’s side and the nearest relatives on the mother’s side. l. regula, §. si, de iuris et facti ignorantia. Therefore, I conclude that the mother succeeds to all the goods.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. One who has discretion from himself by virtue of a superior's mandate, if he proceeds by the force of the mandate, must precisely observe the form of the mandate.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Assuming that the said Lord Caussus has discretion of his own accord, nevertheless he did not act by his own authority, but by the force of a mandate from a superior who prescribed to him a precise and determined form; hence it is not understood that he used his discretion, which ought to be free, for he who had a specific instruction in his mandate is not understood to have imposed a burden, since he does what was mandated to him, as is proven here. D. de arbitris, l. qualem; D. de legibus, l. vnum ex familia, §. et quod non; Inn. de officio delegati, c. si pro debito; and Extr. de appellationibus, c. nouit. And therefore, if the mandants did not have the right to mandate, the proceeding founded upon a mandate without a rescript is null by law itself. C. qui pro sua iurisdict., l. 1; D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. eum, qui omni modo. The words added, namely “by way and right, as we can and ought to do better,” do not stand in the way, because it is always to be understood “by the force of the rescript”: for the title of the case in question is founded upon the title of the rescript, D. de imponendis lucris, disc. l. 1, lib. 10. This is also clear when that rescript strikes down a sentence and is a canon of latae sententiae, when it says, “you must pronounce him suspended.” D. de ritu nuptiarum, l. palam, §. fin. Therefore, this discretion wished to note this: hence, if he could not do so by law, the decree is of no effect. D. qui et a quibus, l. si privatus; and D. de pollicitationibus, l. toties; Extr. de electione, c. osius. And he who cannot deprive entirely cannot suspend even for a time, especially when the cause, which is required in a sentence, is not inserted, as is noted. D. de infantibus, l. 2, §. ignominiae. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a sequestration is made with someone concerning money found in his possession, and while that sequestration stands, a refutation is made by the creditor, and after the refutation another sequestration follows, whether the first is removed by the second, or whether the second is valid after the refutation.
casus: CASE. John Marini Bancherius received and held in his possession from Cechotal a certain quantity of florins. The said quantity was sequestered to the said John for the part of the auditors of exchange at the petition of Manuel the Hebrew, and for the part of the former lords, and for the part of Mansuetus and the associates, officials of the commune of Perugia. Then the said Cechus made a restitution to the said John of the said quantity by the hand of a public notary, and consented that the said quantity be given by the said John to Lord Matthew, son of the said Cechus. And thus the said John promised the said quantity to Lord Matthew by the will of the said Cechus, if and insofar as the said sequestration is lifted. After the sequestration had been made, the said John, regarding the said quantity by the Lords Consuls at the petition of Manuel the Hebrew, creditor of the said Cechus, appeared and narrated the fact as written above. Now, for the part of the said Manuel, it is said that the said restitution could not be made, the first sequestrations made, which then preceded, standing in the way, and that the sequestration for the part of the said consuls for the part of the said Manuel holds, which was made while other sequestrations stood, which, being later lifted, leaves the said sequestration firm. For the other part, it is said that the said sequestration does not hold, the said restitution standing in the way, because the said John was then not in any way obligated to the said Cechus, and it is also said for the other part that the said first sequestration was lifted.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† After a subsequent refutation, seizures are of no effect: because there is nothing in the hands of the sequestrator that belongs to the debtor to such an extent as to justify seizure; for the said John had already been released by Cecho under a condition which is deemed to have existed retroactively, and the said Lord Matthew, although he is a debtor, is nevertheless a cleric, in whose case the Lords Consuls cannot intervene. And although the seizures were valid at the time when the refutation was pending, they are nevertheless deemed to have been lifted, and the matter does not concern those seizures, but new ones, which have no foundation: because they were made at a time when, by legal fiction, he owed nothing to the said Cecho. Nevertheless, because a condition is deemed to operate retroactively (Digest, De solutionibus, l. conditio), and because a conditional delegation creates a conditional debt, which previously was insufficient in the person of the delegator, as in l. pactum (Digest, Si certum petatur), these new seizures were therefore invalid in law, just as the appointment in the name of John is invalid (Digest, De re iudicata, l. a diuo pio, §. si; and Digest, De bonis auctoritate iudicis possessis, l. cum vnus aliter, in the words “post ea” to the contrary effect). There, the case of that question applies to both limbs: namely, concerning the old seizures, which are not removed by a subsequent refutation, and the new ones, which do not invalidate the preceding release and the delegation made to another. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that if one thing has been sold or donated in solidum to several persons, he who has corporeal possession of that thing shall be preferred, provided he has not been notified.
2. When one thing has been donated by someone, with the usufruct thereof retained for himself, and the same thing is subsequently given in solidum without mention of the donation, who ought to be preferred: the donee or the person to whom it was given in solidum?
3. Whether the specification of species narrows the rule, or the preceding words.
4. The word "namely" (scilicet): what it signifies.
casus:
CASE. Whoever shall have sold, donated, or in any way alienated one or more things jointly to two or more persons, without informing the last buyer, or the person to whom the alienation is made, of the first alienation, shall be punished as a forger, and shall suffer other penalties as imposed according to the form of the statute, which instrument was made in person. And that alienation shall be valid, and that person shall be preferred who first obtained true delivery of the alienated thing, or acquired corporal possession with the will of the alienator, and not fictitious possession by legal presumption, such as by constituting himself as possessor in his own name, or by demanding precario, or by conducting a lease or tenancy of another’s property. But if the seller, after making the first sale, remained in true and corporal possession of the said sold or donated thing for one year, we will that he incur the said penalty, etc.

Assuming therefore the aforementioned statute. A certain Mentondus of Racanato donated the ownership of a certain plot of land to Lords Antonio and Colla, sons of Master Vannis of Racanato, generally retaining for himself, the said donor, the ownership of all things for as long as he lived, and the usufruct in the above-mentioned donated things. And after the legitimate insinuation according to the form of the statute of the city of Racanato was made by the said donees, Mentondus gave the said plot of land, donated to the aforementioned Lords Antonio and Colla, to Clarictus Panello Pannulphus without payment. It does not appear that anything was said in the gratuitous transfer made by the said Mentondus to the said Clarictus and brothers about the first donation made to the aforementioned Antonio and Colla. Nor does it appear that the said donees had delivery of the said plot of land, or that they acquired its possession with the will of the donor in any way other than by the act of retaining the usufruct. Now the question arises, considering the form of the said statute, who are preferred in ownership and possession of the said plot of land: the aforementioned donees, or the aforementioned persons to whom it was later given without payment.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

This statute has two parts: the first is penal and general, up to the words “there.” The second is prelatival, which is subdivided into two parts: the real delivery, up to the words “there,” and the special subjection, up to the verse “but if that.” The verse “I do not touch” is omitted, because it is not pertinent to the matter at hand. The question therefore turns on this:

Whether the addition of specific species restricts the preceding words, or not. For if the species are understood as examples, it is established that examples do not restrict the rule, as in D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. scire oportet, §. oportet. But if they are understood in their proper sense as species subject to a genus, they restrict the genus. D. de verbis significatis, l. si cum fundum. In support of the first part is the general reason of the statute. D. de testamento militis, l. in fraudem, §. fin. For the same reason and perfection exist in the retention of usufruct as in precarium. C. de donationibus, l. quisquis. Moreover, the principle of the law is general; therefore, the whole law is general. l. regula, §. fin., de iuris et facti ignorantia. We have a similar case regarding an advocate. I. 1, supra, de suffragio. l. omnibus contractibus, qui suspicione non carent, as noted by Bartolus, D. de donationibus, l. post contractum. Against this is the fact that

† because the word "s." is a restrictive term, and by declaring it narrows the genus to the species, as in Inst. de leg. ag. suc. §. sed quia sane; D. de optione leg. l. 3; and D. de consti. prin. l. beneficium; Inst. de re. diui. §. insula; D. de leg. 2. l. cum ita legatum. §. fin. in the gloss. Nor is the case similar to that of the retention of usufruct, for there true bodily possession is not transferred, but remains with the usufructuary. D. de act. pos. l. naturaliter. And therefore this case, omitted by the statute, remains governed by the common law, as in l. si no. §. de viro. solu. matri. And I hold this, because the enactor of a municipal law, who leaves certain species to the common law, appears to have preserved, not violated, the common law in other species, as in D. de mili. testamento. l. tribunus. §. Iul.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If someone pledges in the name of another, and so on, if it is not finally established whether the pledge can be revoked or claimed.
2. An agreement to repurchase is deemed to constitute a pledge.
3. Whether a thing belonging to another, given as a pledge, can be sold, the statute being in force, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Three things may be revoked in doubt,

First, whether the said prefect can revoke or otherwise claim the said pledged goods, given that there is no proof of the mandate of the said Turinus. Second, whether the said goods are obligated or may be retained for the debt of 150 gold florins. Third, whether, after the pledged goods have been returned to the Perugian citizen, the Jew can subsequently sell them, and whether the general and municipal privilege of the Jews applies where the Jew knowingly accepts another’s property as pledge. Regarding the first point, it must be said that if ratification is established, the goods cannot be claimed unless the debt is paid, as stated in the Digest, *De pignoribus*, law *Eius qui bona*. The same applies if it is established that the transaction was for the benefit of the prefect’s estate or his business, for example, in the trade of arms, as stated in the Code, *Quod cum eo*, law *Ei qui*. However, if none of these matters is proven, then if the lord prefect relies on the aid of this document, he must accept it in its entirety, as stated in the Digest, *De poenis*, law *Publiciana*, in the final paragraph; and in the Digest, *De manumissionibus*, law *Gaius*. But if he were to base his claim otherwise, then according to the common law he could claim the goods, as stated in the Digest, *De conditione indebiti*, law *Servus cuiusdam*. Nevertheless, by virtue of the privilege of the Jews, the claimant must repay the principal sum, and this concludes the first point.

† On the second point, it must be said that by the pactum de revendendo, the said things appear to have been pledged even for the said 150 florins; the text is notable. ff. qui potioribus in pignus habent locum, l. creditor, §. post divisionem. And although according to the common law this cannot be done, namely that a procurator binds the property of his principal for the debt of the procurator himself, as ff. de mandatis, l. creditor, §. fin., nevertheless the statute grants the defendants a right of retention for the principal sum, and thus also for the said 150 florins they have a right of retention. On the third point, I say,

† unless satisfaction is made, [the property] may be sold, observing the time prescribed by the statute concerning Jews, as in D. de manum. l. Emilius Largianus, and D. loca. l. Quaero, §. Inter, to the last pact. I answer, from the above, as in D. de usufr. l. Fundi Trebatiani.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If someone institutes a son as heir and makes a brief substitution in his favor, whether the substitutes are admitted upon the son’s death before the testator, and whether the grandchildren through the instituted son exclude the substitutes.
2. If a posthumous child is born and dies while the testator is still alive, such a testament is revived by praetorian law, and it is necessary to obtain possession of the estate according to the will.
3. Whether the children of the primary heirs come into the inheritance upon the death of those heirs.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. On these points

I say that the institution of Hippolytus was made in a case of caducity, because Hippolytus died after the will while the testator was still alive. C. de causis tollendis, l. sed pro secundo. And because a compendious substitution includes a vulgar one, as noted by Cynus in l. precibus, C. de impuberibus, the second degree, i.e., the vulgar substitution in the persons of the substitutes then living, became applicable; however, because posthumous children were subsequently born, the second degree of the substitutes was broken. ff. de in iure testamento, l. posthumorum.

† Because the posthumous heirs died during the lifetime of the testator, the substitution revived by praetorian law, in which case possession of the estate according to the will is necessary. D. de in ius vocando, l. posthumus. This must be acknowledged before the judge within the useful days, D. de successionibus edicto, l. 1, § quibus. After that, it cannot be acknowledged. D. ad Trebellianum, l. facta, § si quis bonorum. And therefore it must be examined whether the time has elapsed or not, and whether the instituted heirs are excused or not. D. de bonorum possessionibus, l. in bonorum. There is no need to discuss fideicommissary substitution here, because it lapsed due to the death of the instituted heir, not by omission, nor did he add a clause of intestacy. C. de fideicommissis, l. eam, quam.

† It is probable to doubt whether, upon the death of the primary heirs, their children come into the inheritance by virtue of the appellative name, which is extensive up to the time of death. D. de re dubia, l. Si cognatis. And it seems that they do not. D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Qui liberis, §. Hec verba; and this is true, because they do not come by virtue of a transaction. D. de suis et legitimis haeredibus, l. 2, §. Ex pluribus. But they come in their own right, according to the widest signification. Argument: D. de haeredum institutione, l. Lucius. Just as in the institution of an heir of someone, it is observed that, first, the sons come, and if they are lacking at the time of the testator’s death, the grandsons come in the successive order. Argument: D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, §. 1. To the contrary, it is argued that, immediately upon the death of the instituted heir, the case of death designated the persons of the substitutes comprehended by the substitution. Therefore, if they are designated, the share becomes caducous, moving the substitute, as stated in the aforementioned §. Pro secundo. But I answer that it designated them in general, according to the appellative name, and not individually in their proper persons. To this effect: D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. Ex facto, §. Fin.; D. de usufructu accrescendo, l. Si quis nostro; C. de condicionibus insertis, l. 1. And thus I hold, because by the name of heir, according to usage of speech, the son is signified, and by the name of son, the grandson is signified in the legal signification. D. ad Legem Macedonianam, l. Filium habeo. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The pronouncement that the instituted heir be put in possession cannot, strictly according to civil law, be appealed; otherwise, however, according to canonical equity.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It was pronounced that the heir named in the will should be put in possession; the question arises whether an appeal may be taken. It seems that it may not, first on the basis of the general rule which provides that no appeal lies in a possessory action, as in C. de momentanea possessione, l. 1. Secondly, on the basis of the special favor accorded to the execution of testators’ wills, whereby the law specifically and expressly prohibits an appeal in this case, commands that the appeal not be received, and punishes the litigant who appeals contrary to the interdict of the law, as well as the judge who proceeds accordingly. C. quorum appellatio non recipitur, l. quisquis; ff. de appellations recipiendis, c. 1. These laws are canonized in secunda quaestio 6, sunt et quorum. Hence it appears that an appeal may not be taken either under civil law or under canon law. This is supported by the fact that a judgment rendered in a possessory action is more akin to an interlocutory than to a definitive judgment. C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus, omni iudici, l. post sententiam, since it may be verified in a petitory action. Moreover, this pronouncement was based on notoriety, as in C. de edicto divi Adriani, l. si. But in matters of notoriety, an appeal is futile, which is made against the improper voice of one who temerarily appeals; it is not revoked by way of attentatum, hence the execution of the fact is delayed after the words. C. quorum appellatio non recipitur, l. si; C. de appellationibus, l. quoniam nonnulli; de appellationibus, c. Romana, lib. 6; de negotiorum gestione, l. et qui natura, § cum me.

On the contrary, it seems so according to canonical equity. First, because according to the canons, an appeal lies from a judgment rendered in a possessory action, whether mixed or pure, because it imposes a heavy burden, as experience teaches, de restitutione spoliorum, c. ex conquestione. According to Innocentius, who thus decided in c. significatibus, de novo operis, in pretio. Furthermore, it is expressly the mind of Innocentius that when the heir named in the will is not to be put in possession, an appeal may not be taken only when no cause is assigned which is approved by law; otherwise, if a juridical cause is assigned, de officio, de legibus, c. pastoralis, per Innocentius. For what is established by the records is that the will is broken, void, vitiated, or not solemn. Hence the judge cannot rely on the favor of concession; for it is notorious that an appeal does not proceed from the records; rather, if it does not hold by way of appeal, it should hold by way of general recourse to the superior’s mercy, to be pleaded. ar. de officio praesidis, l. illicitas, in principio; de arbitris, l. non distinguemus, § cum quidam.

It must therefore be concluded that, according to the strictness of the law, an appeal may not be taken, for this was introduced by the harshness of the laws due to the common malice of appellants; but according to canonical equity, for an evident and just cause which appears from the records, an appeal may be taken. This is held by Ioannes Andreas in c. pastoralis, in numero.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The acceptance of a legacy, made without knowledge of the entire will or of a part thereof, does not prejudice the legatee in the same manner as if it had been made before the inheritance was entered upon.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If the lady acknowledged the legacy made with the intention of compensation at the time when she could have acknowledged it, and by certain knowledge she was excluded from the recovery of the dowry, as in D. de leg. praest. l. virilis, § non solet, and C. de rei ux. act. l. 1, § sciendum. But if she were ignorant of the tenor of the will in whole or in part, she is not deemed to have acknowledged it, as in D. de tegu. iu. l. in totum omnia; D. de inoff. test. l. iure decedens, § præterea. Moreover, if she acknowledged it before the inheritance was entered upon, the acknowledgment is not valid, nor does it prejudice her, as in D. quorum leg. l. 1, § ait prætor voluntas, for it has the tacit condition that the inheritance be entered upon, D. de leg. 1, l. hæc verba; while the condition is pending, it cannot be accepted, as in D. de leg. 2, l. si ita scriptum, § si sub conditione. Moreover, a legacy which has a burden annexed cannot be accepted in part without being drawn to the whole, D. de leg. 2, l. sed ex duobus, and l. 1 and 2, de acqu. hæred. Hence knowledge of the whole is required; otherwise the acceptance cannot be valid. Since, therefore, the inheritance was entered upon before the alleged acceptance, and it was not alleged and proved that she had knowledge, such an acceptance would not be an obstacle to the recovery of the dowry, if it were so proved. Wherefore the lady has the right, having seen the aforementioned acts. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The succession of the mother is a matter of civil law.
2. Given a statute providing that a brother shall succeed to his brother intestate to the exclusion of the mother, and that the brother is related through the father’s father only, the mother is excluded.
3. Moreover, Paulus first advised on this point in the sixth part of his consilia, number 2, beginning “Quaedam.”
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The words of the statute of the civil law of Cortona are premised, which provides: “Also, if anyone dies intestate, with children surviving him, and any of his said sons or daughters dies without legitimate children, the other surviving brothers, or sisters, or brother, or sister, shall succeed to their deceased brothers or sisters, or to their deceased brother or sister, and the descendants of these brothers and sisters from a legitimate marriage; and not their mother, nor maternal grandmother, or great-grandmother, nor maternal grandfather, or great-grandfather, provided that some male brother, or son of a brother, or some male descendant through the male line from the brother of the deceased survives the said deceased; and the descendants from the said sisters shall in no way succeed: but only the male brother, and the male descendants from him through the male line shall succeed, and not the mother, nor maternal grandmother, or great-grandmother, nor maternal grandfather, or great-grandfather.” It is proposed that a certain Paul Serlacidi of Cortona, having two sons, one from his first wife named Matthew, the other from his second wife called Orlandino, died intestate; then the said Orlandino died in pupillary age. Now there is doubt concerning the inheritance of the said Orlandino, whether it pertains to his mother, or to the brother from the father’s side only. On this point, having been consulted previously, I said that the brother succeeds, excluding the mother, moved by the words and intent of the statute. However, another doctor advised the contrary. Therefore, so that the truth may appear, let us put forward the reasons and laws. Responding against the law, which is very clear, I divide the statute into three sentences. The first differs. The second removes. The third prefers and removes. The first favors brothers, the second opposes mothers. The third, by favoring brothers, opposes sisters and mothers. In the second, “and not their mother.” In the third, “provided.” And I premise for clarity,

† That the succession of mothers is a matter of civil law: because it originated from a Senatusconsultum, and its efficient cause was not the intention of nature; hence, in primitive nature, which produced natural law, such succession, deviating from the origin of natural intention, was by no means present, as is clear. D. and C. ad Tertullianam; and Inst. ad Tertullianam. Just as this succession was born from civil law, so it can be abolished by civil law, and by customs and statutes of places, at least in certain cases, and not always, for example, when a person exists whom the statute prefers, as in c. 1, de natura successionis, feud., col. 10; and arg. C. ad Orphit., l. Non pro numero. For although this statute is contrary to piety, D. de inofficioso testamento, l. Nam et si parentibus, it is nevertheless not contrary to public utility, since it is more in the interest of the republic that families be preserved. D. de venditionibus insipientium, l. 1, § Publico; and per Cynus, C. de adulteriis, l. Publico; and C. de lege sancta. Therefore, against the rule, l. Voluntatem iure non succedat, it is necessary in successions. l. Differentia; note l. Prohibente, as in D. de verborum significatione, l. Lege obvenire haeredi; and D. de petitione hereditatis, l. 2 and 3.

Furthermore, it must be noted that there is a threefold virtue connected in the matter of successions: namely, the inclusive virtue of various persons; the exclusive virtue; and the preferential virtue. It suffices for the legislator to include some only, so that he may appear to have excluded another, and be deemed to have done so, arg. D. de legibus, l. Quod in rerum, § Si quis post. For, so to speak, this is the testament of the law, in which one passed over by the law is deemed disinherited from the succession, arg. D. de solutione matrimonii, l. Si vero, § De viro. Military laws apply, hence the law is compared to a soldier’s testament. For if soldiers serve according to laws, therefore laws apply all the more, because for each thing and that thing more. And in this appears the first error of that consul, who says that the inclusive virtue of brothers is to be referred to the common law according to interpretation, which is not true: because in matter and form not consonant with the common law, but formed in an adversative virtue, as in c. Albertus, de feudorum cognitione, col. 10. Therefore, the inclusion of one is merely the exclusion of another by the virtue of including in a determined manner. D. de legibus 2, l. Cum ita, § In fideicommissis. And this is held by Bartolus in l. 2, D. ad Trebellianam. Nevertheless, here the law proceeds further by expressing what it intends, and this in two ways: first, by saying “and not commonly of theirs.” Here the word “theirs” is weighed, which is of the plural number and of comprehensive signification, as in D. ad Trebellianam, l. Iulius Phebus. From this word, the said consulting jurist said that it is understood as “their mother,” i.e., of the brothers, so that it is required that, just as those joined on both sides, because the double conjunction is more favorable, otherwise the conjunction from the right and from the left, than the right only, which proceeds from the father, or the left only, which proceeds from the mother as weaker: and although he speaks and does not prove, nevertheless this seems to be the case, because the adjective determines the substantive more immediate and proximate to itself in the construction of the sentence, having together to rule in the parts of speech, as C. de fideicommissis, l. Eam, quam; C. de fideicommissis haereditatibus, l. Filium, quem habentem. Hence that adjectival and relative term “theirs” is referred to that word “to their brothers.” But the contrary is the truth itself, for just as we must observe the reason of correct speech, D. de auro et argento legato, l. Plautius, so much more strongly the reason of correct intention, which is the favor of blood. D. de successionibus ab intestato, l. 1, § Largius. Hence it is understood, “and not commonly of theirs,” i.e., of the deceased, and the stepmother is excluded by the stepson, not because he is a stepson, but because he is the brother of the deceased, so that the goods which flowed from the paternal stock may flow back to him, arg. C. de bonis quae liberis, l. Quod scitis. Hence this succession looks to its own stock: because it is imagined by the statute, because this would have been the intention of the father, if he had died testate, arg. D. de pactis, l. Tale pactum, § Si. And thus, as regards the second virtue, he who consulted spoke badly, having understood it poorly: therefore the brother excludes the mother of the deceased, his stepmother: for if a son opposes his mother and is adverse to her, much more will a stepson oppose, because with a stepmother he is not bound to share: and to whom it is more honorable to be adverse: and here the duality is not weighed, but blood and agnatic relationship, as I said. D. de legatis tertio, l. Intestato.

Secondly, the law proceeds further by excluding sisters and mothers simply. Observe that by reason of the conjunction, the understanding of both extremes is given. l. Par intellectus, D. de vulgaribus substitutionibus; l. Nam hoc iure, C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus, l. Si. But it is certain that a consanguineous brother excludes any sister, because so the statute speaks: therefore also any mother of the deceased. Moreover, if the statute prefers a blood sister to the mother, and a brother to a sister: therefore much more strongly it prefers [the brother] to the mother, as in l. Claudius Felix; and D. ad Tertullianam, l. Aequissimum. This statute has its root of words and reason in the paternal line: it excludes the mother by the apt nature of the words, and therefore against the words, reason, and mind, that jurist consulted erroneously: he attempts to gloss, nay, to destroy the statute: hence the truth is that the mother does not succeed, because the determination is general. D. de testamento militis, l. In fraudem, § Si; D. de acquirenda hereditate, l. Si servum, § Non dixit. From the generality of the words itself, therefore, the response to the reason of those [opposing] is clear.

Furthermore, the beginning of the law is general, and the end is placed indefinitely: therefore the whole law has a general sense. D. de iuribus et factis ignorantibus, l. Regula, § Si. And although the middle clause were strictly placed as regards the notification of terms, it would not restrict the breadth of the final and conclusive clause, ad l. Aquiliam, l. Si servus servum, § Inquit lex. Because the genus after the species amplifies, does not restrict: and to this it contributes that often the law repeats, to add what is clear from the nature of the genus, the breadth of which should not be restrained. D. de servorum urbanorum praediisque, l. Si servus; D. de exercitoribus, l. 1, § Generaliter; D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Quae conditio; D. de pignoribus legatis, l. Si; and l. Placet; D. de liberis et postumis, in the words “ex quacumque uxore.” We therefore look to which father, not which mother, they were born, as we also have elsewhere. D. de administratione tutorum, l. Cum plures, § Cum tutor; and what is read, et non, C. de administratione tutorum, l. Non omnes.

I conclude therefore that the aforementioned brother is preferred to the aforementioned mother, namely, this benefit, which the law grants in honor of blood, is to be aided by interpretation, and since the reason of the statute is common, and the breadth of the words expresses this sense manifestly. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A reception into a nun and monastic life by these words is such that a profession is not understood to have been made, whence she may make a will.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It is proposed that in the year 1162, on January 24, Lady Catherine was received as a nun in the monastery of Saint Agnes of Assisi by these words: “they received her as a nun and a monastic.” The question is whether by these words a profession is understood to have been made. It has been said that no: because she did not promise the three substantial vows, neither tacitly nor expressly; hence it is understood that she was received for the year of probation, not for the conclusion of profession. For since this uncle was instituted by law in favor of the monastery and in favor of the one entering, neither appears to have renounced his favor in doubt; this is clear expressly in c. *beneficium*, de re iudicata, lib. 6. Afterwards, however, the said Lady Catherine is said to have remained in the said monastery for more than a continuous year, always saying that she wished to be a nun. And because contradiction is contrary to consent, even if she had declared her will not to become a nun before the sisters or neighbors, she would never be seen as professed by the lapse of time; because the intention is absent, and God and the Church do not receive the unwilling, but one who begs with prayers. For this is an act in which consent is required in any case, just as in marriage, extra, quod meo, c. *j.*, de sponsalibus; c. *cum locum*; and de regulari, c. *ad apostolos* and c. *consulti*. And therefore, according to what is narrated to me, this woman is not a nun; because she never had the intention of making profession, nor the will, but the desire of fleeing. Precepts made to her do not make her a nun who is not one. According, therefore, to what is proposed, she is not a nun, and she had free flight to the secular world, from which she never departed in heart, and with the following signs of will, and she can freely dispose of her own and make a will, because she is not professed. Note in auth. *ingressa*.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a legacy has been made to a woman on the condition that she live chaste and honestly, and she associates in a disgraceful manner, although she does not commit fornication, she is said to live unchastely, and she forfeits the legacy.
2. Where the issue is proving a delict in general, the delict is proved by witnesses testifying individually; otherwise, if it is a specific act.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Because the aforementioned Paganossa lived impudically and dishonestly, it is established that she has fallen from the usufruct bequeathed, and that the usufruct has been consolidated into the ownership. That it has been proven that she lived impudically is evident from the following doctrine:

† For sometimes the issue is proving a general delict, such as heresy, and such a delict is proved by witnesses who testify individually but are consistent in general terms: for example, one says that she denied that Christ was born of a virgin, another says that she denied that Christ was crucified, as noted in C. de hæred. l. quicunque per la. Bu. Sometimes the issue is proving a specific act, and then the witnesses must specifically concur in proving the same act. de fi. instr. ca. cum Ioannes. Now, coming to the point at hand, honesty and chastity are general acts, whereas dishonesty and unchastity, because they are committed in many ways, are not. For even without rape a widow can live dishonestly, for by the very fact that she associates shamefully, she injures the name of chastity, not to mention that rape is evident, as ff. de vsu, et ha. l. non al. and through the rule that what is commonly known is presumed from what is known, to which passage is returned. C. de proba. l. neque natales. per lac. Bu. and others. Therefore, there is no doubt that, having seen the documents and testimonies, an unchaste life in general has been proved. It is supported by what Innoc. noted de accu. c. qualiter. and by Arch. in q. 8. c. nihilominus. ff. de test. l. ob carmen. §. fin. in glo. and quę sit longa consue. c. 2. per Cyn. on the understanding of the said gloss. I therefore conclude from the said documents that the said pagan woman has fallen from the said usufruct, and that it has reverted to her ownership. I, Bal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether general arbitrators can be outlawed by those who have been outlawed.
2. The term "dictio," finally, what it signifies,
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The question is whether, by virtue of a general mandate of arbitration, those who have been outlawed can be recalled, and it seems that they cannot, unless it had been declared simply that it was within their discretion; for this matter is reserved by law to the prince or to the sovereign people. D. de petitione hereditatis, l. relegati. And that it is not so, is noted by Innocentius, X. de re iudicata, c. Cum te. This is supported by what Bartolus writes in D. de decretis ab ordine faciendo, l. In ambitiosa.

On the contrary, it seems that they can, for public enemies can be restored to grace and recognized, when a just cause urges it, as in D. de re militari, l. Non omnes, §. Si; and D. ad legem Iuliam de ambitu, l. 1, ver. Quia lege damnati. Moreover, although the restoration of reputation is reserved to the prince, yet to compromise is not reserved to the prince; for everyone having a general mandate with free power can compromise. D. de procuratoribus, l. Mandato generali, in the gloss; C. de transactionibus, l. Praeses; D. de pactis, l. Item magistri. Someone might say that this is true regarding a debt which has not passed into a judicial decision, if it is liquidated by sentence, as is noted in D. de pactis, l. Contra iuris, §. Fin.; and D. de vi aut clam, l. Prohibere, §. Plene. For it would rather be a dissipation than a compromise, which is not included in any general commission, as in D. pro emptore, l. Qui fundum, §. Si tutor; and D. de transactionibus, l. Post rem; D. de manumis, l. Creditor, §. Si.

Furthermore, by reason of a general commission, something can be done by deferring rather than by prohibiting. D. de verbis oblig., l. Qui Romae, §. Calimacus, in fine; D. de pactis, l. Imperatores. And wherever a contrary provision is found, it is special and should not be extended to consequences. Also, since the sentence has passed into a judicial decision, it cannot be rescinded except by supplication; but supplication cannot be made in a lower court to the prince or to the sovereign people. Auth. Quae supplicatio. Moreover, the sinew of justice is weakened if clemency is shown to criminals with undue facility. C. de privilegiis scholarum, l. Hac lege. And the law and virtue of the city are destroyed if the province is not purged. D. de officiis praesidis, l. Congruit; C. de defensoribus civitatum, l. Per omnes.

But to these arguments it is thus answered, that in our case such allegations cease, because the general assembly has decreed whatever these individuals declare; hence these individuals do not so much restore as declare. D. de rebus dubiis, l. Utrum, §. 1; D. quod cuiusque universitatis nomine, l. Item eorum, §. Si decuriones. Therefore, the general assembly is the author of the true minister, as these are declarers of justice: for even if the restoration of Master John by Innocentius is considered, they subsequently acted prudently and with excellent reason. As in D. de quaestionibus, l. 1, §. Qui ultimo; for from this cause the restoration is most just, as in the said §. de quaest., there: “nisi cui officio etc.” This is cumulative with reason, and another reason, namely the public good, together with the reason of peace, although the reason of the person is resolved on one side; hence the restoration of Master John was possible, authentic, and of equal utility, which are the two roots of reasons to be made. And I say that this dispensation, therefore this compensation, is valid, and that the said Master John is to be cancelled according to the said ordinance.

It is not an obstacle if it is said that in the said assembly special provision was made for certain outlaws, from which it might be understood that it is otherwise in other cases, because indivisible genera usually restrict, as in D. de legibus tertio, l. Heres meus, §. Duae statuæ.

† Item, the word “demum” (finally/only then) appears to be a limiting term, as in C. de procuratoribus, l. ita demum; D. de arbitris, l. ita demum. If all matters were implicitly included, why were certain things expressly provided for to no effect? This seems absurd. But I answer that such specification does not restrict the general, free, and public exercise of discretion for the future, although it confirms the exercise in the past. And those individual items specified were not intended to restrict, but rather to avoid the appearance that the law’s providence had neglected those to whom special provision was due. D. de iniuriis, l. item apud Labeonem, §. hoc edictum. And although there past acts are approved, and in this respect there is speciality of provision, nevertheless future acts are not seen to be prohibited, which can be included, signified, and gathered from the words. Arg. D. de legatis praestandis, l. 1, §. et generaliter. Nor does the word “demum” stand in the way, because it does not signify the restitution of persons, but rather the mode of performance. For thus only then are the former persons, to whom a burden was imposed, brought to liberty, if they pay the imposed burden, and otherwise not. D. de fideicommissis liberis, l. Thais ancilla, §. iura cassanda. Therefore, the said condemnation is inserted by reason of the law. D. de legatis, l. si.

For the tranquil and peaceful state of the men of the city and community of Assisi, and for the preservation of their rights, they established and ordained that no woman of the city of Assisi, or of its county, of whatever condition she may be, can nor ought in any manner to make a will, or codicil, to donate, or to make any last will, or to dispose, or to make a sale, exchange, donation, concession, transfer, or any alienation, or obligation, of whatever kind or condition they may be, without the presence and consent of her husband and father, if she has a husband and father; and if she has only a father and not a husband, without the presence and consent of her father; and if she has a husband and not a father, without the presence and consent of her husband; and if she has neither husband nor father, but male sons, or a son, who can, or can give consent, and are, or is, near the city of Assisi within 30 miles, without the presence and consent of her said legitimate son or legitimate male sons, if she has more than one; and if she lacks a husband, sons, or a son, without the presence and consent, in the manner aforesaid, of her legitimate carnal brother. And if she lacks a carnal brother, without the presence and consent, in the manner aforesaid, of a grandson descending from a son, or brothers, or carnal sisters, in the manner aforesaid; and if there are more grandsons than one, without the presence and consent, in the manner aforesaid, of all her sons and daughters, if she has more; and if the aforementioned persons, or any of them, cannot conveniently give presence or consent in the manner aforesaid, that it is permitted to them to give presence or consent by a procurator specially constituted by them for this purpose. However, it is permitted to the said women, without the presence and consent of the said persons, to make a will, codicil, and dispose of and make a last will concerning their goods and dowries, up to the quantity of 10 pounds of denarii for every hundred pounds of such woman’s goods, all of which they have above the said prohibition in no way obstructing. And if a testament, sale, or alienation, exchange, or cession, and transaction, and any other offer, any obligation, is made without observing the form aforesaid, let them be void, invalid, and of no value, and let all and each of the aforementioned things have place in the present and future. It is also permitted to the said women, if they wish, to constitute one or more procurators, and also a curator, and one or more actors, to sue and defend, the aforementioned prohibition in no way obstructing. It is understood that the husband is he who contracted marriage with the woman, or consummated it, and with her stood publicly as a husband in one and the same house for at least two months, and to prove the consummation of marriage, the oath of the husband and wife suffices.
