And if against the aforementioned form any alienation, sale, cession, donation, or concession, or any other contract is made, or made, or dominion of possession is transferred to another or others, it shall not be valid, nor shall it bind by the law itself, and the Potestas, and Captain, and official of either of them, before whom it shall be demanded, or against the aforementioned form shall have been made, shall hold and must put, send, and deliver into possession the legitimate successor, or successors, to such woman, of the things and goods of the said woman obligated or alienated against the aforementioned form, and shall maintain and defend him, or them, in the said possession, or possessions, under the penalty of 5 pounds of denarii. And no person of such, or such condition, shall dare, or presume, to molest, nor to inquiet, nor to burden the said possessions, or possession, nor to use any right without the license of the said successor, or successors, under the penalty for each one contravening, and for each time, of one hundred pounds of denarii. And whoever should oppose any exception that the said statute was not valid for any cause, shall not be heard by any official, and nevertheless from such opposition of exception he shall be condemned in one hundred pounds of denarii by the Potestas, or Captain of the said community, to be applied to the said community.

Lord Peter, and Lord William, consulted, hold that the said cancellation does not avail, nor has it to take away the testament because of that clause appended in the instrument of revocation of cancellation, which begins, “to the end that the said lady Vicutia, her daughter, may succeed to the same, etc.” which is a disposition, and could not be done without observing the form of this statute. The point is, whether a testament made with the counsel of blood relatives according to the form aforesaid can be cancelled, or cut, without the aforementioned form, and thus the question is, whether he who cancels appears to dispose, and thus the form which is required in disposing, namely the consent of kinsmen, is required in cancelling. And on this is the following opinion.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a woman may not make a will without the counsel of her blood relatives, if the woman makes a will observing the required form, she may revoke it even if the form is not observed.
2. The revocation of a will is not a disposition.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Although the consulting jurists are of great authority, nevertheless I do not depart from what I previously advised. For I said, and I say, that the cancellation of a will is not a disposition of a person, but the removal of a thing disposed; for it is one thing to remove obstacles for those coming to succeed intestate, especially daughters, unless succession is restored to its natural order; it is another thing to dispose. For properly, to dispose is the same as to order, not to be ordered; but he who dies intestate is more ordered than ordering. The dispositive power is given outside, *de testamento*, *cum tibi facit quod non*, *de iustitia et iure*. *L. manumissionis*. It is not an obstacle, *de iure codicilli*, *l. 2* and *l. conficiuntur*, *de legatis 2*. *L. codicilli*, § *penultimo*. For that is by a certain fiction, which has no place in statutes contrary to the common law, as is clear to all, and it is a common saying. Since, therefore, according to the common law, it may be cancelled, nor is it said to be a testament, *C. de testamentis*, *l. nostram* and *persta*, nothing is said about cancellation; therefore we are in the common law, because the act is stronger than the word. For cancellation supplants the will and the proof of the former will, and that instrument was of the testatrix, whence it could be affected, *demil. testa.*, *l. tribunus*, § *ultimo*, *de his quae in testamento delentur*, *l. cancellauerat*. For no one is compelled to die testate or intestate, because this is a matter of free will, *ff. de inofficioso testamento*, *l. posthumus*. Nor is it an obstacle, those words, "for this purpose," etc., because they come constructively, not dispositively, *l. penult.* and *fin.*, *de his quae in testamento delentur*.

And that it is not a disposition is evident, because therefrom does not arise the consequence that, if the bishop is not said to dispose of the benefice by revoking the disposition, but by conferring it, it is also established that legacies cannot be claimed for fame unless they are confirmed by acceptance, which are not due. L. si seruus communis Meuii. in the beginning of the same. ff. de stipulationibus seruorum. C. de fideicommissis. lib. 1. 2. de haereditatibus institutis. L. qui filio. §. seruus. And therefore execution cannot be demanded, because they have a tacit condition, if the inheritance is accepted, whence the condition is an obstacle. ff. quando dies legati cedat. L. quod pure. §. final. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, a dowry is to be provided for children.
2. The legitime does not bear the burden, but rather that which is above the legitime.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It must be known that, when the matter of collation is discussed among children, either the ascendant, whose succession is at issue, has disposed regarding collation, or has passed over it in silence, or has disposed in part and omitted in part. In the first case, the will of the testator must be observed. In the second case, the will of the law must be observed, which is such, namely, that a dowry given or promised is brought into collation, but a dowry left in a will is not brought into collation, as stated in the Code on Collation, in the authority *Ex testamento*, and in the law *Si donatione*, in the jurist’s response. For a legacy from a father is acquired after the father’s death, and therefore it is not brought into collation, but its origin is retained, because legacies are acquired, not brought into collation; these are common legal principles. In the third case, when the testator has imposed the burden of collation on only one child, concerning the others, the conjecture of tacit will resolves the matter; it seems to be said that the others are not bound to bring into collation, for the expression of one not only states the common law but also operates something tacitly from itself, for tacit and conjectured will causes collation to cease, just as express will does, as in the Digest, *Familiae erciscundae*, law *Ex parte*, section *In testamento moriens quenquam*. One could argue to the contrary, namely, that an omitted case presupposes a mental omission by the words, and thus the disposition of the law should be followed, as in the law *Commodissimum* on children and posthumous heirs, especially among children for preserving the equality of collation, as in the Code, *Communia utriusque iudicii*, law *Fin*. As for our case, which is the subject of the question, namely, whether Benevenuta can demand collation: if it is asked concerning legacies, she cannot; if concerning dowries given or promised to her sisters: And here it must be considered whether she succeeds to her father universally. Collation has no place except among universal successors, as in the Code, *De inofficioso testamento*, law *Unde si parens*. And it appears that she does not succeed, because she ceded her rights; hence, if any collation were due, it would be made to the cessionary. But the contrary is true: for the inheritance of a living father could not be ceded, for the father, by subsequently making a will, intended that the daughter should succeed, not the cessionary; hence, he did not persist in his first intention, as in the Code, *De pactis*, law *Fin*. And because the father succeeded to the cessionary, the whole became one patrimony, namely, that of the said Matthew, as in the law *Sed et si plures*, section *Filio*, *De vulgaribus substitutionibus*. Of this he could dispose by will, saving the legitime, and by this means a substantial answer is given to all doubts arising from collation concerning the said Benevenuta and her sisters, namely, that the said Benevenuta must bring into collation her dowry on the occasion of her father’s succession; for the will speaks thus. But from her sisters, the dowries left in the will to the said sisters need not be brought into collation to her. What I have said concerning the dowry, I say the same concerning other gifts made by him, whose succession is in question, unless such a gift has the force of a legacy, as noted in the aforementioned authority *Ex testamento*. These, however, are brought into collation if inequality among the children would result therefrom, for reciprocal collation must be made among them according to the Digest and the Code.

† On another point, it must be said regarding the burden of the mascepta that the burden does not hold within the legitime, but above the legitime, as in l. quoniam in prioribus, de inofficiosa testatione, and fully noted in l. si cum dotem, § si pater, soluto matrimonio. On another point, regarding the dowry returned to Matthew from the succession of Lord Angel, I say that it is common to all heirs, because it is the father’s own patrimony from the said succession. C. de donationibus, l. si auia. Francisca succeeds by pupillary substitution on account of the direct word “if he dies,” substituted to herself, as in c. 1, de testamentis, lib. 6. The form should be in accordance with what is clear from the above. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that whoever associates himself with another and gives aid at the time of a homicide shall be punished, if someone prepares poison and sends it, does he incur the penalty of the statute?
2. One who kills by poison is called a traitor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† That evil would be punishable capitally according to the common law by the Lex Cornelia de sicariis et veneficis and the Digest title On the Lex Cornelia de sicariis, l. 3, in principio, and § legis Corneliae. But it must be considered according to the form of the statute whether this person is said to have committed the act, or to have caused it to be committed by ordering it, or not. And it is certain that he did not commit it, nor did he order it, nor was he a participant in the crime; but he gave aid and the material so that it might be done by another, as in the Digest title On the Lex Aquilia, l. item si obstetrix, in principio. Nevertheless, this case is not covered by the statute, because the statute speaks of aid under different wording, namely by associating and giving favor at the time of the homicide. Although it could be said that this person gave favor, who prepared and sent the material of the poison, I do not believe that the statute considered this terrible case. Codex, title On maleficia and maleficii, l. 1.

† For in poison there is treachery joined with homicide, and it is a most grave crime, if such is the truth of the fact. However, if the truth of the fact were such as to warrant a lighter mitigation, the inquiry should have taken place before the defendant’s response; but since the defendant has confessed voluntarily, nothing can be deducted. Therefore, let the judge be a lover of truth: for since this case was not contemplated by the statute, the judge himself should proceed according to his conscience, by analogy, as it seems to him, because it is a matter of discretion, as stated in D. de legibus, l. non possunt; D. de crimine expilatorum haereditatum, l. 1 and l. hodie; D. de poenis. And the greater part of the counsel of men lies in conscience, which God formed as the inner judge, whom the judge may follow where the law grants the judge a choice. C. de iudicibus, l. rem non nouam. He may therefore also punish pecuniarily, if it seems to him appropriate by analogy, in favor of the opinion or support, since “favor” is a term of general significance; nor does appeal have place in this case, because the evil is most enormous and notorious. C. quorum appellatio non recipitur, l. obseruare. He may also punish with death, because he deserves it; therefore, punish according to your conscience, and do not concern yourselves with appeal. D. de appellations, l. constitutione; and c. Romana, de appellationibus, lib. 6, in the gloss of the Ordo. And it is good caution that you have him renounce appeal and defense as frivolous.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A postponement is invalid when it is granted in consideration of an annual payment or promise.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Proceeding to the truth of law and fact, the aforementioned delay was granted in consideration of the annual payment or promise, which, if valid in law, would mean that the principal could not be demanded in the meantime, as stated in D. de verb. oblig. l. qui Romae, in principio, and C. si certum petatur, l. lecta. But since it is not valid, because it would constitute usury, as noted in D. si certum petatur, l. rogasti, § si tibi, the delay ceases when its final cause ceases, and action cannot be brought immediately, as stated in D. ad Trebellianum, l. filia, § alumno, and D. ad Senatusconsultum Velleianum, § si, l. aliquando. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The protestation of the second creditor to the prejudice of the first is invalid and has no effect.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Notwithstanding Savinus’s protestation, proceedings must continue to further steps at the petition of Amelius, the reason being that Amelius holds an obligation with a mortgage prior in time; hence, a prior creditor cannot be excluded by a subsequent creditor, nor even by a procurator. D. de bonis ante iudicatum possidendis, l. cum unus, where this matter is fully treated; C. eodem, l. si; D. de damno infecto, l. si finita, § si plures; and D. ut in possessorium legatur, l. is cui, § si plures. And the same applies as regards any creditors whatsoever, for a praetorian pledge of one does not exclude the process of another, and in the final conclusion, he who is prior in time in a conventional pledge shall have the stronger right in law, as the rule of both bodies of law states.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When a partnership has been contracted, if one party contributes money and the other contributes labor, the truth of the matter must first be examined before the rule of guarantee is put into execution, on account of the contingencies that may occur.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† As appears from the tenor, the partnership was justly contracted, one party contributing money, namely 400 florins, the other contributing labor for a share of the profit and loss. Hence three cases may arise: first, that there is neither profit nor loss; in which case the entire sum must be returned, and the labor and money will be unproductive. Second, that there is profit; in which case it is common, the capital being saved; because it was acted and agreed upon regarding the sharing of profit, not regarding the bearing of the principal. Third, that there is loss; in which case the share is diminished by half of the loss. And all these are read and noted by the gloss and doctors in the Digest, *pro socio*, l. 1. It therefore appears first that the truth of the matter must be inquired into, before the command of guarantee is put into execution; because the case might be one that would diminish the quantity, for which reason it is placed. l. *huius autem*, § 1, there: "it must be clear to the praetor freely." Digest, *de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, l. *cum servus*, and l. *qui sub conditione reddentur*, Digest, *de statu liberorum*. The praetorian reason, in doubt according to law, should not begin with execution, as in l. *nimis propere macellae*. It is also certain that where a certain form of citation has been given, one cannot proceed with the form omitted; and if one proceeds from an invalid citation, the process is null, as in the law and noted in the Code, *de accusationibus*, l. 4. Moreover, I have said that an undiscussed process is invalid and must be reformed by the office of the judge. Digest, *si mulier ventris nomine*, l. 1, § *debet*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If two persons have received an emphyteusis, so that upon the death of the males it shall pass to one female, and if one of them dies leaving a male heir, while the other dies leaving a female heir, is the female admitted, or the male collateral relative?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Emphyteusis, which Angelus and Peter received for themselves and their male descendants, and upon the death of both, namely one with his male children, and after the other dies with the female, their portion goes to that female, and not to the collaterals. The sole text, very notable, in column 10, *de duobus fratribus a capitaneo investitis*, c. *duo fratres*. And therefore it could not be reaffirmed to the other to the prejudice of the said daughter. Moreover, the husband may go to dwell with his wife in the house where the wife dwells, and use the wife’s goods, against her will notwithstanding, even though others are in possession together with her, as in D. *de usu et habitatione*, l. *certum*, § *mulieri*. And those not placing [the wife] are liable for disturbance by force. D. *de verbis obligatis*, l. *si stipulatus fuero per te non fieri, quo minus*, where this is expressly proven. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A will in which a posthumous heir is passed over is broken, and it becomes valid if the posthumous heir does not die before the testator according to praetorian law, and it is necessary to apply for possession of goods according to the will; if such application is not made, the estate reverts to intestacy.
casus:
CASE NS. In the name of Christ, amen. The fact is proposed in these writings. Angelus Gabrielis from the commune of Bono, of the district of Saint Peter, of the city of Gubbio, in 1348, in the month of September, made a testament, in which he instituted and substituted, as follows below, namely in all his other goods, movable and immovable, rights, and actions, wherever they are and can be found, and could be, in law and in fact, he instituted Augustinus, his son, as his universal heir; and if the said Augustinus, his son, should die at any time without legitimate and natural children legitimately born from his body, he substituted to himself Marinus Gabrielis, his brother, if he should be alive, otherwise the children of the said Marinus, with this condition added, that the said Augustinus may and can, in cases of his necessity, for debts both of the commune and of other special persons, if it should happen that he incurs them, have recourse to the aforementioned goods, and do with them as necessity requires, etc. And in the same testament he submitted or inserted such a clause, and asserted this to be his last will, which he wished to be valid by the law of testament, and if it were not valid, or would not be valid, by the law of testament, he wished it to be valid by the law of codicils and last will, and in every manner, law, and form by which it can best be valid.

After the said testament was made, in which no mention was made of any posthumous child, or child to be born, the said Angelus is said to have begotten a son and a daughter, and from his marriage a son and a daughter were born, who, namely, the son and daughter born after the said testament, died in infancy. However, there is a dispute between the parties whether they died while the said Angelus, the father, was alive, or afterwards, because it is asserted that the said Angelus died in remote parts, so that the certain time of his death could not and cannot be truly known. It is proposed, however, that the said Angelus and his infant children, of whom mention is made above, born after the said testament was made, died; it is now eight years, or thereabouts, as was said of the death of the said Angelus, which arises otherwise from fame, and the said infant children are asserted to have died ten years ago, or thereabouts. Which died first and which later, this consists in fact, it will appear from the proofs: however, the said Martin, brother of the said testator, the testator himself being alive, died newly, a month ago. The said Augustinus, instituted in the said testament, died, having made a testament, and being in perfect age, who in his testament instituted his mother, Lady Catherine, as his universal heir. And having made the said testament, he died without children.

Now it is asked whether the children of Marinus Gabrielis, aforesaid, who are said to be substituted to the said Augustinus in the testament, can claim the inheritance of the said Angelus, the testator, or a part thereof, by the right of fideicommissum or otherwise, and by what right. And if it is true that the said children, born after the aforementioned testament, died while the said Angelus, the testator, was alive, there does not seem to be doubt that the said testament of Angelus is valid, and at least recovers validity by praetorian law, as in D. *de liberis et posthumis*, l. *posthumus praeteritus*; C. *de posthumis haeredibus institutis*, l. 2, and what is noted there. But if the said children, born after the said testament, died after the father Angelus, there would not seem to be doubt that the said testament is null, unless it is said that it can be defended, either because the aforementioned testament was not declared null, or because the clause “if it will not be valid” was added, etc., as above, so that in the testament itself it claims for itself the place of Auth. *ex causa*, with its material.

But as to the first, namely that the said testament seems to subsist, because it was not declared null, as in D. *de inofficioso testamento*, l. *filio praeterito*, it seems to be answered to the contrary that the said children died in infancy, by C. *de posthumis haeredibus institutis*, l. *uxoris abottu*, which has the place of Auth. *ex causa*, with its material. This made me doubt the opinion of the doctors who wish that the said Auth. does not have place in the omission of a child born while the testator was alive: and also the opinion of those who wished that the said Auth. *ex causa* does not have place in paternal omission, or that made by the father, but in omission made by the mother, or by the maternal line. I also consider another altercation, which was a dispute among the doctors, whether Auth. *ex causa* has place in the omission of a posthumous child, or of one who is in the place of a posthumous, namely one born while the testator was alive after the testament was made, who then does not break the testament, by D. *de inofficioso et irritis testamentis*, l. *posthumus*, ver. *sed hi, qui*, and D. *de lege Velleia*, l. *Gallus*, § *nunc*.

Furthermore, it is asked, since the said testament was not declared null by the said omitted children, whether, things being thus, the fideicommissum left in the said testament by the children of the aforementioned Marinus, by virtue of the aforementioned substitution made to the said Augustinus, can be lost by the heirs of Augustinus, which seems to be the case by the said l. *filio*, there: “if the omitted child, omitted by the father, has claimed a part of the inheritance from his brothers.” It is also asked whether it is true that the testament, which was not declared null by the said omitted children, subsists in law or not, and if it is necessary that it be declared null for the impugning of the said testament, whether the right of declaring it null passed to the mother of the said omitted children. It is also asked whether the right of declaring it null was removed by the lapse of a decade or octennium, which passed from the time of the death of the said Angelus, the testator. Finally, it is asked how the said children of Marinus are to be advised concerning the aforementioned testament of Angelus, etc. I, Baldus.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

A testament in which a posthumous child is omitted is broken by the birth of the posthumous child, as established in *l. Gallus*, § *in omnibus*; § *nunc*; *l. inter cetera*; *de liberis et posthumis*; and *ff. de inofficioso testamento*, *l. posthumorum*; *l. 3*, § *ex his apparet*; *l. nam et si sub conditione*, § *rumpendo*; and *Institutes, de exheredatione liberorum*, § *posthumi*, along with countless similar authorities. However, it is revived by praetorian law if the posthumous child dies while the testator is still alive, according to *ff. de inofficioso testamento*, *l. posthumo*. This is to be understood as follows: if the instituted heir petitions for possession of the estate according to the will within the time limit defined in *l. 1*, § *largius*, *de successione edicto*. Otherwise, if he does not petition according to the will, the matter reverts to the case of intestacy. Therefore, possession of the estate according to the will is necessary in this case, for the inheritance cannot be added from the testament, since civil law opposes it, as fully explained in *l. certum*, *C. unde leges*; *ff. de inofficioso testamento*, *l. qui uxore*; and noted in *l. cum in secundo* and *l. filio praeterito*; and *ff. de vulgari substitutione*, *l. si qui*, with § *ult*. Given, therefore, that the said posthumous children died while their father was alive, if Augustus did not acknowledge the will according to the terms, the testament reverts to the case of intestacy, and the edict applies regarding the institution of the heir and the vulgar substitution. However, regarding the fideicommissary substitution, the testament does not lapse; rather, it remains valid by *auth. ex causa*, as in *ff. ad Trebellianam*, *l. ita tamen*, § *quoties*, where there is the ordinary gloss and the opinion of Jacobus de Arena, who states that *auth. ex causa*, under the words "caetera namque firma permanent" [for the rest remain firm], encompasses a universal fideicommissum, or at least a codicillary petition, which has place even in the omission of a posthumous child. On this point, there is a text singularly noted by Jacobus de Arena in *ff. de fideicommissis liberis*, *l. generaliter*, § *testamento*. If, therefore, the said posthumous children died while their father was alive, and finally the father died, and the father's death is certain, the said mother, after deducting the legitimate portion and the Trebellian share, restores the other half. *c. Ray.*, *c. si pater*, with *si*. § If, however, it is uncertain whether the father has died, no action can be brought under his will. The text is in *C. de captivis*, *l. nec nos*, unless death is proven by indications and reputation, as in *l. 2*, § *si dubitetur*, *ff. quemadmodum testamentum aperiri*. If, however, the posthumous children died after the father was dead, the testament is not revived in this case, as in *C. de posthumis haeredibus institutis*, *l. uxoris hortu*. Rather, these posthumous children were intestate heirs, as in *l. 1*, in fine, *ff. si tabulae nullae extant*, and they transmitted [their rights] to the father and mother, as in *ff. de militum testamento*, *l. ex militari*, § *si*, with the following law; *de Castrensi peculio*, *l. haeredes*, § *filius*; and *l. apud hostes*; *ff. de stipulatione servo*, *l. liber homo*, § *ult*. And in this case, because these posthumous children were not burdened in any way, but only Augustinus was named as burdened, the portions of these posthumous children do not fall into the fideicommissum, as in *ff. de iure codicillorum*, *l. si is, qui*; *ff. de legatis 2*, *l. cum pater*, § *cum aestimaret*. For by *auth. ex causa*, one is not burdened either by proper name or by appellative name, but the portion of Augustinus falls into the fideicommissum, because he was burdened by name under his proper name by those words, "and if the said Augustinus, his son, etc." This is noted in *Institutes, de pupillari substitutione*, § *extraneo*; and in *l. precibus*; and in *l. Centurio*. If, however, it is uncertain whether the posthumous child or the father died first, it must be said that regularly he who bases himself on the order of time must prove the time, as noted in *ff. de negotiis gestis*, *l. eum actum*; *C. de probationibus*, *l. matrem tuam*. Hence, it seems that a better composition of the matter is that, in a doubtful matter, favor should be given rather to the defendant than to the plaintiff. However, this rule seems to fail in favor of the fideicommissum, so that in doubt it is presumed in favor of the fideicommissum regarding the order of death, as in *ff. ad Trebellianam*, *l. ex facto*, § *si quis rogatus*, ver. *cum aut suus*, where there is a foreign text. And to the same effect, *ff. de sequestratis tabulis*, *l. qui ex liberis*, in principle. But the preceding opinion seems safer, that the plaintiff must bear the burden of proof, *ff. ad Trebellianam*, *l. eum, qui novissimus*, since here the mother opposes, and the fideicommissary has her resisting and objecting. Other points are not necessary, and it suffices to refer to *l. posthumo*, *C. de contractis tabulis*, through the gloss, which is cited by Cynus. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Balde de Perusio, doctor of both laws. And for the faith of this, I have subscribed and signed with the signs of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that nullity may not be raised as an objection and that proceedings may be conducted summarily and without formal joinder of issue, if a judgment is found in which it is stated that the party was summoned to hear the sentence, yet there is no general appearance of citation in the record, whether such a judgment deserves execution. Personal citation is equivalent to presence.
casus: CASE. A sentence is found in which it is stated that a party was cited to hear the sentence, and nothing else appears in the process regarding the citation. It is asked whether it deserves execution, since by statute nullity cannot be opposed, and the matter may proceed summarily and without contestation. This is the point in effect.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Since citation is a matter of fact and an external formality, because it is an act in itself, it is not presumed unless proven; and where no citation has issued, or it was issued less legitimately, the pronouncement does not bind, as noted in C. de accus. l. 4. For since citation is ordered toward defense, and defense is a matter of natural law, no constitution can be established to the contrary, as in c. pastoralis, de re iudic. in 6. However, in very ancient sentences, due to the lack of proof, the doctors say that it is presumed that the sentence was rendered with the probatory and citatory means observed; which is reported by Cynus in C. de fidei. instrum. l. emancipatione, and by Innocentius in de offi. deleg. c. cum in iure, and by the Speculum in de fid. instru. §. restat, versi. in summa. Nevertheless, we are not in this case, because the time of twenty years is not very ancient, and is contained within the easy memory of men; clear proofs according to the natural course can be had. But that is considered very ancient, concerning which memory cannot easily be had according to the common retention or life of men, as in ff. de probat. l. si arbiter, and in Auth. et constitutio innovat constitutionem, in princ., col. 9. And although the notary attests to the citation, he does not attest to the relation, which is of the substance, as noted by Bartolus in l. multum, de cond. et dem. Moreover, what the notary says is rather renunciatory than solemn, because as regards the citation it does not contain the place or time, and thus it does not have the solemnities of instruments, as noted in c. quam contra falsam, in Novell. Bartolus says that he who seeks to execute a sentence must produce it, otherwise produce the sentence and the acts, ff. de re iudic. l. si cum nulla, unless the sentence was rendered between those present with a mention of the acts, and no appeal was taken, ff. de re iudic. ar., C. de relatione, l. 1, ff. quando appel. sit. l. 1. Furthermore, although one may proceed de facto, nevertheless one cannot judge without hearing the proofs, de const. c. ecclesia sanctae Mariae. But here nothing is shown to be proven, and a judge, to whom nothing is proven, can command nothing, C. de compens. l. 1, de sen. excomm. c. solet, per Innocentius. Indeed, more so, because here the petition is not shown, therefore also c. de fidei. liber. l. 1. Since the day of production is not shown, as in Auth. offeratur. It is true that Innocentius in c. Albericus, de restit. dicit, that if in the instrument there is mention of solemnities and citation, everything is presumed to have been done solemnly. And the same is said there by Johannes Andreae. And it supports what is noted in C. de fid. instr. et iur. hastae fisca. l. 1, lib. 10. And this can be sustained as regards the citation, because it could have been done then for then, since he was cited personally, according to the note by Innocentius in de accus. c. ad peti. But as regards the acts, which cannot be done in the same context, the instrument is not believed, as noted in the said c. quam contra falsam, per Innocentius and Hostiensis and Johannes Andreae. For although the statute does not require judicial order and style, it does require that the wrong be committed, or at least proven as such, as in l. 1, §. illud, ff. ad Sil. Elsewhere Innocentius says that in arbitrations it is presumed for the judge, de eo, qui furti. ordi. susce. c. innotuit. But this is committed to the discretion of the judge not only equitable, but mere and absolute; therefore, the judge’s command must be followed, ff. de offic. praesid. l. illicitas, §. ne potentiores, ff. de offic. procu. Caes. l. 1. And although the proof is not shown, the definitive command is not vitiated, ff. fa. her. l. computarent, ff. de pecu. l. eo tempore. I do not say that anything is presumed concerning the proofs, because citation cannot be presumed, since it is of different kinds; but it is presumed concerning the existence of the sentence: because the statute says that nullity cannot be opposed. Here one must think sufficiently for and against, for this sentence has the form of a sentence from its own series, C. de sen. ex peric. reci. l. 2, de falsis. Nor is the example helped by the statute, which excludes the objection of nullity; therefore, it must be executed. But it is difficult to answer the contrary arguments. Finally, I think, always saving the substance of the truth, that since there was a personal citation, which is equivalent to presence, as in Auth. qua in provincia, and because the statute presumes much for the judge, so that just as a present person who did not contradict seems to have confirmed the assertions, so this most true contumacious person, and thus some presumption is to be made, and it is to be committed to execution by common law and the disposition of the statute joined together. Someone will say, without a preceding process, he is cited personally to hear the sentence; he is cited to an impossibility; therefore, he is not bound to appear, nor is he contumacious due to the express defect of the citation, ff. iudic. sol. l. vir bonus, and in c. 1, de dilationibus, per Innocentius. But I answer, it would be true if negligence were proven, but here it does not appear that it did not precede, and it is presumed to have preceded, as is clear from what has been said, lest the way of saying null be opened, which way is precluded by the statute, which must be observed as it lies, according to the form of another statute; otherwise it would be different under mere common law. Hence, it should be known that either by statute discretion is granted, and the statute does not proceed further, and then by such a statute the party’s messenger is harmed, nor is it presumed against justice, de donat. l. filius, per Bartolus, de admin. tut. l. impuberi filio centurio. Or discretion is granted, the statute presumes for him, and then the burden of proof is transferred to the other party, ar. de leg. 1, l. licet imperator. Or discretion is granted, and it is established for him, and then, provided the words of the statute and its form are observed, one must acquiesce as to the sentence of the law, against which there is no recourse, l. prospexit improba. But since discretion is granted, it is presumed for him, and it is established for him, inasmuch as it is not permitted to say it is unjust or void, sic, ff. de manum. test. l. qui habebat, de except. cum. c. ecclesiasticis, in c. 1, de seques. poss. et fruc. in 6. And the foregoing are confirmed by the example of those in which discretion is granted without writing, in which Bartolus says that the judge’s assertion is believed, C. de sententiis, ex peric. reci. auth. nisi breviores. Also by the example of decrees, for behold, he gives this precept more by decree than definitively, and in interposed decrees solemnities are presumed, as noted in the Speculum in de emph. et ven. §. nunc dicendum, ver. et habetur, and l. si quis missus, ne vis fiat ei, h.C.I.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, by the very fact that it disposes of the succession, it also disposes of the tutelage.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

The statute, which I have seen, speaks of successions, but does not expressly speak of guardianships, as far as I have read; hence there arises a tacit question concerning the tacit understanding of the statute: whether, by the very fact that it disposes of succession, it also disposes of guardianship. And it seems that it does so, by the general rule. D. de regulis iuris, l. quo tutela. By necessary and probable interpretation, as in Inst. de legatis, patrono, tute., §. sed quia, from the express case of the law. Because even a law coming corruptively, by correcting preceding laws in successions, corrects in guardianships, as in Auth. de hereditatibus ab intestato, §. ex his, ex summa prudentia, because, since one hopes for succession, one should guard against the dissipation of goods. D. de legatis, tuto., l. 1. And because whenever something is corrected from which another thing depends, that which depends is also seen to be corrected, as in C. de latiniis, liberis, toleratis, l. 1, in principio. But guardianships are as it were appendages of successions. I believe the contrary to be truer, for this would be to interpret the statute extensively, correctively, and abusively, which would be to interpret [it improperly]; the case and text are in the said §. sed quia. But that this would be an extensive interpretation is clear, for it extends to another matter. Likewise, that it would be a corrective interpretation is clear, because common law is corrected, since it abolished the distinction of agnation and cognation; but this ought not to be done, as noted in Auth. quas actiones, non obstantibus, §. ex his. For there the law proceeds further by correcting even in guardianships, as is clear in the word “sancimus.” Likewise, that the interpretation is also abusive is clear, for if guardianship were conferred in that manner, one would be the guardian of paternal property, another of maternal property, which is absurd, as in l. certarum, de testamento, tute., C. de nuptiis, l. in copulandis. Wherefore, in guardianship we shall observe common law, and the nearest in degree from whichever side shall be guardian, if otherwise suitable, as in the said §. ex his, computing the degree according to civil law, by which law, as many persons as there are, excluding the stock, so many degrees of collaterals there are, and in this one cannot err. Therefore, whoever is nearest, he is preferred, by whatever name he may be called, and from whichever side he takes his origin. And thus I hold and conclude, although the most eloquent advocates on both sides made very beautiful allegations, as is their custom.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In what ways is minority of age to be proved.
2. Reason, and the cause of knowledge, limits, modifies, and restricts the statement of the witness.
3. Testimony of one's own hearing is admitted.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The witnesses and the attestations of the witnesses produced on behalf of Angelo Maffioli of Foligno, examined both in the first and second instance, and produced to prove the minority of the said Catherine and others, having been consulted, whether the said witnesses prove the alleged minority on behalf of the said Angelo.

I premise that reason, and the gloss, limits, modifies, and restricts the said statement. L. Quod dictum, De pactis; L. Adigere, §. Quamvis, De iure patronatus; noted in L. Solam, C. De testibus, together with the authorities cited. And therefore the judge ought to interrogate the witness regarding the cause, and the witness, when interrogated, ought to give the cause of his statement; otherwise the testimony is not valid. The text is noted Extra, De testibus, C. Cum causam, there: "de causa," etc., and there the good gloss; and in the Authenticum, De testibus, in the Corpus, §. Et licet, and there the gloss; and it is noted in the Digest, De transactionibus, L. Cum hi, §. Nihil autem, vers. In causa, etc.; and it is contained in the aforementioned L. Solam. Hence it is that we adhere rather to reason than to the bare statement, as per the said laws, and it is the text in the Digest, De testibus, L. 3, in fine, there: "ad ea, quae interrogaueras," as in L. Ob carmen, §. Si testes, in fine, of the same title.

Having premised these things, I say, as a matter of law, that although witnesses ought to give the cause of their statement through bodily sense, namely a congruent and necessarily concluding one, as in L. Testium, C. De testibus; and in the Authenticum, De his quae veluti falsa, §. Si vero adsunt, col. 1; and the aforementioned C. Cum causam, in the text there: "auditu, visu, et credulitate," etc.; and testimony based on credulity is not readily admitted in a witness, as in the aforementioned §. Si vero, with the authorities noted there; nevertheless, that is true in those matters which can truly be perceived and proved by witnesses through bodily sense; otherwise in those matters which are perceived solely by the judgment of the intellect and are difficult to prove, as is the case in question, namely regarding age. L. Minor 25 annorum ex aspectu, Digest, De minoribus. And although Bartolus in L. De aetate, Digest, De minoribus, posits several modes of proving age; nevertheless, as regards the proposition, I say that the minority of age of the said Do. Catherina was proved by the witnesses of the said Angelo. The first witnesses, almost all of them, deposed that the said Do. Catherina at the time contained in the article was under 25 years of age. Interrogated regarding the cause of their knowledge, they say that they saw her at the time in question and before, and that by their sight, judgment, and aspect of her body, she was a minor. This proof suffices in the cause of knowledge. Digest, De minoribus, L. Minor 25 annorum ex aspectu, and there the text. And although it speaks of judgment, nevertheless the gloss there in L. De aetate, of the same title, and there the doctor and Bartolus hold that the same applies to a witness. Nor does it avail that any of the said witnesses at the beginning of their statement say that they "believe," etc., because afterwards they express the qualification and declare their statement by the reason premised, to which we adhere. And principally this mode of proving is posited and held by Bartolus in the aforementioned L. De aetate. Indeed, more so, because the said Do. Bella and several other witnesses, on the third article, say that if she were alive today, she would not be of the age of 18 years, much less 25. And thus she is optimally proved, because she posits the descent of time noted for proving one to be under 25 years, by Bartolus magisterially in the aforementioned L. De aetate, namely five years, which they subjoin to the first statement. L. Etiam monachis professio, and there the gloss there: "vel dictum," etc., Digest, De testibus; and the same gloss in L. Parentes, Codex, of the same title; and Bartolus in the aforementioned L. De aetate. Nor does it avail that his testimony is added,

† Because although testimony based on what one has heard from another is generally rejected, unless in certain cases, testimony based on one’s own direct hearing is admitted and valid, as stated in the cited chapter *Cum causam*, in the text of the law *De audita*, and in the gloss thereon, as fully explained by Bartolus in the same place, in law 1, § *Idem Labeo*, D. *De aqua pluviae arcendae*; and by Cynus in the Code, *De testibus*, law *Testamentum*; and there also by Jacobus de Arena and by Innocentius in the cited chapter *Cum causam*; and specially in the title *De testibus*, § *Unde*, etc. And because such deposition is admitted from a witness, especially in this case, where proof is difficult and one cannot easily know the truth, as in law 1, in the principle, D. *De ventre inspiciendo*, and where Bartolus notes such testimony in the cited § *Si vero assuit*, D. *De haereditate et falsis*; and in the cited law *Testium*, Bartolus holds in the cited § *Idem Labeo*. By this, I introduce the small but notable gloss in law *Si quis Firmio*, near the beginning, D. *Ad legem Aquiliam*, on the word *videbatur*; and the gloss in law *Utrum*, in the principle, D. *De rebus dubiis*; and *De excusationibus tutorum*, law 1, in the principle, and there by Bartolus, alias Baldus, who make a remarkable point. Moreover, at least such a statement induces a presumption, as the cited gloss in law *Si quis Firmio* states, which presumption shall stand until the contrary is proven, according to the text of law *Non est verisimile*, with its gloss, D. *Quod metus causa*, *De homine libero exhibendo*, law 3, § *Si*, *Cum si*. This presumption is aided by other presumptions, because it is presumed that the person was a minor, since he was otherwise, as noted in the gloss in law *De aetate*. Furthermore, because the said lady was a minor, Lady Marina proves this through witnesses received in the second place, who do not say directly and necessarily that they saw her being nursed and fed by a wet-nurse, and that she was then two years of age, which follows, because children are nursed during such a time, C. *De patria potestate*, law *Nec filium*; D. *De negotiis gestis*, law *Vel alimenta*. When questioned about the time, he says that it was after the year of mortality, which was in 1363. And thus, by making a common calculation of years up to the year of the death of the said lady, it necessarily follows that she was under 25 years of age. This is the mode of proving age, which is necessarily more certain, as explained by the said Bartolus in the cited law *De aetate*, where he treats it fully. Therefore, having reduced the statements of the witnesses and their attestations to one point, I say that minority has been sufficiently proven by the said witnesses, concerning whom also Bartolus notes in law 1, D. *Si certum petatur*, *Audito aetate*, that the party swore to supplement the proof, which could lawfully be deferred by the judge, both at the request of the party and ex officio, as noted in the cited law *Admonendi*, D. *De iureiurando*, and even after the publication of the proceedings. And the same is noted by the said Bartolus and Baldus. And thus, on the foregoing, I advise in law, I, Peter of Asti, Doctor of Laws, to whose faith I have subscribed with my own hand and signed with my usual sign. And thus, as advised above by the eminent Doctor of Laws, Master Peter, I also say and advise, I, Julianus Bini of Perugia, Doctor of Laws. In testimony of which, I have subscribed and signed with my sign.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Witnesses, by stating that someone is a minor, can provide a reason based on appearance.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† From the bodily appearance of a boy, which differs greatly from that of a perfect man, a boy is well recognized by a direct or intuitive cognition. And therefore a reason can be given by parts regarding the appearance, which naturally demonstrates younger age, nor is it called a judgment, but rather sight, if the quality of the appearance naturally demonstrates this, as in the Institution, Quiibus modis tut. finitur, in the beginning; or the counting of years declares this. And because it has been sufficiently alleged by the consultants, I do not allege further, because they speak the truth having seen the acts. I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws, advise the same, and I have subscribed to the faith and signed with the signs of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an heir who has not made an inventory with the legal solemnity is bound to pay legacies in full, and number 2.
2. The inventory of a legatee does not benefit the heir.
3. If the testator bequeaths alimony to his wife, what kind of alimony is due if the heir has not made an inventory.
casus:
CASE

In the name of Christ, Amen. And of His Glorious Virgin Mother Mary. The case ought to be proposed thus, namely, that Jacobus de Faitano, a nobleman of the city of Rimini, having a son from his first marriage, namely Mugiolus, the elder; and a son, namely Annibal, a capable pupil; and daughters from a third marriage contracted between him and my noble lady, made his last will and testament; in which he instituted the aforementioned sons, namely Mugiolus and Annibal, as his universal heirs, and instituted his said daughters in certain quantities, and made such legacies to my said lady in this form, namely:

Item, he left to my said lady, his wife, by way of legacy, her dowries, which were 5 ducats.

Item, he left to my said lady, his wife, by way of legacy, 100 ducats of gold, which he had received from her from the dowries of the late Lady Isabella, formerly the mother of my said lady.

Item, he left to my said lady, his wife, decent alimony from his goods, as long as she shall have observed and maintained a widowed and chaste life, and dwelt with his said heirs; and if she should not wish to stand and dwell, or should not be able to live with his said heirs, the said testator willed that she should have and receive the said legacies from his said heirs. And the said testator died. After his death, my said lady, his wife, as she was bound, made an inventory, as is contained in the positions and responses.

After the said Mugiolus by himself, and the said Annibal, a pupil, with the authority of the tutor appointed in the testament, had entered upon the paternal inheritance without the benefit of an inventory. After the tutor of the said Annibal made an inventory with his own hand, as is contained in the positions, and also the inventory of the tutors, as he is bound by law. And afterwards the said tutor divided the said inheritance with the said Mugiolus, brother of the said pupil. Afterwards my said lady demanded the said dowries for half from the said Mugiolus, and similarly the quantity of the legacies; and also the aforementioned alimony against the said Mugiolus, as is contained in her petition, which we send enclosed.

Afterwards exceptions were made on the part of the said Mugiolus, which we also send with these allegations. And afterwards in the proceedings on the part of my said lady, among other things, it was opposed to these chapters alleged, and on the adverse part it was responded to the said positions, as appears in his response. After the aforesaid, positions and chapters were deduced on the part of the said Mugiolus in this form, and his responses by my said lady, as is contained at the end of them, and proofs were made by witnesses, whose statements and attestations we similarly transmit enclosed in words.

Now the controversy remains concerning the aforementioned alimony; it is only asked, what are the parts now in passing sentence.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be considered that there are certain legacies which have a certain quantity or species, as when ten [units of currency] are bequeathed, or a farm, or Stichus. And in these cases there is no doubt that the heir, who does not make an inventory with the legal solemnity, is bound to pay the full legacies, save that the son, or another to whom a legitime is due, deducts the legitime, as noted in the Authenticum de haereditatibus et falcidia, §. si quis autem non implens, on the word "auferri" [to be taken away], and in §. sancimus. And this is so, in order that heirs burdened [by legacies] may be deprived of the opportunity to commit fraud and to conceal hereditary property and assets to the prejudice of legatees, as the text says there on the word "suscipiunt" [they accept]. Hence, against one who does not make an inventory, dolus [fraud], subtraction, and malice are presumed. And because the law bases its statute on this presumption, it may be called a presumption of law, and one arising by operation of law. And although this is the reason of the letter [of the law], yet, even if this reason ceases to apply, the heir who did not make an inventory is still punished for his negligence and contempt of the benefit of the law. Suppose, moreover, that due to the absence of hereditary assets the heir could not have subtracted anything; nevertheless, the law constrains him to make an inventory, because he who does not make an inventory cannot have the benefit of the inventory. Codex, de iure deliberandi, l. si, §. si autem a locis, and §. cum, n. gemini.

† Certain legacies do not have a fixed quantity, but must be determined according to the quantity of the assets and the means of the testator, in accordance with the intent of both the law and the testator, as is the case with a legacy of alimony, concerning which it is asked, as in D. de alim. legat. l. cum unus. §. alimentis. This was estimated according to the means, dignity, and number of children. arg. D. de leg. 3. l. si filiae pater. and salva rerum substantia. i. from the fruits and revenues of the inheritance. For if a legacy of usufruct, which is more substantial, is understood to be salva rerum substantia, then much more so is a legacy of alimony. D. ubi pupillus educari de l. ius alimentorum. For this was also the custom of the testator. s. to live from the fruits, which ought to be observed. D. de alim. lega. l. mela. §. j. D. de vino lega. l. ex usu. Therefore, the wife is to be treated honorably. D., de leg. 3. l. item in legato. §. parui. however, according to ability, and it is not said that one can do what is beyond one's power, non obst. de ven. in poss. mit. l. 1. §. mulier. and §. diminutio. and de carbo. edic. l. 3. §. an descendi. because there it is understood that one lives from one's own, not from another's. nec ob. de praediis minorum. c. obest. in glo. because there it is promised, not enforced, if it is necessary to alienate the substance and remain stripped. D. qui bo. ce. poss. l. qui bonis. which is the law noted for this purpose. and there by Bar. Therefore, in the case at hand, for one says that an inheritance is wealthy for the solid provision of alimony, which proves due to presumption and legal disposition, as d. §. sancimus.

† Nor does the inventory of the woman avail Mugiolo, because in case of doubt, although the form due for an heir’s inventory is lacking, and perfunctory inventories do not avail, only solemn ones do. C. de iure deliberandi, l. si, §. et si praefatam, in the word, solidauerunt. Moreover, the woman could have acted in good faith, and yet Mugiolo could have concealed assets, as in ff. de pactis, l. tres fratres. Moreover, the matter and confession were conducted between other parties. ff. de in rem actionibus, l. si. And although no immovable property appears, many items could have been unlisted and among things capable of being concealed, as in l. 2, C. quoniam, and qui, quar. pars debetur, lib. 10, l. iniuriarum. Natural equity supports this, because the mistress ought not to be heard alleging that there is more in the estate than in the description, against her own inventory. Her own mandate and concealment are alleged to this effect. C. de arbitrio tutoris, l. si. C. ad Velleianam, l. antiqua. Not without shame does he desire this. ff. de usuris, l. in fideicommissis, §. si. And although the law presumes theft, it can be proven by the concession of the mistress. C. de donationibus ante nuptias, auth. sed iam necesse. And note in Auth. de aequalitate dotis, §. aliud, on the word, scribit. And the testator intended that more be provided than the assets allow, concerning which he also decreed that the children be supported, since he left maintenance for the woman together with them. Nor is it credible that the father intended otherwise, especially because a stepmother ought not to be in a better condition than a stepson, as in l. hac edictali causa, C. de secundis nuptiis. And although the testator, who possessed the dowry, was to provide more generous maintenance, this was because he possessed the dowry; now, however, he is very poor in assets; and therefore the maintenance was to be more meager. ff. de petitione hereditatis, l. si lege, §. si quis, and §. quod autem id, quod totum. Considering all the assets, the judge will arbitrate, so that neither the burdensome woman nor the delicate heir be heard. ff. de pignoratitia actione, l. si seruos pignoratos. I do not say that the edict de alterutro applies here, as in C. de rei uxoriae actione, l. sciendum, but that the maintenance be generous or meager according to the capacity of the true, and not fictitious, patrimony, having regard to the revenues and profits, saving the substance of the ownership, just as if he had left the wife full usufruct, as in l. 1, ff. de usufructu, magis. Note that a legacy of maintenance is considered more binding than a general legacy of usufruct. C. si secundo nupta mulier, l. 1. ff. de usufructu legato, l. uxori. And thus we, the written consultants, have said, joining equity to rigor, principally for three reasons: first, from the condition of the person, because a stepmother, as in l. hac edictali, cannot under the pretext of an inventory not made absorb the entire patrimony; which would be light in the mouths of the indebted. Second, by taxing the maintenance according to the quantity of the patrimony. For if the testator commanded that legacies not be paid beyond the strength of the patrimony, the heir will never be bound beyond that, even if he does not make an inventory. arg. ff. de negotiorum gestione, l. qui aliena, §. libertos. But this taxation is tacitly contained in the legacy of maintenance, de iudiciis, l. fideicommissum, §. tractatum. Third, from the very truth of the things, it is dictated by the inventory of the wife, to which one must adhere. It is the ordinary gloss in the said l. 2, quando, et qui, quar. pars de, lib. 10, on the verse, iurata fide.

The conclusion is this: that, according to the sufficiency of resources, with the truth weighed, alimony is to be provided in a moderate manner. Hence, if the inheritance yields three eggs, because there are three persons whose alimony the testator had in mind, the wife ought to have one egg, of which the stepson ought to pay half. But it ought not be that he lives and the stepmother dies; for other goods whatsoever that the stepmother has are not considered, but are circumscribed. Nor ought it be that the stepmother lives happily and prospers, while the testator’s son dies of hunger; for if the father had been asked about this, he would have wished it so; and it is presumed that he would have wished what he would have answered if asked. D. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. finalis nisi de hoc, ubi de hoc. Therefore, as has been said, let division be made among the said instituted heirs and the stepmother, even if there were only a single sextarius of wheat. And if she cannot keep servants, let her not keep them; and the stepson, if he has children, let him labor to support them, just as he labored for pleasures. D. de falcidia hereditatis, l. si maritus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Debts and the legitime are deducted before all legacies.
2. One who has a legitime must also have the fruits of the legitime.
3. One who makes an inventory on account of the legitime does not incur the penalty imposed on one who makes an inventory.
4. The testator cannot prevent the usufructuary from being sued, if the thing is mismanaged.
5. No one can be restored to his birthright by statute.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

†. Regarding the first point, it must be said that, before all else, the testator’s debts must be deducted from the legacies, and thus the dowry of the said Do. Nicolutia. C. de leg. l. si vniuersae. Likewise, before the legitime. ff. de inoffi. testa. l. Papinianus. §. quarto. And therefore the said Evangelista and John must have the said dowry of their curator before all else. Likewise, they must have the legitime and the fruits of the legitime, expressly noted. ff. de vsufruc. leg. l. vexori.

For a legitimate portion must never be without fruits, even if the heir sui heredes has full ownership of the goods. The statute is not an obstacle, because it does not speak of a testamentary succession, but of an intestate one. Nor are the brothers an obstacle. And this concludes the first points.

† On the second point, I say that they did not incur the penalty by requesting that an inventory be made. For they did this under the pretext of a legitimate right, in which they could not be burdened, nor could a penalty be imposed. D. ad leg. Falcidiam, l. Seius Augerius, where this is expressly stated.

† On the third point, I say that if the dominus is bound, the testator cannot provide that the usufructuary shall not be bound if he makes improper use. The text is explicit. C. si in possessionem leg. l. scire.

† On the fourth point, I say that the statute is invalid as regards a spurious child. On this point, see Jacobus Butrigarius, *De iure annulorum aureo*, l. 1, C. For the rights of birth can be granted by the prince alone; there is the case according to him, and thus holds Bartolus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether and when a substitution made in direct words concerning a specific thing or quantity is extended to the whole estate.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A substitution made with direct words in a certain thing, or quantity, is extended to the whole, just as an institution. D. de vulgari substitutione, l. cohaeredi, §. si. This is true when absurdity does not follow from it. For that which is absurd is not considered to be within the mind of the testator, nor within the mind of the law. Argument: D. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. si non, n. Therefore, it is not necessarily extended to the whole, because the will of the testator does not prevail, as D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. quoties, §. si duo. But it would be absurd that there were so many heirs equally substituted, especially since they are not equally loved, nor equally honored. Hence, it must be said that the conjecture of the will is not extended to the whole; otherwise it would follow that all were heirs in equal parts, although in legacies they were unequal. D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. ex facto. Which is not to be believed to have been within the mind of the testator. Moreover, I hold this from the nature of the words: because the words say, "he is instituted to himself." Although in universal substitution the addition does not restrict it, D. de secundis tabulis, l. si ita, §. si filio, and note in l. 1, D. de vulgari substitutione, nevertheless it is otherwise, because in a certain thing, as C. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. quoties. And because he used the direct word and the common word together, namely "succeed," D. de edendo, l. quaedam, §. is autem, which common word applied to a certain thing is not extended to the whole. D. ad Trebellianum, l. cogi, §. generaliter, and there by Dy. Also, he prefixed the common word to all, when he says, "he made such a substitution and succession." Also, when he wished to substitute in the whole, he expressed it; but where he did not wish, he did not say so, C. de caducis tollendis, l. sin autem ad deficientes. Therefore, it must be concluded that the sister equally related on both sides succeeds the said pupils intestate. It is true that the mother, who remarried, has half the usufruct, as in Auth. ex testamento non obstat statutum; because this is the succession of the brother, not of the father. D. de vulgari substitutione, l. sed si plures, §. filio. It is similar. D. de inofficiosis testamentis, l. Papinianus, §. sed nec impuberis. For the statute must be understood as concerning immediate succession, not mediate. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A donation propter nuptias is not presumed to have been transferred by the husband to the wife in an amount equal to the dowry.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Because if the donation propter nuptias were constituted as true and made by full delivery from the husband, it would follow in the wife, in an equal quantity of the dowry, an absurdity: namely, that the dowry would bring no benefit to the husband. The words of the instrument must therefore be understood correctly. Namely, that the donation was made by constitution, not by delivery, and designatively, not traditively; and therefore it suffices for the husband to raise the exception that he does not owe, nor should he be asked for what he does not have, nor do his heirs have it. This is on account of the gloss on the Institutes, De donationibus, §. Est et aliquid, in the gloss on the word "exequatur," there, n. no., expressly stating that such a donation remains in the possession of the husband, and he enjoys the fruits thereof; therefore, even in money, he retains dominion for himself, because the usufruct of money savors of dominion. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The appellate judge, declaring the procedure to have been conducted improperly, and the sentence therefore void, because a sentence is rendered with a less than legitimate respondent, and the entire procedure is null.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

Having examined the judgment, the appellate judge, who declares that the procedure was conducted improperly and the judgment invalid because it was rendered against a less than legitimate responsible party, and thus not only is the judgment void but the entire procedure as well, must require the plaintiff to commence the action anew from the beginning, as provided in C. de procu. l. licet and C. quo. et quando iudex. l. si vt proponis. For the defect lies not only in the judgment but also in the acts and the procedure. Hence, the lord cannot base his claim on the annulled procedure; rather, the libel must be filed anew from the beginning, and he does not enjoy the benefit of the inventory, which he possessed for a year without having made an inventory: because by possessing and enjoying the estate, he acted as an heir, and the time for making the inventory has elapsed, as stated in l. fi. C. de iu. delib. and ff. de ac. hęred. l. per haeredem. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A confession between a father and a son in his power is valid, especially in the case of a dowry.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† This confession was valid, even between father and son in power, as C. de bonis quae lib. l. cum oportet. §. si autem re. But because it was made for life, it does not exceed, but after death in the manner of a concession. ff. de pac. l. epistola. §. fi. However, through this instrument, a certain confession is induced, and through confession, proof is induced. ff. deposi. l. publica. §. fi. And this confession is valid between father and son, especially in dowry. ff. fa. her. l. Pomponius. Hence it is proven that Casaleno was dotal: nevertheless, necessary and useful expenses must be returned to the heirs of the messenger. ff. de impen. l. 1. et l. quod dicatur. It is also proven that the vineyard was purchased with dotal money, the quantity of which appears upon viewing the purchase instrument. And that quantity must be refunded to the daughter of Luici, unless the property was also made part of the dowry in substitution. C. de rei ven. l. si vt proponis. Because then it would have been united to the said daughter and heir of Luici. I, Bal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that contracts for which the tax has not been paid are null, if someone has sold and delivered the thing, he may claim it back on the pretext of the unpaid tax.
2. A contract is null wherever it is so by reason of public utility; it may nevertheless be said to be null through action, even if the fault is equal on the part of the plaintiff and the defendant.
3. When delicts concern nullity, common fault may be alleged by way of nullity.
4. The nullity of a contract is a certain penalty, which is incurred in its entirety by reason of the unpaid portion.
5. No credit is given to a notary who has not been appointed, where the case is of such a nature as to require a certain and appointed notary.
6. Things alienated in contravention of a prohibition made in favor of public utility cannot be acquired by prescription.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† That it cannot be alleged in bringing an action for an unpaid tax, as declared: because, where both parties are equally at fault, or in cases of death, the position of the plaintiff is worse than that of the defendant. D. de verb. oblig. l. si servum, § sequitur; and D. sol. matr. l. cum mulier, and l. viro, atque uxore; D. ne quis eum, l. nam cum uterque; D. de except. doli, l. apud Celsum, § Marcellus; D. de dolo, § si duo; D. de re iud. l. cum par, § illi; and Extr. de priv. c. petistis, and c. quod nonnullis; and Extr. de usuris, c. quia frustra; C. de inoff. test. l. in arenam.

To the contrary, it seems that the contract is void by operation of law, and by the rule that ownership cannot be transferred by a prohibiting law, the thing can therefore be vindicated from any possessor: although the plaintiff and defendant are in equal fault, the existence of the thing does not exclude the vindication. To this effect is what is noted in a similar case, D. de cond. ob turp. causam, l. 2, § 1. Therefore, neither this preamble and preparatory step to the vindication, in which it is sought to have the contract declared null, is excluded; just as a will can be declared null by petitioning for its nullity, so too can a contract, according to the notes on the doctrine in D. quae sub conditione, § si, de cond. inst. For such a declaration depends on the jurisdiction of the parties, and thus can be sought in court. To this effect is what Innocentius notes in c. 2, de confirm. utili, vel inutili; C. de decur. l. si quis, lib. 10.

Solution.

† Wherever a contract is void by reason of public utility, it may be said to be void in an action, even though the fault of the plaintiff and the defendant is equal. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. Senatus, ver. Plane. And so it is here: because this statute was made in favor of the tax; nor is there here any turpitude, but rather an omission of form and of a certain substantial preamble. And thus the laws which speak of the compensation of delicts do not stand in the way.

† Moreover, when the offenses pertain to nullity, the common conjunction may be alleged by way of nullity. D. de contrah. empt. l. domus, in fine. Although he who incurred the penalty and contemned the law to the contrary cannot bring an action for the penalty. And thus is the response to the first doubt.

† To the second doubt, it is answered that the contract is null in its entirety, because this nullity is a certain penalty which is incurred in whole on account of the part not having been paid, ff. fam. ercisc. l. haeredes. §. idem iuris.

† To the third doubt, it is answered that no notary other than the one appointed is believed, for this is the right of the fisc, l. in fraudem, § neque; and because it was not by right that the solution was given, de prob., c. quoniam, according to Innocentius.

† To the fourth point, it is answered that, since alienation is prohibited in favor of and with respect to public utility, namely, the collection of the tax, such things cannot be acquired by prescription, as stated in the law *Quemadmodum*, Codex, *De agris et censibus*, Book 10. Nevertheless, the price received must be restored, as provided in the Digest, *De rescindenda venditione*, law *Fundus*, and the aforementioned law *Senatus*.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether and when a favor expires by acceptance.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† By the most holy father in Christ, our lord Urban, by divine providence Pope VI, it was provided and mandated to certain executors appointed to John Mascii of Perugia, a poor cleric and rector of the church of Saint Nicholas of Perugia, which church has meager fruits, as is contained in the letters. Regarding the benefit, it pertains to the college and the chapter, which he was to accept within a month from the day of notice of the vacancy, with the usual clauses according to the form of the chapter *cum ei, quem*, § *secus autem*, on the grant of prebends in the clergy, as is more seriously contained in the apostolic letters. Finally, when the church of Saint Lucy of Perugia, pertaining to the aforementioned collation, became vacant, the said John accepted it, not knowing that it had been granted in the meantime to any other priest by the ordinary collators. After a process was conducted by the executors, an appeal was made to the Apostolic See. Seeing, therefore, that the said acceptance would not have final effect, both on account of his poverty and on account of the power of the collator, he renounced the said acceptance, asserting together with the conferring chapter that he had no right. The executor thus declared it so. When another benefit became vacant anew, he accepted it. It is asked whether he can do so, or whether his grace has completely expired.

And it is certain that sometimes the first acceptance is void by law, and then the grace does not expire, as shown by the argument in the Digest, *De iureiurando*, law *Qui per salutem*, and in the Digest, *De legatis primo*, law *Servi electione*, and fully by Innocentius, *De officio*, *De legatis*, chapter *In literis*. Sometimes it is valid by law, but the execution of the fact is quasi impossible. And then some say that he can accept again, because the Pope does not intend to make the grace a mockery and of no effect. Others say that the election expires where the option holds by law. Johannes Andreae says that the first opinion is more equitable, the second more true, as in the said chapter *In literis*. And in the new law I say that either he knew only the difficulty arising, and let him impute it to himself, or he was ignorant, otherwise he would not have accepted if he had known; and then he can choose again, by argument from the Digest, *De fideicommissis*, law *Qui satis* and law *Quaesitum*, when the action for the peculium is annual. And in doubt, ignorance is presumed, Digest, *De probationibus*, law *Verius*.

Sometimes the first acceptance is doubtful, and the matter is sub judice, whether it is valid or not. I say then that a good man, especially a poor one, can pursue the litigation, and having abandoned it, can turn to a new peaceful election, nor is he to be blamed for this, but praised, by argument from the Digest, *De alienis iudiciis*, law *Item si res*, § *Si*. Furthermore, since it was pronounced by the will of the parties that the acceptance does not hold, rightly the pronouncement must be stood by between the parties, Digest, *De re iudicata*, law *Si convenerit*. Nor does the renunciation stand in the way, because it was not general, but regarding the benefit accepted; hence it does not extend further, as in the Code, *Ad Velleianum*, law *Iubemus*. And because the grace endures, even while the executors endure.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A mother may declare a will null when she has been passed over; this right takes the place of the ancient querela (complaint of inofficiousness); and therefore, by accepting a legacy, the will remains valid.
2. A will made in the country is not valid with a lesser number of witnesses when the defendant is near a place of jurisdiction.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A mother who has been passed over may declare the will null, as stated in the Authentica *Ut cum* on the cognition of appeals, § *Aliud quoque capitulum*. Nevertheless, this right to declare nullity succeeds in place of the ancient querela inofficiosi testamenti (complaint of an undutiful will) regarding the passing over of the mother, even though such passing over is considered equivalent to disinheritance. And therefore, if she has acknowledged the will, namely if it has the lawful number of witnesses:

But in this will there are only five witnesses, and therefore it is not valid as a will. Nor does it matter that it was made in the country. C. de testamentis, l. fin. If the rural place is near a place of law, as there, it is still not valid as a codicil, because the mother is owed her legitime, and the Trebellian [portion] is calculated for all intestate heirs; the institution is known. It is converted into a fideicommissum. C. de fideicommis, l. eam, quam, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a mother, appointed guardian of her children jointly with the testator, is bound to make an inventory and not to render an account, provided that she is bound and ought to administer the said estate in good faith and with the consent of the testator’s carnal brothers; and whether, if the said form is disregarded, the mother may accept the guardianship and appoint a representative at her own risk.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

Having seen the testament of a layman, in which he leaves Lady Langueta, his wife, as guardian of Drusiana, their common daughter, stipulating that she is not bound to make an inventory, nor to render an account, provided that she is bound and ought to conduct said administration in good faith with the consent and will of the testator’s carnal brothers, whom he instituted as universal heirs. It is asked whether, if said form is omitted, Langueta can exercise guardianship and appoint an actor at her own peril, or not. And it must be premised that the mother, because she is not a guardian, cannot appoint an actor. D. de negotiis gestis, l. qui alienam, §. quamquam, because she does not have the right of legitimate administration. D. de solutionibus, l. filiae. And it is not only necessary that she have the right of guardianship. l. si, but also that she be able to administer, as C. de arbitris tutoribus, l. si; D. de solutionibus, l. quod si forte, §. 1; D. de auctoritate tutorum, sed si pluribus.
