Therefore, it is necessary that she accept this guardianship with administration; guardianship without administration is not sufficient. Now let us see whether said Langueta, without requiring or having the consent of said brothers, has the administration of said guardianship, or not. And it seems that she does, as D. de administratione tutorum, l. quidam decedens, §. Papinianus. To the contrary, it seems that she does not, as in the same title, l. Titium et Mevium, in principio. The truth of this point depends on the resolution of said laws, and the gloss in said §. Papinianus says that there the mother’s counsel is not necessary, because guardianship and counsel did not fall upon her, since she could not be a guardian; I speak of counsel of authority. Therefore, it is otherwise in law, where counsel and consent can fall, because guardianship can also fall, and this opinion is held by Jacobus de Arena, Petrus, and Cynus. On this, note in l. id quod pauperibus, C. de episcopis et clericis. But in l. Titium et Mevium, it is said that either a colleague and participant in the risk must be required in the administration, and then it must be required and done according to the form dictated by the testator. Or he is not a colleague, and then, since the office resides entirely in the guardian, nothing further is necessary; hence, to require or follow is urbane, but it is not a matter of legal form. And this is held by Bartolus, D. de exercitoria, l. 1, §. si plures. Hence, it must be considered that a form established in ancient times and proper to the limits of guardianship cannot be altered by a testator, because they are of public law; hence, it should not be mixed with private power, nor official with official, nor should legitimate power depend on a person of private authority, but on a colleague who makes an inventory and is a participant in the risk, hence he can reasonably demand it. For it is not in the power of the testator to shape public offices by his own motion. D. de testamento tutorum, l. terrarum. But it is otherwise in colleges, because in those having a symbol, transition and conjunction are easier, and according to this, in this mother there is the fullness of free administration, as noted in D. de appellationibus, l. cum in una, §. tutor. And the acts of the brothers are valid, neglecting consent. Notwithstanding §. si plures, because there it speaks of the inofficious will, which the master has limits by his sole will. D. de manumis, l. diligenter. But the office of the guardian has the limit of legal power, as Inst. de tutoribus, in principio. Also, notwithstanding D. de electione, c. cum in veteri, because there the form was prefixed by a superior. Also, notwithstanding D. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. si qui mihi bona, §. coram, because there, in the acceptance of inheritance, which is regulated according to the will of the mandator, here in the office of the guardian, which is regulated according to the will of the law. Also, notwithstanding Extra de arbitris, c. cum olim, and what Innocentius notes in D. de legibus, l. si pro debilitate, for it is one thing in an arbiter, who can do nothing outside the compromise, D. de arbitris, c. non distinguimus, §. de officio. What then is to be said? Can a testator not command a mother left as guardian, whose counsel is sometimes free, to follow the will of the heirs? For the mother’s guardianship is irregular and abnormal, and for this cause and reason the testator provided for this: partly because she is a woman, partly because she is a relative, partly because she is an heir. D. de legatis tutorum, l. 1; D. ubi pupillus educari debeat, l. 1, §. 1; D. de usufructu, l. in fideicommissum, §. cum Pollidius. I believe that in this administration the mother has no more right than the father wished, D. de administratione tutorum, l. Titium et Mevium, §. quaesitum autem. For just as he will dispense with the partner so that he is not bound to an inventory, so conversely he will restrain her power according to reason and in favor of the ward. Hence, the limits of the testator’s mandate must be carefully followed, and what is done contrary to this, unless done for a cause, is not valid. For the form is to be observed for this reason; but for a cause, the praetor can well permit her to do what is useful for the minor. d. l. 1, in principio, ubi pupillus educari debeat, there, “nonnunquam ratio et c.” The father is also understood, since he spoke thus to the brothers as if speaking with guardians, although they are not truly guardians. And it is similar to D. de auctoritate legatorum, l. liberto. Therefore, the father had two, and hence it is not surprising if they were required, and if their non-requirement is such that whenever acts are done, another doubt arises: whether the protestation is inept, and if a term is given to prove it, the judge proceeds in the meantime against it, or whether the proceeding is valid. And it seems that it is not, C. de dilationibus, l. sive pars. The contrary is true, if it is so in fact: because pending a useful dilatory plea, a useful proceeding should not be impeded, as noted by Innocentius, Extra de electione, cap. quia propter.

CASE. In the name of Christ, Amen. A certain Rigutius promised Bartholus to do and ensure in such a way that Lady Catherine, his daughter, would contract marriage with John, son of said Bartholus, and for said marriage being contracted, he promised to said Bartholus, for dowry and in the name of dowry, one hundred [units]. And said Bartholus promised to said Rigutius to do and ensure in such a way that said John would contract lawful marriage with said Catherine, his daughter, and having received said dowry, to secure her in his goods worth the aforementioned quantity, according to the form of the statute of the land of Gualdo. This was in 1339. Thus, in a manner of speaking, 44 years have elapsed since said promise was made. After this, in said year, said marriage was contracted. After this, in 1341, said Bartholus died, with his son John and his wife surviving. After this, in 1345, said John, husband of Lady Catherine, died, with Lady Catherine, his wife, and Martin and Bartholus, his sons, and Rigutius, father of said Catherine, remaining. After this, said Bartholus and his mother died, with said Martin remaining. After this, in 1355, said Rigutius died, who made his last testament, who among other things left, by right of institution, to Martin, his nephew, formerly son of John Bartholus and said Lady Catherine, his deceased daughter, all that and everything that John and Bartholus had given him in dowry and in the name of dowry at the time of the contracted marriage between John and said Lady Catherine, by the hand of Philip Arrutius, notary, or by the hand of any notary it might appear; and beyond said dowry, in 10 pounds, and in said dowries and said 10 pounds, he instituted him as heir, inhibiting and commanding that he could not ask for more of his goods, and by right of the Falcidian and Trebellian portions or any other right, and in his other goods he instituted his universal heir, Simon, his son, and this was in 1355. After this, said Martin received said legacy and quieted said Simon, heir of said Rigutius. After this, said Simon died in 1363 and made his testament, and instituted his heirs, Angel and Nicholas; and if they should die, he instituted Lady Franceschina, his wife, whose sons died in said year, with their mother remaining, who lady accepted the inheritance of the aforementioned with the benefit of the law, and with citation of said Martin, legatee in said testament of Simon, and finally put herself in possession, with said Martin knowing, and this was in 1364. And from then on, she held said inheritance peacefully and without contradiction from Martin for a period of 16 years. There is a statute in the land of Gualdo that whoever possesses any immovable thing with his entry for 10 years shall be held as true owner and possessor. It is now asked, if said instrument of promise of dowry, which was made 44 years ago, and the marriage was dissolved 24 years ago, is it prescribed? Also, it is asked, if said legacy made by said Rigutius, because he instituted said Martin in the dowries given to said Bartholus or said John, and beyond said dowries, 10 pounds, because this was in 1360, does it break said prescription? Also, it is asked, if said Martin, nephew of said Rigutius and son of his daughter, can sue for the supplement of his legitime in the goods of his grandfather, who died 38 years ago. Also, it is asked, because said lady possesses the things and goods of the heirs of Simon, heir of said Rigutius, for a period of 16 years, with said Martin present and patient and without contradiction, can said Martin, notwithstanding said statute, claim anything against the heir of said Rigutius and the heir of said lady? I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The action for the dowry is prescribed within a period of thirty years; in the same manner, so is the hypothecary action against the debtor or his heir.
2. Whether the supplement of the legitime, which is claimed from an intestate, is extinguished by prescription.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The action for dowry is prescribed by the space of 30 years. C. de iure dotis, l. iuris rebus. But the hypothecary action against the debtor, or his heir, is prescribed by the space of 40 years. C. de praescriptione 30 annorum, l. cum notissimi. And this is true, unless the prescription has been interrupted. For then a new prescription begins from the day of interruption. eod. tit., §. sed et si quis; §. unde evenit. I believe that if the debtor in the meantime bequeaths the debt, it appears that the prescription is interrupted, because the debt was acknowledged in the last will, and it is as if it were his own security; and even if this were not so, nevertheless an action could be brought from the will. ff. de legatis 1, l. si creditori meo. 1. Response: Someone will say that in the case of the present will, the testator bequeathed what was given, not what was to be given, in the name of dowry, and thus nothing comes in this bequest from that which is to be given, but from that which was said to have been given. And this is true according to the strict nature of the words. But otherwise it seems according to the presumed intention of the testator; because otherwise dowry is said to be given by promise. C. de donationibus ante nuptias, autem dos data. And this is true when the word "given" refers to the woman; because it is understood that the dowry is given, i.e., the woman is endowed. But as it refers to the father-in-law or husband, it is not said to be given to him. C. de dote causa, l. 1. et fin. In this, the custom of the speaker must be observed, if it appears from him; otherwise, according to strict law, one must adhere to the proper signification of the words, not to their improper signification. ff. de legatis 3, l. non aliter. And by this, it does not seem that the prescription is interrupted in our case, having seen the words of the will, because he did not acknowledge himself as debtor; because he asserted the contrary, i.e., that he was released by payment.

† On another point concerning the legitime, I do not believe that the supplementation sought from the intestate estate is extinguished by the five-year prescription, if it lasts for as long as the claim for the legitime itself lasts. It is otherwise if one sues for supplementation having been passed over by the maternal line: because then the supplementation takes the place of the querela (complaint of inofficiousness). C. de inoff. test. l. si quis filius. And therefore, it is not granted against a possessor by title after a long time, unless he is bound in a personal action for such relief, as is the case in l. scimus and l. omnimodo. Because a personal action is perpetual, except when it takes the place of a querela, as I said. It supports this. C. de revo. dona. l. fi. Possession according to the form of the statute benefits, so that the thing cannot be evicted, not so that personal debts are not said to be paid. CA SVS. IN the name of God, Amen. Such is the fact, that now 17 years have elapsed, or thereabouts, during which a certain compromise was made between a major and a minor of 25 years of law and fact, into the arbitration of a good man, and a sentence was rendered with an oath against the minor, he being absent and not cited in that year. And at that time a certain statute was in force, which among other things contained that no one should make any contract with any minor of 25 years without the presence of two nearest blood relatives, or a judge, if the contract is detrimental to that minor, and if made, it is null and void, as this form seems to indicate. Now it is asked, if the said person, who was a minor at the time of the said compromise and at the time the sentence was rendered against him, but is not now a minor of 25 years, can it be said now, by virtue of the said statute which was then in force, that the said compromise is null, and the said statutes are null as rendered against a minor, and by virtue of the compromise made with a minor? Furthermore, it is asked, from the form of the statute of the land of Gualdo, it is provided that Mallus of Gualdo must have someone cited outside the court of Gualdo: now a certain person, on a petition for the solution of an oath, causes his brother to be sued before the diocesan bishop; can it be said that he does not incur the penalty contained in the said statute? and c. Bald.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The compromise refers to the statute that was in force at the time of the compromise.
2. What is meant by the Court of the Guard.
body: In the Name of the Lord, Amen.

† Moreover, the statute that was in force at the time of the compromise must be examined. C. de usuris, l. pen. And therefore, the said compromise and award may today be declared null. ff. de servis exponendis, l. si minor. And this concludes the first point.

† Regarding the second point, I say that the temporal court, concerning those matters which properly pertain to the bishop, such as in absolution from an oath, is called the court of Gualdo; for the court resides in the territory of Gualdo, as is noted in the law *Plerique*, Digest, *De in ius vocando*, according to Giuliano da Cuneo, and it is proven in the Digest, *De iustitia et iure*, law 1, section *Publicum*, etc., by Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A minor under guardianship is not said to die intestate; hence he is not included under a statute disposing of those dying intestate.
2. A statute depriving a mother of her right by nature is highly inequitable; and therefore it must be strictly interpreted.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It does not seem that a woman can succeed to an impubes son ab intestato, the statute preferring the sister, and it does not distinguish whether the sister is related to both or not, and therefore we ought not to distinguish either. L. 1, § et generaliter, D. de legibus praestitis. For if the mother is asked in what manner she wishes to succeed, she cannot say otherwise than that she wishes to succeed ab intestato. And thus this statute excludes her. Hence she necessarily concludes against herself, and so holds Bartolus in L. 1, D. de suis et legitimis. In favor of this is the fact that this interpretation is written in the law itself, therefore it must be followed even in the interpretation of statutes using civil words: because such meaning has been attributed to the word by the understanding of the law, whence it can now be said that it is the true signification. D. de legibus 3, L. non aliter. In the contrary opinion are commonly all the doctors, that a pupillus is not said to die intestate according to its proper signification.

And because a statute excluding the mother from the right of nature is highly inequitable, one must adhere to its strict meaning. See *l. non aliter*, *de legatis* 3, together with *si*. And thus I hold that the text of the aforementioned *l. patriae*, at the words "plane," does not obstruct this; nor does the passage in that same law at the words "sed et hoc," because where the matter concerns favor, namely that the mother be called, we adhere to that interpretation; otherwise, it is a matter of irrational hatred and contrary to the law of piety, as argued in *l. cum quidam*, *de lib. et post.* Therefore, the sister by consanguinity being excluded, the mother is called. And the same term, taken in a different sense, includes the mother and excludes the sister; nevertheless, the said sister ought to be endowed with a substantial dowry on account of such a case.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. One cannot renounce a prohibitory law that does not annul the act.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The renunciation was invalid, because one cannot renounce a prohibitory right and one that annuls the act. C. ne fideiussiones dentur, l. 2. And therefore the said donation was invalid from the beginning, because the compromise and the award of the arbitrator have the force of a transaction, as in Auth. ut differentes iudices, §. si vero contingerit. The transaction, or award, was valid. C. de plus petendo, l. 1. and in cap. gravis, de deposito, according to Simon. Nor does the appeal stand in the way, because by paying he renounced the appeal. C. de re iudicata, l. ad solutionem. It is certain that the house, which is in the field, comes with the field, that which accedes to the soil, and because the words say, one field with all and each of the things which the said property has above it. C. de bonis vacantibus, l. si quando tertio 10. And in these cases the brothers do not have the right. ff. de re iudicata, l. non is, §. debeo. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A division made, if it does not hold by reason of an omitted decree, may be confirmed by silence.
2. Whether a division of emphyteutic property can be made without the express or tacit consent of the owner.
3. Emphyteusis received for oneself and for nephews and nieces of either sex descending from males or females, etc., who are admitted to succeed.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The division from the beginning did not hold. L. non solum and L. non vectigale, C. de praed. min. Nevertheless, because only the interposition of the decree had been made, it could be confirmed by silence, in c. si maior functus, l. fi. For a division is presumed to have been duly made, which has been feigned as having been made by long possession, as in C. communi. diui. l. pe., where the glossa ordinaria is found. Thus, therefore, the fund belongs to him, which has pleased for a long time. ff. de aquae hae. l. qui in alienam, C. de pe. hær. l. si filius, de usur. c. cum de in rem verso.

† But that emphyteutic things can be divided among emphyteutic holders is clear. D. de communi diviso, l. cohaeredes, in principio. A division can also be made so that one holds all the emphyteutic rights of one church, another those of another. Or one holds the allodium, another the olive grove, as noted in C. de familia erciscunda, l. familiae, in the glossa ordinaria. But Guillaume holds the contrary, that division cannot take place without the express or tacit consent of the lord. D. de transactionibus, l. cum in § et si pluribus. But the first opinion seems to be followed; in this case there is no doubt, because the church ratified it by receiving the census for a long time. In l. litibus, C. de agris et censibus, lib. 11.

† Having therefore assumed the division, let us proceed to the succession of the emphyteusis. And I premise that commutation is not among those included in the power of succeeding, as in the Authentica de non alienando, §. in emphyteusi, alioquin; and therefore no account need be taken of it. But Jacobutia and Peter are included, for although Peter claims through the female line, he is nevertheless included. The text is in the said §. emphyteusi, where it says, “to nephews of either sex, and descendants from males or females.” And whether the nephews are male or female, it appears that the house belonged in equal parts to Jacobutia and Peter by equal shares of succession; yet because Jacobutia consented, as was affirmed above, her said portion will pass upon her death, as is concluded in column 10 of the chapter Quibus modis feudum amittitur, cap. 1, §. 1. It is therefore concluded that the said house belongs half to the plaintiff and half to the defendant. And so it must be pronounced, and there is no doubt that the building is libellarium, whereas the soil is not, as stated in D. de superficiebus, l. 1, §. quid ait; l. 2, de iure emphyteutico; C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, autem si quis ruinas, since the contract does not contain a stipulation to the contrary.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The questions of the testator's tacit intentions are determined by natural equity.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The legislator determines questions concerning the tacit intentions of the testator by presuming from natural equity. C. de iniusto testa. l. 2. From which presumption I say that he subsequently breaks the will and the codicillary clause, when, according to natural equity, he is afterwards more beloved than the instituted heir. l. sicut certi. l. si cum vel in vtero. de pactis. l. tale pactum. §. fi. de reuocandis dona. l. vnquam. and C. de posthumis haer. insti. l. 1. And therefore the will is broken, and the codicils made to the will do not extend to their own [effect] beyond the greater part of the goods, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If there are two partners, and one executes a deed in his own person, whether it is to be communicated.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Among partners, all things are to be shared simply, notwithstanding that one has made an instrument concerning himself and not the other, as in D. 17.2.1 (pro duobus), in the beginning; D. 5.1.1 (si socius). This partnership, being simple and not qualified, requires acts from which it may be inferred; likewise, it requires persons capable of entering into partnership, upon whom the obligation for fraud and fault may fall according to the nature of the contract of partnership. And therefore, no contract is formed with one who is not capable of fraud. D. 26.1.1 (Titium et Mevium altero). However, if Simon, being a minor but of greater age, conducts business from common assets, then the action pro socio applies, but not negotiorum gestio; what arises therefrom is to be shared, as in D. 3.5.1 (si pupilli), in the beginning. If, therefore, it is to be established, and since there is also added a confession of mind previously given, and these preceded from all things, or from common endeavors, or mutual endeavors in the same or different places, they are to be shared; but others are not to be shared, because they fall outside our partnership. For one who does not contribute labor, money, or property shall not share in any gain, nor even if he does contribute, to the extent that it exceeds fourfold. D. 17.2.1 (si non fuerit), § final, where it is noted, and the words “veniens” etc. were said, not promised, D. 3.4.1 (sciendum). And to further matters, you do not add positoria, D. 7.1.1 (generali), in the beginning, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The property of those who have been denounced, without their property having been confiscated, may be sold by them.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The property of those who have been relegated, but whose property has not been confiscated, may be sold by them, because they are still owners; however, it is sold subject to its legal encumbrance. For if it was pledged to the fisc for a penalty incurred or to be incurred, it passes to the buyer with this burden, and on account of the penalty it may be claimed from the buyers by a hypothecary action, not by a vindicatory action. Therefore, the sale is valid, unless the municipal law provides otherwise, or unless the judge has prohibited the sale. D. de contrah. empt. l. si quis sciens; and D. de interdictis et relegationibus l. relegatorum, § ad tempus; and on this point in l. no. D. de pollicitationibus l. de pollicitationi. Although, therefore, the sale may be binding when it is not prohibited at the time, if afterwards rebellion is committed and the penalty subsequently incurred, if indeed the penalty was the loss of all property, the sale is rescinded, D. de administratione tutorum l. Chirographis, § si; but if it was another pecuniary penalty, the hypothecary action applies, as I have said; but if no penalty was promised or added by the public authority, then alienations lawfully made and sales not simulated are not rescinded against the possessor, as is fully noted, D. de donationibus l. post contractum, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a community, by reason of a transaction, grants a certain place to a monastery, transferring to the said monastery all rights, actions, and the like, it does not thereby appear that mere or mixed imperial jurisdiction, nor the right to impose or exact tolls, duties, and similar charges, has been transferred.
body: The fact, concerning which counsel is sought, is that the men of Chiusi, by reason of a transaction and decision, granted, yielded, and mandated, remitted, and renounced to Lord Foresi, Abbot of the Abbey of Saint Galgano, in the name of the monastery of the said abbey, as recipient, and transferred to the said monastery all rights, actions, and real, personal, useful, and direct claims competent and to become competent to the said commune, or to any member of the said commune, in the wood and in the land, plain, or other things situated near the said monastery in the place called Monteseppio, which is bounded on one side by the flowing river Mersa and on the other by other boundaries; and furthermore, that the said monastery and the said Lord Abbot, for it and its successors, may have, hold, and possess the aforesaid things, and do with them whatsoever they please, by right of full dominion and ownership, without suit or contradiction of the said commune. And the said monastery and the said Lord Abbot, for it, were made procurators in rem in the place of the said commune, and constituted as universal successors, so that they may usefully and directly act, plead, sue, obtain, and defend themselves against any person or party for the said monastery and the aforesaid things, and for them; and whatever possession of the said things the said commune and the men of the said commune had, they held it for the said monastery, etc. The aforementioned contract, which was concluded in 1242, has been used by the said commune of Chiusi from that time until now with high and low jurisdiction and all manner of jurisdiction in the territory granted to the said Abbot and the said monastery, and as it previously used it.

† Now it is called into doubt whether the *merum et mixtum imperium*, jurisdiction, and the right to impose and collect tolls in the aforementioned places were seen as granted and transferred to the said monastery. And first it seems to be said that yes, because one who alienates a thing is seen to transfer every right that he has in the thing to the recipient himself, as in *l. qui tabernas*, D. de contrahenda emptione; *l. si domus*, in fine, D. de legatis 1; *c. cum autem*, de iure patronatus. But the *merum et mixtum imperium*, jurisdiction, and the right to impose and collect duties and tolls in those places belonged to the Commune and the men of Chiusi in that territory; therefore, this right is truly seen to have been transferred to the monastery, which could be done by the person of the Abbot and the notary, as in *c. edocere*, de rescriptis; *c. litterae*, de dilationibus. Also, because in doubtful cases interpretation should always be made against the party who could have spoken more clearly in the law, as in *l. veteribus*, D. de pactis; *l. cum in* and *l. Labeo*, D. de contrahenda emptione. But the Commune of Chiusi in the said contract could have spoken the law more clearly; therefore, interpretation should be made against it, so that the *merum et mixtum imperium* and all jurisdiction may be seen as transferred. Also, that which is comprehended under words is included under the disposition, as in *c. ad audientiam*, de decimis; and in *c. porro*, de privilegiis; *l. 1, §. si is qui navem*, de exercitoria actione. But under the words of the contract initiated between the monastery of Saint Gallus and the Commune of Chiusi, the *merum et mixtum imperium* and jurisdiction are comprehended under the words; therefore, it is clear. For in the contract it is said that the Commune of the men of Chiusi gave, yielded, transferred, mandated, and resigned to the said Abbot all rights and real and personal actions, useful and direct, belonging to the said Commune and the men of the said Commune in the said things by right of dominion or quasi-ownership fully; and that the Commune constituted a procurator and successor in the universal right of the said Commune. If they constituted the said monastery as successor in the universal right, therefore they succeeded in the *merum et mixtum imperium* and jurisdiction; otherwise, it would not be a successor in the universal right, because he who says "all" excludes nothing. *l. Iulianus*, de legatis 3; and *c. solitae*, de maioribus et obediencia. For also those words "universal right" would avail nothing to the contrary. *l. si quando*, de legatis 1.

On the contrary, however, it must be said in law that neither the *merum* nor the *mixtum imperium*, nor jurisdiction, nor the right to impose or collect duties or tolls, are seen to have been transferred to the said monastery, because in a general alienation those things do not pass which one would not verisimilarly have alienated. *l. bonis venditis*, D. de privatis creditoribus; see *l. obligatae generali*, D. de pignoribus; and *l. 1*, C. quae res pignori non subiciantur. It is not verisimilar that the men and the Commune of Chiusi wished to transfer to the said monastery the *merum et mixtum imperium* for so small a price, by which it is conjectured what came into the contract. *l. 1*, D. de re iudicata; *l. quoties*, D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum. Also, a toll cannot be imposed without the license of the prince. C. de nova vectigalium institutione, non posse; *l. 1*, and throughout; *l. vectigalia*, D. de publicanis. If they cannot be established by anyone other than the prince, therefore the monastery of Saint Gallus cannot claim to have the right, from the said contract, to collect tolls in the said places. And it is contradictory: if the Commune of Chiusi conferred the power to collect which it had, it seems that it could not transfer that right which it had to another, but only renounce it in the hands of him from whom it held it. *l. legata*, D. de inofficioso praedicto; and in *c. quod in dubiis*, de renunciationibus. Also, if the Commune of Chiusi had expressly wished to transfer the *merum imperium* given by law to the prince, it could not have done so. *l. 1, §. novissime*, de originibus iuris; note Jacobus Butrigarius in *l. 2*, D. de iudicibus, §. 1, [where he states that] this could be introduced by new custom. For also custom can only confer those things which are of jurisdiction, in *l. 1*, C. de emancipatis liberis; in *c. quamvis*, de foro competenti; in the canon *conquestus*, 8 q. 2. And since custom is the tacit consent of the people, and that which cannot be introduced tacitly by custom, neither can it be expressly by statute, as it is equivalent. *l. de quibus*, and there the notes, D. de legibus 1, according to the said Jacobus Butrigarius. They claim to have the *merum imperium* from the peace of Constantine, the right to mint money, as he notes in the said *l. 2*, D. de iudicibus. And thus it seems that even if the Commune of Chiusi had wished to transfer the *merum et mixtum imperium*, the right to impose and collect tolls, and to mint money, it could not have done so.

Also, this is the will of the words of the contract. For in the contract it is said that the Commune of Chiusi gave, granted all rights and real and personal actions belonging [to them] in the wood, forest, and plain, so that the said monastery might do as it pleased by right of dominion and ownership without contradiction of the said Commune, and made the Abbot of the said monastery and the said monastery procurator, and constituted them successors in the universal [rights]: but it is so that the right of *merum et mixtum imperium*, or jurisdiction, or the right to collect tolls, or to mint money, does not belong to the Commune or the men of Chiusi in the said places by right of dominion and ownership, but by right of jurisdiction and territory. As is clear, because the bishop has ordinary jurisdiction in his entire diocese: as in *c. cum episcopus*, de officio ordinarii, lib. 6; these things, however, in the canon *regenda*, 10 q. 1. And the emperor is lord of the whole world as to jurisdiction, as in *l. deprecatione*, D. ad legem Rhodiam de iactu; and yet they are not lords of all the aforementioned possessions, as noted in *l. bene a Zenone*, C. de quadrienali praescriptione. If the said [argument] holds in the case at hand, although the Commune of Chiusi transfers to the monastery every right that it has by right of ownership and dominion, it is not said to transfer the right of jurisdiction, but of territory, as is proved above. It is not true to say, "I am lord of the estate, therefore I have jurisdiction"; nor conversely. And this is especially so since in the contract it is said that those things which are of custom and usage came [into it]. *l. quod si nolis, §. qui assidua*, D. de aedilicio edicto; note in *l. edictum, §. legatum*.

Also, because after the aforementioned contract was celebrated, the Commune and the men of Chiusi continuously used the said jurisdiction; therefore, it is superfluous to believe that they transferred it. Argument from *l. sicut, §. superuacuum*, D. qui in rem potestatem pigoris vel hypothecae solvere possunt. They are to be preserved in their possession. *l. negante*, C. de actionibus et obligationibus; *l. qui accusare*. Also, and because if these rights had not profited them, they would not have used them for so long, and it can be said that the Commune has prescribed, not beyond the forty-year period. See *De quarta praescriptione*, which is noted in *c. cum ecclesia Sutrina*, de causa possessionis et proprietatis. And I consider this second part, by the laws recently adduced, to be the more true.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. It must be considered that jurisdiction and imperial authority are not appurtenant to the ownership of lands, nor is the right to demand passage, but rather they adhere to the district; under the name of the district of lands, they are held and, as it were, possessed. And therefore, where the district is alienated, jurisdiction is not transferred. Nor does the ownership of lands have anything in common with jurisdiction, because they are not of the same nature, nor of the same definition. Although, if it were seen that a castle, to which jurisdiction was granted, was transferred, the jurisdiction would be transferred; because by the name of the castle, jurisdiction is signified, which is near the walls of the castle, and the lands of its community are nothing other than what it holds within itself. And this is proven by: D. de actionibus emptoris, l. fundi; D. de fundo instrato, l. predia; §. si; D. de restitutione spoliatorum, c. cum ad sedem; D. de probat., c. licet causam. And if it is said that those territories are subject to this jurisdiction, therefore they pass with the universitas, as in D. de contrahenda emptione, l. cum immundicis. I answer that, although those territories are of the right and property of the church, nevertheless the district of the castle remains, and it is the district itself that is subject to the jurisdiction. It supports what is noted in l. plerique, D. de in ius vocando, by Guillaume. It would be foolish to say that if a city donates one field, it thereby relinquishes from itself the jurisdiction within the boundaries of the field and grants it to another, since jurisdiction is a certain integral and indivisible whole. To this effect is what is noted by Innocentius, D. de iure patronatus, c. ex literis. From whose doctrine, rightly understood, this question is determined in favor of this party. And because jurisdiction inheres in the territory, not for the utility of the territory, nor as predial fruits, but for the utility of the fisc, D. locata, l. locare, by Bartolus, this is the truth. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. That which has been acquired by military industry is not to be shared with brothers.
2. Fruits gathered from common property are to be divided, unless one of the partners suffered them to be consumed with the intention of making a gift, which, however, is not presumed.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It is certainly more certain that what is acquired through military industry is not to be shared with brothers, but is the property of the acquirer, whether it be acquired during the father’s lifetime or after his death. D. 36.1.1 § sed nec castrense; C. 6.57.1 § exceptis; C. 6.25.1; and with countless similar authorities. Nor does the commonality of paternal property make any difference, as D. 10.3.1 § si fratres; Speculum Iudiciale, de iudiciis, § sequitur, under the words “quid si duo fratres,” column 10; de fratribus, de novo beneficio investiturae, c. fin. And thus the first question is resolved.

† In the second question, I say that the fruits gathered from the common property must be returned to Bartholomew for his share, or the value of those consumed, unless Bartholomew had endured this with the intention of making a gift; nevertheless, a gift is not presumed in case of doubt. D. de communi diviso, l. 3; D. de familia erciscunda, l. inter haeredes, §. fructus, cum si. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Agreements are not to be observed if they are to the prejudice of a superior, nor when public danger would ensue.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† That the aforementioned franchise does not hold, appears from the text with the gloss in the original chapter *Decurionibus*, law *Vacuatis*, Book 10. Nevertheless, the truth is this: because an official appointed by a superior, for example by the city of Spoleto, may well infringe upon this franchise, but an official appointed by the men of the castle may not contravene it; because the castle is bound to observe its own pacts, which it holds to the prejudice of those who have made peace, as in the Digest, *De pace*, law *Inter debitorem*. Unless there is such great necessity that public danger would result from observing the pact, as noted in law 1, Digest, *De iure immunitatis*. According to Dy. Ray. However, *De foro* holds indistinctly that the pact must be observed, which is more equitable: especially in our case, in which the immunity is confirmed by prescription of time: and thus I hold, without prejudice to the rights of the Abatense fisc, which is the superior authority. Code, *De praescriptione triginta annorum*, law *Comperit*. Nevertheless, if molested by the common fisc of Orzani, it is bound to bear the burdens for it by reason of the pacts, presupposing the mandate of the syndic; indeed, even if it does not appear, ratification appears from the acts, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. No toll is paid under the common law on those things which are carried for provisions.
2. The burden of salt is not of the common law.
casus:
CASS. IN the name of God, amen. The point on which counsel is requested is as follows. Namely, the officials of the commune of Perugia, having an arbitrator from the general assembly, sold the power over Clusium Perusino according to the form of the schedule, in which schedule among other chapters is found a certain chapter of the following tenor, namely, etc. Also that every laborer, peasant, or foreigner who wished to work the said Commune and posts of Clusium, may come to stay, to work, and shall be, and shall be understood to be, exempt from every tax of the commune, and from every reprisal during the said time of ten years, and therefore shall not be understood to be exempt from Castiglione Clusino, and the said salary of the price of the said Castiglione Clusino, and all the fruits that shall be gathered in the said Clusium, shall be exempt and freed from every toll, and from the burden of the commune, both on the part of the buyers, and also on the part of the laborers, and this exemption shall not be understood to apply to those who have land or vineyards in the possessions of the said Clusium, from which land or vineyards they do not render a third to the commune; these shall be bound to pay the toll on the fruits during the said time of ten years, and the buyers of the possessions, where the said land or vineyards are, in that form in which the citizens and the peasants of the other countryside of Perugia pay at present, and that every laborer of such possession shall be bound to pay for their part and that of their lords, so much that the said laborers of the farm may retain so much of the fruits as is sufficient to satisfy what they would pay for him.

Furthermore, there are found among other ordinances of the toll, or communal salary, certain ordinances in this form, namely. Also that the said buyers during the time shall be bound, must keep in the Piazza de sopra muro four doors, or three open, whence they go, and cause the said salt to be sold to whoever wishes to buy it, not being able to constrain, nor force any person to buy the said salt, except as much as it pleases whoever wishes to buy, but they shall be bound to keep the chamber always well supplied with white and black salt, so that every person may have whichever they prefer, and to keep continuously a good, diligent, and faithful servant to sell, so that each person may have their convenience, and similarly they shall be bound to cause the said salt to be sold in the countryside of Perugia in the usual places, and beyond the said places where they give it to whoever has most need, incurring, each time they contravene, the penalty of 200 pounds of silver. And it shall be understood that the places of the countryside, from which they are bound to sell the said salt, are: The Meno. The Castle of the Tratta of the sons of Berto. The Castle of Pauciale. The Castle of Diruta. The Castle of Fossato. The Castle of Marciano. The Castle of Castiglione Clusino. The Castle of Passignano. Also that no person, citizen, or peasant, subject and non-subject, of whatever condition or state, may put salt into the city and countryside of Perugia, either for their own use, or for sale, neither in large quantity nor small, without the license of the said buyers; and whoever contravenes shall incur the penalty each time, or for each load, of 200 pounds of silver, and shall lose the load, and the beast; if it is less than a load, they shall lose for each load 5 pounds, which penalty the buyer shall have.

Now the officials of the salary say that those of Clusium cannot send salt into Clusium without the license of those officials, and the buyers, according to the form of the said pacts of the contract, having seen the said chapters. But those of Clusium say the contrary, on the ground that if they cannot send salt into Clusium, by a certain consequence they would be bound to buy salt from their said officials. Hence, if they could not live comfortably without salt, it would seem they are constrained to buy salt from the said officials according to the form of the said exemption.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Concerning those things which are carried for provisions, no toll is due according to the common law. D. de verb. sig. l. in l. censoria. D. de public. l. si publicanus. §. de rebus. in gl. C. eo. l. universi. Therefore, this faction, or

The salt grievance is not a matter of common law, but is simply a matter of the purchase of the commonality of Perugia. Hence, it must be observed whether the inhabitants of Chiusi are exempt by some law, as is fully noted in the said §. de rebus. But if they were exempt solely by a pact made with the purchasers of Chiusi, the matter acted between others does not seem to prejudice the purchaser of the salt rights. C. res inter alios acta, throughout; C. ad vel., l. iubemus, cum si. And if no law has been made on this point by the Commune of Perugia, but it is a pact made with certain purchasers, it would not bind other purchasers; nevertheless, because that chapter, which speaks of exemption, stands by itself and is placed absolutely, even though it is reduced to one contract, it does not lose the force of a general law. Hence, although the Commune of Perugia never sold, but collected for itself, the Chiusians are exempt according to the tenor of the said chapter, which chapter is a law. ff. de publica, l. Caesar. That this chapter is placed absolutely is clear, because it is, therefore, standing by itself, which is noted in ff. de procu., l. cogendum.

CASE. The fact upon which counsel is sought is as follows: Leonardus Massey of Carbio, having three male sons, namely Mutius and Cola, and one daughter named Blonda, who was married and dowered by the said Leonardus. And because the said Blonda predeceased, the said Leonardus in his testament, among other things, instituted his universal heirs to be his male sons, and instituted the sons of the said Blonda as heirs in the said quantity. And he left to Angelo and Benedict, sons of the said Mutius, certain parcels of lands contained and bounded in the said testament, and made a substitution between Mutius and Cola, that if the sons died, the other surviving brother would succeed. The said Leonardus subsequently died, with the said Mutius and Cola surviving, and with the sons of the said Blonda and the sons of the said Mutius surviving. The said Mutius and Cola took possession of the paternal inheritance and involved themselves in it. Then the said Mutius made his last testament, in which, among other things, he instituted as his universal heirs Angelo and Benedict, his sons, and instituted as heirs Symonellus, Antonius, and Blondella, sons of the late Andreolla, daughter of the late Mutius, in a certain quantity. In that testament, he made a substitution for the said male sons, that if both died without sons, Cola, his natural brother, would succeed. The sons and heirs instituted by the said Mutius both died before the said Mutius, without sons, with the said Cola surviving, and with the sons of the said Andreolla surviving. It is presupposed in the aforementioned point that the said Andreolla was married and dowered by the said Leonardus, her grandfather, and instituted as heir in 20 florins current. Now it is asked, what is the law?

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The heir in a specific thing has the right of accrual.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. If

† If the substitution made by Mutius were merely fideicommissary, Blondelle would acquire the share of the males: because the heir in a specific thing has the right of accrual, and the fideicommissum is due: because it would accrue, although the legitime and the Trebellian portion ought to be deducted; but because the word "succeed" is more appropriate for direct substitution, I say that the substitutes come in by virtue of the vulgar substitution contained in the compendious [rule], as in C. in l. precibus. And therefore, concluding, I say that Cola succeeds by the vulgar substitution without any diminution, because direct substitution is not subject to deduction. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whoever believes with just reason that something is permitted to them does not incur a penalty.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† At the time for extracting promises, things can be extracted whether they were exempted then or beforehand, because all ordinances of the gabelle are silent concerning what happens during the seven excepted days; but those words, "li ditti mercadanti che reuocasse, o conprasse", strongly militate to the contrary. For certain merchandise is lawful by reason of time; otherwise, fraud against the gabelle could be devised. Secondly, just as it is customary for this statute to be understood, so it ought to be regarding laws [in ff. de legibus, l. si de interpretatione]; and it seems that, unless it was previously done in fraud of the statute by defrauding the gabelle, the gabelle ought not to be paid, because the purchase is then contracted when the thing is delivered, as in ff. de pactis, l. ab emptione, and because what is permitted to be done at that time, it is permitted to defer to that time and execute, l. quod saepe, § si quis, ff. de contrahenda emptione; l. in tempus, ff. de heredibus instituendis. And this I hold through what is read in ff. de legationibus, l. cum quaeritur; de pecunia constituta, l. eum, qui, § Iulianus; ff. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. contraxisse; ff. de solutionibus, l. quaero, arguing from place to time. And to this point is C. de nundinis, l. 1, which grants security simply by reason of the market. From these things it is concluded that these men of Castiglione would not be bound to any penalty, and they also believed with just cause that it was permitted to them. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If more persons are named in the libel, one must not proceed, given the statute that no one may accuse more than three persons, etc.
casus: CASE. They dared and presumed to cause damage, and did cause damage personally in a certain vineyard then existing, belonging to the said Nicholas, which is situated in the dependencies of the village of Montis Urni, in the place called "el bullagio." Its boundaries are on one side the road of Vannutius Corradi, and on the other the property of the hospital of the disciplinarians of Saint Dominic of Perugia. Namely, entering the said vineyard with the aforementioned dogs, and there setting nets suitable for catching hares and other animals, and hunting through the said vineyard, as hunters do, and devastating the vines then existing in the said vineyard, and also causing the said vines of Corradi to be damaged by the said dogs and by the dogs themselves, and also gathering pomegranates from a certain tree then existing in the said vineyard, and damaging this tree, committing the aforementioned acts contrary to the form of the law, statute, and order of the commune of Perugia, and contrary to the will of the said Nicholas. Which damage was, and could be, by common estimation and value, 28 solidi and 6 denarii for each of the said accusers, and thus estimated the said Nicholas, the aforementioned accuser.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Because the statute provides that no one may accuse more than three persons from one family in a single accusation or libel, except for one person, however, for damage given below 20 sols or up to the amount of 20 sols inclusive, and if he accuses beyond the said number, the accusation is by the law itself null, void, and inoperative, and no proceeding may be had thereon in any manner, and similarly in the denunciation your parties are to follow the form of the statute and pronounce that no proceeding shall be had.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A person of differing reputation may be investigated on the basis of prior notoriety.
2. The burden of proof in an inquiry lies with the presumption that one always acts with good intent.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

Having examined the acts and allegations transmitted to me, I state that regarding the said offenses, since a differing reputation has preceded them, an inquiry could have been and can be conducted by the court on account of the nature of the crime, on account of the enormity of the crime, and on account of the quality of the place. This delict is principally adultery and the crime of violence. Many offenses are contained therein. Codex, to the Julian Law on Violence, law "Quam multa." For here there was violence, rape, and adultery. Codex, on the Rape of Virgins, law 1. And even if it were only rape alone, or only adultery, which is a kind of sacrilege, an inquiry could be made ex officio of the presiding judge. Law "Congruit." In the Authenticum on Colonists, section "Iubemus," in the words "per se." Innocentius, on Sentences of Excommunication, chapter "Delicto." The objection from law "Quamvis adulterii," Codex, on Adulteries, does not hold, because the judge occupies the place of the principal person when he inquires.

† And the nature of the inquiry is such that it is always presumed that one acts with good intent, as stated in l. 2, C. de inofficiosa iudicatio, and noted in c. accepimus, de aetate et qualitate. For it is an enormous crime, C. de episcopis et clericis, l. 3, de minore, l. auxilium, §. in delictis, and quia in ecclesia, C. de episcopis et clericis, l. si quis in hoc genus. And the penalty is death, as stated in the aforementioned l. quamvis and in Auth. vt nullus iudicum, §. si vero accusatus, §. id quod, in Auth. de bonis damnatorum. The goods remain with the blood heirs, and not with the fisc, and the ban by which they must be revoked from the goods.

CASE. Andreas left to his wife Matilda the use and habitation of the house, and he left her, as is gathered from the will, as usufructuary of his goods, as long as she maintained her widowhood and remained chaste and honest with his daughter Nicolotta. And among other things, he left and disposed of the widow. Finally, he instituted the aforementioned Nicolotta as his universal heir, with this added condition: that if the said Nicolotta should die at any time without legitimate children born of her, half of his goods should be given to the poor, and the other half to the aforementioned Matilda, his wife, and to Benedicta, Angela, Vallutio, and Titia in equal portions. And in the aforementioned will, he ordered legacies to be given. Finally, the case occurred that the said Nicolotta died without legitimate children and heirs born of her, indeed in a pupillary age. From this, a dispute arises between Lady Matilda, the former wife of the testator, on one side, and the poor, as well as the aforementioned Berta, Angela, etc., on the other. For the said Matilda requests not to be disturbed in the use, habitation, and usufruct of the testator's goods, since she lives honestly, has not entered into second marriage, and it does not remain for her not to dwell with her daughter. The poor, and also the aforementioned Berta, Angela, etc., request that the said Matilda be removed from the usufructs and that the last disposition of the testator be observed due to the occurrence of the appended condition, alleging that the aforementioned goods should be divided, half among the said poor, and the remainder among the aforementioned Matilda, the wife, Berta, Angela, etc., in equal portions, as is narrated in the will. The question is, having seen the will and the point, what is the law regarding the premises.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Particular legacies are not transmitted by a universal substitution.
2. If a legacy has been made to a wife, to be enjoyed as long as she lives with her daughter, whether she ought to have the legacy after the daughter's death.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† That Lady Matthiola ought to have the usufruct of all the goods is proved thus: particular legacies are not diminished by a universal substitution, for he to whom the inheritance is restored under the Trebellian law is bound to discharge the legacies. C. ad Treb. l. si; ff. eo. l. 1, §. factum inde Neratius. Therefore, the special legacy to Lady Matthiola, which while the daughter was alive is interpreted as a legacy of alimony, upon the daughter’s death is deemed to be a legacy and usufruct, as noted by the doctors in l. Titia, §. si, de leg. 3, remains firm: although the testator added a universal substitution of herself and others, he did not revoke the singular provision for his wife; but rather he frequently burdened her [with obligations] and pursued her with many favors of diverse kinds and forms. Hence she ought to have all that was left to her, according to what is fully stated in leg. and no. C. de leg. l. cum quod, §. si, and ar. in l. 3, ff. de stip. der. It does not avail that the daughter is dead, and therefore the mother does not remain with her; for she ought no less to have the legacy, as C. de leg. l. 1. To the contrary it seems that, although upon the daughter’s death she ought to have alimony, just as before, she nevertheless does not have the usufruct of all the goods.

And this is clear, holding the opinion of Bartolus, that in the aforementioned law 1 there is a special rule regarding alimony; therefore, the rule is different with respect to legacy of ownership and usufruct, as he notes in the Digest, On Conditions and Demonstrations, in the law "Those freedmen," and to this effect in the Code, On the Insertion of Conditions, in the law "Legacy." Moreover, the shares of others ought not to be devoid of usufruct, as in the law "Ships," in the section On Legacies of Usufruct, and in the law "If to another," and especially the share of the poor. Furthermore, the testator used the phrase "in equal shares," but did not say "equal shares." If the wife were to have the entire usufruct, because the usufruct of a share holds the place of a share, as in the Digest, On Legacies, Title 2, in the law "When the son," section "The owner," she ought to have alimony according to the reasons set forth in the first place; but she ought not to have the total usufruct. Whatever surplus remains beyond alimony, both in ownership and in usufruct, ought to be divided among the substitutes according to the form of the section "On Goods," through the laws and the reasons last set forth.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a legacy to a daughter for her dowry is conditional. The same is discussed below in the next opinion.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Some say that a legacy to a daughter for dowry is conditional, according to the text in the Authentica *De sancta ecclesia*, § *Centum*. But this is the opinion held by Bartolus in the law *Titio*, § *Titio genero*, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*. Others say, as Doctorus says there, that this legacy is under a cause, not under a condition. Nevertheless, such a cause is final, and therefore, although it does not prevent it from being called a cession, its defect leads to the resolution of the legacy. But the truth is that up to the legitime it does not create a condition; because then the testament would be null due to the reason of the omission of an intermediate heir, nor does it create a final cause; because if it were a burden, it is removed in the legitime, *De inofficiosa testamento*, law *Quam in prioribus*, and law *Sancimus*, § *Cum autem*, and noted by Cynus in the Code, *De nuptiis*, law *Sancimus*. Wherefore, up to the legitime, the question is futile, because no supervening case induces repetition, and therefore the agreements must be adhered to. Also, because the transaction was general, expressed in universal words, and with the intent of all inclusive, no question seems to remain. *Digestum*, *De pactis*, law *Emptor*, § *Lucius*. This clearly appears upon inspection of the words of the contract. *Digestum*, *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Quicquid astringem*, word *Nec rursus*. But rather, because the words say "up to the present day," and therefore, by a supervening case, that which was given beyond the legitime can be recovered, and I say that it is not refuted. The action for penalty has no place; because it does not apply against, as in the law *Qui Romae*, § *Duo fratres*, *De verbis obligatorum*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The same as the preceding one.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Whether a legacy of dowry is conditional, or whether it is subject to a final cause, which, if not fulfilled, means that it is otherwise not due, or is found to be paid, or whether it is not simply pure. The learned doctors Dy. and Pe. say that it is not conditional: but casual, or modal, having in itself a final cause, from the defect of which the effect is prevented. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Titio centum, §. sed cum ante nuptias. They say well that this legacy ought not to be paid except at the time of the marriage. C. de nuptiis, l. sancimus. D. de alimentis legatis, l. cum unus, §. si. D. de iure dotium, l. profectitia. This is noted by Dy. D. de administratione tutorum, l. qui negotiationem, §. pupillo. The same is held by Iaco. de Are. that it ought not to be paid at the time of the marriage. D. quando dies legati cedit, l. nec solus, §. si in habitatione. And this is true, according to Iac. de Are., except in the debt of the subsidiary goods, which does not admit of delay of time, or external burden, as he notes in the said l. sancimus. Others say that a legacy in the name of dowry is conditional, by the text in Auth. de sancta ecclesia, §. sed hoc praesenti, there: "if subjected to such conditions," etc., and thus he had made mention of the dowry. Moreover, the day of marriage is an uncertain day, because it is uncertain whether the girl will reach marriageable years. D. de legatis primo, l. si cui legetur. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. cum fuerit. D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. pe. This is held by Bar. in the said §. si cum ante, and he strives to explain that text and to turn it against the substance of the truth, hence I do not believe him, with all due respect, to be speaking the truth, and first because he formally says the contrary to the text which he alleges in the said §. sed hoc praesenti. Hence it must be observed that that text sets forth these cases as different in fact, namely, to leave under the condition of marriage, and to leave for the cause of dowry. And we note that the first case is called under condition, the second case is called under cause. Behold, therefore, what we decline, if, namely, both cases were under condition, the emperor would speak foolishly by distinguishing where no distinction applies. It does not object that he afterwards says "conditions": because it must rightly be understood, i.e., additions, or cases, or times, for the name of condition is taken in many ways, as D. de manumissionibus testamento, l. Mevia. And we note D. pro socio, l. si societatem mecum. Thus we can distinguish: if it is left to a ward, and it is conditional: because it is uncertain whether she will reach marriageable age or not. But if it is left to an adult, then if under a mode, because the day of age has ceased, and providing for the fulfillment of the mode of the legacy: because a minor cannot provide security: because an impossibility is promised for the present, and therefore she can neither sue nor has the day ceased, because the distinction is sufficiently probable, when the title of dowry is ascribed to the legacy, for example, because the testator says for dowry, or in the name of dowry, or for the cause of dowry. But if it does not concern the title of dowry, but certain preparatory matters, which by the consideration of the mind usually lead to marriage, for example, because the testator says, "for this purpose that she may be able to marry, I assign to her a thousand," then it is a pure legacy, argument from C. de iure dotium, l. mulier dotem. Coming, however, to our case, in which a legacy was made to the daughter for dowry, the question is, whether, over and above the legitime, if the minor dies, this legacy is caducous. Bart. says that to the daughter it all seems to be simply pure, and by occasion of the legitime it draws with it the residue: because the will ought not to be divided, for it does not seem that the patron wished to impose anything according to him. And it is answered to §. cum ante, because there in contemplation of a certain marriage, otherwise if uncertain, according to him. It is wonderful, because this distinction is not proved by law or reason. And I concede that the father does not speak with the intention of burdening the daughter, but speaks from affection for his offspring, for this is a natural desire of parents, as D. quod falsum tutor, l. an in patrem. Nevertheless, he wishes the case which he appends to exist, and in this there is a certain delay. Such delay is removed in the legitime, however, and what is more, it is in the power of the father, how he may order and dispose under an equitable final cause. C. de inofficioso testamento, l. quam in prioribus. Nor is the will divided: because it is all uniform under the same final cause: but the power is beyond, which is divided by the authority of law. Wherefore, insofar as it is caducous over and above the legitime, the mother of the ward is heir to that which succeeded in the cause of the caducous legacy, and is to be restored to Cecha for the part which pertains to Cecha, of those very things she would be bound, if a subsequent contract did not hinder Cecha. D. de legatis, l. nuptiarum, §. si. Let us therefore see regarding the contract, whether it hinders Cecha. Therefore, on this second point, because the instrument was not about one lawsuit, but about all that could be for any cause whatsoever, the transaction must be adhered to, nor ought it to be restricted, as C. de transactionibus, l. sub praetextu. And fully noted D. de pactis, l. tres fratres. And l. emptor, §. Lucius. D. de verbis obligatorum, l. quid astringendae, versi. nec rursus. And in the goods, the credulous grandmother excluded the sister from intestate succession on one side only, nevertheless here we are not at the beginnings, but in pacts, and therefore pacts must be observed insofar as they speak.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a rector sues the debtors of a church or altar, he must prove all aspects of his title.
2. Payment is not to be made to one who cannot discharge the payer.
3. If two parties contend over a benefice, such that one is no more in possession than the other, payment is to be made to neither.
4. The patrimony of an altar is distinct from another office, and it consists in administering the altar.
5. If a testator leaves a fixed asset to one altar for the life of a certain priest, what does this entail?
body: In the Name of Jesus Christ, Son of the living God. Amen. Having seen this process and other acts, to the end that I may direct [the matter] in the way of truth,

It must be premised that when someone acts as rector or parish priest of a church or altar against debtors, they are not bound to pay him unless he is sued on the basis of a contract concluded with him. For these administrators are similar to procurators, who, by virtue of their mandate, must first prove their authority; the text is in the Digest, *De deposito*, l. *Si quis inficiatus*. For if he does not prove his title, he is presumed to be an intruder, as noted in c. 1, *De rebus iudicatis*, in the Sextus, to whom no action lies except on his own contract, Digest, *De conditione indebiti*, l. *Si urbana*. And this is fully noted by Innocentius in c. *Nihil*, *De electione*. Just as he cannot alienate, so too he cannot institute an action, Digest, *De iure deliberandi*, l. *Ait praetor*. Nor can payment be made to him, because he does not have the right of a legitimate administrator, Digest, *De solutionibus*, l. *Filiae*.

For he who cannot free the payer is not to be paid. Nor does the contrary apply. L. cogi, C. de petitione hereditatis, where it is said that no one is compelled to state the title of his possession, because that provision speaks of a defendant; but this person, who claims fruits as a curate of the altar, and is a plaintiff, is rightly compelled to state the title of his possession; because he is bound to declare himself a curate, and if he is bound to declare it, he is bound to prove it. C. ordinarii, de officio ordinarii, lib. 6. And no one of any capacity can doubt this understanding.

† Moreover, it must be known that if two parties dispute the title to a benefice, such that neither is more in possession than the other, neither is to be paid during the pendency of the litigation. D. 16, 3, l. 1, § apud Iuliam. And from this it is concluded against Lord Marinus: because, having not shown that his title of institution holds, he obtains a mandate that payment be made to him; and the judge, to whom nothing was proven, could not issue a mandate, nor excommunicate, as noted by Innocentius in c. Solet, at the end, de Sententia Excommunicationis, lib. 6. Nor would it suffice that the title was produced before the judge from whom the appeal lies, as in Auth. De his qui ingrediuntur ad papellam, § Illud, where it is said that victors do not obtain sentences unless they have shown that they are rightly constituted. It supports what is noted in D. 22, 3, l. Quoties, § Si. But let us further presuppose that he was the curate of the altar and had proved his title. The question arises whether the administration of temporalities is due to him, considering the tenor of the testament, from which one must not depart; because, since the testament is confirmed by death, and no one is ordained above another, as the Apostle says, and it is expressly proved in Auth. De ecclesiis, titulis, § Si quis aedificiis, col. 9, where it is mandated that the judgment of the testator be observed to the letter; and Extr. De testamentis, c. Vos quidem. And here it must be considered that the administration of temporalities is separated from spiritualities,

† Hence, one thing is to administer the patrimony of the altar, and another is to officiate at the altar. And if it is committed to someone to officiate, for that reason the full rectory in spirituals and temporals is not committed to him; but rather a certain spiritual ministry is committed, as in the Digest, *De magistro testamento*, l. *Meuia*; *De alimentis legatis*, l. *Servos*. The altar is also said to be for the custody of the temple. Moreover, the altar is said in three ways: in one way, for the church, and then the curate of the altar is, as above, the true and full rector of the church; because the church ought not to stand without a rector of both spirituals and temporals, if it is taken, *Extra*, *De successionibus ab intestato*, c. 1. In another way, the altar is said to be a certain member in a larger church, whence the curate of the larger church is the prelate of that member; because it is not fitting for the members to descend from the head, nor ought the altar to have two curates, but one is the curate as superior, and the other is a mere officiator of the altar, living from the altar. As *Extra*, *De prebendis*, *Cum secundum Apostolum*; 12 q. 2, c. *De his*.

We therefore weigh the words of the will, the form of which is as follows: "I will that the said stable remain to the said altar for the life of one priest of the Mass." What is this statement, "the altar is left to the priest for his sustenance"? It is that the altar belongs to the administration of the church itself; because this whole disposition was made in honor of the Blessed Virgin, and subsequently of Saint James, and was left in contemplation of both. See C. de usufr. l. fi.; C. de iure delib. l. cum aliquis; ff. de cond. et dem. l. filio; and in Auth. de sanct. et hon. eccl. §. si quis in nomine magni Dei. Moreover, the goods are burdened with the provision of sustenance, and the priest must be content within these limits. See ff. de iud. l. fideicommissum §. tractatum. For the testator does not say, "I leave the altar to the priest for sustenance"; for then the priest would possess everything. See C. de don. l. donationes in concubinam §. species; ff. de annuis leg. l. annua §. Titia. But rather, he said the converse, because he leaves it to the altar of the church for the life of the priest. For if anything remains after the priest's life, that belongs to the altar, and consequently, the governance of the surplus belongs to the superior rector of the church; because the word "for," as it pertains to the priest of the altar, imports a certain limitation. Hence, it is said that the excess remains with the church. See extra de constit. c. cum M. Ferrarien.; ff. ubi pu. edu. de. l. ius alimentorum; ff. de us. l. in fideicom. §. cum Pollidius. For this priest of the altar is more of a vicar priest than an ordinary one, and therefore, in administration, he is subordinate in action, as noted by Innocentius, extra de iud. c. cum deputati. And to this point, extra de praeb. c. extirpandae §. pe. ver. nec occasione, and de rescript. in Clem. nam, are most apt, because this altar is annexed to the church of the Holy Annunciation; and therefore, the curate of the altar ought to have a suitable and sufficient sustenance. From these things, it clearly appears that the judge delegated in the appeal case ought to pronounce that the appeal was well taken against the said Marinus, and that judgment was wrongly given for the said Marinus. For this is the form of the sentence. See C. de appel. l. eos. And condemn the said Marinus in costs. Also, the fourth part is due to the bishop; because it is not among the excepted cases. See c. fi. and c. officiis, extra de testam. From the foregoing, it also appears that the rector of the church of the Annunciation may accept the legacy made to the said altar in the aforementioned will; because the altar is a concrete or connected member, concluding, as I said in another opinion, that the one presented and instituted to this altar does not have care of temporalities; but he ought to have a victual stipend; because from the altar, and from that, he ought to be content. Notwithstanding ff. de transac. l. cum his §. cum uni. I answer, as I answered to §. species. It is supported by ff. de transac. l. cum hi §. modus; ff. de alim. leg. l. cum unus §. fi. I therefore take those words of the testator, "for the life of one priest," and they have this sense, which is consistent, that the priest ought to have food; and because the testator speaks only of food, he seems to have denied the remainder to him, as in the cited §. cum Pollidius. For the will of the testator regulates and governs conditions and modes. See ff. de cond. et dem. l. in conditionibus primum locum; and l. pater Severinam §. conditionum.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a certain portion of the month is stipulated in the agreement, and one part pertains to the existence of jurisdiction, and the other part to its non-existence, whether the proceeding is juridical.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It being posited that the portion of the month stipulated in the agreement may pertain to the existence of jurisdiction, and another portion of the month, namely the first three days, to the non-existence, or to the non-absence thereof.

† It is asked whether the aforementioned proceeding is juridical. And it is certain that confession supplies every defect of judicial order, except for the defect of jurisdiction, which is not supplied, as in Extra, De iudiciis, c. Ac si clerici; and De confessionibus, c. Cum super; and De electione, c. Per inquisitionem, according to Innocentius; and De restitutione in integrum, c. Pisanis, according to Albertus and Ioannes Andreae. Hence there are three cases: either it is certain that jurisdiction or the authority of the cognizant judge is lacking, and neither the confession nor the sentence is valid, as in D., De alea, l. 1, § Quod autem; or it is certain that jurisdiction is not lacking, and both are valid. And unless the thief returns the stolen goods, he ought to be retained in prison, as in Auth., Ut iudices sine quoque suffragio, § Oportet enim; and in Auth., Ut liceat matri et aviae, § Illud. It is valid even if one proceeds by inquisition, as in D., De furtis, l. Interdum, § Qui furem. Or it is doubtful whether we are within jurisdiction, or outside the time and limits of jurisdiction, and then this question would have been agitated and settled by the Prince; one should stand by the sentence, as in l. Ex quocunque and l. Si quis aliena. But when a prescription excluding jurisdiction was opposed, whether one presumes in favor of the sentence. It seems that yes, as in Extra, De renuntiatione, c. In praesentia; and according to Innocentius, De probationibus, c. Quam contra. The contrary seems correct, for then one presumes in favor of the sentence when the libel is apt; here the libel of inquisition is inept and does not conclude probably, presumptively, or necessarily. And this on account of the obscurity of the time, as noted by Bartolus in D., De accusationibus, l. Libellorum; and De novi operis nuntio, l. Non solum, § Sed ut probari; and according to Innocentius, De foro competenti, c. Cum sit generale. Nor can an inept libel be validated by proofs, as noted in c. Examinata, De iudiciis, in the Novella: since therefore the foundation of jurisdiction, i.e., the granting of time, is not established, the judgment does not hold, as in D., De adulteriis, l. Accusaturus. But against this allegation, the common reformation of Tudertus seems to openly contradict, which expressly states that those condemned to restitution say they pay, and the reformation does not prejudice those who have been robbed, or from whom things have been stolen by theft: since therefore this is established by confession, no remedy seems available other than that they are bound to pay what was stolen. Glossa ordinaria, C., De in ius vocando, l. Venia. In this question, I doubt that if the maleficium was true, no one having a soul will find the thief; but if the question is asked according to strict law, if the inquisition does not hold, the confession made in the absence of the party does not hold: because the inquisition was not made, since the judgment is null, and the confession tends to bind, as noted in l. 1, C., De confessionibus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The statement of a notary confessing that he had drawn up an instrument falsely is not upheld after he has reduced it to public form.
body: In the Name of Christ Amen. And of His glorious Mother.

After the notary has reduced the instrument to public form, even if he confesses that he made it falsely, his statement shall not be believed: because, since he has already performed his office, he cannot subsequently declare the instrument false or erroneous in its substance, as held by the authorities. §. illud, "Aut erroneum in corpore," D. de testibus; §. quia vero, and Extr. de testibus, c. praeterea. The notary and the witnesses are considered equal. D. de testibus, l. Domitius.
