And this is the opinion of Bartolus, de regulis iuris, l. si librarius, when sometimes, indeed, considering only the strict letter of the law, if judgments were rendered against the notary, it would not prejudice the party who was unaware that the case was being litigated, according to Cynus, who thus notes, C. qui agere non possunt, l. 1. It is supported by D. de infamia, l. Lucius. Although, therefore, the aforementioned statements are true according to the strict letter of the law, nevertheless the judge before whom the matter is debated must consider what weight of credibility should be given to such a notary, just as we say regarding a witness. D. de testibus, l. 3, §. idem divus; and the aforementioned l. Lucius. I, indeed, if I were sitting in judgment, would strive to seek the truth through witnesses and every other possible means; and if I could not have them, I would in no way give credence to such an instrument, since the author of the instrument detracts from it by his own confession, and it is his proper duty to impose credibility upon his own instrument in substance, D. de fide instrumentorum, §. si vero neque, col. 6. For what judge would not doubt the truth of an instrument which the notary has attested to be false before his judge under oath? Therefore, as long as he doubts, the matter will never be clear to him regarding the case; hence he will never be able to render a just judgment, without the burden of his conscience reproaching him, whichever way he might incline, affirmatively or negatively. C. de iudicibus, l. praefendum, §. 1. And that it is within the discretion of the sitting judge what he ought to believe, having weighed the circumstances on both sides, Innocentius expressly notes, de arbitris, c. 1, ver. "ex variis tamen circumstantiis," where this question is decided. From these, I conclude that between the said parties, on the occasion of the said inheritance and goods, there can be a great lawsuit or dispute. For the civil action is converted into a criminal one, in which a most rigorous investigation must be conducted on both sides. C. de falsis, l. ibi fals. And therefore, governed by the fear of the said just future litigation, the governors of the hospital may lawfully compromise with the adversaries. C. de transactionibus, l. praeses; C. de pactis, l. pactum curis; D. de pactis, l. item magistri, l. 2; C. de transactionibus. Therefore, assuming the title of the cause of the transaction, the aforementioned governors should release their adversaries from all right which they had, or could have, by name, cause, and occasion of the aforementioned codicils in the aforementioned inheritance, whether anything was retained by them or given to them; and this way is safe and secure for both parties, and cuts off all lawsuits. And I hold the same conclusively, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws. But that the rector of the hospital may compromise on account of a wounded or doubtful conscience, according to the note, C. de transactionibus, l. praeses, is supported by what is noted by Archidamus, 54. dist., c. generalis; D. de negotiorum gestis, l. at qui natura, §. cum me; D. de actione emptio, l. emptorem. And therefore I have subscribed and signed with the sign of my name. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a merchant who purchases goods to be delivered to him at the time of the fair is bound to pay the toll.
2. Sense and will are incorporeal, and can be present simultaneously and at one and the same time in several places.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Although these allegations are beautiful, I believe it to be most true,

† But if the buyer had purchased goods to be delivered to him at the time of the fair, and therefore goes for the goods at the time of the fair, could he extract them without payment of the toll? Because at that time the day of payment arrives, and then the obligation begins to be in its full effect, not only executory but also obligatory; and although the action arises before the day, the execution is hindered by the dilatory nature of the payment. D. Mandati, l. Si mandauero tibi per me, in principio; and l. Cedere diem, cum sequentibus. And then it is said that the contract is effectively or perfectly concluded with that perfection which consists in full effect: as in l. 3, De bonis auctoritatis iudicis possessorii, cum sequentibus. And therefore that time must be considered not from fiction, but from the understanding of the law, because it arises from consent. And so the contracting parties intend, and therefore I hold that the forum where the contract is made is the true forum, not a fictitious one: as in l. Contraxisse, cum sequentibus. So also regarding place, because the effective place is rather considered than the place of the words: as in l. Unum, Si certum petatur; and l. Finis, De tritico. Just as if a legatee outside the city promised to pay in the city, or vice versa, the place of payment is considered. De iudiciis, l. Si quis delegatus; De arbitris, l. Non distinguemus, §. Item; De constitutione pecuniaria, l. Eum qui, §. 1. And if someone says that the place and time of the utterance of the words should be considered, and not the place and time of the effect of the words: let him suppose that the extraction toll was in force at the time of the contract, but not at the time of extraction. It follows that it must be paid, because the beginning is considered according to his allegation, which is not true, because this burden arises in the execution itself, not in the contract itself: as in D. De publicanis, l. Caesar. Now to the point: since he who is of a different forum buys, it is understood that the act is done, and when he goes or sends for the thing, it is to be paid to him, whether he goes at the fair or at another time, and not before. De constitutione pecuniaria, l. Item illa. Hence, if he goes at the fair, it does not have a necessary consequence except at that time, and not before, and therefore it cannot be drawn back to before, as if it were expressly said, "You shall give when I come." Especially from the quality of the goods: because at that time it was customary to go for that merchandise. D. De iudiciis, l. Sed et si susceperit, §. Si libertis, in verbis "ex genere comparitionis." For that time is tacitly understood when he goes or sends, and this tacit understanding is held as express. l. Cum quid, Si certum petatur. And therefore if he goes at the time of the fair, it is understood that the contract is made at that time, especially regarding delivery and those things which are consecutive to delivery, such as carrying the delivered thing home and the toll of carriage, not of convention. Moreover, then the contract is perfected with the last perfection. Nota in l. 1, De periculo et commodo rei venditae. And therefore I believe this to be the truth, that the thing previously promised can be freely extracted: but delivered at the time of the fair. Nor is this a fiction strictly taken against the truth of nature: but it is truth arising from consent, and thus naturally ensuing, and from the principles of natural law. For although it is a fiction that, while I am in Rome, I should be in Padua, this is as regards the body,

But consent and will are incorporeal, and can be in several places at once and at the same time, as in l. si, C. de praescriptionibus longi temporis; and therefore it is wrongly said that the law speaks in a precise fiction, and that that law has no place in the statute, unless the words of the statute were entirely to the contrary, as in l. ille, aut ille, §. cum in verbis, which here does not seem to me to be the case. That one has bought from a merchant is to be understood in a broad and favorable manner, however the matter may have been bought according to the understanding of the law; for the place from which is not considered, but the place in which payment is to be made, de actionibus emptio venditio, l. ratio, §. final. And therefore I say that he who did not pay did not defraud the toll. Fraud is a name for deceit, and does not apply except to one who knows with certainty that he is bound.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a statute prohibits contracting at a certain time under penalty, and the contract is made at that time, but is perfected at a lawful time, whether the contracting parties incur the penalty of the statute.
2. When the end has a necessary consequence from the beginning in contracts, delicts, and wrongs, the beginning is considered, and not the end.
1. The preambles of statutes are regarded as the reason.
body: In the Name of Christ Amen. And of His Mother the Virgin Mary.

† In the aforementioned question, it seems that, first, according to the law, it should be stated that the said buyers are not bound to any penalty by virtue of the above-mentioned statutes; which is proven as follows. It is equivalent for something to be done at a lawful time, or to be done at an unlawful time and have its substantial effect referred to a lawful time. D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. In tempus; and if it does what it ought not, in l. In fugitivis, C. de plagiariis. But here, although the purchase was made at an unlawful time, it was referred to a lawful time; therefore, it is as if it had been made at a lawful time. Secondly, thus: although a contract was celebrated in one place or at one time, if payment is to be made at some place or time, the time of payment is considered, where the contract is deemed to have been celebrated, as D. de solutionibus, l. Quaero; D. de obligationibus et contractibus, l. Contraxisse; and l. 3, de bonis auctoritatis iudicis possessis, cum si. Therefore, although the contract was celebrated at an unlawful time, yet because its payment was referred to a lawful time, such a contract is valid, and the contracting party does not deserve any penalty, arg. in l. Graecus, C. de adulteriis. On the contrary, it seems that such a contracting party should be punished according to the aforementioned statutes, which I prove as follows:

† When the end has a necessary consequence from the beginning in contracts, the beginning is considered, and not the end, as in D. de minoribus, l. 4, § scio; and this is held by Jacobus. But in delicts, and in matters of maleficia: yet the end of the exportation has a consequence from the very beginning; therefore it is the same as if he had exported at an illicit time. Moreover, the statute privileges those buying at the time of the annual market; but these did not buy at the said time; therefore they ought not to enjoy the privilege. It supports what is noted in l. non solum, § sed ut probari, D. de novo operis nuntiatio; and l. cum actum, D. de negotiis gestis cum eo qui.

† Moreover, the preambles of statutes are regarded as their rationale, as C. de iudic. l. properandum; ff. de haereditatibus instituendis l. Pacumeius. But the rationale of the statute granting the privilege was to increase the annual market, which is not the case in our situation: therefore, the rationale of the statute ceasing, and as Menochius holds, its privilege also ceases. Moreover, care must be taken that statutes and laws are not defrauded: as noted in ff. de legibus l. contra legem. But this could easily result in the aforementioned penal statute being defrauded. For all purchased before the time of the market, and awaited that time so as to transport without payment of the toll; and thus the penal statute could never apply, as if the matter were done in words, and not in deeds, contrary to l. 2, C. comm. de legibus. Moreover, the act of disposition is stronger in its cause than the effect, as ff. de adoptionibus l. si patet in principio; de legibus 2 l. cum pater § dulcissimus; and noted in auth. multo magis. Therefore, the time of the disposition, or contract, ought rather to be considered than that of execution. For the said purchase is perfected by consent alone: as l. consensu, ff. de actionibus et obligationibus; and what is noted in l. 1, ff. de contrahenda emptione. The objection from l. in tempus does not hold, because there it speaks on the ground that the testator expressly stated that he was conferring it at a lawful time; but if the contract was simply celebrated, it is understood in that manner, l. in fuga, C. de plagiariis. For the contracting party provided for himself from the beginning so as not to contract against the law, but in our case he did not. Moreover, the contract was conferred at a lawful time, to such an extent that in the meantime no obligation arose, nor any right; but in our case only the mere execution was delayed. The objection from l. contraxisse and lex 3 does not hold, because that is true by a certain fiction, which fiction does not regularly have place in statutes, as fully noted by Bartolus in l. si is qui pro emptore, ff. de usufructu. Moreover, those laws, l. videntur, do not make against us, for they say that the accusation, or contract, is exercised and celebrated in one place, and the payment is conferred in another, where the payment is distinct: therefore, it does not seem to have been celebrated except there, in the place or time of the thing delivered. From which I conclude that the said purchasers have incurred the penalty of the said statute.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Once the case has been concluded, nothing further may be alleged in law.
2. Whether the conclusion of the case impedes the petition for arbitration.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.
† After the conclusion of the case, Innocentius says that nothing can be alleged either in law or in fact regarding the cause posited in c. Pastoralis. Therefore, it must be considered,

Whether a conclusion in the case precludes the petition for arbitration. For this petition concerns acts, but with respect to acts to be performed, it does not seem that a conclusion can be sought. Moreover, this petition is a kind of declination of jurisdiction, and the way of declinatory pleas is precluded by consent to the judge himself: Digest, De iudicibus, l. sed et si susceperit, in principio. To the contrary, it appears that the statute speaks generally and without distinction; therefore, since it does not distinguish as to time, neither shall we distinguish: Digest, De bonis auctoritate iudicis possidendis, l. in venditione, § de tempore; Digest, De lege praetoria, l. 1, § generaliter. The objection based on Innocentius does not hold, for what he says is true with respect to matters that are of the natural course of the case. For a conclusion in the case pertains to those matters; but this is a certain benefit outside the natural course of the litigation, which has place before sentence at any time; but not after sentence: Extravagantes, De arbitris, c. exposita. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Purchasers of a datium succeed to the place of the fisc.
2. Things that fall into forfeiture are lost by the very act.
3. A datium is taken from all creditors, just like a tax.
4. A special time derogates from a general one.
5. The penalties of statutes are not to be aggravated.
6. One who accepts a datium after the term is bound to renounce it. L. commisso.
7. When a time is not added, it suffices that it be done at any time.
8. A partner ought not to retain in his purse what is owed to the body of the partnership.
9. The official confession is to be believed.
10. The penalty of confiscation does not threaten on account of the unpaid.
11. During the time of fairs, a palificatio is not necessary.
12. Laws are to be reconciled with laws.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Certain evident matters must be premised, and first, that purchasers of property given in lieu of the fisc succeed to the things which fall into forfeiture, as in the Digest, On the Action of Purchase, the law *Creditor* in the beginning.

Secondly, that things which fall into a forfeiture are lost by the very fact, and ownership passes to the fisc or to the revenue collectors, as is stated in the Digest, title "On Public Forfeitures"; nevertheless, possession does not pass by operation of law, as is noted in the Digest, title "On Behalf of the Owner," in the law "When Two," section "He gave the same answer."
Thirdly, it must be premised that the *datium* is taken away from all creditors, just as is the *tributum*. Codex, *Si propter pupillum*, penalty, law 1.
Fourthly, it must be premised that a special time derogates from a general one. Digest, On the General Rules of Law, Law *Ex facto*, Section *Idem quæro*.
Fifth, it must be premised that the penalties of statutes are not to be aggravated; but we ought to be content with the penalties thereof. D. de verb. oblig. l. si ita stipulatus.

Sixthly, it must be premised that whoever accepts a *datium* after the term has expired is bound to renounce the *lex commissoria*. D. de minoribus, l. Emilius. And similarly, one who has accepted a profession after the term appears to have renounced the penalty for not having professed within the term. Arg. D. de verbis oblig., l. Qui Romae, § Calimachus, in fine. And this is true when the right of remission resides in the acceptor or recipient; otherwise, if he does not have the power to remit, as stated in the aforementioned § Calimachus, and l. Si quis professus, in fine, D. de publicanis; C. de pace inter imperatores, l. Commissoria; and D. de lege commissoria, l. Post diem.

† Seventh, that where no time is specified, it suffices that the act be done at any time. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. qui fundum; unless a time is inherent by law, or by nature, or by custom, or an interpellation has intervened. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. nec semel, § si in habitatione; when a day is left to the discretion of the legatee. C. de verbis obligatorum, l. interdum; D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. 1, in fine; de praebendis, c. extirpandae, according to Innocentius.

† Eighth, that a partner ought not to retain in his own purse that which is owed to the body of the partnership; but he ought to offer it in the same manner as if he owed it to an outsider, this being required by the good faith of the parties, for he ought not to intercept what is common. D. 16.3.10 (merito) and D. 17.2.54.1 (si communis).

† Ninth, I premise that the confession of the official shall be believed, as in C. de non numero pecuniae, l. in contractibus, § 1; C. de apocryphis publicis, l. 1; and in Auth. de mandato primo, princ., § coges.

† Tenthly, that the penalty of confiscation does not threaten on account of non-payment, as in c. de mercatoribus, si quis, no. ver. si vero. For on account of the penalty of one hundred solidi, there was a departure from the penalty of confiscation, as in ff. de re militari, l. qui cum uno, §. qui post desertionem. 11
† Eleventh, I premise that in purchases made during the fair period, public proclamation is not necessary, as in c. 1, de forma nundinarum, 12 § 6, which begins "anchora possano," at the end.

Twelfth, and last, is that common maxim: Laws are to be reconciled. C. de inoff. do. l. 1. And distinguish the times, and you will reconcile the texts. not. C. de fur. l. manifestissimi. cum simi. From these matters it is manifestly and clearly apparent, as if whatever can be said for and against by way of allegation, yet in deciding I say that the said cloths did not fall under the offense, by four last evident points, which are here manifestly demonstrated. From which also the response to the contrary arguments is gathered. CASE. The facts are proposed thus: Francis donated irrevocably inter vivos certain goods to Laurentius and Matthaeus, sons of the late brother of the said donor. Regarding this donation, a public instrument was drawn up, in which, among other things, it is contained that the said donor reserved for himself during his lifetime the usufruct of the said donated goods: which goods he declared he held by precarious title for the said donees until they should receive corporal possession of the said goods; the license to take possession thereof by their own authority after the death of the said donor he granted, etc. This donor, after the said donation, lived, possessed, and enjoyed the usufruct of the said goods for a period of one year and more, then he died, the said donees surviving him, as well as Malgia, his wife, and Lucia, his daughter, whom the said donor had married a year before he made the said donation. This wife of the said donor formerly brought an action against the heir. On the first point, it must be said,

† that Petrutius, Andreutius, formerly the said husbands, and specifically against the said do. Lucia, daughter of the said donor, and herself seeking in the court of Arezzo certain things, which she asserted in her petition were due to her by the said do. Lucia, her daughter. The judge pronounced among other things, and granted license and commission to the nuncio, or herald of the commune of Arezzo, or of the court, to give, and that he should give a writ of execution against the goods of the heirs of the said Francis to the said do. Masgia. Who, among other things, issued a writ of execution against certain goods, as is said above by the said Francis, after which, on behalf of the said donees, it was requested before the said judge that the said proceedings conducted and the writ of execution issued, without the said donees being cited and summoned regarding the said goods, be revoked, and that it is null and void, because it was conducted and the said writ of execution was issued without the said donees being summoned, since they claim to be owners and possessors of the said goods, because the commission was made that a writ of execution be issued against the goods of the heirs of the said Francis, and not against the goods of the said donees; now it is asked, what are the parts of the said judge in the said case.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A tenure that has proceeded in fact must be revoked in fact, for example if it was granted after the commission had ceased.
2. A testator cannot make a will in respect of goods in which he has no interest; a judge cannot grant a tenure.
3. The possessor must be summoned when a tenure of the possessed thing is granted.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

The aforementioned holding must be revoked, insofar as it proceeded de facto, and this for three reasons. First, by reason of the cessation of the commission: he did not have a commission over the goods of a third party, and thus the de facto seizure proceeded. C. de iure fisci, l. Prohibitum, lib. 10; and l. Si, de bonis vacantibus, eodem libro. For dominion and possession were with the donee. C. de donationibus, l. Quisquis. For the natural possession, which the donor retained under the name of usufruct, was extinguished by his death, as l. 1, § Is cui, ff. Qui testamento liberi esse iussus fuerit.

Secondly, because the judge’s act is invalid, since it is deemed the act of a party (On eviction, l. si ob causam), but the donor could not make a will regarding that thing (C. de donis ante nuptias, l. si ante; C. de legatis, l. uxor patrui; ff. de usufructu legato, l. Sticho), nor could he dispose of anything to the prejudice of the owner.

Thirdly, because the possessor was not summoned. C. si propter pu. pen. l. si deserta. quibus ex cau. ma. l. cum miles. §. 1. Moreover, it ought to be revoked. per. l. a diuo pio. §. si super. de re iudi. and what is noted, C. ne vxor pro marito. l. ob maritorum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. One cannot claim that what he received from profit is unjust.
2. The disposition of the last statute is to be observed.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having considered the aforementioned point, and having examined the allegations and statutes, I proceed to conclude in a single word,

† namely, that the said Zanobius ought to have the said fourth part: because the commune of Volterra cannot claim that the said condemnation was unjustly incorporated into its assets, since it has derived benefit therefrom; therefore, it cannot challenge it, nor allege the turpitude from which it derives a lucrative cause. And this is established by l. si seruus plurium, § 1, ff. de legatis 1, and ff. pro socio, l. si igitur. What then? Whether just or unjust, it matters not to the point. Furthermore, it is no objection if it is said that he did not condemn except for 75 pounds, having deducted the fourth part on account of the confession. For he was obliged to do so; it appears that he judged the whole matter. And this is supported by l. ff. familiae erciscundae, l. meuius, § arbiter. It accords with what is noted in ff. de re vendicata, l. utique.

† Likewise, contrary statutes do not stand in the way, because the last permission prevails. D. de legibus, l. sed et posteriores; C. de pactis, l. pacta nouissima; C. de latronibus, lib. 1, l. 1, in principio, with countless others.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Executors may declare the testator's intent.
2. When the bishop ought to have a fourth part of what is left by the testator.
3. The lapsed portion accrues to the co-heir joined by words.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. Concerning the first point, it must be said

† that Petrutius, Andreutius, and Franciscus, as executors, having taken an oath to tell the truth, can specify and declare the will of the said testator, especially with respect to pious causes, as in extra de testamentis. c. cum tibi. and l. theopompus. ff. de dote praele.; and if they declare pious places, the bishop must receive the fourth part, unless they declare it for perpetual divine worship, extra de testamentis. c. fi. If, however, they declare certain persons, either by way of consanguinity or of friendship, the bishop ought to receive nothing, neither by law nor by custom. If, however, they declare it under the heading of the poor
†, in that case the bishop ought not to have the fourth part by common law, as noted in c. 2. de sepul., unless there were a custom to the contrary.

† Concerning the second point, it must be said that the share of the son of Nicolaus, as lapsed, accrues to Franciscus Lolii as conjoined in words. ff. de le. 3. l. re coniuncti. And this is the truth. I, Baldus, ASVS.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, when a mother who has entered into a second marriage does not claim guardianship, and the paternal and maternal grandmothers are present, one of whom has assumed the guardianship, the other is excluded from the inheritance of the ward.
2. Grandmothers exclude uterine brothers.
3. The paternal grandmother is preferred in paternal assets, the maternal grandmother in maternal assets.
casus: ASVS. The point of the question, on which a legal opinion is requested, is as follows. A certain Christophanus Nuti of Villa Maginae of Montis Maluae died, survived by his posthumous son Antonius, born of his wife, the said Catherina, who was then pregnant. And the said lady Catherina, mother of the said Antonius, and the lady Clarutia, maternal grandmother of the said ward, who did not accept guardianship, nor did she petition for a guardian to be appointed for the said ward within a year, and she passed to a second marriage, and has three sons from the second marriage, who are uterine brothers of the said ward. Both the said grandmothers, after the marriage was contracted, within which time the mother could have accepted guardianship, and within another year, did not accept guardianship of the said ward, neither she nor the other of them. But after the said two years, the said paternal grandmother accepted guardianship of the said ward, and exercised the said guardianship. The said Antonius, however, died in pupillary age, survived by the aforementioned mother, maternal grandmother, and paternal grandmother, and the said uterine brothers. Now it is asked, to whom, or in what manner, and to whom does the inheritance of the said ward devolve by right?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is proposed that the mother, after the birth of the posthumous child, acted as administrator for about two years, yet she did not assume guardianship; then she married, and after her marriage, the paternal grandmother assumed guardianship before the following year. Then, after the death of the ward,

It will be asked whether the paternal grandmother, who accepted the guardianship, is excluded. And what is the case with the maternal grandmother, who did not accept it? And whether these grandmothers, or one of them, excludes the uterine brothers? It must be said that before the mother remarried, she could also be admitted to the guardianship after the year had passed—not, I say, to the inheritance, as stated in the Digest, *De hereditatibus et tutelis*, in the law *Tutela*, section *Sed et si*, according to the gloss and Bartolus. Therefore, in the meantime, neither of the grandmothers was in delay. Subsequently, within the year, the paternal grandmother accepted the guardianship, which suffices for both grandmothers, because it suffices that the guardianship be administered by one, as noted by Bartolus in law 2 of the Digest, *Qui petere tutelam possunt*. There are also other subtle reasons to prove this, but these clearer ones suffice.
† But it is certain that these grandmothers exclude the brothers, according to the opinion of Bartolus.

The paternal grandmother is preferred in paternal goods, and the maternal grandmother in maternal goods. C. de bonis quae liberis l. quod scitis. § 1. There is a case according to him, as it is said there that the maternal grandmother is preferred in maternal goods, so it should be said of the paternal grandmother and paternal goods, and it is very noteworthy. This dictum does not apply: because the text in auth. defuncto, without distinguishing goods, says that half is called paternal and half maternal, and this is the truth. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 0. Pacts and transactions made by the chapters of mendicant orders and the priors of their places without the intervention of the superior are not valid.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

The allegations are indeed excellent; however, there is a special rule for mendicant friars, whereby agreements and settlements made in good faith by their chapters and local priors are valid, even if the superior has not intervened: as stated in c. si, de pactis, lib. 6. Hence, they could validly settle matters that were not clearly established. C. de transactionibus, l. praeses. And therefore, since hermits are mendicants, it suffices for the prior to settle on behalf of the convent a commission granted by the aforementioned last chapter, de pactis, lib. 6, which speaks generally concerning all matters pertaining to the convent, whether they be tithes or other things. Moreover, it must be considered regarding the interpretation of c. monasteriorum, de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, in that disjunctive phrase “convent or prelates.” I say that this is permitted because that which they never possessed is not said to have been alienated, nor is it established that it was theirs; hence, the composition is rather said to be the excitation of litigation. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a partner has entered the common assets in the cadastre as his own and has made purchases in his own name, to whom shall such assets belong?
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. The following case is presented: Ser Mattheus and Mutius of Corciano were natural brothers, and they lived together and conducted business, and for the most part they contributed all things in common, and thus they were partners. However, the said Ser Mattheus, because he was enrolled in the civic register, had certain possessions, which were in truth common to the said status, inscribed and recorded in his name in his castle. Moreover, he made certain purchases in his own name, because he, as I said, was among the citizens and brought up in the county. Now, after both had died, a matter of dispute arose between their successors, because the successors of the said Ser Mattheus wish to appropriate to themselves the goods registered in the tax rolls and those purchased. The question is asked: what is the law?

I answer that truth has a place, not against the cadastre, as in C. de don. l. censualis; de acquirendo dono, l. quæ quisquam. And since they were partners, everything is said to be shared, as is read, and not in ff. pro socio, l. cum duobus, § si fratres, and in Spec. de iudic. in the 4th part. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A greater portion may not be left to the second wife than to one of the children of the first marriage, or to the grandchildren: and that excess is applied to them.
2. If one coin has been left to the son of the first marriage by way of institution, and the residue to the second wife, whether concurrence occurs with respect to that one coin and the entire legacy is taken away.
3. The grandson imputes to his legitime the dowry of his mother acquired by him through a gift causa mortis; thus do the sons impute, thus the daughter, and thus the mother herself.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† To a second wife, by no title of liberality can more be given or remitted than to one of the children of the first marriage. The same applies to grandchildren, and whatever is given in excess is revoked and applied to the said children or grandchildren, as in C. de secun. nup. l. hac edictali, and in Auth. de nup. §. optime, col. 4.

It must be considered, however, whether, if one coin is left by right of institution to the son of the first marriage, or to the grandson, recourse will be had to that one coin and the entire legacy will be taken away. And it seems that this is so, because the text literally states that that surplus is treated in the case as if not written; therefore, nothing of what is owed to the wife in the case of being treated as not written: because no right arises from being treated as not written. But against this is the gloss on l. hac edictali, which says that if nothing is given to the son of the first marriage, and everything is bestowed upon the spouse, revocation takes place so that the shares may be equal. And if this is so, where the spouse sinned more by giving nothing: therefore, much more strongly where, by giving something, she sinned less, the same reason applies. For the reason of the whole is the same as that of the part. ff. de rei vend. l. quae de tota. Thus, therefore, the whole is not annulled: but it is reduced according to the mode of quality. And following this equity of the gloss, I have otherwise advised thus, because the text in §. optime, insofar as one son has, and with this equity, following the reason and intent of the gloss, I advised by transgressing, and thus I hold, saving the sounder opinion.

Having premised this, I come to the question asked, and first I consider whether the dowry was constituted by the right of this grandson, for such a dowry the grandson acquires by acquisition on account of death, and just as the daughter would impute it to herself, so too the grandson; see what is noted by Bartolus, ff. ad l. Falc. l. in quarta; ff. de coll. bon. l. dedit dotem. What, therefore, is to be said on this point? It seems to be said thus, that the second spouse shall not have more benefit in effect than the said grandson, as stated in the aforementioned §. optime and §. quia vero. Up to this point, in substitutions made to sons, the said testament remains firm, as in Auth. de nupt. §. illud. What is said above regarding fruits, the same must be observed regarding the principal, and this regarding fruits is estimated. ff. de rei vend. l. ex diverso. And also regarding those consumed, insofar as she has been enriched. C. si secundo nup. mulier l. 1. Although it could be said that she acquires in good faith those consumed, as is noted, ff. de re iud. l. fructus. In a woman, error of law is tolerated, and the title gives her good faith. ff. de pet. haer. l. sed si lege. §. sciri. in the gloss.

CASE. Rubric: Concerning those dying intestate without children. Furthermore, we establish and ordain that if any person, male or female, of the land of S. Severino, or its district, should die intestate, male or female, without legitimate children, that all goods and rights of such person dying intestate shall come and devolve to the nearest blood relatives descending from the paternal line, or the line of the paternal grandfather. Since it is sufficiently consistent with reason that such goods return to their original state, from which they are known to have originated, and the aforementioned provisions shall apply to present pending cases and future ones.

IN THE NAME OF GOD, Amen. Having premised the said statute, such a fact is proposed: a certain Angelutius had two sons, namely Nicolutius and Philipputius. From the said Nicolutius was born Peter; from the said Philipputius was born Lippus. From the said Lippus and Catherine, his wife, was born Severinus. From the said Catherine and another prior husband was born Vanna; and from the said Vanna was born Nicolina. The said Lippus died having made his will, and among other things which he disposed in it, he said thus: in all his goods he instituted Francis, Louis, and Severinus, his sons, as universal heirs in equal portions, and if all his said sons should die in pupillarity, or afterwards at any time, I leave to Antonio, son of Nicolutius, and to John, father of Nicolutius, one house with a courtyard, situated, etc. In the event of the said case occurring, to the said Antonio and John, by right of legacy, 100 pounds, which house and the said courtyard were alienated by the said Catherine, guardian of the goods of the said pupils. All these things having occurred, the said Severinus, one of the sons of the said Lippus, and Nicolina, daughter of the said Vanna, uterine sister of the said Severinus, and John, son of Peter Nicolutius, survived. Then the said Severinus died, having certain maternal goods, surviving him the said John Peter and the said Nicolina. Between John and Nicolina arises a dispute concerning the goods and inheritance of the said Severinus, dying intestate without children. For the said John says that the inheritance and goods of the said Severinus pertain to him by right, especially according to the form of the said statute, considering its reason, since it says, "since it is sufficiently consistent with reason," and since the said statute seems to intend that agnates be preferred in such succession to cognates. On the other hand, it is said by the said Nicolina that she ought by right to succeed the said Severinus, notwithstanding the said statute, since the statute speaks of those succeeding from the line of the father or paternal grandfather: but the said John does not descend from them, but from the great-grandfather, and thus the said statute ought not to be extended, since it is of strict law.

It is asked, having seen the said statute and the aforementioned point, and the allegations above mentioned, as far as they can be made, to whom pertains the inheritance of the said Severinus, whether to the said John or to the said Nicolina. And if to the said John, whether he succeeds in all the goods of the said Severinus, both paternal and maternal, and in others acquired from wherever by the said Severinus. And if to the said Nicolina the said inheritance pertains as to the nearer in degree to the said Severinus, ought certain legacies made in the testament to the said John to be claimed by John, and what ought he to have, whether the house with the courtyard, or the price which the said Catherine, guardian, received, that which it now is worth.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that the property of those dying intestate without children shall devolve to the nearest relatives, is the uterine sister excluded from the maternal property devolving to her aforementioned brother, when there exists some person in the line of the great-grandfather?
2. A statute speaking of the line appears to speak of the great-grandfather.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

The opinion of Nicolaus follows that of Severinus, as in the Code, On Legacies and Heirs, the authority "After brothers from both sides." And this is certain according to the law of conjunction. But it is objected against the opinion of Nicolaus regarding the said statute in three ways: first, from the words.

† For the statute speaking of the line, which seems to speak also of the great-grandfather: as in D. de postul. l. si cui. §. item Pompon. Also, from the reason expressed in the statute, from which we argue as from the mind of the law, as is noted by Dy. in c. ultra. de reg. iur. lib. 6. it makes. C. de revo. do. l. is solis. D. de pac. l. quod dictum. de re mili. l. milites agrum. and Inst. de legitima patro. tu post prin. Also, from the distinction of goods, there, when it says, whence they are known to have had their beginning. To this it makes that we note in d. auth. post fratres. But notwithstanding these, the truth is, as I said, that the said Nicolina is stronger in all respects, notwithstanding the words of the statute: rather they make for it, because they speak only of the paternal line, or of the line of the paternal grandfather: but John is not of the line of Philipputius, nor of the line of Lippi: therefore the statute has no place in him, as in D. so. mat. l. si vero. §. de viro. and this is clear to the eye by such a figure: for it is certain from the interpretation of lines, that Severinus is not in the same line of the father, or of the grandfather, with the said John, after the manner of columns: because they are not of the same colonel: as we note in Inst. de gradibus. post prin. Auici. in gl. which begins si pater. Also, the reason of Lippi’s statute does not obstruct: because it cannot be called a true reason, since it departs from reason, as is clear. C. de don. l. si auia. but it is a certain motive of the legislator. N. P. Moreover, correction of laws is not induced, as we note in Authen. quas actiones. From these it appears that the statute does not obstruct, and thus Pe. Lu. advised in a similar case. And to demonstrate, a similar figure makes, let the word “ex” be added, which signifies immediately. l. 1. §. ex incendio. Also, Io. Se. the word “descendentes” and it is clear in itself.

A certain person named Marcellinus Andreoli of Ancona, a merchant, being in the parts of Syria in the land of Damascus, constituted in the last article of death, made a certain testament valid with a solemn number of witnesses, and strengthened: although the witnesses do not appear to have been requested by the aforementioned testator in the private script written below and named: although in their testimony they say they were requested, written by the hand of a certain private person of the said city of Ancona, in which testament, thus asserted by the opposing party, he instituted heirs, no mention being made of his own heirs, but above he simply named those he wished to be heirs, a certain person named Iannellus Portelli, his kinsman, and a certain person named do. Oliueta, mother of the said testator, and beyond the aforementioned, he left legacies to certain special persons of the said city, and among other legacies which he made, he left to a certain person named do. Auiselucia Cionis, his wife, beyond her dowries, 200 gold ducats, nor does it appear by virtue of the said testament that the said Marcellus wished expressly to make a codicil: but only to make a will. Finally, the said testator died in the said place, the said Iannellus and do. Oliueta, heirs described in the said testament, surviving him, and who, Iannellus and do. Oliueta, by virtue of the said testament, entered upon the inheritance of the said Marcellus, and there surviving him were three of his brothers, joined to him by both parents, whom brothers the said testator in a certain other first will of his, solemnly celebrated in the city of Ancona, together with the said do. Oliueta, their mother, and mother of the said Marcellinus the testator, had instituted as heirs. It happened that the said do. Auiselucia, former wife of the said testator, from the heirs described in the said, as is asserted, last will made by the said Marcellinus, in the said place of Damascus, received the said legacy of 200 gold ducats in ordinary judgment, in which judgment, and in every part thereof, as you will see from the acts, the said Marcellinus was always said never to have made the said legacy, and thus to have made the said last will, which is asserted by the said do. Auiselucia, or her curator in this cause, that the said Marcellinus made in the parts of Syria in the land of Damascus, so that not only the will, but also the solemnity of the said testament, and of the said Marcellinus, was totally denied by the said heirs. The curator, however, of the said do. Auiselucia, to prove that the said testament was made in the parts of Syria in Damascus, and its tenor, made certain articles, and upon these, first response having been made by the aforementioned Iannellus and do. Oliueta, he had six witnesses examined, however, from the number described in the said testament asserted by the opposing party. It is alleged that the said testament was thus made, and its tenor, is not sufficiently, as is found in written law, proved by witnesses in the said case upon the said chapters, and examination, both because the said will, denied in the form aforesaid, ought to be validated by a number of 7 witnesses at least, since between the aforementioned parties there was contention about the will, and solemnity: both because two of the said six witnesses examined, one of whom deposed in Florence, the other in the city of Perugia, were not rightly, correctly, nor solemnly examined, according as is required by law, as by exceptions against them, and their statements, and attestations appended, fully opposed against the said witnesses, and their oppositions outside the term given for opposing against witnesses.

From the premises, it is asked, having seen the acts, and things done in the said cause, and others, which in this cause ought rightly to be subtly seen, what are the parts of the judge in judging, and whether in the cause aforesaid there is place for the referral of an oath to the said curator then living, d. d. Emphelitia being in the said cause, and today by the curator of do. Angela, heir of the said lady Auisalutia, her daughter, and legatee, in defect of proof.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a person dies having made two wills, the first in the regions of Soria and the second in Damascus, written in private handwriting with the required number of witnesses, but the witnesses summoned do not appear, and such an instrument cannot be proved except by six witnesses, which will shall be valid, the first or the second?
2. Whether legacies left in a less solemn will are due.
3. Add the following opinion.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† In Damascus, the law of the Romans is not observed; nevertheless, divine law and the law of nations have place there: because, if nothing else is established, it is to be believed thus, as noted by Innocentius in c. 1, quod super, de voto. But by the law of nations and divine law, two good and competent witnesses suffice for a testament, let alone six: therefore, since the custom of the place where the testament was made must be observed, as noted by the doctors in l. cunctos populos and C. de testamentis, l. si non speciali, it appears that the said testament is legitimately proved and valid in all places by reason of the country in which the testament was made. But Jacobus de Arena and Oldradus say that a stranger who tests there by chance and fortune, if he is of the Roman people, i.e., under the Pope or the Emperor, ought to test according to Roman law, because it is absurd that if someone were driven by a storm at sea to the Tartars, he should therefore change his law, and rather give occasion for falsification, j. remotis contra rationem legis ultimas, C. de fidei. But I leave this passage aside,

And I come to another point, and I say that where a will is denied, six witnesses are not sufficient, neither as regards the institution of an heir nor as regards the legacies of the will. Codex, On Wills, l. Si unus; Codex, On Fideicommissa, l. Si. Nevertheless, because the mother was instituted here, it is valid, and the mother succeeds as an intestate heir, and the legacies are due as if from an intestate estate. Codex, On Wills, l. Hac consultissima, § Si quis autem. It is necessary, however, that she accept the intestate inheritance, as noted in Digest, On the Institution of Heirs, l. Qui filio, § Servus. Hence, the mother must be asked whether she wishes to be an intestate heir; and if she affirms this, she is bound to the legacies. Another coheir intestate does not come forward, because he is more remote; therefore, he ought to be absolved as to that part which is claimed from him. Here it must be observed that all these things would be true, unless by virtue of the said statute it appears that the defendants accepted the inheritance; for by this they confess the will and its substance, and therefore, if this appears, they are bound to the legacies, as in Codex, On the Petition of an Inheritance, l. Si. But if it does not appear, what I first said must be observed. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 0. Addition does not supply the defect of solemnity.
body:
Addition does not supply the defect of solemnity. In the Name of Christ, Amen. This is a private writing, and unless it is proved by seven witnesses, it is not valid as a testament; because the will and the solemnity are denied, as noted in the Digest, *de testamentis*, l. *haeredes palam*, in the beginning; in the Code, *de bonis possessionibus secundum tabulas*, l. 2; in the Code, *de testamentis*, l. *si unus*; l. *si non speciali*; in the Code, *de fideicommissis*, l. 1. And although a private writing has intervened, it is nevertheless void as to proof, as noted in the Digest, *quomodo et quando testamentum aperiri debeat*, l. 1, in the beginning; and in the Code, ibid., l. 2; and in the Code, *de edicto divi Adriani*, l. *edictum*; in the Code, *de testamentis*, l. *publicati*. And therefore, by six witnesses, nothing is proved in the form of a solemn testament under Roman law. Hence, it must be observed that the defendants are sued here as heirs under a solemn testament, and the defendants deny the testament, and therefore they ought to be absolved, because it is not proved: I speak according to civil law. It is true that the mother of the testator was instituted. To prove this, five witnesses would suffice, if it had been done in the due manner, and the witnesses were led in that manner, and from that head, as in the Code, *de testamentis*, l. *hac consultissima*, § *si quis autem*; and if the first testament, in which those coming intestate were instituted, had not been made. But because those coming intestate, namely the mother and the brothers, were first instituted in the second testament, the dispositions therein are of no effect; because the testator, what he could do, namely to make a codicil, he did not wish to do. Code, *de testamentis*, l. *non codicillum*. What he wished to do, he could not fulfill; hence, when will and power are repugnant to each other, nothing is done, as in the Code, *de codicillis*, l. *si quis agere*; in the Code, *de fideicommissis*, l. *eam quam*. And that which he wished to bequeath, the mention of heirs makes manifest, as in the Digest, *de hereditate instituenda*, l. 1, § *qui neque*, and § *si autem*. And thus the civil law wills. But according to canon law, there are opinions: Extra, *de testamentis*, c. *cum esses*, and c. *relatum*. And because the testament was made among infidels, who come as we must believe according to the law of nature, as noted by Innocentius, *de voto*, c. *quam super*, and the custom of the place is to be observed. Code, *de testamentis*, l. *sin posset*. It might persuade that legacies ought to be paid at least according to good and right conscience. Digest, *de fideicommissis libertatibus*, l. *in testamento*. But let the mother dispute with herself regarding the forum of conscience; in the forum of civil law, however, I say that the defendants ought to be absolved from the claims: because it is not proved. Nor is there room for the tender of an oath, where not only proof is lacking, but also right and proof are absent: *de fideicommissis hereditariis*, l. *fina*. Since therefore, by imperfect proof, the disposition of the testator is not perfectly proved, the defendants ought to be absolved by sentence. The addition of the inheritance does not obstruct, because addition does not supply the defect of solemnity, according to the note by Bartolus in l. *filio praeterito*, Digest, *de iniusta rupta et irrita testamento*.

CASE: This is the testament of Giulino de Luca, made in the following subscribed form: First, I leave to Vico, and his heirs, Cione, the tutor. I leave my wife in the house, having life, wishing to stay, as is due. And I make my son Luca heir. After the death of the sons, I leave my brother as heir, and his children. After the death of the brother, it remains to his nearest relative. And this son of his died after the death of the father. His daughter was dowered with 50 gold florins by her brother. It is not known whether she is dead or alive. She was a widow, she remained with her, at the toll. Let us suppose that she is dowered, the son is dead, and also she remains with her mother. Then that son is dead. I leave to the wife six gold florins per year. I do not wish to be made to do so from her goods. See if he can do so, and she has not left the house. I can bring her to my house so that she does not lose her right, by removing her from her house, being I made her tutor. Can I excuse myself or not, that I am not?

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The pupil. Substitution excludes the sister and the mother.
2. If it is doubtful whether the substitute is alive, a curator should be appointed for this inheritance.
3. If the wife returns to the household, whether she is to be considered as having a dwelling and provisions, and that she ought not to have anything except provisions.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If such words appear in a public instrument, the mother and sister do not succeed in any respect: because it is a pupillary substitution. D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Centurio; C. eodem titulo, l. precibus; and in c. si pater, de testamentis, lib. 6.

And because it is unknown whether the substitute is alive, a curator will be appointed for the inheritance. C. de cap. l. nec nos. de tutela there is no need to discuss guardianship, because guardianship is terminated by the death of the ward: hence the guardian can no longer administer anything, as stated in Inst. quibus modis tute. finitur.

† And although the wife returns to the house of her brothers, she does not thereby lose or acquire any right, except that she ought not to have habitation, but ought to have maintenance; and if she could not reside honorably in the house, she would have both, namely habitation and maintenance. L. si, where a pupil ought to be educated, according to Jacobus de Arena. CASE. The point on which the advice of a wise man is sought is as follows: Theus Cechi of the village of Ulieto, community of Perugia, died intestate, with his legitimate and natural sons Peter and John surviving him. Then the said John died when he was three or four years of age, with his full brother Peter surviving him, and with Narbo, his maternal great-grandfather, and also Do. Citia, his maternal grandmother, surviving the said John, and also with Clara and Pascutia, full sisters of the late Theus and aunts of the said Theus and John, surviving him. Now it is asked to whom, or to which persons, the paternal and maternal inheritance of the said John the infant has devolved, and in what share. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When brothers and a brother’s grandmother are living, which of them succeeds to the deceased?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The text in the authority *defuncto*, on the word *in gradu proximitatis*, seems to say that only the brother related on both sides succeeds; but the truth is that the brother does not exclude the grandfather or grandmother, and therefore they succeed per stirpes, and thus this brother succeeds in one-third, in another part succeeds the grandfather: namely, in another third, and in the remaining third succeeds the grandmother: because all are in the third degree. And so the gloss holds, and this opinion is commonly approved according to Jacobus de Belvisio, because he says that it should be boldly held, and thus also Bartolus holds it there. However, the uncles do not succeed in any share. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The Emperor is bound to observe agreements.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Moreover, the Emperor is bound to observe agreements, as is fully noted in C. de legibus, l. digna vox, according to Cynus and others; because the prince is above the law, namely civil law, and below the law, namely natural or law of nations. That he is bound to observe agreements, the city commands, but under the laws of conventions. D. de pactis, l. legitima; D. quod cuiusque vivit nomine, l. 1, § quibus; and l. ciuitates; and fully noted in l. semel, de decretis ab ordinariis faciendis. And therefore I would approve the said opinion as true and reasonable. And thus I advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Having granted the privilege of plenary exemption to the brothers of Saint Mary of the Servants, whether they are bound to the canonical portion of wax and other funeral expenses on account of burials chosen at their monastery.
2. Given the aforementioned privilege, if a legacy is not left to the monastery but to a certain brother of that monastery, whether the fourth part is due from such a legacy.
3. From which legacies the canonical portion is due.
casus: CASE: Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons Andrew, prior general, and all the brothers of the Servants of Saint Mary of the Order of Saint Augustine, present and future, greeting and apostolic blessing. The sacred and holy Roman Church, mother of all the faithful of Christ and teacher in the field of the virtues of our order, to whom the Most High Lord has blessed, and in the splendor of the sacred religion under which you devoutly offer service and diligent ministry to the same Lady and her Mother, rejoices and exults; especially when she sees that we, by leading a life of the highest purity through the exercise of good works and the excellent holiness of conscience, by adhering to the word of doctrine and also by example, and by persisting most devoutly in the frequent and celebrated veneration of divine praise, from which the glory of divine majesty is raised, besides us and the aforementioned church, you and your aforementioned order: since therefore we see that you and the same church shine with devotion, embracing you within the confines of our breast with paternal affection, we watch over your good state with all our studies, so that, with God propitious, you may be protected from harms and always receive salutary increases. Therefore, wishing, in view of the aforementioned matters, to adorn you and your places, present and future, with a special favor and grace of extension, and to decorate you with a singular privilege, inclined to your supplications in this matter, we fully exempt and totally free you, your persons, and all your places, both present and future, from all jurisdiction, power, dominion, visitation, charitable subsidy, assistance, and also from the performance of any actions whatsoever, as well as from the removal from synodal and any other congregation of all and each of the Patriarchs, Archbishops, and Bishops, and any other ordinary judges, by special gift of grace; and we decree that you, your persons, and the same places are received into the right and property of Blessed Peter and the Apostolic See, and under their and our special and immediate protection, and that you, your persons, and the aforementioned places are subject solely and immediately to the aforementioned See. We will that the diocesans of the places, or any other person, cannot, as regards your persons or the aforementioned places, which are altogether exempt and immediately subject to the said See, promulgate sentences of excommunication, suspension, or interdict, or other sentences, whether special or general, by ordinary authority, or even exercise any power, dominion, or jurisdiction in any way, on account of any crime, contract, or thing about which it is argued, wherever the crime is committed, the contract made, or the thing itself located, notwithstanding the constitution of Pope Innocent IV, of happy memory, concerning the exempt, which begins "Volentes," and other apostolic constitutions issued to the contrary. We decree null and void any sentences of excommunication, suspension, and interdict, and any processes, penalties, and sentences, general or special, containing any of these, which may be promulgated or obtained against you, or any of you, or the aforementioned places, contrary to the tenor and form of these presents. Let no one at all infringe upon this page of our exemption, liberation, succession, constitution, and will, or dare to act contrary to it. If anyone, however, should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul. Given at Rome, at Saint Peter's, on the 7th of April, in the second year of our pontificate.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The aforementioned privilege is a privilege of plenary exemption, the effect of which is in question. And first, whether the said brothers are bound to the canonical portion of wax and other funeral items given or left on account of burial chosen by parishioners of other churches among them. And it must be said that yes, because although they are exempt, nevertheless they owe this canonical portion, which is due to parish churches by reason of sacraments and divine offices, as in c. *Dudum*, § *Verum*, *De sepulturis* in the Clementines; and noted in c. *Requisitis*, *De testamentis*; and in c. *Officii*. But the episcopal fourth they do not say is due to the exempt, because it is due by reason of jurisdiction. Hence, the exempt would be bound only to the Pope for the fourth payment, and not to the diocesan bishop, because they are not subject to him. Therefore, if the parish church receives a fourth from the bequests to another church, in which someone is buried, and such parish church is exempt, it owes nothing to the bishop, because it has separated from him by exemption and is emancipated, and does not seek the father-bishop. Henceforth it is assimilated to a freedman who has obtained the right of gold rings. Let it therefore be concluded that the brothers are bound to the canonical parish portion, except in privileged cases, which are set forth in c. *Ultima*, *De senatu et nobilibus*. They are not mendicants, to whom the privileged cases do not avail today, as in the aforementioned c. *Dudum*, § *Verum*. They are therefore exempt, but not mendicants. The canonical portion, according to custom, is a fourth, a third, or a half. And thus the decretal fixes its feet in *Extra*, *De sepulturis*, c. *Significari* (or *Certificari*). For where the law fixes its feet, there one must stand, as noted in *Digestum*, *Pro socio*, l. *Si non fuerint*. And this custom must be proved in court, and where custom does not appear, in doubt the canonical portion is understood to be a fourth, according to the doctrine, as in c. *De quarta*, *De prescriptionibus*. I do not dispute here whether it can be diminished or annulled. The truth is that it can be diminished, but it cannot be annulled, lest sacraments be withheld from one who gives no recompense, argument from *Institutiones*, *Ad legem Falcidiam*, in the beginning. It supports *De prebendis*, c. *Cum secundum*. But is it lawful for parish priests to seize bodies, or to snatch them, in order to obtain this canonical portion? It must be said that no. And if they snatch them, they lose all their right, and are compelled to restore the bodies, as in *Extra*, *De sepulturis*, c. *Cum libris*; *Codex*, *De sepulturis*, l. *Si*; and *Authenticum*, *Item qui domum moribundi*. After the body has been buried, the bishop may take the portion, nor is judicial order required, if the bishop permits it, because it is a matter of right and by right. Noted: the bishop compels the exempt, because he could not do so, but he will seize them from the hands of the laymen carrying them, as noted in the aforementioned § *Verum*, in the gloss beginning *Pro hoc dicebat*. And if bodies are taken by rural churches, whose parishioners choose burial for the said brothers in those rural churches, the canonical portion is due, and not to the church to which they are not parishioners. And if the rector of that church does not claim it, the bishop may claim it for the parish church, as noted by Innocentius in c. *Officii*, *De testamentis*. What of one who left to the church of the servants, or to the university of the brothers, and is not buried there? I answer: nothing is due to the parish church, because no injury is done to it. Likewise, nothing is due to the bishop, notwithstanding the exemption; otherwise in non-exempt cases, as in the aforementioned c. *Requisitis*, § *Secus autem*.

† What is to be said concerning one who is buried there, yet left nothing to the place, but rather to a certain brother of that place? It appears that canonical dues are owed, as if it were left [to the place], since they do not have a procurator; thus it is deemed left, as noted in the said §. verum, in the gloss beginning per hoc dicit. I say that if it is left principally in consideration of the person, and is such a thing as adheres to the person, such as food and clothing, no canonical dues are owed, argument from ff. de minoribus, l. 3, §. si quid filio. I say the same even if it does not adhere, for example, if left in contemplation of the person. To this effect is what we note in c. 2, de sepulturis. The objection from l. contraria does not hold, because it speaks of the brothers of the Preachers and the Minorites, and today the same applies to hermits and Carmelites; therefore, the rule is different in other cases, as in ff. de solutionibus et liberationibus, l. si vero, §. de viro.

† Regarding those legacies, I say that a canonry is due from all movable and immovable property, unless it has been left for the perpetual divine cult without fraud, according to the chapter *In nostra* on sepulchers, as interpreted by Innocentius, unless there were a custom that it should not be rendered from immovables; just as, by canonical custom, it can be diminished quantitatively, so therefore regarding the quality of things, so that it may be rendered according to decrees, *De cereo non ar.*, Digest, *De testamento militis*, law *Miles ita heredem*, section *Et quia diximus*. Moreover, if immovables are left for the perpetual cult, Code, *De sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, law *Placet*, nothing is due to the aforementioned parish church, as stated in the last chapter *De testamentis*. Nor is it due to the bishop, especially if exempt, as noted in the chapter *In vestra*, by Innocentius, Johannes Andreae, and Hostiensis, and by the late Federico da Senis in his consilia, consilium 149, beginning *Lo consi.*, 145, which begins *Cum aliqui boni viri*, and consilium 176, which begins *Verba consilii*. And in all these consilia agrees that which I have said, from which this matter, as regards the said brothers, is sufficiently declared. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A legacy having been made to the wife, in which her entire dowry and one plot of land are left to her with this condition, that she may not sell or alienate it unless to the heir of the said testator: whether the dowry, which was owed as to ownership, comes into play, and whether the heir succeeds to the said plot of land intestate.
casus: CASE. The facts are as follows. A husband left to his wife by these words, namely: "Also he left to his said wife, etc., and all his household goods." Also he left to his said wife one piece of land, with this condition, that his said wife could not sell it, nor alienate it, except to Federico, his heir, and his sons, etc. It is asked whether the said piece of land devolves to the brother of the said wife, who succeeds to the said wife intestate. It is asked whether the household goods, which were not the wife's as to dominion, but only as to simple use, are due to the said wife or not.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† This statement can be understood in two ways. In one way, it is to be understood that the testator left the said dowry to his wife, so that the word “his” is a mark of ownership referring to the wife. And such a legacy would be void, because one’s own property cannot be purely bequeathed to another (Digest 45.1, *de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*; Law *Mea res*). In another way, the word “his” is a mark of possession; for, as the grammarians say, it is a possessive pronoun, and then it is understood to refer to the dowry which she holds by the appointment of her husband. Dowry, so to speak, is the treasure of marriage, namely, furs, buttons, movables, and other things which the common people understand under this term, as in § *Asinam*. And in this way the legacy is valid (Digest 32.1, *de legatis tertio*; Law *Hoc legatum*; Digest 33.6, *de auro et argento legato*; Law *Si uxori mundus*; and Law *Vestis*, with *Si*). In case of doubt, however, it must be presumed that the testator intended a legacy that is valid (Digest 50.16, *de rebus suis*; Digest 50.17, *de verborum significatione*; Law *Verbīs legis*; and this is most appropriate, Digest 43.1, *de funerariis instrumentis*; Law *Fundus, qui locatus*), especially since that word cannot be referred to the testator, so that the sense would be that he bequeathed his dowry, i.e., that which he granted to his wife as dowry (Digest 33.6, *de auro et argento legato*; Law *Quintus*; § *Argento*; Digest 24.1, *de donationibus inter virum et uxorem*; Law *Sed et si vir bona*). Otherwise, as I said, he would have bequeathed in vain, as in Law 1, *de regula Catoniana*, which would be absurd to say (Digest 35.1, *de rebus dubiis*; Law *Cum in testamento*). It is credible that the testator, by making a legacy, intended to bequeath something, and that text is sufficiently known for many purposes. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A will having been made, in which the wife is left as mistress and housekeeper, and the sons are substituted as heirs to one another in case of minority, and whenever any other person is substituted in the event of dying without legitimate children, the last of whom having died made a will in which he left his mother as heir, who is to be admitted, the mother or the substitute?
casus: CASE. The point is this: A certain man, coming to his death, made his will, in which he left his wife at home and the Massaria in the house of the said testator, as long as she wished to stay and remain and observe a widow’s life in the house of the said testator. Furthermore, the said testator instituted his sons as universal heirs, and he says that if any of his sons should die in pupillary age, or later, at any time without legitimate children, the goods of his said inheritance shall remain to the other surviving male sons. And if all should die, as stated, in pupillary age, or later at any time without legitimate children, he made certain legacies, after which legacies he said that the residue of the aforementioned inheritance of the said testator, upon the happening of the condition, shall remain to the heirs of Petruccio in equal shares. Now it has happened that the said testator died; after his death, two of the aforementioned sons died in pupillary age. The third remained, who, having reached puberty in his 17th year, died and made his will, in which he instituted his mother and the wife of the said testator as universal heir. Now it is asked from the foregoing whether the goods of the said testator belong not only as to usufruct but also as to ownership to the wife of the said testator and the mother of those sons, or rather to the heirs of Petruccio substituted above, and it is requested from your lordship that counsel be given on behalf of the aforementioned lady, insofar as it can be done according to law, otherwise not.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† This adult had inherited from his brothers by pupillary substitution. The question therefore arises whether that which he received by pupillary substitution comes into the fideicommissary substitution, or whether it truly pertains to the mother. And it seems that it does not come into the fideicommissary substitution, unless he was compelled to accept the portion. D. 36.1. pr. (ad Trebellianam) l. ita tamen. §. qui suspectam. To the contrary, the words of the will are made, because the testator left the residue of the said inheritance, whence he could burden the whole. It is noted that a fideicommissum can be left from a pupillary substitution. D. 32.1. l. si fundum. §. si pater. Solution: Consider the words of the will; the fideicommissary substitution contains the entire inheritance of the testator, but not the personal property of the sons. D. 28.5. l. cohaeredi. §. cum filio. Nevertheless, there is no doubt that when the mother deducts two-fourths from the third at the time of the son’s puberty. C. 6.24.1 (si pater). de testibus. and C. 6.24. Rayn. num. and Rayn. cum si. de portionibus impuberum. Doubt arises, for if we understand that two substitutions were made for the impuberes, namely a pupillary one from the brother, and a fideicommissary one from an outsider, after the death of the father two-fourths are deducted: because the impuberes are burdened by the fideicommissum, and it is deducted from their person. If, however, they are not understood to be burdened themselves, but the puberes as heirs, so that this fideicommissum appears to have been left by the impuberes themselves, then the legitima is not deducted, which is not owed to him: but only the Trebellianic portion is to be deducted from the fideicommissum left in the second wills: as in Auth. de hereditatibus et falcidiis. §. 1. Solution: Because all are substituted together for the benefit of all, the legitima and the Trebellianic portion must be deducted as if burdened by the father in the first wills. And thus this mother deducts two-fourths from the entire inheritance. It supports what is noted in C. 6.25. (de inofficiosis testamentis) l. ex tribus. And if it is said, rather, that nothing ought to be restored: as in §. qui suspectam. I answer, regarding the goods of the impubes, which were not those of the father, nothing comes into the fideicommissum. And thus it speaks there: because it speaks of an impubes whom the father disinherited and deprived: whence the pupillary substitution did not include the father’s inheritance, and therefore rightly the goods of the disinherited impubes do not come into the fideicommissum, ad l. Falcidiam. l. qui fundum. §. qui filios. in fine. And this subtle and useful matter must also be understood from these words of the Lord and Massaria regarding the portion of alimony in the substitution. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The mother, to whom a usufruct has been left, and the inheritance, with substitutes appointed during her lifetime, is not considered the heir in full after her death; rather, the question arises as to who will be the heir at present, whether it is the poor substitutes among whom the distribution should be made, or the commissioners to whom the distribution of the said goods has been entrusted.
casus: CASE: The facts are as follows: Titius died, having passed away with his made testament and last will, in which, among other things which he disposed in it, he instituted A., his legitimate and natural son, as universal heir, and if the said A. should die in pupillary age, or afterwards at any time without legitimate and natural children, then, and in that case, he substituted to the said A. the brother of the said testator, C. and D., his nephews, for certain parts. Titius, the aforesaid testator, dies, leaving the said A., his legitimate and natural son, a pupil, who, through the person of his guardian, accepted the inheritance of the late Titius, his father, and was his legitimate heir. Finally, the said A., the aforesaid heir, became an adult, and after reaching adult age, such A. died with his made testament and last will: in which, among other things which he disposed in that testament, he instituted the womb of his wife as universal heir, if a male were born; if a female, he ordered her to be dowered at the discretion of the executors, and in constituting the dowries, he instituted her as heir, and if it should happen that his said wife is not pregnant, or does not give birth: then, and in that case, he instituted and wished Doña Clara, the mother of the said testator, to be his heir, however, as to the usufruct only, and until the said Doña Clara lives naturally, and he absolved and freed her from all security which his said mother would be bound to provide on account of the aforesaid usufruct. But after her death, the said testator wished that all his goods should come to his undersigned executors, whom he burdened, and that all the goods of his inheritance be sold and distributed to those wishing to buy for a competent price, and that the price received from these be distributed for the soul of the said testator among poor and needy persons, as it shall seem fitting to them, and in marrying poor women and other alms, giving to no poor person more than 5 pounds of Bologna, and to any woman being married, more than 10 pounds of denarii. He instituted and substituted these poor and needy persons, in the quantities and amounts to be given to them by his said executors, as his heirs. I, Baldus.
body: Recently

It is asked whether the said Do. Clara is heir in ownership and usufruct, that is, in full, so that she may be sued and may sue, or whether she is heir only to the usufruct, while the poor, or the commissioners in place of the poor, hold the ownership at present, and whether, upon the death of Do. Clara, by consolidation of the usufruct, she then becomes heir in full, or whether those coming intestate at present are heirs, and she is considered a legatee of the usufruct only.

It appears that she is heir in full right, because no other universal heir has been instituted at present; and thus, removing the mention of usufruct, she is considered simply instituted as heir, as in L. 1, §. si ex fundo, ff. de haeredibus instituendis.
