And because the manifest will of the deceased does not oppose this: therefore also by the force of L. quoties, §. si duo, eodem titulo, and what is said there by Bartolus, and L. si ita quis haeres, eodem titulo.

Against this it is argued, because the testator most clearly willed that the mother should be the usufructuary, such that she should not be the owner; therefore, his will must be observed, as in L. si, C. de fideicommissis, and the authority cited there, and the said L. quoties, §. si duo, according to the reading of Jacobus de Arena and Bartolus. The preceding point is evident from several things. First, from the merely taxative language, where he says "in usufruct." From the fact that he freed the mother from the burden of providing security on account of the said usufruct. From which it evidently appears that he willed another heir to exist in the meantime, to whom security would have been due by law. Second, to the same effect: one instituted in a certain thing is held in place of a universal heir when the thing is certain, as in L. quotiens, C. de haeredibus instituendis, and thus all doctors understand the laws cited above: but this mother is not instituted as heir in a certain thing, but in an uncertain thing, and one which does not yet exist, as in ff. de verbis obligatorum, L. ubi, §. fundus; nor after the death of the testator, before it is constituted, as in ff. de usufructu, L. 3, in principio, and §. 1. Third, because an institution made of a usufruct is made of a thing which, by its nature, must be received and constituted by another, as in the said L. 4; and thus there must be a difference between the constitutor, or giver, and the recipient. Therefore, it follows that, considering its nature, she should not be said to be instituted even by the strict law. Fourth, because one instituted in a certain thing, with no other universal heir instituted, is heir in full by a certain right of accrual according to the doctors; but usufruct does not accrue to ownership. Example: although usufruct consolidates with ownership, and usufruct accrues to the usufructuary, as is clear throughout ff. de usufructu accrescendi. Therefore, in our case, since it is impossible for it to accrue, it must be said that the said Do. Clara is not universal heir and in full right. Fifth, because since usufruct lapses upon the acceptance of the inheritance, as in C. de caducis tollendis, in the newest law, §. excepto, it follows that the heir must be someone other than the usufructuary. Sixth, by reason of impossibility: for how can we say that usufruct draws to itself ownership, which is more powerful than it and can totally extinguish it? And how can it draw it to itself before it exists in reality? I do not see how. Seventh, because the absurdity would follow that this usufruct could not perish by diminution of status, nor by other means.

Therefore, this side seems safer, that the said Do. Clara is merely a usufructuary. And to L. 1, §. si ex fundo, it is responded that the institution was made in the ownership and dominion of the thing, whence attraction and accrual are possible; in our case, it is impossible, as I said.

To the second point, therefore, which asks who is heir at present, I answer, and it seems, that the commissioners of the poor, into whose hands distribution must be made after the death of Do. Clara. Argument from extra de testamentis, c. cum tibi. And this is also supported by the fact that he did not wish all goods to come [to her], etc., and thus in full right and in full: but she does not come even in full, because the mother would deduct the Trebellian portion if she were heir, since the testator did not expressly forbid it. But the contrary seems true, because the poor to be chosen for distribution cannot be chosen before the death of the said Do. Clara, nor are they called simply to the inheritance: but to the distribution of a certain and limited quantity, as is clear in the theme: therefore, for the present, they are not heirs: because they are instituted or substituted after a joined time, whence the time is not subtracted, as noted in L. haereditas, ff. de haeredibus instituendis. That they cannot be chosen before the death of the said Do. Clara is proved in L. cum pater, §. a filia, ff. de legatis 2, and there by Bartolus, and in L. sed an, ff. ad Trebellianum.

Therefore, it seems that those coming intestate, such as the uncle according to the form of the statute, are heirs, and the mother is meanwhile usufructuary, and thus the cause of intestacy draws to itself in our case the cause of testacy on account of the impossibility of the thing in which the mother is instituted. And because those words are of the notary, and not of the testator.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. By reason of preterition, when the person who could break the will is instituted to a specific thing, he cannot be prevented from exercising the right of accrual.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† For clarity, it must be known that when the person who, by reason of preterition, can break a will instituted in a specific thing, cannot be prevented from the right of accrual, as in the Authent. ut cum de appellatione cognos. §. caeterum. For it is valid in its entirety, and by necessary consequence for the whole: since he has no coheir, nor is anyone partly testate and partly intestate. This is noted by the doctors, C. de haer. inst. l. quotiens, after Jacobus Butrigarius. And this is true, unless someone is instituted upon an impossibility, and upon a formal usufruct not given to a coheir: because it is not, nor can it be, in the nature of things. And this is proved by the second and third reasons, most prudently assigned. When it is not, and when the formal usufruct of the one coming into it begins, is to be considered, as the 5th reason proves. And therefore it can be said that the will is null when the mother is pretermitted. §. aliud quoque capitulum. But rather it seems that it is not a will while the mother is alive: because it does not contain the institution of an heir while she is living. For the mother is instituted in a possible thing, and no coheir is given to her. What, therefore, should be said? I answer, according to the form of the statute, one does not succeed as heir, but the uncle, from whom the first degree of intestacy can begin, and upon the occurrence of the case, substitution has place, as in ff. de haer. inst. l. si quis ita haeres instituatur. If that law is read, it does not say this: because it speaks of vulgar substitution. Therefore, it seems that it should be said that the mother, as pretermitted, breaks every degree from every degree, and thus makes way for the statute for other successors, and the substitution of the commissioners, if it is a codicillary clause, is bound to have its place in due time, not in the meantime while the mother lives: but if the mother does not wish to declare it null, she does not open the way of nullity to the uncle, who was not necessarily to be instituted, and then she herself would use it in fact, and upon her death she would come as a direct substitute: because, since those instituted can die, the uncertain day is not removed from them. Someone will say, this mother was instituted, because usufruct is part of ownership, de leg. 2, l. cum filius, §. dominus. I answer, this is true of constituted usufruct, not of impossible usufruct: because that which is impossible is nothing. Here it must be observed, because perhaps the name of usufruct is not placed here formally: but materially, as if it were said, I institute in revenues, which seems more true. And thus the mother, while she lives, is heir in whole by the said §. caeterum. Because the hope of usufruct retained at the time of the testator's death will be sold for at least one coin, it suffices, as in l. si quis priore. The objection from l. quotiens, §. si duo, does not hold: because it must be understood in an outsider, who is not of necessity to be instituted, or disinherited: because this case is more truly one of the subtleties of law. How, however, the substitutes come after the death of the mother, is noted after Guilielmus de Conchis, de haer. inst. l. extraneum. Finally, it must be said that whether it is understood of usufruct formally or materially, that she is not instituted, and substituted to the goods of the testator at the time of the testator's death: because hope alone is not in the substance of goods. ff. ad Treb. l. mulier, §. si heres, and l. 1, ff. de usufr. leg. ff. de leg. 3, l. his verbis, in princ. But it is a matter of chance, as in ff. de act. empt. l. si iactum retis: because the goods might yield no fruit: hence the argument from de inoff. testam. l. quod scimus, §. repletionem, and de condit. et demonstr. l. 1, in fin., ff. de verb. oblig. l. interdum, is not sufficient. And if it is said that all uncertainty and condition is removed, C. de inoff. testam. l. quam in prioribus, I answer, this is true, unless it arises from necessity from the nature of the thing left. Moreover, the legitime must be left by certain judgment, but this is joined: because the mother might die immediately after the death of the son. To this, the note from de inoff. testam. l. Papinia, §. si conditioni, is most apt. Formal conditions, therefore, are removed: but not natural ones, which are outside the nature of things, to which art has deserted. Hence, since at the time of the testator's death there is no certain foundation, no supplement can be made, for the time is considered, de inoff. testam. l. si quis filio exhaeredato. Therefore, whether because she was instituted nullly, or because she was pretermitted, I conclude that we are in a case of intestacy, and that the statute will also have place even against her will, as in ff. si tabulae testamenti nullae ex l. 1, in fin., and C. de contrab. l. posthumo, according to Cynus. And by this, it is necessary that the substitution made in contemplation of the poor be binding: and if it were not binding, it would be annulled as regards the commissioners, nevertheless the distribution to the poor is to be made as in force of a legacy, and is preserved, for which cause, and in due time, the bishop will act.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an episcopal constitution can make someone a manifest usurer.
body: In the name of Christ. Amen. The said portion does not accrue to the brother, but has reverted to the church, as noted by Cyn. C. quando pe. partes. l. 1. and de ver. ob. l. si mihi. et Titio. by Dy. and more fully there by Bar.; and this is the truth. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an episcopal constitution can make someone a manifest usurer.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† The truth is that under the ius commune, according to natural equity and truth, this man is a manifest usurer, and a constitution of the bishop cannot make him manifest when there are no clear proofs concerning him; and therefore his testament is valid. And Federicus de Senis held this by disputation, as appears in his consilia, consilium 18, which begins: "the question is such, whether an episcopal constitution". I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a legacy that has become caducous due to the legatee’s own act can be claimed. I pursue this matter further; it suffices to have concluded the impe
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

The disposition of the said testator, having regard to the ornament of the Republic of Castello and to the honor of the testator himself, whereby the city of Castello may be said to have been honored. Digest, *De legibus*, law *Ciuitatibus*. Therefore, the city of Cassaro itself destroyed [the subject matter], and thus it stood honored by its own act, so that the use is not fulfilled; in no way ought the city of Castello to be heard imposing upon the legacy, which has become caducous and accrued to the city itself by its own act, as in Digest, *De usufructu legato*, law *Quidam praedia*; and Digest, *De legibus secundis*, law *Pater filium*, section *Tusculanus*. And if such a legacy is referred to the Roman Church, it would not suffice in the permutation of the use according to the sentiments of the Castellans. Digest, *De administratione rerum ad ciuitatem pertinentium*, law *Legatum*; and Digest, *De usufructu legato*, law *Legatum*. For it ought to participate in the necessary permutation not as a superior, but as one honored; in the authority *Quae procedit* concerning plenitude of power, it ought to be authorized, because it is supreme, as in chapter *Quia contingit*, *De religiosis domibus*, in the Clementines. And to those not speaking, no lawful use is due.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The property left to a daughter dying in pupillary age passes to the mother, provided that she has requested a guardian, or that she was under twenty-five years of age.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the testament of Ranaldus Sabbatus, and presupposing that first Ranaldus himself died, secondly his brother Andreutius died, thirdly Paulutia died in her pupillary age, with her mother Monaldutia surviving, as well as her paternal grandmother, Lord Florutia, and the full brother of said grandmother, it must be said,

† That two hundred pounds left to the said pupil by the said [testator] to the said Monaldutia, her mother, if indeed the said Monaldutia was under 25 years of age, so that she could not be a guardian: as C. de leg. tute. l. si; and C. si aduersus delict. l. ultra; and note C. ad Tertull. l. matres. But if the said Monaldutia was of legitimate age, and yet did not accept the guardianship within a year, then it may be doubted what the law is. For that the mother is deprived [of the legacy], seems to be proven, as l. sciant, C. de leg. haere.; and ff. ad Tertull. l. 2, §. si mater; and C. qui pet. tuto. l. cum a matribus. To the contrary, because the mother is not bound to request a guardian, as noted in the said l. matres. Also, she is not compelled against her will to accept the guardianship, since this is granted to her as a privilege, as in Auth. matri, et auiae. Moreover, it was not expedient for this pupil to have a guardian on account of the small and meager patrimony. For indeed, 100 pounds could not yet be claimed, but they were in a conditional state, because a legacy given under a condition is considered given under the contrary condition if the condition fails, as appears; the legacy of 200 pounds was revoked under a certain condition, as the testament states: since therefore she could administer nothing in the meantime, the mother, who did not accept the guardianship, is not placed [in a position to claim], ad Tertull. l. 2, §. pe. And if it is said, who was the legitimate guardian? I answer, the consul, as in Auth. de haere. ab intest. §. ex his. To the contrary, it seems that the mother, being of age, is excluded: because it was due to her that the pupil did not have a guardian. For since she precedes the legitimate [guardian]: therefore the pupil did not have a legitimate guardian. For we do not understand "to have" by the law itself, nor by the effect of administration, when the guardianship is not managed, the mother and grandmother being obstacles, which are discussed in the gloss on l. matres. For it speaks of the law of the forums, by which law the mother could not be a guardian. ff. de neg. gest. l. qui alienam, §. quiquam; ff. de solu. l. filiae. But by the law of the Authentica, the guardianship is deferred to her, whence it pertains to the diligence of her office that the pupil not be undefended. C. de admin. tu. l. si, §. personis. And thus holds Bartolus in the said l. matres. The mother is also bound not only to request a appointed guardian, where there is room for an appointed one: but to remove the obstacle from the legitimate guardians: which she can do if she accepted the guardianship herself, or renounced the guardianship within a year: she must therefore either manage it herself, or open the way for another: because it is an equal fault not to request, and not to allow administration by another. d. §. si mater; §. quod si pater. It can be answered to that gloss and otherwise, for that gloss speaks when one has the legitimate [right] with effect, as because, with the mother consenting, or she being cited, the legitimate [guardian] assumed the guardianship within a year, according to the note in l. tutor si petitur, de tu. cu. da. ab his. And from where the words of the gloss "with effect" are to be understood. And according to this opinion, the mother being excluded, the grandmother succeeds, even if the grandmother did not request, or did not refuse, according to the note C. qui pet. tuto. l. nepotibus. For only the first is excluded, and not those who succeed, by the exclusion of the first. ff. ad Tertull. l. 2, §. euindendum. arg. ff. de succes. aedic. l. si. Therefore the legacy devolves, and not under the condition "if he shall have requested a guardian." But Bartolus says the contrary, that the same law and penalty is devolution, for thus the grandmother is punished in the grandson as the mother in the son. d. l. 2, §. quid ergo. But because this is a penalty, and no law provides that those further removed from the first shall incur it, therefore I hold with the gloss, and according to this, in the case of a negligent mother, the aforementioned grandmother succeeds to the said pupil. And thus I hold, especially because even after the year had elapsed, the mother could have accepted the guardianship; the obstacle was in the guardianship, I do not say in the succession: as l. 3, de legi. tuto. per Bartolus. And this is the truth. And in the same way proceeds the succession of Nicolutius to his substitutes, if he did not do what I said, the substitute, for him. For indeed, the necessity does not fall upon the mother preceding them in guardianship; otherwise, if she did not precede, as l. omnes, C. ad Tertull.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When a statute requires proof by means of a written instrument, if such an instrument is produced that does not fully prove the matter, but is corroborated by witnesses who fully prove it, whether this suffices.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the petition produced on behalf of Augustine Gili and true Angelutius before the Massars of the commune of Perugia, the tenor of which appears in the records of the said Massars on account of the presentation of certain murderers; and having examined a certain instrument, in which it is contained that Master Orlandus, formerly Captain of the city of Perugia, confessed that the said murderers had been delivered to him by the aforementioned Augustine and Nerius by the hand of Ser Francis, public notary; and having examined the said witnesses corroborating and verifying the said instrument and the contents thereof; and having examined the instrument in which it is contained that execution was carried out on the said murderers; and having examined the statute of the commune of Perugia under the rubric "On the rewards of those who capture a murderer."

I say, and I, the undersigned Baldus, advise that the reward of the said statute is to be paid to the said captors and presenters by the said Massars. I am moved first by the very truth of the matter, clearly proven; secondly, by the instrument corroborated and verified by witnesses. Hence it must be known that although the law or statute requires something to be proven by an instrument, nevertheless, if such an instrument, which does not fully prove, is verified and corroborated by the conjunction of witnesses who fully prove, such completing proof is attributed to the instrument, and satisfaction is given by viewing the instrument: that is, by viewing such writing proven by witnesses; as appears in the case of a testament written in private hand and strengthened by witnesses, from which testament a commission is made. C. de edicto diuorum Adr. l. edicto. Although therefore the instrument of the said Orlando, in itself and by itself, would not suffice, nevertheless, without doubt, it is made valid and effective by the witnesses, since they make full proof thereof, as ff. de edendo, l. si quis ex argento, § 2; and C. de probat., l. pen. To this effect also: ff. si certum petatur, l. certi conditio, § 1; and what is said there by Bartolus and Jacobus de Belvisio. And if it be said that the statute requires an instrument of presentation, but a declaratory confession made elsewhere and at another time, and outside the office of the said Captain, and therefore does not prove, as noted by Innocentius, extra de probat., c. quamvis contra falsam, I answer that it is true by itself alone; but with the witnesses, as I have said, it proves. de veritate sigilli, l. notionem, § instrumentorum; since the witnesses themselves, who were admitted and published, make the matter notorious, as noted by Innocentius, de filiis presbiterorum, c. constitutus. And it applies to publicans, l. publicanus, § 1; and what is said there by Bartolus; and l. deferre, § idem decreuerunt, de iure fisci, per Bartolus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a testator has made a testament in which he derogates from every other testament in which nothing was written, and afterwards made another which he wishes to prevail over the former, and observed something notwithstanding, whether the first is revoked.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A question arises in the gloss to l. si quis in the beginning, D. de testamento. This case often occurs in practice. The testator says, “I appoint such a person as my heir, and if I make another will, I do not wish it to be valid, and I derogate from it, unless I there write out the entire Psalm Miserere mei Deus with my own hand.” Later he made another will, and states that he wishes it to prevail over the former one, notwithstanding anything to the contrary. Now the question is whether the second will is valid or not.

That the first will prevails is proved thus: just as genus relates to species, so species relates to the individual, as is noted by Dino in c. generi per speciem and c. sed species de rogat generi, and l. si quis in the beginning, D. de testamento. Therefore, a more specific derogatory clause derogates from a derogatory clause that is not so specific. Hence the text says, “unless he has specially stated it by general words”: therefore the first will is valid, and not the second. For that is called special which is restricted by general words, as in l. sed et si quis, §. quaesitum, D. si quis cautio. Moreover, the first will is derogatory: therefore the first prevails, D. de legibus 1, l. si mihi, et tibi, §. fi., and in the Authenticum de testamento imperfecto, §. si quidem.

To the contrary, it seems from the law on codicils, l. diui, §. licet. Moreover, what operates in itself, genus operates in all, as if they had been enumerated, C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. omnes, and D. de administratione tutorum, l. si duo.

Solution: Lord Dino says that the first will is removed only if it is specially revoked, and if the testator says, “I wish this will to prevail notwithstanding such a will,” or “notwithstanding certain derogatory words placed therein”: but if general words are used, “notwithstanding any other will,” the first will seems to prevail, because the text says “specially.” This is the opinion of Dino in the said l. si quis in the beginning, §. et est, and c. quod semel placuit, according to the same Dino.

Moderators therefore hold that the last will prevails, and thus in disputing holds Jacobus de Belvis, and he reports it in the Authenticum de testamentis imperatorum, column 8. And the same in disputing held Lord Cynus. It is sufficiently said that it is special when the will of the testator is established: because not the figure of the letters, but the intellectual sense is considered, and it seems to be said specially because the testator himself specially understood it, and the Moderators commonly approve this in c. de constitutionibus, book 6, and in the Novella. And although the question is disputable, this is the more just part, because the testator says that he revokes every will, of whatever notary it appears. By power and will joined together, the first will fails, and a new one supervenes. A long discourse could be made here from the words of Bartolus in the said l. si quis in the beginning, D. de testamento, and D. de legatis 1, l. si mihi et tibi, §. legatis. Nevertheless, conclusively and briefly, I am of the opinion that I have said, that it is sufficiently explicit that the mind is revocatory and derogatory, and not dispositive of the will, and although the notary who was requested for the first will is not named, nevertheless he should be considered as named, which cannot be understood even of one. D. de liberis et posthumis, l. nominatim, l. si modo vnicus sit.

I, Baldus.

IN THE

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A person produced with respect to the fact to be proven does not establish a confession, nor even half-proof.
2. A surety who has paid the judgment, and a co-litigant, cannot be a witness in that case.
3. One may be said to be content with a debt that subsists.
casus: CASE of Angelo Cioli of Amelia, and Romano of Massano, of the county of Amelia, having seen the acts and proceedings, both in the first cause and the second appeal to the Lords of Amelia, and thirdly, before the commissioner of the great lord, the said lord of the power, it is asked what are the parts of the lords commissioners in sentencing, all things having been diligently seen, inspected, and examined. I, Baldus.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having considered the first sentence given by the judge of Barigiano, which contains that the said Roman is bound to restore half of the fruits received from the penalties contained in the instrument; which sentence was just according to the form of the contract, as in l. 1, § si conuenerit, ff. de deposito; and having considered the other adverse sentence given by the judge of the said Barigiano, which contains in effect that nothing is owed despite the claimed payment, which sentence would be just if it were legitimately established that the formalities were observed, and considering that the satisfaction was not legitimately and sufficiently proven, as it ought to have been proven, ff. de probat., l. quinquaginta and l. in exceptione; it follows that the first sentence, as just, remains firm in declaring the aforementioned fruits, in execution through legitimate proofs or legitimate presumptions, according to no. ff. de edendo, l. 1, in principio. That something was not proven regarding the satisfaction appears from the four witnesses produced to prove the satisfaction, of whom the first is Angelus, one of the individuals, i.e., Angelus.

† And when someone wishes to prove a fact by proving a confession, and thus one witness does not even make half-proof, which is clear: because joined with a witness who was present, it does not fully prove, extra de succ. ab intesta. c. fi. in the word "as not sufficient proving."

† Stephanus does not prove his point, because, being a co-litigant, he, as a surety, has satisfied the judgment. C. de testibus, l. omnibus; and C. de testibus, l. dictantibus, according to Cynus. If Butius says nothing, Butius conclusively annuls the case in his statement of the cause; but because he says that he remained content,

† which can also be the case even when the debt subsists. D. qui sat. cog. Therefore, the aforementioned sentence, being the last one rendered, must be declared unjust, notwithstanding a certain opinion issued without allegations, wherein I am certain that the consultants perhaps erred in fact; for in law, men of such stature could not err, from whom the knots of the laws are accustomed to be unraveled root and branch, and both commissioners must judge together, as in l. sicuti, D. de arbitris. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. To hold and to possess is a continuous act, and not a discrete one.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The inquiry states that he held it continuously. This is not more than one offense, for which he would be liable to a penalty of one hundred shillings.

† to the greater. to hold. n. just as to possess is a continuous act, not a discrete one, as is noted in l. eum qui. §. in popularibus. de iureiurando, the second [author] says that they used the said chapter on each individual day, and does not state how they used it, for they could have used it for other services. Moreover, with a greater measure they can take something moderate by not filling the measure, de dolo malo, l. arbitrio. §. de eo. And therefore this particle does not formally conclude. Follows the third particle of the inquisition, which says, he was taking with the said chapter the multuras. It does not repeat "on each day," nor is it tacitly understood to repeat those words, "on each day," according to the note in l. praetor. ut bonis raptis, through Bartolus, although the contrary is done de fundo instrato, l. Seiae. §. Gayo. But there it is in a dispositive clause, here in a narrative clause. Follows the fourth particle concerning the confession of the vicium, and it is not probable: because the intention of the inquirer was to conclude not according to the narrated facts, but according to the confessed facts, and the conclusion tacitly restricts this inquisition as the final cause of the inquisition. Wherefore ten times in more, i.e., in two, it must be concluded in law that the inquisition is formed. Follows the fifth particle, that all and each of the things contained in the said inquisition were confessed, and it is clear that the first confession is inserted in the inquisition, and is a part of it. Hence, by confessing all and each, he confesses nothing except the complex parts of the inquisition itself. And unless up to this point confessed, and to which, as I said, the conclusion of the inquisition was referred. Hence the restrictive term ten vicium and two is understood to be repeated: because the species declares the genus. de verbis obligatis, l. de clausula. de poenis, l. sanctio legum. And especially so that a contradiction of the response may be avoided, which is to be avoided as far as possible, as extra de beneficiis, c. 1. Hence argue ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. cohaeredi. §. qui discretas. And by this interpretation it equally appears that the parts of the judge in condemning, or in ordering payment, are not more than 12 lib. for each, and in one hundred solidi by reason of the discovery, and he cannot impose a further penalty by using that part of the statute which speaks of 20 solidi for each time. And thus it seems to me, saving the substance of the truth, to which I submit myself.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the solemnities required by public law, which gives a certain form to human acts, can be destroyed by laws.
2. What a substantial form is.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.
† One cannot renounce public law, which gives a certain form to the acts of men. D. de pactis, l. publicum. And the waiver of form vitiates. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. 1, § 1.

† And the substantial form is known constructively, when it gives being to the thing, as in the case of an exhibition, l. Iul. and destructively: because when it is destroyed, the being of the thing is destroyed. ff. de usufr. l. est ulum fructum. And therefore whatever is necessary for the being of the thing, that belongs to the substantial form, whether it is intrinsic or added. Intrinsic. ff. de transac. l. cum hi. §. si praetor. There are therefore certain solemnities that are intrinsic, some substantial and extrinsic; an example of the former is found in stipulation. An example of the latter is found. ff. de pub. l. quaecunquibus. §. fi. C. de dona. l. sancimus. It must therefore be seen whether oaths can destroy these solemnities, so that they are not required in human acts. From what is said by Bartolus in l. si quis. de fideius. such a distinction is gathered, that either the form is intrinsic, as stipulation, and then the oath does not supply the defect of this form, ver. si praepostere stipuletur, and the preceding response, the oath does not make it so that a non-stipulation is a stipulation: or the form is extrinsic, and then either the form is given to the person, and the same argument, l. 1. ne fideiussores dotium dentur. or to the act, and then otherwise. Hence in §. si praetor. it is said that the oath is confirmed by a transaction of alimony made with the solemnity of the intervention of possession, and although he speaks subtly, it should be said otherwise. For either the law expressly rejects the oath, and then it has the force of the apostle, and as remitted it does not bind the oath, as is read, and no. de iu. pa. l. adigere. §. fi. or it expressly approves the oath, and then the oath must be observed, as in Auth. sacramenta puberum. Or the law resists the act, and does not mention the oath, and then either it prohibits consent, and the oath operates nothing: because with consent annulled, the oath has no foundation in natural law, de iur. naturali, de pac. l. iu. gen. §. generaliter. de agri. et cen. l. quemadmo. de leg. 1. l. si quis inquilinus. §. fin. or it does not condemn consent, but confers some benefit or privilege, and then either that benefit is of private utility, and the oath must be observed, or principally public, then otherwise, de pac. l. iure gem. §. si paciscar. Returning to the proposal, from the words of the Pisan constitution it appears that consent is permitted if the solemnity is present, therefore prohibited if the solemnity is absent. ar. C. de procu. l. maritus. de iud. l. cum praetor. Moreover, the solemnity in which consent consists is an intrinsic solemnity, and concerns the act medullarily, the defect of which is not supplied by an oath. And therefore the said oath with false consanguineous relatives intervening is of no moment. ff. de rebus eorum. l. qui neque. Notwithstanding c. mulieres. de iureiu. because there the benefit is broken, but consent is not prohibited. Here, however, the law opposes consent, and therefore the oath has no bond. C. de non nu. pe. l. fi. ff. de act. et ob. l. obligationum substantia. C. de legi. et consul. l. non dubium. and the said l. sancimus. For the productive force of the law and the removal of consent can more than the private temerity of validating an impossible act. Conclusion, where there is force, consent is void, the oath is void.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a contract formed on a certain document, into which words have been inserted, is called a written contract, and whether anything can be added to it.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. First, it must be examined whether the said officials had free power or whether it was limited according to the form of the letter. And it is presupposed by me that they had free power; hence the question is not about their discretion, but about the understanding of the contract.

† And if I consider the matter well, the contract was formed upon the deed (cedula): because the words state according to the form and tenor of the deed. And the deed is inserted word for word into the contract; therefore it can be said that this contract is in writing. C. de fidei instrumentis, l. Contractus. To which one is not permitted to add or detract anything, as noted by Bartolus in de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, §. Idem credendum. It must be known, however, that those things which are said later in contracts derogate from those said earlier, as in ff. si certum petatur, l. Lecta. Furthermore, it must be known that a seller who excepts from the contract the rights of a third party, for example, those of tenants (coloni), is not understood to except his own rights, for example, the rights to pensions. ff. de acquisitione emptionis, l. Si mercedem, §. Si. Therefore, however much the commune excepts from a general sale the rights of tenants, or of purchasers of some portion, it is not understood to have reserved for itself pensions, which are due to the purchaser pro rata temporis. l. Si, de in rem actionibus; de acquisitione emptionis, l. Iulia, §. Si fructibus. And this appears clearly from the tenor of the contract: for the commune sold the universality of the Posta; for a collection of fields is a certain universality. ff. de contrahenda emptione, l. In modicis. And the words in the beginning state that the commune sold the revenues, profits, and rights which the commune has. Under the name of revenues, pensions are contained. ff. de usuris, l. Videamus, and l. 1, and l. Praediorum. Furthermore, it is more evident at the end, because the words which state that of the Posta and its fruits nothing has been given totally or particularly to anyone, such that it could harm the purchaser in the perception of the fruits and revenues of the said Posta, and if it appears that something was given, it was promised to reacquire it by law; and note what it says, "or particularly." Now it remains to respond to those words of the deed which state that others who hold some possession from the commune cannot be burdened. And thus the words of the universal beginning and end must be restricted by the middle: because that which is specifically acted upon does not come into the contract, lest it come. ff. de periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. Si vina; ff. de hae re vel acquisitione venditionis, l. Quod si in venditione. What is said in the middle of the contract seems to be repeated in the beginning and at the end, because it is not likely that one would correct himself immediately, as noted in de contrahenda emptione, l. Pacta conventa. And therefore a determination or restriction once placed determines and restricts the whole contract: because it suffices to have said it once, de pactis, l. Item quia, §. Si. Furthermore, he who excepts a thing is understood to except the emoluments of the thing which arise afterwards. ff. de hae re vel acquisitione venditionis, l. Si, in glossa ordinaria. Therefore, for the excepted things, payment ought to be made to the commune and not to the purchaser of the Posta; but this leads us to an inconvenience. Suppose, for example, that previously the whole Posta, or the greater part of it, had been sold particularly; the purchaser of the Posta would be enormously harmed, which is absurd. ff. de actione emptionis, l. Hanc, l. Item in contractu. It was asserted in the contract that no right had been given to anyone; therefore, what was said and promised must be adhered to. ff. de aedilitio edicto, l. Sciendum, §. Dictum. Furthermore, he who pays a debt is not said to be burdened; hence this is not to burden, but to burden would be if there were disturbance or molestation in the purchase of the thing. And the chapter or clause seems to speak of this, by referring it to the proximate [context], because it ought not to be referred to the contrary: as in l. Si quis id quod, §. Fin., de iudiciis omnium iudicum. We shall therefore satisfy the purchasers, each in his right; but we cannot prefer the seller to the purchaser in these advantages which are included under the universality, de acquirenda re, l. Quaedam. And this is true in law, unless custom were otherwise: because a contract of the fisc would be interpreted according to custom, as in ff. de publicanis, l. Si publicanus, §. In omnibus. Then, the purchaser is not said to be concealed: when he knows, or ought to know, the fact and the custom. ff. de actione emptionis, l. 1, in fine.

CASE. In the name of Christ, amen. The fact is proposed in the following form: Floranus Prenonis of Perugia made certain codicils of the tenor and content written below, namely: Whereas Floranus Prenonis, of the parish of Saint Angel and the parish of Saint Donatus, composed his testament written by the hand of me, the notary subscribed below, and in that testament he made many legacies, and instituted his son Donatus as universal heir; and now at present he wishes to add some things to the said testament in some parts, and to change some things, and to append some conditions by the way and mode of codicils, without revoking or changing the said testament in other parts, except as contained below: but rather confirming it. Therefore, the said Floranus, infirm in body, yet sound in mind, and constituted in good and right knowledge, by way of codicil made the codicils written below in this manner. Namely, that he left and adjudicated to his daughter, Lady Idonea, beyond her dowries, and beyond the legacies made to her by him in the said testament, one thousand pounds of denarii from his goods, computed with three pounds of denarii otherwise left to the said Lady by the said Floranus in his said testament, which he ordered and willed to be and to be computed in this quantity of one thousand pounds of denarii. These one thousand pounds she shall have and ought to have, and she may demand and claim them from the heirs of the said Floranus, and from his goods, if and insofar as the said Lady Idonea shall have contracted with another man and legitimate husband, and shall have married herself, and not otherwise. And if the said Lady Idonea shall die at any time without children from the said marriage contracted by her, if she contracted, during the lifetime of the said Donatus, his son, or the sons of the said Donatus who are male, he substituted them, and then those surviving, in the said one thousand pounds of denarii, namely, the said Donatus, his son, universal heir, and his sons, and the sons of his sons who are male. But if the said Donatus, or his sons, or the sons of his sons who are male, shall die without male children, during the lifetime of the said Lady Idonea, he willed and ordered that the said one thousand pounds of denarii become the property of the said Lady Idonea, and that she may do with them what she wills. Furthermore, he ordered, willed, and commanded that if the said Donatus, his son and universal heir, or his son or sons, shall die at any time without male children, that in that case half of all the goods of the said Floranus shall be and ought to be of the Hospital of Mercy, for the oath, and with the crime of the said hospital in full right, and he instituted the said hospital as his heir in the said half in the aforesaid case.

Now it has happened that before the death of the said Floranus, Francisca, daughter of the said Donatus and wife of Nicolaus Magila, died, surviving two children, one male and the other female. And they still survive, and surviving my daughter of Donatus, and also surviving the said Donatus, the son and heir of the said Floranus, Porronus, son of the said Donatus. Finally, the said Floranus died, surviving the aforesaid, who were surviving at the time of the death of the said Francisca. Afterwards, the said Porronus died, surviving the said Donatus, his father, and surviving Nicolaus, the male son of the said Porronus, and five daughters of the said Porronus who are female. Afterwards, the said Donatus died, and three children of the said Porronus, namely, the said Nicolaus, and two daughters who are female. In pupillary age, now survive the said my daughter, formerly of the said Donatus, and the said children of the said Francisca, and three daughters who are female of the said Porronus, and they are married, and one of them has borne a male child. The said Idonea also survives. Now it is asked, what is the law, both concerning the aforesaid inheritance and also concerning the said legacy of one thousand pounds made to the said Lady Idonea. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The word "sons" conceives and includes daughters.
2. Likewise, the disjunctive "or" is resolved into the conjunctive "and."
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

The condition of the said legacy was obstructed by the following persons during their lifetimes: namely, Donatus, his son, and the male children of the male children of Donatus, or of his son. And briefly, every male from a male, or female from a female, and it is undoubtedly seen that the said Idonea is excluded from the said legacy for three reasons. First, by the disposition of the law, as in C. de fideicommissis, l. cum acutissimi; ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. cum auus. Second, by the disposition of the testator, as in ff. de hereditate instituenda, l. Lucius; C. de conditionibus insertis, l. 1. Third, by the conception of terms: because the word "filii" (sons/children) comprehends also a daughter, as in ff. de legatis tertio, l. Lucius, § quaesitum.

Fourthly, because an alternative [clause] is resolved into a conjunctive one, there, if all. And the law *Filius nepos*, the rest having died, [regarding] the conditions of the said legacy. Fifthly, the law *Maximum vitium* contributes to the same, together with *Si*. Sixthly, that word *filii* contributes to it. For the testator seems to have included all under the plural number, D. ad Trebellianum, law *Iulius Phebus*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. By entering into religious life, the burden of restitution of a fideicommissum left in the event that the testator should die without legitimate and natural children ceases.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A father has three male sons; he instituted them as heirs, and if any of them should die without legitimate children, he instituted and substituted the survivor. After the testator died, one of the said sons, named Mathęoldus, died. Then another survivor, named Antonius, became a monk; but before he made his profession, he made a will, and instituted his brother Herculanus and his sister, Lady Massola, as heirs in equal shares. To the monastery, however, he left a certain quantity; nevertheless, he made his profession, and still lives naturally. Now it is asked whether the said brother Antonius could make a will regarding his entire share, or whether only regarding his legitimate portion and the Trebellianic portion.

And it must be said that by entering religion, the burden of restitution of the fideicommissum was removed, and therefore he could make a will in its entirety, as in the Authentica de sancta ecclesia, §. sed hoc praesenti, column 9; and in the Extravagant de probat., c. in praesentia; and to the Trebellian, Authentica nisi rogati. And therefore the said Massola ought to have only as much as the said Herculanus and the monastery are content with, namely, that they should now have that which would have accrued after the death of Brother Antonius, so that we are not in the question whether natural death is required. Baldus.

The point of the question, in which the advocates of both parties seem to disagree, is this: namely, a certain Carnevale Turcharum of Spello made his last will, in which no express institution of an heir is found, which he wished to be valid by the law of testament, or codicils, or any other last will, in which he left for God and his soul that his house of habitation, situated within certain boundaries, be sold, and the money from it given for God and his soul, and for his brother Iacobutius, etc. And to execute the aforesaid, he appointed as his fideicommissaries Do. Flora, his carnal sister, and certain others expressed in the said last will, as appears in the transcript from the protocols of the late Master Franc. de Spello, notary, by the hand of Franciscus Vannutius Lilli, notary of Spello. It happened that the said Do. Flora contracted marriage by words of the present tense with Valente Nutii of Assisi, and assigned and delivered as dowry and for the dotal fund to the said Valente, her husband, the aforesaid house, as appears in a document copied from the instrument of the said marriage and of the giving or concession for the dotal fund, of which the above has been said. It follows next that the said Lady Flora, as fideicommissary of her said carnal brother, in the name of the fideicommissary and in her own name, by herself and her heirs, sold and delivered the aforesaid house to Brother Carlinus of Master Paul, and promised legitimate defense, as appears by the hand of Antonius de facto Miniato, notary, transcribed from the original by the hand of Petrus Cagni of Spello, notary. Of this house, the said Carlinus, the buyer, had tenure and possession, and dwelt there for many years. And although at times he was ejected from the habitation of the said house, because the said Lady Flora entered and dwelt in the said house in his absence and against the will of the said Carlinus, nevertheless the said Carlinus was restored and put back into possession of the aforesaid house, as appears from the said restoration by transcript and from the said Antonius, notary, from the original by the hand of the said Master Franciscus of Spoleto, notary. But afterwards, in his absence, the said Lady Flora re-entered the said house and sold it to another, who holds it.

It is now asked whether the sale made by the said Lady Flora in the name of the fideicommissary and in her own name stands and is valid, and what is the law in all the aforesaid matters. And this having been seen, the said instrument of the last will of the said Carnevale, signed by A.; and the document in the folio of the good neighbor concerning the dotal fund of the said house, signed by B.; and the instrument of the sale made by the said Lady Flora to the said Carlinus, signed by C.; and the allegations made on behalf of the said Lady Flora, that the said sale does not stand, signed by D.; and the instrument of the restoration and reintegrating made to the said Carlinus of the aforesaid house, signed by E.; and the allegations made on behalf of Ser Nardi, that the said sale stands, signed by F.; and other laws and allegations made regarding the aforesaid, as they are in the mind and knowledge of the most excellent and eminent Doctor, counselor.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Goods left by will, in order that they may be sold and the price distributed among the poor, cannot be given in dowry.
2. A commissioner appointed to distribute cannot distribute to himself.
3. If there are several executors, one alone can execute, and how the sale should be made by them.
4. Where someone sells by the authority of the testator, whether a public auction is required.
5. Bequests and offices for pious causes do not require the acceptance of the inheritance.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The woman could not give the aforementioned house as dowry: because the testator had ordered it to be sold and the price distributed for pious purposes. Hence, it could not be converted to another use, as in the *clausula* *Quia contingit*, at the words *non tamen ea*, *De religiosis dotibus*; nor could it be alienated for another cause, as in the law *Quidam praedia*, *De usufructu legato*, and in the same title, the law *Legatum*, according to Bartolus and others.

† Moreover, a commissioner appointed for distribution cannot distribute to himself, as stated in the Digest, title on mandates, law *Si tibi mandauero*, section *Si tibi centum*, and law *Conditor* at the end. Hence, he could not by himself give [the property] in dowry; therefore, notwithstanding the aforementioned donation in dowry, the said house ought to be sold, and the price distributed according to the form of the will.
† It is necessary, however, to consider how the said sale is to be made. And certainly it must be made by all the executors who have accepted and wish to carry out the execution,

† However, in certain cases, one alone may execute. The first case is if the others are dead. The second case is if the others are in remote parts. The third case is if the others wish to execute, as in c. ult. de testibus, lib. 6, in the text. The fourth case is if the others did not accept the office, but refused it; in this case, no penalty is incurred. The fifth case is if the others wish to execute, but cannot do so due to any of the aforementioned impediments, unless the impediment is of short duration, according to Johannes Andreae. Moreover, by the very fact that the executors do not engage in the office within a year, they are deemed to have tacitly renounced it, as argued in de episcopis et clericis, l. nulli; and in the rubric of l. bonorum. And thus, what is done by one of them is confirmed not by swift preemption, but because they see the other executors are in delay. The delay and the danger inherent in the delay are confirmed by the reasoning of the said cap. ult. de testibus in 6.

Furthermore, it is required that the executor sell for present money. D. de iudiciis, l. si procurator; de re iudicata, l. a divo Pio, §. pen. Hence, a confession of the price is not sufficient to give validity to their sale. C. de nova, l. non abstulit. And this is true, except against the confessor and his successor, for against them the confession stands, as in l. generaliter, de non numero, pen.; and D. de deposito, l. Publia, §. ult.; de re iudicata; and D. de pignoribus, l. si superatus, §. ult.

Furthermore, some say that a public auction is required, because the property of the poor is being sold, l. quod debet inter eos distribui, and the poor are equated with the church and the ward. C. de episcopis et clericis, l. orphanotrophos. And the church is equated with the city, as in l. fi., C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis. Furthermore, with a minor, therefore, etc., as in Auth. hoc ius porrectum; and D. de minoribus, l. sed sine. But this does not seem true where the executor sold having a mandate from the testator; for a public auction is not necessary, for the commission of the testator and the trust placed in the one elected by him suffice. l. 2, C. quoniam decrevit; opus non est; and in l. si quis ad declinandam; and in l. ultima, de rebus eorum. Unless a statute or custom dictates the contrary, good faith is nevertheless required, as in l. creditor, §. Lucius, D. de manumissionibus. However, good faith is always presumed to be present, because it is natural to man, and the reason that creates good faith advises and instills it. l. pro deprehenso, de longis temporibus; Inst. de acquisitione, §. aliae, in the gloss. Hence, unless in cases of malice, and those which are of the nature of malice, good faith is always presumed.

Furthermore, some say that it is required that the buyer be diligent, so that afterwards the money is converted into the very cause, as in Auth. hoc ius porrectum; and l. fi., de exercitoribus; and quod non, D. de nova, l. doli mali, in fine. However, it is presumed if it appears that satisfaction has been made, for it is presumed that the money was converted into that cause, as argued in l. fi., de alimentis pupillorum; and l. si neuter, §. fi., de privatis creditoribus. And it is not required that it be converted immediately, or after an interval, as in D. de in rem verso, l. 3. However, intention is not sufficient unless effect follows, as in l. 3, §. sed si eo, tit. And this seems true when one is simply an executor; but when one is a mixed executor, i.e., executor and heir, as is the case here, the aforementioned formalities are not necessary for the substance of the transfer of ownership. Therefore, ownership was transferred to the buyer by the conjunction of ownership and office occurring simultaneously, and therefore the condition of this first buyer is stronger than that of the one who bought afterwards. Therefore, this latter buyer should be sued by the rei vindicatio or the publiciana, D. de actionibus emptio, l. si ea res, §. ult.; D. de publiciana, l. siue actus, §. si duobus. He can also be sued by the condictio ex canone reintegrandae, because he succeeds and is a spoliator by selling and ceding his rights. And it seems that this right has ceased. D. de peculio haereditario, l. quid si in diem, §. Iulianus; and quod non, Innocentius, de iudicibus, c. quia vero. It also seems that by selling he acted as owner pro haerede, as in Inst. de haereditatibus qualiter et quando differunt, §. fin.

† Although legacies and offices for pious causes do not require the acceptance of the inheritance: because they are held by the office of the judge, as in l. hereditas in fin. de pec. her. and noted in l. eam, quam. and it is the opinion of Speculum that the office of the judge does not require a quasi-contract, and consequently neither the acceptance of the inheritance, as is clear from many examples. ff. de relig. l. si quis sepulturam. ff. de annu. leg. l. pariter. §. aduertendum. ff. de acq. her. l. pro haerede. §. 1. It will be said that where there is no institution of an heir, legacies are not valid; this is a certain error, since such a disposition is codicillary. Hence, legacies are valid even without the institution of an heir, as in ff. de iur. codicil. l. si quis cum maleficium. and l. conficiuntur. and l. ab intest. cum si. and it supports what is noted in l. 1. ff. de testamentis. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, and I have subscribed to the truth and signed with the seal of my name. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. He who can bring a matter to judgment can also cause a stipulation to be committed that he will not further demand the thing.
2. A promise made in his own name that he would do and see to it that, upon reaching majority, he would release the curator from alimony or the amount that he could claim. Also, that he would not raise any controversy concerning these matters, either by himself or through another, under a certain penalty, if the curator were cited and a libel brought against him, and a precept for payment issued, and a transaction made concerning these matters by the said curator with the ward; whether he is bound by the penalty, and if he is bound, whether by one or several.
casus: CASE. A certain Antonius, curator of Petrutia, an adult, compromised in the name of the said adult with Ser Gregorius concerning a certain sum of money, which was said to have been promised by the said Ser Gregorius to the said adult on account of alimony, the said Antonius promising in his own and private name that he would do and see to it that the said adult would release the said Ser Gregorius from the said alimony or sum which she could claim on that account; also that henceforth the said adult would raise no suit or controversy against the said Ser Gregorius, either by herself or by another. And this under a certain penalty contained in the compromise for each chapter of the said compromise not observed, which penalty would be incurred each time, etc., as appears in the compromise itself. Now, after the award was given, not only did the adult not release the said Ser Gregorius, but a certain procurator of hers, legitimately constituted generally, however, in all causes and lawsuits which the said adult had with the said Ser Gregorius, or with any others, etc., as appears in the instrument of procuratorship, raised a controversy against the said Ser Gregorius concerning the said alimony and sum promised on account thereof, at these different times: first, by having him summoned and offering a libel; second, by having a writ for payment issued against him. Whereupon the said Ser Gregorius, seeing himself molested and that the said adult was not observing the award in order to avoid the litigation, which was then dangerous to him, came to a transaction with the said adult, and between them there intervened a full and solemn release, no mention, however, being made of the said Antonius in the transaction. Finally, the said Ser Gregorius, grievously injured by the fact that he had been molested twice concerning the said alimony, brought an action against the said Antonius, claiming the penalty for several chapters of the compromise not observed, and especially because a controversy had been raised twice against him by the procurator of the said adult, although general, and thus for each occasion he says that the said Antonius incurred the penalty, notwithstanding the transaction and release which followed, no controversy having been made. Now it is asked whether the said Antonius incurs the penalty twice, and what is the law, the aforesaid matters being considered. Also, whether the said Antonius ought to be condemned according to the form of the petition of Ser Gregorius, the acts and proceedings in the cause, the instrument, and the rights of both parties being considered, or for what part, if not in whole, he ought to be condemned. I, Baldus.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.
† Everyone who can bring a matter to court causes the stipulation not to sue further to be committed, and the thing by real action and similar. ff. rem. ra. ha. l. procu. cum peteretur.

† But this procurator effectively brought the matter to judgment on behalf of his principal, and therefore it is as if the suspender had brought it himself. *De religiosis*, §. *fi*. But then, without doubt, the penalty would have been incurred. *D. De procuratoribus*, l. *Non solum*, §. *Si status*. *D. Ad Trebellianum*, l. *Lucius*, §. *In haeredem*. *D. De verbis obligatis*, l. *Eadem*, §. *Cato*. Therefore, now the penalty is incurred, and this is true: because one who incurs a penalty has no recourse against the aforementioned procurator who constituted him; for then a general mandate would not suffice. *D. Quod quisque iuris*, l. 1, §. *Si procurator*. And a settlement regarding the principal excludes the penalty between the settling parties. *D. Si quis cautio*, l. 2. But thirdly, it neither benefits nor harms, unless, as I said, he would have recourse, *D. De pactis*, l. *Si unus*, §. *Ante omnia*. It supports this. *D. De verbis obligatis*, l. *Stipulatio ista*, §. *Certum in ratione sui*. *De verborum significatione*, l. *Super quibusdam*, §. *Praeterea*. And *C. Sine censu vel reliquis*, l. *Eos*, in the end, gloss. And this *De usufructu*, as in the gloss. But to the direct servitude contradicts the adverb "freely." *D. De aedilicio empto*, l. *Tibi liberum*, in the second response. Therefore, to whom full liberty of exporting and collecting is given, it is not merely to the performance of a servitude. To the same effect is that "freely" is understood not only from servitude, but without any impediment. *12. q. 6. Omnis oppressus*. And without any other requirement, as in *C. 2. De testibus*, lib. 6. *De officio delegati*, c. *Cum plures*, per Arch. and Io. An. *De officio ordinarii*, c. *Cum episcopus*, per Arch. And in the sum, this adverb abhors all necessity, *De legibus*, 3, l. *Fideicommissa*, §. *Quamquam*. Thus, neither can such liberty be burdened directly, *De restitutione spoliorum*, c. *Pisanis*. *D. De verbis obligatis*, l. *Quinti*. The adverb "peacefully" also perfectly accords, i.e., without controversy of word or deed, *De dolo et contumacia*, c. *Cum olim*. *De testibus*, c. *Ex parte*. *Ne praepositi vices suas*, c. *Ultima*, lib. 6. *De rescriptis et decretis*, c. *Gratiae*, q. d. without force. *D. De vi et vi armata*, and l. *Vim facit*. And without offering, *De procuratoribus*, c. *Non solum*, §. *Si statuae*. And without question, *D. Ad Trebellianum*, l. *Lucius*, §. *In haeredes*. And without revocation into doubt, *D. Quod mei causa*, l. *Extant*, in the gloss. This also the subject word "quietly" clearly demonstrates. For that which is in quiet is that which is not disturbed by any troubles, nor burdened with any extraneous expenses. *C. De episcopis et clericis*, l. *Quisquis*. *Extra. De praescriptionibus*, c. *Sanctorum*. *De probationibus*, c. *Ex literis*. *De sponsalibus*, c. *Impuberum*. *C. Duo pueri*. Therefore, a quiet state is signified by these words, *De poenis*, c. *Multorum*, §. *i*. *In clerico*, *Nil mirum*. Therefore, nothing is to be innovated in any way, lest the debtor impose a law on the creditor: because it ought not to be in the power of my adversary to do what he has with me. *D. Si idem*, §. 1. *De iudiciis omnium iudicum*, in the gloss. But in what manner is it explained in the sense of the case? In no manner, or by any device, *De electione quorundam*, lib. 6, per Arch. *De legibus*, 1, l. *Non quocunque modo*. From which it appears that the true conclusion from the force of the words is, *D. De usufructu legato*, l. *Si alii*, that tolls and pasturage fees for the use of this forest are not due: nevertheless, in this process, nothing else should be mixed in, by which public revenues could be diminished. *D. De aqua quotidiana et aestiva*, l. 1, §. *Trebatius*. It also supports the aforementioned and confirms the third reason touched upon at the beginning of this point. *D. De usufructu*, l. *Proculus*. And it supports. *D. De locato*, l. *Sed Adamus*, §. *Si inquilinus arcaum*, in the word "expenses," s. *locatoris*. And c. *Baldus*.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. To what a custom is equivalent.
2. The right to collect tolls is a real right attached to the territory.
3. The universal heir is bound to enter, or quasi-enter, the vacant possession by virtue of his own authority upon the death of the deceased.
4. Where fraud is alleged, which entails a crime, and thus the fraud ceases, acquittal must follow.
5. To exact tolls without a true or putative cause is an atrocious crime.
6. On what grounds the collector of tolls may be excused.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Because custom is equivalent to truth, as noted in l. 1, de servitutibus et aqua. Moreover, it is equivalent to a privilege, as is read and noted in Extra, de verborum significatione, c. Super quibusdam, § Praeterea, and it appears expressly in ff., de publicaniis, l. Si publicanus, § In omnibus, and in ff., de verborum significatione, l. Nimis propere, pedagia. Therefore, although they properly pertain to the prince, as in c. 1, Quae sint regalia, col. 10, nevertheless, by virtue of the prince’s privilege and of very long-standing custom, they may belong to cities and even to specific persons, as in c. Praesenti, de censibus, in the Clementines, by contrary reasoning; and as noted after Dyther by Bartolus in the aforementioned l. Si publicanus; by Archidamus in q. 14, q. 3, c. Si quis competas; and in Speculum, de causa possessionis, § Quia vero, no. [number]; in Speculum, de locato, § 1, ver. Porro; and in c. Quicumque, de censibus, lib. 6; in ff., de verborum significatione, l. Censoria; and as noted by Hostiensis in Summa, de censibus, § Ex quibus, ver. Et nunquid Rex Franciae, and ver. Quid si quis. It supports what is noted in a similar case in Authentica, de defensione civium, § Nulla, at the end of the great gloss; and what is noted in Speculum, de immunitatibus ecclesiarum, at the end. And on this point, the authors of both laws largely agree. Custom can also confer public right upon a purely private person, de foro competenti, c. Cum contingat. It is supported by ff., de diversis et temporibus praescriptionum, l. Si quisquam; ff., de iniuriis, l. Iniuriarum, § Si cum; l. Sequenti; ff., communia praediorum, l. Venditor; de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. 2, in principio; ff., quod quisque universitatis nomine, l. Nulli. And this is the first point to be premised.

Secondly, it must be premised that the right to collect tolls is a real right, which adheres to the territory in which the toll is levied; therefore, it is a kind of jurisdiction; therefore, it adheres to the territory. C. ubi, et apud quos. l. si. And here it appears that in such a right there occurs a true transmission to heirs. ff. de pec. haer. l. item videndum. §. si. and l. item veniunt. Thus, the deceased was in quasi-ownership, or in quasi-possession, of this right. The heir is not to be prohibited from using the same right; indeed, even if the deceased had not held title for the heir, or for himself, and a just cause for possessing. C. de edict. div. l. si. C. qui ex caus. mai. l. cum miles. in princ. Moreover, possession induces a presumption of good faith, according to the note in de usucap. l. Celsus per Bartolus. Also, public fame. ff. quando ac. de peculio est annalis. l. quaesitum. For it is rightly believed that what is spread by the mouths of all is common knowledge. ff. de fluv. l. 1. §. 1. and the note in l. pe. C. de per. tut. ff. de acqu. haer. l. cum quidam. §. cum dicitur. ff. ad mac. l. 4. C. eo. l. Zenodorus. l. 1. cum concor. In the successor, therefore, good faith is presumed, since he indicates that his ancestors possessed. It supports what is noted by Cynus, C. de servit. l. 1. in 4. q

Thirdly, it must be premised that the universal heir is bound, by his own authority, to enter into the possession vacated by the death of the deceased, or to enter into it quasi, and to perform acts of a possessor. C. unde vi, l. si, de acquisitione possessionis; l. cum haeredes. And even before he apprehends the vacant possession, he is nevertheless deemed to possess. ff. de usucapione, l. nunquam, § vacuum; and l. si homo. And if the deceased possessed as a possessor, the heir is not bound in his own person by an action for the recovery of the inheritance; because, as far as he is concerned, and by himself, he is not a robber; but he is bound only in the person of the deceased, inasmuch as the fault is found in him through the deceased. ff. de petitione hereditatis, l. etiam, § haeredem. It supports what is noted by Dy. in c. 2, de regulis iuris, lib. 6.

Fourthly, it must be premised that where fraud is alleged, which is imputed in the crime, or in the penalty, or especially in the delict, as in torture, and the fraud ceases, an acquittal ought to follow. D. de lib. causa, l. igitur; D. de abig., l. 1, in fine. Moreover, one cannot be criminally punished for every fault, as is noted in C. de epis. et cle., l. si quis. I need not say that no one is bound to relinquish possession without a hearing of the case, or to leave his right undiscussed. D. de pe. hae., l. illud. And he who is in possession does not commit a wrong by using and enjoying it; for this is the nature of possession and his right, D. de ma. et obe., c. inter quatuor, according to Innocentius; D. de resti. spo., c. cum in literis; D. de iure patro., c. consulta, according to Innocentius; and D. de vsur., l. videamus, § 1, there: "therefore," auth. and c.

And having thus premised, I come to the formulated inquiry: and I readily concede that to exact tolls without a true or putative cause is a heinous crime, as is stated in the Digest, under the Julian Law on Public Violence, in the final law, and as noted in the Decretal *Si quis romipetas*. Nevertheless, where there is a just cause or a just error, the crime is not incurred; for legitimate ignorance, so to speak, is not punishable criminally, as held in the Digest, under the title *De poenis*, in the law *Titii ac tutor*, § 1; in the Digest, under the title *De adulteriis*, in the final law; in the Code, under the title *De tabulis*, in the law *Generaliter*; and in Book 10, under the title *Pro vero*. For that which is false due to error is always regarded as true, as noted in the Digest, under the title *De poenis*, in the law *Pro herede*, in the first gloss; and in the Divine Page, where it says: “Your father and I, sorrowing, sought you,” etc.

† Furthermore, I concede that a toll is sometimes exacted contrary to the law. In such a case, fraud is presumed precisely because it is contrary to a prohibiting law, as stated in C. de agris et censibus, l. Tunc praesumitur; and in l. Quemadmodum, D. 11. Sometimes, however, it is exacted in accordance with the law, that is, by virtue of a privilege or by legitimate prescribed custom. In such a case, bad faith does not attach to the lawful possessor and owner of this right. See ff. de re iudicata, l. Qui auctore; ff. de noxalibus actionibus, l. Generaliter. Sometimes it is exacted beyond the law, because the custom was initiated by ancestors in fieri, not in facto esse; that is, it has not yet been prescribed. In such a case, fraud is also not presumed, because fraud is presumed in the invader, not in one who holds even from a non-owner. See ff. de nundinis, l. Utile; §. Vendi, ff. de acquisitione possessionis; l. In probando, nota, C. de praescriptione longi temporis; l. Pluraliter, ff. pro herede, per totum, with the following. Indeed, it can be said that this case is in accordance with the law until the matter has been cognized by a judge, whereby the use of this quasi-possession is determined. See ff. de officio procuratoris, c. Si.

Therefore, considering the proofs, at least of the opinion of the people, that the said passage belonged to the ancestors of the said nobles and to the said nobles themselves, the inquisitors ought undoubtedly to be absolved; hence they ought not to be tortured, and the sentence passed against them was and is most unjust, since ancient possession and good faith excuse them from all criminal penalty. I say no more, lest I repeat what was most elegantly stated by the advocates of the inquisitors. Therefore, they are not to be punished, but are to be maintained in quasi-possession until it is established that they do not have the right. See ff. de itinere, actuque privato, l. 1, §. 1; ff. de aqua quotidiana et aestiva, l. Penultima; Instit. de interdictis, §. Commodum; ff. de libellis causis, §. Finis. And if these inquisitors had nothing else for themselves except the form of ancient documents, this would suffice regarding the evasion of the crime, because reputation excuses from guilt. See ff. de adulteriis, l. Miles, §. Penultimo. This is especially so in inquisitions; see what is noted in C. de solutione matrimonii, l. Si quidam; c. Cum causam, de iuramento calumniae, according to Innocentius. And that which cannot be proved clearly should be proved by arguments and indications. See ff. de re militari, l. Non omnes, §. A barbaris; and see C. de probationibus, l. Non nudis; non epistolis, neque natalibus, ff. de probationibus, l. Finis; C. de fidei instrumentis, l. In sollemnibus. In the gloss on the Ordinance, which states that he who is commonly held and reputed to be privileged is to be maintained in quasi-possession, even if he does not produce privileges.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a libel of this kind shall proceed: I demand that the thing be delivered to me on the ground of sale, and if you do not deliver it, I demand interest.
2. You promised to sell; therefore, I demand that you either sell or provide interest.
3. Whether the libel shall be defeated on account of the ineptitude and impossibility of the time.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The allegations made on both sides are so full and formal that it is not expedient to allege further, but to decide, and the truth is,

† That this libel, in which I ask that the thing be delivered to me on the ground of purchase, and if you do not deliver it, I ask for damages, proceeds, as noted in D. de actionibus emptoris, l. 1. in principio; D. de verbis obligatorum, l. 2. § item si infectio.

And similarly, regarding this petition, I say that you promised to sell; therefore, I demand that you either sell or provide compensation for damages. It is not considered a bare pact, since it is clothed with the obligation of the price. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. Labeo; D. de alterutra venditione, l. 1, in fine; especially according to canon law, X. de pactis, c. 1. And if it is said that this petition is uncertain, it is not true; rather, it is certain, having within itself an order derived from the nature of the contract. And although the event is uncertain with regard to payment, this arises from the act of the party who does not pay. And he cannot object on the ground of such uncertainty. D. quorum legatorum, l. 1, § quod autem; and note, D. de tributoria actione, l. quod in haeredem, § eligere.

It remains to be seen whether the libel is vitiated on account of its absurdity and the impossibility of the time stated. And it seems that it is, for the conclusion of the libel cannot follow from an impossibility, for even by reason: for from an impossibility never follows a possible or necessary thing, even if the defendant confesses; for law and nature regard the impossible. D. de interdictis et actionibus, l. Confessio; fully noted in C. de confessionibus, l. 1. Hence, not only is this libel absurd, but also false and impossible. I say false, not that I examine it as such, but that it arises from the inadvertence of the patron. Wherefore it seems that the defendant ought to be absolved from the observance of the judgment, D. de officio vicarii, c. 1, per Innocentius; D. de inofficioso testamento, l. Posthumus, § Si quis ex his, by contrary sense, where he rejected the right if immediate liberation is granted, and we say something true or false from the time, just as from the place, D. de contraria stipulatione, l. Optimam; D. de re iudicata, l. Habere sane. This libel certainly cannot be sustained without difficulty; nevertheless, for the sake of investigating the truth and considering the simplicity of the woman bringing the action, let us consider that this libel is correct as to the cause, the year, and the name of the month; but it is not true as to the presence of the month; for it is not true that a month which has passed is present, but this falsehood does not vitiate the cause, Extr. de rescriptis, c. Super literis; C. si contra ius vel utilitatem publicam, l. Praescriptione mandatorum. The aptness of the subsequent procedure declares by the very fact the correction of the error, arg. D. de legatis 2, l. Testator, in principio. Moreover, this correction does not touch the substance of the matter; but certain words accidentally added, it can well be done up to the conclusion in the case, D. de noxalibus actionibus, l. In delictis, § Si detracta. Moreover, the judge admitted this correction of the expressed error; therefore, if he had done so in the instance, it is valid, yet the praetor’s decision is upheld, since no appeal was taken from such admission, arg. D. de minoribus, l. Ait praetor, § Permittitur; and Extr. de appellationibus, c. Ex parte. Moreover, these words were said superfluously and do not fall into the essence of the libel; therefore, they do not vitiate it, l. Non solet, D. de re iudicata. Moreover, the proofs are apt; therefore, the judge ought to follow the truth of the proofs; because the libel is not absolutely absurd, but in a certain respect, i.e., in that on which the libel is not founded. Nor is it a matter of form, as it would be in a criminal case, as l. Libellorum. Then it seems not to be valid on account of the defect of form, non obstante. If it be said that the aptness of the proofs operates nothing, but the petition is absurd, as noted in Extr. de iudiciis, c. Examinata; in the Novellae and in the Speculum, de iurisdictione omnium, § Deseruit, ver. Quid si libellus; for that is true when the substantial elements of the libel are lacking, i.e., the thing, the cause, or the action; otherwise, if it has the substantial elements, as here. Moreover, this libel was rather a new production than a new libel; for it was a recapitulation of the old libel aptly conceived, and a certain prosecution of it, as D. de procuratoribus, l. Quae omnia. And therefore it is not false that truth is aided from the beginning, D. de legatis 2, l. Cum filius, § Haeres meus.
