Thus, that word “present” is to be referred, by sound and equitable understanding, not to the day of the new production, but to the day of the truth of the production, as to the beginning of the libel, as D. de legatis 1, l. Talis scriptura; D. de iure codicillorum, l. Pro totiana. Wherefore, I think that adherence ought to be had to the truth of the proofs, D. de officio praesidis, l. Illicitas, § Veritas. Therefore, omitting the absurdities, let us embrace the apt and true things, at least according to canonical equity, as noted in c. Examinata, per Innocentius. It supports what is noted in l. 2, de errore advocatorum.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the time limit for the instance runs when a party is hindered in the prosecution of the lawsuit due to uncertainty regarding the time, the office, or the magistrate.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

First, it must be considered whether, under the common law, the time for the instance runs when a party is impeded in the conduct of the litigation due to uncertainty of time, office, or magistrate. And at first it seems that it does not run by operation of law, as in D. de adulteriis, l. si maritus sit in magistratu, in principio; and this supports the rule in D. de iudicibus, l. 2, § in omnibus; C. de iure deliberandi, l. si, § donec; D. de annis exceptis, l. 1, in fine; C. qui bonis cessis possunt, l. si; and in Auth. ut cum de appellatione cognoscitur, § meminimus, there where it says “but as to other allegations,” as in C. de annis exceptis, l. 2, in fine; and the argument in D. si pendente appellatione mors interueniat, l. fin.; D. de minoribus, l. inter utile tempus; C. de tempore in interdictis restituitis, l. petendae; D. de excusatione tutoris, l. si cum ipse, because he is not harmed by the passage of time, since he was not negligent: D. de inofficioso testamento, l. contra maiores; D. de appellationibus, l. ex ratione; and in Auth. de appellationibus, § sancimus, column 9, and there noted. And if the time runs, at least restitution in integrum should be granted, as in D. de servorum ruinae praescriptione, l. actilanus; D. de minoribus, l. et si sine, § si, there where it says “all ages for all persons,” etc., where it seems expressly stated.

On the contrary, it seems that the time runs and no restitution is granted, lest the law write something uncertain: D. de dolo, l. arbitrio, § dolo, in fine; and this is the glossa ordinaria in C. de tempore appellationis, Auth. item si appellatione, in the gloss; indeed, there where it says: “but in the principal case no restitution is given after the term.” And the reason is that he is secure under the common law through a new instance. It supports what is noted in C. de praescriptione longi temporis, l. 1; C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. si, notwithstanding the laws alleged to the contrary: because some speak of time useful in a qualified sense; others speak of prescription, by which the action or the right of the plaintiff is concluded, but not of the mere end of an instance: D. de in integrum restitutione, l. si; and this supports what is noted by Cynus in C. de iudicibus, l. properandum, § si autem utriusque, although there the gloss varies from another gloss of the said authority. Also a similar gloss is in Auth. ut sponsa largiatur, § huius. Therefore it must be said that under the common law the instance is peremptory, and no further proceedings can be had on it under these circumstances, and any proceeding to further steps would be void: D. de excusatione tutoris, l. scire oportet, § consequens.

Now let us come to the statute, and I premise that the statute was introduced for the sake of brevity and abbreviation of lawsuits, and therefore the time moderated by law should not be extended: D. de iuramento calumniae, l. 2, § fin. Thus it must be understood that legitimate times are not exceeded, as in D. de iudicibus, l. si iudex, and this is gathered from the mind of the law: D. de excusatione tutoris, l. scire oportet, § et si maxime, because what is introduced for diminution should not operate an increase concerning the matter or the time: D. de mandato, l. Titia, § si; D. de legatis primo, l. legata inutiliter. Those words, therefore, “no term, no prescription,” with sound understanding refer to the time established by the statute, not to the time of the term: C. de adulteriis, l. ita pudor; and what is noted in D. ad exhibendum, l. 3, § ibidem, in the gloss de facto in fine, which gloss is noted for this purpose; also the proemium of the statute supports this, there where it says “protractionibus,” etc. For the proemium proves the mutual intent of the law: D. de hereditate instituenda, l. si; and thus the general words of the statute do not correct the common law, nor can they be understood without conception, and the reason of the statute tends to restrict times, not to extend them. And so I hold that by operation of law the instance is peremptory by the lapse of the term after litem contestata, or because thus a certain distinction is applied, the common law and the statute are reduced to a certain consonance: C. de inofficiosa donatione, l. 1; C. de noxalibus, l. 2; Extra de consuetudinibus, c. cum dilectus; and Inst. in prooemio, in the word consonae.

I, Bal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a person commits a maleficium in one territory and in another, he cannot be punished in both territories; it suffices that he be punished once in one of them.
casus: Punctus, thus propose: Certain persons from Carnaro wounded a certain person from Camerino in the territory of Assisi. By the authority of the Castle of Camerario, proceedings were taken against the said Camerines who committed the said maleficium, and similarly by the Captain of Assisi proceedings were taken against them for the aforementioned maleficium. And in the contumacy of the said persons who committed the said maleficium, both by the authority of the Camerario and by the Captain of Assisi, they were condemned for the same maleficium in certain quantities of money, as contained in the condemnations themselves. Now the authority of the Castle of Camerario wishes to carry out execution of the condemnation passed by him. It is alleged on behalf of the said condemned persons that the said execution should not be carried out, since execution of the condemnation passed by the Captain of Assisi has been made in the city of Assisi for the same maleficium, as appears from the cassation of the condemnation and execution, which is transmitted to you on behalf of the commune of Camerario. It is alleged that the execution, which is said to have been made in the city of Assisi, does not prevent execution in the castle of Camerario, since the said execution was made by way of grace. Now it is asked, whether execution should be made in the castle of Camerario or not, having seen the above, and having seen the condemnations passed in the said places. I, Bal.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. This question is doubtful,

† For since in both cases the process has proceeded to condemnation, a right has been acquired by each party; hence it does not appear that the execution against one extinguishes the right of the other, just as when an injury is done to the father and the son is condemned. Each suffers from a different injury by reason of different persons, and although the act was single, it does not appear that one is released by the other, cf. D. de usu, l. 1, § et si usque adeo. Moreover, because the power of the Camerarius arises through citation, cf. D. de iudiciis, l. si quis postea. Moreover, because this penalty has for the most part been remitted, and thus the offense has not been fully punished, and therefore it remains to be punished, cf. C. de sportulis, l. 2, so that crimes do not remain unpunished. Moreover, different territories have different advantages. It is asked, and no one’s right ought to be diminished, l. 2, de his qui sunt sui vel alieni iuris. On the contrary, it seems that punishment pertains principally to the judge of the place where the offense was committed, and if punishment has been inflicted there, it ought not to be inflicted elsewhere: whether because the offender was remitted to that place, or because he paid; for if he ought to be punished in several places, remission would not be made to one place, as in Auth. ut nulli iudici, § si quis comprehensorum. Moreover, a duchy, by its nature, has one governor. Moreover, it has distinct jurisdictions, hence whatever is done merely as a matter of fact, in law suffices once. Moreover, one ought not to be sued repeatedly for vengeance. Moreover, even if more is done in one place than in another according to law, the accused has passed through the Senate’s judgment. Moreover, the remission was not entirely gratuitous, cf. D. de pace, l. si intra. Moreover, the denunciation was presented earlier.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Territory is called terminal in three ways.
2. Ownership is simply ownership joined with patience.
3. Full is said of that to which nothing can be added.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The integral theme to be presupposed is derived from the form of the toll, and having assumed this, it must be premised that the toll is annexed to the soil,

† We call that territory which we term "terminal" in three ways. First, circumscriptively, or terminally. Second, subjectively, or materially. Third, concessively, or rationally. For as regards the first, it is determined by certain boundaries; as regards the second, it is impressed as jurisdiction; as regards the third, because it is privileged, prescribed, and granted, and thus it is in rem, and passes with the territory and its appurtenances, and it is contrary to nature, as with slaves, because naturally all ways are free, Extra, de verbis significatis, c. Super quibusdam, § Praeterea. Although it coheres with the universal soil, it does not cohere with the soil, i.e., with the certain land of any private person; because its signification is taken from a certain power, it does not arise from estates, and therefore it is not a fruit of the field, but is a fruit of that power and of the universal fisc, not of private persons. Note 10, col. Quae sunt regalia, c. 1. Although this power, because it is not divided, is everywhere within the district, just as the fisc, as noted in C. de quadragesimali praescriptione, l. 1, these things are therefore separated, i.e., the jurisdictional and the private. Nevertheless, from these two there is sometimes made a certain quasi-just thing from qualities, or from the appurtenances of qualities, similar to the rule in ff. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. Imperium, § Si mixtum. And therefore in the matter at hand three things are to be considered: the most suitable convenience made into a promise, the full utility made into a concession, and the limitation and cancellation of the pension.

† Regarding the first point, it must be known that sometimes ownership is granted to someone, sometimes mere utility; in the first case, either specifically, or joined with tolerance by way of stipulation. For example: If the Commune of Perugia sold me one hundred bushels of wheat simply, because by the very fact that it gives, it is discharged. But if it is extracted from the district of Perugia, I shall pay the toll, just as others do, because these are separate, and one does not lead to the other. D. de publicanis, l. licitatio; §. si, de serv. pr. urb. praed., l. si domus. And this example is when [it is granted] simply. The example of tolerance joined is if the Commune sold me one hundred bushels with the agreement that it would tolerate my transporting them into my warehouses, which I have outside the district. In this case, it must grant free tolerance, nor do I have to purchase it at a new price, because what is the price of the thing is the price of the agreement, and what is free regarding the thing is free regarding the agreement. D. de act. empt., l. si sterilis; §. si tibi, de contrah. empt., l. fundi partem; D. de donat., l. qui saxum; D. de dolo, l. cum mihi; D. de locat., l. sed si addes; §. inquilinus, in fine. Since the contract is not made upon the utility of the tolerance, the promise appears to be in existence, as noted in D. de usufructu, l. sed et si quid; §. proprietate. Therefore, transport cannot be impeded under the pretext of a toll or pedage, lest the debtor’s sanction bind the creditor and rescind the agreement. For this would be inequitable. C. de pactis, l. pacto cum si. And by this our question is determined, and it is the case of D. de publicanis, l. Caesar, rightly introduced, for Caesar where he does not impose a prohibitory or burdensome law upon lessees, but upon certain persons, and because this was just on the part of the prince, and we ought not to consider it unjust, because Christ’s action ought to be our instruction, and to prohibit and to burden are equivalent; therefore, he who must tolerate cannot burden. l. 1, §. quae honorandae, quarum rerum actio non datur; and l. spadonem, de operis lib.

† Regarding the second point, it should be known that "full" is said of that to which nothing can be added and from which nothing can be subtracted; hence, whenever a faculty is granted, it is understood to be granted with full right, that is, integrally and without diminution, as in c. Apostolicae, de praebendis, lib. 6; D. 8.6, Bene quidam, ff. de alienationibus legatorum; L. Quaero, de bonis quae liberis; L. Si, § Simili quoque modo, ff. de rei venditione; L. Iulianus, in fine. From this it is inferred that no pedagium is due for such use, which would indeed be diminutive. Regarding the third point, it should be observed that an annual pension demonstrates that nothing beyond what has been fixed for the effect of the thing granted is due, ff. de usuris, L. In fideicommissum, § Cum Pollidius, in fine. From the amount thereof it may also be judged that the whole appears to have been granted, arg. L. 1, ff. de rebus dubiis; and what is noted in L. 1, ff. de superficiebus. I therefore conclude, assuming the full thesis, that no pedagium is due, and that the way lies open, full and free, to the redeemer. Many other arguments could be alleged, but it is not expedient to do so at present. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a son born to a natural father is a comitatus member or a citizen, and whether he should be placed in the catalog of citizens.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. This case is to me quite doubtful: because the statute is very strict against the citizens of the county, and those enrolled in the county, and a strict and penal form is prescribed: unless an express license is granted with the consent of the former lords and chamberlains. For this person, concerning whom the question is asked,

† Although he was born in the city, nevertheless his father was from the countryside, and Bartolus says in l. 1 ad Municipales, because one born in the city of a rural father is a *comitativus* (subject of the county) with regard to public duties and functions, and is not to be called or considered a citizen by virtue of a restrictive interpretation: because the father will bind him to the countryside, and inscribes him in the rural roll, as in l. Cum scimus, de Agri et Cens. And this is proven by its contrary: because if someone is generated from a citizen and is born in the county, he is called a citizen, and is not a *comitativus*. And thus the common opinion holds and speaks. Thus, therefore, in these words, proper origin is not considered according to Bartolus. This is of great credibility: they say, because men, both learned and common, commonly believe this: for this obligation proceeds from the father and descends to sons wherever born, even if they were born in another city, arg. ff. de Interdictis et Relegatis, l. 3. Nor should separation of sons from fathers be made, de Leg. 3, l. Uxorem, §. Concubinam. And the free status of the father is considered that of the son, as noted in l. 2, C. Qui Etate, li. 10, where the gloss notes. And we see this in all persons of conditional status, that sons follow their fathers. C. de Decurio, l. Ex omnibus, and l. In successione, and l. Omnes qui. C. Quando et qui, quar. pars debe., l. Si. C. de Munici. et Origina, l. Filius. C. de Metallariis, l. Si. and de Murilegu, l. Qui aliquem. and C. de Fabricem, l. Stigmata. Otherwise, rustics would come to suffer in the city, and material for deserting the countryside would be given, which is absurd. C. de Agr. et Cen., l. Cum satis, §. Nullam. Therefore, a son born in the county in the city is a *comitativus*, and thus cannot be placed in the citizen cadastre for the use of lords, as in C. de Colonis Tracensibus, l. 1, li. 11. To the contrary it seems, because the place of generation makes just as much difference as the father, whence it can be said that the place is a second father. Wherefore the son follows his proper origin. ff. ad Municipales, l. Assumptio. C. de Incolis, l. Cives. But certainly he also follows the paternal origin with regard to duties, and also with regard to forum. Therefore, with regard to duties, he can be called into the county, if the father was a *comitativus*: therefore, his name should not be removed from the county, because the yoke of the father is the yoke of the son. d. l. Assumptio, §. Filius. For the distinction between citizen and *comitativus* is made only with respect to duties: because *comitativi* are presumed to be burdened with heavier and more sordid obligations than citizens, who are better and more worthy than them. It supports what is noted de Manu, l. Prius, §. Sed et suscipientes, in the gloss. Whence, by reason of proper origin, he is not relieved from the attachment of the father’s origin, neither with regard to forum, nor with regard to civil burdens, real, personal, or mixed, as noted by Cynus, de Iu. om. iu., l. 2. And thus it is true in common law, as Bartolus says, as he proved at length. But considering the statutes well, it must be known that the Perugian statute makes mention of *comitatenses* and sons of *comitatenses*, whereas the prohibitive statute makes mention of *comitatenses*, and not of sons of *comitatenses*. i.e., of heads of families, and not of sons of families, who have lived familiarly in the city for 20 years and are artisans. This case, therefore, regarding sons is omitted in the corrective statute: therefore, it remains under the permissive. C. de App., l. Praecipimus. Notwithstanding that both are *comitatenses*: because the last statute is interpreted and understood by the first, so that it is understood of *comitatenses* who are not heads of families, because the statute speaks of these as distinct: because the conjunction falls between distinct things, and thus of the two members of the permissive statute, the corrective statute assumed only one member. The other, therefore, remains uncorrected, especially since proper origin operates something in this distinction of names. For by reason of proper origin, he has some similarity with a citizen, and therefore the transition is easier. Since, therefore, in sons there is some reason of difference to fathers, which is in the proposal, a reason both natural and civil provided against fathers is not extended to sons. ff. de Contrab., l. 3, §. Emancipatus. If, therefore, they have justice according to the form of the statute, prior officials and chamberlains are not necessary: because the law speaks of fathers. ff. sol. ma., l. Si vero, §. de vi 1o. And although this appears to be the truth in that regard, nevertheless I do not wish that officials place him in the citizen catalogue without the counsel of the others aforementioned: because it is more than penal if error were made in this, as appears in d. l. 1. For the cadastre is the sacristy of the Perugians, and must be guarded as a most holy thing and sanctuary, and the life of the city, Baldus.

CASE IN the name of Christ, amen. This is an example, or copy, of a certain contract or declaration found in a certain book of Bonifacio, with membranous covers, written by the hand of Ser Matteo, formerly of Vannis Crarimpoli of Gubbio, to whom such years of the Lord precede the said contract or declaration, namely: In the name of Christ, amen. On the 13th day of the month of September, acted in the house of the heir of Cione Matthioli Guidi, namely Ser Botto Alenutii, with Jacobo Vannelli, Angelo Cecholi, Io. Petrutii, Ioannelli Cauelli, Ioanni Veroli, Partuitio Bocatii Bello, witness of Gubbio, quarter of Saint Andrew, witness to me, I assert the conclusion to subscribe in substance, Lady Nese being called, had, and requested, etc. Since it is so, that Cione Matthioli Guidi of Gubbio, deceased, made his testament, in which, among other things, it is contained that the said Cione, by right of legacy, left to Lady Nese, wife of the notary of Lord Renaldus of Fabria, the goods described below, namely: one farmstead situated in the village of Colonata, county of Gubbio, which is worked by Ventura Berti of Gal., by the ingenuity of his mind, with all its boundaries and appurtenances, with the houses existing therein, and generally all movable and immovable goods which the said testator had in the said village of Colonata and of Saint Justin, within whatever boundaries and confines they appeared and were situated. Also, one vineyard situated in the village of Bagalet, in the county of Saint Clare, with houses and farmsteads existing therein, and stone channels existing therein, the boundaries of which vineyard and house are from two vineyards, other goods and properties of the late Lord Lelli, do. Cau., from Ser Matteo Colle, and the goods of Peter Augunt, and the goods of the Hospital of the Holy Spirit. Also, one villa situated in the village of Vagalae, in the contrada of Saint Gregory, the boundaries of which from one side are a road, from another the goods of the sons of the late Caubii, from four heirs of Ser Mascigioli, and from another the summit of the mountain, as regarding the said legacies made to the said Lady Nese, it appears by the hand of my notary subscribed below, knowing and asserting that the said Lady Nese has well in memory, and has had, from the said Cione, the will and intention of the said Cione, since the said Lady could not, by law, make a will or donate without the express license of the said Lord Nelli, her father, she wished, for her conscience, and for telling and declaring the truth, and declaring the will and intention of the said Cione, lest the souls of the said Cione and Nese hereafter, if the said declaration were not made, suffer any detriment or penalty, in every way, path, law, and form, by which she could best do so, although the aforementioned had been done by the said Cione to the said Lady Nese without any condition by my notary subscribed below: nevertheless, between the said Lady and the said Cione, there were words of pact and condition described below. Namely, that the said Cione said and declared that the said legacies were of Gaspar, son of the said Lady Nese, and son of the said late Cione, with this condition, namely, that the said Renaldus and Nese, Rugus, and Conte, sons of the said Lord Ranelli, together with the said Gaspar, are usufructuaries of the said goods and legacies. And if the said Gaspar dies without sons of the age of 25 years, the goods and legacies are of the said Lords Ranelli, Nese, Rugus, and Conte, saving and reserving that the said vineyard situated in the contrada of Saint Gregory, he wished and declared that it be, and be understood, of Ioan, formerly of Nercoli, father of the brother Andrea, in the said case, provided that the said Nese was in the power of her father, Lord Raynaldus, at the time of the present declaration, and at the time of the death of the said Lady Nese. It is asked, if by law, upon the advent of the case of the death of the said Gaspar, as contained in the said declaration, can Ioannes Nerculi demand the said vineyard from the heirs of the said Gaspar, having seen the said declaration and contents therein, made without the consent and presence of the said Lord Ranelli, father of the said Lady Nese, since it is said by the heirs of the said Gaspar that the said declaration is not valid nor binding by law, even if the father of the said Lady Nese had consented.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A daughter under the paternal power cannot contract without her father's consent.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† Without the father’s consent, this contract did not hold, as in C. de bonis quae liberae, l. si, §. filius autem. So I say, and I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, advise accordingly, and I have subscribed to the truth and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An oblique substitution made in respect of an uncertain thing never extends to the whole, whereas the contrary holds for a direct substitution.
2. Whether a substitution made by the word "succeed" in a certain thing is direct.
3. The word "succeed" is a common term.
casus: CASE. In the name of the Lord, amen. The facts are as follows: in the years of the Lord and so forth, Mandus Andreae, being of sound mind, made his last will and testament, in which, among other things, he made many bequests and legacies. And among other things, in all his movable and immovable goods, rights, and actions, he instituted his son Girard as his universal heir, and if it should happen that the said Girard dies without legitimate children born of his body, or in pupillary age, Rita and Vanna, daughters of Venditi, shall succeed to 25 florins for each of them. In all the other goods, Lucia and Maceutia, daughters of the said Mandus, shall succeed in equal portions. At the time of the making of the said testament, the said Mandus, the testator, had only one son named Girard, who was under pupillary age, whom the said Mandus instituted as his universal heir, and made the following institution for him, namely, that Rita and Vanna, daughters of Venditi, shall succeed to 25 florins for each of them, if the said Girard should die in pupillary age, or without children born of his body. In all his other goods, Lucia and Maceutia, his daughters, shall succeed, as is more fully contained in the said testament. After the making of the aforementioned testament, and after the death of the said Mandus, but before the death of the said Girard, the said Lucia and Maceutia, daughters of the said Mandus, who were substituted to the said Girard by the said Mandus, predeceased. Afterwards, the said Girard died in pupillary age, with the said Rita and Vanna, formerly cousins of the said Mandus, the testator, surviving him, as well as Dame Bartholomeutia, the former wife of the said Mandus and mother of the said Girard; and also with two sons of the said Lucia, formerly substituted to the said Girard by the said Mandus, surviving him. And also with Francesco Massii, the full brother of the said Dame Bartholomeutia, mother of the said Girard, and uncle of the said Girard, surviving him. And also with Agnelella and Colutia, full sisters, related on both sides, of the said Bartholomeutia, aunt of the said Girard, surviving him. It is asked whether the said Rita and Vanna, formerly cousins of the said Mandus, the late father of the said Girard, come to the succession of the said Girard in whole or in part; and if in part, to what extent they come to the aforementioned succession, or not, having seen the narration of the said testament, and having seen the testament of the said Mandus.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. It must be premised for clarity that, just as the institution relates to the instituted heir, as stated in the Digest, to the Law Falcidia, in the law *In ratione*, section *Filio*, and that the heir instituted in a specific thing does not receive the entire estate by accretion if no co-heir is appointed, or if he is appointed in a subtle manner, or excluded, as stated in the Digest, on the institution of heirs, in law 1, section *Si ex fundo*, and in the law *Quotiens*, section *Si duo*, and as noted by Cynus in the Code, on the inofficious testament, in the authentic *Novissima*; so too does the substitute receive by accretion, if the universal substitution has become void, or if no one has been universally substituted, as stated in the Digest, on vulgar substitution, in the law *Cohaeredi*, section *Si*. And this applies in direct substitution; otherwise in

† oblique made in a certain thing, because such a substitution never extends to the whole, as in l. cogi. §. et generaliter. ad Treb. per. Dy. It supports what is appropriate. C. fa. er. de l. quotiens.

† Now, therefore, it must be considered whether the substitution made by the word “succeed” to my son in a certain thing is direct. And it seems that it is, because if it were not direct, the son would not succeed by it, but rather the father, as is noted in C. de inoff. test., l. ex tribus; de vulg. sub., l. cohaeredi, § cum filiae. Moreover, the word “succeed,” in case of doubt, ought to be understood primarily, not secondarily, de vulg. sub., l. qui liberis, § haec verba; ff. si ager vect. vel emph., l. 1, § qui in perpetuum. Furthermore, doubtful words are deemed direct, as in C. de haer. inst., l. si; and it is noted in ff. de vulg. sub., l. verbis civilibus. And thus it seems that to the aforementioned Rita and Vanna everything accrues, as though they were pupillary substitutes, even though they were substituted in a certain quantity; for just as a father cannot die partly testate and partly intestate, so too can a pupillus not. That, however, is certain: that those who died while the pupillus was alive did not transmit by way of substitution, unless they were coheirs of the impubes. ff. de acq. haer., l. si filius, qui patri; it is established in de suis et legat., l. si ex pluribus; de vulg. sub., l. sed si plures, in princ.; and what is noted in l. 1, C. de his qui ante apertas tabulas. To the contrary, it seems that to the aforementioned Rita and Vanna nothing accrues.

†, for the word “succedat” (shall succeed) is a common word. D. de edendo, l. quidam, §. si. A common word added to a certain thing or quantity is never extended to the whole. §. et generaliter. And if it is said that a ward cannot succeed, this word must be placed in a direct sense; therefore, it is direct by necessary reason. The reason is that in pupillary wills legacies can be left; for the son himself is deemed to leave them, and succession takes place from the testament of the minor to the minor himself in the said legacies, D. de legatis 1, l. si fundum per fideicommissum, §. 1. Hence the said argumentation does not hold, because we are not in the primary wills, but in the secondary wills; and for a legatee there is no right of accrual to the heir. C. de fideicommissis, l. eam, quam. And I believe this part to be the more correct, namely, that accrual does not take place to the said Rita and Vanna. What, then, is the case with this inheritance? It certainly seems that it pertains to the children of Lucia; because Lucia was a coheir and substituted by the case of the law qui patri. For certain, she was not properly a coheir; because she was instituted in a certain quantity, and a coheir from the whole reduces her to the understanding of a legatee, except insofar as she may not claim to have been passed over. C. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. quotiens. And noted in l. si quis priore, D. ad Trebellianum. And I think this to be truer. Secondly, that the succession of the said ward is in the case of intestacy, and passes to those who would succeed the ward intestate. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Brothers who are mutually substituted transmit the right of substitution to one another.
2. The legitime portions of brothers who are mutually substituted are divided among themselves and their sisters.
casus:
CASE. In the name of the Lord, amen. The facts are proposed as follows. A certain Mattheolus Guidi of Gubbio made his will, in which he made several legacies, and among other things he left to his son, Lord Thomas, and to the abbess of the monastery of Saint Peter, by way of institution, 25 livres denari Romanorum, and he instituted him heir in the said quantity. Likewise, he left to his daughter, Lady Mita, by way of institution, beyond her dowries, 25 livres denari, and in the said dowries and 25 livres denari he instituted her his heir; but in all his movable and immovable goods, rights, and actions, wherever they might be and could be found, he instituted and made Cione Sparellus and Nicolellus, his sons, universal heirs in equal portions. And if any or all of his said sons should die without legitimate male children born to them, he substituted to him or them, or to the one or ones so dying, the surviving or survivors of their legitimate male sons, if they did not survive, in the place of the predeceased father, in equal portions, however, by stirpes and not per capita. And the said testator willed and ordered that in the restitution to be made on account of the said substitutions, all the goods of the said testator, which had come to him in any manner, should come into account, in whose person the said substitution had effect. But if any of them should die without male children, as has been said, and should have had a daughter or daughters born to him or them, if indeed he had one daughter, he might provide her with a dowry, or leave to her by way of institution up to the quantity of one thousand livres denari Romanorum from the said goods, and no more. But if he had several daughters, he might provide them with dowries, or leave to them, and to each of them, by way of institution from the said goods, 7 livres denari Romanorum, the aforesaid substitution remaining in the other residual goods, as is expressed above.

Finally, the said Mattheolus died, with the said Lord Thomas, his son, instituted heir as above, and the said Lady Mita, his daughter, instituted heir as above, and the said Cione Sparellus and Morellus, his sons, instituted universal heirs in the said will, still living. Finally, the said Lady Mita died, with her son Jacob, and Cione Sparellus, and Nicolellus, surviving her. Finally, the said Nicolellus died, with his son Guido, and the ladies Philippa, Joanna, and Munalductia, his daughters, and the said Cione and Sparellus, surviving him. Finally, the said Sparellus died intestate, and without children, with the said Cione and Guido surviving him. Finally, the said Guido and Lady Joanna died in pupillary age, with Lady Mita, their mother, and the said ladies Philippa and Munalductia, their carnal sisters, and the said Cione, their uncle, surviving them. Finally, the said Cione died, having made a will, in which, among other things, he instituted Gaspar, his son, his universal heir. Afterwards, Gaspar died without children, having made a will, in which he instituted the said ladies Philippa and Munalductia as his universal heirs.

Now it is asked, having seen the aforesaid, in what, or in what portion, could the said Gaspar make a will, presupposing that the said Cione knew of the death of his said brothers, and possessed the goods which remained in the inheritance of the said Mattheus and of his said brothers.

It is also proposed that Lady Munalductia, wife of Nicholas, formerly of the said Mattheolus, formerly made a will, in which she instituted the said Cione, Sparellus, and Nicolellus as her universal heirs, and among other things she judged and left to the said Lady Mita, her daughter, by way of institution, one hundred livres denari, as is contained in the will itself, and substituted to them, as is contained in the will. Afterwards, the said Lady Munaldella died, with the said Cione, Sparellus, and Nicolellus, and the said Lady Mita, surviving her. Finally, the said Lady Mita died, with the said Cione, Sparellus, and Nicolellus, and Jacob, her son, surviving her. Finally, Nicolellus died, with the said Guido, and the ladies Philippa, Joanna, Munalductia, and Cione, and Sparellus, surviving him. Finally, the said Sparellus died intestate, without children, with the said Cione, and Guido, and the ladies Philippa, Joanna, and Munalductia, daughters of the said Nicolellus, surviving him. Finally, the said Cione died, with the said Gaspar, his son, surviving him. And finally, the said Gaspar died, having made a will, in which he instituted the said ladies Philippa and Munalductia as universal heirs.

Now it is asked, having seen the aforesaid, and presupposing that the said Cione entered upon the inheritance of the said Lady Munaldella, and accepted the substitution made in the will of the said Lady Munaldella, and presupposing that the said Gaspar entered upon the inheritance of his father, the said Cione, what ought he to have of the aforesaid inheritance, and of how much can he dispose and make a will of the said inheritance?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The substitution in the will of Mattheolus does not claim a place, except with respect to the share of Supparellus, who died without a son of his. For the portion deducted as the legitime and the Trebellianic share went to Cionus for one half, and to Guidonus for the other half: who transmitted that share to their heirs, as is fully read in the law. And see: ff. de legatis primo, l. cum filio; ff. ad Trebellianum, l. apud Iulium, §. utrum; and §. actitia, C. de fideicommissis, si in persona

The legitime previously devolved intestate to all the brothers and sisters, and to the children of the predeceased brothers of the said Supparello, by representation (in stirpes), not per capita, as in the Authentica Defuncto and in the Corpus, whence it is derived. And if it be asked, how much Philippa and Munalductia may dispose of by will, I answer: of all the goods of Nicolello, and of all the goods of Gaspar, and of that which comes to the said Guido by the aforementioned substitution, from whatever source, considering all the facts narrated in the case, the rights have flowed to them through so many deaths and testaments. Moreover, whatever pertained to Cione and Nicolello from the inheritance of Munaldella belongs to them. But the share of Supparello, who died intestate, receives division into many parts; because all who then survived succeeded to him intestate by representation, as I said, which I say with regard to the nephews, who come in with their uncles by representation. And this applies to those entering upon the inheritance of the said Supparello, as in the Codex, De caducis tollendis, § In novissimo. Now, the legitime of Supparello is one-half of one-fifth part, considering the number of children, as in the Codex, De inofficioso testamento, and the Authentica Novissima. The Trebellianic rule, viewed in the testament of Matthiolus, appears to be prohibited, or rather compensated with the legitime. There it says: "all goods, which in any manner, etc." Furthermore, I do not think that it is to be deducted, by argument from the law Si debitor, ad legem Falcidiam, and the Codex, ad legem Falcidiam, Authentica Sed cum testator. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Property purchased by the fiancé and the father-in-law from the dowry or quasi-dowry money passes into the ownership of the woman, even if she is still under paternal power.
2. If one party confesses that the instruments of such a notary are simulated, and a witness states that he heard from the confessing party about all matters, whether such a witness provides proof.
3. Ownership of the sold thing does not depart from the seller himself if the price is immediately returned to the buyer.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. Between Dominic, acting on one side, and John Martini and his son Laurence, on the other, a question arises concerning several matters, and first concerning a house purchased with the money of the said Dominic, for which money or price of the house the said John and Laurence had a refund made to them by the said Dominic. And although the said purchase was valid and was a true contract, it must nevertheless be considered whether the right acquired ought to be yielded to the said Dominic, and whether possession of the said house ought to be delivered to him or not. And I say that it seems clearly proven that the name of the buyer was attached to the said contract for the benefit and advantage of the said Dominic. And I say further that the right of ownership of the houses was acquired from the very beginning by the said Dominic, both from the series of the instruments and from the nature of the fact itself, nor do we need witnesses in this matter. Take note, because this is a new allegation, and not yet touched upon, that I have heard: and yet

† It is a matter of common law. For it is established that the said house was purchased by the fiancé, and moreover with dowry money, or quasi-dowry money, whereby ownership of the house was immediately acquired by the woman. C. de rei vend. l. si ut proponis, where this is discussed. If, therefore, ownership of the house was acquired by the woman, it can also be acquired by the daughter in favor of the dowry, as in D. de fund. dotali l. Pomponius. Philadelphus follows the opinion that, upon her death, the dowry reverted to the father’s ownership by operation of law, as in C. de iure dot. l. dos a patre. The objection raised by Dominicus regarding the price does not hold, because he ought not to have received the price, which had been converted into a thing, according to the law on dowry, l. ita constante. Nor was the dowry to be returned during the mother’s lifetime. C. si dos constant. matr. l. 1. It therefore appears that since the objection was not made regarding all things, but only regarding the money, the houses themselves can be claimed, even without proof of the simulated objection concerning the price. And if it is said that this was not mandated, certainly the defendant claims that a marriage was contracted by words of present consent and the exchange of rings; although the husband bore no burdens nor took the girl into his home. And if there was no marriage, it suffices that there were betrothals, l. non sine, C. de bonis quæ lib. And if there were no betrothals, because the girl was an infant, nevertheless the hope of a dowry seems to have the same privileges as a true dowry, l. 2 and 3, de priv. cred. and D. de cond. ob caus. l. quod si servus. However, it is not established that she was of such infant age, and therefore at least betrothals are to be presumed, which operate in favor of marriage according to the laws, de fundo dotali l. Iul. And this statement has been made regarding the marriage in itself.

† Regarding the lands, the sale, and the confessed price, I state simply, and this is a new allegation, that although there had been a true sale, nevertheless, because the payment of the price was colorably interposed and the purse was immediately returned to the buyer, ownership did not pass from the seller. And I demonstrate this thus: the things sold and delivered do not become the buyer's in any other way than by the price being paid or credit being given for the price, as in § vendidisse, Institutes, On the Division of Things. However, here the price was not paid; for if he paid it only to receive it back immediately, he does not transfer ownership, as in the law Qui sic soluit, On Payment. Therefore, ownership of the money was not transferred, nor was credit given. Thus, without prejudice to the truth that there was a true sale, nevertheless, because the payment of the price was not true but fictitious, ownership of the thing sold remained with the said Domenico. And so it ought to be declared by the sentence of the judge. And we have more, and now I come to the other allegations made, and I say,

† That the simulation of the instruments is clearly proven in all respects and in every way, according to what is narrated in the petition. And on this point I do not elaborate, because the acts speak for themselves. And I say that if the party confesses that the instruments are simulated by the hand of such a notary, and this indefinite confession is equivalent to a universal one, as in l. pluribus, Unde testis, which states that he who says he has been aided by the confessing party proves all things, De verborum obligationibus, l. quicquid, Astringendae. Thirdly, I answer that there is no reason why it should prove more for one instrument than for another, C. de libellis praetoribus, l. 1. Moreover, the witnesses of the other party prove the simulation in the form and substance of the instruments, because in truth it was not done in that manner. C. de transactionibus, l. cum ea. Therefore, it does not hold as it is written, nor in any other way that would not appear when reduced to the contract: therefore, the present provincial governor should rescind the illicit extortions. l. illicitas, in principio, De officiis praesidis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Simulation is proved by the preambles, even if the contract was otherwise made.
2. Witnesses cannot be produced against exceptions and persons, if it was not protested before publication.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. In the dispute between Dominic and John Martin, it is necessary to speak but briefly: both because the matter is clear, and because the oral pronouncement has been cited on several occasions. Omitting other points that might be called into question due to the subtlety of the advocates, I proceed solely to the proofs. Regarding this, I observe that the said Dominic, in his libel or petition, alleged the simulation of certain instruments of sale of certain immovable properties, and of acknowledgments of receipt of the price, as well as of instruments of lease of the said properties. He requested that these instruments be declared to have been simulated, made for the security of the said lord, and to preserve the rights of the said Dominic, and not to acquire any right for the said John or his son from the said instruments or on account of them, as appears and is contained in the libel. To prove the intention of the said Dominic, several witnesses testified, who directly proved the contents of the libel, and especially Clementis Andructiolus and Nicholas, who state that all and each of the contents of the libel were truly acted and done between the contracting parties at the time the contracts were celebrated, even though something else was written. They state that they were present at the time the act was performed. Therefore, they conclude and necessarily prove the simulation, as in *l. emptor*, *de aqua pluviali arcenda*; and in *l. nuda*, *ff. de contrahenda emptio*; and in *l. emptione*, and throughout the title *C. plus valere quod agitur*.

† Moreover, this simulation is proven by witnesses, who testify that the said contracting parties, before entering into the said contracts, uttered all the words contained in the libel, and agreed upon them, and afterwards had the contracts drawn up in a form different from that which had first been agreed between them, which suffices to prove the simulation. For just as in last wills, the first will, being derogatory, nullifies the subsequent one, as in l. si mihi, et tibi, § 1, de legatis 1, and in l. si quis in principio, testamenti, de legatis 3; so too in contracts, the first will, being derogatory, nullifies the subsequent one. Thus, the gloss in l. pacta novis, C. de pactis, expressly affirms this, as does Jacobus Butrigarius, and there also, through Bartolus and Baldus, Jacobus Butrigarius reports, saying that such preceding words prove the subsequent contract to be simulated; it is similar in l. ac si quis, § plerique, de religiosis et sumptibus funerum. Nor does l. cum plures, § locator horrei, ff. locati conducti, stand in the way, for there the proposal was retained in the mind, and thus the subsequent will prevails. In our question, the proposal was expressed by the parties; therefore, the first will is valid. Thus says Petrus de Bellapertica in d. l. pacta novissima; d. Jacobus Butrigarius answers differently to d. § locator in d. l. pacta non curo. Furthermore, l. finalis, § item si praedixerit, ff. de nautico, chalybeato, et stipticiario, does not stand in the way, for there it speaks of a necessary act, in which a protestation is of no avail unless the adverse party consents; in our case, it speaks of a voluntary case. Furthermore, the said simulation is proven by the confession of the said John, which was made several times after the said contracts were celebrated, and in many and different places, in the presence of the said Dominic, upon his interrogation, which alone would suffice to induce proof without other proofs, as in l. publica Mevia, in fine, ff. depositi; and the gloss and doctors say in l. praesidi, C. de donationibus ante nuptias; and by Cynus, and fully in l. una, C. de confessionibus, in 13 q. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the witnesses are not consistent, and therefore faith should not be given to them, as in l. eos, ff. de falsis, and in l. qui falsa, C. de testibus. For if they are rightly examined, they agree in place, time, and fact; therefore, etc., as in l. ob carmen, § si testes, ff. de testibus. Furthermore, it does not stand in the way if it is said that the witnesses of John prove that the said Dominic changed his will, first, because the first will of Dominic was derogatory of the subsequent one, as has been said above. Furthermore, because the said witnesses do not prove that the said Dominic said nothing or confessed in the presence of John; therefore, he did not prejudice himself, as in l. confessionibus, ff. de interdictis et actionibus, and in l. certum, § si quis absente, ff. de confessionibus. Furthermore, even if it were assumed that the said confession had been made in the presence of John, it suffered from the same defect as the first instruments, because it was simulated, as in l. doli exceptio, ver. diversum, ff. de novis operis nuntiando, and in l. cum ea, C. de transactionibus.

† Likewise, it is not an objection if it is said that the aforementioned John wishes to prove the exceptions produced against the persons of the witnesses of the said Dominic: because the said exceptions were not protested before the publication of the proceedings, and thus he should not now be admitted or heard to prove them, as in the authority *Si dicatur*, Codex, *De testibus*; and in the Corpus, *De testibus*, § *Si vero quis*, column 7; and in the chapter *Praesentium*, Extra, *De testibus*, and there by the Gloss and Innocentius, and Franciscus de Coppolis.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A son burdened by a fideicommissum must receive both his legitime and the Trebellian portion.
2. If two sons are burdened by a fideicommissum, and one succeeds to the other, he may make a will disposing of two legitimes and two Trebellian portions.
3. The father’s will is valid among his children, even if the witnesses were not formally summoned; otherwise, as regards the testator’s brother, formal summoning is required, and it is not presumed that they were summoned, even if the notary states that they were present.
4. Property acquired after the father’s death does not fall within the fideicommissum.
5. The institution or disinheritance of those who are not under paternal power is not necessary.
6. Grandchildren succeed to their grandfather together with their uncle by representation (in stirpes), not per capita.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† He ought to have had both the legitime and the trebellianic portion freely, as in c. Ray. de testamentis, and in c. Ray., and in c. si pater, under the same title, book 6. Similarly, Antonius had the legitime and the trebellianic portion in his father’s goods by the same laws, as noted in de inoff. test., l. Papin. ad fin., and C. ad l. Fal., l. quiqui, and in Auth. de resti. et ea quae pariunt, §. quamobrem, and l. 1, §. si cui plusquam per l. fal., according to Dy.

† He could make a will regarding two legitime portions and two Trebellianic portions, namely his own and his brother’s, and regarding one-half of his father’s estate; because he did not bear the burden in that portion, as stated in the aforementioned chapters and laws, and in the Code, On Inofficious Wills, in the law *Quam in prioribus* and in the law *Scimus*, with the addition *Si*.

† Among the children, the father’s will was valid, even though the witnesses had not been formally requested, as noted in C. de codic. l. si. §. in omni. But with respect to the testator’s brother, the will is not valid under civil law if the witnesses were not requested, nor are they presumed to have been requested, even if the notary states that they were present. ff. de testa. mil. l. diuus. and as noted in l. hac consultis. per Cy. and in l. scendum. de ver. ob. If, however, the word “10” and similar abbreviations were present there, as notaries customarily insert abbreviations, that which is customarily appended would be tacitly included under this. s. de rogitu, as in C. de fideiuss. l. si. and de libe. et posth. l. Gallus. §. quidem.

† Goods acquired after the father’s death do not fall within the fideicommissum, ff. de vulg. subst. l. cohaeredi. §. cum filiae. whence neither [do they fall] within the fideicommissum. For the father could and did wish to make a will concerning his own goods, not concerning the son’s goods, de vulgari substitutione. l. centurio. in ratione sui. C. de leg. l. vxor patrui.

† It is not necessary to institute or disinherit such persons, nor does such omission invalidate the will. C. de inoff. testa. l. fratres. ff. de inoff. test. l. 1. de verb. obl. l. quidam cum filium.

† Grandchildren from one predeceased son succeed to their grandmother together with their uncle per stirpes, not per capita, as stated in the Institutes, On Succession of Intestates, §. cum filiis, and §. et quia placuit; nor could the grandmother have deprived them of their legitime, as in the Authenticum, On the Third and the Half, §. 1. Therefore, either the grandmother did not make a will, in which case both grandchildren succeeded to one half; or, if she made a will, she could have disposed in such a way that the grandchildren received only their legitime. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A father cannot burden his daughter in her dowry, except with regard to that by which the dowry exceeds the legitimate portion.
2. One who pays out another's money may stipulate for himself, although he is bound to return the money to the owner or to assign the rights to him.
3. A ward older than an infant does not transmit an unaccepted inheritance.
4. Whether a minor dying with the inheritance not having been accepted can seek restitution in integrum.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† First, it must be considered whether a father could burden a daughter in the restitution of her dowry, and certain authorities say that he could: because a father can substitute to a daughter, and also in the dowry, as in ff. de leg. 2. l. vlt. §. filię; so Dy. summarizes there, and he understands this to be true when the dowry exceeds the legitima—namely, that in so far as it exceeds it, a substitution can be made to the daughter in the dowry, but in the legitima a fideicommissary substitution is not valid according to Dy. and Old. According to Iac. de Bel. in a certain disputation, he says that if the action concerning the dowry belongs to the daughter alone, or is common to the father and the daughter so that through the death of the father it is consolidated in the daughter alone, the father cannot make a testament concerning the daughter's dowry, namely by bequeathing the dowry to a stranger or to someone other than the daughter; however, that he can make a testament concerning the dowry upon the daughter herself is noted in l. denique. §. sed vtrum ff. de minore. And there is a threefold reason: first, because after the dowry has been given and the marriage contracted, the father cannot by stipulating make the condition of the daughter worse, ff. so. ma. l. quotiens, therefore neither can he by testating. Second, because the dowry belongs to the daughter, not to the paternal estate, C. rem in praesenti. l. videamus. Third, because the daughter has this by benefit of law, not by benefit of the father, de adop. l. arrogator. §. sed an impuberi. Fourth, because the father is a debtor to the daughter in endowing her, de ritu nu. l. qui liberos; but a debtor cannot burden his creditor, C. cer. ve. pi. impe. non posse. l. 1. Fifth, because the cause of the dowry is more powerful than the cause of a fideicommissum, as in auth. res, quae. Sixth, because by a tacit donation inter vivos the daughter is the owner of the dowry after the death of the father, ff. fa. er. l. Pomponius, therefore she cannot be burdened, as noted in de leg. 3. l. similiter. Seventh, because the daughter is permitted not to acknowledge the father's testament and to retain the dowry for herself by full right, as in l. vlt. ff. de coll. dotis. If, however, the father honors the daughter in his testament out of other goods of his, or the action concerning the dowry is by the tenor of the stipulation the proper property of the father and his heirs, then the daughter could be burdened in the dowry; and so §. filiae is understood according to Ia. de Bel. and ff. ad treb. l. a filia, which I believe is truer.

† Second, it must be considered concerning the stipulation of the paternal uncle; and under the ius commune, the stipulation is valid in the form in which it was conceived, as in C. si cer. pe. l. quamuis, because he who counts out another's money can stipulate for himself; nevertheless, he is bound either to return the money to the owner, or to assign his rights to the owner if the owner consents to such an assignment, C. si cer. pet. l. cum si, and de lega. 3. l. si uxo. §. paterfa. supports this; but through the form of the statute, an action was acquired for the woman without any assignment; for the law, or an assignment feigned by law, can effect the same thing that a true assignment effects, C. de act. et ob. l. 1, ff. de insti. l. 1, C. ad Tre. l. 1. §. cum autem.

† Third, it must be considered whether, because the son did not enter upon the inheritance, he transmitted it to his father. And it seems that he did, because a descendant transmits to his ascending heir, as noted in C. de suis, et legi. l. apud hostes. To the contrary appears the text in l. si infanti. §. si non sit tutor, where it is openly said that when a pupillus older than an infant dies without having entered upon the inheritance, it is just as if the pupillus had never been in the nature of things; nor can it be said that the right of deliberating was transmitted, because he survived his mother by many years. Bar. held in disputation that a husband, by delaying for a long time in the restitution of the dowry, is deemed to enter tacitly, because by that very act he declares his intention through l. si peculium. §. sicut. de peculio legato. To me it seems that if he is always silent, he is always deemed to be deliberating, but not entering, C. de iure delib. l. fi.; for he who does nothing is not deemed to act as heir. Iac. de Are., Iac. But., and Barto.

† say that when a minor dies without having entered upon an inheritance, the heir of the minor can petition for restitutio in integrum just as his heir, because he was excluded through absence, de act. haer. l. cum quidam and l. Pontius, C. de testamento mil. l. 1, so that there should not be a greater privilege of absence than of age, de reb. du. l. qui duos; and through Iac. and Bar. there. But Iac. de Bel. held the contrary in disputation in the case of a minor, as he himself notes in Auth. de trien. et semis, and this through the text of the said law si infanti; for there the law establishes that it does not pass to the heirs of the minor, but to the heirs of the mother, and against a statutory provision of law a minor is not restored, as in ff. de admi. tuto. l. si sine. §. Lucius. Therefore, since a restitutio in integrum is neither proposed as petitioned nor granted, things being as they are, I advise that the said paternal uncles can claim the said dowry as heirs and the nearer kin of the woman through the said l. si infanti. If, however, restitutio in integrum were petitioned by the party, I say nothing of my opinion because I am not asked about this; I speak of things as they stand. L. apud hostes does not stand in the way, because it speaks of a paternal inheritance and of a suus heres according to the true understanding of all modern authorities. THE CASE. The point is this: Agnes had a uterine brother named Ventura, which Ventura had a son named Andreas. This Andreas had two sons, namely Vannucius and Franciscus; this Vannucius had a son named Ioannes, who was an infant. This Agnes, coming to death, made a testament in which, among other things, she instituted as universal heir Vannucius her husband, namely for his lifetime; after the death of her said husband, however, by direct words she instituted for herself the aforesaid Ventura, her brother, and Andreas, the son of the said Ventura, if they were alive at the time of the death of her husband; and if they were not alive, she instituted for herself by these words the legitimate sons of the said Andreas, under this condition and burden: that they give, and be bound to give within a year from the death of the aforesaid Vannucius her husband, 50 pounds for her soul. Afterwards, this having been done, the said Agnes died, and the said inheritance was entered upon by the said Vannucius her husband. Later, this husband, instituted heir by the said Agnes his wife, wishing to avoid the hope of catching a death, came to a pact and transaction with the said Ventura—namely, the heir instituted after his death together with the said Andreas his son—to wit, that the said Ventura, without the will and request of the said Andreas his son and co-instituted with him in the inheritance by the said Agnes, remitted to the aforesaid Vannucius all the right that he had or could have in the inheritance of the said Agnes, and bound himself and his heirs not to go against the said transaction or pact under a penalty of one thousand; which transaction was entered into for an amount less by fourfold than the said inheritance of the said Agnes was worth. Afterwards, in the course of time, while the said Vannucius, husband and heir instituted by the said Agnes his wife, was living, the aforesaid Andreas died, that same son of the said Ventura and instituted heir together with the said Ventura by the said Agnes after the death of her husband. Afterwards the said Ventura died, which Ventura instituted as his universal heirs the aforesaid Vannucius and Franciscus, his grandsons by the aforesaid son Andreas, who were instituted heirs in the third place by the said Agnes. With the passage of time, the aforesaid Vannucius, the husband of the said Agnes who had been instituted heir for his lifetime by the said Agnes, died. Now the aforesaid Franciscus and Vannucius come forward, the very ones instituted in the third place by the said Agnes; seeing that they cannot enter upon the inheritance of the said Agnes by virtue of the transaction made by the said Ventura their paternal grandfather, they bought the aforesaid inheritance of the said Agnes, namely, that they did not fulfill the aforesaid condition imposed in the said testament of Agnes. Now comes the aforesaid Ioannes, son of the aforesaid Vannucius and great-grandson of the said Ventura, which Ioannes was conceived and born after the death of the said Andreas his grandfather, and he wishes to claim the inheritance of the aforesaid lady Agnes from the heirs of the said Vannucius, the husband of the aforesaid Agnes. It is objected against him that he cannot claim the said inheritance by virtue of the testament of the said Agnes, because he was not instituted by the said Agnes. It is replied on behalf of the said Ioannes that, on the contrary, he was instituted by virtue of the said testament, and the aforesaid inheritance is owed to him in this manner: namely, because the said Agnes instituted in the third place the sons of the said Andreas. But I am a grandson of the said Andreas, and under the designation of 'sons' grandsons are contained, and thus a right in the said inheritance belongs to him. Secondly, it is objected against him that he cannot claim the inheritance because, although the said Ioannes may be comprehended under the designation of 'sons', yet he was a posthumous child, and under the designation of 'sons' a posthumous child is not included. But he replies to the contrary. In the third place, it is objected to the aforesaid Ioannes that the said inheritance is not owed to him because he did not fulfill the condition, nor did another for him, namely that he give 50 for the soul of the said Agnes within a year from the day of the death of the aforesaid Vannucius. He replies that he is a minor and an infant, wherefore restitution is competent to him against this omission. Secondly, it is replied that, although the inheritance would belong to him, yet because on account of the non-fulfillment of the aditio the inheritance is not owed to him from the testament, it is owed to him ab intestato as the nearest kin, and especially through the renunciation made by the aforesaid Franciscus and Vannucius. The said Ioannes also claims from the heirs of the said Vannucius the fruits gathered by the heirs of the said Vannucius from the inheritance of the said Agnes from the time of the death of the said Vannucius. The said heirs reply that they are not liable for the fruits because they were [not] formally summoned by the said Ioannes or by another on his behalf, etc. Now it is asked what the law is, and what must be done by the said Ioannes in this case, so that it does not prejudice the aforesaid Vannucius his father and heir in part of the said Ventura named above. The heirs of the said Vannucius also say to the aforesaid Ioannes: 'We will sue your father for the penalty, because he did not fulfill the condition placed in the testament of the said Agnes; for if he had fulfilled it, you could not succeed to this inheritance, because Vannucius himself preceded in the succession.' The said Ioannes replies that he was ignorant that this testament was made in this way, and an error of fact, especially concerning another's deed, does not prejudice. It is asked what the law is. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. On the appeal of sons, whether and when nephews come into it; and see also in counsel 362.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Grandchildren are not included. For by the same reasoning, descendants in infinitum would be included, according to certain doctors who hold this in l. Gallus, de lib. et posth. But the truth is otherwise, for either mention is made of the children of the deceased, or of the living. In the first case, the grandchildren of the deceased are not included; or it is said to be made either as a proper name, which is demonstrative of a certain person, or by some other restriction, for example because it is said "the son who will be born to me within ten months," etc., as in l. Gallus. For the time specified there restricts the disposition, and thus the disposition is definite, not indefinite. Secondly, when it matters, if it is established by other proofs that the testator had certain persons in mind, others are not included; and if he had present persons in mind, future ones are not included. ff. de legat. 1, l. qui filiabus. For words are restricted to the intent. ff. de testam. tut., l. si quis ita. Or it is not established, and then a distinction must be made. The affection of the testator is either natural, and ordered according to the degree of consanguinity or affinity; and then grandchildren are included. ff. de verb. sign., l. liberorum. For some understand this when an ascendant disposes, but Bartolus says that the same applies in the collateral line. He cites for the case l. Lucius, ff. de haer. instit. For if the testator had been questioned, he would have specified. ff. de pact., l. tale pact., § fin. Therefore, grandchildren are included by a probable interpretation of the words. ff. de verb. sign., l. iuxta; C. de cond. et demonstr., l. 1. Or the affection is accidental and gratuitous, as when one who is not bound by any natural tie testates, but is moved to testate only by merits; and then grandchildren are not included under the name of children; for words should be understood primarily, and not secondarily. Hence, if I bequeath to the children of Titius, who are entirely strangers to me, his grandchildren are not included; for otherwise "son" is defined differently, and "grandson" differently. l. filium definimus, cum seq. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a woman is excused when the occasion for guardianship arises, if she is a minor and has not requested a guardian, nor after she has become of age.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

The mother succeeds to the estate, considering that when the occasion for guardianship first arose, she herself was a minor, and therefore she is excused from the duty of seeking a guardian, as stated in l. 2, C. si aduersus delictum. For since the law excuses her, the excuse ought to be perpetual, and the immunity perpetual; because whenever the law does not provide that the execution is temporary, the privilege must be perpetual, as is clear in Auth. dedi, §. illud. It is also noted in l. 1, C. in quibus causis in integrum restitutio non est necessaria. And this is the opinion of Speculum in the title de in integrum restitutione, §. si quis autem, under the words "sed si ipsa."

It is not an objection that it is noted in l. Titiam, §. vsuras, de legibus 2, where it is said that when age gives rise to a privilege, the privilege ends when the age ends; for there the privilege involved the odious collection of usury and the impairment of another, whereas here it involves the mere and favorable defense of a minor. Moreover, in usuries, which arise from successive time, it is necessary to consider their respective times; but in matters that are considered at a single point in time, we must look to that moment. Furthermore, as stated in l. quid ergo, in principio, de his qui notantur infamia, cum si. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a legitimate and natural son may claim his legitime from his father while the father is still living.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain man from the island, having a legitimate and natural son under his power, this son asks his father to give him his share; the father does not wish to give him anything.

† It is asked what the law intends regarding this matter. I answer that the father is bound by natural law to provide maintenance for his son, as stated in l. 1, §. pe., D. de iure et iudiciis, and in l. si quis a liberis, C. de liberali actione, and in the Authentica licet. For it is a law of nature that support be provided to one’s offspring. And the father is not concerned with anything else for the son, as long as the father is alive. For while the father lives, the son has no right to the legitime portion. D. de liberis agnoscendis, l. si; D. si quid in fraudem patroni, l. non usque adeo; in the Authentica de haereditatibus et falcidia, §. si vero; D. de vulgari et substituta, l. lex Cornelia. Indeed, even if the father wished, he could not give it to him in ownership, because the peculium profectitium always remains in the father’s dominion, even against the father’s will. C. de inofficiosa donatione, l. 2. This fails in the case of dowry. D. familiae erciscundae, l. Pomponius Philadelphus. And therefore this son ought to be silent in this his petition and not trouble his father. However, the pious father ought not and cannot deny maintenance as a supplement for life, because he is bound to provide it. But I ask, what if the son wishes to support himself? Say, as noted in D. de operis liberto, l. sicut, where it is said that he ought to be supported from where he works. If he does not work for his father, he is not to be supported. And note that law, which says something else, namely, that a woman cannot claim maintenance for that year after the dissolution of marriage unless she works in her husband’s house. And note that gloss. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether and when cancellation proves that a debt has been paid.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In a certain book or quire of accounts it appears that a certain person received from a merchant, whose affairs he administered, certain sums of money, and it does not appear that he restored them to the merchant or converted them into the merchant’s goods; nevertheless, it appears that this account book was cancelled in the possession of his heir.

† It is asked whether, from this account book, one can be sued for the said sums, which are shown to have been received, but it does not appear that they were paid. I answer that cancellation is of two kinds: one is formal, i.e., with a cause, and it is made or approved by both parties; and then the cancellation operates according to what the cause inserted in it suggests. The cause is called the form; therefore, it gives existence to the cancellation, just as we say that an oath is formal when it is with a cause, and informal when it is without a cause, as in l. si duo patroni, §. pe., de iur. dot., and fully noted in Inst., de acq., §. Item si quis postulante. And thus it is stated in ff., de pac., l. emptor, §. Lucius; C., de condi. sine causa, l. dissolutae; C., ad exhib., l. fi; ff., de furt., l. qui tabulas; and l. Fullo, §. vlti. The other kind of cancellation is informal, i.e., without a cause, and then either it appears to have been made by the creditor, and the debtor is released, ff., de pac., l. Labeo, for the writing includes the act itself representatively and contentatively, as in C., de do., l. 1. Or, if it appears to have been made by the debtor, it does not benefit him, just as a liberatory writing would not benefit him, for no one can ascribe anything to himself, C., de prob., l. exemplo; C., de conuenien. fisci. debito, l. item calculus. Or it appears to have been made by a third party, and the same applies even if that third party is a notary, according to Martinus, who says that this must be understood if the cancellation appears to have been made after the instrument was written and the rogation completed. Otherwise, it would be presumed that the parties had disagreed from the very beginning in the making of the instrument, as in ff., de edendo, l. si quis ex argentariis, §. si initium tabularum. Or it is doubtful by whom and why it was made, and then if the instrument is found with the debtor, the cancellation is presumed to have been made by the debtor, and such cancellation is not valid; or if it is found with the creditor, then the cancellation is valid if the creditor was a diligent and circumspect man, and the debtor was a domestic person of good life and good conversation; for from the quality of the persons, a certain distinction must be applied at the judge’s discretion, since the presumption is a matter for the judge, ff., de prob., l. si chyrographum, and noted in ff., de pac., l. postquam, and C., de solutione pecuniae, and l. quod debitori, and in doubt, everyone is presumed to be circumspect, unless age contradicts it. Likewise, everyone is presumed to be good. And therefore, in our case, in all doubt, the cancellation must be upheld, unless it is overcome by another presumption to be proven by the plaintiff, as I said. And if it is said, how can a writing vitiated by cancellation ever prove the payment of annuities, c. cum venerabilis, de edi. diui. Adri., l. fin.? I answer that not every cancellation vitiates the writing, but only a solemn and legally made one, C., de testamentis, l. si vnus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Granted a castle together with all and each of the debts, revenues, and fruits to be collected, whether condemnations made before the grant come with it, see following.
casus: CASE. The point of the question is as follows: our lord the Pope granted to the magnanimous men, Lord Francis and Butius of Urfinis, certain castles situated in the county of Sabina, and to the same persons he granted all and singular debts owed to the Roman Church’s camera, and the revenues and fruits to be collected from them, with full and mixed jurisdiction, and other conditions, as you can see in the rescript. The castle of Turnii, before the said grant, had been condemned by the officials of the Church to a certain sum of money. Now the said officials wish to execute the said condemnation. It is asked whether the said execution can be carried out by right by the said officials of the Church, or whether the execution of the said condemnation pertains to the aforementioned Lord Francis.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It must be distinguished whether the offense was committed within the territory of the said castle, or within the castle itself: in that case, the benefit of the condemnation belongs to the said Lord Francis. Or, if it was committed outside his territory, then it matters whether he himself proceeded by reason of origin and condemned the offenders: in such a case, he may enforce such condemnation. C. *Ubi de crimine agi oportet*, l. 1. Or, if the judge of the place where the offense was committed made the condemnation, then the benefit of the condemnation does not belong to Lord Francis. Nevertheless, this judge could not by himself enter the said territory or castle to seize the immovable goods of the said condemned person located therein, nor de facto incorporate them to himself; because he cannot extend his hand into another’s territory, nor into another’s jurisdiction. L. *Cum unus*, § *Is qui*; and see L. *Cunctos populos*, according to Guillaume and others. And generally it is true that when there are several ordinary judges having territorial districts, one has no power over another, or in another’s territory. D. *De solutionibus*, L. *Quaero*; and see D. *De manumissionibus*, *Apud eum oportet*. Each must preserve his own jurisdiction and his own benefits, and no one’s right should be diminished. C. *De officiis praefecti urbis*, L. 1; D. *De his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt*, L. 2. Therefore, Lord Francis ought to derive every benefit, both personal and real, within the territory granted to him, and those which occur with respect to the inhabitants thereof, or of his own territory. D. *Ad municipalia*, L. *De iure*. And thus it applies to past condemnations, as well as to present and future ones; because territory is a universal entity, and to a universal entity belong all things that are part of that same universality. As noted in D. *De fundo instrato*, L. *Lucius*; and C. *Quae res pignori obligari possunt*, L. *Si prope*; and see D. *De verborum significatione*, L. *Princeps*; and C. *De bonis vacantibus*, L. *Si fundo*, lib. 10.
