For those rights were granted to the chamber, and the chamber granted them by whatever right. Hence, it appears that actions were also granted. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus de Ubaldis, Doctor of Laws. And to the truth I have subscribed and signed with the marks of my name.

CASE. The point of the question is as follows: Our Lord the Pope granted to the Magnificent Lords Francis and Buccio Ursini certain castles situated in the County of Sabina, together with all their territories, appurtenances, districts, waters and watercourses, mills, pastures, possessions, districts, revenues and profits, goods and rights of any kind belonging to the said Lords and to the Roman Church, as well as the mere and mixed empire, and all jurisdiction pertaining to the aforementioned Church, and other chapters, as you may see in the rescript. The Castle of Turni, and certain specific persons of the said Castle, before the aforementioned grant, had been condemned by the vicar of the fictitious community of Sabina, for the Roman Church, to a certain sum of money for certain offenses and crimes committed in the territory of the said Castle, or within the Castle itself. It is asked whether the said execution can be carried out by law by the officials of the Church. Or whether the execution of the said condemnations pertains to Lord Francis.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, according to common, customary, and even statutory law, a dowry provided by the father is to be returned to the one who provided it without any intervening stipulation, when children survive; and what if a stipulation does intervene.
1. In the Name of the Lord, Amen.
body: In the Name of Christ. Because the Apostolic See granted to the said Francis whatever pertains to him and to the Roman Church in the said castles, and condemnations belong to the Camera, although they are not strictly mere personal rights in a certain place, nevertheless they are included under this concession of Niccolò; because they are more personal prestations than mere personal rights. It is known that they are for the benefit of jurisdiction, and jurisdiction is real, and is circumscribed and limited to a certain place. C. where, and by whom. L. if. What, therefore, is committed within the granted boundaries, or was divided at the time of the concession, of which no exception was made by the Roman Camera, pertains to the benefit of the said Francis; because fruits pertaining to the feudatory, and not to the proprietor, as is fully known in §. ex contrario, and in part I advise, I, Baldo of Perugia, V.I.D., and to my faith I subscribed and signed with the sign of my name; because it is not said to be perempted by fruits preceding, but by those perceived, although judgment has been rendered, as in L. nepoti, de fundo instr. and this I hold, always saving the truth of the famous authorities. In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† In common law, there are two doubtful cases in that matter. Whether a dowry proceeding from the father returns to the surviving children begotten of that marriage. The case is where no stipulation intervened, and this case is determined by C. 5. 13. l. dos a patre. The second case is where the father stipulated for restitution to himself; and this case is determined by C. rem in presenti, §. videamus. But in customary law, there are two cases: the first, when no stipulation intervened, and then it remains with the husband for the children, as noted in the said l. dos a patre. The second, when a stipulation intervened, and then one must adhere to the tenor of the stipulation, C. comm. vtriusque iud. l. fi. But it must be observed what the law is if the stipulation is disjunctive, because the father stipulates for restitution to himself, or to whom restitution ought to be made. I answer that, because he placed himself first in the order of the stipulation, and the reason of common law prefers him, if he survives at the time of the dissolution of the marriage, an action is sought for him; but if he were not alive, then an action would be sought for the sons and the heirs of the daughter, d. §. videamus. And this applies to the father, who in giving a dowry is not presumed to make a gift; otherwise in the case of the maternal grandfather, l. Gallus, so. ma. tunc n. an action is sought for the woman, as the text notably says there. But because we are in municipal statutes, it must be said that the husband acquires only one-third part of both the dowry paid and that to be saved; the other two parts belong to the stipulator and his heirs, as in the statute beginning "Item statuimus," ver. et Idem dicimus, which is not corrected by the following statutes, as noted in Auth. de nup. §. hinc nos. And thus say I, Bal., Angelucius, and Mascii.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If an emphyteutic lease is received by several persons for themselves and their male children, and upon their death it is to pass to one female, and if the son of one of them dies without male children, his portion does not accrue to the males, but passes to the daughter of the female.
casus: Petrus, Ioannes Angelucii praedicti, Andreas, and Angelucius, sons of Petrus. Clara, daughter of the above-mentioned Ioannes. The facts are as follows: Pucciolus Nicolae, maternal grandfather of Clara, daughter of the late Io. Angelucius, made a division of the goods of the said Clara, his niece, with Andreas and Angelucius, sons of Petrus, brothers and cousins of the said Clara. This was nine years ago or more. And afterwards the mother of the said Clara went to a second marriage, and the said Clara remained in the house together with the above-mentioned Andreas and Angelucius, after the division made with the above-mentioned, and with the above-mentioned Andreas and Angelucius for a period of five years and more. Afterwards the mother of the said Clara married her off with all her goods without an instrument. Now the said Clara and Dominicus, her husband, demand the goods obtained in the share of the said Clara on account of the division which the said Pucciolus made with the above-mentioned Andreas and Angelucius, the latter contradicting and saying that the said Clara ought not to have anything of the said goods. First, because some are leasehold properties of the Church of Saint Saviour, and are confirmed to them by the said Abbot of the said church. Also, because other goods are their own property, and they say that they possessed and now possess them, and the heir ought not to have them. Also, the said Clara and Dominicus, her husband, have continuously dwelt and now dwell in the house obtained for them in share by the said division, and they do not permit the said Dominicus to enter the said house. But the said Clara gives him food outside the house. It is asked what the law is. Also, whether the said Dominicus, husband of the said Clara, can accuse the above-mentioned Andreas and Angelucius, who do not permit him to enter the said house, or not.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Emphyteusis, which Ang. and Pe. received for themselves and their male descendants, and upon the death of both with male sons, and subsequently upon the death of the other with a female, the portion of the deceased goes to that female, and not to the collaterals. The text is the unique and very notable one in column 10, *de duobus fratribus a capitaneo investitis*, c. *duo fratres*. And therefore it could not be reaffirmed to the other to the prejudice of the said daughter. Moreover, the husband may go to dwell with his wife in the house where the wife dwells, and use the wife’s goods with her consent. It does not matter that the sons are in possession together with her, as in D. *de usufructu et habitatione*, l. *ceterum*, § *mulieri*. And those who do not permit it are bound to the wife for damages, D. *de verbis obligatorum*, l. *si stipulatus fuero per te non fieri quominus*, where this is expressly proven. 20. And thus I say, and I, Bal. de Peru., Doctor of Laws, advise, and I have subscribed to the truth and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a penalty attached to a legacy can be claimed when the legacy is renounced, and vice versa, and when.
casus:
CASE. In the name of the Lord, Amen. The point upon which counsel is requested is as follows. A certain Do. Alenucia, daughter of the late Chichini Do. Marini, being in her last illness, made her testament, in which she bequeathed and left to Ioan. Lipucii, her daughter, a nun of the monastery of S. Bart. de Turpa de Tuderto, for the time of her life, every year, from the day of the death of the said testatrix, 15 pounds of good denarii, with this condition, namely, that if the hereinafter-named heirs, or any of them, should neglect to pay the said legacy, that he or they who should neglect, or has neglected, to pay the said legacy, shall fall, or has fallen, from the said inheritance, and the said Do. Io. shall succeed for the time of her life, and she, Do. Io., by the very right of the legacy, was instituted heir, and she cannot demand or have more of the goods. In all her other movable and immovable goods, rights, and actions, present and future, she instituted, made, and left as universal heirs in equal portions and parts, the ladies Iacobutia, Andreutia, Contessa, Francisca, and Tecla, daughters of the said testatrix, and Ser Gorum Cicholi, her husband. After this, the said Do. Alenucia died, the said testament made by her not being changed, the said ladies Iacob., Andreutia, Contessa, Francis., and Tecla, her daughters, and the said Ser Goro, her husband, surviving and outliving her, and the said Do. Iacoba, her daughter, the aforementioned legatee, surviving. And after this, the said Do. Iacobutia, and Andreutia, and the said Ser Goro, for the parts falling to them by the said testament, entered into and accepted the inheritance of the said Do. Alenucia. And the said Contessa, and Franc., and Tecla renounced the said inheritance for the parts falling to them. And after this, for the part of the said Do. Ioanna, nun of the said monastery, the aforementioned legatee, it was and is acted before the vicar of the lord bishop of Tuderto, and now it is being acted for the said legacy of 15 pounds made to her by the said testatrix in the said testament, against Angelus, son of the late and heir of the said Ser Goro, and against the said Iaco. and Andreu. And it was and is asserted on the part of the said Do. Io., the aforementioned legatee, that the said Ange. and the other above-named heirs instituted in the said testament ceased and neglected, and cease and refuse, to pay the said legacy of 15 pounds to the said Do. Io. And on the part of the said Angelus it is opposed and answered that, since the heirs instituted in the said testament neglected and ceased to pay the said legacy to the said Do. Io., the condition appended in the said testament occurred. For on account of the aforementioned negligence, the heirs instituted in the said testament have fallen, and are considered by law to have fallen from the said inheritance, and that the said Do. Ioanna succeeded and succeeds in the said inheritance, having regard to the words and the form of the said testament. And thus the said Angelus asks that it be pronounced and declared by the said lord vicar of the episcopal court that the said Ange., son of the late and heir of the said Ser Goro, and also the other heirs instituted in the said testament, have fallen from the said inheritance, and that the said Do. Io., the aforementioned legatee, has succeeded and succeeds in the said inheritance, especially because, as is alleged, the said instituted heirs neglected and refused, and also refuse, to pay the said legacy to the said Do. Io., the legatee in the said testament.

Now it is asked whether the said heirs instituted in the said testament, and whether the said Angelus, son of the late and heir of the said Ser Goro, instituted in the same testament, have fallen from the said inheritance of Do. Alenucia, and whether the said Do. Io. has succeeded and succeeds in the said inheritance, and whether the said Ange., son of the late and heir of the said Ser Goro, and the other heirs instituted in the said testament, can ask that it be pronounced and declared by the said lord vicar of the episcopal court that the said Angelus and the other heirs instituted in the said testament have fallen from the said inheritance, and that the said Do. Io., the legatee, has succeeded and succeeds in the said inheritance, on the ground that they neglected to pay the said legacy to the said Do. Io., by the condition appended in the said testament, and whether the said Angelus, son of the late and heir of the said Ser Goro, and the other heirs instituted in the said testament, who entered into the inheritance of the said Alenucia for the parts falling to them, can and ought to be compelled to pay the said legacy to the said Do. Io., presupposing and taking as constant that the said Do. Ioanna, the legatee, wishes the said legacy to be paid to her, and does not wish to succeed in the said inheritance of the said Do. Alenucia. Having seen the aforementioned point and the said testament, counsel is requested in the name of Christ.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A penalty is sometimes attached for the purpose of transferring the delict, so that it is first transferred to the second, and then, once the legacy has been transferred, only the transferred legacy can be claimed, and not the first. D. ad l. Falcidiam, l. 1, § Item si ita; and l. 1, de poenis legatorum; and l. Si poena, quando dies legati cedat. Sometimes a penalty is attached for the purpose of aggravation; and then it is absurd that the penalty should benefit the person who has incurred it. Hence, if the creditor does not wish, he is not bound to remit the principal and to claim the penalty. D. Qui fidem, in the gloss, de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem; l. Commissoria. And the same applies to a private heir. D. de legatis 1, l. Si servus plurium, § 1. Therefore, I believe that the right to claim the said legacy is available to the aforementioned nun; because the penalty was not imposed with consideration of both, but solely due to fault, in order to aggravate the contumacy. C. de fideicommissis, l. Finis; and Auth. Hoc amplius. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Laws. And in faith thereof, I have subscribed and signed with the marks of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a stepfather can be a tutor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† First of all, it must be considered whether a stepfather can be the guardian of his stepson or stepdaughter. On this point there are three opinions. The first is that he can, as in D. de adoptionibus, l. nonnunquam, and l. si, C. de contrahenda iudiciaria tutela. The second is that he can be a testamentary guardian, but not an appointed one, as noted in Auth. de nuptiis, § eiusdem quoque, and c. C. ubi pupillus educari debet, l. 1, and Azo in Summa, ius exemplum in testamentario: because a father left his friend as guardian, who, after the testator’s death, married the latter’s former wife. The third opinion is that he can be appointed guardian before marriage, but not after. For since the mother is excluded due to suspicion regarding her husband, all the more so is the husband himself excluded, because “that for which each thing is, is so to a greater degree,” as in Auth. multo magis, joined with l. lex quae tutores, C. de administratione tutorum. Guillaume de Cuyac in the said l. nonnunquam, and Cynus there in his lecture, state without distinction that he can be guardian, especially if appointed through an inquiry, because an inquiry excludes all suspicion, as in D. de confirmatione tutorum, l. naturali, § 1, and l. utilitatem. And thus I hold, that the said Francis could be appointed guardian of the said pupil, and is a true guardian. But this is opposed by the following argument: it is a matter of law that a female guardian could not be appointed for a female pupil due to second marriages, as in Auth. de nuptiis, § si autem tutelam, and in Auth. sacramentum, C. quando mulier tutelae officio fungi potest. Therefore, she cannot have an assistant, since the principal does not hold; therefore, neither does the accessory office. For the office of an assistant is not principal, but accessory, as in C. quo et quando iudex, l. si praeses quasi desertam. Moreover, the judge appointed the mother and the stepfather together, not separately; therefore, if one cannot serve, neither can the other, as in D. de arbitris, l. Pedius, § unde Iulianus. But I respond that Francis was appointed guardian, and thus principally, as in D. de administratione tutorum, l. decreto, § si duobus, and l. consilio, § si, de curia sua. And although the mother is prohibited, all matters can be carried out without her, as in D. de admissione tutorum, l. quid decedens, § Papinianus, and D. quod falso tutor autem, l. 1, § sed Pomponius. Another objection is raised: for the aforementioned mother had administered the guardianship and was bound to render an account, and the goods of the second husband were bound for the same, as in C. quando mulier tutelae officio fungi potest, l. 2, and C. in quibus causis pignus tacite contrahitur, l. si mater. Therefore, the stepfather is excluded from guardianship due to the obligation of the goods, as Ancharanus in Auth. minoris debitor. To this I respond that it is not established whether the mother is a debtor in any respect, nor whether in a small or large amount, nor whether she herself, as principal, is solvent or not. And therefore, a hypothecary claim cannot extend to an outsider. This is supported by what the doctors note in l. 1, D. si certum petatur, and in the said Auth. minoris in dubio; therefore, Francis is not excluded from guardianship, but rather ought to be admitted to it. And thus I hold, although the mother cannot be a female guardian. Another objection is raised: because they are legitimate [guardians]. I respond that they are excused, as in D. de testamentariis tutoribus, l. si quis sub conditione. And therefore, there is room for an appointed guardian, and thus the said Francis is a guardian according to these writings. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Laws. And to the faith of this I have subscribed and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Those staying in the territory of one city for a year and more with wife and children, and paying the angariae of that city, are not said to have established a domicile, to the effect that they may be punished for a delict committed elsewhere within that time; but what if, with the premeditated intent of committing a delict, they departed from one territory and committed such a delict in another: can they be investigated and punished by the judge where the plan was formed? And at no. 3, 4, and 7.
2. What is required for someone to be said to have established a domicile.
6. What acts are those from which the intention of transferring domicile is gathered.
4. Given a statute providing that the podestà can investigate ex officio, or proceed by inquisition against subjects, can he proceed against the domiciliaries mentioned above? On all these matters, add the consilium of Baldus below, cons. 313.
casus: CASE. The facts are as follows: A certain man from Perugia committed a certain homicide against another man from Perugia in the territory of Assisi. On account of this matter, he was condemned by the official of the commune of Assisi in person. Finally, by the ordinances of the commune of Assisi, he was absolved from the said personal condemnation, on this condition, that the said murderer must pay to the commune of Assisi 50 gold florins; and he has already paid them. It is now asked whether he ought, or can, be condemned by the officials of the commune of Perugia, since, as is said, he was condemned in Assisi. And what is the law?
body: The question upon which counsel is sought is posited to be as follows: Four men, namely Petrus, Martinus, Titius, and Sempronius, Pisan by origin, on account of certain crimes committed and perpetrated by them, were personally banished from the said city of Pisa; and some time after the aforesaid banishments, the said Petrus came to the territory of the city of Genoa and remained there for a year and more, always eating and drinking in two taverns, and kept two natural sons within the said boundary, and went and returned wherever he pleased at his own will, yet for the greater part of the time he stayed habitually in the said territory; and likewise the said Martinus stayed in the said territory for a year and more with his wife, and rented a house for his household, and paid the angariae of the commune of Genoa. Subsequently, the said four departed from the territory of the commune of Genoa and went to the territory of the city of Pisa, and there killed certain banished persons and inhabitants. The judge of the city of Genoa caused the said four to be captured, holds them in his custody, and wishes to punish them for the said homicides.

† First, it is asked whether he can do so, and if he can, whether he can proceed against them by way of inquisition. And, as appears from the aforesaid, two questions are asked. First and principally, it is asked whether the magistrate of Genoa can proceed against the aforesaid four for homicides committed in the territory of the city of Pisa.

† On which question, it is principally to be seen and considered whether these four, by those things which are assumed in fact in the said statement of the case—namely that they are Pisan by origin—are proved to be incolae and are understood to have a domicile in the city of Genoa, or not. For if they were incolae and had a domicile there, it would not be doubtful that proceedings could be instituted and punishment inflicted by the Genoese jurisdiction concerning the said homicides, as is the text and the gloss in l. 1, ubi de crimi. agi oportet, and l. relegatorum, §. interdicere, de interdic. et relega., with similar laws. If, however, they are not incolae, it would be clear that he cannot proceed, since it does not pertain to his jurisdiction, not even by reason of the person of the delinquent, as in l. fin. de iuris. omn. iudi. and l. 3, ff. de offi. praesi., with similar laws. And against the aforesaid Martinus and Titius two points are posited in the statement of the case by which incolatus and domicile seem to be proved: first, because in the territory of Genoa they resided with their wives and household for a year and more, and were residing there at the time the said crimes were committed; secondly, because they paid the angariae of the commune of Genoa. Likewise, it seems proved from continuous living, which almost alone seems to suffice, even if they did not have a domicile there, as is proved in l. 2, §. infan., C. ubi senatores, vel clarissimi, where the text speaks alternatively. And on the aforesaid point, having seen the allegations sent to me, copiously and elegantly drawn up on either side, and having diligently inspected and considered the other points to be examined on either part, having invoked the names and suffrages of our Lord Jesus Christ and of His most holy and glorious Virgin Mother, the counsel of me, Petrus son of dominus Albisi of Pisa, doctor of laws, is such: that proceedings cannot be instituted by the said magistrate concerning the said homicides, since it appears that they are Pisans and it does not appear that they have a domicile in Genoa.

† For in the establishment of a domicile, intention and fact are required, as in l. domicilium, ff. ad municipa.; and residence is required to intervene with the intention that one be and remain there permanently, as in l. ciues, and the law and gloss there, C. de incolis, bk. 10. Such residence does not appear to have intervened here, nor is it presumed prior to the course of ten years, as is noted in the same title, l. 2, especially in residence outside the place of origin, arg. l. fi., C. de praescri. long. temporis. And this opinion is held by Roffredus in the title qualiter declinetur iudicium. Nor does c. ubi senatores, vel claris., cited above, stand in the way of this: because it ought to be understood of a continuous living of ten years, as noted there by Cynus, and well so, whatever Innocentius may say in c. ex parte, Extra, de foro comp., or of a continuous living where it is permanently established there. For this makes the point that residence includes continuous living, as in l. 1, §. habitare, de his qui deie. uel effu., and yet residence alone does not prove domicile, as in l. libertus, §. sola, ad munic. and de leg. 2, and l. 3, C. de inco. Nor does the text in the said §. habitare, in fine, oppose this, because there domicile is used for residence and house. I conclude therefore, as I have said, that proceedings can in no way be instituted by the said magistrate on the basis of the aforesaid. From which the second doubt appears resolved, namely, that much less can proceedings be taken by way of inquisition under the form of the statute of Genoa. Nor does it stand in the way if it were said that proceedings could be taken as against vagabonds and vagrants; this is not true, because vagabonds are not vagabonds in the manner of those wandering and roaming about the world lacking their own residence, as in l. generaliter, C. de sac. sanc. ecc., at the words denegantes etc., and as noted in l. 4, §. praetor, de dam. infect., and by the doctors there; and these men are not such. Likewise, it does not stand in the way that they paid the angariae of the commune of Genoa, because such payment does not prove incolatus, whether it was made under compulsion or voluntarily, as in l. fina., de his spon. num. su. fre., especially if the said payment is made by mere residents lacking a domicile. And this I consider to be true in law, without prejudice to a better judgment, explaining briefly, because truth does not lack anything through the power of words. The point of the question and of the allegations which I received and which I issue with the present consilium sealed with my own ring. Petrus son of dominus Albisi of Pisa, doctor of laws, given on the 1st day of August. Consilium on a similar case: Whether he can punish them, and whether by way of inquisition, the names of Christ and of His Most Holy Glorious Virgin Mother having been invoked. To bring forth the truth from the above-written statement of the case: because from the above-stated case it is sufficiently gathered that the above-written Sempronius, Titius, Seius, and Johannes, with the purpose and intention of committing the said homicides in the territory of Pisa, set out on their journey from the territory of Genoa; and let us suppose without prejudice that deliberately and premeditatedly, having held discussions together in the territory of Genoa concerning the perpetration of the said crimes, they departed from the said territory to perpetrate the said crimes, which crimes, as is supposed, they perpetrated.

† Now we ask whether the aforesaid Sempronius, Titius, Seius, and Johannes may be said to have committed an offense in the territory of Genoa; and in law it seems that they did, because the purpose of committing a crime and homicide, when brought to an external act, completes the crime, as in ff. ad leg. Cornel. de sicar. l. 1, §. diuus, and in the same chapter, l. is qui cum telo; and in homicide, the intention brought to an external act is weighed prior to the fact of the subsequent homicide, as is contained in the said laws, l. uel certe, and l. diuus Adrian., where it is said that in the lex Cornelia the will is regarded, not the outcome. Since, therefore, with deliberate purpose of committing the said homicides, they brought their purpose into an external act in the territory of Genoa, namely by undertaking the journey and perhaps taking up arms, they will therefore be said to have committed an offense in the territory of Genoa, most especially because the effect of any matter ought to be attributed to the part that preponderates, arg. in l. quaeritur hermofroditus, ff. de statu hominum, for which l. adeo, §. cum quis, ff. de acquiren. re. domin. makes. Likewise, this is supported because the mere undertaking of a journey to commit a crime constitutes a crime, C. de serui. fugit. l. si fugitivi. Likewise, this is supported because it is lawful to argue from time to place, as in l. vinum, ff. si cert. peta., and l. ultima, de usu, et ha. But it is established that when an ordination or arrangement is disposed toward one effect, the subsequent effect is attributed to the arrangement in respect of time, but the arrangement is not attributed to the subsequent effect, as in l. qui prior and l. qui balneum, ff. qui potior. in pign. hab., and l. si filius, ff. de verbor. obliga.; therefore also with respect to place, since the plot and deliberation, which is presupposed without prejudice to the aforesaid, took its beginning and existence in the territory of Genoa, the effect of the subsequent homicides arising from the plot and deliberation ought to be attributed to the place of the prior deliberation and plot. Likewise, this is supported because if I ran to kill a man and was unable to, and afterwards out of that very deliberation I kill him, I am deemed to have killed him at once at the time of the first running up, as the text above is in l. quod ait lex, ff. de adul. Likewise, the text seems to support this, because crimes are punished where they are committed or begun, C. ubi de crimine agi oportet, l. 1, where the text is literal. But these crimes of homicide were begun in the territory of Genoa, where the said homicides were deliberated and the journey undertaken to perpetrate the said homicides, assuming this without prejudice; therefore they could be punished in the territory of Genoa. Likewise, this is supported because, assuming without prejudice that the aforesaid, in treating together concerning the homicide to be perpetrated, are seen to communicate with or mandate one another that the homicide be committed, and thus to be bound by mandate, and thus they are held retroactively, as in regula ratihabitio, Extra, de re. iu., bk. 6, l. fi., C. ad Mace., l. bonorum, ff. rem ra. ha. From which it will evidently be concluded that since the aforesaid homicides are said from the premises to have committed an offense in the territory, the podestà of Genoa or the magistrate will be able to punish them and inquire against them, since by municipal law it is lawful for him to inquire against delinquents in a territory not of his jurisdiction, and since the aforesaid committed an offense, therefore an inquiry will deservedly be made against them. Consilium on a similar case. But having invoked the names of Christ and of His Glorious and Most Blessed Virgin Mother Mary,

† notwithstanding the aforesaid, I believe the contrary in law: namely, that the aforesaid, as offenders in the territory of Genoa, are not on this account to be punished by the magistrate in the territory of Genoa. Which I prove: because whenever an arrangement is made between persons or a conjunction is disposed by some in one place, and the effect of the arrangement or disposition is directed to another place, as regards obtaining a forum and the capacity to sue or be sued from the said arrangement, we look to the place to which the arrangement or disposition was directed, but as regards the forum we do not look to the place in which the arrangement or contract was made, as in C. de act. et ob. l. contraxisse, and de bo. auth. iud. pos. l. 3, and C. ubi conue. qui certo loco, l. 1. From which it is concluded that, assuming the said four agreed and arranged among themselves in the territory of Genoa concerning the commission of the said homicides, they did not acquire a forum by reason of the crimes committed in the place where they agreed and arranged, but rather in the place to which they directed their arrangement and perpetrated the crimes; and this is supported because, for the purpose of acquiring a forum, contracts and delicts are equated, as in ff. de iud. l. omnem. Likewise, to bring forth the truth in the premises, it must be considered that the delict or homicide is as it were the principal, and the slayers are deemed principals, whereas counsel, mandate, and assistance toward the delict are deemed accessories, and those who give counsel, mandate, and provide aid are said to be accessorily bound, as in l. non solum, in prin., ff. de iniur., l. non eo minus, C. de accu. Which being premised, let us look at the rule: that whenever an act establishing an accessory obligation and an act establishing a principal obligation concur in the same person or persons, the act accessorily bound is not regarded but is concealed, so that one is not sued upon it, and the act of the principal obligation alone remains, and an action is brought upon that valid one, as in ff. de solu. l. generaliter, and de duo. reis, l. si reus, and de fideiussor. l. vrannius. From which it is concluded that, although the aforesaid four agreed and settled among themselves in the territory of Genoa concerning the said homicides to be committed in the territory of Pisa, because the said slayers are as it were the principal in relation to those agreements and arrangements, and they are found to have performed acts accessory to the delicts and principal acts, namely the crimes themselves, and thus the principal and accessory acts of obligation concur in the persons of the very same men, therefore the principal acts themselves must be looked to, namely the crimes and delicts, not the accessories, namely the agreements and arrangements. Likewise, this is supported because he who persuades, he who arranges, he who mandates a crime to be committed begins to be held then when the crime is committed, and not before, as in ff. de fur. in l. quae seruo, at the words plus Pompei scribit, where the text says that he who persuades someone to harbor a runaway slave, although in the meantime he is not held for theft, nevertheless begins to be held then when he who persuaded the runaway began to be a thief; for which makes ff. de ver. sig. l. cedere in factum. Likewise by this: because whenever from some preliminary acts the shadow of death of a body follows, one is not to be punished for the preliminary acts, but for the death, as in l. illud, in fine, and l. si ex plagiis, ff. ad l. Aqui.; whence it is concluded that although the agreements and arrangements of the aforesaid had been the cause from which the homicides in the territory of Pisa followed, the death and the place where the crimes were committed must be regarded. Likewise for this: because according to the gloss, in public matters we ought not to look to the beginning, as in l. pe., ff. si ex no. cau. agatur, joined with l. 1, de poenis; by which many of the contrary arguments cease to apply. Likewise, this is supported because whenever an arrangement or disposition is made at one time toward an effect capable in itself, and produces an obligation deferred to another time, we look to the effect, not to the preliminary arrangement or agreement, so that action is brought upon that effect, not upon the preliminary arrangement or agreement, as in ff. de ver. obli. l. quidam cum filium, and l. si vero non remunerandi, §. si filiofa., ff. man., where Accursius notes this. It is otherwise if the disposition concerned an act that was not capable in itself of producing an action, as is noted in the said §. si filio; and by this the argument from l. qui potior and l. qui balneum is removed. From which it is concluded that, since these arrangements and agreements of the aforesaid made in the territory of Genoa concerned homicides perpetrated in the territory of Pisa, which homicides were in themselves capable of producing an obligation, the arrangements ought not to be looked to, but the homicides; from which the certain truth premised is sufficiently clear, and by this the contrary arguments, which from the premises would appear removed, do not stand in the way. Nor does l. 1, C. ubi de cri. agi opor., which says that proceedings can be instituted where crimes were committed or begun, oppose this; the gloss there understands 'begun' with respect to judicial prosecution, not with respect to the purpose of committing the offense, as the argument holds. From which it is concluded that by reason of the crime committed and of the forum acquired from the crime, they cannot be sued in the territory of Genoa. But now let us ask whether by reason of domicile a forum is so acquired that one can be punished for crimes perpetrated elsewhere; but in law I say that it is, because delinquents can be sued where they maintain their hearth, or where they possess the greater part of their goods and continuously reside, as is gathered from C. ubi Senato. vel clariss. l. 2, where the text is clear that one has a domicile where one has the greater part of one's fortunes and continuously resides, as is gathered in ff. ad Mace. l. assumptio, §. viris prudentibus; although indeed through the gloss on C. ubi de crim. agi oportet, l. 1, what is noted in auth. qua in prouincia also supports this.

† But now let us see whether the aforesaid four, as posited above in the statement of the case, can be said to have a domicile in the territory of Genoa. For which it must be observed that domicile is established in fact and reality, by act and by intention, as in ff. ad Maced. l. domicilium; and it is not established by fact alone without intention, nor without fact, as is noted in the said l. domicilium. However, the intention of transferring a domicile cannot be truly proved against one who denies it; but the intention of the denier is proved from presumptions, as in l. fulcinius, §. quid sit latitare, ff. qui. ex ca. in po. ea., and l. pro herede, §. Papin., and l. gerit, ff. de acqui. haer.

† But what are those facts from which the intention of transferring a domicile is gathered? I answer that as soon as someone departs from one place with his belongings and transfers himself to another place, he is presumed to have the intention of transferring his domicile, as noted by Innocentius in Extra, de renun. c. tertio. And this because every man is presumed diligent, as in l. liberi and l. omnimodo, C. de inoff. testamen., and it belongs to diligent men to attend to their property, and much more so to their property and household. Likewise, the intention of transferring domicile is presumed if someone cohabits for ten years in one place, even if he had not transferred his belongings; thus l. 2, C. de incolis can speak. Since therefore Johannes, concerning whom it is presupposed above, never resided, nor transferred his property or household, it appears well and evidently that he did not have a domicile in the territory of Genoa. Likewise, it seems that it must be said that a stay of a year or two alone, without the transfer of property or household intervening, does not cause the intention of transferring domicile to be presumed, unless a course of ten years has intervened, as in the said l. 2. Concerning the others, however, namely Titius and Seius, who transferred themselves with their property and household, it does not seem doubtful: namely, that they are to be deemed domiciliaries in the territory of Genoa, according to what is noted by Innocentius; see c. 3, Extra, de renun.

† But now we have to ask whether the podestà or magistrate will be able to proceed against these domiciliaries by inquisition. And it is established that under the ius commune proceedings cannot be taken by inquisition, because no one ought to be punished without an accuser, as in l. rescriptum, §. si quis accusatorem non habens, ff. de mu. et ho.; and Christ said, 'Woman, where are they who accuse you?' Yet that case is excepted which is noted in l. 2, §. qui Lenocinium, ff. de adul.

† But presupposing, as is the case in almost all the cities of Lombardy, that it is enacted by statute in the city of Genoa that against subjects the podestà or magistrate can inquire ex officio or proceed by inquisition, it is asked whether he can inquire against the said domiciliaries, namely Seius, for the said crimes: because whenever it is simply enacted and the power of inquiring ex officio concerning crimes is granted to the podestà, it must be understood of crimes that are committed in the territory of those making the statute, arg. l. rationis, §. is qui, ff. de bo. au. iu. possi.; and most especially because the said power is granted by municipal law, which is contrary to the ius commune and must be strictly interpreted, so that it may impair the ius commune as little as possible, as in ff. de mu. et hono. l. ut gradatim, §. sed si lege, and de noxa, l. 1. And so it seems to me, Philippus de Casalis of Reggio, doctor of laws, actively lecturing and actually appointed to the ordinary chair of the Codex in the general study of Pavia, counselor of the Apostolic Camera and also of the Illustrious and Magnificent Lord, the Count of Virtues, that one ought in law and reverence to give counsel, saving always the better judgment and counsel of any other wise man. CASE. IN the Name of the Lord, amen. The fact upon which counsel is sought is such: namely, an inquisition was drawn up by the lord podestà of the city of Genoa against and facing Petrus Vandi of Poggiobonizio in that and upon that, that the said Petrus, in an evil manner, knowingly, by design, deliberately, and premeditatedly, with the intention and purpose of committing and perpetrating the below-written crime, with a sword which he held drawn in his hands, made an assault and attacked against the person of Corradus Clesius of Cologne from Flanders, servant of Franciscus Scarapa of Genoa; in which assault he struck and wounded the said Corradus with the said sword in the throat on the right side with a great blow and wound, with effusion of blood. From which blows and wound the said Corradus died immediately, and is dead; and these things were committed and perpetrated in the city of Genoa, at the place and time contained in the said inquisition. Which Petrus, answering under oath to the said inquisition, solemnly stated and freely confessed to be and to have been true all and singular the matters contained in the said inquisition, at the place and time contained in the inquisition. To which Petrus a certain term was given and assigned to present his defenses, within which his proctor produced certain exceptions and certain articles for his defense, upon which articles very many witnesses were examined. Now, having seen the said inquisition, and the answer made by the said Petrus, the said exceptions, and the depositions of the witnesses examined, both for the prosecution and for the defense; and having seen all the examinations of the witnesses, who were very many received because of certain doubts arising in the court of the lord podestà, as appears from the acts; having seen the chapters of the city of Genoa speaking of this matter, all of which are presently transmitted: It is asked, with what penalty ought the said Petrus to be punished for the said homicide, and what are the duties of the lord podestà in the aforesaid.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. It is permitted to repel force with force, with the moderation of blameless defense.
2. What is meant by defense.
3. Whether one who has been assaulted is bound to flee.
4. If flight threatens imminent death, such that by fleeing one can easily be wounded and boldly killed, one may turn back. If someone wounded has stood for so long as to be dead, but immediately upon reviving wounds the one who wounded him, whether it is said that he acted after an interval.
5. How proof is made by witnesses that someone made a lawful defense.
body: In the name of Jesus Christ, Son of God. Having examined the records and carefully deliberated, before proceeding to resolve the question, it must be premised for the foundation of the truth.

† That it is lawful to repel force, however, with moderation, so that the repulsion is rather the protection of one’s own body than vengeance. D. de iure et iure, l. ut vim; ad legem Aquiliam, l. scientiam, §. quae cum alter; C. unde vi, l. 1; X. de homicidio, c. significasti, ver. quia tamen; and this is natural; and l. manifestum. For hands are weapons naturally generated for the protection of the human body; this is also evident from the actions of children, in whom malice is not yet formed, nor the impulse of the mind, yet they defend themselves as far as they can, just as irrational animals living by nature alone do. The same quality is seen in natural weapons, such as beaks, or claws, or kicks, or teeth. For nature never gives life without, as it were, giving a natural guardian, and certain defensive arms for one’s own safety; this is clear from natural use, which is the mistress and mother of life. Hence the Apostle, 1 Cor. 11, says, “Nature itself teaches us”; and Aristotle, in the first book of the Minor Works of the Philosophers, confesses that he knows the truth because he boasts of having learned it from nature. The same thing is said by Domitius Ulpianus, D. de verbis oblig., l. ubi autem non apparet, §. illud.

Secondly, it must be premised what is meant by the term "defense," and if I consider this word in its substance, it is the same as protection; but if I consider it in its quality, it ought to consist with modes and times. The moderation, however, consists in three things. First, that it not be done with a notable excess of quantity, if one can otherwise defend oneself. For one must avoid striking with an empty hand differently than with a sword. When it is lawful to use a sword, one repels, and not only the blow, but the assault, in which the fear for one's safety consists. D. ad l. Aquil. l. si explegiis, §. tabernarius; and l. quaeramus, §. si navis alteram. He who defends himself competently is said rather to suffer than to act, because he does not act voluntarily. Hence the crime is attributed to the aggressor. C. ad l. Iul. de vi, l. quam multa facinora. Secondly, that the defense be joined, or as it were joined, to the offense inflicted by the adversary, or to the fear of further injury being inflicted; for from a distance it is not called defense of the person, but vengeance. As noted in the said l. 1, and in the said §. tabernarius, and the said C. significasti. Thirdly, that the cause of defense be just by nature. As noted, C. de his qui ad ecclesiam confugiunt, l. si servus. And it is presumed just from the intent, if the cause of defense be just by nature. Such are understood to be the minds of men, as is the leader of minds in a cause without nature. D. pro socio, l. merito.

Thirdly, it must be premised whether the one insulted is bound to flee, for the gloss in c. 1, de homicidiis, in the Clementines, says that if he can flee or otherwise defend himself without killing, it is not permitted to kill. Cynus on this in the said l. 1 distinguishes; but the Question in the said l. 1, C. unde vi, says the contrary, that he is not bound to flee, because he is not bound to suffer a personal injury, just as he is not bound to suffer a real injury, although the real injury is lesser. For the greatest of real injuries is almost the least of personal injuries. ff. de poenis, l. in seruorum, §. si. According to Bartolus, the text of the law says that he who could not otherwise defend himself, and I understand "otherwise defend himself" as meaning from injury. I prove this thus for the defense of things: although one may kill a man if he cannot otherwise defend his things; therefore, if I cannot otherwise defend myself from flight, it is lawful to kill the one who flees, so that I may not suffer this violence. Nor does it matter whether I could have fled without shame or not; because flight is baseness and a vice of the mind, and ordered charity loves itself first in the sole of the foot, before the adversary in the vertex of the head. But what Scripture says, "flee from persecutors," is to be understood as exemplary and meritorious flight, for which it is fitting for the perfect on the way to heaven; but we are on the way of the forum. I say that if flight is suspect, because the adversary is behind, one is not bound to flee; but if it is not suspect, but is chosen by grave and sensible men, who by ceasing give place to a void and harmless situation, then one ought to flee and hide oneself, and flee rumors, and this is of natural prudence. For a bird by flying escapes to the hiding places it seeks, and thus in man is a more excellent nature, so that greater providence ought not to oppose the madman. It is madness if you can avoid the madman and will not. It is justice to defend oneself. It is temperance to do this with moderation. It is fortitude not to fear, but to resist blamelessly. Prudence is to avoid the greater evil between two evils. c. veni. I ask, can one by fleeing save both thing and person? If, led by shame, he rather enters a duel, will he be excused because he spared his own shame? Far be it from a vulgar man, who daily turns his back when he fears, just as this same one did after the blow. But if he were a great baron or a valiant knight, he would be excused. Argument: if someone omitted, causa testis, l. Iulianus. Because it is divinely more eligible to die than to be despised, hence the Apostle: "it is more expedient to die, than that anyone should empty my glory." Such a one, therefore, and of such standing, will be excused at least from the penalty of death and mutilation of a member. Argument: C. de adulteriis, l. Graecus; and ff. de adulteriis, l. si adulterium cum incestu, §. Imperatores, vers. et magis; and in c. olim casum, in fine, de restitutione spoliatorum, which text is notable for this.

Fourthly, it must be premised that where flight threatens imminent death, such that by fleeing one can easily be wounded or killed, the person may boldly repel the attacker without regard to the distinction of reputation, even if the attacker were the devil or the devil himself, because defense is not denied to him, especially natural defense, as Innocentius states. If therefore he is constrained, he may say, “Do you not know how evil despair is?” and may kill the pursuer without penalty, according to the second book of the Kings, chapter 2, and this is clear in the laws and canons cited at the beginning. For where flight is not safe, one is not bound to choose flight nor to embrace danger to oneself, but ought to choose the safer course and thus preserve oneself, as stated in the aforementioned § Qui aliter and in the aforementioned Chapter 1, De homicidio, in the Clementines, and as noted in the aforementioned Law 1, Code, Unde vi.

Fifth, consider the case where I struck Titius on the head, such that he fell to the ground and remained there, dazed and stunned, for an hour; finally, having come to himself, he immediately struck me. Whether this is said to have been done after an interval, and it seems so due to the interposition of the hour. The truth is that if he feared being struck again, it is said to have been done immediately, and in his own defense; otherwise, if he did not fear being struck again. For then he is said to be starting a new brawl. The effect of the difference is great: for in the first case, I, who struck him again, am punished, even though I acted in self-defense; because I illicitly initiated the conflict, and the entire fault is attributed to me, as the first mover and instigator. In the second case, by no means, since I am not the author of the new brawl, and I am not then said to have acted out of vengeance, and the adversary is then not seen to have defended himself lawfully. I therefore say that the stupor induced by the blow, or by the concussion of the brain, is not said to generate an interval, unless the initiator completely diverts himself from the act and departs from the place. Authority: Codex, De testibus, l. Cum antiquitas. From these, having seen the acts, the solution to the question appears, and do not be troubled by these taxations: because I had made a distinction of persons, and afterwards it was said in law that nothing differs.

† Concluding, therefore, I say that one must proceed to examine the statements of the witnesses, whether they conclusively prove a lawful defense, and a defense simpliciter, which was not accompanied by an offensive act. Regarding this, it appears to be proven simpliciter and conclusively: first, the living constriction of Peter, and this by John, who says finally, when he saw that he could not do more. The text is in the aforementioned §. quæ cum aliter, and the aforementioned c. 1. de homicidio, in the Clementines. Second, because of the living and audacious assault of Conrad. For since Peter was drawing himself back, Conrad did not cease. Likewise, all the doctors determine after him that when the offender flees, the offended party ought not to go after him. And this is noted by Goffredus in the Summa de homicidio. Third, because of the simultaneous striking; for Peter ought not to have waited longer than he did. Indeed, he was foolish, for he ought not to have waited to be struck. As is noted in l. 1. C. unde vi, and de homicidio, ca. significasti. Fourth, because of the discretion of the said Peter; for he fled, but he did so wisely, finally by drawing himself back and wisely; for he did not turn his back. For turning one’s back is to expose oneself to death, since they were separated by a small space. Thus, from the blow of a sword, he could easily die, or be more grievously injured than he avoided by the blow of a stone; therefore, he avoided his own danger and that of his adversary as much as he could; but when he could not do more, he struck the striking aggressor; which seems to have been lawful. Fifth, because of the presumption of law, which our ancestors said, that one who is assaulted and flees is presumed to act in defense. d. §. tabernarius, and §. cum arietes. Sixth, because of the clear vision of the witnesses, who say that they saw that it was for defense, as Francis and Peter. For as Bartolus says in his consilia, it is proven by sight that it was defensive. Seventh, because of the moderation of the directive rule, let him consider, namely, the very one who condemns, whether he himself would have done that, if the case had happened to him. As in the proemium of the Decretals. Eighth, because of the concurrent promise of divine law; for being placed in the desperation of flight, it is permitted to kill oneself in defense, 2 Kings 2. Ninth, because of the open determination of civil and praetorian law. For whether we look to rigor, which pertains to civil law, or to mere equity, one may defend oneself for two reasons: first, for oneself, lest one suffer injury; second, for the good of another, lest one sin against oneself. As is clear in the common laws. Tenth, that Peter does not say that he is worthy of death because of a non-dolous departure, being temperate. For in anger it is impossible where there is no space for deliberation. As I said in the evidential matters. Someone will say, Peter begins: I answer thus, likewise but without iron. Likewise, one flees as a man, face to face, not as a beast, offering the shoulders and kidneys to the sword. Hence, Conrad ought not to have gone after him; for there was no fear of counter-strike; for he who flees is not presumed to return, Inst. de rerum divisione, §. primum. Solution. It could be said that since diverse things are found in the statements of the witnesses, both for and against, it is permitted to the conscience of the judge to arbitrate, presuming against the stronger person from the quality of the persons. Thus the ancients said, and they presumed against the quarrelsome and a man of bad life. But in our case: Peter, who acted out of necessity, ought not to die, nor be maimed. But because he provoked the first matter of the crime, and the substance of the evil deed, he ought to be punished otherwise at the discretion of the judge, and especially because, even if he did not act with a malicious intent, he acted with a bad example in the city and in such illustrious places. Argument, ff. de poenis, l. si quid aliquid, §. qui abortionis. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus de Perusio, Juris Utriusque Doctor. And to the faith I have subscribed, and signed with the sign of my name. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. By reason of laries, a person does not simply acquire a forum.
2. A delict committed outside the territory is investigated by the judge of the domicile, provided the status remains, inasmuch as the authority may investigate against subjects.
3. Having been treated in the territory of the domicile regarding the commission of a certain maleficium perpetrated outside the territory, whether such maleficium may be punished by reason of the treatment.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The aforementioned most excellent doctors have spoken so profoundly that it is not expedient to say many words. For the matter turns into doubt on three points: first, whether by reason of the larium simply, one acquires a forum; second, whether an inquiry may be made concerning a delict committed by such a person outside the territory; third, whether they are to be punished by reason of the tractatus.

† Regarding the first point, it must be said that from mere *lares* (dwellings), unless it is established that one has the intention of making a permanent or long-term residence, a person does not acquire a forum; but if the *lares* are established in a movable manner, they do not constitute a forum, because those who reside there temporarily are not considered to be present there. See D. de pignoribus, l. debitor; D. de haereditatibus institutis, l. ex facto, § reus autem; D. de muneribus et honoribus, l. rescripto, § si; D. de funerariis instrumentis, l. saepe senatus, § praedia, and § Pamphilae. Or, if one has descended with the intention of making a permanent or quasi-permanent residence, and even if he sometimes dwells elsewhere, he nevertheless acquires a forum. See D. de funerariis instrumentis, l. cum delationis, § Sabinus; C. de agris et censibus, l. cum scimus, § si, lib. 11. Or, if there is doubt regarding the intention, it is not presumed except from long residence. See C. de incolis, l. 2, and it is expressly noted in D. ad municipalia, l. eius, § si. And according to the aforementioned distinction, l. 2, C. ubi senatores vel clarissimi, must be understood. And thus the glossa there holds. And it is noted that a person may be interrogated regarding his own intention, and his response shall be relied upon. See D. de probationibus, l. cum probatio, and l. non omnes, § a barbaris, de re militari, cum similibus.

† Regarding the second point, various authors have expressed differing opinions. For Oldradus and the ancient authorities held that inquiry could not be made. Cinus and Bartolus stated that inquiry could be made: on which matter they speak fully in the law *Cunctos populos*. Nevertheless, in the present case, the truth is that inquiry cannot be made, if the statute speaks of subjects, as is presupposed: for, by reason of the offense, although one might be removed from the forum, he is not properly called a subject; thus says the gloss in chapter *Iudicium*, *de foro competenti*, in the Clementines, on the word *subditos*. Which gloss is very notable.

† Regarding the third point, it is said that Cynus held that it is possible for a boy. And it was formerly the case in fact with respect to Lord Alberto de Scala, according to Bartolus in the law *Et si amicis*, *De adulteriis*. He states that either the attempt and the perpetration are the same thing, and one cannot be punished for homicide; or they are different, and then thus: because crimes can be punished where they were commenced, as in law 1, Codex, *Ubi de possessione agi oportet*. It is as if the offense of the place were committed by two persons. In our case, however, the plurality of persons makes it so that what is an attempt with respect to one is [perpetration] with respect to the other. But certainly, only the principalship is considered, as in the Digest, *De furtis*, law *Qui servo*, § *Si*. Therefore, just as it was most correctly advised by the aforementioned doctors, so I affirm and hold. And thus it seems to me, Balde de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, and therefore I have subscribed and signed with the seal of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The mother, together with the children, succeeds to the ownership and the usufruct; if she marries a second time, she holds the ownership, and upon the death of the children, the ownership merges with the usufruct.
2. The son cannot deprive the mother of her legitime.
3. The portion which the husband acquires by virtue of the statute is computed as belonging to another after the death of the deceased.
body: In the name of Christ. Amen.

† John and Jacob’s mother succeeded to one-half in ownership and usufruct. But because she remarried, she lost ownership of the late husband’s goods; yet because the aforementioned Angelina subsequently died without issue,

† the mother recovers that property. C. de secundis nuptiis, auth. ex testamento; and l. foeminae, in fine; and this text, concerning this recovery of property, is not found elsewhere. And in Auth. de nuptiis, § huic vos; and C. ad Tertullianam, l. mater recuperat, so that she may have this consolation for her misfortune, as in Auth. de nuptiis, § pe, si qua mulier, near the end. And this applies as far as the succession made to John and James.

† However, the succession of Angelina proceeds according to her will, saving the legitime due to her mother, which is one-third of Angelina’s assets after deduction of debts owed to others, in which one-third is owed to her husband, according to the form of the statute: because it is a debt owed to others, as in Auth. de nu. §. haec quid est, col. 4, where there is a notable text. Whatever the small gloss says concerning the aforementioned recovery in Auth. ex testamento, when it states “who had only him,” this is rejected by Bartolus and others. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a surety for someone who subsequently changes his condition for the worse can demand that either he be released from such obligation or that sureties be provided for keeping him indemnified.
casus: CASE. In the name of the Lord, amen. The following fact is proposed. John of Florence demanded from Neri of Perugia a certain sum of money, which he had received from him; the latter rightly replied that said coins had been sequestered by the officials of the Roman Church, due to a condemnation made against said John in the city of Perugia. And he said to him: if you wish for this sum of money, I wish to be preserved in such a manner that I suffer no damage, after Jacob of Florence and Simon of Perugia had stood surety for said John and promised to keep said Neri indemnified, after said Neri had restored said sum of money to said John, and said John had kept said Jacob and Simon indemnified in the common form, after said John was and is condemned in said city of Florence for forgery in a certain sum of money and to perpetual imprisonment. After he exited from prison, and to satisfy said condemnation he diminished his own assets greatly, and especially in the moneys he possessed. Now it is asked whether the aforementioned Jacob and Simon can compel said John to release them from the aforementioned obligation and from the promise made by them to said Neri, or at least that he provide suitable sureties for the aforementioned Jacob and Simon, who promise to keep the aforementioned Jacob and Simon indemnified from the aforementioned obligation and from the aforementioned occasion; and whether, on account of the aforementioned occasion, a sequestration can be made of the other goods acquired by said John in Perugia. Furthermore, it is asked: suppose that said John took a wife and received certain dowries from her, which John, together with said Jacob, principally and jointly and severally obligating himself, also promised the restitution of said dowries. After said John was condemned for forgery and diminished his own assets by a great quantity of money, now the aforementioned Jacob wishes to compel said John to release him from the aforementioned obligation, or at least that he provide sufficient sureties for keeping him indemnified and without damage, given that said John had kept said Jacob indemnified in the common form from the promise and obligation to restore the aforementioned dowries.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† These matters could be claimed in law due to the changed condition of the said John, who has fallen into worse fortune. C. man. l. si pro ea. ff. man. item. l. Lucius. ff. de priu. cre. l. si creditores. ff. de iudic. l. in omnibus; and if the said John is contumacious in this regard, sequestration may be ordered on account of contumacy, just as one may proceed to a missio in possessionem, extra de dolo, et contu. c. ex literis. and there by Innocentius. And thus I say, and I, Baldus de Perusio, advise. V. l. D. And I have subscribed to the truth and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A release made under duress or excessive reverence is invalid, and this must be proven.
2. Whether gifts made to a woman by the blood relatives of her husband alone, or made by the blood relatives of the woman, ought to be restored to the woman or to the heirs of the woman.
3. No wages are due to a son who is in the service of his father, unless they have been agreed upon or promised.
casus: CASE. The facts, upon which counsel is requested, are as follows. First, that a certain person named Ser Lippus Baldachini of Cortona, in the year 1371, indiction 9, on the 15th day of the month of November, promised, among other things, in the name of an emancipated son. And in his emancipation, first to Francesco, his legitimate and natural son, 200 gold florins, which 200 florins he had taken from the shop of the wool trade; and the same Ser Lippus wished and ordered that the said quantity of 200 gold florins, and all the profit and advantage, and disadvantage, which was then in the said shop, and which was expected to be in the future in the said shop of the wool trade, should belong to the said Francesco, and as a reward for the emancipation. Finally, after the aforesaid, he promised and agreed, as appears from a public instrument drawn up by a public notary. The same Ser Philip, wishing to attend to and observe the said promises made to Francesco, his son: but rather wishing to be released from the aforesaid, constrained and compelled the said Francesco to make to him a satisfaction, refutation, release, and perpetual pact of not further claiming the said quantity of 200 gold florins, the profit, advantage, and disadvantage aforesaid, with all the clauses which are customarily added in such instruments: as appears fully from the hand of Ser Ludovico, public notary for him: because the said Ser Philip had said that he had incurred many expenses during the time when the said Francesco was under his power, for cloths and garments made, both for the mother of the said Francesco and for his wife, and for other expenses incurred by him, as is mentioned in the instrument of release drawn up by the said Ser Ludovico, written while the said Ser Philip held and possessed, and received, both from the dowries of the said mother of the said Francesco and of his aforesaid wife. Who Francesco, not wishing to contradict the will of his father, nor to contend with him: but rather out of fear and reverence, satisfied and released him from the aforesaid 200 gold florins, and the advantage, profit, and disadvantage received from the same, on the 13th day of September, 1371. Now it is asked, whether the said satisfaction holds, or whether it can be revoked in law, so that the said Francesco may claim the said quantity of 200 gold florins, the advantage, and profit aforesaid, from his heirs instituted in the testament. And whether the aforesaid heirs are bound to restore to the said Francesco the inheritance and donation of his deceased mother. It is also asked, whether after the emancipation made to the said Francesco by his said father, the fruits received by the said Ser Lippus for two years from the dowries and dotal goods of the wife of the said Francesco, then deceased, which dowries remained to Niccolò, son of the said Francesca, the said wife, legitimate and natural son, who succeeded intestate to his said mother, the said heirs are bound to restore, if they exist, or if they do not exist, their sons and heirs. It is also asked, because the same Francesco, after the aforesaid emancipation made to him, remained for a period of three years and more, exercising the art of the wool trade for the said Ser Lippus as his factor, whether he ought, or may, claim a salary for the said time from the said heirs. It is also asked, since a certain person named Iunta Manuti of Cortona bequeathed and left in his testament, by right of institution, to the lady Francesca, formerly of the said Ser Lippo, and mother of the said Francesco, 100 livres tournois, which quantity was paid by the heir of the said lady Francesca to the wife then of the said Ser Lippo. Of which quantity of 100 livres tournois, by mandate, presence, will, and consent of the said Ser Lippo, the aforesaid Francesco, being under the power of the said Ser Lippo, made a satisfaction, release, and pact of not claiming the said quantity of 100 livres tournois from the aforesaid heirs of the said Iunta after the death of his said mother; whether the said Francesco may claim restitution and security for the said 100 livres tournois from the aforesaid heirs of the said Ser Lippo, formerly his father.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the first point, it must be said that if a son releases his father out of fear or excessive reverence, such a release is invalid; however, the son must prove this. C. de dolo, l. si superstite; and ff. quarum rerum actio non datur, l. 1, §. quę honorandum. But if fear or excessive reverence is not proven, then the set-off would be valid, provided that the final cause of the set-off is a legitimate ground for set-off. Here, however, there is no legitimate ground, because the burdens of marriage pertain to the father-in-law who received the dowry, not to the husband who is under his power. See ff. sol. ma., l. si cum dotem, §. transgrediamur; and what is noted in eo. ti., l. si constante, in principio; and ff. de mun. et hon., l. qui orig., §. fi. Therefore, the expenses of the wedding do not pertain to the son, nor is he bound to his father on this account, nor is this a legitimate ground for the son to be required to compensate his father. Thus, the set-off, which has a just cause, is defeated by the replication of fraud.

† On the second point, Bartolus states that if a donation is made to a woman, it remains with the husband if made by the husband’s blood relatives; but if made by the woman’s blood relatives, they say it is to be restored to the woman’s heirs. D. de vulgari substitutione, l. sed si plures, § in arrogato, according to Bartolus. But the better view is that, since the donation is perfected and a right has accrued to the woman, the woman transmits it to her own heirs. C. de donationibus ante nuptias, l. si mater vestra. On the third point, it must be said that half of the usufruct remains with the father, and the other half is due to the son. C. de bonis quae liberis, l. cum oportet, § cum autem.

† On the fourth point, it must be said that no wages are due to a son who is in the service of his father, unless they have been agreed upon or promised. C. de negotiorum gestis, l. Obsequio. On the last point, it must be said that the heir of the husband is not bound to pay those 100 pounds which accrued to the woman, of whom they are not heirs. C. de transactionibus, l. Nec intentio, with similar authorities, unless it were proven that the money came into the hands of the husband. Si certum petatur, l. Si me et Titium. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio. V. l. D. And to the truth I have subscribed and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If someone receives money for loss and profit, and binds himself to prove the loss within the next ensuing month, whether after the month has elapsed he can prove the loss.
2. A renunciation of proof does not prevent proof from being made after the renunciation.
body: In the name of God, amen, and of His glorious Virgin Mother. The point upon which counsel was sought is as follows: Giovanni Valdi Vulgluctii of Todi had and received from Bello Baldelli ten gold florins for a share of the profit and loss in the trade of canvas and coarse cloths, and in whatever other trade he might wish to work; and with the said florins the said Giovanni promised to make profit and trade in good faith without fraud and knowledge of the pact, and to render an account every six months of the principal and of the profit that might be therein; and thence directly he promised concerning the said branch and its loss to prove, that is, of the damage inflicted and loss, within one month then next ensuing, by two or more good, suitable, and trustworthy witnesses; and all and singular the aforesaid things the said Giovanni, having taken an oath, promised to hold, attend to, and observe under a certain penalty.

† It is therefore asked whether, after the said month has elapsed, the proof of the said damage can be made. And at first sight it seems not; because for proving the agreements of contracting parties a certain time-limit is prefixed, which it does not seem lawful or possible to overstep, C. de contrahen. stip. l. magnam; de verb. ob. l. si insulam, and l. ita stipulatus, with its like. This is also corroborated by the general rule introduced by the praetor, who contradicts it where nothing else stands in the way, that terms laid down are to be observed to the letter, ff. de pac. l. 1; nor does there seem here to be room for purging default, since a day and a penalty were added, as in the said l. magnam, and ff. de arbit. l. celsus. I believe the contrary to be true: that the damage can indeed be proved afterwards. A twofold reason moves me to say this: first, because insofar as the proof is not made within the month, it does not appear from the aforesaid words that the way of proving is precluded; for the contracting parties did not go so far as to provide that the said proof could not be made, nor did they speak conditionally, that an account would be taken of the damage and loss if and insofar as proof was made of the said damage in respect of the month—for then it would have to be fulfilled as a condition in its specific form, and thus within the month, as in l. meuius and l. qui haeredi, ff. de cond. et de.—but the parties made mention dispositively of this proof to be made, binding the promisor to the penalty if he did not prove it. Since, therefore, we are not inquiring about the penalty, but whether the said proof can be made, and by common law proof ought to be made when the suit has been contested in the cause, not before, as in the cases set forth in Extra, ut lit. non contest. c. quoniam frequenter; ad l. aquil. l. in l. aquiliana si deletum; C. de prob. l. exceptionem, it appears that neither by common law nor from the form of the pact does the lapse of the monthly term exclude the power of proving.

† Hence it is that a renunciation of proofs does not prevent proofs from being made after the renunciation; and this was the opinion of Giovanni and Accursius in l. Cot. de testi. §. pe. no. in the gloss that begins 'unam productionem'. Furthermore, the power of proof was introduced principally for the public good; it is therefore not to be narrowed, ff. de testa. l. 1; according to l. quoniam in fin., C. de haereti.; whence its form is not harmed by an agreement of private persons, ff. de pact. l. ius publicum, and l. 1, ff. de test. Since, therefore, it belongs to the form and essence of proof that it be made at a certain time, that it be made at another time or otherwise, although the common law disposes it, is not included by the pact or consent of the litigants to the extent that the facilities of proofs are narrowed. In support of this I cite the singular gloss in l. in Cor. ne sine prohi. ma. ram. §. quia nullam, where the doctors expressly determine that, because the facility of proofs cannot be narrowed by an agreement of the contracting parties, an agreement entered into that it shall not be permitted to prove payment of a debt except through a public instrument is invalid. From these premises I conclude that, notwithstanding the said words of the said contract, the loss and damage can be proved after the lapse of the said monthly time.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The requirements for proceeding against someone for arrest.
2. If the defendant is arrested by a judge who does not have jurisdiction over him, such arrest is invalid and has no effect.
3. It is impossible to arrest a person before the debt has been liquidated.
4. What was not alleged before the arrest cannot be alleged afterward to confirm it.
5. Some degree of credibility is required, which reasonably leads the judge to presume flight, so that someone may be arrested as a suspect. See further on this matter below in consilium 338 and consilium 324.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† This arrest is defective on account of the incompetent court, on account of the incongruous mode, and on account of the insufficient cause. The first point is established: because, with this universal pact being circumscribed, the plaintiff must follow the forum of the defendant. C. de iure omnium iudicum, l. iuris ordinem; C. ubi senatores vel clarissimi, l. 2; C. ubi de crimine agi oporteat, l. 1 and fin.; and in Auth. qua in provincia, Pistoriensis. Therefore, he could not be dragged before a Lucan court. D. si quis in ius vocatus non ierit, l. ex quacunque; contractus sit, in vetitio examine; C. de iure omnium iudicum, l. in criminali. Nor does it obstruct that treaties are made among us regarding the exemptions of defendants, and especially where the form of a full treaty provides for the forum, as in D. de captivis, lege non dubito; cum universitas legis habet vigorem, as noted in D. de regulis iuris, l. nec ex praetorio; and l. neque pignus, §. priuatorum; C. de decretis decurionum; lege etiam de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. pe; D. de publicanis, l. Caesar. For this is true when we are within the tenor of the law of the confederation or pact; otherwise, it is separated from the form of the law, as in l. certi forma, de iure fisci, lib. 10; D. ad municipalia, l. constitutionibus; de liberis et posthumis, l. commodissimum; and Inst. l. cuiuscunque, §. non tamen omne, de rebus spoliatis; c. Pisanis, de rescriptis; c. cum dilecta.
