† but the form of this was not observed, nor was the order handed down, whence the irregular seizure is noted. C. de pac. l. si pacto quo poenam. C. de exce. rei iudi. ll. C. de prohi. sequestra. l. 1. de actio. et obli. l. negantes. de bonis autho. iudi. possidem. l. cum vnus. whence also it is declared void, that which proceeded de facto. de ver. sig. c. ex parte in Christo de euic. in men. in prin. and l. 1. §. hoc edictum. ff. si mulier ven. no. imprudenter. n. and lightly done, de facto it ought to be annulled easily. as the text there elegantly says.

It must therefore be noted that it is inadmissible to seize a person for execution before the debt has been liquidated. For if one cannot seize [property], as is stated in C. de vi, l. meminissent, so too one cannot seize a person; because the seizure of a person is a greater burden than the seizure of a thing. D. de iur. ciu., l. magistratus; C. de exact. trib., l. nemo carcerem; C. quibus cess. po., l. 1. For that which is subject to seizure must be clear to the praetor. L. hoc autem, § 1, qui ex cau. in pos. eatur. For a judge to whom nothing is clear can do nothing, as noted by Innocentius, de sent. excomm., c. solet, in fine. Clarity must therefore be established through a preliminary informative narration and subsequent proof of such a kind as is required.

† And it must be known that, when the seizure was based on an interlocutory judgment, that which was not alleged before the seizure cannot subsequently be alleged to confirm the seizure, namely, that it was injurious. For there is no confirmation of an injury, but rather that which proceeded without reason must be invalidated. D. de re iudicata, Si cum nulla; and in C. Appellante, de appellationibus, in the gloss.

Furthermore, it must be known that the omission of the form of a pact, when it has the force of law, renders the act void by operation of law, just as if the form of the common law were omitted. As in L. Prolatam, together with L. Omnes populi; and de muneribus et honoribus, L. Ut gradatim, § Sed et si lege; especially where the form is prescribed by jurisdiction. For, as Innocentius elegantly states, everything that is the cause for conferring jurisdiction must be alleged before proceeding. F. de competentiis, Cum sit generale, especially in extraordinary or anomalous jurisdiction. It supports what is noted by Bartolus, de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, L. Multum interest. It must be established by himself for himself, so that he may be a judge according to the facts narrated to him; otherwise, whatever follows is erroneous. It supports what is noted by Innocentius, Extra, de dilationibus, C. Praeterea.

† Moreover, as I have said, whatever degree of faith is required, which reasonably leads the judge to a presumption of flight. D. ad l. Aquil. l. in l. Aquiliam, si deletum. It follows: because the judge ought not to follow another’s conscience, but his own, informed. As noted, C. de bonis possessionibus secundum tabulas, l. 1. Let us therefore see what was narrated, what was proved, what was done. Certainly, nothing about flight was narrated to the judge: therefore, the capture was not on the occasion of flight. Praetor, n. He was not approached for that cause, but for another. L. habebat, de institutionibus. Where it is also noted that when a narration is considered as a kind of libel, it must be apt and conclusive, just as a libel: but this one is not conclusive for the judge, nor for the defendant. Hence it is begun; this is proved in L. 1, C. de praediis curialium, lib. 10; D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, §. in causa; D. de appellationibus, l. nec ei, §. eorum. And by this, a response is given to the note, C. de feriis, l. si; D. eodem, l. 1, §. fin.; D. de petitionibus, l. quaesitum. Notwithstanding, L. ut praetor, §. si debitorem: because there it speaks of an act of flight, and of a private capture, not judicial and pure. And similarly, a response is given to the note, per Innocentius, de senatu excusando, c. ut fame; per Bartolus, de surro, l. si quis in servitute; and l. interdum, §. qui furem; and l. extat, quod me, cautio, per glossa, C. ubi de crimine vel coactione, l. 1. And it is the gloss, c. quando crimini, actio, on the understanding of that §. qui furem, where the gloss says that that was done de facto. Therefore, the pact speaks of one fleeing with the thing or money of another. Which is not established here, and the words ought to be understood properly according to the nature of the possessive genitive. D., de religione, l. 2, §. in locum; nor ought the improper meaning of its vocabulary to be extended in this pact, which is of strict law. L. si vero, §. de matre, so, ma. Furthermore, an oath against calumny was not taken, which oath is of solemnity and order. D. de iureiurando, l. si non fuerit. Furthermore, the procurators swore on their own souls, when they ought to have sworn on the soul of their principal. C. praesentium, de testibus, lib. 6; c. fin., de iuramento calumniae, eodem, lib. 6. Since therefore the form which gives being to the thing has been omitted, it follows that the captive ought to be restored to his own liberty, and ought to be released from prison altogether as having been captured unduly. For whenever several things are required for the being of something, if one is lacking, the whole collapses. As noted in c. 2, de rescriptis; and de itinere actuque privato, l. unde, §. hic autem a superiori; de probationibus, c. licet causam. And although the statute or pact says summarily and de facto, it is not understood to abolish forms introduced in honor of God. C. saepe, de verborum significatione, in Deum; l. ex quacunque in fine. For and against, it is noted by Bartolus, de donationibus, l. filius. But he speaks of another case, and whether he speaks well or ill, it is not necessary to treat now. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldo de Perusio, Doctor of Laws. And to the faith of this, I have subscribed and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a marriage contracted in the article of death has the effect of legitimating children.
2. Whether one may enter upon an inheritance or act as heir under a condition, unaware of the condition.
3. A substitution made in the event of the failure of children expires when there are children legitimated by a marriage contracted in the article of death.
4. If the testator disposed of property under a condition which fails, and the heir confirms such disposition, whether the disposition will be valid as a disposition or as a confirmation.
5. A universal fideicommissum is transmitted, just as a particular one.
6. The mother is excluded by a pupillary substitution.
7. Whether the term "children" includes a bastard.
casus:
CASE. In the name of God, Amen. The points on which advice is requested are these. First, Matheus Banis Nerei made a will, in which he instituted as his universal heirs Barnabas, his son, and Christophanus, his grandson, with conditions inserted in the said will, with respect to the said Christophanus, by which he made a substitution as appears in the will. Finally, the said Matheus dies, the said Bernardo and Christophanus, his heirs, surviving, and the inheritance having been accepted by them. However, the condition appended in the will was not fulfilled by the said Christophanus; because he did not ratify the acts done by the said Matheus, as was disposed in his will. And thus the acceptance made by him seems to be null. Finally, the said Christophanus died, leaving a single natural son, having made a will, in which he instituted as his heir Benedict, his uncle. And by right of institution, he left certain goods to his natural son. Then the said Barnabas died, leaving a single legitimate and natural son, begotten by him, a free man, and Bilia, his concubine, a free woman, whom he took as his wife at the time of his death, having made a will by the said Barnabas, in which he instituted as his universal heir the lady Beatrice, his mother, and instituted the said his son in a certain part. After whose death, Bartholomew, the said his son, Nifans, died, the said lady Beatrice, universal heir of the said Barnabas, and the said his son, substituted as appears in the will, surviving, and the lady Bilia, mother of the said infant, surviving. Who, Barnabas, wished the substitution made to him by Matheus, his father, to be firm and valid by the words of the following tenor, namely: willing and ordering the said testator, that the substitution made by Matheus Banis, father of the said testator, to the said Barnabas, which has already vanished by the existence of the son of the said Barnabas, be firm and valid, to the said Francis and sisters of the said Matheus, and their sons, as to the part of the inheritance of the said Matheus only, with the condition and mode as contained in the said will. Now it is asked, having seen the aforesaid wills, what is the law.

First, whether by the subsequent marriage between the said Barnabas and his concubine, the natural son of the said Barnabas became legitimate. Since such marriage was contracted at the time when the said Barnabas was physically ill, although of sound mind, from which illness he died, and it was contracted by the procurator of the said Barnabas.

Second, whether the said Christophanus, who involved himself in the inheritance of the said Matheus, and sold many goods as his heir, but did not fulfill the condition under which he was instituted heir, is considered to have been the heir of the said Matheus; because if he was not heir, his part seems to have come to the said Barnabas by right of accretion; if he was heir, then by right of substitution, the diversity of which is the affection. Whether the substitution in the said will of Matheus to the said Barnabas and Christophanus, by virtue of the aforesaid substitution, is admitted to the inheritance of the said Matheus in whole or in part, for which the legitimation of the son of Barnabas, which is said to have been made by the subsequent marriage, is not an obstacle.

Fourth, if by virtue of the said substitution they are not admitted, because it is said to have vanished by the existence of the son of Barnabas, whether by virtue of the approval made by the said Barnabas of the aforesaid substitution as to those named by him, the said approved substitutes come to the succession of the inheritance of the said late Matheus or Barnabas, and for what part.

Fifth, if he is admitted to the aforesaid succession, whether the inheritance of the said Barnabas ought to be estimated, having regard to the time of the death of his father, having regard to the time of the death of the said Barnabas.

Sixth, since some of the aforesaid substitutes approved by the said Barnabas died after the death of the said Barnabas, the aforesaid substitution not being recognized, and before the restitution of the aforesaid inheritance made to him, they transmitted the right of the fideicommissum to their heir.

Seventh, whether the son of the said son of Barnabas, who died in infancy, is admitted to the succession of the said, or to any part, having seen the substitution made to him by the said Barnabas, his father.

Eighth, since Vannes Nerii, paternal grandfather of the said Barnabas, made his will, in which he prohibited absolutely in perpetuity, concerning the right of houses situated in the borough of the Holy Sepulchre, the alienation and distraction of things, and long-term leasing and concession, and every contract from which alienation would follow, or which might be presumed to be made in fraud of alienation, or could be presumed, and this the said testator did because he wished the said houses above mentioned and bounded, and each of them, to come perpetually to his posterity, free from him or from them descending in the male line, and to claim and take possession of his houses and each of them with full power and authority, and sober will of the said testator, in case that against the said prohibition it should come or be done by the said his posterity, free and perpetually descending. And since all descendants from the male line from the said Vannes died, except one natural son of Christophanus Valerii Vannis, the aforesaid, born of a free man and a free woman. It is asked whether the said son Christophanus, by the legacy made of the aforesaid houses to Francis son of Nerii, as contained in the will of the said Barnabas, acquired any right in the aforesaid houses, and whether the said Barnabas could make a will concerning the aforesaid houses, as he did, notwithstanding the aforesaid prohibition.

Finally, the aforesaid lady Beatrice, universal heir of the said Barnabas, says that the aforesaid houses, prohibited from alienation, can be alienated by her as a matter of law, notwithstanding the aforesaid prohibition.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

A marriage contracted in the article of death has the effect of legitimating children, as is noted by Cynus in the Code, *De natura liberorum*, book 1, *nuper*; and it is fully noted by Johannes Andreae in the chapter *Tanta*, *Qui filii sint legitimi*, in the Novellae. And this person, legitimated through marriage, excludes the substitute; because it is the most efficacious form of legitimation, and this is so because it is a legitimation imitating nature, for it derives its origin from marriage. Code, *De natura liberorum*, law *Cum quis*.

† On the second point, it must be said that an heir instituted under a condition cannot enter upon the inheritance or act as heir, unless he knows that the condition has occurred. D. de cond. et demonstr. l. multum; and note in D. l. illud, F. si pars hereditatis petatur. And the portion of him who dies in the meantime accrues to the coheir, as C. de caducis tollendis § pro secundo and note D. de acquirenda hereditate l. nec is § cohaeredes and l. si quis heres; and C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus l. testamento. Here it should be observed that the gloss on the said § heres permits coming in by right of accrual after repudiation of the substitution, and the gloss in l. si quis heres does not permit the coheir to repudiate the vulgar substitution; this passage is difficult. Nevertheless, it is not expedient at present to examine this, since Christopher was not heir and the inheritance of Barnabas was wholly awarded, we are in the law of non-decrementum; all things thus done by Christopher and alienated could not be done nor alienated, since he did not fulfill the condition, D. de cond. et demonstr. l. qui heredi § fin.; D. ad Trebellianum l. sed et si ante. And this concludes the second point.

† On the third point, I say that the substitution has expired, as I stated in the first point. For just as, when marriage is the cause of children, legitimate children born exclude the substitute; so too, when children are the cause of marriage—because one enters into marriage for the sake of children—thus the prerogative of legitimation is established, and they ought to enjoy the favors of marriage. See *l. Cum quis* and *ca. Tanta* *de naturalibus vero meris*. What is the law? Very well noted, *ff. ad Trebellianum*, *l. Ex facto*, § *Si quis rogatus*; *C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus*, *l. Generaliter*, § *Finis*; *ff. de rebus iudicatis*, *l. Si quis praegnante*. And certainly, and simply, a natural child excludes an alien substitute, considering the natural cause and the wish of the parents; which also applies to natural children, unless, due to a contrary and prevailing presumption, the opposite were to be conjectured. But in our case, marriage legitimizes the offspring, and there is no place for the distinction of the said § *Si quis rogatus*; rather, it indistinctly excludes the substitute. For if the mere appearance of marriage does this, as the said *l. Finis* states, how much more should the truth of an effective marriage accomplish the same result.

† On the fourth point, it appears that Barnabone’s disposition would be impossible, because that which has vanished cannot be confirmed; for the nature of confirmation is to find something confirmable. See D. de lib. leg. l. autem, § testamento. But the truth is that it does not operate as a confirmation, but as a new disposition. See D. de leg. 1, l. legata inutiliter; D. de mil. testamento, l. tribunus, § ult.; D. ad Trebellianum, l. si quis posterior. Thus, it derives its force, form, and origin from Barnabone’s testament, as if Barnabone had said: “I do not wish that what my father left under a condition should be due purely.” See D. de aliment. legat., l. 3, § conditio. And because Barnabone’s disposition is a relative disposition, the share is ascertained by the term to which the relation is made. See l. hæc sententia, de sententiis quæ sic certæ quantæ cum similibus. In the rationale of the Falcidian or legitime portion to be imposed, however, Barnabone’s assets are considered, whose inheritance is at issue. See D. ad l. Falcid., l. in quanti. And by this means, the objection is answered.

† Fifth point: Because the aforementioned Barnabas wished that what was to be given to Francis and the sisters of Matthew be provided in the same amount as would have been provided had he had no son, and in that case the legitime and the trebellianic portion would have been deducted, so too is it deducted now. D. de legatis 3, l. Mevio, §. auiae. For he wished to give more than was due, if the condition of the fideicommissum had not failed; D. de legatis, l. legavi; C. de falsa causa, si non designata imputatur. Nevertheless, regarding the weight of the vulgar substitution in this legitime and trebellianic portion, see D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. Marcellus, §. res quae, with similar authorities.

† On the sixth point, it must be said that a universal fideicommissum is transmitted, just as a particular one is, unless it were conditional, which is not transmitted. As is fully noted by Dynus and others. D. de legatis 1, l. cum filio; C. de fideicommissis, l. si in personam; ad Trebellianam, l. apud Iulianum, §. utrum, and §. cum Antistia; C. de his qui ante apertas tabulas, l. 1.

† On the seventh point, it must be said that the mother of the said legitimated son, to whom a pupillary substitution could have been made, is entirely excluded by the pupillary substitution, according to the law *Papinianus*, § *sed nec impuberis*, in the title *de inofficioso testamento*, and in the chapter *Si pater*, in the title *de testibus*, Book 6.

† On the eighth point, it seems that at first glance one should say what was said in the third point, namely that a bastard son is included in the term “children”; and consequently the said houses belong to him and not to Lady Beatrice. D. 32, 1, *Filius*, § *Divi*, with its material. For the testator’s intention is not changed by nature; this is common to both natural and legitimate children, D. 26, 2, *Fin.*; and what is said by Cynus, C. 4, 17, *Libertinum*. Or at least one must resort to the distinction of the said § *Si quis rogatus*. Here consider: it matters greatly whether the testator makes the children less burdened by this, as if he said, “If my son dies without sons, I substitute such a person,” in which case natural children serve to release from the burden of the fideicommissum, as stated in the cited laws; or conversely, whether the condition of the legitimate children is made worse by the natural child, as when we are burdened by their existence, in which we would not be burdened without them, as is the case here. For if natural children are included, the legitimate children are more burdened, because they cannot alienate the houses that have come to them. And thus the prohibition of alienation, made in favor of the children, would be turned against the legitimate children in favor of the natural ones, which is not probable; for it is not to be presumed that the testator had only the natural children in mind, and that he wished to bind the hands of the legitimate children on account of bastards. By them also the honor of the house is not preserved, nor the dignity of the family, to which the testator had regard, and especially because he was a nobleman, as stated in § *Si quis*. Moreover, that testator considered agnation, when he said “from the male line,” which does not apply to bastards. D. 38, 7, *Si spurius*; and D. 38, 7, *Hac parte*. For a bastard follows the mother, and not the father. D. 1, 5, *Vulgo*; D. 50, 4, 1. Therefore I conclude that the said houses do not come to the said bastard, because he is degenerate, as C. 8, 27, *Fin.* From this follows the determination of the last point, that the said houses can be alienated, because no one remains to revoke, even though all legitimate and natural children are dead. As in Auth. *De test. fideicomm.*, § *Manifestum*; and the said § *Divi*, with similar authorities. And this, having regard to the said testator’s will. But having regard to Barnabone’s will, it must be said that alienation cannot be made, and the will of the said Barnabone must be preserved, as in the said § *Divi*. If, however, Francis consented to the alienation, he could not later object, D. 32, 2, *Cum paternae*, § *Libertis*. I also say that the *poderi* [farmsteads] of the vulgar substitution freely belong to Lady Beatrice, notwithstanding any general dispositions made in favor of others. D. 35, 2, *Legata*, § *Qui plures*; D. 33, 1, *Servo manumisso*; D. 38, 2, *Quo*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A conjunctive and alternative appeal is valid if it is valid under civil law; but what is the case under canon law, and number 2.
2. A legate, even without a special commission from the Pope, cannot act against the devolution to the superior.
3. A legate cannot act or decree against the law.
casus: CASE. In the name of God, Amen. After this, sentence having been pronounced against Alsatellus, who appealed for the reasons set forth below, an appeal was also taken in the case of the appeal. A certain instrument was produced, in which it is effectively contained that, after the appeal had been interposed, as stated, within the time in which he was to choose, he chose a procurator for Alsatellus in the absence of the judge and the party. Having had one messenger, he said to him: “Receive these acts and deliver them to Alsatellus, so that he may pursue his case in the court of Lord Alban, to whom I have appealed.” It is objected by the appellant against the said instrument and its tenor that the said choice is therefore invalid, because it ought to have been made in his presence. Also, because it was not made in the presence of the judge; for just as an appeal is interposed before the judge, so also the choice ought to have been made before him. Also, because the choice was made without notice to the party; for by such a choice the appellee was not informed before whom he ought to appear. It is answered to these objections that the first objection does not matter; for an appeal can be taken in the absence of the judge, and consequently, all the more so, a choice can be made in his absence. Also, just as the presence of the party is not required for appealing, so neither is it required for choosing. And also, those laws which say that an appeal interposed conjunctively or alternatively is not valid in benefice cases seem to have their proper place, because the appellee must appear before the judge within certain times, without any other summons.
body: Opinion of Master Simon de Borsano. V. l. excellen. legum. et decretorum doct. Arc. Bon. on the conjunctive and the alternative in an appeal interposed to the Pope. and do. Alba. and to any competent judge

† It is clear in civil law that an appeal is valid and the judge must immediately take cognizance of it: as in the Digest, On Appeals, l. Imperator; and noted in the Decretals, On the Office of Delegates, c. Si is cui, lib. 6. But since we are in the canonical forum,

It appears that the appeal is invalid. Hence, if there are many [grounds] and uncertainty vitiates [the act]. As in D. de iniuriis, l. Praetor, § Quod autem; as in D. de confessionibus, l. Certum, § Pretio; and D. de testamento tutoris, l. Tutor incertus. It supports this: X. de electione, c. 2, lib. 6; and de rescriptis, c. Ad haec; and de arbitris, c. Innotuit. And this is the opinion of Johannes Andreae in c. Si is cui, supra allegated, and in the rule on alternatives, where he expressly holds this. But here it may be objected that Johannes Andreae speaks of an alternative, therefore it is not valid. And thus also speak the laws cited above: because an alternative gives rise to uncertainty. But in the case posited there is no alternative, hence it ought to be valid. As in D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. Recusare, § Totius; and C. de legibus, l. Si, and what is noted there, where a substitution made vulgarly, pupillarily, and by fideicommissum is valid. And for this opinion, regarding the conjunctive, it supports well Speculum, in tit. de appellationibus, § Nunc tractemus, verb. Sed pone, where it seems to hold that it is valid, as in X. de postulando, c. 1, lib. 6; and Inst. de acquisitione, § Aliter.

Furthermore, it may be objected that, although the appellant does not choose within 10 days, the appeal is valid. As in D. de legatis 2, l. Si quis Titio, § Si; and l. Cum quidam; and l. Unum ex familia, § Rogo. Furthermore, it may be objected regarding the constitution of the legate, which seems to intend that appeal should be made only to the immediate judge, and thus reduces it to civil law. Hence it appears that the said appeal is valid, just as it has been said to be valid according to civil law.

To the first objection it is answered that, although it is conjunctive, it nevertheless is not valid, as in X. de constitutionibus, c. Uno, lib. 6. Indeed, it ought to be valid less by virtue of the conjunctive than of the alternative, according to the note by Innocentius in X. de officio delegati, c. Cum contingat, where he says that although one may say a sentence is null or unjust, one may not say it is null and unjust.

To § Totius and to l. Si, it is answered that 'and' is put for 'or', and thus it is in D. de usufructu legato, l. Si Titio. And in that alternative it may be valid, and it is the choice of the substitute, whom he wishes to choose. If it is said therefore that in the same way the appeal ought to be valid in our case, if the appellant were to choose, but it is true within the due time, namely 10 days; afterwards he cannot [appeal] on account of the defect of an outsider, from whom. As in D. de rerum divisione, l. Bonorum; and D. de contrahenda emptione, l. Quod si in diem, § Si sub conditione.

To the opinion of the Speculum, it is answered that it is not true. And also in our case it supports the appellee: because the Speculum holds that the appeal devolved to the Pope; therefore the appellant ought to have prosecuted it before him. And in our case the year has elapsed, and thus the first sentence passed into res iudicata. As in C. de tempore appellationum, auth. Ei qui; and X. de appellationibus, c. Cum sic Romanum.

To the objection regarding probable doubt, it is answered that here there was no probable doubt, for probable doubt is that which arises from the uncertainty of the adversary. As in D. quorum bonorum, l. 1, § Quod ait vel lex. Ignorance of fact is probable, thus it is spoken of, as is noted in c. 1, § Is cui, X. de officio delegati, lib. 6; and what is noted by Johannes Andreae in the Novella. But here it is from ignorance of law, which is not probable. As in X. de regulis iuris, c. Iuris ignorantia, lib. 6, with similar cases.

To the third objection, that it is valid without choice, as in l. Si quis Titio, § Si, with similar cases, the solution is clear. For a legacy is an act which beforehand may be communicated to several, but it is not so in judgment. For the appellee ought not to be dragged before several judges, but only before one.

To the constitution of the legate, it is answered that in our case it does not speak; this also I have seen.

† Moreover, a legate without a special commission from the Pope cannot rule against the devolution to the superior. As stated in the Extravagantes, *De iureiurando*, chapter *Venientes*; and what is noted there by Innocentius. And it supports what is noted in chapter *Foemina*, Extravagantes, *De consuetudinibus*, Book 2, Title 6. And what is noted by Cynus in the law *Si appellaverit*, Codex, *De appellacionibus*. And what is noted by Bartolus in the Digest, *De iustitia et iure*, law *Omnes populi*.

† Moreover, a legate cannot act or decree against the law, as is stated in *Extra*, *De filiis presbyterorum*, chapter *Dilectus*; and also in *De officio praefecti praetorii Africae*, law 2; and what is noted by Modus in the *Clementinae*, law 1, *De electione*; and it accords with what is noted by Bartolus in *Digestum*, *Quod vi aut clam*, law 3, in the beginning. Hence I conclude that the aforementioned appeal is invalid, for the constitution of Urban is an *extravagant* [decree], and it has not been produced in court by the parties. Therefore, one must adhere to the common law, which appears otherwise. Moreover, it could also be said that it does not touch our case, etc. I, Simon de Borsano, thus say and advise, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. By the destruction and demolition of the castle by the authority of the prince, every right of the castle, together with its appurtenances, is extinguished.
2. Whether goods of private persons, having been condemned and confiscated, those goods which were previously subject to servitude and the rights of subjection of the destroyed castle become free.
3. Whether a private person succeeding to the fisc, or to another privileged person, makes use of the privilege.
4. Whether destruction and restitution proceed from the same source.
5. Add the following opinion.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the instrument of sale made by Lord Sabinus to Titius, and having examined another instrument of concession made to Lord Albert by Lord Urbanus Pandere, several matters are to be considered arising from the doubts extracted therefrom.

† First, it must be shown: because, due to the destruction and demolition of the castle by the authority of the prince, especially for an expressly stated cause, namely the rebellion of the subjects and inhabitants, all rights of the castle, together with its appurtenances then granted by special law, are extinguished. This is proven by 25 q. 2 c. fi. and 16 q. 7, and we have written this regarding the signification of words in c. Abbate and c. Cum ex iniuncto de novo operis nuntio, and in both places according to Innocentius and the gloss. Therefore, by the demolition of the castle by the authority of the prince, all rights of the castle and its appurtenances are extinguished. And this is the first conclusion.

† From which it is inferred that, through the confiscation of the goods of private individuals condemned as rebels, those goods which were previously subject to servitudes and the rights of subjection of the castle become free, together with the extinguishment of the rights of the castle. As is deduced below, all rights of servitudes are entirely extinguished, because a servitude is not owed to a thing that does not exist. C. de legibus, l. non dubium; ff. de collegiis illicitis, l. 3; ff. de regulis iuris, l. nihil dolo; ff. de fideiussoribus, l. fideiussor obligari. And this is the second conclusion, namely, that the goods of private individuals condemned by confiscation are freed from the servitude to which they were bound, in the same manner as the church was freed from the servitude to which it was bound by reason of the castle, since, by reason of the castle, they were liable and subject to the servitudes of the church, and especially since they have been incorporated into the fisc of the church, for a thing’s own property does not serve anyone by a formal servitude. From this conclusion is inferred the third conclusion, namely, that when these [goods] are sold, they pass to the buyer with that freedom with which they were with the church at the time of the sale. This is proven by the series of the contract: because the said Sabinus sold [them] with all rights pertaining thereto. And he who says “all” excludes nothing. ff. de officio praesidis, l. praeses; 19. dist.; c. qui Romanorum, de maiore et obedientia; c. solitae. Moreover, because when the principal thing is sold, the accessories pass with it, as the rule states: cum principali, ff. de regulis iuris; and the rule accessorium, in the same title, book 6. Nor is there any doubt or dispute to be made in this case.

Whether a private person succeeding to the fisc, or to another privileged party, should or should not avail himself of the canonical privilege, is fully discussed in the Authentica *Quas actiones*, Codex, *De sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, and thereabouts; and by Cynus, because here, by the force of the contract of sale, all rights and liberties pass which did not belong to the fisc. Certain buyers prove the words of the contract, from which one must not depart unless it were clearly established to the contrary from the intent. Digest, *De legatis tertio*, law *Non aliter*; Digest, *Qui et a quibus*, law *Prospexit*; Digest, *De exercitu*, law 1, section *Is qui navem*, *De proprio privilegio*. And it is so, Chapter *Si Papa*, in the same title, Book 6. And the seller had the power to sell in this manner, as appears from the series of mandates of Lord Innocent and Lord Urban. From these things it is concluded in favor of the said buyers and Lady Berta, their proper heir: by the force of the contract, they hold those goods free from the subjections and burdens concerning which doubt arises here.

† But here an objection will be raised: although the castle was destroyed by the authority of the prince, it was restored by the same authority; for the power to destroy and to build is equal, as stated in the Digest, under the heading *de pauperibus*, in the law *verbum etiam par* (for an equal has no jurisdiction over an equal), in the Digest, under the heading *ad Trebellianum*, in the law *ille*, § *si tempestivum*, under the heading *de electione*, in the chapter *innocentiam tuendam*, in the Digest, under the heading *de actionibus*, in the law *nam magistratus*, and in the chapter *finalis*, under the heading *de rescriptis*, Book 6. Moreover, when a castle is restored, all rights are fully restored. Code, under the heading *de sententiis passim*, law 1, and law *finalis*; Digest, under the heading *de minoribus*, law *quod si minor*, and § *restitutio*; Decretum, Question 4, Chapter 1, chapter *reintegranda*. To this it is answered: that although the castle and the rights of the castle are restored, the restoration is understood, and ought to be understood, without prejudice to the right acquired by a third party, to whom the prince, by simply restoring, is not understood to generate prejudice. Digest, under the heading *ne quid in loco publico*, law 2, § *si quis a principe*; the case is found in the Code, under the heading *de remissione pignoris*, law *finalis*; the case is found in the chapter *quamvis*, under the heading *de rescriptis*, Book 6. Indeed, truly, this is not a true restoration, but rather a mere concession. For an action, once extinguished, never revives. Digest, under the heading *de solutionibus*, law *qui res*, § *aream*; under the heading *de conditionibus*, chapter 4, *quaeris*; and there is a case to similar effect in the said chapter *quamvis*, under the heading *de rescriptis*, Book 6. Therefore, the concession made regarding the castle, and the rights and faculties to absolve banished and condemned persons, does not prejudice the right acquired by a third party, unless the prince expressly states otherwise, which does not appear from the series of the concession. As in law 3, § *si quis a Principe*, Digest, under the heading *ne quid in loco publico*. But here an objection is immediately raised: although the goods, destroyed by confiscation of the castle, were liberated, nevertheless, by Lord Urban, in the concession made to Lord Albert, the ancient extinguished rights are revived. Or he grants new rights of subjection to that constructed castle. For Urban, in his concession, says: “provided, however, that you and the inhabitants are bound to provide cavalry, etc.” Therefore, it seems that he revives rights, or grants them anew. To this it is answered: that it is true that he revives, or grants, the rights of the castle which were previously extinguished; but it should not be inferred: therefore, he grants those rights in any respect. For by that concession, the prince does not intend to derogate from the right of a third party, as by the rights cited above. For it is always understood that a restoration, or concession, is made without prejudice to a third party, unless otherwise expressed. As in the said chapter *quamvis*, and there the case; and law 2, § *si quis a principe*; and law *finalis*, Code, under the heading *de remissione pignoris*. Therefore, those general words are to be understood legally. Decretals, under the heading *de iureiurando*, chapter *veniens*, and chapter *quintavallis*, and chapter 1, in the same title, Book 6; Digest, under the heading *de operis libertorum*, law *si libertus*. Especially since these goods passed with that freedom, by an onerous title, although by way of sale, and thus were bought for a higher price because of the freedom, and thus it is not probable that, by granting so generally, the prince wished to deprive the buyer of his right. It must, however, be noted that what has been said applies to unjust burdens imposed on persons on account of things. There are certain burdens which concern only the persons themselves. The buyer is free, since he is not subject to the castle. As in law *finalis*, Digest, under the heading *de iurisdictione omnium iudicum*; and law *cum bonus*, Digest, under the heading *de bonis auctore iudice possessis*; and chapter 2, under the heading *de constitutionibus*, Book 6. Just as, therefore, from burdens concerning persons, on account of goods, when the person principally subject to the burdens is not subjected, the goods which accrue to the person are not subjected. As in law *principalis*, Digest, under the heading *de regulis iuris*; and law *non dubium*, Code, under the heading *de legibus*; Decretals, under the heading *de fide instrumentorum*, chapter *inter dilectos*; and the rule *accessorium*, under the heading *de regulis iuris*, Book 6. But if the burdens were merely real, they pass to anyone; for the thing passes with its burden. Code, under the heading *sine censu vel reliqua*, laws 1, 2, and 3; Digest, under the heading *de pignoris actione*, law *sane*, and the following law, § *si fundus*; Decretum, Question 23, Chapter 1, *si tributum*; Question 12, Chapter 1, *si tributum*; under the heading *de decimis*, chapter *cum non sit*; under the heading *de pignoribus*, chapter *ex literis*. And this unless those rights were extinguished by the authority of the prince.

CASE. The point of the question on which the advice of a wise man is requested is as follows: that the castle of Corriualdi, in the province of the March of Ancona, was put in ruins on account of a rebellion formerly committed against the Roman Church, and remained uninhabited for a certain time. From this castle, certain men were in heresy, and persons condemned by the officials of the Church, whose goods were seized. For part of the cause, Lord Egidius, Bishop of Sabina, Cardinal Legate, sold them for a certain price to Lord John of Alegio, Rector of the aforementioned province, with all rights pertaining to the said goods and with clauses opportune in the sale. Finally, the said Lord John took possession of the said goods and held them, which he indeed left by right of legacy to his heir, the Lady, or instituted her as his heir in his goods. Finally, after a certain time and a space of eight years, Lord Urban, Pope V, granted the said castle, thus destroyed, in fief to Lord Nicholas of Naples, for himself, his sons, and nephews aforesaid. Therefore, Lord Nicholas, receiving possession of the said castle, restored it, fortified it, and wished the fortress to be garrisoned. He, wishing to have fruits and revenues due, seeks and compels all those possessing and holding possessions in the castle and its territory to pay the general subsidy which is imposed, which part of the Church imposes on all subjects. And chapter *omnibus subditis*. And not only that, but also to pay him collections and dues for the census and lease, which he himself annually pays to the Roman Camera of the Church, and for the salary of the castellan of the garrisoned castle of the constructed castle, for preserving the fidelity of the said Church, as well as to the power and rector of the said castle, and by provision made to Lord Nicholas as the natural lord of the castle of Corriualdi. To which, on behalf of the said Lady, it is objected and opposed, that the aforementioned goods, which were the proceeds of the said condemned rebels, having come into his hands as heir of the said Lord John, he is in no way bound to submit to and contribute to the said Lord in the declared burdens and payments, and that nothing is owed to him from them, and that he is believed to have good rights in these matters, asserting that those goods were bought from the Roman Church, etc., as will be seen in a certain counsel of Lord John of Lignano, a copy of which is sent with the present, and also a copy of the concession of the said castle made to the said Lord, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How the statement of Innocentius in the chapter *Cum ex iniuncto*, *de operibus novis*, is to be understood, namely: if a city, castle, or college is destroyed by the authority of a superior on account of its own offense, thereafter no one is a citizen or burgess there.
2. Whether one who purchases certain possessions from a church thereby also purchases exemption or immunity.
3. A church cannot grant to another the rights which it has sold to one person.
4. A vassal recovers all the rights which he had lost on account of felony, if his lord pardons him.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† First, it must be considered how the statement of Innocentius in c. Cum ex iniuncto, de novi operis nuntiatione, is to be understood, where he prevailed in the opinion that if a city, castle, or college is destroyed by the authority of a superior on account of its own delict, thereafter no one is a citizen or burgess there; for the castle loses all rights, just as one who has suffered death. For in this manner it suffers the greatest diminution of status (capitis deminutio), because it is turned into ashes. As stated in D. Quibus modis ususfructus amittitur, l. Si ususfructus; l. Excepta; and as noted in D. De usufructu legato, l. Ususfructu municipibus. This is especially so when, due to rebellion, they fail and place themselves among the number of enemies. D. De maiestate diminuta, l. Qui deficiunt. And they fall into the crime of lèse-majesté, which is condemned ipso facto. C. Ad legem Iuliam maiestatis, l. Quisquis. Therefore, such rebellions are notorious, whence they do not require a sentence. D. De actione empti, l. Emptorem; and as noted in D. De infamibus, l. Ictus fustium; and in c. Tua; and in c. Vestra, de cohabitatione clericorum et mulierum. And it adds that Innocentius notes in c. Dilecta, de excessibus praelatorum, in the sine, where it is held that they may be destroyed by the mandate of superiors and their word. But when the principal is destroyed, the accessory is destroyed. Hence, when the castle is destroyed, the territory of the castle is destroyed. D. De servitutibus rusticorum praediorum, l. 3, §. Qui habet iustum. Just as a dead and extinguished man has nothing of those things which are held as unwritten. L. Si in metallum, de conditionibus et demonstrationibus; L. Interdictum, ad Trebellianum; L. Ex facto, §. Si quis rogatus fuerit liberis filiis, D. De negotiis gestis; L. 3, §. Haec verba; and as noted in L. Eius qui in provincia, in principio, si certum petatur. Thus, the castle, and its form, and in its essence, being destroyed with its captives, has also lost its forms. D. De secundis tabulis, l. Qui ex liberis, §. Testamento. And it is expressly stated in D. De legatis tertio, l. Pater, §. Tusculanus. And these things are true when it is destroyed with right. See if by chance and by fate. For cases are the judges of fortunes. D. De negotiis gestis, sed in ultimo. Also, if by the providence of a superior, because the castle was weak and on the border of enemies, it was not acted upon for the good. C. De officio praefecti praetorio, l. In nomine Domini. Therefore, the territory agrees with the castle, and the accessory with the principal. D. De collegiis illicitis, l. 1, in fine; for the accessory does not stand by itself. D. De fundo dotali, l. Si cui; D. De peculio legato, l. 2; and as noted in Inst. De legatis, §. Si quis ancillas. Namely, the territory of the castle is called that which corresponds to it in jurisdiction. L. Si pupillus, §. Territorium. Innocentius says in c. Cum ad sedem, de restitutione spoliatorum, which is to be understood regarding pedanean jurisdiction, or customary jurisdiction. As noted in Auth. De defensoribus civitatum, §. Nullam videtur, col. 3, in the great gloss, in fine. It applies in D. De tutoribus et curatoribus datis ab his, l. Ubi absunt. From this jurisdiction they can impose burdens and taxes among themselves for their subsidies and necessities, for example, for paying debts. As noted in L. 1, §. Quibus, quod cuiusque universitatis nomine; and L. 1, D. Quod quisque iuris, per Jacobus de Belvisio. But just as the castle is extinguished, all its jurisdiction is void. C. De caducis tollendis, §. Pro secundo. It supports what is noted in C. De poenis, l. Servus, per Cynus. But nevertheless, these are to be understood when the castle is destroyed by a definitive sentence of a lower court, or by the mandate of the prince. For inferiors, who are subject to laws, cannot inflict capital punishments without a definitive sentence, unless the crime is notorious. L. Divus, de custodia reorum; and L. Quod ad statum, de poenis. Hence, it must be established that the crime exists, and then it is pronounced regarding the right of the fisc. L. Eius qui delatorem. And therefore, if the castle was not demolished by a preceding sentence, nor by the prince—for in the prince the order of law is not required, and therefore the prince is always excepted from the rules of law, as noted by Innocentius in c. In causis, de re iudicata—certainly, demolition made by the impulse of an inferior does not deprive the castle of its rights as to its status; because it does not draw with it the effect that it is in order. D. De re iudicata, l. Si cum nulla. Therefore, the counsel of the said excellent man must be understood in a particular person, by a preceding sentence of demolition, by force or command of the Pope. Otherwise, it would not be true. D. De re militari, l. 3, §. Si ad diem. Especially because corporations do not properly commit delicts, nor do they truly fall into the crime of high treason. D. De poenis, l. Aut facta, §. Si ecclesia. Therefore, how I understand it, it supports what Innocentius notes in c. Dilectus filiae, de simonia. Secondly, it must be seen,

Whether he who purchases certain possessions from a church thereby acquires exemption or immunity from some jurisdiction. It must be said that either he purchases under the name of fields, or under the name of territory. In the first case, no jurisdiction or exemption follows. As noted by Innocentius in *De uno pacto*, chapter *Ex literis*. For jurisdiction is something universal, and therefore it is not contained within a body individually designated. See *Institutes*, *De fideicommissis hereditatibus*, § *Si quis una*; and note *De transactionibus*, chapter *Controversia quamquam*. Although, nevertheless, the signification of "field" does not signify jurisdiction; otherwise, the action of the intellect is judged differently regarding jurisdiction than regarding a field, nor is the definition the same, and therefore they are distinct. Hence, he who purchases a thing from the fisc, although he acquires it with full right, as in *L. Bene a Zenone*, nevertheless must bear public fiscal burdens, and by this he is not exempt or immune. See *Digest*, *De publicis licitationibus*, § *Finis*. This is understood, but not in *L. 1*, *Codex*, *Ne fiscus rem quam vendidit evincat*, Book 10. In the second case, he acquires jurisdiction, that is, the benefits of jurisdiction. For a church cannot sell direct or inseparable jurisdiction. As noted in *Authenticum*, *Quomodo oportet episcopos*, in the beginning; *De re iudicata*, chapter *Cum Bertoldus*; *De contrahenda emptione*, *L. Immodicis*; *De acquirenda domini*, *L. Quaedam*.

Thirdly, it must be known that a church cannot grant to another the rights which are being sold. As stated in l. siue, auth. §. si duobus, de publicis, de legibus 1; l. non quocunque, §. qui Gaium. Moreover, in general terms, those things which are specially assigned to another are not included. As stated in ff. de legibus 1, l. quod in rerum; §. si quis post, de peculio; l. seruo, manu, de funerariis instrumentis; l. Seiae, §. Tirannae. Furthermore, in restitution, those things which do not pertain to the free and equitable power of the person making restitution are not included. As noted in de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, §. et quid si tantum; and in c. quamuis, de rescriptis, lib. 6.

Fourthly, it must be concluded from the foregoing that either Lord John de Angelo purchased the jurisdictional rights, in which case the dominus Nicolaus has no power over the things purchased, nor can he transfer them to another. As stated in l. sicuti, §. aristo, si servitus vendicetur. For then the territory would have been divided from the superior. As stated in ff. de accessione, l. si eadem; ff. de finium regundorum, l. eos. And therefore new boundaries would have to be observed, not the old ones. Or he purchased patrimonial rights, namely the goods formerly belonging to Tirius, and then Lord Nicolaus has that power over these goods which he has over the other goods of the ancient territory. For words which make mention of territory cannot be understood otherwise than of the customary territory. As stated in ff. de auro et argento legato, l. si uxor, mundus, §. 1, in the words "esse solebat"; and by argument from ff. de hereditate instituenda, l. ex facto, §. rerum autem. Otherwise it would follow that he would have power over things which, in no succession or sale, were exchanged for others, which is false: because it removes what is unworthy and restores the benevolent restitution. As stated in the aforementioned l. fina., C. de sententiis passis. Note, as I said, in this case of a legal contract, the buyer acquires no exemption from public burdens. And therefore, that which is not found to be exempt remains included under the law of the universitas. As stated in de militum testamento, l. tribunus, §. fina.; and ff. de fundo instruento, l. quaesitum, §. idem.

He responds again and argues: because before the restitution there was memory, and not the thing itself; and after the restitution made by the prince, there exists both memory and the thing. Note this in l. sicut, §. sed quod cuiusque universi nomine. And he did the same thing that rights ought to do regarding the evils or benefits of a marriage dissolved by mutual consent. For all rights are restored which derived their regime from the former marriage. As stated in ff. de rerum amotione, l. licet, ad fin.; so also in l. peculium, §. uxor. To the same effect is the rule that a legacy extinguished by enmity revives and is restored on account of friendship and good grace. As stated in ff. de adimendis legatis, l. 3, §. fi.; and l. iterum.

† This also supports the same point, namely what is recorded concerning the lord who pardoned his vassal for felony: because the vassal recovers all rights of prohibition. As noted in D. de poenis, l. Peculium, § Si haeres. To the same effect is what is noted in C. de bonis vacantibus, l. Si quando; and D. de constitutionibus principum, l. Beneficium; and D. de contrahenda emptione, l. 1, in fine; and D. de in iustis testamento, l. Si quis filio exheredato, § Penultimus; and what is noted in the aforementioned l. Si, C. de sententiis passis, in the gloss and the doctors. And thus I say, and I, Baldus, advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether and when a person who burns or defaces a written document is liable for the crime of forgery.
2. A witness is not said to give false testimony when his statement can be verified by some interpretation.
3. To succeed to a partnership with someone can be understood in two ways.
casus:
CASE. The question is whether, by virtue of a single accusation of false institution brought by Albert, notary of Variis, of Ponte Pietra, against Laurentius, a certain man of the Lord Marcus de Magistris, before the judge of malefices of the commune of Verona, having seen the acts and proceedings in the said process, and all the individual rights and allegations of the said parties, and the statutes of the commune of Verona alleged and produced by the said parties, the aforementioned Laurentius should be condemned or absolved from the said cause, or what are the duties of the judge of the middle regarding the said accusation and the entire aforementioned process, having first seen all the acts and proceedings as above.

Furthermore, whether by virtue and on the occasion of a single accusation of the production of false witnesses instituted by the undersigned Laurentius de Magistris against the undersigned Albert, notary of Variis, before the undersigned judge of malefices of the commune of Verona, having seen the acts and proceedings in the said cause and in the entire process as above, the aforementioned Albert, notary of Variis, should be condemned or absolved from the said cause, or what are the duties of the judge of the middle regarding the said accusation and the entire said process, having first seen all the acts and proceedings as above.

Furthermore, whether in proceeding on both processes concerning florins, injury was inflicted upon Laurentius de Magistris, who is mentioned in the said processes by the judge of the middle proceeding, and by the judge cognizant of the cause and sentence.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It must be premised for the sake of clarity,

† That sometimes a person draws up a memorandum book for himself alone, so that he may remember matters done by the vision of the writing, it is lawful for him to burn and scrape such writings: because he does injury to no one. Hence it is that a testator can delete his will, and can make it so that it does not appear, nor can it be read or understood. D. 28.5.1 (De his quae in testamento delentur), l. 1; and D. 49.16.5.1 (De militum testamento), l. Tribunus, §. ult.; C. 6.23.1 (De testamentis), l. Vrannius. And he who in such writings, which harm no one, writes falsely, is not liable for the crime of falsification. As noted in C. 9.11.1 (De falsis), l. Clauibus, in the gloss. But why?

Sometimes a person draws up a writing for another only, as a banker and a notary; and then he is liable for falsification if he writes falsely, or commits falsification in another way, as in C. 9.11.1 (De falsis), l. Si quis decurio; C. 3.36.1 (De haereticis), c. Fraternitatis, per Innocentius III; D. 48.10.1.1 (Ad legem Corneli de falsis), l. 1, §. Qui rationibus, with countless similar authorities.

Sometimes a person draws up a writing for himself and for another, as a partner who compiles a book of accounts. D. 12.2.1 (De edendo), l. Quidam, in principio; and as noted in C. 4.20.1 (De usuris), c. 1; and Clem. 5.19.1 (De usuris), Non inuicem. Partners are deemed to mandate each other that each one draw up an account of his acts; for whoever is bound to render an account is also bound to draw it up. D. 26.1.1.1 (De tutelis et rationibus distractis), l. 1, §. Officio; C. 4.19.1 (De edendo), in the gloss; C. 1.17.1 (De rescriptis), l. 1, per Jacobus de Belvis; D. 12.1.1 (De conditione et demonstratione), l. Cum seruus; D. 32.1.1 (De legatis primo), l. Si seruus uetitus; D. 40.12.1 (De manumissione testamento), l. Quod filius, with many similar authorities. And such accounts, if they are probable, create some degree of credibility and give rise to prescription. As noted in D. 12.2.1 (De edendo), l. Quaedam, §. Numularios. And even if they do not create credibility against him, as noted in D. 39.5.1 (De donationibus), l. Nuda, per Bartolus, nevertheless from such a writing the right of proof is acquired by the adversary. And therefore, if falsification is committed therein by scraping or burning, so that the truth does not appear, the doer is liable for the crime of falsification. As noted in the said l. Damnis and the said §. Qui rationibus, at least after someone has used such a writing in court or before an arbitrator. As in C. 4.20.1 (De probationibus), l. Iubemus; and C. 2.21.1 (De fide instrumentorum), l. Fin. For just as the acts are common, so is their production; just as the accounts of the acts, against the producer, create what is noted in D. 12.2.1 (De edendo), l. 1, §. Editiones; and D. 26.10.1 (De administratione tutorum), l. Chirographis; and C. 2.29.1 (De officio delegati), c. Cum in iure; and C. 4.20.1 (De probationibus), c. Quoniam contra falsam, per Innocentius III; D. 48.10.1 (De falsis), l. Quis obrepsit; D. 49.14.1 (De iure fisci), l. In fraudem, §. Quotiens. For after production, that which has been produced always begins to be in the power of the judge. C. 4.20.1 (De testibus), l. Nullum; D. 46.1.1 (Qui satisdare cogantur), l. De die, in principio, per Jacobus de Belvis; D. 47.2.1 (De furtis), l. Sempronia libellus; D. 48.10.1 (De falsis), l. Athletas. To burn accounts that have been produced is not theft. D. 48.10.1, l. Fin., §. Fuit autem, there: "nor with bad faith," etc. And for examining the cause why he burned them, torture is lawful. As in C. 9.11.1 (De falsis), l. Vbi. For this happened by the dolus of the burner, and the dolus is established, since falsity is nothing other than the adulteration of the truth. As in Auth. 3.21.1 (De instrumentorum cautione et fide), circa principium. Concerning the burning, we do not need witnesses: because the defendant confessed spontaneously, although he claims it was lawful to excuse the sin; nevertheless, as I said, it was not lawful, although he had already used it before arbitrators, who are reduced to the status of judges in matters that constitute proof of fact. C. 2.55.1 (De arbitris), l. Pen. This whole matter, namely scraping and burning, because they tend to one end only, namely that the truth does not appear, must be considered as one single offense. C. 11.38.1 (De servis fugitivis), l. Quicumque, per Iac. de Arena, according to D. 9.2.1 (Ad legem Aquiliam), l. Illud, §. Si; and per Dy. in D. 47.2.1, l. Nunquam plura. And by this the first and second points aforementioned are answered; and it supports what is read and noted in D. 43.1.1 (Ad municipalem), l. Titio, §. Cum esset, in principio; D. 4.3.1 (De dolo), l. Quidam.

It remains to be seen what is the law regarding the accusation of Laurentius against Albertus. To this end, it must be premised that a witness is not said to give false testimony when his statement can be verified by some interpretation, as stated in Extra, De testibus, Contumacibus, c. Filii; and noted by Innocentius in Extra, De rescriptis, c. Causamque. Furthermore, it must be premised that

† That one succeeds in a partnership with another can be understood in two ways. In one way, incidentally, regarding the thing itself, for example, if two partners purchase the rights of a third party; or in another way, principally, and by agreement. For example, two persons purchase, or acquire by another title, the rights of one of the same partners. And it is agreed that they are partners therein, and that the partnership nevertheless remains in them. And this is a new partnership, and one departs, and another enters. Or if this was agreed upon from the beginning. D. pro socio, l. cum duobus, § si quis, and § Idem Mela, with many others. According to the first interpretation, the testimony can be verified, as appears from the public instrument. However, it must be considered here that sometimes a witness testifies truthfully and truly, sometimes falsely and truly. For if a witness testifies to the truth as perceived by his senses, then he speaks truly and truthfully. But if he testifies to a falsehood, and says that he was present and perceived it, he testifies falsely and falsely. But if he testifies to a falsehood in itself, in that he did not see it, and asserts that he saw it, he testifies truly regarding the existence of the terms in themselves; however, on account of the false rendering of the cause, he testifies falsely. C. si ex falsis instrumentis, l. 3. But if a witness testifies that something is such as it is commonly seen to be, although it is not, he testifies falsely regarding the thing, i.e., the true intention. For example, if he testifies regarding the office of praetor of Carbone, or regarding a golden chest in a cista, which was in the marrow, and he did not see it. For all senses are a certain surface of the human body, and nothing more is required of a witness than that he testify truly superficially, or to the eye, or to another sense. D. de verbis oblig., l. stipulatio ista, § his quoque; D. de testibus, l. testium officium. The office of a witness is not to decide, but to discern according to the matter of the senses. As noted by Innocentius, D. de testibus, c. cum causam; and C. de testibus, l. testium. Therefore, I do not think that the witness who spoke of the succession in the said partnership told a lie, and consequently Albertus ought to be absolved. It is true that many acts were sent to me, which I could not see all of due to their multitude; but the substantial ones, from which it appears to me principally, are such that the confession, of which it is testified, is an act capable of repetition, and that what was not said once could be said another time. D. de fide instrumentorum, c. cum Ioannes heremita. And because the confession accords with the truth, whence it is presumed in favor of the witness who says that it emanated therefrom. D. de testibus, l. ob carmen, § fi.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Those who enact statutes do not incur any penalty if they do not seek confirmation.
2. Communities can enact statutes concerning their own particular property, nor do such statutes require specific confirmation.
3. One to whom the power of providing has been granted does not need another confirmation.
casus: CASE. In the name of God, Amen. The point of the question is this: a certain Blasius gave in marriage to a certain Peter one of his nieces, namely, the daughter of one of his sons, and promised for her dowry florins of gold in this form, namely, one piece of land with its boundaries, and 30 florins of gold at the request of the said Peter, and 50 florins of gold after the death of the said Blasius at the request of the said Peter. And in the said promise the said Blasius bound himself to the said Peter, present and accepting, by himself and all his goods, and promised to make an instrument of the said promise at the request of the said Peter. Finally, the said Blasius died. After the death of the said Blasius, it was pronounced in the court of the episcopate of Perugia that the said Blasius had been a usurer, and all his contracts were usurious. After the said pronouncement, the said Peter took possession of certain goods which had belonged to the said Blasius, in virtue of the aforementioned promise made concerning the said dowery to the said Peter, which goods the said Peter holds and possesses. Now, certain persons, with whom the said Blasius had contracted usuries for a long time before the said promise of dowry was made to the said Peter, demanded the said usuries upon the said goods seized by the said Peter in virtue of the dowry promised to him, and presupposing that in the said inheritance of the said Blasius a discussion [of assets] was made, and presupposing that the contracts of the said persons claiming restitution of usuries were celebrated for a long time before the said promise of dowry was made to the said Peter, now it is asked, what is the law? I, Baldus.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.
† That the said statutors do not incur the penalty is proved by the underwritten reasons. The first reason is,

† that communities can enact statutes regarding their own peculiar property, nor do such statutes require any other singular confirmation, as is fully noted in ff. quod quisque iuris. l. 1. §. 1. by Iaco. Bu.; for if a private person can impose upon his own property whatever law he wishes, therefore a universitas can as well; and this case is seen in ff. quod ui aut clam. l. prohibere. §. plane. there: "unless a municipal law", etc., as noted by Guli. de Cu. in l. j. post prin. ff. de iusti. et iur. Secondly, this seems to be proved here because in a confirmation the thing confirmed is included, ff. de haer. insti. l. asse toto; de condi. insti. l. illa institutio; but the laws of the commune of Trevi, which spoke specially of the things to be enacted in this case, were confirmed: therefore, etc. Thirdly, it is proved because, since the power of enacting statutes has been granted, it can henceforth be said that what the law itself concedes was sought by prayers in vain, as in l. j. C. de Thes. li. 10; de condit. insti. l. quae sus conditione. §. j.; de origine iuris. l. 2. §. deinde ex his. Fourthly, it proves that when a disposition is made concerning something, such disposition passes to those things which are the consequence of the things disposed, l. Lucius. qui potiores in pig. hab.; but that statute was the consequence of the things granted and approved: therefore, etc. Fifthly, by like reason, if a principal testament is confirmed, an accessory one is also confirmed, ad Treb. l. apud Iulianum. §. inde Iulianus; therefore so it is here. Sixthly, because we deservedly make our own all things to which our authority is imparted, l. 1. de veteri iu. enuc.; but here the authority is present through which they are placed in charge, in ver. 4; therefore, joining all things together, the penalty is not incurred.

† Seventhly, because when the power of providing is granted to someone, from the signification of this word "prouideas" (you should provide), another confirmation is not required; whence we say that persons elected require the confirmation of a superior, but persons provided do not need to be confirmed; this is supported by what is noted by Inn. in c. in literis. de off. de leg., and is supported by de dote praelega. l. Theopompus. with similar texts. Eighthly, and lastly, I adduce specially to this the statement of Iaco. de Arena in l. 2. de orig. iuris, who says that if the provision of some business is committed to someone by a council, and they provide, that it does not appear that it should afterwards be brought back to the council; these are the words of Iaco. de Are. in d. l. 2. §. postea. Moved by which reasons, I believe the penalty of the constitution has not been incurred, saving always the truth, to which I submit myself.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Upon the death of one of the substitutes while the instituted heirs are still living, to whom does the share accrue: to the instituted heirs, or to the other substitutes?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the will of John, son of another John of Tudert, in which he instituted as universal heirs Lady Margaret, his wife, and Jacobellus, his servant, each of them for an equal share, with this condition, that after the death of both of them the said inheritance of his should succeed and ought to succeed to Thomas, his heir, for two parts, and to a certain Andrew for the other third part. And assuming that one of the substitutes has died without surviving children and descendants of the said lady and servant and the other of the substitutes, and with a certain sister of Thomas surviving, it is asked of me, if one of these substitutes were to die, whether then the other instituted heir would succeed, or rather the surviving substitute, or the aforementioned sister.

† As to the first point, it must be said that the coheir does not succeed, but rather the substituting heir who supervenes. For the substituting heir excludes the jointly instituted heir. As stated in Codex, De Cancellatione Tabularum, §. pro secundo. And this is proven by Digestum, Ad Trebellianum, l. Lucius, §. Gayo. And it is noted in the commentary on the Falcidian law, l. haeresedes mei, §. cum ita. And those words “Thomasius, and his heir, etc.” are understood to refer to the descendants of Thomasius, not to his sister, nor to an extraneous heir of any of the substituted persons. For such is the common usage of speaking and understanding. And so it is noted in Digestum, Ad Trebellianum, l. ex facto, §. si. Although certain doctors teach the contrary by means of l. sciendum, De Verborum Significatione, and this is noted by Cynus in Codex, De Operibus Liberatorum, t. liberti libertaeque, and by others in l. ut iureiurando, §. si liberi, De Operibus Liberatorum. Nevertheless, according to the common usage of speaking, the first opinion is more correct. And because it is understood to refer to a similar heir, in whom the testator’s affection falls, i.e., the descendants, and the aforementioned is understood subject to the Trebellianic fourth, which is owed to those instituted. As in Digestum, De Fideicommissis, primo, l. haeredi, and l. Marcellus, Ad Trebellianum, with many similar cases. In which, whether fruits are computed, see Digestum, Ad Trebellianum, l. in fideicommissi, and Codex, Familiae Eriscundae, l. filium quem habentem, and Digestum, De Inofficioso Testamento, l. Papinianus, §. conditioni.

CASE. In the name of God, and of His Glorious Virgin Mother, Amen. The point is as follows. John, formerly of Bartolus, or the Marvellous, of Urbino, made his testament, in which he instituted his son Francis as his universal heir, and ordered that the said Francis, before the age of 25 years, could not sell or alienate any of his movable or immovable goods, without the license of the rectors of the fraternity of St. Mary of Planomercati, and the custodian of the Minor Friars of the said city, except in case of necessity, or adverse judgment. And if he did otherwise, he willed that the said goods sold should devolve to the fraternity of St. Mary, and he commanded that, should it happen, the said Francis made an instrument of sale of certain things formerly of the said testator, with the consent of one rector of the said fraternity, the others being absent and not consulted, and it is said that the said Francis did not receive the price, but that the tutor of the university submitted a tutor, and received him, and after a short interval of time, that rector placed the said rector in his place, and thereafter the said Francis died. It is asked to whom the said sold goods belong, assuming as constant that the sale was made before the lapse of 25 years.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Where a son is instituted heir, with the prohibition that he may not sell before the age of 25 years without the counsel of a certain fraternity, otherwise that the sold goods shall devolve to the fraternity, namely, if he sells with the counsel of one rector of the said fraternity, the others being absent and not consulted, whether the goods devolve to the said fraternity.
body:
On the said point, I consider two things: either the said sale was simulated, which can be proven, and therefore it is invalid; thus, the said goods belong to the heir of the said Francis. C. *plus valere quod agitur*; L. *emphyteusis*; and in the rubric and black letter. Indeed, possession is not transferred by a simulated contract. D. *de aqua et aquae pluviae arcendae*, L. *emptor*.

If the sale was not simulated, but genuine—which is presumed in case of doubt—then, because the said Francis, before the lapse of 25 years, sold against the command of the testator, the sale of the said things was made without the license of the rectors, and then the transfer is made to the said fraternity. D. *de legatis* 2, L. *cum pater*, § *libertis*; D. *de legatis* 1, L. *filius familias*, § *divus severus*, with its subject matter. Although one consented, the consent of one is not sufficient where that of several is required. C. *de auctoritate praestanda*, L. *si*; D. *de servo communi manumittendo*, L. 1, by the argument from the special case.

However, although the said goods have devolved to the said fraternity, if the said fraternity and its members acted otherwise, and if the said goods were deceitfully restored to the heirs of the said Francis as aforesaid, and the rights competent to the same were ceded to the said heirs, it should be believed that his father, wishing to take wholesome counsel for his son—to which paternal piety always inclines and bends, as D. *de adulteriis*, L. *nec in ea*—therefore wished to confer the goods, which were to be sold by the son to the aforementioned fraternity, and to restrain his son by fear of the aforementioned penalty, curbing the youthful heat which is commonly prone to squandering patrimony, as L. *si*, § *filius autem*, C. *de bonis quae liberis*. This was not done with regard to the fraternity itself, since it is probable that the testator did not prefer the fraternity to his son, or another, especially in this case, since he watched with all diligence and careful attention that the said goods should in no way depart from the dominion of his son. To this effect: C. *de fideicommissis*, L. *cum acutissimi*; C. *de institutionibus et substitutionibus*, L. *generaliter in ratione sui*; and C. *de inofficioso testamento*, L. *filius matrem*; and D. *ad Trebellianam*, L. *Imperator*.

And thus I say and advise, I, Angelus de Perusio, doctor of laws. And to the truth of the aforesaid, I have written and subscribed, and signed with my usual seal of my name. And the same I say and advise, and I deem it equitable, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws. And to the truth, I have subscribed and signed with my seal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
0. A legacy is valid if proven by three witnesses.
1. The legitime is deducted from the legatee appointed for pious causes.
2. Property that, after the death of the sons, is subject to institution may be given in dowry by the daughter: and the husband acquires one-half according to the form of the statutes.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. The fact is presented as follows: a certain Francischellus is said to have made a will in which he instituted his children Bartholomew and Letitia as his heirs, and if they died without children, he bequeathed a certain parcel of land to the church of St. Bartholomew. Upon the death of the said testator, Bartholomew died. Letitia, however, married Andrew of Città di Castello, and gave as dowry the said parcel of land and certain others. Finally, the said Letitia died without children; thus, the condition of the said legacy is also said to have materialized. For this reason, the rector of the said church claims the said legacy, namely the bequeathed property, and has proved the legacy through three witnesses. Now it is asked whether the said proof is sufficient, and if it is sufficient, whether the legitime must be deducted; and since by the form of the statute of Città di Castello the husband ought to gain half of the dowry, it is asked whether the said Andrew can defend himself in the said half on account of the said statute. And not going through arguments, I come to the points:
† And I say first that the said bequest is valid, because it is made to pious causes; extra, de testa. c. cum esses and c. relatum.

† On the second point, I say that the legitime can be deducted from this property if there were other bequests that exceeded two-thirds (the bes). And because it is not proved that there were other bequests, the legitime ought not to be deducted; in auth. nov. and l. quam in priorib. On the third point, I say

† that property which, after the death of the children, is subject to restitution can be given in dowry and alienated by the daughter; C. de leg. auth. res quae, pro modo, namely fitting to the station of the persons. Whence the favor of the dowry prevails over the favor of the bequest, from which it follows that the husband ought to have half by the form of the statute de iud. exigere dotem, although it is not entirely clear, because a statute ought not to prejudice the church. Likewise, nor does that auth. res quae seem to be able to prejudice churches; de consti. c. ecclesia S. Mariae. Whence that authentic does not seem to have place in bequests to churches and pious places. To the contrary, that the law and the statute are valid, because this is a legal provision on account of the burdens of marriage, and it is favorable and pious. And the law speaks generally; whence it ought to be understood generally; l. in fraudem, § fi., de mil. test. For even an agreement on gaining entered into in good faith would be valid through the said authentic; therefore, this statute is also equitable enough, lest the father appear to have imposed widowhood upon the daughter, who otherwise would not have found a husband except with a dowry and the expectation of the aforesaid statute; C. de indic. vi. l. 2. and in auth. cui relictum, in the gloss sed an idem. And thus I believe it can be defended in law, although this case is very doubtful. CASE. The fact is as follows: A certain Luculus made a will; among other things that he disposed of in the said will, he left to a certain Peter of Coraduccio certain houses, which the said Peter would and ought to have at his demand after the death of the said lady Paulella, wife of the testator himself and his universal heir; of which houses the said lady Paulella had and ought to have during her life habitation, as long as she lived virtuously and maintained a widowed life, and not otherwise; and that the said lady Paulella, being a widow, cannot and ought not to be molested or disturbed by anyone during her life in the inheritance of the said houses in any way, but that after her death they should devolve by full right, with the aforesaid condition, upon the said Peter. After the death of the testator, the said lady Paulella, instituted universal heir, repudiated the inheritance. It is asked whether the said Peter can have the said houses during the life of the said lady, or whether the said lady ought to have the inheritance of the houses themselves, notwithstanding the aforesaid repudiation.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an heir, having renounced the inheritance, may claim a legacy.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.
