† That the said lady ought to have the said legacy, having repudiated the inheritance by her, since she was the sole heir instituted, appears to be a case according to the letter of the law. D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. Si patroni, §. Quid ergo; and there by Doctorus; and l. Filio, D. de legatis 1, by Doctorus; and l. Qui filiabus, §. Finis, eodem titulo, by Bartolus. The contrary, however, seems to be said by the exception of the codicillary clause. For it is not claimed as from the will, but as from intestacy; and thus, excluded under one head, he is admitted under another. As in l. Lucius, §. Filiam, D. de legatis 2; and l. Filius, D. de bonis liberti. This question is very doubtful on account of the reason of the said §. Quid ergo. Nevertheless, lest the codicillary clause be in vain, I think it more correct that she did not cast off the said legacy made to the wife uselessly from the will, which flowed in; yet usefully from intestacy, D. de legatis 1, l. Legatum, §. Heredi. And therefore Peter cannot claim the legacy while the said lady is alive. D. de usufructu legato, l. Uxori usufructus villae. And so I say, and I counsel. I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, subscribe to the truth and sign with the marks of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If several officials have extorted something, and one of them, on his deathbed, orders that it be restored, it is to be declared by the bishop whether the bishop ought to declare it in solidum or according to shares.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. Certain priors of the city of Todi, with appropriate counsel, imposed a certain tax upon the clerics, which was collected from them. Nevertheless, one of them, on his deathbed, confessed this and, on account thereof, bound himself to restore that sum, which would be determined by the Lord Bishop of Todi.

† It is asked what, and to what extent, must be declared by the lord bishop. The caution contains a certain quantity. It must be considered, however, from where the said quantity descends. For when the obligation descends upon several officials, by common dolus, each is held liable in solidum; but when by culpa, each is held liable pro rata. As in D. de magistratibus conveniendis, l. Magistratibus. Likewise, when several are bound by a delict, each is held liable in solidum. D. de iure omnium iudicum, l. A deo; C. de conditionibus furtivis, l. 1. Because by delict several become debtors in solidum; but if by quasi-delict, each is held liable for his share by reason of office. For office counts as delict. D. de publicanis, l. Si multi; D. vi bonorum raptorum, l. 2, § Si publicanus. Otherwise in persons who do not exercise any office. D. de his qui deiecerunt vel effuderunt, l. 1, in fine, with the following law. But this does not seem true, because a transgressor of the canons cannot be excused from dolus, since he openly acts against the precepts of the canons. X. de immunitate ecclesiae, c. Non nummis; and c. Adversus. Likewise, the priors of Todi, which are considered as clerics, similar to private persons. X. de constitutionibus, c. Ecclesia S. Mariae. And therefore it seems that each who participated and consented may be sued in solidum. And such caution is valid after the death of the delinquent, as in X. de sepulturis, c. Parochi; and in c. Quamquam, de usu, lib. 6. Whatever therefore appears to have been extorted, may be demanded in solidum from any one. But by one pardon or rescript, the others are released from the burden of restitution. As in the said l. 2, C. de conditionibus furtivis. Nor are they excused as individuals; because they sinned as a body. l. 1, § 1, D. de magistratibus conveniendis; l. 1, § 1, D. quod quisque iuris. And therefore it is very dangerous to participate and give one’s voice in such matters. And this supports the above. D. de administratione tutorum, l. Tres tutores; D. quod vi aut clam, l. Semper, § Si in sepulchro. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A paternal uncle on both sides, who is related on both sides, is preferred to a maternal uncle, who is not related on both sides, in the goods of a deceased ward, and even in maternal goods.
casus: CASE. A certain girl named Nouella, daughter and universal heir intestate of the late Andrea, her father, and of the late Helena, her mother, died intestate, and in pupillary age, with surviving in the nearest degree Thomas, her uncle, a priest, brother of the said Andrea, under whose care the said girl remained, and at whose house she died; and Angelino, her maternal uncle, brother of the said Helena, mother of the said girl, but not to the same parents, and two cousins of the said girl, one of whom is the son of the said Angelino. Now it is asked what, and of what kind, is the succession of the same. Likewise, since certain debts and expenses of illness, death, and funeral of the father and daughter of the aforementioned are imminent to the inheritance of the said deceased girl, it is asked whether before all things the debts and such expenses ought to be deducted and paid from the said inheritance.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† The aforementioned uncle is preferred in the said succession: because he is related on both sides. For a double connection is more effective than a single one. As in the Authentica "De consanguineis et uterinis fratribus," §. "Si," where it says that those who avail themselves of a double right exclude those who can avail themselves of only one, Codex, "Communia de successionibus," Authentica "Itaque." Although those laws do not establish this rule except for brothers and the children of brothers: nevertheless, reason being considered, it is perhaps safer. But even assuming that he were not an uncle: nevertheless, because he did not lawfully accept the guardianship, nor did he have another appointed, he would be deprived. Codex, "De legitimis haeredibus," law "Sciant." But cousins do not succeed, because they are more remote in degree. As in the Authentica "Post fratres." As for expenses, and things alienated, there is no doubt that they must be paid before legacies. This uncle did not accept the guardianship within the year. And therefore he seems to be deprived of the inheritance. I answer: this uncle was a priest: and civil law does not bind priests, nor is their guardianship necessary. Codex, "De episcopis et clericis," law "Presbyter," and Authentica "Presbyteros." But the inheritance of the mother, according to the said Novella, pertains to the said uncle: because it was not entered upon in the name of the said girl; therefore it was transmitted to the uncle, unless the uncle, on behalf of the girl, sought restitution in full, as stated in the law "Qui duos," "De rebus dubiis," according to Jacobus de Arena and Bartolus. The year for deliberation has elapsed; so much time has passed after infancy. And thus I say, and I advise. I, Baldo de Ubaldis, Doctor of both laws, have written and signed with the signs of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Agreements of inferiors cannot be made to the prejudice of superiors.
casus: CASE. Finally, in the current year, the Reverend Father and Lord B. Philip, Bishop of Savona, Vicar and co., decreed a privilege, among other things, that concerning all and each of the malefices, excesses, and crimes committed, and which shall be committed in the future, in the City, county, and district of Spoleto, through inquisition, denunciation, or accusation, cognizance shall be taken by the vicar of the said City of Spoleto for the Holy Roman Church, and of all judges, or judges, and that all pecuniary penalties and fines to be imposed on account of the aforementioned malefices, excesses, and crimes ought to come, and do come, into the hands of the chamberlain of the said commune, from which the salaries of the officials are to be paid. It is now asked whether the aforementioned castles are bound to contribute to the expenses of the said commune of Spoleto in proportion according to their capacity, by virtue of the aforementioned first privilege, and whether an estimation of their goods ought to be made, as contained therein, or not. Also, whether cognizance of the crimes committed and to be committed in the said castles pertains to the vicar of the aforementioned city and his judge, and whether the penalties for the aforementioned crimes ought to come into the hands of the said chamberlain of the said commune, as contained in the second privilege, or not. Having seen and considered the said privileges, and pacts, and their tenor and words, the reason for which is stated as constant, as is set forth above.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

The aforesaid matters, concerning which they are established, were in themselves lawful and were to be observed, and are so, provided that in that respect in which the superior ordered the contrary. For from a pact the right of the superior is always understood to be excepted, as in Extra, De iureiurando, in the chapter Veniens. Because the pact of an inferior cannot bind the power of a superior, nor derogate from private right, as in Digest, De pactis, the law Inter debitorem; and De decurionibus, the constitution Vacuitis, Book 6. Nor can subjects put their mouth into the sky, and restrain the power of the Lord Pope or his commissary, since subjects are under the necessity of obeying, not the authority of commanding. I therefore conclude that the superior could order otherwise than what was ordered by the pacts of inferiors, and that the ordinance of the superior is to be adhered to more than the pacts of the subjects; but where the ordinance of the superior does not contradict the pacts, then the pacts are to be observed. De pactis, the constitution Epistola, § Pactum. And thus I have also otherwise advised, that such aforesaid matters are to be observed, unless something else is established by the ordinance of the superior. And it is made. Codex, De iudicibus, the law Omnes pensitare, Book 10, in the Response. Whatever, therefore, the ordinance of the superior contains, the inferior ought to observe. And thus I say and advise, I, Balde de Perusio, doctor of both laws. And to the faith I have subscribed and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A sentence by which it is pronounced that witnesses are to be received is called interlocutory, and an appeal cannot be made from it.
body: In the name of Christ. Amen. Three things are posited: The first is that witnesses be received. The second is that the witnesses be published. The third is that it be pronounced that perpetual credit is to be given to them. Against the first it was excepted that they ought not to be received, because the plaintiff was prepared to bring an action against the defendant, and thus the ordinary route excludes the extraordinary one. Secondly, because a certain suit was pending in another court in which the defendant could prove his right against the opponent, the judge pronounced that the witnesses were to be received; an appeal was lodged. It is asked whether an appeal may be made, having inspected the ius commune and the form of the statute. This is the case between Lady Bamba and Carlinus, thence committed by the lord judge of appeals.

† It must be known, moreover, that that sentence by which it is pronounced that witnesses are to be received, or not to be received, is an interlocutory sentence, as appears in C. de dila. l. a praecedente, C. de testi. auth. si dicatur, and as is noted in ff. de iud. l. de qua re in principio and l. 1, C. de ord. iud., which interlocutory sentence awaits after itself another concluding and decisive sentence, namely that perpetual credit is to be given, which is definitive of the petition, not from the manner of proceeding, but in effect, because it defines the principal matter that is sought. To this tends what is noted in C. de reb. cre. l. generaliter and l. si quis iusiurandum, and what is noted in a similar matter by the gloss and others in ff. de accu. l. cum Titia. And therefore under civil law it does not seem that an appeal can be made, as the ordinary gloss notes in the said l. a praecedente; this is supported by C. de iudi. l. antepe., de app. recipi. l. 2, C. de sen. et interlo. om. iu. l. fi., C. de epis. au. d. l. 2 through the gloss with similar passages. And even posited that it could be appealed under the common civil law or canon law, nevertheless, according to the form of the statute, an appeal cannot be made, because it is purely interlocutory, awaiting after itself what is virtually a definitive sentence; moreover, the causes of this appeal are not legitimate, because this petition is not directed against Carlinus specifically, but generally against all. And therefore the genus is not suspended by one species, C. si vt se ab haere. absti. auth. si omnes. And therefore the judge correctly interlocuted. And so I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of both laws, say and advise, and in witness whereof I have subscribed myself and signed with the seal of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a husband, upon dissolution of the marriage, shall acquire one-fourth part of his wife's dowry, from whomever it may have been given, such disposition of the statute does not apply to a dowry that has been acknowledged.
2. The extension of a statute is not made where the matter concerns the seeking of gain.
casus:
CA SVS.

In the name of the Lord, Amen. The fact, upon which counsel is sought, is as follows. Cola Andreae Necchi, and Flora, wife of the said Cola, and Francis, son of the said Cola and Flora, were confessed and content to have had and received from Stephen, son of Master Peter of Spoleto, giving and paying to them in dowry, and for dowry, and in the name of the dowry of Lucretia, his daughter, and future wife of the said Francis, 100 gold florins, as fully appears from the public instrument, a copy of which we send to you. After the said conflict notwithstanding, the said Stephen promised to the said Cola, Flora, and Francis to pay the said 100 gold florins, for the dowry of the said Lucretia, within 4 years. And he promised that for each of the said 4 years, for fruits and alimony, to give and pay to the said Francis, and his father and mother, 22 pounds of denarii; and he gave until the said Lucretia lived, and the said Stephen, and Bartholomew Miccicarui, at the request and command of the said Stephen, became surety, and bound himself principally, promising the same, that if the said Stephen did not observe all the above-mentioned, he would observe them of his own, as more fully appears from the public instrument, which we send. After the said Francis had brought the said Lucretia to his house as his wife, who Lucretia died without children within the four years contained in the said instrument, the said Francis, her husband, surviving, the said dowries not having been paid by the said Stephen within the said 4 years, nor afterwards, even the said Stephen, father of the said Lucretia, surviving. But because by the form of the statute of the commune of Spoleto, placed under the heading: that the husband shall lose the fourth part of the dowry of his wife, by whomever it was given, without son or daughter from him having, or her having, dying, whenever she shall die, after he has taken her as wife to his house, a copy of whose statute we send to you. Now it is asked, since 4 years have already passed, nor has the said Francis received the said dowry, whether the said Francis can demand the said 100 gold florins from the above-mentioned Bartholomew, so that he may retain the fourth of the said 100 gold florins, or the said dowry, by virtue of the said statute, notwithstanding that the said Lucretia died within the said four years, and whether the said Francis can demand the said fourth in the said, or another way, and whether he can, or ought, to demand from the said Bartholomew, the surety, or from the said Stephen, the principal, and whether he can act for the said fourth against the possessors of the goods, which goods the said Stephen had and possessed at the time of the said contract, and what is the mode of acting.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† Because this dowry was not truly given, nor was it to be given within the time during which the marriage lasted, the words and the intent of the statute cease to apply, even if the dowry was confessed. One thing is a dowry given, another is a dowry confessed, as noted in a similar case: C. Qui potior in pignore habenda est, l. Assiduis; and C. De mandato, l. Pro diversis and l. Ab Anastasio. And although it may seem that the same equity of gaining applies: C. Ad legem Falcidiam, l. Finalis.

† However, because we cannot extend a statute where the matter concerns profit, or in the case of anticipated profit. L. si vero, § de iure, Soluto matrimonio. Nor can the delay in payment be imputed to the debtor. De verbis obligatis, L. qui Romae, in principio; De exceptione doli, L. pater. I say that the aforementioned profit is not due. And so I say, and I advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws. And to the truth I have subscribed, and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a grandson, with respect to guardianship, follows the origin of his grandfather.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The facts are as follows: Master Ambrosius Sungine, as will be stated, was from the castle of Saint Martin in the province of Spoleto, part of the Duchy. However, he departed from there as a small boy and went to the city of Lucca, where he established domicile and begot a certain son named Colocinus, who was a master dentist. This Colocinus went to Genoa, where he established residence and begot John and Anthony. Upon approaching death, he made a testament there, among other things appointing Lady Sanctina, his wife, and Lady Agnola, his sister, as guardians and administrators of the said minors. After his death, one year having elapsed, the undersigned Sanctina entered into a second marriage, first petitioning the official of the said castle to appoint a guardian for her said sons, since she intended to enter into a second marriage. The officials and the judge appointed to her as guardian the one who is now their stepfather and the second husband of the mothers of the minors, on the pretext that the said sister could not be guardian, and consequently that the said minors were in need of a guardian. Now the question arises: Whether the said appointment is valid or not, presupposing that the said Master Ambrosius died twenty-five years ago and more. On these points, legal counsel is requested. Against this appointed guardian, it seems to be said that such appointment is void by operation of law, as made by an incompetent judge.

† And for this it must be known, whether, as regards guardianship, the grandson follows the origin of the grandfather, and it is determined by the Digest and the gloss that he does not. D. ad municipia, l. Assumptio, §. Filius; and C. de municipiis et originibus, l. Filios. Laus de Aretio sometimes said that rather he followed the origin of the grandfather, by l. Libertus, §. In adoptivo, and in the same title; but at other times he distinguished. Either the grandson is born in the power of the grandfather, and he follows the origin of the grandfather, as if in power, like an adopted son, as in §. In adoptivo; and in this way it seems one should say regarding the origin of the great-grandfather, if he were born in the power of the great-grandfather: because law and power effect this, not degrees of immediate proximity. Or the grandson is born in the power of his father, and not of the grandfather: and then he follows the origin of the father, and not of the grandfather. The same if the grandson is born in the power of no one, as a posthumous child. He follows the paternal origin: because the son is a certain part of the father. But he never follows the grandfather’s origin, unless, as has been said, the reason of the grandfather’s power induces this, which is inspected at the time of the grandson’s birth. On this, by Jacobus de Arena and Cynus, C. de iure omnium iudicum, l. 2. I say that when the grandson is conceived and born during the life of the grandfather, then he follows the origin of the paternal grandfather, as in §. In adoptivo. But if he is conceived during the life of the grandfather, but not born, because the grandfather died before the birth of the grandson, as in l. Gallus, §. Nunc de lege, then distinguish: if we speak of a duty which is a burden, for example, whether this grandson can be appointed guardian for another by the judge of the grandfather’s origin, I say that he cannot: because when it concerns the disadvantage of him who is in the womb, he is never considered as born. Or if we speak of favor, for example, whether another can be appointed guardian for him. For this is a favor for wards, and then he is considered as born, and follows the origin of the grandfather. Argument, Institutes, de tutoribus, §. Penult. It is otherwise regarding the great-grandfather: because the law fixes its foot in the father and the grandfather; otherwise you would have to seek the land of Damascus, where Adam was born. But if the grandson is conceived after the death of the grandfather, he never follows the origin, neither in favor nor in disfavor: because improperly. This one is called a grandson, who was never cognate or agnate to the grandfather. D. de suis et legitimis heredibus, l. Item praetor; D. de inofficioso testamento, l. Si quis filio, post princip. From this it appears clearly that the said judge of the castle of Saint Martin, or of Montanea, could not appoint a guardian for the said wards: because not by reason of origin, as has been proven, nor by reason of the grandfather’s domicile, much less the paternal, for the paternal domicile was not there but in Janua; because home, continuous residence, and the greater part of goods demonstrate domicile, as l. 2, C. ubi senatus vel clarissimi; and C. de incolis, l. Aves. But impuberes, and especially infants, as these are, cannot constitute a domicile for themselves by their own will and mind; but nevertheless the law constitutes it for them, if they had the greater part of their fortunes there, as noted by Bartolus in l. Placet, D. ad municipalia; alleg. l. 1, C. ubi pupillus tutorem; and there by Azo in the Summa. It is concluded that the said appointment was void by the law itself. D. de tutoribus et curatoribus, l. 1, in fine; C. qui dari tutores possunt, d. Neque; C. qui petere tutelam, l. In locum. For that law admonishes the mother to seek that a guardian be appointed for her son by the competent judge, not by the incompetent one: unless in that place she has the greater part of her fortunes, for by reason of assets rather than with respect to domicile the law permits this in favor of wards, so that their goods may be administered more conveniently. Therefore, by the law itself, the said appointment did not hold, nor should the judge allow the said administrator to act as guardian, since he is not a guardian, especially with the said sister objecting, who, although not a guardian, is nevertheless otherwise the administrator of the said wards and the executrix of the will, D. de negotiis gestis, l. Qui aliena, §. Quamquam, with similar cases; and it helps, D. de executione tutelae, l. Iurisperitos, §. Cum oriundus. But this is true with respect to origin: because with respect to assets the said appointment was valid, as said l. 1, C. ubi pupillus tutorem, in those words, “or where their assets are,” and the stepfather can be guardian of the stepson. D. de adoptionibus, l. Nonnunquam; C. de contrahenda tutela, l. Si tamen. Elsewhere the gloss says that he cannot be a dativus [guardian appointed by magistrate]: but a testamentary one, yes. Hence, if the father appoints him for the son, although the widow contracts marriage, he does not cease to be guardian. In Authentico de nuptiis, §. Eiusdem quoque; C. ubi pupillus educari debeat, l. 1; and Azo in the Summa there. But custom indistinctly approves that he who was appointed guardian before he became stepfather remains so; for he does not cease to be guardian because the mother of the wards marries him; because no law says this. But if otherwise he were suspect, or administered badly, then he could be removed. The said sister, however, should be, as I said, the educator of the said wards, and she can petition that their maintenance be fixed by the judge. D. ubi pupilli educari debeant, l. Ius alimentorum. Also, she should have the maintenance left to her in the will of her brother, and all else preserved according to the form of the will, except that she cannot be a guardian by common law: but if by the statute of Janua this is permitted to the sister, then she could be a guardian. But I am not aware of this statute, and this sister should have maintenance, whether she marries or does not marry: because maintenance is left to her simply, and the same applies to the education of the boy, since the said brother, when married to that sister, committed the administration to her. Hence, marriage does not make her suspect. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus de Ubaldis, doctor of both laws, and to the faith I have subscribed and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. An appeal cannot be made from an order as to whether a writing is one's own.
body: In the name of Christ. Amen. An appeal cannot be made from an order [inquiring] whether a document is his own or not, because it is not a definitive sentence, nor does it have the force of a definitive sentence, since it is interrogatory, not definitive, de interro. ac. l. 1; otherwise every sentence would be called definitive regarding its own point for which it is pronounced on credited matters, concerning which an oath is to be taken as above, and l. generaliter; which is not true with respect to the matter of appeals, as in l. 1. §. quod in sententiis. quando appel. sit. I, Baldus.

In the Name of Christ. Amen. We hold the opinion that a ward is not properly said to have died intestate, and the mother is admitted, etc. Add this counsel above, counsel 47.

The Archbishop of Prague is a legate a natio, and among other things contained in the privileges of his legation is this clause: “Notwithstanding any privileges, indulgences, constitutions, and exemptions, and non-exemptions, of whatever order or status, even if there is a special mention word for word of their privileges, in non-exemptions, by proper exception, not by our authority, on the pretext of these.”

The same Lord Archbishop, at his synod, summoned the Abbots of the Cistercian Order of the Kingdom of Bohemia, who appeared under protest that they did not intend thereby to derogate from the privileges granted to them by the Apostolic See. Hence, first it is asked: whether, because he is a legate a natio, he has any jurisdiction or any right over the said Abbots and members of the said order, from whatever source it may derive. Second, it is asked: whether this can be done by virtue of the aforementioned clause. Third, it is asked: whether the aforementioned protest defended them. Fourth, it is asked: whether, in the case where the protest was less sufficient, the said Abbots could have renounced, tacitly or expressly, the privileges granted to the entire Cistercian Order. Fifth, it is asked: whether, in the case where this could be done, the said Abbots are considered to have renounced the privileges granted to the entire Order by the single act of attending the synod.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A legate, in whose privilege are the words mentioned here, does not have jurisdiction over the Cistercians.
2. An indefinite term is not equivalent to a universal one, when the reason is not the same.
3. A protestation rather reserves a privilege than neglects it.
4. Individual persons cannot renounce the privilege of liberty granted to the clergy and the order.
5. Whether a privilege is revoked by a single act.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Upon

† On the first point, I say that a native legate has no jurisdiction over the Cistercians, since they are exempt, to such an extent that only the apostolic authority is excepted. For this the Pope reserved to himself. Extra, de rescriptis, c. Cum ordine.

† On the second point, I say that those general words, “exempt and non-exempt,” give rise to ambiguity; because since there are various kinds of exemptions, and it is not clear which are more exempt than others, it is uncertain what the Pope intended, and an indefinite term does not equate to a universal one, since the ratio and condition of participation are not the same, as noted by Dy. de re. iu. li. 6. in rub. Therefore, those who enjoy the greatest exemption, such as the Cistercians, should not be included under the generality, unless they are entirely of the Cistercian order; but they ought to have been specified by name and individually, as stated in ver. cum ordine per lo. An. in nouella. facit. C. de silen. l. decurionibus. li. 12. and ff. de pigno. l. obligatione generali. and ff. si quis cau. l. sed et l. si quis. §. quaesitum. ff. de le. 1. l. legatorum. §. qui plures.

† On the third point, it must be said that a protestation preserves the privilege of the one protesting. For he is not understood to have neglected his privilege who reserves it for himself. This is noted in c. Cum M. Ferraria, de constitutionibus, and in c. Si fideiussor, in principio, ff. Qui satisdare coguntur, l. Finis, §. Item si praedixerit, nautae, cauponae, stabularii, cum si. On the fourth point, it must be said that

† that individual persons cannot renounce the privilege of the liberty of their church and granted to the order. On the competence of judges: c. Si diligenter. On matters judged: c. Suborta. On arbitrators: c. Cum tempore.

† Regarding the last point, it must be said that a single act does not revoke a privilege in all acts. C. de excus. tu. l. voluntarie per Cy. and Pe. It supports what we note in de consti. c. cum accessissent. de vi. et ho. cler. c. ult. de praeb. c. per illorum. Those words in the example, "our authority," do not extend the concession, nor are they applied to those exempted who are entirely included in the generality of these words. As is clear in the aforementioned laws and many similar ones, which will be cited if necessary.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. On the grounds upon which it may be challenged; and see further below, consilium 374, and above, consilium 318.
body: In the case of the imprisoned person

First, it is alleged that he who caused him to be arrested did not swear that he was suspect, and this is expressly provided by the statute; therefore, the order of the same case is self-referential. Therefore, etc. L. *Prolatam*. Second, because he did not prove that he did not possess immovables, which is a negative cause and the foundation of the claimant’s intention to seek imprisonment. Hence, the burden of proof lies upon him. C. *De iure deliberando*, L. *Si*, §. *Licentiae*; *Qui satisdare cogantur*, L. *Si non*, §. *Qui pro rei*. This negative fact is proven by discussion, to which one proceeds summarily, as to arrest, as in *Si debitor*, in Auth. *Presentis*, *De verbis obligatorum*, L. *In illa*, §. *Unico*, according to Jacobus de Arena in his treatise on discussion. Third, it is alleged that the debt alleged, on account of which he was imprisoned, has not been proven. His debt was alleged on the ground of a loan, and nothing has been proven except an indiscriminate confession, which does not bind, as in D. *De probationibus*, L. *Cum de indebito*, §. *Si*; *De interrogatoribus et actoribus*, in the rubric. Indeed, the witnesses assert that he confessed himself to be a debtor by virtue of certain instruments. However, the instruments produced by him who caused the arrest contain a debt not arising from a loan, but from a deposit. Hence, the instrument produced by the plaintiff designates a different cause than that alleged and confounds his claim. *De instrumentis*, L. *Habebat*. And this applies not only in personal actions, but also in real actions brought for a specific cause. *De exceptione rei iudicatae*, L. *Si mater*, §. *Si quis fundum*; *De re iudicata*, C. *Abbate*, Book 6. Fourth, it is an obstacle that it has not been deduced, alleged, or proven that the cause of suspicion has newly arisen. Hence, if the debtor’s condition has not changed, arrest on the ground of suspicion does not apply, nor do any other usual remedies against someone on the ground of suspicion, as in L. *Si creditores*, *De privilegiis creditorum*; as in *Posito legato*, L. *Si is a quo*, §. *Si*, with the following law; *De damno infecto*, L. *Qui bona*, §. *De illo*, unless the contracting party had probably ignored his condition, and thus it would not be imputed to him. The text is joined with the gloss. *De annuis legatis*, L. *Liberto*, §. *Largius*, in the word *vivente*. Although in this case you do not find it expressly determined, perhaps no allegation can be made regarding this ignorance, considering that the arrested person and he who caused the arrest are compatriots, of the same city and neighborhood. And this arrested person was also a neighbor of the arrester. C. *Quando fiscus vel privatus*, L. 2, in the gloss; C. *De nuptiis*, L. *Si vicinus* and L. *Filium diffinimus*. Moreover, if this ignorance were beneficial, it should at least have been alleged. L. *Si adulterium*, §. *Idem Pollioni*, *De adulteriis*; *De usucapione*, L. *Celsus*, which was not alleged here, etc. Fifth, because for the proof of the debt, only a confession made as a usurer is alleged and proven: then, if the confession does not prove that the debt subsists, it is sufficient; or if it proves it, the tax should have been paid according to the form of the tax order. And because it was not paid, the statute provides that the entire proceeding is ipso iure void and invalid. Thus, I heard that the statute speaks, I do not know if it is true. Sixth, because after the arrest, the arrested person now ceded his goods to avoid the penalty of imprisonment, which he may do, as in L. 1, C. *De cessione bonorum*. And although it is objected that after sentence, it does not impugn the sentence, and it arose anew, the laws are such that it could not be done, not to prevent the liquidation of the debt, because he cannot. For it would be dangerous to the creditor, who could not liquidate, and thus the debtor would defraud the debt by being led to greater fortune. D. *De cessione bonorum*, L. 1, in the text and gloss, and C. *Ad idem*.

In the name of Christ, Amen. Although it is established according to the common law that there is a debt, nevertheless, no one can be put in prison for a private debt unless the goods have been discussed. D. *De suspectis tutoribus*, L. 3, §. *Tutores qui*, in the gloss, ordinary. And therefore, according to the common law, the said arrest was not valid. According to municipal law, however, the said arrest does not even subsist if the due order was omitted. D. *De re iudicata*, L. *Si cum nulla*. Moreover, because an arrest made for no cause, or a false cause, cannot be justified by another cause, since it was made, as in C. *Appellante*, *De appellationibus*, in the Clementines. And because that which is null cannot be justified, just as neither can the seizure of things for a false cause. D. *Ne vis fiat ei qui in iudicio vocatus est*, L. 1, §. *Haec verba*; D. *De bonis auctore iudicis possessis*, L. *Cum unus*. And because a cause not alleged in the petition cannot be retained by way of proof. *De petitione hereditatis*, L. *Si quis libellum*, §. *Si*; *De iureiurando*, L. *Si duo patroni*, §. *Idem Iulianus*, because the mode of pleading rather than the mode of proving should be examined. 3. q. 6, C. *Haec quippe*, in the gloss, ordinary; and *De rescriptis*, C. *Super literis*, according to Innocentius, it is clearly apparent. D. *De pactis dotalibus*, L. *Aebellius Marcellus*. And therefore, it must be pronounced that the said arrest is and was ipso iure null, and the said arrested person must be released, or at least, as invalid, it must be revoked by contrary command, as an execution wrongly made, since it appears from the acts that the debt alleged was not proven. And if the judge erred in believing the case was aided by irrelevant proofs, the successor must revoke the error of the predecessor. D. *De testamento tutorum*, L. *Idem fuit* and L. *Quod iussit*; *De re iudicata*, L. *Minore*, in the principle; *De evictione*. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of both laws. And to the faith I subscribed and signed my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A minor under guardianship is not properly said to die intestate.
2. Given a statute that a mother does not succeed to a child dying intestate, whether the mother is excluded from the succession of a child dying while an impubes.
body: The common opinion
† it is, that since a ward is not properly said to die intestate,

† That statute does not exclude the mother when the son is an impubes (a minor under puberty): because he is not said to be intestate, but intestabilis (capable of making a will). As stated in l. 1, de suis et legitimis heredibus. And to this effect it is relevant that in l. 2, ff. qui testamento facere possunt, and in C. de iure deliberandi, l. cum antiquioribus. But it seems that in wills such subtlety should not be considered, but rather the intentions of those who make the will, which are approved by civil law due to common usage of language, and minors are bound thereby. As stated in d. l. 1. For often laws, and especially those concerning pupils, call one intestate. As in ff. qui per tutelam, l. credendum, §. hoc autem; and ff. ad Tertullianum, l. 2, §. si mater. And this subtlety seems to be more scrupulosity and caviling. As in ff. ad Trebellianum, l. 2, §. tractari; and ff. de excusationibus tutorum, l. sed hoc nimium. But this is certain and approved by civil law, and therefore not to be rejected. As noted in Instit. de hereditatibus quae ab intestato deferuntur, in principio, in glossa 1, modo videbatur: because the statute does not weigh age, but children; which condition, namely "without children," is more strongly verified in pupillary age than afterwards. As in ff. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Centurio; and as noted in l. precibus, that an aunt would be called for this purpose. And the reason of the statute supports this, as it is sufficiently appropriate, etc. For reason extends the statement. As in l. de quibus, de legibus; and l. non possunt; and l. illud, ff. ad legem Aquiliam; and l. de fonte, l. 1, §. hoc interdicto; and C. de interdictis, l. 1. For in the reason of the statute it does not matter whether a pupil or an adult dies. And this reason is expressed in the statute; otherwise, if it were not expressed, the pactum odiosum (hateful agreement) would not be excluded. As in l. si vero, §. de viro soluto matrimonio; and l. prospexit, qui et a quibus. That children are the final cause is clear from ff. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. Lucius; C. de fideicommissis, l. cum acutissimi; and ff. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. 1. And for this reason I initially thought in favor of the aunt, saving the legitimate portion due to the mother by virtue of another statute, which I applied to the case of intestacy. Per l. cum quaeritur, de inofficiosis testamentis. Later, upon further consideration, I observed that in that statute concerning those dying intestate and without children, there is no express mention of the mother: although tacitly, if there were no other statute, the mother would be excluded; because the inclusion of others is the exclusion of those not included. As in ff. de legatis, l. quod in rerum, §. si quis post testamentum; and C. de re militari, l. sicut certi. Moreover, by another statute, mention is made of a dowered woman, and mention is made of the mother by including the mother from the will to the legitimate portion. Then I argue thus: if the legitimate portion is due to her from the will, therefore she succeeds intestate. Hence, that statute necessarily makes the mother capable of succeeding intestate. Otherwise, there would be no legitimate portion, which is one-third of what she would be owed intestate. As in Auth. de triennio et sex mensibus, in principio, column 3. And therefore the mother is excepted from the general exclusive statute, for whom special provision has been made expressly from the will, and tacitly intestate. For a tacit special provision derogates from an express general one. As in l. obligatio, nec obligatio ideo statuti: because it is general and not approved by common law. C. de donationibus, l. si cum vestra. And equity accords with this: because the statute was made in favor of male agnates, through whom families are preserved. As noted in C. de adulteriis, l. publico; ff. de venditionibus inspicendis, l. 1, §. de nupta; which are not preserved through females. As in 10. column, qui seu, de possessionibus, c. 1, §. hoc autem notandum. That reason is that succession should be reciprocal, which is sufficiently equitable. As in C. de legatis hominibus, §. cum igitur. And considering equity, I did not remain firm in my first opinion, but changed my mind, and I now think entirely in favor of the mother, always saving the substance of the truth, and the opinion of the stronger counsel. As in ff. qui potior in pignore habeat, l. Claudius. Felix. I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A substitute who dies before the fulfillment of the condition does not transmit the right of substitution.
2. A passed-over mother does not transmit the right to declare the will void.
casus: CASE. The following facts are proposed. A certain lady, Benuenuta, daughter of the late Andrea, gave herself in marriage to Vannes Alexandri, from whom she had three sons, namely Angelo, Iacobutius, and Colla. This Vannes died, the said wife and sons surviving, and this lady assisted in administering the said inheritance together with the said sons for about 20 years. And in the meantime they acquired certain goods by title of purchase, worth about 100 florins. Then she gave herself in marriage to a second husband, from whom she had Ionta and Ursina, and she kept the said sons whom she had from the said Vannes with her. Then the said Iacobutius and Colla died, having made wills, making no mention of their said mother except in substitution. The said Angelo, their brother, survived, instituted heir by them; however, it was believed that he was dead rather than alive, because he was traveling abroad. The mother, believing him dead, held all the goods then belonging to the said Angelo for a certain time, collecting the fruits of those goods, after which the said Angelo returned. Then the said lady Benuenuta died, the said Angelo and the said Ionta and Ursina surviving, having made a will, but not published, in which she instituted the said Angelo, Ionta, and Ursina as her heirs in equal portions. Then the said Angelo died, having made a will, in which he bequeathed to the said Ionta and Ursina the goods of his said mother, acquired by him in any way. In the other goods, he instituted certain of his paternal relatives as his heirs. Now the said Ionta and Ursina claim that they have a right to the goods which belonged to the said Iacobutius and Colla, and to the goods which were acquired after the death of their said father, as well as to the goods which belonged to their said father, in which the said lady Benuenuta succeeded after their death. It is asked what is the law, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The said Benuenuta stated,

† In the goods which had belonged to her husband, she did not succeed to her children, namely James and Cole, who had made a will; and from the will, the mother who had remarried does not succeed, except as any stranger would. C. de sec. nupt. auth. ex testamento. And even if it were assumed that she succeeded in some respect as to the usufruct, these would be extinguished by the death of the woman, as in Inst. de usuf. §. finitur, and C. de sec. nup. l. feminae, §. fi. Nor does it avail that the said mother was substituted in the wills of her children, because she died while the condition was still pending. Hence, the right of substitution does not pass, as noted in C. de his qui ante aper. tab. l. 1, cum.n. She died while Angelus was alive. But in the other goods, which had not belonged to her husband, he ought to have had his legitime, which, if he accepted and transmitted to his children, or if he did not accept, still appears to be the same by tit. de his qui ante apertas tab. and what is noted in C. de suis et leg. l. apud hostes. On this point, opinions are given by l. si quis filium, C. de inof. tes.

And because the passed-over mother did not declare the will of her sons null, it appears to have been tacitly confirmed despite the unjust disposition. L. *Filio praeterito*. And thus her heirs cannot claim it is null, nor can they demand anything against the will; and this opinion is the more correct one if the mother remained silent for a long time and did not declare it null, but died in that state. And so I say, and I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws, advise accordingly. And for the faith of this, I have written and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. On the existence of goods outside the territory subject to confiscation, and when they fall under universal confiscation, and to which chamber the incorporation of said goods, whether movable or immovable, shall be made. Nos. 2 and 3.
2. The chamber of the fisc is twofold.
3. A confession is not valid to the prejudice of the fisc.
4. A mere executor does not adjudicate nullity.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the first point, whether his goods situated outside the territory of the confiscating authority are subject to universal confiscation, it must be said that if such a person is exiled in such a way that he is equated with a deportee, according to the noted institution Qui modis patrimonium soluitur, §. relegati, all his goods fall into confiscation. As stated in C. de poenis, l. deportatorum; ff. de capite diminuto, l. tutela, §. 1, because the fiscus is not divided, but is everywhere; therefore, deportation cannot be local, but extends throughout the entire territory of the authority under which it is carried out, for example, that of the Pope or the Emperor. Nor can he remain in part within the city and in part outside. This is supported by ff. de capite diminuto, l. amissione, §. qui deficiunt; ff. de postulando, l. si ex ea; de iniusto testamento, l. si quis filio exheredato; ff. de testamentis, l. eius qui; C. ad l. Iul. de vi, l. si tulons. In our case, he must be equated with a deportee by the nature of the crime. C. de abolitione, l. 2, in fine; C. ad l. Iul. maiestatis, l. quisquis; and the aforementioned §. qui deficiunt.

† But there is doubt as to the incorporation, to which chamber it should be made, whether where the offense was committed and the condemnation took place, or where the goods are, assuming that both chambers are procurators of the emperor for his own interest. The doctors say, that the chamber of goods, i.e., where the goods are, with respect to the goods, the condemnation is real: because it follows the thing. As the Moderns fully note in l. cunctos populos. And they cite many things, which I do not recite, but they speak of things coherent to the territory.

But in movable things it seems that a distinction must be made, whether they are there as justly established, or only temporarily; because things which are claimed according to place are assigned to that place where they are destined. D. 28,5,1 (Ex facto); D. 20,1,1, § Verum autem; D. 20,1,1 (Debitor); D. 35,1,1 (Huiusmodi), § Legatis. In this case, therefore, where the things have been transferred elsewhere, not for the purpose of bringing them back from where they were transferred, it does not seem that the fisc of this land ought to have them; unless they were transferred after the offense; because then they are claimed as affected on account of the crime of lèse-majesté. D. 48,18,1 (Si). And this is the first point. On the second point, which depends on the first, I say that it must be divided, if the case is one of confiscation to the camera, which claims it; otherwise not.

† because the camera is twofold, namely universal and singular; and the camera of the fisc, which is a member and not a head, has a limited right. As stated in l. extra territorium, de constitutionibus; c. ut animarum, lib. 6. And for this, it was answered in the third point.

† On the fourth point, I say that a confession is not valid to the prejudice of the fisc, as is evident from the noted passage in the law *Post contractum*, in the Digest, under the title *De donationibus*. On the fifth point, I say,

† That a mere executor does not inquire into nullity. But an executor who possesses jurisdiction ought not to execute that which is null. D. de iudicibus, l. si praetor, cum si. A mere executor is one who is bound to obey the command of another; but he who executes by his own authority is not a mere executor. On this point fully, note, through Innocentius, de re iudicata, c. de caetero. ASVS In the name of Christ, Amen. The point is as follows. The testator made a will, in which he instituted his brother as universal heir, and he willed that after the death of said brother, that which should remain at the time of his death, he judged, should be divided into three parts, namely, among Peter, Philosopher, and Martin in equal portions, excepting one-fourth part of said goods, of which part of said goods said heir may do whatever he wishes. The testator died, and the heir entered upon the inheritance and possessed it. While he was in possession, Philosopher and Martin died, with the universal heir and Peter, their coheir, surviving. Afterwards, said universal heir died, who instituted as his heirs Peter and a certain other person in equal portions. It is asked first, to whom the shares of Philosopher and Martin accrue, and to whom they have accrued, whether to Peter the coheir, or to said universal heir, namely, the heir of the testator. Secondly, it is asked, whether said heirs instituted in said will of the universal heir can retain and hold anything in said inheritance by the right of the Trebellian portion, notwithstanding the reason of fruits received, and notwithstanding said fourth part, of which said brother could do whatever he wished.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the share of the substituting heirs who are moving accrues to the instituted heirs or to the substitute.
2. The heir burdened with a fideicommissum, having retained the fourth part, cannot on account of the Trebellian right retain anything else.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† On the first point, it must be said that the share of Philosophus and Martinus has accrued to Petrus as one conjoined by words. C. de cad. tol. §. pro secundo; de ver. sig. l. triplici; de le. 3. l. reconiuncti. etc.

† On the second point, it must be said that the said fourth, which does not fall into the restitution, is imputed to the Trebellian portion. ff. ad l. Fal. l. Titia; what is noted in C. fami. ercisc. l. filium quem habentem supports this; and therefore Petrus ought to have three parts of the inheritance of the first testator by right of fideicommissum, while the remaining fourth pertains partly to him and his coheir as heirs of the second testator. ff. ad l. Fal. l. pater filium etc. CASE. The point of the question upon which counsel is sought is this: namely, Albertus sold to Franciscus certain houses and parcels of land, with no reservation made, for the price of 100 pounds of denarii; which houses and lands the said seller promised and swore legitimately to defend against every man and person, and concerning the aforesaid there appears a public instrument of sale and purchase in proper form. On the very same day on which the said sale was made, the said seller, knowing that he was not bound to the underwritten matters, but wishing to be bound through a solemn pact, stipulated an instrument reinforced with an oath corporally sworn by the seller himself, and promised through another instrument, drawn by the hand of the very same notary, to the said Franciscus the buyer, that if at any time the said Franciscus the buyer, or anyone holding a right and title from him in the aforesaid things or in part of them, should be molested de jure or de facto in the aforesaid houses and parcels of land or in any of them by any person, once the aforesaid lawsuit had been initiated, he would effectively return and restore to the same Franciscus the buyer one hundred pounds of denarii, upon the request and will of the buyer himself after the initiation of the said lawsuit. Now it is asked, having examined the aforesaid point and the instrument of the said promise written by the hand of ser Franciscus Balducii: although the matter has been framed and varied with respect to other persons and another quantity of money than appears in the instrument of the said promise, whether, once a lawsuit concerning the aforesaid property has been initiated, the said seller can return and restore to the said Franciscus the buyer the said one hundred pounds against the will of the buyer himself; and whether, if the said Franciscus the buyer should receive the said one hundred pounds, the above-written sale remains valid, or whether he is bound and can be compelled by law to resell, without any other price, the said houses and lands; and whether the said buyer can renounce the said pact before the initiation of the lawsuit and after, against the will of, or without the knowledge of, or against the objection of the said seller, so that the above-written sale, instrument, and the contents of the instrument of the aforesaid sale remain firm and valid. Let counsel be given in the name of God.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. No one is bound to follow a pact appended in his favor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

This pact was added in favor of the buyer, by those words which say, at the will of the buyer himself. And therefore he is not bound to follow the pact against his will. As in D. de lege commissa, l. ea lege; D. de in diem addendo, l. Sabinus, in the reasoning of the said laws. Hence this sale is not rescinded against the buyer’s will; nevertheless, on account of the defense not being undertaken, the buyer could not sue for more than the said amount by way of damages; because since damages have been agreed upon, one must abide by the agreement. D. de praetoriis stipulationibus, l. fin. I weigh: therefore that word “at the will of the buyer himself” is at the same time a word of dissolution. D. de re iudicata, l. post dotem. If, however, the buyer were to recover the said amount, which was the true price, he would have withdrawn from the contract. C. quando liceat ab empto discedere, l. 1 and 2. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws, and to the truth I have subscribed, and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An arbitrator, by permission of the law for the common good of the parties, may err in a small amount, but not in a large one.
2. A sworn confession is valid, as if it had been made in the presence of the adversary.
3. A petition for reduction is equivalent to an appeal from a definitive judgment.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the case of Lord Louis and Bond, the compromises and the award having been presupposed, and the repetition of the reduction and all the acts of the cause having been considered, three questions are raised. First, whether, in view of the form of the compromise and the oath, a reduction may be sought. Second, if it may be sought, whether the inequity of the award or its nullity has been proven. Third, whether anything has been proven by the said Louis to justify the award, at least to the extent that an uncertain oath of proof should be deferred to him.

And I say that an arbitrator, by permission of the law for the common good of the parties, may cause harm in a small amount, not in a large one. As is noted in the Digest, *De arbitris*, in the law *Si de meis*, § *Recepisse*, and in the law *Sed in seruum*. What is permitted by law may be extended by agreement of the parties to a larger amount; but there is an objection to this, namely that in such a case, unless there was fraud on the part of the arbitrator, a reduction could not be sought. Digest, *De manumis*, law *Creditor*, § *Si*. But Raymond of the Forum and John of Casalis, who both disputed this question, nevertheless their opinion is not well secured; because the entire latitude of an arbitrator’s discretion must be constrained by the discretion of a good man. And note in chapter *Iudicem*, Extra, *De re iudicata*, Book 6, in the glosses; and in the Digest, *De operis liberti*, Book 1, law *Si libertus*, § *Ita*; and in the Digest, *Qui satisdare cogantur*, law *Qui iurata*. If anyone wished to hold even their opinion on account of the oath, he has in his favor all the decretals which require that absolution from the oath be first sought, and thus the complaint be prepared. Extra, *De iureiurando*, chapter 1, § *Re debitoris*, together with the following. To the second and third points

† I likewise opine in favor of Lord Ludouico, who proved the confession of the opposing party through one credible witness. Since this confession was sworn, it is valid, as if it had been made in the presence of the adversary, as stated in the Authentica *De iureiurando a me praestando*, § 1, and in Note 3, Question 6, Chapter *Quoties cordis oculus*. Furthermore, by means of proof, it is presumed that the matter is equitable, issued in good faith, and just, as noted by Dy in the consultation beginning *Tholomeus Manentis facit*, in the Digest *De evictionibus*, Law *Herennius*, § 1. And thus, Lord Ludouico has the presumption of honor and legitimacy in his favor. From these, it is presumed that there is no doubt, and that an oath should be deferred in supplement of proof, should there be any defect, as in Law *Admonendi* and Law *Si duo patroni*, in the principal part.

† For the petition for reduction is equivalent to an appeal from a definitive judgment. And therefore new justifications and challenges are admitted. As in *l. per hanc* and *l. ampliorem*, *de appellationibus*, together with *si*; and *l. non distinguemus*, § *cum quidam*, *de arbitris*. It also moves me that in the testimony given by the aforementioned Ludovicus there is a reservation of rights against the aforementioned Bondus. Hence it appears that the act, by virtue of the absolution, does not extend to him, as in *legi* and noted, *ff. de acceptilatione*; *l. et per iusiurandum*, § *si legatorum*, *ff. de pactis*; *l. nisi*, because it was not a true payment, but a confession having the force of a pact, *ff. de pactis*; *l. tale pactum*, in the principal. Nevertheless, the preceding reasons are better. And thus I say and advise, I, Balduinus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws. And to the faith thereof I have written and signed with the sign of my name. Always saving the truth of the fact. For *tu magis* and the rest, *ff. de testibus*; *l. 3*, § *tu magis scire potes* and the rest.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. He who, on just grounds, believes himself to be the owner, and therefore seizes or secretly takes away the thing, is excused from theft.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† He who, on just grounds, believes himself to be the owner, and therefore seizes by force or stealthily takes away, is excused from theft. As in the Institutes, *vi bonorum raptorum*, § *quia tamen*. The same applies if he is moved by any reasons, even if not just ones; because a just cause excuses from theft and from mutual obligation. As in the law *Iuris error*, Digest, *de abigeis*; law 1, at the end, Code, *de plagio*; law *igitur*, *de liberali causa*. But this messenger probably believed himself to be the owner, and approached with the intention of an owner; because he had a title in his favor. Hence he does not appear to be acting in bad faith. Code, *de furtis*, law *apud antiquos*. And he himself is excused from theft, as well as others who accompanied him; because they acted with the will and command of the owner, or quasi-owner. There is another reason for his excuse: because the said messenger proved that his father possessed during his lifetime, and that he possessed after his father’s death. Hence it seems that both possessions are joined, not because the father’s possession descends to the son by operation of law; but because the son uses the possession of the owner by accession to the father’s possession. Law *cum miles*, *quibus ex causis maior*; and note in law *in suis*, *de liberis et posthumis*. And thus the intermediate possession of a third party is presumed vitious and clandestine. Argument, Extra, *de probatibus*, chapter *licet causam*. Furthermore, the laborers and reapers are even more excused, who did not know that the thing belonged to another, and believed the messenger to be the true owner and possessor of the thing, as noted in Digest, *de rei venditione*, law *in rem*, § *signum*. This is not obstructed by Institutes, *vi bonorum raptorum*, § *sed nedum*; because, with regard to those constitutions intended civilly, bad faith is not required, which cannot be covered by any pretense of cause. As in Code, *de infamia*, law *in furti*.

CASE In the name of Christ, amen. Pollionus of the Mountain made a will, and said, among other things which he disposed in it, that his heirs ought to satisfy, within a year from the day of the death of the said Pollionus, those things which were contained in the wills of his brother by Montanutius and Francis; and if the said heirs did not do the aforementioned, the said heirs would fall from the inheritance. Now it is asked, if the said heirs of the said Pollionus do not satisfy within the year the things contained in the said wills of the said Montanutius and Francis, to whom the said inheritance shall be applied; since the said Pollionus has a certain fleshly niece of his, and one closer to him in degree of kinship. Secondly, it is asked, if before the said year has passed, the said niece, by title of transaction, or sale, or cession, gives and cedes to the heirs of the said Pollionus all right which she has, and could have in the future on any occasion, in the goods and inheritance of the said Pollionus, whether, on this account, although they did not fulfill the will of the said Pollionus within the said time, they ought to have the inheritance of the said Pollionus; and if they ought to have it, the words which ought to be inserted in the said contract to be made by the said niece, or nephew, to the said heirs, are to be written briefly.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. To whom the inheritance shall devolve, when someone is deprived of the testator’s inheritance by legal disposition: because he did not fulfill the judgment of the deceased.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† When someone is deprived of the testator’s inheritance by legal disposition, because he did not fulfill the judgment of the deceased, to whom it shall apply, it is held in Auth. de haer. et fal. §. si quis autem non implens, and C. de fideicom. auth. hoc amplius. But when he is deprived for that reason by the testator’s disposition, either the testator designates who shall succeed, and that person succeeds, or the testator does not designate; then I believe that the said auth. has place, as noted in the same title, l. fi. in fin. According to that auth., where there is a substitution, it goes to the substitute; where there is no substitution, it goes to the coheir, etc. Now in our case there is no substitute. But there are two in a certain thing, who are considered as coheirs at least in name, and therefore I believe that it shall come to them in due time, provided that first and before all else they give adequate security for fulfilling the will of the deceased; because so says the text in the said auth. Hence they cannot yet transfer or alienate, because if they later fail to give security, such assignment would be of no effect. Let him fulfill the will who wishes to obtain its benefit, and it is so in extra de voto, capitulo 2, and extra de testamentis, c. si haeredes, and 11. q. 1. Silvester. And thus I say, and I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of both laws, advise, and for the faith of this I have written and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a tutor may purchase through a secretly interposed person, given a just price, an impending debt, public auctions, and a judicial decree.
2. If the tutor possessed and collected the fruits of the sold property, whether it is presumed that fraud was committed through an interposed purchaser.
3. Whether a general defense raised by the tutor is valid and prejudices the ward in matters not considered, although not in those done secretly.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Titius administered the guardianship of Sempronius, and, the debt being acknowledged, the said Sempronius, with the authority of the said Titius, and by decree of the judge, and with public auctions, sold his estate to Gaius; nevertheless, the said guardian always possessed the said estate after the said sale, and after certain years had the rights remitted to himself by the said purchaser. Then the said Sempronius brought an action for the reckoning of the administration against the said guardian; now, however, the said Sempronius wishes to claim the said estate, alleging that the said guardian secretly and in bad faith purchased the said estate through the interposed person of the said Gaius, and that the name of the said Gaius was inserted in the said simulated contract not so that he might acquire the right in effect, but rather for the said guardian. From this case three questions arise. First, whether a guardian may purchase through a secretly interposed person at a just price and with the debt acknowledged, as with public auctions and by decree. Second, whether it is presumed from the said possession and the said remission of rights that he purchased through an interposed person. Third, whether a general reckoning brought against the guardian hinders the former ward from claiming the said thing.

† Regarding the first point, it must be considered that, among other things pertaining to the substance of the contract of guardians, it is necessary that the tutor acknowledge the goods; and he cannot purchase them unless it is done in good faith, as stated in D. de administratione tutorum, l. Cum plures, §. Quae bona fide; and l. Quotiens, §. Denique; and in C. de administratione tutorum, l. Fin., §. Defensio; and in Auth. Ut hi qui onerantur, §. Fin. Furthermore, it must be considered that the tutor may purchase openly and in good faith, but not secretly; for then bad faith is presumed. C. de contrahenda emptione, l. Si in emptione, §. Fin. And in both cases, the issue is not whether it is done through an interposed person, but whether it is done secretly or openly. For if the tutor openly states, “I wish that Titius purchase for me,” because I wish that my name be written in the instrument, the purchase is valid, provided the other requirements are not lacking; but if he does so secretly, it is not valid. D. de auctoritate tutorum, l. Pupillus, §. Sed si per interpretationem; and §. Sane si quidem. And by this, the question is resolved as to whether the purchase is valid or not. And this concludes the first point.

† Regarding the second point, it must be said that it is presumed that he purchased through an interposed person: because he possessed, and collected the fruits, and finally received the rights, as in C. de repudianda haereditate, l. 2; ff. de actione hereditaria, l. si is, qui bonus; ff. qui modis pignus vel hypotheca solvatur, l. sicut, §. superuacuam; C. si quis alteri, vel sibi, l. cum propriam.

† Regarding the third point, it must be said that a general refutation is valid in those matters which were considered; but it is not valid in those matters which were done secretly. D. de pactis, l. emptor, § Lucius; and l. tres fratres, D. de transactionibus; l. qui tutoribus, § qui per fallaciam; and l. cum Aquiliana, C. de transactionibus; l. ut responsum; and l. in licite, de rebus eorum, etc. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws, and for the faith of this I have written and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In interlocutory matters, it is valid without the recitation of the written document; otherwise, it is in the definitive judgment.
2. Whether a judge can condemn in expenses by an interlocutory sentence.
casus: CASE. Before you, wise and learned man in law and doctor of laws, Lord Nicholas, judge of civil causes of the commune of Perugia, appointed for the gate of Saint Peter by the noble knight Lord Gregory of Schalis, etc., Peter, or Marinus, and the procurator of Lady Vicia, etc., raises an exception and, by way of exception, proposes against Marinus and others certain exceptions and expenses. And first, because it is not established, nor does it appear, that any condemnatory sentence regarding expenses was rendered on behalf of the said Marinus by the said Lady Vicia, which has passed into res iudicata; and therefore execution of the sentence cannot be carried out, because it does not appear, nor is there any, which has not passed into res iudicata. It does not avail if it is said that a certain interlocutory judgment was rendered on behalf of the said Marinus against the said Lady Vicia, for the reason that the said interlocutory judgment was, and is, null by law, especially since the said Lady Vicia was absent and not summoned when it was rendered, and because the said sentence was not rendered in writing, nor definitively, as it ought to have been and must be; for since the libel was presented in the said case, and the issue was joined, and the oath against calumny was taken, a definitive judgment ought to have been and must be rendered in writing, and not interlocutory judgments, and a written sentence. Therefore, the said interlocutory judgment, which was rendered without writing, is null by law itself, and cannot pass into res iudicata, nor can execution thereof be carried out according to the form of the statutes and ordinances of the commune of Perugia, and especially since the nullity is established by inspection of the sentence itself.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† When those words are promulgated in the form of a sentence, etc., all solemnities are precluded, unless they are proven to be present. The doctors place this under the heading of objections regarding truth, in the law *Sciendum*, and regarding legacies, in the third title, in the law *Fideicommissa*, in the first version. But assuming that they were not described by the recitation of the written document, it is asked whether it is valid. I answer that this sentence had two parts: the first part was that it pronounced the defendant to be absolved; and this was interlocutory, because absolution is still hoped for. In the final law, *Ubi et apud quem*, and in the first law of the Code, *Si adversus liberum*, and as regards this chapter, it is not necessary that it was pronounced with the recitation of the written document, as noted in the final law of the Code, *De sententiis ex periculo recipiendis*. The second part, because it absolved definitively, and as regards this chapter, the sentence pronounced without the recitation of the written document was null. In the aforementioned final law and the penultimate law of the same title, and in the Clementine *Saepe*. Nevertheless, a useful part is not vitiated by a useless one. In the Digest, *Si certum petatur*, in the law *Certi conditio*, in the section *Quam*.

But whether he ought to have been condemned in costs, since they do not define the matter, but it is an interlocutory judgment from which he should be absolved. For by reason of victory, it does not seem that anyone should be condemned in costs, except in the final definition, because no one is said to be a victor or vanquished before the definitive judgment. C. de iudic. l. properandum. §. siue autem. However, because no appeal was taken from that condemnatory award of costs, it seems that as to that part it has passed into res iudicata; and if it is said that the condemnation of costs is accessory, and if the principal does not hold, the accessory does not hold. It is answered that its principal here was the interlocutory judgment, which he pronounced for payment, which holds. And thus I counsel, I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of both laws, and for the faith of this I have written and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an acceptance of an inheritance made while a posthumous child is in the womb is valid, and when it is valid, and whether the inheritance is transmitted by such acceptance.
2. When a legacy of several different sums has been made, whether one sum is due beforehand, or two.
3. Doubting whether possession of goods is transmitted.
4. The transmission of the inheritance to the person to whom it was made; that person transmitted the cause to his successor.
5. A minor who did not accept does not transmit restitution in full.
6. Actions may be brought repeatedly on the testaments of different persons.
casus: CASE. On behalf of the fifth party, whether they should remain content with the said legacies made to them of 900 gold florins for each of them by virtue of the testament of the said Raynaldus. And if they should remain content, whether they ought to have the power to demand three hundred gold florins for each of them, left in that testament together with the said 900 gold florins; and if the inheritance of the said Raynaldus was transmitted by the said Francis, by virtue of the said acceptance, to the said Louis, his son, and consequently the said inheritance has devolved to the above-mentioned commissioners by virtue of the testament of the said Francis, etc. Having seen the testament of the said Raynaldus, the testament of the said Francis, and the acceptance of the said inheritance made by the said Francis, and the point being formed, on all and each of which a sound opinion is sought, etc.
body:
In the Name of Christ, Amen. Concerning several transmissions, and first, whether Francis transmitted the inheritance to his son. Second, whether, because the substitution was made in favor of Francis and his sons, Louis could have entered upon and transmitted the inheritance in his own person; and whether he transmitted it to the pupillary substitutes, or not. And whether, as in the first transmission, so also in the transmission of a transmission, the same procedure applies. The first point, upon which this depends, is whether the acceptance of the inheritance made by Francis was valid. For if it was valid, the accepted inheritance is transmitted; if it was not valid, it is not transmitted, as stated in §. in novissimo.

And first, regarding the posthumous child yet to be born: for sometimes he exists and is expected to be born; sometimes he is not in the womb, yet is expected or believed to exist; sometimes he neither exists nor is expected to exist. If the posthumous child is truly in the womb and expected to be born, the right to enter upon the inheritance depends on his birth. Sometimes the inheritance cannot be entered upon, nor does the right of deliberation subsist; for the right of deliberation is like a potentiality, while acceptance is like an act. This is proposed in the Digest, De acquirenda hereditate, l. cum quidem, §. quod dicitur. Moreover, reason dictates that acceptance is an annual movement with a determination of acceptance of the right, accomplished with the aid of a concurrent potentiality. And no one can have full deliberation regarding uncertain matters, nor a certain annual movement and end, as is naturally evident from this reasoning: if he does not exist, yet is expected to exist, in the meantime the inheritance cannot be entered upon due to the defect of the posthumous child, because the counsel of the mind wavers. But if he does not exist, nor is he expected to exist, the acceptance proceeds, because the right and the will concur. A similar point is noted in the Code, De donationibus ante nuptias, l. si filiae tuae.

But if he exists, yet is not expected [to be born alive], the acceptance does not proceed; for truth contradicts it, and truth is the support; and where there is no potentiality, there is no act, because this does not depend on the mind, but on the concurrent truth, as stated in the Digest, De petitione hereditatis, l. antiqui. But if he does not exist, yet men are divided in opinion, some believing he exists, others that he does not, then if the belief of the person entering upon the inheritance is that there is no posthumous child, and the reputation, or, as I think, a just reason, is such that the authority of conscience and reputation concur in the same view, the acceptance is valid; otherwise, it is not, as stated in the aforementioned §. quod dicitur. But if the opinion of the opposing party is that the posthumous child exists, although there is no error, it impedes the mind, so that it cannot will and enter upon the inheritance, as is proven above.

From these points, it is concluded thus: if at the time of acceptance, the person entering upon the inheritance was certain in his mind that a posthumous child was expected, and truth and reputation, or just reason, concurred with his opinion, then the acceptance was valid; otherwise, it was not. However, it must be observed that, although the acceptance was not valid, and the inheritance was transmitted, because this is a special case, as stated in the Digest, De contrahenda stipulatione, l. illud, §. fin., together with the following law, and there noted; and in the Digest, De acquirenda hereditate, l. ventre, and there noted.

It must also be observed that the son of Francis could have come in his own person, because he was instituted heir, and since he died, by his own right, the unaccepted inheritance transmitted the restitution in integrum to the heir, as is held in the Digest, De accusationibus, l. posthumus; and in the Digest, De rebus dubiis, l. qui duos. According to Jacobus de Arena, the cause for motion in entering upon the inheritance is held to be perfect, and against everything done in a childish manner, restitution is granted. But if he is not in delay, then neither is anything done with him, nor does he do anything. How, then, is he restored? But the response is: he who appears not to act, being absent, is undoubtedly restored; for there is his act, namely, his absence.
