This supports what is noted in l. cum quidam, in principio, Digest, De acquirenda hereditate. But if he had transmitted the right of deliberation, restitution would cease, because the injury would be consummated in the adult and in the heir of the minor, unless the heir himself were a minor. Therefore, the benefit of restitution does not seem to fail in our case. The substitute, in the person of the minor, is as if injured at the last breath of life; for acceptance cannot be made by another, therefore also, as stated in the Digest, De conditionibus indebiti, l. vltima, in ratione sui; and in the Code, De testamento militis, l. 1.

And for this, it is not necessary to inquire about the transmission of a transmission, where indeed they do not care for the rules of transmissions, and ignorantly say that they transmit. I believe this to be true in the transmission of the inheritance, as it would be in our case, but in the transmission of the right of deliberation, which does not apply here, I would not believe it, because the right of deliberation does not apply where there is a declaration of fact, as stated in l. sententia non cadit. Moreover, the right is not increased by transmission, just as it does not last longer than its own time. Nor is it certain for others in certain states, but for the present, it is not expedient to distinguish here.

There remains another question, whether two sums or one should be owed to the daughters. It appears that one [sum] is due, from the law *De legatis primo*, l. *Plene*, § *Sed si non corpus*. To the contrary, it appears that two [sums] are due, from the law *De adimendis legatis*, l. *Cum*, D. *De legatis* 1, l. *Si ita scriptum*. Jacobus de Arena says that sometimes the same sum is bequeathed when it is owed once; sometimes different sums, and then all are owed. My master says that what Jacobus said is true when it is bequeathed simply. For the same cause, only the last legacy is owed, from the law *De alimentis legatis*, l. *Libertis*. Hence, since here a legacy of three hundred and ninety was made on account of a dowry, therefore only ninety are owed. I hesitate regarding the testator’s will, and in law it seems doubtful. That both sums should be owed, because the first sum was left purely, the second under a condition. Moreover, the first sum was left by way of institution, the second by way of substitution; and thus there are multiple bequests. For sometimes there are multiple legacies in thing and in word, then all are owed; sometimes in word and not in thing, then it is owed once, as in C. *De legatis*, l. *Cum quaestio*. Sometimes it is doubtful, then it matters whether there are multiple forms of bequeathing, and then there are multiple legacies, because a different form creates a different thing and will, as in D. *Ad exemplum*, l. *Iulianus*. Sometimes there is one and the same form of bequeathing, then although they are repeated often, the same is not the same, unless it is valid. And the same and only once is owed, as I have proven above. It is therefore asked: here there are different forms of bequeathing and different sums, the sole identity of the final cause does not make multiple legacies one, since their time has arrived at different times and is considered under different law. The law *Libertis*, etc., does not obstruct, because the cause of maintenance is different from the cause of a dowry, for a dowry can be constituted often, C. *De donationibus ante nuptias*, l. *Penultima* and *Finalis*. But maintenance is something fixed and is not doubled. And if it is received from a last will, the final cause fails, because he does not need maintenance, because he has been maintained; hence this is from the nature of maintenance. A similar case is D. *De usufructu*, l. *Domus*. Moreover, the case is similar to that one, nor are the legacies of different genus and form. From different testaments, however, we can rightly sue often even for maintenance, because maintenance consists in a genus. Hence multiple lucrative causes can concur in origin and effect from the testaments of different persons, D. *De legatis* 2, l. *Meuius*, § *Duobus*. And it supports D. *De rebus dubiis*, l. *Si is qui*, 200, in the principle. Repeating the aforementioned conclusions briefly, I say first that if it is doubtful whether a posthumous child is born, for this purpose that the inheritance may be entered upon, the necessity of the common and proper opinion of the one entering is required; that these three things are present and concur, namely, that the posthumous child is not, nor is he thought to be; to which opinion belongs the singular opinion of the one entering himself, which opinion can be different at different times. And regarding this opinion, the statement of the one entering is followed, i.e., of his own proper and singular opinion. If these three do not occur together, the entry upon the inheritance does not hold, as in the said § *Quod dicitur*.
Secondly, I say that the person in doubt in this case transmits the inheritance, and the possessor of the goods. On the contrary, see the tabular law, *l. illud*, at the end.

Third, I say that the person to whom the transmission of the inheritance has been made finally transmits it to his successor, as argued from l. 3, l. pater, § 15, ff. quod metus causa; l. videamus. Fourth, I say that a minor who did not accept transmits the restitution in integrum to his successor, as in l. qui duos, according to Jacobus.

Fifth, I say that various sums, bequeathed under different forms and in different cases, are all due; because there are multiple legacies, and one is not merged into another. It would be otherwise if one were merged into the other, or if it caused the final cause of the latter to fail, as in the law *libertus*, non ob. de lega. 2, and the law *Sempronius proculo*, because there he had not bequeathed twice at once, but the legacy had been written twice by mistake. And it supports this, ff. de proba., l. quinquaginta.

Sixthly, I say that from the wills of various persons one may repeatedly bring an action for the same alimony, because they are owed in the generic sense, according to the law 1, the law *plane*, and similar authorities. I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws, say and advise in the aforementioned matters, as is contained above, saving the opinion of the more correct view, and for the faith of this I have written and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A compendious substitution is at all times a fideicommissary one.
2. What is the legitimate portion of the mother of a deceased son, when two sisters are compendiously substituted?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† In giving advice, I have always held the common opinion that this substitution is at all times a fideicommissary one; because it was made without distinction of times or ages, by common words, as is noted in l. precibus and l. Centurio, §. extraneo. Although in §. qua ratione the gloss holds that it is direct in the age of pupillarity, and Cynus in his additions holds the same, and Johannes Andreae in c. si pater, nevertheless I adhere to the common opinion, and not to this singular view of these authors, because the uniformity of the penalty induces a uniformity of the mode of substitution, the penalty being inherent in the substitution; for since it is stated in one and the same voice, it must be understood in one and the same voice; and not because it implies contrary qualities, so that it is both direct and an obligation, as argued in C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. quamvis and l. haereditatem, and C. de testamento militis, l. in testamento, and ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. Lucius and l. iam hoc iure, §. sed si alter. It remains to come to the point: what was the legitimate portion of the mother, whether a third part, or a third of the third part of the sisters of the deceased. And it is remarkable that Jacobus de Belvisus, in disputing, determined that it was a third of the whole, and thus a third of twelve is four. And the mother does not succeed unless in four parts intestate, as in auth. defuncto. Therefore the mother is bound for nothing, because he who succeeds to the whole has the whole. And thus in this case there is no difference between the legitimate portion and the intestate succession, when there is the mother and two sisters with her. And the chief reason of Master Jacobus is that the sisters are not admitted to the legitimate portion; therefore they do not make a share for the mother in the legitimate portion, de legitima, l. l. plane, §. si duobus.

But it must be said that, in this case, the mother’s legitime is one-third of one-third, i.e., one-third of what she would receive on intestacy, as in the Authentica de triennio et semestri, § 1, and Codex de inofficiosis testamentis, l. Cum quaeritur. For the sisters are admitted to a share; therefore they constitute a share, since the sisters succeed together with the mother on a per capita basis; therefore they reduce the mother’s succession, and consequently her legitime, which must be carved out of the substance of the share. The objection based on the disposition of Master Jacobus does not hold, because he is speaking of a different case, namely, when the sisters in no way succeed, but only the mother, as when someone dies testate, having instituted a non-disgraceful person, having instituted the mother in something, and having passed over the sisters. For only the mother brings an action for the supplement of the third part, whereas the sisters count for nothing, as in Codex de inofficiosis testamentis, l. Si fratres, and in the Authentica de haereditatibus et falcidiis, l. 1, and by argument from l. 1, in fine, de contrahenda. But in our question we are precisely in the case of intestacy, where the number of persons introduces a seventh portion. And therefore, in our case, the mother has her legitime, i.e., one-third of her third. Furthermore, to Honorata and Fiora, who are of unsound mind, the Trebellian portion is deducted pro rata, which is restored to them. But to pious causes the Trebellian portion is not deducted pro rata, which is restored to them, according to the opinion which I hold, although Johannes Andreas and the Archpriest in c. Si pater say otherwise. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldo de Perusio, Doctor of Laws. And to the truth I have subscribed and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a testament made before a priest with a lesser number of witnesses, and a legacy made in the said testament, are due, and in the following opinion.
2. A statute and custom may be derogated from. c. cum esses, de testamento, extra.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Since law arises from fact, as stated in the Digest, ad legem Aquiliam, l. si ex plagiis, § inclino, therefore the fact upon which there is hesitation is proposed to be as follows. Among other things which he did, he disposed and left, by right of institution, to Puncepta and Macepta, daughters of Cerchius of Lauciano, sisters and cousins of his own on the paternal side, one hundred [units] for each of them. And in these matters he quieted them, and willed that they could have no more of his goods than they could claim. In all his other movable and immovable goods, rights, and actions, etc., he instituted Ausonius, Andreas, and Bartholomew, his nephews, sons of Benedict, as his universal heirs, etc., and substituted them for one another, etc. In the end, he said thus: “And thus I have disposed, and this is my last will, willing and disposing that it be my last will and my final testament, which I willed and disposed to have effect by right of testament, of donation causa mortis, or of donation inter vivos, and of any kind of last will. And I commanded by right of codicils, and of any other last will, and of my final disposition, cancelling and annulling every other testament hitherto made by me and to be made hereafter. And this present testament, and this present last will and disposition, I ordered and willed to prevail totally over all others, and to have the firmness of strength and authority.” Having thus made and concluded his last testament, and his last will and disposition aforesaid, he commanded and requested the notary, namely a certain Lord Angelus, his priest and kinsman, of whom he was of sound mind and body, to reduce it to writing in his book of protocols, and to set down the year and the day, although the said testator did not then validate the said testament by the publication of witnesses, since he did not have them at that time. This done, the said Dominicus survived for a period of time, having made no other testament; now, however, being seized by a grave and dangerous illness, and seeing the danger of death imminent, in the presence of Lord Corradus, his priest and chaplain, and of his church, in which he had chosen his burial in the said testament, and which pertained by right to the said church as his parish church, and having summoned the said three other witnesses without the said priest, he said to them, with the said persons present and hearing, and thus they testify, namely, that he had made and disposed of his last testament and his last will, of which the said Lord Angelus had been requested, and he willed that it should have and obtain the firmness of strength. In which he had disposed that the said Ausonius, Andreas, and Bartholomew, as heirs and as his heirs, should have all his goods, even if they had all the goods of the world, with the said Lord Corradus, his priest and chaplain, and the three witnesses aforesaid present, summoned, hearing, and understanding. Now it is asked, what is the law: whether the said instituted heirs, and thus named afterwards by the protestation of the said Lord Corradus, produced from the witnesses, succeed as heirs of the said Lord testator in his last will, thus dying and disposing, since he thus disposed in the city of Camerino, because he was a citizen and native of the said city, which city pertains immediately to the Roman Church, and in the ecclesiastical, civil, and temporal forum, by c. Cum esses and c. Relatum, de Testamentis. For c. Illud was ordained for the city of Velletri, which is a city as a city of the Camera immediately subject to the Roman Church; thus it seems to be the case for the said heirs thus instituted and named in d. c. Cum esses and c. Relatum. Thus it seems Alanus holds, and against this in d. c. Relatum, and Barbius, 2 q. 4 c. 1, and Hostiensis in c. Cum esses, and in his Summa de Testamentis, § Qualiter, and by Innocentius, whose opinion it seems to have been in d. c. Cum esses and c. Relatum, who says,

† That, as regards the institution of heirs and as regards pious causes, it suffices that which is said in the cited chapter Cum esses, in the title De terris et locis ecclesiae: because the testament and last will are valid before his priest and three other witnesses in his last will, as was the case here. And it may be alleged on behalf of the said heirs that the said testament is valid by the law of codicils and last will, since the notary who wrote it, and the priest, obtain the place of a witness and of two witnesses, as in the law Servus and the law Domitius, De testibus, in the Digest, and as noted in the chapter Quodam contra falsam, in the gloss, Extra, De probat. And even if another priest intervened with the said three witnesses, and thus there would be more witnesses than are found in codicils and other last wills of the said heir so instituted, and in every civil forum. It is established by what is noted by Cynus, Codex, De testibus, in the law Si unus and the law Hac consultissima, § Ex imperfecto, and by Dyther in the said law Domitius. And in favor of the said heirs is the said clause placed at the end, namely, "and this is his last will," etc. And also the said clause which says: "Furthermore, he left by way of institution to Puncenta and Macepta, etc." and commands at the end of the said legacy that they may not ask for nor have more of his goods, etc. And if the said heirs so instituted and named succeed, whether the legacies made in the said testament are valid, excluding the said Puncenta and Macepta, cousins and sisters of the said testator, to whom he had left by way of institution in the said testament and last will for each of them, etc., and in these matters he had quieted them, commanding that they could not have nor ask for more of his goods: for the said cousin sisters so instituted allege that the said testament and last will are not valid, and that they succeed the said Dominicus ab intestate, etc.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the point of the common law, the said allegations contain the truth, namely that the said testament is valid according to canon law, and in the territories of the Church, because where there is truth, there is solemnity according to canon law, as stated in the chapter *Cum esses* and the chapter *Relatum*. For canon law adheres to divine law, and not to human law; and it walks like a pedagogue of the divine law in divine justifications, and not in human formalities, as it is said concerning good faith that it follows truth, and not subtlety, in the Digest, title *De manumis.*, law *Si fideiussor*, section *Quaedam*. But according to civil law, the contrary holds, because two things are required, namely truth and solemnity, in the Code, title *De testamento*, law *Iube*; Code, title *De fideicommissis*, law *Si veritas*; Digest, title *De testamento militis*, law *Divus*, and the stronger reason; Code, title *De fideicommissis*, law *Si*; and Code, title *Qui testamento facere possint*, law *Hac consultissima*. Hence, the said will would not be valid if not fortified by the due number of witnesses, as in the Code, title *De conditionibus*, law *Si*; section *In omni*; Digest, title *De legatis primo*, law *Venio potest delegationem*; law *Codicillis*, section *Ultima*. But according to the law of custom or the statutory law of the place, custom and statutes are observed, and in the territories of the Church.

And a statute, and the custom of the place, may derogate in that place to those [rules], c. Cum esses, and cap. Relatum, so that a greater number of witnesses is required, as those chapters argue, C. de testibus, l. Si, provided that the statutes are solemnly enacted, or the custom is prescribed; because the Decretals say, each province abounds in its own sense. Conclusion: the will is valid, unless custom or statute repugns. Those words, "in which will, etc.," were the words of the testator, to which one must adhere, as from now on, ff. de donationibus, l. Ex hac scriptura. And thus I say, and I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of both Laws, advise, and to the faith I have subscribed, and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Full faith is given to written documents against the person who drafted them.
2. Full faith is given to the written documents of the fiscal official.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† The written response of Ser Nicolaus de Valdo to the letters of Ser Nattus de Montecatino must be upheld in law against the said writer. And this by the general rule: D. de probat. l. publica, § fin.; C. de probat. l. rationes; C. de conuen. fisci debito, l. inter cartulas, lib. 10. According to the special rule: because it was

† The fiscal official, whose letters are given full faith, as in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. in contractibus, § 1. Thirdly, also by reason of the cause: because the writing contains the cause, eo titulo, l. generaliter; ff. de probationibus, l. cum de indebito, § final; extra de fide instrumentorum, c. si cautio; de exceptionibus doli, l. 2, § circa. It is not an objection if it is said that the said writing is uncertain in itself, because it does not contain a certain quantity. For rather it is certain by reference to another thing, namely, to the books of expenditures of the commune of Assisi. Hence, if the quantity appears from the said books, it suffices for the said Ser Nardo. C. de sententiis, quae sine certa quantitate fiunt, l. haec sententia; ff. de re iudicata, l. in summa, cum si, etc. And thus I say, and I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, give my opinion and counsel. And to the truth I have subscribed and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. What is the effect of union, annexation, and incorporation.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The Lord Pope perpetually incorporated and united the monasteries of the Holy Spirit and of Saint Mary of the Virgins, together with all their rights and appurtenances, in such a way that the two convents, each retaining its privileges as before, shall observe their respective rules and pay the customary census to their superior. Now the abbot of Saint Mary of Fervet, who is the superior of the aforementioned nuns of the Holy Spirit, commands the abbess of the Holy Spirit to expel from the said monastery certain nuns belonging to another monastery of the Virgins, and he does not wish them to reside there.

But on their behalf, the aforementioned union, annexation, and incorporation are alleged. The question is: what is the law? And generally, what is the effect of a union, annexation, and incorporation? On this matter, see Innocentius, *De exceptionibus praeparatoriis*, c. *Dilecta*; and Bartolus, *Extra*, *Ne sede vacante*, c. 1. And I say that a union made from several things creates a certain quasi-mixed entity, just as it is held that two provinces become one. L. 1, C. *De metropolibus*, lib. 10; and in Auth. *Ut iudices sine quoquo suffragio*, § *Illud*. However, disjunctive signs indicate that they are not entirely one body. D. *De assessoribus*, l. *Si eadem*. And because the Pope viewed it in such a way that he wished two monasteries to remain distinct in certain respects, he united them in all other respects. L. *Quaesitum*, § *Idem respondit*, D. *De funerariis instrumentis*. And therefore, it is not said to go beyond the clause which proceeds from one of these places to another place, while preserving its own rule, because they are one house, arg. D. *Ad filiationem*, l. 1. I say this regarding the sentence of its prioress or abbess: because it is in a manner one cloister, and a permissive custody, and the rule being saved, whence discipline follows; and what is said of one of the connected things is also said of the other, C. *De diversis rescriptis*, l. *Libelli*; and D. *De constitutionibus*, c. *Translata*. And the goods acquired and to be acquired would seem to be common due to the union, arg. L. 3, D. *Pro socio*. I, Baldus de Perusio, say so.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A substitution made by these words, "if he should die without sons," is fideicommissary according to the common opinion.
2. To an impubes dying intestate, the uncle succeeds, excluding the paternal uncles.
casus:
CASE. In the name of the Lord, amen. The facts are as follows: A certain man named Pucius, a resident at the gate of Saint Francis in the city of Assisi, made his last will and testament; and therein he made certain legacies, and finally disposed as follows: in all his other movable and immovable goods, rights, and accounts, wherever they are and may be found, he instituted and made his son Baptista, and the son of the late lady Mitia, his wife, his universal heir, with this condition appended: that if the said Baptista, son and heir of the said testator Pucius, should die at any time without a legitimate son or sons, he left to Menechus and Cetha, brothers of the said testator Pucius, for equal shares, one piece of land described in the said testament, and another certain piece of land appended in the same testament. Furthermore, he left to the same Menechus and Cetha, his brothers, in the said case, one enclosed piece of land, with this condition: that from the fruits of the said enclosed piece of land to be collected, the aforementioned Menechus and Cetha are bound in solidum to give each year for the next ten years to the monastery of Saint Paul, for lighting one oil lamp in that church. And in that case he thus disposed, namely, that he wished in the said case, namely if the said Baptista, his son, should die without a legitimate son or sons, the other goods of the said testator, besides two vineyards, apart from the aforementioned legacies made by him in the said testament and left, and which he wished to be made, and he ordered, to be sold by his fideicommissaries and their successors, and the price which would be received from these goods to be given and distributed for the soul of the testator and his deceased ones among those persons, places, and monasteries which he wished to be considered as declared from now on, upon the advent of the said case, and he ordered, which would seem appropriate to his aforementioned fideicommissaries, and this and the rest.

After the said testator Pucius died, with the aforementioned Baptista, his son and heir, and a certain man named Francisco Capi, maternal grandfather of the said Baptista, and the aforementioned Menechus and Cetha, his father’s brothers, surviving him; finally, the said Baptista died in pupillary age, with the aforementioned Francisco, the said grandfather, and the said Menechus and Cetha surviving him. The question now arises concerning the following doubts, and first, who succeeds the said Baptista, whether the said Francisco, or the said Menechus and Cetha. Secondly, what the said Francisco ought to have, assuming that he returned nothing to the said Baptista; and whether, regarding the aforementioned legacies made to the said Menechus and Cetha after the death of the said Baptista, the said Francisco ought to deduct anything for the legitime, the Falcidian portion, and the Trebellian portion, or whether the said Menechus and Cetha ought to have the said legacies intact without any diminution, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The substitution of the poor is to be considered fideicommissary, because by this generality of words, if he should die without children, without any mention being made of the pupillary age, a fideicommissary substitution is signified, which can uniformly be valid at all times, as noted in l. precibus and l. centurio, and it is the common opinion of the doctors and the gloss, although some say the contrary. But I, in giving my opinion, do not depart from the common opinion. Therefore, the poor, and the places, or monasteries, or executors for them, are not substituted pupillarily.

And thus, if an impubes dies intestate, the grandfather succeeds to the inheritance, excluding the uncles, as in the Authentica *De haeredibus ab intestato*, § 2, *Cui debetur legitima*. The remaining goods, however, must be distributed by the executors according to the form of the will, as in the chapter *Si pater*, *De testamento*, Book 6, always saving other legacies which are due to those to whom they were left, after deduction. Finally, the legitima portions are to be taken from all the legitima portions of the years; and if the son had made an inventory, he could also deduct the Falcidian portion from legacies not for pious causes, from which two quarters are deducted, when the son is burdened with a condition of granting land. See the chapter *Rayff* and the chapter *Rayn*, *De testamento*. I, Baldus de Ubaldis.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a legacy made to the tutor who does not accept the guardianship is due, and when.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Although it has been alleged fully and subtly, nevertheless it must be considered,

† That sometimes a legacy is left to a tutor in consideration of the office imposed. Sometimes in consideration of blood relationship. Sometimes as to a creditor, and thus not on account of a future cause, but on account of a past cause. Sometimes there is doubt as to whether it is in consideration of the office, or of the person, or of the credit, or alternatively of various causes.

In the first case, whether the reason of law impedes the guardianship, and nevertheless the legacy is due. C. de leg. l. administratione. Or if it is through negligence that the legacy is left, and the legacy is due, de excus. ut l. quod autem, because where there is no office, the benefit annexed to it ought not to be due, ff. de leg. 1. l. et si. and because he who does not observe the office impugns it, and therefore does not deserve the benefit. ff. de excus. tuto. l. ex his.

In the second case, the legacy is due even if the duties of administration are omitted, because the effect is due by itself, nor is it mixed with another final cause of the legacy, but rather natural proximity. ff. de excus. tuto. l. tutor petitus. §. 1. Therefore, since the natural cause of the defect does not cease, the effect does not cease.

In the third case, if it is established that there is at least a natural debt, and then the legacy is valid and is due, even if the guardianship is not undertaken, because the reason for the legacy was different from the burden of the imposed office, de excus. tuto. l. Nesennius. §. fin. de condi. et demon. l. quibus diebus. §. dominae. And so to speak, due to the uncertainty of the office not undertaken, the legacy is not revoked, argumen. ff. de donat. l. Aquilius regulus. cum glo. sua. and eodem titu. l. si pater. Or if the debt is not established, and then there is doubt in this matter, because although the confession does not prove a true debt, it nevertheless proves the cause of the legacy, insofar as it depends on the intention of restitution: which also the proximate cause of the testament proved, ff. de haere. insti. l. Pacumeius. Hence, since in this matter the intention of the testator is to be considered rather than the effect of proof, it seems that the legacy is due, especially since it was also inscribed; in any case, if the guardianship does not claim a place for itself: therefore it was not inscribed on account of the guardianship, dicta l. Nesennius. For the will of the testator as to intention is proved by bare words, as l. fin. ff. de re. eo. and words are to be understood as if it were true what the testator believed, de haeredi. insti. l. in quo loco. §. 1. and there it is noted in the gloss. For since the testator relied on another cause, the presumption of law ceases that he left it on account of the guardianship, and in view of, or for the sake of, the children. d. l. Nesennius. §. fin. For otherwise he would have left it, de conditio. et demonst. l. illis libertis. and l. in conditionibus primum locum. And it greatly bites the conscience, and is against natural reason, that a creditor should lose his right because he did not undertake the guardianship. It supports this auth. minoris debitor. and de procura. l. pater filio. in glo. unless it is answered that this is true if it were established by decree: but this is not established.

To the contrary it seems, because a confession annexed to a legacy for the purpose of obligating does not prove a contract, because here the legacy is not valid, de leg. 3. l. Lucius. §. fin. quisquis. de liberatione lega. l. Aurelio. §. vltimo. Therefore we are in a simple legacy, hence he who did not undertake the guardianship knowing the fact, let him impute it to himself, because he ought to have followed the judgment of the deceased, and not by his own act impugned it. From this it follows that the said brothers of the testator are excused from contravening, nor does the condition of institution or substitution fail: because those words, "if he did not contradict the legacy," are understood when they would contradict unjustly, but if they contradict justly by the tacit judgment of the testator due to the fault of the legatee, there is no penalty, argumen de legatis secundo. l. cum pater. §. de liber. For if the legatee by his own act gives matter and right to contradict, let him impute it to himself.

What then shall we say? This concession, indiscreet and without a certain cause, does not prove that a debt exists, but proves affection. But to this it is answered that these words, being vague and generally uttered, effect nothing, nor do they prove, but rather require proof, de castrensi peculio. l. si forte. C. de codicil. l. donatione. in glo. And therefore, since they do not aid the intention of the legatee in any way, they are held as not added, hence if they are false, they do not vitiate the legacy, and if they are true, the effect is not increased. C. de falsa causa. l. si non designata. And therefore in every event they add nothing to the legacy.

I believe that when the cause which is expressed, if it were true, would render the legacy useless, it is not to be considered a final cause, but an impulsive one, because if it were considered final, if it were false, the legacy would not fail, de conditio. et demon. l. cum tale. §. fina. If therefore it is not a final cause by legal presumption, it should not be adhered to as a cause, but the legacy should be regarded as simple, which the law interprets in doubt as being in consideration of the office. And this is the fourth case, because here I say that we are in a case of doubt: for laws which do not prove do not exclude doubt, but rather create it, or make doubt present, not absent, because in a case of doubt it is presumed on account of the office, or a mixed consideration of the office and another impulsive cause, provided that the office is the final cause, since no other cause is given which is the final cause of the legacy, or legacy, ergo et c. Otherwise, if the testator had expressed a certain cause why it should be due. d. l. Aquilius. For then he rather wishes the debt to be paid than a benefit bestowed: and therefore it is not a mere legacy, because it does not bestow a benefit, but pays a debt. ff. de haeredita. institu. l. seruo fideicommissaria. §. 1. and argumen. ff. ad legem Falcid. l. sed vsufruc. §. dos. l. cum dotem. For words, to prove, must be certain and clear, as is read and noted, ff. deposi. I. 1. §. si quis argentum. And thus it seems to me according to the strictness of the law, although good equity and good conscience would much persuade the contrary: because a good man adheres not to disputation, but to truth. Nevertheless, in a point of written law, because the confession of debt is uncertain and has no cause, nor its existentials, it can be well defended that the legacy is not due to the daughter born, neglecting the guardianship, in the course of legal proceedings, nothing else being proved extrinsically, because although a cause which is not proved true does not vitiate the legacy, it nevertheless does not increase the strength of the legacy, nor defend it against legitimate impugnations, because a cause which does not appear true cannot effect anything. And if it is said that the judgment of the testator deserved it as a creditor, not as a tutor, I answer that the credit is not established, but in l. tutor petitus. §. i. another cause is established, which was true, but here it is not.

And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws, and to the faith I have subscribed, and signed with the sign of my name, always saving the first truth, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When a clause placed absolutely must be referred to all things.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

A clause placed absolutely refers to all matters, as stated in the Decretals, De Appellatione, chapter 2, "Requiris," unless it would involve a contradiction, as in the law "Si idem cum eodem," §. fin., De Iurisdictione omnium iudicum, chapter "Iudicium," or would introduce some other absurdity, as noted in the Digest, De Legatis primo, law "Talis scriptura." This is true when the clause is perfect and placed simply; otherwise, if it is not a clause but part of a clause and of the sentence, for then it does not refer to other separate clauses to which it does not belong, but only to that to which it is attached, as in law 3, ff., De Liberis et Posthumis, and law "Plures," De Rebus Dubiis, and Codex, De Liberis Praeteritis, law 1, with many similar cases. Now it occurs to me to doubt whether this is a general clause or whether it is part of a clause. Thus, from that verse "et similiter" until the end, there is not more than one clause having two members: first, when the dazia are paid; second, when the dazia are not paid. For if it is a general clause beginning at "et punctam do," there, "et si datia et c.," then it refers to all matters. But if the letter is read suspensively until the end, then it is otherwise, because it would be part of a clause, and thus it would not be understood to apply to adjudications, as in law "Praetor," §. "Erit," Ut Bonorum Raptorum. Which I believe to be more correct, because the first part deserves the privilege of immunity by reason of the conjunction of blood, and therefore I do not believe that those who enacted the law intended to burden them. Codex, De Codicillis, law "Si," §. penultimate; and Codex, De Imponenda Lucris Descriptio, law 1, Book 10. Therefore, when it is doubtful whether it is a clause or part of a clause, this is presumed: because natural equity more strongly dictates that one should presume this regarding the mind of the Legislator. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of both laws, have written this in good faith and have signed it with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether damage inflicted on a thing belonging to a common partnership is common.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the case concerning the general goods taken by Chiaraualle, pending between Francis and Marian, it seems that the following should be said most briefly:

† That the loss was common, because the goods were given in the common property of the partnership without any fault of Marian. For this was a fortuitous event, as is clear: because no prudence of the wisest man could have foreseen it; therefore the loss is common. D. pro socio, l. cum duobus, §. quaedam sacrariam; and §. si in coeunda; and §. fin.; and Inst. pro socio, §. fin. To the contrary it seems that Marian suffered this on account of his father’s name: for the occasion of the paternal name inflicted this loss and caused the enmity, on account of which the generanellos were taken away, which enmity is reckoned as fault, whether just or unjust. D. si merces, §. culpae, locati; D. penult., soluto matrimonio. Moreover, because through the favor of Lord Trinca Marian could have recovered the generanellos; and it is proposed to me that he ought to have done so, and does not do so, and thus he was at fault. Moreover, because he ought to have appeared at Todi and acted against Chiaravalle, because under the pretended name of his he had caused the generanellos to be taken, and if in fact he could not, it was an injury which Chiaravalle was doing in fact to the person of Marian, which ought not to harm another, according to the note in D. nam et si servus, in principio, in 2. gloss., de negotiis gestis. And this seems sufficiently equitable and fitting, yet I doubt whether the first opinion is more correct in law, and therefore I do not advise precisely on this matter, and they would do well to compose among themselves, if, however, the fault of Marian were proved: because, knowing that it could happen on account of the paternal name, he did not foresee it, then without doubt the entire risk would be his, etc. And thus I advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws, and for the faith of this I have written and signed with the sign of my name. The case, however, on which I have now advised, is proposed under this form, which is valid.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A legacy made for the purpose of providing a dowry for marriage, and not for increasing the dowry of a woman already married, is not due.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Because the said legacy was made in aid of marriage, and not for the purpose of augmenting the dowry of the bride by her parents or relatives, I hold that the said legacy is not due to the said daughter in rem, and the words of the testament manifestly exclude her, as well as the defect of the final cause: because the legacy does not apply to the person in question, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. cum tale, § falsam; and D. ad Trebellianam, l. a filia, § alumno. For those words, “so that it should not be exacted,” etc., are sufficiently verified here, because there does not exist such a person as the testator ordered to be given. Hence, it is sufficiently lacking, because it lacks the requisite quality, as in D. de legatis tertio, l. legatis servis, § si ex officio. And this is true if the dowry was constituted at the very inception of the marriage or before. But if she were later endowed after an interval by her relatives, she would perhaps not lose the right to the said legacy by their act, by argument from D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. paterfamilias testamento. It is not an objection, D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. obligamus, § lege, because there it speaks of a father who is bound to endow his daughter by natural law; here, however, it concerns an heir condemned to endow only in aid of marriage; and thus it does not obstruct what I have said above. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of both laws. And to the truth I have subscribed and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If someone is called a false traitor by another, the one who called him is not punished for two insulting words, but for only one.
2. A quality joined to a crime does not give rise to a plurality of crimes.
3. A traitor is said to be so in three ways.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain person said to another, “False coin counterfeiter, traitor.” The question is whether he is to be punished for two insulting words or for one word. And it must be known that sometimes words necessarily signify different crimes, such as “thief,” “adulterer,” “murderer”; then, by the statute which says that one is to be punished for each insulting word, as many penalties would be imposed as there are crimes stated and imputed, D. de privatis delictis, l. nunquam plura. Sometimes words necessarily signify the same thing, as if one were to say to someone repeatedly in the same context, “You are a thief, you are a thief.” And then there is only one crime, because no new offense arises from the repeated utterance of words; rather, it is more a kind of contumacy of speech and a continuing offense than a new offense, argumentum D. de testibus, l. vnum. Sometimes words signify an offense and its quality, as if it were said, “You are a thief, you are a most wicked thief,” or if it were said, “You are a murderer, you committed murder treacherously.” Then there is only one crime, because the quality joined to the offense does not create a plurality of offenses, D. de accusationibus, l. sena; censuit D. de noxalis actione, l. in delictis, § si detractata. Sometimes there are such words that can signify different things, and also not different things; and then, in case of doubt, a plurality of offenses is not presumed, argumentum D. de iureiurando, l. eum qui, § qui popularibus. And this is our case.

For a traitor is said to be so in three ways. First, he who betrays the prince or the public, according to the Julian Law on Majesty, law 3. Second, he who betrays an associate or a friend by killing or wounding him, as noted by Bartolus in the law *Respiciendum*, section *Delinquunt*, on penalties. Third, he who betrays him whom he has received in trust, Digest, on Prævarication, law 3; Digest, on Penalties, law *Si quis aliquid*, section *In scientia*. Now, let us suppose that a false witness gave false testimony against his non-related associate; certainly, the crime of falsity and the crime of treason are incurred. Therefore, since one thing cannot be attributed to another in doubt, the same act is presumed, and not multiple crimes; and thus one penalty should be imposed, and not multiple penalties. Hence, *falsarius proditor* is explained such that *falsarius* is in the force of an adjective, and *proditor* in the force of a substantive, Institutes, on Tutors, in the beginning. And it supports what is noted by Bartolus, Digest, on Rules of Law, law *Item apud Labeonem*, section *Ait praetor*. And thus I say, and I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws, advise. And to the truth I have subscribed, and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the term "son" in wills includes the grandson. See also above, opinion 302, and in opinion 363.
casus: CASE. In the name of God, amen. Cicius Iuncta, son of Martin of Sassoferrato, died having made a will, in which he left the above-mentioned lady and Francesca, his daughters, to whom he bequeathed by right of institution a certain quantity of money for each of them. In all his other movable and immovable goods, rights, and actions, both useful and direct, his own and ecclesiastical, he instituted Nicolaus, Franciscus, and Bartholomew, his sons, as universal heirs in equal parts, and ordered that if any of them should die within the age of pupillage, or afterwards at any time without legitimate sons, that his said goods and inheritance should devolve upon the survivors. And if his said sons and heirs should all die within the age of pupillage, or afterwards at any time without legitimate sons, he ordered that his goods and inheritance should devolve, namely, upon his said daughters, two hundred pounds of denarii for each of them, and his other goods should devolve upon Vannes, his brother, or his sons and male heirs only. Furthermore, he ordered that if the said Vannes should die without legitimate male sons, that his said goods and inheritance, left to him above, should devolve upon the above-mentioned his daughters, and their sons and heirs. The said Bartholomew died in the age of pupillage, the above-mentioned Nicolaus and Franciscus, sons of the said testator, surviving. After this, the said Vannes, the brother of the said testator, the substitute, died, with Angelo, his son, surviving from the said Vannes. Afterwards, the said Franciscus, being of age, died having made a will, in which he left the said Nicolaus, his brother, as his universal heir, and to him he substituted the said Angelo and his sons. Then the said Angelo died, with one male son named Franciscus surviving from him. Finally, the said Nicolaus died having made a will, in which he instituted the said Franciscus, son of the said Angelo, as his universal heir, the above-mentioned two Francescas and Sancta, and certain sons of the said Donna, daughters of the above-mentioned testator Cechius, surviving. Now it is asked, to whom should the goods and inheritance of the said Cechius Iuncta belong: to his said daughters and the sons of his daughter, or to the said Franciscus, son of the said Angelo, son of the said Vannes, brother of the said Cechius? Since it is proposed on behalf of the said daughters of Cechius that the said Vannes and Angelo, his son, died before the said Nicolaus, son and coheir of the said testator Cechius, whose goods are in question, and the rest.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† There are various opinions on whether the term “son” in wills includes a grandson. For Andreas de Pisis, Cynus, and Raynerius, in l. Gallus, §. instituens, say that it does not. Bartolus, in l. liberorum, learned that it does, by virtue of l. Lucius, de haered. insti., where Scaevola says that the term “sons” comprehends the children of a brother. But the term “children” includes grandsons; therefore, etc. And in response to §. instituens, Bartolus replies that there the testator designated the son by his proper name, not by a general and appellative name. I distinguish, or interpret, that if the inclusion of the grandson accords with the natural affection of the testator, then the grandson is included, because it is presumed that every testator, as far as possible, tests prudently, but according to the dictate of natural reason. d. l. Gallus, §. quidam recte. And thus speaks l. Lucius. For there the grandson ought rather to be added than the slave, who is altogether an outsider. This is not an obstacle. §. institutiones, because the testator thinks of a certain person, not of everyone. eo. ti. l. Titius. Or, if the extension of “son” to “grandson” is contrary to the order of natural affection, then it would be a harsh interpretation, and this should not be done, as noted in Auth. de te. fideicommissarii, §. manifestum. The same applies to a disposition implying favor and hatred, or burden, as in inst. qui dare tut. pos., §. si. Now, in the case at hand, to exclude or restrict daughters on account of the children of a brother is contrary to natural affection toward one’s children. And therefore I will not interpret that grandsons are included. It is no objection that the testator says “heirs,” because this comes in a qualifying sense, not an extensive one; otherwise it would follow that even an outsider heir would exclude the daughters, which is false. Moreover, the testator himself declares this when he says, “if Vannes dies without sons,” but does not repeat “heirs.” But if the word “heirs” is placed in the condition, not coming by itself to qualify “son,” but absolutely, it is understood to refer to all children. ff. ad Treb., l. ex facto, §. si. The sense, therefore, is this: that they must be sons and heirs, and not that the term includes other children of a more remote degree. For if this were so, the word “sons” would be superfluous and would effect nothing, which should not be the case. In the first question, it must be said and done, because it is doubtful on account of the undifferentiated term “heir,” for the conjunction is usually held to be ampliative. ff. de le. 3, l. ea tamen. But there the conjunction was not placed in the mode of quality, but between separate substances. And therefore I hold and advise the aforementioned daughters, to whom the share of the predeceased sister accrued, etc. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A judgment rendered, even if contrary to the right of the litigant, must be put into execution.
2. A judgment without a trial is of no effect.
3. The assertion of the judge regarding the trial is not believed.
4. Any judgment from which no appeal has been taken gives the victor a just cause for litigation.
casus: CASE. IN the name of Christ, Amen. The point of fact, on which counsel is requested to be given, is as follows. Against Francis Angelutii of Assisi, an inquiry was formed by the Lord Captain of the said city, to the effect that the said Francis maliciously with a certain iron sword wounded Rufinus with one wound in the left hand of the said Rufinus, with effusion of blood. On account of which wound the said hand remained and will remain weakened. And the aforementioned offenses were committed near a tavern, by two houses of one, as contained in the inquiry. This Francis, after the inquiry was added, confessed that he had wounded the said Rufinus in the left hand of the said Rufinus, and concerning the weakening of the said hand, he said that he wished to abide by the judgment of physicians. According to the form of the statutes of Assisi, a physician was summoned, who judged, pronounced, and declared that the said hand had remained weakened for the future, in the presence of the said Francis and with his contradiction. The Captain of Assisi, seeing the aforementioned, condemned the said Francis in 380 livres of deniers to be given and paid to the chamber of the commune of Assisi, and in 75 livres of deniers to be given and paid to the said Rufinus for the said weakening of the member, by sentence, the penalty being doubled to him on account of the place, according to the form of the said statutes, with a quarter deducted on account of the benefit of confession. It is asserted that this sentence passed into res iudicata. It was produced before the competent judge, and execution of the mandate was requested according to the form of the statutes of Assisi. This Francis, within the term established for him, produced his exceptions before the said judge, which are directed to you: and it is also objected on behalf of the said Francis that the said sentence, condemning him in the said quantity to the said Rufinus, ought not to be executed, since according to the form of the said statute, the said quantity attributed to the said Rufinus by the said sentence ought not to have been doubled, and notwithstanding the statute, which is to be understood as a maleficium, and notwithstanding the statute on the penalty of one who strikes, whereby a member remains weakened, and also the statute that penalties for maleficia are doubled, and because it does not appear legitimately concerning the said weakening of the member, according to what is asserted in the said sentence. On the other hand, on behalf of the said Rufinus, it is said that the said Francis, notwithstanding the objections, ought to execute the said sentence, which was duly rendered, in the said quantity committed to him as due, all the more so because the said sentence passed into res iudicata, and also because the same Francis paid the quantity due to the commune, and thus acquiesced to the said sentence. Now the question is, having seen the petition of the said Rufinus, and the said sentence produced by the said Rufinus, and having seen the exceptions and allegations of the said Francis, and also having seen the aforementioned statutes and other laws of the aforementioned parties, which laws are directed to you, and even to give full faith to them as public, etc. It is asked whether the said sentence against the said Francis ought to be executed in the quantity of the condemnation to the said Rufinus, and thus in whole or in part, or whether the said sentence is null or valid, and what are the parts of the executing judge. On all of which, sound counsel is requested.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† If the statement of the case were true, the said sentence would be valid and ought to be ordered into execution, even if it had been rendered contrary to the right of the litigant in a greater amount, as in ff. de his, qui not. infa. l. quid ergo. §. pę. na grauior. ver. sed si in causa furti., and that whole general rule operates to the effect that a sentence which contains no express error must be executed, ff. de iudiciis. l. si praetor. in princi., ff. fami. erci. l. cum putarem., ff. de peculio. l. eo tempore. in prin., ff. de rei vend. l. ex diuerso. You ought to have appealed, says the Emperor, if the sentence doubled your liability, C. si saepius in integrum resti. postula. l. j.; for remedies of appeal were introduced precisely in order that the injustice of sentences might be corrected, ff. de appel. l. 1. Whence, once the appeal has been omitted, the single remedy is a complaint of nullity, unless the first sentence is null by operation of law, ff. quae sententiae sine appel. rescindatur. l. 1. in prin., C. quando prouo. non est necesse. l. 2., ff. de appel. l. expressi. And having inspected the acts, I do not find an inquest concerning the scar; I find it stated that I am told, and the sentence,

† but a sentence without a process is worth nothing, ff. de re iud. l. si cum nulla., C. de fideicom. liber. l. fi., ff. communi diui. l. vt fundus. For a pronouncement does not pertain to the office of the judge unless it was claimed, or tacitly included under the claim, ff. de aedil. edic. l. ędiles. §. item sciendum., ff. de aqua plu. ar. l. alterius. §. de eo opere., ff. de instito. l. habebat., de app. l. scio.

† nor is credence given to the assertion of the judge concerning the process, as in c. quoniam contra falsam., as is noted in C. de arbit. l. ne in arbitris; and from the acts it appears that there was no inquest concerning the scar, because the acts do not state this, C. de error. aduo. l. errores. Although it may be presumed that there had been an inquest concerning this, the sentence was not valid; nevertheless, the one seeking execution ought not to be condemned in expenses,

† because any sentence from which no appeal has been taken gives the victor just cause for litigation, as in C. de reb. credi. l. generaliter. §. 2., and especially this one of which we speak, because it is founded upon the truth of what was transacted, and in truth an inquest was made: although an error does not truly appear through the acts, yet through the malice of I know not whom, it was such as I have written. And so I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of both laws, declare and advise, and for the faith thereof I have subscribed myself and signed with the mark of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the term "sons" includes grandsons in wills. And see above, opinion 362.
body: The pater familias made a will, in which he instituted his son as his universal heir, and stated that if the said son should die in pupillary age, or at any time thereafter, the said inheritance should devolve upon Titius, or his sons. It happened that, after the testator died, while the instituted son was still alive, Titius died, and his son, leaving a grandson by his son, finally the son died. The grandson of Titius wished to come to the goods; it is asked whether he can. On this question, it seems most doubtful according to l. quod si nepotes, de testamento tutorum et institutione, qui dari tutores possunt, §. fin., and this occurred because of the common appellation.

† Regarding this, we must consider that the term “children” is sometimes used in the sense of a determined person, to whom something is conferred and about whom disposition is made, and sometimes in the sense of a mere appellative and an indeterminate disposition: not as referring to a certain person. And thus, as if it were an appellative substituted for a proper name, by which, as at present, something is conferred under a certain demonstration, so as to signify and demonstrate in place of a proper name, not by reference to or demonstration of any certain individual, but indeterminately with respect to the appellative. Thirdly, it is used not as referring to the person to whom disposition is made, but as a sign and the form of an attached condition. On the first point, see *l. contraria*. On the second, see *l. si Iulianus*, § *mutui*, ad Macedoniam; and *l. filium*, eodem titulo; and *l. iuxta*, de verbis significationibus; and *l. in his*; and *l. solennis*, de conditionibus et demonstrationibus; and *l. si vir uxori*, eodem titulo; and § *si hoc praesenti*, in the Authenticum de sancta ecclesia, de 3; *l. in conditionibus*, de conditionibus et demonstrationibus; and *l. Iulianus*, eodem titulo; and the argument of *l. 3*, C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus. And the plural is resolved into the singular according to intent, as in C. quando dies legati cedit, *l. si uxori*; and *l. non est sine liberis*.

In explaining this, it must be considered that some laws state that the term “children” does not include grandchildren, due to the common usage of the term, as in the aforementioned § *fin.* and *l. quod si nepotes*. Others state that it does include them, due to the meaning of the word, as in *l. liberorum*, § *sed quod Papirius*, de verbis significationibus. And thus *l. iusta interpretatione* could be understood, i.e., the notable expressed meaning, which pertains to the identity of reason, as in the aforementioned *l. sed Iulianus* and *l. filium*. Likewise, the aforementioned *l. iusta* could be understood by taking the word “interpretation” differently.

Secondly, it must be considered that in conditions we pay great attention to intent and effect, as in *l. in conditionibus*, de conditionibus et demonstrationibus; and *l. 3*, § *conditio*, de adimendo legatis. Also, that which is good and equitable, as in *l. in his*, de conditionibus et demonstrationibus. For the decision of this question, it must be known that sometimes this term is used to signify a certain person and to demonstrate the person to whom disposition is made in place of a proper name; and then it seems as if it were the first case. By imposition and usage, it signifies or represents; thus, an appellative placed in the position of a proper name is understood in this way, as in the aforementioned *l. quod si nepotes* and *l. sina*. Just as regarding an appellative placed for the same effect, as is proven in the same title, *l. duo sunt Titij*; and *l. si quis servum*, § *si inter*, de legatis 2; and de manumissione testamento, *l. si ex pluribus*. Sometimes it is used in its proper form as an appellative, not by reference to a certain individual, but to signify according to the force of the appellative; and then the laws speak which say that the term “child” includes a grandson, either by meaning or at least by intent or interpretation of the jurist. Thus is understood *l. sed Iulianus*, § 1; and *l. filium*, § *sed quod Papirius*; and *l. iusta*. Sometimes it is used as a sign and the form of a condition, and in this case one must turn to the rules and numbers of conditions and judge according to them.

The nature of conditions is that in them we look to intent, not words, as in the aforementioned *l. 3*, C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, where a condition of emancipation is attached; and yet, if not emancipation but intervening death equates the disposition due to the same effect and intent, and nevertheless they are not the same, neither by meaning nor by term. Likewise, payment and release are not the same; and in a condition of payment, release is equated, as in *l. Iulianus*, de conditionibus et demonstrationibus. Likewise, a condition of marriage is equated by entry, as in the aforementioned § *sed hoc praesentis*. It is also a rule that in them we look to what is good and equitable, as in the aforementioned *l. in his*.

It is certain that the testator did not prefer Titius’s children as persons to whom disposition is made. But if he had wished, the testator could not confer; yet from this disposition, nothing is conferred to the child or grandson, which is quite clear. Nor does it signify in place of a proper name, nor can it, since he speaks of those to be born, who do not have a proper name, as in *l. maximum vitium*, in fine, C. de libris praeteritis. But they are placed as an appellative, but according to the law, the appellative signifies by the meaning of the word, or at least by intent or interpretation of the word, includes the grandson, as is alleged in the second case. Likewise, they are placed as a sign by the form of the condition, in which we must look to intent; but the intent is the same, because he had no one, or could have no one, known; he loved no one under his own person, because he could not love, but in the appellative. Likewise, because he did not confer to them, but reserved without depriving Titius, it is clear that everything was placed and disposed out of his affection, and that which he had for Titius and his children, to whom he wished to confer or preserve the same goods. But that he equally loves children and grandchildren from his son, as in the Authenticum de haereditate ab intestato, § 1; and Institutiones de haeredibus quae ab intestato, § 2. Therefore, it seems that he disposed of all equally.

Likewise, it cannot be seen that the testator did not love by his own meaning of love those not yet conceived; because they were not yet in existence or conceived during his lifetime, as in the Authenticum de haereditate ab intestato, § plane; ff. unde cognati, *l. 1*, § *pro eo*. But according to what he had for Titius, since they are future children of his children; but that they are equally loved and called. Likewise, there is no reason to give why, for the sake of children more than grandchildren from Titius, who began to hold the place of children and obtain it, and succeed in the goods in place of children, and be called. Likewise, this is supported by what is good and equitable, as in the aforementioned *l. in his*. For which reason, I, Jacobus Butrigarius, in giving counsel, seem to have done so, and I seal this counsel with my seal, and I write it to the faith, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether and when the interpretation of the common law may be alleged in questions concerning statutes.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The texts of statutes, and the opinions of both ancient and modern jurists, are uncertain; therefore, having set these aside, you should say as follows.

† because either the question is about the interpretation of the common law, whether it can be alleged in questions of statutes, or about the interpretation of the municipal law itself. In the first case, it matters, because either the old law is corrected by a new legislator, as in C. de novo codi. confir. l. prima. §. hunc igitur, or derogation is made to the old law similarly by a new legislator, as in C. de lati. lib. tol. in princip. ff. de verborum significatio. l. derogatur. Or something is added to or subtracted from the old law itself, or it is explained by a new legislator, as in ff. ad muni. l. prima. §. qui operas. ff. de verborum significatio. l. uerbis legis. in fin. And then the municipal law could be understood according to another determination of the common law, arg. ff. de sepultu. viol. l. 3. §. diuus. The reason is that it is not said that an interpretation is made, but that the statute of the law is observed, C. de uete. iur. enucl. l. prima. §. iubemus igitur. in prima constitu. C. §. quibus uerbis. versi. adijcientes. and ff. de iusti. et iur. l. ius ciuile. in princip. Otherwise, no common laws could be alleged concerning the matter of statutes, which would be absurd. Or it is a resolution of one act into another, or one species resolved into another, and thus a proper quality and nature is attributed contrary to the proper meaning of the words, and then I cannot, argu. ff. de suppel. lega. l. Labeo. solut. matrimon. l. si vero. §. de viro. and argu. ff. si ager vec. l. prima. §. qui in perpetrum. Because an external act should not be implied, as in ff. de pub. l. quemcunque. §. fina. and not. ff. de verbo. obligatio. l. sciendum. ff. de testamen. milita. l. quod constitutum. and l. fina. and de bono. posses. ex testamento mili. l. 1. de conditio. et demonstrat. l. cum auus. C. de fideicom. l. cum acutissimi. de iure fisc. l. fina. §. Papin. de aqua plu. arcend. l. 1. in prin. de sta. lib. l. 3. §. si quis. and l. Labeo. and in infinite laws which imply or understand new cases, but the words are entirely explained extraneously and most improperly, and contrary to the proper meaning of the words. Or it is a proper explanation of the words, as appears in ff. ad l. Aquil. l. ita vulnetatus. in princip. de uerbo obliga. l. 1. in fi. and insti. eo. §. utrum. and not. ff. de origi. iur. l. 1. in fin. And then I can also, arg. ff. de auro, et argen. l. Plautius. de lega. 3. l. non aliter. de fun. ienstruct. l. cum delanionis. §. 1. de leg. et senatusconsul. l. bensgnius. and l. cum ambigua. If, however, the matter concerns the interpretation of the municipal law itself, then either the words are explained properly and declared according to their proper meaning. And there can be a reason, because such declaration introduces nothing new, but reveals and explains what was already introduced, as in ff. de test. l. haeredes palam. §. si quid. de acque rer. do. l. Labeo. §. cum quis si serui. uen. l. licuti. §. si quaeratur. de rei uendi. l. ex diuerso. §. 1. And this is held by Dy. de uerb. sign. l. j. for which the laws cited above serve. Or it is extended or restricted to another case, and then either to avoid absurdity, and I can, e.g., if a statute prohibits going at night with a light, I will understand it prohibited all the more without a light. Likewise, if it prohibits carrying grain out of the county with donkeys, I will understand the same for those transporting with oxen, with a cart, or with a beast of burden. Likewise, if it prohibits carrying wheat, all the more so flour. Although Dyn. says the contrary in this, and wrongly, ff. de lega. 3. l. quaesitum. §. illud. argum. ad praedicta. ff. ad Maced. I. Iulianus. §. mutui. since absurdity is always understood to be excluded by law, and thus with words omitted, ff. de neg. gest. l. Pompo. de excu. tuto. l. oportet. §. aliud. l. in ambigua. ff. de lega. to which is added C. de condi. inser. l. cum patrem. and de testa. l. hac consultissima criminalia. and de legat. 1. l. si quis a filio. §. 1. ff. de fideicommis. liber. l. fina. de regu. iur. l. aliud. §. absurdum. de publi. l. Caesar. Thus I understand ff. de mun. et hono. l. vt gradatim. §. sed si lege. for there the municipal law is restricted, although Dyn. says that it is simply declared, which is false, as appears expressly there. Likewise, I understand l. 2. C. de noxa. for that happens for the sake of avoiding absurdity, namely, that an innocent person not be punished for the fault of another against the laws. C. de pę. l. sancimus. and thus not. C. de decre. decu. super immun. in rubri. libro 10. and the above are also proven by the fact that no occasion is given for circumvention, argumen. ff. de transac. l. cum hi. §. si cum lis. de rebus eo. l. magis puto. §. si pupillus. cum. simili. Or by the reason of compelling equity, and then either the municipal law is conceived personally, and is not extended to another person, even one having every reason, as in ff. de consti. prin. l. 1. in fi. de re. iu. l. priuilegia. and l. in omnibus. instit. de iure naturali. §. sed quod Principi. Or not personally, yet it disposes in an uncertain case in a certain manner, and then either the equity is written in the body of the law, and I will observe it even in another case in which the same equity is found. Example: if a statute grants immunity from personal offices to those over 25 years old, it will apply all the more to those under 25 years old, because the written equity dictates this, ff. de mino. l. 1. Likewise, if a statute repels those over 25 and under 40 from public council, all the more so those under 25, ff. de mune. et hono. l. ad rem publicam. And the reason is clear, because an absurdity would result in its opposite. To which serves what I said above. Or the motivating equity is not written in the body of the law, for example, because a statute on tolls grants that a creditor, or another non-owner having a right in the thing, may sell without toll, I will not extend this to the owner, although a stronger equity seems to exist in him. Likewise, if it permits the sale of wheat by owners without toll, I will not extend this to wine, although a similar reason of equity exists in it, ar. dictae l. non aliter. de le. 3. l. prospexit. qui, et a quibus. and l. quod constitutum. de testa. mil. ad muni. l. constitutionib. de exercito. l. 1. §. si is, qui. de ver. ob. l. quicquid astringen. C. de leg. et consti. l. 1. and argum. dictae l. si vero. §. de iure. for the legislators do not seem to have had this in mind, argu. ff. de excu. tut. l. ex his. de suppel. lega. l. labeo. in fi. Nor does it obstruct ff. de lega. et sen. consul. l. iura. and de vi, et vi arm. l. 1. §. quod vulgo. and what is not, ff. de re iudi. l. quae per necessitatem. and l. quod contra. and what is not, Dy. in c. in argumentum. lib. 6. because they speak in the common law, whereas here it is in the special and municipal, ar. d. l. priuilegia. and l. in omnib. de re. iu. and in c. priuilegium personale. li. 6. And the reason is that the common law itself grants that, ff. de leg. et sena. consul. l. non prosunt. here the municipal law is not declared from that, because the disposition of the common law would cease. That case would be deceased, which the legislator abhors, arg. ff. de vend. insp. l. 1. §. ex hoc rescripto. C. de vete. iu. enucle. l. 1. §. cumque materia. but in the municipal law, otherwise, because the case provided for by it is left to the disposition of the common law, and is decided by it, per l. si extraneus. ff. de condi. ob causam. and l. commodissime. de lib. et posth. and l. si cum dotem. in prin. ff. solu. matri. and what is not there. And by this it is clear that Dy. has failed in this matter, as in ff. de le. 3. l. qui duos. de ver. si. l. i. Guido de Suza. Nico. de ma. Iac. de Are. have spoken less fully, C. quae sit lon. consue. I. 1. Ray. Baldus. A S IN The name of the Lord, amen. The fact, on which counsel is requested, is as follows. A certain Marinus Beccioli of Trenio died intestate, leaving a wife and a daughter who was a ward, born of the said husband and the said his wife. Finally, the said wife, wishing to enter into second vows, requested a guardian for the said daughter who was a ward, and afterwards, passing to those second vows, she bore another daughter by the said second husband. Finally, the daughter of Marinus died in her wardship, with the maternal grandfather, mother, and sister on the mother's side surviving. The maternal grandfather claims the inheritance of the said his granddaughter, saying that the mother of the said deceased girl was given in marriage before the request for a guardian, and therefore is excluded from the inheritance of the daughter. The mother denies this. The sister of the said girl on the mother's side wants the inheritance, or says that she succeeds in some part. Now it is asked, whether the mother succeeds in whole or in part, assuming it were proven that she was betrothed before the request for the said guardian, although she did not consummate the marriage by carnal union before the said request, and in the said case, whether the said second daughter and sister of the said girl succeeds in whole or in part.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, a mother who enters into a second marriage loses the succession of her son.
2. Whether a uterine brother is excluded from the intestate succession by the maternal grandfather.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A mother who has entered into a second marriage without requesting a guardian, provided she was under 25 years of age, does not lose the succession of her son, C. si aduer. delictum, l. si. If, however, she was over 25 years of age and marries within a year, she is deprived of the succession, in Auth. de nup., §. si autem tutelam, because she ought not to have so hastily entered into a second marriage, disregarding the affection due to her freedmen. If, however, marrying after a year, she requested a guardian, she requested it too late, and is deprived of the succession, as is established by law. And there is no doubt regarding a female guardian that she is deprived of the succession unless she first requests a guardian and renders an account of her administration, as in C. ad tertul., l. omnem. Therefore, this mother is deprived of the succession of her underage son, especially because at the time she made the request, she was married, although not yet cohabiting, l. nuptias, de re iudicanda. For by marrying, she in truth rendered herself incapable of requesting a guardian, and therefore she is deprived of her son’s succession. But certainly this is not clearly established, for the laws speak of a mother who is a guardian and marries, disregarding the guardianship, not of one who is not a guardian, unless we say that rather in the aforementioned §. si autem tutelam, mention is made in the words “and simply equal, etc.” And if it is said that the penalties for marrying within a year have been abolished, as noted by Innocentius in c. vltima, de secundis nuptiis, I answer: it is true when they are imposed solely on account of haste; otherwise, when on account of haste concerning the children, for then they are not abolished. Therefore, she who married with precipitous haste without requesting a guardian, and hindered herself from being able to request one by right, as having become suspect by her remarriage, ought to be punished by the children. And although I hesitate on this point, nevertheless I believe she is deprived.

† It remains to consider another point, namely whether the uterine brother is excluded from intestate succession by the maternal grandfather. It is established that the father and mother are preferred to those related on only one side, as in the Authentica Defuncto, and fully noted by Cynus in the Authentica Itaque, Codex, Common Rules of Succession. However, it does not appear that the maternal grandfather excludes the uterine brother, because both are connected to the deceased by the law of consanguinity, and not by agnation. Nevertheless, the contrary view seems correct, because the maternal grandfather succeeds together with the brother related on both sides, according to the true opinion. Hence, just as the brother related on both sides excludes the uterine brother alone, so it seems that the grandfather excludes him, because the grandfather is equal to the brother related on both sides, according to the common opinion noted in the said Authentica. I do not decide this passage otherwise. Baldus.

CASE. In the name of the Lord, amen. The doubt, on which Matthew seeks clarification by your sound counsel, is as follows. Danellicius Nerii, father of the said Matthew, made his will, which he showed to us reduced into public form, in which he instituted his sons Angelo, Matthew, Anthony, and Catherine as heirs in equal shares; and if any of the said sons should die without children, he substituted the other surviving son or sons. This Catherine, after the will was made but before the death of the testator, died without children, and afterwards the testator died, leaving the said Angelo, Matthew, and Anthony, his brothers. Angelo afterwards made his will, in which he left to Matthew and Anthony, his brothers, between them twenty solidi denarii, and in the said twenty solidi denarii he instituted them as heirs, and they could not claim more of his goods. He also left to Lady Vanna, his wife, for her dowries, 226 pounds. Also for the augmentation of the dowry, which he confessed she had, two Florentine gold florins. In all his goods, however, he instituted the said Lady Vanna, his wife, as his universal heir, etc. After Angelo died, the said Lady Vanna remained in the house and still remains, holds, and possesses it together with the said Matthew, because after Angelo died she entered the house of the said Angelo, and also holds, holds, and possesses the hereditary goods that remained of Angelo, her brother, etc. It is asked what the said Lady Vanna can claim or acquire from the said institution of the inheritance of Angelo, her husband, and to whom belongs the action of claiming from the other. It is also noted that the said Angelo was separated from his said brothers, and the goods that remained of Danellicius were divided among the brothers; Angelo alienated part of the goods of the other, and acquired certain other goods.
