And I say this regarding the legitime and the Trebellian portion, etc. The notary does not wish to give the will of the said Angelo pertaining to the said Lady Vanna, so that we can produce it to you in instruments; but he only showed it, in which I saw among other things the said institution and the legacy made to Matthew and Anthony under the said words written above.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A simple division does not prejudice the fideicommissum.
2. Alienated property is imputed, pro rata, to the extent of its quantity, against the legitima and the trebellianic portion.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A simple division does not prejudice a fideicommissum. On legacies, book 2, l. cum pater, § haereditatem; and fully noted, ff. on the obligation of words, l. qui Romae, § duo fratres; and ff. on transactions, l. qui cum tutoribus.

† In the first place, alienated property is imputed proportionally to the legitime and the trebellianic portion, as in the Authentica de restitutione and ea quae parit, §. quamobrem, and in the Digest, ad Trebellianum, l. Marcellus, §. res quae; hence, in effect, the said brothers ought to have half of the share of the said Angel, notwithstanding the aforementioned division and alienations, as in cap. Si pater, de testamentis, lib. 6, and in the Extravagantes, eodem, c. Raynaldus and c. Raynaldus; the remainder belongs to the aforementioned wife. However, goods which were not the father’s, but were acquired by the said Angel, are not included in this restitution, but are free to the said wife, unless they were purchased with money derived from the paternal estate and exceeded the legitime and the trebellianic portion, as in de vulgari substitutione, l. Cohaeredi, §. cum filiae, vers. nec fideicommissum, and de legatis 2, l. Imperator, §. fin. Furthermore, it must be observed that the payment of the dowry debt does not prejudice the said thesis, because one brother does not bind another brother, l. Si quis in tantam. It does not prejudice the said thesis because he first committed the repulsive violence against Vanna, etc. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws, and for the faith thereof I have written and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the fourth part is due to the Parish Priest and to the Bishop from those bequests.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Regarding a legacy left to another person or to a pious place, the fourth part is not due to the parish priest, unless it is a legacy left to that Church where the testator is buried, cap. In nostra, de sepultura. For regarding such a legacy, even if that Church were exempt, the fourth part is then due to the parish priest, and from that fourth part the Bishop must have his fourth, so that it is a fourth of a fourth, unless that Church were exempt from the Bishop, as noted above, in the same book, consilium 142. And the aforementioned is true, that the fourth part is due to the parish priest, unless it is left in those privileged cases, of which in cap. Finis, de testibus. Know that even in those cases the parish fourth is due when it is left to any of the mendicant orders, such as the brothers of Saint Francis, or Saint Dominic, or Saint Clare, or the Carmelites, as in Clem. Dudum, § Verum, de sepultura, and according to the notes there by the doctors. However, the episcopal fourth seems to be due when it is left to churches exempt from the jurisdiction of the Bishop; but if not exempt, it is due only in the cases noted in the said cap. Finis, de testamentis. And regarding this matter, see in this book, consilium 142, in the book of consilia.

CASE. In the name of Christ, Amen. A certain man gave a dowry for a woman, and stipulated that the dowry be returned to him, and in the event of his death, that if the marriage were dissolved without children, and what dowry was to be returned and restored, a pledge of land was sealed, and license was given to enter the tenement and possession of the said piece of land in the case of the dowry being returned, to hold and possess the said land until satisfaction had been made for the dowry, etc. And it is stated in the instrument drawn up therefor, that the fruits are not to be computed into the principal, but that he gave and donated them as to a friend, in gratitude for acceptable services received from the said [woman], as is stated in the instrument, having had and received them, and he renounced the exception, etc. The marriage being dissolved, and in the case of the dowry being returned, the aforementioned dowry-giver entered into possession of the said piece of land pledged and hypothecated, and from it he received the fruits of several years. Now the recipient of the dowry wishes to restore the said dowry, and says that the fruits received from the said piece of land ought to be computed into the principal, and that the donation of the said fruits inserted in the said instrument is presumed to have been made in fraud. It is asked, what is the law?

Furthermore, it is asked: by statute it is provided that if the wife predeceases in marriage, the husband acquires one-third part of the dowry for the marriage constituted. Now the father had dowered his daughter, constituting for her a certain dowry; afterwards the father, coming to death, by law, by right of institution, left upon the said dowry his [property] for the augmentation of her dowry, for which 50 pounds he had three acres of land, which land the husband had, held, and possessed for six years, with the knowledge and will of his said wife. Furthermore, he alleges that during the subsistence of the marriage the said husband confessed to having had and received from his said wife 93 pounds for the payment of the dowry, which he asserted had come to his wife from her father's goods, and which he promised to restore to his said wife in the case of the marriage being dissolved. Now the said marriage is dissolved by the death of the woman. The aforementioned husband wishes to restore one-third part both of the dowry constituted in the first place, and also of the others which are said to have been given in augmentation by virtue of the said testament. It is asked now, whether he may do so by law, or not.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether fruits diminish the principal and the dowry.
2. Whether interest is permitted in dowries, and when.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† In the first point, I say, and it seems that, omitting the arguments, one should say that the said fruits diminish the principal, and thus the dowry, as in D. soluto matrimonio, l. Titia, where the case is that, if it is said that the said fruits were donated, one responds that this should not be considered a true donation, but rather a placement, as in C. mandato, l. Ab Anastasio; D. de transactionibus, l. Cum Aquiliana; and it is clearly proven by what is read and noted in D. si certum petatur, l. Rogasti, § Si tibi; and D. de pactis, l. Si tibi decem, in principio, and there by Guillaume and Cynus. For what happens to the principal is interest, and although interest is lawful when it is owed to the husband for the burdens of marriage, as in Extr. de usuris, l. Salubriter, and l. Insulam, § Usuras, soluto matrimonio.

† Moreover, since a woman may recover her dowry up to the amount of her maintenance, as stated in C. rem in praesenti, §. exactio, and l. penultima, in the title "In possessione legatorum"; nevertheless, when an outsider recovers a dowry, usury is not permitted. This is supported by the note in C. de usuris, Authent. ad hæc, because the recovery granted to an outsider is of strict law, as in Inst. de actionibus, §. fuerat. Regarding the second point, the case is that the same rule applies to the increment, as in ff. de pactis dotalibus, l. inter socerum, §. cum inter; and C. de iure dotium, l. etiam, with similar authorities. I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a libel, if not requested, should compel such a person to be condemned, or whether the proceeding should continue.
2. Whether a contract is proved by witnesses testifying as in this case.
3. The term *prosoneta* is used in two senses, and when it may serve as a witness.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Three doubts are raised. The first, concerning the petition, whether it is incompetent or not. The second, whether the contract has been proved or not, considering the form of the witnesses' depositions. The third, whether James Bagnoli can be rejected as a prosoneta.

† On the first point, Master Bartolus says in l. 1, C. de executione rei iudicatae, that the libel does not proceed if one says, “I ask that such a person be compelled,” unless one asks that he be condemned; for he cannot be compelled unless he is condemned, and he cannot be condemned unless it is asked that he be condemned, as in l. si, C. de fideicommissis libertatis. I say, however, that if the necessary facts are narrated and the conclusion is drawn in the form “I ask that it be given or done to me,” even though I do not say “I ask that the defendant be condemned,” the petition proceeds. And the ordinary gloss says that the libel would be so. And it says that all other words are superfluous, in Auth. de exhibendis reis, § sancimus. And so it was here, if the petition is properly examined.

† On the second point, I say that two witnesses prove by bodily sense that the agreement was not erroneous, hence the contract was perfected by consensus, as is noted in C. de contrahenda emptione, l. in emendis. Moreover, because the earnest money was given as part of the price, the thing was not entire, as is noted in ff. de contrahenda emptione, l. quod saepe; nor could it subsequently be dissolved by the dissent of one party, as in l. ab emptione, de pactis.

† On the third point, I say that a *prosoneta* [broker] is called so in two ways: in one way, he who receives a price; in another way, he who, although without charge, nevertheless through whom there is an agreement and a forum. But where there is a forum between the principals themselves without an intermediary, he who brought the parties together or summoned witnesses is not called a *prosoneta*; because this person does not provide any service to the contract, nor does he thereby merit a brokerage fee. And thus stands the common understanding, and it is proposed in Auth. de testib. §. quoniam vero, and in ca. 1. de testib. lib. 6, and what is noted in l. eleganter. de dolo. in prin. Hence, Jacob was not properly a *prosoneta*, because he did not provide an intrinsic and substantial service, but an extrinsic one in gathering the parties in one place. Hence, I do not believe this person is properly called a *prosoneta*, to whom no brokerage fee corresponds, but he is indeed a friend, as l. sciendum. ff. de vsu. Nor do I believe the reason for prohibition applies to him, because the contract is not by his arrangement or for his benefit, but for the benefit of the principals. Hence, as l. repellit eum, nor does utility, as an effect, which are two reasons indicated in d. §. quoniam. in glo. For one is not bound by that which was done by another and not by oneself, and no law provides that this person be repelled. Therefore, and c. l. 1. ff. de testib. But if he proves at least the agreement, although he does not prove another doubtful point: because he says he gave it, and in this he was an intervener and minister. It supports what is noted in l. deferre. §. 1. de iure fisc. and what is noted in c. Romana. de testi. lib. 6. in gl. sing. And thus, one is believed regarding another’s act as regarding his own act; but as a witness, he is not believed: because these are separable. And according to the gloss of Accursius in d. §. quoniam, one is believed regarding the whole, if he does not hope for gain: because he is admitted, although not compelled. But the glosses of canon law say that a *prosoneta* involved is not admitted unless by the will of both parties, as noted in q. 1. si quis episcopus. de testi. cogen. c. dilectorum. per Barto. Whatever may be said about the *prosoneta*, I say that in the earnest money of the agreement, this person was not a *prosoneta*: because the parties agreed by themselves immediately, and from the acts of both parties it can be weighed by the judge, who must investigate all things, that this was the truth of the matter: and therefore the points should be observed, as extra de pac. with similar cases, the praetor says, I will keep the pacts. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Words of this kind, appended in a mandate granting free and full power and administration, etc., for recovering, acquiring, maintaining, and enjoying fruits, restrict the free mandate to the will of the principal.
2. One holding a mandate with free power cannot make a donation.
3. An abbess receiving something by express agreement for the admission of nuns commits simony. And see below, consilium 373.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the tenor of the aforementioned instruments of mandate and of the donation made to the abbess and convent of the said monastery, by which the undersigned Master Adam was appointed procurator for Master Thomas de Luto concerning the dowries of Joanetta Venectua and Jacobuta, and for their entry and reception together with the provisions contained in the said instrument, it is valid in law; and the goods donated, valued at 500 florins and more, may be claimed by the successors of the said Master Thomas once one of the said nuns has died. This has long since occurred, and the successors of the said Master Thomas were not required to choose and receive another nun into the said monastery in place of the deceased, according to the pacts contained in the said instrument. It seems that, in law, it must be said that the aforementioned donation was not valid in law and did not hold, and that the donated goods can be recovered by the abbess and convent of the aforementioned monastery. Which I prove by the laws and reasons set forth below.

And first, that the words appended in the instrument of mandate for recovering, acquiring, maintaining, and enjoying fruits for the benefit of Master Thomas, and for converting what is contained in the instrument of mandate, should not be extended to diminution or alienation, or to a contrary effect, ff. de adiectis legibus, l. legata; and de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. cum tale, §. si. And although it is contained in the said instrument of mandate that the said Master Thomas gave to Magister Adam, his procurator, full and free power and administration of goods, nevertheless the statute determines that clause, restricting it to the aforementioned goods, namely, those to be acquired, recovered, and kept for his benefit. For free power is restricted, and especially a mandate, to the aforementioned and other causes and matters which he had and would have in the district and estate against his adversaries. And thus the generality preceding is to be understood according to the distinction and determination under the same series and continuation of words contained in the said instrument. de verbis significandis, l. sicut fundus; and de legatis 2, l. cum pater, §. dulcissimis.

Secondly, because even assuming that the said procurator had a simple mandate with full discretion, he nevertheless could not make a donation unless this had been specially granted to him, as stated in D. de donationibus, l. filius; D. de pactis, l. quae iure; and X. de officio vicarii, c. fin., lib. 6. The reason is given in the aforementioned laws, namely that to donate is to lose. In support of this, see D. quae in fraudem creditorum, l. si pater filio; D. de peculio legato, l. qui peculii. And although a dowry is not a title of gain, but onerous as regards the recipient of the dowry, D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. ex promissione, nevertheless, as is well proven, C. de rei uxoriae actione, § accedit, in fine; D. de administratione tutorum, l. cum plures, § pen., and there in the gloss beginning "donatio," the person in question here was one who was not compelled to donate, as stated in l. si extraneum. And therefore it was a donation, because that is considered donated which is granted without any legal compulsion, D. de regulis iuris, l. donari, cum si.

Thirdly, because the agreement made between the said procurator on one part, and the abbess and convent of the said monastery on the other, concerning the reception of the said nuns into the monastery in exchange for the aforementioned lands and possessions, and concerning the substitution and religious profession of others in the place of the deceased, according to the modes and conditions contained in the said instrument, contains a manifest appearance of simony, and therefore was invalid by law, as is clear from the text in Extra, De simonia, c. Tua nos. and c. Quonam symonia; since in spiritual matters all agreement must cease, Qu. 2, c. 2, Quamvis; and De pactis, c. Cum pridem. For this reason, it is not excused by the pretext of any custom, as stated in De simonia, c. Iacobus. Therefore, such a mandate of a procurator, however full and general, cannot be extended to such illicit and prohibited acquisitions, as held in D. De conditione indebita, l. Si procurator, § Celsus. Such an agreement was also contrary to the laws expressly, namely that Master Thomas, his heir, and successors would have the right to elect and substitute in the said monastery other women in the place of the deceased; whereas even in secular collegiate churches, canonical laws have abhorred the right of election belonging to laymen, as stated in De electione, c. Sacra sanctae ecclesiae and c. Massana. Therefore, much more so in regular orders, in which not only are they elected by the abbess and convent, but also tested by the mother and mothers entering, which could not be the case in the present instance according to the agreements contained in the said instrument, according to which they were to receive those to be substituted in every event. And therefore it is concluded that agreements contrary to laws and canons are held as void, C. De legibus, l. Non dubium; and De iureiurando, c. Quae contra iura, lib. 6. And the successors of the aforementioned Master Thomas can demand the said goods from the abbess and convent of the said monastery, since dominion was not transferred to them by the said procurator, who did not have a special mandate for this purpose, C. De procuratoribus, l. Si procurator; D. De nova, l. Non abstulit; and Quod cum eo, l. Subuentum. It is therefore held as not given, that which was given by one who could not give it by law, D. De officiis proconsulis, l. 3, § fin.; and De iure patronatus, c. Quod autem. And thus, in every event, it is concluded that the successors of Master Thomas need not concern themselves with prescription against the aforementioned monastery, because it was interrupted doubly, and because they lacked good faith, having purchased against the laws, as the rule of law states, Qui contra iura, lib. 6, etc. I, John of Canon, deceased.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Granted emphyteusis in perpetuity, up to which generation and for how long it extends.
2. The term "in perpetuity" is explained in various ways.
3. If emphyteusis is granted up to the third generation, the first recipient is counted in the number, as discussed in consilium 315.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the time of the divine Emperor Frederick, a certain Abbot of Saint Peter of Rasenna lawfully granted in emphyteusis to the ladies Dialta and Sardamora of Euf. and their heirs in perpetuity certain lands and possessions. Afterwards, many encumbrances remained upon the aforementioned ladies. And now today there exists Lady Lucia, proceeding from the lineage of Lady Sardamora by legitimate succession.

† Now the question arises concerning those words, "in perpetuum," up to which generation and time they extend. To which it is briefly answered that they are understood to mean as long as the pension is paid, as in D. si ager vectigalis vel emphyteuticarius, l. 1. qui in perpetuum; and Inst. locati conducti, §. adeo.

† This phrase, "in perpetuum," is explained in various ways. First, for the life of someone, ff. pro soc. l. 1. Second, up to 30 or 40 years, insti. de perpe. et tempo. act. in prin. Third, without a fixed time limit, as in l. pure. in fi. de exce. doli. Fourth, it was formerly understood in the context of ecclesiastical emphyteusis for three generations, in Auth. de non alie. §. emphyteosim. But today, since the Church can grant perpetual emphyteusis, it is understood to apply to all generations; indeed, it is said more strongly: that it applies to all heirs, even strangers, as long as the pension is paid; just as in private law emphyteusis, or civil law. But if the generation is legitimate, it has the right that subsists from the genus, as from a certain source of memory, de verb. sig. l. prouinc. §. fin. and this is expressly noted in Authen. de non eligen. §. alienationis. glo. which begins, hic not.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one holding a general mandate with full discretion may make a donation to a monastery for the admission of nuns, and whether such a donation is valid. See also above, consilium 371.
1. What is required for a person to be considered suspect so that he may be arrested. See also above, consilium 338.
2. One suing another as an heir must prove that the defendant is an heir.
3. One suing as an heir must declare himself to be an heir; it is not necessary that this be attested by an instrument.
4. Whether a procurator holding a mandate to take an oath may render the oath regarding the suspicion of the debtor's flight, notwithstanding a statute, etc., as here.
5. Whether an oath is presumed to have been tendered by the judge concerning suspicion and flight.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. Having seen the content of the said instruments, the question is whether the acts performed by the said Master Adam as proctor of Master Thomas de Luco in the form shown by the tenor of the said instruments could by law have been done or not, and whether the successors of the said Master Thomas can recover the said property.

† And it seems it must be said in law that the said mandate was not sufficient for the aforesaid acts that were carried out. For whether the said mandate relates to judicial proceedings and matters connected with judicial proceedings—just as a mandate to demand relates to receiving payment that is made voluntarily, according to the true opinion—or whether it relates to transactions entirely separate from judicial proceedings, such as to contracts; nevertheless, according to the true opinion, it ought not to be extended to a gratuitous alienation, because initially a mandate is considered to be given, not a concession: ff. quod vi aut clam, l. prohibere, §. plane; ff. de pact., l. contra iuris ciuilis regulas, §. si filius; ff. de sol., l. si is cui, §. Flauius. And if it is said that it indeed fell within the mandate because he did this from a just cause—for the cause of a dowry is a most just cause, ff. de ver. ob., l. a Titio; and just as a dowry is given for the burdens of marriage, so it can be given to a monastery for the burdens and sustenance of the person entering it; nor does simony seem to be committed if it is done on account of the necessity of sustenance and of the monastery, as is noted in extra. de simo., c. non satis, and ca. tua nos, because it ought to be understood as done rather by way of alms and aid than by way of simony, as in ff. pro soc., l. merito; and especially if it were applied upon the property of the person entering, because it seems to be tacitly inherent, as in auth. ingressi; and here it first appears to be done from the property of the person entering, and afterwards it is delivered by himself to the monastery, by the argument of ff. si cer. pet., l. singularia, and ff. de dona. inter virum, et vxo., l. 3, §. sciendum—yet I respond that it is not true that there is a just cause with respect to the proctor unless it is a cause that lies upon the principal of the business, as is noted in the said §. filius, and de admin. tu., l. cum plures, §. in primis. Likewise, every agreement in such matters is reproved unless it is applied with the knowledge and disposition of the law: de elec., c. significasti; de praeben., c. nisi essent; de simonia, c. cum satis, and c. nobis, and c. tua nos; and as is noted in 1, q. 2, in summa. Nor under the pretext of poverty ought simony to be committed or a crime to be perpetrated; whence the mandate of a proctor does not extend to such matters by any interpretation of law unless it is mandated by specific words, as in ff. quod quisque iur., l. 3, §. si procu., and ff. si quis ius dicenti, l. 1, §. si procu., and in quæ in frau. cred., l. si pater, with similar texts. Therefore, because in donations, as in l. filius, de dona. et delic., the law requires a specific mandate, and here it was general, therefore it does not suffice: ff. de condi. indeb., l. si procur., §. Celsus; ff. de pecu., l. qui peculii, with countless similar texts. First, it must be noted in this regard that he who has a mandate to conduct the business of a principal, and let the principal be called Titius, does not have a mandate to conduct the business of Seius: ff. de neg. gest., l. 3, §. apud Marcellum; note also ff. mand., l. si mandauero, §. si curator. But this proctor, in acting thus, did not conduct the business of the principal, but rather that of the one who gives: ff. de manu., l. ab agnato; ff. de in rem verso, l. et nihil, with the following law; therefore it did not fall within the mandate. But if it is proved that the principal ratified it, then the heir could not recover, whether the cause was honest or base, because in such a cause the condition of the possessor would be stronger once ownership was transferred: ff. de condi. ob tur. cau., l. idem est, and l. si ob turpem, §. fin.; and that ownership is transferred even from a base cause is clear, because if ownership were not transferred, the condictio ob turpem causam would never lie, since no one condicts his own property, except from a thief: ff. vsufruc. quemadmo. caue., l. fin. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that no person may make a will unless he has expressly observed the right of the community, whether a will made by a person of the said community is valid, where the said reservation has not been made elsewhere.
2. Whether executors appointed for the purpose of building a hospital are said to be in default after the lapse of two years, even if they have not been summoned.
3. It is enacted in the City of Eugubium that no person
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† The question is whether the arrest made of Matteo di Cechutio at the petition of the proctor of Lady Cobutia, as a suspect and absconding debtor, was rightly and duly made, or not, having inspected the acts and proceedings in the case, and three statutes of the commune of Todi: one under the rubric on the precept of guarentigia; another under the rubric on him who had the protocol; a third under the rubric on those who appoint guardians. And it must be premised that, for an arrest to be made as of a suspect debtor, the statute requires: first, that the debt appear by an instrument of guarentigia; second, that that instrument was shown to the judge; third, that the creditor, his heir, or their assignee confirmed by their oath that they held the debtor to be suspect. And understand that this oath must be tendered by the judge, and this is by virtue of the first statute. By the second statute, it is required that the protocols of a deceased notary that are exemplified must contain in themselves a public form and be marked with the mark of the deceased notary. By the other statute, a general necessity is imposed upon certain judges concerning the interposition of decrees. Likewise, I premise that here three instruments seem to have been produced: one original of the principal debt or contract, and others copies—if the testament and the acceptance of the inheritance are not called copies—made upon the commission of the deceased notary in his testament. Now, from the aforesaid, many doubts arise: first, since the arrested man denies that he is the heir, and consequently the debtor, whether it is proved from the aforesaid that he is the heir of the debtor; second, whether the plaintiff, who seems to have acted in part as heir, ought to have proved that he was the heir in a manner other than that by which he did prove it; third, whether the aforesaid oath, having regard to the form of the statute, could be taken by a proctor having a mandate to swear; fourth, whether the said oath is presumed in doubt to have been tendered, or not.

† And this is premised as most certain: that he who sues someone as heir must prove that the defendant is the heir. And the text says that the said proof is sometimes difficult, ff. de interro. act. l. 2; for that someone has accepted the inheritance of another is a matter of fact, and is not presumed unless it is proved, as noted in ff. sol. ma. l. si cum dotem. §. transgrediamur. Nevertheless, here this seems sufficiently proved by the instrument of the testament and of the acceptance of the inheritance; for such an instrument of acceptance of an inheritance benefits absentees just as it benefits those present, as noted in l. fi. ff. de interro. ac., because by accepting he quasi-contracts with the creditors, as in §. eorum, and in quasi-contracts the presence of the persons is not required, as appears in the actions of negotiorum gestio, ff. de ne. go. ge. l. si quis absentis, and throughout, and de reg. iu. l. semper qui not. And that faith must be given to this copy appears from the fact that it was drawn according to the form of the statute, and the person copying it attests that it was taken from a public document: therefore, that it was from one sealed with the valid mark of the notary, for otherwise it would not be public, as in C. de accesso. l. fi. and as noted in Inst. de publ. iudi. l. item lex. cum si. And this concerning the first point.

† On the second point, I say that he who sues as heir must show that he is the heir; nor is it necessary that proof of this be made by an instrument, because that he is the heir is not the principal transaction upon which an instrument ought to be drawn, but is rather an effect of that transaction. For the right that he has by virtue of the guarentigiated instrument is not transmitted even to an intestate heir, because it belongs to the law of succession, as in ff. de pe. hae. l. 2. et 3. and ff. de eden. l. quaedam. §. is autem. And therefore, if summary proof has been made that he is the heir, it seems to suffice, arg. ff. de exi. l. thesaurus, provided that if it is later denied, it be proved, as noted in ff. de bo. pos. l. 3. §. pe. and ff. de leg. prae. l. filium. §. si quis. But certainly, in our case I find that proof has in no way been made; and the law says that it ought to be clear and apparent to the praetor concerning the right of the plaintiff and the obligation of the defendant, ff. qui. ex ca. in pos. ea. l. hoc autem, and ff. ne vis fiat ei. l. 1. §. haec verba; and if it is not clear, that which was done must be revoked as void, l. fi. §. fi. quod me. cau. and de bo. auth. iu. pos. l. cum vnus. And therefore, as to that part for which he sued as heir, I do not see that, proof having been made, the arrest is valid; but as to the other part, yes, because whenever suit is brought under several titles, the matter can be valid as to the part of one title and not valid as to the other, ff. de iudi. l. non idcirco, and ff. de ap. l. si pro lusorio, and l. asinam. §. si habes. Nor does l. thesaurus stand in the way, because it speaks of a judicial proceeding, or of a point preparatory to execution, whereas here it is for enforcement.

† On the third point, there is a doubt, because the statute seems to require the oath of those who pursue their own cause; therefore, the oath of a proctor does not suffice, as in C. de iur. calum. auth. principales; for the true conception of the words opposes it, and that which is to be done by oneself cannot be done through another, C. de cad. tol. §. ne autem. Likewise, this statute is against the common law, ff. de re iud. l. de vnoquoque; therefore it ought to be understood of their oath properly speaking, not interpretatively, because we ought to restrict, not enlarge. But to the contrary I say: if the proctor has it in his mandate to swear, ff. de iureiu. l. iusiurandum. §. fin., because this is an oath in place of proof, not of calumny. To this makes what is noted in c. vt circa. de ele. lib. 6. And because the oath must be taken before joinder of issue in matters concerning possessions and arrests, it can be taken by a proctor, as noted in ff. de dam. infec. l. qui bona. §. si alieno; for here one does not swear according to the formal course of a judicial proceeding, since, because a citation of the adversary is not required, it cannot be said that the form of a judicial proceeding is present there, as noted in said l. 3. §. pe. de bo. pos. Nor does it stand in the way that the words of the statute are said to be understood and taken properly and strictly; for a praetorian oath is properly taken for the principal, upon whose soul the oath is sworn, and not by the proctor, because the law refers this principally and more properly to the principal, thus in ff. de ma. vin. l. pater.

† On the fourth point, I say that, from the fact that the judge received it, I presume that he tendered and exacted the oath, arg. C. de rela. l. 1. in fi., ff. de fidei. tu. l. cum ostendimus. §. vlti., and as noted in de dote praele. l. Theopompus. To this makes what is noted by Innocent on de eo, qui fur. or. suscepit. c. innotuit. I presuppose that the procuratorial mandate is in order, and that the commission is established; because a commission is not presumed, as in l. 1. de man. prin. and C. de exhi. re. l. neminem, and C. de iu. fis. l. prohibitum. lib. 10. I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
0. If an emphyteusis is granted or accepted up to the third generation, the first person receiving it is not counted; but what if it is stated for the third generation, or up to the third completed? Number 1. Also, what if it is granted in simple terms? Number 3.
1. A pact in doubt should be presumed real, and not personal. Also, personal, and not most personal.
2. If an emphyteusis is granted in perpetuity, up to which generation does it extend? Above, in counsel 372.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† An emphyteutic right was granted to someone until the third generation, both male and female, is completed. Now it is asked whether this first recipient is counted in the generation or not. And it seems that the ordinary gloss says that he is counted, in Auth. de non alienando, § alienationes, in gloss 2, which begins “hic no.” at the end, joined with § alienationes. For the gloss understands that the third generation includes the son and the grandson. This is supported by the fact that the word “until” must here be taken exclusively, not inclusively, arg. ff. de pace, l. veteribus; ff. de verb. oblig., l. quicquid astringendae. Hence, although the person receiving is not counted, nevertheless the great-grandson cannot be understood to be included. This is further supported by the rule that words in doubt should be referred to the nature of the contract, ff. de usuris, l. si stipulatus; and note per Dy., ff. ad Trebellianum, l. ex facto, § si; ff. de verb. sign., in conventions. And emphyteusis of the church has this nature, as stated in § emphyteosim. Therefore, etc. It is also supported by what is noted in ff. sol. matr., l. etiam.

On the contrary, it is argued that the recipient is not a generation of himself, because nothing generates itself, as is clearly evident, since everything that is generated is generated by another: therefore, he is not counted in the number. Thus we say in degrees that the stocks are not counted in the number, as noted in ff. de gradibus, l. Iurisconsultus; Instit. de successionibus liberorum, § sed nostra; and de consanguinitate et affinitate, c. non debet. And this is clear in the tree of consanguinity and affinity. And this is also proven, because if he were counted, and the word “until” were taken exclusively, the grandson would not be included, because the recipient would be one generation, the son the second, the grandson the third: but the third is not included. Therefore, we would directly conclude against § emphyteutic.

And therefore, the truth seems to me to be that the first person, or stock, is not counted in the number, because he is not a generation, but the cause of generation: just as husband and wife are not affines, but the cause of affinity, as in Instit. de emphyteusi, § affinitatis; de conditionibus ob causam, l. quod servus.

† Therefore, the doubt does not lie in whether the first person is counted as the first generation, but rather in whether the words “up to the third generation” are to be understood inclusively or exclusively. The gloss and the preceding authorities expressly hold that they are to be understood exclusively. But I say that when an emphyteusis is granted for the third generation, it is certain that the third generation is included; the same applies if it is said “up to the third generation completed.” For the term “completed” indicates that it shall last until the end of the third generation. And since the entire third generation is included by the force of the words, because under the latest law an emphyteusis may even be granted in perpetuity, as noted in the aforementioned § alienationis, the objection based on the said § does not hold.

† But if emphyteusis were granted in simple terms up to the third generation, and it was not stated as finished, nor stated as begun, then it is doubtful whether this wording, which is added concerning the degree, is placed by a person inclusively. For when it is added concerning the degree by law, it is certain that it is placed inclusively, as in Inst. de succ. agnat. §. si, and note C. unde leg. l. certum, and it is proven in d. c. non debet, de consanguinitate et affinitate, and in c. statutis, de haereditate, lib. 6. But when it is added by a person, in an obligatory contract it seems to be added, arg. l. veteribus. I believe that it is placed inclusively, because it is presumed in doubt that the recipient did not wish to acquire even for the third generation, ff. de probat. l. si pactum, and arg. C. de legat. l. in animalibus. And it supports what is noted by Cy. C. de operis liberti, libertaeque, according to the opinion of La. de Ra. Notwithstanding l. ne tribus, because that is understood in what would increase the obligation; here it is not increased, but makes it more transmissible.

† And this is supported by the fact that a pact is presumed to be real rather than personal; and by the same reasoning, it ought to be presumed to be personal rather than strictly personal. D. de pactis, l. iuris gentium, § pactorum; and l. qui in futurum, § fin. And it is supported by what is noted by Cynus, according to Petrus, C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. veteris. I, Baldus de Ubaldis, Doctor of Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A ban has the force of a citation. See also below, in opinion 433.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. On the said point, it seems to me that Baldus, Volume I, Digest, is valid and assists the plaintiff, and this for two reasons; the first reason being,

† That a ban, with the assignment of a term, has the force of a citation and can be called a citation. For since a ban is said to be a proclamation, as in Extra, Qui matrimonium accusare possunt, c. Cum in tua; and since a denunciation is said to be a citation, as in Codex, Quomodo et quando iudex, l. Tres denunciationes; it follows that a ban can be called a citation. And this is clearly apparent from the nature of the assigned term, insofar as it is of the nature of a citation, as in l. 2, Codex, De iure dotis imperatoris. To the same effect is the fact that a citation is sometimes made by a herald, as in Auth. Quo semel, Codex, Quomodo et quando iudex. Therefore, if within the term of a hundred days from the day the ban was issued, a concord has been given, it follows that it must be valid. The second reason is that it seems permissible to anticipate the hundred days, and that diligence in anticipating does not render the act invalid in that which proceeds from the will of the parties, as is the case with a concord, as in Codex, De fideicommissis, l. Post mortem. And thus I, Baldus, say.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether and when a person who has been dispossessed may bring an action for eviction.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The facts are as follows. Simon, son of Angelo of Cortona, took as his wife Lady Benucia, and there were promised to her by the said son of Angelo one thousand [units of currency] by way of dowry. After the death of the said son of Angelo, with the said Simon and John, son of the said son of Angelo, and Bartholomew, his nephew through another predeceased son, surviving, the said Simon was appointed general procurator of the said John and curator of the said Bartholomew. This Simon, in their common name, received in payment of the said one thousand certain possessions situated in the territory of the castle of Fogiano. Finally, wishing to proceed to a division, they chose arbitrators among themselves, who made an accounting and division between them, and assigned the said possessions to the said Simon for the said dowry, and the said Simon possessed them for many years. Finally, he was dispossessed of the aforementioned possession, taken advantage of by a certain Carcasion on the occasion of a restitution in integrum granted to him. Now, because an action for eviction was promised, the said Simon wishes to bring an action against the said Carcasion, who in fact occupied the possession, and he notifies his brother and nephew that they should assist in the case, and he protests against the damage and interest arising from the eviction.

† It is asked whether they are bound to this, or not. And this question consists in the understanding of two laws which seem to contradict each other. One says that if the buyer, or one similar to him, renews litigation against another, his warrantor is liable for eviction if the buyer succumbs, D. de evictionibus, l. si euicta, § duplae. The other says that if the buyer fell from possession through his own fault, he has no recourse against the warrantor, D. de evictionibus, l. si rem quam, § si culpae. This Simon either fell from possession due to negligence, and then he is at fault, or by violence: and this too is reckoned as fault, and eviction is not owed. C. de actione empti, l. impulsos; D. de locato, l. si merces, § culpae; and l. in his, Sol. Mat. et. Also, this Simon does not seem able to sue, because these possessions seem to have been merely common, but were also properly adjudicated to him before the award; therefore, what was done to the said Simon regarding his own property is not valid, but if the principal is not valid, the accessory is not valid. I.e., eviction is not owed, D. de contrahenda emptione, l. suae rei; C. de locis, l. qui rem; D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. mea res. But it seems that he can sue against the warrantor, l. contra fratrem, and nephew, from whom he has the cause by division, which things were common, D. de evictionibus, l. si plus, § mota quaestione. And if it is said that he lost possession through his own fault, I answer: he does not thereby lose the right to sue for eviction, unless when through his own fault he lost both possession and right, for example because the thing is prescribed, or he held it as stolen. D. de evictionibus, l. si intentati. Therefore, the plaintiff must assist and defend the buyer, or one similar, in the petitory action against the invader, d. l. si euicta, § duplae. And if it is said that the thing assigned to Simon was his own, I answer: let it be so, yet this can be done by sentence, C. de familiae erciscundae, l. si maritus; l. Pomponius Philadelphus. And eviction applies, because this was expressly permitted. Or it can be said, if it is proven true what is supposed in the case, that those possessions were not his own, but common, because they were acquired in common voice and common peril; hence, the eviction was rightly valid, C. de familiae erciscundae, l. si familiae; D. eodem, l. inter cohaeredes, § 1. And therefore it seems to be concluded that if Simon sues by petitory action, and the aforementioned facts are proven true, that John or Bartholomew are bound either to defend Simon, or, if Simon succumbs, to indemnify him for eviction. From the foregoing it appears that fault committed with respect to true possession does not exclude eviction with respect to ownership, although the text in l. si rem quam, § si culpae, cited above, makes much against this, but understand it as I said above, always saving the sounder understanding. Azo also in his Summa, C. de evictionibus, § fin., seems to say that he who lost possession through his own fault is repelled, but if this is understood generally, the gloss in § qui duplae would be superfluous; hence it must be understood when something of right is lost, not if the bare fact of possessing is lost, which does not prevent action. See C. de actione empti, l. vi pulsos. But I concede that the seller is not bound to defend against violence, but in court, thus. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a peace agreement, in which the quality of the offense is omitted, benefits the accused.
2. Although an offense may be repeatable, nevertheless repetition is not presumed unless it is proven.
3. When the offense is remitted, its quality is also considered remitted.
casus: CASE. The point is this. The judge of malefices of the commune of Gubbio inquires against Jacob Petrucii in that he struck Thomasutius Masceti with a certain stone, one blow to the face with effusion of blood, and the aforementioned were committed by the said Jacob at night, namely after the sound of the bell which is rung in the morning for the day, which Jacob obtained peace from the said Masceti, within 10 days from the day the malefice was committed, in which instrument it is said simply that the said Thomasutius made peace with the said Jacob regarding the said blow made by the said Jacob against the said Thomasutius in such month of December, the day not otherwise declared, at night time. Now it is said by the officials that that peace does not avail the producer, because it was not made regarding the malefice about which inquiry is made, since in the instrument of peace it is not said simply on such day, and thus, one malefice seems to be that about which inquiry is made, and another that about which peace was made on such day. It is answered on behalf of the said Jacob that the appellation of day does not comprehend night; it is understood according to nature. To this it is said by the office that this would be true where the statute did not distinguish day from night: but the statute distinguishes in the instrument of peace on such day, it is understood of the artificial day according to the distinction of the statute. To this it is answered on behalf of the said Jacob that that addition of day was not added in the instrument of peace because of the statute which speaks of doubling of penalties, but because of another which speaks of peace and its benefit. It is now asked whether the omission of that quality, namely night, has the effect of harming, so that the aforementioned instrument of peace is not understood regarding the malefice about which inquiry is made, and where it would not be added. If the notary, who was requested regarding the said peace, can supply it without prejudice, having seen the aforementioned inquiry and the statute, of which mention is made above.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It seems to me, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, that the said peace benefits the said inquisit, although the instrument of peace does not mention the time of the offense. And this for three reasons. First, because the instrument of peace refers to the process of inquisition, and thus by reference to another thing it becomes certain, as in l. in summa, de re iudic., as in l. haec sententia, de sententiis, quae sine certa quantitate prosequuntur.

Secondly, although the delict is repeatable, repetition is not presumed unless it is proved, as noted in D. de iureiurando, l. eum qui, § in popularibus; and D. de fideiussoribus instrumentis, c. cum Ioannes Heremita. And therefore the peace cannot be understood to refer to anything other than this specific instance. To this effect: D. de fundo instrato, l. fundus, qui locatus.

Thirdly, because when the delict is remitted, even though no mention is made of the quality, the quality appears to be remitted as well, since the quality is accessory. And therefore, when the principal is removed, the accessory is also removed; but nothing was said about the accessory, or about the quality, regarding the noxal liability. L. in delicto. §. si detracta. de legibus iuris. L. cum principalis. with similar authorities. And thus I advise, and I have written this in good faith, and I have signed it with the seal of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the entire inheritance accrues to an heir instituted in a specific thing, if the heir instituted universally dies during the testator's lifetime, or if his acceptance is otherwise impeded.
2. If the testator instituted an heir in a specific thing and restricted his institution to that heir, it is certain that he is deemed tacitly satisfied and content, and cannot demand more; the question is whether the institution in a specific thing expires if the universal heir dies before restitution.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. The fact pattern upon which advice is sought is as follows: Titius made his will, in which he instituted his sister as heir in the amount of 20 ducats and inserted this clause, namely, that the said sister must be quiet and content with those 20 ducats, and that she may claim nothing more from his estate. But as universal heir he instituted a certain uterine brother of his, which brother died before the testator's death, with the said testator's knowledge; the said testator then survived for about five years or thereabouts. Thereafter, the said testator died with no other will having been made. Now comes the sister, instituted heir in 20 ducats, and says that the entire inheritance belongs to her by right of institution, while against her it is said that she claims this by no right. It is therefore asked what the law is; and for the clarity of understanding, divide the questions.

† And let the first question be this: whether the entire inheritance accrues to an heir instituted in a specific thing if the universally instituted heir dies during the testator's lifetime, or his acceptance is otherwise prevented. And it is argued that it does not, by such reasoning: that one instituted in a specific thing or in a specific amount is regarded in the place of a legatee, C. de haered. insti. l. quotiens. But an inheritance not accepted by the institute does not accrue to a legatee, but rather causes the legacy to fail, C. de fideicommissis. l. eam quam. and l. si nemo. de reg. iur. And there is an ordinary gloss on the institute in a specific thing that, where there is a certain universal institution, the institution from a specific thing is vitiated, ff. de except. doli. l. liberi. Furthermore, you will say either that this happens on account of the right of accrual, or from a presumed universal institution, or because the testator cannot die partly testate and partly intestate. It does not happen by right of accrual; which I prove thus: a share accrues to a share, and where someone does not have a share, it cannot accrue to him, ff. de vulg. substit. l. ex facto. l. Iulianus Longinus. and noted in ff. de acq. haere. l. si totam. But the one instituted in a specific thing does not have a fractional share; therefore it does not accrue to him, because a specific thing does not give a fractional share to an heir. This is clear from what is fully read and noted in ff. de transa. l. controuersia. C. de rei vendi. l. cum a iure. ff. ad Treb. l. 1. §. si haeres. and l. cogi. §. generaliter. Nor does it arise from a presumed universal institution, because there a co-heir has been given. In the universal whole the presumption ceases, so that the institute may not have everything that the testator intended, ff. de vulga. subst. l. verbis ciuilibus. by its own reasoning. For what is assigned to an heir universally is not tacitly prohibited and taken away from another, de leg. 1. l. quod in rerum. §. si quis post. in fi. Nor is it to be considered whether the prohibition attains the effect of acquisition, because it nevertheless has the force of adoption, ff. de adi. leg. l. et si transferam. Likewise, if the institution in a specific thing is extended to the whole, that is from the presumed intention of the testator, because whoever institutes someone as heir is not presumed to wish to die intestate, C. de testamentis. l. non codicillum. extra de testamentis. c. cum tibi. But this presumption regarding the institute in a specific thing is removed by the express universal institution made of another, arg. ff. de iudiciis. l. cum praeter. For an express provision makes a tacit and presumptive one cease, C. de pac. conuen. l. fi. Note also that the testator might die partly testate and partly intestate; indeed, he dies wholly intestate, since a specific thing does not make a fractional share in him who is instituted in a specific part, whence this reasoning ceases. And note C. de secun. nup. l. 1. and note de acqui. haere. l. si seruus communis extero. And therefore it seems astonishing that Dinus and other doctors note in said l. quotiens. and auth. that the rationale of that §. si ex fundo. is lest the testator die partly testate and partly intestate, because a specific thing does not make a share. Whence, this being posited—that it does not accrue—the cause of testacy and intestacy is not divided perpetually, but we are wholly in a cause of intestacy. Yet the text seems to favor the doctors and the gloss, ff. de test. mili. l. si miles vnum ex fundo. where it says that because a soldier can die partly intestate, it does not accrue; therefore in a civilian it accrues for the reason that he cannot die partly intestate. And thus the rationale of the gloss and the doctors seems to be established by that text. From the aforesaid, therefore, it seems that the institution from a specific thing, where the universal heir repudiates or is excluded, is not on that account extended to the whole. And this is confirmed, because that a legacy should be extended to a universal institution seems impossible, just as it is impossible that what is oblique should become direct, argu. not. de vulg. substi. l. verbis ciuili. I respond: likewise, between an heir and a legatee no joinder induces the right of accrual; on the contrary, the legacy and fideicommissum expire, C. de fideicommis. l. eam quam. for an accessory does not give strength to the principal, but the reverse, de iure codi. l. quod per manus. And it is confirmed that no law here says that there is a right of accrual between a universal heir and a quasi-heir instituted in a specific thing. For §. si ex fundo. does not say a word that sounds in the right of accrual or of non-decrease; but it says that the farm added is held as not added, as we say that the useless addition of a farm from the very beginning does not restrict a valid disposition. Whence, just as it is said that there are two precepts of an arbiter, so there are two of a testator: first, universally to be heir, that is, to be the legal successor, de haere. institu. l. quot. §. hęreditat.; but to be so in such an estate is, first, by its nature suited to the whole; the second is by its nature suited to a legacy. But an heir cannot be bequeathed to himself, nor subtracted, ff. de haered. instit. l. si quis ita haeres institutus excepto fundo. and l. si sub conditione. §. fi. in the reasoning of the text. Therefore, the specification of a certain farm does not signify an institution, de ali. legat. l. Lucius. But when the testator from the beginning gave a universal co-heir, there were not two precepts of the testator, but only one specially applied to a specific thing; and the nature of specific things is that in them the time of the testament is looked to, and they are not augmented after the fact, ff. de fun. instru. l. Lucius. ff. de lib. lega. l. Aurelius. §. testamento. Let those therefore who turn to the right of accrual or of non-decrease cite any text saying this, if they can, and if they are not ashamed, in Authem. de trien. et semis. §. consideremus. C. de colla. l. illam. Further, let us suppose the testator died while the institute in a specific thing was living, and while the universal heir was living; and then I ask whether ownership of the thing left was transferred ipso iure, and it cannot be denied that it was, ad l. Aquil. l. huic scripturę. de furtis. l. a Titio. Suppose then that the universal heir later repudiates, and thus as a legacy the ownership expires by right of accrual; therefore, find one to whom it can accrue. Likewise, how do two contrary or incompatible qualities concur in the same subject? de leg. 1. l. legatum. §. hęredi. C. de codi. l. fi. To the contrary: that the institution in a specific thing is drawn to the whole if the institution in the whole is in the state of lapse, just as if from the beginning a co-heir had been given, or had been given in a clause held as unwritten; and I prove it thus: it is the same thing for a co-heir not to have been named, or to have been named uselessly and to be written, for an act is not interpreted as done which has no effect, nor can it have an effect where the useless and the null are found together, ar. ff. de leg. 1. l. si duobus. §. hęres. ff. de suis, et legi. l. 1. in prin. But where from the beginning he does not have a universal heir, he claims the whole; therefore the same applies if an intervening circumstance after the fact shows him alone entitled to the succession. And we argue from that rule: he who is not admitted, nor expected to be admitted to a share, does not make a share, said l. si duobus. §. fi. Thus he who is not admitted to the inheritance does not exclude another from the inheritance, instit. de l. ful. can. Secondly, because I prove this: it is clearly provided by law that one instituted from a specific thing has the right of accrual, ff. de hęre. insti. l. Titius fundi Corneliani. For since that law considers the right of joinder, therefore by consequence it considers the right of accrual. Thirdly, I prove this through what is noted by Cynus and Iacobus de Arena in auth. nouissima. in q. where it is said that a son instituted in a specific thing has the right of accrual. And if it is said that this is the reason because a specific thing is reduced through legal interpretation to the whole, or to the legitime, as the text says in Auth. vt cum de app. cognoscitur. §. cęterum. and so Mar. responds; if I respond, this response is null, because the legitime is not a true fractional share in the inheritance, since it does not include burdens, and therefore the legitime alone does not make a son an heir in anything, as is subtly noted in C. de rei uendi. l. cum a matre. and is proved in ff. de bonis libertorum. l. si libertus. §. quid ergo. where both the concurrence of the institute and the substitute is removed, because it is not properly a concurrence; for although the institute has the legitime, he is not properly an heir, and in the first degree, because an heir in the legitime alone, properly speaking, does not constitute a degree, which is not found elsewhere. That, therefore, the right of accrual effects: for the institution is of right, not of the nature of the legitimate portion. Furthermore, an heir instituted in a specific thing has the name of heir and the onerous title of an institution, as noted in l. filium. §. sed si portio. de legat. praestan. whence by reason of the name—which name ought not to be in every respect in vain, as noted in ff. de actio. haereditariis. l. pro haerede. §. Papinianus—it deservedly accrues to him. And, to speak more subtly, it is not properly to accrue, but is strengthened in virtue, so that what was in name is now in fact and name; and thus to the name the effect of the thing is added, ff. ad Trebel. l. si haeres institutus. To this is added the gloss arg. in l. ius nostrum. de reg. iur. and C. de sec. nupt. l. 1. But what is noted in ff. de adopt. l. si arrogator. in the great gloss, at the word 'sed pone', applies even more strongly. Further on this, see the ordinary gloss on C. de testa. mili. l. 1. in the great gloss, at the word 'si autem vnus ex vna re' etc., through which glosses I hold that on behalf of the universal heir who died before the testator, or who repudiates, the entire inheritance belongs to the institute in the specific thing, and perhaps this also from a certain tacit substitution. For the right of accrual is said to arise from a tacit substitution, as in l. Titius, et Męuius. §. Iulianus. de leg. 2. nor is a text found elsewhere saying this. And this is the solution to the first question, which opens the way to the second question, by which

† it is asked: if a testator instituted an heir in a specific thing, and restricted his institution by commanding her to be quiet and content and not to be able to claim more, does the institution in a specific thing expire upon the death of the universal heir before restitution, or is it indeed enlarged to the whole? And that it fails, and does not draw the whole to itself, seems expressly proved in ff. de haere. insti. l. quot. §. si duo. at the end of the §, where I said that where the intention of the testator is opposed, it is not drawn to the whole. But here the testator openly resists this, because he speaks by setting a limit and by prohibiting, and this seems to be the nature of restrictive words, which impede the right of accrual, as in ff. ad Treb. l. Lucius. §. quae habebat. Furthermore, in a specific thing there is a universal institution by interpretation of the testament, not by the open nature of the words. But that which comes by tacit interpretation is easily removed by any contrary presumption, as in ff. de leg. 2. l. fi. in princ. Furthermore, that institution in a specific thing is easily drawn to the nature of a legacy or pre-legacy, ff. de haered. insti. l. ex facto. §. dicebam. But in legacies a testator can prohibit the right of accrual, as in ff. de vsufruc. l. domus. Therefore so it is here. Furthermore, an institution in a specific thing is a certain implicit disposition toward an institution and a legacy, and through this the testator's intention can be drawn to two things; and whichever of them the testator rather wishes, that will have to be followed, ar. ff. de serui. l. si tam August. To the contrary are several points: because those restrictive words were evidently uttered in favor of the heir, ar. ff. de lega. 1. l. si seruus. §. qui Margaritam. and in respect of that which would come to be claimed under that heir, not in respect of that which will be claimed through the heir's death. And this seems to be the case in ff. de legat. 3. l. paulo Calimaco. §. Pomponius Euriperus. and to the same effect ff. de hęredi. instit. l. si quis ita haeres institutus excepto fundo. For excessive restriction contrary to the nature of the act does not impede a favorable act; and the institution of an heir is a very favorable act, as in l. cum quidem. ff. de libe. et posth. What is noted in ff. de adop. l. si pater. in prin. supports this. To the same effect: if the rationale of the right of accrual is because one cannot die partly intestate, then the right of accrual is so necessary that it cannot be prohibited, as is noted in said l. si seruus. de acqui. hęre. And this is confirmed, because the cause of testacy draws to itself the cause of intestacy, except when there is the defect of nullity; for nullity is an indivisible defect, and the void cannot be drawn to this, because there is no path from privation to possession, but there is a path that leads from possession to privation, de iniu. test. l. si ego. and de statu ho. l. homo liber. Likewise, an interpretation is to be made more benignly, so that what is left may be valid rather than lapse. Likewise, the word 'instituo' must effect something, ff. de hęred. insti. l. quot. From which it seems that the said sister is admitted to the whole, because the testator does not seem to have thought of this case. For he merely preferred the brother to the sister, nor is any other intention of his perceived, ff. de hęred. insti. l. Lucius. §. si duo. does not stand in the way, because there the testator, by prohibiting it from being drawn to the whole, did not wish to die intestate because he had made no universal heir; therefore the will of intestacy is deservedly not drawn to the will of testacy, ff. de hęred. insti. l. si quis ita hęres instituatur, si leg. and what is noted in C. de test. l. nostram. But here in our case he wished to die testate. Likewise, there it can be valid upon intestacy, here it cannot; and therefore let it be valid here in the manner in which it can, because it is more just that it stand than fall. On this point the solution is not easy, because the question is first of all one of intention. Next, by law, some hold that there is no place for the right of accrual, in favor of whom is the fact that the testator, speaking thus, seems rather to disinherit than to institute, as noted in ff. de hęre. insti. l. qui volebat. But the disinherited do not have the right of accrual, in Auth. de hęred. et fal. §. exhęredat. But I respond and deny that it is a modified institution rather than an odious deprivation. Likewise, I respond through the cited §. Pompo. and ar. de condit. et dem. l. publius. §. 1. and ar. ff. ad Treb. l. a filia. §. alumno. For when the cause of delay or restriction ceases, the delay or restriction ceases, as if the final cause ceased, arg. to this effect ff. de testa. tute. l. fin. To the aforesaid may be added ff. de fideicom. l. Panthonius. Likewise, when an exclusion concerns the favor of another, when the reason for the favor ceases, the effect of the exclusion ceases, as in ff. de au. et ar. leg. l. medico. §. fin. Therefore, words regarding the exoneration of a universal heir, upon the occurrence of a case in which exoneration does not apply, ought not to effect anything; to which ff. de contratab. l. si post mortem. §. liberi. contributes excellently in its rationale. Furthermore, I bring in the gloss on l. quotiens. C. de hęr. insti. applied to the text on this side, for the law speaks when the testator left one thing and ordered the heir to be content; and the gloss says that if he did not have a co-heir, he would have the whole; but this sister has no co-heir; therefore she ought to have the whole. The gloss there seems to be ordinary, if subtly referred to the text. To this, the conjecture of intention sufficiently adds weight, because the testator was able to change his will and did not change it; whence he seems to have set his foot firmly, de proba. l. cum tacitum. and l. quinquaginta. C. de inoff. test. l. 3. C. de testa. l. sancimus. Certainly on the first point I am clear enough, but on this second I fear lest the intention of the testator be offended; and therefore I doubt considerably; yet by law subtly considered I think that the aforesaid sister upholds the side more defensible in law, and excludes every other intestate succession, although dominus Baldus [recte: Bartolus] affirms the contrary side; but in invalidating opinions he was also too bold. And from the aforesaid it is clear that neither he nor anyone else has truly and perfectly chewed over these passages. I, Baldus de Perusio, so state and advise, and have signed to attest.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an executor appointed in a will with full and free authority to sell, without contradiction by the heir, may sell without first requesting the heir’s consent.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† Concerning that which is asked, whether an executor appointed in a testament with full and free power of selling without the contradiction of the heir, as was in the testament of the lady co-heir Rucia, can sell without consulting the heir, in view of the full and free power granted to him. It seems it must be said by law that he can sell, although he has not consulted the heir: because if he can sell against the will of the heir, therefore also without his knowledge. For such power given to the executor by the testator is valid, de ali. lega. l. alio haerede, and noted in l. 2. C. quando decreto opus non est. Nevertheless, if he should sell for less than a fair price, such executor is bound to the heir, and the same if other fault should be involved, because he laid hands on the better thing when he could sell the worse, ar. ff. de nego. ge. l. 3. §. haec uerba, with the like. If he should sell through fraud by colluding with the buyer, then the contract is void ipso iure if the heir wishes it not to be valid, ff. de act. emp. l. Iulianus. §. si quis colludent; for fraud is not deemed to have been permitted, de his, quę in frau. cre. l. si pater; ff. man. l. creditor. §. fi., with the like. Yet I do not deny that it is always safer to inform the heir, just as when an alienation is made by a lawful executor, or the heir is to be informed by him; to this makes extra de testamentis. ca. uos quidem; de lega. 2. l. si tamen quibusdam; de in diem ad die. l. necesse; C. de autho. pręstan. l. fi.; de nata. resti. l. 2.; de hęrede, et si. to the same §. si quis autem non implens. Yet in a mere executor I do not think it is necessary by law that he inform or advise the heir, as I have said; if with fault he administers usefully, he is held liable to the heir: nevertheless the sale and execution is valid, unless it were done contrary to the form of the mandate, ff. de neg. ge. l. quae aliena. §. libertos. Likewise, regarding that which is asked, whether Iaconellus ought to gain a portion of the dowry under the form of the statute—which indeed is said not to be confirmed—or under the form of the testament, it seems that he should not, because in the testament there is left the portion owed, if nothing is owed, in l. legatur. de leg. 2. and l. Maeuio. §. a me. I believe that this is contrary to the mind of the testatrix, and contrary because I presuppose not only a statute, but a prescriptive custom concerning the gaining of this portion: which custom does not need confirmation, since it draws its strength from time, as l. de quibus, and de elec. ca. Cumana. By force of custom, therefore, this is rather than of statute. I, Baldus, so say and advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether some burden may be imposed on the said donation after the donation has been perfected.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

The facts are as follows: The Lord Cardinal of Todi appointed certain of his procurators to give and donate irrevocably inter vivos to Lady Machalta, his sister, and to certain others, certain specific goods of his, under these conditions: that the said Lady Machalta, before the aforementioned donation is made to her, shall give and pay to the Lord Bishop of Todi, the Lord said Cardinal’s [relative], 7 gold florins; and this for the payment of legacies and debts of the father, brothers, and sisters of the said Lord Cardinal, or of nephews and cognates; and furthermore, if any legacies should appear to be due by the same father, brothers, sisters, nephews, and cognates, that the said Lady Machalta is bound for one-third part of the said legacies and debts, as more fully appears from the public instrument drawn up therefor. After the said Lady Machalta had paid the said 7 gold florins, and finally received the donation of the said things according to the form of the mandate given to the said procurators, after which mandate the said Lord Cardinal made certain codicils, in which he left to the Commune of Todi 1500 gold florins for all and everything in which he might be bound to them, whether from the succession of his father, brothers, sisters, and nephews, or in any other way. After his death, the Commune of Todi demanded from the said Lady Machalta 10 florins of the said sum. It is now asked whether the said Lady Machalta, or her heirs after her death, are bound for the residue of the said third part, etc.

On these points, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Law, consulted, say that the said Lady Machalta, or her heirs after her death, are not bound, except to those burdens which are expressed in the contract of donation. On this point, I consider: First, the nature of a perfected act. Second, the strength of an act inter vivos. Third, a vested right. Fourth, the force and power of legacies. Fifth and last, the quality of the possessor.

And first I argue thus: This donation was a perfected act; hence it does not thereafter receive a burden or a mode, nor could a burden be imposed outside the form, since a burden could not be imposed outside the form of the contract, C. de donat. quae sub modo, l. perfecta.

And secondly thus: A contract inter vivos is more powerful than a preceding or subsequent testament; hence an alienation by the testator made inter vivos derogates from the testament and codicils, not vice versa, de leg. 3, l. 11, § si rem; de alien. legat., l. rem legatam. And especially because this contract was not lucrative, but onerous; hence another burden outside the contract could not be superadded by the will of only one contracting party, C. de cond. ob causam, l. si in rem repetendi. For contracts are regulated by the will of two, not of only one, as l. in emendis, and noted in l. 1, C. de pact.

From the third it is argued thus: A vested right arising from a contract cannot be taken away, or diminished, or burdened by the will of the other party alone. Let all the laws be added which speak of a vested right not being taken away. C. locat., l. si cum Hermes; ff. de pact., l. si; de contrah. empt., l. si post mortem, § si. Hence, since this was a vested right arising from a contract according to the form of the contract, it could not thereafter be altered or overridden by codicils, nor could a new burden be inserted.

From the fourth thus: The force or power of legacies, when a quantity is bequeathed, is to bind the universal heir by a personal obligation. Moreover, it creates a hypothecary obligation, C. commun. de legat., l. 1 and 2. But this cannot create a personal action against Lady Machalta, because she is not an heir, ad Trebell., l. 1, § si haeres; nor a hypothecary action, because the goods which she possesses were not the testator’s at the time of his death, d. l. 1, in fin., commun. de legat. Therefore, she can be sued by no right. Moreover, she could not be burdened with that which she possesses by right of contract, not by right of legacy, C. de fideic., l. ab eo; de adopt., l. si arrogator, § sed an impuberis; and ff. ad l. Falcid., l. pater filium.

From the fifth and last, because she is a singular possessor, against whom neither a personal nor a real action lies, because she does not possess the hereditary corpus. For what was alienated before death, the heir holds by right of the donee inter vivos. Hence she is not bound to acknowledge, except the burden of the contract, not the burden of the codicils. For contracts diminish legacies, not vice versa, l. si universorum, de inoff. testam.; l. Papinianus, § quarta.

I conclude therefore that by virtue of the codicils of the Lord Cardinal, Lady Machalta, while living, or her successors after her death, cannot be sued, nor can the origin of the petition be taken from the said codicils. But if other legacies made by the father, or brother, or sisters of the Lord Cardinal appear, in this regard the faith of the contract of donation must be observed according to the form of the contract, C. de donat. quae sub modo, l. 1; ff. de donat. haeredit. pet. I, Baldus de Perusio, say this.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When multiple articles are contained in an award, and a reduction is sought, and judgment is rendered partly in favor of the petitioner and partly against him, whether the penalty may be claimed in its entirety.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† When several clauses are contained in an award, and a reduction is sought, and it is pronounced partly for the petitioner and partly against the petitioner, whether afterwards it may be sought, so that it is equal to succumb in the whole, and in something to win, and in something to lose, as far as the penalty to be allowed was concerned. Sometimes an award has only one clause, sometimes it has several clauses. In the first case, if something is reformed regarding that clause, the penalty is not incurred. For since it has been acted upon legitimately, it does not deserve a penalty, *de verbis obligatis*, l. *quidam cum filio*, ff. *locato conducto*, l. *quaero*, §. *inter locatorem*, ff. *ad legem Falcidiam*, l. *Seius et Aurelius*. And thus holds Dyonisius in the rule *scienti*. In the second case, when there are several clauses, either separate, which do not proceed by the same reason, or contiguous, or connected, so that they should be regarded as one, in the first instance one can uphold the right in one clause, and not uphold justice in another, ff. *fando hereditatis petitione*, l. *quaedam mulier*, ff. *de iure patronatus*, l. *Carmelia*, ff. *de minoribus*, I. *etiam*, §. *ex causa*. Nor does the equity of one clause excuse the temerity committed with respect to another clause, *de legatis secundis*, l. *qui solidum*, in the beginning. Or they are connected, and then they are held in place of one clause, d. I. *etiam*, §. *ex ca.*, and ff. *de appellationibus*, l. *appellanti*, per Dyonisius. Since therefore the clauses are distinct and separate, although in some it has been acted upon well, afterwards it is incurred with respect to some, in which it has been acted upon unjustly. Which I prove thus: this petition for penalty from the form of the compromise is taken not only from the whole, but also from some part; therefore it suffices for verifying the penal stipulation that in some part it has been agreed, *de rebus dubiis*, l. *si is qui*, 200, §. *utrum*, and *iudicatum solui*, l. *cum quaerebatur*, ff. *rem raptoram habere*, l. *si procurator*, from which I infer that the penalty is incurred.
