It is true that some say that Johannes Andreas in the title *de arbitris* in his additions in §. *sequitur*, in the version *in addi.*, which chapter Dyonisius in the rule *scienti* and others say, that if he who sought the reduction of the award had a just cause for litigation, and this proves that he is excused from the penalty, although he succumbed in the cause of reduction. And by this it makes what we note, *inst.* *de actionibus*. Also mixed is the action against them, and what we note, C. *quorum appellatio non recipitur*, l. *ab executione*, and argument *de regulis iuris*, l. *qui in alterius*, and *de verbis obligatis*, l. *ad idem*, and l. *cum filius*, §. *in haec*, in the gloss of the text; however, there it makes to the contrary. Also if the judge, to whom recourse is had for reduction, pronounced badly, that this may hinder the repetition of the penalty, noted gloss, ff. *de verbis obligatis*, l. *qui Romae*, §. *duo fratres*, in the great gloss, version *si autem duc.*, that he says badly from that gloss, it may also be argued to the contrary, in the words *sed quid hoc casu*. And by this *de rei venditione*, l. *ex diverso*, that the same judgment is of the principal and the penal, and by one judgment another is ordered and liquidated. And this is against Johannes Andreas, and makes to this gloss *ordinaria*, ff. *quod metus causa*, l. *si cum exceptione*, §. *haec autem actio*. But my own opinion, which is more equitable, makes that the penalty is sought from the contract, not from the sentence: and when action is brought by personal action, and from contract, every exception seems saved, and every old defense, as noted, ff. *de exceptione rei iudicatae*, l. *duobus*. Whatever this is, it is not alleged, nor proved even in our case. And therefore I say the penalty is incurred from particular convention: the allegation does not stand, that the compromise was null due to the uncertainty of the third party, which allegation seems founded by l. *item si unus*, §. *si in duos*, ff. *de arbitris*, and extra *eo*, c. *innotuit*. For that §. is understood when the said electees disagree. Then indeed the compromise vanishes according to the moderns, and according to the gloss; and then it does not vanish: but it is valid by the protection of the praetor, not by the force of uncertain arbitration; the agreeing parties are compelled to choose a third party according to the gloss in the same l. §. *paterni*. For the reason, because the text says it does not hold, is founded on account of disagreement. This reason ceases, if they consent to each other of their own motion without a judge, argument *de legibus primis*, l. *huiusmodi*, §. *fi*. Nor in your documents is it questioned about that which they do concordantly, because the substance of the compromise is not disapproved, but the quality, or mode, as elsewhere noted, C. *eo*. Or we would say, this clause added to increase should not operate the destruction of the compromise, if they agree according to all, nor disagree according to the gloss; according to the moderns not all, according to some the compromise expires, because the judge is not bound to supply where the party wished to provide for itself; even where an useless provision is impeded by the subsidiary office of the judge. For the parties by choosing the way of providing seem to have deserted the legal promise, C. *de iure deliberandi*, l. *fin.*, §. *pe*. Also let the judge not protect the ineptitudes of the contracting parties, which can sufficiently be defended, argument C. *de pactis conventis*, l. *fi*. On the connection of the clauses I say that those are not connected which are not ordered to each other, but have a different reason. C. *de rebus creditis*, l. *generaliter*. And argument ff. *de legatis secundis*, l. *neminem*, and l. *si ex duobus*. Those therefore, of which one is equitable, another inequitable, are not connected, but each is decided by itself. Baldus de Perusio, *legum doctor*, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a petition is said to be correctly drawn up.
2. A conventional penalty may be claimed together with the principal claim.
3. When there are two special statutes, which statute must be observed when they concur on the same matter.
4. A day and a conventional penalty, where default has occurred in obligations to give or to do, do not admit of purification.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. First, three matters appear to require examination: first, regarding the libel, whether it is properly drawn up; second, regarding the procedure, whether the case should be pursued by way of compromise or not; third, regarding the substance of the petition, whether the penalty has been incurred, and whether the delay can be purged or not.

† Regarding the first point, whether the libellus is properly drawn up, it is alleged as follows: that libellus is properly drawn up where the conclusion follows from the facts narrated by the plaintiff. The opposing view holds, and this is the principal rule in the matter of libelli, as noted in D. de exceptionibus doli, l. 2, § circa. But here, from the facts narrated by the plaintiff and conceded, the conclusion follows for the condemnation of the defendant; therefore, the libellus is most suitable. Secondly, it is proven thus: however a libellus may be tolerated, it is said to be suitable. These are the words of Innocentius in De iudiciis, c. Examinata. But this libellus can be tolerated; therefore, it is suitable. To the contrary, that the libellus is unsuitable, or the petition, is proven thus: in the libellus mention is made of two months, within which he promised to perform. And the beginning of the time is not expressed in the libellus. And, the beginning being unknown, we are uncertain about the course of the action; for he who is ignorant of the terminus a quo, when the term is measured by time, is also uncertain about the middle and the end, as noted by Oldus in D. de edendo, l. 1, § diem; and by Bartolus de Assis in C. de testibus, l. Testium. It accords with what is noted in D. de testibus, l. Ob carmen, § si; and D. de minoribus, l. 3, § minorem; and D. de testamentis, l. Qua aetate. And it is naturally evident that time is the measure of motion, and of those things which are in motion. And motion is from an external terminus a quo to an external terminus ad quem. Therefore, it is necessary that the beginning of time be certain, so that those things which follow after the beginning may be certain. But this is a certain beginning of time; therefore, the libellus is uncertain. For a certain species of unsuitability is the uncertainty of the libellus, if it is opposed, as noted in C. de annua exceptione, l. Si; especially in petitions for penalties, where everything ought to be more certain, as in D. de codicillis, l. Testamento, § si.

† Secondly, it is proven, because in the same libel the claim for the penalty and for the principal fact are cumulated: although this seems impossible, because those things which are such that they are extinguished by the action or by the judge’s absolution cannot be cumulated: D. 2. l. filius. §. variis. ff. si fa. fur. fe. dica. l. 1. in fin. ff. de excep. l. fundum Titianum. and l. fundi. But it appears thus here, for the principal sum and the penalty are extinguished by election, even where there is no novation, as in l. rescriptum. §. si pacto. de pac. and de except. doli. l. apud Celsum. §. Labeo. where the case seems to be found. Likewise, the principal sum and the penalty are extinguished by the action, for if the principal sum is paid, the penalty is not due; and if both could be claimed considering the concurrence in the birth, ff. de arbitr. l. Celsus. Likewise, if it is pronounced that there was no contract regarding the principal sum, this is an obstacle to the example in the penalty; and if the contrary is pronounced regarding the principal sum, the defense in the penalty is excluded, as noted in ff. de ver. obl. qui romę. §. duo fratres. in fi. magnae glos. Likewise, that two judgments are required, the first for the principal sum, the second for the penalty, is supported by what is noted in ff. quod met. caus. l. si cum exceptione. §. haec autem actio. Since therefore the rules preventing cumulation have place in our case, cumulation is prevented. And when those things which cannot be cumulated are cumulated, the libel is considered null, as in ff. de adult. l. si maritus. §. fina. For the declaration of this point, it must be known that sometimes the penalty involves the rescission of the act; then it cannot be in the same libel, nor is it due together with the principal, as in l. commissoriae. de pac. inter emp. Sometimes it does not contain the accretion of rescission, but a new obligation; and then it matters whether such a penalty cannot be claimed together with the principal, and then the libel does not proceed for both, but must be formed for one or the other, as in §. Labeo. Or it can be claimed together with the principal, and then it is a legal penalty, and the connected claim proceeds simultaneously. de re. and c. c. poena. C. loca. l. conductores. and C. vnde vi. l. cum ab re. and as noted on both sides. And if the penalty is not yet incurred, the penalty can be claimed conditionally: founded on the principal judgment in the claim for the principal sum. For in the condition alone the process cannot be founded, nor can the cause of action be divided. For just as the condition, or its existence, is not in act but in potency, and therefore does not found a judgment, as in ff. de vsuris. l. 1. in prin. Or it can be claimed together with the principal, and it proceeds from legal disposition, as in the penalty for contempt; and then both cannot be claimed: although delay cannot be purged against the will of the plaintiff, because the plaintiff is not forced to accept the principal sum, yet if he accepts it voluntarily, he is seen to have receded from the penalty, as in l. Celsus. and noted in l. 2. de iure emphy. And therefore he cannot conclude conjunctively in the libel for the exaction of both. It fails. C. de transact. l. vbi pactum. and l. si quis maior. Or that both can be claimed and exacted together is expressly agreed between the parties, and then the form of the pact must be followed, so that both can be claimed and exacted together. As noted in de ver. obl. l. cum stipul. sit mihi a proculo. according to the opinion of Rof. And in the same libel regarding the connection of causes, it seems that both can be claimed. And the rule of the law, fundi and fundum, ceases here. To this, it is well supported, and noted in de verb. ob. l. 2. Likewise, if in the fact in the gloss. ordi. and de act. emp. l. 1. in prin. l. si cum except. §. haec autem actio. per Gul. C. de iudi. l. 1. and what is noted in extra de testa. ca. Rayn. in glo. Ber. For this is our case. Hence it seems that the libel is well conceived. The argument from uncertainty does not obstruct, because the instrument was issued regarding the facts on a certain day, and ff. vt in pos. le. l. postquam. §. si dies. And the libel, whenever declared, proceeds, as in ff. de rei vend. l. idem Pomponius sembit, si frumentum. §. vltimo. And this is for the first point. And the foregoing are confirmed, because the form is in the mode of acting. Hence if the contract is alternative, an alternative claim proceeds from it. As in eo, quod cer. lo. l. non vtique. If conditional, a conditional libel proceeds, not beginning with the condition, but with the disposition. For that which is in the obligation must be in the claim, de solu. l. si stipulatus. §. fi. And the reason is, because it is a certain penal covenant having two heads, the principal sum and the penalty, admitting a double claim, so that what is cumulated in the contract may be cumulated in the claim, as I have proved at length above. And it is supported by C. de e. trah. et committ. stip. l. nuda. Regarding the second, concerning the mode of proceeding on the claims

It must be considered, after it has been said regarding the form of the petition: and this question depends on the understanding of the statutes. For the statute concerning the execution of a precept and a public instrument wishes it to be expedited quickly within the shortest delays. Another statute concerning forced arbitrations, because this law was born conditionally on account of the partnership, seems to urge towards arbitration. Here it must be considered, because each statute seems principally to favor one thing: one the cause of the instrument and precept, the other the persons of the partners and heirs; which of these special provisions derogates from the other; and whether the statute concerning execution has application to an instrument that is not liquid; and whether it has application where an instrument is produced, but not where a precept is produced. On this point, it must be premised that, just as a species derogates from a genus, so the most specific species derogates from a species that is not most specific, and individuals derogate from a species, according to law 3, *Heres meus*, § *Duae statuae*. If, however, the species in the statutes were equal, that species which is more benign and has more special consideration should be added, because it ought not to be weighed heavily, as we say, when several parties concur as if privileged, that one is stronger in which the power of favor is found, C. *Qui potiores in pignore habentur*, l. *Assiduis*, § *Decepti*; Ff. *Qui potiores in pignore habentur*, l. *Interdum*; *De privilegiis creditorum*, l. *Si ventri*, § *In bonis*. Therefore, it must be considered which name is more specific: the name of instrument or the name of partnership. And they seem to relate to each other as exceeding and exceeded, for instrument is predicated of the instrument of partnership and of other contracts. Again, partnership is sometimes with an instrument, sometimes without. And thus it is divided into members, and the members, as it were individuals, are joined under the species of law. The name of partnership seems to be the most specific, for whether an instrument is of partnership or not is not a division into inferior species, but into modes of proving; on this ground, it seems that there is room for arbitration.

On the contrary, to ask that the cause be referred to arbitration is a certain species of evasion and declination of judgment, C. *De iudiciis*, l. *Penultima*. But where the debt is clear, reason dictates that mere dilatory tactics be decided against, C. *De temporibus appellationum*, l. 2. Moreover, a provision with a certain time makes the debt of the penalty liquid by the mere passage of time. Nor is it necessary for the creditor to prove the negative in any other way, *De probationibus*, l. *Quinquaginta*; *De verbis obligatis*, l. *Hoc iure*. Cynus, *De iure emphyteutici*, l. 2; *De actionibus*, c. *Super his*. According to Innocentius and the Archdeacon, C. *De litis contestatione*, auth. *Offeratur*. There it is said that not only, etc. Also, if it is a certain exception, it ought to have been opposed before the joinder of issue, C. *De exceptionibus*, l. *Finis*. And what is noted in c. *Finis*, *De exceptionibus*, in c. *Pastoralis*, according to Innocentius. Therefore, it seems that arbitration cannot be requested, because it seems to be requested with malice. Hence, since the petitioner must swear that he does not request it with malicious intent, and malice is clearly apparent, his petition ought not to be admitted, Ff. *De iureiurando*, l. *Iusiurandum*. For, as Innocentius says, it is the same to request ineptly and to request evidently unjustly, c. 1, *De officio vicarii*, according to Innocentius. And then the petition is challenged on its own face: whether the error appears from the form or from the matter, arg. Ff. *Ne quis eum qui sub tutela est*, l. 1, § *Offilius*; *Iudicium solutum*, l. *Vir bonus*; *Ne quis vel a rege*, l. 2, cum si. Also, no one can decline the judge in execution, Extra, *De appellationibus*, c. *Novit*. Also, arbitration ought to be of a doubtful matter, when it is transferred to an arbitrator, just like a transaction. But here there is no doubt, when it is certain from the contract and the passage of time. And if it is said that the business makes the matter doubtful, as in l. *Finis*, *Qui ad libertatem proclamare non licet*, I answer: it is true that it makes the matter to be proved doubtful, but not the matter already proved. For proof confounds the one denying penalties with the guilty. Moreover, occasion is twofold: from the prior, as in l. *Calphurnia*; and from the posterior. Occasion is called an ordered case, in a way contingent, as C. *De legatis*, l. *Non dubium*; *De incendio, ruina et naufragio*, l. 1, § *Ex incendio*; *Quod vi aut clam*, l. *Alius*, § *Est et alia*. And it supports what is noted, Ff. *Rerum amotarum*, l. *Similiter*; *De dolo*, l. *Cum quis poenarum*, l. *Conclusio*. Occasion occurs in acts naturally tending in order to a penalty: for the act is considered, and its effect is said to occur occasionally, Inst. *Ad legem Aquiliam*, l. *His autem verbis*; Ff. *De poenis*, l. *Utrum*. Since, therefore, in our case the penalty was inserted outside the nature of the contract, it is not said to be an occasion, unless so remote that it must be considered, as Ff. *De furtis*, l. *Verum*. And thus we are entirely outside the case of the statute.

Also, the privilege that was in the action for a partner seems to have been lost by the interposition of a stipulation, Ff. *De novazione*, l. *Alia* and l. *Emptor*. What is to be said? This reason weighs with me: for to understand the statute concerning executions as applying to uncertain and non-liquid instruments could induce great absurdity: for what is conditional and uncertain requires liquidation and proof, C. *De compensatione*, l. *Finis*; C. *De sententiis quae sine certa quantitate fiunt*, l. *Finis*, there especially; and it must be clear and certain to the praetor regarding the event of the condition, *De iudiciis*, l. *Sed si restituatur*; Ff. *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, l. *Quae sub conditione* and l. *Qui haeredi*, § *Finis*; *De pignoribus actionibus*, l. *Si rem*, § *Finis*; and noted, Ff. *De dolo*, l. *Filius*; *Qui ex causa in possessionem eant*, l. *Haec adiit*, in principle; and in c. 1, *De officio delegati*, in the end; in clem. And in non-liquid matters there cannot be a uniform delay, nor a reason for terms.

Also, the statute makes mention of instruments and precepts; hence from this conjunction it is understood, and it speaks of instruments similar in the reason of execution to precepts. But this is not the case except in liquid matters, to this effect Ff. *De legatis 3*, l. *Finis*, § *Cui dulcia*; and arg. Ff. *De re dubia*, in l. 1. For a conjunction placed by the law is presumed to couple equals, not contraries, as is certain and uncertain, arg. Ff. *De legatis*, l. *Non possunt*; C. *De revocatione donationum*, l. *Is solis*. Perhaps it could be distinguished: either the arbitration was requested before the liquidation was made, and then it was rightly requested, and the statute concerning forced arbitrations has application; or the liquidation has already been made, and then the request for arbitration does not proceed, arg. C. *De adulteriis*, l. *Quamvis indubitati*. And this I believe to be equitable and just, whether the plaintiff or the defendant requests arbitration. In this case, however, a term was given by law for proving, and nothing was placed or articulated. And consequently, nothing was proved. Hence, if in this, namely in the acts of the case, there is no error, I believe the requested arbitration should be made. The term of the statute does not obstruct, because the statute assigns a certain term in non-liquid matters. And because that limit, if any is prefixed, would be for the judge, not for the party, and therefore it does not close the mouth of the party. And noted, doc. C. *De iudiciis*, l. *Properandum*, in principle; and *De excusationibus tutorum*, l. *Scire patet*, § *Consequens*, according to Jacobus and Oldradus. For it is one thing to refer to the exclusion of the father, C. *Ut omnes tam civiles quam militares*, l. 1.

† Now follows the third question, in which I do not state what I think, because we are not in a definitive calculation, from which the case ought to be referred to arbitration. Nevertheless, I hold one point, which I maintain according to the opinion of the gloss: that where there is a fixed day, and conventional delay has been incurred in obligations to give or to do, it does not admit of purification. And because this article concerns the subtleties of the law, and the article concerning ignorance or difficulty, whether it excuses, I refrain for the present. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What usufruct is, and what the benefit of fruits is.
2. Usufruct cannot be ceded; it is otherwise with the benefit of the fruits.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† On this point it must be considered that usufruct is one thing, and the benefit of the fruits is another. For usufruct is something inseparable from the person, which cannot be ceded under the new law, l. vsus f. ff. sol. matrimo., l. si vsus fructus, in stip. de vsufruct. §. finitur; for things naturally inseparable cannot be ceded, ff. de iu. do. l. si mulier. §. ex asse. The benefit of the fruits, however, can indeed be ceded, de periculo, et commo. rei ven. l. necessario. §. fin. Likewise, it must be considered that a formal usufruct was bequeathed to Ciola and Agnodella, ff. de vsus fr. l. si quis ita, and noted there; and upon the death of Agnodella, to Ciola, ff. de vsuf. accrescendo. l. 1. §. interdum.

† It must therefore be seen whether in the cession which Ciola made, the right and action of this usufruct are included. From the aforesaid it sufficiently appears that they are not: because the right of usufruct cannot be ceded, though the benefit can indeed be ceded. But the words of the instrument signify a right, not the mere fact of the gathering of fruits; and therefore it does not seem to include the usufruct in question. Nor does the oath stand in the way, because an oath has the force of confirmation, whence it extends [not], but corroborates, de lib. le. l. aurelio. §. testamento. Likewise, a cession is not valid except up to the amount which one in truth paid, C. man. l. per diuersas, and the costs of that lawsuit, as noted there; whereas now the right of usufruct would be included. Likewise, one is not deemed to cede a right against oneself, as in l. 1. in fi. de no. ope. nun. Wherefore, if the right of usufruct is included, it will either be contrary to l. per diuersas [or] l. 1. in fin. The question is sufficiently doubtful, but in law I believe as I have stated above. I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What usufruct is, and what the benefit of fruits is.
2. Usufruct cannot be severed, whereas it is otherwise with the benefit of fruits.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† The counting out of this money made for trading for the common benefit induced a contract of partnership, because it is a partnership if one puts in money and the other labor, as is fully noted in C. pro so. l. 1. And that partnership is dissolved by renunciation; whence he could lawfully renounce the partnership and demand the money, ff. pro so. l. actione. §. renun., and especially because it was expressly said: both upon his petition, and at the term. It is otherwise in a contract of loan for use (commodatum), in that the thing loaned for use cannot be reclaimed before the use is finished, as noted in C. conmoda. l. 2. A doubt arises in this question, because the quantity does not seem to be liquidated, since an accounting has not been rendered, nor is it apparent what the remnants/balances are. But I respond: on the contrary, it is certain from an inspection of the form of the instrument, unless a loss is proved; for a loss is not presumed unless it is proved. And what is noted in C. de sen. quae sine cer. quan. l. 2 supports this, as is noted there. I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute that daughters must be married from the *parage*, whether equality must be observed in marrying sons.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Having considered the said point, it seems that one should say that the words of the statute, which state that daughters must be married with a dowry (paragium), are to be understood as meaning that equality is to be assessed in light of the condition of the person, the quantity of the patrimony, and the number of children, as in D. 35.2.12 (Si filiae). Thus, a good man ought to determine the measure of the dowry, as in D. 26.1.14 (Si ex causa), § In dotis. In this matter, general custom is to be observed more than the custom of a single part, as supported by what is read in D. 29.1.11 (Cum delationis), § Asinam; D. 35.2.1 (Liberorum), § Quod tamen Cassius; D. 50.16.189 (Tugurii); and D. 50.16.190 (Ut Alfenus). Although equality must be preserved among children, if it can be preserved, as in C. 2.12.1 (Ultima), nevertheless, in our case, she who is undowered ought to be dowered no less than the father did not marry two others with a decent dowry; just as, conversely, if a father, out of singular affection for one of his daughters, had given a dowry beyond the proper measure, as in D. 35.1.1 (Cum filius), § Haeres meus, we would not therefore follow this path for the other daughters. Therefore, the middle course must be taken, and it is not to be weighed according to what the father gave, but according to what reason dictates; therefore, the condition of the person must be examined, especially in these and many other cases, as in D. 7.1.1 (Plenum), § Equitii; D. 44.7.1 (Finis). It is clearly stated that she marries an equal who marries an equal. And it is relevant in D. 2.13.1 (Si rogatus), § Matrimonii. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a peace is made between two enemies by mutual compromise not to harm each other in person or in property, and one of them is killed and robbed, whether the sureties are bound both for the robbery and for the offense of the killing.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It is proposed that peace was made between certain enemies, and it was promised on both sides not to offend in person or in property under a certain penalty to be incurred as often as the agreement is violated, and sureties were given. Finally, two from one party killed another from the other party, and after they had killed him, they went to the house of the said deceased and robbed the house. Now, two penalties are sought from the sureties of the offenders, one on account of the homicide, the other on account of the robbery. And this is so because there are multiple offenses; the number of offenses induces the number of penalties, C. de accus. l. si quis homicidii; de privatis delictis l. nunquam plura. Moreover, there are two heads: one concerning the offense against the person, the other concerning property. And in each, it was agreed, therefore a penalty is due from each head, since it was provided that it should be incurred repeatedly, as in l. si duo, re, §. fina., ff. de arbitris.

To the contrary, because this person was first killed, and thus the party ended by death: hence, from then on, the peace can be broken with the dead, arg. de bonis libertorum l. qui libertus, §. posthumus; and in Auth. de nuptiis, §. deinceps. For the contract of peace ends by death, arg. ff. de rapinis l. non a patre. Therefore, all clauses of the contract and all penalties for future breaches end, arg. no. ff. de minoribus l. verum, §. 1. But it could be said that rather the dead person is offended, and an injury is done to the corpse, as in C. de sepulchris violatis l. qui sepulchro, in the word "dominus defunctorum"; ff. de iniuriis l. 1, §. quotiens. And the deceased is said to have friends and enemies, arg. in l. 1, §. eleganter, de ventre in possessionem mittendo. What is to be said?

I answer: I admit that if the house had first been robbed, and then the person killed, there would be two penalties, because two heads of the agreement would have been violated. But if the homicide was committed first, and then, after an interval, the house was robbed, this robbery is not a breach of the peace, because that which does not exist cannot be broken, de iniustis testamento l. nam si sub conditione, §. post defectum; de verbis obligatorum lib. 10. To this effect, de negotiis gestis l. 3, §. haec verba, in the reason of itself. And de servitutibus legatis l. pater. If, however, the killing and the robbery were committed simultaneously, then I would believe that two penalties should be imposed, because everything appears to have been perpetrated during the time of peace, ff. de manumissionibus testamento l. qui duos autem. Therefore, the robbery precedes, or the homicide follows, and if it follows, either immediately or after an interval. And this is supported by ff. de actionibus et obligationibus l. nunquam actiones; and what is noted in c. 1, de regulis iuris 6, in the Novels. And there we have this distinction, ff. de adulteriis l. quod ait, §. fin.; ff. quod vi aut clam l. si alius, §. est et alia. However, I understand "immediately" to mean when there is no interval of time, and in the same place, so that the acts are continuous, as if someone kills and immediately strips the body; for the inheritance would not suffer violence, nor theft, ff. si quis testamento lib. esse iussus fuerit l. 1, §. Scævola. Thus I, Baldus, say and advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Governors appointed by the prince, or confirmed, have jurisdiction to try and punish light crimes.
2. What crimes are called atrocious, and which are light. No. 3. And add below, consilium 412.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If the prince does not wish it, and the cities or nobles of the university have no jurisdiction, they all the less can possess the university; for jurisdiction is granted solely by the permission or tolerance of the prince, and is held from the prince as it were by precarious tenure, and when the prince wills otherwise, it shall cease to be; and therefore the places of statutes and customs are in the power of the prince, according to the law *De sepulchro violato*, l. 3, § *Diuus*, in the Authentica *Cassa*, and in c. 1, *De constitutionibus*, lib. 6. For the Emperor is the lord of laws, and can abolish and reform them, as in l. *Constituta*, C., § *Quibus*, and *Apostolus*; he who is the prince of princes and lord of lords. Nevertheless, in our case there is no doubt, nor ought there to be any, because the said inquisition proceeded, since the statutes were confirmed, and among those confirmed is our statute, as in D. *De militum testamento*, l. *Tribunus*, § *Iulius*. For it is not said that the crime is grave on account of the kind of penalty, because it is a small pecuniary one, nor because it concerns the prior, is it therefore enormous, because the prior and the decurion are equated, and not every injury done to a decurion is a grave crime, especially since it is not stated that it was done in contempt of the office.

† A crime is said to be atrocious in several ways: in one way, every crime that is committed with intent, as stated in the Digest, title *De regulis iuris*, law *Auxilium*, section *In delictis*; and in the Digest, title *Ad ea*, law *Ad ea*. In a second way, crimes are called atrocious or slight according to the quality of the punishment, as stated in the Digest, title *De publicis iudiciis*, law 2; and in the Digest, title *De securitate*, law *Leuia*. And therefore a delict is considered slight if the law punishes it lightly, as stated in the Codex, title *De defensione civium*, section *Aud

And it can be said that every crime is minor, from which a pecuniary penalty is imposed below 300 gold florins, in the same title, §. et iudicare. And therefore, concerning such matters, inquiry may be made by the rector of the place, if the superior forbids it; I understand this to refer to the prince, who can forbid, not to the provincial governor, who cannot order what is just and lawful under inferior jurisdiction. As noted by Atexius, ii. q. i. de persona. Custom, however, grants jurisdiction or emanates from liberty, l. 1. ff. de iurisdi. om. iu. l. minor maiorum. de du. om. iuros. cum si. And it supports what is noted by Innocentius, de const. c. cum accesserint, and ff. de iu. c. 2. §. is datur. de fo. comp. c. cum contingat. And Privilegium, de cu. in l. si in praecium. de iuris. om. iu. cum si. It is therefore concluded that the rectors of the said commune, who are appointed or confirmed by the superior, have jurisdiction to cognize and punish minor crimes. And I understand "minor" to mean those for which a mere and small pecuniary penalty is imposed. And it is proven, as noted in the said §. in delictis. Baldus, de reu.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What makes a pignorative contract actionable.
2. Whether several indications are required, or whether one suffices to induce a presumption of simulation and fraud of the contract.
casus: CASE. The fact is as follows, and is proposed. A certain Dominicus, on behalf of and in the name of Cola Sacebi of Insula Calae, sold a certain vineyard and certain other possessions to Federico Serbelli and Petrucia Constagionis for the price of 42 gold florins, as appears from the present instrument, which I send to you. However, at the same place and time, and with the same witnesses, an agreement was made between the aforementioned parties, that if the said sellers neglected to redeem the aforementioned possessions for the said price of 42 gold florins within a certain term, it would be permitted to them, and that the buyer should gain half of the future vintage of the said vineyard, as appears from the said pacts in a certain other instrument, a copy of which I send to you. The said sellers never declared their intention to redeem the aforementioned possessions within the said term, nor can they; rather, the said Cola and his heirs always held the said possessions peacefully and quietly. Now, the said Constagionis says that he wishes to redeem the said possessions for two parts, that is, for his part and that of the aforementioned Petrucia, who granted the said Constagionis during her lifetime, and the said Constagionis says that all fruits should be computed into the principal, since the said contract was in truth a pawn contract (pignoratitius), and to prove this he produces only the aforementioned instrument with the said pacts, as contained in the aforementioned copy, which I send to you. And he says that the said possessions were worth more than 80 gold florins at the time of the said contract, and he does not prove this. On the part of the heirs of the said Cola, it is said that the said possessions were sold purely, although with the said pacts. Furthermore, they say that the said possessions were not worth more than 50, and at most 52, gold florins at the time of the said contract. And this the said heirs prove. Furthermore, Ser Federico, one of the aforementioned sellers, says that the said possessions were sold purely, although with the pacts written below; and this is against the notary who wrote the aforementioned documents. Now it is asked to be declared whether the said contract should be judged as a pawn contract (pignoratitius) or not.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† That the said contract ought to be judged as a pignoratitious contract appears to be proved by this reasoning: when something is received for the resale beyond the price given, such a contract is considered pignoratitious, as in Extra de pign., c. ille. But here something beyond the price is received, namely half of the fruits; therefore it ought not to be considered a pure sale, but rather a pledge. Secondly, it is proved thus: when an agreement conforms to the nature of a purchase, then from the agreement a purchase is presumed; but when it conforms to a purchase, yet to a usurious contract, then a pledge is presumed. So note Cy. and Iaco. de Aret., plus valere quod agitur, l. emptione. But that agreement, by which the fruits, whether pending or not pending, are to be gained, is alien to the nature of a resale, in which, if indeed the fruits have been gathered, they are not included except by delay, as in l. 2, C. de pact. inter empt.; if they are pending, all are included, as in l. fi, §. pe., quae in frau. cred. Hence the division of fruits, of which the instrument speaks, at no time and in no way pertains to the nature of a pure resale, but rather to the nature of usury; because even if the principal is returned the following day after the contract, nevertheless by the form of the agreement half of the fruits ought to be gained. Certainly whatever is added to the principal is usury, ff. si cer. pe., l. rogasti, §. si tibi. And such a contract is presumed to be of the kind that is declared by the agreements, ff. de contrah. emp., l. qui manu sata, §. nemo.

To the contrary, that it ought to be judged a true purchase, as is proved: for in doubt every contract is presumed true, and not simulated, as in C. de proba., l. cum precibus. Therefore this contract is presumed true. Secondly, this is proved because the confession of one of the co-debtors, and the acknowledgment of the debt, harms the other co-debtor, as in C. de duo. rei., l. fin. But one of the parties bound jointly and severally acknowledges that it was a true contract; hence we must adhere to his statement, since it is presumed that he acts in good faith, as in ff. manda., l. quintus.

† Thirdly, it is proven by the saying of c. illo nos. For that chapter presumes simulation from indicia. For judgment is not rendered from one indicium, since one judgment is less than half-proof, as noted in ff. de probat. l. probatio. Therefore, when three indicia, or at least two, concur, then the contract is presumed to be simulated; but if only one indicium occurs, then it is otherwise, especially if another indicium is to the contrary, as is the case here: for it cannot be denied that the said Correi makes at least an indicium against Correi, as in C. de fidei instru. l. 2. I declare what it means to say three indicia, two, and one: three indicia are present when fruits are computed into the principal, when something is added beyond the principal, and when someone is a partner of the moneylender. From these three, two suffice, because the effect is increased by indicia concurring from several sources. And thus it is said from two, not from only one. Likewise, from several concurring indicia, it is indicated in c. nostram, de emptione et venditione. For there, one indicium was that he did not wish to accept a loan, whereas the contract had preceded from lending. A second indicium was that the thing was of much greater price; fraud is not presumed from the pact alone, unless perhaps another indicium concurred with it, which was that he was accustomed to be a moneylender; this would not suffice, as noted by Ia. de probat. l. 1, § pro certo. Even in this contract there are presumptions for and against; nevertheless, finally I believe that if one of the sellers in court recognized and confessed that the contract was true and not a pledge, that this confession should be upheld against them, by the case of the said l. ultima, C. de duobus rebus. And I hold this opinion by the said l. ego Bal. de Per. legum doc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a fund is sold with a formula reserved, which is in the fund itself, whether such reservation is understood as to dominion or as to servitude.
2. Whether access is open to someone to their own thing, and when.
casus: C A The facts are as follows. A certain Brother Ubaldus, Syndic and procurator of the monastery of Saint Mary of the Scholars, sold to Cechus Matheoli a certain piece of land for a certain price, in which land there is a certain channel, through which water used to flow, which came out of a certain Mill of the said brothers, situated on the said land in another part of the land of the said brothers, and in this the said brothers reserved for themselves the said channel, as appears by the hand of Ser Matthaeus Ioannes de Eugino. And after the said sale, the said brothers came to certain pacts with the said Cechus, the buyer, as appears by the hand of Ser Nuccius Niger, notary of Eugino. We send you these instruments of purchase and pacts in public form. Now, the brothers, seeing that the Mill is destroyed, sold themselves another land where the place of the said Mill was, and also sold all the rights they had in the said channel. Now, that buyer says that the said channel is his, and that he wishes to use it for another use than for the flow of water. It is responded by the said Cechus that the said channel is appointed only for the flow of water, and that they cannot use it for another use, and that he, Cechus, offers to fulfill separately all that is contained and to which he is bound according to the form of the instrument of the said pacts. Now, the question is, having seen the aforementioned instruments and the point above written, what is the law in the aforementioned matters: whether the said buyer of the said Mill can use the said channel for another use than for the use of water, because he wishes to work it and sell it, whether it belongs to the said Cechus, and whether he can enter the said channel against the will of the said Cechus.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† This question presents two doubts. The first point is whether the said reservation of the said channel was made with regard to ownership, or with regard to the servitude of conducting water through the sold estate. And it appears that it was made by way of servitude, and thus it is not permitted to change it to another use; this seems to be the case in D. de serv. rust. pr. l. qui duo praedia. To the contrary, it appears that full ownership was reserved, such that it is lawful for the owner to use it for whatever purpose he wishes, as in D. de pact. l. nemo videtur; the case in D. de leg. 1. l. si fundum sub conditione, §. qui fundum. And this appears to be true, for the words state that he reserved for himself a channel of a certain width, etc., whence these words suggest an exemption or exclusion; indeed, it expressly states that the channel was not included in the sale, etc. Therefore, it rightly did not pass in the sale, as argued from C. de peric. et comm. rei vend. l. si vinea. And thus he did not depart from the convention of the grantor, and it was done by measurement: and the said channel was not measured, nor was any price paid for its soil, or area, or bed. Therefore, rightly, that which is alienated is retained in the original dominion, arg. D. quibus ex caus. mai. l. nec utilem. This creates doubt for me, because the surface appears to have been excepted, in that the form of a certain width was reserved; for if ownership had been reserved down to the center of the earth, the reservation would extend its force, just as upwards to the sky. Hence, from this pact it seems to be inferred that only the surface was reserved, arg. D. de serv. rust. pr. l. Lucius Titius Gaio. For additions sometimes enlarge, as in D. de usufr. l. Proculus; sometimes they limit, D. de verb. sig. l. si cum fundum. To the same effect, D. de act. et obl. l. obligationum fere, §. placet, ver. sic et in contrahendo. But I do not say that it is a servitude of water, but that the useful dominion of the surface was reserved. Sometimes something is reserved principally for itself, and then the reservation is interpreted as full right, if the nature of the words permits, D. de vend. pr. l. si in venditione; D. de leg. 1. l. si quis legaverit fundum Cornelianum. Sometimes it is reserved accessorially: and then sometimes it accedes to a servitude, and is considered reserved by way of servitude, as in the aforementioned l. qui duo praedia; or it accedes to ownership, as here the channel accedes to the Mill: and then it appears that at least the useful dominion and the surface are exempted. And so it is in our case. Therefore, whether ownership or surface was reserved, it could be alienated to another, D. de superf. l. lege propria, §. quod ait. And this concludes the first point, regarding which I conclude that it is not a servitude, but ownership, or at least useful dominion; and certain things are not inserted, and yet with regard to something they are included in the sale, D. de acq. her. dom. l. maritus.

† On the second point, whether access to that formula is open to the seller, or to his successor, it must be considered that sometimes one wishes to enter one’s own field through one’s own place, sometimes through another’s place, sometimes through a public road. In the first and third cases, access is lawful; and if the public road is destroyed, then the law *si locus* must be observed, §. *si*, ff. *quemad. serui. amit.* In the second case, when I wish to pass through another’s field, then either by using a servitude granted by the owner of the field, and I may do so against his will, as in ff. *de ser. urb. praed.*, l. *olim pon.*, and ff. *de vsufru.*, l. *sed si quid aedificauerit*, §. *proprietatis*; or by using ownership, and I may not, as noted there. In this question, the tenor of the agreements must be considered, for the agreement states that access is then lawful for the seller if the buyer does not purge the formula; therefore, by contrary reasoning, it is not lawful if the buyer purges it. And this is so because the said ditch was enclosed by a wall, hence the wall could not be broken, as noted by Innocentius in c. 1, *de immu. ecc.* And I hold this, because such agreements must be observed, as noted in C. *de pac. inter emp.*, l. *fina.*, and the argument from contrary reasoning in agreements has the force of an express agreement, as in ff. *de pact. dot.*, l. *inter socerum*, §. *cum inter*. Moreover, the agreement to maintain the formula was made for the benefit of both parties. For from this the buyer derives utility, because he can purge the gardens purchased. Hence this advantage cannot be taken away from him, *de aqua plu. ar.*, l. *in concedendo*. Nor can he be prevented from holding the formula purged, if such is the quality of the emphyteutic lease that he derives benefit therefrom. I, Bal. de Per.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a disposition made among sons, grandsons, daughters, and granddaughters shall be valid and firm, and may not be rescinded, whether the action for supplement is thereby excluded.
2. A statute is not understood to deprive of or diminish the right to the legitime, unless it makes specific mention of the legitime.
3. A statute may diminish the legitime. How much the legitime of children is.
casus:
CASE

In the name of Christ, Amen. The point of question, on which counsel is requested, is substantially found to be as follows. A certain citizen of the old city, named Lucius Bartolocii, having a sole legitimate and natural daughter named Catherine, married and delivered to her husband, from whom there are several children, and a certain fleshly granddaughter of his, from a deceased daughter, married, dowered, and delivered to her husband by the said Lucius, and a certain fleshly grandson of his, from his deceased daughter, as is said above, dowered and delivered to her husband, being in extremis, drew up his testament, in which, among other things, by right of institution, he left to the citizens a certain quantity, as you can see with your own eyes in the testamentary instrument itself; he instituted the said Catherine, his daughter, as his universal heir in all his goods. Which testament is transmitted to you, as it lies.

It is opposed, and it is said on behalf of the said nephews of the said deceased testator, that the said Lucius could not burden his said nephews in the due portion which falls to them, or is due to them, in the goods of the said testator by natural right, and by the Trebellianic right, or by any other right, etc.

Now it is asked, on the above matters, having seen the said testament and certain statutes of our commune, which we transmit to you, what is the law, and whether the said testament holds for the heir, from the said legacies it must be observed, or what portion is due by law to the same nephews of the said testator in his goods, and by what right, or what should be done by his heir for the preservation of his right.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

It must be premised that, although the statute states that a disposition made among sons and grandsons, and daughters and granddaughters is valid and firm, and cannot be retracted, nevertheless by these words the action for supplementing the legitime is not excluded; for this action was introduced so that testaments may be more secure and not overturned, as is stated in Codex, De inofficioso testamento, l. omnimode and l. sancimus.

† Moreover, by a statute, the right to the legitimate portion is not understood to be taken away or diminished, unless the statute makes special mention of the legitimate portion; and even then, it may diminish it in whole, but cannot take it away entirely, because the legitimate portion is as if of natural law, and cannot be entirely abolished. However, the measure, or the entire legitimate portion, is of civil law, and therefore formerly it was smaller, now it has been increased in the Authentica de triennio et semestri, § 1.

† Moreover, it may still be diminished by statute. See Dy. in c. indultum. Cf. C. de nuptiis, l. sancit. However, if the statute employs general words and not specific ones, general words are not extended to the legitime. C. de inofficioso testamento, l. si, quoniam, §. si. It supports what we hold. Ff. de transactionibus, l. de his. According to Guillaume de Cuy. Moreover, the aforementioned statute is understood as not being subject to revocation on account of a defect of solemnity or of the number of witnesses; but if a father disinherited his son, it could properly be revoked. Ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. Titia. And it supports what is noted in auth. ex causa. Having premised this

I come to the question asked, and I say that, considering the number of children, which is three, one-third of all the goods is due to them as their legitime. First, the testator’s debts, which the testator owed, must be deducted, as in § 4. Therefore, to each of the grandchildren is due one-third of one-third, that is, one-ninth part of the entire inheritance, by dividing it into nine parts. For example, if the entire patrimony of the testator, after collation in the computation of dowries, is worth nine thousand, one thousand is due to each of the grandchildren. In these one thousand, the granddaughter through the son imputes the dowry given to her, and the grandson through the daughter imputes the dowry given to his mother, as in C. de collationibus, l. illam, § final. For example, if the dowry was 500, the grandson retains those 500 without burden, l. uxor, § pater naturalis, de legatis 3, and the other 500 are supplied to him by the universal heir from the other goods of the testator. But if the dowry had been one thousand, nothing would be due to be supplied; if, however, it were more than one thousand, he would not be compelled to restore that excess in common, because it is excluded from the goods of the donor, as in l. dedit dotem, de collatione bonorum, de trebellianica. No mention need be made of the grandchildren regarding the Fideicommissum Trebellianum, because the right of the Trebellianum cannot apply to those instituted in a certain quantity where there is a universal coheir, ad legem Falcidiam, l. lex Falcidia, § unquam; ad Trebellianum, l. 1, § inde Neratius.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A substitution made by a common word is valid at all times.
2. The mother is not excluded from the succession of her son by reason of the non-claim of the fideicommissary heir, when she lived only a short time.
3. Alienated property is imputed to the legitime.
4. Renunciation in certain cases does not cause an increase to the coheirs.
5. Whether faith should be given to the instruments of a notary deported on account of his own confession.
6. Delay occurs by the thing itself in the case of a minor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

On the first point, namely whether the said substitution is pupillary or fideicommissary, adhering to the common opinion, because it was made by a common word, and because the testator did not distinguish the times, I say that it is at all times fideicommissary, as is noted in l. precibus and l. centurio, and in Inst. de pup. sub. § extraneo, especially because the mother was in the middle, although Cynus in l. precibus in the new additions, and in the gloss in qua ratione, seems to hold that it is pupillary within the time of puberty, and the text also in c. si pater de test. lib. 6. And I do not respond according to the mode, because the discourse would be prolix. Therefore, I do not depart from the common opinion, especially because the mother was not in the middle, as in the aforementioned l. precibus. On the second point, whether the right of the said substitution belongs pro rata to Peter, son and heir of Cecilia, I say that it does, not by virtue of paternal transmission, but because the testator substituted the heirs of the substituted persons, ff. de usufr. ad Treb. l. si quis Titio; ff. de verb. oblig. l. stipulatio ista § si quis ita.

† On the third point, whether the aforementioned mother is excluded from succession on account of not having requested a tutor, I say that she is not, because she is excused by the death of the son who survived, C. de leg. hær. l. sciuit amiti. For the period is one of three months, as appears from l. si debitorum de iud. joined with l. si C. de exec. rei iud. It is also proved by l. 1 ff. de iu. deli. where mention is made of one hundred days. It is also proved in the aforementioned l. sciant where mention is made of a year and c.

† On the fourth point, whether property alienated by the mother is to be imputed in the deduction of the legitime, I say that alienated property is imputed in the legitime, as in the Authentica de testibus and in the constitution ea quam, §. quam ob rem, just as in the Trebellianum, as in the Digest ad Trebellianum, l. Marcellus, §. res quae.

† On the fifth point, whether anything accrued to the said Peter from the renunciation of Angelo and Thomas, I answer that nothing accrued, because this renunciation in certain things is not a renunciation of a universal fideicommissum, but rather a special pactum de non petendo concerning certain things. Hence, since the said Angelo and Thomas are still admitted to the universal fideicommissum, which is not caducous, or quasi-caducous, it does not accrue to another, as in § pro secundo. And that it is not a universal renunciation appears from l. neminem, de leg. 2, ff. de acquisitione hereditatis; l. 1 and 2. Also, it makes in a similar case C. ad Velleianam, l. iubemus. On the sixth point, whether fruits of his share are due to Peter by reason of minority, I say that they are, from the day the inheritance was accepted by the mother, because delay occurs ipso facto for a minor, i.e., by the very fact that payment is not made to him, and this is a special favor for the minor, as in C. qui causae in interdicto restitui non est necessaria, l. in minorum; and l. Titia Seio, § usuras, de leg. 2; and noted in l. mora, ff. de usuris, etc.

† On the seventh point, whether the instrument of the said notary is valid, having seen the inquisition, confession, and sentence, as it stands, it seems to be said that it is not, because the confession brings infamy just as a sentence does, as in *l. quia* [D. 3.1.1], *de infamia*; and because a sentence of deportation has been passed, which excludes all honor, and the deported person loses all rights and is considered dead, as in *l. 1* [D. 48.22.1], *ff. de contrahenda empt.*; furthermore, because the infamy of the act seems to disqualify him from the trust of his office, *ff. de senatu* [D. 50.1.1], *l. Cassius*; *C. de susceptis* [C. 10.32.1], *l. si aliquid*. To this effect also serves what is noted in *de probat.* [D. 22.5.1], *l. iubemus*; *ff. de edendo* [D. 49.14.1], *l. si quis ex argentariis* § 1; *ff. de infamia* [D. 3.1.1], *l. 2* § *miles*. To the contrary, it is argued that in a criminal case, a confession does not have the force of a sentence, because a sentence is awaited, *ff. de custodiendo reo* [D. 48.16.1], *l. si confessus*; *de poenis* [D. 48.19.1], *l. quod ad statum*. Moreover, the objection regarding the sentence does not hold, because it does not appear by whom it was passed, hence impersonality, i.e., uncertainty of the person, vitiates the act, *de testibus* [D. 22.5.1], *l. duo sunt Titii*; *de legatis 3* [D. 35.1.1], *l. si quis servum* § *si inter duos*; *C. de constitutionibus petendis* [C. 3.31.1], *auth. si quinque*. I do not believe that full faith should be given to this instrument, because he is a sordid person to be counted among the infamous, *l. eadem* [D. 3.1.1], § *hac* [D. 3.1.1], especially in wills, in which the integrity of the proof of faith is required. Therefore, this is true, unless it is proven that he subsequently exercised the office of notary; because then the instrument is upheld, as noted in *Auth. de tabellionibus* [C. 4.19.1], *in fine*, col. in the gloss, which gloss is not found elsewhere. And note by Bartolus in the said *l. eadem*, although he did not recall the said gloss; for they excuse those ignorant of the said process, just as if it were clandestine. I, Baldo de Ubaldis of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The risk of a fortuitous event occurring before the condition is fulfilled lies with the seller; once the sale and purchase are perfected, it lies with the buyer.
2. Given the ordinance that the one who offers more shall obtain the tax farm, if in the first round of bidding something is offered, and in the second round more is offered before deliberation, and if a hailstorm supervenes, whether the one who offered more in the second round is bound to accept it, considering that in the third round of bidding, due to the hail, nothing or very little was offered.
3. The price is due when one is bound to another for mere forbearance, and has received a certain sum for that forbearance alone, even if nothing was expressly stipulated.
4. If the commune lets or sells a tax farm, whether it is bound to mere forbearance.
casus: CASE. In the name of Christ, Amen. The point is as follows: It was reformed and obtained in the council of the people of the commune of Eugubium in the month of June just past, that the tax on the collection of wine for the present year should be sold for one year, beginning from the day of the Kalends of the month of October next future, and should be put up to auction, so that it would be granted and conceded to the highest bidder. And the said reformation, obtained in the aforementioned council, the said tax was put up to auction with the condition that whoever offered more for the said tax, or promised more for the said tax, would receive from the aforementioned commune one florin. Under this condition, a certain person in the said council promised one thousand gold florins for the said tax. After the aforementioned events, a few days later, the aforementioned council was again assembled, in which the aforementioned tax was also put up to auction under the condition that whoever promised more than the aforementioned one thousand florins for the said tax would receive, for each florin, two denari of the Republic. Under this condition of two denari, many were promising, among whom a certain Orsellus Ribaldi promised, who offered more than all the others, and offered 1500 gold florins. And after this promise was made, the aforementioned council departed, and the said Orsellus was not invested with the said tax, nor was the said tax delivered or granted to him at the time of his promise, nor did it rest with him. On another day, a great hailstorm came over some parts of Eugubium and caused considerable damage to those parts, namely by devastating two [vines/areas]. And after this damage and the arrival of the said hail, the aforementioned council was again held, and in it the said tax was put up to auction under many conditions imposed, but no one offered. Now, on behalf of the commune, it is said that the said tax should be granted and delivered to the said Orsellus as the highest bidder, and that the said Orsellus is bound to pay the commune the price he promised, namely 1500 florins, in the terms declared in the aforementioned council, and to buy the aforementioned tax and to provide suitable sureties for paying the aforementioned price, notwithstanding the aforementioned damage and hailstorm, since whoever promises more for the tax of the said commune, according to the custom of the said city, is bound to buy the said tax and pay the price he promises. And this is derived from custom and from the form of the ordinances of the commune of Eugubium, and that no tax is granted to anyone unless it is put up to auction in several councils held on different days. On behalf of the said Orsellus, it is alleged that, since the hailstorm came while he was not invested with the said tax, and the said tax was damaged due to the hailstorm, while it remained in the hands of the commune, he is not bound by law to buy the said tax against his will; since the said tax is not in the same state as it was at the time of the promise made by the aforementioned Orsellus. And that the said Orsellus did not find sureties, that he greatly inflated or overvalued the aforementioned tax, and that the purchase of the said tax was not perfected. Now it is asked whether the said Orsellus, due to the said damage, can withdraw from the aforementioned promise by law, or not; and whether he must buy the said tax against his will and pay the price he promised, or not; and if, and to what extent, he cannot withdraw from the said promise and is bound to buy the said tax notwithstanding the said damage and hailstorm, whether compensation should be made to him by the commune, and how, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having premised two rules, the first of which is,

† The first rule is that the risk occurring before the condition is fulfilled is that of the seller. The second rule is that the risk occurring after the sale and purchase are perfected is that of the buyer, whether he buys a certain thing or an uncertain hope, as stated in the law *necessario*, On the risk and burden of the thing sold, and in the Code, in the same title, law 2. And the aforementioned other rule is that there, in the future perception not yet made, damage occurs by divine judgment, as when hail comes in a contract of lease, there is remission, as noted in the Code, On lease, law *damnum* in the first section.

† First, it must be seen what kind of contract this is, whether lease and hire, or sale. Second, whether it is a perfect contract under a tacit pact of addition for a day, or rather imperfect: and whether this first promise, before the establishment, is a certain future undertaking by the seller: which, if it were a contract, would not be in the species of a perfect sale: these are the doubts. Also, another doubt is whether a distinction should be made between usual and unusual hail, as in l. fistulas, §. frumenta, de contrah. empt. And I say that this contract seems from one side perfect, immediately made upon the promise, because there precedes an interrogation, if anyone promises, and follows a response. Hence it is properly not a bare undertaking, but rather a certain stipulation. On the contrary, let there be an interrogation, therefore a promise, and follows a response. Hence it is properly not a bare undertaking, but rather a certain stipulation. On the contrary, let there be a general and uncertain interrogation: afterwards the respondent is from a special and certain person, when anyone says if this is a stipulation: therefore there is obligation on both sides. I answer that, by the nature of obligation, it is that the promisor is bound, not the stipulator. I say that here both are bound, but in different ways: for the promisor is bound precisely, but the fisc is not bound so precisely, because it can add to another offering a better condition. But if another offers, the promisor is bound to add, C. de fi. instr. and iure hastę fis. l. si tempora. I concede, however, that this contract is a preamble to a future sale to be made purely and fully, because so it is agreed between the parties. For in the auction are placed words of the future time, e.g., whoever however shall promise, hence it shall be sold. Hence it does not seem immediately that a sale is made, but to be made, C. de contrah. emp. l. sed in emendis. there in the gloss. It makes what we note, ff. de pet. hęr. l. in extima. Against this opinion, Bartolus thinks in l. licitatio, in prin., ff. de pub. and by the same, Baldus in cons. 404. Others say that immediately a purchase is made, although afterwards it is reduced to writing. Which does not please, rather it is a certain preparatory thing, from which, the principal contract having followed, no action lies, because it is confused in the principal, arg. ff. iudic. sol. l. cum quaerebatur. de ac. emp. l. exempto. §. si is, qui vina. From this, because the obligation is perfect, it seems to be the loss of the promisor, but on the contrary it seems, because the purchase is imperfect, it seems to be the loss of the seller: moreover, this contract is sometimes called a lease, although it is called a sale. That it is more properly a lease, thus I prove, because the dominion of the principal thing remains with the seller; therefore it is properly not a sale, ff. de contrahen. emp. l. cum manu sata. §. pe. sicut. n. From a corporeal thing, for example from a fund, fruits are perceived, so from an incorporeal thing, for example from the right of collecting a toll, an annual, or monthly, or daily fruit is perceived. Since therefore this right is not alienated, nor separated from the fisc, but granted to another for a time, this contract is properly called a lease: and thus where it is called a sale, because fruits can be sold, I say that with respect to the fruits it is called a sale, with respect to the principal right it is a lease: and when loss emerges, it concerns the thing itself, and the owner: therefore the loss ought to be the owner's, not the promisor's. They prove this, ff. de pub. l. quotem. §. qui maximos. and l. Cęsar. ff. loc. l. quem fideiussor. ff. de iu. do. l. si vsus fruc. there, let him sell, or let him lease, etc. ff. lo. l. 1. insti. locati. §. adeo. de bo. auth. iud. pos. l. in venditione. C. de vec. l. si quis. and l. si. C. loc. l. si cum hermes. cum si. Perhaps it could be distinguished, whether by reason of hail the injury is beyond half the just price, then the promisor is not compelled to fulfill the contract, otherwise yes, l. domum. de contrah. emp. But there, at the time of the contract, the form of this thing was not changed, for the law seems express that fruits sold, the peril of hail is the buyer's, unless another pact has been made, d. §. frumenta. Also unless something is bought in genus, not from a certain body: I will see. n. As if it were a gamble, as l. si iactum retis. But to that law it can be answered that in another, and in the casting of the net, the peril does not adhere to the thing of the seller, but is outside the thing, here however it is intrinsic to the thing itself, because it is worse, in which less is perceived: just as less is the peculium which has accrued, yet that hope seems bought, makes extra de vsuc. c. nauiganti. ar. ff. loca. l. opus. de nau. fęn. l. periculi. This question is very doubtful, and the reasons are for and against.

† Finally, however, I state that sometimes one is bound to another only to passive tolerance (patientia), and for such tolerance alone receives a certain sum; and then, even if nothing is actually received, the price is still due. Hence, if I sell to someone a servitude, say, of an aqueduct for one or more years, although the water is not conducted due to drought, the price is owed, because it suffices that the seller provides only passive tolerance. See *De servitutibus*, l. *Quoties*. But sometimes one is bound to another regarding a servitude to make some positive performance; then, if he does not perform, he does not act [or: the action does not lie]. See *De contrahenda emptione*, l. *Si debitor*, § *Verisimile*. And this is true when the performance is commensurate, or commensurable, with the price. But if it is not commensurable, as in the casting of a net, then, even if nothing is caught, the price is owed, as if for the labor and industry of casting the net, not for the thing itself, provided a promise was made, as in l. *Nec emptio*, *De contrahenda emptione*. For the price is promised, or the wage is mixed with tolerance and performance, because the lessor is bound to tolerance, namely, to suffer the tenant to collect; and while the tenant collects, he becomes the owner of the fruits, because the owner is deemed to deliver the fruits to him. See *De furtis*, l. *Si servus*, § *Locavi*. And thus, fictitiously, there intervenes a performance of fruits for money, because tolerance is the place of delivery. See l. *Quaedam mulier*, *De re vendicata*, and l. *Minus instructus*, *De aqua pluviae arcendae*. If, therefore, this quasi-delivery cannot take place due to divine judgment or some other fortuitous event, a remission is rightly made at the discretion of a good man. I do not give force to the species of contract, whether a true or fictitious future performance arises from it, for the law is written, and in a contract other than lease, as is read and noted in l. *Excepto*, § *Locati*.

† Now it must be considered whether one who sells or leases a tax farm is bound to mere passive tolerance by the commune, or whether what is received from the payer is first paid to the commune and then transferred by the commune to the buyer: which I believe to be true, arg. ff. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem and l. profectitia de iure dotis and l. si singularia ff. si certum petatur and d. §. locavi. Hence, for this contract there is not only mere passive tolerance, but a certain bare and fictitious performance: which, if severed by accident, the price too ought to be severed, if sterility has arisen by chance. C. locatio conductio l. licet. arg. in a similar case ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus l. Plautius. where it is said that when the benefit is severed, the burden is also severed. And this is supported by natural equity: therefore the buyer is not compelled to complete the contract, unless account is taken of the diminution, if the diminution, or damage from hail, has exceeded a tolerable limit. Bartolus, however, holds that no diminution is made: but his opinion is too rigorous, and contrary to equity, which the nature of the contract desires: and especially where the purchase is in fieri, and not in facto esse, as is in our case. I conclude that this promisor is not compelled, unless the price is diminished at the discretion of a good man.

CASE. Rubric of the statute l. That the notaries of the college, namely the consuls, may make a comparison of letters. Wherefore, since sometimes the notaries of the city of Castello, its county, and district, as inhabitants thereof, having been prevented by death, or some other cause, do not write their rogita and protocols in the quaternions of their rogita and protocols, whether extended or not extended, but in certain sheets, papers, or some other quaternions, which results in no small damage to private persons, we have statuted and ordained that the aforementioned rogita, protocols, and writings made in the quaternions of the deceased notaries, not being placed, upon comparison of those rogita in the quaternions of the aforementioned notaries not written, or of those writings to the writings of the rogita in the quaternions of the deceased notaries written by all, or at least three, of the consuls of the notaries of the city of Castello, and declaring them to be of the hand of the aforementioned deceased notary, ought to be reduced to public and formal shape, and authenticated by a notary appointed, or to be appointed, for publishing or authenticating the rogita and writings of the deceased notaries, to whom full faith ought to be given as to the public authenticity of the present statute.

In the name of Christ Amen. A certain Jacopo, wishing to make a testament, employed a notary, who was to be requested for this. It appears that the said notary wrote in a certain folio the testament of the said Jacopo, which, however, does not appear public because the subscription and sign of the said notary, who is deceased, are lacking. A certain Francesco, who claimed the benefit of the said testament, sued the daughters of the said Jacopo and their mother and guardian, and because the aforementioned writing was not authentic, he had it done by the consuls of the college of notaries by comparison of letters from the letters of the said folio, but not from other authentic writings of the same notary, and wishing to prove that the testament had been made by the said Jacopo, he made one production thus: that the said Jacopo made a testament in his last will written by the hand of such a notary, and the said wife, responding to the said position, denied it. Finally, the inheritance of the said Jacopo came to the said Francesco by another right, and the said wife, in her own name, sues the said Francesco by virtue of the said testament. It is asked, whether the said writing is valid as a testament: and it is asked, whether the said guardian, suing in her own name as perjured, ought to be repelled from her intention, having seen the statute set forth above, that the notaries of the college, etc. Furthermore, it is asked, if she is not repelled as perjured, whether she is repelled from the usufruct which she says is due to her, because she sold part of the goods in which she says she has a usufruct, or whether she loses only the usufruct of the thing sold by her. Furthermore, counsel is requested to be given on another point, which is this: the said Francesco sold a certain house of his for a certain price, now he says he was deceived in the aforementioned sale by more than half the just price, and now he sues for rescission of the said contract. It is opposed to him that he cannot sue, the words of the said contract and the statute of guarantee of the said city standing in the way. Now it is asked, whether the words of the contract and the statute of guarantee stand in the way, having seen the said contract and the aforementioned statute, or not.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that notarial documents of deceased notaries are to be given credence upon comparison of the handwriting by the consuls, if the document is found without a subscription and seal, does it have the force of a will after such comparison has been made?
2. Whether variation and the allegation of contradictory positions are admissible in different lawsuits.
3. Whether a perjurer is to be heard.
4. A seller of part of his property, in which he holds a usufruct, prejudices himself as to the usufruct of the part sold.
5. The benefit of L. 2, C. de rescindenda venditione is not granted to a seller who has knowledge.
6. Credence is given to an instrument stating that something was done with certain knowledge and not by mistake.
body: In the name of Christ. Amen. On the first point, whether the said writing is valid as a testament,

I say that if a comparison of the letters was made by the consuls of the college, and their declaration was given according to the form of the said statute, the said writing ought to have been, and ought to be, reduced to public form. And from now on, it makes the same point as C. de testi., l. publicati; and Extra, de fide instrumentorum, c. cum P. The statutes and customs of places in such matters ought to be observed, as C. quemadmodum testamenta aperiantur, l. 2; and Extra, de fide instrumentorum, c. cum dilectus, § 1.

† On the second point, I say that in various lawsuits variation and the allegation of contradictory positions are admitted, as in D. 38.2.1 (Aurelius), § si etiam si sint contraria, even if they are incompatible; how much more so when it has connection with the first case. He denied that a guardian acting in her own name harms herself, so that she may assert the contrary in a second lawsuit concerning what she stated in the first, as in D. 29.6.1 (filius). And see the argument from D. 44.2.1 (ia, qui haeres non erat), § si, and what is not permitted according to D. 44.2.1 (modestinus).

† On the third point, whether a perjurer should be heard, I say that he should, because that is an oath of calumny, from which neither an action nor an exception arises. And that a perjurer should be heard in another case is noted in D. de iureiurando, l. alias. And it is proven in C. de non numerata pecunia, auth. contra quod propriam. And see the argument in D. de minoribus, l. Papinianus exul.

† On the fourth point, I say that the sale prejudices the usufruct of the part sold, not of the other part, D. de pactis, l. sed si unus, § ante omnia; C. ad Velleianam, l. iubemus; de his qui ut indigni, l. rescriptum.

† On the fifth point, I say that the vendor cannot bring an action on the ground of deception for two reasons: first, on account of knowledge, for the benefit of l. 2 C. de rescindenda venditione is not granted to one who has knowledge, eo. tit. l. si voluntas.

† Secondly, the donation was not made by mistake. For it is believed from the instrument that it was made with certain knowledge and not by mistake, according to C. de prob. l. cum precibus. And thus that law 2. argu. ff. si quis cau. l. sed et si quis. §. fi. ceases to apply. I, Baldus de Peru.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A woman ought to be restored to the possession of her dowry, or of the dotal property, when the possession has come to another in a vitious manner.
2. Title does not excuse an unjust possessor who, from the beginning, had knowledge that the thing was alien.
3. Proof, and how an exemplification are to be made.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† In the case of the lady Prima against Agnolellus, it appears that the said Prima ought to be restored to possession of her dowry, or of the dotal property. And this is proven thus: because possession of the dotal property came to the said Agnolellus vitiously, with fraud and bad faith, since he knew the thing to be dotal, as is proven by his own confessions. For dotal property cannot be alienated, as is stated in C. de iure dotis, l. si praedium; and in C. de rei uxoriae actione, l. 1, §. et cum lex.
