Since therefore he began to possess with defect and bad faith, he is bound to relinquish possession, according to c. reintegranda; c. saepe, de restitutione spoliatorum; and notably C. de agris et censibus, l. si coloni; and l. ideo, §. Neratius, de condictione furtiva. For according to the canonists, it is the same whether possession comes with defect or with fraud, d. c. saepe, according to Innocentius. And he is in fraud who knowingly purchases a prohibited thing, C. de agris et censibus, l. quemadmodum, lib. 11.

† and the title does not excuse a possessor in bad faith, who from the beginning had knowledge that the thing was another’s. Likewise, it has not been proven by means of the fruits received that there is a title, since the instrument is so uncertain,

† That it is not established with certainty who the person is or what the specific place is, as argued in the Digest, *de iure fisci*, law *ita fideicommissum*. Moreover, proof is not made by means of an exemplification, unless two conditions are present in the exemplification: that the party has been cited, and that the judge interposes a decree, as noted in the Code, *de edendo*, authentic *si quis in aliquo*. Nevertheless, even though the title was proven, it is not regarded as a title, as in the law *si in emptione*, section *item si emptor*, *de contrahenda emptione*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Those who possess jurisdiction, who may grant statutes, and from what causes.
2. Whether a statute of laymen, by which the benefit of the Church is taken away and the benefit of laymen is increased, is said to be against the liberty of the Church.
body: That the aforementioned statute is valid appears, first, from the standpoint of those who enacted it; second, from the standpoint of those upon whom the burden of the twelfth is imposed; third, from the reason and purpose of the statute; fourth, from the natural rule of ordered charity; fifth, as if by way of the cases of the laws.

† From the first, it is argued thus: the commune of Spoleto has temporal jurisdiction, which it exercises, as is supposed in the point at issue; by reason of its jurisdiction, it can make statutes, as stated in the law *Omnes populi*. Also, by a good consequence: a city has jurisdiction; therefore, it can make statutes. For making statutes is an act of the power to legislate, as is clear from the definition of jurisdiction given for the cause, and also in law 1, Code, *De iurisdictione omnium iudicum*. From the second, it is argued: a statute binds inferiors; thus, subjects are bound to obey the law of their superior, law 1 and 3, Digest, *De legibus*; law *Finis*, Digest, *De decretis ab ordinario factis*; and Code, *De constitutionibus principum*, law 2, in the end. Therefore, since this right is general, it must be observed in all places; for from the difference of places, etc., and thus jurists give reasons for almost every praetorian edict, but the best reason is that provisions not be exported, lest the price of grain rise, so that frauds may be prevented. These reasons are probable and necessary, since they are written in the law, as is added, which is noted in Code, *De aedificiis privatis*, law *Si quis post*; Code, *De naufragiis*, law *Cum proponas*; Code, *Quae res exportari non debeant*, law 2; Code, *De minis*, law 1; Digest, *Ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis*, law 3, with the following. For public and private reason urges that frauds be prevented, Digest, *De iure publico*, law *Si liberius*. And a contract made in fraud of a ward is condemned, Code, *Quae res vendi non possunt*, law *Nonnunquam*. From the fourth, it is argued: just as on account of speciality one can, nay, is bound by the ordinance of charity, to look more to oneself and one’s necessities; for many burdens are supposed to fall on the commune, which cannot be discharged without money, Code, *De vectigalibus et commissis*, law *Finis*. Hence, if the commune makes a law for obtaining greater revenues from the purses of laymen, although the revenues of the bishop are diminished accidentally, it ought not for that reason to be called an unjust law, which is simultaneously fostered by charity and natural reason, as in Code, *De servis et aqua*, law *Praeses*, and there noted. For the commune does not insert its sickle into another’s harvest, but only into its own subjects, upon whom it can impose a collection and a tax, Digest, *De mutationibus et huiusmodi*, law *Rescripto*, § *Finis*. For from the fact that the commune of Spoleto does not have its own mills, it could impose a burden on those willing, Code, *De vectigalibus et commissis*, law *Si omnium rerum*, and law *Ex praestatione*, and law *Vectigalia*. For just as the King of Hungary could have free governance, and what is done by the commune of Spoleto with his permission seems to be done by his authority, Code, *De postulatione hereditatis*, law *Si filius*, and law 6, Digest, *De acquirenda hereditate*, and Code, *De veteribus iuribus enucleandis*, and law 1, § *Omnia*. From the fifth, it is argued thus: it is the same to do something in my place, as in my subjects, arguing from place to persons, which argument is lawful. These are similar: place, time, and person, and often one infers from one to another by argument, as in law *Unum*, Digest, *Si certum petatur*; *De vulgaribus substitutionibus*, law *Qui plures*; *De militum testamentis*, law *Miles ita*, § *Et quia*. But it is most certain that in my place I can do what I wish principally, so that I may profit myself, although it may harm others consequently, as in Digest, *De damno infecto*, law *Proculus*. But if it would not profit me, and would harm others, I cannot do it, Digest, *De aqua pluviali arcenda*, law 2, § *Inde Neratius*. Therefore, what is true of place is also true of person.

† so that the city may promulgate a law useful to its republic: it is permitted. Even if its revenues are thereby diminished more or less, it is bound to the bishop by no obligation to preserve the revenues due to him: but only by a certain general equity, which ordered charity concludes. And it is established in D. si quis omissa causa testamenti, l. quia autem, §. si patronus, in the reason of itself. Thus the city could indirectly derogate from the archbishop’s entrance fees (introitus) by admitting those going to the city mill; for example, where the archbishop causes the twelfth part to be taken, they would cause the twentieth part to be taken. For although a premium would be offered to those coming, it is not said to be done to the injury of another, but for one’s own advantage, arg. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Titio centum, §. 1. And the same could the lord archbishop do to his temporal subjects: even if it derogated from the city’s entrance fees. And one ought not to demand in something what, on the contrary, would not have been demanded as a right against oneself, as in C. de rescissis venditionibus, l. ratas. And thus I hold, that the said statute is valid, and those coming to the mill ought to pay 12 to the commune, even if by this men go to the mills of the commune, and not to the mills of the archbishopric. But against this it is objected, and truly, that the said statute is not valid by c. eos qui, de immunitate ecclesiarum, lib. 6, where it seems expressly stated. But I answer, that I induce the reason of that chapter for myself; the reason of that chapter is, when such fraud is presumed from the book of the church of the one asking. Hence, whether it be explained with ‘cum’ for ‘when’, or by ‘because’: where another reason ceases, the said rule ceases, as in l. adigere, §. quis, de iure patronatus. But in our case the reason for presuming fraud ceases, because, as has been said, he does not seem to commit fraud who loves himself more than another, or who intends to repel the fraud of another, D. de legibus, l. cum pater, §. Titio. And here is the distinction: either the statute is directly prohibitory, that no one go to the mills of the church, and it is not valid, d. c. eos, because it thrusts the sickle of prohibition into another’s harvest. And thus speaks d. c. eos. But the statute tends to this by a certain consequence, and then it matters whether the antecedent is licit and permitted, and it draws the consequent to itself, and the penalty of that c. eos ceases, arg. D. de libellis, l. si is, qui duos; D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. Seyus et Augerius. And thus it is in our case. Or the antecedent is not licit, for example in some case in which the public would not perceive advantage, and the church would perceive detriment; then such a statute would not be valid, because it would be odious and illicit, arg. D. quarum rerum actio non datur, l. 1, §. quae honorandae; and d. §. variis; and D. de doli exceptione, l. 1, in fine. But in our case the statute seems to have been made in good faith for the good of the city, which is equal to the good of the churches, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. 1. And although in acquired rights laymen cannot derogate by any device from the church or the rights of churches, as in c. ex Ecclesia S. Mariae, de constitutionibus; nevertheless in rights to be acquired, if laymen do not do this by evil device, but simply by good faith, so that they may profit themselves, not principally so as to harm others, it seems that this may be done. Moreover, the twelfth part due to the archbishop is due by work, and is in a condition; if he has made this condition in his mill, that the commune does not exist, he can impede it, if it is in the interest of the commune, as is in our case, D. de conditionibus ob causam, l. 3, §. quamquam. And where a premium or advantage is proposed to two, one can preempt it, if it is due alternatively, as in runners for a prize, as noted in D. de verbis obligatorum, l. executus, §. 1. And because the commune is not subject to the archbishop in temporals, he cannot forbid the exercise of his temporals over his subjects, arg. 11. q. 1, c. de opera; and D. de deposito, l. bona fides; and arg. D. de solutionibus, l. si stipulatus, §. si tamen. And if it be said, what justice is this: for justice gives to each his right, this does not render his right to the archbishop. I answer: rather, because he has no more right than has been stated; for by consequence sometimes the right of another is derogated, D. quod vi aut clam, l. si aliis, §. est et alia. Again, if it be objected from auth. cassa, and d. c. noverit, de sententia excommunicationis, or from c. non minus, de immunitate ecclesiarum, in which it is said that statutes against the liberty or rights of the church directly or indirectly are not valid, to which also contributes c. statutum, de haereticis, lib. 6. I answer, as I answered above, because in our case the principal right of the twelfth part of the city through its subjects is valid; although the church is injured by a certain consequence, because men do not wish to go to the mill of the church, lest they pay another twelfth part to the millers of the Church. Again, if it be objected that this is against ancient custom, by which men went here or there to the mill, and are not impeded, which ought not to be done, as in l. si quisquam, de diversis et temporibus praescriptionibus; and l. venditor, contra praedicta; and D. de usucapione, l. 1. I answer, this custom ought not to be said to be prescribed. This, because it pertains to a natural faculty, which is not prescribed, D. de malo publico, l. viam publicam. If anyone should say it is not permitted, let him beware of this law: l. haberi. By the same reason it is said that it is not permitted for the city to have a mill, because by this the revenue of the church is impeded, which it would receive more if the church alone had mills, which nevertheless no one of sound mind would say, D. de fluminibus, l. quominus. And if it be said, this statute is most bad, that what is due to the church is paid to the city. I answer, that which is not demanded is not due. And if it be said that the commune draws all the water to its mill, and dries up the water, l. redditum ecclesiae. I answer, this water arises in its own source, i.e., from its subjects, and from their purse. Hence it is lawful to draw it all, from l. praeses. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an instituted heir who contests the will is excluded from the inheritance.
2. Whether one may bring an action or controversy arising from the contract itself, in cases where contracts are prohibited from giving rise to litigation or dispute.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be said in law that the said heir is not excluded from the said inheritance, although he brought suit against Blandinus; because, since he obtained judgment, he appears to have brought the suit justly; for it is always presumed that he who prevails by judgment upholds justice, as in C. de iud. l. remnouam; §. si, de euic. l. Herennius; §. Gaya, extra de renun. c. in presentia. This victory had its cause after the death of the testator; because the legatee did not accept the guardianship, de excu. tu. l. sed hic nimium. Hence the testator does not appear to have considered the supervening cause, as in ff. de confir. tu. l. utilitatem. For a prohibitory disposition of the testator is not extended to new cases, ff. de ann. leg. l. liberto; §. largius cum prauus. For such a controversy arises from the mind of the testator, whence the testator does not appear to have prohibited it, since he tacitly established it, arg.

† That one who is prohibited in contracts from raising a lawsuit or controversy may raise a controversy arising from the contract itself, On the True Meaning of Words, l. venditores. Hence, he who does not observe a testament by failing to fulfill the imposed burden ought not to hope for benefit from the testament; and if he demands it illicitly, therefore defense is lawful, and it holds that one may lawfully resist another, and no penalty is incurred, On the True Meaning of Words, l. in executione, §. si; to the Law of Falcidia, l. Seyus, and Augerius; and D. loc. l. quaero, §. inter locatorem; to this effect D. de rescindenda venditione, l. si; C. de non numerata pecunia, l. si; nor is he said to be offended who deserved to be offended, On the True Meaning of Words, l. qui servus. It appears, and whatever the point of law was before sentence, whether the said legacy is due or not, as in l. Nesennius and l. ab Anastasio; nevertheless, since sentence has been passed, it is deemed as if for it, and it must be adhered to, since it has passed into an irrevocable effect, as in Trebellian, l. debitor, §. si; D. de rei venditione, l. ex diverso, §. 1. And therefore I conclude, since the cause of the testator repels the cause of the intestate, C. communi de usucapione, l. antequam, the said heirs, because they have not become heirs by condition, are called to succession by the testament, and the mother is entirely repelled; nor do these heirs seem to have merited succession because they are tutors, and because they are brothers; therefore, although the tutorship is neglected, they are nevertheless heirs of the testator, D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. tutor petitus, §. 1. And thus, notwithstanding, D. l. 1, in fine, D. ubi pupillus educari debet, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A substitution in which words of this kind are placed, "if he should die without sons and children," is considered, both in law and in fact, to be a fideicommissary substitution.
2. Grandmothers and sisters succeed in the male line: a sister succeeds intestate. And a grandmother, if they neglected to request a guardian within a year, is repelled.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It must be stated that the aforementioned substitutions are fiduciary and oblique, not direct: because the words are more suited to a fiduciary substitution than to a direct one, as noted in l. precibus, l. centurio, and Inst. de pupillari substitutione § extraneo. For where the clause “if he should die without sons and children” is appended, it appears that, both in law and in fact, a fiduciary substitution has been made, since the testator did not specify a time limit; and this is the common opinion of all, although some hold the contrary by virtue of c. Si pater, de testibus, lib. 6, and by the gloss in Inst. de pupillari substitutione § qua ratione. But the first opinion is the common one and the one followed in judicial practice. Secondly, it must be noted that the substitution made by the testator with respect to the person of Iouaccimus has expired, because Iouaccimus died while his son Jacobus, a male child, was still alive; and thus the condition has failed, as stated in de hæredibus instituendis, l. Lucius, de institutione et substitutione, l. generaliter, and the preceding law; and de fideicommissis, l. cum acutissimi, de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. cum auus, ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. hæredes mei § cum ita.

Thirdly, it is noted that the aforementioned Jacopo, dying intestate, is succeeded by his grandmothers and his sisters per stirpes, as stated in the Authentico *Defuncto*, cited by Cynus and others. Moreover, the grandfathers cannot be charged with the neglect of not having requested a tutor, because Jacopo died within a few days. Indeed, the grandmothers are not charged with such neglect if they did not precede the request for a tutor with precipitous haste, as held in the Digest, *Ad Tertullianam*, law 1, § *Si mater*, and § *Confestim* at the end.

Fourthly, it is noted that the substitution in the person of Jacopo takes effect by the law of fideicommissum; therefore, the aforementioned grandmothers and sisters are bound by the law of fideicommissum to restore to the substitute the inheritance of Jacopo, and the particular legacies, after deducting the legitimate portion, because the burden of the fideicommissum did not attach to that portion. See the Code, *De inofficiosis testamentis*, law *Ex tribus*, and law *Qui in prioribus*; and the Digest, *Ad Trebellianam et Falcidiam*. There is doubt on this point, but I believe that if the testator did not expressly prohibit the deduction, as in the chapter *Raynerius*, *De testibus*, book 6, nor does it matter that he said "in the entire residue," because this is understood tacitly, according to law *Titia*, *Ad legem Falcidiam*. It would be otherwise if he had said "I forbid" or "I prohibit the deduction," because this is not understood tacitly. And thus speaks the Authentico *Sed cum testator*. The same applies if he had said "the whole without any diminution," because then these words, "without any diminution," are prohibitory words and must have some effect; and the prohibition causes the Falcidian and Trebellian fractions to cease, according to the common opinion. Others say the same in both cases, because the testator appears to prohibit, which can sufficiently be said through the gloss *Ordinaria*, which is found in law 10, *De fideicommissis libertatis*, a gloss not found elsewhere.

Fifthly, it must be known that the sister succeeded the girl dying last intestate, not the grandmothers, who are repelled because they neglected to request a tutor for the underage girl for a year; but, after deducting the legitimate portion due to the girl, the remainder is owed to the substitutes. And thus, only the legitimate portion is at issue, not the Falcidian or Trebellian fraction, which is not owed to a legatee or to one instituted in a certain thing or quantity, as held in the Digest, *Ad legem Falcidiam*, law *Lex Falcidia*, § *Nunquam*; and *Ad Trebellianam*, law 1, § *Inde Neratius*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Regarding the procedure when it does not appear, and what is presumed and what is not in trials or judgments: a judgment is not presumed.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Nor is a sentence presumed, unless the proceedings appear, as noted by Innocentius, De officio, De legibus, c. Cum in iure; De probationibus, c. Quam contra falsam; De eo qui fuisset ordinem suscepit, c. Innotuit. And therefore he who seeks to have a sentence executed, if the proceedings are denied, must produce the proceedings. Hence, the words of Innocentius are well considered, three things are to be weighed: either because they come by way of the foundation of jurisdiction, such as delegations and subdelegations, and these, if denied, must be proved by him who asserts them; some come by way of the foundation of the judgment itself, such as the libel, or the price of the contestation of terms, the assignment of terms, the citation of the party: and if these are lacking, they render the judgment null, and they are not presumed, unless they are proved, because they are of fact, and this in contemptuous jurisdiction. C. De arbitris, l. Ne in arbitris, § 1. Some come by way of justice, and these are presumed, such as that the sentence is equitable, this is presumed, unless it has been appealed, as noted, ff. De evictione, l. Nerennius, § Gaya; De renunciatione, c. In presentia. Also, if it has emanated, it is presumed to be held in Italy, unless it is established that the pronouncement was duly made, ff. De re iudicata, l. Si cum nulla. And therefore the judge should not execute it, for by his office he ought not to execute that which is null, as noted, C. De transactione, l. Ubi pactum. I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a city can abolish the jurisdiction of a castle subject to it, and by counsel; that the right to demand passage tolls cannot be abolished by purchase, by ancient prescription, and by custom, except by
2. the Pope.
3. Whether a donation made by the syndic of a castle of the castle itself is valid.
4. The clause that there be as many donations as there are things.
5. A defective instrument, with the passage of much time, having observed those things contained in the instrument, fully proves, and in many similar cases.
6. The Emperor cannot grant any right in the lands of the Church.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the first point, let us first consider, for those things which are done for the commune of Eugubium, and first it is done, that the Castle of Pergola was said to be in the commune of Eugubium, and thus it seems that it can prohibit there that a toll be exacted. Secondly, it is done for the said commune the donation, which the syndic of this Castle of Pergola made to the commune of Eugubium, granting the Castle and all rights situated. Thirdly, it is done, that to the said commune of Eugubium the declaration last made by the said four men of Eugubium, of which mention is made above. On the contrary, for the part of the commune of the Castle of Pergola it is done,

† because he has the right to demand passage both from the purchase made, from those to whom it was due, and from ancient prescription and custom, the memory of which does not exist, as is proposed in the case. And thus it cannot be taken away from him by any superior below the Pope. The case is found in the words of the sign, c. super quibusdam, § 1. And thus the first allegation does not stand, assuming that the Castle of Pergula belonged to the community of Eugubium.

† Notwithstanding. The donation made by the syndic of the community of Pergola to Eugene. For in said donation there was no intervention of the consent or decree of the Rector of the Province, nor did the individual inhabitants of said Castle separately express their will regarding the aforementioned donation; and thus said donation was null, as C. ne re. d. l. si. in fi. lib. 10. Likewise, the aforementioned donation exceeded the sum of 500 gold florins and was not insinuated, and thus it is null, as l. sancimus. C. de do.

† Nor does it matter that in the aforementioned instrument it is stated that there are as many donations as there are things. Those added words appear to be in fraud of the law, as noted in the Speculum, De donationibus, § 1, at the words "quid si aliquis." This is proven to be true by the law *Quemadmodum*, Codex, De agris et censibus, Book 11, where a similar fraud is posited. Moreover, if one carefully examines the law *Sancimus*, § *Si quis autem*, Codex, De donationibus, in the text and gloss, it is established that for a single donation to be said to exist and require insinuation, only this is considered here: whether it was made at one time or at different times; even if, at the time of the donation, several things are named, or several prestations are to be made, as in the same § *Si quis autem*. And § *Sequenti*. The declaration made by the said four men does not stand in the way, because they had no authority, as is evident from the narration. Regarding the second point, which is claimed for the Commune of Gubbio, that the said Commune of Pergola shall bear the expenses of the stipendiaries for the Commune of Gubbio, the laws cited above support this. Furthermore, the penalty attached to the said contract supports this, because the Castle was built, and especially in that it promised that the Castle of Pergola would provide horses to the said Commune of Gubbio, as contained in the said instrument. To the contrary, for the said Commune of the Castle of Pergola, the words of the said instrument are effective, which state that the men of that rebellious Castle of Pergola shall observe the precepts of the Commune of Gubbio, except in taxes and levies, to which they ought not contribute more than six denarii per hearth, in which it is expressly stated that they are not bound to contribute to the said expenses. I admit, however, that when the Commune of Gubbio is in need of horsemen, it may denounce to the said Castle that it must provide horses and horsemen, and they are bound to do so in such manner as a good man would judge. But if the Commune of Gubbio raises horsemen from its own resources, and afterwards requires the Commune of Pergola to contribute to the expenses, it cannot do so, just as a patron cannot demand the valuation of services from a freedman, except in the cases provided in the Codex, De operis libertorum, law 1, with its sequel. Nor does the foregoing stand in the way of the above,

† that the aforementioned instrument of the said parties is not found to be authentic, nor solemnly exemplified, nor even an instrument of syndicate: for the said instrument is so defective, given the passage of such a long time, as is expressed in s., and the observance of the aforementioned matters during the said time, as has been fully proven, as in D. de usu, l. cum de in rem verso; no. D. de serv. l. si servitus rusticorum; and no. D. de aqua pluv. arc. l. 1, §. si. Just as if a son held an inheritance devolved upon him, it is long presumed that the father’s command preceded and that acceptance followed, as in D. de acq. haer. l. qui alienam, ver. non adierit; and C. de pet. haer. l. si filius. Moreover, an invalid emancipation is considered valid with the passage of time, as in D. de adop. l. post mortem; C. de pat. pot. l. 1, and there no. 1. An invalid testament operates with the passage of time to effect what it would not otherwise effect, as in C. de test. l. sancimus. Furthermore, from the fact that they stood thus for so long, and that the commune of Eugubium and the commune of Pergula jointly performed many things together, it is presumed that a remission was made, as in D. de prob. l. pericula. Moreover, that example which we give, that it is a private writing, will prove with other supporting evidence, as in C. de prob. l. instrumenta, and per ibi no. And our question serves the aforementioned matters optimally, per gl. C. communi div. l. penult. Furthermore, such an instrument, although invalid, operates so that it appears that the commune of Pergula stood during the said time in the said manner by the right of its own liberty, which suffices for prescription, as in D. de itin. actuque priv. l. 1, §. 1, in the gloss beginning iure servitus; and what is noted by Cy. C. de serv. et aqua, l. 1, in 4. q. And for this part there is an express text, C. de fun. pa. l. si, lib. 11, near the end, where someone alleged a concession made to him of a reduction of the canon, and there was doubt about this: but if possession of 40 years is proven, it suffices. Since therefore it has been legitimately proven that those who were outside the territory came to dwell in the Castle of Pergula under such a pact and such an agreement, faith must be kept with them; the case is D. de iure immut. l. 2, in princ. And from these things it appears that a response is given to what is said concerning the said penalties entered into first, s., in the foundation of the said Castle. Also, a response appears to what is said, that it is in the territory of the city of Eugubium, because they come into the said territory with the said pact, and they are not bound to the said burdens. Also, a response appears to what is said concerning the donation made to the commune of Eugubium, because that did not hold, as has been said. Also, concerning what s. says, that the commune of Pergula had at some time participated in the expenses of the commune of Eugubium, this does not hinder, for it is presupposed that the commune of the Castle of Pergula had already been for so long in the said liberty, such that prescription or custom had been induced and completed, and thus the said right is not taken away by one subsequent act, as in l. nemo, quae temporales, D. de re iud. and there no. per gl. and Io. And. extra de consuet. c. cum tanto. Moreover, since the said commune of Pergula participated in the said burdens for the state of pronouncement, it did not do this on account of a right owed to the commune of Eugubium, as is clear from what has been supposed above. And thus from these things the commune of Eugubium can say nothing, as in l. 1, §. 1, D. de itin. actuque priv. and de postul. c. bonae.

Concerning the third point, it helps for the commune of Eugubium, as its allegation is, s., that the Castle is in the community, that the aforementioned donation was made, and if. On the contrary, for the part of the said Castle of Pergula, it is alleged that the castle has the aforementioned jurisdiction, and it cannot be taken away by the commune of Eugubium, since now the commune of Eugubium has conceded, and in the constitution of the said Castle of Pergula, that it may choose for itself a power and a rector, even from the City of Eugubium. Also, since it has been conceded to them that they have statutes, as appears from the form of the said instrument made at the time of the constitution, in which it is said that the said penalties are placed among their other statutes, and since the aforementioned cannot exist without jurisdiction, therefore it seems to concede that they have jurisdiction. Moreover, the said Castle of Pergula, by the said ancient prescription and custom, of which there is no memory of the contrary, if it had not been under the said jurisdiction, nor could it be taken away by the commune of Eugubium, as has been proven above in the said articles. And if it is said that the commune of Eugubium exercised jurisdiction there, and there was room for prevention, it is answered that this is contended by the commune of Pergula, but let each remain in his right of ownership and possession, as is said in the last l. D. uti poss.

Concerning the fourth and last point, regarding bulls and measures, it must be said the same as above, that since the commune of Pergula was in possession, or quasi-possession, of the said right during the aforementioned time in the said right, it cannot be molested or disturbed by the commune of Pergula, as has been expressed above, nor do the aforementioned, or any of the aforementioned papal privileges, of which mention is made above, hinder, because they contain a certain confirmation made in common form without cognition of the cause, nor do they grant any right, as in extra de confirm. utili vel inutili, c. examinata, and c. penult. and si. Also, imperial rescripts or privileges do not hinder, because the said Castle is not under the jurisdiction of the Prince, but of the Church; therefore

† An Emperor could not grant a right to another, when he does not possess that right, as is stated in the Digest, *De acquisitione rerum dominii*, in the law *Traditio*; and in the Digest, *De iuribus omnium iudicum*, in the law *Extra territorium*; and this is proven in the Decretals, *De rebus iuratis*, in the chapter *Pastoralis*. Moreover, privileges of a prince must be understood as being without prejudice to another, as in law 2, § *Merito*, and § *Si quis a principe*, in the Digest, *Ne quis in loco publico de eius libertate*, in the law *Nec auus*. Furthermore, if a prince wished expressly to take away the right of another, it is not valid, unless he stated, "notwithstanding," as in the Code, *De precibus Imperatoris offerendis*, in the law *Quo*, and there noted; and if against the law or public utility, in the Digest, *De constitutionibus principum*, in law 1, at the end, and there noted; and this is the truth. And thus, as has been said above, I say and advise. I, Bartolus de Saxo Ferrato, doctor of laws, have written this to the truth, and affixed my seal, etc.

Allegations of Lord Cini of Pistoia. And it seems that the answer is no, for several reasons. First, by virtue of the said pacts, which pacts do not bind the said Castle, or the inhabitants of that Castle, nor the crime, except as to certain factions, to which the inhabitants of the said Castle do not deny allegiance; as to other matters, they appear to be immune and exempt, as evidently appears from the form of the said pacts. Hence, since the said pacts are not contrary to good morals, nor contrary to canons or laws, they must be observed, as in the Digest, *De pactis*, in the law *Iure gentium*, and *Praetor ait*; and in the Decretum, question 20, cause 1, in the chapter *Puellae*, at the end. This is not obstructed by the fact that instruments of the syndicate of those who made the said pacts are found, because the said communities, in whose name the aforementioned pacts were entered into, ratified them by the thing itself and by the very fact; for the aforementioned commune of Gubbio, following the form of the said pacts, sent its power and its people to build the said Castle, and once it was built, sent its officials to the said Castle; and the community of the said Castle did the same, because according to the form of the pacts, the aforementioned community at least transferred itself to the place where the said Castle of Pergula was built, and remained in that same Castle until now, and received the officials hitherto sent by the commune of Gubbio into the said Castle, and rendered to those same officials due obedience and due salaries; and consequently, the said commune of Gubbio and the community of the said Castle of Pergula by the very fact approved the acts done in their name; for ratification is retroactive and is compared to a mandate, as in the Code, *Ad Macedonianam*, in the law *Si filius*; and in the Decretals, *De transactionibus iuratis*, in the chapter *Ratihabitione*, book 6. It does not matter whether something is done by word or by the thing itself, as in the Digest, *De rerum repetitione*, in the law *Paulus*, otherwise *Non tamen*; and in the Decretum, question 20, cause 1, in the chapter *Quem progenitores*. Indeed, it is more significant that something is done by fact than by words, as in the Digest, *De legibus*, in the law *De quibus*; and in the Decretals, *De appellationibus*, in the chapter *Dilecti filii*.

This is not obstructed by the fact that the original of the said pacts is not presented, or that the exemplification, where the said pacts are written, was not authenticated with the authentic judge, as is otherwise required to be done, as in the Authenticum, *Ut sponsa*, *Largitionum*, § *Hoc instrumentum*, column 9. First, because those pacts have already been approved by the aforementioned communities by the very fact, as has been said, and consequently it seems that faith has been accommodated to the said exemplification, as in the argument from the Code, *Qui potest in pignus habere*, in the law *Scripturas*, and there noted; this supports the aforementioned in the Digest, *De iudiciis fideicommissorum*, in the law *In fraudem*, § *Neque instrumenta*, and what is noted there. Second, because the aforementioned exemplification was made in a place where there is no copy of the pacts, and thus such solemnity is not required, for in rural areas there is much simplicity, as in the Authenticum, *De fide instrumentorum*, § *Haec autem omnia*. The custom of one place is observed, as in the argument from the Digest, *De usu*, in law 1.

Furthermore, assuming without prejudice that the said pacts were not proven by the said instrument, nevertheless, since it was so according to the truth of the matter, and because this is a very long time, since the said pacts were made, exceeding the memory of any long human life, it could be proven by mere fame or by hearsay, as is held in the Code, *De senatus consulto Macedoniano*, in the law *Si quidem*, with the notes there; and in the Decretals, *De testibus*, in the chapter *Licet ex quodam*. To this supports the Digest, *De bonis possessionibus secundum tabulas*, in law 1, § *Si Rosae*, there, "or of antiquity," etc., where, notwithstanding the defect which occurred due to antiquity, possession of goods according to the tablets will be granted, which otherwise would not be granted if it had occurred without antiquity.

Furthermore, this is not obstructed if it is said that the aforementioned pacts were not made except with those of Ser Alta, which did not extend to other communities with which they were not made. To this it can be answered in several ways. First, because those pacts seem to have been made in the name of all those communities, and all other communities seem to have held those pacts as ratified, because all communities transferred themselves to the said Castle, and dwelt in it, and received the officials, and observed the aforementioned pacts together with the aforementioned inhabitants and communities; and thus also accepted and suffered the community of the city of Gubbio, because the aforementioned pacts seem to benefit not only those of Ser Alta, but also others. To this supports the Digest, *De manumis*, in the law *Qui patitur*; the Decretals, *De regulis iuris*, in the chapter *Qui tacet*, book 6; the Code, *De diversis rescriptis*, in law 1; and the Digest, *De appellationibus*, in the law *Si quis separatim*, § *Quod enim respondet*. And the second reason of the said community was already committed, and especially due to the passage of a very long time, for now a hundred years or so have passed, because the inhabitants of one could not be distinguished from the inhabitants of another; and therefore in doubt we must incline towards liberty, as in the Digest, *De re iudicata*, in the law *Inter partes*, in private matters; furthermore, in doubt we must incline towards that which benefits, not towards that which harms, as in the Digest, *De liberto causa*, in the law *Liberis*, § *Si duo simul*.

Furthermore, the said community of Ser Alta, as is commonly reported, was larger than the others of the said communities, and the greater draws to itself the lesser, and the lesser accedes to that which is greater, as in the Digest, *De auro et argento legato*, in the law *Et si non sunt*, § *Perueniamus*. Furthermore, because the said community of Ser Alta, or that in whose name the said Castle was founded: hence all other communities seem to have acceded to that same community of Ser Alta, as to that which was principal, and the accessory follows its principal, assuming without prejudice that the said pacts did not have force by virtue of the said instrument which the said pacts contain. It is certain that from the beginning everyone was free, and liberty is not presumed unless servitude is proven to have been imposed, because every virtue is imposed from the beginning, as in the Institutes, *De iure naturali*, § *Ius autem gentium*. For servitude is either imposed by contract or in the last will, as in the Institutes, *De servitutibus*, § *Finis*. And that liberty is presumed, or is found imposed by law or custom, and in two places you have examples, as in the Digest, *De aqua pluvia arcenda*, in law 1, § *Denique*, up to the end.

It does not appear that the aforementioned Castle of Pergula, and the inhabitants of that castle, and its curia, are bound to another commune of Gubbio, and to its rectors and officials, to do and perform what they have hitherto been accustomed to do, or promised; nor can the commune of Gubbio, and its officials, impose any new work on the same commune and the inhabitants of the said Castle of Pergula, or extort it from them against their will, as in the Code, *De nova vectigalibus*, in laws 2, 3, and 4; and in the Decretals, *De censibus*, in the chapter *Prohibemus*. Furthermore, in the state in which they are found, they must be preserved and judged, and not in a harsher one, unless it is proven that they ought to do otherwise, as in the Code, *Ubi causa status*, in law 2; the Digest, *De liberto causa*, in the law *Liberis*, § *Pe*, at the end. And there is another reason, that the said Castle and its curia have stood for so long a time in their liberty in not paying or performing any other duties to the commune of Gubbio, or sustaining any other burdens, other than those of which mention has been made above without any contention: which they have now prescribed, which can be written, not only in the space of 100 years, but also in the space of 20 years; a city prescribes against the fisc, as in the Digest, *De diversis et temporibus praescriptionum*, in the law *In omnibus*; and against rights, which they have to impose anything, or to perform in giving or doing, is prescribed in the space of 30 years or 40 years; and against the Church it is prescribed in the space of 40 years, as in the Decretals, *De praescriptionibus*, in the chapter *Audi*, and *Ad aures*; and against the Roman Church in the space of 100 years, as in the Code, *De sacris sanctis ecclesiis*, in the law *Inter diuinum*; and in the Decretals, *De praescriptionibus*, in chapter 2, book 6. In which prescriptions, not only is good faith without title sufficient, provided there is some good beginning, as in the Decretals, *De praescriptionibus*, in the chapter *Si diligenti*, there noted by Bartolus and Innocentius; and to this supports what is noted in the same title, chapter 1, book 6; and by Lord Ioannes Andreas, Cyrensis.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether agreements are consumed by reason of their antiquity, or remain perpetual.
2. Whether the Prince can abolish the right of sinners.
3. An ancient custom cannot be abolished, except by the Prince.
4. If a certain castle is bound to provide a cavalry service of horses, whether a monetary fine can be imposed in place of said cavalry service.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Regarding the question whether the most ancient pacts made between the commune of Eugubium, acting as a universitas, and the men of the Altieri family, who subsequently transferred themselves to the Castle of Pergola, are to be observed, or whether they are, as it were, consumed by their antiquity, it must be said that agreements are not consumed by the mere lapse of time, but are perpetual, as stated in the Digest, under the title "Of Acquisitions and Obligations," in the law "Obligationum fere," § "Placet"; in the Digest, under the title "Of Urban Servitudes," in the law "Eum debere columnam"; and in the Code, under the title "Of Witnesses," in the law "Sancimus." Indeed, the more ancient they are, the more efficacious they are, provided that observance has prevailed. Those things which have always been observed must not be changed, as stated in the Digest, under the title "Of Preventing Rain Water," in law 1, at the end; under the title "Of Water in Summer and Winter," in the law "Hoc iure," § "Ductus aquae." And it should be noted here that, although when we speak of observance, the last observed practice is preferred to earlier ones, as in the law "Mela," § 1, under the title "Of Aliments and Foodstuffs for Legatees," and in the Code, under the title "That the Status of the Deceased Shall Not Be Changed," in the law "Si mater," nevertheless this is true only in those matters which can be changed by bare will. Certainly, in other matters, one must look to the concurrent support in which the right is contained. Therefore, the first observance prevails, unless there were a prescription against it, as noted in the law "Nemo," § "Temporalis," under the title "Of the Rules of Law," and in the chapter "Cum de beneficio," under the title "Of Prebends," Book 6. This is supported by the chapter "Cumana," under the title "Of Elections," and the chapter "Procula," under the title "Of Proof." In our case, however, nothing is alleged to show that the parties have departed from the ancient form of the contract; therefore, one must adhere to the ancient form. I prove this thus: conventions newly received into the municipal body are to be observed, as in law 2 of the Digest, under the title "Of the Right of Immunity." But immunities cannot be granted to citizens against the public utility without the consent of the community, as stated in the Code, under the title "Of Decurions," in the law "Vacua," Book 10. Since, therefore, these pacts were originally made with free men, with citizens, and not with serfs, these pacts are to be observed perpetually, especially because they were not gratuitous pacts, but fell into the category of "I do so that you may do," that is, "from one, so that you may dwell," or "having dwelt, so that you may depart from one." Hence, the commune of Eugubium cannot revoke such pacts, by the best argument from the Digest, under the title "Of Fraud," in the law "Si cum mihi permisisses," because an obligation is a bond of law by which we are bound by necessity, not by will, as stated in the Institutes, under the title "Of Verbal Obligations," in the beginning. And this is supported by the law "Priv." under the title "Who, and from Whom," and the law "Totius" under the title "Of Decrees by Ordinaries," and the law "Quod semel." Otherwise, no one would contract with cities if they could rescind agreements, as stated in the law "Et potest sine," § 1, under the title "Of Minors." And this is supported by the law "Quibus" and the law "Civitates" under the title "Of the Rules of Law," and the law "Nec ex praetorio."

† Indeed, no one can abrogate this right except the Prince, and not anyone inferior to the Prince, because it is a right of the law of nations, because agreements must be kept. Moreover, there is even doubt regarding the Prince, for natural rights and natural obligations cannot be abrogated by rescript, as noted in l. 1, de constitutionibus, in principio, and Codex, si contra ius, vel utilitatem publicam, l. final. Unless such agreements, arising from the circumstances of our cases, tend toward public damage, then the Prince can, both in law and in fact, rescind them, and grant a right to one against another; for it is proper to the Prince alone, de vulgari et technica, l. ex facto, in principio. The conclusion is that, until the Lord Pope changes the ancient agreements and the ancient custom, the commune of Eug. or its officials cannot change them; but they are not bound to observe the agreements, nor can they increase the assessed rates, Codex, de annuis et tributorum, l. final, lib. 10, where no official can assess or change on behalf of the Prince.

† Custom, and the most ancient one arising therefrom, cannot be abolished by a subordinate of the Prince, as stated in the Digest, under the heading "de verborum significatione," in the law *super quibusdam*, unless the reformer of the Province, considering utility and the necessity of the fatherland, should see fit otherwise, as we note in the aforementioned law 2, according to Doctorus, because he is not bound by pacts not made with him. Hence, obedience is due to him without prejudice to the pacts, as argued in the Digest, under the heading "qui in possessionem in pignus habent," in the law *Claudius Felix*, at the end.

† Furthermore, regarding the question whether, in place of the horseback service (caualcata), which is no longer in use today, a monetary fine may be imposed, and the act estimated, and the estimation exacted: it must be known that a debtor of an act is not bound to pay a sum of money, unless by reason of delay, according to the rule "obligations are not divided" (de verbis oblig.), § Celsus (de re iudicata), l. Si quis ab alio; or by reason of difficult performance, when the difficulty concerns the person of the debtor, as in l. 2, in principio (de actionibus emptoris et venditoris) and de verbis oblig., l. Continuus, § Illud. But here neither of these applies; therefore, the debtor is not bound to anything other than what he promised. And thus he is not bound to pay one thing for another, as in l. 2, § 1 (si certum petatur). This is expressly stated in the Codex, de agris et censibus, l. Dominis praediorum, lib. 11. And this is the common opinion. Ego, if he wished to impose the caualcata upon them, he could do so, provided that he imposed it in good faith according to the necessity of the time. For works are not to be exacted if it is not expedient for the patron to have them performed, as in l. Medicus (de operis liberto). And the contract is to be interpreted for the common good of both parties, as in ff. de solutionibus, l. Si cum Stichus. I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a person punished in one court may be punished in another with a heavier penalty.
2. Municipal magistrates may adjudicate minor crimes.
3. A minor crime is judged by the quality of the penalty.
casus:
AS VS.

In the name of Christ, Amen. The point is this: the Podestà of the Castle of Monte Franchi, in the district of Spoleto, condemned a certain Cola Cerretani of the said Castle, because he had wounded a certain Pietro Ioannutii of Arrone with several wounds. After this condemnation had been made, the judge of malefices of the general court of the Duchy proceeded similarly against the said Cola, as is said, for the same offense. Now, this Cola obtained from Lord Albano that, since he had once been condemned for the said wounds by the Podestà of the said Castle, it would please him to provide for his indemnity. For which reason, Lord Albano issued a commission to the Vicar of the city of Assisi, to inquire according to law whether the said Podestà of Monte Franchi had the authority to condemn, and thus to annul the condemnation of the judge of malefices of the general court, and to proceed against him. Now, it is brought into doubt, from those things which have been proved and pleaded before the said Vicar-commissioner in the aforementioned matters, whether the said Podestà of Monte Franchi could legally condemn, and which sentence should be confirmed, since it is alleged by the advocates of the Roman Curia and the Church that the said Podestà had no jurisdiction to make the said condemnation, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Although there was doubt in law whether one punished in one court could be punished with a greater penalty in another court—on which point reference is made by Cynus in *l. qui sepulchro*, *de sepulchris violatis*, and in the *Codex* *de secundis nuptiis* and *de testibus*, *l. nullum*, and it is touched upon in the *Codex* *de sponsalibus*, *l. 2*, and by Bernardus *de iudiciis*, *c. at si clerici*, and by Petrus de Modo in *l. Senatus censuit*—nevertheless, because this doubt has been resolved by the letters of the said Albani, it ought not to be reopened into question.

And it remains only to be seen whether the authority of the said Castle had jurisdiction or not. And here I shall briefly dispose of the matter. Since the statutes of the castle have been confirmed by the superior, it follows that the authority possesses jurisdiction; and it would be of little avail to have statutes if there were no magistrate to execute them, D. de off. iud. l. 3 § post originem. Moreover, the authority is appointed by the superior, and by law municipal magistrates may take cognizance of minor crimes, Auth. de defensione civitatis § audientia et civitatis; and a castle is called a municipality, as is noted, D. qui ex causa maiestatis l. legatis. And if it be said that these crimes are not the subject matter, where so many wounds have occurred, as in l. is qui cum telo and l. 1 D. ad l. Iuliam de vi publica.

I answer that, according to the common law, [matters] are not slight, neither by the quality of the fact nor by the type of penalty. But because, by the form of the statutes, a slight and pecuniary penalty is imposed, and the crime is judged to be slight, *de publicis iudiciis*, l. 2. Furthermore, if it is said that these statutes, insofar as they would prejudice the jurisdiction, have not been confirmed by the superior, I answer that the statute does not prejudice, but the prevention of jurisdiction does. It is said that the superior is not prejudiced because jurisdiction is attributed to the inferior, as in *Codex*, *de officio praefecti urbis*, l. 1, in the final paragraph, where there is a text on this point. I therefore conclude that, since the power has jurisdiction, it ought to pronounce judgment according to the form of the letters of Lord Alban for the inquiry. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the mother is bound to petition that the tutors be compelled to administer.
2. Whether, testamentary tutors having been appointed, the mother is bound to accept the guardianship.
3. Whether a legacy in lieu of dowry is conditional or casual, and whether a burden can be imposed upon it, and whether it is transmissible.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It seems that, prima facie, one should say that the mother is deprived of succession for two reasons: because she did not petition that the tutors be compelled to administer, ff. ad Ter. l. 2. §. si mater; and because she proceeded to a second marriage, disregarding the guardianship and without rendering an account of the administration, C. ad ter. l. omnem. And thus the inheritance came into the power of the next of kin in degree after the mother, C. qui petant tuto. l. nepotibus. To the contrary, it seems that the mother is not bound to petition that she be compelled to administer, unless the tutors requested by the mother herself were not appointed in the will, C. de adm. tu. l. fi. §. in personis; and there by Cynus.

† Moreover, the mother did not accept the guardianship, nor was she bound to do so, since she had appointed testamentary guardians in the will, C. de te. l. si mater. Hence it cannot be said that she ought to render an account, if she did not involve herself in the administration of the guardianship, and thus the provision in Auth. de nup. §. si autem tutelam does not stand in the way. And this is the more correct opinion. And therefore I do not believe that, according to the matters proposed, the mother is deprived of the succession.

Whether a legacy for a dowry is conditional, casual, or neither: note this in *l. Titio centum*, § *non licet*, with the preceding text, *de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*; and according to Cynus, *Codex de nuptiis*, *l. sancimus*. Whatever the case may be, it is owed to the daughter up to her legitime, without burden. And the daughter freely transmits this to the aforementioned mother. On this point, note *Codex de nuptiis*, *l. sancimus*, in the four questions by Cynus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a statement is taken as a whole, with respect to its proper meaning, every part must be true.
2. The legitima and the trebellianica do not apply in a fideicommissum made conditionally.
3. In ecclesiastical territories, under canon law, two witnesses suffice in wills.
4. A witness duly examined is not believed if he first said one thing and later says the contrary.
5. Although a witness lies in one part, he is nevertheless believed in another.
6. If a legacy is left in a will under a condition, and the legacy is repeated in codicils without mention of the condition, and it is claimed pursuant to the codicils, there is no need to fulfill the condition.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It must be premised for clarity that when a statement is taken universally as to its proper meaning, every part must be true in fact. Digest, Title 2, Law: *Si is qui ducenta*; Section: *Utrum*. However, in a fideicommissary substitution, a distinction is made: either someone survives, in which case, by the presumed will of the testator, the substitute is excluded, and then the substitute is not called; or no one survives, for example because the last one died without children, in which case the substitute is called as to his share and right, as in the Digest, Title: *Ad Trebellianum*, Law: *Heredes mei*; Section: *Cum ita*. And this distinction, based on the presumed will of the testator, has been accepted against the proper meaning. Or, if the condition is taken from any one, then it is verified by any one; the same applies to a disjunctive condition, Digest, Title: *Ad Trebellianum*, Law: *Lucius*; Section: *Gayo*. Having premised this, it must be considered that among the brothers there was inserted a substitution with a condition taken from any one, such as "if any one," etc. Hence, it is undoubtedly decided that, dying without legitimate male children, because so says the will, the surviving substitutes, e.g., A and B, died without legitimate male children; C and D succeeded by fideicommissum. Then D died with a son; as to this part, it is not to be treated. C died without sons; this share comes into the fideicommissum, after deducting the legitime and the Trebellian portion of what this C received by institution.

† which the legitime and the Trebellian portion do not come into a conditional fideicommissum, as in c. Rayn. and c. Ray. Therefore, it is clear that in the person of the last dying without children, the subsequent substitution has effect; but the legitime and the Trebellian portion must be deducted. And on this point, see l. pater filium, § duobus, ad l. Falcidiam, and C. de impuberibus et aliis subiectis, l. pen., and c.

† On the second point, the common opinion is that, according to canon law, two suitable witnesses suffice in the territories of the Church. And this is proved in the text, in the reasoning of the text, on testaments, c. Cum esses, and c. Relatum, unless otherwise provided by statute or local custom.

† On the third point, I say that if a witness duly examined said one thing, he is not believed if he later said the contrary; otherwise, if he was not duly examined, as noted in c. Cum causam, De testibus, by Ber.

† On the fourth point, I say that although it is false in part, it is nevertheless believed in another part, D. de falsis, l. filius, § sequens quo; and C. de testibus, l. iubemus; de transactionibus, l. si ex falsis; and l. querela, C. de falsis; and note, de hereditatibus, c. fraternitatem, according to Innocentius.

† On another point, it must be considered that a legacy to a witness is special, and the condition of a fideicommissum in codicils is universal, and the condition of making a refutation is not repeated. Hence, if action is brought on the basis of codicils, it is not necessary to make a refutation, as stated in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. nam ad ea. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If an instrument is true in some respects and false or defective in others, whether it is to be believed in any respect.
casus: CASE. In the name of Christ, Amen. The point of the question is as follows. A certain person named Puccius offered himself and his goods to the hospital and the Church of St. Mary of the Rose, with certain goods excepted; and he reserved for himself, as appears in the said offer. Then he donated the said reserved goods to the same hospital and Church in this manner, that by reason of the aforementioned donation they should give to a certain Church 50 pounds of denarii, if a cleric resided there. The notary, requested to draw up the aforementioned instruments, published the second donation as public, and did not add the aforementioned condition; however, it is found written in the protocol, or first draft. Now it is asked whether the aforementioned public instrument is valid or not, etc. I, Baldus.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Thus, if an instrument is true in some respects and false and defective in others, whether it is to be believed in any respect. The glossator states in l. si ex falsis. The doctors commonly hold that if the clauses are separate, the useful and true is not vitiated by the useless and false. And this seems to be proven. D. de falsis, l. filius, § sequens quaestio; and C. de testamentis, l. subemus. Innocentius says that such an instrument is not believed, D. de haereditatibus, c. frateritatis. I say that either the falsity concerns the solemnities or the transaction. If it concerns the solemnities, because it touches the force of the entire instrument, it is of no effect, C. de falsis, l. si creditor concluderes; D. de fide instrumentorum, l. petita. If it is false in that which constitutes the entire fact, then the instrument is of no effect. And if the falsity is in the manner or substance of the entire transaction, as in Extr. de fide instrumentorum, c. cum Ioan. haeremit., or if it is some false particle which does not touch any part nor inform it, then the false is vitiated and that which is true remains valid, as noted in C. de falsis, l. querela. I do not say that the true is never excluded by the false, but rather that proof is excluded, because it cannot be made from a discredited instrument. Therefore, the truth, which is not proven, is suppressed. That which does not appear is not presumed to be true, as in l. 3 and l. ruptilia. And it supports its own reasoning in D. de verborum obligationibus, § cum adiecit; and Dist. 9, si ad scripturas; and C. de fide instrumentorum, si ex his. It appears from this that the said instrument is not relied upon in any respect, but the plaintiff is dismissed. Well, it stands, because it contains mere truth, in Auth. de, § si falsum est, not only when something is added, but also when something is detracted from the truth, C. de episcopis et clericis, l. presbiteri. But that which is notable is that if one party produces an instrument, this production suffices for both parties, as noted in D. de editionibus, l. 1, § editiones; and D. de censibus, c. olim, according to Innocentius. But if the instrument exists, yet is produced by no one, such an instrument operates for nothing in court, D. de minoribus, Auth. mona. and l. minores, 25 annis omissam; and noted in D. de probationibus, l. quoties, § si. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The plaintiff is bound to prove that which he has set forth in his libel.
2. What the witnesses produced concerning the sale of wine are bound to prove.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It must be premised that if the plaintiff fails to prove his case, the defendant is absolved, as stated in the law *Actor, quod asserat*, in the Digest, title *Qui accusare possint*. Therefore, it must first be examined what it is incumbent upon the plaintiff to prove, and whether it has been proven or not.
It must be known that he must prove what he alleged in his libel, as stated in the law *Habebant* under the title *De Institoria*. In the libel, however, he narrates

† On the sale of a certain quantity of wine for a certain quantity of price. Also, the promise to give a merchant as promisor to the said seller: and finally, the articles were drafted very wisely. The first article concerning the sale does not appear to be proven by Cola Benicase, the witness, because at the end he says he does not know what quantity of wine lay in the large casks and small casks; and thus he does not know what quantity was sold; therefore it is not proven, because he lacks certainty. For the knowledge of the witness must be certain, not conjectural, as noted in § si plures. Also, regarding the price, he disagrees with the plaintiff, because he says that the price of all the wine was equal, whereas the plaintiff says it was different. And if a witness testifies against the truth on one point, he is not believed on any point, as in c. pura et simplex. Also, the second good witness does not prove it, because he says he does not remember the number of large casks and small casks, and thus he is ignorant of whether the statements are true; and uncertainty in the container generates uncertainty in the content, as in l. omnia, § cum ita. However, because at the beginning he says that it was not stated within the term, which is contrary to the allegations, the plaintiff must stand by this, as in l. cum pretium. Hence, the plaintiff necessarily has to admit that the witness is defective. Also, because regarding the quantity of wine, this witness does not give a cause of knowledge from sight, but from hearing from the plaintiff, and thus he does not prove it, as in l. solam. Also, Angelucius Mancini does not prove it for the same reasons. Also, Sancius Petri did not testify on the first article. Also, Vagnolus says he heard it, but he does not say that one confessed in the presence of the other. Also, because he testifies against the article of Petrus Andrioli, nor does Bar. prove the contract on the first point; and every proof must be certain, as noted in l. 1, § si quis ar. deposuit, and in c. in praesentia, de probat. Hence, saving the truth, it does not seem to me that the sale of a certain quantity of true wine for a certain price is proven; and consequently, the promise to give a merchant cannot be proven; because if the debt does not appear, that which accedes to the debt cannot be proven, l. 1, § debitum, de constit. pecunia, and as noted in l. sciendum, de verb. oblig. Also, since a copy was made of the peace agreements, and that copy, due to the fault of the plaintiff to whom it was handed over, is not produced, how can the defendant be condemned on an uncertain matter? For it is presumed against the one who does not produce the document, as in l. fi., C. de fid. instr. Also, it does not appear that delivery, measurement, or offer of the wine was made at the legitimate time; therefore, the plaintiff is repelled, as in § offerri, and as noted in de aedil. edict., l. aediles, § fi., and in l. si in lege, § colonus, and l. quaero, § inter locatorem. For these reasons, I believe the defendant should be absolved. I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The statute of the Florentines does not bind the Paduans, and thus foreigners.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It is absurd to doubt whether the statute of the Florentines binds the Paduans, who neither contracted in Florence, nor committed a quasi-contract, nor committed a delict, nor a quasi-delict. For the Emperor cannot bind non-subjects, nor can the Pope. Nor by any reasoning does this person acquire a forum in Florence; hence, he can be bound by no law and no equity. For no one can impose a law except upon his own subject and one who has acquired a forum, as established in the law *Cunctos populos*; and *Extra territorium*; and *Extra qui filii sint legitimi*; chapter *Per venerabilem*; and in chapter *Pasto*, *De restitutione in integrum*; and in the *Clementina*; and in chapter 1, *Ideo constitutum*, Book 6; and in chapter *Postulasti*, *De foro competenti*, according to Innocentius; and *De sententia excommunicationis*, chapter *A nobis*, according to Innocentius. For to make statutes is a matter of jurisdiction, as is proven in the *Differences of Jurisdiction*. Therefore, a statute cannot be made against one who is not within the jurisdiction. It is relevant to the matter of duties and honors, the law *Rescripto*, § *Si*, Code, *De decurionibus*; the law *Diversorum iuris*, with countless others, and so forth. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The oaths of minors have effect not only in contracts, but also in dispositive acts.
2. Whether an oath supplies for the defect of a statute that requires the consent of blood relatives.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Regarding the question whether the sons of Dulceta succeed to their grandfather Biennus, their grandmother Paulucia, and their aunt Francisca, and in what share, and whether, because Dulceta concluded and entirely renounced, they are excluded and the sons of Matthew, who are first cousins of the sons of Dulceta, succeed in their entirety: having examined the statutes of the Fabricis and Dulcetis, and the testament of Paulucia, it seems to be said that, according to the common law, the said Dulceta, being of age, could transact and make an agreement with an oath,

† because the Authentica *Sacramenta publica* applies not only to contracts but also to dispositive acts, as is noted in l. 3, § *De contrario iudicio tutoris*, D.; and since the law itself received his son as his heir, they have no right under the common law, because the preceding law released those to whom it put an end.

But there is doubt on account of the statute, which requires the presence of blood relatives and annuls the contract; yet, because the statute does not expressly disapprove of an oath, the renunciation with an oath seems valid, since the oath makes it stronger, and therefore the statute ceases to apply, as it speaks of minors, as in Auth. sacramenta, and as noted in l. 2, C. de rescind. vendit. For civil law requires the presence [of relatives] and a judicial decree, which is more than the presence of blood relatives. And yet, without a judge, it is valid on account of the oath. It must be observed, however, that the renunciation speaks of succession and paternal goods, and therefore it does not seem to extend to the succession of others. But I answer that these sons of Dulceta do not have a right in the goods of their aunt by marriage through the person of Dulceta, because she did not transmit the inheritance not yet accepted, C. ad orf. l. nam pro numero. Where it appears that they have a right through their own person on account of the edict concerning succession, de inoff. testam. l. si is qui, C. de success. edict. l. fina., unless one says that by making an agreement she seems to have accepted, and as an heir made a pact not to claim in the goods possessed by Matthew. For it was not a mere renunciation, but a pact not gratuitous, which cannot be made concerning the name and right of an heir, de acq. haer. l. pro haerede, §. Papinianus. Concerning the inheritance of Vannis, there is no doubt on account of the renunciation. Likewise, concerning the inheritance of Paulutia, there is no doubt, because it does not appear to have been renounced, nor accepted. Hence it seems that the sons of Dulceta succeed in equal shares with the sons of Matthew; but one opinion is per stirpes, according to another, which is the more correct, as noted, satis de haer. ab intest. §. si igitur defunctus. Nor does the statute impede, because it does not speak in this case. Likewise, the renunciation does not impede, C. de transact. l. si de certa, ff. eodem, l. cum Aquil. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that accusations for crimes must be brought within a certain period, whether an accusation may proceed after the expiration of that period.
2. Although the proof is clearer than daylight, or there is a confession by the offender, the exception of prescription of the accusation for the offense may be raised.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† In the case of the accusation instituted by Benecasani against Gestantium, concerning which mention is made in these records and others, it must be said that, according to law, the said Gostantius ought to be absolved. And this is because the law provides that time extinguishes a crime: to such an extent that after a long time no punishment can be inflicted, even if the crime were clear, D. de iniuriis, l. sed si vnus, §. si ante iudicem. But here the time for accusing has lapsed, not the time of a year, from which it can be said that the injury was inflicted within a year, D. quod met. causa, l. fi, cum exceptione, §. 2. For this statute defines this time. And therefore, after the time has passed, the accusation does not endure, D. de mino, l. auxilium, in principio. Likewise, the lapse of five years, which is established by common law in cases of adultery, D. de adulteriis, l. mariti Lenocinium, §. quinquennium. Hence this exception was raised, and it undoubtedly stands in the way, as is fully read and noted in C. de adulteriis, l. ita pudor. And if it is said that here the act was one of rape, I answer that rape is not proven, because to rape is to lead away or seize by force or seduction, as l. 1, in fine, C. de rap. virgi., states; to lead away or to seize, D. ne quis eum in iudi. non est, l. sed eximendi. Certainly, neither is adultery proven, but there is strong evidence against Gostantium regarding adultery.

† but on account of the lapse of time, impunity is prescribed, even if the proof were clearer than daylight; indeed, even if there were a voluntary confession made in court, nevertheless the exception of prescription could be raised, as in the aforementioned laws. It follows, therefore, that the said Gostantius is to be absolved from rape, because it was not proven, and from adultery, because it is prescribed. I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A testament in which a child is passed over is null.
2. A sui heres who is passed over transmits the right to declare the testament null, unless he tacitly or expressly approves the testament.
3. Whether one who suffers time to lapse is deemed to have tacitly renounced the right to declare the testament null. For how long the right to declare the testament null endures.
4. If a daughter who has been passed over declares the testament null, it benefits her, because she will receive a dowry on intestacy, given the statute that a male succeeds, not a dowried female.
5. Given the statute that female daughters do not succeed while males are present, and if some of them die before being provided with a dowry, the dowry becomes lapsed and remains with the brothers.
6. Given the statute that female daughters do not succeed while males are present, whether their dowry, which succeeds in place of the legitime, is transmitted to their successors.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† First, it must be examined whether the will is void or valid. And there is no doubt that, according to the common law, it is void by operation of law itself, as stated in the Digest, *De liberis et posthumis*, in the law *Gallus*, § *in omnibus*; and in the law *Inter caetera*; and in the law *Maximum vitium*; and in the Institutes, *De exheredatione liberorum*, in the beginning; and in § *Aliud quoque capitulum*.

† Moreover, there is no doubt that a passed-over *sui* heir transmits the right to bring an action for nullity, as in C. de posth. hęredi insti. l. uxoris ab ortu, just as in the case of a complaint. C. de inoffi. testa. l. si quis filius, unless he had tacitly or expressly approved the father's will, ff. de iniusto test. l. filio praeterito.

But it is well to be in doubt whether the right of speaking has been tacitly repudiated, since she suffered a long time to elapse, and the fact was known to the pious, and she peacefully possessed it for a long time. It seems that this is so, as stated in the aforementioned law *Filio* and in the Digest, title *De probationibus*, law *Pericula*; and in the Digest, title *Ad Carbo*, law *Si impubes*, section *Quaesitum*. And according to this, a testament cannot be said to be null after long patience, by argument from the Code, title *De petitione hereditatis*, law *Si filii*; and in the Digest, title *De actione hereditaria*, law *Qui in aliena*, section 1; and what is noted in the Code, title *Qui admittuntur ad bona possessionem*, post, law 1. For long time does not of itself do this, but here other indications joined to time do it. And what is noted in the Code, title *Communi dividundo*, law *Pe*; and the aforementioned law *Procula*.

† For by its very nature, the right to declare [a witness] null does not endure for any period longer than thirty years, as is stated in C. de iure delib. l. licet. For the past is connected with the present, so that to declare nullity is to speak of what has passed. And it adds in C. de repud. haered. l. 3: “Moreover, it endures for as long as the action for the inheritance endures,” namely thirty years, ff. quibus ex causis maior. l. non solum; C. de edict. divi Adriani tollend. l. 2 and l. final in fine. Moreover, if the right to declare nullity is a judicial office, it endures for thirty years. And note C. de praescript. 30 annorum l. sicut. But by accident, through suppression, a shorter time may induce a presumption, not from time alone, but from acts or acquiescence, arg. de usuris l. qui semisses; de donatione inter virum et uxorem l. si servus communis. From the foregoing I say that, according to the common law, the said Laurentia may declare the witness null, unless something else is proved externally; otherwise, if it pertains to the proof or confirmation of the will, for the said pupil could not have made the will according to the aforementioned rules.
But let us see what benefit this brings to her. For, intestate, she does not succeed according to the form of the statute, but the male does. I answer: in the dowry, so that there may be a statute.

† What, therefore, regarding sisters who died as unmarried wards? I answer that the dowry has become caducary, by argument from *de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, l. *Titio centum*, § *sed cum ante*; and thus it remains with the brother, C. *de caducis tollendis*, § *pro secundo*, and without burden, because the obligation to provide a dowry and to support are personal and do not admit of the right of accretion, C. *de caducis tollendis*, § *ne autem*; ff. *de usufructu*, l. *domus*. Moreover, it was lawful for the daughter to repudiate the inheritance, as in c. 2, *de pace*, lib. 6; therefore, it seems that the conclusion should be drawn against the woman in favor of the man. This is supported by *de adultis*, l. *publico*, according to Jacobus and Cynus.

† It could nevertheless be said that it is not probable that the statute intended to entirely deprive women of what is due to them and their successors as a legitime. For the dowry, of which the statute speaks, appears to be assigned in place of the legitime and substituted in place of alimony. Therefore, transmission should be made up to the amount of the legitime. This is supported by what is noted by Rycardus and Cynus in C. de nuptiis, l. Sancimus. And this is very equitable and fitting, as stated in l. Cum ratio naturalis, de bonis damnatorum. I, Baldus de Perusio.
