consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A statute against robbers who forcibly seize or injure does not apply to those who have possessed for a long time with title. A less legitimate citation and a null citation are equivalent, and they render the proceeding null.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

Let us begin with the principles, namely, whether the statute speaking of notices to be placed in the chest applies against those who have possessed with title for a long time. And I believe that it does not, considering the words of the same statute. For it appears to speak only of a robber, or a forcible dispossessor, and an injurer, and therefore it should not be extended to lawful possessors. For lawful possessors are not to be ejected by the decrees of the city councils, but they must first be convicted by legally constituted judgments before being deprived, ff. qui, et a quibus. l. si priuatus. and l. quotiens. de pollicita. and de act. et obl. l. negantes. de pactis. l. si pacto, quo pęnam. C. vnde vi. l. meminerint. C. si per vim, vel alio modo. l. fi. Furthermore, considering the words of another statute concerning one who has possessed for ten years with title, the statute protects the possessor; hence, even if the statute speaking of notices were to apply to a possessor with title, this would be true only before the ten years, not after the ten years, as in C. de censoribus. l. apud eum, where it says, “we wish there to be no beginning of recovery.” lib. 11. Then let us come to the procedure of the judge, and I say that the writ of trespass, or sorgerium, was expressed less legitimately,

† For where the citation is invalid by the law itself, neither is anything done by the judge valid, because a less legitimate citation and a null one are equated. And thus, where there is no citation, there is no process, as in l. ita diuus and l. de vno quoque. Thus, when the citation does not hold by the law itself, as in l. i. ff. de feriis, and noted diffusely by Innocentius extra de dila. c. 1. But the citations made against Segerius were null by the law itself, not because they were made at his house, but on account of the brevity of time. For since it appears that he was in Castiglione d’Arezzo, as it were banished, how could he be cited in the morning for the evening? It was an impossible command, Inst. de ver. ob. §. loca. Which sentence, sine appel. rescin. l. Paulus. Furthermore, the citation did not come to his knowledge, as the law requires, C. vbi in rem actio. l. 2. and l. 1. §. item cum ex edicto. Thirdly, we come to the petition of Segerius, and I say that his petition is founded on the common law, because the injury done previously by the judges, or predecessors, or any officials whatsoever, is to be revoked by the office of the judge, and noted ff. de euic. l. emi. noted and C. de iur. fis. l. prohibitum. li. 10. de purga. c. significatibus. Moreover, it is founded by the chapters of Laudus the First, which is still intact, l. 4. §. si ex conuen. de re iudi. For since by the law itself the process was null, as this may be made clear by the opening of the process and notarial instruments concerning a certain and doubtful matter, it ought to be composed more carefully, but that which was done wrongly is to be revoked. It serves in the reasoning of his case ff. ad exhi. l. 2. §. sciendum. As in pos. lega. l. is, a quo. ad Treb. l. ille, a quo. §. si de testaoo. cum si. From these, and others which can be alleged, I conclude for Segerius: Nor does it avail the opponent to object that it was done while he was ignorant, since he was absent through fear, as in l. i. f. qui es cau. maio. and there noted Odofredus de expul. ciuitatis Veronae. And because this proceeding savors more of a possessory cause than a petitory one. And although possession is restored to Segerius, saving the right of the adversaries regarding ownership, arg. in l. fi. C. quorum bono. de acq. pol. l. exitus etrouersia. de re iudi. l. diuo. §. si super. de praescrip. 30. anhus si quis emp. §. fina. I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In how many ways a crime is said to be light and grave. And above, similarly
2. and 402.
body: And thus I say, and I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Laws, advise accordingly; and I have written this in good faith, and have signed it with the sign of my name.

And it is true that what I touched upon regarding the cases below, concerning civil causes, is found expressly in criminal ones. The text says that they cognize of light delicts, but does not open otherwise, and therefore it is still doubtful: for a light crime and a grave one are said in several ways. In the first way, by person, time, or thing, or by the place of the person, or by the place of the delict. These five modes are set forth in D. de iniuriis, l. Praetor edixit, §. Si, with the following law. In the second way, all chapters are called grave delicts, and no others, as noted in l. Ad ea, de regulis iuris. In the third way, a grave delict would be one committed with dolus, not one committed with culpa, as noted in D. de minoribus, l. Auxilium, §. In delictis, and l. Si ex causa, §. Si mulier. In the fourth way, it is called light or grave according to the genus and quality of the penalty, as fully noted by Dy. in D. de accusationibus, l. Levia. And in that respect speaks Auth. Nisi breviores, C. de senatu ex periculo recipiendo, where Cy. says that they are light wherever they do not exceed 100 gold coins. And he also says there that, moreover, proceeding in causes, the custom of the forum is observed. How, therefore, shall we understand a light delict here, whether according to the genus of the penalty or according to the intent? And I distinguish: either the delict is committed without true dolus, or with interpreted dolus; and I consider this delict light, when the Prefect of the Vigiles cognizes it, l. Si, D. de officiis Praefecti vigilarum, and l. 3, §. Cognoscit, eod. tit. Or, if with dolus, then it matters: either such a delict is capital, but the ius commune then, although the statute diminishes the penalty, does not yet call it light, as if for adultery the statute imposes a penalty of 100 pounds, for the crime itself in itself is enormous, d. §. In delictis. Likewise in homicide, falsity, and so forth. It supports what is noted in §. Publice, by Iac. But. It also supports, because these pertain to judges who have greater imperium, and who have the power of the sword, as l. Congruit, D. de officiis praesidis. It supports l. 2, C. de sportulis. Or, according to the ius commune, the delict is otherwise not capital, but it is capital by the form of custom or statute, and the same reason applies, because statute and custom can make a delict more atrocious than it is according to the ius commune, as D. de extraordinariis criminibus, l. Facultati, §. Sunt quaedam. Or such a delict is not capital, neither according to the ius commune nor according to the ius municipii. Then I sub-distinguish: either the penalty is above 300 gold coins, and it is not called light, but grave, as in §. Audientia, and therefore the defensor or municipal magistrate does not cognize. Or it is below 300 gold coins, and then I say that the defensor of the municipality is legitimately conformed, [and] is cognized by the superior. And he posits, because this cognition and punishment belongs to the magistrate by right. And this is the mind of the gloss in l. Imperium, de iure omnium iudicum. And it displeases me that Ped. iud. according to the gloss of the Ord. confirms the opinion of Cyn. in Auth. De manibus principum, §. Sit tibi, and Gul. de Cu. confirms in l. Imperium that lighter causes are called those below 100 gold coins, which is safer. And thus I would practice: by which it appears that in our case the potestas had jurisdiction. It does not obstruct l. 2, C. de sportulis, because it speaks of delegates. Likewise it does not obstruct De modo mulctandi eos, because it speaks of a mulcta, not of a penalty. Or it can be greater or less than 300 gold coins, as the penalty of confiscation, for in a poor man it is less than 300 gold coins, because he does not have so much in goods indistinctly, if it were less. And I say that in this doubt he would not have jurisdiction, as C. Ne sine iussu principis certis iudicibus liceat confiscare, l. Unica. It does not obstruct De appellationibus, l. Ampliorem, §. Fina, because there it speaks in civil causes. And thus I say, and I, the aforementioned Baldus, advise, and I declare my advice, and I consider the aforementioned to be useful and sufficiently known. I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether grandchildren are included under the name of children in a substitution.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the will of Bozzano of the Burg, in which he instituted his daughters, Lady Mutia and Lady Vanna, as universal heirs to all his goods, and provided that if any of his said daughters should at any time die without issue, he substituted the other surviving daughter to the deceased; and if she should not be living, he substituted to himself the sons or daughters surviving him; and if both his daughters should die, either not existing or leaving some sons, then in that case he substituted to them the Brotherhood of Saint Bartholomew of the said Burg. Then the testator died; then one of the daughters died without issue; then the son of the other daughter died, leaving a son of his own surviving.

† It is asked, if one of the daughters dies leaving a grandson surviving, whether there is room for the aforementioned substitution or not. The word "sons" creates doubt. For under the name of sons, grandsons are not included in a strict sense, nor is a great-grandson included under the name of sons, as in D. de lib. et post. l. Gallus, §. instituens; and D. de excus. tutor. l. sed et milites, §. 1, ver. hoc autem. To the same effect is Inst. qui et in quibus ordinibus ab intestato succedunt, §. si. On the contrary, because under the name of sons grandsons are also included, since such a word is used by an ascendant: D. de verb. sign. l. liberorum, §. sed quod Papi.; to the same effect D. de ritu nupt. l. senatus. For where there is an equal reason of law or affection towards a son and a grandson, there, according to interpretation, grandsons are included under the name of sons: D. de verb. sign. l. iuxta. I say that the grandson excludes the substitute, because there mention is made of sons conditionally; and grandsons, and all descendants, are included: D. de haer. inst. l. Lucius, where the case is to the same effect; D. ad Trebell. l. ex facto, §. si, joined with the text and gloss, where it is the same to say "without sons" and "without descendants." Therefore, although the substitute would not be excluded here by an express condition, he would be excluded by a tacit one: D. de cond. et demonstr. l. cum auus; D. de fideicom. l. cum acutissimi; D. de inst. et subst. generaliter. And this is the truth. And it supports C. de cond. insert. l. 1.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a notary may impose an obligation on goods, even if he is not one in another matter.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Since, by statute, greater regard must be had for the style and custom of the notary than for the abbreviations, and the briefest series and the custom of the notary are undoubtedly presupposed, it seems to me, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, that the said instrument can be perfected with an obligation of goods; indeed, even if it is not expressly stated, it is understood. And I prove this by the last law, Codex, On Guarantors, because the law is true to this effect: but if we did not have the style, the custom, and the statute of the contract, nor would they be extended to a new hope of obligation, it supports what is noted in the gloss, Codex, On Falsehoods, law *Satis aperte*, and see the gloss there. It also supports the extrajudicial provision, On Faithful Instruments, chapter *Cum P. tabellio*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, a person may excuse himself in a capital case.
2. Inquisitio is a remedy outside the ordinary course, and of special law, and common law.
casus:
CASE. Point of the question. A certain Ser Ambrosius of Corneto is alleged to have struck a certain John of Bitotio with a certain woman from Suzza, from which beating he died in the year of our Lord 1371, in the month of July. And by the Vicar of Corneto, and his judge, and the court, a process was undertaken against the said Ser Ambrosius for homicide, dolus, and by inquisition. Upon which process, the procurator of the said Ser Ambrosius appeared by mandate of the Lord Cardinal Bictu, Vicar. Since it was alleged by the said Ser Ambrosius that he had killed the said John by accident, and he was admitted by the said judge and Vicar to respond to the said process, and to other proofs and defenses, the said procurator of the said Ser Ambrosius, in his name, as appears from the records, after the aforementioned Vicar and judge, having seen the defenses of the said Ser Ambrosius, condemned the same Ser Ambrosius pecuniarily for accidental homicide, and absolved him of dolus, and the aforementioned condemnation was paid, as appears from the records. Now, by the judge of malefices of the general court of the Patrimony, and its court, a process is being undertaken against the said Ser Ambrosius by inquisition. It is alleged on behalf of the said Ser Ambrosius that he has been preempted in the said court of the commune of Corneto legitimately, namely by legitimate citation, and also according to the subsequent definitive sentence, and the preceding litigation with payment, because he cannot be drawn to the said general court in first-instance civil or criminal cases, according to the privilege of exemption granted to the inhabitants of Corneto by the late Lord Pope Urban V. Now it is asked, what are the legal grounds for the judge of malefices of the said general court of the Patrimony, having seen and considered the aforementioned matters.

On behalf of the judge of the court of the Patrimony, it is alleged that the case is capital, and thus the procurator should not have been admitted; for a procurator intervenes in vain in a capital case, and thus preemption cannot be alleged, since the process conducted in Corneto was not legitimately conducted, as the legal constitutions require, etc. It is also alleged that before the judge of malefices of the court of the Patrimony, Ser Ambrosius has not yet appeared personally, which is necessary, since the case is capital. It is also alleged that preemption by a procurator should not be preferred, since it is expressly stated in the constitutions that no exception in a civil or criminal case shall have the power to impede the litigation, and that Ser Ambrosius must necessarily appear personally, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† That the general civic judge cannot proceed against the said Ser Ambrosius: although in the first trial he excused himself through a procurator, this is proven, because I say that, with the permission of the Pope, or of him who acts in his stead, one may plead a capital case through a procurator. See the gloss in q. 6, *hec quippe*. But here Ser Ambrosius had a special privilege of the *domus victurae*; therefore he duly appeared through a procurator, and thus conducted his case. Secondly, it is proven, because even under the *ius commune*, the act holds in a capital case in favor of the absent party, when through his procurator up to the sentence, inclusive, as in C. *de adulteriis*, l. *quamuis indubitati*, and in c. *iuris ambiguum*, de *regulis iuris*, lib. 6. It was therefore held that the act was done in favor of the said Ser Ambrosius. Thirdly, it is proven, because the outcome of the case sometimes demonstrates whether the procurator or minister intervened correctly in the case or not, de *damnis infectis*, l. *praetor*, § *si controversia*, according to Jacobus, and note C. *de petitione hereditatis*, l. *si putas*. But here the outcome of the controversy contains a condemnation to pay money; therefore, even if it were so that the procurator intervened improperly from the beginning, he is deemed to have intervened properly by subsequent ratification. For elsewhere, what was improperly begun is cured afterwards, ff. *de inofficioso testamento*, l. *si non mortis*, § *fi*. Fourthly, it is proven, because from any truth, since it has been proven that fraud is absent, fraud should not be imputed anew, or called into doubt, which has been made notorious by legitimate proofs, and especially by inquisition. For with inquisition, infamy must precede, as in *inuscissiones* and in c. *qualiter*, and c. *licet Ely*. And here infamy has been abolished by legitimate proofs, and it is notorious; the inquisition has no basis from which to consider infamy, and must be in the place of the debtor. But this is not infamy; therefore the inquisition ceases. Moreover, an absolving sentence, and if an innocent person is absolved, removes infamy. And here he was absolved from fraud; therefore fraud cannot be inquired into. Fifthly, it is proven, when the way to inquire into the same crime is open to two, preference is given to him who began first, ff. *de officiis consulis*, l. 1, and note in l. *sive contra*, § *j*, de *libero agnoscendo*, according to Dyther. But here from the beginning the way was open to the official of Corneto and to the general judge; hence the officials of Corneto, presuming to claim the entire office for themselves, acted, so that not, according to Archid. 11 q. 1, c. *de persona*. Sixthly, it is proven thus: from the first sentence arose the exception of *res iudicata*, and the exception of payment also arose from the subsequent payment; from the first chapter arises the exception of *res iudicata*, which can be opposed to the procedure through a procurator, because it is declinatory, according to the note in c. *venientis*, de *accusationibus*, according to Innocentius, and de *procuratoribus*, c. *in nostra*, according to Innocentius. From the second chapter, full liberation arose, de *exceptione rei iudicatae*, l. *si quis cum totum*, § *plane*. It supports what is noted de *praescriptionibus*, c. *super his*, according to Innocentius. Seventhly, it is proven, because the same delict should not be inquired into repeatedly, even if something is added or even subtracted, ff. *nautae, caupones*, l. *licet*, § *possumus*. Eighthly, it is proven, because all inquisitions are known to be instituted for vengeance, and in remedies instituted for vengeance, a lesser penalty derogates from a greater or more atrocious one, ff. *de iniuriis*, l. *quod senatus*; ff. *de accusationibus*, l. *senatus censuit*; C. *quando civilis actio*, l. 1, and note C. *de testamento*, l. *nullum*, according to Cynus.

† Ninth, this is proven by the theory of the gloss on the Institutes, *Si qua pauper*, §. *Si quae*, which is noted and commonly cited to the effect that an inquisition, because it is an extraordinary remedy and of special law, not of common law, as is noted in §. *Si publico*, is more easily excluded even in that which exceeds. Thus should that gloss be applied to our case. Tenth, this is proven because no one has a right in vain, D. *De inofficioso testamento*, l. *Si sub hac*; therefore, the judge of Corneto does not act in vain, although he does not have office, for he does not bear the sword without cause, as the Apostle says, and consequently his sentence is not in vain. And then it necessarily follows that it benefits the said Brother Ambrose. Eleventh, this is proven by l. *Sepulchri violati*, in the beginning, where, when the order of admitting persons is inverted, one must adhere to the sentence, and no account should be taken of the plurality of reasons. And thus says Dy and Guido de Summo through that law. Twelfth, and lastly, this is proven by l. *Qui de crimine*, C. *De accusationibus*, for one ought to be sent to the same judge on account of the same matter, not to be dragged before different judges, yet he absolved him. To this effect it is noted by Innocentius, *De constitutionibus*, c. *Cum M. Ferrariem*, and 2 q. j., in the beginning. And that the aforementioned are true for the last conclusion, see Innocentius in c. *Cum dilectus*, *De purificatione canonica*, where he holds this expressly. And I believe the same, namely that against the said Brother Ambrose one cannot proceed by the general court as a matter of law. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a church or a place for minors may be left to a corporation,
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the substitution of Raramont, in which he universally substituted the place of the Minor Friars, it is called into doubt,

Whether a legacy may be left to a church or to a place of the Minor Friars by a universal disposition, or not. For the text in the chapter *Exiui*, de Paradiso, § *Quia igitur*, in the title *De successionibus*, states that brothers and the order are not capable [of receiving legacies]; but it does not speak of a church. If, however, nothing is said regarding a church or a place, we adhere to the disposition of the common law, that the legacy is valid, in the Authenticum *De ecclesia*, title § *Si quis in nomine*, Codex *De sacris sanctis ecclesiis*, law *Si*; and such a legacy will not be contracted by the brothers themselves, nor will they touch it, nor apply anything to their own uses, because this is forbidden to them; but the procurator of the fisc, i.e., of the church, will take it, law 1, Digest *De iure fisci*. And thus holds Bartolus in his *Minorica*, an opinion which, with due respect to learned men, has never seemed sound to me, nor consonant with the minds of the statutes, saying that he considered leaving to the Roman Church, which is supremely rich and opulent, that which is left to the supremely poor, i.e., the church of the Minor Friars. Nor do I believe that, if the testator had been questioned about this, he would have admitted or consented to it; for if he wished to leave to the Roman Church, it was easy for him to say so, Codex *De caducis tollendis*, § *Si autem ad deficiendum*, *De pactis*, law *Tale pactum*, § *Si*.

Therefore, either we must say that by the name of the Church of St. Francis is signified the universal Roman Church. And this is against the mind of the testator, and against the nature of the species, which signifies itself; but it does not imply the prediction of law or of a universality, *De legibus tertio*, law *Si quid eorum*, § *Inter emptum*. Or [we must understand] a special church, as the words sound, and the mind of the testator. And then either of a church, i.e., of walls, and then that the walls take [the legacy] was an opinion condemned, which was held by Archbishop Moses, as noted in law *Sicut*, *Quod cuiusque universitatis*, number. Or of a church, i.e., of the collection of brothers, and then the Church is not capable, just as the order is not, said § *Quia igitur*. And it supports what Azo notes in the Summa, Codex *De sacris sanctis ecclesiis*, § *Videndum ergo*.

Moreover, it is ridiculous to say that it cannot be left to the brothers, but it can be left to the Church and the custodian of the altar, as Bartolus says; for what else is this but to cavil at sacred words and to profane the mind of the law? When rather, § *Mens*, *Quid dicatur animadvertendum*, Digest *Ad exhibendum*, law *Pe*, Digest *Ad Tertullianam*, law 2, § *Tractati*. And it would be to commit fraud from name to name, Codex *De secundis nuptiis*, law *Hac edictali*, at the end of the beginning; and *De legibus*, law *Fraus*, with the following. Whence it can be said to it: "Your letter kills, but the spirit gives life," Question 1, *Marizore*. Pope John renounced such acquisitions, as in the Extravagant *Ad conductorem*, § *Si*. And thus notes Johannes Andreae in chapter *Ultima*, *De pactis*, book 6, in the Novels. And thus the truth is, that such a substitution is not just.

But I think that it should be expended on pious uses, as law *Legatum*, *De iure legatorum*, *De relictis*, chapter *Quia contingit*. And from this chapter something may be converted to the pious uses of the Church and the brothers by the authority of the distributor, not by the mere judgment of the testator, as in the decretal *Dudum*, § *Vetum*, *De sepulturis*. For to pious uses of ornaments, or of buildings, of divine sustenance, and also to divine worship, they will be able to take, as is said in the said § *Quia*; the use itself takes, not the brothers.

I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If the testator makes a private substitution and does not state to whom it should be applied, it ought to be applied to the heir.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Magister Benedictus died while the testator was still alive; Nicolutius died twenty-five days after the testator, being over fourteen years of age, or intestate, survived by his sister Thomassutia; then, one month after the death of the testator, Massiolus died, and his heir demanded that mention be made of the orders given by the testator, leaving behind two pupillary substitutes and his own sons, who hold the property.

† It is asked, what is the law, whether they ought to be deprived of the said inheritance, or not, and to whom it ought to devolve. But it must be considered that the said substitution, which was made to the said Nicolutius, was fiduciary (fideicommissary), especially because Nicolutius died in adult age, as we read in l. precibus, and l. centurio, and in §. extraneo, and in §. qua ratione, and on this there is no doubt. Furthermore, it must be considered that a fideicommissum can be directly taken away and revoked, C. de fideicom. l. fideicommissum; de leg. 1, l. si ita scriptum; Inst. de codicil. §. 1. Thirdly, it must be considered that when a testator revokes a legacy or a fideicommissum, then such fideicommissum or legacy is removed from the equation, and the heir is released from its performance, as Inst. de adim. leg. §. 1, and the other authorities cited above. And by these points our question is resolved: for the testator, by depriving him who was substituted by fideicommissum, although he did not state to whom it ought to go, nevertheless there is no doubt that it reverts to the heir of the heir, to whom also provision ought to have been made regarding the manner of performance, as l. si tibi, de leg. 3; and C. de indic. vidui, auth. relictum supports this. In a direct substitution, there is greater doubt, per l. militis, eo. §. neratius, de mili. testa.; but in a fiduciary substitution, there is no doubt among those who have understanding. It appears, therefore, that the inheritance reverted to Tomassutia, because she is the legitimate heir of the said Nicolutius; but there is doubt, because these sons were pupilli, and the heir of Massioli, whether they have restitution in integrum. And it seems that they do, ff. de mino. l. 3, §. si quid filio. To the contrary, it seems that time runs in favor of the claimant, and it is a statute of time established by man, hence it runs without the aid of restitution, as is read and noted in ff. de mino. l. emilius largianus; and in law, the truth appears by equating testaments with contracts, ff. de leg. 1, l. quod in rerum, per Dy. Although this opinion seems very harsh, it is true in law. Therefore, the fideicommissum reverted to the sister, but with the burden of the other legacies, C. de cadu. tol. §. pro secundo, and §. in nouissimo. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a statute regulating wills applies to that which is outside the territory.
2. The right of deliberation may today be transmitted by one capable of dolus, and the authority of a tutor is not required.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the first point, it must be known that when a statute regulates mere solemnity, as when it states that two witnesses suffice in a will; or sometimes it regulates a certain capacity, as when it states that a woman cannot make a will without the presence of certain persons; or sometimes it regulates some performance, for example, that the heir must pay a tax. In the first case, the statute does not apply to acts performed outside the territory, because the place where the act is performed is considered with regard to the order of the act. In the second case, the statute applies even to acts performed outside the territory; otherwise, it would be easy to leave the territory and make a will there. For capacity and incapacity inhere in the person and follow the person, as stated in the law *Ex ea*, *De postulando*. In the third case, the place of the person is considered, not the place of the act, because the obligation refers to the person. Now, our case concerns the second member, and therefore a woman from Todi must observe the form prescribed by the statute of Todi in all places. But let us see that the lady was not a native of Todi in her own right, and her husband then had his domicile outside Todi; for the wife follows the domicile of the husband, according to the law *Exigere dotem* and the Code *De incolis*, laws *Miles* and *Cum quaedam puella*. It appears that, considering the domicile, the will made according to common law is valid. This is supported by the Code *De testamentis*, law *Si*, whereby in this case the origin of the law of her own city is not considered, but rather the pure domicile, as stated in the Digest *De capite diminuto*, law *Amisi*, section *Qui deficiunt*. And I believe this to be true, that the will of such a lady was valid, because such a woman was not subject to the law of the people of Todi, but to the common law, and therefore, being free from the statute of Todi, she could not be incapacitated by it. And even assuming that Lord Tarlatus was a true citizen of Todi, counted among the citizens and not among the enemies, it is nevertheless more true that domicile is to be considered in law, even with regard to the wife, rather than the origin of the law, as stated in law 1 of the Code *De mulieribus* and *In quo loco*, book 10. And by this, the answer regarding the will is resolved.

But it remains to be seen whether Franchius transmitted the unaccepted maternal inheritance. It must be said that he did not; rather, he could transmit the right of deliberation. Or, if he did not transmit it, his heir could, by operation of law, seek restitution in integrum, provided the four-year period allows it; otherwise, not, according to the rule on doubtful matters, *l. ad vos*. Nevertheless, I believe that the right of deliberation may today be transmitted by a ward capable of dolus, for this is such a favor that it cannot constitute any damage. Hence, the authority of the tutor is not required for such transmission, although it would have been otherwise under the old law, as in *l. si infanti*, § *si vero*, *de iure deliberandi*, and *l. cum antiquioribus*. And it is pertinent to the Code, *ad Orphition*, *l. non pro numero*. And it should be known in this regard that, under the common law, since there are no brothers united on both sides, nor children of brothers united on both sides, Pelionus, the uterine brother, succeeds. *Auth. post fratres*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether condemnations made before the concession are included when a castle is granted with high and low justice and full jurisdiction.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Our Lord the Pope granted to the noble and distinguished knight and doctor, Lord Nicholas, as perpetual Vicar, certain castles with high and low justice and with all temporal jurisdiction; and he granted to him the power to collect and apply to his own use all the fruits, revenues, and profits of the said castles, etc. It happened that before this concession, the community of one of these castles had been condemned by the Roman Camera to pay a large sum of money; now the Camera wishes to enforce that condemnation and collect the debt. To the contrary, on behalf of the said Lord Nicholas, it is argued that the Camera transferred all its right, both for the future and for the past, concerning the matters committed, granted, and entrusted to be collected, to the said Lord Nicholas; and that the said execution belongs to him, not to the Camera.

† The question is asked: what is the law? It is alleged on behalf of the Camera as follows: This penalty had been incurred before the donation of the castles, and therefore it does not appear to be included in the donation of the castles, D. Quod vi aut clam, l. Is qui praesentem, § Si postea. Moreover, this penalty was an external revenue arising from nothing, but was not a natural or quasi-natural accession; therefore, it does not pass by succession, by argument from D. De petitione hereditatis, l. Ac ubi. Furthermore, this is not a rent or revenue of the castle, since it is not collected by the Camera of that castle; just as in the peculium of a slave, that which the slave owes to his master is not said to be part of it, and when a slave is granted to Peter, or a slave is granted with his peculium, it is not understood that what is owed to the master is granted, as in D. De peculio legatorum, l. Si peculium, § Sicut, and l. Sciens.

To the contrary, that which appears to have been granted, is proved thus: This penalty is a fruit of jurisdiction, because they are renewed, according to Cynus in l. Divortio, § Si in fundo, Sol. Mai. and Eo. Tit. l. Si, per Bartolus, which the Church grants in that castle; because if it did not have jurisdiction, it could not impose a penalty. Moreover, it is a fruit not separated from the soil, since no collection has been made. But the castle granted to Lord Nicholas was granted with its fruits; therefore, these fruits are included and contained in the grant, because they still adhere to the soil, as in l. Si, D. De iure fisci, and in l. Fiscum, § Si, D. Quae in fraudem creditorum. Moreover, jurisdiction is a universal thing, and bans are natural advantages, natural revenues of jurisdiction; therefore, all things seem to have been granted, by argument from D. De petitione hereditatis, l. Item veniunt, § Fructus, and D. De usufructu, l. Usufructus, and l. Omnes. Moreover, with the universality, all rights pass, D. De contrahenda emptione, l. In modum; D. De acquisitione rei dominii, l. Quaedam; D. De re iudicata, l. Cum Bertoldus; D. De iure patronatus, c. Ex literis, per Innocentius. Moreover, benefits of princes, where they do not derogate from an alien, are to be interpreted most broadly, D. De constitutionibus principum, c. Beneficium; C. De bonis vacantibus, l. Si quando. Moreover, a prince, by granting goods, is deemed to grant rights and actions, D. De verborum significatione, l. Princeps bona. Moreover, this castle ought to be delivered free, not subject to any obligation or mortgage. For if this is so in a legacy, as in l. Si res obligata, D. De legatis primo, therefore much more so in benefits, which extend more broadly. Moreover, for this reason, therefore, he granted all things, D. De officio praefecti urbis, l. 1, § Cum urbem. Moreover, because the vicar acts in place of the owner, and is similar to a procurator, by argument from D. De fideiussoribus et rebus creditis, l. Si pignori, in fine; but a procurator appointed for the affairs of that castle can demand a debt contracted there; therefore, Lord Nicholas can also demand it, D. De solutionibus, l. Quaero, Sol. Quod supersit. It is to be consulted with our Lord the Pope, who should declare how he wishes his benefits to be, D. De re iudicata, l. Neratius. And that in the meantime such castles, on account of the said debts, cannot be molested by general collectors, since that which is specially granted and assigned to Lord Nicholas seems to be denied to others, D. De legibus, l. 1, l. Quod in rerum, § Si quis post, and there by Iacobs. Moreover, it is not probable that the prince wished to grant a castle emptied of debts, but a castle full of revenues. For the munificence of a prince ought to be free from diminution, as the text says in Auth. Constitutio, Qui dedignatur, § Illud.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A criminal act of maleficium is not proven unless the place and time are proven.
2. The place is proven in two ways.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Because a criminal act of maleficium is not proven unless the place and time set forth in the bill of accusation are proven, it must be examined whether, in our case, the place has been proven. For if it has been fully proven, condemnation must follow according to the proof; if it has not been proven on this point, acquittal must follow, as in C. de probat. l. sciant cuncti; C. de accusat. l. tunc convenit; and note, Extra de accusat. c. qualiter et quando, according to Innocentius. And this is clear from the example of Daniel, as noted in C. de testib. l. testium.

It must therefore be known that a place is proved in two ways, or its boundaries, by addition, as in the Digest, On Restitution, l. forma, and there the glossa ordinaria which begins, no. or cetera, and by special circumlocution, as in l. centum, Digest, If a Certain Thing is Demanded. But if the circumlocution is not certain, there is no place for punishment, as in l. optimum, Digest, On Conditions, and l. in testamento, ibid. l. 1, at the end, as in n. non procedit libellus, where the place is not bounded or restricted, much less does the statement of a witness hold, because the statement of a witness ought to be clearer than the libel, as noted in Digest, On Deposit, l. 1, § si quis argentum. Having premised these things, I come to our case. Two witnesses. Ruffinus says that the assault was made at the house in which Paulus lived; he does not say that it is the house bounded in the accusation. It is true that the word follows in the said house, etc., and this expression was made relative; nevertheless, it does not appear that the witness referred himself to the accusation, but to his own statement, and his own statement is uncertain; hence it proves nothing, unless he is recalled ex officio curiae to clarify his statement according to some, as noted in Authentica, On Witnesses, § quia vero, and Extra, On Wills, c. cum clamor, through Innocentius. And just as the libel would not proceed by saying that the assault was made at the house where he lived for the exercise of his art, without bounding the house or stating in which gate or parish it is, as noted in the said l. forma and the glossa ordinaria, so much less does the proof hold when it is uncertain, as in Extra, On Proof, c. in praesentia, and argument in l. si domus, On Legacies, 1, and it is read and noted in l. si, Digest, On Pretorian Stipulations. And thus it is concluded that the statement of Ruffinus does not prove, because he testifies about an uncertain place, nor does he refer himself to the place confirmed by the accusation, but speaks indefinitely, and from his statement it is not clear what place this is, and where the other witness is. Lucia suffers from the same disease. She testifies about an uncertain place, and not distinguished by boundaries. The libel of Coradus is that of one witness, and the statement of one is not believed, as in l. iusiurandum, or even of this there is sufficient doubt, but not clearly, although he speaks obscurely. My counsel therefore is that, things being thus, it is not proved, and the accused is to be absolved, etc. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Having received an emphyteusis for himself and his descendants, if the usufruct of the emphyteutic thing is left to the wife, and the sons do not wish to be heirs, but to have the emphyteutic thing, whether the usufruct is due.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A certain person received from a certain church an emphyteutic lease for himself and his descendants up to the third generation, without any mention being made that he received it as for heirs, but simply. Then, the emphyteuta dying, left to his wife the habitation of the emphyteutic property, while the sons wish to be the heirs of their father, but they wish to hold the emphyteusis by right of contract. Now it is asked whether the said wife ought to have the said habitation or not. To which I answer and say that the said emphyteusis passes to the sons, even if they are not heirs, and this is the opinion of Speculum in Speculum de locato, § nunc aliqua, verb. 158. And this is posited by the modern doctors in l. ut iureiurando, § si liberi, de operibus libertorum, and de verbis oblig., l. quod dicitur. And therefore the father could not bequeath the thing of the sons, if they are not heirs, as is fully read and noted in C. de rebus venditis, l. cum a matre. For who can accept a contract and repudiate an inheritance? C. de inofficioso testamento, auth. unde et si parens. I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, when a thing is sold together with its entire territory and district, all its integral parts are included, even if they are located in another territory.
2. On these points, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws, was consulted.
body: I will argue both for and against, so that the truth may appear more clearly, and then I will respond with that which I finally believe.

And it appears that what was first placed in the district of Humani is not included, because the territory of the Castle of Humani is set as a boundary; and therefore, when it comes to delimiting and limiting, it is not included in the contract, as in D. de contrahenda emptione, l. cum servo, §. fin. Response 2. When the boundaries of a father’s farm are established by designation, as in D. de coniuncto praedio, l. si quis duas, §. plane, and regions can likewise be divided, as is said there, rightly, nothing comes under the appellation of this except what is included within the designated region. And although the words in the first part of the contract were general, they are restricted by the subsequent ones, arg. D. de verbis oblig., l. si cum fundum. And although false boundaries do not vitiate the contract, nor do false names, as in D. de legibus 3, l. patronus, §. sempronio, nevertheless true boundaries limit and declare the contract, just as measurement does, as in D. de contrahenda emptione, l. ruptilia polla. And it supports D. de censu, l. forma, cum si. On the contrary, it is not so, because the words say “with the whole territory and district.” Therefore, all parts, both integral and adjacent, to the holding and castle come into the contract, because he who says the whole excludes no part, and parts are easily included, as in D. de procuratoribus, l. procurator tutorum, and D. de legibus 3, l. uxore, §. legaverit, and §. qui bene facit. And although the word “holding” is placed in the district of Aquapendente, not by way of restriction, but by way of demonstration of place, it has great force taken from the consideration of the price, as was prudently alleged, as in l. 1, de rebus dubiis, and l. 1, §. 1, de superficiebus, in the gloss. Secondly, I say that everything is concluded, because the words say “in the holding and castle situated in the contrary and district of Aquapendente, according to the thing and c. and other boundaries, and with the whole territory and district.” Hence, if one carefully observes the breadth of the territory and district, it is not here confined or restricted, but the breadth of the holding is principally sold and well bounded; therefore, because of that addition, “with the whole territory and district,” adjacent possessions come into it, to which no restriction can be applied, saving the reason of right speech, arg. D. de auro et argento legato, l. Plautius. Here let that conjunction “and other boundaries” be added, which is accustomed to enlarge, D. de legibus 3, l. ea tamen adiectio. I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Property subject to a fideicommissum may be alienated for the purpose of a dowry, and may be alienated up to the amount of the legitime.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† To Francischina, who died in pupillary age, her sisters, namely Vinera and Agnesa, succeeded by direct right, and without the deduction of any legitime or Trebellianic portion, because in direct succession the deduction does not apply. Agnesa, because the testament was null due to the omission of the mother, although under ancient law it was otherwise, but it must be purged by a querela inofficiosi testamenti, as in the Authentico de haeredibus et falsis, §. hereditas, and by Dy. in l. Gallus, §. in mag. distinct. Vinera could not succeed in the testament, nor come in as a testamentary heir, if the mother declares it null; but they succeeded intestate. s. mater. i. Dialtutia, and sister. l. said Vinera, as in the Authentico defuncto. Nevertheless, the mother was obliged to restore to Dialtutia, by virtue of the fideicommissum, one half, or she could retain the other half of the half for the legitime and Trebellianic portion on behalf of the daughter. s. Agnesis, because the legitime and Trebellianic portion are transmitted to the heir; nevertheless, it must be observed here that, however Agnesa Martini, formerly of the said, succeeds, the Trebellianic portion of the dowry is excluded by the form of the statute: because it is permitted to the daughter to alienate for the cause of dowry, as in the Authentico res quae. It is also permitted to alienate or bequeath up to the legitime, as in the Authentico de restitutione et ea quae parit, §. quamobrem. And therefore the husband must have the said third part computed in the said profit of Viviana. The mother and Nicolaus succeeded by right of the fideicommissary substitution made by Cana; the goods of Cana must be divided in effect as follows: because, after deducting the legitime and Trebellianic portion, if an inventory was made, otherwise the Trebellianic portion will not be deducted according to one opinion, or rather it is always deducted according to another opinion, reputed in the said legitime and Trebellianic portion, the said third part of the goods belongs to Agnesa: because it was left by her to her husband from paternal goods; the remainder that is left over is due for one third part to the mother, for two thirds to the fraternity, because of the fideicommissum double was left to the fraternity as well as to the mother, and that quarter to Andrea and Francis, because it was caduc, accrued by verbal conjunction in the manner aforesaid, because in the right of accrual the whole is the same as in the right of express substitution, C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutis, l. 1. and l. testamento, cum si. Moreover, I say that the Trebellianic portion is not deducted from the fraternity, because for pious causes the Trebellianic portion ceases according to the common opinion of jurists, but the legitime is deducted. Conclusion concerning all that touched Viviana by the testament of Cana: the mother has one half, from which she must restore two parts to the fraternity, after deducting a third of the two parts by name of legitime, and Nicolutius has the other half, from which he must restore to the said mother one half of a third, because he retains the other half for the legitime and Trebellianic portion, and to the fraternity two parts after deducting a third for the legitime. Let them make this computation from the abito. I, Bal. of Perugia, doctor of laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a will made before the taking of a wife and the acceptance of children is broken as regards the institution of an heir and as regards legacies.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Assuming that the said testator took a wife after making his will, and that two children were born to him, namely Ugolino and Magdalena, lawfully begotten by the said spouses, and that finally the said testator died while they were still living.

† Therefore, whether the said testament is broken as regards the institution [of an heir] and the legacies, or only as regards the institution of the heir, while the legacies remain valid, seems to be proven by the Authentica *Ex causa*, which has application in the case of the omission of a born child according to all authorities, and also in the omission of a posthumous child, as noted in *l. 1*, C. *de codicillis et fideicommissis libertatibus*; *l. Generaliter*, § *Ex testamento*, ff. *de manumissionibus testamento*; *l. Uxorem*, ff. *de captivis*; *l. Bona*, in the gloss, *pe*. Secondly, it seems to be proven by that clause: “If it is not valid by the law of testaments, let it be valid by the law of codicils.” For what is left over in the event of the failure of the testament remains valid, even though the testament is attacked by an omission. The case is found in the aforementioned § *Ex testamento*, ff. *de in iustis testamento*; *l. Posthumus*, § *Si paganus*, *de legatis* 2; *l. Lucius*, § *Filiam*. And thus holds Dyonisius. However, the gloss holds the contrary in the Authentica *Ex causa*, and Guillaume holds it in *l. Si*, C. *de codicillis*; others have it, according to Guillaume, in the aforementioned *l. 1* of that title.

To the contrary, that the legacies are not due, is proven first, because the Authentica *Ex causa* does not apply in the interpretation of a posthumous child, when the testator in no way considered burdening his children, according to the true opinion, C. *de posthumis haeredibus instituendis*, *l. 1*. And this is proven thus: a testament that is broken on account of an omission does not operate more than one that is not broken, such as a military testament, in which, however, there is the defect of omission? But the conjecture of the will dictates that the legacy is not due to the omitted posthumous child, whom the testator did not consider, as C. *de militum testamento*, *l. Sicut certi* and *l. Si cum vel in utero*. Moreover, a donation is stronger than a legacy, and yet it is revoked, C. *de revocatione donationum*, *l. Si nunquam ad diem*; ff. *de pactis*, *l. Tale pactum*, § *Ultimo*. Furthermore, here one would be acting against the omitted person, which ought not to be done, as ff. *de legatis* 3, *l. Ex filio*. Secondly, because that clause has words of the present tense, “If it is not valid,” etc., which condition is false, since the testament was valid from the beginning, as *l. 3*, *de in iusto testamento*. And thus the clause operates for nothing in the omission of a posthumous child, *de legatis* 2, *l. Si ita scriptum*, according to Dyonisius. And thus hold all the doctors. Indeed, some say that when there was no consideration of burdening the children, which is expressed by words of the future tense, the formed clause operates for nothing; because the will of the testator regarding the law of codicils is lacking, *l. Is qui*, and argumentum ff. *de militum testamento*, *l. Miles*, eo, § *Miles in supernis*. For in our case, the testator did not have a wife, and therefore he did not consider legitimate children. And thus ceases the will to burden the children, to whom all things according to the wish of the parent ought to obey, as *l. Testimonium*, *certa est conclusio mea*, that from the said testament nothing can be claimed by the said children, because that clause, proven by one ignorant and not considering the children, operates for nothing to the prejudice of the children, especially since it is proven by words of the present tense. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a tutor has promised a surety to keep him indemnified, to pursue his own claim, and to release him from the obligation, and has begun to act improperly in his conduct during the guardianship, whether the surety can be sued to be discharged from the said suretyship.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

The question arises as to whether, if a guardian has promised a surety to keep him indemnified at his request and to release him from the obligation, and subsequently the guardian began to conduct his affairs improperly, whereby during the guardianship the surety seeks to be discharged and preserved, this petition is valid or not. And it seems that it does not proceed, because there is no action for things that are impossible, nor can judgment be pronounced upon the impossible, as in *l. non solum*, *de actionibus et obligationibus*; and *l. Paulus*, *quae sententiae sine appellatione rescindantur*; and *l. si decesserit*, *qui satisdare cogantur*. But it is impossible for the surety of the guardian to be discharged during the guardianship, because the guardian himself cannot be discharged, *Digestum*, *de minoribus*, *l. minor viginti quinque annorum*, *ex aspectu*; and *Codex*, *eadem*, *l. de tutela*. And just as the guardian cannot be discharged, so neither can his surety. Moreover, the surety can then seek to be released as long as he remains in an obligation effective for bringing an action; otherwise, if it was not effective, *l. facere potest*, *solum modus*; and there by Jacobus, *Codex*, *mandati*, *l. pro ea*; and there by Cynus. But the guardian cannot be sued during the guardianship; therefore, the surety fears in vain in the meantime, *l. nisi finita*, § *finis*, *de tutoribus et curatoribus*; and the reason, *de distractione*. Moreover, here there was an act of disobedience, *de negotiis gestis*, *l. si quis mandato*. But an action cannot be brought on an act if it cannot be done by law, *Digestum*, *de legatis*, *l. apud Iulianum*, § *finis*. Since therefore the surety cannot be released during the guardianship, therefore an action cannot be brought for this.

On the contrary, because although he can be released, the surety can nevertheless clearly secure indemnity for himself, as in *l. si creditores*, *de privilegiis creditorum*. Hence, it is interpreted that what is promised is that which can be done, not that which cannot be done, argument from *de iureiurando*, *l. sed et si priori*, § *sed si rerum*. And this I believe to be true, that he ought to be kept indemnified in the manner in which it can proceed by law, namely by adequate security, not by release. And thus I say, and I, Baldus of Perugia, advise. I, Doctor, and to the faith of the aforesaid I have written, and I have signed with the seal of my name, always saving the substance of the truth, and the counsel of another who may judge better and more correctly.

I, Ser R., having been added by the said Lady Dialcutia, and by her special and express mandate, in place of the said Dialcutia, who is an heir and cannot write, I subscribe in her stead and name, affirming that the said inventory was made and perfected in good faith according to my conscience and in my presence, and that I am not aware of any malice. And therefore I have written according to the form of the law, I, such-and-such, a witness added and requested to attend the making of the said inventory, attended all the aforesaid in place of the absent creditors and legatees, and I have written: there ought to be at least three such witnesses. And I, such-and-such, notary, wrote and completed the said inventory in the presence of the said witnesses, who are of good repute from the said place, possess immovable property, and affirm that they know the said Viniana, and know the said Dialcutia as heir, and state that they are not aware of any malice, being requested, and I appended my usual sign. Two other witnesses ought to be added, whose subscription is not required. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
0. Whether emphyteusis follows the son, or daughter, or children, if they enter a monastery.
1. Whether it may be provided by agreement that one entering a monastery shall not succeed to the emphyteusis.
2. Whether a monastery is regarded in the place of a child, and to the prejudice of any church.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. On the aforementioned point, many arguments have been put forth by others with great wisdom, which I do not recount, but I come briefly to the facts.

† And it must be considered that, according to the true opinion, emphyteusis follows the son or daughter and children, if they enter a monastery, as noted in the Authentico *Ingressi* at the end, in the great gloss, and by Innocentius in the Extravagantes, *De probat.*, c. *In praesentia*. And it remains with the monastery, as the person of the monk, as long as the monk lives naturally, from the argument of *De legibus*, l. 2, l. *Peto*, § *Praedictum*, D. *De pignoribus*; l. *Vectigali*, D. *De locato conducto*; l. *Si quis domum*, § *Et hoc subiungi potest*. And similarly we say in usufruct, for the monastery is rather said to have the benefit of the usufruct than the usufruct itself, which is inseparable from the person, D. *De periculo et commodo rei venditae*, l. *Necessario*, § *Finis*; D. *De nova operis nuntio*, l. 4; D. *De solutionibus*, l. *Si usus fructus*. And this is a good similarity, because the gloss equates in the said Authentico *Ingressi*. Secondly, I premise that simple natural possession of a thing can be changed by pact, because contracts assume the law from agreement, D. *De deposito*, l. 1, § *Si convenit*. And in emphyteusis it is expressly stated that pacts are to be formally observed, and those which are outside the nature of the contract, as C. *De iure emphyteuticario*, l. 2. And especially the pact not to alienate is to be observed, as in the Authentico *Emphyteusis*, § *Sanctissimos*, and from the argument of C. *Ne rei dominicae vel temporariae*, l. *Universos*, and noted in C. *De conditionibus ob causam*, l. *A lege*, in the great gloss.

It remains, therefore, to see whether, through the two aforementioned pacts, or any of the aforesaid, an impediment is presented to the said monastery by the person of the said nun intending [to sue]. And it seems that this is so. First, because that pact whereby the said Lord Ugucio was to succeed in the goods, and vice versa, seems to confine and restrict the succession, so that it does not take place among the others, but only between those two, as in D. de vulgari et pupillaria substitutione, l. cohæredi, §. qui discretas, and §. qui patrem; and D. de verborum significatione, l. si cum fundum. Secondly, it seems that that other pact, whereby the said house could not be sold nor granted to a religious place, similarly stands as an obstacle: for he against whom this pact is opposed is bound to do and ensure that it does not go to a religious place, as expressly noted in D. de verborum obligationibus, l. si ita quis, §. ea lege; and it supports D. de legatis 2, l. peto, §. fratre; and D. de verborum obligationibus, l. in illa stipulatione per te non fieri; and D. de locato conducto, l. in lege; and D. de pactis, l. non impossibile. Moreover, it must be understood regarding any alienation, as expressly noted in l. 2, C. de usucapione pro emptore; and C. de fideicommissis, l. voluntas; and D. de testamentis liberis, l. statu, liberis a cæteris, §. quintus. For the word "grant," which is uncertain in the pact, has a general signification, D. de legatis 3, l. iusta, §. uxori, and l. uxor, §. 1; and it supports what is noted in D. de donationibus, l. pe. Furthermore, because the canon [rent] was not paid in the name of the said nun previously, therefore the case falls under the canon, whereby the monastery could confer [the property] to another, nor did it prejudice him to whom it had previously granted it by subsequently accepting the canon, as in D. quomodo et a quo, l. si partem, §. 1; D. de bonis liberis, l. octuaginta. For since the emphyteusis had expired, it could well be granted to another, D. de aqua quotidiana, l. 1, §. promittitur; and Extravagantes, de donationibus, c. per tuas.

† To the contrary, it is argued, because the glossa states that a monastery is regarded in the place of a son, so that the emphyteusis passes to the monastery as to a son, as the learned Doctor Dy. says; and this is true if one enters the monastery. Thus they say in the said §. ea lege. But this reason does not seem true in the case of an ecclesiastical emphyteusis: because, to the prejudice of another church, a monastery is not regarded in the place of a son, as in Auth. de sancta episcopali, §. hoc praesenti, and Cod. ad Trebellianum, auth. nisi rogati, in fine. Moreover, that statement is true only unless the case is expressly determined, from which action is brought by the form of a pact or testament. But here it is determined that the monastery cannot succeed; therefore, etc., as noted in ff. ad Trebellianum, l. Lucius, §. tres haeredes. Furthermore, if the monastery were regarded in the place of a son, even after the death of the son, the emphyteusis would remain with the monastery in its own person, because it is regarded in the place of a son; but that is false and contrary to glossa 3, auth. ingressi. For upon the death of the monk, it ends, by argument from ff. de usufructu, l. Sticho; Cod. de legatis, l. uxor patrui; ff. de contrahenda emptione, l. qui tabernas. What, then, should be said? Is it said that he sold or granted to a religious house by entering the monastery? And consider that this is not so, because this is done by law, not by the consent of the one entering, by argument from de legibus, l. ab administratione. Nor is the grant prohibited by law, but by human regulation, as in l. 2, ff. de rebus ecclesiasticis. And since the entry is lawful, therefore whatever necessarily follows from it is also lawful: because when something is permitted, it seems that whatever follows from it is permitted, provided it does not require some other external and separate act from that which was promised, as noted by Cy. in the said auth. ingressi, and Cod. de locato conducto, l. certi iure, in 3. quaestio, and by the glossa in ff. de pactis, l. Item, because of the similarity, on the contrary. And see Cy. in l. 1, Cod. si rector provinciae, and it is established in ff. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. 2, and there noted in ff. si ususfructus petatur, l. 1, §. 1, and ff. de servis rusticis praediis, l. 3, §. si haeres institutus. Moreover, the monk is more properly here the one enjoying the benefit than the emphyteuta, as in the said l. necessario, §. finis. And I consider this part to be true, that as long as this nun lives, her monastery has this benefit. Nor does it matter that she does not pay the canon, for another pays it, and it does not matter in whose name it is paid, because where we are dealing with the preservation of a right, it does not matter how it is done, as noted by Dyn. in ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. cum servus, and de usufructu, l. arboribus, §. quid tamen, and ff. quemadmodum servus amittitur, l. qui fundum. Moreover, the pact of succession between the first parties does not matter, because it does not thereby restrict the real pact between successors, as in ff. de servis rusticis praediis, l. cum fundo, which is very notable for this purpose. And I confirm the foregoing thus: a pact that is tacitly contained, if expressed, operates nothing, as in Cod. de fideiussoribus, l. non recte. But it seems to be tacitly contained, so that it not be alienated to a more powerful or another church, as in Auth. de alienationibus et emphyteusibus, §. si vero contigerit quemlibet. And yet, by entering the monastery, the right, or at least the benefit, is transferred to the monastery by the entry; therefore, etc. I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a voluntary witness, who is not adverse to the principal party, may object to a delegation made for a distance exceeding one day’s journey; a neighboring city is said to be such if it differs by ten miles.
body:
In the Name of Christ, Amen.

The most Reverend Lords of the Archdiocese seem to wish to commit the article of jurisdiction. On our part, it has been objected and said that the delegation is invalid, and that neither the Lord Bishop, nor the Clergy of Florence, nor Lord Simon can be drawn into this jurisdiction, since they are located beyond one day’s journey. But they reply and say that, although the Lord Bishop of Florence, his chapter, and the clergy have their domicile in the city and diocese of Florence, and that said city and diocese are distant from the diocese and city of Perugia by more than one day’s journey, and that even Lord Simon has his domicile in Florence, or elsewhere within the district, nevertheless the said mandate of jurisdiction was valid with respect to him, because the Lord Bishop of Florence, his chapter, or the clergy were not made parties to the suit, nor were they cited in the case; hence they are not necessary parties, nor indeed parties in any way, as noted by Innocentius in *de exceptionibus*, chapter *Cum inter priorem*. And thus they are not drawn in, but draw themselves in by making themselves voluntary opponents.

Furthermore, a person coming from the side does not change the forum, as stated in the Digest, *de iudicibus*, law *Venditor*; and in the Code, *ubi in rem actio*, law 1. Although this is not admitted unless he comes for his own interest, as in the Extravagant, *de testibus*, chapter *Veniens*; Code, *de litigioso*, authentic *Nunc si haeres*; Digest, *de inofficioso testamento*, law *Suspecta*.

Furthermore, their cause should not be said to be their own, from which they are not cited in judgment, nor are they masters of the suit, as in the Code, *de appellationibus*, law *Dominus litis*; Digest, *de appellationibus*, law *Ab exceptione*, section last.

Furthermore, they say that this cause is not even that of Lord Simon, nor does it concern him in any way, because the benefit does not pertain to him, nor is he cited as injured in his office, but rather on account of certain acts, albeit wrongly performed, and by judgment from a commission made to him. And he asserted injury by the then General and Apostolic Nuncio, and thus the entire circumference and entire breadth within which the city of Perugia is situated must be considered. And with respect to this, the delegation was not made beyond the proper limits, but within the limits. And that said Simon is not the principal adversary here, they prove because it is not concluded against him that he be condemned to anything, but only that the act performed by him be declared null or rescinded; from which rescission he is in no way obligated, nor damaged in any respect. And thus properly he is not a party, nor is he cited as a party, but because by his office he burdened the party, he is cited in the case, as in chapter *Venerabilem*, section 1, *de sententia excommunicationis*, book 6; and as noted by Innocentius in *de transactionibus*, chapter *De caetero*. If he wishes to defend his act, he may do so, but he is not compelled, especially here, because it is said that he had a special mandate from the Lord General, and thus it was not Lord Simon who burdened, but the Lord General, as in the Extravagant, *de appellationibus*, chapter *Novit*; and the argument in the Digest, *de legibus* 2, law *Unum ex familia*; Digest, *de mandatis*, law *Pater ex provincia*. For a mere minister is like a magpie and an instrument, and is not properly said to burden, as in the Digest, *de evictionibus*, law *Si pignori*; and as noted similarly in the Code, *si quis alteri vel sibi*, law *Multum*; and as noted by Doctorus in *de regulis iuris*, law *Quod quis mandato*.

Furthermore, they say, even if Lord Simon is the principal defendant, he can nevertheless be drawn here, considering under what name he is drawn, because he is drawn, so to speak, under another’s name, namely as commissary of the Lord General, who has a general domicile, or is without domicile, because he does not have fixed homes; therefore he can be drawn anywhere, as argued in *de damno infecto*, law 4, section *Abesse*, words *quod si nec habitationem habeat*.

First, they say that in this judgment a party is not required, nor does it have the form of a judgment, and one can proceed without a party, as otherwise happens in the Code, *si quis se ab haereditate abstinerit*, authentic *Si omnes*; Code, *ad Trebellianam*, law *Iubemus*; and in the Authentic *Et haeres et falcidia*, law *Si vero absunt*; Digest, *de bonis possidendis*, law 3, section *Pe*; *ille, cuius interest, videtur a iure*; law *Qui grauatos*. For that which was done by office without a party and without the form of a judgment must be revoked by the contrary office of the superior, as in the Code, *de accusationibus*, law *Absentem*; Digest, *de evictionibus*, law *Minut*; Digest, *de administratione rerum ad civitatem pertinentium*, by law 3, section *Graui*; Digest, *quod metus causa*, section *Suo*; Extravagant, *de purificatione*, chapter *Significantibus*. By the foregoing, they extend [the rule], although they do not allege such laws, they nevertheless allege reasons.

But I make this foundation to the contrary, and I say that the highest authority is in a contradictory judgment, but in every contradictory judgment the person of the judge, the plaintiff, and the defendant, otherwise it does not have the form of a judgment, as in *de iudiciis*, law *Inter litigatores*. Then I ask, who is the defendant here? If it is said that no one, the judgment does not proceed. Furthermore, if it is said that Lord Simon is the defendant, then I ask, who is the plaintiff? Then I ask, is he principal or accessory? If he is not adhering, because he is alone, therefore he is principal. If principal, then I have my intent, because a principal defendant is drawn beyond one day’s journey, contrary to section *Cum autem*, chapter *Statutum*, *de rescriptis*, book 6.

Furthermore, against Lord Simon directly a petition was offered, citation made, and it is an interpretation of the letters, and thus, considering the supplicatory, conventional, and citatory libel, he is a party, he is the defendant, he is treated as such, and the text in section *Cum autem* prohibits that they be drawn. And from this alone, that he is drawn beyond the terms thereof, therefore the rescript is invalid by the law itself, as in that section, and chapter *In si*. For there the treatment is prohibited, and the reason of that section is founded on the fact that one should not be vexed with so many labors and expenses. That reason seems to apply here.

First, I say that not only Lord Simon, but the Lord Bishop of Florence himself and the clergy are directly touched by this cause; it is in the interest of the bishop, chapter, and clergy to have coadjutors; and conversely, they could seek execution of the mandate and distribution for their own interest, just as a coheir acts against a coheir and contributes to the expense of a monument, as in the Digest, *de annuis legatis*, law 5, section *Pomponius*; Digest, *familiae erciscundae*, law *Is consequenter*, section *Celsus*. And from this mandate to contribute, a right is sought for the Florentine clergy to this collation; thus, and otherwise, the collation is sought by right of action or by the office of the judge, as argued in the Code, *de codicillis*, law *Si soror*. Since this judgment comes directly to the prejudice of the Florentine clergy, and to their greater burden, and since they are acting to avoid damage, therefore it principally concerns them, because interest is emerging damage, etc., as noted in law 1, *de sententiis*, *quam pro eo*. And although they are not cited by word, they are cited by the fact itself, because they know their cause is being acted upon, and also because he whose interest seems to be at stake is cited by law, because he knows, as in the Digest, *de re iudicata*, law *Saepe*. Therefore he is a necessary defendant, at least by the necessity of the cause, if he does not wish to lose his right. Why, therefore, is he drawn by the fact itself? Therefore they can oppose in writing, just as if a tutor were given to a ward by office, and the tutor appealed. For the ward, because his benefit or detriment is at issue, is said to be the defendant and principal party, as in the Digest, *de minoribus*, law *Verum*, section *Ex facto*; Code, *si de falsis allegatio*, throughout. And this cause, although it originated from the office of the judge, is nevertheless said to be the cause of the ward, and in it the ward, treated before the delegate, could defend himself by section 2, *Cum autem*. For there it is not cared for whether action or office is intended, nor is there any force in this.

Furthermore, it cannot be denied that the aforementioned bishop and clergy are provoked to judgment, as noted in *de opere novo*, law *De pupillo*, section *Qui remisit*; *de procuratoribus*, law *Non cogendum*, section *Si*; *de bonis*, authentic *Iudicium possit*, law *Si pupillus*, section *Defendere*; and as argued in the Digest, *de in ius vocando*, law *Libertus*, section *A patrono*, *quae benefaciunt*. Nor does the statement of Innocentius in section *Cum inter* stand in the way, because he speaks of an accessory person who is incidentally touched; here it is of a principal person, without whom the judgment cannot be founded. But a person coming from the side is not of the essence of the judgment, therefore he is not said to be drawn.

Furthermore, in every appeal there is an appellant and an appellee. I ask, who is the appellee here? The General? Not, because there is no mention of him here. Lord Simon, as his commissary? Not, because he performed his office of commissary, as in the Code, *de procuratoribus*, law *Inuitus*; *de solutionibus*, law *Hoc iure*; *de pactis*, law *Sed si tantum*; *de re iudicata*, law *Admonemus*, in the beginning; and law *Iudex*, *de arbitris*, law *Dicere*, section final. Therefore, either Lord Simon in his own name, or as the chapter and clergy, and in either way the rescript is invalid, nor can it be said that he is the appellant and not the appellee in this cause; because appellant and appellee are correlatives, or relatively applied. Hence one is not found without the other, as in the Digest, *de re permutatione*, law 1; *de acceptilatione*, law *Si*.

Furthermore, it does not seem that this process can be founded otherwise than if there is someone to receive the judgment, but outside the aforementioned there is no one, and if they are compelled to receive the judgment, by that very fact they are drawn to the forbidden examination, as in the Digest, *de iudiciis*, law *Sed et si restituatur*, section *Ex quibus*; and law 2, *de arbitris*, law *Non distinguimus*; and law *Item si quis*, Code, *de assertionibus tollendis*, law 1; Code, *de iurisdictione omnium iudicum*, law *In criminali*.

Furthermore, it is not true that said Simon is not damaged; indeed, he is damaged if he succumbs, as in the Code, *de excusationibus tutorum*, law *Si servitus*; and *de sententia excommunicationis*, chapter *Sacro*. Furthermore, it is a disgrace to him, which is not more than interest, as in the Digest, *si quis omissa causa testamenti*, law *Iulia*.

Furthermore, section *Secus* directly supports this party, because there it says that he who acts by office is to be sued if he commits [an error], therefore he is drawn. For if the Lord Bishop excommunicated someone by office, for this reason he could not be drawn beyond one day’s journey; because this limitation is general, as in the Digest, *de militum testamento*, law *In fraudem*, section *Si*.

But our adversaries greatly exaggerate this fact, and burst forth into one, saying that it is worthy to aid them. Then, from a false cause, they say they are burdened, because the city of Retina is not nearby, nor certainly situated; but is distant from our said place by six days’ journey and more.

† I do not know this measure, but in law we have that neighborhood is sometimes said, if it is distant by one hundred miles, as noted in ff. de damno infecto, l. 4, §. si tam vicinum. Concerning the hundred placed, I do not believe that it would be extended so much, as in extra de feriis, c. 3. See ff. de dominio, l. 1, §. 1. Whatever this article may be, it does not expedite us, nor the Lord Archdeacon, although I consider him a good and just man; nevertheless, he seems too arbitrary, and wishes to commit this step over the jurisdiction of the council of wisdom, and wishes to give suspected and consulted persons with deceit, unless I have it from you. And therefore I beg your lordship that it be written to me what I shall do, whatever I can: I doubt because of what I said, and because the fact is said to be by opinion: but this does not seem to obstruct, because although it is opinion as to the fact, i.e., mandate, nevertheless as to dividing the prestation and contribution of damage, it was done by Lord Simon. Also, as to the right of salary, it pertains to the recipient, ff. de mandato, l. idemque, §. idem Labeo, and ff. ad legem Falcidiam, l. cum dotem. And although they say that they committed by certain knowledge, because there is a distance of places: nevertheless these are true, because in l. apparet per acta, nor is knowledge presumed. And perhaps it is not sufficient, because that decretal has a derogatory clause. I, Bal. de Per.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A compendious substitution has the force of a vulgar substitution if the inheritance is not accepted.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Because the substitution made in favor of Marino and Antonio contains a vulgar substitution, since it was a concise substitution, which, even without the inheritance having been accepted, has the force of a vulgar substitution, as noted by Cynus and all the doctors in *l. precibus*, I say that if none of those instituted became the heir of the mother, the aforementioned last substitutes come in by virtue of the vulgar substitution, as in *C. de caducis tollendis*, *l. unica*, § *pro secundo*. And the reason is that when the testator makes several degrees of substitutes, excluding uncles, the second-degree substitutes come in, and the testament begins from the latter degree, as in *ff. de liberis et posthumis*, *l. 3*, § *fin.*, and as noted in *l. si posthumus a primo*, § *itaque*, and in *de vulgari substitutione*, *l. quaedam testamento*, and *l. si mulier*, § *ulti*. Because, however, we wish to argue from the text or from the glosses: if from the text, there the substitute is repelled because he succeeded from the first degree; taking the argument from the gloss of the said *l. si mater*, § *ultim.*, there it is said “therefore,” because the first substitution, and consequently the second, was limited in time, even if the son dies during the lifetime of the testator. Hence, if the first one dies, the condition fails, *ff. de liberis et posthumis*, *l. commodissimum*, and *l. Gallus*. And here there was no other limitation except that one, if he should die within 20 years, which condition was fulfilled. And if it is said that the substitution was made in some order, let it be exceeded; nevertheless, this does not prevent the substitution from beginning from the second degree of the substitutes, as in the said § *pro secundo*.
