For if the substitution is in the case of a lapsed legacy, the first substitution goes to that substitute, just as an institution does, as there. And it supports this, *l. §. in primo*, with similar cases. And it supports the institution in *de vulgari substitutione*, in the beginning, and *ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, *l. Publius*, *ff. de ventre in utero*, *l. pen.* And by this it becomes clear what is the law regarding the substitute appointed by Lady Vaneta. For, the facts being thus, they succeed, at least others besides the younger brothers; because regarding them there is doubt whether the substitution appears to apply to them, whatever some may say. Nevertheless, the friend does not succeed as a substitute, being excluded by the inheritance not having been accepted, nor transmitted by the instituted heir, nor by the right of deliberation. Regarding the paternal substitution, it is certain that the one who has obtained it succeeds, because in the vulgar substitution made by the said women, the goods of the impubes do not come in, *ff. de vulgari substitutione*, *l. si mater*, in the beginning. I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 0. The confession of the prelate alone is valid and constitutes proof in matters that pertain solely to him and his exclusive benefit.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Because it is the common opinion that, in matters which pertain jointly to the prelate and the chapter, the consent of the prelate and of the entire chapter is valid and establishes proof, as noted in the Authenticum *Hoc ius porrectum*, although the contrary is noted in the Authenticum *De non eligendo*, § *Si vero*. And we must say this: that in matters which pertain to the prelate alone and to his sole benefit, the confession of the prelate alone is valid, especially to effect a release, and it creates faith and proof; and above all, a confession made by a bishop is more to be presumed [valid] than one made by inferior prelates. It is not similar in the case of a tutor or a procurator, because the benefit or detriment does not pertain to them, and they are mere ministers, Codex, *De nova*, l. *Non abstulit*. But in the bishop, this is presumed to be his own right, at least beneficially, and therefore I believe that such confession proves [the fact], and it must be adhered to. And what was done rightly ought not to be retracted, especially concerning those things which can be called certain fruits and acquisitions, as in the Codex, *De administratione tutorum*, l. *Sancimus*, § 1. Moreover, the said confession was general, and it ought to be valid generally, Digest, *De poenis*, l. *Emptor*, § *Lucius*. Although it is not stated that satisfaction was made in money, it appears that satisfaction was made regarding 25 florins; nevertheless, satisfaction is proposed in another manner, which term is broadly interpreted, as in l. *Solutum*, § *Solutum*, cum sequentibus. And from custom, we generally see that bishops make such confessions, and they ought to have force in them, as if they were judicial confessions, so that they have compulsory effect. And it supports what is noted in l. *Certum*, § *Pe.*, *De confessis*, and in the Codex, *De transactionibus*, l. *Praeses*, cum sequentibus. I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a judge who formed an inquisition on the 19th day, based on a citation issued on the 20th, is said to have preempted the superior judge, who formed an inquisition on the 18th day, based on a citation issued on the 20th, given that the said judge formed the inquisition concerning the wound on the 17th day, based on a citation issued on the 18th day.
2. Whether one execution extinguishes another, when the penalties are not to be applied cumulatively to the same person for various offenses.
3. Whether cities of the Church possess the *merum et mixtum imperium* (full and mixed jurisdiction).
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Regarding the first point concerning prevention, having examined the inquiry formed by the authority of Narni, first concerning the wound, which was formed on 17 April from a citation made concerning it on 19 April, and another inquiry made concerning the homicide, or concerning the death resulting from the same act and wound, on 19 April from a citation made concerning it on 19 April, and having examined the inquiry made by the general chapter of the province, and concerning the same homicide, and against the same person on 18 April, and the citation made concerning it on 20 April; and having examined the constitution of the Lord Legate, which begins *Nonnulli*, in the end of which it is contained that if on the same day a citation of any official of a territory concurs with the general citation of the official of the province, so that nothing appears regarding the priority of time, the citation of the higher court is to be preferred, as having greater authority. The doubt arises whether the authority of the territory of Narni prevented in the process against the said inquisited persons, or not. If it prevented, it seems this can be proven from the fact that it is certain that in that inquiry concerning the wounded person, the said authority of Narni prevented in time. And this seems sufficient, because from the same act, concerning which the inquiry was made, the penalty of death ensued; hence, since it prevented concerning the act, it seems it also prevented concerning the right, and concerning every effect which can result from that act, as in D. de iureiurando, l. Duobus, §. Colonus, and §. Exceptio. Also, because in the first process the death seems to be included, since in the first inquiry mention was made of a mortal wound. And this is noted in D. de confessionibus, l. Qui Stichum, according to the third reading. Also, because the death is traced back to the day of the wound, as in D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. Ita vulneratus. Hence, since the right has supervened, it is feigned to have been well done from a past cause, as in D. de pignoratitia actione, l. Si vendidit, §. Ultimo. And this seems true, especially according to those who say that from the same process, and from the same instance, condemnation for the killing can follow, when mention is made that the wound was mortal. From which, as noted by Jacobus de Arena in D. de damno infecto, l. Damni, §. Sabinus, laws can be alleged for and against, which are alleged in Speculum, de actore, §. Viso, vers. Sed pone, and vers. Si quid vulnerasti, and the following.

To the contrary, it seems more true for the reason that the instance has been changed by the new inquiry, and the crime has been changed, because one species of crime is homicide, another is wounding; they are punished by different laws, and with different penalties: and the citation made concerning the wound does not bind concerning the homicide; therefore, it does not induce prevention of jurisdiction, because action is brought anew for another end, and for another effect; hence, the citation made in the first judgment is not valid in the second, and especially because the second judgment could not be instituted, since death had not ensued. Also, because the form of the process, and the form of the terms, has been changed, and a changed form seems to change its entire substance, as in D. ad exhibendum, l. Ultima; and supporting the above are D. de institoria, l. Habebat; D. de adulteriis, l. Denunciasse, §. 1; D. vi bono raptu, l. Praetor, §. Docere; D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. Si vulnerato servo. Nor from a confession made concerning the wound could condemnation for homicide be made without a new process, because there can be another defense which excludes condemnation for homicide, and not the penalty for wounding, as in D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. Huic scripturae, §. 1. And therefore I believe that neither by the process, nor by the confession concerning the wounded person, was the said prevention induced concerning the different process of death, because they are processes of different genus and form; and this concerning the first point.

† Regarding the second point, it seems to be said that one exception does not bar another, because although different punishments should not arise from the same act, yet here the penalties are not to be applied to the same fiscal treasury, but to different ones, due to the authority and force of the sentences; each merits its own execution, because they must impute to themselves the fact that they did not use the defenses which they could have used, since a sentence from which no appeal is taken cannot be retracted once it has become res iudicata. And although there would be inequity here, nevertheless all this proceeds due to the strictness of judgments and the authority of the sentence, as has been said: for they ought not to have omitted their defenses. Moreover, they ought to have appealed if the sentence displeased them, C. si saepius in integ. resti. postu. l. 1; C. sententiam rescin. non pos. l. 1; C. de re iud. l. 1, in the first response. But several actions for vindication should not concur in execution, as ff. de iniuriis, l. praetor edixit, § 1, and l. quod senatus; and all criminal penalties are forfeited for vindication, and the execution of one impedes the execution of another. This is true if the defendant has used his defenses; but if he has suffered himself to be condemned several times to different penalties to be applied to different fiscal chambers, and did not make his defenses, something is to be imputed to his own fault, argumen. ff. iudica. sol. l. iam ante, in the beginning; and ff. de cond. inde. l. qui ob rem non defensam. Hence he suffers this penalty not from the mere nature of the offense, but with the added fault of omitted defense. And this concludes the second point.

Regarding the third, I say that the said constitution does not prevent inquiry by the general court of the province; because the constitution was not enacted for the exoneration of delinquents, but only for syndics who were not denounced. Hence every month is appointed, not for commencing the inquiry, but so that in the meantime the syndic is not said to be in default. Similarly, because a term does not extend itself to anything else except that for which it is established, as C. de reb. credi. l. generaliter, § 2; and arg. ff. ad Ireb. l. a filia, § a calum.; and C. de leg. haere. l. sciant, joined with l. 2, § confestim, ad Tert.

† On the fourth and last point, I say that the cities of the Roman Church do not have mere and mixed empire, but the rectors appointed by the Roman Church have mere and mixed empire, in Spec. de iuris. om. iud. §. expedito, ver. ergo potestati. For this appears from the form of the privilege, which confers mere and mixed empire to the power, and although by custom mere empire may be acquired, as in l. iurisd. and no. in l. imperium, yet according to Guillaume, custom is never stronger, although the lords of the Popes in their lands, since he can abrogate and annul said custom and any other in the territories subject to his temporal jurisdiction at will, as he is of greater authority than custom, as in l. 2. C. quae sit long. consuet. ff. de sepul. vio. l. 3. §. diuus. C. de fur. auth. nauiga. and in auth. omnes peregrini. C. comu. de suc. cum si. For the absolute power of the prince cannot be restrained by the custom of an inferior, because an inferior has no power over a superior, as ff. de arbit. l. nam magistratus. And I believe the same of the lord legate, because the customs of the territories of the Church, which he can refer in any way, he could remove and abrogate: so far. Such customs are tolerated insofar as they are tolerated by the superior, as proved above. And I conclude this. On the said fourth point, I say that according to the tenor of said privilege, the power of said territory has such and such jurisdiction as the words of said privilege allow, from which one must not depart, as extra de priuil. c. posito, etc. I, Bal. de Peru.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When fraud is alleged in an accusation, if the fraud is not proven, acquittal must follow.
2. Causes that excuse from disturbance of possession.
casus: CASE. In the name of Christ, Amen. The fact on which counsel is sought is as follows. Having seen the accusation presented by ser Girardus cęterant. de saxofer. against Nasius perlegatum vitam lotale, and lady flor. and the acts and proceedings on said accusation, and the instruments produced by both parties, which are the parts of the judge.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Because in the accusation instituted by Lord Girard, fraud has been alleged. And where the case is brought with the addition of fraud, if fraud is not proven, acquittal must follow, as is read and noted in the Digest, *De furtis*, l. 1, § *Divus*. Therefore, I believe the accused should be acquitted. For although the constitution does not require fraud, yet where the accused binds himself and acts in the name of fraud, then fraud is of the substance of the proof; because the sole cause of action in the judgment is fraud, as in the gloss, *Oratio est*, in the said § *Divus*. And here fraud has not been proven, nor knowledge, and neither of these is presumed unless proven, Digest, *De probationibus*, l. *Quoties*, § *Qui dolo*, and l. *Verius*.

The second reason is that the possession of the lady of Florence prior to the month of March has been proven; and thus, since the time of the alleged offense merely continued said possession during the month of March, and although it was improper, it is not said that she committed a delict, especially now, until she is prohibited by the authority of the judge, as in l. 2, C. si per vim, vel alio modo; l. 2, ff. uti possidetis. The third reason is that it has been proven that the lady of Florence had an earlier possession than that of the accuser. Hence, she is not said to be using force, but rather suffering it, as in extra de probat., c. licet causam; and noted in ff. uti possidetis, l. si duo, in principio. The fourth reason is that the guardian appears to be excused by reason of her office, unless dolus (fraud) is proven, as in the notable argument of ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. athletas, § calumniator. The fifth reason, on behalf of the other accused, is that their defense adheres to the defense of the guardian, since their accession was with the said lady, as is gathered from the tenor of the accusation, inasmuch as we commit ourselves to the fact that they are accused as if of the same act. ff. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. si famulus; ff. quod vi aut clam, l. semper, § in sepulchro. Hence, the said lady provides them with sufficient defense, just as the master does for the craftsman, as noted in ff. de rei venditione, l. in re, § tignum. For by the right of friendship and familiarity, it was permitted for them to join, ff. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. qui iure; it supports what is noted by Dy. in ff. de verbis oblig., l. si stipulatus fuero per te non fieri, quo minus, in § ultimo; and ff. de religione, l. ossa, in fine. And possession can be retained through friends, ff. quemadmodum servus amittitur, l. qui fundum; and what is done through friends is as if done by yourselves, as in the argument of de verbis oblig., l. cum servus; de negotiis gestis, l. libertos, § fine. The sixth reason is that disturbance (turbatio) is not only of fact, but also of law, just as possession. And here there does not appear to have been an intent to disturb, but rather to use the possession according to her right, as in the argument of ff. pro socio, l. merito. For even if the reason is unjust, true possession excuses from dolus, as in C. de plagio, l. plagii; ff. de liberatione causa, l. igitur. Hence, therefore, the reason is that, assuming that the other accused did not use the aid of the defense of the lady of Florence, they can still say that the plaintiff did not prove possession, since it is proven that another could have possessed it: whose possession is not compared with that of the plaintiff, as in l. si ut certo, § si duobus vehiculum; and in l. 3, § ex contrario, ff. de aqua pluviae arcendae. The seventh reason is that the knowledge, patience, and will of the lady of Florence, since the matter pertains to her care and likeness, has the force of a mandate with respect to the others who joined, ff. de mandato, l. qui pater. For she appears to have used their help and service, and the society of the journey. Hence, if the access was permitted to the lady of Florence, it was permitted to those associating with her, as in C. de adulteriis, l. Graccus. And it is read and noted in ff. de vi et vi armata, l. cum fundum, according to the true opinion; and l. 3, § cum igitur qui corpus.

Notwithstanding the objection that it might be said that these things were ecclesiastical and returned to the church, because this is so with regard to law, but with regard to the fact of possession it was otherwise, since the possession was occupied by the said guardian, and since our question is one of fact and possession, not properly of law, l. 2, ff. si servi venditi. I therefore say that the aforementioned should be absolved, because even where there are several co-possessors who litigate with each other and equally prove possession, if one disturbs the other, he does not incur a crime; nor even if he expels from possession, because, all other things being equal, the contradiction of the thing is stronger, as in l. si servum, § sequitur; and it is the counsel of Speculum, that he who can, let him expel the adversary. Moreover, the said lady of Florence does not possess by force, or secretly, or by precarious title from the accuser; therefore, she ought to be absolved. ff. uti possidetis, l. 1, in fine; C. eodem, l. 1. And the others avail themselves of similar protection, as I have proven above.

I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The sons and daughters of brothers and sisters succeed together with the brothers and sisters.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

†. It is proposed that, upon the death of the testator, Bal. first died, being perhaps seven or eight years of age. Also, Catherine died, surviving her son Francis. Afterwards, the boy finally died in pupillary age. Now it is asked whether, since he died intestate, only his surviving sister, Floretta, succeeds him, or whether Francis, the son of another sister, also succeeds together with the said Floretta. On this point, I, Bal. of Perugia, doctor of both laws, consulted, say that the said Floretta and the said Francis succeed in equal shares; because the sons of brothers and sisters are called to the succession together with brothers and sisters, as in the Authentica "Ut fratrum filii," in the rubric and the black text, and in the Authentica "Cessant," C. de legatis hereditatibus, cum si, and at the end. I have subscribed and signed with the seal of my name. And I presuppose that the last substitution made to children and others was not direct, and therefore is not drawn to the whole, as noted by Dy., ff. ad Trebellianum, l. cohaeredi, §. et generaliter. And thus it does not oppose, ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. cohaeredi, §. ultim. I, Bal. of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether one who has peace within eight days from the day the ban is issued is considered to have it within eight days from the day of citation.
casus: OASV. The point is rational. Christophanus Lelli struck Ioannellus, servant of Thomas, in the face with effusion of blood. The offense was committed in the month of December. In the month of January, he obtained peace from the offended party. And after the peace instrument was celebrated, when the peace proceeded in the said month of January against the said Christophanus, a sentence having been passed on the said offense, within ten days the said Christophanus produced before the said Captain the instrument of peace. The Lord Captain refuses to admit it, on the ground that it was not made within eight days from the day the inquisition was formed, or citation issued, or excuse given. It is answered on behalf of the party that the said instrument ought to be admitted by the Captain, that it sufficiently satisfies the intent of the statute: when the instrument of peace is made after the offense is committed, and before the inquisition is formed, or citation issued, or excuse given. Now it is asked whether the said Captain ought to admit the said instrument or not. Having seen the statute of the community of Assisi placed under the rubric "That peace may be made for any offense, and concerning the benefit of confession," which statute is transmitted to you. I, Bal. of Perugia.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† I had previously given my opinion in the case of one who made peace within eight days on the day the ban was issued, and I said that it appeared to have been made within eight days from the day of citation: because a ban with the assignment of a term is a kind of citation, as is expressly shown in 15. q. 4. placita. He also alleged other laws, as above in consilium 366. But the case seems to be entirely different, because here the peace was made outside the term of the statute, and therefore I do not see it being valid by operation of law, as in D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. scire oportet, § consequens. But I believe the truth to be this: if it had been made after the term had elapsed, it would not be valid. For one must not depart from the form of the law and the term, and delay is harmful to everyone; but if someone is more diligent and anticipates the legal term, this diligence should not be harmful to him. Nor does it seem to be the intent of the law that one may not come forward before the time and provide for oneself as a precaution against future events, D. quam in fraudem creditorum, l. pupillus. Moreover, a peace made before the term endures during the term and after the term, D. de iure communi, l. placiana; D. de verborum significatione, l. verbum erit; and not D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. 1, § veteres. And therefore the peace was made within the term, just as we say then, now the term is captured. And this is supported by, if one knows the judge, D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. si iam facta. And therefore, let it be put, considering the intent and reason of the statute, and the other things mentioned above, that the said peace is valid and ought to be admitted by law. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When a deadline has been set by the agreement of the parties for raising objections, whether another postponement should be granted to the other party, or whether he should be admitted to raise objections.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Regarding the matter which is in question and brought into doubt in the case and controversy, it is argued before the learned man Marino Martini of the Castle of Mount of Saint Martin, arbitrator and umpire elected by Vannes Thomas on one part, and Andreas Vannutii, syndic of the chapter of the nuns of Saint Lucy of the said Castle, on the other part. Again, having seen the terms given by the said arbitrator and umpire to the said parties, and especially having seen the production made by the said Vannes of certain documents on the 21st day of the month of February, and the term subsequently given by the conscience and will of the said parties to oppose, whether after the said term another delay should be granted to the other, or the party admitted to oppose and prove against the said instruments produced, since Andreas asks for a new delay. Briefly

I answer that, since the aforementioned term was peremptory, and after the said term the said Andr. is to be admitted not to oppose, because he did not oppose within the said term, as noted in *qui accusare non possunt*, l. *si eo*, ff. *de operis legatis*; l. *mancipiorum*; and fully noted in c. *saepe*, de *veritate sigilli*, in the Clementines; *ad iuvenem facit*, ff. *de feriis*; l. *oratione*; and what is noted in the same title, l. *si*, and ff. *de accusationibus*, l. *cum Titia*. And this is true, unless the said Andr. alleges and proves that he was impeded within the said term, as noted in the said l. *oratione* and in the said l. *si*, ff. *de feriis*. A just cause of impediment is the absence of the advocate, as noted in ff. *qui ex causa maiestatis*, l. *ab hostibus*, § *final*, with the following law; and C. *rem publicam bona possidere*, l. 1. Or unless the said syndic petitions in the name of the monastery for restitution in integrum, as in extra *de restitutione in integrum*, c. *coram Felici*. Of which the arbitrator can incidentally take cognizance, C. *ubi et apud quos*, l. *si*. And the same is said of probatory terms, and that a term cannot be admitted for proving, unless impediment is proved or by way of restitution, as has been said. And the proofs subsequently made by witnesses admitted with that protestation, if and insofar as he is bound by law, and otherwise not, since the said witnesses ought not to be admitted by law, are invalid by law according to the said laws and arguments, ff. *de compensatione*, l. *quod in diem*, § *si rationem*. If the arbitrator were aware of the impediment, because it was publicly notorious, or even known to him, because the arbitrator ought to adhere more to truth than to scrupulosity, and before him a formal process is not required, as noted by Innocentius in c. *Quintavallis*, and noted by Dyther in the consultation beginning *Tholomaeus Manentis*. For if the arbitrator can take from the right of one party and give to the other, not in a large quantity, as noted in § *recepisse*, therefore much more can he impose a burden regarding a term, arguing from a matter of temporary nature, as ff. *de milite testamento*, l. *miles ita haeredem*, § *et quia*. And we say, ff. *de verbis obligatis*, l. *qui Romae*, § *Calimachus*. I, Bal. de Peru., doctor of laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A deceased person who leaves behind grandsons through a daughter is not said to die without children.
2. The right of children in intestate succession is prior and stronger.
3. Whether granddaughters through a daughter are excluded from intestate succession when a grandson through a brother exists, given a statute providing that, upon dying without children, the nearest person of the said agnation up to and including the third degree shall succeed to those surviving him, or to any person surviving him. Also, given another statute providing that no daughter, granddaughter, and other persons inscribed therein shall see [inherit], as you have seen.
4. If a substitution has been made, and one of the heirs died without sons, whether another or others succeed, or whether they succeed to the last one dying without sons, or whether, when granddaughters through a daughter are admitted, the sons of other brothers are admitted to the exclusion of granddaughters through a daughter.
5. A fideicommissary substitution is not transmitted.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The point on which legal opinion is requested is as follows. A certain person named Ugolino Oduccio Pauli of Todi died intestate, with nephews born of his daughter surviving and living after him, and with a nephew born of his full brother also surviving and living after him. It is now asked to whom, according to law, the inheritance of the said Ugolino belongs: whether to the nephews through the daughter, or to the nephew born of the full brother, having regard to the statute of the commune of Todi concerning intestate successions, which statute is transmitted to you. On the aforementioned point, it must be preliminarily stated for clarity,

† That he who dies leaving surviving grandchildren through a daughter is not said to have died without children, as in C. de condicione inserta, l. 1, and there noted. Secondly, it must be premised that in intestate succession, where collaterals are excluded,

† The prior and stronger reason is that of the children, by virtue of which they succeed in preference to all others, as in the Authentica *De haeredibus ab intestato*, § 1; and in the Code *De suis et legitimis*, l. *final*; and in the Authentica *In successione*. Thus, according to the *ius commune*, there is no doubt that the nephews through the daughter succeed to the said Ugolino, who died intestate, to the exclusion of the brother’s son without a nephew in the transverse line.

But a doubt arises in the present case from the form of the statute of Todi, and likewise from the form of the testament of the said Oduccio. For the statute of the city of Todi provides that if any person of the city or county of Todi dies intestate without surviving children, or without any persons surviving him up to the third degree of his agnation, inclusive, the nearest relative of his said agnation shall succeed him, etc. By which statute cognates seem to be preferred to cognates. Hence it appears that the sons of a brother are preferred to the grandson and the daughters. Likewise, another statute provides that no daughter, granddaughter for a granddaughter, or from a granddaughter of any of the persons listed below, concerning whose succession it is treated, nor any person of whatever sex or degree, descending from such a person through the female line, shall succeed, or ought to succeed, or be able to succeed intestate in any of his father, mother, grandfather, grandmother, great-grandfather, great-grandmother, from grandfather, from grandmother, intestate deceased, or deceased woman, nor shall she be heard in the said succession by suing or pleading, while any of the aforementioned persons, thus deceased, has any legitimate and natural son of a lower degree descending through the legitimate and natural male line from such deceased person, concerning whose aforementioned succession it is treated, and accepting that succession, etc. Likewise, the testament of the adopted son contained as follows, etc.: In all his other movable and immovable goods, rights, and actions, wherever situated, he instituted Ugolino, Masciolo, John, Napoleon, and Polutio, his sons, and each of them, and for an equal portion, as his heirs, with this condition added,

† namely, that if any one of them should die without legitimate children born of him, he substituted another, or others, who survived. From this substitution it may be called into doubt whether the son of the predeceased brother should be admitted to any share upon the death of the said Ugolino, as is proposed. For according to the glossa ordinaria on the Digest, De acquisitione et oblatione hereditatis, in the law Is cuius liberti, conditional legacies are transmitted. But it seems to me that, notwithstanding the said statutes, in the said testament, I say that the nephews through the daughter are to be preferred to the said nephews through the brother. The first foundation of the claim of the said nephews is from the common law, which suffices for them, unless something is proved that excludes them from the benefit of the common law, as in the Digest, De probationibus, in the law Ab ea parte. But here nothing of the sort is proved; therefore, the common law must be followed. For the first statute concerning intestate successions does not stand in the way, because it speaks of a case where someone died intestate without children; but in our case, he died with children, because the nephews through the daughter are among the children, for they are descendants, who are included in the appellation of children, as in the Digest, De verborum significatione, in the law Cognoscere, section Liberorum; Digest, De gradibus, in the law Iuriscosultus; Digest, De liberis praeteritis, in the law Maximum vitium; in the Authenticum, De hereditate ab intestato, section 1. Hence, the said statute does not stand in the way. Furthermore, another statute, that female daughters do not succeed intestate when a male survives, does not stand in the way, because it speaks of a case where males surviving through the male line are present; but here they are not present; therefore, the statute does not claim a place in our case, because when the males cease, the favor towards them and the exclusion of females and descendants from them cease, because whenever one person is the immediate cause of the exclusion of another, when that person ceases, the exclusion ceases, as in the Digest, De iniusta testamento, in the law Posterum; De liberis et posthumis, in the law Gallus, section In omnibus; and in the law Inter cetera; Digest, De inofficioso testamento, in the law Pater filium; and in the law Si is qui. Furthermore, the testament of Oductius does not stand in the way, because from the last survivor no substitution was made; hence, the last survivor is free from the cause of substitution, as in the Digest, Ad Trebellianam, in the law Haeredes mei, section Cum ita.

† For neither is a conditional substitution transmitted. For just as a direct conditional substitution does not admit of transmission, as in the Digest, title De suis et legitimis heredibus, law Si ex pluribus; so also does a fideicommissary substitution, as in the cited section Cum ita; and in the Code, title De fideicommissis, law Cum si; and law Si in personam; and in the Code, title De caducis tollendis, law Si autem, section Aut quid; and section Pro secundo; and noted in the sole law of the Code, title De his qui ante apertas tabulas. And especially where the testator says, “I substitute the survivor.” For he considers the order of death, and it appears from the nature of the words that the substitution is made in the name of the last to die; afterwards the condition of the substitution fails, because it lapses with the children, as in the Code, title De conditionibus insertis, law 1; and title De institutionibus et substitutionibus, law Generaliter, last section, with many similar authorities.

I, Baldo de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A usufruct first left under a condition, and secondly by way of substitution, if the substitution takes effect, is due, even though the condition under which it was first left has failed.
2. Whether a usufruct in alienated things accrues to the usufructuary.
casus:
CASE. In the name of Christ, Amen. The point of the question is this: A certain servant of Manerto made his will, in which he left several legacies; among others, he left to Clarutia, his niece, 200 livres for her dowry, so that she might marry, and ought to marry; and if she did not wish to marry, but wished to remain in the house chaste and honestly without marriage, she should have food and clothing. Furthermore, he instituted his son Francis as universal heir of all his goods; and if the said son should die without legitimate children, he left the usufructuary ownership to Savina, the wife of the said testator. Finally, the son died without children. Now, this Clarutia, being a usufructuary together with the wife of the said testator, alienated certain usufructuary possessions without the consent of the other usufructuary, namely, the wife of the said testator. With the passage of time, this Clarutia gave herself in marriage with the dowry left to her by the testator, as above. It is now asked, first, whether she, being a usufructuary before she married, could sell the said possessions, or the usufruct, and whether the sale was valid; and if she could then sell the right of use, whether now, being married, the said sale is rescinded and reverts to the other usufructuary. Second, whether this Clarutia can now in any way claim anything from that usufruct. Third, whether that usufruct accrues to the other usufructuary.

I, Baldo de Perusio.
body: In the name of Christ. Amen.

† Because the usufruct left by way of substitution to the aforementioned granddaughter and wife was not left to the grandson himself on the condition that he should not marry, but freely, I believe that even if he married, he ought to have the usufruct, so that he does not lose it by marrying, ff. ad Trebellianum, l. mulier, §. cum proponeretur. But because Clarutia alienated [the property], it must be seen whether the usufruct of hers perished in the alienated things and accrued to the wife of the testator. For sometimes the usufructuary alienates the very right of usufruct, and then the usufruct perishes, consolidating with the ownership, or accrues to another joint usufructuary, as in Inst. de usufructu, §. finitur. Likewise, sometimes he alienates the simple benefit of the fruits, and then the usufruct does not perish, de periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. necessario, §. finalis. Sometimes he wishes to alienate the ownership itself, and yet I believe that he intends to fully eradicate it from himself, so that the usufruct in such alienated thing perishes, arg. l. finalis, C. de iure emphyteuticario.

And therefore I believe that it accrued to the wife, to the prejudice of whom an alienation could not be made, as stated in the law *Fundus Trebonianus* and the law *Is qui* regarding usufruct. Unless the alienation was made for the purpose of the legitime, if any is due to such a grandson as a descendant, because it may be deducted by way of alienation in a single thing, as noted in the Authenticum *De restitutione* and *Ea quae parit*, § 1, and in the Authenticum *Res quae*, according to the doctors. But if the grandson was the son of a brother or sister, then the legitime has no place. And thus I say, and I, Baldus of Saxoferrato, doctor of both laws, advise. And to the truth I have subscribed and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A remission must be granted to the lessor if he could not use the leased thing due to superior force.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the lease of the mills made by Brunitia of Cisiola, which appears from the public instrument of Francis, son of Peter,

And assuming that, by force majeure to which no resistance could be offered, he was unable at a certain time to collect the fruits from the said Mills due to the division of the said Mills made by the members of the Angelic society, I say that a remission of the pension, or of the coctium, ought to be made pro rata temporis, as in D. 19.2, l. item quaeritur, §. extra; and D. 19.2, l. si merces, §. ius maius; C. 4.65, l. excepto sed. Although it may seem to be glossed otherwise in C. 4.65, l. damnum, the truth is as I first stated. And regarding l. damnum, say that there the damage occurs to the tenant’s goods, not to the leased thing, as there by Cynus, no. Baldus.

USAGE.

In the name of Christ, Amen. The fact, concerning which counsel is sought, is as follows: A certain man died, leaving surviving his mother, wife, infant son, and father-in-law. The said wife, without having a guardian appointed for the said infant son, entered into a second marriage. Afterwards, the said pupil son died after the death of his father, after many years, leaving surviving his mother, paternal grandfather, maternal grandmother, and full uterine brother. Now it is asked, which of the aforementioned shall succeed to the inheritance of the said pupil, now deceased in the manner aforesaid.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a deceased person leaves behind a surviving mother, wife, infant son, and father-in-law, and the wife, without having appointed a guardian, enters into a second marriage, and if the said son subsequently dies leaving behind a surviving mother, paternal grandfather, maternal grandmother, and a uterine full brother, who is to be admitted to the inheritance of the ward?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

This question is sufficiently doubtful, for since the maternal grandfather was the legitimate tutor, he does not seem to be excluded, because the ward had a legitimate tutor, as noted in the commentary on the law *Matres* in the title *De senatu consulto Tertulliano*. The mother is preferred to the grandfather and grandmother in succession according to the prerogative of degrees. Likewise, she is preferred to the uterine brother, as in the *Authenticum Defuncto*, and as noted by Cynus in *Communia de successionibus*, *Authenticum Itaque*, verse 3, case. But my teacher says that, since the mother has the right of preference in guardianship, if she does not petition for another, or if she herself does not administer the guardianship, she loses the succession; for she ought to have done one of two things: either petition for another, or accept the guardianship herself, *Digestum*, *Ad senatum consultum Tertullianum*, law 2, § *Si mater*, verse *Quid si pater*. It cannot be said that she has a legitimate tutor as long as the mother is present and is capable of guardianship. She is all the more repelled from the succession if, by marrying, she spurned her son, *Codex*, *Ad legem Iuliam*, law *Omnem*. For those who sin more by not petitioning and by marrying than those who merely do not petition; yet she does not marry, as argued in the *Authenticum De nuptiis*, § *Si autem tutelam*. If we hold that the Gloss speaks also according to the new laws, these laws apply in this case. The objection from the verse *Quid si pater* does not hold, for there was no legitimate tutor there, since the mother was a potential testamentary guardian; for she could have obtained from the prince her confirmation as testamentary guardian, just as she had been left as such by her husband. It appears that the mother renounced the guardianship ipso facto by marrying, as argued in the *Digestum*, *De divortiis*, law *Quod ait lex*. Hence the legitimate heir succeeded immediately, especially here. However, according to those who say that the legitimate heir is preferred to the one petitioned by the mother, it was in vain that she did not petition, and it is not imputable to the mother that she did not do what would have relieved her of any burden. The objection from § *Si autem tutelam* and law *Omnem* does not hold, for there the mother was guardian, hence the one petitioned by the mother succeeds in the mother’s place in guardianship; therefore he is rightly petitioned and excludes the legitimate heir. Since he can be petitioned with effect, the mother is punished if she does not petition. Moreover, she ought to have rendered an account of the administration, as in law *Omnem*. What Cynus notes in the *Authenticum Matri et aviae* in the 8th question supports the foregoing. If the mother had accepted the guardianship and married in the manner described, I say she is repelled from the succession of her son, as in law *Omnem*. But if the mother was not guardian, I do not believe she is repelled from the succession. For she is not excluded by the fact that she did not petition, because she had no right to petition due to the existence of a legitimate tutor, or because she did not administer it; nor is she repelled for this reason, because she abstained by permission of the law, since guardianship in the mother and grandmother is voluntary. But who shall succeed where the mother is excluded? I answer that here it cannot be said that the grandmother is excluded on account of the tutor not being petitioned, for two reasons: first, because the grandfather is the legitimate tutor, to whom she is not preferred; second, because he who has the way open by reason of the tutor not being petitioned will not be excluded by another if he himself does not petition, *Digestum*, *Ad senatum consultum Tertullianum*, law 2, § *Si*. Likewise, the grandfather is not excluded, for he was so by law itself, although he did not administer it in fact, as argued in the *Digestum*, *De excusationibus tutorum*, law *Nensenius*. Likewise, the uterine brother is not preferred to these, nor does he concur with them, as in the *Authenticum Defuncto*. I therefore conclude that, the mother being excluded, the grandfather and grandmother succeed, and the uterine brother is referred to the right of the son and the guardianship, as stated. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Sole faith, and the singular error of the contracting parties regarding a prohibited degree of kinship, does not render the marriage valid.
2. Whether a legacy made to someone with a false quality inserted therein is valid and binding.
3. An exception that must be proved before the bishop may be raised before a secular judge.
4. Whether the provision of a statute applies to a citizen not originally residing within, even outside the territory of that statute.
casus: CASE. The fact upon which counsel is sought is as follows. Lady Joan of Santa Flora married John Vignali, a citizen of Siena, and had a daughter by him named Catherine. Then the said John died, the said Lady Joan and the said Catherine surviving. Afterwards, the said Lady Joan contracted marriage with G. of Santa Flora, a citizen of Siena. This G. was related to the said Joan in the third degree according to canon law, and lived with the said G. as his wife for many years. Then the said Joan died, having made a testament by which she left to the said G. certain possessions situated in the County of Siena and in the Castle of Santa Flora, in which consisted half of the assets of the said Lady Joan, and she instituted the said Catherine as heir. It is proposed that the said Castle of Santa Flora is not part of the County of Siena, and that the said testament was made in the Castle of Santa Flora. It is further proposed that by some the said Lady Joan was considered the wife of the said G., and was held and treated as such. Several questions are asked. First, whether the said legacy made to the said G. by the said Joan held in law, and can be exacted from the heir of the said Lady Joan, assuming that the said G. and the said Lady Joan were ignorant of their kinship; and what if it is proved that there was public fame in the Castle of Santa Flora concerning the kinship of the said Joan and G. at the time of the contracted marriage and before. Second, assuming that the said legacy is not due in law, whether before the secular judge, before whom the heir of the said G. claims the said legacy from the heirs of the said Lady Joan, he can oppose the kinship and prove it before him, or whether this must be proved only before the ecclesiastical judge. Third, it is asked whether, assuming that the said G. was capable of receiving the legacy, the said Catherine or her heirs can say that they are not bound by the name of the said legacy except up to the fourth part by virtue of the statute, which is transmitted to you; or whether, notwithstanding the foregoing, the legacy is due up to the dodrans. It is alleged that the testator was not originally a citizen of Siena, nor did he make the testament in the city or commune of Siena, and therefore the disposition of the statute does not claim place in the present case, nor in the goods which are in the city or commune of Siena. On all these matters, with the laws alleged, counsel is requested.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the first point, it must be premised that good faith alone, and the singular error of the contracting parties regarding a prohibited degree of kinship, does not render the marriage valid, when it is prohibited by the impediment of consanguinity or affinity, as is stated in C. de incest. nupt. l. cum ancillis; ff. de ritu nupt. l. qui in provincia, §. diuus; and extra de clandest. despons. ca. cum mihi, together with si.

Secondly, it must be premised that when something is left to someone with a false quantity inserted, either the true quality induces a legal prohibition, and the legacy is invalid, as if the testator were to bequeath to a spurious child whom he considered legitimate, as in Auth. quibus modis naturalis effectus legitimi, §. ultimo, and D. de probat., l. qui testamentum; or the true quality does not induce a legal prohibition, and then either that putative quality concerns the affection of the testator, or it does not. In the first case, either the testator knew that the quality did not exist, and then the legacy or bequest is valid, D. de hered. instit., l. nemo qui, §. 1; or he was mistaken, and then it is invalid, C. de hered. inst., l. nec apud; C. de fideicomm., l. eam quam; or it is doubtful, and then either the knowledge of that quality consists in fact, and error is presumed, and the bequest is invalid, whether this quality is natural or accidental, as noted in C. de hered. instit., l. si pater, and l. non ideo; C. de testib., l. neque professio; or the knowledge of that quality consists in law, and knowledge is presumed, and the bequest is valid, C. de hered. instit., l. non ideo. If, however, the quality does not concern the affection of the testator, the demonstration of falsity does not vitiate, D. de hered. instit., l. quoties; D. de condit. et demonstr., l. demonstratio falsa. From this it is concluded that in this case, the lady Joan left [something] to William as her husband, although he was not of consanguinity and affinity, having [the impediment], such that such a bequest is invalid by law, as is proven by the aforementioned laws. Moreover, if the woman and the man knew that the impediment still existed, the bequest is nevertheless invalid, as in C. de incestis nupt., l. si quis incesti.

† On the second point, I say that if the exception did not hold, the said legacy may be pleaded before a secular judge; but proof of affinity must be made before the bishop, Extra, de ordine cognitionis, c. Tuam, cum si. On the third point, because the question does not proceed on the basis of a proven impediment to marriage, there is no need to deliberate. But because condi.

† It is asked, what is the law, if the aforementioned G. were capable of receiving a legacy: for anyone is presumed capable unless the contrary is proved, as is well known. D. de legatis 1, l. Lucius, §. ultimo; and D. de probat., l. ab ea parte, because the common law is written with respect to persons, unless certain persons are proved to be excepted. I answer, and I premise, that marriage has the force of origin: for the origin of the husband is considered to be that of the wife through the union of the sacrament of marriage, because the wife is joined to the husband as to the more worthy one, and the condition of those united is the same, as is noted. C. de municip. et origin., l. originis. It is relevant, C. de incolis, l. mulieres; D. de minor., l. mino.; l. filii libertorum, §. 1; and l. eaque, noted. Hence it is that statutes, which bind the husband by reason of origin or domicile, bind the wife, as D. de iudic., l. exigere dotem. Likewise, marriages which are not valid in law do not change the forum, as is noted in l. cum quaedam puella, D. de iurisd. omn. iudic.; and D. ad municip., l. fin. Since, therefore, the statute of the commune of Siena disposes concerning the person, prohibiting that she not dispose beyond the fourth part, or it seems that the prohibition adheres to the person, wherever the act is done, and concerning whatever goods it is done, since it is a defect of the efficient cause, as is noted. Gul. in l. cunctos populos. Others say that this prohibition, as being odious, has no place in an act exercised outside the territory, arg. D. de postuland., l. ex ea; nor in goods situated outside, D. de bonis autem iudicis possess., l. cum unus, §. is qui. But someone will say that this is not principally a penalty, but a provision for the children of the first marriage, C. de secundis nupt., l. hac edictali; and noted by Innocentius, de secundis nupt., cap. pen. and l. fina.; and the same by Hostiensis; and therefore it seems that favor should be extended, and it ought to be aided by interpretation, not restricted. And if it is said that this lady was no longer under the law, because she remained at the place of origin properly, and in word and deed had transferred her domicile, and things easily return to their nature, D. de poenis, l. si unus, §. quod et in spem; and it seems absurd that a widow could not change the forum of her first husband, since with the death of the husband she is released from the law of the husband. It is answered that she will not be seen to have changed her domicile with respect to the Sienese domicile by marrying in the Sienese territory, although in fact, arg. D. de peculio legato, l. cum filius, §. ultimo. And thus, since she is still under the Sienese law, she is restricted by the same law. Briefly, if the second marriage were valid, she would follow the domicile of the said husband G., the second husband, and his city, as is noted. C. de incolis, l. cives. And the prohibition of the Sienese statute can be adapted to both as subjects, and the legacy would not be valid unless up to the fourth part, holding that this prohibition is favorable: because it was not made absolutely, but with respect to the children, arg. D. de condit. et demonstr., l. sed si hoc, §. ultimo, in the goods of the Sienese territory, as I will say below. If the marriage did not hold, then it is valid in no way, or by reason of error, or by reason of the invalid marriage, as has been said. One could also doubt where the marriage would hold, because in this woman two qualities concur, natural, or original: but because she is not subject to it, nor bound by that law, and accidental, hence it seems that the natural cause is rather considered, D. de tutel., l. qui habet; l. fi. de his qui pro donato, l. si me. But I say the contrary, because in obligations the subsequent act is considered, C. de pactis, l. pacta nouissima. But this is an accidental act, therefore. And so forth. Likewise, where nature and act are divided, nature is considered; where they are contrary, the accident is considered. D. de postuland., l. 1, §. bestias; D. de assess., l. si eadem; D. de iure iur., l. si manus. Sometimes the accident is disordered against nature, but to supplement and corroborate: for even then in an absolute disposition we consider the natural cause, but if it is relative to the accident, then we consider the accidental cause, C. de his qui vet. aet., l. fina.; D. de liber. et posthum., l. filio, quem patrem; D. de condit. et demonstr., l. fideicommissum. But still someone will say that four reasons support the legacy, namely: the origin of the woman, the place where the testament was made, D. de evict., l. si fundum; C. de testib., l. fina.; C. quemadmod. testa. aper., l. 2; goods situated outside the territory. And I argue thus: a sentence binds more strongly outside the territory than a law, as noted by the doctors in c. vt animarum, de constit., lib. 6. But the sentence of a judge does not bind goods situated outside the territory, as l. cum unus, §. is qui. Therefore, neither does the sentence of a statute make the generality of the law apply outside the territory, D. de iurisd. omn. iudic. Likewise, because it is not permitted to interfere in another’s affairs, l. sicuti, §. aristo, si serui vendi. Likewise, because the custom in the Castle of Santa Flora is according to the common law: therefore the common law is to be observed there, and not the statute of the city of Siena. And the fourth reason is, although the second husband, who was a native of Santa Flora, was a citizen of Siena, perhaps by statute this was with respect to civil duties. And although the wife follows him with respect to the forum, since he did not have a forum in both places, D. ad municip., l. assumpto; no law seems to say that she follows the husband with respect to the prohibition of testating. Join these, because he who is not a subject in a place, in things not subject, is not bound by the Sienese statute. First, this statute seems injurious, as C. de contrahend. empt., l. dudum, because it binds the hands of the owner. Likewise, it impedes the free making of a testament. Likewise, it is contrary to the common law, therefore it must be restricted, and not extended to things which are outside the territory: because odious things ought not to be extended, D. de liber. et posthum., l. cum quidam. Likewise, if it were said to be favorable, this would be in privilege of the children: but neither ought a privilege to be extended where it redounds to the injury of another, as in §. si quis a principe, de auctor. et usu pallii, ca. ex tuarum; and D. de administ. tutor., l. impuberi filio centurio. And if it is said that the statute disposes concerning the person, let it be conceded, but it disposes concerning the person with respect to the things, therefore it does not extend to things situated elsewhere, arg. de mun. et hon., l. rescripto, §. fina.; C. de milit. testam., l. 1. But someone will say, rather it disposes with respect to an indivisible act, namely testating: and therefore it extends to all goods, because wherever they are situated, they follow the condition of the person. D. de acquirend. haered., l. paulus, §. paulus, §. ultimo. Hence the same testament ought not to be judged by different laws. Noted in l. precibus, with similar. Otherwise if it were a case of intestacy, because it does not concern an indivisible act, since there is no act of the testator there, nor is the capacity of the deceased person required in a case of intestacy, and therefore there one can rightly distinguish by local distinction according to Gulielmus. But to this it is answered: for since guardianship is something indivisible in itself, and with respect to the right of guardianship, D. de administrat. tutor., l. inter tutoris; and the effect of the appointment of guardianship is not extended, nor claimed, unless insofar as the jurisdiction of the deciding authority is claimed, D. de excus. tutor., l. iurisperitos, §. cum oriundus, and there noted. But there they speak of a curator, who is given principally for the things, secondarily for the person; otherwise in a tutor, who is given principally for the person, as in l. propter, §. fina., eod. tit., where it is said that the appointment is a necessary excuse: therefore the appointment holds, unless you say excuse. l. contradictio, because it ought not to be felt: for it is an excuse of law, and by law, when one is not bound to obey, arg. iudicatum solvi, l. vir bonus; D. si quis in ius voc., l. ex quacunque, in the gloss. But this exposition is not permitted by the letter, because it does not presuppose that he is tutor in both places by law itself, and not in effect, and this is what it says, that to one having a tutor another is given. For by law itself it would not be claimed, elsewhere he would not have a tutor: and therefore another would be given to one not having one there, and it would be of the rule, not of the exception: in this sufficiently difficult question the opinions of the doctors can be induced on both sides: nevertheless consider. It seems to me, all things considered, that assuming the capacity of the said G., the legacy made to him was valid in the goods which are not of the territory of Siena, insofar as l. hac edictali permits. However, in the goods existing in the Sienese territory, the statute of the city of Siena prevails, arg. D. de solut., l. quæro. That statute, however, is somewhat obscure, because it seems to speak where another disposition preceded, then the prohibition of the statute has place; otherwise if another did not precede, thus C. de testam., auth. hoc inter liberos. However, the rubric, which summarizes the black [text], is more general, to whose generality it seems one should adhere: because the rubric has the force of the text, as is noted. C. ob chirogr. pecuniam, cum sim. In this the customary practice is to be observed, if it does not appear from the style or practice, the rubric, auth. per text., is noted in the prologue of the Sextus, in the word. Otherwise if the subscription were not authentic, but demonstrative, arg. C. de relig., l. monumentorum. I, Bal. de Peru.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that the officials of commerce have jurisdiction over all matters of commerce and debts arising therefrom, whether such officials are competent to hear a case concerning a loan made to a certain partnership.
2. Whether a question of nullity impedes the execution of a sentence.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having premised the words of a certain statute in the vernacular, which reads thus: “Let the officials of the merchant court have cognizance of every merchandise and debt arising therefrom.” The question arises as follows: The aforementioned transferee borrowed from the company of the Vascones of Arezzo one thousand gold florins. A certain person, by virtue of a cession of right, demanded these gold florins before the said officials of the merchant court, and a sentence was rendered. Finally, proceedings were instituted for the nullity of the sentence, on the ground that it is alleged that the said officials lacked jurisdiction. Now, it is asked, first, whether jurisdiction pertained to the office of the said officials. Second, it is asked, whether the cause of nullity impedes the execution of the said sentence.

† Regarding the first point, a doubt arises that the cause of the trade in the loan was not uncertain; hence, since a loan may be taken for various causes, it follows that it does not appear to have been taken for that cause which would assert jurisdiction for the said officials. For the cause is here of the substance of proof with regard to jurisdiction: therefore, it must be proved specifically. Let all the laws be added which speak of the proof of the cause. D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § causa, and § si praetor; C. de aedificiis divi Adriani, l. finalis, cum si. I believe the contrary to be true, namely, that since it was loaned to their society of merchants, the law presumes that it was received for the cause of trade, C. ad Macedonianam, l. finalis, § si, and there by the doctors; and this is a presumption of law, which is held as liquid proof, as noted in C. de periculo et commodo tutorum, l. tutor. And therefore I believe that the jurisdiction was that of the said consuls, who could proceed according to their statutes and customs, C. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. iniquum; C. de constitutione pecuniae, l. 2, in fine; in Auth. de fideiussoribus, § argentariorum.

† On the second point, it seems to be said, first, that the question of nullity impedes the execution of the sentence: because it is a prejudicial question, C. si ex falsis instr. l. fin.; ff. de re iud. l. 4. §. condemnatum; C. de procu. l. licet. For a sentence, which is null, does not deserve execution, nor the name of sentence, C. de sententiis ex periculo reci. l. 2. and l. fin.; and the pending judgment, which the sentence operates, ff. de exce. l. fundi. et fundus; and a sentence passed on nullity would impede execution: therefore, a lawsuit is moved. It supports what is noted, ff. de appel. l. si expressum; ff. quae sententiae sine appel. rescind. l. j. §. j. cum si. On this, the doctors say: either the nullity can be proven immediately, and then execution does not take place, C. de falsis. l. satis aperte; ff. de iudi. l. si praetor. §. Marcellus; ff. de re iudi. l. diuus; ff. de excep. l. qui agni; and noted by Innocentius, de offic. delegat. c. cum in iure. in prin. For this distinction, it supports what is noted, ff. de iureiuran. l. nam et postea. in princi.; ff. ad exhibend. l. 3. §. idem; C. de compensa. l. fina. And this is held by Speculum, de libellorum conceptione. §. nunc dicendum. versi. 1. Applying to the proposition, I say thus: either the judge, before whom the nullity is pleaded, is a competent judge, and then the aforementioned distinction survives; or he is incompetent, then such a motion of litigation operates nothing, C. ne de sta. defun. l. si pater; C. de assertio. tol. l. prima in fin. And the competent judge in a case of nullity principally intended is the same ordinary judge who issued it, C. quomodo, et quando iudex. l. si vt proponas. el primo. in vltima glo.; C. de senten. et inter. omn. iudi. l. 1. Also, the superior to whom the subordinate pronounces, C. de accusa. l. absentem; and d. l. si vt proponis. in text. Also, the successor, ff. de rebus eorum. l. quamuis. Also, if the cause of nullity arises in appeal, the appellate judge, ff. de iure patronat. l. fina.; ff. famil. ercisc. l. quaedam mulier; and noted in l. prima C. quando prouo. non est ne. And he to whom appeal does not pertain is not called superior, so that with respect to such a cause he has greater administration; it supports ff. de mino. l. minor autem inagistia. And it can be said, according to Jacobus de Arena, that he alone can declare the sentence null, and he alone is the judge of nullity who could restore in integrum against the sentence: because he alone ought to be able to declare, who can, by rescinding the judge, ar. l. fin. C. de leg. Thus holds Jacobus Butrigarius in l. 3. C. si aduer. rem iudica. If it pertains by right of superiority to the power, who is held in the place of the praeses, then he would be the competent judge in nullity, and by common law this seems true, C. de iur. dot. l. fina. in fine. But if by statute the cognition of the grievance in the proconsules’ latifundia were assigned to another, then the power, the judge, is incompetent, and the process conducted before him would operate nothing, nor even his sentence, C. si a non compe. iud. l. fi: for what is specially granted to one seems taken away from another, ff. de lega. 1. l. quod in rerum. §. si quis post. in fin. and what there by Jacobus de Arena. Concluding, if the judge is competent, or the plaintiff offers proofs of nullity prepared, and execution is delayed; or a deeper inquiry is required, which the nature of execution does not permit: and then execution takes place, saving the right of retracting the sentence and execution, if it appears later that the sentence is null, de purga. vulga. cap. significantibus. It supports what is noted in cap. calumniae. de re iudica. in clem. ad finem. And this regarding execution, which ought to be done by a man; but regarding execution of law, proof is not considered: but truth. Hence, a sentence, which is truly null, never draws with it the execution of law, ff. de iniusto testamen. l. si quis filio. §. quod si quis. For the law always imitates the existence of the thing in that which it does by itself, ff. de condic. ob causam. l. si pecuniam. §. si seruum. Although in the contrary, it supports d. Dyn. ff. de acquir. posses. l. 3. §. si seruus. But that is true, which is presumed for the sentence, that it is some, and excuses the erring one, ff. de euict. l. Herennius. §. 1. Yet it does not draw with it the execution of law, because the insertion of mode, or form, even in a favorable act, impedes legal disposition, ff. de verbo. obli. l. qui Romae. §. flauius. If, however, the cause of nullity is moved before an incompetent judge, it is the same as if it had not been moved, C. de iurisdi. omn. iudic. l. in criminali. et l. nemo. cum sim. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the substitute comes into his inheritance, where a son was instituted as heir, and the father substituted to him in this manner: "If my son should die in pupillary age, or afterwards at any time, I substitute Titius to him by way of vulgar, pupillary, and fideicommissary substitution," if he dies during the lifetime of the testator, who afterwards dies without altering the will.
body: The testator said in his will as follows,

† namely, if my son should die in pupillary age, or afterwards at any time, I substitute Titius to him by vulgar, pupillary, and fideicommissary substitution. Now this pupil dies while the testator is alive. Finally, the testator died without having made any other testament or last will. Now the question arises whether Titius, the substitute, is admitted. And there is doubt: because the instituted heir died while the testator was alive. And briefly, Baldus, now in the city of Assisi, and also in his first opinion, which he ever rendered, was consulted on the first point, and always held that the substitute is admitted: although the instituted heir dies while the testator is alive. For on this matter there is a gloss in l. Gallus, § 1, de liberis et posthumis, where in the case of an express vulgar substitution it claims for itself a place even when the instituted heir dies while the testator is alive; but a tacit vulgar substitution does not: which, if it does not claim for itself an express place, for example an express pupillary substitution, therefore neither does a tacit one, that is, a tacit vulgar substitution contained in an express pupillary one: although there are opinions regarding the tacit vulgar substitution, as noted by the gloss and doctors in l. lex Cornelia, ff. de vulgaribus et pupillaribus, nevertheless the truth is as I said. Now returning to the point at issue, in our case I say that the express vulgar substitution claims for itself a place because of those words, “I substitute to him vulgarly, pupillary, etc.” And this from that head, because he cannot be heir. For a vulgar substitution has two heads, namely, if he will not be heir, that is, if he will not, or because he cannot, as is the text in C. de hereditate instituenda, l. cum proponas. Where, when the testator had said to himself that if my son should die in pupillary age, or afterwards at any time, I substitute such a person, and had not said “vulgarly,” and so forth, then in such a case the substitute would come by virtue of the tacit vulgar substitution comprehended in the pupillary one, which has no place when the instituted heir dies while the testator is alive, as Baldus said. Thus he held in the aforementioned opinions.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a daughter may make a will regarding her dowry.
body: The point is that Arcolanus confessed that he had received from the lady Paula, wife of Peter, who gave and paid from the money of the said ser Peter, 40, and this for the marriage contracted between the said Arcolanus and the lady Thomasa, daughter of the said ser Peter and the said lady Paula, namely for the dowry of the said lady Thomasa, which dowry the said Arcolanus promised to restore to the said lady Paula stipulating for the said ser Peter, if the said marriage should be dissolved without children. The said lady Thomasa, after the death of her said father, having made a testament by which she instituted her said husband as her universal heir, died without children. Now the sons and heirs of the said ser Peter, and brothers of the said Thomasa, demand from the said Arcolanus that the aforesaid dowry be restored to them. The husband and heir aforesaid pleads in exception that she could dispose by will of the aforesaid dowry after the death of her father, because she succeeded to the said dowry, and it was acquired to her as his heir. Now the question is, what is the law? This question is one of the subtleties of the law,

† And it is examined in C. de rei uxoriae actione, l. unica, which begins "rem in praesenti," §. videamus, after Cynus; and in l. penultima, soluto matrimonio, by Dyaco; and in l. post dotem, in the same title, by Bartolus. And here, if anyone wished to set forth arguments for and against, many folios would not suffice. But conclusively and determinatively, this must be said: either this Thomasa succeeded to Peter together with her brothers, and then it is the common dowry of all of them, and it does not consolidate to her alone, C. communia utriusque iudicii, l. finalis; or she did not succeed, because perhaps the statute does not wish that a dowried daughter succeed when males are extant. And thus she is in a manner disinherited by the statute in consideration of the dowry, as in l. qui volebat, de hereditatibus instituendis; and then it consolidates to the daughter herself, and she may make a will concerning it, as in the aforementioned §. videamus, and l. ultima, ff. de collatione dotis. And if this daughter were not given a dowry, her legitimate portion could not be denied to her, and she could make a will concerning it. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether it is considered a wrongful act if one spurs a horse vigorously with sharp spurs, and the horse, running as a result of such spurring, strikes someone.
2. In such a striking, if the person struck falls, and the horse, with its hoof, both strikes and inflicts two wounds, whether this is considered one wrongful act or multiple.
3. Given a statute providing that when blood flows from a blow, a settlement is not valid, if no blood flows from the blow mentioned above from the accused, but from the animal itself, the statute will not apply.
4. [Continuation of point 3] ...from the accused, but from the animal itself, the statute will not apply.
5. An injury is not strictly said to occur where there is no intent.
body: Before you, noble and powerful knight, Lord Michael of Vulterris, Captain of the commune and people of the city of Perugia, and your judge and that of the said commune, Lord John, appointed for malefices, it is denounced and affirmed by Franciscus Paulutii, syndic of the village of Santa Maria de Villigenis, and Andreutius Meneci, syndic of the village of Santa Crucis, and the community of the village of Illligenis, against Cola, merchant of Nursia, an outsider, because Cola this year on the last day of the month of June just past, spurred a certain mare upon which he was sitting with spurs, so that the said mare began to go quickly and ran, in which course Bernard, a villager and citizen of Perugia, was struck on the chest by the breast of the said mare. From which blow the said Bernard fell to the ground, and the said mare struck the head of the said Bernard with its foot in a single blow, from which blow two wounds were made in the head of the said Bernard, and the aforesaid are said to have been such, from which blood flowed from two places on the head of the said Bernard. And the aforesaid are said to have occurred in a certain lane bordering the said villages, within the common district of the said villages of Santa Maria de Villigenis and Santa Crucis de Villigenis, the boundaries of which lane and place are, on one side, the properties of the church of Saint Laurentius, which are on one side of the said lane, and on the other side, the properties of Bartholomeus, son of Gielloli, which are on the other side of the said lane. First, it must be seen whether this is a maleficium. Second, whether it is one or several. Third, whether it is entirely extinguished by concord.

† Regarding the first point, it must be known that spurring a horse is in itself no wrongful act; nevertheless, it can be a certain precursor to a wrongful act, and this is to be judged from the circumstances. Just as cutting down a tree is not a wrongful act, but cutting it down when people are passing by, so that it harms another, is a delict (Digest, *ad legem Aquiliam*, l. *si putator*); likewise, digging a pit is not in itself a delict; yet digging it in a place where there is a thoroughfare for people, if someone is thereby injured, is a delict (Digest, *ad legem Aquiliam*, l. *qui foueas ursorum*). Also, sailing swiftly is not a sin, but if thereby another ship is overwhelmed, one is liable, unless such force was made unexpectedly that it could not be restrained (Digest, *ad legem Aquiliam*, l. *quod ad quem modum*, § *si navis alteram*). Thus it is to be said concerning a horse, because sometimes the fault of the rider is imputed for an accident happening to another, not as in the Decretals, *de homicidio*, c. *dilectus filius*, a *capellanus*, where it says, "nor by will, nor by act did he perpetrate homicide," etc., as you have signified. And certainly, from the facts narrated, considering the form and the nature of the fact, a proper wrongful act does not result; and this is regarding the first point.

I come to the second point, assuming that a harmful result ensues, whether it is one or many. It appears that there are many, considering the end, as noted by the doctors in *l. si gemina* [arborum furtim cesarum]. To the contrary, there is one, considering the beginning, for there is one fault, not multiple faults; because the injury to the horse was not within the power of the man. And therefore, the number of wounds to an irrational animal did not aggravate the man’s act, because they are not multiple, as stated in the aforementioned *l. gemina* in the text. And therefore, a distributive penalty according to the number should not be imposed; but rather a single and comprehensive penalty, if any arises therefrom. And this concludes the second point, because a single act, as stated in *c. dilectus* in the word “act,” speaks in the singular number.

† Regarding the third point, it must be said that all penalty is entirely removed by the settlement, because here no blood was shed from the blow inflicted by the accused or the person under inquiry, but rather by the animal itself; and thus no penalty remains, as stated in the Digest, title *Si quadrupes pauperiem fecerit*, law 1, section *Ideoque si equus*. For in that section, since the nature of the wording is lacking, the case is expressed clearly to any observer, and this is considered in light of the general statute concerning settlements. As for the objection based on another statute, which states that if a settlement is made with a foreigner by a citizen regarding those injuries, half of the penalty remains: that statute speaks of injuries.

† Properly and strictly speaking, an injury is not said to occur where there is no intent to harm (*dolus*), as stated in the Digest, under the Lex Aquilia, in the law *Sed et si quaecumque*; and in the Digest, on injuries, in the first law, section 1. But here there was no intent to harm, nor is any alleged, as indicated in the law *Si praeses* under the title On Penalties. Therefore, the act is entirely valid. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a tax be paid on every contract of sale at the rate of so much per pound or ducat, if anyone buys a thing for a price to be declared by another, the tax ought not to be paid.
2. Whenever a right of the republic is acquired from a future declaration, such declaration must be made, as in the case of dowries for the poor and of last wills.
body: Since the substance of a sale consists in the price, as is stated in the Digest, On Contracting Sale, in the law *Pacta conventa*, section *Paulus*.

† And here it is not declared that a certain derivative, namely, the price of the compromise, from which this declaration depends as to its very substance, exists; and thus there are two extremes, namely, the primitive and the derivative. Without doubt, the contract fails in substance, not in its consequences. And since the tax (gabella) is assessed with respect to the price, and the price is not certain, the tax is not truly due; and this is expressly held by Guillaume. D. de pace, l. ab emptione. To the contrary, it seems that it matters greatly whether the tax is assessed with respect to the agreement, or with respect to the obligation, or with respect to the transfer of ownership. In the first case, when it is assessed with respect to the agreement, the obligation or ownership does not seem to be taken into account, cf.
