D. de periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. qui in venditione; and so here. In the second and third cases, the statement of Guillaume applies.

† Moreover, since the right of the republic is acquired from a future declaration, such a declaration ought to be made in favor of the republic, just as it is made in favor of a dowry, and in favor of the poor, and in favor of a last will, ff. de leg. 2. l. quidam. and l. i. ff. de iure do. l. cum post. §. gener. ff. de epis. et cler. l. 1. And therefore, if the arbitrators are unwilling or unable to arbitrate, the matter proceeds on an equal footing. Furthermore, the republic, and one having a cause from it, ought not to be defrauded under any collusion, nor under any artifice or fiction; rather, such fraudulent artifice deserves a greater penalty, as ff. de iure patro. l. si libertus minorem. Moreover, fraud is presumed on account of a lower price. C. man. l. per diuersas. Furthermore, the act of private individuals does not harm the republic, ff. de pact. l. inter debitorem. It therefore appears that the price ought to be declared entirely, not for the interest of the contracting parties, but for the interest of the republic, to which the tax is owed on every quantity declared and to be declared. And thus, C. de contrahen. emp. l. fi. does not stand in the way, which speaks with regard to the action of purchase and sale, not with regard to the right of the tax; for since it appears that the matter stands by the conclusion of the contracting parties, it ought to be considered as done, ff. de contrahen. emp. l. labeo scribit, si mihi bibliothecam. And thus, the incidental obligation is incurred, and yet the principal obligation is not drawn along: because they do not come from the same source, ff. de contrahen. emp. l. senatus. I doubt, because a contract is defined as arising from equity, an obligation can arise on both sides. de verb. sign. l. labeo. §. contra. But here it cannot arise, d. l. fin. de contranen. emp. Hence, it will not be called a contract, except abusively and without understanding of the law. And therefore, the tax is not owed on this account. It is not an obstacle that the statute says "declared, or to be declared"; because henceforth there is no quantity to be declared: d. l. fi. Furthermore, it is not an obstacle if it is said that here the arbitration is not about the substantial matters: because it is not about the formal price. For rather it is about the substantial matters, because by this means one arrives at the substantial price, which otherwise is uncertain, d. §. paulus. And this is the truth, that the tax ought not to be paid; nevertheless, an oath of purgation ought to be administered to them, that they have simulated nothing to the prejudice of the tax. C. de his, qui ad eccle. confu. l. praesenti. cum simil. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who does not acknowledge a superior is bound to observe the order concerning the imposition of reprisals against non-subjects.
2. Justice cannot be administered regarding that which is uncertain.
3. What the term “districtualis” signifies.
4. A subject who is not a subject simpliciter, but secundum quid, is not called a subject.
5. A city is considered in three ways.
6. Those who are not bound to public burdens are not truly subjects.
7. Given a treaty or convention between the City of Venice and the Commune of Fano, and whether the Commune of Venice is bound to treat the citizens of Fano equally in protection, and whether, if reprisals have been granted by the common Duke of Venice against Lord G. de Malatestis, his subjects, and his faithful followers, the citizens of Fano are included therein, even though they are subjects.
8. What is the form of reprisals.
1. The form of reprisals in Venice.
body: Four matters are to be investigated with respect to the proposal: the order, the cause, the judge, and the form. Regarding the order, Bartolus says.

† That he who does not recognize a superior is not bound to observe the order, and that no solemnity is required, thus neither a libellus, nor another order, nor writing. And that he who has reprisals from him does not have to prove another process: but it suffices to show only the concession. All other things are presumed as if solemnly acted by the royal hand. Thus he says in his treatise. The Venetians do not recognize a superior from true and ancient civic liberty. Therefore these reprisals are founded on presumption. This adulterous theory remains for the ignorant. For since reprisals are granted against non-subjects, it is foolish to say that one should believe the one who declares the law. For as to non-subjects, he himself recognizes a father, as in the law "de manumissionibus," l. "apud eum"; and therefore it must be established that the order contained in divine law is observed. Ask, and you will receive. And it is confirmed by canon and civil law, hence it must be established that an ordinary, or at least quasi-petition, was made beforehand in the forum of the defendant, before the defendant is bound to follow the forum of the plaintiff. It is true that this petition can be made by letters of the Lord Duke, which concerns the subjects, and the authentic letters of the same are considered as a petition, de re iudicata, c. "ad apostolicae," de electione, c. "venerabilem," ad municipia, l. "de iure," de appellatione, c. "dilectis." And it must be established that these letters were presented to the most noble Lord. 6. Regarding the cause, it is certain. The cause must allege the fact of a certain person. For regarding an uncertain one, not

† justice can be administered, ff. nautae cau. l. licet. §. possumus. quod me. causa. l. si cum exceptione. §. in hac. unless the people were held liable for uncertainty, or the contrada, l. ne quid. de incen. rui. et naufrag. But certainly this is unjust, that the contrada be punished, unless it ceased to oppose or apprehend the robbers in a more sound festival, as we see in Aut. vt nulli iudi. §. quin vero. col. 9. For the contrada ought not to be held liable for the acts of travelers or pirates, nor the lord of the place. ff. furt. aduer. nautas. l. 1. For what justice can be rendered, unless apprehension takes place? Certainly none. Where therefore there is no certainty, or there is inability, there is no reason or cause for seizing another’s property: because there was no juridical key, but nature, if it may be so said. And thus there is no ground for reprisals. Regarding the judge, it appears to be a retrogression: because the defendant, having abandoned his own forum, is dragged to the plaintiff’s judge, who grants reprisals against the law and the order of law, C. de iurisd. om. iud. and it becomes so that he who offends in the forum, but outside, whence reprisals bring the sickle into alien territory and against alien and innocent persons, against all natural reason, in Aut. ut non fiant pign. col. 5. and in c. si pignorationes. de iniur. et dam. dato. Regarding the form, it must be considered that the form of these reprisals contains four persons, namely the lord G., his faithful, his subjects, and his districtuals; this person, about whom inquiry is made, is not a faithful of lord G., nor his subject, nor districtual. That he is not a faithful is evident from his original free birth, and because neither he nor his parents ever swore fidelity, nor does he receive any fruit from lord Galeo. That he is not districtual is evident

† because this term, *districtualis*, sounds and signifies origin, ff. de tut. et cura. l. 1. de ver. sign. l. sed reprobari. Moreover, by the reason which follows, that he is not a subject, it is clear. For either we shall say that he is a subject of Fano, and then he does not suffer reprisals, because a native of Fano is regarded as a Venetian by treaty. Or we do not say so, and then know that by contract and tacit agreement with the city of Fano, he acquires jurisdiction and is bound by his promises: nevertheless, he is not truly and properly called, nor is he, a subject.

† Moreover, because he is not subject in an absolute sense, but only with respect to the promises made, as is noted in c. 1, de fideiussionibus et compendiis, arguing from de verbis obligatoris, l. quidam cum filium. Certainly, nothing was specifically promised here; rather, he was simply made a citizen of Fano with immunity for twenty-five years. This supports what is noted in de senatu et excommunicatione, c. a vobis, in the gloss, which states that, insofar as they are their subjects regarding this matter, they have been made citizens with respect to privileges.

But civility can be considered in three ways. In the first way, with regard to favors; in the second, with regard to burdens from which one is exempt under the common law; in the third, with regard to accidental burdens contrary to the common law, and with regard to these it does not seem to be extended, cf. C. de legibus, l. quod favore. And so in the case at hand.
† Moreover, since they are not bound to public offices, they are not merely and truly subjects, l. 1. ff. ad municip. even if they have their household and domicile there, and this is the very truth.

It is therefore clear that this person is not included under reprisals, and thus cannot be molested in his person or property. For either he is regarded as a citizen of Fano, and cannot be seized by way of reprisals, because the commune of Venice is bound to treat the citizens of Fano on equal footing with its own citizens in terms of protection, and the treaties have not been altered; or he is regarded as not being a citizen of Fano, and is therefore not a subject: and thus neither the words of the Doge of Venice, nor his intent, nor reason include this person about whom the question is asked, cf. D. 40.4.1 (Gallus), § ult. Between contrary interpretations, one must be chosen, D. 12.1.1 (Titia), si non nupserit: and whichever is chosen, reprisals do not extend to this person about whom the question is asked, who wears the toga of Fano and has his substance in Forlì, D. 49.14.1 (Sed si accepto usu togae). Hence I conclude that reprisals do not include this person about whom the question is asked. Moreover, considering that the matter of reprisals is to be restricted for the sake of civility, so that the republic may flourish for many citizens, and to be expanded for the sake of civility, which is to be preserved as a kind of possession, together with its cause and its defects, namely its honors and burdens, and that contradiction is to be avoided: hence either this person is to be held as a citizen of Fano, and is not included in reprisals, or not, and then even less so, as I said above. And considering the treaty between the cities, which ought not to be violated, but rather supported, D. 49.15.1 (Non dubito etc.). I, Baldus.

† We, Antonius Venerio, Duke of Venice, etc., with our counselors above the consuls, judges, and advocates of the commune, order and decree that a pledge shall be made on all the goods of the most noble lord Galeotto de Malatestis of the city of Rimini, etc., Vicar-General of the Holy Roman Church, and also on all the goods of all his faithful subjects and those of his districts, and against their persons, for the satisfaction to be rendered to the underwritten citizens and our faithful subjects, namely, Franciscus de Cale, Iacobus a Fornacibus, and Betinus de Pone, who have been damaged in the parts of the district of Pesaro of the aforementioned lord Galeotto, and also to Christophorus Faxuol, likewise a citizen and our faithful subject, who was condemned by the officials of the said lord Galeotto in the said city of Pesaro, and against right and justice was robbed of damages inflicted upon him amounting to the sum of 337 pounds, 2 solidi, and 2 grossi, and more, as has been proven and assessed by our extraordinary officials appointed for such matters. However, a great deduction has been made from the said citizens and our faithful subjects regarding those things which they ought to have, to their greatest loss, as is clearly evident to you. We hoped, indeed, and without doubt held, considering our just petitions, that without delay provision would have been made by him in such a way that we and our citizens, as they have reported to us, would have received something; yet they have never received anything, nor do they claim to have received anything, despite continuous and numerous petitions to the aforementioned lord Galeotto. We are not a little astonished, seeing that in such manifest justice of our citizens, the said lord Galeotto has shown himself difficult. Our predecessors and we, desiring and willing that our native citizens might recover the underwritten 337 pounds, 2 solidi, and 2 grossi, assessed by the said our extraordinary officials, wrote repeatedly to the aforementioned most noble lord Galeotto, requesting that it please him to provide in such a way that the said our citizens might be satisfied. And although lord Galeotto has alleged and alleges certain excuses and delays, he has by no means denied the said damages and robberies inflicted upon the said our citizens, nor has he cared to make or cause to be made any satisfaction to the said our citizens for the aforesaid, nor does he care, nor has he wished, nor does he now wish, for a long time, to give effect to our letters and our prayers, which are so just, indeed most just, to the no small detriment and burden of the aforementioned our citizens. Since the law rightly binds us to grant aid to our citizens and faithful subjects in their grievance, and especially to those for whom the right of proof and the aid itself intercede, considering that long expectation redounded greatly to the loss and detriment of the said our citizens and faithful subjects, and furthermore, at the continuous and assiduous complaint and petition of our said faithful subjects, we have diligently examined the laws, letters, and all other things pertaining to this matter. Having diligently examined and duly considered these, seeing that the said our citizens could not, nor can, come to satisfaction for the aforesaid otherwise than by real and personal pledge on all the goods of the aforementioned most noble lord Galeotto, and also of all his faithful citizens, subjects, and those of his districts, and against their persons, we have deemed it proper to grant the aforementioned pledge to the said our citizens and faithful subjects in the following manner, namely, that if from the day of the presentation of our letters, lastly to be sent and presented by our sworn messenger, to whom we shall give full faith regarding the presentation thereof, until three months next ensuing, satisfaction is made for the 2 solidi and 2 grossi assessed by our aforementioned extraordinary officials on account of the said damages, although they amount to a higher sum, and if satisfaction is made, this is good and will greatly please us. Otherwise, until the aforementioned sum of 337 pounds, 2 solidi, and 2 grossi, we grant full and complete power to the said our citizens and faithful subjects, and their successors, to pledge all the goods of the aforementioned most noble lord Galeotto of the city of Rimini, Vicar-General of the Holy Roman Church, and also of his faithful citizens, subjects, and those of his districts, and their persons, which we will and command to be observed inviolably. However, it is to be understood that whatever is exacted must be distributed and given pro rata, pound for pound, among the said our citizens and faithful subjects according to the assessment made for them by the said our extraordinary officials on account of the aforementioned goods, namely: Franciscus de Cale for 94 pounds, 2 solidi, 2 grossi; Iacobus de Fornacibus for 100 pounds; Betinus de Pone for 137 pounds, 6 solidi; Christophorus Faxuol for 6 pounds, 4 solidi. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, in the case of goods descending from a father, the maternal grandfather and grandmother are preferred to consanguine brothers, or vice versa.
body: By this opinion

It would be said that consanguine brothers are preferred to the maternal grandfather and grandmother in goods descending from the father, as we say in the case of brothers, as noted in the Authentica *Post fratres*, Codex, *De legatis hereditatibus*. And as some say, that the paternal grandfather is preferred in paternal goods, the maternal grandfather in maternal goods, as in the law *Quod satis*, Codex, *De bonis quae liberis*, according to one reading, which Bartolus notes; and if they are not preferred, at least they will be admitted equally, because all are in the second degree, and all from one side. However, against this equity is the written law, to which one must adhere, that the grandfather and grandmother are preferred to brothers from one side, as in the Authentica *De haeredibus ab intestato*, § *Si igitur defunctus*, where it says, "except only brothers from both parents." And therefore in the intestate succession

†Savoryta and Samaritana, who are the maternal grandfather and grandmother, are preferred over Gilio and Rogerio, who are brother and sister on one side only; because the inheritance is more properly due to ascendants than to collaterals, *de inofficiosa testamento*, l. *nam et si parentibus*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that if anyone dies intestate without maternal descendants, no one may succeed to his estate except to the extent of one-fourth of the inheritance, while the remaining property shall pass to those who would have been entitled to succeed on the paternal side if the mother had not survived: a certain person died survived by his mother, his grandmother, and a certain blood relative on the paternal side; who is to be admitted to the succession?
2. Whether excluding the mother also excludes the grandmother.
3. There is no shame in changing one’s opinion whenever truth and justice are evident.
body: Statute

† It is provided that if anyone dies intestate without children, the mother cannot succeed to the goods of the deceased, except in one-fourth part of the inheritance. The remaining goods shall go to those who, on the paternal side, ought to succeed to the aforementioned inheritance, if the mother did not exist. Now, a certain person has died, survived by his mother and maternal grandmother, and by a certain blood relative on the side of his father’s father. I ask, which of these shall succeed to the intestate estate, the mother and the grandmother, or the said blood relative, having regard to and considering the words and meaning of the aforementioned statute. And it seems that the mother succeeds to the whole, because the mother has a foundation in the common law, as in the Authentica *De haeredibus ab intestato*, § *Consequens*, and in the Institutes *Ad Tertullianam*, § *Cum antea*. Nor does the statute stand in the way, because it does not speak of our case, since there are no persons on the paternal side who ought to succeed to the inheritance if the mother were not in existence. For if the mother were not in existence, that blood relative would be excluded by the grandmother, as stated in the said § *Consequens* and in the Authentica *Defuncto*. For the statute does not speak absolutely of the blood relative; but it qualifies him, and requires him to be such a one as would succeed intestate if the mother were removed from the equation. But here, if the mother were not in existence, this blood relative would not succeed intestate; therefore, the statute does not speak of him. For what is said expressly and under a certain qualification of one person is not extended to another, D. *De liberis et posthumis*, l. *Commodissime*.

† Someone might say that the statute excludes the mother, except in the fourth part; therefore, it all the more strongly excludes the grandmother, just as when it excludes the daughter, it all the more strongly excludes the granddaughter, as is fully noted by Cynus in l. 1, C. quae sit longa consuetudo. But to this I respond that the law speaks of the mother, not of the grandmother. Nor does the aforementioned argumentation hold, as in Inst. ad tertulianum, §. postea, where it states: "to the mother, but not also to the grandmother." That text is noted for this purpose, for the name "mother" denotes both degree and person, and by no derivation of any meaning can it comprehend the grandmother, as is clear in that ancient possession of goods called "unde liberi" [from the children], as in Inst. de bonorum possessionibus, §. autem. Nor is it similar to the case of the daughter and granddaughter, because by a certain broad meaning a grandson can be called a son, as in De verbis significandis, l. liberorum. Hence there, the largeness of meaning concurs with the greater weight of reason. This is what the doctors emphasize there.

Furthermore, someone might say that this statute, by virtue of the inclusion of agnates, excludes the maternal grandmother and all cognation, as in Inst. ad tertulianum, in the beginning. For the inclusion of one is the exclusion of others, as in De legibus, l. quod in rerum, §. si quis post testamentum, and noted by Bartolus in l. 2, §. videndum, ff. ad tertulianum. But to this it is responded that it is not true that the statute includes this agnation, due to the nature of that restrictive term "who ought to come," etc. For this one is not among those, therefore it clearly appears that it does not hinder the mother; and if it does not hinder the mother, then the mother succeeds in whole, since no one can make a share for her by concurrence, ff. de haeredibus institutis, l. si te solum, and l. si quis ita facit, which is noted in C. de secundis nuptiis, l. 1, in the gloss beginning "nec etiam inter vivos."

To the contrary, it seems by such a rule: if I exclude the one who excludes you, I similarly exclude you, and you do not exclude me, as in l. aequissimum, ff. ad tertulianum, where the grandfather, excluding the mother of the deceased, excludes the mother whom the father was excluding; and he is not excluded by the mother, by whom he would be excluded if the father were not in between. So in the present case, the agnate excludes the mother, the mother excludes the grandmother; therefore, the agnate excludes the mother and the grandmother. For this grandmother, who does not succeed, does not pertain to the understanding of the agnate's exclusion, ff. ad trebellianum, l. si post mortem, §. liberi.

However, that the grandmother does not succeed is apparent. For either the mother accepts her portion, and then there is no place for the successor edict, since the first degree hinders the second. Or she repudiates, and it accrues to the agnate, by argument from ff. de coniunctione cum emancipatis liberis, l. eius, l. 1, §. si quis ex nepotibus. And if it is said that the agnate would succeed if the mother did not exist, I respond: rather, the grandmother would not be in a state of exclusion, as she is now. For the grandmother who does not succeed is just as if she were not in the nature of things. But this grandmother now does not succeed; therefore, she does not hinder the agnate. And if it is said that this agnate is not among those who, etc., I respond: rather, assuming the exclusion of the grandmother, as is now said, such a grandmother, as she is now, if excluded, does not hinder the agnate, ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. si is qui, and l. pater filium. For if you argue from an unexcluded grandmother to an excluded grandmother, the fallacy of accident is committed.

This question is subtle, and it has been deeply consulted; nevertheless, I am of the opinion for the agnate, by the aforementioned l. aequissimum and §. cum antea in the recitation of ancient constitutions and their ancient affection towards similarity, from which the statute in question emanated. And this seemed to me because agnates are substituted in the place and right of the mother, and, so to speak, enter her degree; therefore, they exclude the grandmother. But others thought the contrary, because the intention of the statute does not exclude the grandmother; hence, if the mother cannot succeed, the following degree comes, that is, the grandmother, ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. si is qui, in the word "non possit," where the case seems to be. It supports what is noted in Auth. de funere by Cynus, which is more equitable, because if the mother did not exist, the grandmother would succeed, not these agnates. And thus the statute ceases to apply, because it does not speak in our case, ff. de legibus, l. filius, §. cum quis.

† Nor do I feel ashamed to change my opinion whenever I see another person holding a better view; rather, I rejoice, and shall continue to rejoice, in following the truth and justice. And because in doubtful cases it is safer to follow the more equitable side, I finally hold against the agnates, since equity more strongly urges this course. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Upon the death of one of the partners, the partnership is dissolved with respect to all, unless the surviving partners have restored it by new consent.
2. How the partnership is regarded as renewed by the others upon the death of one partner.
3. Time, just as much as the sum, is a part of the partnership.
body: The point on which counsel is requested is as follows. In the year 1382, in the month of May, Matthew Cecholi, Antonius Paulutius, and John of James contracted a partnership for the purpose of trading, and for trading the art of commerce and exchange. This partnership was contracted in this manner and form, namely, that the said Matthew was a partner for one share, and the said Francis for another share, and the said Baldus for another share, and Antonius Paulutius and John for two shares, for a period of five years. Now it happens that in the second year, in the month of October of said year, the said Francis died, and the said Paulutius, after the accounts had first been settled and the calculation balanced for the first year during the lifetime of all the above-mentioned. And in the aforementioned second year, after the death of the aforementioned [partners], in the month of January, the surviving partners reviewed the accounts and calculated the accounts of said fund for the purpose of assigning the portion to the children or guardians of the aforementioned deceased Francis. And having reviewed the accounts and calculation, they said to the children of the said Francis or their guardians: “There falls to you from the partition, or portion, of said fund such a quantity for your share.” And then the said surviving partners had the said children or guardians of the said Francis summoned before the consuls of commerce, so that they might come to hear the pension due to them assigned. Who appeared before the consuls and said that they were content that the consuls of the merchants pronounce according to the pension assigned to the said children of Francis; and they were content to adhere to the portion assigned to them by the said surviving partners. But the matter remained such that the consuls did not pronounce on this on account of a dispute over the payment of the tenth. Then, after the death of the aforementioned Francis and Paulutius, up to the present day, the fifth day of September, the said surviving partners remained in the partnership and traded together the said art of commerce and exchange, both in this city and outside, just as they first traded before the death of the aforementioned [partners], and all letters sent outside the city by the said partners were for said partnership and for said art under the name of the said Matthew, Baldus, and partners. Then, after the aforementioned events, in the month of August just past, the said surviving partners reviewed and calculated the accounts of said fund, and to each was assigned a fourth portion for his share, just as it pertained at first before the death of the said Francis and Paulutius, removing and annulling the share of the said Francis. Now it is asked, having seen the aforementioned, whether said partnership contracted between the aforementioned partners is firm and valid, and reaffirmed for the period of five years, notwithstanding the death of the aforementioned Francis and Paulutius with respect to the survivors, so that the said surviving partners ought to abide by the aforementioned partnership.

It must be known that, although there are many partners, the partnership is terminated with respect to all upon the death of one of them, unless the surviving partners have restored the partnership by new consent, as stated in D. 17,2,1, § morte, and D. 17,2,1, § plane, si hi; or unless it was agreed that the partnership would remain intact for the survivors upon the death of one partner, as stated in Inst. 3,25, § soluitur.

† If, therefore, the partnership has been continued or reinstated among the surviving partners, it must be inquired under what terms and for what duration this occurred. And if they have agreed among themselves regarding the terms and duration, their agreement shall stand, as provided in C. pro soc. l. pen. But if this does not appear, because the partnership has been tacitly renewed and nothing has been expressly stated regarding the terms and duration, it is presumed to have been renewed with all the same terms, agreements, and duration as it was originally established. For this renewal is a certain consequence and continuation thereof. And therefore, the subsequent event is shaped from the beginning of the title. Although in contracts of lease and hire, in urban leases, as long as the tenant resides, and in rural leases, for a year, a renewal is understood to have taken place (in locatione n. et conductione), in leases the fruits of the thing are considered, which nature yields annually; but in partnership this consideration cannot be applied, because it consists more in labor, to which no certain time can be assigned, except that which was established from the beginning and is now in effect. And things said in preambles are understood to be repeated in the consequences, as stated in ff. loca. l. Item quaeritur; §. qui impleto, ff. de arb. l. labeo; ff. sol. mat. l. in his; §. vxor. And thus, from the nature of the extension, it is understood.

† Since time, as the principal part of a partnership, is [governed by the rule that] if a new form had been given by agreement, then nothing would be understood to have been repeated, as in D. 19.2.13 § dicta. It is necessary, however, that these social and renewing acts have continued. But if, after the acts of formation, they had performed acts of dissolution, for example by receiving a portion of the shares, the partnership would have been dissolved anew by division; otherwise, if only the profits had been divided while the capital remained in the partnership. D. 17.2.1. Therefore, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, when the alienation of immovables is prohibited, the alienation of movables appears to be permitted.
body: The point is as follows. In all his other movable and immovable goods, rights, and actions, wherever they are and may be found in any way, he instituted his son Francis for one-half, calculated after deducting all legitimate portions or Falcidian shares that may touch the said son under any law, and Lady Amatus, the wife of the said testator, for the other half, during the life of the said Lady, provided she lives chastely and does not enter into second vows or second marriage, as universal heirs in equal portions. And if the said son should die in puberty, that is, within the period of 14 years, within which he could not make a will, or at any time intestate without legitimate children, surviving the said Lady Amatus, the part of the said son’s inheritance shall devolve upon the said Lady during her life, provided she lives chastely, as aforesaid. And if the said Lady should not wish to cohabit with the said son, or should wish to enter into second vows or second marriage, he left to the same Lady, by way of legacy, 100 pounds of Perugian denarii from his goods. And nevertheless, whenever the said Lady should die, or should not have lived chastely, as aforesaid, with the said son surviving, the Lady’s part of the said inheritance shall devolve upon the said son. But if both the aforementioned Francis and Amatus should die, namely, the said Francis in puberty, that is, within the period of 14 years, within which he could not make a will, or at any time without legitimate children, and the said Lady Amatus should die without the said son surviving, or if she should not have lived chastely, as aforesaid, he substituted Peter Locopelli Bonacursi, his carnal brother, as universal heir to him in all his goods and possessions, however, only in immovable property, or his surviving children, coming into such case, if the said Peter should not have survived, provided that the said Peter nor his children, nor any other person or persons to whom the present substitutions might devolve, may not nor ought to sell or exchange the said immovable goods in any way, and they are bound and ought to give every year for the soul of the said testator three tunics of woolen cloth worth three gold florins, to whatever poor Christians his underwritten fideicommissaries shall see fit and please. And for the execution and carrying out of all and each of the aforesaid things, he left the said Lady Amatus, the Guardian of the place of Saint Francis of the Castle of Preggio, and the prior of the fraternity of Saint Mary of the said Castle, whoever they may be for the time being, as his fideicommissaries. To whom he gave full license and free power to sell from his goods, both movable and immovable, with bans and without bans, and without the license of any judge, up to the full satisfaction of all the aforesaid things. And this is his last will and his last testament, which he wished to have effect by the law of testament. Which, if they do not have effect by the law of testament, let them have effect by the law of codicils, and of any other last will, canceling and invalidating any other testament formerly made by him, written by any notary, so that this testament he wished to prevail over all others.

It is asked whether the said Amatutia, with respect to movable goods, may exercise her own will, so that after her death they ought not to be restored to anyone; and it seems that she may not, since they are subject to restitution. First, on account of the universal substitution, as appears in the words “he substituted a universal heir”: for when he said “heir,” he included everything, especially since he added “universal,” as in D. de verb. sign. l. nihil aliud. Second, on account of the disposition of law, because substitution extends to the whole, just as does institution, D. de vulg. sub. l. cohaeredi, §. fin. Third, on account of the institution being restricted as to time: for Amatutia was instituted only during her lifetime; therefore, after her death, it seems that provision was made for the testator’s brother; otherwise, the temporal limitation would have no effect, D. de test. mil. l. miles ita heredem, §. et quia diximus.

To the contrary, because those words “immovable goods” are placed in the place of a specification, and therefore do not include money nor movable goods, as in D. de verb. sign. l. mouentium. Since, therefore, the said substitution is a fideicommissum, as in Inst. de pup. sub. §. extraneo, nothing comes into it except what is specified, as in D. ad Treb. l. cogi, §. generaliter, and l. Lucius, §. quae habebant. And if it be said, whose are these immovables after the death of the lady? I answer, they are those of the heir of the said lady: for the inheritance given directly for a time is given in perpetuity, the defect of time being removed, as in D. de hered. inst. l. haereditas ex die. Someone may say that those words “in movables” nevertheless refer to possessions, not to other goods: for he had previously said “in all his goods.” But I answer that whatever is held is possession, D. de acq. poss. l. si rem mobilem. Moreover, the following restriction binds all the preceding words, together with all those coupled in the same sentence, D. de verb. sign. l. si cum fundum. Therefore, money and other movables are not found in the aforementioned substitution, nor does immovable property purchased by the lady from that money come into the fideicommissum, but it is her own free property, because it succeeds in place of the free money.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The time within which the right to bring an action, whether real or mixed, is prescribed.
1. Prescription is not proved by possession and the continuity of time, unless something else is proved.
2. A woman is heard when she wishes to revoke a confession that she made without understanding the article.
body: On

† In the first point, two prescriptions must be considered: one is the prescription of the right to accept (ius adeundi). For after thirty years, the inheritance cannot be accepted, even by a son, as is noted in C. de iure deliberando, l. licet. The other is the prescription of the right to bring an action (ius agendi), and the same applies, as in C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. sicut. And therefore it seems that the prescription stands as an obstacle to the first point. But it must be said that there was no prescription against the right to accept, because it is clear that he intervened within the lawful time by taking possession. Likewise, there is no prescription against the right to bring a real or mixed action, because the adversary’s possession has not been proven to have continued for a very long time without title, or for a long time with title, as in C. de petitione hereditatis, l. petitio.

† On the second point, I say that the prescription has not been proven, because the defendant must prove it, and it does not appear to have been proven by possession and the passage of time, ff. de usuc. l. 3.

† On the third point, it must be said that the response is prejudicial to the said lady who responded and confessed; nevertheless, if it appears from the records that the case is otherwise than she confessed, and she retracts her confession as having been made through a failure to understand the article, this position is legally sound: because a woman ought to be heard, C. de iure, et fact. igno. l. cum falsa, and ff. de iure, et fact. igno. l. regula. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. See, because the following opinion is not complete, it will be completed below in the opinion beginning *quis melius*. 455.
body: I understand that the aforementioned Meus, John, and Philip died being over 18 years of age and under 20 years of age; therefore, by virtue of the substitution, Thomas and Gabriel ought to have received one-half of their respective shares. The other half is divided into three parts, one of which belongs to Lady Angiola, and to Thomas and Gabriel. C. ad Tert. l. matres; and in Auth. defuncto. To Gabriel, who was an impubes, Thomas succeeded by virtue of a pupillary substitution. Regarding the succession to be made to Thomas: if he indeed died as a pupillus, the mother is excluded, as C. ad Tert. l. omnem; but if he died as an adult, the mother is not excluded, but rather she would succeed to him in all of his goods. In case of doubt, it is not presumed that he died as a pupillus, unless it is proven. And if it has been proven before the arbitrators, they must rule against the mother. S. si probatum est, quod decessit pupillus, which is proven by disproving the time of birth, de mino. l. de aetate; on which point the arbitrators must follow the truth of the fact, ff. de proba. l. cum de aetate. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a universal heir may enter upon and continue the possession of the deceased by his own authority. Likewise, whether he may pay legacies notwithstanding that executors have been appointed in the will.
body: Because

† Lady Catherine is the universal heir of Polidamassus; she may, by her own authority, continue the possession which Polidamassus held, unless it has been occupied by another: for then she ought to be put into possession by the judge, according to the law *Edicto*, in the title *De edicto divi Adriani*. And if the judge were unavailable, she could, by her own authority, administer justice to herself, if there is danger of the destruction of the possessions and the dissipation of the fruits, as is stated in the law *Ait praetor*, section *Si debitorem*, in the title *Quae in fraudem creditorum*. And because this Lady Catherine is the mistress of the inheritance, she may discharge the legacies of the daughters to them, notwithstanding the executors appointed, and give them in satisfaction of the legacy of the hereditary things, without prejudice to others, according to the law *Quidam testamento*, section *Si scriptus*, in the title *De legatis*. And she may put them into possession occupied by others. And the same may be done in the person of the daughters as in her own person, with regard to the giving of possession. But as to ownership, it is clear that she may give it to them: because she is the mistress, with a certain induction into possession, according to the law *Si fundum*, in the Digest, title *De fundo dote*, and *De acquisitione possessionis*; and the law *Cum heredes*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. What an impediment is, and how it is to be proved.
body: What must the appellant do in order to be said to pursue the appeal?

† A certain judgment cannot be rendered unless the fact is established by the credibility of the proofs. Credibility regarding impediments may be established by presumptions, as in D. de excus. tutor. l. scire oportet, § sufficit; and D. de re milit. l. non omnes, § a barbaris.

† However, an impediment is said to be that which cannot be remedied by any means, or can be remedied only with great difficulty. D. 50.17.129 (de re iudicata, Quaesitum); D. 49.3.2 (si quis cautio, l. 2). Moreover, the appellant must constantly attend to the case, either in person or through a procurator, as in Auth. de his qui ingrediuntur ad appellationem, § 1, according to Jacobus de Belvis. Therefore, it must be established that the pursuing party has shown diligence (instantia), D. 43.1.1 (de libellis diuisoriis, l. 1); and D. 20.1.130 (de pignoris actione, l. si, § si); D. 22.1.14 (de usuris, l. mora). It is not sufficient to appear once, but one must appear again and again, D. 27.1.1 (qui ex causa maiorum, l. non enim); and perhaps even a third time, D. 20.1.130 (de pignoris actione, l. si convenit); D. 50.17.129 (de verbis obligatorum, l. qui Romae, § cohaeredes). Therefore, one must prove diligence, for wherever the court proceeds, the procurator should have been present to interpellate, D. 4.4.1 (de minoribus, l. Papiensi exuli). Otherwise, negligence is presumed from the lapse of time, as in X. 1.33.1 (de rescriptis, c. ex parte) and c. plerunque. And the appeal would be considered abandoned, C. 7.62.1 (de appellations, l. eos, in principio). The authority Auth. sed lis does not obstruct this, because it is written: "Knock, and it will be opened to you." For one perfunctory appearance is not sufficient, as I have proved above, and it is clear, D. 26.10.1 (de executione tutorum, l. scire oportet, ver. ideoque si representauerit quis). See also what is noted in C. 7.62.1 (de temporibus appellationum, Auth. si tamen); X. 2.28.1 (eodem, l. ex insinuatione) and c. ex parte, according to Innocentius. Moreover, one who has a procurator in court but does nothing through him is considered to be in default, and the procurator’s delay harms the principal, D. 49.4.1 (quando appellatio sit, l. 1, in fine); X. 2.5.1 (ut lite non contestata, c. 1), according to Innocentius; D. 17.1.1 (de mandato, l. si procurator, § si tutores). For he who chooses a negligent procurator is at fault, and he must be questioned about himself. For he should not prolong the litigation through his own negligence to the prejudice of the adversary, as in D. 42.1.1 (de iudicibus, l. sed et si quis, § si). And therefore, unless something else is proved, the said appeal is considered abandoned. And so it must be pronounced, if the matter is concluded regarding proofs, as in Auth. de iudicibus, § appellationes. And he who has a procurator in court cannot plead the dangers of the roads, D. 50.17.129 (de verbis obligatorum, l. fin., § fin., inter eos). And so I, Baldus, say.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the Friars Preachers are capable of receiving a devolved inheritance.
2. Restitution in integrum is not granted after four years according to canon law.
body: Point

† A certain woman had two sons, whom in her last will she instituted as her universal heirs, as legitimate and natural, and in equal shares, with this condition appended, that if either of them should die without legitimate children, the share of the deceased should devolve upon the survivor. The testator, having not otherwise changed her will, dies. The elder of these two sons, having taken a wife, begot children. The younger became a brother of Saint Dominic. Some time later, after the younger had entered the aforementioned order, the elder dies, leaving behind some young children, with their mother remaining as their guardian. The younger, after the death of the elder, with the consent and will of the entire chapter, made a certain composition and transcription with the aforementioned minors, the mother receiving the composition for them as their guardian. The composition was as follows, namely, that the said guardian, or another person for the said minors, is bound to give to the said brother certain sums of money annually, and if the money were not given within certain terms, as was contained in the instrument of composition and transaction, that the said composition and transaction should be considered now, as from then, as not made, and that the said parties should remain ipso facto in that state in which they first were before the aforementioned contract of composition and transaction. Now neither the said guardian nor another person for the said minors has paid to the said brother the said quantity of money within the said terms, as was contained in the said instrument. This payment not having been made to the said brother, the Church of Saint Dominic seeks to be remitted into tenure and corporal possession of one-half of all the goods of the father of this brother, by virtue of the institution made by him in his last will, on the ground that the agreements were not observed towards him. And also, as the said composition was injured beyond one-half of the just price, it seeks restitution in integrum as one holding the place of the minors: notwithstanding that it has to act with the minor.

† If four years have elapsed from the day of the composition, the church cannot seek the benefit of restitution in integrum, as stated in c. ult. de restitutione in integrum, lib. 6. Nor can it allege in the contract of transaction that it was injured beyond half of the just price, as per ff. ad Trebellianum, l. Lucius, § fin. But because the agreements were not observed, the church ought to be put in possession of the aforementioned goods, according to C. de edicto divi Adriani, l. fin., and C. de pactis, l. cum proponas; C. de transactionibus, l. cum proponas, and l. ut responsum. And I presuppose that the Friars Preachers are capable [of acquiring property] by the general custom of the entire order, which they cannot properly be ignorant of, or by apostolic privileges. And thus it is no obstacle that their order is called mendicant. Moreover, they can acquire by law in order to sell, although the rule is different for the Friars Minor, as per de episcopis et clericis, l. Deo nobis, according to Jacobus de Arena and Cynus, because the Clementina Exivi does not speak of the Preachers, nor of their rule, but only of the Minorites. And therefore it has no application to the Preachers, nor to the Hermits, nor to the Carmelites, although they are mendicants.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How age is to be proved, and what if witnesses disagree concerning age.
2. Whether testimony is to be admitted concerning the age of relatives.
3. Whether three men are to be believed more than four women.
body: Who

† He had better established the age in the preceding opinion, which is above in one document, and begins: “I understand that the said, etc.” Therefore, I could not express [my view], because the attestations of both parties were not transmitted to me; but now, having seen the attestations, and considering that three men testify to the minority, while three women and two men testify to the majority of age, and both sides endeavor to prove [their case] by visual inspection, it is necessary that one party testifies falsely. However, it seems that in case of doubt, one should adhere to the number of witnesses; for five witnesses disprove three witnesses, as is noted in the Institutes, *de inutilibus stipulationibus*, § *item verborum*. But certainly there are not five, but four, because the natural brother is regarded as no one according to the form of the statute; although this is so, nevertheless four are more credible than three. Indeed, if there were three and three, because the testimonies would confuse each other, we would judge in favor of the mother, inclining to the more lenient and pious part, D. *de inofficioso testamento*, l. *si pars*. To the contrary, it seems that men are more credible than women, for a man is more worthy of faith, for women are fragile, as D. *de fidei instrumentis*, l. *fin.*; nor does that contrary witness [object],

† because his credibility is somewhat weakened on account of affinity, which is stronger than fervent friendship, which weakens the credibility of a witness, D. de testibus, l. 3, in principio. Therefore, one must resort to evident and ocular justice before the judge himself, to whom it will be said: “You can know better how much credibility should be accorded to the witnesses,” D. de testibus, l. 3, § tu magis. He will inform his mind as much from the quality of the witnesses as from their number, D. de testibus, l. ob carmen, § si testes. He will also weigh the fact that the witnesses of the lady Petrutia do not speak of a confused vision, but specifically refer themselves, with particularity, to a certain time.

And therefore men are better and more credible than women, concerning whom there is also suspicion that they may have been suborned, because they utter the same words word for word, as if they had conferred with one another. The arbiter, therefore, to whom it is permitted to follow his own conscience when faced with conflicting proofs, should consider the matter discreetly, keeping before his eyes only God as judge, and render his decision; for, due to such obscurity and contradiction among the witnesses, arbitrators may compromise between the parties for the sake of peace. But given that the facts stand thus, I say that greater weight should be given to those who render their account more clearly. For those women, when they state that they gave birth at the said time, if reference is made to the month of March, prove nothing: because they said they did not know the year of that month, or at least they testify obscurely, according to the chapter *In praesentia* on proof. And therefore the witnesses of the lady Petrutia are preferable, because they render a clear, certain, and undoubted account. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. By those words, he instituted his wife as usufructuary owner for the entire duration of her life; whether she appears to have been instituted as heir.
2. Whether, and what may be done concerning matters pertaining to the execution of the deceased’s will before the inheritance has been accepted.
3. Point: Among other things, which the testator disposed of in his [will].
body: In his will, etc. Moreover, he made, instituted, and left to himself and to all his movable and immovable goods, and to all other goods whatsoever, as universal usufructuary owner, after first satisfying and discharging the above-mentioned and below-mentioned sums, judgments, and legacies, his wife, Lady Joanna, and a certain daughter of Agnolino of Lucca, generally in all his individual goods, for as long as she shall live, notwithstanding any statutes and ordinances of the city of Lucca which might in any way bind or restrict the said lady in the aforementioned usufruct. Indeed, generally, she shall have the usufruct of all his goods for her lifetime, provided that the above-mentioned and below-mentioned judgments and legacies are paid. To these statutes and ordinances, in this part, he wished to be and to be understood as having totally derogated, to such an extent that the said Lady Joanna cannot or ought not, for as long as she lives, in the aforementioned usufruct, be in any way disturbed, harassed, required, or constrained by the below-mentioned heirs of the testator to draw up any inventory, or otherwise to give security, or to do anything else in any way whatsoever. If his heirs should act to the contrary, they shall ipso facto be deprived of his inheritance, and in that case, the same testator substituted for himself as universal heir the Hospital of the Holy Cross of Lucca, with the same burdens and conditions under which the below-mentioned heirs of his are, as is set forth below, substituted. Moreover, he judged and left to Lady Nicolosa, etc. So copiously, so excellently, and so subtly has it been alleged that it is more expedient to proceed to conclusions than to allege.

† It must be considered, however, whether the lady Joanna was instituted as heir during her lifetime, by those words: “he instituted and left [her] universal usufructuary lady, etc.” And it seems that, although [this is the case], first on account of the word “instituted,” which is civil, and even direct, as in the entire title of the Codex *De haeredum institutione*; Codex *De sacris sanctis ecclesiis*, l. *Si*; Codex *De secundis nuptiis*, l. *Feminae*; and l. *Hac edictali*. Second, on account of the word “lady,” which is understood as referring to direct and universal dominion, and thus to heirship, Digest *De haeredum institutione*, l. *His verbis*. It supports what is noted in Codex *Familiae erciscundae*, l. *Quoties*. Third, on account of the implied term. For when it is said “I institute,” “heir” is implied, Codex *De fideicommissis*, l. *Verbum volo*. Fourth, on account of the necessity of law. For if she were a formal usufructuary, it would follow that the bequest was useless. For before the inheritance is accepted, the day of the usufruct of a legacy does not pass, Codex *De caducis tollendis*, l. 1, § *Excepto etiam usufructu*. And the inheritance cannot be accepted by another while the wife is alive; therefore, such a disposition is as if the wife had been left the usufruct after his death. Such a legacy is invalid, Digest *De usufructu*, l. *Titio cum morietur*. Hence, lest the testator’s will be rendered useless, it seems one should say that the wife is understood to be heir during her lifetime. Nor does it matter that it says “usufructuary,” because usufruct is sometimes used for ownership, and is understood as accidental, Digest *De usufructu*, l. *Proculus*; Digest *De donationibus*, l. *Donatis in concubinam*, § *Species*. Likewise, it does not matter that he instituted other heirs in solidum, namely the hospital and the poor. For that second institution must be considered a substitution, and indeed a fideicommissary one; it cannot be direct, Digest *De vulgari substitutione*, l. *Verbis civilibus*, unless it be said to be special for pious causes, whereby one may be directly substituted after the inheritance has been accepted, just as it may be done by a soldier, Digest *De testamento militis*, l. *Miles ita haeredem*, § *Et quia diximus*. That opinion would be very equitable, if it could be defended by written law.

On the other hand, that the said woman was not instituted as heir by the said words appears most manifestly, because the testator did not say “lady” simply; but he added “usufructuary lady,” that is, lady of the usufruct. For without a conjunction, when two adjectives are placed, the latter is placed as a substantive, as is instituted in Digest *De tutela*, in the beginning. Likewise, the testator expressly said that she should have the usufruct. Likewise, because the immortal heir is instituted, who, by the defect of time, can immediately accept, that is, the poor and the hospital, l. *Haeredem ex die* and l. *Extraneum*.

† And if she could not immediately accept the inheritance, the executors seem able to carry out the will in order to preserve the testator’s intent. And equity, derived from natural justice, would dictate this, as also does law 12 of the Tables, in the Digest, *De verbis significationibus*, in the law *Verbis legis*. But written law seems to oppose this, because nothing written in a will is valid unless confirmed by acceptance of the inheritance, as in the law *Si servus communis meus* and *Castrensis peculii*, in the beginning, in the Digest, *De stipulationibus servorum*. Hence, the act of an executor, unless confirmed, is invalid unless the inheritance is first accepted, saving that in those matters which by their nature precede the acceptance of the inheritance, such as funeral expenses, and in legacies left for the soul, because spiritual matters are not confirmed by temporal ones, but stand by themselves as superior and not dependent on lesser things, in the law *Eam quam*, in the Code, *De fideicommissis*, in the gloss, and in the law *Nulli*, in the Code, *De episcopis et clericis*. If therefore the lady is not an heir, how could she have discharged the obligation as an heir? Not because the substantial form of an heir is to be an heir, but because this person is not an heir, nor an executrix, not because she was not confirmed as executrix without having accepted the inheritance, in the Digest, *De executione tutorum*, in the law *Si is qui tres*, § 1. O illustrious science of civil law, if the testator ordered his money to be thrown into the sea, it could be done with impunity without accepting the inheritance, in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, in the law *Melius*. And if he orders it to be distributed prudently, it cannot be done: because the civil obligation, which is confirmed by acceptance, or rather induced by it, is lacking. But it is not new that before the inheritance is accepted, the testator’s will should be carried out, in the Digest, *De conditionibus institutionum*, in the law *Mulier*, § 1. And the executor is like a certain procurator of the deceased, in the Digest, *De mandato*, in the law *Si vero non remunerandi*, § final. I answer briefly, that the discharge was valid, not as from an heir, because she was not an heir, nor as from a usufructuary, because she did not give security. The case is regarding the usufruct of a name in law 1 of the Code, *De usufructu*. But as from an executrix, who had the mandate to pay out from what was received: but she received the sum, and thus she could pay out from the sum. Likewise she received the rest, and could pay out from the rest. And these are connected matters, in the Digest, *De manumissione testamento*, in the law *Qui filium* and the law *Si ita fuerit*. It also appears that the expenses were rightly made in the payment of legacies, especially for the soul, in the Digest, *De administratione tutorum*, in the law *Lex quae tutores*, in the Code, *De alimentis pupillorum*, in the final law, and the last law, in the Code, *De pignoribus*, and in the law *Si ventri*, at the end, in the Digest, *De privilegiis creditorum*. For since by this way we come to the fulfillment of the mandate, it is necessary that this be permitted, whether it is impossible to fulfill or not so conveniently. The laws are common. To this is added also the commission of free administration. And it helps, in the Digest, *De solutionibus*, in the law *Vero procuratori*. And the trust chosen and approved by the testator, in the Digest, *De legatis secundis*, in the law *Unum ex familia*, § *Item imperator Marcus*, and in the Institutes, *De satisdatione tutorum*, in the beginning. That also the said lady did as a usufructuary and executrix, one should not say that as a usufructuary she could not: because the discharge is valid in that mode and name in which it can be valid, in the Digest, *De acceptilationibus*, in the law *An inutilis*, in the Digest, *De testamento militis*, law 3. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a witness who testifies that the creditor made a settlement with the debtor and confessed that he had been satisfied proves the payment.
2. Whether and when the testimony of a witness outside the articles is valid or not; this is a beautiful opinion and a matter of daily occurrence.
3. The judge must make the witnesses swear on the articles given and the entire case, so that if any speak outside the articles, they may be said to have testified without having sworn.
4. The statutes of the consuls bind outsiders by reason of contract.
body: The case is stated as follows. Francis of Nursia brought an action before the podestà and the judge of the territory of Nursia against John, procurator of Nicholas, and demanded 130 florins on account of the sale of certain cloths sold by the said Francis to the said Nicholas in the city of Perugia for the price of 237 florins. The procurator of the said Nicholas confessed to the contents of the said petition. However, he stated that the said Francis had been paid the said sum of 130 florins by the said Nicholas through the hands of Guido Albizzi in Perugia. The judge ordered the said procurator to pay the said Francis the said 130 florins within ten days on account of the matter contained in the said petition, saving the right of the said procurator to prove the said satisfaction of the 130 florins within a term of twenty days. The said procurator, before the podestà and the judge of the said territory, drew up certain articles for the proof of the said payment. The aforementioned judge committed the examination of witnesses on the said articles to the Captain of Perugia and his assessor, and notified the said Francis to appear in the city of Perugia to witness the receiving of the oaths of the witnesses. The witnesses, having been cited, took their oaths and testified on the said articles, as appears from their depositions. Furthermore, the written record of the book of the aforementioned Nicholas, in which appear certain payments made to the said Francis, was approved by the consuls of the merchant guild of the city of Perugia, according to the ordinances of the said guild. The question is, having considered all these matters, what are the duties of the judge and the podestà of the said territory of Nursia in the said case. I answer that John, the aforementioned procurator, ought to be definitively absolved from the petition of the said Francis. For, as appears from the depositions, Peter Antonii, a witness produced, proves how Francis confessed, in the presence of Nicholas, that he had received through the hands of Guido 130 florins. Moreover, the aforementioned Peter Antonii and Philip John, another witness, prove the settlement of accounts made between the said Nicholas and Francis, and upon the settlement of the said accounts, Nicholas remained debtor to Francis only in the amount of 100 gold florins of the aforementioned sum.

And although the first witness proving the confession does not have a corroborating witness, nevertheless, regarding the balance of the account, the said Peter Antonii has Philip as a corroborating witness. According to the law, if the defendant alleges that he has paid the creditor, it suffices to prove that the creditor confessed to having been satisfied, or that the creditor settled the account with the debtor. For one alleging a fact suffices to prove the confession regarding that fact, when one and the same fact results from the proof of the truth of the fact and from the proof of the confession regarding the fact, *de successionibus ab intestato*, chapter *finis*, where the case is found. Nor does it avail to object what is noted by Guido in the *Speculum*, *de testibus*, § 1, under the words "but suppose," where he says that if I sue on a loan of 10, because I lent, it does not suffice for me to prove the confession regarding the loan; because I ought to prove the delivery of the money, and not the confession, *l. testium*, Codex, *de testibus*, *de non numerata pecunia*; *l. si ex cautione*, Codex, *de solutionibus*; *l. 1*. And because the judge ought to proceed according to the allegations, and here nothing was said about the confession, for there one and the same loan does not result from the proof of the truth of the fact and from the proof of the confession regarding the fact. For where a loan is truly made, it is a natural loan. But where a confession regarding a loan emanates, and then it is a civil loan, *Institutes*, *de litterarum obligationibus*. Therefore, it is one thing to prove a natural loan, another to prove a civil loan. For these differ from each other as distinct and separate species, and one does not include the other, and therefore, to one alleging one, it does not suffice to prove the other. But in our case it is not so, because to the debtor alleging that he has paid, it suffices to prove the confession regarding the satisfaction, or regarding the balance of the account; because from all these is included payment and satisfaction, *Digestum*, *de pigneraticia actione*, *l. si rem*, § *omnes*.

† Moreover, the aforementioned objection does not hold, because in the articles upon which the witnesses testify, no mention is made of a confession or a settlement of accounts, but rather of a payment which Nicolaus claims to have made through the hands of Gutius of Florence. And thus it appears that the testimony is not valid, except insofar as it is contained in the articles; it seems that other matters have been waived by the parties, as stated in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Cum ita*. Nor ought the notary to have exceeded the form given, as stated in the Digest, *De iure fisci*, law *Certa*. For the examiner ought not to examine on any matter other than the articles transmitted, as stated in the Decretals, *De testibus*, chapter *Praesentium*, Book 6. Nor ought a witness to testify outside the articles, as stated in the Digest, *De petitione hereditatis*, law *Si quis libertatem*; in the Code, *Qui legitime personis*, final law; in the Digest, *De iureiurando*, law *Si duo patroni*. And note the gloss in the Decretals, *De testibus*, chapter *De testibus*, under the title *De testibus*. For that statement is true when the article upon which the witness testifies is irrelevant to the case; otherwise, if it is pertinent to the case. Hence, Speculum states in the title *De testibus*, section 1, that if the articles are not fully composed, yet the witness fully testifies regarding those matters which pertain to the case, the testimony is valid; because witnesses ought to declare for both parties whatever they know, as stated in the Code, *De episcopis et clericis*, authentic *Sed iudex*. For it matters not whether the witness states the truth spontaneously or when questioned, as stated in the Digest, *De codicillis*, law *Si duobus*, section 1. And a witness is deemed to have been summoned to testify on all matters which pertain to the case, as stated in the Code, *De agris et censibus*, law *Cum scimus*. And it is not to be disapproved to question a witness outside the articles, since it is not contrary to law, as stated in the Digest, *Quod metus causa*, final law; in the Digest, *De condictione indebiti*, law *Eleganter*, section *Penultimus*; in the Digest, *De interdictis et relegatis*, law *Legatorum*, section *Ad tempus*. Nor does it seem that by submitting articles one waives other matters, because if witnesses testify on the generality of the case, as stated in the Digest, *De publicis*, law 2; in the Digest, *De haereditatibus iustis*, law 1. It supports what Innocent notes in the Decretals, *De testibus*, chapter *Pastoralis*, where, if the plaintiff demands money from the defendant as being due to him, and it appears through witnesses produced by the plaintiff that the debt exists, he says that this will benefit the defendant; because although the witnesses were not summoned for this purpose, nevertheless the principal matter of the case has occurred, as stated in the Decretals, *De accusationibus*, chapter *Inquisitionis*. The above is well supported by what Innocent notes in the Decretals, *De testibus*, chapter *Per tuas*, where he says,

† That the judge makes the witnesses swear upon the articles given, and upon the entire cause, so that if they say anything beyond the articles, they are not said to have deposed without having sworn, as in the Decretals, De testibus, c. De testibus. The same William in the Speculum, De testibus, § Illud. Jacobus de Arena in the law Si, C. Qui legibus personis, distinguishes: either the witness deposes on another matter or cause, and it is not valid; or on the matter in dispute, but otherwise than the articles state, and then, if he swore only upon the articles, it is not valid. But if he swore upon the entire cause, or to answer the interrogatories, then it is valid, De accusatione, c. Cum dilecti. Here, however, the witnesses swore not only upon the articles, but also upon the cause; therefore, the testimony is valid in all matters pertaining to the cause, as is proved above. It is established, moreover, that since we are here dealing with the liberation of the debtor, which is brought about by the payment of the debt, or by the creditor’s confession of payment, or by the settlement of accounts, all these things pertain to the principal cause and to the liberation of the debtor. Furthermore, great weight must be given to the sentence of the consuls approving the written record of the said book, which could be approved by them according to the ordinances, arg. l. 2, De constitutionibus pecuniariis; l. fin., C. De iure omnium iudicum.

† which statutes bind the same Fran., although he is a foreigner, because with regard to those matters which were transacted in the place of the contract, they bind him, 2. dist. c. Nos consuetudinem. and c. Illa. D. de iudiciis. l. Exigere dotem. D. de postul. l. Ex ea. D. de eo, qui mit. in pos. c. Cum uenuissent. c. Cum si. From these I conclude that the said Nicolaus ought to be absolved from the petition of the said Fran. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether sacrilegists and robbers of ecclesiastical property may be apprehended anywhere. Likewise, whether they ought to be remitted to the judge of the offense.
body: These sacrilegious persons

† Robbers of the goods of monasteries or churches may be apprehended anywhere; nevertheless, they ought to be remitted to the place of the offense, so that they may be punished there, as in Auth. ut nulli iudicum, § si quis vero comprehensurum; and l. desertorem, in principio, de re militari; and Codex, de raptu virginum, l. 1, § si autem. Therefore, the apprehension could have been made for the purpose of remission to the place of the offense. However, such remissions are not according to custom; therefore, neither are such apprehensions, as is noted in c. pastoralis, de re iudicata, in the Clementines. And thus, as regards the procedure of the judge, it was rightly judged by Lord Adotianus. Nevertheless, it is established that the said 40 florins ought not to be restored by the Lord Abbot; the text is in l. si, § fin., Digestum, quod metus causa. Moreover, the aforementioned magnific Lord ought not to suffer this, even by his mere office; Codex, de episcopis et clericis, l. si quis in hoc genus; in Auth. ut iudices sine quoquo suffragio, § oportet, in the word reddantur futura; and in Auth. ut liceat matri et aviae, § illud valet, column 8. Aid ought not to be given to evildoers; Codex, de defendendis civibus, l. per omnes. And it serves well against the said sacrilege; Digestum, de accusationibus, l. si cui, § cum sacrilegium. And thus I, Baldus, say.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one can be condemned for the crime of usury after death.
2. How it is proved that someone is a usurer. And nos. 9 and 10.
3. A manifest usurer is detected in two ways. And nos. 8 and 10.
4. What is called legitimate proof.
5. Proof made against a usurer after the usurer's death does not prove that he was manifest.
6. It does not follow that, because someone was formerly a usurer, he is therefore presumed to be a usurer today. And no. 12.
7. Intent alone is not sufficient for someone to be called a manifest usurer, but an act is required, that is, to receive and to make usury.
8. "Manifest" is understood in two ways. And no. 3.
9. When an act without quality requires someone to prove it.
10. Regarding the subject matter of this opinion, add below opinion 365.
body: Having examined the petition, the articles, and the attestations, four points are made by the plaintiff against the defendants: first, because certain witnesses prove that John committed and practiced usury; second, because another witness proves that John committed usury; third, because certain witnesses prove that they heard it said that he committed usury; fourth, because they prove the reputation that he was a usurer. These seem sufficient for John to be pronounced and declared a manifest usurer. For we have arguments and corroborations in the statements of the witnesses who say that he committed and practiced usury. Arguments and corroborations, together with reputation, seem sufficient for him to be declared a manifest usurer, *de usur.*, c. *Cum in tua*; and in the same title, c. *Ult.*, lib. 6. Moreover, we have the confession of the party, for John confessed that he had committed usury, which confession establishes notoriety in law, *de verb. sig.*, c. *Cum olim*. But I will show that he cannot be pronounced a manifest usurer.

† An action for the crime of usury cannot be brought after death, except on account of property, which occurs when the action is brought for the restitution of usuries to be made to the plaintiff, as in c. Cum tu; or so that the testament may be void, and thus the property be restored to the plaintiff, or to the intestate heir through those instituted in the testament, as in c. Quanquam; or so that the usurer may not be buried, or if buried, may be exhumed from the grave. And in these cases the accusation proceeds, and proof is admitted after the death of the usurer. But in our case, upon inspection of the petition, the action is not brought on account of property, because this is not expressed in the repetition, and thus the action is brought ineptly. And the ineptitude is an objection raised against the plaintiffs; therefore, the defendant ought to be absolved, de iudicibus, c. Examinata. It is supported by C. de annua exceptione, l. Si. But even if the petition proceeds from the proofs, nevertheless the defendant cannot be condemned.

† I demonstrate this as follows: to prove someone a manifest usurer, two things must be proved, namely, the fact and the quality of the fact. The fact is the usurious contract itself, because contracts are facts, D. de cura furiosi, l. consilio, § si. The quality, however, is the very manifest nature. For notoriety and manifestness relate to the fact or contract by way of quality, D. de officio delegati, c. 1, lib. 6, where by the gloss and by Innocentius; D. de cohaeredibus, c. tua. But in our case neither is proved, for the fact, i.e., the usurious contracts, is not proved, because the witnesses testifying about the usurious contracts are singular with respect to the contracts, with respect to the places, and with respect to the times, when one testifies about one contract, another about another contract. One testifies about a contract celebrated at one time, another about a contract celebrated at another time. One testifies about a contract celebrated in one place, another about a contract celebrated in another place, as appears from the attestations. But singular witnesses are not believed, D. de electione, c. bonae; D. de accusationibus, c. cum dilecti. Moreover, the quality, i.e., the very manifest nature, is not proved, because no witness testifies about such quality.

† This quality, i.e., the very manifest nature, is discovered in two ways. First, from the evidence of the fact: for example, because he publicly and openly lent money, or kept a ready table for lending, as the glossa says in de usuris, c. 1, lib. 6; and in this case no witness testifies. Second, the manifest nature is discovered from the disposition of the law, as in one who is condemned, confessed, or convicted, de veritate, sigillum, c. cum olifam; similarly, none of these is proven: not condemnation, because it was not issued; not proof,

† because legitimate proof induces notoriety of law, as in c. cum olim, cited above. But that proof is not legitimate which is made through individual witnesses, as in the aforementioned c. bonae; nor is it a confession, because the one proving the confession is an individual witness, as appears from the attestations. Moreover, that confession regarding the crime of usury was made outside of court and in the absence of the adversary; therefore, it is not sufficient for condemnation, as stated in ff. de adult. l. capite quinto; de excessib. praela. c. quam sit graue. For a confession to be prejudicial, it must appear that someone publicly confessed before a priest and witnesses that he is a usurer, and ordered the restitution of usuries, and handed over a ledger of accounts, as the glossa says in c. quanquam; none of which occurred here. Since, therefore, by the disposition of the law, one is required to prove two things, namely, to prove the fact, i.e., the contract, and to prove the quality, i.e., that it is manifest: if neither is proven, the defendant is absolved, de ese c. si forte, li. 6; de ver. sig. l. cum eo; l. vbi casus; similarly de proba. c. licet causam. Therefore, the aforementioned proofs are not sufficient for condemnation, because through individual witnesses and through witnesses testifying from hearsay and reputation, condemnation cannot follow for a crime, whether it is prosecuted criminally or civilly, de testib. c. tam literas, in prin. vbi casus. Nor is it proven manifestly, although it is proven by reputation that someone is a usurer; because it is one thing to prove the fact or the quality, and another to prove the reputation concerning the fact or quality, de accu. c. inquisitionis, §. quaumsti.

† Moreover, it must be carefully observed that proof which is produced against a usurer, after the death of the usurer, does not prove him to have been a manifest usurer.
