This proof, from which a presumption of law is induced, induces this notoriety on the part of the proof, and induces it as manifest, but does not induce it retroactively as manifest, as is stated in the question *fortè*. Where, if after the death of the usurer his books are found, it would not be said that he was a manifest usurer. And therefore, for the aforementioned reasons, it cannot be judged that he was a manifest usurer at the time of his life and death. But if proofs are received during the lifetime of the usurer, then, if the proof were legitimate, it would constitute him a manifest usurer.

It is also to be carefully observed that, since the aforementioned witnesses state that he formerly committed usury, expressing an ancient and long time ago, because some expressed that it was already 30 years ago, some that it was already 22 years ago, some that it was already 20 years ago, it could not be judged by such proofs that he was a manifest usurer after those times, and especially at the time of his death. For this notoriety does not have perseverance in itself, as the gloss says in *de usuris*, c. *cum in diec.* For it is not notoriety of a permanent fact, but notoriety of a transitory fact. And sometimes a usurer does not continue this crime. But where he continues it, and publicly, then it is notoriety of an interrupted fact, as Speculum says in the title *de notorio*, § *tam notorio*, under the word *ceterum*. But in our case, it has not been proven that this John continued the crime of usury publicly; therefore, it cannot be said that he was a manifest usurer after those times, nor that he was a manifest usurer at the time of his death.

† Nor does it follow that because he was formerly a usurer, he is therefore presumed to be a usurer today, as in the law *semel malus*. For there is not such a strong presumption as would lead to condemnation. Moreover, that presumption pertains only to the criminal intent, as Dy and Ioan say in the rule *semel*.

But the mind alone is not sufficient for one to be called a manifest usurer; but a deed is required, i.e., to make and receive usuries, as in the cited chapter *Quamquam*. Therefore, since the aforementioned arguments and supporting evidence, together with proof of hearing and reputation, are not sufficient for condemnation, nor can it be pronounced from them that he was manifest, in the Council of Lucdon, *de usuris*, chapter *Quicumque*, book 6.

I answer that "manifest" can be understood as synonymous with "notorious," which possesses an evidentiary quality of fact that cannot be concealed by any evasion. The evidentiary quality of fact is said to exist, for example, when one keeps his altar prepared, and keeps a table or chest ready to lend money to anyone at usury, as the glossa states in *De usuris*, c. 1, lib. 6. Similarly, the evidentiary quality of fact is said to exist when one publicly, openly, and commonly in the house in which he dwells lends money and receives pledges, as the Archipresbyter states in the same chapter. It is also said that the evidentiary quality of fact is manifest when one can be convicted by his apparent books concerning the extortion of usurious wickedness, as the Archipresbyter states in the same chapter *Quiquid*. Hence, Federicus de Senis stated in consilium 7 that "manifest" can be understood as that whose proof lies in the evident. For example, defects of sight, hearing, and knowledge do not appear openly to everyone, and yet by subjecting the person to examination, such defect is found evident and manifest, *De electionibus*, c. *Si forte*; *De verborum significatione*, c. 2, lib. 6. Thus, in the case at hand, although someone did not exercise usury openly and notoriously, nevertheless by a prompt and easy examination it will become manifest, for example, because his books of accounts appear, regarding which there is no doubt that they are the books of the usurer himself; such proof can be called clear and manifest, as the Archipresbyter states in the same chapter 2. This is supported by Question 27, c. *Omnes feminae*.

In another sense, "manifest" can be understood as notorious in law. Notorious in law is said to be the case when someone publicly confesses before a priest and witnesses that he is a usurer, orders the restitution of usury, and hands over his books and account ledger to the diocesan bishop; therefore, he is also said to be a usurer notorious in law when he has been condemned for the crime of usury, as the glossa states in *De usuris*, c. 1, lib. 6; or when he is published in the church by the bishop as a usurer, as Hostiensis states in *De usuris*, c. 1, lib. 6. And the same is stated by Goffredus in the same chapter 1, who adds that he is considered by law a notorious usurer who is published in the church by the bishop as a usurer. It is otherwise if he were still tolerated in the church, *De cohabitatione clericorum*, c. *Vestra*.

If, however, they are manifest by reputation, yet not notorious, then there is no place for the penalty of that consilium by the law itself, but rather by publication, for which publication it suffices that those summoned confess, or that it be proven by witnesses.

Furthermore, "manifest" can be understood as that which is notorious and above mere reputation (*famosum*), for example, because it can be proven, and beyond customary proof it is *famosum* and public, yet not to such an extent that it could be called notorious in law. *De cohabitatione clericorum*, c. *Cum in tua*. For "public" does not necessarily include "notorious," *De cohabitatione clericorum*, c. *Tua*, as Federicus states in the same consilium, who concludes that "manifest" is taken for "notorious," which has the evidentiary quality of fact, or is notorious in law by sentence or by the judge's publication, by clear and undoubted proofs. And note carefully this word, which says "by clear and undoubted proofs"; therefore, the proof must be clear, undoubted, and legitimate, *Codex, De probationibus*, l. *Sciant*. And thus, singular witnesses are not sufficient.

It is also to be known that "manifest" in the cause of the chapter *Quamquam* is taken for "notorious," as Hostiensis states in *De usuris*, c. *Cum tu* and c. *Quia in communibus*. And Speculum in the title *De notoriis criminibus*, § *Sequitur*, and in § *Iam de notorio*, versi. *Notorium*.

Reducing therefore all the aforesaid

† It is clearly demonstrated by the aforementioned proofs that he cannot be judged to have been a manifest usurer. And therefore his will is valid, since he is not a manifest usurer; for the aforementioned proofs of the witnesses are not legitimate proofs, for seven reasons. First, because the witnesses are singular with respect to the contracts about which they testify, and with respect to place and time; for one witness testifies about one contract, and one place, and one time, another about another contract, and another time, and another place; therefore, as singular witnesses, they are not believed, *de electione*, c. *bonae*. Second, that proof is not legitimate, because when it is required to prove someone a manifest usurer, two things must be proved, namely, the fact, that is, the usurious contract, and secondly, the quality, which is the very state of being manifest, *de officio delegati*, c. 1, according to Innocentius, *de cohabitatione clericorum*, c. *tua*. But the fact has not been proved, since the witnesses are singular. Moreover, the quality, which is being manifest, has not been proved; because no witness testifies about this quality. Here it should be noted that such a quality is ascertained in two ways. In one way, from the evidence of the fact, because he publicly keeps a ready table, *de usuris*, c. 1, lib. 6, which has not been proved here. In another way, he is ascertained to be manifest by the disposition of the law, as in one who is condemned, or confessed, or convicted, *de verbis significatis*, c. *cum olim*. None of these is present here. For he is not condemned, because this man was never condemned for the crime of usury. Moreover, he is not proven, because proof then induces notoriety when it is legitimate, as in the cited c. *cum olim*. But here the proof is not legitimate, as has been said above, and will also be said below. Moreover, there is no confession of the party here. For although one witness testifies about a confession, it has no corroborating witness, nor is that confession prejudicial. Nor can a sentence follow from it, because the confession was made outside of court, and in the absence of the adversary, as in *ff. de adulteriis*, l. *capite*; *de excessibus praeparatorum*, c. *quam sit*; *de iudiciis*, c. *at si clerici*. Third, the proof is not legitimate, because for the will of a manifest usurer to be null, it must be proved that he was a manifest usurer at the time of the will. For the decretal states that although the wills of manifest usurers are void, the quality joined to the word is determined according to the time of the word, *de statu hominum*, l. *in servorum*; *de noxalis actione*, l. *in delictis*, § *si detracta*. But it has not been proved that he was a usurer at the time of the will; nor even at the time of death; therefore the will is valid. Fourth, the proof is not legitimate for this notable reason, if

† After the death of the usurer, proof is admitted that he practiced usury; this proof now, from the time of the proof, induces notoriety, but does not make it notorious retroactively. From such proof, notoriety is induced by the death of the usurer; therefore, let it be drawn back to the time of the usurer’s life, 24 q. 2, Si forte, where it is said that if after the death of the usurer account books are found, nevertheless he is not thereby called a manifest usurer. For the finding of such books induces manifestness from the time when the books are found, but does not fictitiously make him manifest at that earlier time. And this is also held by Johannes de Usuris, c. Cum in diœcesi. And thus it is clear that it has not been proven that he was a manifest usurer at the time of the testament, nor at the time of death. Fifthly, it is not legitimate proof, because here a crime is in question, where proof must be clear, De probationibus, l. Sciant. Nor do singular witnesses with reputation suffice for condemnation, De testibus, l. Tam litteris, ubi casus. Nor does it suffice to prove reputation, where the proof of the truth of the fact is in question, De accusatione, c. Inquisitione, § Quæsiuisti. Sixthly, it is not legitimate proof,

† because when it falls upon a party to prove the fact and its quality, it is not sufficient to prove the fact without the quality, ff. de instructione, l. habebat; and this is a case of election, cap. si forte, book 6. But this quality of manifestness has not been proven.

Seventhly, this is shown thus: the witnesses testify concerning an ancient fact, that is, concerning usurious contracts celebrated from ancient times, and this criminal act is a transitory act, not a continuing act. Nor is the continuation of the crime of usury presumed, because continuation is a matter of fact, and facts are not presumed, D. de publ. l. quaecunque; and thus the crime is not presumed to have continued at the time of the testament, nor even at the time of death. Nor does it avail to object that one who was once evil is presumed to be evil today, as in the rule semel [malus semel malus]; for this is true of a presumption which is one of intent, as Dy. and Io. say there. But to induce and prove someone to be a manifest usurer, it does not suffice to prove by a presumption which consists in intent. Rather, proof of the fact is required, as in the cited chapter quamquam, just as is the very extension of usuries. Eighthly, the petition must be carefully considered, where it is simply concluded and argued that he be pronounced to have been a manifest usurer. This petition does not proceed, because after the death of the usurer, no action can be brought concerning the crime of usury unless there is an interest of the plaintiff, and the plaintiff has an interest either because he seeks the restitution of usuries, or because he alleges that the testament of the usurer is null, and thus that his inheritances ought to pertain to him. But for none of these effects is action brought, as appears from the form of the petition; therefore, the plaintiff is not heard, because he does not express any cause of his interest in the libel, and the exception of non-interest precludes the way for the plaintiff. D. de testib. c. ex parte. I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the seller is liable if proceedings have been unjustly brought against the buyer.
2. Things are sold in many and various ways.
3. An action for eviction may be brought on three grounds.
4. In which cases the seller is not liable for eviction.
5. The seller follows the forum of the buyer.
body: The facts of the case

† Such is the case: Ser Paulus of Butrio sold one farmstead to Benedictus Guidutius of Sigillo, and promised to legally defend it for him, as appears in the instrument of sale itself. A dispute is said to have arisen concerning the said farmstead against the said Benedictus in the City of Perugia. And he was condemned in the libel, as is more fully contained in the sentence, which is transmitted to you, and an appeal was taken by Benedictus, and the sentence was confirmed. But Paulus says that he is not bound to defend the said farmstead in the said case, nor for its eviction in the said judgment, for the reasons set forth in the allegations, which are transmitted to you. Now the question arises, what is the law, having regard to the aforesaid.

† Things are sold in many and various ways: sometimes by one’s own right, sometimes by leasehold or census right, sometimes partly by one right and partly by another, with a distinction between the parts. And sometimes without distinction, but with a certain condition, as is fully noted in Speculum, De emptione et venditione, § 1, “hoc etiam scias.” For the understanding of many forms, and the contract fell under the second form, as appears from the instrument. And it must be presupposed that this contract does not aim at the alienation of the Church’s property, but at the alienation of the right of a private person, D. De contrahenda emptione, l. Qui tabernas. Such alienation may be made by reason of custom, by reason of an agreement made with the Church, by reason of the lord’s required custom, by reason of the lord’s consent, and by reason of his ratification, C. De iure emphyteutico, l. 2 and l. Si. And assuming that the transfer of emphyteutic right is invalid, nevertheless the agreements are valid, C. De evictionibus, l. Si fundum Stichus; C. Communia utriusque iudicii, l. Si fratres. And so says Speculum, supra, and this is the truth.

Secondly, it must be premised for clarity that in this matter the action proceeds on three grounds. For if the action is brought on account of possession evicted, in which no right is contained, then the action is brought by the action on the contract of sale, because it is not the thing itself, but bare possession, that has been evicted, as in D. de actione empti, l. Ratio, in principio. But if it is brought on account of the thing evicted, or on account of the eviction of ownership, or quasi-ownership, then the action is brought by the action on stipulation, D. de evictionibus, l. Habere licere, and the aforementioned l. Si fundum, with its si clause. But if it is brought on account of the thing not defended, because the buyer promised to defend it and did not defend it, similarly the stipulation is invoked; however, the seller is not bound to defend against force and injury, whether judicial or extrajudicial, C. de actione empti, l. Finis, and note in Speculum, d. § 1, ver. Ecce primum pactum, and note and concordances. And this is true when the force and injury are directed against the buyer. But when they are directed against the seller himself, then the seller is indeed bound, because injury done to the seller ought not to harm the buyer, D. de fideiussoribus, l. Exceptione, in ratione sui; D. de locato conducto, l. Si merces, § Culpa; D. de solutionibus et liberationibus, l. In his, § 1; D. de hereditate vendenda, l. 2, § Solet ei. It is considered that he succumbed to what was not due, as stated in the aforementioned laws.

Thirdly, it must be premised that the seller is not liable for future events occurring after the contract of sale has been concluded. Therefore, an eviction arising from new laws disposing of matters contrary to or beyond the common law does not fall to the detriment of the seller, as stated in the text of the aforementioned law *Lucius*. It is also established that laymen cannot make statutes concerning the rights of the Church, because a subordinate does not make law for a superior, as set forth in the chapter *Ecclesiae S. Mariae* on constitutions. Nevertheless, without prejudice to the Church, they may well make statutes and agreements among themselves, as provided in the law *nec ex praetorio* on the rules of law.

† Moreover, it is certain that the seller follows the forum of the buyer, D. de iudiciis, l. venditor; C. ubi in rem actio, l. 1. And regarding the law and the order of the forum, he ought to follow the buyer, as is evident there. From these premises, I conclude that the sentence passed here was rendered in a possessory action, not against the dispossessor, who is said to be the abbot, but against the possessor, as in c. saepe and c. reintegranda. Laymen could not proceed against the abbot, de foro competenti, c. si diligenti. Furthermore, I consider that if the abbot had not been paid for that pension, the judge acted rightly, C. de iure emptionis, l. 2, unless something else was stipulated in the agreements, as in the text there. Therefore, if the buyer did not avail himself of such a defense, let him impute it to himself, not to the seller. The same applies if he did avail himself, but was not heard by the judge due to the power of the opposing party. However, if the sentence were founded on truth, eviction would be owed at least under the clause for failure to defend the thing: because the seller, having been notified, did not defend, and because this is gathered from the records of the eviction case. It is necessary to examine the records, for without having seen them, a definitive opinion cannot be given. But once they have been seen, what law must be upheld will appear from the foregoing: because if the proceeding regarding such injury was unjust, the seller is not bound, D. de evictionibus, l. si per imprudentiam. I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Civil Law.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether goods purchased by one of the partners during the partnership are to be shared.
2. Where no instrument appears for the giving of a dowry, it is proved by two witnesses.
3. A person related to both parties who gives the dowry is admitted as a witness when the suspicion of bias ceases.
body: Lippus had three sons, namely Lipputius, John, and Augustine. Lipputius went about trading, and sometimes he made a profit, sometimes he incurred losses. But John and Augustine remained at home with their father and performed manual labor. They also made profits and paid out of the common funds large sums of money on many occasions for the said Lipputius, who had been captured, and they did all things as partners. Nevertheless, the said Lipputius purchased certain goods and executed instruments in his own name. Cechus died, and a certain girl also remained from the said Lipputius, who likewise passed away.

† It is asked whether the aforementioned goods purchased during the said partnership are to be shared by each for a third part. I answer: yes, as in D. 17,2, l. si societatem universarum. It is also proposed that the learned Margarita, their mother and wife of the said Cech, had a dowry given to the said Cech by the present brother of the said learned [Margarita].
† It is asked, when the instrument does not appear, by how many witnesses it can be proved. I answer, by two. D. de testibus, l. ubi numerus.

† But whether the said brother, who provided her with a dowry, will be a competent witness against his nephews and the said girl, his great-granddaughter. I answer: yes, because, since he is related to both parties, all sinister suspicion ceases, ff. de ritu nuptiarum, l. non solum, § de uno. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the university binds each individual, and whether each individual is liable for the expenses and burdens that arise, is distinguished.
body: Point. Certain men from a certain village purchased a certain plot of land in the said village, or in another nearby, for the purpose of building a certain fortification thereon for a certain price, and these men were not two parts, and they purchased for themselves, and for the men, and persons, and households, and the community of the said village, assembled in a public and general meeting of theirs, and they deliberated that whatever was done by the said men who purchased the said plot for the purpose of building the said fortification, and that all expenses made and to be made in the said fortification, were done lawfully, and whether all the men and persons of the said village are bound to contribute to the said expenses according to their share. Now two of the said men, one of whom dwells in the said village and there has his share, who was not among the men present at the said assembly, refuses to pay the expenses for his share. Likewise another, who has his share in the said village, yet did not dwell there for many years before, nor does he now dwell in the said village, but in another village distant from it, refuses to pay even the said expenses and the said assessments for his share.

† It is asked whether they are bound to the said expenses, both those incurred and those collected, or not. And having seen the statute of the commune of Perugia, placed in the first book of statutes under the rubric "The majority binds the minority, when the act is useful and necessary to the community," and of this utility the individual members of the community, who are subject to contribution, are participants. For it is according to nature that he who shares in the benefits should bear the burdens, and not another. But if it is due to him that he does not participate, then let him impute it to himself: provided that they cannot transfer their domicile unless those who consent do so, as in l. domicilium, de municip. Therefore, either the said thing was purchased in the same village or its district, and the purchase was made for the public good of all, and all are bound to contribute; or it was purchased outside the village and the district of the village, and then otherwise, because only those who obligated themselves are bound to contribute. Likewise, if it does not regard the public good, nor bring utility to others, but only to those consenting, they are bound: for it is rather a monopoly than a public right, de constitutionibus, c. cum omnes, C. quae sint lon. consuet., l. 2, in gl., de reg. iur., l. aliud, §. refertur, C. de monopoli, l. 1, ad munic., l. maior, C. de iure delib., l. nec emeret, ff. magistr. conuen., l. j, §. j, et quod no, ff. de pac., l. maiorem, and l. rescriptum, and l. Item magistri, in gl. or. And from these it appears that a response must be given to the questions with distinction. I, Bal. de Per.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. That rivers are [things of common use].
2. What a bank is, and whose it is.
3. A mill, or the dam of a mill, and whether it is lawful to construct them; if two persons unjustly build, neither is enjoined against the other.
4. What a shore is.
5. What a riverbed is, and whether it is lawful to build upon it.
6. Whether and when one may use water, or alter its course, or obstruct it; with the clause, "if you feel yourself aggrieved."
body: Four

There are the bank, the shore, the riverbed, the water, and the rivers. There are two kinds: navigable and non-navigable. And again, the non-navigable is twofold: one kind that makes another navigable, and another kind that does not make another navigable, to which a navigable one flows out, such as one that has an outlet to the sea, or one where a non-navigable flows into another similarly non-navigable.

† A bank is a place sloping or descending from the level ground to the water, as stated in the Digest, On Rivers, l. pe. These riverbanks are the property of those who hold contiguous estates adjacent to the bank; nevertheless, the use of the banks is public, that is, common to the people, by the law of nations, which all nations employ, Digest, On the Division of Things, l. riparum; and Institutes, ibid., §. riparum.

† First, therefore, it must be considered whether it is lawful to establish a mill or a mill dam on this bank. And it has been said that it is so, if it harms neither the public nor a private person; otherwise, if it were harmful to the public utility of navigators, or if it were made to the detriment of a neighbor contrary to law. Cf. *vicini*. The first point is proven by natural equity, because that which harms no one and benefits the doer is deemed to be done in the air, D. de aqua pluv. arc. l. 2, §. item Varus; and D. ne quid in flum. publ. l. 1, §. sunt qui putant. It is also proven by the authority of the jurists, D. de fluminibus l. quominus. And also from the edicts of the praetors, D. de damno infecto l. si finita, §. deinde ait; and D. de fluminibus l. 1, §. non autem. The second point is proven by D. ne quid in loco publ. l. 1, §. merito; and §. si quis a principe. However, if there are two builders, each acting unjustly, neither is enjoined against the other; the text is in that law, §. idem ait. And it is a notable text, for since both act contrary to the edict, the condition of the defendant is the better one, D. de damno in sec. l. qui bona, §. si quis; D. de usuris l. quia frustra; D. ne quis cum l. 2.

Secondly, it must be considered regarding the shore, that is, that space which the winter or summer tide uncovers and erodes, so that no fruits are gathered there. For the shore is called as if "washing away," whatever is sown there; hence we say the shore is plowed, that is, in vain. D. 50.16.189 (l. littus). This shore is public, C. 4.31.3 (l. littus), D. 41.1.2 (l. 2).

Thirdly, it must be considered regarding the bed of a public river and the land under the water, which is called the riverbed, which is like a field, and the water is like the surface, as the text says that it is impossible for the bed of a public river not to be public, ff. de fluminibus. l. 1. §. si insula. ver. ille. And although according to the strict law no one would be allowed to make works on the shore or in the bed of a river, because it is not permitted to encroach upon another's property, as l. sicuti. §. Aristo, si ser. vent. And what is alien is that which does not belong to the builder, C. unde vi. l. fi. nevertheless, the most equitable praetor does not forbid it if it harms no one. For example, because the river is not navigable, as are countless small streams, such as our Perusia and Cayna: for what purpose would he prohibit something that benefits no one but is publicly harmful? It is sheer madness to harm many and benefit no one, d. l. quominus. From this it appears that weirs can be made in these small streams, and mills can be established. And thus custom is preserved without prejudicing the right of possession by another previously. And it should be noted, because I weigh the right, which is considered in two ways: one way in possessing, another in prohibiting. Some have the right to prohibit, for if you have a house or inn, and earn much, and I build another inn next to you, and do not encroach upon yours, even though fewer people come to you, you have the right to possess, but not to prohibit. But if you had by privilege or custom that you alone could then prohibit, l. venditor. communia praedio. de usuc. l. fi. de diuer. praescr. l. si quisquam. Thus one craftsman does not prohibit another from practicing his craft, nor does one soldier obstruct another from seeking pay, because the gifts of genius, fortune, and goods are open to all. For the common things of the world are common to all, because nature is common, ff. de no. ope. nun. l. 1. §. quod si in mari.

Fourthly, it must be considered regarding water, and there is no doubt that water, if considered in itself, is open to the use of living creatures. And it would be foolish to deny to men what is available to livestock, D. 8.3.1.1 (§ si). However, if the question concerns water to be drawn from its usual course for the sake of some profit arising therefrom, it is established that if the flow of water is impeded, one may not do so, D. 43.12.1.1 (§ non autem). But if it is not impeded, then it is permitted, provided no prejudice is caused to the right of another. What, therefore, if the upstream owner prejudices the downstream owner, or vice versa? It is answered that it matters greatly whether this prejudice arises from particularity, that is, from the concurrence of neighbors, or in a natural manner, or from a change in the course of the water from the previous season. The first is lawful, just as it was lawful for someone to be born in the world after me and to take a share that he would not have taken if he had not been born. And just as it is lawful for those standing at a cutting board to eat. For, so to speak, the common benefits which nature sets before us are common to all for eating, placed by the divine nurse, nature itself. The second, however, is not lawful, as noted in C. 11.3.1 (Si manifeste) and D. 47.10.1.1 (§ si initium tabularum). But this can be discerned by the eye of the prior owner, with experts in the art also being consulted, as in Auth. 10.1.1 (§ quod autem) and D. 49.16.1.1 (Semen). From these it appears when it is lawful to build a mill and a dam, and where mention is made of a mill and a dam, D. 43.24.1.1 (§ 1) in the gloss, which says that he called it a dam. Now, however, let us come to the interdict of new work, because a new work was denounced. And this denunciation was made in multiple ways. First, to the praetor, who, upon the appearance of the denunciation, reduced the command to a simple citation, i.e., he revoked it.

† From this, the party appeared, because the clause had been appended: “if you feel yourself aggrieved, appear.” L. de pupillo. §. meminisse. In the gloss, it is said: the judge, or do not build, or appear. And thus the choice was given to the cited party, who, by appearing, satisfied the mandate and consumed it. Otherwise, if the judge had commanded conjunctively in this manner: “I command that you do not build, and that you appear,” unless someone says that the mandate is a commination or a letter, and not a sentence, since no cognition of the cause preceded. C. comminationes, vel epistolae. L. interlocutio. Whatever may be said about this, let us come to the acts of the case. From the acts it appears that a surety was given for the demolition of the work, if and insofar as it should be established that the building was erected unjustly; but the judge, without receiving sufficient and conclusive proofs, commanded the demolition. Hence he commanded unjustly. De novo opere nuntiando. L. de operis. The very satisfaction of the obligation opened the way for building, unless the other party had immediately ready negative proofs and had proved that this was not done here, as in the first cause, nor in the cause of appeal. Certainly, neither party proved anything of their private right in due manner by those things which I have seen. And therefore I do not see on what right the precept is founded, and from it the obligation to demolish, for it ought to have a cause, of which there is no certainty. Moreover, the builder did not allege that he was doing something on his own bank, nor where he had fixed, so to speak, the root of the mill, so that from such a just and customary beginning it might be lawful to go further. He who possesses land next to the river cannot make a dam, although it is otherwise in the sea, as in Inst. de rebus divisis. §. littorum. The other party also proved nothing of their singular right by those things which I have seen. Hence it is not clearly established that they built contrary to law conclusively and necessarily; nor yet does it appear from the opposite side that it was built contrary to right, because the substantial matters were not proved by either party. In doubt, therefore, let us favor the defendant who is building, since it regards public utility. Arg. de damno infecto. L. si finita. §. si publicis. And arg. ff. ne quis in loco publico. L. 1. §. si quis nemine. That which is most certain is that when building is done contrary to law in a public place, anyone can interdict the new work. Ff. de novo opere nuntiando. L. 3. §. fi. But if it is doubtful whether it will be done according to law or not, it is lawful to build, provided caution or satisfaction is given for the thing. Ff. eo. L. 1. L. non solum. §. fiendum. And finally, if after cognition of the cause it is found that it was built contrary to law, it is for the praetor to command that the work be destroyed, as in ff. ne quid in flumine publico. L. 1. §. hoc interdictum. Someone will say, therefore, if this is so in the present case, because the builder did not prove that it was lawful for him by law, custom, or privilege, as in ff. nequid in loco publico. L. 2. in principio. But to this it is answered by the said L. quominus, where on that word “let water be led,” Jacobus de Aretio says, for irrigation or when the course of water is impeded, as above L. proxima. §. sed Labeo. And §. si in mari. in fine. Jacobus de Aretio. And if it is lawful to lead water, by consequence it is lawful to make a dam through which it may be led, as in ff. de aqua quoties et aestimatio. L. hoc iure. §. ex flumine. And §. fi. Moreover, the other party did not show that they had their mill by right, and therefore the right to forbid does not belong to them, as noted by Cynus in the said L. si manifeste, because they are in equal cause, as in ff. de fluminibus. L. 2. §. 1. there where it says, “we have as much right to obtain” etc. But against this it seems ff. de fluminibus. L. fi. where it is not lawful for one having lands on both sides of the river to make a bridge of private right over the water itself: therefore much less over the water itself and the bed, ff. ne quis in loco publico. L. 2. §. tractatum. The answer to §. tractatum is clear from the reason of that §. and to that final law the answer is clear from that word “private right.” For this dam, which is in a public river, is not entirely of private right, but the passage is open to all through it, considering the circumstances; therefore, it seems that the order to demolish the work was wrongly given, notwithstanding extra de officio delegati. C. cum olim abbas. And C. conventus, because the solution is clear, and that word “in their land.” I wished to examine this matter not so much for the reason of the present case, as for the reason of perpetual utility. This counsel is in the case of Peter, lord of Francis, and his adversaries concerning the dam. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. An instrument whose protocol or bastardellum does not appear. Likewise, in which the words are in the third person, not in the first, principally by the notary subscribed below, it does not say "by me, the notary." Likewise, because it is on paper. Likewise, when it ought to say "in the time of Urban the Sixth" and it says "the Fifth," it is not thereby vitiated, if it is established that the notary was a person of good standing and that the instrument is written in his own hand.
body: It is doubted,

Whether the aforementioned writing is valid, when the protocol, which in the vernacular we call the *bastardellum*, does not appear. And it seems that it is not valid, as in the Authentica *De tabulis*, in the rubric *In rubro et nigro*; for the original writing must be the matrix, which is the root testifying to the truth, but here the matrix writing is not found; therefore, it is not valid. Moreover, this writing appears suspect, because it speaks first in the third person, when it says, "by the undersigned notary"; it does not say, "by me, the undersigned notary." And afterwards it follows, "and I, etc.," in the first person. For it is not the custom of notaries to speak in such a style in the same instrument. Hence suspicion arises, *De probationibus*, l. *Iubemus*. Moreover, the writing is on paper, whereas it is customary to make it on parchment for perpetual memory, *De secundis tabulis*, l. *Carere*. Moreover, the name of Urban V is placed, and the name of Urban VI ought to be placed. Therefore, the name of a Pope long since dead is placed, and not the name of the living Pope, as in the Authentica *Ut praeponatur nomen Imperatoris*, verse *In documenta*. And thus the instrument is deficient; therefore, it is vehemently suspect. But notwithstanding these objections, I say that if it is established that the notary was a person of good repute, and that the writing is in his own hand, that the said writing is valid, and is legitimate and solemn. And in doubt, it is also presumed to be true, and to emanate from the protocol, even though the protocol does not appear; indeed, this itself may be the protocol. Nor does it matter that he erred in saying "Pope V," because the name of the true Pope is established by the year and the indiction. Therefore, etc., l. *Si liberaveris*, *De regulis iuris*. But it pertains to the judge to ascertain the truth from witnesses, if anything were alleged to the contrary. But in doubt, one must stand by the instrument, as in the Codex, *De probationibus*, l. *Cum precibus*. Finally, I conclude that truth must always have its place; we have sufficient regard for solemnity. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. He who wishes to prove a certain quality must first prove the substance in which that quality is grounded.
2. It is impossible to prove that someone is a manifest thief unless it is first established that he is a thief.
3. Just as accidents cannot exist without subjects, so too can they neither be proved nor understood.
4. When a public prostitute is to be proved, and what she is.
5. Who is to be called a usurer.
6. Whether one who pays usury should be admitted as a witness against a usurer to prove him to be a usurer.
7. Wherever general proof suffices, witnesses prove individually in the specific instance, but collectively in the general sense.
8. Whether manifest knowledge can arise from a single competent and credible witness.
9. Accursius is the master of the sciences.
10. Reputation can be so strong that by itself it suffices for proof alone, and so weak that it does not even constitute an indication.
body: Having examined the aforementioned articles and the testimony of the witnesses, the question is doubtful to me with certainty. And the cause of my doubt principally lies in this,

†because he who wishes to prove a quality must first prove the substance in which that quality is grounded. For if the substance is unknown, the quality is also unknown. This is stated by the gloss in the Digest, *De probationibus*, in the law *Arbiter*. It says, indeed, that it is impossible to prove by memory that a work of hand does not exist, unless the work of hand is first proved, which can be understood from the very ancient structure of the work. And it gives the aforementioned reason concerning substance and quality by the same reasoning.

† It is impossible to prove that someone is a manifest thief, unless it is first established that he is a thief, as is noted in the Digest, *De furtis*, law *Is qui opem*. Therefore, if it is not proven that he is a thief, the whole world could not prove that he is a manifest thief.
† because just as accidents cannot exist without subjects, so too they cannot be proved or understood: for the being of an accident is to inhere. D. 7.1.2

† Nor can it be proven that anyone is a public prostitute unless it is first established that she is a prostitute, l. palam de ritu nuptiarum; nor that a wound is mortal unless it is first established that there is a wound, ff. ad Sillan. l. 1, § illud; ff. ad leg. Aquil. l. Item Mella, § si plures; and l. huic scripturae. Therefore, it cannot be proven that anyone is a manifest usurer unless it is first, that is, as a settled fact, placed and proven, and made clear, that he is a usurer. Then I argue: by singular witnesses, something is not proven simply; therefore, neither is something of this kind proven, as noted in C. de testibus, l. testium; ff. eodem, l. 3, in the glossa, it is said. Since, therefore, all witnesses are singular with respect to usurious contracts, about which they testify individually, they therefore do not prove this person to be a usurer. Therefore, it is impossible to say that he is manifest, since the witnesses are various and singular both in their dispositions and in their acts.

† For this, in order that the usurer be manifest from the acts, the quality of the acts is required, namely that he has openly usured in the presence of many; but in order that he be manifest from the proofs, the quality of the proofs is required, namely, that it has been proved clearly and not conjecturally, nor presumed. Extra, De verborum significatione, c. Cum olim; Ut electo, libro 6, C., De poenis, l. Cum reus. Hence it is written that the fourth act, which is manifest, we cannot deny. To the contrary it is made, because the Speculator says in c. Quamquam, in the commentary, that a manifest usurer is he against whom public fame labors, if any arguments appear, because fame alone would not cause them to be judged usurers. Extra, De usuris, c. Cum in dioecesi.

But here any witness provides an indication, or argument. And all arguments, being of the same kind, strengthen one another, according to the note in l. 2, § 1, ff. de erciscundis. And although there is diversity in the specific case, nevertheless there is the same quality in the general sense. And all these acts have their tails tied together with respect to the same genus, namely turpitude; hence they are not witnesses entirely singular, because the knowledge represented in the minds of those witnesses through the said acts is common, and not merely singular. It supports what is noted in ff. de testibus, l. ob carmen, § fin. And it is confirmed by the aforementioned Jacobus Butrigarius, who says,

† That wherever general proof suffices, there singular witnesses prove in the specific instance, but concurring witnesses prove in the general sense. And he gives an example in heresy. For that someone is a heretic in the general sense is proved by witnesses asserting heresy in various ways, for example because one says he is a heretic because he says, "I do not believe in the Trinity, and One." Another, because he said, "I do not believe in the Incarnation from the Virgin," and similar things. And to this effect is the said Bartolus in the law *De minore*, § *Tormenta*, D. 48.18, *De quaestionibus*, where he says that reputation is proved by witnesses, one of whom speaks of one place, another of another. But this seems contrary to the gloss of the doctors in the third law, D. 22.5, *De testibus*. Also contrary to what the same Bartolus notes in the law *Labeo*, D. 47.11, *De suppositione*, and in the second law, D. 28.1, *Quemadmodum testamenta aperiantur*. Whatever may be said about the statements of Bartolus, I return to the proposition,

Whether it can be manifestly established by one suitable and credible witness, for example, if one notable man says that he saw a scholar in bed with Berta, and did not keep silent about it, but made it public; hence everyone calls and holds Berta to be an adulteress. The question is whether she is thereby called a prostitute. And what if another man saw her with the monk Piloso, and also with a Teuton, so that from these reports she is firmly held and called a prostitute. It seems to be said that manifest knowledge cannot arise from the voice of one person, because the voice of one is the voice of none. To the contrary, it seems from the ordinary gloss on the Digest, *De probationibus*, in the law *Si arbiter*, in the great gloss, under the words “but in the first case I ask,” where the gloss says that memory, and the manifest knowledge of that memory, is proved by one witness believed by many who testify based on their recollection. For one witness does not do this by himself, but with the added opinion and belief of many. And I held this view in my writings in the first law of the Code, *De testibus*, as anyone can see, and will find there many arguments for and against alleged. Finally, what I held there, I now hold even more firmly, saving the advice of a wiser council. Whether it is manifestly proved: because it is not simple fame, because it does not originate from fame, but gives life to fame and causes it to pass over entirely, as if it were notorious.

† as the master of sentences, the excellent glossator Accursius, says, because the root of this reputation proceeded from the truth established by many, and through the mouths of many, and not once, but often, and very often. And these witnesses are not singular in a simple sense, but in a qualified sense: because they agree in one end of the same reason and expression. All. For they confess that he lent at interest in the presence of many, and not only do they testify that he was a usurer, but they assert that he was like a circle to the tavern, and to signify what kind of person he was, they call him by the appellative name, he was a usurer, and that by this he was known.

† From this, note the vehemence of reputation. For, as Bartolus elegantly states in his consilia, consilium 27, beginning “Domino paci,” reputation can be so vehement that it suffices by itself for proof alone, as in C. de iudiciis, l. Ubi adhuc; so in C. de maleficiis, l. Si constante; ff. de fluminibus, l. 1, § 1; C. de maleficiis, l. Siquidem. And it can be so weak that it would not even constitute an indication, according to Bartolus. In our case, however, the reputation appears vehement, since it has passed into the appellative name among the multitude of those who know. And this reputation, said to have arisen from the frequency of acts, is asserted, for the frequency of acts makes the truth more known, just as a heap of stones would be seen more clearly than a single stone, as noted in C. de surrogatione, l. 2. Moreover, we should not restrict ourselves to one species of proof, because certainty and clarity are increased by many concurring factors, ff. de testibus, l. 3. That which Bartolus says about reputation alone would not be true in the present case; this is shown by what is noted in Cyriacus, de accusatione, l. Ea quidem, nos. 3 and 4. But because the reputation is strengthened by so many and such great indications, such that everyone’s opinion is caused and clothed by the senses, then it is true, as I have said in my judgment, because “manifest” is nothing other than truth made public among the people. As for the other points of this case, I do not involve myself, but only with the point “manifestly,” etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a creditor, in the absence of the debtor, confesses before friends that he has been paid and satisfied, such confession has the force of proof, not the force of inducing liberation.
body: The question is,

† Whether, if a creditor, in the absence of the debtor and in the presence of friends, confesses that he has been paid or satisfied, such confession is valid or not. And it seems that it is not valid, because the rule is that a response is required in releasing just as in obligating, D. de regulis iuris, l. nihil tam est naturale; D. de solutionibus, l. prout quisque; D. de negotiis gestis, l. Pomponius scribit, ver. nam quoque; D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. consensu; C. de donationibus, l. nec ignorans; and note D. de contrahenda emptione, l. 1; C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. illud. Moreover, the rule is that presence is required, D. de confessionibus, l. certum, §. si quis absentis; and note D. de confessionibus, l. 1. Moreover, unless the debtor suspects a pact, or another acts for the debtor, the exception of fraud is not sought, D. de pactis, l. rescriptum, §. fin.; and l. si tibi, §. si pactum; and note in the same title, l. idem in duobus; and l. haeredi, §. nos autem. Moreover, this is expressly held by Bartolus, D. de liberatione legata, l. non solum, §. si liberationis verba.

To the contrary is the common opinion, namely, that a confession made between absent parties is valid for releasing, as noted in C. de confessionibus, l. 1; D. de interdictis et actionibus, l. 1; D. de iureiurando, l. Labeo; C. de pactis, l. postquam liti. And this is in favor of release; otherwise there would be no difference whether the confession is made to release or to obligate, which is false. Moreover, this seems to be expressed in Auth. de testamento, §. licet. Moreover, in support of this is the extraordinary gloss in the said §. si liberationis. Moreover, this is held by Guillaume de Coucy in the said l. Pomponius. Bartolus says, as I said, that the confession is not valid. For if it were valid, it would follow that if in a will the testator confesses that he has been satisfied or paid, that such confession would not have the force of a fideicommissum; the consequence is false, as in l. 1, C. de falsis causis adiectis legatis. Therefore, the said confession is not valid, unless it is made in a will, because then it is valid by the law of fideicommissum, according to Bartolus.

The objection from l. postquam does not hold, because there it speaks of when it is done in court before a judge deciding and supplying the absence of a party, as noted in C. de confessionibus, l. 1, by Petrus and Cynus. Nevertheless, Bartolus says that one can renounce a real right in the absence of a party, because it can be considered as abandoned. Otherwise in an obligation, according to him. Also, the objection from §. et licet does not hold, because it must be understood as before neighbors, i.e., with the party present, according to Bartolus. The objection from l. Labeo does not hold, because there a messenger or letter intervenes, according to Bartolus. The objection from what is noted by Innocentius in c. veniens, de renuntiatione, does not hold, because there it speaks because a real right is renounced, not a personal obligation, according to Bartolus, who sows these words in the said §. si liberationis. But after this sowing of his, I go with an extirpating hoe, because he speaks poorly.

Consider, namely, that either someone alleges a pact made between absent parties. And then the gloss speaks in l. duobus. And the laws alleged for this part, as he alleges that he is bound to simple proof, induce proof with cause. And then he has the exception of fraud, not of confession, because it is presumed to act with fraud, who denies with his own voice or that of his author. And thus says the gloss, noted and true, in the said §. si liberationis verba. But if the confession had no cause, as in l. tale pactum, then the opinion of Bartolus could be sustained, that it is valid for releasing between present parties, or as if not entirely between absent parties, and this between living persons. In a last will, a confession is presumed to be made liberally and gratuitously, hence it does not prove, arg. D. de liberatione legata, l. Aurelio, §. fin.; D. de legatis 2, l. Titia, §. Gaius; and the said l. 1, de falsis causis. And thus Cynus feels, C. de non numerata pecunia, l. generaliter, in 4. q. there, when he says that confession, as regards the act of disposition, is to be understood as valid as regards the act of proof. Thus concerning usury, with what has been converted into the thing, l. autem. Bartolus, that another thing in real law is lacking in understanding, as appears in Speculum, de confessionibus, §. nunc videndum, ver. porro.

I conclude, therefore, that the confession is valid in the force of proof, not in the force of introducing release. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A statute providing that, upon the death of a wife without issue, the husband shall acquire one-third of the dowry, does not distinguish whether it applies to a wife who has not yet been brought into the husband’s household and has not been cohabited with.
2. What is the meaning of the word “perceperat” (had received
body: The fact is found to be as follows. A certain Do. Cecha, wife of Accursinus, formerly had two legitimate and natural daughters, namely Bartholomaea and Petrutia, and she gave certain goods as dowry for the said Do. Bartholomaea to a certain Peter Vannutii, stipulating for Ser John, her future son-in-law, Ser John aforesaid, if it should please God. And then she was betrothed by the said Ser John, and in the course of a short time, not having been known carnally by her said husband, she died, her mother Do. Cecha and her full sister Petrutia surviving her; and the said Bartholomaea, thus betrothed, did not go to the house of habitation of her said husband, nor did Do. Ver. go to the house of habitation of Do. Bartholomaea. And in the said inheritance, Do. Petrutia, her sister, succeeded upon the death of Do. Bartholomaea and Do. Cecha, and by other rights. Then Do. Petrutia died, leaving two legitimate and natural sons surviving her. Now the same Ser John, notwithstanding that the marriage was not consummated between Do. Ser John and Bartholomaea by carnal copulation, claims a portion of the dowry of the said Do. Bartholomaea, which he says he has acquired by virtue and under the pretext of the statute of the commune of Castrum Sartianum, whence the said Do. Bartholomaea and Petrutia are from, which statutes are transmitted to you. Moreover, the said Ser John intends, insofar as any portion is due to him by virtue of the said statutes, to claim that portion which would fall to him if he had usufruct or a part of the fruits of the said portion from the day of the death of the said Bartholomaea; for the said Bartholomaea died intestate eleven years ago and more, her full sister Petrutia, from both parents, surviving her. Upon these matters, you are requested to advise what the law is, and to return your opinion sealed with your seal.

† It is asked whether a man, who did not take a wife, nor knew her carnally, nor bore the burdens of marriage, ought to have the profit, of which the said statute speaks, which begins: "If a married woman"; and it seems that he should, because marriage is made not by cohabitation, but by consent, as in l. nup. de re. iu. Also, because just as he would profit from an agreement, as in C. de epis. et cle. l. deo nobis, so he ought to profit from a statute, ff. de pac. l. non impossibile. And this seems to be held by Bartolus in l. nihil. rerum amo. per l. cum hic statutus. §. si maritus. de don. inter vir. et vxo. with similar authorities. I also say in l. deo nobis, that if the statute says that the husband profits one-third part of the dowry, it is understood indistinctly, because the statute does not distinguish whether she was taken in marriage or not; and where the statute does not distinguish, neither do we distinguish. To this effect is C. de bo. quae lib. l. non sine. For it is not alleged that the husband stood firm, hence he ought to be considered as having passed over, ff. de condi. insti. l. vter ex fratribus. Also, this seems to be decided by Guillaume de Cuy in vxore in contracto matrimonio, otherwise in sponsa, i.e., in a marriage not contracted, d. l. non sine. On the contrary, it seems that this profit regards the burdens of marriage, just as the profit of fruits, as in l. dotis fructus. de iure dotium. and no. in l. si donatarius. §. fi. de condi. ob causam. Also, this profit is accessory, and the dowry is principal. But the dowry itself could never be claimed; therefore neither can this profit, since it is claimed by the action of dowry, l. si socer. §. Lucius. sol. mat. Also, the mind and reason of the statute regard a woman married with effect, not a woman married in name only, ar. in l. adigere. §. quamuis. de iur. pa. and C. de nup. l. sancimus. Solution: considering the words of the said statute, it must be said thus: either this man received the dowry, and then he profits; or he did not receive it, but stood within the bounds of the promise, and then he does not profit. The case is in this statute in the word,

† perceperat: because this word means to have in one’s possession, D. de usufr. l. si fur decesserit, in the word “percipiantur”; and D. qui mod. usufr. amit. l. si fructuarius missioni, in the word “percipi”; D. de rei vend. l. fructus, in the beginning; and l. si navis, with many others. Moreover, the following clause of the statute, in the word “venientibus,” seems to require the act of leading (the bride), and thus it clarifies the preceding clause. D. de pe. her. l. utrum; D. de coniung. cum eman. l. nihil. I hold that if she was neither led nor was the dowry paid, the husband does not acquire anything. And I consider this most true, because no delay in payment was committed before the leading, but after the leading; and the delay is acquired even if the dowry was not paid. So holds Bartolus in cons. 83, which begins “Statuto communis Sartiani,” etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a woman, who has other means from which to provide herself with a dowry out of her father's property, can revoke or diminish a fideicommissum.
body: A certain man, having two daughters, made legacies to each of them, then instituted them as his heirs, and substituted in the legacies only the survivor to the one who died first without children. Finally, one of them married Titius and gave her legacy as dowry. By statute it is provided that if the wife dies before the husband, the husband acquires a certain portion of the dowry. Afterwards, this married woman died without children, and the condition of the fideicommissum occurred. Hence, the other sister claims the things given in dowry. The husband raises the exception based on the statute; the sister replies, saying that the fideicommissum could not be diminished, because the married woman had other goods from which she could provide herself with a dowry without diminishing the fideicommissum.

† It is asked, what is the law. I answer that she, who has from elsewhere the means whereby to provide herself with a dowry from her father's goods, cannot, for the purpose of the dowry, overturn or diminish a fideicommissum; the text is in C. communia de legatis, Auth. Res quae, from the contrary sense; and in Auth. de restitutione, and in ea quae parit, §. Quamobrem, ff. de petitione hereditatis; but l. Sed si lege, §. Quod autem, ff. ad Trebellianum; l. Titius rogatus. And if it be said, therefore the husband will gain nothing. I answer that this third part, which is due to the husband, is evicted by the right of the fideicommissum. And therefore it is due from the evictor as dowry evicted, C. de iure dotis, l. 1. The husband will therefore bring an action for eviction against the remaining goods of the woman. And in this way he will be satisfied from her other goods. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one ought to present oneself within a month to the prior and the convent, or otherwise whether such an abbot should provide for it, and whether this time period runs if the convent is dispersed to pious places on account of wars or pestilence.
2. If impeded by a fortuitous event, the time period does not run.
body:
Pope Honorius, of most holy memory, ordained that when the prior of the hermitage of Virgiliano dies or is removed, the brothers of the same hermitage, together with the abbot and the chapter of the royal convent, shall commonly elect a prior from within the same convent within one month. If they fail to do so within that time, the abbot shall freely appoint from his own convent someone who knows how to govern and benefit the community according to the Rule of St. Benedict, and shall place him as prior over the hermitage, to whom the brothers of the hermitage shall owe obedience and reverence.

Now it has happened that, after the death of the said prior of the hermitage, the brothers of the said hermitage requested the said lord Abbot to appoint a prior for their community, but they did so unanimously only after the expiration of one month, because they could not have the presence of the chapter of the convent due to wars. Therefore, since the month has elapsed, the question arises whether the said candidate should be appointed as prior, or whether the power to create the prior remains freely in the hands of the aforementioned lord Abbot.

For the said lord Abbot argues that he is not bound by law to admit the aforementioned postulation, since it ought to have been made by the abbot and the chapter together. But here it was not made by the chapter; therefore, after the lapse of the month, the power has devolved upon the lord abbot.

On the other hand, it is argued that this occurred because the monks, who constitute the chapter, had left the monastery on account of the wars, nor could they safely return to the monastery.

† It is asked, what is the law, against the claimant principally two things are made, namely, the form not being observed, and the lapse of time. For the claimant only one thing is made, l. impedimentum.

For when time is impeded by a fortuitous event, it does not run, as is stated in the Digest, *De publicis*, law *Caesar*; in the Code, *Qui petant tutelam*, law *Cum amatrix*; in the Code, *De appellationibus*, law *Praeses*; and in the Authenticum, *De his qui ingrediuntur ad appellandum*, § 1; in the Decretals, *De electione*, chapter *Cupientes*, § *Quod si*, in the 20th title of Book 6; in the Digest, *De excusationibus tutorum*, law *Scire oportet*, § *Sufficit*, at the words "if it can be said," where it appears that the case is joined literally; § *Consequens*, in the same law, *Putastud accidit*, because it happened due to a supervening case in the person of the defendant, since on account of wars he withdrew from the monastery, and the individuals went their separate ways. For it cannot be said that there is a chapter where there is almost no one of the chapter, as noted by Innocentius, *De non operante*, now chapter *Ex iniuncto*. And the rule of law is that when a case supervenes in the person of him to whom something must be done, it is as if it had been done, because it ought to have been done, as is fully noted in the Code, *De institutionibus et substitutionibus*, law 1, *Praesentatio*. It depends on the act of those who present, and is called a presentative condition. And therefore it is held as fulfilled if it does not depend on them, but on a case, Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *In testamento*. Thus, the laws which distinguish from whose side the fortuitous event occurs are applicable to this, Digest, *De locato conducto*, law *Si uno*, § *Item cum quidam*; and law *Peregrinus*, § *Navem*; Digest, *De adiectis*, law *Die sancto*. I believe that as long as the impediment of wars lasts, this month does not run. But when the impediment ceases, it runs, because there are two precepts, namely, to present the postulation, and to present within a month, Digest, *De arbitris*, law *Celsus*, § *Idem ait*. And therefore it must be done without a dilatory monitorium, since the confirmation pertains to him together with the abbot by consequence, whence the abbot alone could not confirm. And the chapter could not confirm, even if presented to itself, because the Apostolic See has statutorily required both collectively and jointly, when it said, "by the abbot and the convent." And the act of both is required, Digest, *De manumissionibus testamento*, law *Si ita fuerit*; *De arbitris*, law *Pedius*, § 1; *De electione*, chapter *Cum in veteri*; *De rescindendis*, chapter *Cum te*; *De testibus*, chapter *Praesenti*, Book 6; *De praescriptionibus*, chapter *Veniens*. For these words, "if they have not done," etc., are understood, i.e., if they have been in delay in doing, Digest, *De constituenda pecunia*, law *Si duo*, § *Si*. It is said that this text is very notable for this purpose. Moreover, relief is granted to one impeded by the necessity of fortuitous events, Digest, *Si quis cautio*, law 2, § *Quod diximus*; *De appellationibus*, chapter *In ratione*; Digest, *Quibus ex causis maior*, law *Non enim*; Digest, *De re iudicata*, law *Quaesitum*. Furthermore, as long as the chapter is not assembled, which is within the power of the Abbot, who is universally to be required on this matter, time does not run, as in the Digest, *De libertate universitatis*, law 1, and there a notable point is collected by Jacobus de Arena. And it is supported by the Decretals, *De electione*, chapter *Ne pro defuncto*; and chapter *His quibus*; *De concessionibus praebendarum*, chapter *Quia universitatem*; *De annuis exceptionibus*, law 1, § *Si*, Question 2, Cause 6, *Anteriorum*. For these times, which regard the provision of churches as to what is useful, do not run for those impeded, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How the paternal and maternal grandfathers succeed to the grandchildren.
2. Whether the same applies to a dowry given by the father.
body: The point of the question is as follows. A certain person named Bubalus gave in marriage to a lady named Pe. the daughter of a certain person named An., with a dowry, guarantees, and other paraphernal goods agreed upon and settled between them, and the marriage between them was consummated. From them were born two children, a son and a daughter. Then the said An. died, survived by the said lady Pe., his wife, and by the said son, and by the aforementioned Bubalus, father of the said Pe., and by Theobald, father of the said An. After the death of the said Anthony, the said Pe. died, survived by the said children, or wards, and by the aforementioned Theobald, paternal grandfather of the said children, as above, and by the aforementioned Bubalus, maternal grandfather of the said wards and children, as above. Finally, the said two children died as wards, one after the other, survived by the same Bubalus, maternal grandfather, and by the same Theobald, paternal grandfather of the said wards. It is therefore asked, what is the law in the aforementioned case: whether the said Bubalus or the said Theobald succeeds to the aforementioned rights which belonged to the said lady Pe., and which of them succeeds to the whole or to a part, and to a quarter share.

† Every dispute among uncles turns on the question of who shall succeed to the nephews. Some say that in the goods coming from the paternal line the paternal uncle succeeds, and from the maternal line the maternal uncle. And this is according to the law *Quod scitis*, Codex, *De bonis quae liberis*, according to one reading, which Bartolus holds. Others say that by the Authentica *De hereditatibus ab intestato*, § *Ex his*, both succeed together in all. But this is not our matter, because here it is not precisely a question of the goods of the nephews.

But regarding the dowry advanced by Bubalus, and the other items given as paraphernalia, it must be considered that if Bubalus’s daughter had died during the marriage, i.e., while Antonio survived, the rule would apply, as noted in *l. dos a patre*, that the dowry would remain with the son-in-law for the common children. But since the son-in-law died first, the action for the dowry became that of the father and the daughter; and upon the daughter’s death, it became solely that of the father, as in *c. rem in praesenti*, § *videamus*, C. *com. utriusque iudicii*, *l. fin.* And therefore, after the nephews subsequently died, all the aforementioned property would revert to Bubalus, C. *de bonis quae liberos*, *l. quaecunque.* And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The formality required in contracting is also required in rescinding the contract.
2. If an act was performed at the time of the first contract regarding its rescission, this rescission is not a rescission, but rather the execution of the first contract, which was validly celebrated.
3. Allegations of law without facts.
body: That solemnity,

† What is required in contracting is required in rescinding the contract, C. de praediis minorum, l. si. ad resoluendum. And note in l. 1, C. si adversus transactionem. But there is a great difference between the rescission of a contract and its observance.

For if, at the time of the first contract, it was agreed to rescind, this rescission is not a rescission, but rather the execution of the first contract as celebrated in words, even if otherwise simulated in writing, as in D. de manum. l. 4, § si ab ignoto, and l. 2, in fine, D. de reb. eor. Nevertheless, it must be proved by witnesses that this came about at the time of the said simulated sale; once this is proved, the said Do. Iacoba has the stronger right, C. de re indi. l. quoties. And therefore, the opinion of Master Angelus in this case is not the truth.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Mere cohabitation does not create a partnership.
2. One who receives money in good faith and openly does not incur a crime, but is bound to return the money.
3. Secret donations, although suspect, are nevertheless valid.
4. The action for a partner is not prescribed by ten years.
body: On

† On the first point, because cohabitation does not create a partnership, the goods pertain freely to the purchaser, ff. pro socio, l. cum duobus, § si fratres. But if a partnership were proven, the purchased goods would have to be shared, eo. ii., l. si societas universorum. On the second point, if neither Philip nor his sons assisted, the property accrues to Andreutius and his heirs, C. ad orf., l. quod minor. I say the same on the third point, as C. quando non pet., par., l. 1.

† On the fourth point, if they have openly and in good faith taken [the money], and not with the intention of contracting, they do not incur a crime, but are bound to restore the money. But if they had secretly taken it with the intention of withholding it, they are liable for the crime of plundered inheritance, if they did so before the inheritance was entered upon. But if they did so after the inheritance was entered upon, they are liable for theft, as in C. de furt. l. de his.

† On the fifth point, although clandestine donations are suspect, they are nevertheless valid, c. 1, ut eccles., de beneficiis, s. usque ad quingentos aureos, even if they have not been insinuated. C. de donat., l. si quis argentum. On the sixth point, if Andreutius died before Philip, the substitution has lapsed, C. de caducis tollendis, l. si autem, and the property must be freely awarded to the mother. But if Andreutius survived, then, the legitime and the Trebellian portion being retained, the mother must restore the residue to the heirs of Andreutius, as in C. de fideicommissis, l. in personam. The seventh question was answered in question 1.
† Moreover, the action for partnership, which is personal, would not be prescribed by a period of ten years if the partnership were proven, l. 1. C. de consti. pecu. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If, while the mother is still living, the brother has been instituted as a pupillary substitute for the ward, either by direct institution or by fideicommissum, to which of these two does the right to demand the appointment of a guardian for the ward belong? Furthermore, whether, if the mother is excluded, the grandmother is
body: The burden of guardianship falls upon the pupillary substitute, as stated in C. de legit. haer. l. sciant. It is otherwise in the case of a substitute by fideicommissum, as in l. credendum, qui pe. tu. And therefore, if the said elder brother was substituted pupillarily, he was deprived [of succession], because he did not duly administer the guardianship, and the mother succeeds. But if he had been substituted by fideicommissum, he himself succeeds, and the mother would be deprived, as noted by Bartolus in l. 2, qui pe. tut. Observe in our case that, whatever the nature of the brother’s substitution may have been, the mother appears to be excluded, because the brother, having common property with the said brothers, could not by law be appointed to the statutory guardianship by virtue of the existence of his heir, as in auth. minoris debitor. Therefore, the guardianship devolved upon the mother, and if she did not accept it, she does not succeed. But certainly, the aforementioned distinction regarding substitution is true. For if the brother was pupillarily substituted, the mother was not bound to accept the guardianship. But someone will say that neither was the brother bound, because the mother preceded him in the guardianship. This is the question that Bartolus has already discussed in the aforementioned l. 2. And I say that the pupillary substitute must ensure that the ward does not lack a guardian; however, this question does not arise here, because the substitution was by fideicommissum, not direct, hence the brother is called to the fideicommissum without doubt, holding the common opinion, since the substitution is by fideicommissum. But regarding the statutory and Trebellanian succession, the question remains whether it pertains, to the exclusion of the mother, to the grandmother, or to the consanguineous brother only, i.e., who succeeds an underage person intestate. If certainly the grandmother succeeds, unless the same equal fault of not requesting a guardian can be imputed to her, as in auth. defuncto, and the aforementioned l. sciat, and l. 2, §. videndum, ad Ter. The legacies, however, left to the said wife should be had according to the note by the doctors in l. 1, si secundo nu. mulier, and l. Titia, §. 1, ff. de leg. 2, by Bartolus, because she does not lose the legacies, l. tutor petitus, §. qui tutorib., ff. de excu. tut. I, however, said in l. precib., C. de impu. et ali., and now I say that the above-mentioned authorities do not apply, which proceed according to the opinion of Bartolus, that the mother is excluded from guardianship by death, renunciation, or by entering a second marriage. And then, if the grandmother was subsequently negligent for a year, she is deprived of succession. Or, the mother is not excluded from guardianship, but only from the hope of succession by the lapse of a year, and then the grandmother is not excluded. And thus I conclude in favor of the grandmother, saving the right of the fideicommissum due to the surviving brother, as stated, and saving the legacy of the wife, as in the aforementioned l. credendum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that no person may make a will unless he has expressly reserved the right of the commune, whether a will made elsewhere away from the right of the said commune is valid without the said reservation having been made.
2. Whether executors appointed to build a hospital within a two-year period are said to be in default once the two-year period has elapsed, even if they were not warned.
3. It is provided by statute in the City of Gubbio that no person [?]
body: he might make a will, unless he expressly reserved the right of the commune of Gubbio, as the whole said statute is written above. 11. A certain Marianus Bartolelli of the City of Gubbio, being in the City of Fano, made a will, for which a certain notary of Sant'Angelo in Vado, acting as an inhabitant of Fano, was requested to draft the instrument, in which will it is not expressly stated, "saving the right of the commune of Gubbio"; the will is produced in court, and the party against whom it is produced says that the will is invalid because the right of the commune of Gubbio was not reserved. And the party producing it says that it was not necessary, since it was made in the City of Fano, and in decisive matters regard must be had to the place where the act was celebrated, not the place of the judgment.

† Now it is asked whether the said will is valid notwithstanding the said ordinance and statute, or not. Likewise it is asked, since the said Agnesola died now six years ago or thereabouts and the said hospital has not been built by the said friars of Sant'Anna, whether the lapse of that two-year period applies to the said friars of Sant'Anna, and whether it ran immediately from the day of the death of the said Agnesola, or whether it was necessary that notification be given to them, so that they could then be said to be in default, or not; and if they are in default, whether the bishop can now cause the aforesaid hospital to be built, or whether the goods of the said testator are devolved entirely upon the said Ser Cechus according to the intention of the said testator. Likewise it is asked whether the right that now belongs to the said Ser Cechus belongs to his sons, since Ser Cechus died three years and more after the death of the said Lady Agnesola, nor does it otherwise appear that the said Ser Cechus, while he lived, acknowledged the said inheritance. The statute provides in rem with respect to things that are subject to tribute; whence the place of the things themselves is considered, and not the place where the act was made, as is fully noted by the Doctors on l. cunctos populos; l. 1 C. ne liceat potent. patrocin. litig. facit. For that statute was made for the benefit of the commonwealth, and therefore it must not be contravened by a change of place, otherwise an open path would exist for defrauding the security of the commonwealth, which is absurd. But I raise a doubt as to whether that statute speaks when the property passes by universal title; and it seems that it does not, as in l. quaedam de acq. rer. dom. To the contrary speaks the fact that the statute speaks generally, as in l. fi. C. de reb. alien. non alien., and this is truer through l. si quis prioris § certam C. de secun. nupt.; nevertheless, through that statute, I do not believe that the substitution made concerning the Church of Sant'Anna is hindered, extra de consti. c. Ecclesia Sanctae Mariae.

† Likewise, the hospital can and ought to be constructed, because the friars of the said Church were not in default of building it, especially because they have not yet had possession of the property, C. de episc. et cler. l. nulli; and on this account there is no question concerning Ser Cechus if the friars were not negligent; but if they had been negligent, the question stands whether the said will is valid as to Ser Cechus, or not. I said above that it is not valid, the said statute prohibiting it. And so I say and advise.
