If the will was made elsewhere, where that statute is not in force but the common law is, the will seems to be valid, saving however the right of the commune of Gubbio, since the goods are tributary, because the commune of Gubbio has no interest in other things, since it does not bind outside its territory. To the contrary it seems, because the statute invalidates the testator's power over those censual goods unless the form of the statute has been observed. And where a form is given to capacity and power, it ought to be observed in any place whatever, as in l. cunctos populos. What therefore shall we say? Certainly the will is valid as to the remaining property not subject to the statute, because they are not tributary, but censual. In censual things, however, it is not valid. Tell me, to whom will they belong? For if it is valid, the legacy remains with the heir as if unwritten. But in place of the heir is the universal fideicommissary. Secondly, if the church was in default, it ought not to have the bequest, and it is deprived of its benefit. But whether the censual property is assigned to the substituted kinsman is doubtful, because the substitution of the kinsman does not seem to have been valid in those censual things. What therefore shall be done? It seems that the universality draws the rest to itself, de acq. rer. dom. l. quaedam. And since the will is valid in its universality, those coming from intestacy can do nothing. And it is as if an heir had been instituted with an estate excepted, and nevertheless the estate passes not by the judgment of the testator, but by the judgment and authority of the law, ff. de hered. inst. l. 1 § si quis heres. And therefore, the friars being in default, the one substituted to them succeeds. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who consents is said to prorogue jurisdiction to a judge who is not his own.
2. Whether the judge to whom prorogation has been made ought to proceed according to the law of his own forum, or according to the common law.
body: Peter, an operator of the trade of the cerdoni, although entirely enrolled in the register of the said trade, sued Martin, who was not an artisan, before John, the Chamberlain of the aforementioned trade of the cerdoni. Martin, through error, omitted to raise the exception of declination of the said judge and of his jurisdiction before the joinder of issue; but he raised it afterwards, and before the publication of the proceedings.

† Now it is asked whether jurisdiction is said to have been prorogated. And assuming that it had been prorogated, the aforementioned Martin, who is the defendant, wishes that the case be decided according to the *ius commune* and the statute of the entire people and of the same city; whereas the plaintiff wishes that it be decided according to the ordinances of the said guild of *cerdoni*. It is asked according to which laws the said John, the chamberlain, ought to adhere and decide the case. Where there is an error of law, prorogation ceases, L. 2, D. *de iudicibus*; and L. *si per errorem*, where this matter is treated more fully. The same applies if it is due to doubt, as in L. *manifestus*, § *si autem defunctus*.

† And although jurisdiction has been prorogated, it nevertheless appears that by virtue of the prorogation he assumes the office of proceeding according to the law of his own forum. That is, the office of deciding according to the law by which the city is commonly governed, for artisans do not use it, since he is not one of them, l. 2, C. de constit. princ. et de foro comp., c. quod clericis.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, in the event of non-payment of the canon, the husband prejudices the wife, at the time the dowry was given and the stipulation for its restitution was made, with respect to the property given to him as dowry.
2. Whether the husband may prejudice the wife or her heirs in ecclesiastical emphyteutic goods given in dowry, and whether the husband acquires a share thereof by virtue of the statute, etc.
body: From the acts and facts before the arbitrators between Vincentius and Paulus, the following point is stated, namely, that the said Cuctisa, having certain emphyteutic goods pertaining to the monastery of Saint Christopher of Castro Durante, and certain other goods of her own, married Vincentius Zannis of Castro Durante, and delivered to him in dowry the said emphyteutic goods. Vincentius, during the marriage, had himself renewed in the said goods for the canon paid by the said monastery, the said lady Cuctisa, his wife, being absent, for whom he promised ratification for the price of 16 florins, in this form in effect, namely: in the year of our Lord 1300, and so forth, when the underwritten plots of emphyteutic land of the monastery of Saint Christopher of Castro Durante, to which the dominion and ownership of the same pertained and pertains, were and are legally devolved and reverted to the said monastery because the pension and canon paid to the said monastery for ten years by the said Cuctiola, daughter of the late Cecholus Perusinus, on account of the aforesaid matters, was and is accepted and held by a syndic, and possession of the said things was and is held by the said monastery peacefully and quietly for one year and more after the apprehension of the said holding, and the fruits were collected by the said monastery for the time of the said possession; therefore, the Reverend man, Lord Angelus, Abbot of the said monastery, renewed the said things as devolved to the said monastery by emphyteutic right, and re-granted them to Vincentius Zannis, present and receiving for himself, and on behalf of and in the name of the said Cuctiola, his wife, for their sons and grandsons, for the price of 16 florins, and so forth. And this the said Lord Abbot did because the said Vincentius promised ratification for the aforesaid lady Cuctiola, and so forth. Then, the concession having been made in the said form, it appears that after some time the said lady Cuctisa died, having made a will, in which she instituted Paulus, her son, whom she had by another husband, as heir. This Paulus, as appears from the acts, claims from the said Vincentius the said emphyteutic goods, which were given in dowry by their said mother, by an action for dowry. The said Vincentius, by way of exception, alleges that he has a right of quasi-ownership in the said goods by virtue of the said concession for one-half, thereby raising a question of ownership against the said Paulus for the said one-half, alleging that he acts fraudulently in what he claims, which he would be restoring. Secondly, because he says that by virtue of the statute and custom of the said Castro, he ought to gain one-third part of the dowry. On the part of Paulus, it is replied and denied that there is a statute and custom in the said Castro that the husband gains one-third part of the dowry when the wife predeceases, especially when the matter concerns immovable things. And against the aforesaid, it is said and denied that the monastery was in possession of the fruits perished from the said things, as contained in the said instrument. And for this, it is alleged by the witnesses of the said Paulus that the monastery never possessed, nor collected the fruits, and it is excepted that the said instrument was not valid to the prejudice of the said lady Cuctiola, who was absent and ignorant. And because it appears that she ratified the right, as Vincentius promised. Furthermore, it is excepted against the said instrument that it is not valid, because it is fictitious and simulated, as appears from the smallness of the price, because if the things had been devolved, the said Vincentius would not have given nor renewed them for 16 florins, things worth a certain sum and more. Moreover, it is replied against the exception of the said Vincentius: granted that the said Vincentius had a right to one-half in the said goods, nevertheless the rule "he who acts fraudulently" does not apply, because to one bringing an action for dowry, the exception of ownership cannot be opposed, as appears from the chapters of the said Vincentius, in which it is stated that the said Vincentius, from the time of the said concession, possessed by right of the renewal obtained from the said monastery. But this is not proved; rather, it appears from the proceedings that he possessed as husband. The said Vincentius does not prove that in the said Castro there is a statute that the husband gains one-third part of the dowry. Hence, although he strives to prove that some observed it, or even granted that it is a custom, because he alleges statute and custom conjunctively, it is not sufficient to prove one, yet in truth it is that there is no statute by which this is provided. Regarding the own goods, the contention is whether they were given, because Paulus denies that they were given in dowry, and demands that an account be rendered to him of the fruits. Vincentius seems to prove by two witnesses that all the goods were given in dowry, both own and emphyteutic; if they speak the truth, God knows.

† Arbiters ought to possess justice and discretion, and it matters greatly whether it is established that the property was returned to the wife due to the fault of the husband, because he did not pay the canon while he possessed it, as stated in the law *neque stipendium*, under the title *De impensis in rebus dotis factis*. And then the wife retains her right in its entirety, because the husband ought not to profit from his own fraud and harm the wife and the wife’s heirs. For it is established that the husband is held liable for fault, in the Digest, under the title *Solutio matrimonii*, in the law *etiam*, section *licet*.

† and he is bound to the thing itself. Or it is established that it was the wife’s fault, because before she gave it to her as dowry, she had ceased to pay the canon for two years, and then the contract entered into between the husband and the church must be upheld, even to the prejudice of the wife, D. de evictionibus, l. si rem quam, in principio. Or nothing is established on this point, except that the abbot so said. And then it must be considered whether credit should be given to his denial. On this point, see Cynus in l. 2, de iure emphyteuticario, and it seems that credit should be given. For the woman must prove that she paid, D. de probationibus, l. quinquaginta. For the husband succeeds in the place of the abbot, and it is not necessary for the abbot to prove that the canon was not paid, but rather the passage of time, as the noted doctors teach, D. de verbis obligatorum, l. in illa stipulatione, § si calendis, and l. hoc iure.

To the contrary, that the husband is absolutely bound to restore the possession which he received as dowry, it seems to follow because the husband ought not to interrupt the wife’s possession, C. de locato et conducto, l. si quis conductionis; C. de acquisitione possessionis, l. ex liberis. And he ought to have received her, l. creditor, C. de distractione pignorum. And because whatever comes to him by reason of the dowry, he is also bound to restore, D. de iure dotium, l. quoties; D. de solutione matrimonii, l. si alienam. And because he has his cause from her, who, as regards him, holds the place of the owner, C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. male agitur. Such a contrived retention in a dowry of this kind is prohibited, c. rem in praesenti, § placet. Otherwise, it would be easy for a husband to acquire a title from someone and to say that that person is the owner, and to delay the restitution of the dowry after many years. And this is when he acquires his cause from a non-possessor. For the emphyteuta does not have a cause in civil possession, but in natural possession, and the church was not bound naturally. For if the thing and natural possession had reverted to the church, and this were established, then the husband would have a right, but this is not the case here.

But as to the profit of the third part, there is no need to dispute: for even if the custom had been proved, nevertheless the husband and wife do not succeed to the ecclesiastical emphyteusis, unless mention was made of them in the concession made by the church, which was not done here. See in the first concession, as in Auth. de non alienando, § emphyteuta, column 2. And what the noted doctors say in l. cogi, C. de petitione hereditatis, supports the foregoing. And lest husbands be given an opportunity to deceive and circumvent their wives, this is the just and holy opinion in a doubtful case. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that if the wife predeceases her husband without issue, the husband acquires one-third of the dowry and must restore two-thirds, and that no agreement to the contrary shall be valid, what is the outcome if there are surviving children?
2. Whether an argument from the contrary sense (*a contrario sensu*) is to be drawn in statutes, and whether one may renounce it by agreement or custom. See nos. 3, 6, and 8.
3. Whether a new statute extends its force to old dowries, since the restoration was to be made according to the old law.
4. A contract regarding the dowry, while the marriage subsists, is valid in law.
5. Bartolus, according to Baldus, was a mere schoolboy.
body: The point of the question is as follows. A certain man gave a dowry for his daughter, and during the subsisting or consummated marriage, he stipulated that the dowry be returned to him, a copy of which instrument is sent to you. At the time of said stipulation, a certain old statute concerning the restitution of dowries was in force, a copy of which is shown to you. And while said statute was in force, said marriage was dissolved. Now, because the woman has died, with common children from the aforementioned marriage still living. Then a new statute is enacted, also disposing of the restitution of dowries, and differently from what is contained in the old one. And while said new statute is in force, under whose observance the children who were born from said marriage die, with the father surviving, a copy of which new statute is also sent to you. Now, two things are asked. First, whether said dowry ought to be returned, and which statute ought to be observed. For it is said by the stipulator that the old statute and the marital agreements ought to be observed, since the new statute does not extend to past events, and the old law must be observed in the decision of the lawsuit. To this effect, the law *Leges et constitutiones*, Codex, *De legibus et constitutionibus*, is alleged, with the notes thereon by the doctors, and on this point a certain opinion given by Master Rosellus will be shown to you. On the other side, it is said that the dowry ought not to be returned, but ought to remain with the father according to the form of the new statute. And this seems to us so, according to Cynus in the law *Unica*, at the end, Codex, *De re uxoria actione*, and according to Bartolus in the repetition of the law *Omnes populi*, Digest, *De iure et iuramento*. And therefore, because the action for claiming the dowry arises from the death of the child, but said action for claiming the dowry did not arise at the time of the old statute, but at the time of the new one. And although the opinion given in the above-mentioned point does not in any way contain what is asked secondly, since said stipulation was made during the subsisting marriage, and such promise and contract celebrated therein has the force of a donation, and is presumed to be simulated, because every contract which is between husband and wife, or between others who have a husband and wife under their power, is presumed fictitious and simulated, and conceived in fraud of the law. And thus, no faith ought to be given to such an instrument, unless it otherwise appears that the dowry was constituted and agreed upon before the marriage was consummated, as is noted by Cynus in the law *In contractibus*, Codex, *De non numerata pecunia*. It is asked, what is the law on both points. In the name of Christ, amen.

† The first statute provides that, if there are no children, the husband, upon the predecease of his wife, shall acquire one-third part and shall restore two-thirds, notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary. The question now arises whether, when children are present, anything is to be restored according to the circumscribed custom mentioned in the law *dos a patre*. It appears that the entire dowry is to be restored, as noted in the law *Beblius*, *de pactis dotalibus*. For the case of children is a case unforeseen by the statute; therefore, the custom ceases, and the rule of common law applies. Thus, it ought to be restored, as stated in the final law of the Code, *communia utriusque iudicii*, and in the text of the aforementioned law *dos a patre*. On the contrary, it seems, taking an argument from the contrary sense of the statute itself, *de pactis dotalibus*, law *intra socerum*, § *cum inter*, that it remains with the father for the children. This is supported by what is noted by Dy. in the chapter *quod ob gratiam*, *de regulis iuris*, book 6, and in the law *quod favore*, *de legibus*, according to Cy.

† I hold that from this status an argument *a contrario sensu* is to be drawn, as if from the contrariety of the final cause. For the final cause why the two parts ought to be restored when children exist is the lack of children; therefore, when children exist, the contrary final cause produces the contrary effect: *non obstat* so. ma. l. *Si cum dotem*, because there the unforeseen case was not contrary in the final reason for the restitution of the dowry to the case expressed in the contract; here, however, it ought not to be said,

Whether one can renounce this argument *a contrario sensu* by pact, just as one can renounce the custom of the law regarding the dowry given by the father. It seems that yes. D. de pactis, l. pacisci. To the contrary it seems, for the statute prohibits renouncing its own provision. This contrary sense appears to be in the text of the statute itself; hence a pact which speaks against the contrary sense of the law speaks against the law itself. S. contra textum legis loquendo ad intellectum, D. de testamento, l. qui testamento, §. mulier. And if this is true, even under the old statute the dowry remains for the children with the father, notwithstanding a stipulation made to the contrary by the father of the woman. The second statute, newly issued, contains this expressly.

But it is doubted whether this new statute extends to old dowries stipulated by the father before the statute in the case of the death of the children. And it seems that the new statute does not know the old stipulations, C. de leg. l. leges. §. decurio. l. pe. C. man. l. per diuersas. §. fi. with infinitely similar ones. To the contrary it seems, because the restitution of the dowry is of the future, although the stipulation is of the past, as noted by Cy. C. de rei ven. l. rem in praesenti. §. fi. and Bar. in l. omnes populi. and to this effect, ff. de pact. do. l. si inter vi. et vxo. So, if this new statute is understood to be declaratory of the old statute, or obtained as if tacitly contained under the old statute from the contrary sense of it. And where the statute speaks directly or tacitly, there any clause of it speaks, even a derogatory one, because it is common; then there is no doubt that it has place in past matters, ff. de lib. le. l. Aurelius. §. Sticho. and in Auth. de fil. ante dotis instrumentanatis. §. fi. But if we say that it is entirely new, then either the condition of restoring the dowry had occurred, and that right acquired by the statute arriving is not taken away; nor does it seem to be the mind of the statutors to take away natural equity and natural obligation already founded, as in Auth. ex libra. et ascriptio natos. post prin. col. 5. or it had not yet occurred, and because the son of the daughter was still alive at the time of the new statute, although the marriage had been dissolved before, and then the new statute is to be observed, because the statute preceded the case to be disposed of by the statute. That is, the retention to be retained by the statute. And this is a certain succession of the future similar to that from intestacy. For the statute ordains that the son succeeds in the dowry of the mother notwithstanding the pact. And it does not distinguish between factum or fiendum. And it is sufficiently clear there, when it says, notwithstanding any form of the dotal instrument. That is, facti, vel fiendi. For when past matters have in their being a dependence on the future, we judge of them as of future matters as far as the decision of future matters is concerned. Hence the statute on the profit of the dowry has place even in dowries given before the statute, the condition of which to be restored arose after the statute, l. leges. per Cy. and all the doctors. And the reason is, because the condition of the death of the children, just like a conditional acquisition causa mortis, does not fix retroactively. Hence, the new statute impeding, the preceding death of the children, the stipulation of restoring the dowry cannot be committed: because the time of the condition, and not of the contract, is considered, as ff. ad Sil. l. 1. §. serui. and l. i. ff. de reg. caton. ff. de haeredi. insti. l. sed si in condi. §. solemus. And thus the force of the new law reaches the case of restitution, and the law is to be followed. And by this our question is decided either to one part or to the other, according as the order and process of the facts stand. And granted that the stipulation had value from the beginning, nevertheless the hope of it could be elided, and an exception from the new law could be prepared, just as from a new custom. The example is clear in the new prescription newly introduced, which regards even old obligations: because it does not dispose of the origin of the exception. And this is held by Cy. expressly in his own terms. C. de rei vxo. ac. l. 1. §. fi. I know your cunning wisdom does not recall such a learned doctor.

† On the second point, a childish doubt is raised, because by law the contract is valid even during the subsistence of the marriage. C. de donat. ante nup. l. si; ff. sol. matr. l. quoties; and it is not presumed to be simulated. Let those who understand the law speak, for men of dull intellect do not grasp subtleties. One must, however, understand why in l. Beblius, ff. de pact. dot., the husband is repelled, since by that condition, "if without children," etc., half of the dowry ought to be retained if they died after the marriage was dissolved. Therefore, by necessary consequence, if with children, the entire dowry, as in l. intra, § cum inter, de pact. dot. You know well why this is so. Hence the gloss filius legis, which states that the husband does not gain the entire dowry because he had a daughter, in the major gloss and in the minor gloss beginning "ideo."

† Hence, if an argument from the contrary sense were formed in this way: “When there are no children, the husband profits by one-half; therefore, when there are children, he profits by the whole,” such reasoning would be false, as if proceeding from his own provident mind, because in the case of children the husband profits nothing in his own person. And therefore that husband acts wrongly and fails in his claim by alleging a tacit pact in his own person; for the tacit pact does not speak of Marillus the husband himself. But if the argument from the contrary sense is formed in this way: “When there are no children, the husband profits by one-half and restores the other half; therefore, when there are children, the daughter profits by the dowry for her children, and nothing is to be restored to the father,” this is the best argument. The text and the gloss are in the said § cum inter. And it may be said that this is not the case, for the reasons which I am about to state, in the same law, where it is said that the woman, daughter of Marcellus and wife of Marillus, made testamentary disposition of the entire dowry. Hence, nothing was to revert to the father’s heirs, because it was provided for her children, § cum inter. And see the argument in the Digest, De heredibus instituendis, l. Lucius, ver. nam prudens. And if you do not believe me, believe Jacobus de Belvis, who disputes this point and says so; and if you wish to see the disputation, I will send it to you; and also Bartolus, who recites and confirms this in l. si cum dotem, in principio, Soluto matrimonio.

† I know, however, that your wisdom is so great that you do not care about these little doctors, and although in another case, when omitted, there is an action for the common dowry of the father and daughter: nevertheless, in this case, where the father of the woman provided for himself under the condition, if children did not exist, if they exist, nothing is due to the father, the case is in the said §. cum inter. It cannot be answered. Apollo would not answer. And if you know, say with one sensible and wise word. Someone will say, rather it is the case in the said l. beblius. because there the daughter of Marcellus, wife of Marillus, testifies by the right of prelegacy, not by tacit pact, as there in the word, fideicommissi. Take heed, lest you fight, as that Marillus fought. For the argument from the contrary sense is taken in the same condition, not in another. For example, if in the case of divorce it is argued from the contrary if with children, and thus also if in death the condition is inserted, if not similarly in death there will be a contrary condition, if so. But where in the case of death it is conceived, and not by death, but by divorce it is dissolved, or vice versa, just as it does not have an expressed place due to the different species of the case, so neither does it have a tacit one from the contrary sense, and because in the said l. beblius. the pact was formed in the case of death, and that case did not occur, but of divorce, it was rightly necessary to have a prelegacy, although today it would not be necessary, by l. C. de rei ux. ac. l. 1. §. videamus. It suffices for you, if you do not understand more, the authority of the said doctors.

† I have stated that an argument *a contrario sensu* is drawn from the contrariety of the cause, as set forth in the final paragraph of the Digest title *De pactis*, in the law *Tale pactum*, § *Si*. On this argument, I spoke at length in the law *Conuenticulam*, Codex, title *De episcopis et clericis*, and there among the ancient authorities in the law *Testamento*, § *Mulier*, Digest, title *De testibus*. Otherwise, it follows that the dowry would be restored on account of children, and retained without children, which would not be said of a single beast. See, therefore, what you have studied in the law *Dos a patre*, together with its gloss, Codex, title *De solutione matrimonii*. I have said enough, and even too much, for do not contend with verbose persons by words. Therefore, I confirm my opinion with the first seal. And if there is doubt about anything else, I beg you to write back to me, for I never give counsel while dreaming, by the grace of God. For I do this not so much for worldly honor, but for conscience and the inquiry into truth itself. And yet I am not so foolish that I do not always submit myself to the judgment of those who possess the sense of the laws, from whom I always desire to be taught, nor do I shrink from learning. I.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In what the administration in spiritual matters consists.
2. In what the administration in temporal matters consists.
3. A visitor appointed by the Pope may do everything himself or through another, as a bishop may, except that he cannot alienate immovable property.
4. What matters fall under the jurisdiction of law, or diocesan jurisdiction.
5. The clause regarding temporal and spiritual matters is greatly restricted in the case of the bishop’s vicar.
6. Although the bishop’s vicar cannot deprive anyone of his benefices, he may nevertheless declare that the possessor does not have a just title to the benefice.
7. In what the power of the spiritual sword consists.
8. The appeal of a censure does not include deposition or degradation, and what these contain.
9. What ecclesiastical reproof is.
10. One who has the power of judging is understood to have ordinary power.
11. What ecclesiastical reproof and the ecclesiastical sword are.
12. What an ecclesiastical censure is, and canonical severity, and what it contains.
13. How manyfold the sword is.
14. Whether a patriarch can deprive offending clerics of their benefices, and compel clerics to teach according to their canonical institution.
15. What a patriarch can do.
body: It must be premised that sometimes administration is granted in both temporal and spiritual matters, as stated in *de electione*, chapter *Cum nobis*, and in *de regulis iuris*, chapter *Nihil est* at the end; in *de relictis domibus*, chapter *Cum inter*; in *de privilegiis*, chapter *Cum venerabilis*; in *ne clerici vel monachi*, chapter *Quoniam*; and in Book 6, chapter *Si liber*. Sometimes it is granted in temporal matters only, as stated in *de officio delegati*, chapter *Ventus*; in *de electione*, chapter *Indemnitatibus*; in *de suppleto ne praedae*, chapter *Penultimus* and the last. Sometimes administration is granted in spiritual matters only and temporal matters, as stated in *de ordine*, chapter *Cum nullus*, Book 6. Sometimes administration is granted simply, as stated in *de officio*, chapter 1 and 3; in *de consuetudine*, chapter *Imputamus*; in *de officio ordinarii*, chapter *Romana*; in *de appellationibus*, chapter *Romana*; in *de officio*, chapter *Si contra unum* at the end; in *de praebendis*, chapter *Statutum*; in *de habitibus*, chapter *Ut officium*; and in Book 6, chapter *Si*. It is also relevant in *de institutionibus*, chapter 3; in *de Romano*, chapter *A*; in *de situ*, chapter 1.

Secondly, it must be premised that administration in spiritual matters consists in this, namely: to excommunicate, to suspend, to interdict, to confer benefices, to institute, to confirm, to elect, to present, to visit, to correct, and to punish. The conferral of sacraments, the entire power of the penitential forum, the dispensation of vows, and the commutation thereof, make this clear, as stated in *de ver. sig.*, c. *quaerenti*; *de re iud.*, c. *ad probandum*; *ne praela.*, vi. su. eo. ti.; *de simonia*, c. 1; *cum in ecclesia*; c. *insinuante*; c. *eaque veniens*; c. *ex tuae*; c. *ad aures*; *de regularibus*, c. *cum audiuimus*. For all things that are spiritual, when exercised by someone capable of spiritual matters, are said to be exercised by spiritual administration, as stated in *de iudi.*, c. *decreuimus*; and c. *quanto*; *de ordi. cogni.*, c. *tuam*; *qui fi. sint leg.*, c. *lator*. And what things are spiritual is clear from *de rel. do.*, c. *constitutus*; *de elec.*, c. *massanna*, and c. *sanc.*; *de consti.*, c. *cum rem*; *de sen. excom.*, c. *iudex laicus*, lib. 6; and in the decretal *dispendiosam*; *de iu. facit.*, ii. q. i.; in the *summa*. Therefore, administration in spiritual matters is recognized from the nature of that which is administered, because that which is administered is spiritual, therefore the administration is spiritual, and of a spiritual matter.

† The administration in temporal matters consists in judicial acts and in extra-judicial acts. In judicial matters, when the superior holds a city or a castle in which he had temporal jurisdiction by full right, which pertains to the mere and mixed empire and to all jurisdiction, as stated in *Conquestus*, de foro competenti; *Ne clerici*, de clericis laicis; or *Mortuis*, de mortuis; or when he has a certain and limited jurisdiction, as stated in *Cum contingat*, de officio ordinarii; *Dilectus*, de praescriptionibus; *Ad audientiam*, de praescriptionibus. Extra-judicially, however, this administration consists in every species of alienation. Likewise, to lease, to grant in emphyteusis, or to let out at a fixed rent censuses, revenues, and pensions, and to collect them, as stated in *De rebus ecclesiae*, l. *Si quis presbyterorum*, ne praedae; *De rebus ecclesiae*, clerici priv.; C. *De administratione*, l. *Lex quae tutores*. It should be known, however, that although the matters mentioned are contained under the clause "in temporal and spiritual matters," nevertheless the meaning is restricted according to the diversity of persons. Sometimes it is restricted greatly, sometimes moderately, sometimes very slightly: for it is restricted in the person of the visitation and of the administration granted by the Pope.

† For he, by himself or through another, can do all that the bishop can do, except that he cannot alienate the immovable property of the church, as stated in the chapter *Is cui*, De electionibus, Book 6. The bishop, however, can do all that pertains to jurisdiction and order, as held in the chapter *Transmissa*, De electionibus.

† Moreover, he may do all things that pertain to the law of jurisdiction and to the diocesan law, and whatever is of the law of jurisdiction or diocesan law, is held to be of office. See *Conquerente* and *Dilectus*. And according to Innocentius, *De statu monasterii*, cap. 1. But in the person of the chapter, during a sede vacante, the clause concerning spiritual and temporal matters restricts more than in the case of a visitation. For he cannot confer, elect, or present. And there are many cases in which it is doubtful whether they pass to the chapter during a sede vacante, whether they are spiritual or temporal, whether they are exercised in judgment or outside it. See *Ne sede vacante*, cap. 1 and the last, *De eo de quo plene* by Innocentius, *De maiestate et obedientia*, cap. unico, lib. 6.

† Moreover, this clause is most significantly restricted in the person of an official or a vicar general of a bishop, to whom such office is generally committed, if from such commission he may have cognizance of civil, temporal, or spiritual causes, as in c. 2, de officio vicarii, lib. 6; de foro competenti, c. 1; and also if he has power over those matters which are held, de haereticis, d. c., vt officiales, in fine; and c. si. Nevertheless, he does not have the power to inquire into, correct, or punish the excesses of anyone, or to remove anyone from their benefices or administrations: as stated in the aforementioned c. 2; nor can he confer a benefice, as c. si, eo titulo, de officio vicarii, lib. 6. From this, however, it follows that a vicar may institute and confirm, as the glossa says there; and this is the case in de institutione, c. 3.

It must be noted, however, that although the vicar of the bishop cannot, on account of a crime, deprive someone of his benefices, he may nevertheless declare that the possessor of the benefice does not have a just title to it, when this is sought by way of an action. And thus a personal action is established. Note this. Innocentius, *De electione*, c. *Querelam*; and what is noted by Johannes, *Ut lites non contingant*, c. *Quia maior*, § *Porro*. For since the vicar of the bishop has cognizance of carnal marriage, *De frigiditate*, c. 1, he therefore has cognizance of spiritual marriage, as Johannes Andreae says in the aforementioned c. 2, *De officio vicarii*, lib. 6. But concerning the above, attention must be paid to two matters contained in the said apostolic letters. First, concerning the spiritual jurisdiction granted to the Lord Patriarch by the Lord Pope, when it is said: "We, wishing that you may be able to freely exercise the power of the spiritual sword and spiritual jurisdiction in the same province."

† Regarding this, it should be known that the power of the spiritual sword appears to consist solely in the sentence of censure, as stated in the chapter *Dilecto* under the title *De sententia excommunicationis*, where the spiritual and ecclesiastical sword is taken to mean the sentence of censure. Under the name of censure, however, come excommunication, suspension, and interdict, as is expressly stated in the chapter *Quaerenti*.

And there John says that the term "cessation" does not include deposition or degradation. For those penalties are odious and therefore must be restricted, according to the rule of law in the chapter *In poenis*. Those, however, of which the Decree speaks in the chapter *Quaerenti*, are favorable. Moreover, the latter are temporal, whereas the former are perpetual. Although, therefore, from that clause he cannot punish a contumacious person with any other penalty than that which the text there expressly states, the Patriarch himself, by virtue of the commission, receives jurisdiction and thus coercive power; wherefore he can inflict the penalty written in the law. And where no certain fine is found, he may punish at his discretion, according to the chapter *De causis* in the title *De officio delegati*. And thus is understood the chapter *Pro humani* in the title *De homicidiis*, book 6. But the said clause seems to be understood differently, for the Pope, wishing the administration of justice to be maintained in that province, so that the subjects may rest in peace, and so that the way of offending may be barred to the audacious, as in the chapter *Congruit* in the title *De officio praesidentis*, wishing that province to be pruned by the power of the spiritual sword, ought to have granted spiritual jurisdiction to the same Patriarch. Therefore, the Lord Patriarch can wield the sword of ecclesiastical censure against offenders. For this pertains to the administration of justice, according to the law *Sancimus* in the Code, title *De poenis*; the law *Congruit* in the title *De officio praesidentis*; and the chapter *Quaesiuit* in the title *De his quae fiunt a maiore parte*. Censure

† "Ecclesiastical" sometimes denotes the imposition of many penalties, as is clear in c. Pro humani, De homicidio, lib. 6, where Johannes says that although the term "censure" contains only three things, as in the cited c. Quærenti, this is understood when it is written to a delegate, or when it pertains to his jurisdiction, who cannot do more if more is not stated in the letter. Hence, he cannot deprive of benefices, depose, impose a new fine, nor inflict other penalties, as discussed in the cited c. Pro humani. Although he may subdelegate and condemn in expenses, De officio delegati, c. In literis, De dolo et contumacia, c. 2, De eo qui mittitur in poenam, c. 2, nevertheless, the ordinary ecclesiastical judge may do all things, unless it is proven otherwise, De clericis non residentibus, c. Ex tuae. Hence, since the bishop has jurisdiction and may exercise it judicially, therefore he may impose fines, De iudicibus, l. 2, §. Si non obstat, l. 2, in principio, 10, De iure omnium iudicum.

† For what is said there, that he who has the power of judging can inflict a great penalty, is understood with reference to ordinary power, ff de ver. sig. l. aliud. and l. si qua poena. Therefore, the ordinary judge can punish in money, de deli. pue. c. 2. de offic. ordi. c. dilectus. And this is a fitting punishment, de pęnis. c. dilectus. Provided, however, that he takes care not to allow his subjects to remain in their offenses for the sake of monetary gain, de poenis. c. licet. de offici. ordi. c. irrefragabili. ad fi. If, therefore, it is believed that a subject is better corrected by a temporal than by a spiritual penalty, he may safely inflict the former, as stated in the aforementioned c. pro humani, where this is expressly treated. And since the delinquents can be struck by the sword of ecclesiastical punishment,

† It should be noted that the laws sometimes grant someone the power of punishment, which punishment is understood as ecclesiastical censure. At other times, they command that someone be struck with the sword of ecclesiastical discipline, 16 q. 2, visis, in the end, de puritate, c. inter, where the sword is explained as degradation. For in the Church of God there are two swords, temporal and spiritual, de sententia excommunicationis, c. dilecti, 12.

It is also an ecclesiastical censure, which contains those three matters referred to in the chapter *Quærenti*, *De verborum significatione*; and canonical severity, which pertains to temporal punishment, as stated in the chapter *In quibusdam*, *De poenis*. It is an ecclesiastical reproof, which consists in degradation and delivery to the secular court, as stated in the chapter *Novimus*, *De verborum significatione*, as is said in the chapter *Cum quidam*, Book 6, of the *Archidecisions* (or *Archidecretals*), *De exceptionibus*.

† Although there are indeed two swords in the Church of God, namely the spiritual one, as stated in Dist. 15, question 6, and the *Authentica*, and in the title *De sententia excommunicationis*, chapter *Dilecto*, Book 6; nevertheless, it may be said with authority that the spiritual sword is subdivided and is twofold: one is eradicating and mortal, namely degradation, as found in the title *De purificatione*, chapter *Inter*, and in the title *De homicidio*, chapter *Pro humani*; the other is disciplinary or medicinal, namely excommunication, as stated in Dist. 2, question 1, chapter *Multi*, which is also referred to as a sword in Dist. 16, question 2, chapter *Visis*, in the title *De rebus ecclesiasticis*, chapter *Non alie*, and in the title *De clericis excommunicatis*, chapter *Si qui presbyterorum*. And concerning this twofold sword, it is spoken of in the title *De sententia excommunicationis*, chapter *Cum medicinalis*, Book 6.

First, it is called the eradicating or mortal sword because it is inflicted not only for correction but also for punishment, and dispensation is not easily granted in such cases, as stated in the title *De clericis non residentibus*, chapter *Ex tuae*. And this sword is the most special prerogative of the bishop; hence, no one who is not ordained a bishop can wield it, as stated in the title *De electione*, chapter *Transmissa*.

Secondly, it is called a sword because it separates a person from God, that is, it declares separation from the communion of men, as stated in Dist. 3, question 4, chapter *Ultimo*, and in Dist. 11, question 3, chapter *Cum excommunicato*, and in the title *De clericis excommunicatis*, chapter *Si celebrat*. It is called disciplinary and not mortal because it is wielded not for punishment, but solely for correction, as stated in Dist. 2, question 1, chapter *Multi*, and in Dist. 24, question 3, chapter *Notandum*, as explained by Johannes in the aforementioned chapter *Dilecto*, and in the title *De purificatione*, chapter *Inter*.

These matters having been thus premised, it seems that the following should be decided according to law:

† Since the said Patriarch is the general vicar in temporal matters in the Duchy of Spoleto, and thus holds from the Lord Pope a temporal province and ordinary jurisdiction. Moreover, he holds ordinary and spiritual jurisdiction, as it is stated in the Speculum in the title *De officio ordinarii*, that he may deprive offenders of benefices, since that clause of spiritual jurisdiction is added more strongly for the punishment of crimes, declaring that those holding benefices who do not have a canonical title do not have a canonical institution. And this is also stated by Johannes in the cited chapter 2, *De officio vicarii*, Book 6. However, to what I said, that he may deprive of benefices on account of a crime, much is objected by the cited Decretal 2, *De officio vicarii*, Book 6, and by what is noted by Johannes *De officio vicarii*, chapter *Si*, where it is said that the vicar of the Pope appointed in the city cannot remove from benefices on account of a crime.

† But certainly these rights do not stand in the way, because since the Lord Patriarch has ordinary temporal jurisdiction over the entire province, by reason of which ordinary jurisdiction he has mere and mixed Empire, as will be said below, and thus he can cognize and punish crimes, therefore he can also remove from benefices. The objection from chapter 2 does not hold, because there [the judge] could not cognize nor punish crimes, therefore neither could he remove from benefices, since such removal comes by reason of the crime. For when a pronouncement is made upon the crime, the person is said to be deprived of the benefice, when it is such a crime for which one is deprived of the benefice. And Innocentius says this in *de accusatione*, chapter *Cum oporteat*; and chapter *Qualiter*; and *de foro competenti*, *postulatum*; and if he cannot cognize the crime, therefore he cannot deprive of the benefice. The Lord Patriarch, who is vicar in temporal matters, has that jurisdiction which vicars have by common law and by custom: by common law, mere Empire seems to have been transferred, which is delegable according to the canon *de raptoribus*, chapter *In Archiepiscopatu*; *ne clerici vel monachi*, chapter *Ultima*, book 6. And it supports what is noted by Guillaume in the *Speculum*, *de iudiciis*, *omnium iudicum*. Furthermore, he has that power which vicars have by custom, which custom grants and amplifies jurisdiction. Law 3, *de emancipatis*, *liber de iudiciis*; chapter *Novit*, *de foro competenti*; chapter *Cum contingat*. And it should be noted that the temporal jurisdiction attributed to the Lord Patriarch in the city of Spoleto in the province of Spoleto, Duchy, includes clerics and laymen, *de foro competenti*, chapter *Dilecti*, where the case makes what is noted by Johannes *de officio*, *de legibus*, chapter *Finis*, book 6. The objection from *de rescriptis*, chapter *Sedes*, does not hold, because there an expression was made regarding laymen, therefore clerics are not included in the general clause, since they are more dignified; and just as that temporal jurisdiction includes clerics, so too does the spiritual jurisdiction attributed to the said Lord Patriarch. And from that apostolic commission, I say that the Lord Patriarch has ordinary jurisdiction and mere Empire in the province. *Digestum*, *de officiis praesidis*, law *Illicitas*, section *Qui universas*; it supports *Codex*, *de episcopis et clericis*, law *Raptorem*; *Codex*, *de appellationibus*, *praecipimus*; *Codex*, *de raptu virorum*, law *Unica*, which laws speak of a vicar. And therefore, from that power, he can deprive offending clerics of benefices, and he can compel clerics to prove their canonical institution, *de officiis ordinarii*, chapter *Ordinarii*, book 6; *de regulis iuris*, chapter 1; *de procuratoribus*, chapter *Ex insinuatione*. And he can declare that those possessing benefices do not have a just title to the benefices, since their canonical institution does not appear, as stated in the said chapter *Ordinarii*; or if they have intruded themselves into benefices, *de praebendis*, chapter *Eum qui*, book 6; or if the title is reduced to no title, for example because they are deprived of the benefice by sentence of law or of a man. Regarding sentence of law, it is clear from *de praebendis*, chapter *De multa*, and in the Extravagant chapter *Execrabilis*. Regarding sentence of a man, it is clear from *de dolo et contumacia*, chapter *Veritatis*; *de excessibus praeparatorum*, chapter *Ex literis*. However, the Lord Patriarch could make those committing capital crimes suffer for those crimes, and have them thrown into prison, *de poenis*, chapter *Quamvis*, book 6; *de sententia excommunicationis*, chapter *Si clericos*. And furthermore, he can compel clerics who have no title to benefices to make restitution of fruits. The same applies if they had a title to benefices, and the title was reduced to no title by sentence of law or of a man, and such clerics had received fruits. *de causa possessionis*, chapter *Cum super*; *de praebendis*, chapter *Dilecto*; *de iure patronatus*, chapter *Cum dilectus*. It supports what is noted by Innocentius *de restitutione spoliatorum*, chapter *In literis*, in the large gloss, word *quinimo*, with many similar authorities. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a father provides a dowry and immediately stipulates that it be returned to himself and his heirs, whether, upon his death, the action for the dowry consolidates in favor of the living daughter.
2. Whether a father is presumed, in case of doubt, to provide a dowry from his own goods or from those of his daughter.
3. Whether a father may substitute for his daughter in the dowry.
4. The legitime is not owed to natural children only.
body: When

† When a father provides a dowry and immediately stipulates it for himself and his heirs, it has been variously written by the learned in the context of the action for the wife’s property, in l. 1, § videamus, whether, upon his death, the action for the dowry consolidates in favor of the surviving daughter. But the truth is that the tenor of the stipulation prevails, C. communia vtriusque iudicii, l. 1, and this is fully noted by Bartolus in l. post dotem, sol. matr. And this applies when the father dowers his daughter from his own patrimony, because, although he is bound to provide a dowry, the law permits him to stipulate for himself, ff. sol. matr., l. quot. But if the father dowers his daughter from the daughter’s own goods, the father is compelled to cede the action to the daughter and her heirs, ff. mand., l. idemque, § cui.

† In case of doubt, it is presumed that the dowry was provided from the father’s goods, C. de donationibus promissis, l. si. But the statute decides the contrary, namely that it was provided from the woman’s goods. I understand this to apply unless there is an express mention in the instrument that it was from the father’s goods, by argument from Auth. de aequalitate dotis, § 1, in the gloss; for the presumption of the statute can be derogated by a contrary confession. Hence, this statute greatly favors the heirs of the woman. Another statute also favors them, under the rubric “that daughters and granddaughters,” where it says, “and the aforesaid shall not be understood to apply to dowries.” For the statute intends that in the dowry the daughter shall not be bound to follow the father’s judgment. To the same effect: C. de inofficioso testamento, Auth. unde si parens; and l. si, ff. de collatione dotis.

† And this pertains to the second point, whether a daughter can be substituted in the dowry. For if it proceeds from the father, she can be substituted to the extent that it exceeds the legitime, otherwise not, ff. de leg. 2. l. si. §. filiae. ff. ad Treb. l. filia. and l. Lucius. §. filiam. and §. maritus. But if it were adventitious, the father could not substitute in it. Also, if the father gave the dowry, and did not stipulate it, he could not substitute it to himself, because, the stipulation ceasing, custom gives it to the children, as we know in l. dos a patre. C. sol. ma. and C. de colla. l. illam. Having seen the tenor of the stipulation, because it does not say from whose goods. And having seen the statute, that it is presumed given from the goods of the daughter for the heirs of the daughter, I am of the opinion, but according to the common law, one should adhere to what Dy. and Cy. say in d. §. videamus. and Bar. in d. §. maritus. s. that beyond the legitime it could be burdened.

† It must be known, however, that a legacy left to natural children is not considered to be from another’s property, because by the will the father is not bound to leave anything to them, as is stated in the gloss beginning “subaudi” in the principal part of the title *Ad Trebellianam* in the Digest. Hence, no legitime is owed to natural children alone. And this is a singular gloss. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Spoils must also be restored to a pirate who is being deprived of them.
2. The owner of a granary who holds another’s grain in the granary, if he does not have the key, is not bound to accept sequestration, and therefore is not liable.
body: This question

† good faith can be determined by law. S. Incurrit, D. de deposito, where it is said that even to a robber the spoils which he deposited must be restored, otherwise if the owner did not demand them. But here the owner did not demand them, and he made a sequestration, having jurisdiction and power, indeed even a manus iniectio over the thing itself. Therefore, the sequestrator acted wrongly in restoring it, and is bound to surrender the sequestered thing to the owner, L. oleum, D. de dolo. To the contrary it is argued,

† Although the grain was in his granary, he nevertheless did not have any detention of it, since the person who deposited the grain had the key to the granary, and it was within his power, as stated in the law and noted in the law 2, l. Titia, § Gaius. Hence, that person could refuse to act as a sequestrator, nor was he bound to accept the office of sequestrator in a contentious matter, nor to involve himself in the litigation, C. de iure dominii imp. l. si, ad fin. Therefore, if this is so, the owner of the granary is not liable, because he never had the grain in his power, nor was he bound against his will to accept the office of sequestrator, especially when done without any examination of the case. But this person, who accepted it and delivered it, or caused it to be accepted or sold, undoubtedly is liable. It supports what is noted by Innocentius de testibus, c. cum in officio. Moreover, the one who granted the granary by precarium or leased it was not bound to resist the removal of the grain which had been stored there, and which he held and possessed, especially if he was unaware when it was being removed; but if the owner of the granary had possessed it, then he ought not to restore it, as noted in C. depositi, l. si. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A legacy of alimony for the life of a certain person is pure for the first year, but conditional for the subsequent years.
2. Witnesses may be received and published regarding a conditional legacy, or one deferred to a future day, for the perpetual memory of the matter, provided that the reception of the witnesses is upheld.
3. A notary, by virtue of his office as a scribe, cannot receive witnesses for the perpetual memory of the matter, but he may do so by commission of a judge.
4. A commission for the reception of witnesses issued by a judge to a notary has the force of an interlocutory judgment.
5. The debtor of alimony is not discharged, even if the legatee to whom they are left has lived off other resources.
6. When witnesses are received for the perpetual memory of the matter, the case is said to be ordinary, and not summary.
7. Whether an action arises from the statements of the witnesses.
body: The following are all and each of the acts, agitated, and held in the case by Nardutia and Catherine, daughters of the late Petrutius Augustinus of the land of Malleano, sisters and heirs of the late John, son of the said late Petrutius Augustinus, against Franceschina, wife of the said Petrutius Augustinus and mother of the said John. Copy of the libel. Before you, noble man Jordan of Pistionibus of the city, good man, podestà of the land of Malleano, specially appointed by the Roman people, and your jurisdiction. Nardutia and Catherine, daughters of the late Petrutius Augustinus and sisters of the late John Petrutius Augustinus, without revoking their procurators, propose and act against and adverse to Francesca, wife of the late Petrutius Augustinus, intestate heir of the said John, and against any other person legitimately intervening for her in judgment, saying that John Petrutius Augustinus, son of the said late Francesca and late full brother of the said Nardutia and Catherine, in the year of our Lord 1382, indiction 7, during the time of the most holy father in Christ and our lord Urban, by divine grace Pope VI, on the 23rd day of the month of May, sick in body but sane in mind, in the presence of the underwritten witnesses, namely Angeletus, Tutius, Nannus, Andreutius, Nardutius, Falconera, Hennufrius, Pangratius, Lord Angelus, Petrutius, Cecharellus, Rolandus the Clerk, Angeletus, John Fuxice, Antonius, Master James Patrochus, John, Master Jacobus, Lord Angelus, Antonius, John Lellecola Lella, and Brother Tutius of Anania of the order of hermits, and prior of the place of Saint James of Malleano, specially summoned and requested, made his last will and disposition as follows, namely that to the aforementioned Nardutia and Catherine, his sisters, he left by right of legacy for the whole time of their lives, and of each of them, a continuous habitation or receptacle in one of the houses of the said John located in the quarter of Saint John, and that also for the whole time of their lives Nardutia and Catherine should be maintained from his own goods. And this after the death of Augustinus, the said Nardutia and Catherine, and their common brother John. Which disposition and will the said John wished to be valid by right of last will and disposition, and in every way by the right and cause by which it could be best. They also say and narrate, the aforementioned Nardutia and Catherine, that the aforementioned Francesca, mother of the said John, was present and consented to the aforementioned. They also say that after the aforementioned, the said John died, now three months and more having passed, with the said Francesca, his mother, surviving and living, and with the said Nardutia and Catherine, his sisters from one parent only, namely the father, surviving and living. And also with the said Augustinus surviving and living. They also say that after the aforementioned, the said Augustinus died, with the said Nardutia and Catherine, his sisters, who now live, surviving and living, and with the said Francesca surviving and living. They also say that the said Francesca asserted and said and affirmed, and says, that the inheritance of the said John, her late son, was devolved to her, and that she was and is the heir of the said John, and that the said Francesca entered upon the inheritance of the said late John, her son, and that she acted as his heir. They also say that the said Francesca, heir of the aforementioned late John, her son, refuses to deliver and assign to them the habitation of one of the houses of the said John located in the aforementioned quarter of Saint John, and also to maintain Nardutia and Catherine from the goods of the late John, as the said John disposed and left, as is expressed above. And now she refuses unjustly and wrongfully. And since the aforementioned are true, therefore the said Nardutia and Catherine, without revoking their procurators, request through you, the aforementioned lord podestà, and your sentence, that the aforementioned Francesca, heir of the said late John, for past times ought, and in the future ought, to deliver and assign to the said Nardutia and Catherine the habitation of one of the aforementioned houses of the late John located in the aforementioned quarter, and also that she ought, and in the future ought, to maintain the said Nardutia and Catherine from the goods of the late John for the whole time of the lives of the said Nardutia and Catherine and of any of them, and also to deliver and assign to them, Nardutia and Catherine, the aforementioned habitation, and to maintain them, Nardutia and Catherine, from the aforementioned goods, the said Francesca, heir of the aforementioned, both for the past time, for which, all things computed, by common estimation for each month 10 florins, which also for the future she should be condemned and compelled. And they request the aforementioned to be done by you according to law and the form of the statute and ordinance of the said land of Malleano, and in every way, by right, form, and cause by which it can be best, with expenses made and to be made until the end of the case, saving to them, Nardutia and Catherine, always the right of access. And for the verification and proof of the aforementioned, among other things, the said Nardutia and Catherine intend to produce and do produce a public instrument written and published by the hand of Romanus Nardolus of Calvis of the city, public notary. The present petition was asserted, exhibited, and produced together with a certain instrument written by the hand of Romanus of Calvis, public notary, before the noble man Jordan of Pistionibus, the aforementioned podestà, sitting on the tribunal, etc., by the aforementioned Nardutia and Catherine for the memory of the thing, with the aforementioned Francesca personally cited by the liberarius of the castle of the commune of Malleano, and all the officials of the jurisdiction of the said lord podestà present, and receiving a copy of this libel. Who, the lord podestà, to the said Francesca, present and hearing, fixed and appointed a term of 8 future days to oppose and otherwise act according to the form of the statute of the commune of Malleano. And requesting also their antecedent admission to the reception of the said libel, which said podestà admitted, if and insofar as he is bound and ought by law. Before you, noble man Jordan of Pistionibus of the city, good man, podestà of the land of Malleano, and your court. Francesca, late wife of Petrutius Augustinus of the said land of Malleano, without revoking her procurators, and who is asserted to be heir to the underwritten Nardutia and Catherine, heirs of John, late son of the said Petrutius, excepts and by excepting opposes against and adverse to Nardutia and Catherine, asserted to be daughters of the said Nardutius Petrutius, and against a certain libel or petition, if it can be so called, exhibited before you on the part of the said Nardutia and Catherine. In which, in sum, it seems to request from the said Francesca, as heir, a certain legacy of a certain habitation of a certain house and of certain alimony, in which in the said libel it can be so said, and as is mentioned therein, and of which it is said to appear in the acts of your court: and against the aforementioned, a certain public instrument she asserted to be written and published by the hand of Romanus Nardolus of Calvis of the city, notary, as she asserted public, saying that the said lady Francesca does not merit the said libel or petition by the name of libel and petition. And the said instrument, which she asserts to be produced in judgment by them, is ineffective and altogether of no value, for the following main causes and reasons. And first, because the said libel or petition, if it can be so called, is uncertain, alternative, general, and obscure in many parts of it, as evidently appears from the reading of it, and especially in that part where it is said, habitation or receptacle. For the word 'or' is alternative by law. And an alternative creates obscurity by law, as in many other parts of it: and especially where it is said, in one of the houses of the said John. And it is not declared which one, nor are boundaries set, which ought to be done by law. And thus the said libel or petition does not proceed. Furthermore, saving the premises, that the said cause begun by the said Nardutia and Catherine is ordinary, and thus they ought not to have requested pronuntiatio by you. For pronuntiatio does not require litem contestatam, which an ordinary cause, if the libel proceeded, requires. s. litem contestatam. Furthermore, saving the premises, because as from the tenor of the said libel, if it can be so called, the said Nardutia and Catherine request alimony for the past time, which they could not do, considering especially that they did not live on air during the past time. Furthermore, saving the premises, because the narration, as it is narrated therein, and the contents, as they are contained, were not and are not true, by which exception of prescription, not with the intent of contesting the lawsuit, the said Francesca does not propose, but if the said libel proceeded, which she does not believe, the said Francesca is content that the lawsuit be contested upon it at its proper place and time. Furthermore, saving the premises, because the said instrument written, as it is said, by the hand of the said Romanus, who is asserted to have been a notary, does not proceed, for the main reason that a commission to a notary to examine witnesses cannot be made by law for examining, although perhaps as to writing only it could perhaps be made, as noted by Innocentius in c. cum Bertoldus, col. 2, extra de re iudicata. The text seems to be in auth. apud eloquentissimum, de fide instrumentorum. And if by any law a commission to a notary to examine witnesses could be made, which is not true, nevertheless it could perhaps be made by the express consent of the parties, but in the examination, which is said to have been made by the said Romanus, there was no express consent of the said Francesca. Therefore the said commission could not be made by law. And if it could not be commissioned, therefore the examination of any, which was said to have been made by the said Romanus, did not proceed and was not valid, because witnesses ought to be examined by the judge and not by the notary, as the aforementioned noted by Innocentius in c. cum causa, extra de testibus. Furthermore, saving the premises, that the examination of the witnesses, who are said to have been examined by the said Romanus, was and is without effect for another reason, because witnesses ought by law to be examined after the lawsuit is contested, for then proofs come by law, and not before. And thus because they were examined before the lawsuit was contested, such proof and examination was not valid, if the said witnesses, who are said to have been examined, had proved anything in effect, and they did not prove. And it is not true that the said examination was made in cases which were said by law to be able to be made before the lawsuit was contested, as the aforementioned are proved extra ut lite non contestata in c. quam frequenter. Furthermore, saving the premises, and positing without prejudice that they were of cases in which witnesses can be examined before the contestation of the lawsuit, which was not, since the publication of the said witnesses could not be made within a year from the day of examination, as noted by Innocentius in c. significavit, extra de testibus. And the text seems to be in the decretal quam frequenter. And if it is said that, positing that the said witnesses, who were, as it is said, examined, were in the case and of the aforementioned cases, as noted in the said c. quoniam frequenter, nevertheless they were examined in the case lest the right of the one causing them to be examined perish. And in such a case witnesses could be published immediately, as in c. significavit, de testibus. Nevertheless they could not be examined at the petition of a person who could act by law, as noted by Innocentius in the said c. significavit, in the beginning. And thus in the case the examination was invalid. And the said instrument, which is said to be written by the hand of the said Romanus, was without effect, considering especially that the said Nardutia and Catherine could, if they believed they had a right, petition and act. Furthermore, saving the premises, because it was not true for the time when it is said that the said John made a legacy to the said Nardutia and Catherine, positing without prejudice that it appeared, nevertheless in truth the said John was not of sound mind, but rather was in contrary health. Furthermore, saving the premises, because the said witnesses, who are said to have been examined, if they were examined by the said Romanus, did not prove those things for which they were induced, and especially since the said John, at the time when it is said that he made the said legacy, was of sound mind, which were not true, nor did they prove at least the time posited in the articles of the said Nardutia and Catherine. But in the proofs they totally and completely failed. And thus the said instrument, which is said to be written by the hand of the said Romanus, does not avail the said Catherine and Nardutia. And from now on the said Francesca is content that the reservation of her exceptions by you, lord podestà, be made in the said cause, litem contestatam, reserving the said exceptions after litem contestatam. Furthermore, saving the premises, because the said witnesses did not speak the truth, and especially because when asked if they were related to the said Nardutia and Catherine, they answered commonly that they were not, for saving the peace of them, and especially Angelus, Tutius, Andreutius, one of the said witnesses examined, who said that they were not related, and in truth they were related at least in affinity, and those examined were the husbands of the said Nardutia and Catherine and some of their blood relatives. And when asked about relationships, they said that they were not, which is not true, as the said Francesca will prove at her legitimate and proper time. And now she is ready and offers herself to be willing to prove the relationship. And because they said among themselves that they were not related, they did not speak the truth. And a witness who does not speak the truth in one thing is not believed in any of his statements. Indeed, by law all his attestation is derogated and arrogated by law. And thus the said witnesses examined by the said Romanus are without effect, and they are not believed, for a witness who does not speak the truth in one thing is considered not true in all. Proves Innocentius in c. fraternitatis, extra de haereticis. She opposes these, saving others, offering herself ready, the said Francesca, to prove the said exceptions and any of them before you, lord podestà, within a competent term at her proper time to be fixed by you, which she now requests to be given to her by you to be legitimately proved. Exhibition of the exception on the part of Francesca. The aforementioned exceptions were exhibited and produced by the aforementioned Francesca before the said lord podestà sitting on the tribunal at his usual bench of law, as is the custom, against the said Nardutia and Catherine, and against the libel and instrument produced by them, in her presence, Ser Valentine, and the procurators of the said Nardutia and Catherine, present, to whom, and to each of them, the said lord podestà fixed a term of 8 future days to contradict, etc. And he admitted the said exceptions insofar as by law. Constituted Nardutia and Catherine, daughters of the late Petrustinus, and Ser Valentine, their procurator, to the said lord podestà sitting on the tribunal, to the exhibition made by Francesca, wife of the late Augustinus, of a certain writing, as the said Francesca asserts, produced in the form of exceptions, if they can be so called, and the public instrument written by the hand of Romanus of Calvis of the city, public notary, produced in judgment by Nardutia and Catherine before you and your court, on Monday, the fifth of the present month of September. They say that the said Francesca, regarding the said writing, as it is promised, produced by her in the form of exceptions, if it can be so called, against the said libel and the said instrument, ought not to be admitted by you, lord podestà, and your court, since especially in the term of 8 days assigned to the said Francesca by you, lord podestà, and your court, to oppose and otherwise act against the said libel and against the said instrument according to the form of the statutes of the commune of Malleano, the said Francesca produced nothing of her rights against the said libel and against the said instrument, and thus she was and is contumacious by law, and of debt of pronuntiatio, that the said Francesca ought not to be heard henceforth regarding the said libel and public instrument, and that she be condemned and compelled to give and deliver to the aforementioned Nardutia and Catherine alimony and maintenance according to the form and tenor of all and each of the things contained in the said libel and written and published by the hand of the said Romanus in the said instrument. And thus from now on the said Nardutia and Catherine and the said Ser Valentine, their procurator, request and protest through you and your court that pronuntiatio be made and that the said Francesca be nevertheless condemned to give and deliver the said alimony and maintenance to the said Nardutia and Catherine by virtue of the said libel, contested therein, and by virtue of the said instrument published and written by the hand of the said Romanus and produced in judgment before you, as is premised above, protesting also that the said Nardutia and Catherine and the said Ser Valentine, their procurator, save their exceptions and rights to be produced by the said Nardutia and Catherine and by the said Ser Valentine, their procurator, at their proper place and time, and especially in the term of 8 future days by you and your court, asserting, etc. And they request all and each of the aforementioned to be done for them by you, lord podestà, and your court, in every way and by right by which you ought and are bound to do best, according to the form of the law, statute, and ordinance of the commune of Malleano. Before you, noble man Jordan of Pistionibus of the city, good man, podestà of the land of Malleano by the sacred Roman people, and your court, Nardutia and Catherine, daughters of the late Petrutius Augustinus and sisters of the late John Augustinus of the said place, without revoking their procurator, and Ser Valentine, procurator of the said Nardutia and Catherine, and in the procuratorial name of them, replicate and by replicating oppose against and adverse to Francesca, wife of the late Petrutius Augustinus, aforementioned, heir of John, son of the late said Petrutius, and against certain exceptions, if they can be so called, frivolous and not true, opposed by the said Francesca against the petition and instruments or documents produced by the said Nardutia and Catherine before you against the said Francesca, heir of the aforementioned, saying that the said exceptions do not obstruct and ought to be rejected and repelled for the following main causes and reasons. And first, because the first exception written in the order of the said exceptions does not obstruct, for the reason that it contains no truth in fact nor in law, for the reason that the petition produced by the said Nardutia and Catherine, against which the said Francesca seems to wish to oppose, is well and aptly conceived and formed, and consists especially according to the municipal law of the said land of Malleano. And for the reason that it is not true that the word 'or' is regularly alternative. And positing, but not conceding, that it were, nevertheless the said petition would not be vitiated thereby, since the aforementioned part of the petition narrated the form of the legacy. And positing that even the same were placed in the petition, nevertheless it would not obstruct, since this arises and proceeds from the nature and form of the aforementioned legacy and the obligation descending from it, in which case it is permitted to place, narrate, and request alternatively according to the laws. Nor does it obstruct that the boundaries of the house, of which mention is made in the said petition, are not set. The reason is that in the aforementioned legacy by the aforementioned John the boundaries were not expressed, and nevertheless the legacy is valid, as l. si domus, in the beginning, ff. de legatis 1. Especially since the said John, who thus made the legacy, had several houses in the said quarter. Furthermore, the second exception written in the order of the said exceptions does not obstruct, for the reason that it lacks all truth of fact and law, for the said cause begun and instituted by the said Catherine and Nardutia against the said Francesca is not ordinary, but executory, and has execution ready, since it is established by public documents of the things requested by them, and thus the said Francesca, heir of the aforementioned, ought to be compelled and constrained by you in person and goods to pay to the said Nardutia and Catherine the contents and things requested by them in the aforementioned petition by virtue of the statutes and ordinance of the land of Malleano, placed under the rubric, how a debtor is compelled, and according to the form of the aforementioned statute, the said Nardutia and Catherine request through you that the said Francesca, heir of the aforementioned, be constrained to deliver, assign, and pay to them the things requested by them in the aforementioned petition. Furthermore, the third exception written in the order of the said exceptions does not obstruct, for the reason that it lacks the truth of law. It is not doubtful in law that by the alimentary action, i.e., by him to whom alimony ought to have been provided, if it was not provided, although they did not live on air, the said alimony can sometimes be requested, sometimes the estimation of them. s. in the proposal the estimation can be requested according to the laws, as l. si usus fructus mihi biennium, ff. de usufructu legato. And such estimation, as in the proposal is requested, appears, that the said exception does not obstruct. Furthermore, the last exception written in the order of the said exceptions does not obstruct, for the reason that the narrations and contents in the aforementioned petition are true and ought to be done, nor in the aforementioned causes is there place for the exhibition of the libel nor for the contestation of the lawsuit, since they are established by public documents, and thus there is no place for the exhibition of the libel nor for the contestation of the lawsuit, but it is to be proceeded according to the form of the said statute placed under the rubric, how a debtor is compelled. Furthermore, nor do the certain exceptions appended against the public document written and under the hand of the said Ser Romanus, notary, produced by the said Nardutia and Catherine against the said lady Francesca, heir of the aforementioned, obstruct, for the reason that they contain no truth of fact nor of law. And especially the first, for the commission made to the notary to examine witnesses was made in a case in which it could be made legitimately, as the said Francesca was present and consenting, or at least not contradicting, of which commission it is legitimately and fully established even by a public instrument written by the hand of Antonius Blaxius Cola of Nepi, public notary, which instrument they now exhibit and produce before you. For the inspection of whose instrument the laws alleged to the contrary do not obstruct. Furthermore, the second exception appended against the said public document does not obstruct, for the reason that it contains no truth of fact nor of law. Since in the aforementioned causes the lawsuit ought not to be contested, as is said above, and also because even if it ought to be contested, they were examined for a sufficient and legitimate cause, for which they could be examined before the lawsuit was contested, as clearly and purely appears in the said public documents.
