Furthermore, the third exception appended against the said public document does not obstruct, for the reason that it lacks the truth of fact and law. For the said Nardutia and Catherine could not then act, for the time was a holiday, partly because of the pestilence and mortality which then was, partly also because of the harvests, and partly because of the statute of the commune of Malleano aforementioned, placed under the rubric, of holidays. And positing, but not conceding, that they could then act, nevertheless the examination and publication of the said witnesses could be made, and is held and valid by the said c. significavit, alleged and noted in it under the rubric, word monumenta. Furthermore, the fourth exception appended against the said document does not obstruct. For it contains express falsity. For the said John was of sound mind, and is presumed to have been of sound mind. Furthermore, the 5th exception written in the order of the exceptions opposed against the said document does not obstruct. For it lacks all truth, for the said witnesses prove fully and well those things for which they were induced. And positing that it was not proved that the said John was of sound mind, nevertheless since they do not prove the contrary and unsound mind, it does not obstruct that there is a presumption of sound mind according to the laws, but that is not submitted in the said exception, and from now on he is content, etc., to be altogether rejected, not to be done, for the reason that in the said cause the lawsuit ought not to be contested, as is said above often. Furthermore, the last exception written in the order of the exceptions appended against the witnesses does not obstruct, for the reason that it lacks all truth. For the said witnesses were and are suitable, and nothing could nor can be opposed against them on account of consanguinity or affinity, nor any other reason or cause that would have or would have them repelled by law, and the statements and attestations of the said witnesses by them were and are true in fact and valid in law. They oppose these by replicating, saving others, etc. The aforementioned replications were asserted and produced together with a certain instrument written and published by the hand of Ser Antonius Blaxius Cola of Nepi by Nardutia and Catherine, daughters of the late Petrutius Augustinus and sisters of John, son of the late said Petrutius Augustinus, and by Valentine, their procurator, aforementioned, and in the procuratorial name for them, before the aforementioned lord podestà sitting on the tribunal at his usual bench of law of civil causes, as is the custom, against and adverse to the aforementioned Francesca, and against certain exceptions, if they can be so called, produced by the said Francesca against the petition made and produced by the said Nardutia and Catherine before you and your court, the said Francesca present, nevertheless legitimately cited by this by the liberarius of the castle of the commune of Malleano and your court simply to her house of usual habitation by the said lord podestà and me, the notary underwritten, and thus referring. Which replications and the said public instrument the said Nardutia and Catherine and the said Ser Valentine, their procurator, request through you, lord podestà, and your court, to be admitted and to pronounce that the said Francesca ought to be compelled to give, maintain, and alimony, and habitation of the house, and both for the present and for the future, according to the form and tenor of the petition of the said Nardutia and Catherine and the document written and published by the hand of Romanus Nardolus of Calvis and produced by the said ladies on the 5th day of the present month of September. And they request the aforementioned to be done for them by virtue of the statute of the commune of Malleano placed under the rubric, how a debtor is compelled, and in every way, by right, and form by which they can best. For the lord podestà admitted the said replications and the said public instrument insofar as he is bound and ought by law, in the presence of the lady Francesca, to whom Francesca fixed a term of 8 future days to prove her rights and to contradict and oppose before you, noble man Jordan of Pistionibus, good man, podestà of the land of Malleano. Francesca, late wife of Petrutius Augustinus of Malleano, without revoking her procurators, duplicates and by duplicating opposes against certain frivolous replications opposed, although less legitimately, against true and veridical exceptions opposed on the part of the said Francesca against Nardutia and Catherine, and against their petition, of any petition, exception, replication, not obstructing the true and juridical exceptions of the said Francesca, for the following main causes and reasons. And first, the first replication does not obstruct, for it is not true in law, and less in fact. For it is certain in law that the word 'or' is alternative, as in l. si quis uxori, ff. de auro et argento. Or it is certain that an alternative word creates generality and obscurity, as in l. praetor, in §. si praetor, ff. de iniuriis. And there it is contained that an alternative libel does not proceed. And if it is said that thus it was in the obligation and with the legacy, for thus the testator made the legacy, although he made no legacy with one, since in requesting in the petition he ought to have requested what was clear. And although without prejudice it was thus in the legacy, nevertheless in the petition he ought specifically to choose and express what he requested. And it seems noted by the gloss in the said l. qui uxori. For the petition ought to be clear and similar to the thing requested, coherent, as in l. forma censualis, ff. de censu. And there by the doctors, l. si domus, in the beginning, alleged in the replication, saving the peace of the allegator, says the contrary, for although the testator had several houses, as if he had bequeathed one of his houses, although the election was of the legatee, he ought to have chosen and, having made the election, to request a certain thing and with similar coherence, as in the said l. forma. And in l. si res, ff. de re vendita. Just as the republic. Does not obstruct. And the exception is valid, fully established by Innocentius in ca. significavit, extra de libello obligatorio. The second replication does not obstruct, for it is verbose and lacks truth. Nor is every cause regularly ordinary, as in c. auth. offeratur. And because positing without prejudice that there was a statute in Malleano that the underwritten be committed to execution, that they have part of execution, nevertheless in the said cause no instruments were produced which could be so considered, and the statute speaks of the underwritten, wherefrom obligation arises on both sides, for thus it is. And therefore the aforementioned Nardutia and Catherine did not request against Francesca the exception of any instrument. But they requested her to be condemned by you, lord podestà, which would not be done when execution of an instrument was requested. For condemnation presupposes that a libel preceded and the lawsuit was contested, so that condemnation could be made, which was not done here on the part of Nardutia and Catherine. And thus the said petition does not proceed, and sentence and condemnation of the said Francesca cannot in any way be made by law, therefore, etc. The third replication is without flavor and does not proceed by law. For it is not alleged that past alimony can be requested extraordinarily, for the petitioner already had alimony. And it is not to be said that the estimation of the thing is in the obligation, but in the principal thing itself, when that which ought not to be owed in our law is owed, and l. si usus fructus and de usufructu speaks, for thus the usufruct is not found in the nature of things, and this because of the delay of the deceased, if it leads, but here it is not presupposed, for the principal thing would not be found. And that someone was dilatory and because of someone the thing was perished, and the aforementioned are proved by the noted by the doctors in l. fi, de actione empti. Therefore the replication does not proceed. The last replication proceeds. And first, because the contents in the exception of Francesca are true, and the contents in the replication are not true. And because, as is said, regularly, for every cause is ordinary: as in the said auth. offeratur. And because it is not that in the said case the statute has place, which is alleged in the replication, and it was not intended in the petition of the said Nardutia and Catherine, the said statute could not be intended, but condemnation was requested, that it be made of Francesca, and condemnation presupposes that the libel was presented and the lawsuit contested, and without the lawsuit contested, the process and sentence would be null: as noted by Innocentius extra de dolo et contumacia, c. proponit. Furthermore, the replications which are opposed against true and juridical exceptions opposed against certain writings, which the part of the lady Catherine and Nardutia say were documents and public instruments, which they are not, do not obstruct. And because it is not true that a commission can be made to a notary to examine witnesses, although it could almost be made for writing. And this is proved by Innocentius in c. cum Bertoldus, extra de re iudicata. And it is held in the laws alleged in the exception of Francesca, to which, or to any of them, no response was made, nor could be made by law. And thus the replication does not obstruct. And positing that Francesca was silent when the commission to the notary for the examination of witnesses was made, it does not follow that she consented, the letter which is silent does not necessarily confess, etc., as in c. qui tacet, extra de re iudicata, lib. 6. And there by the lord Dy. And thus such commission was not valid, as is said, as is proved by Innocentius in c. causam, de testibus. And it is not a response to the laws if it says l. non obstat, but it ought to allege why it does not obstruct. And positing without prejudice that the said writings, which are said to be underwritten on the part of Nardutia and Catherine, were public acts, nevertheless not instruments, as l. in fraudem, ff. de iure fidei commissi, there, where acts and instruments. And noted the word 'and', which is placed between diverse things, as noted by the gloss in the rubric de iure et facto ignoto. And thus the statute has no place in acts, for it speaks of the exception of an instrument, and there is a difference between acts and instruments, as says Innocentius in c. 1, extra de probationibus, circa fidem. The second replication does not proceed, and lacks the truth of law and fact, and regularly witnesses come to be examined after the lawsuit is contested and not before, and in the case in which they were examined, in the present question they could not be examined, for Nardutia and Catherine could act, and one cannot cause witnesses to be examined, but ought to act, and then after the lawsuit is contested cause them to be examined. This is the determination of Innocentius in c. significavit, extra de testibus. And if it is said that they were examined according to the form of c. quam frequenter, it is not true, and positing without prejudice that it were true, the witnesses could not be published within a year, and the podestà ought to have pronounced the time for the witnesses and that faith ought to be added to their attestation, as there by Innocentius, which was not done, therefore, etc. The third replication does not proceed. First by the allegation in the next preceding, doubly. And because one wishing to act cannot cause witnesses to be examined before the lawsuit is contested, as there determines Innocentius in the said c. significavit, to whose saying the adverse part ought to have responded, if it could, to which it could not, it is said not to be true that the writing, which is said to be public documents, that they are thus, as is said, for as is said, there is a difference between acts and instruments, of which perhaps the statute speaks. The fourth replication does not proceed, for it lacks the truth of law and fact, and because it is false that it is said that the said John, of whom mention is made in the replication, was of sound mind. And it is not true that it is denied, especially that one is of sound mind, as was in our case, that one is presumed to be of sound mind, but when it is denied, it is necessary that he who alleges that one was of sound mind prove by law that he was of sound mind, which was denied and not proved. And c. quia, as is said, he made himself such, of whom mention was made in the underwritten replication, and the documents are not. The fifth replication does not obstruct, for it lacks truth, and because of the things said in the next preceding duplication, and in others, it is not true that when it is denied that one is of sound mind, that he is presumed, but he is not presumed, but it appears by law, as is said, that it be proved. The last replication does not obstruct, for it is not natural. And because some of the said witnesses were altogether not true, for when asked if they were related to the said Catherine and Nardutia, they answered that they were not, they were related, and some of them were the husbands of the said ladies, and if husbands have affection for their wives, it is known, and thus as not true they are rightly to be repelled, those of whom mention is made in the last exception of the lady Francesca. And if relationship is denied, at least of faith, let it be seen what Bartolus terminates in l. haeres palam, de testamento. She opposes these alternatively and copulatively, as they make better for the said Francesca, saving others, etc. The aforementioned duplications were exhibited and produced on the aforementioned day and in the evening hour by the aforementioned Francesca before the lord podestà, etc., in the presence of Ser Valentine, procurator of the said Nardutia and Catherine, and requesting a copy with a term to oppose and contradict for the defense of their rights, who the lord admitted the duplications if and insofar as he is bound by law, and otherwise not. And to the said Ser Valentine he fixed a term of 8 future days to receive a copy and to oppose and contradict, etc. Before you, noble Jordan of Pistionibus of the city, good man, podestà of the land of Malleano by the sacred Roman people specially appointed, and your court, Nardutia and Catherine, daughters of the late Petrutius Augustinus and sisters of the late John of the said place, without revoking their procurator, you and Ser Valentine, procurator of the said Nardutia and Catherine, and in the procuratorial name of them, replicated and by triplicating opposed against and adverse to Francesca, wife of the late Petrutius Augustinus, heir of the late John, son of the late Petrutius, and against certain duplications, if they can be so called, frivolous and not true, oppositions by the said Nardutia and Catherine before you against the said Francesca, heir of the aforementioned, saying that the said duplications are not true in law, and less in fact, and do not obstruct for the following reasons and causes. And first, the first duplication of the duplications produced by the said Francesca does not obstruct, for it is not true in law, and less in fact, as clearly appears from the form of the replications produced by the said Nardutia and Catherine. And because the said Francesca is obliged to deliver the habitation or receptacle as heir of the said John, the testator, and in the alternative, the election is of the debtor, as l. plerunque, in the end, ff. de iure dotis. Or we can otherwise say that when two substantives are placed in narration signifying one substantive added, we will say, if those two substantives, habitation or receptacle, such exposition is by the gloss in l. 1, ff. de petitione. And thus the said libel is not alternatively conceived, although the response made in the mutation is sufficiently sufficient, which to repeat again is superfluous. And thus the first duplication does not obstruct. Secondly, the second duplication does not obstruct, for it is not true in law, and less in fact, and lacks altogether all truth. For by common law and by municipal law there are many summary proceedings, as is read and noted in c. saepe contingit, de verbis significandis, in the cle. And l. Thesaurus, ff. ad exhibendum, as noted by Bartolus in the constitution ad reprimendum, in the 11th column. Therefore it is not true that every cause is ordinary, as the second duplication says. Nor is it true that which is said in it, that the statute of the land of Malleano is to be understood of those from which obligation arises on both sides, for that statute would have place in an instrument of loan and in an instrument of deposit, and of similar things, in which only he who receives the loan is obliged, and only he who receives the deposit is obliged. For if the said duplication were true, the said statute would not have place in the said contracts, which to say is to dream in Parnassus. And in entering upon the inheritance as heir, obligation is contracted, therefore the said statute has place, since the heir is debtor to the legatee, therefore without contradiction execution ought to be made against the said Francesca, although by the second replication it is sufficiently shown. The third duplication does not obstruct, as was clearly and lucidly responded in the third replication on the part of the said Nardutia and Catherine, rightly understanding, which I do not repeat here. And thus the said duplication is rather dreaming than explaining that law, which speaks clearly, and it is sufficient that the heir is in delay if he does not provide that which is left by the testator, for he incurs a penalty, for heirs ought to provide, as in Auth. de haereditate et fideicommissis, §. si quis autem implens. Therefore the third duplication does not proceed. Furthermore, the replication which begins, 'last replication,' does not obstruct, as was responded above in the second triplication, which I do not repeat here. And that noted by Innocentius in c. proposuit, extra de dolo et contumacia, has place when the cause is ordinary, as noted by the doctors in l. prolatam, C. de sententiis. But this cause by the form of the statute is not ordinary, therefore the said Innocentius is alleged in vain. Furthermore, that duplication which says, 'Furthermore, the replication does not obstruct,' does not obstruct, for it has already been responded to by the replications, as it ought to be examined at the time of allegations, it might rightly be said that he who wrote had the will of occupying paper. Furthermore, another duplication which begins, 'second replication,' which is the 6th in order, does not obstruct. For we could always versate in the same speech, that witnesses are to be examined before the lawsuit is contested, to which it was sufficiently responded by the replication, for these are sufficiently declared by cap. quoniam frequenter, extra ut lite non contestata, often alleged. For these are rather allegations than duplications. And whether it was a case of examining witnesses, it is sufficiently clear to barbers and tonsors, when men did not come from one day to another. Furthermore, another duplication which begins, 'third replication,' which is the seventh in order, does not obstruct, for it is not true in law, and less in fact, as was shown above in the second triplication. Furthermore, another duplication which begins, 'fourth replication,' which is the eighth in order, does not obstruct, for it is not true in law, and less in fact, since the said John was of sound mind at the time of the making of the testament, as is sufficiently clearly shown in the replication. For the burden of proving that he was not of sound mind lies upon him who says so, since the said John was always of sound mind. Therefore one is presumed to be in that state in which he was, if it is not proved that he changed. Furthermore, another duplication which begins, 'fifth replication,' does not obstruct, for it is not true in law, and less in fact, and by law everyone is presumed to be of sound mind, unless the contrary is proved, as was sufficiently clearly responded in the replication. Furthermore, the last replication, which begins, 'last, etc.,' does not obstruct, for it is not true in law, and less in fact. For the witnesses examined most clearly prove that for which they were induced to prove. And although it is said that relatives are of no account, for what laws prohibit relatives from not being witnesses in a testament? Certainly none, as is read and noted in l. parentes, C. de testibus. Therefore, not obstructing the said publication, it is to be proceeded to the execution requested on the part of the said Nardutia and Catherine. In a legacy of alimony for the life of someone, this is to be held according to the gloss in l. 4, de annuis legatis.

† that which is public for the first year is conditional for the subsequent years, to the same effect: ff. when the day of a legacy vests, l. si cum praefinitione; and ff. concerning annual legacies, l. a vobis.

† And regarding conditional or future-dated matters, witnesses may be received for perpetual memory and published, as noted in the Authenticum *Si quis ab aliquo*, Codex, *De testamento*; in the Authenticum *De testamento*, § *Penultimus*, Digest, *De testamento*; *L. Curent*, Digest, *Ad legem Aquiliam*; *L. In legem Aquilianam suum dilatum*, Codex, *De usuris*; *L. Pupilla*; *L. Pupillus*, Extra, *De testamento*; *C. Significavit*; and *C. Albericus*. It is established by what is noted in the Codex, *De testibus*, *L. Publicati*; *L. Gesta*, *De re iudicata*. And therefore one step is expedited. However, this would be true regarding publication only if the reception of the witnesses had been valid.

But it seems that they did not hold, because they were not received by the judge, but by the notary. But to this it must be said that the notary, by virtue of his office as a scribe, that is, by his own authority, cannot receive witnesses, as is noted in C. de test. l. hac consul. §. penulti. But with the commission of the judge, he can in a civil case, especially with the express or tacit consent of the party, as is fully noted in C. de fid. instru. Auth. apud eloquentissimum. and de proba. c. quoniam contra falsam. and noted in c. 1. de offic. de le. in the Clementines. And the party who was present, if he remained silent, is understood to have consented, as in ff. de fideicom. tu. l. cum ostendendus. §. fi. C. de rela. l. i. quando appellam. sit. l. fi. ff. ad Mace. l. filius. ff. rem ra. ha. l. quo enim. §. 1. quando appellatum sit. l. fi.

† Moreover, this commission has the force of an interlocutory decision; hence, if it displeased him, he ought to have appealed, according to l. 1, si sepius, in the interpretation: resti. postuletur. And another passage is expedited concerning the commission and reception.

It remains to be considered regarding the claim for alimony for the past period. It is said that he has already lived; therefore, he does not claim what has already passed. But certainly, the debtor of alimony is not thereby released from his obligation because the person entitled to alimony has lived off other resources, as stated in the Digest, *De alimentis legatis*, law *Libertis quos*, § 1, where it reads: "both for the past and for the future time." There is the text in the Code, *De fideicommissis*, law 1, and another passage is declared.

It remains to be seen whether this case is summary, considering that the statements of the witnesses have been recorded in public records. And it appears that it is so, according to the ordinary gloss on the Code, *De edicto divi Adriani*, in the law *Edicto*.

† He states that from such attestations there arises a *missio* under that edict, and that the procedure is summary, as he proceeds to argue below. To the contrary is the ordinary gloss, which holds that from the statements of witnesses no action arises, nor execution. D. 12.2.1 (*Sed et si possessori*), § *pen.*; and this is not found elsewhere in the law. This is the truth: this case is not summary, but ordinary, because this new instance requires the usual order. C. 4.20.1 (*Si*). Moreover, the purpose of such an examination is not that an action be derived therefrom, or that its effect be increased, but solely so that the means of proof may not be lost through fortuitous events, as Innocentius noted in the aforementioned chapter. And another step is expedited. Nevertheless, I do not deny that the libel can sufficiently stand, provided that one proceeds juridically upon it, just as a judgment is valid in which it is declared that something is due. D. 4.8.1 (*Quid tamen*), § *Si arbiter*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a legatee who is called upon, and is not a mere minister, is bound to satisfy the legacy unless after two years.
body: Because the aforementioned

† Actus was called by name and acted as a legatee, and not as a mere minister; he transmitted the said legacy with the burden, namely, of sale and satisfaction of the legacies, as in the Digest, *De alimentis et cibariis legatis*, law *Cum onus*, in the beginning. And he is not bound to satisfy [the legacies] until after two years, according to the form of the testament, Digest, *De legatis primo*, law *Talis scriptura*. And the fruits in the meantime are [his], Digest, *Ad Trebellianam*, law *Mulier*, section *Si heres*. And beyond what is relegated, that which remains is freely theirs, namely, the action for the inheritance, Digest, *Mandati*, law *Si mandauero tibi*, section *Si tibi*.

But concerning that which Actus placed in secret regarding that residue, it must be known whether it is lawful and can be proved, law *Theopompus*, *De dote praelegata*; Digest, *De rebus dubiis*, law *Quem heredi*. I understand this to apply when it is for the soul; otherwise, it is different, as in law *Captatorias*, *De hereditatibus institutis*, and Extravagant, *De testibus*, chapter *Cum tibi*. Others say indiscriminately that this disposition is captatory and is not valid, nor is the heir bound to abide by the statement of the executors regarding this secret, unless they testify as witnesses, which is the more correct opinion, following the statement of Cynus and Ricardus, namely, that it is valid if it is proved that the testator spoke the truth; otherwise, it is not. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an oath is valid when the form prescribed by the statute has not been observed in the refutation.
2. Whether a municipal judge may remit an oath and impose a penalty.
3. A statute cannot make it lawful to commit perjury.
body: Having seen the statute placed under the rubric concerning alienations made by a minor, and having seen the first refutation made by the said Francis Bellezano to his father on the 14th day of the month of September 1483, and having seen the second refutation made by the said lady Francis to the same lord father on the 19th day of the month of November of the same year, it seems to me, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws.

† that, because the form of the said statute was not observed, the said refutations were invalid, nor could they be confirmed by the oath of the said minor. And this for several reasons. First, on account of the form not being observed. D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi. §. si praetor. Second, on account of presumed fraud. C. de in integrum restitutione minorum, l. de tutela. Third, on account of the deficiency of cause. For the last refutation contains a false cause, and this appears upon examination of the first refutation, and its cause, and the amount of the dowry. D. de exceptione doli, l. 2. §. diuersum. Fifth, on account of excessive reverence. l. 1. §. quae onerandae. quarum rerum actio non datur. in the gloss, ordi.

Sixthly, the power of the municipal law can condemn a statute and remit an oath, just as the Apostolic See can, as noted in *l. adigere*, § *fi*, *de iure patronatus*. Seventhly, because where the law repudiates an oath, it is not valid, *de legibus*, *l. quis inquilinos*, § *fi*. Eighthly, because it is lawful for municipal law to feign and to induce a presumption of law, as in *l. omnes populi*, *de iustitia et iure*, and in the matter of the law *siue possideat*, C. *de probatibus*. Ninthly, by the general rule of the law *non dubium*, at the end, C. *de legibus*. Tenthly, by another rule, because an oath was not invented to be a bond of iniquity, as in *Authentica sacramenta*; and therefore *Authentica sacramenta* excepts force and fear. And this is confirmed by the note of Bartolus, ff. *de fideiussoribus*, *l. si quis pro eo*. And even if it were assumed that the oath were binding, it ought to be relaxed by the bishop, as is fully read and noted in 15 q. 6, c. *authoritatem*. And fraud may be proved by the authority of the statute. For presumptions of law are equivalent to the clearest proofs, ff. *de legibus*, *l. licet*, in the beginning, and noted in *l. si tutor*, *de periculo tutoris*. And I say this presupposing that the contract is presumed to have been made with fraud before the cause of the contract, and as the aforementioned statute speaks, to which statute, and its fiction and disposition, I say that one must adhere. Although it is safer to seek absolution,
† because a statute cannot make it lawful to commit perjury: for this would be contrary to divine law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A person to whom alimony has been bequeathed in a house cannot claim it outside the house, unless he is prevented from remaining in the house due to cruelty and the conduct of the heirs.
2. The meaning of the word "cum" (when/with).
3. Whether a daughter, to whom a legacy was made in a nuncupative will, can allege ignorance, and whether she is to be believed.
body:
The case is as follows: A certain Simon Nerii, in the year of our Lord 1387, in the month of July, made his will, in which he disposed, among other things, in this manner, namely: Furthermore, he wished, commanded, and ordered that if any, or one, or all of his daughters, whether married or to be married, should remain widows, that they have and ought to have, in the event of their widowhood and that of each of them, the income and habitation of one of the testator’s properties, in which he currently resides, from the heirs, as well as food and clothing with the heirs and from the heirs of the said testator, suitably according to the means of the testator and his heirs. And he instituted as his heirs Sandinus, Nerius, and certain other sons of his. Afterwards, the said testator died. Afterwards, Lady Agostantia, one of the daughters of the said testator, remained a widow; it is now thirty years and more, and she did not dwell with the heirs of the said testator, nor in his house, nor with them, except that now she has demanded something from the said alleged legacy, alleging that she was ignorant that the aforementioned legacy had been made for her. It is asked whether, at present, for the past time, she can demand and ought to receive from the heirs, or from the inheritance of the late Simon, the said legacy, and what is the law regarding the said legacy.

Furthermore, Sandinus, son of the said late Simon Nerii, in the year of our Lord 1366, in the month of May, also made his will, in which, among other things which he disposed, he left by way of legacy to the said Lady Agostantia, and to Guerriera and Elisabetta, his sisters and daughters of the said late Simon, for the whole time of their lives, and to each of them, the usufruct of certain goods and of a certain house for the whole time of their lives; and after their death, he wished it to come and to pass to his heirs. And the said Sandinus died; it is now twelve years and more, and afterwards the aforementioned Guerriera and Elisabetta died, the said Lady Agostantia surviving, and no caution was ever provided by them, or any of them, to use the said goods according to the discretion of a good man, nor was any other caution provided. It is asked whether the said Lady Agostantia can demand the said legacy, and if she can, what, and how much, and for what period of time.

In the counsel of Master Bartolus, namely in counsel 71, which begins “quidam sibi filios,” it is contained literally as follows:

Whether he to whom alimony has been bequeathed in the house can demand it outside the house. And it seems that he can demand it outside the house, for the favor of the legatee is presumed in case of doubt; thus it is noted by Dynus on the rule of law *Imputari*, and in the Code, on legacies, law 1, by the gloss and doctors; on annual legacies, law *Annua*, with similar provisions in the beginning; and law *Seiae* in the beginning, in the Code, on institutions and substitutions, law 1. Since therefore it is added in favor of the legatee, he is not compelled to observe it, according to the law *Titio centum* in the beginning, on conditions and demonstrations.

On the contrary, it seems that this also regards the favor of the heir, who more easily and with less expense provides alimony in his own house than outside the house, as the evident facts teach. And therefore, concluding, I say that he cannot demand alimony outside the house if he can conveniently reside in the house. Otherwise, if he were hindered by the act or severity of the heirs. This is expressly proven in law *Qui concubinam*, section *Uxori*, on legacies; 3, on administration, law *Meuvia* in the beginning and section 1, on alimony and food bequeathed; law 4, section final, from the contrary sense.

The contrary opinions do not stand, because I say that in doubt I understand it in favor of both the legatees and the heir, and thus in favor of both. And therefore, if the legatee is hindered, as I said, he can demand that it be provided to him outside the heir’s house, according to the cited laws. These are the words of Bartolus, faithfully transcribed word for word. He holds the same opinion in the aforementioned law 4, on alimony bequeathed. And he also adds that another favor of the heirs lies in the fact that they provide marital or convivial services in taking care of and attending to the household.

This counsel being presupposed as true, because it is merely to say that he is to be fed with the heir, that is, among the heirs, in their house and family, it clearly appears that the said legacy of the said Lady Agostanzia, if she knew of the said testament, is not due.

† And the word "with" here joins together those who dine together, or are to dine and live together. C. communia utriusque iudicii, l. patronum. And this is in accordance with the intention and the words of the testator, and especially by what he says about the return.

It remains to inquire, since the said lady alleges ignorance, what is the law? And first it must be seen whether the said lady obtained anything from the will itself. For by reason of a part, the whole is presumed to be known, D. de transactionibus, l. non est ferendus. Moreover, it is not credible that a daughter would be ignorant of a nuncupative will, especially one publicly known, as in l. de tutela, D. de in integrum restitutione minorum, and l. Octavi, D. unde cognati. Furthermore, if she is ignorant, it is gross and supine ignorance. For she ought to have inquired and investigated, and since it then concerns a gain to be obtained, let her impute it to herself if she did not exercise common and ordinary diligence, D. de iuris et facti ignorantia, l. Respublica. Therefore, I conclude against her that she cannot bring an action, without prejudice to the sounder judgment. As for the word "cum," it is not expedient to allege it, because there are innumerable laws, and it has as many meanings as aspects. And it is supported by D. quibus ex causis maiores, l. si quis Titio, in ratione sui.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the equipment and implements of a farm pass under a legacy of the usufruct of the farm.
2. What are called the implements and equipment of a farm. If the testator bequeaths the use and convenience of all movable goods, of the holdings of the massarii, and of the harness existing in the house, what passes under such a legacy. Also, whether the word "existing" refers to the time of death or to the time of making the will.
3. Whether a species restricts a genus.
body: He who bequeaths

† the usufruct of a field, or bequeaths the power of using the equipment and the instrumentum of the field, ff. de vsufru. l. sed et si quid. §. proprietatis, and there noted in the ordinary gloss, prudently cited by the other party alleging it. And the same holds in another disposition which looks to the use of the thing, not to the ownership, ff. loca. l. sed addes. §. aliud nobis. Nevertheless, the usufructuary must give security for returning their appraised value, l. j. et 2.; and this concerning the first point, and concerning the instrumentum and equipment.

† What, however, if the instrumentum and equipment of the field? The text speaks in l. quaesitum. de fund. inst. in prin. and through many paragraphs; and thus there come the instruments of the estate which were for the sake of the estate, not on the estate just as on the estate, provided they were for the work of the estate, ff. de fun. instr. l. cum quidam duos, and the example is clear there.

† I come to the other conclusion, which states that under a bequest made thus: "I bequeath the use and enjoyment of all and singular movable goods and household goods (massaritiae) and furnishings (arnesia) existing in the house," there is contained the usufruct and enjoyment not only of household furniture, which we commonly call massaritiae, and of arnesia—which word must be understood according to the usage of speech of that region—but also of all certain movables.

† Outside the aforesaid, doubt may be raised here because when a species follows a genus, the species then restricts that genus; otherwise if it precedes it, as noted in c. generi. de reg. iu. and l. quaesitum. §. pe. de fun. inst. de leg. 3. l. haeres meus. §. duae statuae. ff. de verb. sig. l. si cum fundum. de leg. 2. l. legatorum. §. fi. Nevertheless, I believe it is to be understood of all things, as in ff. de penu leg. l. fin. ff. de suppel. l. legatum suppellectili. in prin. In this legacy, however, all things come, with the exception of those which were brought in without the knowledge of the testator, ff. de leg. 2. l. cum ita; and with the exception of those which the testator had assigned elsewhere, de haere. instit. l. ex facto. §. reum. ff. de pign. l. debitor; with the exception of merchandise for sale, de vsufruc. leg. l. generali. §. vxori. Debts (nomina debitorum) also, because they are not circumscribed by place, do not come, de leg. 2. l. Gayus. in princ. Moreover, that participle "existing," which can be understood as of the time of the testament or of the death, is understood in doubt as of the time of the testament, so that the intention of the testator may fall upon something certain; this is supported by what is noted by Petrus and Cynus, C. de ser. l. non modus, and l. fi. quae res pig. obl. pos. Nor does l. Lucius. de fun. instr. stand in the way, because there it concerns a universal legacy, here a general legacy; supported by de au. et arg. l. si ita, with its subject matter. Security, however, about which I spoke above, must always be provided.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a promise of identity for a delict is valid or not, and if so, when.
body: When

† If indemnity is promised for a delict to be committed, the promise is invalid. D. de fideiuss. l. si a reo. §. quod vulgo. Lest anyone be induced to commit a wrong. But if the wrong had been committed through fault and not through dolus, because the disciple believed his preceptor, then the promise of indemnity is valid. For one can bind himself to a penalty committed by another, as D. pro socio l. si igitur. This seems contrary to the text in l. 2. §. plagii. D. de verb. oblig. where a promise for a wrong already done is invalid, just as for one to be done. But there it speaks where dolus intervenes, because it speaks of plagium; here, however, this disciple was simply led by his master, believed him, and was obedient. Hence, although he ought not to have believed, he nevertheless fell into fault, not into dolus, l. seruos. C. ad l. Iul. de vi publica. And therefore he did not wrong from intent, but that master wronged from intent. And he confessed this there, when he said, I know well that I am bound to pay, and not you, etc. To this effect is what is read and noted D. de rei vend. l. in rem. §. tignum. If, therefore, this one was in fault, he fell into it through the dolus of the master, being circumvented by him, and therefore the promise was not for a turpis causa.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Who is said to be an accomplice in crime, and in what manner, and how an accomplice in crime is punished, or not.
body: It must be considered

† that someone accompanies another in many ways: for sometimes he accompanies him before the crime to perpetrate or arrange it; sometimes at the crime and in the very act of the crime to perpetrate it; sometimes after the crime to continue the crime; sometimes after the crime for the delinquent to escape or to rescue him. And these four cases are punishable, as is clear from what is fully read and noted in c. 1 de poe. in Cle. However, none of these cases is alleged here, but two entirely different things are alleged, namely, the visit to the house of the aforesaid Master Franciscus, and the accompaniment to bring back the sheep to the sheepfold, that is, that poor woman to her monastery. But the visit and the stay, because they do not touch the crime in question, since they are not directed to any other act proceeded with by the person investigated, do not import guilt in the crime, and consequently neither in punishment. Just as if someone shares food and drink with an excommunicated person, he does not on that account incur the major excommunication, nor is he punished criminally, since he is not a partner in the crime. In this way also, certain persons can be partners, and if they are not partners in the crime, the delinquent alone is punished, ff. pro so. l. cum duob. §. fi. et l. seq. But nevertheless, partnership in crimes is punishable, ff. de fidei. l. si a reo. §. quod vulgo. But in our case neither the partnership nor the sharing was criminal in the house or at the table; moreover, the accompaniment to bring back that nun to the cloister was not faulty in itself, C. de insti. l. reprehendenda. versi. redde igitur ad maritum tuum; just as counsel is lawful, so aid and favor are lawful, as noted by Inn. in c. solet. de sen. exc. Wherefore, according to what is put forward, the law raptores, C. de epis. et cle. and l. 1 de rap. vir. are not to the point, nor under those chapters can that person investigated be punished, whether we consider the common law or municipal laws speaking of criminal jurisdiction to the ultimate penalties, and from like to like, because between a delinquent and a non-delinquent there is no similarity, since similarity is nothing other than the same quality in multiple delicts or facts, ff. vi bo. rap. l. 2. §. homines. at the word ad hoc. Likewise, this person investigated, having been questioned as to why, where he had been, and what he had done, ff. de re mili. l. qui cum vno. §. fi., answered everything without any mark of crime: for as to why, he answered that he had been there because he had been invited to dinner, for it is lawful to dine even with publicans and sinners; as to where, he answered in the house of Master Franciscus; as to what he did, he said that he accompanied her to bring her back to the due place. Nor does that response harm him, because he was not an accomplice to another's wickedness, since he did not consent to the wickedness—that is, he neither brought aid, nor counsel, nor favor to the wickedness, but gave his effort to a lawful escorting. And because he did none of those things that are subject to punishment, ff. de adul. l. qui domum. et l. si amicis. and de min. l. auxilium. §. in delictis., he is deservedly not punished, as read and noted in ff. de re. iu. l. culpa caret. and Extra de rest. spo. c. cum ad sedem. and ff. de fur. aduersus nau. l. 1. §. fi.; and because, being ignorant of the beginning, he joined them, and this is supported by ff. de adul. l. mariti lenocinium. in prin., ff. de abig. l. 1. in fi., C. de plagia. l. plagii quidem., C. de tab. l. generali.; whence his approach was not deceitful, nor his departure villainous, nor was anything attempted immodestly by the said person investigated.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a testator, if in his first will he instituted Titius as heir and in it stated that he owed him a certain sum, and later revoked the will, the confession contained therein remains valid and an action can be brought on its basis.
body: In a certain testament of a certain Simon, it is contained as follows. Moreover, he left by right of restitution to John of Puti, asserting that he was bound to him, if Fiordelisa, his daughter, should die within the present age of 25 years, and the said John receiving four hundred pounds of denarii; then the testament was changed,

† It is asked whether, from the said confession, a claim or proof can be founded, such that the said revocation of the said testament does not prejudice the said John. This question is sufficiently common and well-known, and it is evident from the words of Cynus in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. generaliter. Some say that such a writing proves; others say that it neither proves nor obligates. The former base their argument on l. publica, §. fin., ff. de depositi; the latter base theirs on the fact that in a last will one can pass to a contract, and irrevocably, as noted in l. haeredes palam, §. fin. A third group bases their argument on l. Aurelius, §. fin., de liberatione legata. However, those holding the first or second opinion respond that in l. Aurelius, the party did not participate in that confession, whereas here they did, so that in this case it may be valid as a donation inter vivos, as it seems from the ordinary gloss in ff. de donationibus, l. ex hac scriptura. But against this it seems to be argued, because this confession is indiscriminate, since it did not express the cause why he is bound. Hence, even in a true contract, it is not valid as being informal, l. cum de indebito, §. fin., de probationibus. But to this it can be responded, because rather it was made with a cause, although the cause is not expressed, because he said he was bound, and added, on account of, or by right of restitution, ff. de legibus, l. cum pater, §. fidei suae committo uxori. This question could be reduced to the matter of the second law, §. circa, de exceptione doli, namely that it is a donation inter vivos, at least between closely related persons, and therefore cannot be revoked. This seems to be the opinion of Bartolus in l. cum quis decedens, §. codicillis, de legatis tertio, where he treats this matter fully and beautifully. And there he did not cite the gloss of the said law ex hac scriptura; but in the said l. ex hac scriptura, Bartolus holds that if the father was present, a donation inter vivos is presumed. But that law speaks when the testator made mention of a donation, which is threefold, as noted in l. legatum, C. de legibus, libro secundo. And in the stronger sense it is understood as a donation inter vivos. Here, however, he made mention not of a donation, but of restitution. But to this it is responded by l. si divortio, de verbis obligatis. I believe it cannot be revoked, because a cause is inserted. For being obliged to restore is a cause, although the cause of the cause is not specified. Or perhaps, especially if these indications occur, as in extra de successionibus ab intestato, c. cum dilectus, unless it were proven that the testator erred or was circumvented in this confession, as noted in C. de iuris et facti ignorantia, l. cum testamentum. Given the aforementioned, if the condition, and if, not always, but often, is taken in place of a cause, ff. de verbis obligatis, l. a Titio, and l. si intra, de pactis.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When several tutors are appointed in a will, among whom is the mother, who wishes to enter into a second marriage, is she required to petition the judge for a tutor to be appointed in her place?
2. Whether the judge is bound to appoint the one whom the mother requests, or whether it suffices for him to appoint a suitable person.
body: The point of the question, on which legal opinion is sought, is as follows. A certain man named Bartoluccio Cola of Ancona, having made a will, in which by right of institution he left to each of his said daughters dowries of 600 gold florins, and instituted the womb of his wife as his universal heir, if she should bear a male child. Finally, to his said daughters and to the posthumous child, he left as guardians a certain man named Marchione Nicola, Filippo Nutii, and Lady Margherita, his wife. And the said testator willed that the said Lady Margherita, together with one of the said guardians, should act and administer. After the aforesaid, the said testator died, with his said daughters, who were minors, and the said guardians surviving him. Finally, one of the said guardians died, with the said Marchione and Lady Margherita surviving him, who acknowledged and accepted the guardianship of the said daughters, and formally, as required by the order of law and the statute of the commune of Ancona. And subsequently they administered the goods of the said minors and involved themselves therein in good faith. Finally, the said Lady Margherita, being over the age of 25, testamentary guardian, as above, wishing to enter into a second marriage, petitioned before the ordinary judge of the commune of Ancona that a certain man named Francesco be given and decreed as guardian to her said daughters, or to one of them, who today survives at the age of one and a half years. On the other side it is said, explained, and narrated by the said Marchione, one of the said guardians, that the said Peter, named as guardian by the said Lady Margherita, nor any other, ought to be given while she survives and administers the guardianship, and wishes to administer it; since a testamentary guardian by law excludes any other legitimate or appointed guardian. From the aforesaid it is asked: whether, while the said Marchione, testamentary guardian, exists and administers the said guardianship thus lawfully and in good faith, a co-guardian ought to be given, or not. Secondly, if a co-guardian is to be given, whether the judge is obliged to give the one whom the said mother named for herself and requested to be given, or whether the judge may give another, not following the mother’s will in giving the said co-guardian, if there are several testamentary guardians, among whom is the mother, who intends to enter into a second marriage.

† First, it must be considered whether the mother is bound to request a tutor in the ordinary manner upon withdrawing from the guardianship. And it appears that she is, as in Auth. de nupt. §. si autem tutela; and C. ad Tertul. l. omnem; and C. in quibus causis pignus tacite contrahitur, l. si matre; and ff. ad Tertul. l. 2, §. quid ergo si non fuerit. For since it is the intention of the testator that the guardianship be administered by several persons, another must be substituted in the place of the one who fails, ff. de testamentaria tutela, l. si quis sub conditio, §. plane; C. qui pet. tutores, l. in locum Solu. aut ceteri. Or, if the others who remain are sufficient for the administration of the wardship, the mother is not bound by necessity to request that another be substituted, but she ought to notify the judge that she wishes to enter into a second marriage, and renounce the guardianship in the hands of the judge, and render an account of the administration to the co-guardian. Thus is understood what is noted in C. de testament. tute. l. 1, in the very notable gloss ordinaria; and in the aforementioned §. quid ergo; and this by l. credendum, ff. qui pet. tuto., there: “because the number…” But if the survivors are not sufficient for the administration, then she is bound to request another in her place and have him appointed. And thus are the laws cited for this part understood.

Secondly, it is asked, when the mother is bound to petition, or petitions voluntarily, whether the judge is compelled to grant the one whom the mother petitions, and whether in the aforementioned law *Si quis sub conditione* it is held that this is so. And it seems expressly stated in the aforementioned section *Si autem tutelam*, and noted in the Code, *Quando mulier officio tutelae fungi potest*, by Anthonius in *Sacramentum*. To the contrary, it seems that the judge is not bound to grant this one, but ought to grant a suitable one according to the judge’s discretion. The aforementioned law *Credendum*. And thus holds Cynus in Anthonius, *Matri et aviae*, Code, *Quando mulier tutelae officio fungi potest*, and Jacobus de Arena and Bartolus in the aforementioned law *Si quis sub conditione*. Let us therefore suppose that the judge, not following the mother’s petition, appointed another; therefore, the mother did not fulfill what she ought to have done, because she did not have another appointed, and thus she will be deprived of succession. Digest, *Ad Tertullianum*, law 2, section *Igitur si forte*. Also, because the laws say that the mother causes [a tutor] to be appointed. But how will she cause [him] to be appointed, if it is permitted to the judge not to appoint, if a tutor is given against the mother’s will? Law *Unica*. To the same effect is what is noted in the Institutes, *De curatellis*, section *Interdum*. The solution depends on the first question. For whether another, or others, suffice for the administration, and then it is in the judge’s discretion, or not. And then either the mother petitions for a suitable one, and the one petitioned by the mother must be granted, and not another; or he is not suitable, and then another must be granted. Digest, *Ad Tertullianum*, law 2, section *Non solum*; Digest, *De ventre in possessionem missa*, law 1, section *Elegatur*; Code, *Quibus causis tutorem habenti*, law 1. And thus it must be held regarding this matter. The statute of Ancona, however, can sufficiently be understood in this article according to the common law, because it refers to it, when it says “under legal pacts.”

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether daughters, who are not admitted to succession by statute, constitute a portion for the son succeeding in the legitime.
body: The statute provides that daughters are bound to observe the father's testament when male sons survive, and because a male was here instituted as universal heir, the female daughters do not exist as universal heirs to the father.

But it must be considered whether they make a part for the son in the legitime. For there are five females and one male. For if they make a part, the son’s legitime would be a third, as in the Authentica *De triente et semisse*, in the beginning, column 3. On this point, however, a distinction must be made: either the daughters, who are found to be excluded by universal law, have something which, by its nature, is imputed to the legitime—for example, because they have been dowered by the father whose succession is in question. For dowry is imputed to the legitime, and then they make a part for the male son, because they are admitted to a part, i.e., to the dowry, which succeeds in place of the legitime portion, as in C. *De inofficioso testamento*, l. *Quoniam*, Novella. Or they have something which, by its nature, is not imputed to the legitime, or they are excluded by statute even though they have nothing: then they do not make a part according to one opinion, l. 1, in fine, ff. *De contrahenda tutela*, gloss. *Sic dicit statutum*. Thus, the statute says that a daughter dowered by the mother shall not succeed to the father in anything, and the father dies, and the father’s succession is discussed. These incapable daughters do not make up the number, and therefore the male, as the sole successor, will have a third for his legitime. And this is not by right of accretion, because then he would have a half for his legitime, and the number of children would be more than four. He therefore then has a third, as if the females were not in the nature of things. Not that the portion accretes, because there is no such portion, since the law does not grant them anything. Of this it is touched upon in Accursius, ff. *De legatis* 1, l. *Plane*, § *Si duobus*. In the case of our question, however, because the succession of the father is discussed, and the daughters were dowered and instituted by the father in a certain quantity, they make a part for the male son, whence his legitime is one-twelfth only: because there are five daughters and one son. But the Trebellianic fourth of the universal institution, and thus he will have one ounce for his legitime from what remains after the legitime portions of the said daughters, and from that said ounce he will have a fourth, and the mother, instituted by him, has those institutions. The remainder pertains to restitution on account of the fideicommissum, as appears in the testament of the father.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the house of a neighbor is consumed by fire arising in my house, whether I am bound to make reparation for the damage and loss.
2. In doubt whether fault or accident is presumed in a fire that has arisen.
body: The point on which legal advice is sought is as follows. A certain man named Restorus de Corbonio, who owned a house near the house of Matthew Pauli, through slight negligence on the part of the said Restorus, his house was burned down, and the fire grew so much that the neighboring house, and that of the said Matthew Pauli, was likewise burned down, from which burning the said Matthew suffered great damages. Now it is asked whether, according to law, the said Restorus is bound to restore to Matthew the damages and interest for the house and things burned. On this point it must be said thus,

† That a fire sometimes arises by chance without any other fault, and affliction should not be added to the afflicted. Hence, from such a fire, one is not bound to another. D. 16.3.12 (Cum duobus). Damna fatalia, and in this case the neighbor, whose house is burned or demolished on account of the fire, cannot bring an action. D. 9.2.27.1 (Si quis fumo). Quod dicitur. And D. 43.29.1 (Si alius). Est et alia. And there by Bartolus expressly. No. However, Jacobus de Belvisio said that when one house is demolished for the safety of the whole neighborhood, so that the fire does not consume everything, that contribution is to be made to this damage by all the neighbors, just as in the case of jettison of goods for the saving of the ship, l. 2, D. 14.2.1 (Ad legem Rhodiam de iactura). And he speaks of demolition, not of burning. And both of these say what is true. Sometimes a fire arises from fault, and then either it is the fault of a certain person, or of an uncertain person. If indeed from the fault of a certain person, he is bound to repair the damage of the burning: because fault even in one’s own thing, preceding the accident in another’s thing, is accustomed to bind, as D. 9.2.1 (Qui occidit). In hac. And D. 9.2.27.1 (Si servus servum). Si quis insulam. Because the act of one should not draw others into danger, D. 9.2.27.1 (Si sornicarius). And there noted. But if the fault of a certain person cannot be discovered, the owner of the first house burned is not bound: because the act of a certain person must be proved, D. 14.2.12 (Licet). Si nau. cau. sta. Since this action, on the part of the plaintiff, contains a mere penalty. In doubt, however, those are presumed to have made the fire who are accustomed to make fire there, and from them the truth about culpable fault should be inquired. D. 19.2.1 (Domus horreorum).

† But whether, in case of doubt, fault or accident should be presumed in the event of a fire arising. For usually, as a rule, it is due to fault, as in l. 3, ff. de officiis praefecti vigilum, and ff. de periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. si vendita. It may be said that if it is not established by any judgment who set the fire, and the owner was accustomed to be watchful and diligent, the owner is not liable in case of doubt, as in ff. de re militari, l. non omnes; §. a barbaris, ff. commodati, l. argentum. Otherwise, if he was a man of little circumspection, or if it is established that he himself made the fire, he is liable, ff. locati, l. si quis fundum, §. si colonus. For he ought to have been diligent in himself and in his household, ff. ad legem Aquiliam, l. si servus servum, §. proculus; ff. furti adversus nautas, l. 1, §. extraneorum. Nor does he answer for the act, nor for the accident of the winds, if on account of the force of the winds the fire burned more than usual, d. §. in hac; facit de incendio ruinae naufragii, l. qui edes, §. si vero, with its material; and Codex ad legem Aquiliam, l. 2; and Institutes ad legem Aquiliam, §. capite tertio. And therefore, if the fire arose from the quality or quantity of the fire, which is presumed from the place by the effect, and the owner or tenant did not exercise the diligence that careful men are said to exercise, he is liable for this damage given by reason of fault. But if this happened by chance and misfortune, he is not liable. In case of doubt, however, if his own act or fault is established, because perhaps he kept children there who set the fire, he is liable; otherwise, he is not.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How the children of the first marriage succeed together with the children of the second marriage in the dowry of the mother.
2. An infant transmits an inheritance not yet accepted.
body: The point on which the opinion is sought is as follows. A certain woman named Margatita had

First, a man, from whom she had one son and two daughters. After the death of her first husband, the said Margaret married John as her second husband, from whom she had two daughters. Later, the said Margaret died intestate, survived by the said children, and the two daughters from her first husband, and the said two daughters from her second husband. After this, one of the said two daughters of the second husband died within six years of her age, survived by her said father, the second husband, and her said sister, related to her on both sides, as well as by the said son and two daughters from the first husband, her brother and sisters on her mother’s side, and by a certain brother on her father’s side. Later, the second husband died, survived by his said daughter from the said Margaret, who was provided with a dowry in the testament of her said father, and by a certain son from another wife, instituted as universal heir. Finally, the said second daughter born to the said Margaret and the second husband died under the age of twelve, intestate, survived by her said brother on her father’s side, and by the said son and two daughters, her brother and sisters only on her mother’s side. The question is: to whom does the dowry of the said Margaret belong? To the said son of the second husband, brother of the last deceased on his father’s side? Or to the said son and daughters of the said Margaret from her first husband, brother and sisters of the last deceased? And for which party, and what should be done with the said dowry? It should be known that both the children of the first marriage and those of the second succeed both in the mother’s dowry and in other maternal goods, each according to their share, as in Auth. de nuptiis § illud quoque col. 4. And on this point it must be considered whether they entered into the mother’s inheritance or not, and whether they transmitted it or not; because those who do not enter into the inheritance nor transmit it are not counted in the number, as in C. ad orficianum l. non pro numero.

† Moreover, the aforementioned girl, who died as an infant, transmitted her share to her father and to her sister, who was related to her on both sides, as provided in the law *Si infanti*, Codex, *De iure dotium*. Nevertheless, even here it must be examined whether the father or the sister accepted the inheritance or not, as stated in the Codex, *De iure deliberandi*, in the law *Quoniam sororem*. For, after the death of the second husband, another daughter of the second marriage died, and in her share, which she held in the dowry and in all the goods of her mother, the uterine sisters succeeded, and not the brother who was related only by blood. However, in the dowry given by the father, only the brother related by blood succeeds, according to the doctrine of the doctors, in the Codex, *De legitimis haeredibus*, in the authentic *Post fratres*, *De suis et legitimis*, and in the authentic *In successione*, as interpreted by Cynus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether loss in a partnership is common. And whether. 2.
2. How chance is to be proven in the loss of capital money.
3. If purchased goods are lost, whether they are presumed to have been purchased with partnership funds. And if not, how this is to be proven.
4. Whether a partner who has been dispossessed is said to have lost the aforementioned money or goods by fortuitous event, by reason of partiality.
body: Loquacity has always been displeasing, while soundness has always been pleasing. Two persons entered into a partnership in the following manner: one deposited two hundred [units of currency] for a share in the profits and losses; the other contributed his labor, promising to trade with the said money and to render an account each month. And if any loss were incurred, he was to prove it within a month.

† It is asked first, if the capital is lost or diminished by chance, whether the loss of the lost capital is common. I said that it is so, by that which is read and noted in the Digest, *pro socio*, l. *cum duobus*, § *damna*, where it says that the loss is common; there is the text to the letter. Moreover, there is no doubt because of the express words of the agreement: for the words say "to the part of the loss," which cannot be understood except as referring to the loss occurring in the capital, as in the Digest, *pro socio*, l. *Mutius*, where is the text. For a partnership is sometimes profitable, sometimes barren, sometimes loss-making. And there cannot be a loss unless the capital is not safe, as is clearly apparent there. And this is also clearly proven in the Digest, *pro socio*, l. *si non fuerint*, § *ita cohiri*, where it is said that if one puts in money and the other labor, then the one putting in labor does not participate in any other loss than that of the lost labor, when it is so specially agreed between the partners. And the question is also raised there, whether such an agreement is valid against the natural equity of the partnership. And it is decided there that it is valid. Therefore, if no agreement had been added, the loss would be common. And thus holds Jacobus de Arena in l. 1, Codex, *pro socio*, and this is the truth, notwithstanding the gloss placed there, which seems to say the contrary, namely, that the money perishes to the one putting in money, and the labor perishes to the one putting in labor. For here it was expressly agreed that the risk of the money should be common, and this suffices in our question.

But we wish to know what would be the case if no agreement had been added. There are opinions. For the glossa says that the loss there is proper, not common. Jacobus de Arena says that it is common. And the same is held by Rosfredus in his libelli in the title De actione pro socio. Petrus and Cynus, from a certain equity of their own, distinguish otherwise, as is shown there by them. I say that where the capital, in which the substance of this partnership consists, is not preserved, having perished by chance, which perished to both, namely, that which was the capital communicated, which is certainly owned by each as co-owner. Otherwise, if ownership was not transferred, as in the case of an institor, for if the principal is the institor. But in the profit of the partnership, the risk is that of the owner. And thus is understood that glossa. And these things are true, whether the chance event occurs in the money itself or in goods purchased elsewhere. And I have said this succinctly. In the first part of my opinion, I saw the opinion of a certain other opposing party, who neither examined the agreement nor weighed the nature of the partnership, with his audacity intact; yet he ought not to be blamed, because of natural infirmity: as many heads, so many opinions. And also because the glossa ordinaria is a great authority; but where there is a case of law, the text prevails over the glossa. And there is a text in the said § Damna, according to Jacobus de Arena. But whatever may be the case with the opinions of the doctors on this point, care must be taken, because the agreement opposed in the contract resolves this question, as is shown there. It remains to be seen, if it does not appear

† Regarding the case which was to be proved within a certain agreed time, whether execution may be sought on the principal sum itself. And it seems that not, because it is not liquid, unless a calculation is made and the accounts are examined, as in l. cum seruus, de conditionibus et demonstrationibus. But if the contrary is true, because the instrument contains three cases within itself, s. damni, and this case is to be proved by the defendant, 4Ce3 Svaquuudt acui permittitur excipere de casu lucri. And certainly in the principal sum it is liquid, but the profit is to be liquidated by the plaintiff, even if they do not produce the account book. And there is a third case, when there is neither profit nor loss, and yet the instrument in this case is to be executed. Either therefore the defendant proves the loss: and then the instrument ought not to be executed, except for the half part, in which the instrument is liquid in every event, as I said above in the first step. Or the defendant proves nothing, and then execution is made in full: because the writing says, all florins with half the profit, etc. For this writing has two parts. l. de sorte certa, and de lucro incerto. Hence, that which is certain ought to be executed, de statu libe. statu. li. l. rationem, de probationibus. l. quinquaginta. And it ought to be executed, I say, after a term has been set for the defendant to defend himself, and his defense not having been proved by the defendant. This is therefore the correct mode, that execution be sought in the quantity aforesaid. And that the defendant be cited, that he oppose, and a term be set for proving, and if he proves nothing, execution be made of the promise of the certain quantity specified in the aforesaid promise. Nor is the judge ignorant of that from which the form of jurisdiction arises, rather he knows it from the reading of the instrument. Nor is any other proof required on the part of the plaintiff, although by negation and exception the matter might become doubtful. ff. de transactionibus. l. post rem. But the exception, if it were proved, is not excluded by the statute, because it arises from the tenor of the instrument, vt leg. et no. de senatu. l. cum eorum. It follows to see whether the case was not proved. And certainly this case was not proved, because it is alleged in the very body of the coins, but the defendant was ordered to prove that it happened in the goods bought, and in those coins. Certainly I have already advised, that it did not appear to me to be proved, because that those goods were bought with that money, no one attests by bodily sense, nor could anyone attest, unless he had been present at the counting of the money and the purchase, seeing that money converted into that, which proof is most difficult, and almost impossible, unless it were proved by the confession of the parties, or by legitimate and undoubted account books. Since therefore this is not conclusively proved of necessity, there remains

† so that we may see what is presumed by law. And briefly, the case is that of the law: if they were purchased immediately, it is presumed from that money; otherwise not, since they could have been purchased by them from elsewhere. The text is noted in D. de privilegiis creditorum, l. Venter, §. fin., and C. pro socio, l. 2, vers. sane. But this is not proven here, therefore, etc. But certainly these goods were not purchased out of thin air, l. fin., C. ubi pupillus educandus debeat. And they are presumed to have been purchased in the common name because of the preceding contract of partnership, D. de administratione tutorum, l. Qui negotiationem. And the partner, because he places these goods in common, is not bound to pay from his own funds, but from the common funds; therefore, at least it is proven that the loss must be common.

But certainly there is a great difference between a universal manager and a particular or limited partner. For from a particular partnership, let us say of two hundred, it is not presumed that anything purchased is bought in the common name. Therefore, it cannot be presumed that a partner of two hundred purchased everything in the common name, nor even this or that, because of the uncertainty of a fact not determined to this or that thing. What if a thousand thousand are purchased, and the partnership’s money and labor were around sixteen? Nevertheless, in universal administration, it may be presumed that something is purchased; not in a general partner who is limited to one quantity, nor in one who trades in one species, in that which can relate to several species: for example, if he is a partner in cloths, and buys wool for the purpose of making cloths, and it enters into the partnership, or for the purpose of reselling the wool itself, and it does not enter into the partnership, in doubt the burden of proof lies on him who says it was purchased for the purpose of making cloths.

Therefore, since there are two patrimonies, namely the social and the personal, it is presumed in doubt that it is from the social, as in C. arbitrium tutelae, l. Quicquid; D. de testamento, c. Cum inofficiosum, per Innocentius; it supports D. de petitione hereditatis, l. Sed si lege, §. Quod autem; D. ad Trebellianum, l. Titius; C. eodem, auth. Contra rogatos. Because one is more affected to have his own property than common property, l. 2, C. quando et quibus quarta pars debetur, lib. 10; it supports D. de solutionibus, l. Et magis; and what is noted in C. de bonis quae liberis, l. Cum oportet, in principio; it supports D. de peculio, l. Hinc quaeritur, §. Potest.

Moreover, the law expressly says that what a partner purchases simply is his own: but by the judgment of the partnership he is compelled to share it. Therefore, if he is bound to share it, he purchased from the common funds; otherwise he would not be bound to share it. And with this it is established that he appears to have purchased in his own name, the text is in D. pro socio, l. Si quis socius societatem contraxerit, that what he purchases is his, not common, etc. For whether he purchases in his own name or simply, he is not understood as an external person; it supports D. de verbis obligatorum, l. Si ita stipulatus, §. Grisogonus, in fine. Therefore, it is not true that it is reduced from personal to common by the sole will of the purchaser, but will and act are necessary, as in D. de peculio, l. Non statim, and l. Finis; D. si pars hereditatis petatur; D. si certum petatur, l. Si socius, vers. Quod si communem.

It appears that it is not proven that the money was converted into goods, that it is not owed as much, relatively speaking with regard to the hope, but simply, as in l. Incendium, cum sequentibus, D. si certum petatur.

It remains to be seen, assuming that the case (casus) has been proven most clearly, for example by the confession of a party, whether, since the latter was dispossessed on account of the particular partiality of the lord Cathalan, this damage is that of the dispossessed alone or common. That consultant says that the damage is common, because the violence of robbers is said to be a fortuitous event, as in D. 17,2,3, § damna, in the rubric latrocinio; and not only in a common thing, but also in one’s own thing, if on account of the partnership a common damage was inflicted, as in the same law, § quidam sagariam, and D. 17,2,2, Iulia, in the same title. The contrary is the truth itself, because these partialities seem to have the character of a monopoly, which is condemned and prohibited by law, C. 4,54,1. And thus fault precedes the case. And therefore the entire risk pertains to the one at fault, D. 17,2,3, § si, because these partisans place themselves in a brawl and provide the cause of the damage. Moreover, when private enmity is the cause of the damage, such damage is attributed to fault, D. 19,2,13, § culpae; D. 24,3,1, in his. And that the cause of enmity was the cause of the damage appears from the partiality itself. Either therefore the damage is inflicted on account of the things, or on account of the person, or by a mixture on account of enmity and of the things or the person. In the first case, the damage is common; in the second and third, it is proper to the sufferer, C. 6,42,1, ex repudiatione, in the text of the letter. And I say that in the third case, that which is more significant is considered, D. 7,2,1, Fulcinius, § quid ergo, two. And if my friend’s opinion proceeds in order from beginning to end, it is manifestly contrary to the law in all points, his peace being saved. This I say with regard to the substantial points of the question; however, in certain other matters he spoke probably and copiously, which is clear from the noise. Therefore, what I have already advised is most true, and I advise it again and assert with full truth that the defendant is in a case of condemnation or execution, and that he is not to be absolved by proof, his defense not concluding any substance. And it supports what is noted in Speculum, de fideicommissis, § fin., ver. attamen; and there it is clear that if he who contributes only labor does not wish to be bound by the case of money, he must agree to this separately. Finally, it is known that the case of money is not presumed unless it is proven; because, given the delays and having discussed this, it has not been proven, whence the quantity remains pure and liquid. And thus to say, as he says, that nothing appears in the rest, is not true, because no diminution appears, no case being proven. The laws are known to the blind and to barbers. And beyond the common laws, C. 4,10,1, si de bonis, supports this very well. I, Baldus.
