consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The usufructuary must provide security for using and enjoying the property according to the discretion of a good man. The father is excluded by the substitutes appointed for the underage ward in a pupillary substitution.
body: After death

† Juvenalis, the said Catherine, so long as she lives, ought to have the usufruct of all the goods of the said Ser Matteo, upon giving security for using and enjoying them according to the discretion of a good man, and for restoring them upon the termination of the usufruct, as is fully set forth in the law and notes in l. Titia, § fin., de legatis 2, according to the doctors, especially Bartolus. Nor does it avail that it was left to her together with the children; because, upon the death of the children, the children’s portion, that is, that of Juvenalis, accrues to the mother, as in ff. de usufructu accrescendi, l. si mulieri cum liberis. Likewise, it does not avail that I said she was to share the dowry with them during the son’s lifetime, for this clause, being referred to the son, does not extend to the substitutes of the son; and therefore, upon the death of the son, she ought freely to have the usufruct for the whole time of her life, C. de legatis, l. 1. And this is the first point. And as regards the goods of Ser Matteo, she has this nature only with respect to that which accrued to Juvenalis from the paternal goods, from which the mother ought to have no usufruct.

† On the second point, it must be said that this mother does not succeed to the impubes son in anything, neither in the goods of Master Matthew nor in the goods left to the impubes by his uncle, because all these goods, however acquired, pertain to John and Master Angel, who were substituted for the impubes by pupillary substitution. C. de impube. et aliis substi. l. precibus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Within what time the power of an arbiter or arbitrator is terminated.
2. What the word "secundum" signifies.
body: Having presupposed the validity of the submission to arbitration and the election of the third party, whether after the two months predetermined by the statute an award could be rendered, or not.

† On this matter, therefore, it is asked of me whether by reason of time the arbitral award is null, because it was rendered after a year. On which point it must be known that under the ius commune the power of arbitration is not terminated by a year, ff. de arbi. l. sed si compromissum, but remains within the power of the arbitrator. Baldus says that it is terminated by a year, as noted by Bart. in l. si quis arbitratu. de verbo. ob. I have held, and hold, that if a submission is made concerning a lawsuit or a controversy to be decided, the submission to an arbitrator is not terminated by a year, as in C. de temp. appel. auth. si tamen in medio. and in c. quamdiu. de appel. in cle. And therefore the said award would be valid even though rendered after a year, and especially from the power of an arbitration (arbitrium), not merely an arbitrament (arbitramentum). Those words, "according to the form of the statutes," do not stand in the way, for those words serve as a qualification of those words, "in law and in fact," not as a designation of any time, ff. de bonis auth. iud. poss. l. in venditione. §. de tempore. And because that statute speaks of a necessary submission, which differs from a voluntary one, as in C. de iudi. l. pen. in fin. And because it is not properly called a statute of Gualdo, but a statute which a father makes for his son and a lord for his subject, as in c. licet de sepul. li. 6.

† And because the word "according to" (secundum) requires an antecedent to which it properly refers, otherwise it operates nothing, in c. Abbate. extra de verb. sig. Furthermore, the boundary of time was not imposed by the statute for terminating the submission, but for punishing a negligent arbitrator—provided, however, that his negligence is established, and not otherwise. And therefore, if nothing else stands in the way, the said award ought to be ordered into execution.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute that every lessee of a mill suitable for making oil shall pay 10 to the commune as a gabelle: whether one leasing such a mill from the church is bound to pay the gabelle.
2. Not only are statutes that are made directly against ecclesiastical liberty invalid, but also those that derogate from ecclesiastical liberty in any respect.
3. Just as laymen do not take away the liberty of the church, so neither do clerics take away the liberty of laymen.
4. When a statute of laymen is said to concern clerics so that it is invalid, he distinguishes.
body: The point of the question is as follows. By a statute of the city of Montefalco newly made regarding the matter of a newly instituted gabelle, now a year ago, it is provided that for every mill suitable for making oil there shall be paid to the commune of the said city 30 solidi for each year. And that whosoever contracts with any exempt person, or with another who cannot be sued, such contractor shall be bound to pay the gabelle for both sides, both for himself as contracting party and for him with whom he contracted. Now a certain lay citizen contracted with the dean, canons, and chapter of the church of Montefalco, namely by leasing from them a certain mill suitable for making oil, as above, for a fixed annual rent; and the said dean, canons, and chapter promised the said lessee to defend the said mill against every troublesome person, as appears in the instrument of lease. Recently, the said lessee is being compelled and constrained by the commune and the official of the said city to pay to the commune itself the said 30 solidi under pretext of the said statute. It is objected by the aforesaid dean, canons, and chapter, and asserted that the said lessee is not bound by law to pay the said 30 solidi, and consequently ought neither to be compelled nor constrained by the commune itself to pay; and especially because the said mill thus leased belongs to the church and to the dean, canons, and chapter themselves, and ecclesiastical persons and their property are not bound by law to pay such things, since the said ecclesiastical persons and their property are not under the power of laymen, nor is a statute of laymen extended to clerics or their property; indeed, it was enacted contrary to ecclesiastical liberty, and if so, those who enact such things incur the penalty of the canon, and nothing pertains to laymen concerning those who are outside. If it is said that such a statute concerns the person of the contractor, not the thing contracted for, this is not true, because the lessee is sued by reason of the thing in question, that is, of the mill itself. And he is compelled to pay for the mill itself, which is an ecclesiastical thing, and an ecclesiastical thing is not bound, therefore, etc. For if the mill is removed, the gabelle is removed, and thus it is by reason of the thing in question, etc., not by reason of the person of the contractor; wherefore, etc. It is replied on behalf of the commune that the Roman Church had, or has, salt-pans in parts of Romagna, which it leases annually, or sells to secular merchants, who cause salt to be carried to be sold in certain provinces; the cities and other communities through whose territories the said salt is carried demand transit-tax and gabelle for the said salt; it is alleged on behalf of the merchants and defendants that the Roman Church is not bound to pay road-toll nor gabelle, nor consequently are the purchasers and lessees of the said salt-pans, upon which the said commune says it has obtained legal counsel.

† finally, because it says, the lessees were bound to pay the gabelle and transit-tax. Likewise, the commune itself says that the lords Bar. and Iac. de Aret. hold this opinion, though the said commune does not allege the laws upon which the aforesaid consultants base themselves. Now, the said statute, the point, the laws, and the allegations of both sides having been examined, it is asked of the consultant what the law is.

† Not only statutes that are directly contrary to ecclesiastical liberty, but also those that in any way derogate from ecclesiastical liberty, and even those through which fraud is committed from person to person, are invalid; nevertheless, laymen are not thereby prevented from using their own advantages and benefits against their subjects who lease from churches or buy possessions or revenues from them.

† Because, just as laymen cannot take away the liberty of clerics, so neither can clerics take away the liberty and jurisdiction of laymen over their lay subjects, nor can a commonwealth do so any less than a private person, who can command his servant and say, 'I wish you to work my vineyard and not that of the priest'; nor can the church command the contrary to a layman, unless the layman acts maliciously, perceiving no profit therefrom, but solely inflicting injury on the clerics or churches, because then it would not be permitted on account of the evil and fraudulent intention, as is proved in c. dos, de immu. eccl., lib. 6, and c. quamquam, de censi., in the same compilation, and c. fi., de immu. ecc., in cle., and ff. de condi. et dem., l. haeres meus, § in fraudem, and in auth. cassa, et irrita, C. de sacros. ecc., with its subject-matter. And therefore the said statutes are not odious, because they do not principally contain odium, but favor for the fiscal interest against subjects alone: ff. de dam. infe., l. proculus; ff. de serui., l. manifeste. And because the world so approves it, I do not dare to condemn it: for as the wise man says, take heed that you do not despise the judgment of the universal people; and therefore I follow the dance. As to what other doctors can allege for that side, there is to this purpose ff. de pub., l. licitatio, § mercatores, and there by Dyn.; and agreeing with Dy., in Spe., de censi., § nunc dicendum, both Speculator and Ioan. An. in the same place; also relevant are ff. de verbo. obl., l. si ita quis, § ea lege, and de iure dot., l. promittendo, in principio.

† Three cases, however, must be weighed. For either the statute directs its words against non-subjects, and clerics or churches are not included, because it would be directly contrary to the liberty of the church, which is free from these extraordinary burdens: C. de sacros. ecc., l. placet; de immu. eccl., c. non minus, and c. aduersus, de sen. exc., c. nouerit, per Inn.; de condi. insti., l. si quis sub condi., per Bart. Sometimes the statute expressly says thus: 'whosoever contracts with a cleric, each shall be bound to pay the gabelle, and for the cleric the layman may be coerced', and then it is not valid as to the cleric, nor as to the layman for the share of the cleric, because the obligation of the layman is posited as a consequence of an obligation that is void, as in quarum rerum actio non datur, l. 1, § exceptiones. Sometimes the statute does not burden the cleric in anything, but burdens the layman doubly, so that the portion of the layman is burdened in solidum, but the portion of the cleric in nothing; then the liberty of clerics is not infringed, although indirectly some advantage is taken away from them, namely, because the lessee on account of that burden would not wish to agree except for a lesser rent, as in ff. de ser. expor., l. si venditor, § fi.; nevertheless the commonwealth, which is equated with the church, as in C. de sacros. eccl., l. vt inter diuinum, is not bound to find difficulties for itself for the benefits of others, because 'he seeks in the Alps', etc., and it is so practiced everywhere. Yet this opinion somewhat troubles my conscience, because the intention of the enactors is implicitly directed to their own advantages and to the harm of the churches. But it is natural that the generation of one thing is the corruption of another; and yet by the primary intention of nature it is to generate and not to corrupt. And relevant is what is noted in ff. de auth. tu., l. 1, in fine, and ff. de via publica, l. aediles, and ff. de priuil. cre., l. antiocensium.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a donation is revoked by operation of law on account of ingratitude, or whether the act of a judge is required.
body: If it is asked,

Whether, by the last law and the final law of the Code on the revocation of donations on account of ingratitude, which is true and proven in court, the donated property returns to the donor by operation of law, or whether it is done by the office of the judge. And there Peter and Cynus say that it is done by the office of the judge. But in our case, because the donee consented to the revocation and yielded and granted the rights, there is no need for a praetor. And therefore what has been done is valid, and by the distribution the rights of the contract have been lost, because although there was no retransfer, there was a cession for a just cause. It supports what is noted in the Digest on the topic of peace, the law "From the buyer"; in the Code on when it is permitted to withdraw from a buyer, law 1; in the Digest on donations, law 1, in the great gloss; and in the Code on heirs or actions sold, the final law; and in the Digest on no new matter to be introduced, law 1, section "The same is asked." I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When the mother and grandmother are alive, when does the year begin to run for the grandmother to petition for a guardian?
2. When are expenses considered to have been incurred out of piety or for the sake of the soul, so as to be recoverable?
body: Opinion

† The opinion of Master Bartholomew is this: that when the first year has elapsed for the mother, the second year begins to run for the grandmother, and when the second year of the grandmother has elapsed, the third year begins to run for the uterine brother, or others similar, who are called subsequently. Hence, in this case, all these persons, concerning whom the question is asked, would be excluded from the succession. And thus the mother is protected rather by possession of the goods than by the very right of inheritance. And so it is held in l. 2, Qui petant tutores, D., and C. eod., l. Nepotibus. But the gloss says there that the first is excluded, but not the subsequent ones; hence, according to the gloss, the grandmother would succeed. And this is by l. 3, § Videndum, D., ad Tertull. I say thus: if indeed the mother is excluded from the succession and from the guardianship, for example by passing to a second marriage, because she becomes suspect, then the duty of solicitude falls upon the grandmother. And from that time, if she neglects it for a year, the grandmother is deprived of the succession. But if the mother is excluded from the hope of succession, but not from the hope of guardianship: for even after a year the mother can exercise the guardianship, and she excludes the grandmother from the guardianship. In this case the grandmother is not punished, and the reason is this: because if the ward has a legitimate guardian, the woman ought not to be punished, as noted in C., ad Tertull., l. Matres. But here he has a mother, who is a legitimate guardian, or else quasi-legitimate; therefore the grandmother is not punished. But if the mother had renounced the guardianship, or had passed to a second marriage, then this reason would cease, and the grandmother would be punished. And so I have often advised, and of this I spoke in l. Precibus, C., de Impuber. Concerning the second point, it must be said,

That expenses are understood to have been incurred out of piety, if they were made concerning the person of a minor and are small expenses. But if they are made concerning things, they are understood to have been incurred with the intention of recovering them. C. de negotiorum gestorum, l. 1, through the gloss and doctors; ff. ibid., l. Nesennius Appolinaris. Follows the constitution of Lord Egidius, Cardinal of Spoleto and legate of the Lord Pope. And because we know that the commune of the aforementioned city is burdened with heavy expenses, we will and command that the communities, inhabitants, and residents of all the castles, territories, and places of the aforementioned district are bound to contribute with the said commune in the firming (tax farming).

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Under the common law, garrisons, nor cities, do not possess the power of the sword.
2. Only the governors of provinces, and not those inferior to them, hold the command of the sword; hence, the authorities of cities and garrisons do not, under the common law, possess the command of the sword.
3. Garrisons to which a city sends authorities who adjudicate only civil and criminal cases in which a pecuniary penalty is imposed are not said to be within the district of the city.
4. That is properly called such which is simply such, not one that is such in a certain respect.
5. Three kinds of district are found.
6. Whether an inferior to the prince may impose new burdens in districtual matters.
body: It is proposed that these castles receive the powers (potestates) sent by the commune of Spoleto for the government of said castles, who, however, have jurisdiction in civil matters and criminal cases, for which monetary condemnations are imminent. But where the penalty of blood is inflicted, said powers, or the commune of Spoleto, have no power, but the rector of the duchy alone must have a certain share of the monetary penalties of said powers. It is therefore asked, whether said castles are said to be within the district of the city of Spoleto, so that they are included under said constitution of Lord Egidius, on account of what has been said, or also because they are bound to make host, and cavalry service, and give wax, and are bound to have friends for friends, and enemies for enemies. Secondly, it is asked whether said Lord Cardinal could make said constitution, and bind said castles to more than what has been abstracted from the commune of Spoleto by pacts. Thirdly, it is asked, since said constitution has not yet been in use, whether it is abrogated. Fourthly, it is asked whether said constitution, by its nature, is perpetual.
† And concerning the first point, it must be known that cities, not to mention fortresses, do not have the power of the sword by common law.

And therefore, the authorities of cities or castles do not, by common law, have coercive power, but only the governors of provinces, and not those inferior to them. D. de officiis praesidis, l. illicitas, § qui universas; and in Aurne, de defensione civitatis, § audiant; and noted in Speculum, de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, § ei pedetento, ver. quod potestates; and by Rossetti, in title qui possunt iudicare. And yet it is established that cities have territory, boundaries, and district, D. de restitutione spoliatorum, c. cum ad sedem; D. de electione, c. tupeculium, lib. 6; and c. cum Romani, de electione, in Clementinis; D. de episcopo et ecclesia, c. nulli, 16 q. 1; ca. 1; and noted in C. ubi de possessione agi oportet. Hence, the inference is not sound: [because] it does not have in itself the power of a castle, therefore it is not a castle within the district.
† It is therefore alleged that the said castles are within the district of Spoleto. To the contrary, it is said,

† For that is properly called such which is simply such, not in a certain respect. D. de leg. 3, l. hoc legatum. But camps are distinguished in a certain respect. Therefore they are not within the district. Regarding the second point, it should be known

It is that the district is threefold. First, conventional, when a castle governs itself and submits itself simply to a certain city for the protection of its body, without prejudice to the Prince. D. de iuris et iurisdictionis omnium iudicum, l. est receptum. Second, privileged, when the Prince has granted a castle to a certain city for the district. C. de legibus, l. nam humanum. And third, prescribed, when jurisdiction and empire are prescribed over the castle itself. C. de diuersis officiis, l. viros, lib. 12; and de foro competenti, c. cum contingat. Now we are in the first member, namely, the conventional district, and in a certain respect.

It is asked whether a subject may be subjected to a heavier servitude than was agreed upon by a superior below the Prince. And it seems that this is so, because an immunity granted to someone is infringed upon account of unforeseen cases, as noted in l. 1, de iure immunitatis, by Dominus Dynus. To the contrary, it seems that one who is burdened beyond the agreement has a negative action, or the office of the judge, whence it cannot be removed by an ambitious decree of the judge: l. ambitiose, de decretis ab ordinario facienda. Also, because it is tacitly agreed that they shall not be burdened further: de negotiorum gestione, l. qui alienos, § libertos. And rescripts or statutes cannot remove the natural rights of agreements. Also, because the mandate given by the Pope to the Lord Legate does not extend to this, as l. si pater, quae in fraudem creditorum, John Andreas in the Speculum, de censibus, cites Dynus and notes and confirms; but certainly there is a great difference between a gratuitous immunity, of which Dynus speaks, for this is a kind of donation, and if the donor is in danger, namely if for the public utility he can do this, and between an agreement of strangers, and this cannot in any way be violated, as noted by Rosset in the Rubricella de re commenda. Moreover, mention is not made of the said agreement in the constitution of the Lord Legate, and therefore the agreement is not removed by it: C. de testamento, auth. hic inter liberos. Furthermore, the Legate could not impose servitude on free estates; therefore, much less on free persons. For this the Prince himself can scarcely do: C. de nova vectigalia, l. 1. And it is well supported by ff. quod vi aut clam, l. prohibere, § plane, and C. de rescissione venditionis, l. ratas; for the firmness of human acts would be of little value if it were removed by rescripts. And to this point many laws and reasons, nay, the cries of the truth of the immortal laws, can be adduced; and because this is the very truth, the deceased cannot personally contend with others. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The canonical portion is twofold, namely, parochial and episcopal.
2. When a legacy is left to minor hermit preachers, not absolutely, but for perpetual use and divine worship, does the parochial or episcopal canonical portion apply?
3. If a person has chosen burial in a church, but by chance is buried elsewhere, is the rector of the parochial church bound to pay the canonical portion, not as if he had been buried where burial was chosen?
4. If someone is buried by chance in a church to which he had bequeathed a legacy, although he had not chosen burial there, does the parochial church have the canonical portion?
body:
The point of the question turning between Barthol. Blasii, Vicar, and the governor of the church of Saint Severus of Perugia, which is a parish church, acting on one side, and the chapter and convent of Saint Mary New, their syndics, defending on the other side, is as follows, namely:

Lady Genola Cecholi Ioannelli of the Castle of An., and then wife of Barthol. Monoli of the Gate of the Sun and of the Gate of Saint Severus, in the year of our Lord 1362, on the 2nd day of the month of November, made her will in this manner, namely: First, she wished her body to be buried at the church of Saint Mary New of Perugia. Furthermore, she left and ordered that 4 gold florins be spent from her goods on the funeral of her body at the time of her burial. Furthermore, she left to the brothers of Saint Mary New for her soul 25 pounds of denarii. In all her other movable and immovable goods, she instituted John and Anthony, her sons, and any posthumous child to be born from her, if it should come to light, as her universal heirs in equal portions, provided that within the term of 25 years all her said sons, both born and to be born, both male and female, should die without legitimate children. And she left her goods to the place of the brothers of Saint Augustine for one-third part, to the place of the brothers of Saint Francis for another third, and to the place of the brothers of Saint Mary New for the other third part. And in the aforementioned case, she instituted and substituted the said places as her universal heirs.

Finally, the said Lady Genola died during the existence of the marriage between herself and the said Barthol., with the said Barthol., her husband, and her said legitimate children surviving her. And the said Anthony and the said Barthol. died in the county, namely in the castle of Andria, which is distant by five miles from the city of Perugia, from the said church of Saint Severus. And she was buried at the church of the said castle, in which was the burial place of her ancestors, the choice of burial not being changed, and not at the church of Saint Mary New. Finally, the said sons died within the term of 25 years without legitimate children. And thus the case of the substitution of the said legacies occurred, namely those of Saint Augustine, Saint Francis, and Saint Mary New.

Now, two questions are asked: First, since the said Lady Genola lived with her said husband at the Gate of Saint Severus, whether the said church of Saint Severus is the parish church of the said Lady Genola’s inheritance contingent upon the place of the brothers of Saint Mary, and also of the said 25 pounds of denarii, namely the canonical portion, notwithstanding that she died outside the said parish, namely in the said castle of Andria, and was buried at the church of the said castle.

Second, it is asked whether the place of the brothers of Saint Francis is capable of the said substitution and institution for one-third part, and thus whether the place of Saint Mary, at which the said Lady Genola chose burial, succeeds in the one-third part of the said inheritance, and thus whether the said parish church ought to have the canonical portion of the one-third part of the said inheritance and of the said 25 pounds of denarii. Or, in the case that the said place of Saint Severus is not capable, whether the whole of the said inheritance from the said part of the said sons belongs and ought to belong by right of accretion to the said places of the brothers of Saint Augustine and Saint Mary New, namely to each for one-half. And thus, of such one-half of the said inheritance contingent upon the place of Saint Mary New, whether the said church, or the place of Saint Mary New, is bound to pay the canonical portion to the said parish church of Saint Severus.

† There are two kinds of canonical portions: episcopal and parochial. The episcopal portion is due to the bishop on account of the episcopal burden incumbent upon him, which consists in celebrating solemnly, conferring orders, confirming with chrism, consecrating and blessing holy oil, and so forth. The parochial portion, however, is due to the parish priest of the church on account of the parochial burden, which consists in celebrating Mass and so forth. Nevertheless, this is the difference in the nature of these canonical portions: sometimes the canonical portion is due to the bishop, but not to the parish priest; sometimes it is due to the parish priest, but not to the bishop, according to one opinion; sometimes it is due to both the parish priest and the bishop. And this happens in two ways: either because the bishop is entitled to a quarter of the fourth part, or because two quarters are deducted, one by one person and the other by another. Hostiensis, in his Summa, De sepulturis, §. Et utrum canonica portio. An example of when the episcopal portion is due, but not the parochial, is when the parochial portion is claimed only from the church in which the deceased chose burial; whereas the episcopal portion is claimed from all pious places to which a simple legacy has been left, even if the testator was not buried there. See De sepulturis, c. Cum liberum; c. In nostra; and c. Ab testamentis. De verborum significatione, c. Ex parte, lib. 6, according to Hostiensis and all the doctors after him.

† Example concerning the second point, when a legacy is left to the minor orders, to hermits, and to the Carmelites, not simply, but for perpetual use and divine worship, etc., where the canonical right of the bishop and the decree *Si* do not apply, but rather the parochial right, as in *c. Dudum*, § *Verum*, *De sepulturis* in the Clementines. And some say that in this case the bishop has nothing, so that the parochial church is not bound to the bishop for the fourth part of the fourth part, because it is free from the bishop. Hence it may be said, as far as you are concerned, "I have free buildings," as in *l. Loci corpus*, § *Competit*, D. *Si servus venditus*. But the contrary is true, as noted by Lord Federicus in his work, *Consilium* 6, which begins "Testator elegit." But that statement has a flaw, for by what reasoning could one demand the fourth part of the fourth part from the curators, by the same reasoning, to avoid circularity, could one demand it from the heirs of the testator, d. § *Verum*. The glossator said by this that it is against the text of the said § *Verum* in privileged legacies, but in non-privileged legacies there is no doubt that the bishop must have from the curates the fourth part of the fourth part. But if the opinion of Hostiensis were true, bishops would first have their full fourth part, then from the church to which it was left, and then have the fourth part of the fourth part of the curates from the curate of the church where one is assumed, and in another legated church buried, and the bishop would have with his churches a leonine and predatory partnership, and one greatly diminishing the pious considerations and wills of descendants. And therefore it must be said that either it is a case in which the fourth part is due solely to the bishop, and then it is due to him in full, *De testamento*, *c. Requisisti*, § *Secus*; or it is a case in which the fourth part is due to the parochial church, and then the bishop is not due more than the fourth part of that fourth part, D. *Si cui plus quam per legem Falcidiam*, *l. 1*, § *Interdum*. Otherwise, suppose that by canonical custom it is half; if the bishop has half and the curate half, nothing will remain for the church where the burial is chosen, or if anything remains, it will be half of half, and beyond that the bishop will have from the curate half of half of half, which is false. And Hostiensis here had bad knowledge and worse conscience. For the church which the testator deemed worthy by his liberal judgment would have less than the bishop, of whom the testator did not think, and, so to speak, the disinherited or passed over would have more than the instituted and honored, contrary to *l. Maximum vitium*, C. *De libellis praetextis* and *De legatis praestantibus*, *l. Salvius Aristio*. These things being premised, such a question follows,

Whether, if burial was chosen in a church, but the deceased was buried elsewhere by chance, the rector of the parish church is entitled to the canonical portion, as if the deceased had been buried where the burial was chosen. And it seems at first that the entire legacy is void, as if the final cause were lacking, as in D. de adimendis et revocandis legatis, l. Alumnae, § Seia. But certainly this substitution was made simply, not on account of the burial; and therefore it must be considered whether the canonical portion is due to the parish church, as if the testatrix had been buried there where she chose her burial. And on this point there are expressly contrary opinions. Some say that the event is to be awaited; others, the intention of the testator. The first opinion is held by Master Federicus of Siena in his consilia, consilium 10, which begins “Casus talis est.” Because, since a fourth is due to the parish church in compensation for a certain injury committed by burying elsewhere than in that church, it is said that the injury is received when the burial takes place, because where the body lies with funeral rites, there the injury is said to be committed. For burial requires an act, not merely the designation of a person, D. de religiosis, l. 2, § Sepulchrum; and l. Os; and l. Cum in diversis. Others say the contrary, lest it be within the power of the blood relatives, by burying elsewhere, to deprive the parish church of the fourth, as in D. de arbitris, l. Nec in potestatem; D. de iuris et de facto ignorantia, l. Si quis; and l. Inquisitum. And this is held by Paulus de Castro and Innocentius. It seems this is held in X. de sepulturis, c. In nostra. And that we should not consider a casual event, but only the event that ought to have followed, is clear from the laws stating that it is not inspected what was done, but what ought to have been done, D. de officio praesidis. But Pope [Benedictus] will say that the church which has not performed the duty of burial ought not to have more than if it had obeyed the judgment of the deceased regarding burial, D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Mulieri et Titio; and l. Titiae si non nupserit. Moreover, although this fourth is not according to the judgment of the testator, it is nevertheless executory of his judgment, and from it it takes its form and origin; hence, it is not the event, but the mode of this obligation to be removed or imposed, but the disposition of the testator together with that of the law. And in a manner, the testator is punished as ungrateful according to the judgment of the testator, as in the said § Verum. Furthermore, even if we say that the event is to be considered, it is understood as the event of damage, not the event of burial, D. si quid in fraudem patroni, l. 1, § 1.

† What, therefore, conversely, if he was buried by chance in the church to which he had bequeathed, yet had not chosen burial there? Certainly, the parish church ought to have the canonical portion, according to the opinion of Federicus de Senis; otherwise, not. What if, by chance, it does not appear where he is buried, for example, because he died at sea? Will the parish church be defrauded of its canonical portion? Certainly, this too does not seem to be said. Let us therefore look to the intention and not to the chance event, according to that of Ovid: "I wish him to lack success, whoever thinks that deeds should be judged by the outcome." D. de negotiorum gestione, l. sed in ultimo, §. si.

Or, if we speak of funeral expenses annexed to the funeral, regarding these, the parish church must simply have the fourth part from the church where he had intended to be buried. For the testator's intention creates the right. D. de hereditatis institutione, l. ex facto, §. rerum autem Italicarum; C. de mortuo inferendo, l. 1; C. de religiosis et sumptibus funerum, l. si quis enim; D. de legato primo, l. certa, §. si; and D. de actione emptionis, l. fundi nihil, §. ult., and l. grauaria, in fine. And this is especially true if it is due to the fault of the legatee church that the body is not claimed. For this right of claiming is held as if the body had already been claimed and obtained. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. Labeo scribit, si mihi bibliothecam.

From the foregoing, a clear and lucid solution to the question appears, saving the opinion of the majority, as in l. Claudius Felix. I, Baldus.
